case_prompt:
A 44-year-old man with a history of colonic diverticulitis presented with acute abdominal pain. On examination, his abdomen was distended with right lower quadrant tenderness. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed small-bowel loops dilated up to 4.3 cm in diameter, with a transition point in the mid-lower abdomen concerning for moderate enteric obstruction and asymmetric wall thickening of some ileal loops, along with a few borderline mesenteric lymph nodes. Diagnostic laparoscopy identified a nonperforated Meckel diverticulum in the mid-ileum that appeared prominent, inflamed, and indurated. 

Histologic examination of the resected diverticulum showed a true diverticulum lined by intestinal mucosa without ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue. Microscopy revealed extensive infiltration of sheets of small lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm (monocytoid B-cells) forming lymphoepithelial lesions in the mucosa and submucosa and focally involving the serosal adipose tissue. In some areas, there were nodular proliferations with occasional reactive germinal centers and an expanded marginal zone. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the lymphocytes were positive for CD20 with weak coexpression of CD43 and positive for BCL-2, and negative for CD10, Cyclin-D1, CD3, and CD5. The reactive germinal centers were BCL-2–negative and BCL-6–positive, with no evidence of follicular colonization by tumor cells. In situ hybridization for kappa and lambda showed scattered polyclonal plasma cells, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was less than 5%.
title: Extranodal Marginal Zone Lymphoma Presenting within the Meckel Diverticulum as Diverticulitis: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 37-year-old man was admitted in early November 2014 with intermittent fevers of one month’s duration, peaking at 39.6°C, accompanied by night sweats, mild cough, and a 7-kg weight loss over two months. Initial mycobacterial studies were negative, and a bone marrow smear showed yeast-like organisms, but culture was unrevealing. He received moxifloxacin for ten days and voriconazole for three days without improvement. He worked in a blood bank with frequent plasma donation and had recent soil exposure through farm work in his home region along the Yangtze River; he had never traveled abroad. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C), tachycardic, and ill-appearing, with no lymphadenopathy, but hepatomegaly (2 cm below the costal margin) and splenomegaly (3 cm below the costal margin). Laboratory studies revealed progressive pancytopenia (WBC 1.86 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 86 g/L, platelets 2 × 10^9/L), elevated C-reactive protein (43 mg/L), abnormal liver enzymes, low CD4 count (320 cells/μL), and positive CMV IgM and HSV antibodies; HIV serology, PPD, and T-SPOT were negative. Blood and sputum cultures were repeatedly negative. Abdominal CT demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly with retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy; chest CT showed only minimal chronic inflammation. PET-CT revealed increased glucose uptake in bone marrow and spleen without evidence of malignancy. He was treated with ganciclovir for ten days and received supportive IVIG and thymalfasin, but fever and cytopenias persisted with further hepatosplenomegaly.
title: Disseminated histoplasmosis: a rare clinical phenotype with difficult diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and moderate aortic regurgitation was referred for resection of a newly diagnosed left adrenal mass after 3 months of spells characterized by anxiety, agitation, headaches, pallor, palpitations, and hypertensive crises. An abdominal CT scan showed a left adrenal nodule compressing the splenic vein. Elevated urinary normetanephrines and metanephrines confirmed a catecholamine-producing tumor. He received 30 days of doxazosin and bisoprolol before surgery and was hemodynamically stable on admission. Preoperative ECG showed sinus tachycardia with T-wave inversions in lateral leads. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an LVEF of 55% without regional wall motion abnormalities.

He underwent laparoscopic left adrenalectomy. Gentle tumor manipulation elicited transient blood-pressure spikes to 180 mmHg until the main adrenal vein was ligated. Immediately after tumor removal, he became hypotensive to 50/30 mmHg and developed a new left bundle-branch block. Emergent coronary angiography showed no obstructive atherosclerotic disease (TIMI 2 flow, no vasospasm). Left ventriculography revealed circumferential midventricular akinesia. Repeat echocardiography demonstrated midventricular and apical akinesia with an LVEF of 25%. Cardiac biomarkers peaked on postoperative day 2 (troponin 21.9 ng/mL [URL 0.2 ng/mL]; NT-proBNP 7000 pg/mL [URL 300 pg/mL]).
title: Takotsubo syndrome during surgery for pheochromocytoma: an unexpected complication

case_prompt: A 52-year-old white man presented with a 4-year history of recurrent, intermittent rash of symmetrically distributed, red annular patches on non–sun-exposed areas of the trunk and extremities. The lesions gradually expanded in concentric rings with scale over several months, were mildly pruritic, and associated with arthralgias during flares. His only medication was a proton pump inhibitor. Lyme disease testing was negative. Initial treatment with topical and systemic corticosteroids resulted in only temporary improvement. On examination, pink-red, symmetric, concentric annular patches with trailing scale involved 10% to 15% of his body surface area without lymphadenopathy. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits. A punch biopsy and a broad shave biopsy from the leading edge of a lesion showed a superficial perivascular and lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate with exocytosis of small lymphocytes with mild nuclear contour irregularities, minimal spongiosis, vacuolar alteration at the dermoepidermal junction, and papillary dermal fibrosis. Immunohistochemical staining revealed a predominantly CD3⁺ infiltrate with an approximately equal ratio of CD4⁺ to CD8⁺ cells. Periodic acid–Schiff diastase staining was negative for fungi. No perivascular cuffing, interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate, or significant red blood cell extravasation was seen. Loss of CD7 on lymphocytes was estimated to be approximately 40%.
title: Mycosis fungoides presenting as symmetric concentric patches mimicking figurate erythema

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of mild lumbar and right hip pain without fever, chills, or weight loss. On examination, lumbar flexion was 60°, extension 10°, lateral bending 10° bilaterally; mild tenderness was noted near the L4 spinous process. Neurologic testing, including cervical reflexes, femoral nerve stretch, and straight leg raise (45° on the left, 50° on the right), was unremarkable except for hypoesthesia of the left lateral leg. Routine tumor markers (CA 19-9, CEA, AFP, NSE, and others) were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the lumbosacral region revealed a well-demarcated, homogeneous soft-tissue mass (3.2 × 7.5 cm) within the right multifidus muscle. Noncontrast attenuation was 55 HU, with heterogeneous enhancement (arterial phase 61–85 HU; venous phase 67–95 HU) and a central low-density area. The mass compressed but did not infiltrate the sacrum; the adjacent bone showed compressive sclerosis without destruction.

MRI showed an intramuscular lesion from L4 to S3. On T1-weighted images, the mass was isointense to muscle with patchy hypointense areas. STIR images demonstrated slightly hyperintense signal with patchy low-signal foci. Post-contrast sequences revealed heterogeneous enhancement with lamellar nonenhancing regions.

At surgery, the tumor was found within the right multifidus muscle, firm, poorly circumscribed, infiltrating surrounding muscle but without bone destruction. Grossly, it measured 7.5 cm, was yellowish-gray and slightly firm.

Histologic sections showed large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, marked nuclear pleomorphism with prominent nucleoli, and approximately 2 mitoses per 10 high-power fields; there was no definite invasion of nerves, vessels, or bone. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for S100 protein, SOX-10, MDM2, and Bcl-2, and negative for Desmin, MyoD1, Myogenin, CD99, Synaptophysin, CK-pan, CD34, ERG, and CD163. The Ki-67 proliferation index exceeded 10%.
title: Malignant granular cell tumor of the multifidus muscle: Case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man presented with a six-week history of sharp, left-sided chest pain worsened by inspiration and lying down. He also reported progressive back pain exacerbated by walking, constipation, and lower-limb weakness and numbness suggestive of spinal cord compression. He had no history of smoking or significant past medical conditions. On examination, vital signs were stable. There was abdominal distension without hepatomegaly, minimal lower-limb weakness, and otherwise normal cardiovascular and respiratory findings.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 138 g/L, white-cell count 5.14×10^9/L with a normal differential, platelets 256×10^9/L, normal renal function, and normal serum calcium. Contrast MRI of the spine revealed widespread skeletal lesions with at least three large thoracic paraspinal soft-tissue deposits, including one at T4/T5 causing significant cord compression. A chest radiograph demonstrated a left upper-lobe opacity. Contrast CT of the chest confirmed a 75 mm lobulated mass in the left upper lobe with invasion into the chest wall (involving the left third rib and adjacent muscle), a mild to moderate left pleural effusion, and CT evidence of vertebral and pelvic bony lesions.
title: Rare case of plasmablastic myeloma diagnosed on lung biopsy

case_prompt: A 37-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of pain in the toes of her left foot. The pain was persistent, worse with movement, and associated with numbness, tingling, and a bluish-pale discoloration of the left toes. She had no prior medical history or medication use. On examination, heart rate was 102 beats/min; left femoral pulsation was weakened, distal pulses were absent, and the left toes were dry, cold, and pale. Motor function was intact, but sensation was reduced in the left foot. Electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, and transthoracic echocardiography showed no abnormalities or intracardiac thrombus. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated triphasic flow in the right superficial femoral artery, and a thrombus in the left common femoral artery with poor distal flow. Laboratory studies revealed a platelet count of 812 × 10^3/μL; other routine blood tests were normal. Peripheral blood smear showed marked thrombocytosis with giant platelets, leukocytosis, and immature granulocytes. A JAK2 mutation assay was obtained.
title: Acute Limb Ischemia in the Young: A Rare Case of Essential Thrombocytosis

case_prompt: A 22-year-old Malay woman presented with an 11-year history of asymptomatic, unilateral brown patches on the right arm, right side of the trunk, and right leg. She reported no preceding skin lesions or inflammation and had no significant medical or family history. On examination, there were linear hyperpigmented, slightly atrophic patches following Blaschko’s lines on the right arm, extending over the trunk to the right buttock, and down the right thigh and leg; no induration or active inflammation was noted. Routine laboratory investigations—including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, renal and liver function tests, and a panel of antinuclear and extractable nuclear antibodies—were all normal or negative. A skin biopsy from an affected patch showed mild upper dermal perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, reduced dermal thickness, and more compact dermal collagen; adnexal structures were unaffected.
title: Linear atrophoderma of Moulin

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia presented with a 2-day history of continuous, progressive epigastric pain that began after a heavy meal. He described the pain as sharp (10/10), radiating to his back, and worsened by leaning back or lying down. He reported nausea and several episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. He denied recent dietary changes, binge drinking, hospitalizations, or medication changes.  

Home medications included fenofibrate 48 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, insulin glargine 30 units at bedtime, and insulin lispro 7 units three times daily. He admitted occasional noncompliance with his medications and poor adherence to a diabetic diet. He led a sedentary lifestyle.  

On examination, temperature was 98.9 °F, heart rate 91 bpm, blood pressure 127/84 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. He sat leaning forward in mild distress. He was alert and oriented. Lung fields were clear. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding; there was no peripheral edema.  

Chart review revealed a hospitalization 2 years earlier for diabetic ketoacidosis complicated by hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis.  

Laboratory studies on this admission showed a normal complete blood count, blood glucose 256 mg/dL, an elevated anion gap >17, and a beta-hydroxybutyrate level of 74.5 mg/dL. Serum lipase was 257 IU/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a normal gallbladder and no dilation of the common bile duct.
journal: Journal of Community Hospital Internal Medicine Perspectives
title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hypertriglyceridemiainduced Pancreatitis: Can the Perfect Storm Happen Twice?

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old G2P1 woman presented 4 days after an emergency caesarean delivery with a 1-day history of headache and new-onset generalized tonic–clonic seizures. Her antenatal course was unremarkable. During labour she received what was noted to be a difficult lumbar epidural, although no dural puncture was recorded. Post-operatively on day 1, she developed a frontal, postural headache that responded to bed rest, intravenous fluids, and simple analgesics, and she was discharged on day 3.

On day 4, she returned with nausea, headache, and generalized seizures. There was no history of visual change, fever, tinnitus, or neck stiffness. Paramedics administered diazepam en route. On arrival her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 8/15; pupils were equal and reactive, and peripheral neurological reflexes were normal. She was afebrile; pulse 114 beats/min; blood pressure 108/46 mmHg; SpO₂ 98% on 5 L/min oxygen. Chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Obstetricians administered magnesium sulphate and obtained a head CT scan, which did not reveal any abnormality. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL; WBC count 15.9×10⁹/L; platelets 102×10⁹/L; normal electrolytes, renal and liver function tests; uric acid normal; and no proteinuria. Her mental status improved to GCS 15/15 over several hours, and magnesium was discontinued. A lumbar puncture with a 27-gauge needle revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid, elevated protein (715 mg/L; normal 120–600 mg/L), and no cells. She was started on phenytoin, with no further seizures. Over the next 24 hours her only symptom was a severe postural headache, worse upright and relieved supine. Neurology consultation prompted magnetic resonance imaging and MR venous angiography of the head, and both studies were reported as normal with no intracranial pathology.
title: Seizures in the early post-partum period: A diagnostic dilemma

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old woman was referred for refractory hypertension and acute kidney injury secondary to suspected renal vascular disease. Two weeks earlier, she had presented with a hypertensive emergency (blood pressure, 249/99 mm Hg) and altered mental status attributed to posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. At that time, her serum creatinine was 5.4 mg/dL (baseline, 0.9 mg/dL). Her blood pressure was controlled with intravenous nicardipine, and hemodialysis was initiated urgently.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography revealed a large segment of calcific plaque extending from just below the superior mesenteric artery to the inferior mesenteric artery, involving both renal arteries. Both renal arteries were occluded at their origins, with distal reconstitution via collateral vessels (right greater than left), and a subacute thrombus was noted at the orifice of the right renal artery.

On transfer, aortography confirmed extensive calcific plaque in the visceral aorta and bilateral renal artery occlusions. Given the severity of calcification, stenting was deemed unfeasible, and aortic endarterectomy was considered to carry high morbidity.
journal: Journal of Vascular Surgery Cases and Innovative Techniques
title: Hepatorenal bypass resulting in dialysis independence in case of acute renal failure

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old woman presented with a 2–3 cm hard, irregular lump in the lower outer quadrant of her left breast. She had no hormonal symptoms, weight loss, or family history of breast cancer. Three-year-old bilateral mammograms were normal. Current imaging showed an asymmetrical density on the left mammogram (BI-RADS M4), and tomosynthesis confirmed an ill-defined 28 mm mass. Ultrasound demonstrated a suspicious ill-defined lesion (U4) with normal axillary nodes. An image-guided core biopsy revealed a grade 2 invasive carcinoma interpreted as apocrine carcinoma (B5b); ER and HER2 were negative. 

The patient underwent wide local excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Grossly, there was a well-defined pale tumour measuring 22 mm. Microscopically, the neoplasm was well demarcated with foci of papillary architecture, comprising large tall cells in solid nests with central fibrovascular cores and luminal histiocytes. The cells had eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei, and cystic spaces contained luminal eosinophilic secretions. Notably, in several areas the nuclei of the tall columnar cells were located at the luminal surface rather than the basement membrane (“reversed polarity”). Focal luminal calcifications were present. No lymphovascular invasion or lymph node involvement was identified.

Immunohistochemical studies showed strong CK7 positivity, ER and HER2 negativity, and no myoepithelial layer around lesional structures on p63 and CK5 stains. GATA3 demonstrated moderate nuclear positivity; CK5 was patchy; calretinin was positive; and TTF1 was negative.
final_diagnosis_raw: Tall cell carcinoma of the breast with reversed polarity
title: Tall Cell Carcinoma with Reversed Polarity: Case Report of a Rare Special Type of Breast Cancer and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 66-year-old man with a history of Whipple disease, heart failure with cardiomyopathy, cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, and pulmonary hypertension was referred to the clinic. He was severely malnourished and in cardiogenic shock. Two months earlier, an intestinal biopsy had confirmed Whipple disease, which was treated with 4 weeks of ceftriaxone followed by oral trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. On presentation, he had anasarca. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 46%, severely reduced right heart function, and severe aortic and mitral valve regurgitation; the left ventricular end-diastolic dimension was 57 mm and end-systolic dimension 44 mm. Right heart catheterization revealed a right atrial pressure of 32 mm Hg, mean pulmonary arterial pressure of 55 mm Hg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 27 mm Hg, and pulmonary vascular resistance of 10 Wood units. Results of Whipple polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in blood culture were negative. Right ventricular endomyocardial biopsy showed no myocardial inflammation or involvement by Whipple disease.
title: Valvular Endocarditis and Biventricular Heart Failure in the Setting of Tropheryma whipplei Disease

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old girl presented with a 7-day history of diffuse abdominal tenderness. She had no chronic illnesses, no alcohol or drug use, and no known tuberculosis exposures. Vital signs were normal. On examination, she had moderate ascites without other abnormalities.

Laboratory studies showed: 
- Normal blood counts and chemistries  
- CRP 39 mg/L (0–5)  
- ESR 42 mm/h (0–20)  

Chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal ultrasound revealed free fluid with septations, multiple small nodular implants on peritoneal surfaces (largest 16 mm), and a septated left ovarian cyst measuring 39 × 27 mm. Paracentesis yielded lymphocyte-predominant fluid without malignant cells, with a serum–ascites albumin gradient <1.1 g/dL.

Thyroid function tests were normal. Serum tumor markers were: 
- AFP 2.48 ng/mL (0–7)  
- CEA 0.39 ng/mL (0–3.8)  
- CA15-3 26.15 U/mL (0–26.4)  
- CA19-9 1.14 U/mL (0–27)  
- CA125 107.5 U/mL (0–35)  

Brucella and viral serologies were negative. Tuberculin skin testing was anergic, and QuantiFERON PCR and acid-fast staining of ascitic fluid were negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, and abdomen showed bilateral cervical, supraclavicular, paratracheal, subcarinal, anterior diaphragmatic, and cardiophrenic lymphadenopathy; nasopharyngeal soft-tissue thickening; omental nodularity with peritoneal implants; ascites; a 23 × 18 mm left ovarian cyst; and mesenteric lymph nodes. Ascitic fluid adenosine deaminase was elevated at 62 U/L (0–30). Abdominal MRI confirmed bilateral ovarian cysts, dilated fallopian tubes, nodular peritoneal opacities, and moderate ascites.
title: A Case Report of Peritoneal Tuberculosis: A Challenging Diagnosis

case_prompt: A 90-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of a gradually enlarging left-sided nasal mass. He had no prior sinus disease or surgery. On examination, a voluminous mass was prolapsing through the left nostril, causing complete obstruction of the left nasal cavity and deflecting the nasal septum to the right; there was no cervical lymphadenopathy or facial deformity. Nasal endoscopy via the right naris revealed a smooth, grayish mass filling the left choana and extending into the nasopharyngeal space, displacing the septum. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a homogeneous mass completely occupying the left nasal cavity and extending to the nasopharynx, displacing the medial wall of the left maxillary sinus; erosion of the nasal septum and the left lamina papyracea was noted, along with complete opacification of the left maxillary sinus.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Solitary Fibrous tumor of Nasal cavity: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 44‐year‐old Hispanic woman with insulin‐dependent diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with 3 weeks of progressively worsening nonradiating chest pain, fatigue, and exertional dyspnea. She also reported melena, gum bleeding with tooth brushing, nausea, and loss of taste; she denied fevers, chills, hemoptysis, weight loss, neurologic symptoms, or diarrhea. Her mother had myelodysplastic syndrome. 

Vital signs were notable only for a blood pressure of 138/92 mm Hg. On examination, she was obese with conjunctival pallor and multiple ecchymoses on the lower extremities; there was no hepatosplenomegaly and no neurologic deficits. 

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hemoglobin 5.4 g/dL, hematocrit 16.4%, MCV 116.3 fL, WBC 3.5×10^3/µL, platelets 28,000/µL.  
• Peripheral smear: macrocytes, schistocytes, and teardrop cells; no hypersegmented neutrophils.  
• Troponin I <0.03 ng/mL; total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL; AST 52 U/L; LDH 1647 IU/L; haptoglobin <30 mg/dL.  
• CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis: no splenomegaly or evidence of neoplastic disease.  
• Coagulation studies: PT 11.2 s, fibrinogen 349 mg/dL, aPTT 24.6 s.  

She received two units of packed red blood cells, was started empirically on prednisone and daily plasmapheresis due to concern for TTP, and had hematology consultation on admission day 1. On hospital day 2, ADAMTS13 activity was 85%, an ANA screen was negative, and flow cytometry showed no PNH clone. The patient had no improvement in blood counts or symptoms after two days of plasmapheresis.
title: Pseudo-Thrombotic Microangiopathy Secondary to Vitamin B12 Deficiency

case_prompt: A 53-year-old woman with no family history of cancer presented with a lump in her left breast. Physical examination revealed a movable, painless, 3 cm nodule between the upper and lower inner quadrants of the left breast, without inflammatory signs or nipple retraction; the axillae were clinically negative. Mammography demonstrated a nodular lesion with irregular contours and peripheral calcification, classified as BI-RADS 4. Ultrasonography confirmed a 32 mm hypoechoic nodule with irregular, polylobed margins in the same location. An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy was performed. Histopathological examination showed spindle cell proliferation without hemorrhage or necrosis. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed positivity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3 and smooth muscle actin, a Ki-67 labeling index of 25%, and nuclear p63 expression. The pathology report concluded a spindle cell carcinomatous proliferation.
title: Rare variant of metaplastic carcinoma of the breast: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
An 88-year-old woman with arterial hypertension, osteoporosis, and degenerative lumbar disk disease presented with six months of worsening left low back pain radiating to the left lower limb, partially relieved by analgesics. Home medications included indapamide, enalapril, isosorbide mononitrate, and alphacalcidol. She denied smoking and alcohol use.

On examination, she appeared pale and hypertensive (190/80 mmHg); heart rate was 90 bpm, with a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, a grade 2/6 apical systolic murmur, and bilateral carotid bruits. Lung fields were clear. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, with a palpable, non-tender mass in the left flank; there was no edema.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 5.9 g/dL (MCV 66.4 fL; MCH 19.5 pg), serum iron 12 µg/dL, TIBC 221 µg/dL (transferrin saturation 5.4%), ferritin 36.6 ng/mL, creatinine 1.23 mg/dL (eGFR 39 mL/min/1.73 m2), and NT-proBNP 10 545 pg/mL. Inflammatory markers and other studies were normal.

Abdominal ultrasound showed a 100-mm heterogeneous mass adjacent to a calcified aortic wall and next to a 90×50-mm cyst-like structure with internal septations; Doppler detected minimal flow in the mass. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a normal right kidney and, on the left, a 27-mm cortical cyst plus a giant (109×102×94 mm), saccular, almost completely thrombosed left renal artery aneurysm with parietal calcifications and a small nodular calcification. The aneurysm compressed the pelvis, causing severe hydronephrosis and extreme parenchymal thinning to 2 mm. CT angiography showed scant contrast filling of the aneurysm.
title:
Giant Renal Artery Aneurysm With Hydronephrosis and Severe Atrophy of
the Renal Parenchyma: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old man from Sri Lanka presented with 3 weeks of high-grade fevers, drenching night sweats, anorexia, and a 6-kg weight loss. He denied cough, bowel changes, headache, or known tuberculosis exposure. His past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, he was febrile (39.8 °C), mildly pale, and had soft, nontender hepatosplenomegaly without lymphadenopathy or meningism. Blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg; other systems were normal.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, leukocytes 840/μL (neutrophils 640/μL), platelets 112×10^3/μL, C-reactive protein 206 mg/L, and ESR 135 mm/h. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Chest radiograph was normal. Renal function and coagulation profile were within normal limits. Serum albumin was 26 g/L. Liver enzymes were elevated (ALT 318 U/L, AST 444 U/L), with normal bilirubin. LDH was 1620 U/L. CSF analysis was unremarkable. Serologies for melioidosis, hepatitis, HIV, and a malaria smear were negative. Mantoux test was negative. Ultrasound and contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed only mild hepatosplenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy or lesions. 

He was treated empirically with meropenem and teicoplanin but remained febrile with worsening cytopenias. A bone marrow biopsy was obtained.
title: Fever with pancytopenia: unusual presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 71‐year‐old Japanese woman with severe dementia was found by her caregiver on her bed in the morning with a fluorescent pink liquid spilled over her head and an altered level of consciousness. She lived in a supervised facility, and all detergents and disinfectants had previously been removed after a suicide attempt 1 month earlier. She had no known medications aside from those managed by the facility. 

On presentation to a secondary hospital, she was hypotensive (systolic blood pressure < 60 mmHg) and received 2 L of extracellular fluid, 20 mL of 50% glucose for a blood glucose of 66 mg/dL, and 250 mL of 7% sodium bicarbonate for presumed acidosis. Three hours later, she was transferred to our emergency department. 

On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 9 (E3V2M4); pupils were sluggishly reactive. She was tachycardic at 128 bpm in sinus rhythm; other vital signs and the physical examination were unremarkable. 

Laboratory tests showed: white blood cell count 18.3 × 10^3/µL; sodium 160 mmol/L; chloride 114.8 mmol/L; creatinine 0.73 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed pH 7.083, bicarbonate 3.2 mmol/L, and an anion gap of 38.8 mmol/L. The calculated plasma osmolality was 334.9 mOsm/kg H_2O. 

A chest radiograph was normal. Noncontrast head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality.
title: Anion gap‐opening metabolic acidosis and urinary findings in the early diagnosis of ethylene glycol poisoning: A case report

case_prompt: A 64-year-old man presented with haematuria and urinary retention after his long-term catheter, placed for benign prostatic hyperplasia, fell out 2 days earlier; he had not passed urine for 24 hours. His history included benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension, treated with ramipril; he was an ex-smoker and did not consume alcohol. On examination he was diffusely tender in the lower abdomen, had an enlarged prostate on digital rectal examination, and a temperature of 37.8 °C. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 179 mg/L, a white-cell count of 8.5×10^9/L with neutrophils of 7.3×10^9/L, urea of 13.9 mmol/L, creatinine of 222 µmol/L, and blood glucose of 14 mmol/L; a subsequent HbA1c measurement was 7.8%. Urine dipstick revealed blood, nitrates, and white cells. Blood cultures were sterile after 5 days; urine culture showed heavy mixed growth without a definitive organism. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis, an incidental 2.7 cm renal cyst, and heterogeneous echogenicities around the bladder consistent with gas. On day 3, CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a thick-walled bladder, a large right-sided bladder diverticulum containing a gas–fluid level with intramural gas, and extraluminal free gas in the pelvis and right paracolic gutter.
title:
An unusual cause of free air in the abdomen: emphysematous cystitis
with bladder diverticulum perforation

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old woman presented with acute severe dyspnea. Eight and thirteen years earlier, she had undergone coronary artery bypass grafting: the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) to the left anterior descending artery, the right internal mammary artery (RIMA) to an obtuse marginal branch, and a saphenous vein graft to the distal left circumflex artery. Her medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.5%–6.7%), hyperlipidemia (LDL 100 mg/dL), and a bilateral neck bruit noted two years ago. MR angiography at that time showed <50% stenosis of both carotid arteries and 50% stenosis of both subclavian arteries. Ankle–brachial indices were elevated (ABI 1.62 on both sides), attributed to arterial stiffness, and she was asymptomatic without inter-arm blood pressure difference or arm claudication.

Six months before admission, she developed exertional chest discomfort. Two months later, her systolic blood pressure fell from 126/70 mmHg to 94/60 mmHg. ECG showed worsening ST-segment depression and QRS widening; echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 40% (previously >55%). Treatment with pimobendan led to slight improvement. One week before admission, her blood pressure measured 70/40 mmHg in the right arm and 80/50 mmHg in the left arm; antihypertensive medications were discontinued.

She was scheduled for cardiac catheterization but presented first with severe dyspnea. In the emergency department, respiratory rate was 30/min, heart rate 86/min, temperature 36.0°C, and bilateral arm blood pressures were difficult to measure. Chest radiography showed severe bilateral pulmonary edema. ECG demonstrated diffuse ST-segment depression with non-specific intraventricular conduction delay. Cardiac troponin I was positive; creatine phosphokinase rose from 66 U/L to 720 U/L. Renal and liver functions were normal.

She was intubated, admitted to intensive care, and started on intravenous dobutamine and furosemide. Dyspnea improved rapidly, and urine output was 950 mL in the first 4 hours and 50–100 mL/h thereafter. Despite vigorous treatment, systolic blood pressure remained low at 60–70 mmHg in both arms, but femoral pulses were easily palpable.
title: Pseudo-hypotension with acute pulmonary oedema due to simultaneous bilateral subclavian artery stenosis in a patient with coronary artery bypass graft surgery using bilateral internal mammary arteries: a case report

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man with a history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, hypertension, stable lung nodules, and a prior right thalamic ischemic stroke (treated with thrombolysis) presented after multiple witnessed seizures. The events began on awakening with headache and progressed to brief (<1 min) focal motor seizures of the left arm and leg, occurring every few minutes with preserved awareness; there was no incontinence, tongue biting, or postictal confusion. He reported left-sided tingling and numbness but denied visual, speech, or cognitive changes. He had been compliant with levetiracetam since a single seizure at the prior admission and had no further events until this presentation.

In the emergency department, he was hemodynamically stable. Examination revealed repeated left-sided shaking involving the neck and extremities with preserved consciousness, a left upper-extremity pronator drift, and 3/5 strength in the left lower extremity; the rest of the neurologic and general exam was normal. Lorazepam and a loading dose of levetiracetam controlled the seizures. 

Noncontrast head CT showed sulcal effacement with isodense material suggestive of a leptomeningeal process. EEG demonstrated cortical hyperexcitability with focal seizure activity over the right frontocentral and parasagittal regions. MRI of the brain ruled out acute infarction but revealed focal right frontal pachymeningeal and leptomeningeal enhancement.

Laboratory tests, including CBC, electrolytes, liver function, hepatitis B and C panels, vitamin D, HIV, angiotensin-converting enzyme, proteinase 3, C3, C4, extractable nuclear antigens, immunoglobulin G4, myeloperoxidase, rapid plasma reagin, and anti-dsDNA, were all negative. Rheumatoid factor was mildly elevated; anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody was >250 U/mL. 

Lumbar puncture showed normal cell counts, protein, and glucose. CSF studies—including rheumatoid factor, angiotensin-converting enzyme, Lyme serology, syphilis testing, Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, adenosine deaminase, cytology, and flow cytometry—were negative, and bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures showed no growth. 

CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed only small stable pulmonary nodules; MRI of the spine was unremarkable.
title: New-onset seizures: an unusual neurologic manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis

case_prompt: A 26‐year‐old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive lower-limb weakness. She initially walked with crutches, but by presentation she was wheelchair bound and had bladder and bowel incontinence. She denied trauma, fever, or prior medical comorbidities. On examination, she had a palpable thyroid nodule and hirsutism. Neurologic examination showed increased lower-limb reflexes, clonus, hypertonia, a positive Babinski sign, and paraparesis worse on the right. There was a T4 sensory level, diminished anal sphincter tone, and reduced perianal sensation. Her upper limbs and cranial nerves were intact, and there were no signs of infection or spinal tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed negative CEA, negative antinuclear antibodies, negative HIV, normal thyroid‐stimulating hormone, thyroxine, triiodothyronine, parathyroid hormone, CA-19-9, CA-125, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase, and normal urine electrophoresis with Bence-Jones protein of 0. Surveillance CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no primary lesion. Thyroid ultrasound confirmed a solitary nodule. Spinal CT demonstrated expansile osteolysis and collapse of the T2 and T3 vertebral bodies with residual trabeculae, a sclerotic rim, and segmental kyphosis. Sagittal and axial MRI showed vertebral collapse involving posterior elements, high-grade cord compression, lesions that were T1 isointense to gray matter, slightly T2 hyperintense, and demonstrated gadolinium enhancement. CT-guided biopsy of the thoracic lesion and fine-needle biopsy of the thyroid nodule were performed.
title: Primary Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma of the Spine: A First in Africa. A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old woman with hypertension, lupus nephritis, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, coronary artery disease, and prior Libman-Sacks endocarditis (status post coronary artery bypass graft and aortic valve replacement) presented with one week of lightheadedness and two days of recurrent nausea, vomiting, and poor oral intake. She also noted two days of right calf pain only when ambulating. She denied chest pain, back pain, or abdominal pain. Her medications included warfarin, and she required hemodialysis. 

On examination, blood pressure was 171/91 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 37.1 °C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She appeared comfortable, alert, and oriented. Neurologic examination was normal. Lungs were clear, and cardiac examination revealed regular rate and rhythm without murmur. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, and non-distended. Lower extremities were warm and well perfused, with normal range of motion, no swelling or calf tenderness, and symmetric palpable peripheral pulses.

Initial working diagnoses included an acute viral process or foodborne illness. However, given her right calf pain in the context of a chronic procoagulant state, a point-of-care ultrasound two-point compression examination of the right leg was performed.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Iatrogenic Aortic Dissection Presenting With Leg Pain Diagnosed With Point-of-care Ultrasound

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman was referred by her dentist for sudden onset of pain in the right mandible and numbness of the right chin. Her medical history was notable for an early breast carcinoma diagnosed in 2008 (pT1a N1a, estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive, HER-2 negative) treated with wide excision, axillary lymphadenectomy, adjuvant chemotherapy (3 cycles of FEC-100 and docetaxel), radiotherapy, and subsequent letrozole (2 years) and tamoxifen (5 years). In the same year, she underwent a total nephrectomy for a stage T1a clear-cell renal carcinoma. In October 2015, pulmonary and osteoclastic bone metastases from breast cancer were identified, and treatment with monthly zoledronic acid began in January 2016; she also received exemestane followed by fulvestrant after disease progression. 

In June 2016, she noted right mandibular pain and chin numbness, without involvement of the lower lip. Examination revealed no cervical lymphadenopathy. Intraoral inspection showed a firm bony elevation in the region of the right first and second premolars; the lower right second molar was tender to percussion but pulp sensibility was intact. A panoramic radiograph was unremarkable. Cone-beam CT and PET-CT were obtained; the PET-CT demonstrated bony radiolucent areas in the right mandibular ramus suggestive of osteoclastic lesions. Skeletal scintigraphy revealed diffuse metastases in the spine, ribs, pelvic bones, sacrum, proximal femur, and right mandibular ramus. MRI of the head was performed to evaluate possible trigeminal involvement and showed a small lesion in the right cavernous sinus, interpreted as a hemangioma or leiomyoma, with no apparent role in the patient’s neuropathy.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Numb chin syndrome as a sign of mandibular metastasis: A case report

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman with a 17-month history of schizophrenia was admitted for adjustment of antipsychotic medication. Her regimen had been switched from risperidone to perospirone, and over three weeks the perospirone dose was increased to 40 mg/day. Shortly after reaching this dose, she developed tremor, muscle rigidity, akathisia, heavy sweating, difficulty swallowing and speaking, tachycardia, fluctuating blood pressure, a fever of 39.8 °C, restlessness, and confusion.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 18.3 × 10^9/L, serum sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, creatine phosphokinase 813.2 U/L (normal 26–140 U/L), and myoglobin 486 µg/L (normal 12–76 µg/L). A lumbar puncture revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid. Neuroimaging was unremarkable. Electroencephalography demonstrated diffuse slow waves, consistent with metabolic encephalopathy.
title: A case of neuroleptic malignant syndrome induced by perospirone

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman with a 4-year history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia treated with fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab presented in May 2021 for induction therapy of newly diagnosed, therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia (decitabine plus a 21-day venetoclax ramp-up). Prophylactic levofloxacin, isavuconazonium, acyclovir, and allopurinol were started for neutropenia and tumor-lysis risk. On cycle 1 day 3, she developed neutropenic fever and was switched to meropenem; a CT pulmonary angiogram showed a pulmonary embolism, small bilateral pleural effusions, and basilar atelectasis. Chemo was held on day 4 due to persistent tachycardia and rising oxygen requirements; a repeat chest CT revealed worsening patchy infiltrates in the upper and middle lobes and consolidation versus atelectasis in the lower lobes. Pleural effusions improved with diuresis, but tachypnea persisted despite broad antibiotics and sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim for Pneumocystis coverage. She was discharged after stabilization.

Twelve days after chemotherapy was held, she returned with acute, left-sided facial swelling in the setting of neutropenia. Dermatologic exam revealed a solitary subcutaneous nodule without epidermal ulceration. An initial biopsy was non-specific, showing mild inflammation but no evidence of infection, leukemic infiltration, or neutrophilic dermatosis. Two days later, similar erythematous plaques appeared on her right eyelid and eyebrow; a repeat biopsy showed dense neutrophilic infiltration consistent with Sweet syndrome, with negative bacterial and fungal stains. Prednisone was started, and the skin lesions improved rapidly.

In October 2021, approximately four months later and on day 35 of azacitidine plus venetoclax, she developed facial pain, fevers to 38.1 °C, and neutropenia (ANC 390 cells/μL). She had bilateral purpuric papules on the lower extremities and periorbital tenderness. Bone marrow biopsy showed 2% blasts. Empiric cefepime, doxycycline, acyclovir, and isavuconazonium were instituted, and prednisone 30 mg daily plus topical hydrocortisone were added for presumed recurrence of cutaneous Sweet syndrome. Maxillofacial CT demonstrated maxillary sinus opacification with hyperdense material and orbital fat stranding, prompting amphotericin B and daptomycin. Nasal endoscopy suggested bacterial sinusitis but cultures remained negative. Despite optimized antimicrobials, fevers and dyspnea persisted. Chest CT revealed new bilateral ground-glass opacities in the upper and middle lobes with consolidative opacities in the lower lobes. She developed increasing oxygen requirements, ultimately requiring high-flow nasal cannula. Bronchoscopy with cultures was unrevealing.
title: Unique challenges to diagnosing sweet syndrome following induction chemotherapy for relapsed Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML): A case and brief-review

case_prompt: A 40-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a 6-week history of exertional dyspnea and cough. He had worked in construction for 18 years, had a 23 pack-year smoking history (quit 6 weeks earlier), and a 12-year history of allergic rhinitis. He was afebrile. Vital signs: heart rate 86/min, blood pressure 137/87 mmHg, respiratory rate 27/min, oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Lung auscultation was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed leukocyte count 3150/µL, lactate dehydrogenase 394 U/L, C-reactive protein 4.48 mg/dL, and Krebs von den Lungen-6 435.2 U/mL. Immunologic studies were normal except an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:40. Sputum and blood cultures were negative for pathogens. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed centrilobular ground-glass opacities predominantly in the right lung. Pulmonary function tests showed a mixed ventilatory impairment (VC 53.6% predicted; FEV1/FVC 64.3%). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cultures were negative for bacteria, viruses, and fungi. BALF analysis demonstrated a total cell count of 6.994 × 10^5/mL with 61.3% lymphocytes, 37.5% macrophages, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.81; there was no alveolar hemorrhage. Transbronchial lung biopsy revealed alveolitis without malignancy, granulomas, or fibrosis.
title: Arc-welders’ pneumoconiosis with atypical radiological and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid findings: A case report

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman presented with multiple episodes of coffee-ground emesis over 24 hours, preceded by nearly 20 episodes of greenish, nonbloody emesis beginning 3 days earlier. She reported a 7-month history of similar 2- to 3-day episodes of moderate, continuous, dull, midline abdominal pain associated with nausea, anorexia, and a mild headache without visual changes or aura; these episodes required three prior hospital admissions. Between admissions she was symptomatic enough to need assistance with activities of daily living. She denied fever, chills, bowel‐habit changes, weight loss, or skin findings. Her medical history included coronary artery disease treated with a drug-eluting stent 2 months earlier; she was on aspirin and ticagrelor. Prior outpatient therapies (omeprazole, ondansetron, sucralfate, meclizine, scopolamine, topiramate) had failed. 

On examination, her abdomen was soft, mildly distended, and tender in the epigastric and periumbilical areas without guarding or rebound. Initial laboratory studies showed potassium 3.0 mEq/L, glucose 264 mg/dL, anion gap 20 mEq/L, venous pH 7.412, HCO3 18.6 mmol/L, and beta-hydroxybutyrate 2.25 mmol/L. Management for presumed starvation ketosis and possible diabetic ketoacidosis corrected her metabolic abnormalities. Low hemoglobin and coffee-ground emesis raised concern for an upper GI bleed, so aspirin was held and intravenous fluids and antiemetics were administered.

A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a small hiatal hernia and no acute changes in the bowel or mesentery. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed no ulcers, strictures, or active bleeding, and biopsies were negative for malignancy. A gastric-emptying study was normal. Brain MRI demonstrated only a stable chronic cerebellar infarct without new findings. Blood cultures and urinalysis were normal, and chest radiography showed no pulmonary process. Cardiac evaluation revealed a normal ECG and negative troponins.
title: Fifty‐eight‐year‐old female with abdominal migraine: A rare cause of episodic gastrointestinal disturbance in adults

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old Thai woman, G1P0 at 31 weeks’ gestation, presented with 6 hours of fever and severely painful swelling of her wrists, hands, and feet. She was unable to make a fist and had difficulty walking. She also reported a headache but denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or myalgia. A pruritic, erythematous rash was noted on her abdomen. She lived in a community where neighbors had experienced fever and arthralgia in the past week. She was not on any medications, had no recent hospitalizations, and no family members were ill.

On examination, temperature was 38.1 °C, blood pressure 100/40 mmHg, pulse 126 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Maculopapular rashes were present on the forehead, cheeks, nose, and abdominal wall. There was arthritis of both wrists, ankles, and all metatarsophalangeal joints. Arthrocentesis of the left wrist yielded clear yellow synovial fluid with high viscosity; Gram stain showed no organisms.

Laboratory studies revealed: hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL; hematocrit 33%; white cells 9300/mm3 (91% neutrophils); platelets 180 000/mm3; BUN 8.3 mg/dL; creatinine 0.38 mg/dL; total protein 6.2 g/dL; albumin 3.5 g/dL; globulin 2.7 g/dL; total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL; direct bilirubin 0.1 mg/dL; AST 15 U/L; ALT 8 U/L; ALP 102 U/L; ESR 52 mm/h. Serology for dengue NS1 antigen and IgM and IgG antibodies was negative.
title: Atypical skin manifestation in severe acute chikungunya infection in a pregnant woman: a case report

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old Nepalese man presented with a more than 5-year history of insidious onset weakness of his right upper limb. He initially noted difficulty sustaining his grip when holding objects, which gradually progressed to impairments in fine motor tasks, including buttoning clothes, writing, combing his hair, and using utensils. Over the same period, he observed a tremor and progressive reduction in muscle bulk of his right hand. After 2 years of right-hand symptoms, he began to notice tremors in his left hand without accompanying weakness. His symptoms progressed over the first 3 years but have been static since then. He denied neck pain, sensory changes, autonomic symptoms, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. There was no history of trauma, surgery, medication use, vaccination, or toxin exposure. He is a university student working part-time and has no family history of neurologic disease.

On examination, vital signs were stable. General examination was unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed normal cranial nerves, coordination, sensation, and gait. Motor testing showed atrophy of the right hand, most prominently in the first dorsal interosseous, with sparing of the brachioradialis. Muscle strength (Medical Research Council scale) on the right was 2/5 in the interossei, 3/5 in wrist flexion and extension, and 4/5 in elbow flexion and extension; left upper-limb strength was normal. Tone was reduced around the right elbow and wrist. Minipolymyoclonus was present in the fingers bilaterally (more pronounced on the right). Deep‐tendon reflexes were symmetrical and normal except for a brisk right supinator response. Plantar responses were flexor bilaterally, and Hoffman signs were absent. Sensation and gait were intact.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, thyroid function, inflammatory markers, creatine phosphokinase, viral serologies, and autoantibodies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA), were within normal limits. A cervical spine radiograph was unremarkable. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated motor axonal neuropathy with reduced compound motor action potentials in the right median and ulnar nerves; findings were normal on the left. Needle EMG showed neurogenic discharges with fibrillations and fasciculations in bilateral first dorsal interossei and the right biceps and triceps. Cervical spine MRI, including flexion T1-weighted contrast and neutral T2-weighted sequences, showed no dural enhancement, no anterior displacement of the posterior dural sac, and no cord atrophy or signal abnormality. A prior MRI performed 2 years earlier was also normal.
title: The diagnostic quandary of magnetic resonance imaging-negative Hirayama disease: a case report

case_prompt: A 42-year-old man with HIV on HAART (undetectable viral load), a history of anal condylomas, intersphincteric fistulas, perirectal abscesses, and ischemic proctitis 6 years earlier presented with 1 day of severe rectal pain, subjective fevers, nausea, multiple episodes of bloody and brown emesis, diarrhea with bright red blood mixed with clots, and fecal urge incontinence. He engages in receptive anal intercourse and takes prophylactic medications for HIV and herpes simplex virus. On examination, he was febrile (38.9°C), had abdominal distension and tenderness in the lower abdomen, and poor rectal sphincter tone. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis (WBC 29,000/mm3) and elevated lactate (2.5 mmol/L). Abdominal CT demonstrated severe proctocolitis. Empiric antibiotics were started after obtaining blood, stool, and rectal swab cultures. Sigmoidoscopy revealed a 5 cm submucosal, circumferential, nonbleeding mass 15–20 cm from the anal verge suggestive of an abscess. Pelvic MRI confirmed a 10 cm segment of circumferential intramural abscess with hemorrhage near the rectosigmoid junction. Stool studies and infectious serologies were negative. The patient improved clinically, was afebrile with normalized WBC count, and was discharged after 1 week; diverticulitis was presumed to be the etiology. Six weeks later, he underwent laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy with primary stapled anastomosis. On postoperative day 3, he developed sudden abdominal pain, ileus, and rising WBC count and C-reactive protein. CT with rectal contrast showed no leak but segmental colitis. He underwent abdominal washout and diverting loop colostomy; exploration revealed ascites and adhesions without stool or purulence, and proctoscopy under water showed no air leak. Pathologic examination of the resected sigmoid colon showed patchy mild active colitis with focal perivascular lymphocytic inflammation and chronic vasculitis involving intramural and mesenteric arteries, with “no evidence of diverticular disease, granulomas, or viral cytopathic changes.” Rheumatology evaluation revealed bilateral L4 dermatome numbness. Serologic testing showed elevated p-ANCA titers, normal serum protein electrophoresis and complement levels, and negative anti-Ro, anti-LA, double-stranded DNA, and PR3-ANCA titers. Creatinine and urinalysis were normal, suggesting no renal involvement.
title: Clash of the -itises: An Unexpected Case of Sigmoid Colon Vasculitis

case_prompt: A 66-year-old man presented with a 9-day history of progressive abdominal fullness, a 3-day history of obstipation, and night sweats for over 1 month. He had no prior episodes of bowel obstruction. His medical history was notable for sarcoidosis diagnosed by transbronchial biopsy 12 years earlier. On examination, his vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count with differential, electrolytes, liver enzymes, and lactate, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple small-bowel air-fluid levels and a 6.1-cm mass at the ileocecal region with adjacent pericolonic lymph nodes up to 2 cm in diameter, consistent with mechanical obstruction. Given the acute obstructing colonic mass and high suspicion for malignancy, the patient was taken directly to surgery for right hemicolectomy.
title: Ileocecal IgG4-Related Disease: A Case Report Mimicking Malignancy

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman with a history of ovarian cancer completed six cycles of postoperative chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. After her 5th and 6th cycles, she developed myelosuppression and received filgrastim (75 µg/day) for 3 and 4 days, respectively. On the night after her last filgrastim dose, she developed high fever. 

She was prescribed acetaminophen and levofloxacin as an outpatient but remained febrile and was admitted on day 4. She had no cough, chest pain, abdominal pain, rash, or visual symptoms. Her temperature was 38.0 °C, blood pressure 92/50 mmHg, pulse 70 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. The head and neck were without bruit or tenderness, chest and cardiac auscultation were unremarkable, and the abdomen was soft without tenderness. There were no skin lesions or peripheral edema. 

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 8780/µL, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelet count 70,000/µL, and C-reactive protein 19.39 mg/dL. Serum ferritin was elevated (883 ng/mL), β-D glucan was normal, and blood cultures were negative. Serologic tests including STS, tuberculosis interferon-γ, and viral panels were negative. Autoimmune serologies were negative (MPO-ANCA <1.0 U/mL, PR3-ANCA <1.0 U/mL, fluorescent ANA negative, IgG4 21 mg/dL). 

Electrocardiography, echocardiography, and chest radiography were unremarkable. Abdominal aortic ultrasonography demonstrated circumferential wall thickening with a surrounding hypoechoic rim. Contrast-enhanced CT showed new soft-tissue stranding around the aortic arch and abdominal aorta compared with pre-chemotherapy images. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed thickening and enhancement of the aortic wall and periaortic tissue. These imaging findings suggested active inflammation of the aorta.
title: Granulocyte colony stimulating factor-associated aortitis evaluated via multiple imaging modalities including vascular echography: a case report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old female high–level soccer player twisted her right ankle during a match and immediately noted pain, swelling, and difficulty bearing weight. She had no prior history of tibial, tarsal, or ankle disease or injury. In the emergency department, radiographs of the right ankle were interpreted as a displaced medial malleolus fracture and demonstrated an os subfibularis. 

On transfer to our department, examination of the right ankle confirmed swelling, functional impairment, and intense medial malleolar pain but revealed no ankle laxity, instability, or pronation pain, and flexion-extension was preserved with only slight discomfort. Twenty-four hours later, she reported a marked reduction in pain and swelling and improved range of motion. 

To investigate the discrepancy between the initial radiographic interpretation and the unexpectedly benign clinical course, a comparison radiograph of the left (uninjured) ankle was obtained and showed a similarly shaped medial malleolus fragment without an os subfibularis. 

Because the clinical findings and bilateral radiographs were incongruent with a typical acute fracture, a bilateral CT scan was ordered.
final_diagnosis_raw: congenital pseudoarthrosis of the medial malleolus
title: Congenital Pseudoarthrosis of Medial Malleolus in A Young Soccer Player - Diagnosis in Clinical setting of Ankle Sprain

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of slowly progressive vision loss in both eyes, which had markedly worsened over the past 3 months. He also noted floaters and a rapid decrease in vision in the left eye. His medical history was notable for chronic kidney failure from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (on peritoneal dialysis and erythropoietin) and well-controlled systemic hypertension (blood pressure 115/80 mmHg on beta- and alpha-blockers). He denied diabetes, prior ocular surgery, or significant eye disease; he was allergic to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination showed clear corneas, rubeosis iridis, and mild nuclear sclerotic cataracts. Funduscopic examination revealed engorged, pale retinal arterioles; attenuated venules; diffuse RPE pigmentary changes; small vitreous hemorrhage and subhyaloid hemorrhage sparing the fovea, with neovascularization of the optic disc in the right eye; and old inferior vitreous hemorrhage with fibrovascular proliferation on the optic disc in the left eye.

Fluorescein angiography demonstrated a leopard-spot pattern of choroidal hyperfluorescence, optic-disc neovascular leakage, and peripheral capillary nonperfusion in both eyes. Spectral-domain OCT showed posterior vitreous detachment with hyperreflective intraretinal flecks, and visible hyperreflective arterial vessel walls. Enhanced depth imaging OCT revealed thickened choroidal vessel walls and lumenal enlargement.

The working diagnosis was bilateral proliferative retinopathy from an occlusive retinal vasculopathy. Laboratory studies showed normocytic normochromic anemia, elevated creatinine (12.9 mg/dL), elevated alkaline phosphatase, and hypoalbuminemia. Syphilis serologies and tuberculosis testing were negative. ANA, RF, anti-Sm, antiphospholipid, ANCA subtypes, complement levels, anti-DNA, anti-RNP, anti-Ro, and anti-La antibodies were all negative. A thrombophilia panel for factor V Leiden, protein C and S deficiencies, and antithrombin III deficiency was negative. Carotid and orbital Doppler ultrasonography showed mild carotid and vertebral artery stenosis with reduced flow in the ophthalmic and central retinal arteries.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Secondary hyperhomocysteinemia-related occlusive retinal vasculopathy: A case report

case_prompt: A 12-year-old boy presented for evaluation of a scalp rash. Three years earlier, he had sustained a third-degree burn of the scalp treated with an autologous skin graft. Two years after the graft, a rash developed over the grafted area and gradually worsened over the following year. The patient reported pruritus and erythema, and he noted development of a thin film over the site. Treatment with topical 5% doxepin relieved the itch, but multiple courses of topical antibiotics and antibacterial soaps produced no improvement, prompting consideration of regrafting for presumed infection. His history was notable for atopic dermatitis; his mother had hidradenitis suppurativa. On examination, approximately 70% of the scalp radiating from the vertex showed diffuse erythema, weeping shallow erosions with overlying yellow-brown crusts, and atrophic skin bordering the graft. Prior bacterial cultures obtained at the burn hospital were all negative.
final_diagnosis_raw: Erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp
title: A case of erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp in a pediatric patient

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old man presented with headache, psychomotor retardation, and left hemiparesis. Laboratory evaluation revealed HIV infection (CD4+ T-cell count 20 cells/μL; plasma HIV RNA 301,000 copies/mL) and positive serology for Toxoplasma gondii. A brain CT scan showed multiple scattered parenchymal lesions with perilesional edema, mass effect, and ring contrast enhancement. He received anti-toxoplasma therapy without corticosteroids, with clinical and radiologic improvement, and initiated HAART one month after diagnosis (regimen as per institutional protocol). Toxoplasmosis therapy continued (followed by suppressive dosing), and MAC prophylaxis was maintained.

Three months after HAART initiation, he reported abrupt onset of right lower-limb numbness that progressed over one month to involve his entire right lower limb and right hemi-abdomen. He denied fever or other systemic symptoms and affirmed full adherence to all therapies. On examination, mental status and cranial nerves were normal. Apart from his prior left hemiparesis, there was a distinct sensory level at T9 on the right, with loss of touch and pain sensation below this level; strength, proprioception, and reflexes in the affected areas were preserved. 

A follow-up brain CT scan revealed that some prior lesions had improved, others had slightly worsened with ring enhancement and edema, and several new lesions had appeared. MRI of the dorsal spinal cord demonstrated T2-weighted hyperintense lesions extending from T3 to T9, with a probable posterolateral lesion at T7–T8. At this time, CD4+ T-cell count had risen to 128 cells/μL and plasma HIV RNA had fallen to 121 copies/mL. CSF analysis showed 5 cells/μL, protein 58 mg/dL, glucose 51 mg/dL; Gram and acid-fast stains, microbiological cultures, cryptococcal antigen, VDRL, and PCR assays for JC virus, BK virus, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, human herpesvirus 6, varicella-zoster virus, and enterovirus were negative. CSF PCR for T. gondii was not performed. EBV PCR was positive, but a normal CSF lymphocyte phenotype and a whole-body PET scan showed no hypermetabolic cerebral or medullary lesions. HTLV-I/II serology was negative.
title: Toxoplasmosis-associated IRIS involving the CNS: a case report with longitudinal analysis of T cell subsets

case_prompt: A 41-year-old multiparous woman (G6P5) with a history notable only for an open appendectomy at age 12 years presented in active labor. Seventeen hours after admission she had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with 400 mL blood loss and received methylergonovine and misoprostol for uterine atony. On postpartum day 1 she tolerated oral intake, voided, and ambulated. Approximately 11 hours after delivery she developed severe, cramping, generalized abdominal pain. Vital signs were: temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 147/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 100% on room air, and blood glucose 98 mg/dL. Examination revealed moderate tenderness in all quadrants without rebound or guarding. Bedside abdominal ultrasound showed a thin endometrial stripe, a well-contracted uterus, and no free intraperitoneal fluid. Hemoglobin was 11.7 g/dL. She was treated conservatively with antacids, soft diet, and analgesics with initial symptomatic improvement. On postpartum day 2 she became intolerant of oral intake, with persistent pain. Electrolytes, liver function tests, amylase, and lipase were normal; white-cell count was 15.2 × 10^9/L. An abdominal radiograph showed mildly distended, gas-filled large bowel loops and absence of gas in the rectum, “possibly due to ileus or early obstruction.”
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Small Bowel Obstruction in Postpartum Vaginal Delivery due to Prior Abdominal Adhesions Case Report

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man presented for routine follow-up of sigmoid colon cancer. Two years earlier, he had undergone laparoscopic sigmoidectomy for a pStage I, moderately differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma with submucosal and venous invasion. His father died of gastric cancer. 

He was asymptomatic, with no abdominal pain, palpable masses, or lymphadenopathy on examination. Laboratory studies showed:
- Lactate dehydrogenase 239 U/L (elevated)
- Creatinine 1.14 mg/dL (elevated)
- Carbohydrate antigen 19-9 41 U/mL (elevated)
- Other serum biochemistry and tumor markers within normal limits
- Urine cytology: no atypical cells (class II)

Enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 30 × 13.7 mm soft-tissue mass involving the left ureter at the level of the common iliac bifurcation; the lesion had grown from 16.7 × 10.3 mm over 17 months. There was no hydronephrosis or lymphadenopathy. FDG-PET–CT showed focal uptake in the same region (SUVmax 8.93) and no other abnormal accumulations. Ureterography and colonoscopy were unremarkable.

Given the slow growth and significant FDG uptake, concern arose for lymph node recurrence or peritoneal seeding of colon cancer, and a decision was made to proceed with laparoscopic excisional biopsy of the mass.
title: IgG4-related focal retroperitoneal fibrosis in ureter suggestive of colon cancer recurrence and resected laparoscopically: a case report

case_prompt: A 48-year-old woman with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, premature ventricular contractions, and anxiety underwent elective right renal cyst aspiration for right upper-quadrant pain. Under ultrasound guidance and moderate sedation, an 18-gauge needle yielded 170 mL of clear yellow fluid. She reported symptomatic relief and was initially stable. One hour later, she developed severe abdominal pain. Examination revealed a soft abdomen and cool, dry skin. Vital signs showed bradycardia and hypotension. Intravenous fluids and Trendelenburg positioning were started, but she became unresponsive and pulseless. Advanced cardiac life support was initiated with CPR and intravenous epinephrine. After return of spontaneous circulation, she complained of severe chest pain. Bedside ultrasound showed no right flank haematoma or pericardial effusion. An ECG demonstrated ST-segment elevations in the anterolateral leads and depressions in the inferior leads. A chest radiograph was normal. Initial laboratory studies showed normal troponin, serum glucose, and serum potassium levels. She was taken emergently for coronary angiography, which demonstrated angiographically normal coronary arteries.
title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy following ultrasound-guided renal cyst aspiration

case_prompt: A 68-year-old woman was diagnosed with sigmoid colon cancer and was scheduled for laparoscopic colectomy the next day. On the evening before surgery, she reported left preauricular pain and difficulty opening her mouth. On examination, the maximum interincisal opening was 13 mm. Palpation of the temporomandibular joints revealed no pain or erythema, and there was no joint clicking. Schuller’s radiographic views of the left temporomandibular joint showed that the mandibular condyle did not translate anteriorly in the open position; there was no evidence of bony ankylosis or mandibular fracture. Dental examination revealed tooth mobility and loss from periodontal disease, with deviation of the occlusal plane.
title: Diagnosis and management of temporomandibular joint dysfunction before surgery: a case report

case_prompt:
An 88-year-old man with hypertension and chronic kidney disease presented with progressive dry cough, dyspnea, fever, and chills. Twenty-five days earlier, he had started a herbal medicine, Sai-rei-to, and symptoms began two weeks after initiation. He was an ex-smoker, took no other medications, and had no history of pulmonary disease or allergy.

On examination, temperature was 38.0 °C; respiratory rate 20 breaths/min; blood pressure 189/91 mmHg; heart rate 72 bpm; and oxygen saturation was 99% on 12 L/min via reservoir mask. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral late inspiratory crackles, and bilateral pretibial edema was noted.

Laboratory tests showed WBC count 8000/mm3 (78.8% neutrophils, 7.8% eosinophils), platelets 155,000/mm3, BNP 406 pg/mL, CRP 10.51 mg/dL, KL-6 374 U/mL, and SP-D 339 ng/mL. Coagulation was normal. Bacteriological tests were negative; Mycoplasma complement fixation titer rose fourfold, and single-sample Chlamydia pneumoniae antibodies were non-diagnostic. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed severe hypoxemia. Echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 60% with normal wall motion.

Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities. High-resolution CT confirmed bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities, infiltrative shadows, and pleural effusions. Nasal high-flow oxygen therapy was initiated.

Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage with a neutrophil predominance (total cell count 325,000/mL: 62% neutrophils, 26% lymphocytes, 12% macrophages; CD4/CD8 ratio 0.49).

Given the lack of known interstitial lung disease, the temporal association with Sai-rei-to, and the exclusion of obvious infection or cardiac failure, all oral therapies including Sai-rei-to were discontinued, and the patient was started on methylprednisolone pulse therapy (1000 mg/day for 3 days), furosemide, ceftriaxone, and azithromycin.
title: Severe acute respiratory failure due to Sai-rei-to-induced lung injury successfully treated by multi-modal therapy including immunosuppressive therapy, plasma exchange, and intravenous immunoglobulin: A case report

case_prompt: A 56-year-old woman was evaluated for 8 months of symptomatic hypoglycemia associated with syncope, relieved by carbohydrate intake. She had type 2 diabetes managed without medications since 2018 and had undergone Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 3 years earlier. On examination, her body-mass index was 29, and the abdominal examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 33.9%, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, plasma glucose 114 mg/dL, c-peptide 4.71 ng/mL, insulin 27.9 μU/mL, and hemoglobin A1c 4.9%. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a large gastrojejunostomy anastomosis but no pancreatic mass. A selective arterial calcium stimulation test showed a fourfold increase in insulin secretion localized to the gastroduodenal artery. During a supervised 72-hour fast, her glucose level remained above 60 mg/dL. She was discharged on octreotide and a low-carbohydrate diet. Two weeks later, she presented with a blood glucose level of 44 mg/dL. CT of the abdomen again showed no enhancing pancreatic mass but revealed intrahepatic biliary ductal dilation and a pancreatic duct dilated to 4.3 mm concerning for a head mass.
title: Non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglycemia syndrome due to nesidioblastosis following bariatric Roux-en-Y gastric bypass

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man presented with 3 months of lower-jaw and submandibular pain occurring only with eating. He described acute, sharp, stabbing pain (8/10) over the lower jaw and submandibular glands, more pronounced on the right, triggered by the first bite of each meal, subsiding over subsequent bites and resolving minutes after the meal. Episodes lasted less than 2 minutes with no associated hoarseness, facial sweating, rhinorrhea, odynophagia, or dysphagia. Symptoms were independent of time of day or position. He had no history of surgery, trauma, underlying disease, medications, or family history of similar symptoms. Vital signs were normal. 

Head and neck examination revealed dentures in place, no ulcers, deformities, masses, or lymphadenopathy. The pharynx, tonsils, soft palate, tongue, parotid glands, nose, temporomandibular joint, and neck were all normal on inspection and palpation. 

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, viral serologies, fasting blood sugar, thyroid-stimulating hormone, inflammatory and rheumatologic markers, electrolytes, and renal function, were all within normal limits. 

Contrast and noncontrast CT scans from the skull base to the neck showed no space-occupying lesions, masses, or other pathologic findings.
title: Successful management of an idiopathic first bite syndrome: A case report and review

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old man with longstanding fibrostenotic Crohn’s disease presented with a one-day history of fever and abdominal pain. One week earlier, he had a surveillance colonoscopy showing progression of his disease, and azathioprine 125 mg daily was started after TPMT levels were found to be intermediate. His history included iron deficiency and benign prostatic hyperplasia; he had no known allergies. Current medications were azathioprine 50 mg daily, budesonide, tamsulosin, and ferrous gluconate.

On admission, he was febrile, tachycardic, and hypotensive; intravenous fluids were given. A working diagnosis of sepsis led to empiric ceftriaxone. Chest radiograph, blood and urine cultures, and CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed no source of infection. Azathioprine was held. Over the next three days, he remained febrile with persistent tachycardia, progressed to distributive shock and acute renal failure, and required piperacillin-tazobactam, vancomycin, stress-dose methylprednisolone, and norepinephrine.

On hospital day 4, he developed an acute erythematous rash with pustules on the torso and extremities. A skin punch biopsy was obtained. With clinical improvement and reduced concern for infection, azathioprine was restarted on ICU day 7. Twelve hours after a single re-challenge dose, he redeveloped vasodilatory shock and a decline in consciousness requiring intubation, fluid resuscitation, and vasopressors. ECG showed transient ST elevations in the inferior and septal leads, and high-sensitivity troponin T was 1290 ng/L (upper reference limit, 14 ng/L). Urgent cardiac catheterization revealed no obstructive coronary artery disease.
journal: Allergy, Asthma, and Clinical Immunology : Official Journal of the Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
title: Severe distributive shock, neutrophilic dermatosis, and ST-elevation myocardial infarction in the setting of azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome

case_prompt: A 66-year-old man with familial dilated cardiomyopathy and a CRT-D device presented with transient faintness and palpitations. His history included juvenile sick sinus syndrome treated with a permanent pacemaker at age 25; his son died of juvenile dilated cardiomyopathy. On examination, pulse was 90 beats/min and systolic blood pressure 102 mm Hg. A 12-lead ECG showed a regular wide QRS rhythm at 90 beats/min, QRS duration 200 ms with a right bundle branch block pattern, marked left axis deviation, and no obvious P waves. Device interrogation revealed ventricular sensing without CRT pacing at a V-V interval of 700 ms, which was shorter than the regular right atrial rhythm. The CRT-D did not classify this as ventricular tachyarrhythmia because its detection zone was programmed for rates over 150 beats/min. From these observations, the initial speculation was that this was an accelerated idioventricular rhythm with ventriculoatrial dissociation, and catheter ablation was planned to restore effective CRT pacing.
title: Left atrial reentrant tachycardia with interatrial dissociation mimicking accelerated idioventricular rhythm in a patient with a cardiac resynchronization defibrillator

case_prompt: A 2-year-old girl, the third child of healthy nonconsanguineous parents, was born at 38 weeks by elective Caesarean section weighing 3.01 kg. Apart from mild neonatal jaundice, her infancy was uneventful. By age 3 months she tracked at the 99.9th centile for height and weight and exhibited an insatiable appetite. Development was mildly delayed at 18 months but normalized by 2.5 years. For weight management, two separate TSH levels were found to be elevated with normal free T4. At referral, her weight was 20 kg (>99.6th centile), height 93 cm (>99.6th centile), and BMI 23.2 (>99.6th centile). On examination she had a round facies, flat occiput, and central obesity. Serial electrolytes showed normal calcium and phosphate with persistently elevated PTH, and thyroid tests remained abnormal. Mild primary hypothyroidism was suspected and confirmed on a TSH stimulation test.
title: Duplication of 17q11.2 and Features of Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy Secondary to Methylation Defects within the GNAS Cluster: Coincidence or Causal?

case_prompt: A 57-year-old woman with no prior cardiac history was admitted for newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia.
