On arrival, laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis of 31.9×10^9/L with an eosinophil count of 7.66×10^9/L and normocytic anemia. Baseline echocardiography demonstrated preserved biventricular function without valvular disease. She began induction chemotherapy with cytarabine and daunorubicin. Two days after starting systemic chemotherapy, she developed chest pain. She had cardiovascular risk factors of hypertension and a smoking history. An ECG showed anterior and inferior ST-segment depressions, and troponin I was elevated at 690 ng/L (normal <14 ng/L) alongside an eosinophil count of 33.3×10^9/L. Because of thrombocytopenia, she underwent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging instead of immediate catheterization. Stress perfusion CMR revealed a new left ventricular ejection fraction of 32% with global hypokinesia and extensive sub-endocardial hypoperfusion in all coronary territories. T2 mapping was at the upper limit of normal. The study was terminated early due to severe dyspnea, and no late gadolinium enhancement images were obtained. Given her risk factors and perfusion findings, a working diagnosis of severe triple-vessel CAD or vasospasm was made. Coronary angiography demonstrated no atherosclerotic disease. Despite medical therapy for heart failure, the patient’s severe LV dysfunction and troponin elevations persisted.
title: Eosinophilic myocarditis during treatment of acute myeloid leukaemia: cardiac magnetic resonance in the very early phase mimicking triple-vessel coronary artery disease: a case report

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old man with a 5-year history of poorly controlled hypertension was admitted 10 days ago for a spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage managed nonoperatively. He was discharged after 3 days on analgesics and an anticonvulsant. He re-presented with 2 days of profound asthenia and dyspnea that acutely worsened on the day of admission. He also noted excessive polyuria over the preceding 3 days.

On examination, he was alert (GCS 15), hypotensive (74/30 mm Hg), tachycardic (135 bpm), mottled, and had cool extremities. He was tachypneic; cardiac and lung auscultation were unremarkable. He had dry mucous membranes and visible skin-fold dehydration. His weight was 65 kg (10 days earlier, 71 kg). Urine output was low (0.3 mL/kg/h).

ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a collapsible inferior vena cava, preserved LVEF (65%), and no tamponade. Arterial blood gas showed metabolic alkalosis and lactate of 3.64 mmol/L. Chest radiograph was normal.

After 30 mL/kg of saline, he remained hypotensive and required norepinephrine. Six hours later, blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg, lactate had fallen to 1.8 mmol/L, and urine output improved.

Laboratory studies showed hemoconcentration, hyponatremia (123 mmol/L), hypochloremia (54 mEq/L), hypokalemia (2.3 mmol/L), low plasma osmolality (254 mmol/kg H₂O), elevated creatinine (120 μmol/L), and elevated urea (0.97 g/L), with normal inflammatory markers. Urine studies revealed natriuresis of 62 mmol/L and urine chloride of 64 mmol/L.
title: Cerebral Salt Wasting Syndrome (CSW): An unusual cause of hypovolemia after spontaneous cerebral hemorrhage successfully treated with fludrocortisone

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old Japanese woman was brought to the emergency department with severe chest pain and transient loss of consciousness. She had no history of smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, connective-tissue disease, or prior cardiac disease. Four days before presentation, she noted exertional chest discomfort that gradually worsened, sometimes with diaphoresis. On the day of admission, she developed severe chest pain with diaphoresis, fainted at a local clinic, and was transferred to a nearby hospital. 

Electrocardiography showed marked ST-segment elevation in lead aVR and widespread ST-segment depression elsewhere. Echocardiography revealed diffuse left ventricular hypokinesis with preservation of basal inferior wall motion. On arrival at our hospital, she was hypotensive and agitated (GCS E1V1M5), heart rate 113 bpm and irregular, jugular venous distension, coarse crackles bilaterally, and no murmurs. 

Laboratory studies revealed WBC 19,400/μL, CRP 8.18 mg/dL, CK 1100 IU/L, CK-MB 89 IU/L, troponin T elevated, lactic acidosis (pH 7.016, lactate 10.3 mmol/L), normal lipid profile, and negative autoantibodies. Chest radiograph showed pulmonary congestion. 

During evaluation, she developed pulseless electrical activity and ventricular tachycardia. VA-ECMO was initiated, and emergent coronary angiography demonstrated 99% stenosis of the left main trunk. Intravascular ultrasound showed no calcification and a poorly defined three-layered structure with concentric thickening of the vessel wall. A 3.5×12 mm bare-metal stent was placed with restoration of TIMI grade 3 flow. An intra-aortic balloon pump was instituted, and she was admitted to the coronary care unit.
title: New-onset Takayasu's Arteritis as Acute Myocardial Infarction

case_prompt: A 56-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of right lumbar pain, intermittent hematuria, and weight loss. He is a chronic smoker (11 pack-years) with an otherwise unremarkable medical history. On examination, there was a palpable right flank mass appreciated bimanually. Routine laboratory studies were normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 25 × 11 × 8 cm heterogeneous mass replacing the right kidney and extending into the right renal vein lumen, with compression of the inferior vena cava; no other intra-abdominal abnormalities were noted. Chest CT showed multiple nodular lesions suggestive of metastatic disease. The patient underwent a right radical nephrectomy with resection of the thrombus in the right renal vein.
title: Leiomyosarcoma of the Renal Vein Mimicking a Primitive Renal Cell Carcinoma: Case Report of an Unusual Presentation

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman with a 23-year history of thyrotoxicosis treated intermittently with antithyroid drugs presented with recurrent symptoms two weeks after total thyroidectomy. On initial evaluation she had bilateral exophthalmos, an enlarged thyroid with nodules, and an elevated TSH-receptor antibody level of 3.86 IU/L (normal < 1.00 IU/L). A Tc-99m thyroid scan had shown diffusely increased uptake with one hyperfunctioning nodule in the right upper pole and a hypofunctioning nodule in the right midlobe. Histopathology of the 57.7 g thyroidectomy specimen confirmed Graves’ disease and benign nodules.

Two weeks after surgery, she developed symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. Thyroid-function testing confirmed elevated free T4 and suppressed TSH. A radioiodine uptake in the thyroid bed was 0.2 % (reference, 15 %–45 %). An I-131 whole-body scan demonstrated intense radiotracer uptake with a “star” artifact in the pelvic region. SPECT/CT of the pelvis revealed an 8.5 × 7.2 cm mixed cystic–solid mass with internal calcification in the right adnexa. The plasma cancer antigen 125 level was 48.55 U/mL (reference, 0–35 U/mL).
title: Coexistence of Graves’ disease and unilateral functioning Struma ovarii: a case report

case_prompt: A 49-year-old white woman with a remote history of sarcoidosis was referred for evaluation of an incidentally noted nodular liver during laparoscopic ovarian cyst surgery. She reported no fatigue, hematemesis, abdominal pain or distension, ankle swelling, pruritus, jaundice, or encephalopathy. She denied alcohol use. Vital signs were normal. Examination showed no icterus, spider nevi, clubbing, ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, or peripheral edema. Laboratory tests revealed a mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase level, a slightly prolonged prothrombin time, and mild thrombocytopenia. Serologic testing for hepatitis A, B, and C, antinuclear antibody, antimitochondrial antibody, anti–smooth-muscle antibody, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, and α1-antitrypsin were all within normal limits. A percutaneous liver biopsy showed cirrhosis without granulomas and demonstrated sinusoidal dilatation. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an enlarged inferior vena cava but was otherwise unremarkable. Left heart catheterization showed normal coronary arteries. Right heart catheterization revealed a right atrial pressure of 12 mm Hg, pulmonary-artery pressure of 32/15 mm Hg (mean 21), pulmonary-artery wedge pressure of 18 mm Hg, left ventricular end-diastolic pressure of 18 mm Hg, and a cardiac output of 5.2 L/min. Over the next weeks, she developed progressive exertional dyspnea. Pulmonary function testing showed mild restriction; chest radiography was unrevealing. Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography ruled out pulmonary embolism and demonstrated scattered pericardial calcifications. A contrast echocardiogram showed no right-to-left intracardiac shunt.
title: An Unusual Case of Cirrhosis

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old Taiwanese woman with a family history of Sjögren’s syndrome presented with two weeks of daily fevers, arthralgias, sore throat, and a macular rash. Initial evaluation at a district hospital included negative viral tests and bacterial cultures. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (13 060/μL with 85.5% neutrophils) and marked hyperferritinemia (12 585 ng/mL). Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor were negative. Gallium-67 inflammation scanning and abdominal CT demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes; an excisional lymph node biopsy excluded lymphoma. She met Yamaguchi criteria for adult-onset Still’s disease. 

Because of a history of NSAID allergy, on hospital day 8 she received intravenous betamethasone (8 mg/day), which was transitioned to oral prednisolone (20 mg/day) two days later. Her fevers and arthralgias resolved. On day 10, ALT was 150 U/L and AST was 119 U/L; by day 15, levels peaked at ALT 1473 U/L and AST 722 U/L. Under suspicion of drug-induced liver injury, all medications were stopped. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis were excluded by serological tests, and liver enzymes declined. Corticosteroids were resumed on day 17, and she was discharged on prednisolone 20 mg/day. 

Five days after discharge, she was readmitted with acute severe hepatitis (ALT 1652 U/L; AST 766 U/L). Prednisolone was halted immediately while silymarin and lactulose were maintained.
title: Corticosteroid-Induced Liver Injury in Adult-Onset Still’s Disease

case_prompt:
A 66‐year‐old African‐American woman, 4 years after bilateral lung transplantation for end‐stage pulmonary fibrosis, presented with 2 months of progressive dyspnea, wheezing, and 4 weeks of cough productive of scant blood‐tinged sputum. She denied fever or weight loss but reported nightly sweats for 6 months. Her immunosuppression regimen consisted of tacrolimus (goal trough 8–10 ng/mL) and prednisone 5 mg daily; azathioprine had been discontinued years earlier because of pancytopenia. Her medical history included chronic pancytopenia, stage IV chronic kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, and gastroparesis. 

On examination, she was afebrile, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air; focal end‐expiratory wheezes were heard over the left lung. Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (WBC 0.9×10^3/mL, hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, platelets 134×10^3/mL) and elevated creatinine (2.37 mg/dL). CMV and EBV PCR were undetectable. 

Chest CT showed a 2.2×1.1×0.9 cm polypoid soft‐tissue lesion arising from the roof of the left mainstem bronchus at the anastomotic site, with severe luminal narrowing to 3 mm and tree‐in‐bud nodularity in the left lower lobe. 

Rigid bronchoscopy revealed a fibrinous mass protruding into the left mainstem bronchus proximal to the anastomosis. Multiple biopsies were obtained, and a bronchial wash was performed; samples were sent for histopathologic and microbiologic evaluation.
title: A novel presentation of Mycobacterium avium complex in a recipient of a lung transplant: a case report

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old woman with HIV-1 infection presented with a 10-day history of diffuse maculopapular rash, fever, myalgias, arthralgias, choluria, pruritus, and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Three days before admission she developed nausea, vomiting, and decreased oral intake. Her HIV had been well controlled on zidovudine, lamivudine, and lopinavir–ritonavir for the past three years, with CD4 counts consistently >500 cells/mm3. Forty-five days before presentation her regimen was changed to zidovudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine because of gastrointestinal intolerance. Twenty days after starting nevirapine the rash and jaundice began. 

On examination: temperature 39.0°C; blood pressure 95/66 mm Hg; marked conjunctival and skin icterus; diffuse maculopapular rash covering >50% of body surface; no lymphadenopathy; abdomen soft with tenderness in the right hypochondrium; no hepatosplenomegaly; neurologic examination normal.

Laboratory studies showed: normal complete blood count and differential; normal glucose, electrolytes, and pancreatic enzymes; elevated aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase; acute kidney injury with a threefold increase in serum creatinine and a 75% decrease in estimated glomerular filtration rate. Testing was negative for cytomegalovirus antigenemia, hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B and C antibodies. An electrocardiogram was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a liver of normal size and shape with homogeneously increased echogenicity of the parenchyma.
title: DRESS Syndrome due to Nevirapine Treated with Methylprednisolone

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old African woman, with three prior full-term pregnancies and recent immigration from East Africa, presented with a large, tender left axillary mass. She first noticed a small, nontender lump 3 years earlier—6 months after placement of a left-arm etonogestrel implant, 8 months after her most recent delivery, and 2 years after arriving in the United States. The mass grew slowly without pain, drainage, skin changes, or neurologic symptoms, and did not interfere with breastfeeding. Six months before presentation, the mass enlarged rapidly and became tender, limiting full adduction of the left arm. Her implant had been replaced 2 months before this acceleration. She denied breast symptoms, trauma, infection, systemic complaints, or other exposures; her only medication was the implant device.

On exam, there was a softball-sized, mobile, nonreducible mass in the left axillary fossa with overlying skin striations; no regional lymphadenopathy; intact vascular, sensory, and motor function; and mild discomfort with arm adduction. Vital signs and the remainder of the examination were unremarkable.

Prior MRI of the left axilla (with and without contrast) demonstrated a 16 × 11 × 11 cm multiloculated subcutaneous cystic lesion displacing but not invading adjacent structures, without intrathoracic communication or lymphadenopathy. MR lymphangiogram—after subcutaneous contrast injection into the interdigital web spaces—showed no lymphatic communication with the mass, although lymphatic drainage led to nodes over the lesion. Echinococcal IgG antibody testing was equivocal. Initial laboratory studies were otherwise unremarkable, without evidence of systemic infection.
title: New-onset axillary lymphangioma: a case report

case_prompt: A 63-year-old woman underwent left knee replacement and was discharged on enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily for thromboprophylaxis without planned platelet monitoring. Fifteen days later she presented with fever (39.5 °C), headache, acute right-sided weakness, and a 2-minute episode of altered consciousness with focal tremors in her right leg and abdomen. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Brain MRI showed an acute infarct in the left precentral and postcentral gyri and a subacute infarct in the right parietal lobe. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, platelet count 43 000 × 10^9/L, and D-dimer 34 800 ηg/L; other values were within normal limits. She had no history of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, or estrogen use. Physical examination noted right upper quadrant pain without hepatosplenomegaly or mucocutaneous bleeding. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm, and echocardiography showed a nondilated left atrium with a normal ejection fraction (65%), excluding atrial fibrillation or intracardiac thrombus. Carotid duplex ultrasound was normal. CT pulmonary angiography revealed pulmonary emboli in the left main and segmental arteries. Abdominal CT identified filling defects in branches of the right suprahepatic vein. Venous ultrasound of the left leg showed nonacute thrombosis of the superficial femoral and popliteal veins. A repeat platelet count using citrate-anticoagulated blood confirmed thrombocytopenia.
title: A “Catastrophic” Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old man presented in January 2014 with a solitary yellowish plaque on the right temple that had been stable for 5 months and was mildly itchy on touch. His history was notable for a superficial spreading melanoma excised from the right upper leg in 2012; there was no history of pediatric cutaneous mastocytosis. Physical examination revealed a solitary plaque on the right temple without other skin lesions or systemic abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed a normal serum tryptase level (2.9 μg/L; normal <11.4 μg/L). 

A punch biopsy of the lesion revealed diffuse sheets of epithelioid cells in the dermis without epidermal involvement. The cells had abundant, finely granulated cytoplasm and slight nuclear polymorphism, with scattered spindle-shaped and bilobed/multilobed nuclei. Mitotic activity was low (up to 1 mitotic figure/mm2). Giemsa stain highlighted metachromatic granules. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD117, tryptase, and MiTF; CD30 showed heterogeneous positivity; a few cells were CD25 positive; CD2 was negative. Next-generation sequencing of the lesion showed no KIT mutations (exons 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 17).

In July 2014, the lesion was excised. The histopathologic features were similar but with increased nuclear pleomorphism, up to 9 mitotic figures/mm2, and a Ki-67 index of 29.5%. CD117 and tryptase staining demonstrated small clusters of mast cells extending into the resection margin. No clinical or imaging evidence of systemic disease was found. 

Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of mastocytoma was made.
title: Case report of a clinically indolent but morphologically high‐grade cutaneous mast cell tumor in an adult: Atypical cutaneous mastocytoma or mast cell sarcoma?

case_prompt:
A 56‐year‐old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and a history of multiple myeloma treated by bone marrow transplantation presented with a painful ulcer on the lower leg clinically consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). A biopsy showed a benign ulcer with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate, and stains and cultures for bacteria, acid‐fast bacteria, and fungi were negative. Over the next decade, she had recurrent PG flares on her extremities managed with systemic and intralesional steroids, adalimumab, cyclosporine, mycophenolate, and anakinra, during which her rheumatoid arthritis also improved.

Ten years after her initial PG diagnosis, she was hospitalized with new shortness of breath and worsening cutaneous PG. She was afebrile. Laboratory studies showed a C‐reactive protein level of 14 mg/L and a leukocyte count of 17,000 per cubic millimeter with 80% neutrophils. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography revealed a moderate pericardial effusion and multiple large, bilateral, cavitary pulmonary lesions as well as splenic abscesses. She was treated empirically with broad‐spectrum antibiotics and her immunosuppressive therapies were discontinued, after which her clinical status deteriorated.

Mycobacterium fortuitum was isolated from a sputum sample. Bronchoalveolar lavage, transbronchial biopsy, and two lung wedge resections showed only abscess formation with no evidence of infection by stains, cultures, or molecular studies. An antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody test was negative. Despite initiation of broad‐spectrum antibiotics and systemic antifungal therapy, her condition continued to worsen.
title: A case of extracutaneous pyoderma gangrenosum in a patient with persistent cutaneous and systemic symptoms: Implications for differential diagnosis and treatment

case_prompt: A 51-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus status post pancreas transplant presented for evaluation prior to kidney transplant and right native nephrectomy. She had developed a right ureteral stricture managed by a nephrostomy tube and nephroureterostomy stenting every two months, with progressive decline in right renal function and recurrent complicated urinary tract infections. Her past surgical history included left native nephrectomy at age 2, for unclear reasons. She denied any history of renal calculi. Preoperative contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen demonstrated an atrophic right kidney with extensive lipomatous proliferation of the renal sinus fat and marked inflammation within the collecting system. A percutaneous drainage tube was in place.
title: Renal Replacement Lipomatosis Presenting in the Setting of Ureteral Stricture with Absence of Renal Calculus Disease

case_prompt:
An 86-year-old woman was referred for several months of worsening vision. She had cataract surgery two years earlier and a 25-year history of open-angle glaucoma treated for seven years with brimonidine tartrate 0.1% twice daily in both eyes and artificial tears. She denied contact lens use or lid disorders and had no history of corneal disease. She reported gradual vision decline since her cataract surgery, most noticeable over the past three months, and experienced photosensitivity in both eyes. She had no history of hyperlipidemia or systemic disease.

On examination, best-corrected distance visual acuity was 20/60 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left. Manifest refraction was +0.75–1.00 × 160° OD and +0.50–1.25 × 165° OS; intraocular pressures were within normal limits. Slit-lamp examination revealed dermatochalasis, superficial punctate keratitis, and bilateral peripheral corneal opacities from the 4- to 5-o’clock and 7- to 8-o’clock positions with overlying neovascularization. Crocodile shagreen was noted bilaterally, with no guttata or lattice lines. Dilated fundus examination showed a blunted macular reflex in both eyes and cup-to-disc ratios of 0.65 OD and 0.75 OS.

An infectious and autoimmune workup was performed, including CBC with differential, ESR, CRP, ANA, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, rheumatoid factor, anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, PPD, interferon-gamma release assay, chest radiography, ACE and lysozyme levels, MRSA swabs, stool ova and cysts, Lyme titers, syphilis testing, and review by the primary care physician for systemic rheumatologic disease. All test results were negative or within normal limits, and there were no systemic symptoms to suggest autoimmune disease.
title: Bilateral Lipid Keratopathy in the Setting of Brimonidine Tartrate Use

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old Japanese man presented with three weeks of left chest pain and a rash on his hands and feet. His history included allergic rhinitis; he smoked 5–10 cigarettes per day and drank socially. Three months earlier, he had sexual intercourse with a commercial sex worker; he had not traveled abroad. 

He denied fever, cough, sputum production, or weight loss. A local plain CT scan performed three weeks earlier showed multiple nodular shadows in the left lower lobe, and metastatic lung cancer was suspected. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT one week later again showed multiple nodular shadows in the left lower lobe, slight enlargement of left mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes, and a small left pleural effusion; upper and lower endoscopy were normal. He was referred for further evaluation.

On arrival, temperature was 36.8°C, pulse 85/min, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg, and SpO2 99% on room air. Examination revealed several millimeter oral aphthae, numerous soft, non-tender cervical lymph nodes bilaterally, and multiple pale red, scaly, nodular erythematous patches 3–8 mm in size on the palms and soles. Heart and lung examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 10,600/μL, platelet count of 621,000/μL, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase of 161 U/L, C-reactive protein of 3.13 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 62 mm/h, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor of 1180 U/mL. Tests for HIV antigen/antibody, hepatitis B and C, HTLV-1 antibody, and tumor markers (CEA, SCC, CYFRA, Pro-GRP, NSE) were negative. β-D glucan, rheumatoid factor, MPO-ANCA, and PR3-ANCA were all negative.

Chest radiography showed blunting of the left costophrenic angle without discrete lung field opacities. Doppler ultrasonography of the neck confirmed multiple enlarged lymph nodes with preserved hila. PET-CT demonstrated high uptake in bilateral cervical, subclavicular, axillary, mediastinal, and pelvic lymph nodes but no abnormal uptake elsewhere.

Cervical lymph node biopsy revealed lymphoid follicular hyperplasia, enlarged germinal centers, paracortical dilation, vascular proliferation, and fibrosis. Bacterial and acid-fast bacillus smears and cultures were negative, as was PCR for Mycobacterium DNA. Immunostaining of germinal centers was negative for B-cell lymphoma, and flow cytometry and genetic studies supported reactive lymphadenopathy.
title: Secondary Syphilis with Pulmonary Involvement

case_prompt: A 78-year-old Swiss-born woman presented with a 10-kg weight loss, progressive weakness, and intermittent night sweats over 6 months. Her history was notable for seronegative rheumatoid polyarthritis treated with methotrexate and then leflunomide, switched to adalimumab in September 2021 after a negative interferon-gamma release assay and normal chest radiograph. On admission in April 2023, examination was notable for mild splenomegaly. Laboratory testing revealed hypercalcaemia and acute renal impairment. PET-CT showed multiple hypodense, intensely hypermetabolic lesions in the spleen and liver, small bilateral hypermetabolic pulmonary nodules, and hypermetabolic lymph nodes at the hepatic hilus. Splenic biopsy demonstrated non-necrotizing granulomatous splenitis. PCR for mycobacterial DNA and panfungal PCR from the biopsy were negative. In June 2023, systemic corticosteroids were started for suspected sarcoidosis, resulting in clinical improvement. Further evaluation showed elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme, soluble IL-2 receptor, and neopterin levels. Bronchoalveolar lavage cultures and lymph node biopsy showed no granulomas. Serologies for Treponema pallidum, HIV, Bartonella henselae, Coxiella burnetii, Francisella tularensis, Brucella spp., and dimorphic fungi were negative. A repeat T-SPOT.TB was positive. Liver biopsy again showed non-necrotizing granulomas; PCR and blood cultures for mycobacteria were negative. Adalimumab was stopped and steroids tapered, but hypercalcaemia and renal failure recurred, prompting re-initiation of steroids and adalimumab. In October 2023, she was readmitted with fever, dyspnoea, disorientation, and new bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on CT.
title: Disseminated, fatal reactivation of bovine tuberculosis in a patient treated with adalimumab: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 25-year-old woman with a history of chronic headaches and Kawasaki disease presented with lethargy, blurred vision, confusion, and headache. Her serum sodium was 127 mmol/L; other metabolic and hematologic studies were normal. Non-contrast head CT showed a 2.2 cm heterogeneous mass in the pineal region without calcification, with resultant obstructive hydrocephalus and transependymal CSF resorption; an external ventricular drain was placed. Subsequent brain MRI demonstrated a mildly lobulated, well-circumscribed mass that was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on FLAIR, with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement except for a small nonenhancing anterior component. On the ADC map, the lesion’s mean ADC was 1077.01 ×10⁻⁶ mm²/s (±191.14 ×10⁻⁶ mm²/s), higher than normal brain. MRI of the spine showed no evidence of drop metastases.
final_diagnosis_raw: Pineal parenchymal tumour of intermediate differentiation
title: Pineal parenchymal tumour of intermediate differentiation: a rare differential diagnosis of pineal region tumours

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of worsening scleral icterus, abdominal distension, and fatigue. Her only medical history was acne vulgaris treated recently with minocycline. She denied high-risk behaviors and had no family history of liver disease.

On examination, she was afebrile; blood pressure was 119/79 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She was alert and oriented. Physical findings included icteric sclera, a mildly distended abdomen without shifting dullness, and 1+ pitting edema of the lower extremities.

Initial laboratory studies revealed:
• Mild elevations in alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase  
• Increased total bilirubin  
• Hypoalbuminemia  
• Elevated international normalized ratio  

Hemolysis laboratories (haptoglobin, direct Coombs test, and lactate dehydrogenase) were within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound showed mild ascites but was otherwise unremarkable.
title: Fulminant Wilson's Disease Managed with Plasmapheresis as a Bridge to Liver Transplant

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old Palestinian woman was admitted with vertigo and fatigue. She had infantile cerebral palsy, mental retardation, and a body‐mass index of 15.3. Vital signs were stable; she appeared pale, with no evidence of bleeding.  
Laboratory tests showed:  
• Hemoglobin 4.6 g/dl (MCV 58 fl)  
• Platelet count 1703 × 10^3/μl  
• Leukocytes 11.45 × 10^3/μl; differential normal  
• Blood smear with anisocytosis, low reticulocyte fraction, micro- and macro-platelets  
• Ferritin < 1.5 ng/ml; serum iron 0.4 μmol/l; transferrin 3.8 g/l; transferrin saturation 0.4%  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 4.75 μmol/l; vitamin B12 112 pmol/l; folic acid normal  
• Erythropoietin 854 mU/ml; C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate normal  

Upper and lower endoscopy and gynecological examination were negative for bleeding. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable except for a spleen length of 12 cm.  
Bone marrow smear and biopsy showed markedly increased megakaryopoiesis with juvenile megakaryocytes, occasional clustering, few hyperlobated forms, increased non-dysplastic erythropoiesis, and depleted iron stores; cytogenetics were normal.  
Over ten days, after four red-cell transfusions and iron supplementation, hemoglobin and serum iron normalized, erythropoietin declined, and the platelet count returned to normal without other intervention.
title: Severe thrombocytosis and anemia associated with celiac disease in a young female patient: a case report

case_prompt:
A male infant was born at 36 + 2 weeks of gestation to a 22-year-old G2P1 mother whose antenatal scan at 32 weeks demonstrated polyhydramnios and left-sided fetal pleural effusion. The baby’s birth weight was 2290 g (AGA). Apgar scores were 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes. At 30 minutes of life, he developed grunting and mild subcostal retractions. In the NICU, respiratory rate was 65/min, SpO2 was 80% on room air, and Downes score was 4/10. There was decreased air entry on the left, with otherwise normal cardiovascular and abdominal examinations.  
A chest radiograph confirmed a large left pleural effusion. A chest tube was placed, and 200 mL of straw-colored fluid was aspirated. Pleural fluid analysis showed: protein 1.2 g/dL, glucose 97 g/dL, LDH 82 U/L, triglycerides 13 mg/dL, cholesterol 50 mg/dL; RBC count 10/mm3, WBC count 100/mm3 (30% neutrophils, 70% lymphocytes). Serum studies revealed WBC count 15 000/mm3, LDH 750 U/L, and serum protein 5 g/dL.  
Echocardiography showed a small atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunt, no pericardial effusion, and no signs of cardiac failure.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?
title: Neonatal pleural effusion associated with pulmonary sequestration: A case report

case_prompt: A 33-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of progressive weakness and difficulty swallowing. He had daily heroin use administered by skin popping and untreated hepatitis C. On arrival, he could open his eyelids only 2–3 mm with marked ptosis, had diplopia, pooling of secretions after 1–2 words, dysarthria, difficulty holding up his head, and proximal upper-extremity weakness (4/5 bilaterally). Vital signs were blood pressure 136/80 mmHg, pulse 106 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, temperature 36.5°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Five deep-cavity abscesses over his hips and thighs were incised and drained, and wound cultures were obtained. Over the next few hours, his neck and extremity weakness worsened and breathing became very shallow, prompting intubation for airway protection and impending respiratory failure. A urine drug screen was positive for amphetamines, opiates, and acetone. The constellation of symptoms was suggestive of botulism, with differential diagnoses that included Guillain–Barré syndrome and myasthenia gravis. The patient denied ingestion of bulging canned food and recent travel.
title: Wound botulism caused by Clostridium subterminale after a heroin injection

case_prompt: A 63-year-old obese African American woman with asthma, hypertension, congestive heart failure, obstructive sleep apnea, and obesity presented with sudden onset of bilateral facial and tongue swelling and progressive shortness of breath. She had minor fruit allergies but no history of anaphylaxis. Initial vital signs were blood pressure 127/67 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturation 100% on 6 L nasal cannula. She received epinephrine, diphenhydramine, and solumedrol for presumed anaphylaxis and was intubated for airway protection. On examination, there was extensive laryngeal edema. The right pupil was dilated and unresponsive; the left pupil was pinpoint but reactive. Emergent head CT showed bilateral effaced sulci with small ventricles and narrowed basilar cisterns, consistent with increased intracranial pressure. Initial arterial blood gas analysis on controlled ventilation (tidal volume 600 mL, respiratory rate 12, FiO2 50%) revealed pH 7.22, pCO2 85 mmHg, pO2 109 mmHg, and bicarbonate 33 mEq/L. A neurosurgeon recommended no surgical intervention. Mannitol was not administered, as there were no clinical or laboratory signs of an osmotic disturbance. The patient remained unresponsive with a dilated right pupil and blurred disc margins bilaterally.
title: Hypercapnic cerebral edema presenting in a woman with asthma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old Iranian woman presented with a 3-year history of bilateral vision loss and photopsia. Three years earlier, she had accidentally ingested four 1250 mg boluses of veterinary niclosamide. A few days after ingestion, she noted visual disturbances and was treated empirically with a short course of high-dose oral corticosteroids for presumed bilateral optic neuritis; her vision neither improved nor worsened. Over the next 3 years, her visual symptoms remained stable. She denied other medication use, alcohol, smoking, night blindness, or photophobia. There was no family history of vision loss or retinal disease, and parents were nonconsanguineous. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Best-corrected visual acuities were 20/50 in the right eye and 20/63 in the left eye. Color vision and pupillary reactions were normal. Anterior segment and vitreous examinations were unremarkable; intraocular pressures were normal. Fundus examination revealed pink optic discs, cup-to-disc ratios of 0.2, and parafoveal retinal pigment epithelial atrophy manifesting as bilateral bull’s-eye maculopathy. Fundus autofluorescence demonstrated annular hyperautofluorescence in the parafoveal region. Optical coherence tomography showed parafoveal ellipsoid zone disruption, outer retinal thinning, and relative foveal sparing (“flying saucer” sign). Full-field electroretinography revealed decreased scotopic and photopic amplitudes with normal waveforms in both eyes. Electrooculography showed Arden ratios of 240% (right eye) and 202% (left eye).
title: Presumed veterinary niclosamide-induced retinal toxicity in a human: a case report

case_prompt: A 57-year-old Fitzpatrick III woman with a history of numerous basal cell carcinomas since 2015, cervical polyps, uterine fibroids, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, arthritis, and decreased visual acuity presented with numerous growths on her eyelids for several years. She denied a family history of basal cell carcinoma, although her mother had breast, bladder, and colon cancer and her maternal grandmother had breast cancer. She denied lesions on the genitals, seizures, dizziness, learning difficulties, dental abnormalities, hoarseness, hypotrichosis, hypohidrosis, or macroglossia; her hair turned gray at age 13. On examination, she had numerous 2 to 6 mm pearly papules scattered on the face and bilateral strings of pearly papules along the upper and lower eyelid margins. Dermoscopic examination of the eyelid lesions revealed arborizing vessels, brown-gray globules, and aggregated yellow-white globules in all lesions. Additionally, a dermatofibroma and a plantar verruca were noted. There were no palmar pits, skeletal abnormalities, macrocephaly, or jawline deformities. Four facial papules were biopsied, each showing infundibulocystic basal cell carcinoma with follicular differentiation. A fifth lesion on the forehead demonstrated a collision of a nodular basal cell carcinoma with a blue nevus.
title: A case of Gorlin syndrome like phenotype with multiple infundibulocystic basal cell carcinomas in a moniliform blepharosis arrangement

case_prompt: An 84‐year‐old man presented with acute onset abdominal and back pain that began during the night without vomiting or gastrointestinal disturbance. One day earlier he had completed a 10-day course of clindamycin for left calf cellulitis. His medical history included atrial fibrillation, congestive cardiac failure, ulcerative colitis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and antiphospholipid syndrome with recurrent deep vein thromboses; he was on maintenance warfarin. On examination he was afebrile, blood pressure 200/132 mm Hg, heart rate 68 beats/min, and capillary blood glucose 9.1 mmol/L. Chest auscultation was clear; abdominal examination showed mild to moderate epigastric tenderness with normal bowel sounds; mild resolving cellulitis of the right calf was noted. Admission studies revealed hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, white blood cell count 12.9×10^9/L, platelets 303×10^9/L, INR 6.8, urea 8.7 mmol/L, creatinine 111 μmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, CRP 75 mg/L, calcium 2.02 mmol/L. ECG showed a paced rhythm and chest radiograph demonstrated slight fluid overload, cardiomegaly, and interstitial shadowing. The initial impression was possible gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Warfarin was withheld, vitamin K administered, and intravenous fluids started. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed subtle, non-specific bilateral adrenal enhancing lesions. His INR normalized to 2–3, but he remained hypotensive with ongoing abdominal pain, nausea, lethargy, and abdominal distension; capillary blood glucose remained normal despite withholding diabetic medications. A short synacthen test showed no appreciable rise in cortisol (baseline 95 nmol/L; 60 min 113 nmol/L; 90 min 132 nmol/L).
title: Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage presenting as epigastric and back pain

case_prompt: A 49-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department with 48 hours of rapidly progressing, ascending weakness of all four extremities and increasing difficulty breathing. She had no prior similar episodes, no recent trauma, vaccinations, infections, or toxin exposures, and denied drug use. On examination, she was alert but in acute respiratory distress, using accessory muscles and receiving oxygen via face mask. Vital signs were: blood pressure 140/90 mmHg, heart rate 98 beats/min, respiratory rate 40 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on supplemental oxygen. Chest auscultation was clear. Neurologically, she had hypotonia in all limbs (lower > upper), muscle strength of 1/5 in the lower limbs and 3/5 in the upper limbs, absent deep tendon reflexes, and equivocal plantar responses. Sensation and cranial nerves were normal. Her abdomen was distended with absent bowel sounds without tenderness. A provisional diagnosis of Guillain–Barré syndrome was made, and she was intubated for worsening respiratory distress. Laboratory studies revealed: serum potassium 1.72 mEq/L (arterial blood gas potassium 1.38 mEq/L), metabolic acidosis (pH 7.12, HCO3- 12.5 mmol/L, BE –15.8 mmol/L, pCO2 38.5 mmHg), sodium 149 mEq/L, calcium 8.8 mg/dL, and normal renal, liver, coagulation, and glucose profiles. Hemoglobin showed moderate anemia; ELISA tests for hepatitis B, C, and HIV were negative. ECG demonstrated ST depression and T-wave inversion.
title: 49-years-old women with unusual presentation of severe hypokalemia mimicking Guillain-Barré Syndrome: A rare case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man first noted right calf muscle cramps in 2013. Twelve months later, he developed right foot drop, fasciculations in the right leg, and wasting of the right anterior compartment. Neurological examination in 2014 showed 2/5 strength of the right ankle extensors, right leg amyotrophy, brisk reflexes in the lower limbs, a positive right Babinski sign, and no sensory deficits.

By 2015, fasciculations were present throughout the body, painful cramps and weakness appeared in the left shin, and thigh muscle atrophy developed. Deep tendon reflexes remained brisk except for absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally; Hoffmann sign was positive. There were no bulbar or respiratory symptoms.

In 2015, T2-weighted MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a slitlike syrinx (central canal dilation) extending from T3 to T9 without Chiari malformation or extramedullary compression; brain and cervical MRI were normal. EMG in 2015 revealed fibrillation potentials, fasciculations, and large‐amplitude, long‐duration motor–unit potentials in both upper and lower limbs without conduction block. GM-1 and GM-2 antibody titers were negative, and routine blood and CSF studies were normal. Follow-up spinal MRI in 2016 and 2019 showed no change in the cavity size.
title: Clinical cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis concurrent with hydromyelia

case_prompt: A 67-year-old Saudi man, retired elementary school teacher, with hypertension and longstanding benign prostatic hypertrophy, was referred to a psychosomatic service for evaluation of chronic anxiety. Three years earlier, he began repetitive checking behaviors—specifically, re-examining his underwear for residual urine—which interfered with his prayer duties. He developed progressively intrusive worries about religious rulings and family inheritance, accompanied by continuous fear and sleep disturbance that evolved from intermittent awakenings to persistent insomnia. His sons noted a diurnal pattern: severe anxiety with palpitations or occasional numbness at dawn, failure to return to sleep, gradually worsening fatigue by sunset, and appreciable relief each evening. There were no identifiable triggers, no specific phobias, flashbacks, avoidant behaviors, or irritability, and mood was not persistently low. Appetite was normal until the last few weeks. He denied suicidal ideation and had no personal or family psychiatric history. Premorbidly, he was an introverted but religiously observant man. He also described chronic sensations of “chest heat,” attributed by his family to anxiety. Over this period, he was seen by several psychiatrists and received sequential trials of paroxetine, escitalopram, mirtazapine, fluvoxamine, and sertraline at therapeutic doses; there was no meaningful clinical response. Because of his persistent, cyclically worsening anxiety, he was referred to a tertiary center and electively admitted for further evaluation.
title: A case of anxiety associated with miliary tuberculosis

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man with known chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) diagnosed in July 2009 underwent staging studies that revealed a large substernal multinodular goiter (volume ≈82 cm3) on chest CT. In October 2009, an ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of a thyroid nodule was suspicious for carcinoma; serum thyroglobulin was 936.9 ng/mL. CLL required no treatment at that time.

On January 5, 2010, he underwent total thyroidectomy with removal of 29 regional lymph nodes. Pathology showed a 1.2-mm follicular variant of papillary thyroid microcarcinoma confined to the right lobe, with metastases in 8 of 29 nodes but no extrathyroidal extension or vascular invasion. He was referred for radioiodine ablation.

One month later, before I-131 therapy, he was off thyroid hormone replacement. Investigations included:
– Chest radiograph: normal.  
– Neck ultrasound: bilaterally enlarged lymph nodes in levels I, II, and VI, interpreted as inflammatory.  
– CT of chest and abdomen: enlarged axillary and retroperitoneal lymph nodes, attributed to CLL.  
– CBC (Jan 27): 4.74×10^6 erythrocytes/mm^3; 19,200 leukocytes/mm^3 (72.7% lymphocytes); 265,000 platelets/mm^3.  
– Serum (Jan 23): TSH 63 mIU/L; thyroglobulin 93.4 ng/mL; anti-thyroglobulin antibodies negative.  
– Pretherapeutic I-131 whole-body scan (WBS): tiny thyroid remnant uptake (<1% at 24 h); no definite uptake elsewhere, with very faint questionable activity in both axillae.

On February 2, 2010, he received 7,400 MBq (200 mCi) of I-131. A post-therapy WBS on February 6 showed expected cervical uptake and new, definite uptake in both axillary regions and small foci in the inguinal regions. SPECT/CT of the chest localized radioiodine concentration to enlarged axillary lymph nodes, particularly one in the left axilla.
title: Normalization of lymphocyte count after high ablative dose of I-131 in a patient with chronic lymphoid leukemia and secondary papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Case report

case_prompt:
A 60‐year‐old man with no history of liver disease, pancreatitis, or abdominal trauma was admitted for severe anemia (hemoglobin, 4.8 g/dL) after one episode of hematemesis and two episodes of melena over the prior 24 hours. He was hemodynamically unstable (pulse, 110 bpm; blood pressure, 100/50 mmHg) but afebrile, with an unremarkable abdominal examination and no stigmata of portal hypertension. Digital rectal examination revealed melanic stool. Other laboratory tests, including coagulation, liver, and renal function, were normal.

After resuscitation with transfusion and high‐dose proton‐pump inhibitor, emergent esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed. A moderate amount of fresh blood was aspirated from the stomach. In retroflexion, the gastric fundus showed varicose‐shaped, pulsating, tortuous submucosal vessels without active bleeding, and a small erosion over one vessel suggested recent rupture. There were no endoscopic signs of portal hypertension.

To further characterize the lesion, computed tomography angiography was obtained. There was complete thrombosis of the splenic artery and tortuous arterial structures arising from the left gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries and coursing into the gastric fundus. No active contrast extravasation was seen.
title: Massive bleeding from gastric submucosal arterial collaterals secondary to splenic artery thrombosis: A case report

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old man with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with three months of progressively worsening dyspnea. He had been treated elsewhere for presumed congestive heart failure with diuretics but had no clinical improvement. He denied chest pain, cough, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, back pain, fever, weight loss, bladder dysfunction, or sensory disturbances. He reported progressive difficulty walking and leg weakness. He was a nonsmoker, drank alcohol occasionally, and had no recent viral symptoms.

On examination, blood pressure was 161/106 mm Hg. Neurologic findings included symmetric proximal and distal muscle weakness (4/5 in the upper extremities, 3/5 in the lower extremities), decreased distal pinprick sensation, and hyporeflexia (1+ in all limbs). Cranial nerves were intact; there was no muscle atrophy or fasciculations. A fasting glucose level was 229 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pO2 60 mm Hg, pCO2 58 mm Hg, and SaO2 89%, consistent with chronic respiratory insufficiency.

A chest radiograph showed clear lung fields without evidence of fluid overload. Serum electrolytes and thyroid function tests were normal. B-type natriuretic peptide level and two-dimensional echocardiogram findings were inconsistent with heart failure. Despite achieving adequate glycemic control with insulin, repeat arterial blood gases remained unchanged on hospital day 1.
title: Not Just Another Cause of Dyspnea: Common Complaint Leads to a Rare Diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old Caucasian man, a non-smoker, presented with a 3-month history of 12 kg weight loss and recent generalized pruritus and jaundice. Serum biochemistry and abdominal ultrasonography confirmed obstructive jaundice. Contrast CT of the abdomen showed a 4.6×4.1 cm mass in the head of the pancreas without radiologic evidence of distant metastases. He underwent ERCP with stent placement, followed two months later by a pylorus-sparing pancreaticoduodenectomy, with an uneventful recovery.

Gross examination revealed a 5.5 cm lobulated tumor in the pancreatic head extending to the superior mesenteric vessel margin; the entire lesion was submitted for histology. Microscopically, the neoplasm consisted of large nests of basaloid cells with central necrosis and scattered small foci of squamoid differentiation. There was no morphologic evidence of glandular or acinar formation. The tumor showed extensive intravenous and intralymphatic invasion, foci of perineural invasion, extension into the duodenum, ampullary region, pancreatic duct, and peripancreatic fat, and microscopic involvement of the superior mesenteric vessel margin. Metastatic deposits with similar morphology were identified in 6 of 43 regional lymph nodes.
final_diagnosis_raw: Squamous cell carcinoma of the pancreas
title: Primary squamous cell carcinoma of the pancreas: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 19-year-old previously healthy male presented with chest pain and fever. Initial evaluation revealed an enlarged cardiac silhouette on chest radiograph, ST-segment elevation in leads aVF and III on ECG, and a 2.2 cm pericardial effusion on transthoracic echocardiography. He was diagnosed with acute pericarditis and treated with ibuprofen and colchicine; colchicine was continued after discharge. One month later, echocardiography showed persistent pericardial effusion (0.7 cm) and ongoing fatigue. Seven months after initial presentation, he experienced recurrent pericarditis with effusion and asthenia, prompting cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR). CMR demonstrated a 54×42 mm mass adjacent to the epicardial surface of the basal and mid anterior left ventricular wall that was hypointense with a peripheral hyperintense rim on T2-weighted images, hyperintense on T1-weighted images, and showed peripheral gadolinium enhancement with a nonenhancing central core; diffusion-weighted imaging showed no signal increase. Contrast-enhanced cardiac CT confirmed a hypervascular mass with a central hypodense scar and showed that the proximal left anterior descending artery coursed through the lesion without chamber invasion. Laboratory testing revealed marked elevations of plasma and urine 3-methoxytyramine and increased chromogranin A levels.
title: Role of integrated imaging in the diagnosis of an atypical and unresectable cardiac paraganglioma: a case report

case_prompt: An 81‐year‐old man with a history of grade 2 prostate adenocarcinoma diagnosed one year earlier (managed with watchful waiting) presented with five months of progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, peripheral edema, and painful knees and thighs that limited ambulation. He reported a 10-kg weight loss and anorexia over six months but denied chest pain or hemoptysis. His medical history included hypertension, TURP six years prior, and a 50-pack-year smoking history. On exam, blood pressure was 150/80 mmHg with an irregular pulse of 96 beats/min. He had dullness and diminished breath sounds over the left lower lung field consistent with pleural effusion, normal heart sounds, no hepatomegaly, and pitting edema of both hands and lower extremities. The hands were noted to be remarkably large. There was no vertebral tenderness. Laboratory tests showed ESR 35 mm/h, CRP 134 mg/L, hemoglobin 6.3 mmol/L (MCV 82 fl), leukocytes 8.6×10^9/L with 90% neutrophils, normal platelets, electrolytes, and liver enzymes; creatinine 77 μmol/L; alkaline phosphatase 285 U/L; calcium 1.95 mmol/L with albumin 23.9 g/L; normal phosphate; and chronic compensated respiratory acidosis with O₂ saturation 80%. ECG showed atrial fibrillation and LBBB as before. Chest X-ray confirmed a large left pleural effusion and cardiomegaly without pulmonary lesions. Thoracentesis removed 4.5 L of lymphocyte‐predominant fluid with negative cytology, biochemistry, and TB cultures. Echocardiography showed good LV function. Abdominal ultrasound showed a dilated IVC. CTA excluded pulmonary embolism but confirmed the left pleural effusion. Given the elevated alkaline phosphatase, bone pain, and known prostate cancer, a skeletal scintigraphy was obtained. It showed a “super scan,” with diffuse increased uptake throughout the entire skeleton. However, the prostate-specific antigen was within the normal range at 1.4 μg/L (normal <4.4).
title: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy as the cause of a super scan of the bone in a patient with prostate cancer: a case report

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man was referred for evaluation of right upper chest pain, progressive malaise, generalized weakness, loss of appetite, and an unintentional 10-lb weight loss over 2 months. His medical history was notable for rheumatoid arthritis treated with weekly etanercept injections for 10 months, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a 60-pack-year smoking history. He denied cough, dyspnea, fever, chills, night sweats, or known tuberculosis exposure. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine laboratory studies revealed no significant abnormalities.

A chest radiograph demonstrated a right upper lobe density. Chest CT showed a 1.5 × 2 × 1 cm pleura-based consolidated mass on the lateral aspect of the right upper lobe and a 2.5 × 3 × 3.5 cm thick-walled cavitary lesion in the superomedial apex of the right lung. Background emphysematous changes were present without bronchiectasis or lymphadenopathy. Subsequent 18F-FDG PET imaging revealed hypermetabolic foci in these lesions with standardized uptake values ranging from 7.4 to 12.8, features considered consistent with pulmonary malignancy.

Bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial lesions. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cytology did not demonstrate malignant cells. BAL Gomori methenamine-silver stain and fungal cultures were negative.
title: Pulmonary Mycobacterium kansasii Infection Mimicking Malignancy on the 18F-FDG PET Scan in a Patient Receiving Etanercept: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of painless, gradually progressive swelling of the upper and lower lips and of the gums.
She had no relevant medical history and no history of allergy to foods, drugs, or cosmetics; no asthma or eczema; and no family history of similar findings.
On extraoral examination, there was diffuse, soft, nontender swelling of both lips with normal temperature, with mild fissuring and a cobblestone appearance of the upper lip.
Intraoral examination revealed enlargement of the gingiva extending from tooth 13 to 23, involving marginal, interdental, and attached gingiva to the mucogingival junction; the gingiva was red, smooth, shiny, and lacked stippling. Probing revealed bleeding on probing, mild local deposits, and false pockets without clinical attachment loss.
Panoramic radiograph showed no alveolar bone loss in the maxillary or mandibular anterior region.
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, differential, platelet count, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level, were within normal limits.
Chest radiograph was unremarkable, and the Mantoux test was negative.
title: Orofacial granulomatosis affecting lip and gingiva in a 15-year-old patient: A rare case report

case_prompt: A 72-year-old woman with a 12-year history of refractory Mycobacterium intracellulare pulmonary disease was referred for further treatment. She had a prior history of pulmonary tuberculosis. Four years ago a cavitary nodule was detected, and she subsequently received multiple macrolide-containing multidrug regimens without sustained culture conversion. At presentation, chest radiography and computed tomography showed fibrocavitary-type lesions in the upper lobes. Sputum cultures grew macrolide-resistant M. intracellulare (minimum inhibitory concentration for clarithromycin >32 μg/mL; for amikacin 8 μg/mL). She was continued on clarithromycin 400 mg/day, ethambutol 500 mg/day, and moxifloxacin 400 mg/day, and inhaled amikacin liposome suspension (ALIS, 590 mg/day) was added. Three weeks after starting ALIS, she developed fever, cough, and loss of appetite. Repeat chest radiography and CT revealed multiple infiltrative opacities in the left upper lobe and bilateral lower lobes, with decreased thickness of the cavity wall and bronchial walls.
title: Diagnosis and Management of Drug-Induced Interstitial Lung Disease Associated with Amikacin Liposome Inhalation Suspension in Refractory Mycobacterium Avium Complex Pulmonary Disease: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 50-year-old Chinese woman with a 9-month history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was admitted for fever and relapsing abdominal pain over the same period. Initial SLE had been diagnosed on the basis of fever, recurrent abdominal pain, bloating, leukopenia, positive antinuclear and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, anti-Smith and anti-RNP antibodies, and polyserositis, and responded to prednisolone and mycophenolate mofetil. As steroids were tapered, she redeveloped fever (38.5°C), abdominal pain, hair loss, dry mouth, and reduced defecation; she denied photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthralgias, or Raynaud’s phenomenon. Examination was notable only for tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Her history included osteoporosis and a tuberculous infection treated with rifampicin and isoniazid for 3 months without relief of abdominal pain. Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (WBC 2.56 × 10^9/L), anemia (hemoglobin 102 g/L), normal ESR, CRP, and procalcitonin, and negative blood cultures. Immunologic tests revealed rheumatoid factor 153 IU/mL, low complement C3 (0.71 g/L), positive ANA (1:320), and positive anti-Smith, anti-dsDNA, and anti-RNP antibodies; a TB-spot test was positive. A PET-CT scan showed no abnormalities. After exclusion of infection, intestinal tuberculosis, and malignancy, SLE-related mesenteric vasculitis and intestinal obstruction were considered. Treatment with methylprednisolone (120 mg/day for 11 days), cyclophosphamide, gastrointestinal decompression, and nutritional support resolved her fever and normalized her WBC count, but her incomplete intestinal obstruction and decreased bowel movements persisted. An abdominal X-ray showed multiple air-fluid levels. Enteroscopy demonstrated a small intestinal ulcer with luminal stenosis. Contrast CT of the small intestine revealed segmental dilatation with wall enhancement and multiple air-fluid levels.
title: Coexistence of Crohn’s disease and systemic lupus erythematosus: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 25-year-old man presented with difficulty fitting his right ocular prosthesis. He had undergone enucleation of the right eye at age 4 for retinoblastoma in France; no orbital implant had been placed. On examination, the right anophthalmic socket showed a thickened bulbar conjunctiva with a central, translucid, round area that was vascularized, and an associated inferior symblepharon. Orbital computed tomography revealed a bilobated, cyst‐like structure in the right orbit, with hyperdense walls and hypodense content. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an ovoid cystic structure with an increased anteroposterior diameter, a T1 signal identical to that of an atrophied optic nerve, and no contrast uptake to suggest an expanding lesion. Comparison with a CT scan obtained six years earlier showed no such lesion.
title: Giant Conjunctival Cyst of the Orbit in a Patient with Previous Enucleation

case_prompt: A 56-year-old Puerto Rican man with untreated HIV infection and hypertension presented with 3 months of left upper jaw swelling and pain, difficulty swallowing, a 9-kg weight loss, and nonproductive cough. On examination, temperature was 97.8°F, blood pressure 147/95 mm Hg, heart rate 116/min, and respiratory rate 16/min. He had oral thrush, palpable cervical lymph nodes, a mass in the posterior left maxillary region, and a generalized maculopapular rash on the upper chest and back. Laboratory studies showed an HIV viral load of 162 500 copies/mL and a CD4 count of 27 cells/μL. MRI of the brain revealed a 3.9 × 5.8 × 4.3 cm soft-tissue mass in the posterior left maxilla with erosion into the maxillary sinus. Biopsy of this mass demonstrated sheets of granulomatous tissue with macrophages containing well-demarcated fungal spores. Chest CT revealed hilar lymphadenopathy and bilateral adrenal enlargement (left, 4.8 × 3.7 cm; right, 4.7 × 2.3 cm). Laboratory testing showed hyponatremia (serum sodium 126 mEq/L) and mild hyperkalemia (serum potassium 4.9 mEq/L). A 250-μg cosyntropin stimulation test yielded a baseline cortisol of 7 μg/dL, an adrenocorticotrophic hormone level of 86 pg/mL, and a 60-minute cortisol of 9 μg/dL, consistent with primary adrenal insufficiency. Twenty-one-hydroxylase antibody levels were undetectable.
title: Histoplasmosis: An Unusual Cause of Adrenal Insufficiency

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman presented with abdominal discomfort. She had undergone laparoscopic myomectomy 8 years earlier and was otherwise healthy with no medications. There was no known family history of endocrine or inherited disorders.

Vital signs were normal, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine biochemical tests, including serum calcium and intact parathyroid hormone, were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a multilocular 21 × 19 mm mass in the pancreatic tail. MRI showed the lesion to be low signal on T1-weighted images with heterogeneous high signal at the margins. Doppler endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated increased blood flow in the lesion and identified three additional tumors in the pancreatic body and one in the uncinate process.

EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration of one of the tumors confirmed a neuroendocrine tumor. Serum levels of gastrin, glucagon, insulin, and other endocrine studies were normal.

Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with nonfunctional multiple pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs).
title: A Novel Pathogenic MEN1 Gene Variant Identified in a Family With Multiple Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man with advanced non–small-cell lung cancer and pleural metastasis had been treated with carboplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab for nine months, followed by pembrolizumab alone for four months, after which therapy was suspended because of good disease control. Three months after discontinuation of pembrolizumab, he remained asymptomatic without abdominal or back pain. 

Contrast-enhanced CT showed localized enlargement of the pancreatic head with delayed enhancement compared to baseline, and hypoattenuating areas in the pancreatic body. Laboratory studies revealed normal pancreatic amylase (50 IU/L), lipase (50 IU/L), and C-reactive protein (0.05 mg/dL), but an elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9 level (148 U/mL); serum IgG4 was 22 mg/dL (normal). 

MRI demonstrated enlargement of the pancreatic head with a hypointense T1 signal, hyperintense T2 signal, and marked diffusion restriction. MR cholangiopancreatography revealed multiple stenoses of the main pancreatic duct and stenosis of the intrapancreatic bile duct. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed hypoechoic pancreatic parenchyma with scattered hyperechoic foci and stranding in the enlarged head. ERCP confirmed focal narrowing of the main pancreatic duct at the head, irregular ductal caliber at the tail, and intrapancreatic bile duct stenosis. 

Pancreatic juice cytology, bile cytology, and brushing cytology of the bile duct stricture were all negative. Based on the history, pembrolizumab-induced pancreatitis was considered highly probable, but pancreatic tumor and mass-forming pancreatitis, including autoimmune pancreatitis, could not be ruled out. Therefore, endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration was performed for histopathological diagnosis.
title: Pembrolizumab-induced Focal Pancreatitis Diagnosed by Endoscopic Ultrasound-guided Fine-needle Aspiration

case_prompt:
A 13-month-old girl with no prior health issues was found unresponsive at home following 2 days of vomiting and 1 day of lethargy. Paramedics recorded a Glasgow Coma Score of 3, and she was intubated and transferred to a regional hospital. A noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. On admission she was hypothermic (core temperature 33.2 °C). Initial laboratory studies revealed:  
• Arterial pH 6.6, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L  
• Urine ketones positive; blood glucose 33 mmol/L  
• Platelet count 99 × 10^9/L; hemoglobin 106 g/L; creatinine 82 μmol/L  
• Fibrinogen, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time within normal limits  

She was managed according to DKA protocols and transferred to a tertiary pediatric ICU. Over the next 48 hours, serum ketones normalized and blood glucose ranged 6–12 mmol/L, but metabolic acidosis persisted and she remained obtunded without fever. By day 7 she developed oliguria with urea 27.5 mmol/L and creatinine 175 μmol/L; renal ultrasound showed bilaterally enlarged kidneys, and she developed pulmonary edema with pleural effusions.  

By day 5, platelet count fell to 20 × 10^9/L and hemoglobin to 77 g/L despite transfusions. Blood film demonstrated red cell fragments and fibrin strands; reticulocyte count was 0.2%; coagulation studies remained normal; lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 800 U/L.  
These biochemical features in conjunction with her clinical symptoms of renal failure and decreased neurological function led to a presumptive differential diagnosis of thrombocytopenia-associated multiorgan failure.
title: Thrombocytopenia‐associated multiorgan failure occurring in an infant at the onset of type 1 diabetes successfully treated with fresh frozen plasma

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man presented with fever and loss of consciousness. Five days earlier, he had acute watery diarrhea. Overnight he developed a high fever (105.8 °F) and altered consciousness. He reported recent household exposure to COVID-19; his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive on admission. He had no underlying disease, drug allergies, or trauma.

On examination, blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg, pulse 90/min, respirations 18/min, temperature 98.6 °F, and O2 saturation 95%. He opened his eyes to pain and withdrew his limbs (GCS 10/15). Pupils were equal and reactive; gag reflex was intact. Bronchial breath sounds were heard bilaterally; abdominal and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Initial labs showed sodium 117 mEq/L, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, BUN 11 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, WBC 6900/μL, platelets 132 000/μL, INR 1.3. His consciousness normalized as sodium corrected to 137 mEq/L (GCS 13/15).

On hospital day 2, neurologic exam revealed bilateral facial weakness (House-Brackmann grade V), reduced eyelid closure, drooling, and inability to raise eyebrows, puff cheeks, or keep food in his mouth. A nasogastric tube was placed. Other cranial nerves, limb strength, reflexes, sensation, and gait were normal.

Brain CT and MRI without contrast performed one day after onset of facial weakness were normal. Lumbar puncture showed glucose 67 mg/dL, protein 69 mg/dL, and no cells or organisms. Serologic tests for HIV, Epstein–Barr virus, syphilis, HSV, and CMV were negative. Ear–nose–throat examination revealed no neoplasm or local infection. Rheumatological tests (ANA, ANCA, C3, C4) were negative.
title: Bilateral peripheric facial nerve palsy following SARS‐CoV‐2 infection: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of progressive limb weakness and muscle cramps. Five years ago she had been diagnosed with possible amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) after developing intermittent cramp-like chest sensations, numb neck pain, and then objective weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations of the upper limbs with extremely brisk tendon reflexes. No sensory deficits had been documented initially. Electromyography at that time showed abnormal spontaneous activity in multiple upper-limb muscles and signs of chronic denervation; a cranial MRI was normal. A bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome was also presumed based on increased distal motor latencies of the median nerve.

On current examination, cranial nerves were intact with no bulbar signs. The arms showed distinct proximal atrophy and mild fasciculations in the supraspinatus, deltoid, biceps, and finger extensors, with motor strength 3–4/5. The legs had mild weakness (4/5 in foot dorsiflexion) and gait ataxia. Vibration sense was reduced in all limbs, and there was hyper- and dysesthesia over the shoulders and proximal arms. Deep tendon reflexes were symmetric and extremely brisk; plantar responses were flexor. Abdominal reflexes were present. There was no bladder or bowel dysfunction, but she reported persistent neck pain, numbness, and clumsiness of both arms. Proximal arm atrophy in combination with sensory dysfunction and pain prompted reconsideration of spinal pathology.
title: Cervicothoracic Intradural Arachnoid Cyst Misdiagnosed as Motor Neuron Disease

case_prompt:
A 9-year-old Limousine beef cow, non-pregnant and 4 months postpartum, was referred for a 10-day history of moderate hyperthermia (39.5–39.6 °C), dry feces, decreased rumination and appetite, an arched back, and attenuated heart and lung sounds. Initial treatment with amoxicillin and dexamethasone produced no improvement.

On arrival, the cow was depressed but in fair body condition (BCS 3.5/5) and weighed 738 kg. She exhibited complete inappetence (rumen-fill score 2), a persistently arched back, dewlap edema, and bilateral jugular distension with a positive jugular compression test. Mucous membranes were pale. Vital signs: heart rate 105 bpm, respiratory rate 44/min (costo-abdominal breathing), rectal temperature 38.7 °C. Right-sided pulmonary auscultation was attenuated; cardiac auscultation revealed a duplicated S1, loud on the left and attenuated on the right. Rumination was absent. A wither-pinch test elicited pain. External lymph nodes: moderate enlargement of the right superficial cervical node. Rectal and urine exams were unremarkable; feces appeared normal.

Laboratory studies showed normal plasma fibrinogen, mild hypoalbuminemia, increased total protein (chronic inflammatory syndrome), leukocyte count at the upper limit with neutrophilia, and lymphopenia. 

A right-sided thoracic ultrasound revealed a 30 cm × 25 cm echogenic mass severely compressing the right heart, reducing right ventricular size, and an adjacent anechoic pleural fluid collection; the pericardium and valves appeared normal. Reticular ultrasonography showed normal structure but absent contractions. Pleural fluid, aspirated under ultrasound guidance, was moderately cloudy, orange-brown; analysis indicated a non-specific septic exudate.
title: Thoracic Tumor Associated with a Unilateral Empyema in a Beef Cow: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 23-year-old Asian man with no significant medical history presented with sudden onset of diplopia followed by left-sided facial asymmetry for 3 days. He was alert and fully oriented. Visual acuity and color vision were normal bilaterally. Pupils were equal and reactive without a relative afferent pupillary defect. On extraocular-movement testing, there was a complete left conjugate horizontal gaze palsy. On attempted right gaze, the left eye could not adduct past midline and the right eye showed horizontal nystagmus. These deficits did not improve with the oculocephalic (doll’s-eye) maneuver. Prism cover testing showed 30 prism diopters of left esotropia. There was no ptosis and convergence was intact. Funduscopy was unremarkable. Cranial-nerve examination also revealed a left lower motor–neuron facial palsy, with inability to wrinkle the left forehead, lagophthalmos, and flattening of the left nasolabial fold. All other neurologic findings were normal. Brain MRI showed multifocal T2 FLAIR hyperintense lesions without restricted diffusion in the bilateral periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial regions, including the left pontine tegmentum. A focal gadolinium-enhancing lesion with an open ring sign was noted in the left frontal juxtacortical region.
title: Eight-and-a-half syndrome as the first presentation of multiple sclerosis in an Asian male: a case report

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old Afro-Caribbean man with a 5-year history of ulcerative colitis was admitted with a 1-week history of intermittent stabbing chest pain radiating to the neck and left arm, which worsened over the previous 24 hours. He reported no dyspnea or pleuritic component. Two and a half weeks earlier, during a flare of bloody diarrhea and malaise, his therapy was changed from steroids to azathioprine after a normal thiopurine‐methyltransferase assay; he was also taking mesalazine. He denied smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, illicit drug use, and had no family history of coronary artery disease.

On examination he was afebrile; blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg; heart rate 80 bpm; respiratory rate 18 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Heart sounds were normal; jugular venous pressure was not elevated; lungs were clear. The abdomen was soft with diffuse tenderness. He had reduced abduction of the right hip consistent with sacroiliitis; no rashes were present.

Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 80 bpm with pathological Q waves in the inferior leads and tall R waves in leads V1–V4. Troponin I was elevated at >50.00 mg/mL. Laboratory studies revealed anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL), thrombocytosis (465×10^9/L), hypoalbuminemia (31 g/L), and a marginal eosinophilia (1.1×10^9/L). Blood cultures were negative. Serologies were negative for Echo, Coxsackie, EBV, CMV, and streptococcal infection. Rheumatoid factor was positive (31 IU/mL); antinuclear, mitochondrial, smooth muscle, and liver microsomal antibodies were negative; complement C3 and C4 were normal. High‐titer antiproteinase-3 ANCA (10.2 U/mL) was detected; perinuclear ANCA was negative. Chest radiograph was normal; urine dipstick showed no blood or protein. Flexible sigmoidoscopy revealed mildly active distal colitis without ulceration or granulomas.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved overall systolic function, inferolateral and anterolateral wall hypokinesia, mild mitral regurgitation, and no pericardial effusion.

Differential diagnosis at this stage included inflammatory-bowel-disease–related giant cell myocarditis, drug-induced hypersensitivity myocarditis, acute lymphocytic myocarditis, and late-presentation myocardial infarction.
title: Acute Myocardial Infarction Complicating Active Ulcerative Colitis: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old Sri Lankan female law student presented with multiple episodes of nonbilious, nonprojectile vomiting over two days, associated with burning chest pain and regurgitation. She reported a 3-year history of similar cyclical vomiting episodes—each lasting 4–5 days with 4–6 daily episodes—followed by symptom-free intervals. These episodes were managed as gastroesophageal reflux disease with proton-pump inhibitors and prokinetics without full investigations. She denied abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, or bulimic behaviors; there were no signs of an eating disorder. She had reduced appetite, generalized weakness for 3 years, and secondary amenorrhea since age 20. She had psychosocial stressors, including a recent breakup. On exam, BMI was 16 kg/m^2, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
- Serum sodium 110 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, chloride 74 mmol/L (repeatedly low)  
- Serum osmolality 223 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality 266 mOsm/kg; urine Na+ 14 mmol/L  
- Random serum cortisol 105 nmol/L (measured at 1 a.m.)  
- TSH 0.209 µIU/mL, free T3 1.32 pg/mL, free T4 0.98 ng/dL  
- FSH 1.4 mIU/mL, LH 0.4 mIU/mL  
- Serum prolactin 90.8 ng/mL after dilution  

She was euvolemic, denied polydipsia or polyuria, and had a normal urine output.
title: A Nonfunctioning Pituitary Macroadenoma Presenting as Cyclical Vomiting and Severe Hyponatremia in a Young Female

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old man with known diabetes mellitus presented with a 3-month history of intermittent fever, night sweats, and a 6-kg weight loss. He noted a hard swelling in the right parotid region that had rapidly enlarged over the past 2 weeks. On examination, a right supraclavicular lymph node was palpable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed multiple hypodense liver lesions, bilateral small pleural effusions, a right apical lung nodule, and axillary, mediastinal, peripancreatic, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Skull and spine radiographs showed no osteolytic lesions.

Fine-needle aspiration of the parotid swelling yielded hypercellular smears composed predominantly of large plasmacytoid cells with central to eccentric nuclei, perinuclear halos, less condensed chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and abundant basophilic cytoplasm. Binucleated and trinucleated forms and atypical mitoses were noted, along with mature plasma cells, scattered neutrophils, eosinophils, and apoptotic bodies. 

Based on these findings, the preliminary differential diagnosis included plasmablastic lymphoma, plasmablastic plasmacytoma/myeloma, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation.
title: Cytological Diagnosis of Plasmablastic Lymphoma Involving the Parotid Gland: A Case Report with Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 43-year-old man with no prior lung disease presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset left-sided chest pain and progressive shortness of breath. He was afebrile, mildly tachycardic, and normotensive. On examination, breath sounds were decreased bilaterally and pulse oximetry showed an SpO2 of 90% on room air.
