Supplemental oxygen was started, and chest CT revealed a simultaneous bilateral pneumothorax that was larger on the left side. In addition, there were numerous elliptically shaped lung cysts of various sizes distributed bilaterally, predominantly in the basilar medial, basilar lateral, and subpleural regions. Bilateral chest tubes were placed, resulting in full reexpansion of both lungs with no persistent air leak after 48 hours. Radiographic findings suggested an underlying multiple cystic lung disease. Family history was notable for a maternal aunt with bullous emphysema and two episodes of pneumothorax and a deceased grandfather who had an unspecified pulmonary disease.
title: Simultaneous Bilateral Spontaneous Pneumothorax Revealed Birt-Hogg-Dubè Syndrome

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old woman with a history of recurrent patellar dislocations and progressive right anterior knee pain underwent patellofemoral arthroplasty with concomitant medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction. The surgery was uneventful. Four weeks postoperatively, she noted an erythematous, blanchable rash around the arthrotomy incision, associated with warmth, swelling, and stiffness limiting range of motion to 0–30°. She was afebrile, and vital signs were normal. A 7-day course of trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole was initiated for presumed skin and soft-tissue infection. Two days later, she returned with increased pain, persistent rash with mild urticaria and warmth, tenderness along the joint line, and a trace effusion; the surgical incision sites were well healed. She was referred to the emergency department, where she received intravenous vancomycin and diphenhydramine. Laboratory tests showed normal inflammatory markers, and MRI of the knee showed no evidence of infection; the rash and swelling subjectively improved.  

Over postoperative weeks 7 through 21, she had recurrent episodes of knee warmth, swelling, a reticular rash over the limb, and throbbing pain rated up to 10/10 with activity, significantly impairing daily activities. At week 14, she presented to the emergency department with fatigue and headache; workup for infection and thromboembolism was negative. Outpatient allergy evaluation considered implant allergy, mastocytosis, and hereditary angioedema; patch testing was negative, and serum C4 complement and tryptase levels were within normal limits. Vascular surgery evaluation for May–Thurner syndrome and popliteal entrapment included MRI angiography and abdominopelvic CT with contrast, which demonstrated patent vasculature. On further questioning, she reported intermittent bloating, fatigue, and headaches. Allergy specialists recommended maintenance of a rigorous food diary before pursuing further testing.
title: Non-classical Celiac Disease as an Unrecognized Cause for Post-operative Knee Swelling following Patellofemoral Arthroplasty: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 42‐year‐old right‐handed man was admitted with a 6-year history of painless, progressive stiffness and wasting of the back and proximal limb muscles. He reported increasing difficulty with walking (short‐stepping gait), rising from supine, bending in any direction, lifting his arms, and abducting his thighs beyond 20°. He did not experience weakness, sensory changes, spasms, or pain.

Six years earlier, he began self-injecting pentazocine (60 mg daily, intramuscularly into buttocks and upper arms) combined with promethazine for abdominal pain and continued in a dependent fashion. He never injected the thighs, calves, abdomen, shoulder girdle, or forearms. He stopped the injections 6 months after symptom onset. He had a 13-year history of alcohol dependence but had been abstinent for at least 6 years. He was normotensive and non-diabetic.

On examination, there was marked wasting and woody induration of the deltoids, biceps, glutei, quadriceps, and paraspinal muscles. Active range of motion was markedly reduced: arm abduction to 45–50°, thigh abduction to 20°, elbow flexion to 15°, and thigh flexion to 10°. Distal joint movements were normal. Muscle power was full within the limited ranges, and sensation was intact. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function, serum calcium, phosphate, and creatine phosphokinase, were within normal limits. Roentgenograms of the lumbar spine, pelvis, thighs, knees, chest, and shoulders revealed multiple soft‐tissue calcifications with muscle hyperdensity. Electromyography of affected muscles was normal.
title: Calcific myofibrosis due to pentazocine abuse: a case report

case_prompt: A 25-year-old Indian woman presented with sudden severe lower abdominal pain for 2 days. She denied fever, vomiting, bowel, or urinary symptoms. She reported onset of breast development at age 11 and pubic hair development at age 12 but has never menstruated. Since age 13 she has experienced infrequent dull cramping abdominal pain that became cyclic at 45–50-day intervals by age 16, managed with occasional analgesics. She is unmarried, sexually inactive, with unremarkable medical, surgical, and family histories. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable, with normal height, weight, and body habitus; Tanner stage 4 breasts and pubic hair; and mild right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding or rigidity. Pelvic ultrasound showed blood within the right uterine horn and multiple small ovarian cysts. Pelvic MRI without contrast demonstrated a bicornuate (likely unicollis) uterus with heterogeneous myometrial signal suggestive of adenomyosis in both horns, a single angulated cervix with suboptimal visualization of the uterocervical junction, a blind upper half of the vagina, and polycystic-appearing ovaries with multiple peripheral follicles and thickened stroma.
title: A rare variant of mullerian agenesis: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old nulliparous Hispanic woman with an uncomplicated antenatal course presented in active labor at 40 weeks of gestation. Twelve hours after an uneventful vaginal delivery, she developed chills, diaphoresis, right-sided back pain, and a fever of 40.0 °C. Her heart rate was 110 beats/min, blood pressure 136/85 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Examination revealed marked right costovertebral tenderness. Laboratory evaluation showed a WBC count of 18,000/µL; urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood, 3+ leukocyte esterase, and 49 WBCs per high-power field. She was started on intravenous antibiotics for presumed pyelonephritis. 

Thirty-six hours after delivery, she became dyspneic, with a nonproductive cough and malaise. Her temperature rose to 40.5 °C, heart rate to 136 beats/min, blood pressure 136/82 mm Hg, respiratory rate 32 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 76% on room air. Chest radiography showed poor aeration at both lung bases and large bilateral pleural effusions. Blood and urine cultures grew Escherichia coli. Forty hours after delivery, she was intubated. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes; troponin levels were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed biventricular hypokinesis and an ejection fraction of 35% with normal end-diastolic chamber size and normal valvular function. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed bilateral airway disease and no pulmonary embolus.
title: Severe postpartum sepsis with prolonged myocardial dysfunction: a case report

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old man presented with progressively worsening shortness of breath over 1 month, on a background of exertional dyspnea for 1 year and increasing fatigue. Recently, he developed orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and progressive bilateral leg swelling. He was treated with furosemide 40 mg twice daily and enalapril 5 mg twice daily with no improvement; enalapril caused dizziness and worsened fatigue. He has no personal or family history of hypertension or diabetes and denies syncope, neurologic symptoms, joint pain, or autonomic symptoms.

On examination, blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 110 bpm, respiratory rate 23 /min. Lung auscultation revealed bibasilar dullness and decreased air entry, more on the right. The jugular venous pressure was elevated; the precordium was quiet, and there was a systolic murmur at the left sternal border. The liver was enlarged 6 cm below the costal margin and tender, with shifting dullness; there was grade ++ bilateral pitting edema.

Laboratory tests showed normal renal function, electrolytes, liver function, and urinalysis. Hemoglobin was 11.7 g/dL (MCV 91, MCH 29). Serum troponin was elevated at 656 ng/L and 578 ng/L (normal < 100 ng/L). Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatic congestion with hepatomegaly, ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions. Chest X-ray confirmed a right pleural effusion. ECG showed low-voltage limb leads with a pseudoinfarction pattern in precordial leads and ST-segment depression with T-wave inversions in V4–V6.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed biatrial enlargement and biventricular hypertrophy (IVS 22 mm, LVPW 21 mm, RV wall 14 mm) with interatrial septal thickening and granular “sparkling” myocardium. Left ventricular ejection fraction was 65% with no regional wall motion abnormalities. Doppler indices showed a restrictive filling pattern (E/A ratio 11, septal e′ 3, E/e′ 18) and atrial arrest. Mitral, aortic, and tricuspid valves were thickened; the IVC was plethoric, and there was minimal pericardial effusion.
title: Navigating the Diagnostic and Management Challenges of Suspected Cardiac Amyloidosis in Resource‐Limited Settings: Ethiopia Experience

case_prompt: A 47-year-old Japanese woman with no breast symptoms was referred after screening mammography revealed clustered pleomorphic calcifications in the left breast. Her mother had bilateral breast and ovarian cancer. On examination, there was no palpable mass or nipple discharge. Serum tumor markers (CEA, CA15-3, NCC-ST-439, BCA225) were within normal limits. Breast ultrasound showed a 13×12×7 mm irregular, hypoechoic mass with clear margins and internal high-echogenic foci in the left breast. MRI demonstrated a 14×11×12 mm lesion with early arterial enhancement in the same region. PET-CT revealed focal uptake (SUVmax 3.54) in the left breast without abnormal uptake elsewhere. Core-needle biopsy of the mass showed ductal carcinoma in situ, nuclear grade 2, negative for ER, PgR, and HER2, with a Ki-67 labeling index of 32.4%. Given her family history, hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome was considered, but the patient declined genetic testing. The patient elected to undergo total left mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy.
title: Sebaceous carcinoma of the breast predominantly characterized by intraductal growth: a case report

case_prompt: A 7-year-old female presented with a 12-month history of progressive bilateral neck swelling, intermittent fever, night sweats, and weight loss. She had no known tuberculosis exposure or similar family history. On examination, she was pale and undernourished (BMI 10.24 kg/m2) with multiple rubbery, mobile, non-tender lymph nodes in the submandibular, submental, and posterior cervical regions (largest 4 × 3 cm), as well as inguinal nodes; no hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (14.57 × 10^9/L) with neutrophilia, microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL; MCV 64.7 fL), and thrombocytosis (974 × 10^9/L); ESR was 36 mm/h, CRP 641.8 mg/L, and ferritin 256 ng/mL. Peripheral smear demonstrated hypochromia, anisocytosis, microcytosis, rouleaux formation, and no blasts. Gene-Xpert testing on lymph node aspirate and sputum was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, as was urine LF-LAM. Chest radiography revealed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. CT imaging of the neck, chest, and abdomen showed generalized lymphadenopathy without extranodal masses. She was started empirically on anti-tuberculous therapy.
title: An Unusual Cause of Lymphadenopathy: Rosai Dorfman Disease in a 7-Year-Old Female Zambian Child: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 29-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with epigastric abdominal pain. He reported a 1-week history of tea-colored urine, pale stools, and diffuse pruritus that preceded the development of a new rash. He denied taking any medications, including over-the-counter herbal supplements or analgesics. He drank alcohol occasionally (2–3 standard drinks several days per month). He identified as a man who has sex with men and reported unprotected sexual encounters with multiple partners several months before symptom onset. On examination, he had a diffuse papular rash involving the palms, soles, trunk, face, and groin, as well as scleral icterus; the abdomen was soft, without hepatomegaly or tenderness. Laboratory studies showed an alkaline phosphatase level of 279 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 70 U/L, alanine transaminase 167 U/L, total bilirubin 5.6 mg/dL (conjugated bilirubin 3.7 mg/dL), and serum albumin 2.6 g/dL. Urinalysis revealed 3+ bilirubin and 4+ protein; serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL. The random urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 6,667 mg/g, and a 24-hour urine collection showed 13.3 g of protein. Five days before presentation, antimitochondrial antibody and antismooth muscle antibody had returned positive (AMA 57 U; ASMA 31 U). Hepatitis A, B, and C serologies were negative. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated moderate intrahepatic biliary dilation and heterogeneous perfusion of the liver. Hepatology was consulted and recommended evaluation for systemic infectious or inflammatory etiologies and repeat autoantibody testing.
title: Secondary Syphilis Can Simultaneously Mimic Cholestatic Liver Injury and Glomerular Nephropathy

case_prompt: A 26-year-old woman was admitted with a 3-week history of fever and painful right-sided neck swelling. She first noted a painful right cervical node, then developed fever up to 40 °C, nausea, and fatigue despite courses of amoxicillin–clavulanate, metronidazole, clindamycin, and naproxen. She had no comorbidities, recent travel, or relevant family history. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable and had three tender enlarged lymph nodes on the right side of her neck; the overlying skin was normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.4 × 10^3/mL, C-reactive protein 77 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm/hr, and lactate dehydrogenase 519 U/L. Blood and urine cultures showed no growth, and a tuberculin skin test was negative. Serologic tests demonstrated evidence of past Epstein–Barr virus infection but were negative for HIV, hepatitis B and C, toxoplasmosis, VDRL, ANA, and rheumatoid factor. Chest radiography and CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were unremarkable. Ultrasound and CT of the neck revealed multiple lymph nodes bilaterally extending to the base of the neck and intraparotid region; on the right, posterior-triangle nodes measured up to 18 × 14 mm with rim enhancement and central hypodensity, and on the left, nodes up to 12 × 5 mm appeared reactive. An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of an affected lymph node was performed.
title: Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease in an Iranian Woman; a Rare but Important Cause of Lymphadenopathy

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old man with no significant medical or family history presented with a 2-week history of progressive abdominal distention associated with generalized abdominal pain, myalgia, fatigue, decreased oral intake, nausea, and unintentional weight loss. On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed distention with shifting dullness; cardiopulmonary, skin, and scleral examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed:  
- White-cell count 10.6 × 10^9/L  
- Hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL  
- Platelet count 557,000/µL  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated moderate ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, and a 4.7 × 3.3 cm lobular omental mass in the lower pelvis. A diagnostic paracentesis yielded 3.2 L of grossly bloody fluid with a low serum–ascites albumin gradient. Ascitic-fluid analysis showed:  
- Red-blood-cell count >900,000/µL  
- Total nucleated cells 3,382/µL (41% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, 0% eosinophils, 1% monocytes, 28% other cells)  
- Negative bacterial cultures  
- Cytology revealing mononuclear cells of possible mesothelial origin, inflammatory cells, and histiocytes in a hemorrhagic background
title: A Rare Presentation of Omental Lymphangioma Masquerading as Malignancy in an Adult Patient

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old man presented with mandibular discomfort and pus discharge beneath the chin. Four years earlier, he had been diagnosed with mandibular osteomyelitis and underwent sequestrectomy; since then he had received antibiotics and conservative care. On examination, a fistula with purulent discharge was present in the mental region. He had no significant medical history. He exhibited macrocephaly, frontal bossing, a broad nasal bridge, and ocular hypertelorism; hearing and facial nerve function were normal. Intraorally, the maxillary teeth were very mobile with sequestra noted in the mandibular midline; a retained deciduous tooth and a few permanent teeth were present. Oral hygiene was poor, and there was an anterior crossbite with a narrow maxillary arch. 

Panoramic radiography showed decreased radiolucency on the left mandible compared with four years earlier, increased radiolucency on the right, and generalized increased radiopacity of the maxilla and mandible; several maxillary teeth were impacted. A whole-skeleton radiograph demonstrated linear sclerotic striations in the long bones, and bone scan revealed increased uptake in both the maxilla and mandible. Maxillofacial CT confirmed mandibular and maxillary sequestra and revealed marked sclerosis of the cranial base, including the Eustachian tube and internal auditory canal.
title: Osteomyelitis in an Osteopathia Striata with Cranial Sclerosis Patient

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old Caucasian woman reported 4 days of right ocular pain and progressive blurred vision. On initial evaluation, best corrected visual acuity was 20/32 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure measured 32 mmHg in the right eye and 16 mmHg in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed marked ciliary injection, mild corneal edema with diffuse keratic precipitates, and an anterior chamber reaction (cell grade 2+, flare grade 0). Funduscopic examination was unremarkable. The left eye was normal. She was diagnosed with hypertensive anterior uveitis presumed herpetic and started on oral valacyclovir 1 g three times daily, topical dexamethasone every 2 hours, topical cyclopentolate, and brinzolamide twice daily, with progressive improvement of the uveitis.

Two months later, while on valacyclovir 500 mg daily, she developed a tender, reddish scleral nodule at the 11 o’clock position of the right eye. Biomicroscopy showed a clear cornea and anterior chamber, with normal fundus findings. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory therapy (ibuprofen 600 mg twice daily) produced no change. Laboratory studies revealed a normal blood cell count, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and normal angiotensin-converting enzyme levels. Immunological tests were negative for rheumatoid factor, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and antinuclear antibodies, but positive for HLA-B27. An infectious workup—including tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, herpes simplex, and Borrelia—was negative. Therapy was switched to oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg/day, which led to some improvement of the scleritis but plateaued over several weeks without further resolution.
title: Nodular Scleritis Associated with Herpes Zoster Virus: An Infectious and Immune-Mediated Process

case_prompt: A 24-year-old Japanese man was referred for evaluation of hypocalcemia. He was born at low birth weight (1114 g) with ptosis and joint contractures but without neonatal asphyxia or cerebral anomalies. At age 4, he was noted to have moderate bilateral sensorineural hearing loss requiring hearing aids. Beginning around age 10, he experienced facial spasms, tetany, and leg cramps, which improved during puberty but recurred in adulthood, prompting evaluation. Initial testing showed adjusted serum calcium 6.1 mg/dL (normal 8.8–10.1) and phosphate 5.4 mg/dL (2.7–4.6), and he was started on oral vitamin D and calcium, which normalized his calcium and relieved symptoms. There was no family history of parathyroid disease, tetany, deafness, kidney dysplasia, or congenital anomalies. On admission, while on supplementation his serum calcium was 8.3 mg/dL, phosphate 4.9 mg/dL, and intact PTH was low at 15 pg/mL (18.5–88.0). Other hormones were normal. Renal function was normal without proteinuria or hematuria. Neck ultrasound showed no thyroid or parathyroid abnormalities. Brain CT demonstrated multiple basal ganglia calcifications, and abdominal CT showed morphologically normal kidneys.
title: A case of hypoparathyroidism, deafness, and renal dysplasia (HDR) syndrome with a novel frameshift variant in GATA3, p.W10Cfs40, lacks kidney malformation

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman presented three weeks after an insect bite to her left thigh that evolved into a deep ulcer requiring surgical debridement and antibiotics. Following treatment, she remained listless and reported bilateral proximal muscle weakness in her upper and lower limbs, with several prior exertional episodes of similar weakness.

On examination, blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg and heart rate 80 beats/min; she was normotensive. Renal function was normal (serum urea 13 mg/dL; creatinine 0.72 mg/dL). Laboratory testing revealed serum potassium 1.31 mmol/L, metabolic alkalosis on arterial blood gas analysis, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone levels were modestly elevated.

By history, surreptitious diuretic use, diarrhea, vomiting, and a recent hypercapnic state were excluded. Spot urine studies showed chloride excretion >20 mEq/day and potassium excretion >30 mEq/day. There was no family history of Bartter’s syndrome. Urine calcium excretion was low. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no nephrocalcinosis. Electrocardiography and stress echocardiography were normal.
title: Diuretic loading test and use of Bartter's Normogram in diagnosing a case of Gitelman's syndrome: Relook into pathophysiology

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a two-week history of left lower extremity swelling and pain that improved slightly with leg elevation and NSAIDs. She denied shortness of breath, recent trauma, fever, chest pain, or unexplained weight loss. Her medical history included inflammatory polyarthritis (on methotrexate and adalimumab), hyperlipidemia, hypertension, asthma–COPD overlap, osteopenia, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation managed with warfarin (therapeutic INR). She had a three–pack-year smoking history, quitting 40 years prior.

On examination, the left lower extremity had pitting edema; peripheral pulses were strong, and the abdomen was soft and nondistended. Laboratory studies showed hypokalemia (2.8 mEq/L), which was repleted, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/hr, and a C-reactive protein level of 30.1 mg/L. Doppler ultrasound of the left leg was negative for deep venous thrombosis. Computed tomography angiography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large heterogeneous left pelvic retroperitoneal mass centered at the left iliac chain, measuring 8.7 × 6.9 × 8.5 cm, with probable compression or occlusion of the adjacent iliac vein. Based on imaging, the differential diagnosis included sarcoma, lymphoma, ovarian neoplasm, or germ cell tumor.
title: Primary Retroperitoneal Malignant Melanoma with Involvement of Iliac Artery and Vein

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old White man presented with a 2-year history of episodic fevers and tender erythematous rash predominantly on his trunk. Flares were preceded by prodromal flu-like symptoms, low-grade fever, sore throat, and arthralgias; during these episodes he also reported intermittent diarrhea and severe headache. Each flare lasted 3 to 7 days and recurred approximately every 3 weeks, at times rendering him bedbound. He had a history only of seasonal allergic rhinitis and no family history of autoimmune disease.  

Biopsies of the rash demonstrated a perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate without evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis. The patient had trialed multiple antihistamines, oral prednisone, and monthly omalizumab injections without improvement. Further laboratory evaluation showed mildly decreased C4 (12.8 mg/mL), normal C3, negative antinuclear antibodies, negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, negative rheumatoid factor, normal thyroid hormones, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, negative celiac serologies, normal serum IgA, serotonin, chromogranin A, and tryptase levels, negative hepatitis, HIV, toxocara, and tuberculosis screening, normal urinary catecholamines, metanephrines, 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, and a normal chronic urticaria index (while receiving omalizumab).  

Because of his gastrointestinal symptoms, a colonoscopy was performed and showed no evidence of inflammatory bowel disease.
title: Treatment of refractory Yao syndrome with canakinumab

case_prompt:
A 21-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of painful swelling over the inner angle of the left eye. She reported occasional epiphora since childhood, without trauma or discharge. Visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, and ocular examination was normal. External examination of the left eye showed upper and lower eyelid edema and erythema, with superotemporal displacement of the globe; the caruncle was thickened, and the medial canthus appeared rounded. There was no conjunctival hyperemia and no discharge from either punctum. Mild mechanical limitation of adduction was noted. 

After a 1-week course of anti-inflammatory and antibiotic medications, the pain and erythema improved but the inferomedial swelling persisted and appeared to progress. Lacrimal irrigation demonstrated a patent lacrimal drainage system. Given the inferomedial location of the lesion, associated preseptal cellulitis that subsided, and the history of lifelong epiphora, a lacrimal sac diverticulum was suspected.

Computed tomography of the orbits and paranasal sinuses revealed a large, heterogeneous, radiolucent mass in the inferomedial aspect of the left orbit, indenting the globe, and containing a radiopaque solid structure attached to the inferior orbital rim near the lacrimal sac fossa, without bony remodeling.  

With a revised clinicoradiological diagnosis of an orbital foreign body granuloma or cyst, surgical exploration was planned.
title: Dentigerous Cyst Masquerading as Lacrimal Sac Diverticulitis

case_prompt: A 35-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of mobile teeth in the lower left molar region and progressive difficulty chewing associated with pain and reduced mouth opening. She had hypothyroidism managed with medication; no history of trauma, familial bone disease, or systemic symptoms. On panoramic radiography, an initial patchy osteolysis of the left mandibular condyle was noted. Over 18 months, serial orthopantomograms demonstrated slowly progressive osteolysis extending from the condyle through the angle toward the mandibular body on the left side. Laboratory studies showed hypocalcemia (serum calcium 4.9 mg/dL), low vitamin D (52.14 nmol/L), and low intact parathyroid hormone (14.81 pg/mL). Investigations—including serologies and imaging—were performed to exclude rheumatoid arthritis, multiple myeloma, eosinophilic granuloma, and other systemic diseases. A whole-body PET scan revealed no additional lytic lesions. Cone-beam CT with three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed the extent of mandibular bone loss confined to the left hemi-mandible.
title: Diagnostic Dilemma of Vanishing Bone Disease - A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old man was referred to our hospital because of an abnormal finding on screening colonoscopy. He had a history of tuberculosis-related lung destruction with pneumothorax and an 8-year smoking history; there was no other relevant family or medical history. He had no gastrointestinal symptoms. On examination, his vital signs were normal and laboratory tests, including alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9, were within normal limits.

Colonoscopy revealed an approximately 10-mm yellowish, sessile protruding lesion in the proximal ascending colon covered by intact mucosa without a rolling sign or cushion sign. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a 10-mm homogeneous hypoechoic-to-isoechoic mass mainly in the mucosal layer with irregular extension into the submucosal layer; the muscularis propria appeared intact. On the basis of the EUS features, a colonic carcinoid tumor was initially suspected. Abdominal CT did not detect the lesion or any enlarged lymph nodes. An endoscopic biopsy specimen was consistent with a granular cell tumor, although the possibility of a malignant tumor could not be completely excluded based on the endoscopic evaluation.
title: Experience of surgical treatment in a granular cell tumor in the ascending colon: a case report

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman was referred with progressive generalized fatigue, proximal muscle weakness, insomnia, flushing, hypertension, impaired concentration, memory difficulties, and hypomanic symptoms. She reported a 5-kg weight loss over several months despite features of Cushing’s syndrome. Her history included breast cancer 16 years earlier and a superficial melanoma with no recurrence.

On examination she had moon facies, supraclavicular fat, a buffalo hump, chin hirsutism, and proximal myopathy. Laboratory studies showed a 24-hour urinary free cortisol of 1300 nmol (reference <183 nmol), serum cortisol levels of 600–1000 nmol/L without diurnal variation, and plasma ACTH levels of 30–45 ng/L throughout 24 hours. There was no suppression on 1-mg or 8-mg dexamethasone tests.

An MRI of the sella turcica showed no pituitary lesion. Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling after CRH stimulation demonstrated no central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient and no ACTH increase. Fasting CRH was normal at 3.5 pmol/L. Urinary catecholamines and hydroxyindoleacetic acid were normal. Chromogranin A was mildly elevated.

A CT scan of the neck, chest, and abdomen revealed only slight enlargement of the left adrenal gland with an attenuation of 25 Hounsfield units. A whole-body planar 111In-pentetreotide somatostatin receptor scintigraphy scan demonstrated no uptake typical of an ectopic ACTH source.
title: Atypical or typical adrenocorticotropic hormone-producing pulmonary carcinoids and the usefulness of 11C-5-hydroxytryptophan positron emission tomography: two case reports

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old Japanese man with a history of gastric ulcer treated with esomeprazole presented with 2 days of fever to 40 °C, headache, myalgia, fatigue, and vomiting starting 2 days after a finger laceration during sewage-plumbing work. Influenza A/B tests were negative; he received amoxicillin and ibuprofen without improvement. 

On day 6, he was alert with temperature 38.5 °C, heart rate 88 bpm, blood pressure 133/69 mmHg, neck stiffness, positive Kernig sign at 60°, and tender bilateral cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. White blood cell count was 8200/mm3 (6.0% eosinophils). Serum creatinine was 0.91 mg/dL; BUN 6.0 mg/dL. ESR was 55 mm/hr; CRP 11.58 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed no protein or cells. Head CT was normal. CSF opening pressure was 235 mmH2O; CSF had 1 cell/µL, glucose 66 mg/dL, protein 31 mg/dL; Gram stain and cultures of CSF and blood were negative. Oral levofloxacin was started.

Despite CRP falling to 0.67 mg/dL by day 17, creatinine rose to 2.74 mg/dL and peripheral eosinophils reached 12.5%. Levofloxacin and esomeprazole were stopped on day 17. He was transferred on day 20 with creatinine 2.09 mg/dL, urinary β2-microglobulin 1589 µg/L, N-acetyl-β-d-glucosaminidase 7.9 IU/L, and FeNa 2.1%. Renal sonography was unremarkable.

Renal biopsy on day 22 showed focal interstitial edema, mononuclear and eosinophilic infiltrates, mild tubulitis, and four noncaseating granulomas; glomeruli and vessels were preserved. Immunofluorescence was negative. Acid-fast and Grocott stains were negative. ACE level was normal. Chest X-ray and CT were normal; gallium scan showed no uptake. Autoantibodies including ANA, ANCA (MPO and PR3), anti-SS-A/SS-B, anti-dsDNA, and anti-GBM were negative; viral serologies (HIV, hepatitis, EBV, CMV, mumps) were not consistent with acute infection.

On day 29, he developed bilateral eye pain, conjunctival hyperemia, photophobia, and blurred vision. Best-corrected visual acuity was 1.2 OD and 1.5 OS; intraocular pressures were normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed bilateral iritis with keratic precipitates and anterior chamber cells (1+ OD, 0.5+ OS). Dilated funduscopic exam was unremarkable.
title: Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome following meningitis and systemic lymphadenopathy with persistent Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M: a case report

case_prompt: A 62-year-old Indian man with recently diagnosed p16-negative posterior oropharyngeal wall squamous cell carcinoma (stage IVb, T3N3bM0) and comorbid hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and ischemic heart failure (ejection fraction 23% with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator) underwent elective feeding gastrostomy. His thyroid function was normal at initial cancer staging. Three weeks later, he developed fever, tachycardia, and stridor. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy showed near-complete oropharyngeal obstruction; an emergency tracheostomy was performed. Examination under anesthesia revealed rapid progression of the tumour into a circumferential oropharyngeal stricture. Despite 17 days of piperacillin-tazobactam, his fever persisted (maximum 39.6 °C) and heart rate remained 110–120 bpm. Extensive cultures (blood, urine, sputum, gastrostomy site), HIV and cryptococcal tests, echocardiography, and brain CT were negative. Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 243.3 g/L and a white-cell count of 18,400/mm3 (75.1% neutrophils). Chest radiography demonstrated a small right pleural effusion. Neck CT revealed worsening pharyngeal disease with invasion into bilateral thyroid lobes and new bilateral lung nodules. On examination, there was central neck tenderness without a palpable goiter. Thyroid function tests showed triiodothyronine 8.0 pmol/L (reference 3.5–6.0), free thyroxine 54 pmol/L (reference 8.0–16.0), and thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.01 mIU/L (reference 0.45–4.5). Antithyroid peroxidase, thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin antibodies were negative. Thyroid ultrasonography showed reduced vascularity without abscess formation.
title: Refractory Thyrotoxicosis in Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma Invading the Thyroid Gland

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old right-handed man with essential hypertension and a history of COVID-19 infection 3 weeks earlier presented with a 1-day history of acute bilateral lower extremity numbness, paresthesia, paraparesis, and urinary retention. He felt mildly headachey but denied fever, chills, respiratory, chest, abdominal, or gastrointestinal symptoms. 

On examination, he had no voluntary movement against gravity in either lower extremity; deep tendon reflexes were normal and symmetrical. Pinprick sensation was diminished bilaterally beginning one fingerbreadth below the umbilicus. Upper extremity strength, sensation, and coordination were normal. A Foley catheter was placed, and urinalysis showed no infection.

SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed on admission by nasal swab antigen testing and RT-PCR; lung imaging was deferred in the absence of respiratory symptoms. Initial MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral spine (with and without contrast) and CT and MRI of the brain showed no lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed protein 90 mg/dL, red blood cells 40/mcL, white blood cells 9 cells/mm³ with 14% neutrophils, and no oligoclonal bands. A comprehensive antinuclear antibody panel was negative.

He was admitted with a working diagnosis of acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy versus postinfectious radiculopathy and started on intravenous immunoglobulin, which was discontinued after development of subsegmental pulmonary emboli. He then underwent five sessions of plasmapheresis. 

On hospital day 15, repeat MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine demonstrated diffuse increased T2 signal throughout the spinal cord and multiple enhancing lesions with edema extending over most of the thoracic cord, consistent with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis. He was treated with a 5-day course of IV methylprednisolone with slight improvement.
title: Post-COVID-19 Longitudinally Extensive Transverse Myelitis with Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antibodies

case_prompt:
A 29‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of recurrent cutaneous xanthomas. She had developed xanthomas before the age of 10 years, which were resected multiple times during her teenage years. On re-presentation she had nodular xanthomas over the elbows, palpebral xanthomas, and thickened Achilles tendons, but no palmar xanthomas or corneal rings. She smokes 10 cigarettes per day and drinks minimal alcohol. Her mother died suddenly at age 60 (possible premature coronary artery disease), and her sister had childhood xanthomas and persistent hypercholesterolemia (LDL‐C ~140 mg/dL) despite statin therapy. 

On examination: temperature 36.0°C, blood pressure 108/68 mm Hg, pulse 60/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies showed: total cholesterol 429 mg/dL, LDL‐C 357 mg/dL, HDL‐C 45 mg/dL, triglycerides 136 mg/dL, lipoprotein(a) 20.2 mg/dL, sitosterol 3.9 μg/mL, lysosomal acid lipase activity 18.1 μM/h/disk (normal ≥14.9), thyroid‐stimulating hormone 1.53 μIU/mL, free T3 2.1 pg/mL, free T4 0.99 ng/dL, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 30 U/L, HbA1c 5.7%, albumin 4.1 g/dL. Urinalysis was normal. 

Radiography of the Achilles tendons showed thickness of 15 mm. Coronary computed tomography angiography revealed no coronary artery disease, and there was no evidence of aortic stenosis.
title: Phenotypic homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia successfully treated with proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors

case_prompt:
An 11‐week‐old intact male mixed‐breed dog was referred for severe anemia and suspected babesiosis. Three weeks earlier, he had been transported from Texas. One week after transport, he developed acute lethargy and fever (40.4°C). In‐house CBC showed severe microcytic, normochromic, non‐regenerative anemia (HCT 0.147 L/L; RI 0.373–0.617 L/L) and severe thrombocytopenia (23 × 10^9/L; RI 148–484 × 10^9/L). He received 15 ml/kg pRBC over 4 h and was discharged on omeprazole, sucralfate, and amoxicillin/clavulanate. The next day, PCV was 23%. Eight days later, he was lethargic with PCV 15%; a blood smear was suspicious for Babesia, and clindamycin was started. When he became too weak to stand, he was referred.

On presentation, the dog was nonambulatory, pale, mildly icteric, and splenomegaly was noted. Weight was 5.75 kg; temperature 38.2°C; heart rate 150 beats/min; respiratory rate 60 breaths/min. Point-of-care testing showed PCV 14%, total protein 5.4 g/dL, and compensated metabolic acidosis with lactate 5.2 mmol/L. Ultrasound revealed volume contraction, no effusions or pulmonary B-lines, and subjective splenomegaly. He was blood‐typed (DEA 1.1 positive), cross-matched, and transfused with 14 ml/kg pRBCs. Cytologic evaluation demonstrated intra-erythrocytic piroplasms consistent with Babesia canis. He was treated with IM imidocarb and IV fluids.

After the first transfusion, PCV remained 13% and lactate rose to 8.2 mmol/L. He received diphenhydramine for suspected transfusion reaction and an additional 13 ml/kg pRBCs. Fourteen hours after admission, his respiratory rate exceeded 100 breaths/min; he was placed in an oxygen chamber, then developed diarrhea and hypersalivation treated with atropine. Tachypnea worsened further, necessitating emergent endotracheal intubation. During intubation, a large volume of serosanguineous/icteric fluid was produced through the endotracheal tube. Initial manual ventilation with 100% FiO₂ yielded SpO₂ values of 88%–92%, after which he was transitioned to mechanical ventilation.
title: Successful treatment of suspect Babesia‐induced ARDS in a dog using lung‐protective positive‐pressure ventilation and neuromuscular blockade

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old Filipino man was referred for evaluation of progressive shortening of his fingers. Over 30 years ago, he noticed “map-like” hypopigmented patches on both hands and wrists with tingling in cold weather. Over the past 20 years, he observed gradual shortening of his fingers without pain, pruritus, or ulceration. He reported one episode of bluish discoloration of a left finger that resolved spontaneously. One year before presentation, he developed bilateral ankle and foot swelling, a sensation of skin thickening over the extremities, and occasional hand tingling. Three months ago, he noted inversion of his feet causing difficulty walking. He denied systemic symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss, morning stiffness, gastrointestinal or genitourinary complaints. His medical history was notable only for remote burn injuries to his left hand and right arm; family history was negative for similar extremity abnormalities. He quit smoking several years ago and drank alcohol in moderation. For 30 years, he worked as a painter, laborer, and cleaner at construction sites, including a five-month stint at a PVC factory where he cleaned containers and transferred chemicals without gloves.

On examination, he had hypopigmented patches on the hands, wrists, knees, and ankles without telangiectasias or salt-and-pepper changes. Oral aperture was three fingerbreadths without perioral furrowing. Bibasal crackles were heard in the lungs; cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. There was non-pitting edema of the lower extremities. Multiple finger contractures were present. The remaining fingers showed no skin thickening or sclerodactyly. Sensation was reduced by 50% up to the knees, and there was muscle atrophy of the hands.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 83 g/L, white blood cell count 13.3 × 10^9/L (85% neutrophils), platelets 173 × 10^9/L, creatinine 86.7 μmol/L, BUN 4.7 mmol/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 2.44 mmol/L. Chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, and right lower-lobe infiltrates. Chest CT confirmed bilateral pneumonia with right loculated pleural effusion and emphysematous and bronchiectatic changes. Renal ultrasound indicated chronic kidney disease. Echocardiography demonstrated a dilated cardiomyopathy (EF 38%) and moderate pulmonary hypertension. Radiographs of the hands revealed complete resorption of distal phalanges of multiple digits, fusion of phalanges, cortical sclerosis, and subchondral cystic lucencies. Foot films showed lytic and erosive changes of the metatarsals and tarsal bones.
title: Acro-osteolysis in a Filipino Male with Vinyl Chloride Exposure: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of fever and a 7-day history of cough, dyspnea, and a painful swelling over the right side of her neck. She had a 10 pack-year smoking history and no significant past medical or family history. On examination, multiple firm, palpable right cervical lymph nodes were noted, and prominent dilated veins were visible on the right anterior chest wall. No other abnormalities were detected on systemic examination.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 13,000/mm3 with 510 eosinophils/mm3, an IgE level of 779 IU/mL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/hr, and a positive C-reactive protein. Tests for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, antiphospholipid antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, protein C and S, antithrombin III, factor V Leiden, and homocysteine were all within normal limits or negative. Two-dimensional echocardiography revealed a mild pericardial effusion. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Sputum studies, including acid-fast bacilli smear, GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Gram stain, KOH mount, and cultures for pyogenic bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi, were negative.

Neck ultrasonography demonstrated multiple necrotic right cervical lymph nodes and thrombosis of the entire right internal jugular vein. A chest radiograph revealed right middle lobe collapse and consolidation. A CT venogram of the neck and chest showed multiple heterogeneous lymph nodes in the cervical, pretracheal, and mediastinal regions; thrombus in the right internal jugular, subclavian, brachiocephalic veins, and superior vena cava; compression of the right internal jugular vein by an enlarged lymph node; extensive collateral venous channels; a small right pleural effusion; and mild pericardial effusion.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of a right cervical lymph node yielded few lymphocytes and histiocytes, with no granulomas or malignant cells. Staining and GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and cultures were negative.
journal: Lung India : Official Organ of Indian Chest Society
title: Rosai–Dorfman disease presenting as internal jugular vein thrombosis and middle lobe collapse-consolidation

case_prompt: A 24-year-old Bangladeshi man from a rural area presented in early 2008 with progressive bilateral dimness of vision (worse on the left), headache, nausea, and left-sided deafness. Despite evaluation by ophthalmologists, his vision deteriorated to complete blindness. On referral, he was normotensive, nondiabetic, and had no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, leukocyte count 8.8 × 10^9/L, and ESR 14 mm at 1 hour. Chest and sinus radiographs were normal. Audiometry revealed normal hearing on the right and no response on the left ear except for vibrotactile sensation. MRI of the brain demonstrated hypointense lesions adjacent to the cavernous sinus and retroocular region of the right orbit, findings suggestive of an inflammatory lesion or neoplastic mass (e.g., meningioma). An endoscopic endonasal transethmoidal biopsy yielded fragmented soft tissue, chronic inflammatory cells, and a single focus of oval cells forming a whorled pattern. The lesion was reported as an inflammatory pseudotumour with a differential diagnosis of lymphoplasmacyte-rich meningioma.
title: Isolated Intracranial Rosai-Dorfman Disease

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman underwent uterine curettage for fetal death at 9 weeks and 6 days of gestation. Six days later she developed fever up to 39.8 °C, generalized arthralgia without joint swelling, muscle fatigue, and dyspnea on minimal exertion. Initial laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (moderate microcytic anemia with circulating myelocytes), C-reactive protein elevated, procalcitonin normal, elevated D-dimer and ferritin levels. Vaginal swab grew Acinetobacter baumannii. ECG showed no right-ventricular overload or left-ventricular dysfunction. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 65% and no pericardial fluid. Chest CT angiography revealed no emboli but an 11-mm pleural effusion. Broad-spectrum antibiotics yielded minimal improvement despite sterile blood cultures. Bone marrow biopsy showed reactive changes with cells containing eosinophilic amorphous nuclear material. Further tests revealed hypoalbuminemia, decreased C3 and C4 complement, ANA with granular fluorescence at 1:1280 (anti–SS-A and SS-B positive).  

After 16 days she was transferred to rheumatology, reporting persistent fatigue, arthralgia with 1-hour morning stiffness, dyspnea on minimal exertion, and low-grade fever up to 37.4 °C. Exam showed limb muscle weakness, decreased breath sounds at lung bases, tachycardia (100/min), and bilateral lower-leg edema. Labs: WBC 3.05×10^3/mm^3, hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, platelets 117×10^3/mm^3, ESR 27 mm/h, CRP 199 mg/dL, procalcitonin normal, D-dimer 21 μg/mL, ferritin 953 ng/mL, NT-proBNP 798 pg/mL, triglycerides 268 mg/dL, fibrinogen 142 mg/dL, C3 0.67 g/L. ANA ≥1:10,000, anti-dsDNA 1:3200, lupus anticoagulant slightly elevated, anticardiolipin IgM positive, proteinuria 0.7 g/24 h. ANCA negative, CK normal, Coombs test negative, cultures negative. She met 2018 ACR/EULAR criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (score 24).  

She received heparin prophylaxis, antipyretics, IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 6 days, then oral prednisone 1 mg/kg. Despite this, she developed worsening dyspnea, right-upper-quadrant pain, increased leg edema, and fever. Exam again showed reduced breath sounds at lung bases and epigastric tenderness. Repeat labs demonstrated rising ferritin, fibrinogen falling to 94 mg/dL, further cytopenias, NT-proBNP rising to 4600 pg/mL, and troponin T at the upper limit of normal. CT showed pleural effusions widened to 25 mm and small pelvic fluid; abdominal organs were unremarkable. Echocardiography again showed no right-ventricular overload or left-ventricular dysfunction, with only mild mitral regurgitation. The calculated H Score was 195, corresponding to an 80–88% probability of macrophage activation syndrome.
title: Acute Heart Failure in the Course of Macrophage Activation Syndrome Due to Newly Diagnosed Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Case Presentation and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old Hispanic woman was referred for progressively worsening blurry vision, right eye greater than left. Her past ocular history included bilateral epiretinal membranes. Medical history was notable for nonspecific joint disease managed with low-dose prednisone and methotrexate, and pulmonary symptoms of unclear etiology for which she was also on low-dose prednisone. 

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left. Intraocular pressures were 13 mm Hg OU. Slit-lamp examination showed nuclear sclerotic cataracts OU (2+ OD, 1+ OS) without cell or flare. Dilated fundus examination revealed 0.5+ vitreous haze OU and mild vessel attenuation OU. Spectral-domain OCT showed preserved foveal contour without sub- or intraretinal fluid. Wide-angle fluorescein angiography demonstrated mild bilateral peripheral perivascular leakage.

Initial laboratory tests including liver function, basic metabolic panel, hemoglobin A1c, angiotensin-converting enzyme, lysozyme, QuantiFERON, syphilis serologies, anti–dsDNA, and chest radiography were within normal limits, except for a positive antinuclear antibody titer of 1:80. Complete blood count showed leukocytosis (11.6 K/µL) and anemia (hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL; previously 10.2 g/dL one year earlier).

Methotrexate was discontinued; the patient was started on mycophenolate mofetil 1000 mg twice daily and prednisone 20 mg daily. Two months later, visual acuity remained stable (20/25 OD, 20/20 OS), but repeat fluorescein angiography showed worsening peripheral perivascular leakage.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Bilateral retinal vasculitis associated with cold agglutinin disease treated with obinutuzumab and infliximab

case_prompt: A 52‐year‐old man with Addison’s disease on lifelong corticosteroid replacement and a history of lateral epicondylitis presented with a 7‐day history of severe redness around his right elbow accompanied by intense burning and stinging. The redness began after he had been gardening on a cloudy summer day. Over the next days, his elbow became swollen, blisters formed and then ruptured, leaving crusted lesions. His general practitioner suspected cellulitis and prescribed dicloxacillin. Two days after starting antibiotics, he developed an itchy rash on his chest and abdomen. On examination, there was a bright red, edematous, crusted erythema over the right elbow and a maculopapular rash on the trunk. Laboratory studies, including C‐reactive protein and complete blood count, were within normal limits.
title: A phototoxic drug reaction due to topical NSAIDs

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old nonpregnant woman presented with a 2-year history of low back pain that had worsened over the preceding 2 months. Her medical history was notable for a laparoscopic myomectomy for uterine leiomyoma 5 years earlier. Physical examination findings were unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 3.6 × 2.5 cm hypoechoic solid mass in the posterior right lobe of the liver; the remainder of the abdominal and pelvic ultrasound examinations was normal.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a patchy, slightly low-density area in the peripheral zone of segment VI of the right liver, with heterogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase.  
Laboratory studies, including liver function tests and tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA19-9, CA125), were within normal limits. Serologies for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C virus antibodies were negative.  
What is your differential diagnosis?
title:
Extrauterine adenomyoma of the liver with a focally cellular smooth muscle
component occurring in a patient with a history of myomectomy: case report and
review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old African American man presented with a one-month history of worsening low back and bilateral leg pain, intermittent night sweats, and a 32-kg unintentional weight loss over one year. He denied saddle anesthesia or bowel/bladder incontinence. He was treated empirically for sciatica with prednisone 10 mg daily without relief. He then experienced an episode of leg weakness and was admitted for evaluation. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. There was no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Neurologic examination showed intact strength and sensation in both lower extremities. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, normal serum electrolytes, and a normal serum calcium level of 8.1 mg/dL. HIV serologies were negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine demonstrated multiple enhancing lesions in the T11, T12, L3, and L4 vertebral bodies, right sacrum, and ilium, with retropulsion causing effacement of the lateral recesses at L3–L4 and L4–L5; a small epidural lesion was noted at T5 without significant cord compression. Additional osseous lesions were seen in the sternum and multiple ribs.

Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, mild cardiomegaly, a dilated main pulmonary artery (3.6 cm), hepatomegaly (18.1 cm), splenomegaly (12.4 cm), and multiple enlarged pelvic sidewall, external iliac, and inguinal lymph nodes. Testicular ultrasound was normal. Serum protein electrophoresis, urine immunofixation, β-hCG levels, and fecal occult blood testing were all negative.

A CT-guided core biopsy of a left iliac crest lesion revealed noncaseating and necrotizing granulomas; Grocott’s methenamine silver and Ziehl–Neelsen stains were negative. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration of a mediastinal lymph node demonstrated nonnecrotizing granulomas without malignant cells; fungal and acid-fast cultures were negative. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was 62 U/L (reference 14–82).

One month later, an excisional biopsy of a left inguinal lymph node again showed necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous lymphadenopathy without evidence of fungal or acid-fast organisms. An ^18F-FDG PET scan revealed extensive hypermetabolic osseous and nodal uptake.
title: A Case Report of Sarcoidosis Mimicking Vertebral Metastasis

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute onset confusion and transient left-arm tingling that resolved before arrival. Initial head CT and CT angiography of the head and neck were normal, and he was discharged. Two weeks later, he returned with fever, headache, and altered mental status characterized by waxing and waning attention. On examination, he was delirious but had no focal neurologic deficits; there was a diffuse petechial rash on his extremities. Laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 7,000/mcL, hemoglobin of 10.6 g/dL (baseline 15.6 g/dL), lactate dehydrogenase of 817 U/L, and haptoglobin less than 10 mg/dL. Serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate was greater than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2. He was started on high-dose steroids and plasmapheresis, and an ADAMTS13 activity assay was sent.

On hospital day 1, a brain MRI (1.5T) demonstrated multiple patchy T2- and FLAIR-hyperintense lesions in the right perisylvian white matter, right thalamus, left lentiform nucleus, and right midbrain. Susceptibility-weighted imaging showed punctate low-signal foci in these regions, consistent with microhemorrhages. No abnormal enhancement was seen. Review of prior imaging revealed bilateral parotid calcifications and cysts, raising concern for Sjögren’s syndrome. Differential considerations based on MRI included atypical posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome related to TTP or viral encephalitis. A lumbar puncture showed clear cerebrospinal fluid with 2 WBCs/dL, glucose 67 mg/dL, protein 48 mg/dL; cultures were negative, and viral PCR and antibody panels for West Nile virus, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, and enteroviruses were negative.
title: Atypical posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in a case of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with Sjogren's syndrome

case_prompt:
A 59‐year‐old woman was referred after an incidental finding of a brain mass on CT performed for evaluation of labyrinthitis. She was asymptomatic, with no neurologic deficits. Her medical history included hypertension and diabetes mellitus; there was no history of seizures. Laboratory studies were unremarkable.

Noncontrast head CT showed a well‐circumscribed hypodense mass in the temporal horn of the right lateral ventricle, with tiny hyperdense foci suggestive of prior microhemorrhages. Brain MRI demonstrated a lobulated intraventricular lesion measuring approximately 4.0 × 2.8 × 2.7 cm. On T1‐weighted imaging, the mass was hypointense relative to gray matter; on T2‐weighted imaging, it was heterogeneously hyperintense, with mild adjacent temporal lobe hyperintensity. Susceptibility‐weighted imaging confirmed punctate hypointense foci within the lesion. There was no or only minimal enhancement after gadolinium administration. High‐resolution 3D‐CISS sequences revealed internal cystic components. Short‐echo‐time proton spectroscopy of the lesion showed a partially decreased N‐acetylaspartate peak, a normal choline peak, and an increased myoinositol peak.
title: Temporal horns subependymomas: A report of two cases of an intraventricular neoplasm in an atypical location

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of right-sided abdominal pain. MRI of the abdomen revealed a 9.7 × 9.2 × 8.0 cm right renal mass invading the hepatic lobe. Chest CT demonstrated multiple small bilateral pulmonary nodules. He underwent cytoreductive right nephrectomy with partial hepatic resection. Pathology showed 10 cm clear-cell RCC, Fuhrman grade 4 with sarcomatoid differentiation, lymphovascular invasion, direct liver capsule invasion, negative margins, and pT4 N0 M1 stage.

Six weeks postoperatively, CT showed progression of pulmonary metastases. He was intermediate risk by the IMDC model and started sunitinib. After two cycles, he developed severe right upper-quadrant pain. CT at 12 weeks showed increased bilateral lung nodules, an 8 × 5 cm recurrence at the nephrectomy bed, multiple new liver lesions, and a 3.4 cm heterogeneous filling defect in the right ventricle. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 5.6 × 3.0 cm echogenic mass extending from the RV inflow to outflow tract with mobile components, and a separate 4.0 × 2.2 cm mass in the RV apex; right and left ventricular size and systolic function were normal, ejection fraction 50%, inferior vena cava and pulmonary valve uninvolved.

Cardiac MRI at 1.5 Tesla showed a large RV lesion invading 47 mm of the interventricular septum and extending into the RV outflow tract with no IVC involvement. Further tissue characterization revealed: (a) isointense signal on cine, low intensity on pre-contrast T1-weighted images; (b) high T2 signal intensity with absent first-pass perfusion; and (c) heterogeneous enhancement after contrast.
title: Rare Case of Intracardiac Renal Cell Carcinoma Metastasis with Response to Nivolumab: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old homeless African American man with hypertension presented with 1 week of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. He had presented 6 days earlier with similar symptoms but left against medical advice. On arrival, he reported intractable nausea, vomiting, fatigue, headache, photophobia, anuria, and myalgia; he denied cough, fevers, chills, or night sweats. He used cocaine regularly but denied alcohol, tobacco, and intravenous drugs. He had no recent travel.

Vital signs: afebrile; blood pressure 177/65 mm Hg; heart rate 77/min; respiratory rate 16/min; oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination revealed scleral icterus, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice of the soft palate, and a supple neck. Cardiopulmonary exam showed a heaving, laterally displaced point of maximal impulse with regular rate and rhythm. Abdominal exam disclosed epigastric tenderness without guarding or rigidity, normal bowel sounds, and a negative Murphy’s sign.

Laboratory studies showed: 
• Lipase >3× upper limit of normal  
• Mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic liver injury (elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT)  
• Thrombocytopenia  
• Acute renal failure (creatinine 10.4 mg/dL)  
• Elevated creatine kinase  

Urinalysis revealed hematuria, pyuria, leukocyte esterase, and hyaline casts.

Initial differential: hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).  
• Peripheral-blood smear: thrombocytopenia without schistocytes.  
• ADAMTS13 activity: normal.  
• Stool cultures: negative for Escherichia coli, Shigella, and Salmonella.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia was suspected but anti–platelet factor 4 antibodies were negative. Serologic and PCR testing for CMV, EBV, and HIV were negative. Workup for glomerulonephritis and other autoimmune renal disease (ANA, anti–dsDNA, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, complement levels) was unremarkable. Evaluation for chronic and autoimmune liver disease, including hepatitis panel, QuantiFERON, CMV, EBV, HIV, α₁-antitrypsin, and ceruloplasmin, was negative.

Given elevated lipase and epigastric pain, acute pancreatitis was diagnosed. Investigations for causes of pancreatitis included autoimmune markers (negative), urine toxicology (negative), undetectable blood ethanol level, abdominal CT (only subtle gallbladder sludge vs small stones), and MRCP (unremarkable).

Right upper-quadrant ultrasound demonstrated isolated hepatofugal flow in the right portal vein suspicious for portal vein thrombosis, whereas the left portal vein had normal directional flow.
title: Leptospirosis as an unusual culprit of acute pancreatitis and portal vein thrombosis in a New Yorker

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old healthy woman of Turkish ancestry was referred for persistent ocular symptoms. One month earlier, she had acute redness, purulent discharge, and discomfort in the left eye (OS), with the right eye (OD) affected four days later. She was diagnosed with bilateral bacterial conjunctivitis and treated with topical moxifloxacin 0.5%/dexamethasone 0.1% every 2 hours for one week. Three weeks after completing that course, she developed ocular pain, severe photophobia, mild hyperemia, and decreased vision in OS; intraocular pressure (IOP) was elevated. She was diagnosed with presumed autoimmune hypertensive uveitis in both eyes and treated with topical prednisolone acetate 1% every 2 hours, atropine 1% twice daily, a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor/β-blocker, and oral steroids (1 mg/kg/day, tapered over 3 weeks) with no improvement.

On examination at our clinic, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/200 OS, with intact color vision. Slit-lamp examination revealed severe pigment dispersion in the anterior chamber, diffuse iris transillumination defects, and mydriatic atonic pupils in both eyes. There were no keratic precipitates or anterior chamber cells, and corneal sensation was normal. Gonioscopy showed wide-open angles with heavy trabecular meshwork pigmentation and no peripheral anterior synechiae. Despite ongoing topical and oral antiglaucomatous therapy, IOP was 30 mm Hg OD and 45 mm Hg OS.

Fundus examination showed tilted discs with increased cup-to-disc ratios in both eyes. In OS, there was optic disc edema and peripapillary retinal hemorrhages suggestive of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, findings confirmed by optical coherence tomography and high-frequency B-scan ultrasonography. Fluorescein angiography showed no signs of inflammation.

Laboratory evaluation including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (11 mm/h), VDRL, FTA-ABS, herpes simplex virus and cytomegalovirus serologies, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, homocysteine, anticardiolipin antibody, lupus anticoagulant, antinuclear antibody, and HLA-B27 testing were all negative. Chest, orbital, and brain MRI and magnetic resonance angiography were unremarkable.
title: Bilateral Acute Iris Transillumination Syndrome after Topical Moxifloxacin/Dexamethasone Initially Misdiagnosed as Uveitis: Case Report

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old farmer from Kankossa, Mauritania, presented with severe chronic arthralgia of both hands and bilateral perforating ulcers on the soles, evolving over 7 years. His symptoms began with hypopigmented maculopapular skin lesions and paresthesia at the finger and toe tips and on the plantar surfaces. He had seen multiple dermatologists and traditional healers without improvement despite analgesic, antibiotic, and topical therapies. 

On examination, there was distal phalangeal atrophy with severe hand deformities, hypochromic anesthetic macules on the skin, atrophy of the metatarsals and phalanges with marked foot deformity, and bilateral plantar perforating ulcers. Palpable thickening of the ulnar and popliteal nerve trunks was noted. Visual acuity was normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Radiographs of the hands and feet demonstrated osteoporosis.
title: Two Cases of Delayed Diagnosis of Leprosy in Mauritania

case_prompt:
A previously healthy woman was admitted with a 20-day history of recurrent headache and fever and a 3-day history of dyspnea. Twenty days before admission, she developed intermittent left occipital headache lasting 2–3 minutes per episode, followed by low-grade fever, sore throat, and dry cough. Initial outpatient treatment provided only transient relief. Fifteen days before admission, fever recurred (to 38 °C), with marked fatigue, persistent dry cough, nausea, and non-projectile vomiting. One week before admission, she noted memory loss, bilateral hearing loss, and limb weakness; urinary incontinence developed the next day without altered consciousness. Three days before admission, dyspnea worsened, and she was transferred to the MICU after rapid progression to severe hypoxemia and lethargy, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation.

Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine) and chronic hepatitis B (on entecavir), with normal thyroid and liver function pre-illness. She had no diabetes, head trauma, psychiatric disease, tuberculosis, or malignancy. She denied smoking, drug abuse, recent travel, tick bites, and any known contact with birds, poultry, or horses.

On MICU admission (day 1): temperature 39.0 °C; pulse 128 beats/min; respiratory rate 20 breaths/min; blood pressure 105/78 mmHg on dopamine infusion; SpO₂ 96.4% on FiO₂ 0.90. She appeared lethargic under sedation. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds and bilateral wet rales; no murmurs, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, or definitive neck stiffness; Kernig sign was equivocal.

Laboratory results: WBC 6.37 ×10⁹/L (neutrophils 94.7%); CRP 175 mg/L; PCT 6.87 ng/mL; ESR 65 mm/h; lactate 1.3 mmol/L; albumin 29.4 g/L; AST 218 U/L; ALT 97 U/L. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.378, PaO₂ 79.4 mmHg, PaCO₂ 32.8 mmHg, PaO₂/FiO₂ ≈ 88.2. Interferon-gamma release assay was negative. Hepatitis B serologies showed HBsAg+, HBeAb+, HBcAb+; HBV DNA 610 IU/mL. Tests for influenza A and B viruses, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Toxoplasma, rubella virus, and herpes simplex virus were negative. Cryptococcal antigen, galactomannan, and β-D-glucan tests were negative. Autoimmune panels (ANA, anti-ENA, ANCA) were negative. Lymphocyte subsets: CD3 76/mm³, CD4 44/mm³, CD8 28/mm³. 

Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 212 mm H₂O; CSF clear; WBC 6 ×10⁶/L; RBC 124 ×10⁶/L; protein 0.267 g/L; glucose 5.83 mmol/L; chloride 125.9 mmol/L; ADA 1 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Chest CT showed multiple patchy shadows in both lungs with bilateral pleural effusions. Head CT was normal. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures during febrile episodes were negative.
title: A case of chlamydia psittaci caused severe pneumonia and meningitis diagnosed by metagenome next-generation sequencing and clinical analysis: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 54-year-old woman presented with one day of unconsciousness, fever, nausea, and vomiting. Over the past decade, she had been hospitalized repeatedly for similar symptoms and complained of chronic headaches. On admission, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 7, and meningeal signs were present. Renal function, liver biochemistry, and peripheral white-cell count were normal. A head CT scan was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 200 mm H₂O; CSF analysis showed 374 white cells (80% neutrophils), protein 324.6 mg/dL, glucose 0.91 mmol/L, and chloride 109.5 mmol/L. CSF cultures were negative, and CSF metagenomic next-generation sequencing did not identify a pathogen. She was treated empirically with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ceftriaxone. By day 12, her symptoms and CSF indices (pressure 190 mm H₂O; white cells 20; protein 80.8 mg/dL; glucose 2.18 mmol/L; chloride 119.6 mmol/L) had improved. On day 17, she redeveloped fever, headache, nausea, and vomiting. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure > 300 mm H₂O; 2911 white cells; protein 178.2 mg/dL; glucose 1.82 mmol/L; chloride 118.6 mmol/L. CSF cultures grew hemolytic streptococcus, and she received meropenem and norvancomycin. To investigate recurrent meningitis, a brain MRI was obtained. It demonstrated multiple symmetric hyperintense signals in the periventricular white matter around the fourth ventricle, brainstem, posterior limbs of the internal capsules, and cerebral hemispheres. Additionally, there was a partially empty sella, distended optic nerve sheaths, flattening of the optic papillae, and narrowing of the ventricles.
title: Case report: Meningoencephalocele and recurrent bacterial meningitis in chronic idiopathic intracranial hypertension

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old woman noted a subcutaneous mass in her left lumbar region that had grown gradually over 5–6 years. She experienced pain and restriction of trunk movement, particularly flexion, extension, and rotation, and was concerned about its appearance. She had no other symptoms, took no medications, and had no family history of similar lesions. Her weight had decreased by about 20 kg on a low-calorie diet, and her body–mass index was 31.8. 

On inspection, there was a large mass altering the silhouette of the left flank; the overlying skin was normal. Palpation revealed a subcutaneous bulk that was painful to touch but mobile over underlying structures. Routine laboratory tests and a lipid profile were within normal limits.

Ultrasound of the left lumbar region showed an oval, echogenic, non-homogeneous image with a fibrolipomatous aspect, measuring approximately 210 × 49 mm. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 22 cm subcutaneous, round mass with regular, sharp borders and a lipomatous signal; there was no evidence of infiltration into the abdominal wall or underlying muscles.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Approach and management of a giant lipoma in the left lumbar region

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of microscopic hematuria and a rise in creatinine from a baseline of 59 to 94 µmol/L. Over three months, she had developed a bilateral petechial rash on her lower extremities, intermittent right knee swelling and pain, and a two-year history of subjective fevers and night sweats. A short course of oral prednisone produced transient improvement in her rash and systemic symptoms, but these recurred on tapering. She was restarted on prednisone 30 mg daily one week before nephrology consultation for concern of vasculitis or connective tissue disease.

Her medical history included a left femoral crossover graft (2005), gastroesophageal reflux, dyslipidemia, depression, and at least six months of microscopic hematuria with normal cystoscopy. Medications were rabeprazole, ASA, simvastatin, citalopram, and bupropion. On exam, she had palpable petechiae on her lower extremities and warm moderate effusions in the right knee and ankle; vital signs were normal.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 102 g/L, WBC 11.1×10^9/L, creatinine 94 µmol/L, ESR 115 mm/hr, CRP 94 mg/L, and rheumatoid factor 176 IU/mL. Urinalysis had trace protein, 58 RBCs/HPF with acanthocytes, and 7 WBCs/HPF. ANCA, C3, and C4 were normal. A skin biopsy demonstrated leukocytoclastic vasculitis with dermal capillary IgM and C3 deposition. Knee arthrocentesis was noninfectious and noncrystalline.

Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and syphilis were negative; blood cultures were negative. SPEP showed no monoclonal protein; cryoglobulins and anti-CCP were negative. Kappa and lambda light chains were modestly elevated. ANA was weakly positive with RNP 1.1 AI, dsDNA was negative, and lupus anticoagulant was normal. Twenty-four–hour urine protein was 0.32 g. Renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys.

Because her creatinine and symptoms initially improved on prednisone, biopsy was deferred. Upon prednisone withdrawal, her creatinine rose to 111 µmol/L and symptoms recurred, prompting a renal biopsy. Light microscopy revealed diffuse global mesangial hypercellularity. Immunofluorescence showed trace mesangial IgG and kappa, 1+ IgM, lambda, and C1q, and 2+ C3. Electron microscopy demonstrated mesangial electron-dense deposits. These findings were thought to be consistent with mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis, although her clinical and serologic profile was atypical.

She was treated with prednisone and azathioprine, then mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab in various combinations, each time showing creatinine improvement on steroids and relapse on tapering. Given her atypical clinical features and inability to wean prednisone, the lupus diagnosis was reconsidered. Repeat transthoracic echocardiogram, CT of the abdomen and pelvis, and blood cultures showed no infectious focus. She was referred for further infectious evaluation.
journal: Canadian Journal of Kidney Health and Disease
title: Q-uestioning the Diagnosis: An Educational Case Report

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old right-handed man presented for presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant seizures. He had experienced bilateral tonic–clonic seizures at awakening beginning at age 16. After initiation of antiseizure medications, he continued to have focal hyperkinetic seizures with mild impairment of awareness, occurring 4–8 times per month despite lacosamide (600 mg/day), levetiracetam (3000 mg/day), and valproate (1000 mg/day). 

Brain magnetic resonance imaging at 1.5 T showed increased T2 and FLAIR signal intensity in the right frontal lobe “due to possible gray matter heterotopias or focal cortical dysplasia.” Long-term video-EEG monitoring with surface electrodes over three days captured five seizures lasting 16–30 seconds, localizing the epileptogenic network to the right frontal region. 

Subsequently, subdural grids, strips, and depth electrodes were implanted over the right frontal lobe to delineate the caudal boundaries of the seizure focus and to map motor cortex. After further video-EEG recording and cortical stimulation, a tailored resection of the right frontal lobe respecting the kinetic area was performed.
title: Epileptic Patient with Mild Malformation of Cortical Development with Oligodendroglial Hyperplasia and Epilepsy (MOGHE): A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 19-year-old woman presented after an accidental ground-level fall with direct head trauma. She noted a tender, unilateral soft-tissue swelling over the left temporoparietal region extending into the periorbital area, causing facial asymmetry and compromised opening of the left eye. On examination, she was alert, hemodynamically stable, and neurologically intact; facial sensation and motor function were preserved, though her chin deviated leftward with some dental malocclusion. Brain CT showed no intracranial injury but noted deformation of the left zygomatic arch. Further history revealed excision of a tongue neurofibroma in childhood and multiple café-au-lait spots; physical exam confirmed NF1 with a congenital lateral neck mass. Facial bone CT and orthopantomogram demonstrated left mandibular hypoplasia with osseous defects, a thinned zygomatic arch, and an enlarged mandibular canal and mental foramen without signs of infection. CT angiography excluded ruptured aneurysms but revealed a 75 × 45 × 97 mm ill-defined lobulated lesion in the left suprahyoid neck, infiltrating multiple neck spaces and encasing the jugular vein and internal carotid artery. Over the next 6 hours, the facial swelling rapidly increased in size, and the overlying skin became tense with punctate hemorrhagic spots.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Minimal intervention for neurofibromatosis type I manifestations: A case report

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old girl presented with involuntary movements of her upper limbs that were triggered by running. She was born full term, with normal developmental milestones and a history of febrile seizures at age 1 year. There was no family history of endocrine disorders or epilepsy. At age 7 years 2 months, she exhibited involuntary lifting of the left hand, dropping of the right hand behind her back, and flexion of both wrists with running. By 7 years 4 months, these movements increased in frequency, and jerking of the lower extremities occurred upon walking, without alteration of consciousness. An interictal electroencephalogram was normal. On the basis of these findings, carbamazepine was started, and the dyskinesia resolved.

Two months later, she was hospitalized with fever (38.6 °C) and a 3-minute generalized tonic convulsion. On examination, she was 114 cm tall (–1.4 SD), weighed 19.8 kg (–0.8 SD), and had no features of Albright’s hereditary osteodystrophy.
