Blood pressure was 109/73 mmHg, heart rate 127 beats/min, and SpO2 96% on room air. Laboratory studies showed sodium, glucose, and renal function within normal limits. Serum calcium was 5.5 mg/dL (normal 8.7–10.2), phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL (3.9–5.8), intact parathyroid hormone 343.1 pg/mL (10–65), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 74.3 pg/mL (20–60), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 13.5 ng/mL (>20). Thyroid function was normal. Brain CT revealed multiple bilateral calcifications in the basal ganglia and frontal cortex. Ophthalmological examination showed cataracts, and electrocardiography demonstrated QT prolongation with QTc 0.496 msec.
title:
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B with involuntary movements: a case report
and literature review

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old girl presented with a 5-year history of gradually progressive diminution of vision in both eyes, associated with mild ocular pain and photophobia. She denied ocular trauma, surgery, or contact-lens use and had no family history of eye disease. She had a 7-year history of migratory joint pains with swelling; rheumatic fever had been ruled out, and she had been on treatment for over a year.

On examination, visual acuity was finger counting at 5 meters in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination revealed a circumferential peripheral corneal lesion in both eyes, characterized by an overhanging epithelial edge (more prominent in the right eye), peripheral subepithelial stromal infiltrates with scarring, and corneal thinning; there was no fluorescein staining, no vascularization crossing the area, no descemetocele, and no scleral involvement. Corneal sensations were intact; intraocular pressure and extraocular movements were normal. There was no uveitis, dry eye, or blepharitis, and the fundus examination was unremarkable.

Anterior segment optical coherence tomography showed, in both eyes, areas of thinned, hyporeflective epithelium overlying focal stromal hyperreflectivity with a sharp demarcation; these changes were more pronounced in the right eye.

Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level <6 mg/L and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 24 mm/h. Antinuclear antibody testing was positive; rheumatoid factor and anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibody were negative. Complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, serum electrolytes, total protein, albumin, and infection screening (Mantoux, VDRL, HIV, hepatitis B and C) were all within normal limits or negative. Chest radiography and electrocardiography were unremarkable.
title: Bilateral peripheral ulcerative keratitis in a child with juvenile idiopathic arthritis

case_prompt: A 16-year-old Iranian girl presented with sudden-onset bilateral horizontal gaze palsy that developed overnight. She reported paresthesia in both feet beginning 2 months earlier, progressing over 2 weeks to her trunk at the level of the umbilicus, and a similar episode in both hands about 1 year prior. She had no significant past medical history, took no medications, and denied illicit drug, tobacco, or alcohol use. On examination, she had complete bilateral horizontal gaze palsy in the horizontal plane while vertical gaze was intact aside from slightly decreased saccadic velocity. Pupils were midsize and reactive; there was no nystagmus, diplopia, or blurred vision. Mild bilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy was present. Hyperreflexia was noted in all four limbs without clonus; plantar reflexes were downgoing; muscle strength, tone, and coordination were normal. Brain MRI showed multiple hyperintense subcortical and periventricular lesions on FLAIR and T2-weighted images, and bilateral hyperintensities in the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) at the level of the pons. Spinal MRI revealed two hyperintense lesions, one at C7 and another adjacent to T4. After gadolinium, the PPRF lesions did not enhance, whereas the T4 lesion enhanced. Visual evoked potentials were normal. Serum anti–aquaporin-4 and anti–myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies were negative. All other laboratory tests and routine studies were unremarkable.
title: Complete horizontal gaze palsy due to bilateral paramedian pontine reticular formation involvement as a presentation of multiple sclerosis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 79-year-old woman presented with five days of right orbital pain. She had a ruptured vesicle at the right nasal root (the Hutchinson sign) and was diagnosed with herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO); oral famciclovir was started. On hospital day 2, she developed nausea, malaise, right conjunctival hyperemia, right upper-eyelid swelling with ptosis, and dysesthesia in the ophthalmic nerve distribution; there was no extraocular movement restriction or pupillary dilation. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed no pleocytosis or elevated protein, but PCR was positive for varicella-zoster virus DNA. Oral famciclovir was changed to intravenous acyclovir (30 mg/kg/day). She then developed neck pain, CSF pleocytosis, and elevated protein, consistent with meningitis, and received intravenous methylprednisolone. By day 23, CSF PCR was negative for viral DNA.

On day 32, despite ongoing acyclovir, she abruptly developed diplopia and right eye pain. Visual acuity and fields were normal; there was no relative afferent pupillary defect and no pupil dilation. On the right, abduction was moderately restricted, and adduction and elevation were slightly restricted. Tendon reflexes were diminished; Romberg sign was negative. Serum autoantibodies (antinuclear, ANCA, SS-A/Ro, aquaporin-4, anticardiolipin) were negative. Repeat CSF showed a normal cell count, elevated protein, negative PCR for VZV, and negative oligoclonal bands. Brain MRI with gadolinium showed no orbital apex mass, no cranial nerve enhancement, no extraocular muscle swelling, and no brainstem signal abnormalities. Neurophysiological studies were normal aside from known left carpal tunnel syndrome. A blink reflex study showed absence of right R1 and prolongation of bilateral R2 upon bilateral stimulation.
title: Delayed Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome Arising More than One Month after Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus and Meningitis

case_prompt: A 49-year-old man was referred for evaluation of two liver tumors detected on routine abdominal ultrasonography. He had no medical history, medication use, alcohol intake, or known viral hepatitis. On examination, he was afebrile, had no stigmata of chronic liver disease, and his body-mass index was 22.7. Laboratory tests, including alpha-fetoprotein and protein induced by vitamin K absence-II, were within normal limits. Abdominal sonography showed two well-circumscribed, hypoechoic lesions measuring 2.1 cm in segment 8 and 2.2 cm in segment 7 in a mildly fatty liver. Plain CT demonstrated both lesions as iso- to hyperdense relative to liver. On contrast-enhanced CT, the lesions showed arterial‐phase enhancement with delayed washout in the portal venous phase. On MRI, each lesion exhibited high-intensity rims and low-intensity centers on T1-weighted images, low intensity on T2-weighted images, and signal drop on opposed‐phase compared with in-phase images, indicating intralesional fat. Both lesions retained ethoxybenzyl contrast on hepatobiliary-phase imaging. Based on these findings, well-differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma was suspected, with benign nodules such as nodular regenerative hyperplasia or focal nodular hyperplasia–like lesions in the differential diagnosis.
title: A rare case of liver regenerative and non-neoplastic lesion resembling a well-differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma

case_prompt: A 28-year-old Caucasian woman was brought to the emergency department with a 5-hour history of progressive impairment in consciousness and slurred speech. Her medical history was unremarkable; she did not smoke, drink alcohol, take medications, or use illicit drugs. There was no history of head trauma. On examination, blood pressure was 140/70 mmHg, pulse 90 beats/min, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, and temperature 37.1 °C. She was stuporous, with no focal neurologic deficits, no neck stiffness, and bilateral downgoing plantar reflexes. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, white-cell count 9100/mL³, platelets 270,000/mL³, normal electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, and coagulation studies. Serologic testing, including VDRL, was negative. Urine microscopy was normal. Blood and urine toxicology screens for cocaine, opioids, and amphetamines were negative. A 12-lead ECG was normal. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed bilateral hypodensities in the corpus striatum and a small hyperdense focus in the anterior right globus pallidus.
title: Progressive obtundation in a young woman with bilateral corpus striatum infarction: a case report

case_prompt:
A 79-year-old white man presented with sudden onset of right-sided ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, and ptosis accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and headache. The symptoms began two days after receiving an inactivated seasonal influenza vaccine containing A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1N1)-like, A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2)-like, and B/Malaysia/2506/2004-like viruses. 

He had no history of diabetes, glucose intolerance, arterial hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, systemic vasculitis, smoking, obesity, or other vascular risk factors. There was no personal or family history of neurologic disorders. 

On examination, temperature and other vital signs were normal; blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg. Neurologic examination revealed right oculomotor nerve palsy with pupil sparing; all other cranial nerves were intact. Motor strength, reflexes, tone, coordination, sensation, gait, and Romberg test were normal.

Laboratory studies showed normal red and white blood cell counts, platelet count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, electrolytes, renal function, lipid panel, fasting glucose, glucose tolerance, and glycosylated hemoglobin. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Noncontrast head CT, brain MRI, and MR angiography were unremarkable.
title: Transient Oculomotor Palsy after Influenza Vaccination: Short Report

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old girl was admitted with a 5-day history of fever (to 39.5 °C) and a 2-week history of unilateral clear tearing from the right eye. She had been treated elsewhere for presumed bacterial conjunctivitis with topical ofloxacin without improvement. Over the previous 4–6 weeks she had chronic nasal obstruction, noisy breathing, and rhinolalia, and for 7 days she had purulent anterior rhinorrhea.  
On examination, she had erythematous, tender, and edematous right upper and lower eyelids with an S-shaped palpebral swelling and overlying erythema at the site of the lacrimal sac. There was painful palpation at the nasal canthus but no ocular discharge. Nasal mucosae were swollen. Bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy was present, more marked on the right. Neurologic examination, ocular motility, and funduscopy were normal, with visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally and no proptosis or relative afferent pupillary defect. Throat and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count with a left shift, C-reactive protein 22 mg/L, and normal procalcitonin.  
Contrast CT of the head revealed right preseptal soft-tissue infiltration and a well-delimited ipsilateral 11 × 18 × 13 mm collection with rim enhancement suggestive of a periorbital abscess; there were no signs of acute sinusitis or intracranial extension. Multiple bilateral cervical lymph nodes were also noted.  
Intravenous co-amoxiclav (100 mg/kg/day) and topical neomycin–polymyxin B were initiated. Over the next 3 days, fever persisted, and a fluctuating lump developed in the nasolacrimal region. Systemic corticosteroids were added. No spontaneous purulent discharge occurred, and blood cultures plus eye-swab cultures remained negative. Surgical drainage was considered, and EBV serology was sent.
title: Epstein–Barr virus-related dacryocystitis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman with no history of cardiac disease presented with 3 weeks of confusion, anorexia, a 20-lb weight loss, and fatigue. She denied fever, headache, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, or edema. In the emergency department her blood pressure was 92/52 mm Hg, heart rate 129 beats/min, and she was lethargic but without focal neurologic deficits. Examination revealed small, painless supraclavicular and inguinal lymph nodes; heart and lung exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 88 000/μL, creatinine 4.8 mg/dL, and corrected calcium 21 mg/dL. Peripheral smear demonstrated atypical lymphocytes. Additional studies were consistent with tumor lysis syndrome. Imaging revealed diffuse lytic bone lesions and enlarged lymph nodes. Bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry confirmed a T-cell clonal neoplasm, and HTLV-1 serology was positive, establishing acute adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL). A baseline transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and function, with an ejection fraction of 65%.

After stabilization of tumor lysis syndrome, she was started on inpatient EPOCH chemotherapy: continuous infusions of etoposide, vincristine, and doxorubicin, followed by cyclophosphamide and prednisone. Ten hours into the infusion of doxorubicin, etoposide, and vincristine, she developed acute hypoxia (70% on room air), tachycardia (152/min), and tachypnea (40/min), prompting endotracheal intubation and discontinuation of chemotherapy.

An electrocardiogram showed new nonspecific T-wave inversions in leads V2-V3. A bedside echocardiogram revealed apical ballooning with severe hypokinesis of the anterior and anteroseptal walls, mild hypokinesis of other walls, and an estimated ejection fraction of 20%. Chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary edema and an enlarged cardiac silhouette. N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide was 7000 pg/mL (normal <125 pg/mL), and peak troponin was 0.7 ng/mL (normal <0.01 ng/mL). 

She was started on intravenous dobutamine for hemodynamic support.
title: Doxorubicin‐associated takotsubo cardiomyopathy in a patient with adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of pain in the right laterocervical region over the carotid bifurcation. The pain was a severe dull discomfort radiating to the ipsilateral ear and was triggered by head and neck movements. He had mild fever, fatigue, and myalgia at the onset but denied migraine or other neurological symptoms.

On examination, he was afebrile and in good general condition. There was localized swelling and tenderness at the right carotid bifurcation, worsened by palpation. No carotid bruits were audible. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy or induration along the jugular vein.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9910/mm3, C-reactive protein of 0.10 mg%, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/h. All other laboratory parameters were within normal limits.

Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated an asymmetric hypoechoic thickening of the right distal common carotid artery extending into the proximal internal carotid artery. No intimal plaque or stenosis was present, and Doppler studies showed normal flow parameters. The thyroid, parathyroid, and salivary glands appeared normal; no neck mass or cervical lymphadenopathy was seen.

MRI of the neck revealed a thin rim of hyperintense tissue surrounding the right carotid artery on STIR sequences, which showed diffusion restriction on DWI and marked enhancement after contrast administration. There was no significant luminal narrowing.
title: “TransIent perivascular inflammation of the carotid artery (TIPIC) syndrome” as a rare case of laterocervical pain: Multimodal diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old Asian woman was transferred with a two-month history of episodic chest pain, dyspnea, bilateral lower-extremity swelling, cyanosis, and transient loss of consciousness. Two years earlier she had undergone an abdominal hysterectomy for uterine fibroids. Two months before transfer she had a brief loss of consciousness; two weeks before she noted gradual pleuritic chest pain and leg edema; and one day before she developed shortness of breath and a nonproductive cough. She had no known risk factors for thromboembolism.

At the outside hospital she appeared cyanotic and hypotensive, with a heart rate of 110 bpm, systolic blood pressure of 70 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 34 breaths per minute, and dusky skin. An electrocardiogram and serum troponin were normal. Arterial blood gas on 100% oxygen showed pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 22 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 506 mm Hg. The leukocyte count was 12.9×10³/μL; other hematologic, renal, liver, and coagulation studies were within normal limits. A head CT scan was normal. Venous duplex ultrasonography revealed a right proximal deep venous thrombosis, and unfractionated heparin was started.

On transfer, a CT scan of the chest identified a 3.1-cm hypodense filling defect traversing the right atrium into the right ventricle, with small bilateral pleural effusions and atelectasis but no pulmonary embolism. Abdominal CT showed distension of the inferior vena cava with a similar-density lesion and subtle linear enhancement. Pelvic CT revealed a 6.2×3.9-cm lobulated pelvic mass inseparable from the internal iliac vein. Transthoracic echocardiography in the apical four-chamber view demonstrated a 3.5×3.0-cm tissue-density mass filling the right atrium to the plane of the tricuspid annulus.
title: Obstructive shock in a 47 year old female with a deep venous thrombosis due to intravascular leiomyomatosis: a case report

case_prompt: A 45-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of malaise and upper respiratory symptoms for which she had taken ibuprofen and pseudoephedrine. On initial assessment she was febrile (38.5 °C), hypotensive, and tachycardic with a heart rate of 250 bpm. Vagal maneuvers and escalating doses of intravenous adenosine did not affect her rhythm. At the community hospital her ECG showed a narrow QRS tachycardia up to 280 bpm. She received several liters of crystalloid and an infusion of IV diltiazem without sustained slowing, and six attempts at electrical cardioversion under sedation failed to terminate the tachycardia. Over the next hours, control was attempted with IV esmolol, digoxin, magnesium sulfate, and a 150 mg loading dose of amiodarone. As she developed increasing oxygen requirements and pulmonary edema, she was given IV furosemide and transferred to the cardiac ICU at a tertiary center. There she received a second amiodarone load, three more unsuccessful cardioversions, and boluses of lidocaine and procainamide with only transient rate slowing. With worsening respiratory status she was intubated, cooled to 35.5 °C, and placed on infusions of esmolol, lidocaine, and procainamide. Her heart rate slowed to 130 bpm and ECG demonstrated atrioventricular dissociation.
title: Successful radiofrequency ablation of junctional ectopic tachycardia in an adult patient

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of gradually increasing lower abdominal pain and irregular vaginal bleeding. She was postmenopausal (age at menopause, 56), with no significant medical, surgical, or family history. She had no history of HPV vaccination.

On examination, she was pale and underweight. Abdominopelvic CT without contrast showed an enlarged uterus. Laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 32,200/mm3, a C-reactive protein level of 17 mg/dL, and hemoglobin of 5.5 g/dL; 6 units of red blood cells were transfused. Tumor markers were elevated: SCC antigen, 5.3 ng/mL (normal ≤2.5); CA-125, 112.7 U/mL (normal ≤35).

Speculum examination demonstrated a large bleeding tumor occupying the vaginal canal; bimanual exam revealed an enlarged, fixed uterus with the fundus midway between the symphysis pubis and the umbilicus. Contrast-enhanced CT showed multiloculated, thick-walled cystic lesions in the uterus and pelvic fluid suggestive of an abscess. Empiric antibiotics were begun.

Pelvic MRI revealed an 11×9-cm mass with central necrosis confined to the cervix; the endometrial cavity was spared and distended with fluid. There was no parametrial, vaginal wall, or rectal involvement on MRI; bladder mucosal invasion was not excluded.

Colposcopy-directed biopsy of the cervical lesion showed endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was diffusely positive for vimentin and estrogen receptor, almost negative for progesterone receptor, and patchy positive for p16. Tests for high-risk HPV (16 subtypes) and microsatellite instability were negative. Cystoscopy confirmed intact bladder mucosa.
title: Large cervical endometrioid adenocarcinoma mimicking endometrial endometrioid adenocarcinoma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old Caucasian man with a 10-year history of biopsy-proven EGPA, who declined maintenance immunosuppression and was managed intermittently for asthma flares, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of sudden onset sharp right-sided lumbar back pain beginning after moving a heavy object. He also reported periumbilical pain worsened by meals, associated with nausea and loose stools.  
On examination: temperature 36.6°C; blood pressure 129/77 mm Hg; pulse 79 beats/min; respiratory rate 12 breaths/min. The abdomen was soft with periumbilical tenderness; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 14,240/μL (4,000–10,000) with 2% eosinophils, neutrophils 82%; C-reactive protein 104 mg/L (0–5); procalcitonin 7.4 ng/mL (0–0.25); normal renal function; alkaline phosphatase 217 U/L (40–150); normal transaminases. ANCA panel and ANA were negative; IgG4 was 125 mg/dL (2–96). Blood cultures were negative.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed an asymmetric fusiform dilation of the infrarenal abdominal aorta measuring 3.6 × 3.2 cm along the right lateral and anterior margin at L4, with focal wall calcification and surrounding hazy soft-tissue stranding, findings interpreted as consistent with a mycotic aneurysm.
title: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis Polyangiitis (EGPA) Masquerading as a Mycotic Aneurysm of the Abdominal Aorta: Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old Italian boy presented with a six-month history of recurrent episodes of fever, vomiting, dizziness, headache, tinnitus, and ataxia. He had no significant past medical or family history. On day 7 after symptom onset, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was normal. A vestibular viral neuritis was diagnosed, and oral steroids were given with partial improvement.

On admission he was afebrile (37 °C), normotensive, and alert. He had persistent dizziness and horizontal nystagmus aggravated by head movement. He was unable to sit or stand unassisted. Romberg’s sign and the head-thrust test were positive. There were no visual deficits, meningeal signs, or pathological reflexes, and tympanic membranes were normal.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h, C-reactive protein of 4.5 mg/dL, and neutrophilic leukocytosis. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 3 nucleated cells per field, normal glucose and protein levels, and negative tests for Herpes simplex virus 1–2, enterovirus, and Borrelia burgdorferi. Cultures of CSF, blood, urine, and throat swabs were negative. Serologic tests for varicella-zoster virus, Borrelia burgdorferi, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein–Barr virus were negative. Anti-nuclear and anti-cochlear antibodies were absent. HLA-B52 haplotype was detected.

Audiometry demonstrated bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Chest radiography, abdominal ultrasonography, and repeat brain MRI were unremarkable. Electroencephalography was normal.

An autoimmune audio-vestibular disease was suspected, and methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day) was initiated.
title: Autoimmune sensorineural hearing loss as presenting manifestation of paediatric Behçet disease responding to adalimumab: a case report

case_prompt: A 51-year-old multiparous perimenopausal woman presented with a painless right breast mass noted on self-examination. The mass had not changed in size since detection, and there was no associated pain, nipple discharge, skin discoloration, or axillary swelling. Her medical history was notable for well-controlled hypertension. On examination, there was a nontender, mobile 2 × 2 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, free from the overlying skin and chest wall, and no axillary lymphadenopathy. Two weeks after detection, a blind core biopsy with a 14-gauge needle yielded inadequate tissue for diagnosis. Three weeks later, a repeat blind core biopsy showed acute-on-chronic nonspecific inflammation with fat necrosis and no evidence of malignancy. Three weeks after the second biopsy, because the mass persisted and the patient experienced some discomfort, a breast ultrasound was performed. B-mode imaging demonstrated a thick-walled anechoic lesion measuring 2.07 × 1.02 × 0.9 cm with a pulsating anechoic center. Color Doppler examination revealed swirling flow within the center of the lesion.
title: Pseudoaneurysm of the breast following blind palpation-guided core needle biopsy: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 77-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of a left breast lump. She had a history of heart disease, treated for 4 years. On examination, there was a 3 × 2 cm firm, mobile, non-tender mass in the outer quadrant of the left breast; the skin, nipple, and areola were unremarkable. There was no axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy; the right breast was normal. Mammography showed a 2 × 2 cm ill-defined mass with irregular margins in the left upper outer quadrant and no microcalcifications; the right breast was normal. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was inconclusive. She underwent a lumpectomy with frozen-section analysis.

On gross examination, the specimen revealed a firm, grey-white, fibrous, unencapsulated nodular tumor measuring 2 × 1.2 × 0.8 cm with infiltrative borders; the closest margin was 0.5 cm from the base. Frozen sections showed a spindle cell proliferation with mild atypia in a sclerotic stroma infiltrating adjacent fat; a low-grade sarcoma was favored, and no axillary staging was performed at that time.

Permanent sections demonstrated an infiltrative spindle cell tumor with prominent sclerosis reminiscent of keloid formation. The cells were arranged in fascicles with tapering nuclei, mild anisonucleosis, and inconspicuous mitoses. Occasional plump epithelioid cells formed small clusters. Interspersed foci of benign ductal hyperplasia and papillary hyperplasia, including a micropapilloma without atypia, were noted. No squamous differentiation or ductal carcinoma in situ was seen.

Immunohistochemistry revealed tumor cells diffusely positive for cytokeratin (CK), CK7, high molecular weight cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, and vimentin. They were negative for gross cystic disease fluid protein, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, S100, desmin, CD34, and HER-2/neu. Smooth muscle actin and p63 showed focal positivity. Ki-67 labeled fewer than 5% of tumor cells.
title: Fibromatosis-like carcinoma-an unusual phenotype of a metaplastic breast tumor associated with a micropapilloma

case_prompt: A 40-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension presented in Pemba, Mozambique, with a 2-day history of fever, chills, malaise, general weakness and prostration. He denied headache, arthralgia or myalgia at onset. On admission, temperature was 38.2 °C, blood pressure 110/75 mmHg, and a diffuse, undifferentiated rash was noted without hemorrhages or edema. A rapid diagnostic test for Plasmodium falciparum was negative. Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 15.7 × 10^3/mm^3 (lymphocytes 6.9 × 10^3/mm^3), hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 33 × 10^3/mm^3, alanine aminotransferase 245 U/L, glucose 9.11 mmol/L, and urea 14.2 mmol/L. No blood cultures were available. He was started on ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin and ampicillin. Over the next two days, fever persisted and he developed headache, dizziness, symmetrical polyarthralgia and melaena. On hospital day 2, hemoglobin fell to 6.2 g/dL and platelets rose to 56 × 10^3/mm^3. On day 3 he was transferred to the ICU and received three units of whole blood. On day 4 he became comatose. Repeat malaria tests remained negative, and urinalysis was unremarkable. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were continued without improvement.
title: Severe Chikungunya infection in Northern Mozambique: a case report

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old self-employed man presented with a 5-year history of “allergic rhinitis and sinusitis” managed without standard therapy and a 3-year history of an indeterminate lung shadow. Over four years he had recurrent upper abdominal pain, anorexia, and 10 kg weight loss. Laboratory testing showed a marked peripheral eosinophilia (peak 64.5 × 10^9 cells/L, 78.2%). 

Serial gastroscopy and biopsies demonstrated moderate chronic gastritis, focal glandular epithelial atypia, and eosinophil-rich exudate. Pancreatic head biopsy showed bloody effusion with eosinophils and neutrophils. Abdominal CT and PET-CT revealed a bulky pancreatic head (interpreted as pancreatitis) and mild gastric wall thickening (inflammation versus lymphoma). Chest imaging showed multiple patchy and cord-like pulmonary opacities and mildly enlarged mediastinal nodes.

On admission for evaluation of the lung shadow and hypereosinophilia, his oxygen saturation was 90% on room air, and he had a scattered erythematous rash on both lower limbs. A bronchoscopy with right lower lobe biopsy showed abundant eosinophils, histiocytes and lymphocytes in the alveolar interstitium, and eosinophilic infiltration of small vessel walls. Immunohistochemical findings were CD3(+), CD5(–), CD4(–), CD8(individual+), CD56(–), CD20(–), CD30(+), Ki-67 30%+, with EBER(–) and negative fungal and acid-fast stains. 

Based on these findings, the provisional differential diagnosis included eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, pending characterization of sinus lesions, and eosinophilic gastritis.
title: Misdiagnosis of lymphoma as vasculitis: A case report

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with sudden, severe abdominal pain 60 minutes earlier, preceded by anchovy ingestion 48 hours before. She also reported weakness, diaphoresis, and hypotension. Her pain was rated 8/10 and was diffuse, with maximal tenderness in the periumbilical and epigastric areas associated with guarding.  

Her blood pressure was 84/49 mmHg, pulse 110/min, respirations 20/min, and SpO2 98% on room air. She was pale and diaphoretic. The neck was supple, chest clear, and there was no abdominal ecchymosis or palpable masses.  

She had a 6-month history of epigastric pressure unrelated to food, with intermittent nausea and vomiting; surgical causes had been previously excluded. Medical history included hyperlipidemia, hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and type 2 diabetes; she was on fluvastatin, lansoprazole, irbesartan, metformin, and aspirin. She had no history of trauma.  

Four months earlier she had elevated serum-specific IgE against Anisakis simplex. On admission her white blood cell count was 13 160/μl with eosinophilia, hemoglobin 7.9 g/dl, hematocrit 22.4%, C-reactive protein > 67 U/L, and D-dimer 550 ng/ml. Other laboratories were notable for normal liver enzymes and coagulation studies.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a splenic subcapsular hematoma with loss of normal splenic architecture and perisplenic free fluid, consistent with acute spontaneous splenic rupture, and a thickened, inflamed retrocecal appendix with mesenteric fat stranding, suggestive of acute appendicitis.
title: Spontaneous splenic rupture and Anisakis appendicitis presenting as abdominal pain: a case report

case_prompt: A 29-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of progressive vision loss in her left eye. She had a 15-year history of headaches with documented bilateral optic nerve head swelling and possible optic disc masses. At age 14, she had been diagnosed with pseudotumor cerebri and underwent an extensive negative work-up, including left optic nerve sheath fenestration, without improvement. On presentation, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/150 in the left. Initial genetic testing by whole exome sequencing was negative for mutations in von Hippel-Lindau, hypoxia-inducible factor-2α, neurofibromatosis, and tuberous sclerosis genes. Over the next several years, she received monthly then biweekly alternating intravitreal bevacizumab and aflibercept injections, along with bimonthly intravitreal steroid implants, with only limited response in the right eye. The optic nerve head lesions progressed to involve the papillomacular bundles. By early 2017, visual acuity had declined to 20/400 in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Optic nerve head reactive retinal astrocytic tumor treated with photodynamic therapy

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old girl presented with a 10-day history of left-sided otalgia, otorrhea, and ipsilateral hearing loss. On the day of admission she noted binocular diplopia and strabismus. She had taken paracetamol and ibuprofen regularly, had a single day of fever on day 4 of her illness, and vomited the night before presentation without headache or ocular pain. Her past medical history was unremarkable.

On examination her temperature was 38.0°C. Otoscopic examination showed a suppurative left-sided acute otitis media. Tuning-fork testing demonstrated bilateral conductive hearing loss. Neurologic exam was notable for an ipsilateral abducens nerve palsy; trigeminal sensation was intact, there were no other focal deficits, and meningeal signs were absent.

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 26,200/µL with 93.4% neutrophils and a C-reactive protein level of 88.8 mg/L. Renal function and coagulation studies were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head demonstrated left mastoiditis, left petrous apicitis (apical petrositis), ipsilateral septic cavernous sinus thrombosis, and infectious arteritis with stenosis of the internal carotid artery. MRI confirmed diffuse enhancement of the left mastoid air cells and petrous apex with extraosseous extension to the adjacent dura, approximately 50% stenosis of the petrous, lacerum, and cavernous segments of the internal carotid artery, and enhancement and swelling of the cavernous sinus.
title: Gradenigo's Syndrome with Carotid Septic Stenosis

case_prompt:
A 9-year-old Ugandan girl with no significant past medical history presented with an 8-day history of persistent high-grade fever unresponsive to antipyretics and severe abdominal pain localized to the periumbilical and right iliac regions. Five days after symptom onset she also developed profuse, nonbloody diarrhea (7–10 stools/day), vomiting, and malaise. On day 7 she noted a generalized maculopapular, non-pruritic rash without conjunctivitis or mucosal changes. One day before transfer she developed a dry cough and dyspnea.

Two days after initial symptoms, she was treated at an outpatient facility with paracetamol and oral amoxicillin–clavulanate for presumed infection after a CBC showed neutrophilia, but her abdominal pain, fever, diarrhea, and vomiting worsened. An abdominal ultrasound was reported as normal, yet an empiric diagnosis of appendicitis led to a laparoscopic appendectomy; the appendix appeared grossly normal. Postoperatively, she remained lethargic with persistent fevers despite IV fluids, analgesia, antipyretics, and broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin–tazobactam). She developed photophobia. A nasopharyngeal swab tested positive for SARS-CoV-2. Her oxygen saturation fell from 98% to 82% on room air, and she was diagnosed with COVID-19 pneumonia and transferred for further care.

On arrival she was febrile (39.5°C), tachypneic (RR 35/min), tachycardic (PR 70/min), and required 3 L/min supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO₂ 95–97%. Examination disclosed oral thrush, a maculopapular rash, and tenderness in the right iliac fossa and epigastrium without guarding. Neck was supple; Kernig’s sign was negative.

Laboratory studies showed lymphopenia (720 cells/μL; normal 1.0–7.0), elevated C-reactive protein (103 mg/dL; normal <1.6), and ferritin (344 ng/mL; normal 20–250). A chest CT scan demonstrated multifocal peripheral ground-glass opacities and consolidation in both lungs, with basal and apical predominance.
title: SARS-CoV-2-Associated Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in a Child in Uganda: A Paediatric Experience in a Resource-Limited Setting

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old man was followed for mild bilateral renal cystic disease when surveillance imaging showed interval enlargement of an endophytic right interpolar Bosniak III cyst measuring 1.9 × 2.0 × 1.6 cm. He was asymptomatic, with no hematuria or flank pain. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type II diabetes, and gout; his baseline glomerular filtration rate was 77 mL/min. He had a 22–pack-year smoking history but no family history of genitourinary malignancy. Laboratory studies were normal. He elected to undergo a robot-assisted right partial nephrectomy without complication. 

Gross examination revealed a well-circumscribed renal mass composed of multiple cysts ranging from closely packed small tubules to larger simple cysts within fibrous stroma; focal papillary architecture was noted. On light microscopy, the cysts were lined by predominantly a single layer—and occasionally multiple layers—of cells with variable eosinophilic cytoplasm resembling oncocytic cells. In some areas, cells exhibited a hobnail appearance and focal intracytoplasmic vacuoles. Nucleoli were prominent (grade 3). Ovarian-type stroma was absent.
title: Unusual Suspect: A Case Report of Tubulocystic Renal Cell Carcinoma with Features of Cystic Renal Oncocytoma

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man with sleep apnoea and a history of junctional tachycardia ablation presented with acute dyspnoea shortly after undergoing urgent percutaneous coronary intervention for an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. His medications included aspirin, clopidogrel, bisoprolol, atorvastatin, and ramipril. Initial examination prior to PCI was unremarkable, and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed no valvular abnormalities. Coronary angiography revealed a complete occlusion of the distal right coronary artery, which was stented without difficulty, despite a shepherd’s crook configuration of the proximal vessel.

Soon after the procedure, he developed shortness of breath and a short decrescendo early diastolic aortic murmur. NT-pro–brain natriuretic peptide was 1784 pg/mL. Chest radiograph was normal, and CT angiography excluded dissection and pulmonary embolism. Repeat TTE showed new moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation (vena contracta 0.6 cm; jet >50% of outflow tract; pressure half-time 340 ms) with an abnormal mobile structure on the aortic valve. Left ventricular ejection fraction was 45% with inferior wall hypokinesis.

Transoesophageal echocardiography identified a 17 mm fine, filamentous mobile lesion attached to the non-coronary cusp, causing a coaptation defect and severe eccentric regurgitant jet. The valve was tricuspid without root dilation. There was no clinical or laboratory evidence of infective endocarditis. After multidisciplinary discussion, the patient was referred for surgical evaluation.
title: Iatrogenic aortic valve fenestration rupture following coronary angiography: a case report

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 5-year history of persistent headaches and nausea. Over this period, she noted progressively worsening vision in both eyes and short-term memory loss. She was born in Honduras and continues to travel there regularly; she has no history of fever, night sweats, weight loss, rash, oral or genital ulcers, or sick contacts. Her past medical history is unremarkable; she does not smoke and has no pets.

On examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologic examination revealed decreased peripheral vision in both eyes; the remainder of the neurologic and general physical examination was normal. Formal ophthalmologic evaluation showed no signs of ocular cysticercosis.

Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• White blood cell count 7000 cells/mcL  
• Hemoglobin 12 g/dL  
• Platelets 333,000 cells/mcL  
• Creatinine 1 mg/dL  
• Glucose 109 mg/dL  
• Aspartate aminotransferase 111 units/L  
• Alanine aminotransferase 149 units/L  
• Morning cortisol 1.1 mcg/dL (low)  
• Adrenocorticotropic hormone 5.8 pg/mL (low)  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a partially calcified suprasellar and parasellar mass with both solid and cystic components, the largest segment measuring approximately 1.0 × 1.3 cm in the right parasellar region.
title: Neurocysticercosis mimicking craniopharyngioma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome underwent ascending aortic replacement and mechanical aortic valve insertion 8 years earlier. She presented with a 2-week history of rhinorrhea, progressive dyspnea, and central chest pain radiating to the back. Over the preceding two nights she developed night sweats but had no fever or rigors. Her only medication was warfarin, and outpatient records suggested that her international normalized ratios had been within the therapeutic range.

On arrival at the tertiary cardiac ICU, she was fully conscious but in cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Respiratory rate was 50 breaths/min with coarse crepitations over all lung zones and oxygen saturations of 85–88% on supplemental oxygen. She was tachycardic (sinus rhythm at 145 beats/min) with a blood pressure of 109/65 mmHg. Laboratory tests showed an INR of 1.3, APTT ratio 0.95, troponin I 4289 ng/L (normal <50), ALT 115 U/L (normal 0–40), CRP 67 mg/L, white blood cell count 28.2×10^9/L (neutrophils 25.4×10^9/L), hemoglobin 146 g/L, and platelets 233×10^9/L.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severely restricted excursion of the bileaflet aortic prosthesis with no obvious thrombus or vegetations, a peak transvalvular gradient of 128 mmHg, and a hyperdynamic, non-dilated but impaired left ventricle. Chest radiography showed bilateral pulmonary edema.

The differential diagnosis was thrombosis, pannus formation, or—least likely—infective endocarditis.
title: Acute obstruction of a mechanical aortic valve in a young woman: case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 43-year-old premenopausal G4P3 woman with no significant past medical history presented with acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain without vaginal discharge, bleeding, or systemic symptoms. Her serum hCG was negative. An abdominal CT scan revealed a 7×4×4 cm soft-tissue and fluid-containing structure with a 2.5 cm rim-calcified component, most likely representing the right ovary with a contained dermoid cyst. A pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a 6.5×3.0×4.5 cm lobulated solid mass, partially calcified (2.8 cm) and partially solid with color flow, located in the posterior cul-de-sac adjacent to but seemingly separate from the right ovary; etiology was thought to be para-ovarian versus bowel. Review of pelvic ultrasounds from 9 years earlier showed a 4.0×2.0×2.0 cm heterogeneous solid-appearing right adnexal mass with areas of increased echogenicity, felt to possibly represent a broad ligament fibroid. Laboratory studies revealed CA-125 10 U/mL, CEA 1.6 ng/mL, and CA 19-9 7 U/mL. The patient’s pain was controlled with NSAIDs, and she was referred to gynecologic oncology for surgical management.
final_diagnosis_raw: Female adnexal tumor of probable Wolffian origin
title: Female adnexal tumor of probable Wolffian Origin – A report of two cases at one institution

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old girl presented with a 4-day history of increasing difficulty swallowing solid foods and a painless globus sensation. She denied ingestion of caustic substances or foreign bodies. An ENT examination was unremarkable; she could swallow saliva and small amounts of water. A barium swallow study the next day was normal.

Two weeks later, her dysphagia persisted. She was limited to soft foods and liquids, with no weight loss or reflux. She described three choking episodes in the month before her first visit and anxiety about solids lodging in her throat. She denied additional trauma. Her history included mild anxiety and depression managed in outpatient psychiatry after self-harm one year earlier; she had no current psychiatric treatment. Repeat ENT examination was again normal; she declined fiberoptic endoscopy but agreed to evaluation by a speech and language pathologist (SLP).

Three weeks later, SLP assessment showed normal oral sensorimotor function, an EAT-10 score of 10/40 (normal <3), and a prolonged swallowing capacity of 150 ml water in 26.9 s (normal <15 s). A video fluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS) performed four weeks later was inconclusive: she could ingest only minute solid or semisolid pieces, and liquids were within normal limits but taken in very small sips.

At a pediatric clinic consultation, neurological, cardiac, ENT, and abdominal examinations were normal. Laboratory studies, including electrolytes, liver enzymes, blood count, thyroid function, vitamins, and celiac serology, were all within reference limits. She was referred for gastro-esophagoscopy with biopsy and psychological evaluation. Endoscopic biopsies of the esophagus were normal.
title: Swallowing difficulties in adolescents: A case report and suggestion of treatment model

case_prompt: A young woman presented to the emergency department with a several-week history of difficulty breathing and shortness of breath. She was ambulatory on arrival and was awake, alert, and oriented. Her past medical history included diabetes, anemia, hyperlipidemia, and asthma; surgical history was notable for endometrial ablation and multiple kidney biopsies. Medications included simvastatin, low-dose aspirin, lisinopril, metformin, and inhaled asthma therapies. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, chest auscultation, palpation, and percussion were unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed microcytic anemia and a mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia; other results were unremarkable. An initial chest radiograph showed two possible granulomas in the left lung base but was otherwise normal. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest demonstrated a 4.5 × 3.3-cm mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the right posterior mediastinum at the cardiophrenic angle, separate from the orthotopic liver; the radiology report suspected an enlarged lymph node or an esophageal mass.
title: Ectopic Hepatic Tissue Presented as a Posterior Mediastinal Mass

case_prompt: A 5-year-old boy was brought with a 40-day history of pain, swelling, and redness in both legs. He had been treated 30 days earlier elsewhere with a 10-day course of oral antibiotics for fever. He had no history of chronic illness or trauma. On examination, both legs showed swelling, erythema, warmth, and purulent discharge from the proximal tibiae. Vital signs were within normal limits except for mild tachycardia. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 15,640/mm3, C-reactive protein 5.29 μg/mL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 63 mm/h. Serologic tests for Brucella and Salmonella and purified protein derivative tests for tuberculosis, previously negative twice, were again negative; chest radiograph was normal. Radiographs of both tibiae showed cortical destruction and periosteal reaction at the proximal tibiae and distal left tibia. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated bone-marrow edema throughout both tibiae, purulent debris within the medullary canals and metaphyses, and adjacent pyomyositis. Radionuclide bone scanning revealed increased technetium uptake in the metaphyses of both tibiae.
title: Bilateral acute tibial osteomyelitis in a patient without an underlying disease: a case report

case_prompt: A 52-year-old woman with known unrepaired Type II tricuspid atresia with d-transposition of the great arteries, hypoplastic right ventricle, unrestricted atrial and ventricular septal defects, and multi-level pulmonic stenosis presented with sudden-onset severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or dysuria. Two months earlier, she had flu-like symptoms treated with doxycycline, and she reported poor dentition with no dental care for two years. On examination, her blood pressure was 90/54 mmHg, she was afebrile, heart rate was 80 bpm, and oxygen saturation was 79% on room air. A grade-2 systolic ejection murmur was heard at the left upper sternal border. She had cyanotic fingers bilaterally but no Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, or splinter hemorrhages. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 17.9 g/dL and C-reactive protein 2.2 mg/dL; lactate, white blood cell count, and creatinine were within reference ranges. Computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated an acute right renal infarct; cerebral computed tomography was negative. She was anticoagulated with heparin.
title: A case report of infective endocarditis in a 52-year-old female with unrepaired tricuspid atresia and d-transposition of the great arteries

case_prompt: A 44-year-old man was referred for evaluation of several weeks of constipation without abdominal pain or fever. He had a history of similar symptoms 10 years earlier with a normal colonoscopy at that time. His only medication was for hypertension. On examination, a hard, palpable mass with local warmth was noted in the lower left to mid‐abdomen. The white blood cell count was 6500/μL and C‐reactive protein was 2.7 mg/dL. Colonoscopy from another hospital showed significant edema of the sigmoid colon mucosa and narrowing of the lumen, preventing passage of the scope. Initial contrast‐enhanced CT demonstrated edematous thickening of the bowel wall from the splenic flexure to the rectum, a thin, cord‐like inferior mesenteric vein, and ectatic mesenteric venous branches, while the inferior mesenteric artery was patent. There were no arterial or venous thrombi, arteriosclerotic changes, or calcifications. Clinically, inflammatory bowel disease and eosinophilic enteritis were suspected, but an endoscopic biopsy showed only mildly inflamed mucosa without significant eosinophilic infiltration. The patient was managed conservatively. One month later, he developed lower abdominal pain for 1 week and self‐medicated with NSAIDs. On examination he had left lower‐quadrant tenderness with guarding and a temperature of 38.0°C. The white blood cell count rose to 18,600/μL and CRP to 20.5 mg/dL. CT angiography was performed to evaluate suspected vascular abnormalities.
final_diagnosis_raw: idiopathic myointimal hyperplasia of mesenteric veins
title: Idiopathic myointimal hyperplasia of mesenteric veins: radiological evaluation using CT angiography

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old Caucasian woman with hypertension and glaucoma presented with a three-month history of a productive cough and progressive dyspnea. She was initially treated for bronchitis with antibiotics and a methylprednisolone dose pack without improvement; allergy testing was negative. She denied fevers, chills, weight loss, chest pain, palpitations, hemoptysis, gastrointestinal symptoms, asthma, rash, arthritis, recreational drug use, bird exposure, or occupational exposures (silicon, beryllium, asbestos). Medications included timolol eye drops, losartan, and pantoprazole.

On examination, her blood pressure was 128/68 mm Hg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 98.8 °F, and oxygen saturation 84% on room air. Pulmonary exam revealed bibasilar rales; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood counts and chemistry panels. Blood cultures remained negative for 5 days; sputum cultures were negative for acid-fast bacilli, fungi, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Chest CT demonstrated a slight mosaic attenuation pattern suggestive of air trapping. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed ground-glass opacities and a mosaic pattern consistent with bronchial air trapping. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) showed 89% neutrophils, 8% lymphocytes, 2% monocytes, and 1% macrophages. Transbronchial biopsy revealed focal giant cell reaction without malignancy; the CD4:CD8 ratio was 2.8:1. Pulmonary function testing showed an FEV1 of 75% of predicted and a decreased DLCO, consistent with restrictive physiology.
title: Timolol-induced interstitial lung disease

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old girl presented with a 3-week history of bilateral mandibular swelling and morning purulent oral discharge. She was otherwise well, with stable vital signs. On examination, there was bilateral facial swelling in the mandibular region, multiple dark brown nevi on the palms and soles (unchanged in size for ≥5 years), and clinical macrocephaly. Intraorally, there was bilateral buccal cortical expansion in the posterior mandible with moderate pus discharge adjacent to tooth 36; teeth were firm and without paresthesia.

Orthopantomogram showed expansile radiolucent lesions in the mandible bilaterally, extending from the first molar region to the coronoid processes, with impacted second and third molars displaced into the coronoid areas and cortical thinning and erosion at multiple sites. A smaller radiolucent lesion with an impacted third molar was seen in the maxilla. 

Incisional biopsy from multiple sites revealed a parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelial lining, six to eight cell layers thick, with surface corrugation and basal cell palisading, and a moderately collagenous fibrous capsule. The mandibular lesions were initially marsupialized; three months later, enucleation specimens showed similar histology plus budding of basal epithelial cells, keratin-filled daughter cysts, odontogenic epithelial islands, and focal crowding with mild atypia of basal and parabasal layers.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head demonstrated calcifications within the falx cerebri. A chest radiograph was normal.
journal: Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology : JOMFP
title: Frameshift mutation in exon 17 of PTCH1 gene in Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome: A case report

case_prompt:
A 21-year-old woman presented with a 12-hour history of sharp, central chest pain that awoke her from sleep and worsened to 9/10 in severity. The pain was associated with brief dyspnea on minimal exertion and three witnessed syncopal episodes. Two weeks earlier she had a viral prodrome with generalized malaise and a 30-minute episode of similar chest discomfort that resolved spontaneously. Her past medical history was significant for clinically diagnosed Cutis Laxa since age 17. She had a family history of maternal diabetes and hypertension, was an active smoker (1 pack-year), and took no regular medications.

On examination, her heart rate was 52 beats per minute, blood pressure 101/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The physical examination was unremarkable. ECG showed sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. D-dimer was normal. Initial troponin T was mildly elevated at 17 ng/l (<14 ng/l), rising to 33 ng/l after 2 hours.

She underwent an ECG-gated CT angiogram of the aorta, which demonstrated no aortic dissection or central pulmonary embolus. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left and right ventricular systolic function without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Her chest pain resolved over 2 hours, and there were no ECG changes thereafter. She was admitted for observation on telemetry. On hospital day 2, repeat troponin T was significantly elevated at 731 ng/l, although she remained asymptomatic.
title: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection in cutis laxa

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old Caucasian woman, a non-smoker with no relevant drug history, presented during routine follow-up for bullous pemphigoid (in remission) with progressive, asymptomatic blackish pigmentation of both buccal mucosa. She also reported a 7-year history of brownish-black pigmentation of several fingernails. No family members were affected. 

On examination, there was a regular, brownish, reticular pattern on both sides of the buccal mucosa. Multiple longitudinal pigmented bands were present on her fingernails and toenails. Potassium hydroxide preparation and fungal cultures were negative. Digital dermoscopy of the nails showed a pseudo-Hutchinson’s sign, with homogeneous brownish and grayish longitudinal bands and lines with ill-defined margins on the nail plate.

Laboratory tests—including erythrocyte sedimentation rate; complete blood count with differential; urinalysis; lipid profile; renal and liver function tests; serum amylase, lipase, and lactate dehydrogenase; tumor markers (CEA, AFP, CA 19-9); and immunology parameters (antinuclear antibodies, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins)—were all within normal limits. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. Colonoscopy revealed no tumorous formations. Endocrinologic evaluation, including cortisol levels, antipituitary antibodies, and an ACTH stimulation test, was normal. The patient declined biopsy of the oral lesions.
title: Laugier-Hunziker syndrome - Case report*

case_prompt:
A 46‐year‐old woman with intractable complex partial seizures presented with increasing episodes of sudden falls over the past 2 years. She had been diagnosed with epilepsy at age 21 and, despite maximal antiepileptic drug therapy, continued to have monthly seizures. A left‐sided vagal nerve stimulator had been implanted in 2004, with a generator change in 2012; over the past 2 years, the output current had been gradually increased to control breakthrough seizures.  

Her new spells occurred randomly, without prodrome or postictal period, were not position related, and were not accompanied by urinary or bowel incontinence. She reported brief loss of consciousness and an average of two falls per month, resulting in injuries. This pattern differed from her prior episodes of blank staring and automatic behavior.  

On examination, vital signs were normal. Cardiopulmonary auscultation was unremarkable, and there were no signs of heart failure. Brain MRI showed left mesial temporal sclerosis and increased signal in the posterior right frontal region. Three prolonged EEG studies demonstrated spikes in the F7–T3 distribution, consistent with her known hemispheric epileptiform focus. A Ziopatch monitor disclosed no arrhythmias; ECG showed normal sinus rhythm; echocardiography and myocardial perfusion stress testing were unremarkable.  

The VNS settings were adjusted (decreased current strength and increased OFF time), but her spells persisted. A LINQ implantable loop recorder was placed, and on interrogation several sinus pauses of 10 to 12 seconds were documented. Review of her records showed that these pauses corresponded exactly to the times of her falls and injuries.
title: Late-onset asystolic episodes in a patient with a vagal nerve stimulator

case_prompt: A 15-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of a right lower limb deformity. He was born at term following induction; growth parameters were normal. On examination, the right foot had medial splaying and duplication of the hallux with mild anterolateral bowing of the right tibia. The left index finger had radial deviation. There were no café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, or other cutaneous stigmata of a neurocutaneous disorder. Initial radiographs of the right leg showed anterolateral bowing of the tibia, a medullary cyst, and duplication of the first ray; the fibula appeared straight. At 7 months of age, an MRI of the brain and right lower extremity was performed: the brain was normal; the right tibia showed midshaft cortical thinning with continuous anterior cortex and posterior callus formation without evidence of pseudarthrosis or medullary canal duplication; a supernumerary digit arising from the first cuneiform was noted.
final_diagnosis_raw: Congenital anterolateral tibial bowing and polydactyly
title: Congenital anterolateral tibial bowing and polydactyly: a case report

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism presented with two weeks of progressive temporal disorientation and unsteady gait. Her rheumatoid arthritis had been treated for 10 years with prednisolone (10 mg daily), leflunomide (20 mg daily), and weekly methotrexate (7.5 mg). Two months earlier, adalimumab (40 mg every two weeks) was added due to worsening joint pain and deformity.

On examination, she was afebrile. Neurologic assessment showed moderate left hemiparesis (Medical Research Council grade 3) without sensory deficits or cranial nerve abnormalities. Laboratory tests revealed a normal white-cell count (9100/µL) with neutrophilia (89%) and lymphopenia (7%), hyperglycemia (136 mg/dL), and an HbA1c of 6.9%. HIV testing was negative. Toxoplasma serology was IgG positive and IgM negative. Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph were unremarkable.

Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated a focal hypodense lesion in the right basal ganglia with surrounding edema and mild midline shift. Brain MRI showed a heterogeneous T2/FLAIR lesion with peripheral gadolinium enhancement and perfusion‐weighted imaging revealed decreased cerebral blood volume in the lesion.
title: Cerebral Toxoplasmosis as an Uncommon Complication of Biologic Therapy for Rheumatoid Arthritis: Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of severe, global headaches (10/10) that worsened over the past 2 years. Eighteen months ago, she developed polydipsia of approximately 15 L per day with matching polyuria, waking 10 times per night to urinate. She also reported secondary amenorrhea for 18 months, a weight loss of 10 kg over the past year, and intermittent epigastric discomfort. She denied trauma, surgery, radiation exposure, fever, cough, or osmotic diuretics. Menarche occurred at age 13. She had no personal or family history of diabetes mellitus or other endocrine disorders. Medications included occasional antacids and analgesics.

On examination, vital signs were normal; BMI was 16 kg/m2. Axillary and pubic hair were normal, and the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Initial labs: urine specific gravity 1.005; random urine osmolality 150 mOsm/kg. After overnight water deprivation, serum osmolality rose to 298 mOsm/kg while urine osmolality remained low at 210 mOsm/kg; urine output was 3 L over 8 h and urine specific gravity 1.006. Desmopressin challenge by IV was unavailable; however, on low-dose oral desmopressin, her urine specific gravity normalized to 1.020 and urine osmolality to 600 mOsm/kg.

Additional labs: βhCG 1.2 mIU/mL, AFP 7 ng/mL, IgG4 28 mg/dL, soluble IL-2 receptor 203 U/mL; anterior pituitary hormones (TSH, T3, T4, prolactin, cortisol) were within normal limits.

Brain MRI showed partial filling of the pituitary fossa by CSF with a flattened pituitary gland measuring 3.68 mm, consistent with a partial empty sella. There was no evidence of intracranial hypertension. Pelvic ultrasound was normal.
title: Arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) with partial empty sella: a case report

case_prompt: A 59-year-old man with no significant medical or surgical history presented with a 6-week history of an enlarging, painful mass on the dorsum of his right hand. Six weeks earlier, he had sustained a penetrating injury from a galvanized culvert, resulting in a small laceration. Despite antibiotic therapy for presumed Staphylococcus abscess, the lesion continued to enlarge. On examination, there was a 2.5 × 2.0 cm solid, mobile mass over the dorsal right hand. The lesion was nonpulsatile, nonfriable, nonfluctuant, not adherent to underlying structures, and appeared limited to the cutaneous and subcutaneous tissues. There was no surrounding erythema, no expressible drainage, and no palpable lymphadenopathy. A central area of keratinaceous-appearing material was noted. Radiographs of the hand were unremarkable, and routine laboratory values were within normal limits.
title: Post-traumatic keratoacanthoma of the hand: A case report

case_prompt: A 43-year-old Hispanic woman with a history of left-leg monoparesis from poliomyelitis, long-standing diabetes mellitus, hypertension requiring three agents, nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy, proteinuria, and osteoporosis was evaluated for suspected Cushing’s syndrome. She first underwent evaluation 13 and 5 years earlier, including inferior petrosal sinus catheterization, without localization of an ACTH source. Three years ago she presented with an 18-month history of polymenorrhea, and examination showed moon facies, buffalo hump, prominent supraclavicular fat, purple striae on arms and abdomen, truncal obesity, an umbilical hernia, and proximal muscle wasting. Laboratory evaluation revealed urinary free cortisol 186.5 μg/day, morning serum cortisol 21.8 μg/dL, midnight serum cortisol 16.1 μg/dL, serum cortisol after a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test 16.6 μg/dL, and plasma ACTH 32.6 pg/mL. An 8 mg high-dose dexamethasone suppression test showed cortisol suppression to 2.69 μg/dL (84.8%). Thyroid function was normal. Two pituitary MRIs were reported as normal. Abdominal CT revealed a 68 × 60 × 76 mm bilobed intra-abdominal mass protruding through the umbilicus, adjacent to a small-intestinal loop, with unenhanced attenuation of 3, 7, and 45 HU rising to 6, 16, and 88 HU postcontrast, raising the possibility of a mesothelioma. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed uterine fibroids but no ovarian masses. Exploratory laparotomy was planned.
title: Ectopic ACTH secretion (EAS) associated to a well-differentiated peritoneal mesothelioma: case report

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old right-handed woman was evaluated for recurrent seizures that began in early 2014. The initial events were dyscognitive and progressed to secondary generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Some weeks before the first seizure, she developed subacute bifrontal headaches and noted progressive short-term memory impairment. In May 2015, her husband observed a transient personality change with disinhibited behavior, which did not recur. 

Her medical history was notable for Crohn’s disease diagnosed in 2006 by ileocolonoscopy, treated with steroids and mesalazine until 2008, then methotrexate (15 mg weekly) through 2016, with no gastrointestinal symptoms since 2013. She smoked 25 pack-years and had no other comorbidities, family history of neurological disease, or exposures. 

In early 2014, a transient dyscognitive event was interpreted as a transient ischemic attack, and a head CT excluded hemorrhage. By August 2014, after a secondarily generalized seizure, MRI showed multiple supratentorial Gd-enhancing cortical lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed pleocytosis (14 cells/μl) with negative oligoclonal bands. Bronchoalveolar lavage and chest CT were normal. Laboratory studies showed normal levels of IL-2 receptor, ACE, neopterin, calcium, ANCA, ANA, and antiphospholipid antibodies; an interferon-gamma release assay was negative.

Two months later, MRI demonstrated progression of cortical lesions. Methotrexate was supplemented with prednisolone, leading to stable lesion load on MRI in February 2015. Seizures recurred intermittently without changes in therapy. In August 2016, MRI revealed increased bihemispheric cortical and deep gray matter hemorrhagic lesions, gadolinium enhancement in multiple cortical and limbic regions, and bilateral hippocampal atrophy with hyperintensity. Repeat CSF showed pleocytosis (8 cells/μl), elevated protein, and now positive oligoclonal bands. Extensive serologic and CSF testing for neural autoantibodies (including paraneoplastic and autoimmune encephalitis panels) was negative. Complement levels, rheumatoid factor, and immunoglobulins were normal. Neuropsychological testing showed depressive symptoms with attentional, executive, and memory deficits.

In September 2016, further evaluation included CSF testing for Borrelia burgdorferi, Treponema pallidum, PCR for HSV-1/2, VZV, Tropheryma whipplei, and HIV (all negative). Ultrasonography of extra- and intracranial arteries showed no large-vessel vasculitis. Sarcoidosis biomarkers, PR3-ANCA, p-ANCA, and blood cultures were negative. Fluorescein angiography of the retina excluded small-vessel vasculitis or Susac’s syndrome. Given the progressive cortical lesions and nondiagnostic noninvasive workup, a stereotactic brain biopsy was planned.
title: Cerebral granulomatosis as a manifestation of Crohn’s disease

case_prompt: A 73-year-old woman with a history of poorly differentiated caecal adenocarcinoma (T4N2M0) treated by right hemicolectomy, incomplete adjuvant chemotherapy, and radiotherapy to para-aortic lymph nodes, presented three years after radiotherapy with a rapidly enlarging, painless, left-sided neck lump. She had no dysphagia, odynophagia, dysphonia, weight loss, or appetite change. On examination, there was a smooth, nonfluctuant, non-tethered 6-mm level IV lymph node. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function, were normal; carcinoembryonic antigen was elevated at 24.0 mg/L (normal <2.5 mg/L). Ultrasound of the lump showed a 6-mm level IV cervical lymph node with intranodal calcifications, loss of hilar architecture, and increased vascularity. Fine-needle aspiration cytology demonstrated clusters of atypical cells with pleomorphic nuclei and moderate cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical analysis of the cell block preparation showed cells positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3 and CDX2. Whole-body PET-CT revealed elevated tracer uptake in an 8.4-mm left level IV node and a 7-mm left supraclavicular node, with no further evidence of thoracic or abdominal disease.
title: Case Report: Colorectal cancer metastasis to a cervical lymph node – an unusual source of a neck lump

case_prompt: A 54‐year‐old Hispanic woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and peripheral vascular disease presented with a 3‐day history of severe watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and altered mental status. Her medications included metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril, metoprolol, pravastatin, aspirin, hydrochlorothiazide, and nightly insulin detemir; she had not administered her prandial insulin for the preceding 24 hours due to poor oral intake. In the emergency department, her serum glucose was 47 mg/dL, for which glucagon was administered. She was hypotensive (70/39 mmHg), confused, and disoriented, with dry mucous membranes and decreased bowel sounds. Shortly after arrival, she became unresponsive and developed pulseless electrical activity; return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after 3 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation, including intubation and mechanical ventilation. In the intensive care unit, her blood pressure was 98/37 mmHg on norepinephrine (0.3 µg/kg/min). Laboratory studies showed arterial pH 6.57, serum bicarbonate 2 mEq/L, anion gap 30 mmol/L, osmolar gap 21 mOsm/kg, lactate 16.3 mmol/L, hemoglobin A1c 7.3%, and creatinine 8.07 mg/dL (baseline 0.86 mg/dL two months earlier). A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed only nonspecific gallbladder wall thickening. Vasopressin was added to maintain a mean arterial pressure above 60 mmHg.
title: Metformin-Associated Lactic Acidosis: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue, treated 16 months earlier with hemi-glossectomy and chemoradiation, presented with a 1-month history of progressively worsening severe, sharp, constant right shoulder and chest pain, associated with right arm numbness, productive cough, and dyspnoea on exertion. The pain was exacerbated by right arm movement. She denied trauma or travel.

Her medications included pembrolizumab and recent head and neck radiation. She had a 1.5-year smoking history (0.5 pack per day), social alcohol use, and no significant family history of cancer aside from a grandmother with brain cancer.

On examination, she appeared frail with weight loss. Vital signs: heart rate 86 bpm; blood pressure 121/74 mm Hg. Pulmonary auscultation revealed coarse rales and rhonchi in the left lower lung field. Cardiac examination showed a regular rhythm without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. She had tender right supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and swelling with erythema over the right suprascapular area.

Laboratory studies showed haemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, haematocrit 28.8%, total calcium 10.5 mg/dL, ionized calcium 1.51 mmol/L. Admission ECG demonstrated ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads and T-wave inversions in the anterolateral leads. Troponin I peaked at 0.29 ng/L (normal <0.05 ng/L). Chest radiograph revealed a left lower lobe infiltrate, progression of a known left upper lobe cavitary lesion, and a new right clavicular lesion.

Differential diagnosis at this point included acute coronary syndrome, myocarditis due to pembrolizumab, and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy in a cancer patient.
title: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to the heart: an unusual cause of ST elevation—a case report

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressively enlarging bilateral parotid gland swellings, dryness of the mouth and eyes, and a dry cough. She reported a transient enlargement of her bilateral submandibular glands that resolved spontaneously. She denied fever, sputum production, or known exposure to tuberculosis; however, she noted decreased appetite and weight loss. 

Two months earlier, a chest radiograph had shown bilateral hilar prominences. A fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the parotid swellings performed at that time was inconclusive, and polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacterium tuberculosis on the parotid aspirate was negative.

On examination, both parotid glands were diffusely enlarged without palpable lymphadenopathy. Repeat FNAC of the parotid glands revealed smears containing noncaseating epithelioid granulomas and multinucleated giant cells against a background of lymphoid cells and salivary ductal and acinar cells. A few giant cells contained refractile crystalline structures. There was no evidence of caseous necrosis, and an acid-fast bacillus stain was negative.
journal: Journal of Cytology / Indian Academy of Cytologists
title: Bilaterally enlarged parotids and sicca symptoms as a presentation of sarcoidosis: Pivotal role of aspiration cytology in diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 41-day-old female infant was referred for evaluation of recurrent electrolyte disturbances. She was born at 37 weeks’ gestation to consanguineous parents by uncomplicated vaginal delivery (birth weight 3 kg). At 6 days of age, she developed poor feeding, lethargy, and frequent vomiting. In the emergency department, she was severely dehydrated with an arterial pH of 7.20, serum bicarbonate 11 mmol/L, serum potassium 10 mmol/L, and serum sodium 119 mmol/L. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was required, and she was intubated. Initial hormonal studies were obtained, and she received hydrocortisone (stress dose), a fluid bolus, sodium bicarbonate, and measures to lower potassium. She was admitted to the neonatal ICU, tested negative for sepsis and metabolic disorders, and was discharged on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone without sodium supplementation.  

At 20 days of age, she was readmitted with recurrent vomiting, poor feeding, and lethargy, again with hyperkalemia and hyponatremia. Treatment included hydrocortisone, fluid resuscitation, sodium bicarbonate, potassium‐lowering measures, and emergency peritoneal dialysis.  

Upon transfer at 41 days, she was alert, well hydrated, with normal female genitalia and no dysmorphism. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 5 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 23 mmol/L; urinalysis and urine culture were normal. Fluorescence in situ hybridization was negative for SRY, and karyotype was 46,XX. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography were normal. Repeat hormonal studies were inconsistent with congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and she did not respond adequately to corticosteroids, requiring ongoing mineralocorticoid therapy.
journal: Journal of Clinical Research in Pediatric Endocrinology
title: A Novel SCNN1A Variation in a Patient with Autosomal-recessive Pseudohypoaldosteronism Type 1

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old boy with mixed gonadal dysgenesis and a two-stage proximal hypospadias repair as an infant presented with 2 days of lower abdominal pain and dysuria. He had occasional vomiting, loose stools, and had had a fever 1 day earlier. In the ED, he was afebrile, with mild lower abdominal distension and suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis showed turbid urine with too numerous to count white blood cells; a urine culture was sent. He was discharged on oral cephalexin for presumed UTI.

He returned 2 days later with persistent end-of-void suprapubic and right lower quadrant pain, dysuria, urgency, frequency, and foul-smelling urine. He denied fevers or chills; diarrhea had resolved. He reported decreased appetite and small, clumped stools but denied chronic constipation. His mother noted a small amount of urethral discharge. On exam, he was afebrile, with lower abdominal tenderness; genitourinary exam revealed a circumcised penis, an absent left testis, and a mildly tender right testis with normal lie and reflexes. Repeat urinalysis again showed too numerous to count white blood cells, though the previous urine culture had no growth. Peripheral white count was normal and CRP was 20 mg/dL.

Scrotal ultrasound showed a normal right testicle with normal flow. Abdominal ultrasound did not fully visualize the appendix and showed no secondary signs of appendicitis. Retroperitoneal ultrasound revealed normal kidneys and bladder but reported “circumferential wall thickening of the rectum with an air-fluid level.” The differential diagnosis included UTI, appendicitis, scrotal pathology, severe constipation, or gastroenteritis.
title: An Enlarged and Infected Prostatic Utricle as a Rare Cause of Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms in Adolescent Males

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old man presented with a one-month history of worsening nasal bridge pain and intermittent fever. A primary care physician prescribed oral faropenem for presumed infection without improvement. His medical history included a childhood small intestinal obstruction requiring surgery. 

On examination, he was in moderate distress. Vital signs were: temperature 36.4°C; blood pressure 112/60 mmHg; heart rate 64 beats/min; respiratory rate 14 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He had tenderness over the nasal bridge without external deformity. 

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 15 500/μL, hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 53 U/L, C-reactive protein 16.4 mg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 70 mm/h. Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses revealed thickening of the left frontal sinus mucosa. A tentative diagnosis of acute sinusitis was made, and he received oral amoxicillin–clavulanate for 10 days without improvement.
