His nasal pain worsened, and he was admitted for further evaluation. After admission, he developed generalized joint pain and severe diarrhea. Repeat sinus CT showed resolving mucosal thickening but edema and inflammation of the nasal septum and adjacent cartilage, findings that were confirmed on contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging. All serological tests, including rheumatoid factor and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, were negative.
title: Early Stage Relapsing Polychondritis Diagnosed by Nasal Septum Biopsy

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman with a 27-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus and secondary antiphospholipid syndrome presented with painful, non-healing ulcers. Her initial lupus manifestations included recurrent pneumonitis, malar rash, and biopsy-proven lupus nephritis. She had recurrent deep venous thromboses at diagnosis, was positive for lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 3 months apart, and was anticoagulated with warfarin targeting an INR of 2.0–3.0. Additional thrombophilia testing (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C/S, antithrombin III) was negative.

Her comorbidities included obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, stage 3B chronic kidney disease, and previous endometrial cancer in remission. Medications were warfarin, hydroxychloroquine, atenolol, and analgesics.

Two months before admission, she noted small bruises at sites of abdominal ultrasound probe pressure, which progressed to ulcerative lesions on the anterior abdominal wall. Wound swab grew multidrug-resistant Enterobacter cloacae, and she was treated with ciprofloxacin and wound dressings. Her INR was 2.5 on admission, and over the prior 8 months had ranged between 2.3 and 3.6. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable and had five ulcers on the anterior abdominal wall; the largest had irregular margins, surrounding erythema, and a clean base.

She was discharged on antibiotics and warfarin. Eleven days later, she returned with worsening pain and non-healing ulcers. Examination showed progression of the largest abdominal ulcer (11 × 7 cm) with black eschar and yellow exudate, plus new ulcers on the left breast and interscapular area. Wound cultures grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococci; blood cultures were sterile. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis, rising CRP, stable renal function, and mild worsening of anemia. Serologies were positive for lupus anticoagulant but negative for cardiolipin IgG, anti–β2-glycoprotein I, cryoglobulins, ANA, ENA, and ANCA; complement levels were mildly elevated. 

A skin biopsy from an abdominal ulcer showed ischemia and necrosis of subcutaneous fat, granulation tissue in the dermis, and thrombo-occlusive material but no evidence of vasculitis or calciphylaxis. A second biopsy revealed numerous microthrombi in small subcutaneous vessels and a recanalizing thrombus in a medium-sized vein, with no vasculitis.
title: Extensive abdominal wall ulceration as a late manifestation of antiphospholipid syndrome: a case report

case_prompt: A 54-year-old woman presented in 2023 after discovering a firm, movable, nontender mass in her right breast. She had no systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or dyspnea. She underwent breast-conserving surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy; pathology showed invasive carcinoma, ER 5%, PR negative, HER2 0+, Ki-67 45%, pT2N0M0, with a close margin (<1 mm at 3–6 o’clock). She received one cycle of docetaxel and then, at our institution, five cycles of docetaxel (120 mg/m2 q3w) plus cyclophosphamide (600 mg/m2 q3w) and pembrolizumab (200 mg q3w). After the fifth cycle, she noted numbness in her hands and edema of her lower limbs, followed by swelling and fibrotic changes of the skin on both lower extremities. On examination, there was bilateral leg skin induration without sclerodactyly, Raynaud’s phenomenon, or dysphagia. Laboratory testing revealed negative antinuclear antibodies. A skin biopsy of the lower leg demonstrated perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and thickened collagen bundles.
title: Scleroderma-like Lesions in a Patient Undergoing Combined Pembrolizumab and Routine Chemotherapy: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman presented with a history since February 2008 of painful left axillary lymphadenopathy accompanied by low-grade fever. Initial excisional biopsy showed changes suggestive but not diagnostic of Castleman’s disease. A CT scan revealed an 8×6 cm colliquative mass in the left axillary and supraclavicular regions, smaller reactive nodes in the right axilla and inguinal areas, and subcentimeter nodules in the lung and liver. Repeat lymph node biopsies through 2010 demonstrated nonspecific necrotizing lymphadenitis; microbiologic and virologic studies, including HHV-6 and HHV-8, were negative. A subsequent CT scan confirmed persistent axillary and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, bilateral inguinal enlargement, and a perianal mass. Review of prior histology noted necrotizing lymphadenitis with epithelioid and giant cells and vasculitis without lymphoproliferation.  

In January 2011, rheumatologic evaluation revealed nasal chondritis with crusted lesions, chronic conjunctivitis, violaceous purpuric areas on the extremities, ulcerative palmar and gluteal lesions, and persistent evening fevers. Examination showed mobile, nontender axillary and inguinal nodes. Nasal mucosal biopsy demonstrated acute and chronic inflammation but no vasculitis or granulomas. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis and elevated acute-phase reactants. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, whereas IgG and IgM anti–β2-glycoprotein I and anticardiolipin antibodies were positive. Cytomegalovirus IgM and Epstein–Barr virus IgM were detected, but antigenemia was negative and PCR non-significant. Bartonella henselae serology returned a titer of 1:128.
title: Beyond Cat Scratch Disease: A Case Report of Bartonella Infection Mimicking Vasculitic Disorder

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old man presented 4 weeks after coronary artery bypass grafting to the left anterior descending and posterior descending arteries and bioprosthetic aortic-valve replacement, with a 1-week history of dyspnoea on exertion, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and progressive oedema. His medical history included multivessel coronary artery disease, severe aortic stenosis (status post-AVR), paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and hypercholesterolaemia. He had no prior pericardial or myocardial disease, autoimmune conditions, or history of arrhythmia symptoms.

On examination, he was euvolaemic except for pitting oedema extending to the abdomen, jugular venous pressure markedly elevated with a positive Kussmaul’s sign, and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases. Heart sounds were dual without murmurs.

Laboratory studies showed an N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide level of 3034 ng/L (normal < 126 ng/L). A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions without pericardial calcification. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm without ischaemic changes or low-voltage QRS complexes.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal chamber sizes, preserved left ventricular systolic function, and normal prosthetic valve function without regional wall-motion abnormalities. A bright, thickened pericardium and a small pericardial effusion were noted. The inferior vena cava was dilated without respirophasic collapse. Respirophasic septal motion (“septal bounce”) indicating ventricular interdependence was observed. Mitral inflow velocity varied by > 25% with respiration, and tricuspid inflow velocity varied by > 40%.
title: Early-onset post-cardiotomy severe constrictive pericarditis: a case report

case_prompt: A 46-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 1-month history of worsening dry cough and slight loss of appetite without weight loss. She had no significant medical or family history, was a non-smoker, and drank alcohol socially. On examination, vital signs were normal, lung and heart auscultation were unremarkable, there was no peripheral lymphadenopathy or skin lesions, and neurologic findings were non-specific. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed bilateral anterior uveitis. Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 5300/µL, hemoglobin 14.7 g/dL, platelets 201 000/µL, C-reactive protein 0.76 mg/dL, serum calcium 9.7 mg/dL, angiotensin-converting enzyme 35.1 U/L (elevated), soluble interleukin-2 receptor 1693 U/mL (elevated), and normal antinuclear antibody. Urinalysis was normal. Blood and sputum cultures were negative. A Mycobacterium tuberculosis–specific interferon-γ release assay was negative, but serum anti-glycopeptidolipid core immunoglobulin A antibody for MAC was positive. Tests for Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, beta-D-glucan, Cryptococcus antigen, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, and HIV were all negative or within normal limits. Chest radiography showed upper mediastinal widening. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT demonstrated enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes with low-density areas and hepatosplenomegaly. Bronchoscopy revealed edematous bronchial mucosa, but endobronchial ultrasound‐guided needle aspiration yielded insufficient tissue. A surgical biopsy of a mediastinal lymph node was performed. Histology showed epithelioid cell granulomas with marked necrosis. Ziehl–Neelsen staining and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and MAC on the biopsy specimen were negative.
title: Sarcoidosis with marked necrosis in enlarged lymph nodes mimics mycobacterial infection: a case report

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old African American woman presented with 3 days of progressive abdominal and pelvic pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Two months earlier, she had been hospitalized for possible rheumatic fever with polyserositis and cardiac tamponade requiring pericardial drainage. Medications included colchicine, lisinopril, proton-pump inhibitors, ranitidine, tramadol, penicillin G, and albuterol; she had recently quit smoking. Family history was significant for hypertension.

On examination, she was tachycardic (112 beats/min) with a 2/6 systolic murmur. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (41×10^9/L), hemoglobin 107 g/L, hypoalbuminemia (28 g/L), and serum creatinine 53 µmol/L. Urinalysis revealed 1+ protein. Abdominal CT demonstrated colitis and mild ascites. A presumptive diagnosis of sepsis related to Clostridium difficile colitis was made, and she received IV metronidazole, oral vancomycin, and IV fluids.

Four days later, serum creatinine rose to 159 µmol/L, leukocyte count to 60×10^9/L, and platelet count fell to 71×10^9/L; hemoglobin remained stable. She was evaluated for possible acute tubular necrosis and vasculitis. A peripheral smear then showed schistocytes and LDH was elevated at 3.69 µkat/L. A diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) was presumed, and she was started on high-dose steroids and daily plasma exchange. Dialysis and mycophenolate mofetil were also initiated. She subsequently developed seizures treated with levetiracetam.

Shortly thereafter, she reported vision loss. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed bilateral disc, macular, and retinal hemorrhages, central retinal artery and vein occlusion, and vitreous hemorrhage with a best-corrected visual acuity of 1–2 feet. Outpatient dialysis and plasma exchange were continued three times weekly without improvement. On September 2, her ADAMTS13 activity was found to be 61%.
title: Case report of atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome with retinal arterial and venous occlusion treated with eculizumab

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old girl with congenital intellectual disability and blindness presents with primary amenorrhea and a 2-year history of cyclical lower abdominal and pelvic pain lasting 5 days each month. The pain has worsened over the past 2 months and is partially relieved by oral analgesics. She exhibits irritability, reduced attention span, impaired perceptual reasoning, and limited functional independence. A sister has a similar clinical profile.

Vital signs: blood pressure 100/60 mmHg; pulse 96/min; respiratory rate 18/min. Examination shows pallor, moon face, submental fat, height 151 cm, weight 85 kg (BMI 37.2). Post-axial polydactyly is present on the left hand. Tanner stage 5 secondary sexual characteristics. Genital exam reveals vaginal atresia, a rudimentary uterus, and a transverse vaginal septum. Ophthalmologic exam shows astigmatism, strabismus, and on funduscopy numerous whitish-yellow equatorial spots, optic nerve pallor, retinal vessel constriction, and macular degeneration.

Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography demonstrates a 13.9-cm cystic structure posterior to the bladder within the vaginal canal, communicating with a small amount of fluid in the endometrial cavity. MRI confirms hematometrocolpos with moderate bilateral hydrosalpinx. Laboratory studies reveal normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL); renal, hepatic, metabolic profiles, and electrolytes are normal.
title: Primary Amenorrhea in a 15‐Year‐Old Girl Leading to the Diagnosis of Bardet‐Biedl Syndrome: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 51-year-old woman with Crohn’s disease on infliximab presented with a 2-day history of a bullous rash on her left arm, axilla, and lateral chest wall accompanied by subjective fever. Two days before presentation, she received her second dose of the recombinant adjuvant Shingrix vaccine. She denied new medications or topical products and had no prior similar rashes. Her Crohn’s disease was at baseline with intermittent loose stools. On examination, there was diffuse erythema and swelling from the midchest to the axilla and upper arm, with multiple bullae, some with central dusky areas; mucosal surfaces were spared. She was referred to dermatology and underwent punch biopsy; PCR testing of a bulla for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 and varicella zoster virus was negative.
title: Bullous fixed drug eruption following administration of the recombinant adjuvant Shingrix vaccine

case_prompt:
A 50‐year‐old woman on maintenance hemodialysis for end‐stage renal disease (initiated in 1987) presented during routine dialysis with several months of pruritus and productive cough. Her history was notable for hypertension and prior parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism; she remained dialysis‐dependent. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. Skin turgor was normal without rash or ecchymoses. There was no jugular venous distention, lymphadenopathy, or palpable neck masses. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral rales without wheezing.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, creatinine 8.4 mg/dL (0.5–0.9), parathyroid hormone 1891 pg/mL (10–69), and calcium 10.3 mg/dL (8.6–10.2). Thyroid‐function tests (TSH, free T4) and thyroglobulin were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph revealed bilateral pulmonary opacities. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated multiple well‐defined nodules in both lungs, the largest measuring 1.35 cm. A 99mTc‐MIBI scan showed dominant uptake in the pulmonary lesions. Neck ultrasound identified a multinodular goiter but no discrete parathyroid glands, and CT of the neck failed to localize any parathyroid tissue.

What is your differential diagnosis?
title: Hyperparathyroidism presented as multiple pulmonary nodules in hemodialysis patient status post parathyroidectomy: A case report

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old man with hypertension underwent aortic valve replacement for severe aortic regurgitation. After induction and placement of a transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) probe, initial TEE confirmed severe aortic regurgitation with holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta. Measurements in the midesophageal aortic-valve long-axis view showed an aortic root diameter of 3.0 cm, a sinus of Valsalva diameter of 4.0 cm, and a sinotubular junction diameter of 2.7 cm. The eccentric regurgitant jet had a vena contracta of 5.3 mm. Left ventricular ejection fraction was 39%, with only trivial mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. A patent foramen ovale was identified and closed before cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB).

A 23 mm stented bovine pericardial valve was implanted supra-annularly using a non-everting mattress suture technique with pledgets. The patient was weaned from CPB on low-dose dopamine and dobutamine. Post-bypass TEE in the midesophageal long-axis view showed a well-seated prosthesis with good leaflet mobility, but color-flow Doppler revealed a perpendicular turbulent jet originating from between the stent post and the sewing ring. In the midesophageal short-axis view, there was a considerable flow convergence adjacent to the stent post originating from outside the sewing ring. Further color-flow Doppler demonstrated a second turbulent jet arising from outside the sewing ring, running perpendicularly below the ring toward the left ventricular outflow tract. These findings suggested that both transvalvular and paravalvular leakage existed in close proximity.
title: Perpendicular and turbulent flow after aortic valve replacement: paravalvular or transvalvular leakage? – a case report

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman presented 2 weeks after cesarean section with a 2-week history of cough, dyspnea, and head and neck swelling. Symptoms had begun in pregnancy and worsened over the last few days. The cough was nonproductive, with no hemoptysis. She had no history of cardiac or pulmonary disease or risk factors such as alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drugs.

On examination, heart rate was 110/min, blood pressure 110/75 mmHg, and she was afebrile. There was slight respiratory discomfort but no cyanosis. Lung fields were clear; heart sounds revealed wide fixed splitting of S2 without murmur. There was no clinical evidence of right heart failure.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a severely dilated right atrium and right ventricle, a nonmobile 6.5 cm² mass attached to the right atrial wall, and a secundum-type atrial septal defect measuring 2.44 cm with a left-to-right shunt (QP/QS 2.9). A large extracardiac mass (8.7 × 4.3 cm) anterior to the ascending aorta was also noted.

Chest CT and pulmonary CT angiography demonstrated a lobulated anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass (105 × 46 mm), suggestive of thymoma, teratoma, thyroid goiter, lymphoma, or germ cell tumor, with extension of thrombosis into the brachiocephalic veins, superior vena cava (SVC), and right atrium, as well as multiple pulmonary nodules. Abdominal and pelvic CT were unremarkable. Serum alpha-fetoprotein was 5000 ng/mL; blood cultures were negative.

At this point, by considering the findings of physical and laboratory examinations, echocardiography, thoracic CT scan, and pulmonary CT angiography, a mediastinal malignancy with cardiac and lung metastasis was at the top of our differential diagnoses. Atrial thrombosis was another potential diagnosis due to the hypercoagulable state because of the post‐partum period and the mediastinal probable malignancy. On the other hand, the absence of fever, negative blood culture, and no history of IV drug abuse made endocarditis vegetation a less likely diagnosis.
title: Metastatic right atrial mass in the presence of atrial septal defect: A rare clinical coincidence

case_prompt: A 67-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer treated three years earlier presented with progressive perioral numbness and dizziness of 16 days’ duration. She was initially treated as an outpatient for presumed vertebrobasilar stroke with carbasalate calcium. On admission, MRI of the brain showed intact cerebral vasculature but diffuse fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense lesions around the fourth ventricle extending into the pons and medulla oblongata. A lumbar puncture revealed 240 cells/μL (30% lymphocytes) and a CSF glucose of 3.7 mmol/L; blood and CSF cultures were negative. Empiric acyclovir and dipyridamole were started for presumed herpes encephalitis with secondary vasculitis, but the patient deteriorated. A second CSF sample showed 102 cells/μL (96% lymphocytes) and a glucose of 3.2 mmol/L. Initial Borrelia serology was negative, but on day 15 IgG seroconversion (negative IgM) combined with a recent tick bite led to a presumptive diagnosis of Lyme disease; ceftriaxone and dexamethasone were administered. Four days later the patient developed spiking fever, complete left hemiparesis, and cranial-nerve palsies. Three weeks after admission she was transferred to our center. On arrival she was somnolent (GCS 14), febrile (40.2 °C), hypertensive (167/70 mmHg), tachycardic (100/min), and tachypneic (25/min), with a full left-sided hemiparesis. Rapid deterioration necessitated ICU transfer and intubation (GCS 7). A repeat CSF sample showed 23 cells/μL and a glucose of 3.4 mmol/L.
title: A case report of iatrogenic deterioration of yet undiagnosed Rhombencephalitis; always be careful with corticoids

case_prompt: A 22-month-old Caucasian girl presented with low-grade fever, cough, decreased activity, poor oral intake, and bilateral jaw-line swelling. She was born at term without complications; her maternal aunt had autoimmune disease. Vaccinations were incomplete (no MMR, varicella, or fourth DTaP). History included recurrent otitis media (with tubes) and eczema. Initial tests showed positive mumps IgM; elevated IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE, and IgG subclasses; positive rhinovirus and enterovirus; negative CMV, HIV, and hepatitis panels. She was leukopenic with cold-agglutinin autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Exam revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly and small mobile cervical nodes. EBV serologies indicated acute infection, with plasma EBV load 9 000–20 600 copies/μL. Flow cytometry showed reduced B, T, and NK cells. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics and symptomatic improvement, chest radiography and CT demonstrated persistent bilateral perihilar and right middle lobe infiltrates. One month later, she was readmitted with febrile neutropenia, rash, elevated soluble IL-2, but did not meet five of eight HLH criteria. Lymphocyte proliferation studies showed poor response to PHA but normal response to pokeweed mitogen.
title: Pediatric Pulmonary Epstein-Barr Virus-Positive Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman with a >20-year history of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus complicated by dialysis-dependent renal failure, retinopathy, and neuropathy presented with sudden onset of left thigh swelling and constant severe pain for 7 days. She denied trauma, vascular interventions, fever, or weight loss. Her medical history included coronary artery disease, stroke, hypertension, and mild cirrhosis from hepatitis C.

On examination, the left thigh was erythematous, edematous, and tender on the medial aspect, with a circumference 9 cm greater than the right. The overlying skin was otherwise normal, and she was afebrile. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 11 000/μL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/h, a C-reactive protein level of 1.3 mg/dL, and a creatine phosphokinase level of 338 U/L.

Plain radiography of the thigh showed no gas or calcification. Lower-extremity arterial and venous Doppler studies showed no vascular occlusion, and blood cultures were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the left thigh demonstrated diffuse fat stranding and a heterogeneous appearance of the vastus medialis muscle. An MRI with gadolinium contrast was then obtained after hemodialysis; T2-weighted images revealed an irregular, enhancing 20 × 5 cm lesion with surrounding edema in the medial vastus medialis, containing areas of muscle breakdown. Imaging alone could not exclude a soft-tissue sarcoma, and a biopsy was planned.
journal: Journal of Community Hospital Internal Medicine Perspectives
title: Diabetic myonecrosis: a diagnostic challenge in patients with long-standing diabetes

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old previously healthy man presented with four days of progressive weakness of all four limbs, dysphagia, drooling, nausea, and vomiting. One month earlier, he had received the first dose of an inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. In the days after vaccination he developed lethargy and intermittent myalgia with partial improvement. He had no recent infection, no known COVID-19 exposures, and a negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR. 

On examination, temperature was 37.0 °C, heart rate 88 bpm, blood pressure 115/80 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20 /min. He was alert and oriented. Cranial-nerve examination showed bilateral facial paralysis; pupils were 3 mm and reactive bilaterally. There was no sensory level. Muscle strength was 2/5 in all four limbs, reflexes were preserved, and plantar responses were extensor. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, WBC 11,600/µL, platelets 305,000/mm3, PT 17.5 s, PTT 37.2 s, INR 1.27, ESR 23 mm/hr, negative CRP, and normal chemistry. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 2 WBCs, 32 RBCs, protein 56 mg/dL, glucose 97 mg/dL (serum glucose 159 mg/dL), and no oligoclonal bands. Chest radiography and ECG were unremarkable.

On hospital day 2, brain MRI revealed poorly marginated T2-FLAIR hyperintense foci in the left cerebral peduncle, bilateral pons, and medulla with slight T1 hypointensity and faint contrast enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed restricted diffusion in the pons. MR spectroscopy showed elevated choline and myoinositol peaks. Cervical spine MRI was normal.
title: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) after SARS- CoV-2 vaccination: A case report☆

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, pleuritic chest pain, abdominal distension, and peripheral edema. One year earlier, coronary angiography for chest pain was normal. Six months before admission, thoracentesis revealed a lymphocyte-predominant exudative right pleural effusion; cytology was nondiagnostic, and pleural biopsy was nondiagnostic.

Over the past 10 days, he noted worsening abdominal distension and pain. On examination, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 78/min, jugular venous pressure was markedly elevated, and heart sounds were muffled. Right lung base breath sounds were diminished. Abdominal examination showed mild hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema.

Laboratory tests were within normal limits. Analysis of ascitic fluid demonstrated protein 4.1 g/dL and serum–ascites albumin gradient 1.6 g/dL. Abdominal ultrasound showed congestive hepatomegaly, mild splenomegaly, ascites, and signs of portal hypertension; upper endoscopy revealed no esophageal varices, and viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Chest and abdominal CT demonstrated right pleural effusion, pericardial thickening with calcification, ascites, and inferior vena cava dilation.
title: Chronic Constrictive Pericarditis

case_prompt: A 71-year-old man with coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout, and benign prostatic hyperplasia was transferred from a long-term acute care facility with a 2-day history of right wrist and hand pain, tenderness, and swelling. Eighteen days earlier, he was admitted for COVID-19 pneumonia with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring high-flow nasal cannula and bilevel positive-pressure ventilation. During a 16-day ICU stay at the referring hospital, he underwent frequent arterial blood gas sampling from both radial arteries, multiple venous blood draws, and peripheral IV placements but never had an indwelling arterial line. He reported fatigue, shortness of breath, generalized weakness, and easy bruising and bleeding. His medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, carvedilol, lisinopril, sublingual nitroglycerin as needed, and therapeutic enoxaparin 90 mg subcutaneously twice daily. On admission, his temperature was 96.7°F, blood pressure 158/70 mm Hg, heart rate 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on 10 L nasal cannula. Examination revealed diffuse bilateral inspiratory crackles, anasarca, and mild tenderness and swelling of the right wrist and hand with bruising on the volar wrist. Radial and ulnar pulses were palpable; sensation and motor strength were intact; the right fingers felt cool. Electrolytes and renal function were normal. The admission chest radiograph showed bilateral infiltrates consistent with COVID-19 pneumonia.
title: Development of Compartment Syndrome after Radial Artery Puncture in a Patient with Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure due to COVID-19

case_prompt:
An 81-year-old right-handed man presented with a two-week history of gradually worsening headache. His medical history included lung cancer treated with chemotherapy and radiation two years earlier, with no evidence of recurrence. On examination he was afebrile and normotensive. Neurologic examination was normal except for an active vesicular eruption over the left C4 dermatome. Initial laboratory studies showed a normal CBC and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 79 mm/hr. Noncontrast head CT showed small bilateral subdural hygromas. He was discharged with analgesics, prednisone, and famciclovir.

Twenty-four hours later he returned with visual hallucinations and progressive obtundation. Temperature was 99.0°F and blood pressure was 136/79 mm Hg. He was mildly obtunded and agitated, nonverbal, and unable to follow commands. Neck stiffness was present without overt meningeal signs. Pupils were equal and reactive; cranial nerves were otherwise intact. Motor examination revealed symmetric movements of all extremities. Reflexes were 1+ with bilateral upgoing plantar responses.

Laboratory studies on return showed a WBC count of 12,700/µL (84% neutrophils) and a negative HIV antibody test. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 240 mm H₂O and hazy pink cerebrospinal fluid. Tube 1 contained 3600 WBCs (78% neutrophils), 2800 RBCs; Tube 3 contained 6500 WBCs (92% neutrophils), 24,900 RBCs; protein was 501 mg/dL and glucose was 31 mg/dL. CSF bacterial cultures and cytology were negative; qualitative CSF encephalitis panel was positive for varicella zoster virus antibody.

Electroencephalography showed disorganized high-amplitude delta activity with occasional theta waves. Brain MRI demonstrated symmetric T2 hyperintensities in the body and splenium of the corpus callosum extending into the posterior parietal-occipital white matter with vasogenic edema. On T1-weighted imaging with gadolinium there was enhancement of the corpus callosum. MRA revealed moderate stenosis of the right intracavernous internal carotid artery, hypoplasia of the right A1 segment, and minor irregularity of the distal right posterior cerebral artery. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy of the right parietal-occipital white matter showed elevated lipids, reduced N-acetyl aspartate, and a choline-to-creatinine ratio of 1.7. The initial radiology report concluded this appearance was most consistent with a “butterfly glioma.”
title: An unusual case of varicella zoster encephalitis mimicking a glioblastoma on magnetic resonance imaging and magnetic resonance spectroscopy

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old Moroccan man with a history of cocaine and alcohol abuse and a 10–pack-year smoking history, detained for 3 months, was referred after prison doctors noted severe anemia (hemoglobin 43 g/L). He reported 2 months of progressive fatigue, arthromyalgia, mild abdominal pain, upper finger paresthesia, left ear tinnitus, and recurrent headaches. He denied fever, bleeding, or bowel changes.

On examination he was afebrile (36 °C), blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 80 bpm, and oriented. Findings included pallor, slight epigastric tenderness, and a left tympanic membrane perforation. There was no lymphadenopathy, purpura, or hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic exam was normal except for mild finger paresthesia.

Laboratory tests showed: hemoglobin 36 g/L, MCV 87 fl, hematocrit 10.8%, RDW 27%, neutropenia (0.59×10⁹/L), and a normal platelet count (15×10⁹/L). Creatinine was 176.8 μmol/L with azotemia of 24.9 mmol/L. Peripheral smear showed marked anisopoikilocytosis and 10% schistocytes. LDH was 19.7 μkat/L, haptoglobin <1 mg/L, and total bilirubin 17.1 μmol/L. Coagulation studies were normal except for D-dimer 2.63 nmol/L. Direct Coombs test was negative. Reticulocyte production index was 0.061. Ferritin was normal.

He received intravenous saline and five units of packed red cells. Renal function improved, but anemia persisted with ongoing hemolysis (schistocytes, rising LDH, low haptoglobin). Platelet count fell to 46×10⁹/L and neutropenia persisted, without peripheral blasts.
title: Vitamin B12 deficiency-induced pseudothrombotic microangiopathy without macrocytosis presenting with acute renal failure: a case report

case_prompt:
A woman in her seventies with a history of appendectomy, hypothyroidism, and cataracts underwent endoscopic papillary balloon dilatation and later sphincterotomy for recurring choledocholithiasis. She presented for surgical management of recurrent gallbladder stones. On examination, she had no jaundice or anemia; her abdomen was soft and nontender. Laboratory tests showed no inflammation, normal hepatobiliary enzymes, and normal levels of carcinoembryonic antigen and CA 19-9. 
Abdominal CT demonstrated a low-attenuation area within the gallbladder wall, suggesting a cyst, with attenuation values lower than the gallbladder lumen. DIC-CT revealed no contrast filling of the cystic area, and ultrasound showed bile sludge but no wall thickening apart from the cyst and a 15 mm gallstone. 
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed without difficulty, and the gallbladder appeared to have a normally reticulated mucosal surface. On the serosal (liver) side of the gallbladder fundus, a slightly elevated, whitish submucosal lesion was noted. On gross sectioning, multiple small cysts (3–5 mm) were visible within the gallbladder wall at that site, containing clear serous fluid without bile. 
Histologically, the cysts were located in the subserosal layer, each lined by a monolayer of cuboidal to low columnar cells without atypia, with small round nuclei and clear or weakly eosinophilic cytoplasm. No Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses or mucosal invaginations were seen around the cysts. The cysts were surrounded by dense fibrous tissue lacking elements of the usual gallbladder fibromuscular layer and without a muscularis propria. Scattered small tubular structures lined by low columnar epithelium were present around the cysts.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Intramural cyst originating from Luschka’s duct in the gall bladder: A case report

case_prompt: A 56-year-old man with idiopathic hypertension presented with a 1-month history of right aural fullness and subjective hearing loss. Examination and audiometry confirmed a conductive hearing loss consistent with otitis media with effusion; on placement of a ventilation tube, the effusion was thick and viscid with a red–yellow hue. CT of the temporal bones showed partial opacification of both the middle ear and mastoid cavities; incidental findings suggested chronic rhinosinusitis. Nasal endoscopy was unremarkable and his nasal symptoms were mild. Despite spontaneous extrusion of the first grommet and placement of a larger tube, otorrhea persisted; a swab was negative and a biopsy of the postnasal space showed nonspecific inflammation. MRI with gadolinium demonstrated a large T2-hyperintense, T1-hypointense effusion in the right middle ear and mastoid with patchy mucosal enhancement extending along the Eustachian tube into the nasopharynx and sinonasal cavity. The extensive mucosal inflammation, persistent effusion, and lack of clear infectious or atopic cause raised suspicion for an autoimmune process. Blood tests showed normal RF, ANCA, ANA, serum IgE, CCP, renal and liver function, and ESR; ACE was elevated, as was total IgG (16.21 g/L; normal 6.2–14.4 g/L). A chest radiograph and QuantiFERON Gold test were unremarkable, and repeat ACE testing normalized.
title: IgG4 disease of the ear: Report and review

case_prompt: A 69-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (peritoneal and hepatic metastases) enrolled in a trial of SBP-101 combined with nab-paclitaxel and gemcitabine presented with a 6-month history of progressive blurred vision and visual field loss. She had no diabetes or hypertension. Baseline ophthalmologic evaluation before SBP-101 showed 20/20 visual acuity (VA) in both eyes, normal intraocular pressures, and normal macular structure on optical coherence tomography (OCT). After the second monthly cycle of SBP-101, her VA fell to 20/50 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed pigmentary changes in the macula, with punctate hypo- and hyperautofluorescent spots on blue-autofluorescence. OCT demonstrated ellipsoid zone disruption and hyperreflective material between the Bruch membrane and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in both eyes. SBP-101 was discontinued, and intravitreal dexamethasone was administered bilaterally without improvement. One month later, VA was 20/50 OD and 20/32 OS. Full-field electroretinography (ERG) showed normal scotopic responses and photopic amplitudes at the lower limit of normal. Serum anti-recoverin and anti-enolase autoantibodies were within normal limits. Over the next five months, VA declined to 20/5000 OD and 20/4000 OS, with photopsias and severely impaired central vision. Ultra–wide-field fundus photographs revealed bilateral roundish macular areas of irregular pigment loss extending beyond the vascular arcades, with scattered dot-blot hemorrhages. Blue-autofluorescence showed central hypoautofluorescence surrounded by a ring of alternating hyper- and hypoautofluorescent dots. OCT of the macula demonstrated incomplete RPE and outer retinal atrophy with signal hypertransmission to the choroid, ellipsoid zone disruption, and perifoveal hyperreflective sub-RPE deposits; choroidal thickness was reduced. Optic nerve OCT and RNFL thickness were normal. Visual fields showed bilateral central relative scotomas (VFI 26% OD, 31% OS). ERG per ISCEV standards revealed preserved dark-adapted 0.01 cd·s/m2 and mixed rod–cone responses, relatively preserved a-waves on light-adapted single flashes, but reduced amplitudes and slightly prolonged implicit times on 30 Hz flicker.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Rapidly progressive central retinal pigmented epithelium atrophy after Ivospemin (SBP-101) treatment for pancreatic adenocarcinoma

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man with Gorlin syndrome and a 10-year history of daily vismodegib therapy (150 mg) for locally advanced and metastatic basal cell carcinoma presented with worsening watery diarrhea. Two years after starting vismodegib, he developed loose stools 2–3 times daily (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade 1), with no interruptions in therapy. A colonoscopy after 5 years of vismodegib was unremarkable; at 9 years it showed mildly granular mucosa with loss of vascular pattern in the ascending and transverse colon, and random biopsies exhibited chronic inactive colitis without erosions, ulcers, granulomas, metaplasia, or dysplasia.

At 10 years of therapy, he had grade 2 diarrhea only partially responsive to loperamide (up to 5 doses daily). He also had alopecia, dysgeusia, and muscle spasms, although these did not correlate with diarrheal episodes. He denied abdominal pain, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel with electrolytes, thyroid-stimulating hormone, tissue transglutaminase antibody, immunoglobulin A, and a multiplex stool PCR panel for bacterial and viral pathogens, were normal or negative.

A repeat colonoscopy revealed diffuse mild ileal edema and granularity with punctate erosions and exudate, as well as colonic edema, granularity, and loss of vascular pattern. Ileal biopsies showed mild villous blunting, active ileitis, chronic lamina propria inflammation, and epithelial apoptosis. Biopsies from the right colon, left colon, and rectum demonstrated crypt architectural distortion, mixed inflammation, epithelial apoptosis, and a crypt abscess. Immunostains for cytomegalovirus were negative.
title: Characterization of intractable diarrhea resulting from vismodegib treatment for basal cell nevus syndrome

case_prompt: A 75-year-old Albanian man with benign prostatic hypertrophy underwent an ultrasound for prostate evaluation, which incidentally detected a focal liver lesion. He denied symptoms, and his physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests, α-fetoprotein, and viral hepatitis serologies, were within normal limits or negative. Contrast‐enhanced multidetector CT of the chest and abdomen showed a solitary focal lesion in the right hepatic lobe without cirrhotic changes, other masses, or lymphadenopathy. For further characterization, a 1.5-T MRI of the upper abdomen was performed with T1-weighted in-phase and out-of-phase sequences, T2-weighted images with fat suppression, and dynamic contrast‐enhanced sequences. On MRI, the lesion was hypointense relative to liver parenchyma on T1-weighted images but isointense to spleen; on T2-weighted fat-suppressed images it was moderately hyperintense relative to liver yet isointense to spleen. In the arterial phase after gadolinium administration, the mass showed mild homogeneous enhancement, and in delayed (90-second) images it demonstrated mild perilesional enhancement.
title: Magnetic resonance imaging findings in primary lymphoma of the liver: a case report

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman was found unresponsive and diaphoretic by paramedics. A point-of-care blood glucose measurement was 18 mg/dL. She received 12.5 g of intravenous dextrose, regained consciousness, and her glucose rose to 109 mg/dL. 

On arrival at the hospital, she was alert. Vital signs were blood pressure 117/68 mm Hg, heart rate 73 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination showed mild distress, moist oral mucosa, and a nonfocal neurologic examination with normal pupils.

In the emergency department, her venous blood glucose was 15 mg/dL. She received two additional doses of dextrose 50% in water, improving her glucose to 45 mg/dL, followed by an infusion of dextrose 5% in water, which raised her glucose to 96 mg/dL.

Once stable and alert, she reported that the previous evening at 5 pm she took two light blue pills given by a friend for anxiety, believing they were diazepam. She felt unwell overnight with nausea and diaphoresis, awoke at 4 am with tremulousness, improved after a large lunch at 11 am, then used cocaine and consumed three beers before losing consciousness at dinner around 7 pm.

Her history was notable for substance use disorder and anxiety. She denied personal or family history of diabetes or use of hypoglycemic medications. Current medications included methadone; she had no allergies. Social history included daily tobacco use and occasional beer consumption.

Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines, ethanol, and cocaine. Laboratory studies revealed a blood glucose of 44 mg/dL, insulin level of 47.4 mIU/mL (normal 2.6–24.9), and C-peptide of 5.4 ng/mL (normal 1.1–4.4). Morning cortisol, thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, and insulin antibodies were within normal limits.
title: Hypoglycemia After Ingestion of “Street Valium” Containing Glyburide, Alcohol, and Cocaine

case_prompt: A 15-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a 3-day history of dizziness, gait instability, nausea, and headache. On examination, he had mild diplopia on left lateral gaze and on convergence, an inability to sustain upward vertical gaze, mild right upper- and lower-extremity weakness (Medical Research Council grade 4), right-sided hypoesthesia, and mild gait instability without frank cerebellar signs. Brain MRI showed a well-defined, lobulated cystic lesion in the right middle cerebellar peduncle adjacent to the fourth ventricle, causing mild mass effect on the cerebellar vermis. The lesion contained multiple thin septations and was uniformly isointense to cerebrospinal fluid on all sequences, with no definite enhancement or diffusion restriction. There was mild surrounding edema in the right middle cerebellar peduncle. Single-voxel proton MR spectroscopy demonstrated unremarkable concentrations of N-acetylaspartate, choline, and creatine, with normal choline/creatine and choline/N-acetylaspartate ratios.
title: Posterior fossa giant tumefactive perivascular spaces: 8-year follow-up in an adolescent

case_prompt: A 48-year-old man of African descent was brought to the emergency department unresponsive after a generalized tonic–clonic seizure. On examination he was comatose with a blood pressure of 178/121 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3 of 15; he required intubation and ICU admission. He had no history of epilepsy, head trauma, recreational drug use, smoking, or alcohol consumption. His medical history was notable for resistant hypertension diagnosed 20 years ago, treated with atenolol 50 mg, spironolactone 100 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, and valsartan 160 mg daily, with poor compliance, and for type II diabetes mellitus treated with a sulfonylurea. Family history was positive for hypertension but negative for renal disease or adrenal tumors. Body mass index was 31. Thyroid and visual-field examinations were normal, and there were no cushingoid or acromegaly features. Initial laboratory studies showed a potassium level of 2.6 mmol/L (normal 3.6–5.1), creatinine 113 μmol/L, metabolic alkalosis on blood gas analysis, urea 5.7 mmol/L, and creatine kinase 2.2 μg/L. Urinalysis was negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrites. A chest radiograph showed no signs of heart failure. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm. Troponin-T and BNP were within normal limits. Calcium was 2.46 mmol/L. CT of the brain showed no lesions, and MRI the next day revealed no mass-occupying lesion; EEG was normal. Repeat potassium remained low at 2.6 mmol/L; plasma aldosterone was 36.2 ng/dL (normal 2.8–15.8), and plasma renin was < 0.081 ng/dL (normal 0.4–2.3). A 24-hour urine collection excluded Cushing’s syndrome and pheochromocytoma. Renal ultrasound and cardiac echocardiography excluded renovascular and cardiac causes of secondary hypertension.
title: Seizure and coma secondary to Conn’s syndrome: a case report

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man presented with an asymptomatic, diffuse swelling on the right side of his face and neck. He reported similar, smaller swellings over the past 3–4 years that would spontaneously regress. He could not relate episodes to trauma, meals, dental pain, or systemic symptoms.

On examination, a 7 × 3 cm firm, non-tender, mobile swelling extended from the midface to the right submandibular region and from the oral commissure to the anterior masseter border. The overlying skin was normal. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Oral opening, salivary duct flow, cranial nerves, and neck movement were normal. There was no trismus, dysphagia, or dyspnea.

Initial differential diagnoses included buccal‐space infection, dermoid or epidermoid cyst, branchial cleft cyst, lipoma, vascular malformation, recurrent lymphadenitis or sialadenitis, salivary tumor, and cyst/pseudocyst of salivary origin. The absence of inflammatory signs and normal intraoral findings argued against infection.

Fine-needle aspiration yielded yellowish mucoid fluid. Microscopy showed cystic macrophages in a mucoid background, culture was negative, and the fluid had a high amylase content. Ultrasonography reported 7–9 mL of slightly echogenic fluid with irregular margins anterior to the right mandibular angle, with no calcifications.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the face revealed a well-defined, lobulated 5.5 × 4.5 × 2.5 cm cystic lesion that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with thin peripheral enhancement and a few septations. The lesion lay anterior to the right submandibular gland, lateral to the mylohyoid muscle, and extended over the masseter, without invasion of the parapharyngeal or sublingual spaces. The submandibular and parotid glands appeared normal. There was no “tail sign” toward the sublingual gland.
title: A rare cause of lateral facial swelling

case_prompt: 36-year-old gravida 2 para 1 woman at 30 weeks’ gestation presented with fever, productive cough, and central cyanosis for 2 days. Two weeks earlier, she was diagnosed with multibacillary leprosy based on hypoaesthetic annular plaques on the trunk and limbs, a positive slit-skin smear (morphological index 3.2%; bacteriological index 4.3%), and was started on clofazimine, rifampicin, and dapsone 100 mg daily. She denied headache, chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, chemical exposures, or unprescribed medications. On examination, her temperature spiked once on admission; vital signs were otherwise stable without respiratory distress. Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry was 84–88% on room air, and both radial arterial and venous blood appeared dark. Arterial blood gas on room air showed PaO₂ 111 mmHg and calculated SaO₂ 98%. Laboratory tests revealed normal hemoglobin, bilirubin, LDH, and leukocyte count. G6PD activity was normal. Chest radiograph and sputum studies for bacterial culture and acid-fast bacilli were unremarkable. Administration of 100% oxygen failed to correct the cyanosis, and repeat arterial blood gas values remained unchanged.
title: The mystery of ‘saturation gap’: a case of dapsone-induced methaemoglobinemia in a pregnant mother with leprosy

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old Japanese man presented with a one-month history of bilateral wrist pain and swelling. Two weeks before referral, he had been seen by an orthopedist, was noted to have bilateral wrist swelling and a positive rheumatoid factor, and was referred for further evaluation. He was a farmer with a 40–pack-year smoking history and was treated for ulcerative colitis with mesalazine and low-dose prednisolone.  

On examination, his blood pressure was 104/64 mmHg, pulse 101 beats/min, and temperature 36.6 °C. The left wrist was markedly swollen on both dorsal and palmar surfaces, and both wrists were tender. Sensation was decreased in the left palm, and Tinel’s sign and Phalen’s test were positive on the left. There were no skin lesions or injuries.  

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9,040/mm3, C-reactive protein 4.78 mg/dL, matrix metalloproteinase-3 199.2 ng/mL, rheumatoid factor 63 IU/mL, anti-citrullinated protein antibody 0.7 U/mL, and β-D glucan 9.1 pg/mL. Renal function and glucose levels were normal. Wrist radiographs demonstrated soft-tissue swelling without bone erosions.  

Musculoskeletal ultrasonography of the left wrist revealed marked thickening of the flexor and extensor tendon sheaths with power Doppler signals at the margins and multiple isoechoic rice bodies within the tenosynovium. Aspiration of straw-colored, cloudy synovial fluid yielded no crystals or microorganisms, and polymerase chain reaction analysis for Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA was negative.
title: Sporotrichal Tenosynovitis Diagnosed Helpfully by Musculoskeletal Ultrasonography

case_prompt:
A 72‐year‐old man with metastatic castration‐sensitive prostate cancer (PSA, 89.8; Gleason 5 + 5; cT3aN0M1 with multiple bone metastases) was started on apalutamide (240 mg daily) along with a gonadotropin‐releasing hormone antagonist. His past history included transverse colon cancer, chronic glomerulonephritis, and remote cerebral infarction; he had no known drug allergies. Forty-one days after initiating apalutamide, he developed multiple small erythematous patches on his face and trunk without fever. Topical corticosteroids were ineffective, and apalutamide was discontinued 3 days later; an oral antihistamine was started. Nine days after drug discontinuation, he became febrile (38.1 °C) and hypotensive (77/50 mmHg). Examination showed edematous erythema with numerous small pustules spreading over the trunk and limbs, covering > 30% of the body surface; there were no mucosal erosions, and Nikolsky’s sign was negative. Laboratory studies revealed C-reactive protein 3.30 mg/dL, leukocytes 11 610/μL with 8 816/μL neutrophils and 8.5% eosinophils, and normal liver function tests; no atypical lymphocytes were seen. Echocardiography was unremarkable. A drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test for apalutamide was negative, and no other medications had been introduced. He required ICU admission for hemodynamic support, and all drugs were held. A skin biopsy was obtained.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?
title: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis during apalutamide treatment in a patient with prostate cancer

case_prompt: A 28-year-old woman with Turner syndrome (karyotype 45,X/46,X,+mar), diagnosed at age 16 for amenorrhea, was referred after abnormal brain MRI. She denied alcohol, tobacco, or drug use and had no family history of neurologic disease. On arrival, her temperature was normal, blood pressure 180/130 mm Hg, and heart rate 89 bpm. She was obese (BMI 27.3 kg/m2). Neurologic examination showed no focal deficits. She had had sudden-onset severe headache with a recorded blood pressure of 240/140 mm Hg. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Diffusion-weighted MRI demonstrated restricted diffusion in multiple lesions involving different vascular territories. Cerebral MRA and carotid ultrasound revealed no extracranial or intracranial arterial stenosis. Chest radiograph and ECG were normal. Laboratory tests showed a fasting glucose of 219 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1C 11.0%, and LDL cholesterol 189 mg/dL.
title: A Case of Turner Syndrome with Multiple Embolic Infarcts

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old woman reported a 5-year history of recurrent febrile episodes every 6–8 weeks. Each episode featured a temperature of 38.5–40 °C lasting up to 7 days, accompanied by sore throat, cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy and pain, headache, myalgia, fatigue, and dysphagia. She was asymptomatic between episodes and could predict their onset. She had a history of childhood tonsillitis treated with tonsillectomy. She worked in black metal analysis for over 30 years.  

During episodes, laboratory studies showed CRP 64 mg/L, serum amyloid A 140 mg/L, leukocytes 2.94 × 10^9/L, and neutrophils 3.19 × 10^9/L; procalcitonin, immunoglobulins, and ANA titres were normal. HIV, CMV, EBV, and other infection indicators were negative, and blood and throat cultures showed no growth. PET-CT demonstrated increased glucose metabolism in the sigmoid colon, but colonoscopy was normal. Pharyngoscopy revealed pharyngitis with white exudate. Ultrasound showed enlarged bilateral cervical, submandibular, and supraclavicular lymph nodes (up to 21 × 6 mm), and a supraclavicular lymph node biopsy revealed reactive hyperplasia. Bone marrow biopsy and cytogenetics were unremarkable. Despite multiple courses of antibiotics, febrile episodes persisted.
title: Neglected adult PFAPA syndrome

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man presented with severe acute‐onset myalgia affecting his hips and shoulders. Three months earlier, he had been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. He described proximal myalgia and stiffness in the upper limbs more than the lower limbs; the pain was severe enough to disrupt sleep and had no diurnal variation. His primary‐care physician had prescribed morphine and, subsequently, a 5-day course of prednisolone 30 mg daily, which produced significant symptomatic improvement. 

On examination, he had nonspecific myalgia and arthralgia but no neurological deficit or other systemic findings. His medical history included fatty liver disease and type 2 diabetes; he was not taking metformin or atorvastatin. He was a retired executive, a nonsmoker, and drank little alcohol; there was no relevant family history.

Laboratory studies showed normal or negative results for complete blood count, PSA, immunoglobulins, renal function, vitamin D, and bone profile. He had mild chronic elevations of alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transferase. Inflammatory markers were elevated (CRP 103 mg/L [< 5], ESR 45 mm/hr), and creatine kinase was 811 IU/L (30–200). Immunological tests (ANA, ENA) and viral serologies (hepatitis B and C, HIV, dsDNA), as well as an expanded myositis autoantibody panel, were negative. MRI of the spine was normal; upper‐limb muscle MRI showed nonspecific atrophy without edema.

A working diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica was made, and a tapering prednisolone regimen (initial dose 20 mg) was started. An initial EMG was limited by pain but suggested a possible symmetrical myopathic disorder. A muscle biopsy was offered but deferred when his symptoms resolved on corticosteroids.

Fourteen months later, off steroids, he reported episodic brief myalgias, considered baseline. After strenuous activity, his CK rose to 3473 IU/L while CRP was < 5 mg/L. A repeat EMG demonstrated an active symmetrical myopathic process with short‐duration motor-unit potentials and fibrillation potentials in the right deltoid, with a proximal-to-distal gradient of severity. A muscle biopsy was then performed to further evaluate the myopathy.
title: Late Presentation of McArdle's Disease Mimicking Polymyalgia Rheumatica: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman with a 5-year history of episodic unresponsiveness characterized by akinetic mutism lasting hours to days with postictal amnesia was transferred to our neurology service for evaluation of possible non-convulsive status epilepticus. She had been diagnosed elsewhere with schizoaffective disorder and catatonia. Episodes occurred roughly every 2 months without identifiable triggers, and she had no dietary preferences.

On day 3 of hospitalization, she was comatose with eyes closed. Continuous, generalized, frontally predominant 2.5 Hz sharp and slow-wave discharges were recorded on EEG. A trial of 10 mg intravenous diazepam abolished the sharp waves, and she partially aroused to painful stimuli. No focal neurologic deficits were present. Based on the EEG frequency and apparent benzodiazepine response, she was diagnosed with probable non-convulsive status epilepticus and started on intravenous valproate (1500 mg/day).

On the following day, she remained unresponsive and continuous EEG showed the same 2.5 Hz generalized discharges. Intravenous midazolam, levetiracetam, phenytoin, and oral topiramate were sequentially added, along with pulse-dose methylprednisolone for presumed autoimmune encephalitis, without clinical or electrographic improvement. Brain MRI, CSF studies, and an autoimmune encephalitis antibody panel were unremarkable.

Laboratory tests revealed mild hyperammonemia with normal liver-function tests. Valproate and topiramate were discontinued, and she was started on 10% dextrose infusion and intravenous sodium benzoate and sodium phenylbutyrate. Hemodialysis was initiated for rising ammonia levels. Brain CT showed diffuse cerebral edema, and EEG became nearly isoelectric as she awaited plasma amino acid analysis.
title: Encephalopathy mimicking non-convulsive status Epilepticus

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old man presented in March 2020 with a 1-day history of fever (38.5°C), dry cough, and sore throat. Eight weeks earlier he had a mild, PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. He had received two doses of the Sputnik-V vaccine, at 16 and 12 weeks before admission. On presentation, he was hemodynamically stable. Basic laboratory tests (CBC, creatinine, CRP, and liver enzymes) were normal; chest CT showed no abnormalities; and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. He was treated with ceftriaxone and antipyretics, and over the next 2 days he remained intermittently febrile (≤39.5°C) but stable.

In the early morning of hospital day 3, he became drowsy and oliguric and developed hypotension and hypoxemia (GCS 13/15; HR 110 bpm; BP 70/30 mmHg; RR 45 breaths/min; SpO2 85% on room air; T 39.5°C). Chest examination revealed bilateral coarse crepitations. He was transferred to the ICU, started on IV fluids, norepinephrine, and oxygen support. ECG showed sinus tachycardia; echocardiography and cardiac‐enzyme levels were normal. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis, worsening renal function, elevated liver enzymes, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, elevated CRP, ferritin, D-dimer, IL-6, and creatine kinase. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidation.

Further testing revealed negative results for respiratory viral PCR panels (including influenza, Mycoplasma, Legionella), negative blood, sputum, and urine cultures, and negative viral hepatitis and autoimmune screens. SARS-CoV-2 serology was positive for IgG antibodies. An abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and grade I nephropathy.
title: First confirmed case of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in adult in Egypt

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of progressive anorexia, general malaise, and a 15 kg weight loss that left him unable to walk. His medical history was notable only for intestinal volvulus surgery at age 14 years. On admission, he was alert; temperature was 36.9 °C, blood pressure 124/86 mmHg, pulse 60 beats/min. He appeared cachectic (BMI 16.4 kg/m2). Neurologic, respiratory, cardiac, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:
- Hypoalbuminemia (2.1 g/dL) and low total protein (4.9 g/dL)
- Elevated C-reactive protein (2.75 mg/dL)
- Elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor (1,950 U/mL) and interleukin-6 (20.7 pg/mL)
- Hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL; other values notable for normal LFTs and renal function.

Abdominal CT demonstrated thickening of the small-intestinal mucosa and intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy. Upper endoscopy revealed yellow-white, shaggy mucosa in the duodenum; biopsy specimens showed no specific abnormalities. The patient received intravenous hyperalimentation without improvement. Given the high sIL-2R and IL-6 levels and lymphadenopathy, oral prednisolone (25 mg daily) was initiated, leading to improved appetite and weight gain. He was discharged on day 33. One month later, he lost his appetite again and was readmitted for further evaluation.
title: Whipple's Disease with Long-term Endoscopic Follow-up

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old right-hand–dominant man originally from Afghanistan presented with over 3 months of progressive right wrist pain. Seven years earlier he had immigrated to the United States; during the current illness he moved between Florida and Canada. Initial wrist pain followed minor lifting trauma. He was first diagnosed with a wrist sprain and treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, then with primary osteoarthritis without improvement. He re-presented with continued pain and new fluctuance over the volar wrist.

On admission he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers; HIV testing was negative. Radiographs of the right wrist demonstrated diffuse destruction and osteopenia of the proximal and distal carpal rows with scattered cystic changes of the distal radius, ulna, and carpal bones. Physical examination revealed an erythematous, desquamated, fluctuant lesion on the volar right wrist, pain with small arcs of motion, and hyperreflexia of the upper extremities but otherwise intact neurovascular status.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the wrist showed diffuse T2-weighted enhancement of the carpal bones and a subcutaneous fluid collection communicating with the radiocarpal joint. Synovial aspiration yielded grossly purulent fluid, which was sent for cytology, Gram stain, aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, acid-fast cultures, and crystal analysis. A chest radiograph was unremarkable for pulmonary disease, and MRI of the cervical spine showed no syrinx. He was admitted for presumed septic arthritis and taken for open irrigation and debridement of the wrist, during which extensive purulence, synovitis, severe bony erosion, and cartilage loss were encountered. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics were initiated.
title: Rare septic arthritis of the wrist and carpus primary osteoarticular manifestation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis: A case report

case_prompt: A 68-year-old woman was referred for gradually increased facial hirsutism and deepening of the voice over 6 months. She had entered menopause at age 52 and had an unremarkable family history. Her medical history included hypertension managed with telmisartan and osteoarthritis treated with topical NSAID creams. On examination, blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg, pulse 84 beats/min, and temperature 36.9 °C. She had plethoric facies and terminal hair growth on the upper lip, chin, and upper abdomen (Ferriman–Gallwey score 4). There was no clitoromegaly or temporal balding. The remainder of her examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed polycythemia (hemoglobin 18 g/dL, hematocrit 54%), normal electrolytes and biochemistry, and a serum testosterone level of 25.40 nmol/L (normal range for women, 0.38–1.97 nmol/L). Further testing revealed a 17-hydroxyprogesterone level of 302.57 pmol/L and a cortisol level of 2.7 nmol/L after a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test. Pelvic MRI showed ovarian dimensions of 22×12 mm and 22×14 mm without masses, and adrenal CT demonstrated normal gland size and configuration. Serial measurements on hospitalization days 4, 6, 8, and 10 showed a decline in testosterone levels to 12, 7.4, 4.3, and 2.1 nmol/L, respectively.
title: An Interesting Cause of Hyperandrogenemic Hirsutism

case_prompt: An 87-year-old man from Isfahan presented with asymptomatic, progressive facial lesions of 3 years’ duration. He noted onset after an overnight outdoor camping trip; his son concurrently developed a leishmanial nodule on his leg. Lesions gradually extended over the nose, cheeks, upper lip, and periorbital areas, with confluent erythematous plaques, induration, ulceration, crusting, and purulent discharge compromising vision. Routine blood tests and chest radiography were normal. PPD was negative. Over 3 years, multiple skin biopsies showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and mixed inflammatory infiltrates with occasional noncaseating granulomas; special stains and cultures for fungi and mycobacteria, Giemsa smears, and PCR for Leishmania were repeatedly negative. Empiric courses of antibiotics, antifungals, intralesional antimonials, antituberculous therapy, and systemic corticosteroids produced no durable improvement. The most recent biopsy of the upper lip lesion revealed actinic cheilitis. In our clinic, three punch biopsies again showed noncaseating tuberculoid granulomas without identifiable organisms. A nasal skin biopsy demonstrated prominent epidermal hyperplasia with cellular atypia, increased mitoses, invasion of squamous nests, and keratin pearls, consistent with well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Staging revealed no metastases. Culture of purulent discharge grew Staphylococcus aureus, but a 10-day course of cloxacillin yielded no significant change; botryomycosis was excluded due to antibiotic nonresponse. Otolaryngology and oncology consultations were obtained, and a surgical plan for SCC was scheduled.
title: Two cases of neglected leishmaniasis with marked facial disfigurement: A diagnostic conundrum

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old man with ischemic heart disease and a bioprosthetic aortic valve implanted in 2009, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, stage 4 chronic kidney disease, and peptic ulcer disease presented with a 2-week history of worsening exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and intermittent presyncope. His medications included lifelong clopidogrel, antihypertensives, statin therapy, and insulin.

Initial ECG showed a stable borderline left bundle branch block without ischemic changes. He was admitted for intravenous diuresis. A few days later, he awoke with new right-sided visual disturbance. Vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologically, he had a right homonymous hemianopia; tone, reflexes, cranial nerves, strength, and sensation were otherwise normal. Cardiovascular examination revealed a regular rate with no rub, gallop, or murmur; there were coarse crepitations at the lung bases and bilateral ankle pitting oedema. Abdominal and dermatologic findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 102 g/L, white-cell count 15.3×10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 121 mg/L. Five sets of blood cultures were negative. Serologic tests for Coxiella and Bartonella were unremarkable. Coagulation studies, a prothrombotic panel (protein C, protein S, factor V Leiden), and blood film were normal.

Diffusion-weighted brain MRI demonstrated a left occipital lobe infarct at the junction of the posterior and middle cerebral artery territories without hemorrhage or old infarcts. Transoesophageal echocardiography revealed a 10×7.5 mm heterogeneous mobile echogenicity attached to the bioprosthetic aortic valve with moderate stenosis, severe paravalvular regurgitation, and leaflet degeneration; no valvular abscess was seen. Cardiac positron-emission tomography showed no FDG uptake at the bioprosthetic valve.
title: Nonbacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis of Bioprosthetic Aortic Valve Presenting as Cardioembolic Stroke in a Patient without Predisposing Systemic Disease

case_prompt:
A 3-month-old male infant with failure to thrive and a cardiac murmur was found on echocardiography to have an isolated 6 mm × 9 mm perimembranous ventricular septal defect with an unrestrictive left-to-right shunt, pulmonary plethora, congestive heart failure, and left heart volume overload. There were no other cardiac or extracardiac anomalies. Despite maximal medical therapy, he remained symptomatic and underwent surgical VSD closure with a porcine pericardial patch via a right atrial approach under standard heparinization, cold-blood cardioplegia, and cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) (CPB time 47 min, aortic cross-clamp 35 min).

After separation from CPB, a routine epicardial echocardiogram demonstrated no residual VSD and normal ventricular function but revealed an unexpected single, well-circumscribed, globular, homogeneously hyperechogenic mass within the left atrium. On multiple planes, the mobile mass measured 10 mm × 11 mm, had a tongue- or finger-like appearance without a peduncle, and extended from the free wall of the left atrium. With each cardiac cycle, it protruded closer to the mitral annulus in diastole. Colour Doppler interrogation showed no obstruction of pulmonary veins or mitral inflow. An intracardiac thrombus was the primary differential diagnosis; however, he was adequately anticoagulated, the activated coagulation time was maintained in the desired range throughout, and no thrombi were observed in the CPB circuit.
title: Inverted left atrial appendage mimicking potential left atrial thrombus in an infant following cardiac surgery: a case report

case_prompt: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with abnormal vaginal bleeding. Hysteroscopy identified and resected a 2 cm polypoid mass in the right lateral uterine wall. Histologic examination of the biopsy showed mucinous adenocarcinoma with glandular and solid architecture, intra- and extra-glandular necrosis, neoplastic cells with pale eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, variable intracytoplasmic mucin, mild to moderate nuclear atypia, and a high mitotic rate with atypical figures. Immunohistochemistry revealed diffuse positivity for CK20, CDX2, and p16; focal positivity for CK7 and PAX8; negative estrogen and progesterone receptors; a wild-type p53 pattern; focal (< 10%) chromogranin A and synaptophysin positivity; and intact MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, and MSH6 expression. A diagnosis of high-grade adenocarcinoma with mucinous features, highly suspicious for metastatic origin, was initially rendered. Subsequent ultrasound demonstrated only a superficial minimal residual endometrial lesion without myometrial or adnexal involvement. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, PET, and MRI were all unremarkable.
title: Gastric (gastrointestinal)-type endometrial adenocarcinoma presenting as a solitary endometrial polyp: a case report and literature review on a novel and potentially aggressive endometrial cancer histotype

case_prompt: A 21-year-old man was admitted with a 1-week history of swelling and pain in both knees, both ankles, the right shoulder, and the right wrist, accompanied by fever. Physical examination revealed redness, swelling, and a subcutaneous hematoma over the right ankle with increased local skin temperature. He reported an antecedent “cold” and had experienced watery diarrhea 3 days before the onset of joint symptoms. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 11.78 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 82.9%), platelet count of 384 × 10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 77 mm/h, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein of 176.49 mg/L, uric acid of 250.5 µmol/L, activated partial thromboplastin time of 44.60 s, fibrinogen of 6.74 g/L, D-dimer of 10.67 µg/mL, and factor VIII activity of 203.7%. Aspiration of the right ankle yielded bloody fluid with numerous leukocytes and red blood cells. Debridement of an ulcerated, necrotic subcutaneous hematoma was performed and cultures of joint fluid and wound secretions were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right ankle suggested inflammatory arthritis. Tests for rheumatic factor, antinuclear antibodies, HLA-B27, stool cultures, and other infectious agents were negative. On hospital day 3, he developed severe left perianal pain with localized skin redness and swelling, and a diagnosis of perianal abscess was made.
title: A case of reactive arthritis caused by a perianal abscess

case_prompt: A 59-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of sore throat, cough, hoarseness, and a 10-kg weight loss. She was a never-smoker, had undergone left quadrantectomy for ductal carcinoma, and had been treated for stage II pulmonary sarcoidosis with hydroxychloroquine (400 mg/day) and oral prednisone (15 mg/day) for 5 years. Physical examination was unremarkable, and laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. Flexible laryngoscopy showed a centimetric polylobulated lesion on the free border of the epiglottis, inframillimetric lesions on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis, and a millimetric ulcerated area on the right arytenoid mucosa; vocal-fold and arytenoid motility were preserved, and neck examination was normal. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the neck demonstrated a small low-enhanced lesion of the epiglottic border without other laryngeal enhancements. Whole-body PET-CT revealed multiple ground-glass lung masses and bilateral nodules increased from prior imaging of known sarcoidosis.
title: Isolated laryngeal tuberculosis complex infection: expect the unexpected

case_prompt: A 15-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of progressive erythematous, edematous papules and plaques arranged in a linear pattern on the left side of her body. She had congenital amniotic band syndrome but no personal or family history of autoimmune disease and denied systemic symptoms. On examination, violaceous dermal papules coalesced into blaschkolinear plaques from the left medial arm to the wrist, from the left side of the abdomen to the flank, and from the left posterior thigh to the lower leg. Laboratory studies showed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320 (homogeneous pattern); tests for anti–double-stranded DNA, ENA panels, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, cardiolipins, rheumatoid factor, and acute‐phase reactants were negative. Complement levels were normal. A punch biopsy of a lesion demonstrated focal vacuolar interface change; mild superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation; and increased superficial and deep interstitial mucin deposition on Alcian blue and colloidal iron stains.
title: A teen with blaschkolinear tumid lupus erythematosus

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old Caucasian man was admitted with six days of cough, fever, myalgia, and chills. He had tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 three days after symptom onset. His only medical history was hyperlipidemia managed with atorvastatin; he had no known allergies and denied tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use. On admission his renal function was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed diffuse bilateral ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, moderate pleural effusions, and normally sized kidneys with preserved perfusion.

Two days later he developed acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring intubation, prone positioning, and empiric amoxicillin–clavulanate; hydroxychloroquine was also given after exclusion of G6PD deficiency. His course was complicated by atrial fibrillation, paralytic ileus, and oliguria. By hospital day 9, he had acute kidney injury with a serum creatinine peak of 519 μmol/L and severe metabolic acidosis, prompting initiation of continuous veno-venous hemodiafiltration.

Over the next two weeks he developed a maculopapular rash on his trunk and lower extremities and a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, high lactate dehydrogenase, undetectable haptoglobin, and transfusion dependence. Laboratory studies revealed ferritin >11,000 μg/L, elevated C-reactive protein and procalcitonin, worsening hypoalbuminemia, persistent proteinuria (urine protein/creatinine ratio 72.6 mg/mmol), microscopic hematuria, but minimal leukocyturia and no marked eosinophilia. Serologic screening for HIV, hepatitis B and C, antinuclear, anti–DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, and anticardiolipin antibodies, complement levels, and ADAMTS13 activity were unremarkable. Echocardiography showed preserved ventricular function; imaging excluded urinary obstruction. In the absence of renal recovery, nephrology was consulted on hospital day 26 to consider renal biopsy.
title: Granulomatous interstitial nephritis in a patient with SARS-CoV-2 infection

case_prompt: A 63-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging cervical mass. He had no personal or family history of neoplasms. Laboratory evaluation showed a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 56 µIU/mL (elevated), free T3 of 2.4 pmol/L, and free T4 of 10 pmol/L; antithyroglobulin antibodies were within the normal range. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 4.5 × 4.0 × 4.5 cm calcified mass in the left thyroid lobe causing tracheal compression and deviation, as well as two smooth, homogeneous nodules in the right thyroid lobe. MRI demonstrated that the epicenter of the left-lobe mass was within the thyroid gland, with no invasion of the adjacent thyroid cartilage. The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with cervical lymph node dissection. Gross examination showed a gray, lobulated, firm mass with calcifications occupying most of the left lobe, and two gray, firm, oval nodules in the right lobe.
title: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with chondrosarcomatous differentiation: a case report

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old Asian woman presented with a 3-week history of constant bilateral heel pain and difficulty walking. She also reported migratory pain involving her ankles, knees, and hips of the same duration; the pain worsened with activity and was not associated with morning stiffness.
