She had no history of sexual activity, no family history of tuberculosis or rheumatologic disease, and had received BCG vaccination at birth. 

On examination, she was afebrile. There was mild swelling of the left ankle without erythema, tenderness, or limitation of movement; all other joints and the remainder of her examination were normal. Initial complete blood count and creatine phosphokinase level were normal; radiographs of the hands and knees showed no erosions. She was treated with NSAIDs and other symptomatic measures, but her pain worsened over the next week, now involving her wrists and small joints of the hands bilaterally. She failed to respond to escalated analgesic therapy, and developed low-grade fevers to 37.8 °C, anorexia, fatigue, a 2-kg weight loss, and a mild nonproductive cough. 

Laboratory testing revealed an ESR of 72 mm/hour and a CRP of 4.9 mg/dL. A tapering course of corticosteroids produced partial relief of pain but persistent daily fevers. Ten days after steroids were discontinued, she returned with worsening polyarthritis, fevers to 37.8 °C, an additional 2-kg weight loss, and cough. Her ESR was 70 mm/hour, CRP 5.3 mg/dL, and ferritin 204 mg/dL; ANA was positive, but ASMA, AMA, anti–dsDNA, and RF were negative. Chest radiography revealed patchy right perihilar and lower-lobe infiltrates without lymphadenopathy or effusion. A PPD skin test showed 22 mm of induration at 72 hours, compared with a negative test 2 years earlier. Attempts to obtain sputum and synovial fluid for AFB were unsuccessful, and the patient declined invasive procedures.
title: Poncet’s disease: two case reports

case_prompt: A 70-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, eczema, and obstructive sleep apnea presents with 4 days of fever and chills, with a maximum temperature of 104 °F, though she is afebrile on admission. Vital signs are normal. Initial laboratory studies reveal troponin 14 552 ng/L (0–30), C-reactive peptide 96.2 mg/L (< 8.0), ESR 23 mm/h (0–20), BNP 895 pg/mL (≤ 100), CK 2 584 U/L (25–190), and WBC count 8.7 × 10^3/µL (3.7–11.0). Peak absolute eosinophil count is 0.67 × 10^3/µL (≤ 0.50). Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Cardiac MRI demonstrates diffuse mid-wall to near-transmural patchy late gadolinium enhancement of the left ventricle without subendocardial enhancement in a vascular distribution, consistent with nonischemic myocarditis.
title: Eosinophilic myocarditis: Case report and brief review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man with a history of nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (stage IA treated with radiotherapy five years earlier) presented with three weeks of fatigue, jaundice, and intermittent epigastric pain. He denied fevers, sweats, weight loss, alcohol excess, toxin or mushroom ingestion, intravenous drug use, recent travel, or new medications apart from an over-the-counter multivitamin. There was no family history of liver disease.

On examination, he was alert and oriented but visibly jaundiced, with mild epigastric tenderness, ecchymoses, and no stigmata of chronic liver disease or asterixis. There was no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or ascites. His BMI was 28.7 kg/m^2.

Laboratory studies showed: total bilirubin 156 μmol/L (normal <20), direct bilirubin 100 μmol/L (<4), ALT 2190 U/L (≤45), AST 1750 U/L (≤35), ALP 143 U/L (30–110), GGT 214 U/L (<55), albumin 36 g/L (35–50), INR 1.9 (0.9–1.2), hypoglycemia (<3 mmol/L), ferritin 3380 μg/L (40–440), CRP 8.4 mg/L (<5), globulins 26 g/L (25–45). Complete blood count was unremarkable. Viral serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, HIV, EBV, CMV, and HSV were negative. Antinuclear, smooth-muscle, antimitochondrial, and anti–liver/kidney microsomal antibodies were all negative. Alpha-1-antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, and copper studies were normal. Peripheral blood flow cytometry showed no monoclonal B-cell population.

Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous liver (span 14 cm), gallbladder wall thickening without cholelithiasis or biliary dilation, patent portal vein, nonvisualized hepatic veins, and splenomegaly (15 cm). Contrast CT of neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed heterogeneous hepatic enhancement without discrete lesions, multiple enlarged upper abdominal lymph nodes, and splenic lesions; portal and hepatic veins were patent though the left hepatic vein was poorly visualized. There was no biliary obstruction and echocardiography showed normal cardiac function.

Given the acute hepatocellular pattern with coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, and negative noninvasive workup, the leading considerations were lymphomatous infiltration of the liver, Budd–Chiari syndrome, and autoimmune-mediated hepatitis. On hospital day 2, a transjugular liver biopsy with hepatic venous pressure measurement was performed.
title: Relapsed nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma presenting as severe paraneoplastic hepatitis: a case report

case_prompt:
A term female newborn (3.700 kg) was born vaginally without prenatal complications. Family history was negative for heart disease. Before discharge, transthoracic echocardiography showed moderate tricuspid regurgitation due to valvular dysplasia; all other findings were normal. She was discharged for follow-up.

On day 6 of life she was admitted with tachypnea, sweating, and failure to thrive; weight was 3.220 kg. Signs of heart failure and respiratory distress were present: O2 saturation 96% on 6 L/min, venous blood gas revealed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.03, pO2 46 mmHg, pCO2 29 mmHg, HCO3– 12.3 mmol/L, BE –19). Mechanical ventilation was initiated. On arrival: BP 70/30 mmHg, HR 130 bpm, diuresis preserved. Examination showed a grade 3/6 systolic murmur, weak femoral pulses, and hepatomegaly (liver palpable 3 cm below costal margin).

Laboratory studies: high-sensitivity troponin T 1001 ng/L, CK-MB 37.4 mcg/L; venous blood gas on admission pH 7.1, pO2 65 mmHg, pCO2 28 mmHg, lactate 14.8 mmol/L. Viral studies were negative. Chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly and mild pulmonary venous congestion.

ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm at 133 bpm, right atrial enlargement, inferior Q waves, and lateral repolarization abnormalities. TTE revealed a normal-sized left ventricle with hypokinesis of the inferior wall, dyskinesis of the septum, and mildly depressed ejection fraction; the right ventricle was enlarged with mildly impaired systolic function. Moderate mitral regurgitation and severe tricuspid regurgitation were present. The right coronary artery origin was normal; the left coronary artery was not well visualized.

Selective coronary angiography confirmed normal origin and anatomy of both coronary arteries and normal hemodynamic parameters. With mechanical ventilation and diuretics, hemodynamics improved and heart failure resolved. Within hours, the patient was weaned from ventilation; ECG normalized except for a prolonged corrected QT interval (480 msec). Cardiac markers fell (high-sensitivity troponin T 163.2 ng/L, CK-MB 5 mcg/L). TTE showed normal biventricular systolic function, no wall motion abnormalities, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and no mitral regurgitation.
title: An Unusual Case of Suspected Microvascular Angina in a Newborn

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old Nigerian woman was referred with a one-month history of recurrent dyspnea, central chest pain, headaches, visual blurring, and dizziness. She reported orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, progressive bilateral leg swelling, and reduced urine output. She had been diagnosed with hypertension five years earlier but was noncompliant with medications; there was no family history of hypertension.

On examination, she was in respiratory distress and pale, afebrile (36.8 °C). Vital signs: blood pressure 220/120 mmHg, pulse 118 beats/min, respiratory rate 50 breaths/min. BMI was 23.8 kg/m^2. Cardiovascular exam revealed arterial wall thickening, a fourth heart sound, and a loud A2. Lung auscultation showed reduced breath sounds in the left lower zones and bibasal fine crepitations. She had bilateral pitting edema to the knees, grade III hypertensive retinopathy, and asterixis. No focal neurologic deficits were noted.

Laboratory studies showed serum creatinine 900 µmol/L (normal 53–115), urea 30 mmol/L (2.1–7.1), Na 136 mmol/L, K 4.0 mmol/L, Cl 98 mmol/L, HCO3 28 mmol/L. Liver viral markers and HIV were negative. Urinalysis revealed ++ proteinuria without hematuria.

Renal ultrasound and Doppler findings:
- Right kidney: 8.63 × 4.59 × 5.07 cm, loss of corticomedullary differentiation; renal artery velocity 73.9 cm/s, resistive index 0.9.
- Left kidney: upper margin appeared intrathoracic and poorly visualized; hypoechoic with loss of corticomedullary differentiation; renal artery velocity 195 cm/s consistent with stenosis.
title: Ectopic Thoracic Kidney and End-Stage Renal Disease in a 38-Year-Old Nigerian

case_prompt: A 71-year-old man with advanced renal cell carcinoma treated with ipilimumab (1 mg/kg) and nivolumab (240 mg) presented four days after his second infusion with an asymptomatic, sustained mild rise in serum creatine phosphokinase. On the seventh day after infusion, ST-segment elevations were noted on his cardiac monitor. Twelve-lead electrocardiography showed ST-segment elevation in all leads. Laboratory testing revealed elevated inflammatory markers and myocardial biomarkers (creatine kinase MB-isozyme, 23 488 U/L; troponin-I, 100 680 pg/mL; NT-proBNP, 15 964 pg/mL). Echocardiography demonstrated an akinetic apex, a hypokinetic septum, and an ejection fraction of 50% (baseline 72%). Emergency cardiac catheterization excluded relevant coronary disease, and left ventriculography showed that the left ventricular apex was nearly akinetic while the remaining left ventricle was hyperkinetic.
title: Myocarditis as an immune-related adverse event following treatment with ipilimumab and nivolumab combination therapy for metastatic renal cell carcinoma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old African American woman with a history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and Rai stage 1 CLL, diagnosed 8 years earlier on routine evaluation, presented with progressive lymphadenopathy, intermittent fevers, a 5-lb weight loss, and worsening respiratory status requiring airway management. Initial CLL had been managed with observation; rheumatoid arthritis therapies had included hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, prednisone, and rituximab infusions. 

On CT imaging, there was a soft-tissue mass in the nasopharynx representing enlarged adenoidal tissue, diffuse palatine and lingual tonsillar hypertrophy with airway narrowing, and bulky cervical, supraclavicular, and axillary lymphadenopathy. PET/CT showed intense FDG uptake in the nasopharyngeal mass (SUVmax 18.7), level IIB cervical chain nodes (SUVmax 20.7), and bulky FDG-avid lymph nodes in the axillary, periaortic/retroperitoneal, and iliac regions. 

Complete blood count revealed leukocytosis (WBC 40.7 × 10^3/mm^3; 24% neutrophils, 75% lymphocytes), mild hypochromic-macrocytic anemia (Hb 11.8 g/dL; MCV 97.6 fL), and normal platelet count. The peripheral smear showed numerous atypical lymphocytes consistent with persistent CLL. Serologic and viral studies were negative, including HIV, hepatitis A/B/C, COVID-19, influenza A/B, RSV, and QuantiFERON-TB Gold. 

CLL prognostic testing revealed CD19-positive lymphoid cells (87% of lymphocytes), ZAP70 positivity 1%, CD38 positivity 20%, unmutated IGHV3-21 status, normal karyotype, and negative FISH for trisomy 12 and deletions of 6q, 11q, 13q, and 17p. Beta-2 microglobulin was 2.27 mg/L. These features indicated unfavorable CLL prognosis. 

At presentation, the leading clinical consideration was Richter transformation of her CLL, and an ultrasound-guided core biopsy of an enlarged cervical lymph node was performed.
title: Transformation of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia/Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma to Histiocytic/Dendritic Cell Sarcoma

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old previously healthy girl presented with fever, bilateral foot pain, and a mottled purpuric rash. Over the prior 6 months, she had intermittent episodes lasting 2–3 days, improving with ibuprofen. In the weeks before presentation, she developed fatigue, hip and calf pain attributed to sports, and an episode of abdominal pain with diarrhea and emesis. She denied headaches, visual changes, oral ulcers, or other systemic symptoms. Family history was negative for autoimmune disease. 

On examination, temperature was 39.2 °C, heart rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate 20 bpm, blood pressure 114/62 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She had blanchable, retiform violaceous patches with areas of true purpura on her lower extremities and duskiness of the right second toe. Cardiac, pulmonary, joint, and neurologic examinations were otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies showed elevated creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, C-reactive protein, and transaminases. A skin biopsy of a purpuric lesion demonstrated subtle ischemia, vascular congestion, purpura, and focal eccrine gland necrosis without evidence of vasculitis. Direct immunofluorescence was negative. An extensive work-up—including hepatitis panel, cryoglobulins, lupus anticoagulant panel, cardiolipins, beta-2-glycoprotein, complements C3 and C4, antistreptolysin O titers, anti-DNAse B, and aldolase—was unremarkable. Abdominal and renal Doppler ultrasonography showed no abnormalities.
title: Rare presentation of an atrial myxoma in an adolescent patient: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 68-year-old woman presented with a dry cough of more than 1 month’s duration, associated with dyspnea, fever, chills, myalgia, and intermittent diarrhea. She had type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a history of COVID-19 diagnosed by PCR 40 days earlier that required hospitalization and treatment with antipyretics, corticosteroids, anticoagulants, and intravenous fluids. She denied known exposure to tuberculosis. On examination, she had crackles in the right lung, an oxygen saturation of 80% on ambient air, a blood pressure of 118/80 mm Hg, and a pulse rate of 97 beats per minute. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 33 000/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 194 mg/dl. A chest radiograph demonstrated a cavitated density in the right upper lobe. Computed tomography of the thorax revealed bilateral diffuse parenchymal densities, two cavities in the right lung (one in the right upper lobe and one in the right lower lobe), and residual ground-glass opacities.
title: Activation of tuberculosis in recovered COVID-19 patients: a case report

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old previously healthy boy presented with three weeks of mild dyspnea, chest pain on exertion, and a newly detected cardiac murmur. He denied syncope, palpitations, fever, weight loss, recent infections, and had no history of central lines or tattoos. Family history was negative for congenital heart disease, cardiomyopathy, sudden death, or thrombophilia.

On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 95 bpm, blood pressure 96/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100%. He had a grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, normal S1 and S2, no gallops or rubs, and mild hepatomegaly. Peripheral pulses were normal. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 43 U/L, normal renal function, coagulation profile, C-reactive protein, and troponin, but an elevated NT-proBNP of 4019 pg/mL. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. 

Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm, right bundle-branch block with repolarization abnormalities in the right precordial leads, and isolated monomorphic premature ventricular contractions often in a bigeminy pattern. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 3.5 × 4.0 cm rounded, lobulated mass with clear margins and inhomogeneous content, attached by a pedicle to the infundibular septum and causing severe obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract with a peak gradient of 80 mmHg. The right atrium and right ventricle were dilated, with severe right ventricular systolic dysfunction (fractional area change 18.6%). 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed a heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass occupying the right ventricular outflow tract without evidence of pulmonary embolism.
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
title: New Onset Cardiac Murmur and Exertional Dyspnea in an Apparently Healthy Child: A Rare Localization of Obstructive Myxoma in the Right Ventricle Outflow Tract without Pulmonary Embolization—A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old man with no past medical history developed fever, headache, and a painful left-sided neck swelling while working offshore. He denied cough, dyspnea, chest pain, or recent travel and had no known COVID-19 contacts. On admission: temperature 41 °C, heart rate 115 beats/min, blood pressure 119/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 12–22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Physical examination revealed a tender, non-fluctuant swelling extending from the left mandibular angle to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and a red area on the posterior palate; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
ECG showed sinus tachycardia with moderately flattened T-waves. Chest radiograph was normal. Arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.55, pCO2 3.9 kPa, pO2 8.4 kPa, HCO3 23 mmol/L). Laboratory studies revealed CRP 230 mg/L (0–5), procalcitonin 2.1 µg/L (0–0.10), WBC 7.1 × 10^9/L (3.5–11.0), troponin T 90 ng/L (0–15), and NT-proBNP 160 ng/L (0–85).  
Contrast CT of the neck showed left-sided subcutaneous edema with multiple enlarged lymph nodes up to 2.7 cm. Transthoracic echocardiography on admission demonstrated normal ventricular function without hypokinesia. On day 2, echocardiography revealed a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%, while CRP rose to 344 mg/L and procalcitonin to 12.9 µg/L, with persistently normal WBC count.
title: COVID-19 myocarditis and postinfection Bell’s palsy

case_prompt: A previously healthy 3-year-old boy from Gorakhpur was admitted with 12 days of high-grade fever, generalized tonic–clonic seizures for 6 days, and altered sensorium for 1 day. On examination, his temperature was 103°F, pulse 158/min and feeble, respirations 54/min, blood pressure 56/32 mm Hg, and Glasgow Coma Score 4. He had hepatosplenomegaly, bilateral chest rhonchi, tachypnea, tachycardia, extensor plantar responses, and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Initial laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, normal leukocyte count, platelets 180 000/mm^3, SGPT 109 U/L, blood urea 87 mg/dL, and blood glucose 50 mg/dL. CSF analysis revealed 68 cells/mm^3 (72% lymphocytes), protein 68 mg/dL, and a normal glucose level. Given the prolonged fever with hepatosplenomegaly, a rapid diagnostic test for malaria was performed and was positive for Plasmodium vivax and P. falciparum; peripheral thick and thin smears confirmed both species with a parasitic count of 6%. Widal test, acute hepatitis viral markers, and blood cultures were negative, and chest radiography showed right-sided heterogeneous opacities. A head CT scan on day 3 was normal. The child received a 7-day course of intravenous quinine and doxycycline, but on day 8 of admission his fever persisted. A repeat peripheral smear on day 7 of antimalarial therapy was negative for malarial parasites.
title: Concurrent infection of Japanese encephalitis and mixed plasmodium infection

case_prompt: A 26-year-old previously healthy Caucasian man presented with a 3-week history of dry cough and progressive dyspnea. He reported dizziness, retrosternal chest pain, and one febrile episode. Physical examination was notable only for hypophonetic heart sounds. Chest radiography showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large pericardial effusion without signs of tamponade. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed multiple rounded hepatic lesions, all hypodense and hypovascular, the largest measuring 3 cm in segment IVa. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia and elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 95 mm/h; C-reactive protein, 92 mg/L); liver and thyroid function tests were normal. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C viruses and HIV were negative; rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody tests were also negative. An ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy showed lobular necrosis and perisinusoidal fibrosis without granulomas or neoplastic cells. During hospitalization he developed fever, night sweats, and weight loss, and was started on empiric therapy for extrapulmonary tuberculosis with corticosteroids. Two months later, pericardial effusion had resolved but liver lesions persisted. He was readmitted in hemorrhagic shock due to bleeding from the hepatic lesions, underwent unsuccessful embolization of the right hepatic artery, and died shortly thereafter.
title: Multiple hepatic metastases of cardiac angiosarcoma

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old girl was referred with gross hematuria and altered mental status after 6 hours of symptoms. Two days earlier she was well; she had sudden abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and three episodes of vomiting. Her mother had given her two tablespoons of areca nut powder and ibuprofen syrup for presumed diarrhea and fever. Immediately thereafter, she became pale, developed cold extremities, gross hematuria, and two generalized tonic–clonic seizures (10 and 3 minutes in duration). On arrival, temperature was 39.4°C, heart rate 140/min, respiratory rate 40/min, blood pressure 90/50 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 85%. She was pale, febrile, had non-exudative conjunctivitis, and gross hematuria.  
Initial laboratory tests showed normal electrolytes except for potassium 3.8 mEq/L, C-reactive protein >150 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase 3570 U/L, fibrinogen 611 mg/dL, a negative direct and indirect Coombs test, and sufficient G6PD activity. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.43, PCO2 14.3 kPa, HCO3 9.6 mEq/L. Echocardiography was normal. Renal function was normal (BUN 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.42 mg/dL). Liver enzymes were elevated (AST 2670 U/L, ALT 970 U/L, INR 1.76) with normal total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase. Urinalysis showed 4+ blood and 2+ albumin. Stool examination revealed 3+ occult blood and numerous white blood cells. Blood cultures showed no growth. Virology tests for HBV, HCV, HAV, SARS-CoV-2, and HSV 1 and 2 were negative.
title: Acute toxic effects of areca nut on central nervous system and liver: A case report

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old amateur athlete presented with 3 weeks of exercise intolerance manifesting as exertional dyspnoea and dizziness. He denied syncope, had no family history of sudden cardiac death, and took no medications. He had traveled to Iran and, 3 months earlier, had an inguinal bullous skin lesion treated briefly with topical steroids without recurrence.

On examination: heart rate 61 bpm, blood pressure 122/77 mmHg, temperature 36.5 °C; cardiac and pulmonary exams were normal. Laboratory tests showed normal leukocytes (4.89 g/L) and CRP (0.8 mg/L). Resting ECG revealed an incomplete right bundle branch block and first-degree AV block; rhythm monitoring showed intermittent 2:1 AV block. During spiroergometry, exercise-induced high-degree AV block was documented.

Transthoracic echocardiography raised suspicion of inferobasal septal wall-motion abnormalities and, retrospectively, a mass; left ventricular ejection fraction was normal. Coronary angiography excluded coronary artery disease, and chest CT revealed no pulmonary pathology. Cardiac MRI demonstrated a 5 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm mass in the inferobasal septum with late gadolinium enhancement but no active perfusion. FDG-PET showed intense uptake in the inferobasal septum and no extracardiac uptake.

Further evaluation revealed normal sIL-2 receptor, ANA, ANCA, serum calcium, and ACE levels. Blood cultures (aerobic, anaerobic, mycobacterial) and serologies for Brucella, Bartonella henselae, Treponema pallidum, Borrelia burgdorferi, Coxiella burnetii, and HIV were negative. PCR for tuberculosis and mycobacterial cultures were negative. Dermatologic full-body exam showed only non-specific skin changes.

Because there were no extracardiac manifestations, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography-guided endomyocardial biopsies were performed, but all samples were non-specific.
title: Exercise intolerance — from spiroergometry to transdiaphragmatic myocardial punch biopsy: a case report of isolated cardiac sarcoidosis

case_prompt:
A woman in her late 70s presented with a 2-week history of progressive bilateral leg weakness, unstable gait, and fluctuating drowsiness with moments of confusion. This followed a 4-week history of progressive bilateral lumbosacral herpes zoster infection that spread to her right groin and right leg. Her medical history included primary biliary cirrhosis with two liver transplants, immunosuppression with tacrolimus, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder in remission, and chronic pancreatitis.

On examination, she was drowsy but could converse and obey simple commands; when verbal stimulus ceased, she fell asleep, indicating hypersomnolence. Cranial-nerve evaluation revealed bilateral upward gaze palsy and horizontal nystagmus on smooth pursuit. Deep-tendon reflexes were absent, plantar responses were extensor bilaterally, and there was a symmetrical flaccid paraparesis (2/5) of the lower limbs with preserved tone and power in the upper limbs. Sensory testing showed a non-painful glove-and-stocking paraesthesia; otherwise, sensation was intact. There was no history of foreign travel or tick exposure.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, liver and renal function, and undetectable SARS-CoV-2 RNA; tacrolimus level was 3.3 µg/L (reference 5.0–15.0). Serum anti-mitochondrial M2, anti-M2-3E, and anti-Ro52 antibodies were strongly positive. MRI of the brain and spinal cord with and without contrast was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed protein 0.37 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, and zero white cells; viral PCR for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, enterovirus, and adenovirus was negative. Nerve conduction studies at 8 weeks after symptom onset showed no demyelinating or axonal features. Serum anti-ganglioside testing was positive for anti-GQ1b IgM and negative for anti-GM1 and anti-GD1b subtypes.
title: Bickerstaff’s brainstem encephalitis mimicking herpetic encephalomyelitis in a liver transplant patient with anti-GQ1b antibodies

case_prompt:
A 44‐year‐old previously healthy man presented with chills for 3 days and arthralgias in the knees and hips, preceded by several days of unproductive cough and headache. One week before presentation, he had been treated with a macrolide antibiotic and an NSAID. His medical history was notable only for smoking; there was no family history of cardiovascular disease or long‐term medications. 

On examination, temperature was 38.5°C, heart rate 113/min, blood pressure 126/64 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Auscultation revealed no pericardial rub or crackles; there was epigastric tenderness. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with first‐degree AV block (PQ 210 ms). Laboratory studies demonstrated WBC 13.4×10^3/µL, CRP 16.9 mg/dL, ESR 95 mm/h, and high‐sensitivity troponin T 656.2 ng/L; the differential count showed no eosinophilia. Electrolytes, liver, and kidney function were normal. Blood cultures, serology, and PCR for pathogens were negative; vasculitis‐associated autoantibodies were absent.

Chest radiograph showed mild peribronchial cuffing. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved LV function, a 9-mm pericardial effusion, and slight IVC dilation; coronary CT excluded obstructive disease. He was treated empirically for pneumonia with pericarditis.

Over 2 days he developed worsening dyspnea and congestion, requiring noninvasive ventilation and diuretics. Repeat echocardiography showed an LV ejection fraction of 35%. On hospital day 4, cardiac MRI demonstrated myocardial edema with multifocal subepicardial and subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement and pericardial inflammation.

On day 8 he had syncope from complete heart block, was treated with isoproterenol, but progressed to low‐output state requiring dobutamine and a temporary pacemaker. Right heart catheterization revealed a cardiac index of 1.65 L/min/m^2, mean PCWP 34 mmHg, and LVEDP 29 mmHg.

A total of eight endomyocardial biopsy specimens were obtained from the left ventricle.
title: Eosinophilic myocarditis complicated by permanent atrioventricular nodal block: a case report

case_prompt: An independent octogenarian with hypertension, coronary artery disease, and prior Bell’s palsy was last seen well at 10 :00 AM but found ‘confused’ at 12 :40 PM with new speech disturbance, right facial droop, and right‐sided weakness. On arrival at 1 :40 PM, his NIH Stroke Scale score was 19, with severe aphasia, impaired command following, visual inattention, near‐unintelligible speech, and right hemiparesis. Blood pressure was 155/88 mm Hg. Baseline blood tests and electrolytes were unremarkable; finger‐prick glucose was normal. Noncontrast CT of the head showed chronic small‐vessel ischemic changes and arterial calcification without hemorrhage or acute infarct. Intravenous alteplase was administered 26 minutes after referral. During infusion, CT angiography revealed no large‐vessel occlusion. CT perfusion imaging demonstrated relatively reduced time to peak and time to maximum, and increased relative cerebral blood volume and flow in the left hemisphere compared with the right, findings interpreted as compatible with seizure activity.
title: CT perfusion: stroke, seizure or both?

case_prompt: A 42-year-old Asian woman presented with a 5-day history of fever and chills and a 2-day history of jaundice. Three months earlier she had undergone laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholangitis due to gallstones. She had no family history of hemolytic disease. On examination, she was alert, temperature 39.3 °C, blood pressure 122/61 mmHg, pulse 119 beats/min, and respiration rate normal; skin and sclera were icteric, with no abdominal or costovertebral-angle tenderness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, reticulocyte count 25.0%, white-cell count 10,580/µL, platelets 125,000/µL; total bilirubin 10.9 mg/dL (direct 6.0 mg/dL), AST 49 IU/L, ALT 65 IU/L, ALP 441 IU/L, LDH 550 IU/L, and GGT 301 IU/L; coagulation tests were normal. Blood cultures grew Escherichia coli. Abdominal contrast CT revealed splenomegaly and a distended left kidney, with no biliary-tract obstruction. Urinalysis showed leukocyte esterase 3+, nitrite 2+, hemoglobin 3+, bilirubin 2+, and urobilinogen 3+; sediment contained white cells, bacteria, and 5–9 erythrocytes per high-power field, and urine culture grew E. coli. Further testing showed haptoglobin 8 mg/dL and negative direct and indirect Coombs tests. A peripheral blood smear revealed spherocytes.
title: Previously undiagnosed hereditary spherocytosis in a patient with jaundice and pyelonephritis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 10-year-old boy was evaluated for a swelling on the dorsal surface of the tongue that had appeared 3 years earlier as a small, localized lesion and gradually increased to 1.5 × 1.5 cm. He reported no pain but had difficulty eating. There was no history of fever or other medical problems. On examination, the lesion was an oval, firm, nonmobile nodule with a smooth, nonulcerated surface.

Differential diagnoses included mucocele; benign mesenchymal tumors (lipoma, fibroma, hemangioma, lymphangioma, granular cell tumor); parasitic cyst; and minor salivary gland adenoma.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology was performed with a 22-gauge needle, yielding 1 ml of clear fluid containing pearly white flakes. Smears stained with May–Grünwald–Giemsa and hematoxylin–eosin showed a mixed inflammatory infiltrate composed of numerous eosinophils, plasma cells, and palisading histiocytes.
journal: International Journal of Clinical Pediatric Dentistry
title: Oral Cysticercosis in a Pediatric Patient: A Rare Case Report with Review

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man with primary hyperparathyroidism due to a right parathyroid adenoma was scheduled for focused parathyroidectomy under general anesthesia. His medical history included asthma managed with long-term inhaled steroids leading to severe osteoporosis of the spine, and chronic left shoulder impingement with limited elbow extension from a remote injury. He had no hypertension, diabetes, smoking history, or cardiovascular disease. He weighed 64 kg (BMI 19.8 kg/m2) and was ASA class II. Preoperative airway examination showed Mallampati I without restriction or pain on neck extension, though a note advised careful extension due to osteoporosis. 

Anesthesia was induced with fentanyl, propofol, and remifentanil without neuromuscular blockers. Intubation with a conventional laryngoscope in slight neck extension revealed a Cormack–Lehane grade II view. The patient was supine with a small pillow under the shoulders for slight neck extension and arms alongside the body. A bilateral SCPB was performed using anatomical landmarks with 10 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine (5 mL per side). The 103-minute surgery was uneventful, and vital signs remained stable. The patient was extubated and transferred to recovery. 

Shortly after transfer, painless left arm weakness was noted. Neurological examination 3.5 hours after surgery showed strength 2/5 in shoulder elevation, 4/5 in elbow flexion/extension, and 4/5 in finger abduction and wrist extension; fist closure was normal. There was no headache, altered consciousness, dysarthria, or leg weakness. Vital signs were normal. Given the mild symptoms and absence of signs suggesting stroke or cervical spine complication, no CT or MRI was performed.
title: Transient unilateral brachial plexus block following landmark-guided superficial cervical plexus block: A case report

case_prompt:
A 79-year-old white man with PD-L1–positive stage IV non–small cell lung cancer began pembrolizumab, 200 mg every 3 weeks. His history included a 50-pack-year smoking history, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypothyroidism, and oral lichen planus managed with doxycycline, 20 mg daily, with good control. He had no prior cutaneous lichen planus or history of skin cancer.

Approximately 6 weeks after starting pembrolizumab, he noted a mildly pruritic, enlarging rash on his arms, legs, and upper back. On examination, there were innumerable hyperkeratotic, necrotic papulonodules and ulcerations on the extremities and scattered multicentimeter, serpiginous, nonscaly, erythematous annular plaques on the upper back and forearms. Concurrently, his oral lichen planus flared, and his doxycycline was increased to 40 mg twice daily. He denied genital lesions or systemic symptoms.

Punch biopsies of an extremity papulonodule and an annular plaque were performed.
title: Programmed cell death protein-1 inhibitor–induced granuloma annulare and hypertrophic lichen planus masquerading as squamous cell carcinoma

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man presented with fever and confusion. One month earlier, he had been admitted for slurred speech, right hemiparesis, and weight loss; MRI at that time showed multiple left temporoparietal enhancing lesions, and biopsy diagnosed glioblastoma (WHO grade IV), for which he received radiation and temozolomide. His past medical history included diabetes mellitus.
On current admission, temperature was 39.7 °C, pulse 88/min; examination revealed left facial weakness and decreased strength in the right upper and lower extremities. Laboratory tests showed WBC 0.4 K/mm3 (absolute neutrophil count 0.2 K/mm3), hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, and platelets 20 K/mm3; other routine tests were unremarkable. Chest radiograph suggested a possible right lower lobe infiltrate.
Noncontrast head CT demonstrated stable left frontal and corpus callosum abnormalities compared to prior MRI. He received platelet transfusion and was started on meropenem for febrile neutropenia; dexamethasone was tapered. After platelet count rose, lumbar puncture showed 0 WBC/mm3, 0 RBC/mm3, protein 100 mg/dL, glucose 33 mg/dL, LDH 38 IU/L, and negative Gram stain. EEG revealed generalized background slowing with left frontotemporal low-amplitude sharp waves. Repeat brain MRI with contrast showed a new signal abnormality in the right temporal lobe.
title: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1) Encephalitis Mimicking Glioblastoma: Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 62-year-old Hispanic woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-week history of progressive dyspnea, palpitations, profound weakness, new hot flashes, and right flank pain. Vital signs showed a heart rate of approximately 100 beats per minute and a temperature of 37.7 °C. Examination revealed pale conjunctivae without erythema or exophthalmos, a thyroid gland of normal size without nodules, a systolic tricuspid murmur, decreased basal breath sounds, and tender hepatomegaly extending 5 cm below the right costal margin. Neurologic examination demonstrated hyperreflexia and tremor. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 3054 U/L (122–222), alkaline phosphatase 434 U/L (40–129), elevated total and free thyroxine levels, and suppressed TSH. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed pulmonary hypertension (65 mmHg), right atrial and ventricular dilation, tricuspid regurgitation, preserved left ventricular function, and an atrial septal defect with right-to-left shunt. Contrast-enhanced 18 F-FDG PET-CT demonstrated hepatomegaly (22 cm) with multiple FDG-avid liver masses up to 12 cm (SUVmax 13.5), FDG uptake in the gastric antrum (SUVmax 9.4) without corresponding wall thickening, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and small pulmonary infiltrates. A technetium-99m pertechnetate thyroid scan showed diffusely increased uptake, and assays for thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin and TSH receptor antibodies were negative. The patient was started on propranolol and methimazole for thyrotoxicosis.
title: Severe thyrotoxicosis as initial presentation of gastric choriocarcinoma: a case report

case_prompt: A 72-year-old man with a history of retroperitoneal fibrosis presented with a 1-week history of swelling and pain in his left lower extremity. Magnetic resonance angiography demonstrated occlusion of the left common iliac vein. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 3.37 mg/dL and a D-dimer level of 3.50 µg/mL. Plain computed tomography revealed a soft-tissue mass encasing the terminal abdominal aorta. Unexpectedly, noncontrast CT also demonstrated increased wall thickness of the ascending aorta. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a circular high-attenuation lesion in the ascending aorta, approximately 5.3 cm in maximum diameter with a wall thickness of 15 mm; no entry tear or intimal flap was identified. The patient was afebrile, with normal blood pressure and heart rate, and denied any chest or back pain. Transthoracic ultrasound showed no intimal flap or aortic valve abnormality. Given the absence of typical features of aortic dissection and his history of retroperitoneal fibrosis, the team elected to observe the ascending aortic findings without surgical intervention.
title: IgG4-Related Periaortitis Initially Suspected of Being an Aortic Intramural Hematoma in the Ascending Aorta

case_prompt:
An 11-year-old spayed female Golden Retriever was referred for evaluation of an incidentally detected hepatic mass. Five days earlier, she had pollakiuria and mild abdominal discomfort; abdominal ultrasound then showed a 5.2 × 5.0 cm round hypoechoic mass in the left lateral liver lobe and a smaller hypoechoic lesion near the right middle lobe. Urinalysis was notable only for struvite crystals and mild proteinuria; empirical amoxicillin resolved her urinary signs. CBC and serum chemistry were within reference limits. 

Her only chronic issues were bilateral elbow osteoarthritis and cruciate ligament injuries, for which she was receiving tramadol, amantadine, meloxicam, and supplements. On presentation, she was bright, alert, obese (BCS 8/9), with a left forelimb lameness. Abdominal palpation and peripheral lymph nodes were unremarkable. Repeat abdominal ultrasound confirmed a 4.5 × 5.7 cm heterogeneous, well-vascularized hypoechoic mass in the left lateral liver lobe. Thoracic radiographs were normal.

Ultrasound‐guided fine‐needle aspiration of the hepatic mass yielded a mixed lymphoid population: predominantly intermediate‐sized lymphocytes (12–15 μm, indented nuclei, coarse chromatin, pale blue cytoplasm) and fewer small lymphocytes (8–12 μm, condensed chromatin). There was a lymphoglandular background, few hepatocyte clusters with mild hydropic change, and no expanded lymphocytes in adjacent parenchyma. The cytology was most consistent with lymphoma, and marked inflammation was deemed unlikely.

Flow cytometry on the aspirate demonstrated predominantly small CD3+ T cells (mixed CD4+ and CD8+), about 5% small CD21+ B cells, and 15% CD45+ MHC class II+ leukocytes lacking lineage markers. PCR for antigen receptor rearrangements (PARR) revealed a reproducible clonal immunoglobulin heavy‐chain rearrangement and polyclonal T‐cell receptor rearrangements.
title: Indolent T‐cell‐rich small B‐cell hepatic lymphoma in a Golden Retriever

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old Hispanic woman with acne, asthma, and psychosocial distress presented to the ED with lightheadedness, generalized weakness, diaphoresis, diarrhea, and vomiting. 

First ED visit:  
• She reported a home glucose of 53 mg/dL, rising to 80 mg/dL after eating.  
• Triage vitals: BP 98/65 mmHg; HR 81 bpm; RR 18/min; SpO₂ 100% on room air; T 37.0°C.  
• Exam: well-developed, obese woman in no acute distress.  
• Point-of-care glucose was 60 mg/dL (confirmed by lab); other labs and examination were unremarkable.  
• She received IV saline, ondansetron, dietary advice for hypoglycemia, and was discharged.

Second ED visit (next day):  
• Found unresponsive at home with prehospital glucose 46 mg/dL treated with D50W.  
• Triage vitals: BP 122/75 mmHg; HR 100 bpm; RR 18/min; SpO₂ 100%; T 36.7°C.  
• Exam and labs again unremarkable. She was treated symptomatically and discharged.

Third ED visit (three weeks later):  
• Found unresponsive at work with glucose 23 mg/dL; EMS administered D50W to 172 mg/dL.  
• In the ED her glucose repeatedly fell despite multiple D50W boluses and escalating dextrose infusions (D5½NS then D10W), prompting ICU admission.  
• She had recurrent episodes of weakness, confusion, diaphoresis, palpitations, and altered mental status.  
• ECG: normal sinus rhythm, no acute changes.  
• Laboratory studies across visits showed hypoglycemia with otherwise normal hematologic, renal, and electrolyte panels (Table 2).  
• A standard drug screen was negative.  
• Further tests: hemoglobin A1C 5.1%; C-peptide 9.9 ng/mL; free insulin 370 mIU/L; total insulin 377 mIU/L.  
• Noncontrast head CT: no intracranial abnormalities.  
• Abdominal CT: right ovarian cyst; no pancreatic mass.
title: Hypoglycemia secondary to factitious hyperinsulinism in a foster care adolescent - a case report of munchausen syndrome in a community hospital emergency department setting

case_prompt: A 32‐year‐old Asian man presented with a 1‐year history of a right neck mass. His past medical history was noncontributory. On extraoral examination, there was a soft, slightly movable mass in the right submandibular region with normal overlying skin; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Computed tomography of the neck revealed a well‐defined, mixed‐density lesion measuring approximately 5 × 3 cm adjacent to the right submandibular gland. Subsequent image segmentation suggested that the lesion contained components of fat, connective tissue, and osteoid. Primary differential diagnoses based on imaging included pleomorphic adenoma of the submandibular gland, teratoma, and osteo/chondroid lipoma.
title: Ossifying Fibromyxoid tumor of soft parts in head and neck: case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 9-year-old girl was referred for an irregular heart rate noted at an incidental well-child visit. An electrocardiogram showed a prolonged QTc of 485 ms and runs of non-sustained bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. There was no family history of arrhythmogenic disorders, congenital heart disease, or sudden death; the mother and maternal grandmother had syndactyly. Physical examination revealed short stature, low-set ears, mild micrognathia, wide-spaced eyes, dental abnormalities, and left iris heterochromia. Vital signs were age-appropriate. Holter monitoring revealed a ventricular ectopy burden of 40%. Laboratory studies, including a CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, cardiac enzymes, and thyroid function tests, were normal. Exercise stress testing showed no significant increase in ectopy from baseline at higher heart rates. Transthoracic echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a structurally normal heart with no evidence of ventricular dysfunction.
title: Asymptomatic ventricular tachycardia: diagnostic pitfalls of Andersen–Tawil syndrome—a case report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old boy presented with headache, convulsions, blurring of vision, and vertigo. His vital signs were stable, and he was fully conscious and oriented. Pupils were 2 mm bilaterally and equally reactive. There were no cranial nerve, motor, or sensory deficits. He had scattered melanocytic nevi over his back since birth, none larger than 1 cm, and no family history of melanoma. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain revealed a heterogeneous high-density mass in the anterior left temporal lobe with contrast enhancement. MRI of the brain showed a T1-hyperintense and T2-hypointense mass in the left temporal lobe with perilesional edema, no dural attachment, and mild heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. The imaging prompted consideration of a hemorrhagic brain tumour.
title: Primary Intracranial Melanoma with Early Leptomeningeal Spread: A Case Report and Treatment Options Available

case_prompt: A 53-year-old otherwise healthy man presented with a 4-month history of swelling of the right foot and ankle. He denied trauma, fevers, weight loss, or claudication. On examination there was non-pitting edema of the right foot and ankle without erythema or warmth. Duplex ultrasound of the leg veins excluded deep vein thrombosis. Radiographs of the ankle and serologic tests were unremarkable, with no evidence of arthritis. One month later, because of progression of the edema to the entire leg, a CT scan of the pelvis and groin was performed and revealed a hyperechogenic structure in the right groin compressing the common femoral vein and causing focal venous narrowing. Duplex sonography confirmed a 3 cm mass dorsal to the common femoral vein. MRI of the groin showed a 26×24×54 mm lesion that was mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, isointense to muscle on T1, and demonstrated slight contrast enhancement. A fine-needle biopsy revealed proliferating spindle cells but did not provide a definitive diagnosis.
title: Incidental deep soft tissue leiomyoma of the groin – a case report and comprehensive review of literature

case_prompt:
A 12-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of progressive weakness and generalized edema, which began in the feet and later involved the abdomen, and a 1-week history of progressively worsening dyspnea at rest. There was no fever, headache, rash, or other constitutional symptoms. She had no prior serious illness. 

On examination, she was in severe respiratory distress, markedly pale, with bilateral pitting pedal edema and mild dehydration. Respiratory rate was 40 breaths per minute. Chest examination revealed stony-dull percussion notes in the mid and lower lung zones bilaterally, decreased vocal and tactile fremitus, vesicular breath sounds of reduced intensity, and a few basal crepitations. 

Cardiovascular examination showed a low pulse volume, pulsus paradoxus, raised jugular venous pressure of 11 cm H₂O, tachycardia at 120 bpm, hypotension (60/30 mmHg), an impalpable apex beat, and very distant heart sounds. Abdominal examination revealed tender hepatomegaly 7 cm below the right costal margin and mild ascites. Other systems were normal. 

An initial diagnosis of congestive cardiac failure with bilateral pleural effusions and large pericardial effusion—possibly secondary to viral myocarditis or pericarditis, with tuberculosis to be ruled out—was made, and she was started on anti–heart-failure therapy. A chest radiograph confirmed bilateral pleural effusions and an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Bilateral pleural fluid aspirations yielded clear fluid with chemical analysis suggestive of a transudate. A Mantoux test was negative. Full blood count and film were unremarkable except for a packed cell volume of 23% (hemoglobin, 7.6 g/dL).
final_diagnosis_raw: Hemorrhagic pericardial effusion from blunt chest trauma
title: Late onset hemopericardium with cardiac tamponade from minor blunt chest trauma – a case report

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman presented with half-day episodes of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting that began 3 weeks prior and recurred weekly. The pain was dull, poorly localized across the central abdomen from the epigastrium to the lower quadrants, intense enough to interrupt her daily activities, and resolved spontaneously after approximately 12 hours. She denied diarrhea, constipation, weight loss, photophobia, phonophobia, or visual auras. Her medical history included migraine since age 30 and an ectopic pregnancy; her mother and brother have migraine. She had a recent episode of infectious enteritis treated symptomatically. Initial treatment by a local physician with lansoprazole, bifidobacteria probiotic, and daikenchuto provided no relief; subsequent outpatient therapy with oxethazaine, dimeticone, and domperidone also failed, and the pain recurred multiple times over one week.  
On examination: temperature 36.6℃, blood pressure 122/73 mmHg, heart rate 74/min, respiratory rate 18/min. The abdomen was soft with mild tenderness from the epigastrium to the lower abdomen without rebound or guarding.  
Laboratory tests revealed a slight amylase elevation (157 U/L) and otherwise normal blood counts, chemistry, liver enzymes, pancreatic enzymes, and CRP. Serologic testing for Helicobacter pylori IgG was negative.  
Abdominal ultrasound, contrast-enhanced CT, and upper and lower endoscopy (performed during pain episodes except colonoscopy) showed no abnormalities.
title: Abdominal Migraine in a Middle-aged Woman

case_prompt:
An African woman in her early 40s presented with 4 years of gradually progressive visual loss, beginning in the right eye and then involving the left, associated with eye pain that worsened with movement and throbbing bitemporal headache. There was no fever, seizures, or altered mental status. She was initially diagnosed with idiopathic intracranial hypertension despite a normal brain MRI and normal CSF opening pressure, and underwent ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement after acetazolamide failed.

One year after the shunt, she developed numbness in her lower and upper extremities. She noted progressive difficulty standing from sitting, climbing stairs, sitting unsupported, handling objects, writing, buttoning shirts, and combing hair. She also developed bladder and bowel incontinence. There was no history of joint pain, weight loss, skin changes, or preceding respiratory or gastrointestinal illness.

Her medical history included 6 years of hypertension, well controlled on medications. Obstetric history was notable for 11 spontaneous pregnancy losses before 24 weeks and one living child; menstrual history was otherwise unremarkable. There was no history of preeclampsia, thrombosis, or similar family illnesses.

On examination, she was alert with normal cognition and no meningeal signs. Cranial nerves were intact except for the optic nerves. Ocular motility was full; visual acuity was light perception only in both eyes, intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg (right) and 18 mmHg (left), pupils were dilated and nonreactive, and fundoscopy showed bilateral optic disc pallor with peripapillary atrophy and otherwise normal retinal background. Motor examination revealed normal bulk, strength 2/5 in upper limbs and 1/5 in lower limbs, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Sensory examination showed decreased pinprick, fine touch, temperature, and vibration below the C4 level; spine palpation was unremarkable. Other systems were normal.
title: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder co‐existing with antiphospholipid syndrome: A case report

case_prompt: A 26-year-old woman with a history of unspecified bipolar disorder and recent antipsychotic treatment was brought to the emergency department after 10 days of worsening mental status. Collateral history revealed progressive fatigue, inability to feed herself, and dependence for activities of daily living. On arrival, she was unresponsive; blood pressure was 175/108 mm Hg, heart rate 170 beats per minute, temperature 37.8 °C, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had adequate urine output but required assistance with toileting. Physical examination showed rigidity of all four extremities, areflexia, inability to follow commands, and warm skin. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 12,000 per mm³ and a creatine kinase level of 6,500 IU/L. A noncontrast CT scan of the head was unremarkable. The initial differential diagnosis included neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant catatonia, encephalitis, and sepsis.
title: An Abnormal Case of Malignant Catatonia in a Previously Healthy Young Female With Unexplained Neurological Symptoms

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old woman was referred for constant right proximal thigh pain that had progressed over 8 years. She had no other medical conditions, menarche at age 13, and no family history of bone disease. The pain was worse at night, somewhat relieved by activity and cold baths, and required daily NSAIDs, paracetamol, and weak opioids. She had a leg-length discrepancy managed with shoe inserts and was on sick leave due to her symptoms. At age 11 she had hip joint pain with an ultrasound-guided aspiration revealing sterile fluid; pain resolved. Six months prior, she was hit by a car at knee level, with no fracture diagnosed, after which her thigh pain worsened.

On examination, there were no skin lesions, café au lait spots, erythema, heat, or swelling over the right thigh. Leg lengths were slightly unequal but within normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging and PET–CT showed significant increased cortical thickness of the right femoral diaphysis with partial medullary obliteration and an uneven sclerotic surface. A Tc-99m bone scan demonstrated increased uptake in most of the right femoral shaft. Biochemical bone markers, including alkaline phosphatase, were normal. Genetic screening in blood for the GNAS1 R201 mutation and for SQSTM1 mutations was negative. Bone biopsy of the lesion revealed thickened bone trabeculae with preserved lamellar structure, accentuated cement lines, and no fibrosis, inflammation, alcian positivity, malignancy, or neoplasia.
title: Clinical improvement in a patient with monostotic melorheostosis after treatment with denosumab: a case report

case_prompt: A 64-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an abdominal mass incidentally detected on routine examination 6 months earlier. She denied fever, abdominal pain or distension, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, or changes in bowel habits. Her history was notable only for type 2 diabetes mellitus of 10 years’ duration; she had no tobacco or alcohol use. Physical examination was unremarkable. Urinalysis showed leukocytes 2+; fasting blood glucose was 6.97 mmol/L; complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, and tumor markers were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a dumbbell-shaped, moderately inhomogeneous soft-tissue shadow measuring approximately 3.6 cm × 1.8 cm in the region of the stomach’s lesser curvature, with apparent origin from the gastric wall, and a mesenchymal stromal tumor was suspected. Two months before planned surgery, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed chronic superficial gastritis without evidence of mucosal lesions or malignancy, and colonoscopy showed no abnormalities, ruling out colorectal metastasis. The tumor’s extraluminal location and lack of mucosal involvement reduced suspicion for a primary gastrointestinal lesion. Preoperative three-dimensional reconstruction showed a 4 cm × 2 cm × 1 cm dumbbell-shaped mass encircling the left gastric artery, splenic artery, and splenic vein to guide surgical planning. Preoperative diagnosis: abdominal mass (suspected gastric stromal tumor) and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
title: Primary Adenocarcinoma of the Lesser Omentum: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old woman with no prior medical history was referred for evaluation of suspected early breast cancer. She was asymptomatic. On examination, there were no palpable masses in the breasts, axillae, or abdomen. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and serum tumor markers (CEA 1.8 ng/mL, CA15-3 11.4 U/mL, BCA225 30.7 U/mL, NCC-ST-439 1.3 U/mL, soluble IL-2 receptor 322 U/mL), were all within normal limits.

Mammography revealed a high-density mass with clustered microcalcifications in the inferior lateral right breast. Chest CT confirmed a well-enhancing right breast mass without axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of the breast lesion yielded class V cells, consistent with malignancy.

As part of staging, abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass with internal blood flow signals arising from the splenic periphery. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 40-mm well-circumscribed splenic lesion with less enhancement than the surrounding parenchyma in the arterial and portal phases, becoming isodense in the delayed phase. MRI of the abdomen revealed a lesion isointense to the spleen on T1- and T2-weighted images, with slow centripetal enhancement reaching parity with the spleen at 10 minutes post-contrast. PET-CT showed no significant FDG uptake in the splenic lesion.

The preoperative differential diagnoses for the splenic mass included benign vascular neoplasms (hemangioma, lymphangioma, littoral cell angioma, hamartoma, inflammatory pseudotumor), angiosarcoma, solitary splenic metastasis of breast cancer, and primary splenic lymphoma. Given the inability to establish a definitive diagnosis noninvasively, the decision was made to perform a partial mastectomy with sentinel node biopsy and a simultaneous laparoscopic splenectomy for therapeutic diagnosis.
title: Sclerosing Angiomatoid Nodular Transformation of the Spleen: Lessons from a Rare Case and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral hypoglycemic agents was referred for evaluation of a presumed soft-tissue tumor in his lower left leg. He had no known diabetic nephropathy, retinopathy, or sensory disturbances. He first noted a painless, palpable mass on the anterior aspect of his left lower leg 6 months earlier; it gradually enlarged and developed large blisters. 

On physical examination, there was swelling over the anterior lower left leg without tenderness. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 0.05 mg/L, a white-cell count of 4,580/mm3, a creatine kinase level of 164 IU/L, and a casual blood glucose level of 298 mg/dL. 

A radiograph of the lower left leg showed moderate soft-tissue swelling without bony abnormalities or soft-tissue calcifications. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a large mass (maximum diameter, 7.2 cm; length, 21.0 cm) with cystic areas within the tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus muscles; the mass and cysts did not enhance, while the anterior tibialis artery was well visualized. 

MRI demonstrated heterogeneous signal intensity of the mass on T1- and T2-weighted images and homogeneous signal of the cystic areas on both sequences; there was no perifascial, intramuscular, or subcutaneous edema. Fat-suppressed gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images showed slight heterogeneous enhancement with focal hypointense nonenhancing areas. The ankle–brachial index was normal.
title: Diabetic Muscle Infarction of the Tibialis Anterior and Extensor Hallucis Longus Muscles Mimicking the Malignant Soft-Tissue Tumor

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old Namibian man was referred for evaluation of anemia, thrombocytopenia, and back pain. Seven months earlier, he developed insidious low back pain that gradually worsened, radiated to the lower limbs, and was aggravated by walking and relieved by rest. Four months before admission, he noted exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and palpitations. He also reported weight loss, fevers, malaise, and urinary symptoms including straining, frequency, and dysuria. He had no history of trauma, cough, gastrointestinal symptoms, smoking, or alcohol use.

On examination, he appeared pale and mildly wasted. The right shoulder joint was swollen, tender, and had a limited range of motion. There was percussion tenderness over the thoracic and lumbar spine without deformity. Digital rectal examination revealed an asymmetrically enlarged, nodular, and hard prostate with diffuse firm areas. Other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed a normocytic, normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 5.4 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (42×10^9/L), a reticulocyte count of 101 500 cells/µL (index 1.1), hypercalcemia (2.9 mmol/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (509 IU/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (547 IU/L). Renal and liver function tests were normal. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed no M-protein, and urine was negative for Bence Jones proteins. Urinalysis showed mild proteinuria and microscopic hematuria; urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to cefuroxime. The prostate-specific antigen level was >100 ng/mL.

Radiographs of the right humerus demonstrated osteolytic lesions. Computed tomography of the spine, pelvis, and femur showed multiple osteolytic lesions. A lateral skull radiograph was normal.
title: Cancer of the prostate presenting with diffuse osteolytic metastatic bone lesions: a case report

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a cardiac mass identified during work-up for hypertensive urgency. She reported chest tightness and malaise. Her history was notable for well-controlled hypertension, dyslipidaemia, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and gallstone disease; there was no fever or signs of infection. Physical examination was unremarkable. Electrocardiography and laboratory tests excluded an acute coronary syndrome. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an echo-lucent, partially calcified lesion measuring 28×24×21 mm at the posterolateral mitral annulus, without mitral regurgitation or stenosis and with normal biventricular function. Given the irregular borders of the mass, further evaluation was undertaken.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an 18×23×31 mm heterogeneous mass adjacent to the posterior mitral annulus. First-pass perfusion sequences showed no perfusion of the mass, and late gadolinium enhancement revealed contrast uptake only at the periphery. Native T1 mapping showed a hyperintense central region with elevated values, and T2 mapping was also elevated. 

Transesophageal echocardiography excluded mobile vegetations. An atherosclerotic plaque was noted in the aortic arch on imaging.
title: Big mitral annular calcification: a case report of a dynamic liquefaction necrosis as a potential source of embolism

case_prompt: An 84-year-old woman had an incidentally discovered simple liver cyst one year earlier. She was asymptomatic, and physical examination was unremarkable. Liver function tests were normal, and hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen was 5.0 ng/mL and CA19-9 was 43.5 U/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-defined, low-attenuation cystic lesion that increased in maximal diameter from 41 to 47 mm over one year, with an irregularly shaped mural nodule demonstrating progressive contrast enhancement and no biliary duct dilation. Enhanced ultrasonography revealed a 14 mm isoechoic irregular nodule with a distinct feeding artery and gradual enhancement. MRI depicted a homogeneous water-intensity cystic lesion; the mural nodule showed peripheral low intensity and central high intensity on heavily T2-weighted images and contrast enhancement on portal venous–phase T1-weighted images comparable to intrahepatic vessels, with hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging. PET/CT demonstrated no abnormal ^18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the nodule.
title: Hepatic hemangioma in a simple liver cyst mimicking biliary cystic neoplasm

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old Japanese man was evaluated for several months of progressive anorexia. His medical history was notable for sublingual adenocarcinoma treated with resection and radiation 6 years earlier, supraclavicular lymph-node metastasis resection and radiation 5 years earlier, and subsequent lung and bone metastases treated with platinum-based chemotherapy. He was currently receiving nivolumab. He had no history of smoking or significant family illnesses and was taking sertraline. 

On initial evaluation, laboratory testing demonstrated secondary adrenocortical insufficiency and secondary hypothyroidism without evidence of diabetes insipidus. Serum IgG4 was 52.0 mg/dL; angiotensin-converting enzyme, 13.6 U/L; soluble interleukin-2 receptor, 684 U/mL; and T-SPOT was negative. 

Magnetic resonance imaging showed an isointense, homogenously enhancing enlargement of the pituitary gland and stalk with extension into the cavernous sinus and the planum sphenoidale dura, without compression of the optic chiasm. No other intracranial lesions were identified. Autoimmune hypophysitis related to immune checkpoint inhibition was suspected, and the patient was started on glucocorticoids and thyroid hormone replacement. 

One month later, he returned with new right-eye visual impairment (visual acuity 20/200) attributed to invasion of the optic canal. Pulse corticosteroid therapy was administered as a diagnostic treatment. Repeat MRI showed no clear reduction in the pituitary lesion, and he subsequently developed a right oculomotor nerve palsy.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Pituitary metastasis of salivary gland carcinoma mimicking hypophysitis: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old man with chronic hypertension and gout presented to the emergency department with acute-onset chest tightness and a burning sensation radiating from the chest into both upper extremities, accompanied by sensory impairment at the T4 (nipple) level. Minutes after arrival, he developed bilateral arm weakness. He reported receiving a fourth dose of the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine three weeks earlier. Cardiovascular and vascular etiologies were excluded on initial evaluation.

Over the next few hours, his left lower extremity strength declined from 5 to 2 on Lovett’s scale, followed by progressive weakening of the right lower limb (to 3/5) and both upper limbs (to 3/5). Cervical spine MRI revealed an inflammatory focus centrally at C5–C6 without contrast enhancement; brain and thoracic spine MRI were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed elevated protein (0.91 g/L) and albumin (656.7 mg/L) levels without intrathecal oligoclonal band synthesis. CSF culture and PCR for pathogens were negative. Serum aquaporin-4 antibody was negative. Anti–myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibody titers were 1:10 on October 13 and <1:10 on October 18. A connective-tissue–disorder workup was unremarkable.
title: Case Report: The Rehabilitation of a Patient with Acute Transverse Myelitis after COVID-19 Vaccination

case_prompt:
A 77-year-old overweight woman presented with a 4-hour history of abdominal pain and rhythmic abdominal wall and bilateral lower limb jerking movements after she forcefully pulled a blanket toward her with her left arm while supine. Her history was notable for mild cognitive impairment, a hiatus hernia, and Factor V Leiden deficiency. Three months earlier, she had undergone implantation of a dual-lead permanent pacemaker for recurrent syncope due to sinus node dysfunction.

On arrival, she denied chest pain, presyncope, or heart-failure symptoms. Examination revealed a pulsating contraction of the abdominal wall; the lower-limb jerking had ceased. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. A computed tomography aortogram excluded the suspected diagnosis of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. A chest radiograph demonstrated displacement of both pacemaker leads, with the atrial lead migrated to the superior vena cava and the ventricular lead within the right atrium. Electrocardiography showed intermittent atrial pacing, under-sensing of the ventricular lead, ventricular pacing spikes occurring after the QRS complexes, and absence of ventricular capture. The rhythmic 60-beats-per-minute abdominal contractions resolved after deactivation of the pacemaker.
title: Reel syndrome, a diagnostic conundrum: a case report

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of progressive leg weakness. He reported right foot slap and tripping on uneven ground, later developing bilateral foot drop, exercise-related leg fatigue, and mild difficulty climbing stairs or rising from a low chair. There was no bulbar or upper-limb involvement. He also described sensory loss in both feet to mid-shin level with mild superficial dysesthesia. A prior workup suggested bilateral L5 radiculopathy, but lumbar MRI was normal.

On examination, there was no obvious muscle atrophy. Manual strength testing revealed isolated distal lower-limb weakness: ankle dorsiflexion 2/5 on the right, 4–/5 on the left; inversion and eversion 4/5; plantar flexion difficulty when standing on toes. Hip girdle and thigh strength were 5/5. Pinprick and light-touch sensation were reduced in a length-dependent distribution; vibration and proprioception were intact. Reflexes were 1+ in the upper limbs and absent at the knees and ankles.

Laboratory studies showed normal CBC, vitamin B12, TSH, serum protein electrophoresis, hemoglobin A1c, paraneoplastic antibodies, and renal and liver function tests. Creatine kinase was mildly elevated at 508 U/L. A 30-gene Charcot–Marie–Tooth panel was negative. Because EMG showed myotonic potentials, genetic testing for myotonic dystrophy types 1 and 2 was performed and was negative.

Nerve conduction studies revealed mildly reduced peroneal and tibial CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities. Sensory nerve conduction studies were within normal limits. Needle EMG demonstrated fibrillations, positive sharp waves, and polyphasic, long-duration motor-unit potentials with reduced recruitment in the tibialis anterior (most prominent) and gastrocnemius. Prominent myotonic discharges were also noted in several muscles. The biceps brachii and vastus lateralis were normal. Overall, these findings were interpreted as consistent with a predominantly motor length-dependent polyneuropathy.
title: Myofibrillar Myopathy Mimicking Polyneuropathy

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man with a 7-year history of refractory anemia–type myelodysplastic syndrome presented in 2008 with macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 114 fL), a normal white-cell count, normal platelets, and a low reticulocyte count; B12, folate, TSH, and liver function tests were normal, and bone marrow biopsy showed refractory anemia with blasts <5%. By 2011, his hemoglobin fell to 7.0 g/dL and platelets to 50,000/µL despite normal vitamin and thyroid studies; repeat marrow showed hypercellularity with dysplasia, blasts <5%, and a normal karyotype. He required monthly red-cell transfusions to maintain a hemoglobin >8 g/dL and occasional platelet transfusions. 

In October 2013, he noted painless gross hematuria. His hemoglobin was 7.5 g/dL, platelets 13,000/µL, and coagulation studies were normal. CT urography revealed a 16 mm lobulated lesion near the left ureteral orifice. With transfusional support, cystoscopy demonstrated five superficial bladder tumors; transurethral resection showed low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma without invasion. After resection, transfusion requirements decreased but did not resolve. 

Beginning March 2015, he received intravesical BCG (weekly ×6, biweekly ×4, then monthly ×12). While receiving BCG, his hemoglobin rose to 13.7 g/dL, platelets to 317,000/µL, and he became transfusion independent.
title: Transitory Spontaneous Remission of Myelodysplasia in an Elderly Man while Receiving Intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin for Bladder Cancer: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, stroke, and hypothyroidism presented with altered mental status, nausea, multiple episodes of nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting, and dizziness. She reported a three-month history of intermittent night sweats, diffuse body aches, and 10 lb of unintentional weight loss. She denied fever, chills, respiratory symptoms, excessive dairy or antacid use, recent travel, or sick contacts. Her medications included vitamin D supplements, last taken three months earlier. 

On admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed dry oral mucosa and multiple painless, mobile, firm lymph nodes measuring 2–3 cm in the left anterior cervical region, right axilla, and right inguinal area. 

Initial laboratories showed: microcytic anemia, monocytosis, acute kidney injury with a prerenal pattern (BUN/creatinine ratio > 20), hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, and a serum calcium level of 16.5 mg/dL (corrected to 16.7 mg/dL). She was started on intravenous saline, calcitonin, and bisphosphonates. 

Further evaluation of her hypercalcemia revealed:  
• PTH at the lower limit of normal  
• PTHrP within normal range  
• 25-hydroxyvitamin D at the high end of normal  
• 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D elevated
title: Unforeseen Hodgkin Lymphoma Hidden behind Hypercalcemia

case_prompt: A 7-month-old intact female Maine Coon kitten was evaluated for a 2-month history of severe regurgitation occurring seconds to minutes after eating or drinking, with episodes ranging from twice weekly to twice daily. Weight loss was noted over this period despite a normal appetite, water consumption, and activity level. Previous treatments—including maropitant, cimetidine, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, and gastrointestinal diets—had no effect. The kitten had a history of chronic vomiting of undigested food and bile from age 3–5 months and a self-resolving episode of acute vomiting at 5 months. No regurgitation or vomiting occurred before 3 months of age. On presentation, the kitten was bright, alert, weighed 2.5 kg with a body condition score of 2/9, and had stunted growth; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Thoracic radiographs obtained before and after oral contrast demonstrated severe and diffuse oesophageal dilatation consistent with generalized megaoesophagus, with persistent contrast and aeric distension of the oesophageal lumen and apparent loss of continuity between the distal oesophagus and the stomach. No aspiration pneumonia was evident.
title: Surgical treatment of a distal oesophageal stricture by mucosal radial incision and dilation in a kitten with secondary megaoesophagus

case_prompt:
A 10‐year‐old girl with a history of SLE diagnosed at age 6 (initial features: polyarthralgia, facial rash, oral ulcers; ANA 1:320; anti-dsDNA 21.3 IU/mL; normal complement; SLEDAI 9) had been well on hydroxychloroquine. She presented with a 2-day history of fever up to 39.5°C, headache, and repeated vomiting. On examination, she was alert, without focal deficits or seizures; Brudzinski’s sign was positive. 

Noncontrast head CT showed an extensive hypodensity in the left temporal lobe without edema or hemorrhage. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 29 cm H₂O, CSF WBC 485 cells/mm³ (91.7% polymorphs), protein 1526 mg/L, and glucose 3.6 mmol/L; gram stain and CSF cultures were negative. EEG demonstrated focal slowing with a sharp wave over the left posterior temporal region without epileptiform discharges. 

Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and antivirals were started, but fever and meningism persisted. Blood tests showed CRP 14.7 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/hr, C3 0.27 g/L, C4 < 0.1 g/L, ANA 1:2560, and anti-dsDNA > 300 IU/mL. Anti-NMDA, anti-NMO, and anti-MOG antibodies were negative, as were lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies. Multiplex PCR and antigen tests for common meningitis pathogens, plus specific viral, mycobacterial, and fungal studies, were all negative.

Brain MRI revealed T2-weighted hyperintensity in the left temporal subcortical and deep white matter with mild cortical swelling; susceptibility-weighted imaging showed petechial hemorrhages. MRA and MRV were normal, and MR spectroscopy showed no lactate peak.
title: Aseptic Meningitis and White Matter Disease in Childhood-Onset Neuropsychiatric Lupus

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old Caucasian man with an eight-year history of well-controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus (average blood glucose 150 mg/dL; hemoglobin A₁c 7.5%) presented with a three-month history of an unintended 22-pound weight loss. He denied abdominal pain, diarrhea, changes in diet or exercise, palpitations, heat intolerance, neck soreness, or other thyroid-related symptoms. His diabetes regimen (insulin pump plus pramlintide) and glycemic control were unchanged. 

On examination, he was well-nourished and in no distress. Blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/minute. There was no lid lag, proptosis, thyroid enlargement, tenderness, cervical lymphadenopathy, or tremor. 

Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, electrolytes, liver and kidney function. Thyroid studies revealed a suppressed TSH level of 0.033 mIU/L (reference 0.4–5.0 mIU/L) and a free thyroxine level of 33 pmol/L (reference 7.7–15.4 pmol/L). An anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody was elevated at 13.2 SD (normal <2.0 SD). A thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) assay was undetectable. Serum thyroglobulin was within the normal range.
title: Hyperthyroidism from autoimmune thyroiditis in a man with type 1 diabetes mellitus: a case report

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old woman from Eastern Nepal presented with a 10-day history of painful erythematous nodules along the radial border of her left hand, forearm, and arm, and a 5-day history of swelling of the left hand. For the preceding 10 months, she had been treated with oral corticosteroids, methotrexate, and hydroxychloroquine for presumed pain in the left arm and forearm. She denied any antecedent trauma.
