On examination, there were six tender, warm, erythematous nodules in a linear distribution along the radial border of the left upper extremity, with edema extending from the proximal third of the fingers to the wrist joint. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Laboratory investigations revealed a normal complete blood count, blood glucose, chest radiograph, urine microscopy, and serum cortisol. C-reactive protein was elevated; rheumatoid factor and serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. Liver transaminases were mildly elevated (1.6× upper limit of normal), and vitamin D level was low. A wound swab culture was sterile, and a microfilaria test was negative.

An incisional skin biopsy was performed and sent for histopathology and tissue culture for bacteria and fungi. Histopathological examination showed lymphohistiocytic infiltrates admixed with neutrophils and activated macrophages forming epithelioid aggregates and ill-defined granulomas, with acid-fast bacilli on staining. A slit-skin smear for Mycobacterium leprae and sputum examination for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Culture of the biopsy specimen yielded no growth.
title: Sporotrichoid lymphocutaneous pattern in a fish‐merchant under immunosuppressant medications: Clues to differential diagnoses

case_prompt: A 27-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks and 6 days’ gestation presented three hours after an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery following a second stage of labor lasting 2 hours and 22 minutes. She complained of constant central chest pain and shortness of breath on standing. Her heart rate was 120–145 beats per minute; blood pressure was 130/75 mmHg; respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute; oxygen saturation 98% on room air; she was afebrile. On examination, subcutaneous emphysema was palpable over both clavicles and into her neck; chest auscultation revealed good bilateral air entry. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia. A venous blood gas sample showed pH 7.416, pO₂ 47 mmHg, lactate 4.59 mmol/L, and HCO₃⁻ 19.6 mmol/L. A chest X-ray demonstrated pneumomediastinum with subcutaneous emphysema at the base of the neck and no visible pneumothorax. A computed tomography pulmonary angiogram excluded pulmonary embolism, showed pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema within the neck and right chest wall, and revealed no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.
title: Pneumomediastinum following a prolonged second stage of labor – an emphasis on early diagnosis and conservative management: a case report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old girl was admitted with a 12-hour history of pulsatile frontal headache accompanied by nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. One hour after headache onset, she developed diplopia, difficulty adducting the right eye, dysarthria, and subtle imbalance. She had a history of migraine with visual aura since age 10: episodes of scotomas, blurred or tunnel vision lasting up to 60 minutes, with complete resolution, but no prior diplopia or ataxia. She denied fever, other neurologic complaints, or use of oral contraceptives.

On examination, she was tachycardic, blood pressure was 150/80 mmHg, and temperature was normal. Neurologic examination showed right-eye adduction paresis on left gaze, binocular diplopia, slow saccadic abduction of the left eye with horizontal nystagmus, and preserved convergence. Other cranial nerves were intact. Strength, sensation, and reflexes were symmetric. In standing, she swayed backward (worse with eyes closed). She had an ataxic gait with a leftward fall tendency. Diadochokinesis and the finger-to-nose test were normal, but the left heel-shin test was dysmetric. 

Noncontrast head CT and CT angiography were normal. On hospital day 2, headache and nausea improved but diplopia persisted. Brain MRI demonstrated a focus of diffusion restriction in the paramedian right dorsal midbrain, corresponding to the ipsilateral medial longitudinal fasciculus, with T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity and no contrast enhancement.
title: Migrainous infarction: a rare and often overlooked diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with hypothyroidism and cochlear hydrops took nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for presumed uncomplicated urinary urgency and frequency. She had no prior exposure to nitrofurantoin. 

In less than 24 hours, she developed abrupt fever (101.7 °F), chills, lightheadedness, chest congestion, pleuritic chest pain, generalized weakness, and hypotension (90/51 mm Hg). In the emergency department, she received 2 L normal saline, ceftriaxone IV, ondansetron, and had blood and urine cultures drawn.  
– WBC 17.1 × 10^3/µL (83% neutrophils, 9% bands)  
– Lactate 1.4 mmol/L  
– CMP notable only for K^+ 3.4 mmol/L  
– Urinalysis: 2+ blood, trace leukocyte esterase, 5–10 WBCs, 0–4 RBCs, 1+ bacteria  

She was discharged on levofloxacin for suspected acute pyelonephritis. All symptoms resolved within 24 hours, and she completed 7 days of levofloxacin.

Two months later, she again took nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for similar urinary complaints. Within 24 hours she developed fever (102.6 °F), chills, myalgias, pleuritis, weakness, nausea, vomiting, hypotension (80 mm Hg systolic), and tachycardia (120 beats/min), with a positive tilt test but no rash or urticaria. She received 2 L normal saline and was again prescribed levofloxacin after blood and urine cultures were obtained.  
– WBC 22 × 10^3/µL (94% granulocytes)  
– Urinalysis: 500 leu/µL, 250 ery/µL  
– CMP notable only for K^+ 3.2 mmol/L
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome Secondary to Nitrofurantoin

case_prompt:
A 3-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of left thigh swelling. The swelling was insidious, progressive, and painful—worse at night and aggravated by movement—and was accompanied by fever, local warmth, weight loss, and anorexia. There was no abdominal pain.  
On radiographs of the left femur, there was an ill-defined expansile lytic lesion of the diaphysis and distal metaphysis with lamellated (“onion-peel”) and focal sunburst periosteal reactions; no fracture was seen.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7220 cells/µL, hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, hematocrit 24%, platelets 190,000/µL, C-reactive protein 81.5 mg/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 468 U/L.  
High-resolution ultrasonography of the thigh revealed a vascular soft-tissue mass with spiculated sunburst periosteal reaction.  
A provisional diagnosis of a primary bone tumor was made.
title: Metastatic Neuroblastoma Masquerading as Ewing’s Sarcoma on X-ray: An Imaging Puzzle in Pediatric Oncology

case_prompt: An 85-year-old woman was admitted with acute abdominal pain. Laboratory tests showed elevated cholestasis parameters and a C-reactive protein level of 99 mg/dL (reference <5 mg/dL). She was treated empirically for suspected acute cholecystitis with cefuroxim and metronidazole, but her abdominal symptoms improved only moderately. During her hospitalization, she reported diffuse pain attacks, malaise, and fatigue. She then developed bizarrely shaped, violaceous, figure-like patches on the right side of her neck that did not disappear with diascopy. She also complained of a new right-sided headache, scalp tenderness, intermittent blurred vision in the right eye, and rushing sensations in her ears. Ophthalmologic examination revealed anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated leukocytosis (12.2 × 10^9/L; reference 3.6–10.5 × 10^9/L) and persistently elevated C-reactive protein.
title: Localized livedo racemosa as an indicator for giant cell arteritis

case_prompt: A 41-year-old Iranian woman with no known immunodeficiency presented with a 10-month history of slowly enlarging, crusted, painful ulcerative lesions on her lower lip. She had no history of smoking, alcohol, opium use, trauma, cosmetic lip tattooing, or burns. She had intermittent bronchitis treated with a corticosteroid nasal spray. On examination, there was an ill-demarcated, tender, thick-crusted ulcer measuring 3 × 1 cm on the lower lip, which discharged fluid when pressed. There were no signs of onychomycosis or interdigital intertrigo; she was afebrile, with no lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of her exam was unremarkable. HIV antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody tests were negative. An upper endoscopy performed for dysphagia was normal. Despite local wound care, topical antifungal and antimicrobial therapies, and empiric immunosuppressive and antibiotic treatments, the ulcer worsened. Clinical differential diagnoses included squamous cell carcinoma, other malignant lesions, ulcerative leishmaniasis, ulcerative mycobacterial infection, erosive lichen planus, immunobullous disorders, and opportunistic fungal infection. Two incisional biopsies of the lip lesion showed parakeratotic hyperkeratosis, severe acanthosis, spongiosis, exocytosis of inflammatory cells in the epidermis, and a mixed dermal infiltrate without evidence of malignant transformation. Direct immunofluorescence was negative for immunobullous diseases. A direct smear for leishmaniasis was negative, and the nitroblue tetrazolium test was normal.
title: Fusarium proliferatum-induced chronic lip ulcer: successful treatment with itraconazole: a case report

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old woman, a former health professional with a history of treated depression and a prolactin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma managed by transsphenoidal surgery in 2010 (with normalization of prolactin and no glucocorticoid replacement), presented in 2013 with episodic features of Cushing syndrome, including weight gain, new-onset hypertension, and diabetes.  
Laboratory evaluation using chemiluminescence immunoassay showed a 24-hour urinary total cortisol of 12 200 μg/24 h (normal 50–310 μg/24 h) but a normal morning serum cortisol of 12 μg/dL (normal 5–25 μg/dL). Midnight salivary cortisol by ELISA was elevated above the normal range. Plasma ACTH was 14 pg/mL (normal 10–46 pg/mL), and serum DHEA-S was low at 208 ng/mL (normal 988–3400 ng/mL). Abdominal CT revealed normal adrenal glands. A pituitary MRI showed a 1–2 cm cystic lesion in the sella, described as similar to her prior tumor but also possibly an arachnoid cyst. The patient denied any use of exogenous glucocorticoids.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?
title:
RETRACTED ARTICLE: Fatal factitious Cushing
syndrome (Münchhausen’s syndrome) in a patient with macroprolactinoma and silent
corticotrophinoma: case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 70-year-old man with a history of clear cell renal cell carcinoma treated by nephrectomy and multiple prior lines of therapy for spinal metastases was started on axitinib 5 mg twice daily for progressive disease. Ten days later, he reported severe fatigue; a complete blood count showed a platelet count of 4 × 10^9/L (baseline 245 × 10^9/L). Axitinib was discontinued, and he was admitted for evaluation. Viral serologies (hepatitis, CMV, HIV) were negative; renal and hepatic function were normal. Prothrombin time, INR, activated partial thromboplastin time, fibrinogen, and D-dimer levels were normal. Direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. ADAMTS13 activity was 42.5% (normal > 10%). The serotonin-release assay was normal (<1). Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a spleen of normal size. Bone marrow biopsy was normocellular, without metastatic disease or increased blasts, and showed a normal proportion of megakaryocytes. He received six units of platelet transfusions, but the platelet count remained between 12 and 15 × 10^9/L.
title: A Case Report with Severe Thrombocytopenia Induced by Axitinib

case_prompt:
– A 72-year-old man with a 12-year history of idiopathic Parkinson disease presented with progressively worsening low back pain.  
– Eight years earlier, he developed chronic back pain aggravated by movement, which became associated with bilateral radicular leg pain and weakness.  
– His past medical history included coronary artery disease, a pacemaker, and hemochromatosis.  
– Neurologic examination showed 3/5 strength in the right L4 and L5 myotomes and hypoesthesia in the L4 dermatome.  
– Electromyography demonstrated irritation of the right L4, L5, and S1 nerve roots.  
– He underwent L3–L5 laminectomies for presumed degenerative lumbar stenosis, with only transient relief; six months later, low back pain and right leg pain recurred with right foot drop.  
– Over the next three years, medical therapy and epidural corticosteroid injections failed to provide lasting benefit, and thoracolumbar kyphosis developed.  
– Plain radiographs revealed extensive destruction and collapse of the L2 vertebral body with paravertebral hypertrophic ossifications at the superior margin of the prior laminectomy.  
– Dynamic radiographs showed gross instability at L2–L3.  
– Computed tomography of the spine demonstrated severe lateral dislocation of the L2–L3 articulation and a reduction in the local kyphosis angle.
title: Charcot Spine and Parkinson's Disease

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old man presented with several years of incomplete bladder emptying. He denied dysuria, hematuria, incontinence, weight loss, or bone pain.  
On CT urography, there was a 13.4 × 10.6 × 13.0 cm thick-walled, predominantly cystic pelvic mass with solid-enhancing mural nodules located inferior to the bladder. No lymphadenopathy or distant metastases were noted. He was started on tamsulosin and referred for further evaluation.  
An ultrasound-guided needle biopsy of the mass showed bland smooth muscle cells with no cytologic atypia, no necrosis, and mitotic activity <1/50 high-power fields, consistent with leiomyoma. Active surveillance with a CT in 3 months was recommended.  
Three months later, he presented with urinary retention requiring catheterization. Repeat CT showed slight increase in tumor size. His AUA symptom index was 35. Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) performed 2 weeks later again showed leiomyoma.  
Over the next 2 years, his PSA remained 1.13 ng/mL, and his creatinine rose to 1.4 mg/dL. MRI of the pelvis demonstrated a well-marginated, complex solid, cystic, and septated mass with multiple enhancing areas and restricted diffusion, appearing to communicate with the bladder neck.  
The patient opted for surgical excision of the mass.
title: Leiomyosarcoma of the prostate: a novel approach to treatment—case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old obese woman with chronic migraines, recurrent sinusitis, and allergic rhinitis presented for evaluation of a possible sinus infection. She reported a 2-month history of copious clear rhinorrhea, purulent postnasal drainage, and cough. She also experienced self-limiting episodes of clear nasal discharge at the onset of her menstrual cycles, each preceded by severe menstrual migraines. 

A 2-week course of antibiotics, antihistamines, and steroid nasal spray provided mild relief of her cough, but the clear rhinorrhea—more copious on the left—persisted. A subsequent 4-week trial of ipratropium nasal spray yielded little benefit. Several months prior to the current symptoms, she had developed a chronic severe pounding headache in the frontal and bitemporal regions, accompanied by tinnitus and visual disturbances; these symptoms resolved with the onset of her copious clear rhinorrhea.

Anterior rhinoscopy was unremarkable, and the patient declined nasal endoscopy. Computed tomography of the sinuses revealed an isolated air–fluid level in the left sphenoid sinus without masses, nasal obstruction, or obvious skull base defects. The patient noted that the nasal drainage worsened with lifting, bending over, and upon waking in the morning. This history and imaging prompted evaluation of the nasal fluid for cerebrospinal fluid.
title: Intermittent spontaneous CSF rhinorrhea exacerbated by hormonal fluctuations associated with menstrual cycles

case_prompt:
An otherwise healthy 8-year-old Bajau boy from Malaysia was evaluated for gradually developing pigmentation over his nails and mucosa. Over the past two years, he noted longitudinal and diffuse melanonychia of all fingernails and toenails. Over the past year, he also developed discrete, asymptomatic brown-black macules on the lower lip and tongue and a well-defined pigmented macule on the nasal aspect of the right sclera. He denied fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, palpitations, or other systemic symptoms. There was no relevant medication history, no consanguinity, and no family history of pigmentary disorders or intestinal polyposis. 

On examination, all 20 nails showed longitudinal melanonychia without dystrophy. There were multiple brown-black macules on the tongue and lower lip, and a single pigmented macule on the right sclera. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, liver function tests, serum cortisol, and adrenocorticotropic hormone—were all within normal limits. Chest radiograph, abdominal ultrasound, electrocardiogram, and echocardiography were unremarkable. The patient had undergone esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy eight months earlier, both of which yielded normal findings.
title: Laugier–Hunziker Syndrome in an 8-Year-Old Boy with Scleral Melanocytosis, Lingual Pigmentation, Labial Pigmentation, and Melanonychia Striata

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old G1P1 Hispanic woman presented with 3 months of gradually worsening left breast pain, swelling, chills, night sweats, skin discoloration, and a self-detected mass. Five years earlier she had a similar left-breast episode that resolved spontaneously. Three months before presentation, she was diagnosed elsewhere with mastitis and treated with meloxicam and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. She is on norgestimate/ethinyl estradiol and has no tobacco, alcohol, or family history of cancer.

On examination, vital signs were normal. The left breast showed a nodular mass in the outer quadrants with brownish discoloration and edema, but no nipple discharge, peau d’orange, or regional lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies (CBC, LFTs, renal function, urinalysis, serologies, lipid panel) were normal.

A 3D mammogram and targeted ultrasound were reported as BI-RADS 5, highly suspicious for malignancy. A percutaneous needle biopsy showed no invasive carcinoma but revealed fibrohistiocytic and florid inflammatory reactions with multinucleated giant cells. One week later she developed an abscess at the biopsy site; incision and drainage were performed, cultures were negative, and tuberculosis testing was negative. She remained on TMP–SMX and NSAIDs.

An incisional (wedge and Tru-Cut) biopsy of the breast mass showed granulomatous inflammation of the lobules with well-formed granulomas and multinucleated giant cells. Periodic acid–Schiff and Grocott’s methenamine silver stains were negative for fungi, a special acid-fast stain showed no organisms, and Gram stain showed no bacteria.
title: Red flags for the differential diagnosis of granulomatous mastitis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old woman with a history of intermittent headaches and a half–pack-per-day smoking habit presented with subacute intermittent right-sided hemi–body numbness and recurrent transient word-finding difficulties. She had an intrauterine device, was not taking oral contraceptives, and reported multiple sexual partners; her last syphilis screen 6 years earlier had been negative. On arrival, her blood pressure was 138/50 mm Hg; during hospitalization it ranged from the 90s to the 130s systolic. Neurologic examination revealed expressive aphasia, dysarthria, and decreased fine-touch sensation over the right forearm. 

Noncontrast head CT showed ill-defined hypodensities in the left posterior parietal lobe with hemorrhagic transformation and additional hypodensities in the left frontal lobe. CT angiography demonstrated focal moderate-to-severe stenosis of the left M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery. Brain MRI with and without contrast revealed numerous diffusion-restricted foci involving both white and gray matter of the left cerebral hemisphere, with correlating FLAIR hyperintensity suggestive of acute to subacute infarcts, some with hemorrhagic transformation; a left basal ganglia focal enhancing lesion with T1 hyperintensity and no diffusion restriction was also noted. 

Routine stroke workup, including transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study, 48-hour Holter monitoring, and laboratory tests (CBC with differential, serum electrolytes, CRP, ESR, and liver function tests), was normal. Given her young age and unusual presentation, vasculopathy versus vasculitis was suspected; HIV and Lyme disease antibody screening, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), proteinase 3 (PR3), myeloperoxidase (MPO), and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies were all negative. She was started on verapamil for concern of reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS). 

Diagnostic cerebral angiography showed a distal left M1 segment stenosis with partial improvement in caliber after administration of 10 mg of intra-arterial verapamil.
title: Neurosyphilis presenting with focal middle cerebral artery stenosis and acute ischemic stroke: A case report

case_prompt: A 31-year-old Mestizo-Mexican woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of asthenia, adynamia, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, food intolerance, impaired visual acuity, and abdominal pain. Fifteen years earlier, she had episodes of idiopathic pancreatitis with normal exocrine and endocrine function between ages 12 and 16. More recently, she developed alopecia, malar rash, and oral ulcers; a skin biopsy indicated discoid lupus. One week later she had focal motor seizures and was diagnosed with neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE; SLEDAI 18). Initial therapy included three daily 1-g doses of intravenous methylprednisolone, followed by discharge on chloroquine, levetiracetam, phenytoin, lorazepam, a tapering prednisone regimen (initially 1 mg/kg daily), and monthly cyclophosphamide boluses. Seven days after the sixth cyclophosphamide dose, examination revealed tachycardia (125 beats/min), tachypnea (27 breaths/min), drowsiness, dehydration, a normal body-mass index, and no dermatologic stigmata of insulin resistance. Laboratory evaluation showed: serum glucose 1240 mg/dl, sodium 127 mEq/L, potassium 5.56 mEq/L, chloride 86 mEq/L, arterial pH 7.07, bicarbonate 3.0 mmol/L, urinary ketones 80 mg/dl, effective serum osmolarity 322.8 mOsm/kg, and anion gap 43.56. Liver tests, amylase, and lipase were normal. Fluid resuscitation with 0.9% saline and continuous intravenous insulin infusion was initiated.
title: Difficult-to-diagnose diabetes in a patient treated with cyclophosphamide – the contradictory roles of immunosuppressant agents: a case report

case_prompt: A 74-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of dyspnea and bilateral chest pain, continuous and worse on exertion; she denied cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Her past medical history included glaucoma, hip arthrosis, and cystocele repair. She was a non-smoker with no relevant exposures. Medications: boric acid and timolol eye drops. Physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed WBC 4860/μl, hemoglobin 133 g/l, platelets 205 000/μl, normal PT and aPTT, D-dimer 5360 ng/ml, calcium 2.35 mEq/l, albumin 4.3 U/l, potassium 4.3 mEq/l, CRP 3.4 mg/l, creatinine 0.852 mg/dl, LDH 306 UI/l, and normal liver tests. Chest radiography revealed multiple bilateral nodules. CT pulmonary angiography confirmed bilateral pulmonary emboli and multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, some calcified, the largest measuring 35 mm in the right middle lobe. She was anticoagulated with enoxaparin. Flexible bronchoscopy was normal; bronchoalveolar lavage was nondiagnostic, with no AFB on microscopy and negative cultures for bacteria, nocardia, mycobacteria, and fungus. CT-guided lung biopsy demonstrated amorphous eosinophilic material with surrounding plasma cells and no neoplastic cells. 18F-FDG PET-CT showed intense uptake in all pulmonary nodules (SUVmax 8.8) without hypermetabolic lesions elsewhere. Autoimmune serologies were negative (ANA, ANCA); ACE was normal. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis were normal, but immunofixation revealed an isolated monoclonal kappa IgM. Bone marrow biopsy showed 3% plasma cells and 9% lymphocytes with slightly reduced cellularity. Pulmonary function tests and arterial blood gases were normal.
title: Pulmonary nodules associated with pulmonary embolism: A rare and misleading presentation of amyloidosis

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man presented with a several-year history of purple spots on both feet that gradually increased in number and size. He had well-controlled hypertension for 10 years. Dermatologic examination revealed multiple purple-colored plaques and papules, 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter, some with crusted surfaces on the dorsum of the feet and around the ankles. He had no systemic symptoms, lymphadenopathy, or visceral involvement. Laboratory and serologic tests, including HIV-1 serology, were unremarkable. A punch biopsy was obtained from a lesion on the dorsum of his foot.

Histopathological examination of hematoxylin and eosin–stained sections showed a dilated, blood-filled vascular proliferation lined by flattened endothelium, extending from the papillary dermis under hyperkeratotic epidermis to the reticular dermis in a lobular pattern. A few thick-walled vessels were interspersed within predominantly thin-walled vascular spaces. Hemosiderin pigment was noted in vessel walls and surrounding stroma. Chronic inflammatory cells were present, and focal areas of immature vascular structures forming clefts, containing extravasated erythrocytes, and mild endothelial cytologic atypia were identified, especially in the papillary dermis. No spindle cell proliferation was observed.
title: Cavernous Hemangioma-Like Kaposi Sarcoma: Histomorphologic Features and Differential Diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 21-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of dry skin and generalized spiny skin lesions. She had been treated empirically for eczema with a medium-strength topical corticosteroid without improvement. She had no other medical problems, medications, atopy, allergies, or family history of similar skin findings.

On examination, she had multiple minute, digitate, folliculocentric hyperkeratotic papules symmetrically involving the face, neck, trunk, and upper extremities. There was no perilesional erythema, palmoplantar keratoderma, scarring, alopecia, or signs of nutritional deficiency.

A 3-mm punch biopsy from the back showed keratin plugs in hair follicle infundibula, sparse perifollicular lymphocytes, and cystic spaces in the outer root sheath of hair follicles and sebaceous glands. Alcian blue–periodic acid–Schiff stain highlighted mucin within these spaces. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated CD3- and predominantly CD4-positive small T lymphocytes, few CD8-positive T cells, and inconspicuous CD20-positive B cells and CD30-positive cells. T-cell receptor gene-rearrangement testing failed for technical reasons.
title: Generalized lichen spinulosus and secondary follicular mucinosis

case_prompt: A 23-year-old previously healthy Caucasian man presented with a 4-day history of confusion, extreme restlessness, and diffuse cognitive deficits. He developed aggressive self-harming behavior, paranoia, suicidal thoughts, and motor restlessness. He had no history of substance use or psychiatric illness and no recent infection or vaccination. On examination he was afebrile (37.1°C), with normal vital signs. Neurologic exam revealed decreased motor function of the right lower extremity and an ataxic gait; there were no signs of myopathy. Mental status testing showed agnosia, inability to recognize his mother or girlfriend, unreal and irrelevant thoughts, and increased latency when answering. Initial laboratory studies showed normal hematology, electrolytes, infection markers, and thyroid tests (including thyroid antibodies). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 5 mononuclear leukocytes, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, protein 0.56 g/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, normal IgG levels, and negative oligoclonal bands; PCR for herpesviruses and Borrelia was negative, and CMV IgG was negative. CT of the head showed multiple low-density lesions without hemorrhage, ischemia, or mass effect. MRI of the brain demonstrated multiple fulminant contrast-enhancing ovoid lesions—both nodular and ring-enhancing—in both cerebral hemispheres (including the callososeptal interface) and in the left pons and medulla oblongata, raising suspicion for acute demyelination (eg, ADEM or MS), malignancy, or neuroinfection. MRI of the cervicothoracic spine showed no lesions.
title: A case report revealing acute onset psychosis and cognitive impairment as primary manifestation in relapsing‐remitting multiple sclerosis

case_prompt:
A 10-year-old spayed female domestic shorthair cat was evaluated for a 2-day history of anorexia, vomiting and lethargy. There was a 1-year history of suspected weight loss and intermittent reduced appetite. The cat had outdoor access, was up to date on vaccines and anthelmintics, and was fed a commercial diet. On presentation the cat was lethargic but alert; body condition score was 4/9. Vital signs showed mild tachycardia (200 beats/min), and there was mild diffuse discomfort on abdominal palpation.

Complete blood count was within reference intervals, but blood smear evaluation showed toxic and hyposegmented neutrophils. Serum biochemistry revealed a severe elevation in alanine transaminase activity (456 U/l; RI 12–130), mild hyperglobulinaemia (53 g/l; RI 28–51), moderate hyperbilirubinaemia (14 µmol/l; RI 2–6) and a severe elevation in serum amyloid A (138.6 µg/ml; RI 0–12).

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a diffusely hypoechoic liver with thickening and dilation of the intrahepatic biliary tract and cystic duct. In the common bile duct, a hyperechoic spindle-shaped structure measuring 12 × 2.5 mm with linear interfaces and mild acoustic shadowing was seen. A second linear hyperechoic structure extended into the duodenal papilla without distal common bile duct dilation. Severe gallbladder wall thickening (2.1 mm) consistent with cholecystitis was also noted. The ultrasonographic appearance of the two spindle-shaped structures was suggestive of vegetal foreign bodies (grass awns) or a conglomerate of biliary sludge; biliary worms were deemed unlikely given the geographical location.

Fine-needle aspirates of liver and bile showed rare plasmacytes and lymphocytes in liver tissue and septic suppurative inflammation in bile. Culture of bile yielded Escherichia coli sensitive to marbofloxacin, doxycycline, amoxicillin and sulfatrimethoprim. The cat was hospitalized for IV fluids, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, antiemetics, analgesia and assisted enteral feeding.

Despite 8 days of treatment, the cat remained lethargic and anorexic. Repeat biochemistry showed persistent elevations in liver enzymes and the development of severe ionized hypercalcaemia (1.87 mmol/l; RI 1.1–1.4) with an increased phosphorus concentration. Follow-up ultrasound supported retrograde migration of the spindle-shaped structures within the biliary tract.
title: Ionised hypercalcaemia in a cat with extrahepatic biliary tract obstruction secondary to a bile duct vegetal foreign body

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old boy of Brazilian descent with autism presented with an 8-month history of painful oral ulcers. He had a one‐time perianal ulcer, folliculitis on his scalp and buttocks, intermittent fever, and bloody stools. He had no genital ulcers. He was initially treated as PFAPA with steroids, but symptoms recurred when steroids were tapered. Family history was noncontributory.

On examination, he had multiple large oral ulcers on the tongue, palate, and lips. Abdominal examination was normal, with no tenderness or masses; there were no perianal ulcers, arthritis, or other skin findings. An extensive workup for systemic lupus erythematosus, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, tuberculosis, cyclic neutropenia, primary immunodeficiencies, and periodic fever syndromes was unremarkable. Ophthalmological examination was negative, with no pathergy. Buccal biopsies showed chronic inflammation with granulation tissue, no granulomas, and grew Fusobacterium periodontium.

Prometheus IBD sgi testing demonstrated a pattern consistent with Crohn’s disease (positive anti-A4-Fa2 IgG, anti-Fax IgG, ATG16L1 heterozygous, NKX2-3 heterozygous, ICAM-1, SAA 179, elevated CRP; ASCA and ANCA negative). Multiple endoscopies and colonoscopies with ileal intubation were negative. Capsule endoscopy, CT of the abdomen, and MRI enterography showed no abnormalities.

Despite treatment with steroids, colchicine, infliximab, and methotrexate—later escalated to high-dose infliximab—the patient’s bloody stools worsened and he developed severe malnutrition (BMI z-score −2.38). At month 18, a fourth colonoscopy revealed large, round ulcers in the terminal ileum with granulation tissue and chronic inflammatory infiltrates, but no granulomas or cobblestoning.

Treatment was switched to ustekinumab, after which gastrointestinal symptoms improved. At month 19, he developed bilateral hip effusions and later presented with headaches, emesis, and fevers. A lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 39 cm H2O; brain MRI/MRA/MRV revealed extensive thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, and proximal right transverse sinus. A hypercoagulability panel was negative.
title: A Challenging Case of Oral Ulcers and Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Crohn's or Behçet's Disease

case_prompt: A 53-year-old woman had a 3-year history of a burning sensation in her mouth and esophagus, leading to a 50-pound weight loss, followed by the development of skin lesions. On examination, there was diffuse intense erythema of the oral mucosa—most pronounced on the gingiva and cheeks—with a reddish, glazed tongue without atrophy and a crusted cheilitis. There was also diffuse vulvar erythema and an anal marisca. The skin of the trunk, pubis, and limbs showed crusted, hyperkeratotic follicular plaques, open comedones, and papulopustules. Both palms and soles had well-demarcated erythematous plaques. Gastroscopy revealed linear ulcerations of the esophagus. Antifungal therapy with oral fluconazole and amphotericin B solution was ineffective. Laboratory studies showed no vitamin B12 or iron deficiency, and serum zinc levels were normal. Topical and systemic corticosteroids did not help. Colonoscopy was normal. Serum glucagon levels were normal, and pancreas CT and MRI showed no abnormalities. Direct and indirect immunofluorescence studies were negative, and antibodies against desmoglein 1 and 3, envoplakin, and periplakin were undetectable. A thoracoabdominal and pelvic CT scan was normal.
final_diagnosis_raw: folliculotropic and syringotropic CD8 mycosis fungoides
title: Folliculotropic CD8+ mycosis fungoides associated with diffuse mucosal involvement

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man presented with two days of worsening pain in the left posterior thigh associated with an enlarging mass. He reported that the mass had been slowly growing for 12 years but had only recently become painful. He denied trauma and was not on anticoagulation. On examination, there was a large, firm, tense, relatively non-tender mass in the left posterior thigh. Strength and range of motion at the knee were full, and sensation was intact distally without paresthesias.

Contrast CT and MRI of the thigh demonstrated a 16.0 × 13.7 × 17.1 cm multiloculated, cystic mass in the posterior compartment with fluid–fluid levels, a thick fibrous rim, and splaying of adjacent muscles; the femoral cortex was abutted without invasion. Proximal and distal segments of the sciatic nerve were visualized, but the nerve was not seen at the mass level. The radiology report favored a chronic hematoma.

Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded 1.8 L of serosanguinous fluid. Cultures were negative. Cytology showed scattered lymphocytes, blood clot, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages without atypical cells, again suggesting chronic hematoma. Within 48 hours, the fluid had reaccumulated.

An open irrigation and debridement with biopsy was performed. Approximately 1.5 L of bloody fluid was evacuated through a rind-like capsule, and small areas of solid hypertrophic tissue at the periphery were sampled. No large bleeding vessel was identified, but diffuse capillary oozing prompted specimen collection for pathology. A vacuum-assisted closure device was placed.

Four days later, repeat irrigation and debridement revealed another substantial blood collection despite the VAC. Two dilated, thrombosed vessels were debrided, and fibrin sealant was applied to all exposed surfaces. Two drains were placed, the hamstring was imbricated to obliterate dead space, and multilayered closure with compressive wrapping was performed.
title: Ancient Schwannoma with Hemorrhagic Degeneration Causing Chronic Intramuscular Hematoma: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man was referred for evaluation of proteinuria. He had noted occult blood in his urine since age 24. At age 37, hypertension was diagnosed, and laboratory tests showed microscopic hematuria and proteinuria of 0.4 g/g creatinine. Over the next eight years, proteinuria gradually increased to 1.16 g/g creatinine, prompting hospital admission.

He denied episodes of gross hematuria or flank pain. He was born at term; birth weight was unknown. There was no family history of kidney disease. Medications included losartan (25 mg daily), amlodipine (5 mg daily), and febuxostat (20 mg daily). He weighed 98.7 kg and was 177 cm tall (BMI 31.5 kg/m^2) and had been overweight (BMI >25) since adolescence. Blood pressure was 140/78 mm Hg.

Physical examination was unremarkable. Urinalysis showed proteinuria of 0.7 g/g creatinine, 10–19 red blood cells per high-power field, and red-cell casts. Serum creatinine was 0.69 mg/dL, cystatin C 0.74 mg/L, albumin 4.1 g/dL, uric acid 6.3 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 144 mg/dL, and HbA1c 5.5%. Estimated GFR was 97.6 mL/min/1.73 m^2. C-reactive protein, IgG, IgA, complement levels, and ANA were within normal limits. ECG and chest radiograph were normal. Renal ultrasonography showed bilaterally normal-sized kidneys with preserved cortical thickness.

With a clinical suspicion of IgA nephropathy, a kidney biopsy was performed.
title: Clinicopathological Implications of Proteinuria after Long-Term Isolated Hematuria due to Thin Basement Membrane Nephropathy and Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis

case_prompt: Ms L is a 47-year-old woman referred for respiratory assessment and flight testing because of recurrent, predictable symptoms occurring only during airplane flights. She had flown in the past without incident but, beginning in 2003, developed on five separate flights a sudden, severe, left-sided, stabbing pleuritic chest pain radiating to her back, associated with a severe tightness across her forehead and painless left arm weakness preventing her from lifting a cup. There were no facial weakness, dysphasia, visual disturbances, or arm discoloration. Symptoms began as the airplane reached cruising altitude (flights lasted 2.5–4.5 hours) and fully resolved on descent; forehead tightness occurred in only one episode, while chest pain and arm weakness were always present. She did not receive oxygen or other treatment in flight. Medical history included eczema, treated depression (fluoxetine), mild childhood asthma, and social smoking (one cigarette per month); she denied anxiety attacks or claustrophobia. Family and occupational histories were noncontributory. On examination, respiratory, cardiovascular, and neurological findings were normal; oxygen saturation was 100% on room air and did not change with posture or exertion. A chest radiograph showed a subtle reduction of vascular markings in the left mid and upper zone. CT pulmonary angiography revealed a solitary left apical bulla measuring 10×8×8 cm and mild peripheral bronchiectasis in the middle and right upper lobes. A head MRI was normal. Pulmonary function tests showed normal spirometry, normal lung volumes by helium dilution, and a normal transfer factor.
title: Recurrent inflight chest pain due to a solitary bulla

case_prompt: A woman in her 70s with longstanding mild systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)—manifested by discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp, positive anti–double‐stranded DNA antibody, and otherwise quiescent systemic disease—presented for treatment of a recalcitrant scalp lesion. Physical examination revealed a single well-demarcated red-purple scaly plaque on the scalp with follicular plugging and scarring alopecia, consistent with active DLE. No other classic DLE lesions were noted on the head or neck. On the right lower eyelid, there was a focal area of erythema involving the temporal lid margin and adjacent palpebral conjunctiva, without loss of lashes. A biopsy of the eyelid margin showed atrophic lichenoid inflammation with basement membrane thickening, consistent with a lichenoid presentation of DLE. The patient was started on hydroxychloroquine, with partial improvement of her lesions, and topical plus intralesional steroids were used for her scalp. Over the next 3 years, she experienced recurrent inflammation of the right lower eyelid accompanied by right-sided episcleritis. She ultimately developed a focal symblepharon between the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva. Because the etiology of the ongoing ocular inflammation—active mucosal DLE, friction or trauma from her prior biopsy, or another process—remained unclear, a diagnostic conjunctival biopsy of the symblepharon area was planned.
title: Cicatricial conjunctivitis secondary to discoid lupus erythematosus

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old man with a history of heart failure with recovered ejection fraction (60%), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus presented with 2 days of severe, exertional, pressure-like chest pain rated 9/10. His physical examination was unremarkable. Vital signs were: heart rate 60 bpm, blood pressure 119/58 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. Initial laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 16 g/dL, platelet count 380 K/cm3, white-cell count 8.1 K/cm3, creatinine 2 mg/dL, high-sensitivity troponin >5000 ng/L, and B-type natriuretic peptide 2810 pg/mL. He was admitted for management of non–ST–elevation myocardial infarction and started on a heparin drip and antiplatelet therapy. 

On hospital day 2, he developed severe left lower abdominal and thigh pain. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed marked swelling of the left psoas and iliacus muscles with heterogeneous density, consistent with hemorrhage. Anticoagulation and antiplatelet agents were discontinued, and a CT angiogram revealed active contrast extravasation into the left psoas muscle. Interventional radiology performed angiography, which showed no arterial source of active bleeding. After stabilization, his hemoglobin rose to 18 g/dL.
title: Polycythemia vera with acute coronary syndrome and bleeding as initial presentation: A case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 63-year-old woman with metastatic myoepithelial carcinoma of the left parotid gland, type 2 diabetes (managed with metformin until recently), hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and hypothyroidism presented for routine chemotherapy infusion and was found to have a preinfusion serum glucose level of 30 mg/dL. She reported several episodes over the past week of morning and evening confusion and tremulousness after fasting several hours; finger-stick glucometers confirmed values in the 30s and symptoms resolved with sugar-containing foods, fulfilling Whipple’s triad. Metformin had been discontinued after hypoglycemia began. On admission, renal function was normal. Liver enzymes were stably elevated, with normal bilirubin, INR, and a mildly decreased albumin. During a hypoglycemic episode (glucose 33 mg/dL), laboratory evaluation showed insulin <1 μU/mL (reference 3–25), C-peptide <0.5 ng/mL (reference 1.1–4.3), β-hydroxybutyrate <1.0 mmol/L (reference <3), and random cortisol 23 μg/dL (reference morning 8–25). Thyroid studies showed TSH 8.3 mIU/L (reference 0.3–4.7) and free T4 0.80 ng/dL (reference 0.80–1.70), and her levothyroxine dose was increased. Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) was 15 ng/mL (reference 41–279), and IGF-2 was 147 ng/mL (reference 180–580), yielding an IGF-2:IGF-1 molar ratio of 10.
title: A Case of Nonislet Cell Tumor Hypoglycemia Due to Metastatic Salivary Myoepithelial Carcinoma

case_prompt: A 58-year-old woman with no significant medical history noted a left laterocervical mass enlarging over 3 months. CT imaging showed a 25 × 28 × 44 mm laterocervical mass. In September 2019, a core-needle biopsy was reported as paraganglioma. Octreotide scintigraphy revealed uptake in the left cervical region and in the body of the stomach; endoscopic biopsies of the stomach were negative. In October 2019, the cervical mass was resected, and the initial diagnosis was extraosseous Ewing sarcoma. Upon referral, an anatomopathological review described a well-demarcated tumor composed of oval cells with clear eosinophilic cytoplasm arranged in nests separated by thin fibrous septa. Immunohistochemistry was positive for S100, SOX10, synaptophysin, and CD57; negative for Melan-A, HMB45, MITF, CD99, and multiple other markers. FISH detected an EWSR1 rearrangement that next-generation sequencing confirmed as an EWSR1-ATF1 t(12;22) fusion. A diagnosis of malignant gastrointestinal neuroectodermal tumor (GNET) was rendered. In January 2020, PET-CT showed uptake in the left laterocervical surgical bed consistent with local recurrence.
title: A Clear Cell Sarcoma Case: A Diagnostic and Treatment Challenge, with a Promising Response to Trabectedin

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old girl presented with a one-week history of persistent low-grade fever and slight cough treated with ibuprofen. A general practitioner noted an increase in abdominal girth from a giant palpable mass and referred her urgently. She reported progressive abdominal enlargement for one year, associated with intermittent mild pain; her menstrual cycles were normal. On examination, she was afebrile; there was a giant, tense, relatively mobile abdominal mass with a regular surface, an umbilical hernia, and a brown-black lesion on the right thorax. 

Abdomino-pelvic ultrasound showed a thin-walled, multilocular cystic mass occupying nearly the entire abdomen and pelvis, with transonic fluid and multiple septa; the ovaries were not visualized, and there was no free fluid. MRI demonstrated a well-defined 115 × 224 × 350 mm cystic tumor originating from the right ovary, multiloculated, containing some T1-hyperintense loculi, with moderate mural and septal enhancement after gadolinium; the suggested diagnosis was ovarian cystadenoma.

Laboratory results revealed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, hematocrit 29.4%, platelets 656 × 10^3/µL, CRP 26.45 mg/dL, D-dimers 1.21 mg/L, ALP 213 U/L, ferritin 480 ng/mL, iron 28 µg/dL, AST 70 U/L, ALT 77 U/L, GGT 353 U/L. Endocrine studies, including thyroid function, were normal. Tumor markers CEA, AFP, β HCG, LDH, and CA 19-9 were normal; CA 125 was elevated at 124.7 U/mL. Urine culture and nasal and pharyngeal swabs were negative, and chest radiography was normal.

On hospital day 3, she developed high-grade fever (up to 39.5 °C) unresponsive to intravenous antibiotics and antipyretics, without localizing symptoms. Otorhinolaryngeal, respiratory, digestive, urinary, and cutaneous sources were excluded; blood cultures and SARS-CoV-2 testing were negative. Intracystic hemorrhage or infection was suspected, but abdominal ultrasound showed unchanged cyst contents. A pediatric oncology consultation raised concern for paraneoplastic syndrome and sepsis, and she received meropenem, gentamicin, and metronidazole; her temperature normalized after 2 days. Given a presumptive diagnosis of serous or mucinous cystadenoma, surgical removal of the cyst was planned.
title: Giant Benign Struma Ovarii with High-Grade Fever, Elevated CA 125, and Hormonal Function in an Adolescent Patient

case_prompt: A 73-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a painless swelling on the tongue that had gradually increased in size. She denied dysphagia, odynophagia, speech changes, or breathing difficulty. Her medical history was notable for well-controlled hyperthyroidism. Examination revealed stable vital signs and no lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there was a 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm pale-pink, round, soft-to-firm, sessile, nonpulsatile, nontender, slightly mobile nodule with intact mucosa on the dorsum of the tongue near the left lateral border. Oral hygiene was good, with a broken lower molar and sharp opposing cusp noted. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Based on the clinical presentation, a benign fibrous lesion was suspected, and a broad differential diagnosis was considered. After informed consent, an excisional biopsy under local anesthesia was performed.
title: Solitary Encapsulated Neurofibroma Not Associated with Neurofibromatosis-1 Affecting Tongue in a 73-Year-Old Female

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old Iranian female presented with a 1-month history of progressive thickening, itching, and swelling of the skin involving the trunk and both upper and lower limbs, with sparing of the face, hands, and feet. She denied fever, Raynaud phenomenon, dysphagia, gastroesophageal reflux, dyspnea, or cough. There was no history of diabetes mellitus, febrile illness, or family history of autoimmune or connective tissue disorders.  

Initial evaluation in hematology and dermatology clinics revealed hemoglobin 14.4 mg/dL, white blood cell count 8.6×10^3/mm^3 (eosinophils 10.7%), platelet count 264×10^3/mm^3, and normal serum protein electrophoresis. Tests for HIV antibody, HCV antibody, and HBs antigen were negative. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography was unremarkable. Tumor markers (CEA, CA-125, CA 19-9, CA 15-3, and AFP) were negative. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were normal. PCR for JAK2 mutation and genetic evaluation for PDGFRA, PDGFRB, and FGFR1 rearrangements were negative.  

On rheumatologic examination, she had generalized non-pitting skin thickening, swelling, and hyperpigmentation sparing the hands and feet; other system examinations were unremarkable. Echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 60% and normal pulmonary artery pressure. Nailfold capillaroscopy was normal. Immunologic studies including ANA, anti–dsDNA, anti–Scl-70, anti-centromere, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, anti-Ro, anti-La, ACE level, C3, C4, CH50, anti-CCP, and rheumatoid factor were all negative.
title: Treatment of scleredema adultorum of Buschke with intravenous immunoglobulin and mycophenolate mofetil in a 14-year-old girl: a case report

case_prompt: Patient is a 40-year-old man with a history of reactive arthritis, Graves’ disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, mitral valve prolapse, and Gilbert’s disease who presented with one month of progressive jaundice, fatigue, lightheadedness, and exertional dyspnea. He described dark urine and dark brown to black stools. He denied fevers, chills, or recent transfusions and had no history of hepatitis, alcohol or intravenous drug use. His medications included etanercept, methimazole, niacin, and aspirin; he had discontinued metformin and pioglitazone more than one month before symptom onset. Family history was notable for autoimmune hemolytic anemia in his mother and anemia of unknown cause in his maternal grandmother. On examination, he was jaundiced with scleral icterus; vital signs showed heart rate 102 beats per minute and normal blood pressure, respiratory rate, and temperature. There was no lymphadenopathy. The thyroid gland was non-tender without enlargement or exophthalmos. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed mild hepatomegaly without splenomegaly. A vesiculobullous rash was present on the plantar surface of the right foot. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL, hematocrit 18.7%, MCV 107.5 fL, reticulocyte count 23.4%, total bilirubin 13.6 mg/dL (direct 0.6 mg/dL), LDH 369 U/L, and undetectable haptoglobin. Hepatitis serologies, antinuclear antibody, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins, and HIV were negative. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Peripheral smear showed spherocytes and bite cells without schistocytes. Direct antiglobulin test was positive for IgG and negative for C3; indirect antiglobulin test was negative. G6PD level and thyroid-stimulating hormone were normal. Lumbar spine radiographs showed sacroiliac joint ankylosis. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed probable anterior mediastinal enlargement, mild splenomegaly, and multiple small hypodensities in the liver and kidneys.
title: Concurrent reactive arthritis, Graves’ disease, and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia: a case report

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks’ gestation presented with a 4-day history of suprapubic pain and intermittent left flank pain, plus headache, nausea, and vomiting over the preceding 24 hours. She had no fever, vaginal bleeding, or changes in bowel habits and reported normal fetal movement. Her prenatal course was uncomplicated. She had a remote history of urolithiasis and a urinary tract infection two years earlier. 

On examination she was afebrile with normal vital signs and had mild left flank tenderness without peritoneal signs. A urine dipstick showed moderate leukocyte esterase, 6–10 squamous cells per high-power field, no blood, and no nitrites; urine culture later showed no growth. Her white blood cell count was 12 900 cells/mm3, creatinine was normal, and liver and biliary function tests were normal. Fetal fibronectin was negative, and cardiotocography showed rare contractions every 30 minutes with a reactive fetal heart rate. Betamethasone and a course of magnesium sulfate were administered for fetal lung maturity and neuroprotection, respectively, after which contractions resolved and flank pain improved.

On hospital day 3, she developed acute, colicky left flank pain with nausea and vomiting. Given the negative urine culture, absence of fever, and stable white blood cell count, infectious processes were considered less likely. A renal ultrasound showed mild left pelviectasis not out of proportion to normal pregnancy and small areas of echogenicity in the left kidney without shadowing; no definitive stones were visualized. Repeat urinalysis showed trace blood and trace leukocyte esterase. Gastrointestinal causes were deemed less likely given the location of the pain, good bowel sounds, lack of distention, and normal gastrointestinal and liver function tests. She was managed with intravenous fluids and analgesia, with symptom improvement. 

On hospital day 5, she experienced a recurrent episode of left flank pain, prompting urology consultation and a repeat renal ultrasound, which showed unchanged mild hydronephrosis without discrete stones or abscess. An MRI was obtained for further evaluation.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Preterm Delivery in the Setting of Left Calyceal Rupture

case_prompt: A 40-year-old woman presented with concern for a right breast lump following trauma. Screening mammography was abnormal and concerning for malignancy. Core-needle biopsy revealed granulomatous mastitis. She received a 2-week course of cephalexin without improvement, followed by a prednisone taper with only transient symptomatic relief, and then an oral course of doxycycline with persistent symptoms. On examination, there were multiple red, indurated, tender areas on the right breast, including a suspected fistula on the lateral aspect of the nipple. In-office breast ultrasound identified multiple complex abscess cavities and a fistulous tract. Two aspirations of fluid collections yielded negative wound cultures. The infection did not resolve with further penicillin administration, and concerns for multidrug-resistant organisms and acid-fast bacilli were raised. After more than one year of progressive symptoms, the patient underwent operative incision and drainage with debridement; perioperative antibiotics included vancomycin and a gentamicin/clindamycin irrigant. Intraoperative cultures again failed to isolate an organism.
title: Granulomatous mastitis secondary to Corynebacterium requiring surgical intervention: a complicated diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hypertension presented with several weeks of cramping abdominal pain, vomiting, and frequent watery, nonbloody diarrhea. The pain began as generalized cramping and later localized to the epigastrium without radiation; there were no alleviating or aggravating factors. She denied dysphagia, odynophagia, fever, chills, rashes, joint pains, recent travel, sick contacts, or antibiotic use. She had been admitted twice previously for similar symptoms; a prior CT scan showed fluid‐filled bowels and colonic wall thickening, and she received empirical antibiotics without improvement.

On examination, she appeared uncomfortable. Blood pressure was 146/93 mmHg, pulse 88/min, temperature 36.5 °C. The abdomen was tender, worst in the epigastrium, without rebound or distention; bowel sounds were normal, and there was no organomegaly. Other systems were unremarkable except for xanthelasmas on the eyelids.

Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 9,000/µL with 28% eosinophils (absolute count 2520/µL). Hemoglobin was 14.7 g/dL. Lipase was 2831 IU/L (previously 2415 IU/L five days earlier). Alkaline phosphatase was 391 IU/L, AST 57 U/L, ALT 54 U/L; bilirubin, kidney function, lactate, and electrolytes were normal. ESR was 10 mm/h and CRP 0.673 mg/dL. Peripheral smear demonstrated mature‐appearing eosinophils without atypia. HIV test was negative; IgG4 was 40 mg/dL (normal <86). Chest X-ray showed no infiltrates or adenopathy.

Stool PCR panel was negative for bacterial and viral pathogens; ova and parasites were negative. Review of her medications excluded drug-induced eosinophilia. Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed diffuse fluid-filled loops of small and large bowel without obstruction; the pancreas appeared normal.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with biopsies from the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and jejunum was performed. Histologic examination revealed eosinophilic-predominant mucosal inflammatory infiltrates in all specimens. Helicobacter pylori testing was negative. No villous abnormality, cryptitis, or crypt abscesses were identified.
title: Successful use of montelukast in eosinophilic gastroenteritis: a case report and a literature review

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old man, a US service member, was referred for chronic neuropsychiatric and vestibular symptoms years after deployment to East Africa. Two weeks after starting mefloquine 250 mg weekly for malaria prophylaxis, he developed anxiety and vivid dreams, progressing over two months to disequilibrium and confusion. He continued mefloquine for six months; four months into deployment he experienced enemy gunfire but reported no change in symptoms after this trauma. On return, he had emotional lability (anger, irritability), difficulty concentrating, anhedonia, short-term memory loss, word-finding difficulty, persistent “sea legs,” and episodic vertigo (4–5 times daily, 20–30 min), relieved by eye closure, without autonomic symptoms. He also had constant “spinning” dizziness, falls, insomnia with vivid dreams and nightmares, and daily headaches without aura or photophobia. He denied significant environmental exposures, illicit drugs, or head trauma; alcohol use occurred during deployment but was later limited.

He was diagnosed with anxiety and PTSD by psychiatry and treated with prazosin, clonazepam, lorazepam, venlafaxine, diazepam, clonidine, and psychotherapy, with partial improvement in mood but persistent vestibular and sleep symptoms. Physical examination showed mild right cervical lymphadenopathy and balance loss on rising and tandem gait; neurologic exam was otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies were notable for negative infectious and heavy metal panels, normal inflammatory markers, and normal endocrine and tumor markers. Neck ultrasound–guided lymph node biopsy showed benign reactive tissue. MRI of the brain and internal auditory canals were unremarkable. Vestibular evaluation demonstrated hyperactive vestibulo-ocular reflex gains and abnormally low phase on rotary chair testing, consistent with a central vestibulopathy.
title: Prolonged Neuropsychiatric Symptoms in a Military Service Member Exposed to Mefloquine

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man was referred with a 6-week history of a left-sided scrotal swelling that was not painful but had increased in size. His medical history included hypertension, eczema, and a right orchidectomy with chemotherapy for seminoma 25 years earlier. On examination, he had a large left hemi-scrotal swelling with an impalpable left testis.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 131 g/L, normal inflammatory markers, lactate dehydrogenase 743 IU/L (elevated), alpha-fetoprotein 4 ku/L (normal), and β-hCG 3 IU/L (upper limit of normal 2 IU/L).

Scrotal ultrasound revealed a grossly enlarged left testicle with heterogeneous echotexture, loss of normal architecture, and chaotic intratesticular perfusion on color Doppler. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a left testicular soft-tissue mass extending through the left spermatic cord into the left gonadal vein up to the level of the left kidney, with an additional large left suprarenal soft-tissue mass. 

FDG-PET showed intense uptake in the left testicular mass, the extending gonadal-venous soft-tissue, and the left suprarenal mass.
title: A case of primary testicular lymphoma with continuous spread along the gonadal vein and spermatic cord

case_prompt:
An 85-year-old man was admitted after three episodes of collapse with transient loss of consciousness at home. He reported only mild, diffuse abdominal discomfort and no trauma. His medical history included severe aortic stenosis, type 2 diabetes, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and a prior duodenal ulcer bleed. Medications were aspirin, bisoprolol, omeprazole, and ramipril. He was a former smoker (quit 35 years prior) with minimal alcohol intake and lived independently.

On examination, he was afebrile with an oxygen saturation of 100% on room air, blood pressure of 80/40 mmHg, and remained hypotensive despite aggressive fluid resuscitation. Cardiac exam revealed an ejection systolic murmur; jugular venous pressure was not elevated and there was no peripheral edema. The lungs were clear. Abdominal exam showed mild epigastric discomfort without peritoneal signs. Rectal examination was normal.

Initial laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL (reference 13–18), white cell count 11×10^9/L, and platelets 136×10^9/L; coagulation profile, renal function, and liver function tests were within normal limits. Chest radiograph was unremarkable and ECG showed left ventricular hypertrophy. He was admitted to a monitored unit given concerns for syncope related to aortic stenosis. An urgent echocardiogram demonstrated aortic stenosis but no critical obstruction, with an ejection fraction >55% and good biventricular function.

A repeat full blood count revealed a hemoglobin of 4.9 g/dL, and he was transfused with blood products. Given the possibility of a dissecting thoracic aneurysm extending into the abdomen, he was transferred to the ICU and underwent an urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen, which showed normal thoracic and abdominal aortas without dissection but revealed a large volume of free intraperitoneal fluid and areas of low attenuation in the right hepatic lobe consistent with metastatic lesions.
title: Bleeding from ruptured hepatic metastases as a cause of syncope in an octogenarian: a case report

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old Japanese man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnea and productive cough. Several days before symptom onset, vildagliptin (100 mg/day) was initiated for uncontrolled diabetes.  
On admission, temperature 35.8 °C, blood pressure 120/79 mmHg, heart rate 66 bpm, and oxygen saturation 98% on 2 L/min oxygen. On chest auscultation, fine crackles were heard bilaterally; there were no signs of connective-tissue disease.  
Laboratory studies showed elevated serum IgE (4216 mg/dL; normal <400 mg/dL) and KL-6 (9781 U/mL; normal <500 U/mL). Autoantibodies including ANA, anti-RNP, anti-Smith, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB, anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase I, and anti–tRNA synthetase antibodies were all within normal limits.  
Arterial blood gas on 2 L/min oxygen showed pH 7.450, PaO2 111.6 Torr, PaCO2 32.1 Torr, and HCO3– 21.8 mmol/L.  
Chest radiography revealed reduced bilateral lung volumes and diffuse reticular shadows. Chest CT demonstrated extensive ground-glass opacities with irregular reticulation in a peribronchovascular and basal-dominant distribution. Pulmonary function testing showed a restrictive pattern with FVC 43.2% of predicted.  
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis revealed 23% macrophages, 57% lymphocytes, 5% neutrophils, and 12% eosinophils; microbiological studies were negative.  
Transbronchial lung biopsy specimens showed atypical multinucleated regenerative alveolar epithelial cells, infiltration of eosinophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells, and interstitial fibrosis around thickened alveolar walls, consistent with subacute interstitial pneumonia showing organizing pneumonia with an acute alveolar injury pattern.
title: A case of vildagliptin-induced interstitial pneumonia

case_prompt: A 55-year-old Chinese woman was admitted with a 2-week history of fever and 1 week of bilateral thigh edema. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was marked edema and diffuse induration of both thighs, with prominent dendritic-like telangiectasia overlying the skin. Multiple firm subcutaneous nodules were palpable in the thighs without tenderness. There was no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or neurologic deficit; her mental status was normal. Her temperature fluctuated between 36.2 °C and 39.2 °C. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 98 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 3971 IU/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 120 mm/h, C-reactive protein 137 mg/L, and β2-microglobulin 2.74 mg/L; other tests, including infection workup, were normal. Bone marrow biopsy revealed hypercellular marrow without abnormal cells. MRI of the thighs demonstrated soft-tissue swelling and thickening. Chest CT revealed a solitary low-density nodule in the left upper lobe; abdominal CT was normal. Brain CT and MRI showed a 3.2 × 1.9 cm extra-axial mass in the left parietal region, suspected to be a meningioma. One week after admission, two biopsies of the indurated skin were performed: the first showed mild epidermal keratosis, and the second revealed small lymphocytes around dermal vessels, suggesting possible vasculitis. She was started on intravenous methylprednisolone 40 mg daily. After one week, her fever resolved, but the telangiectasia rapidly spread to the abdomen, chest, and neck, and new subcutaneous nodules appeared on the right arm.
title: Generalized Telangiectasia as a Hallmark of Intravascular Lymphoma: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 30-year-old G1P1 woman presented with a vaginal mass first noted at the time of a vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery 4 years earlier. She reported no change in size until 1 month of worsening watery yellow–pink discharge, occasionally blood-tinged, and entry and deep dyspareunia. She denied bowel or urinary symptoms, fevers, weight loss, or systemic complaints. On examination, there was copious serosanguinous fluid in the vaginal vault. A well-circumscribed, smooth, cystic structure approximately 4 cm in diameter was palpated along the posterior vaginal wall, with a 0.5×1.0 cm exophytic lesion overlying it, draining serosanguinous fluid. On bimanual and rectal examination, the mass was separate from the cervix and located in the rectovaginal septum; there was no rectal invasion. Biopsy specimens showed fibrous tissue with acute and chronic inflammation and squamous debris, without a definitive diagnosis. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a complex vaginal mass inseparable from the cervix, measuring 5.1×3.8×5.4 cm, with minimal peripheral vascularity on color Doppler. MRI demonstrated a 4.7×4.8×4.9 cm mass arising from the posterior vaginal wall, separate from the cervix, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on T1-weighted images, and on postcontrast sequences showing wall enhancement, absent internal enhancement superiorly, and bulky, nodular hyperenhancement inferiorly, consistent with a complex cystic mass.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Vaginal Angiomyofibroblastoma: A Case Report and Review of Diagnostic Imaging

case_prompt: A 33-year-old Moroccan man presented with a left-sided laterocervical mass of four months’ duration. He had no personal or family history of note and denied smoking, alcohol use, irradiation, fever, chills, or weight loss. On examination, the left parotid gland was enlarged and firm, with cervical lymphadenopathy; no overlying skin lesions were observed. Ultrasonography and CT revealed a solid mass in the parotid gland. A biopsy showed a poorly differentiated carcinoma. The patient underwent excision of the tumor. The resected mass measured 21.5 × 9 × 6 cm, with a cut surface that was firm, tan-gray, and lobulated, measuring 6 × 5.5 × 5 cm, with apparently normal salivary gland tissue at the periphery. On histologic examination, the tumor was lobulated, with nests of large foamy cells containing centrally located nuclei and vacuolated clear cytoplasm surrounded by smaller basaloid cells, and areas of squamous islands with keratin pearl formation. Periodic acid–Schiff staining was negative in the foamy cells. Immunohistochemical studies showed expression of EMA, pancytokeratin, and p63 in all neoplastic cells and focal β-catenin, with negative staining for CK5/6, CEA, S100, CD10, vimentin, melan A, and CD45.
title: Parotid gland, an exceptional localization of sebaceous carcinoma: case report

case_prompt: A Caucasian man in his early 20s with schizophrenia spectrum disorder and a history of monthly crystal methamphetamine use was transferred to a forensic psychiatric unit for aggression and erratic behavior. He had been on oral ziprasidone for several weeks but stopped it briefly and then restarted at a lower dose. Over the next month, he refused medications, and his behavior worsened. He was switched to oral aripiprazole, with low‐dose clonazepam added. After a requested increase in aripiprazole, his irritability improved. Two weeks later, staff noted that he was wearing a thick pullover despite warm temperatures, was sweating, and refused to speak, responding only by head movements. Concerned about oversedation, clonazepam was reduced. Over the next two days, he developed bizarre persecutory delusions, undressed, paced, and became noncompliant. A single dose of intramuscular zuclopenthixol was given; the next day he was calmer but had increased paranoia, vague suicidal thoughts, slowed movements, and disordered thinking. He was thought to be in a psychotic state with catatonic‐like features. That night, he exhibited ambitendency and mild posturing. His temperature and blood pressure were at baseline; heart rate was 135 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed mild rigidity of the arms. To rule out neuroleptic malignant syndrome, blood was drawn for measurement of creatine kinase.
title: A ‘benign’ extrapyramidal side effect masking a life-threatening neuroleptic malignant syndrome

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman presented with recurrent fevers and painful leg ulcers for two months.
Eight months earlier she developed vertigo and a fullness sensation in her left ear; audiometry confirmed left sensorineural hearing loss.
Two weeks later she had fever with chills; chest radiograph showed a right‐lung infiltrate and ESR was elevated; her symptoms improved with oral antibiotics.
Subsequently she noted gingival hypertrophy. CT of the paranasal sinuses revealed subcutaneous thickening of the right buccal area, and she improved with ibuprofen.
Her history included hypothyroidism on levothyroxine. She denied recent travel but cared for sick pets.
On examination, temperature was 37.5°C, blood pressure 139/69 mm Hg, pulse 78/min, respirations 16/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Tender erythematous nodules were present on both lower extremities; otherwise normal.
Laboratory tests showed normocytic anemia with normal white‐cell and platelet counts, normal renal and liver function, and an unremarkable urinalysis.
Blood and urine cultures were negative. The test for latent tuberculosis by interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) was also negative. Serology for Brucella abortus and melitensis also came negative. Serological tests for connective‐tissue disease were negative as was the serum angiotensin converting enzyme level.
Abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple hypoechoic cystic lesions in both liver lobes. Contrast‐enhanced CT confirmed multiple oval hypoattenuating hepatic lesions.
Liver biopsy showed cholestasis and large irregular necrotic areas palisaded by epithelioid cells with granulomatous inflammation and plasma cells; acid‐fast bacilli culture remained negative at six weeks.
She continued to spike fevers up to 101°F, and her leg lesions progressed to central necrosis with purulent discharge. Pus cultures were negative for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial growth.
Skin biopsy demonstrated surface ulceration, fibrinoid necrosis and vasculitis of superficial and deep dermal vessels with granuloma formation, neutrophilic infiltration, and debris. Immunohistochemistry and PCR for mycobacterial species on the biopsy were negative.
title: Cutaneous Ulcers as Initial Presentation of Localized Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old boy was evaluated for a 1-year history of a slowly enlarging mass in the right cheek. He reported no pain, tenderness, dysphagia, dysphonia, dyspnea, trauma, or systemic symptoms. No relevant medical, family, or psychosocial history was noted.

On examination, there was a 3 × 2 × 1 cm firm, non-tender, non-fluctuant, non-pulsatile mass on the right cheek, extending from the right oral commissure to the pterygomandibular raphe. The overlying mucosa was normal in color, margins were distinct, and the lesion was freely mobile between the buccal mucosa and skin. Aspiration yielded no fluid. No submandibular or submental lymphadenopathy was present.

Ultrasonography confirmed the presence of a soft-tissue mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the right cheek demonstrated a well-defined, hypodense lesion within the muscle layer. Complete blood count and metabolic panel were within normal limits.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Non-pancreatic pseudo cyst of oral cavity-case report

case_prompt:
A 15-week-old male domestic longhair kitten was evaluated for a 1-month history of intermittent generalized tremors and progressive abdominal distension. The kitten was fully vaccinated, dewormed, had not travelled outside the UK, and was fed a constant mixture of three commercial kitten diets according to manufacturers’ recommendations. No treats were given.

On examination, the kitten was bright and responsive, weighed 1.2 kg (body condition score 3/9), and had moderate muscle wasting. Heart rate, respiratory rate and temperature were normal. The long bones were visibly bowed but non-painful on palpation. The abdomen was markedly distended; palpation revealed a faeces-filled colon. Neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable.

External haematology showed a mild leukocytosis and monocytosis. Serum biochemistry revealed hypocalcaemia (total calcium 1.42 mmol/L; RI 2.3–2.5) with a mildly decreased creatinine and mildly increased alkaline phosphatase. Pre- and post-prandial bile acids and total thyroxine were within normal limits; serum phosphorus and total protein were considered normal.

Further evaluation demonstrated ionized hypocalcaemia (0.78 mmol/L; RI 1.2–1.4), elevated parathyroid hormone (120 pg/mL; RI <40), normal magnesium, normal feline pancreatic lipase immunoassay, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 (75 nmol/L; RI 127–335), and high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (670 pmol/L; RI 90–342).

CT of the chest, abdomen and long bones revealed generalized marked osteopenia with abnormal metaphyseal mineralization and normal physes; the right femur, left shoulder and left stifle were most affected. There was a markedly distended colon with faeces and a subjectively narrowed pelvic canal. No malformation of the pelvic canal bones or pathologic fractures were identified.
title: Unusual presentation of vitamin D3-dependent rickets type II in a kitten

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old woman underwent surgical tricuspid valve replacement for symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation. Ten days later, she developed acute left-sided hemiplegia, dysarthria, right-gaze preference, and a left facial droop. Her history included idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis with prior pacemaker placement and postoperative atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban. Noncontrast CT and CT angiography of the head showed an occlusion of the right distal internal carotid artery and an acute right middle cerebral artery infarct in the insula and temporal lobe. She did not receive IV thrombolysis because of anticoagulation and underwent mechanical thrombectomy via stent retriever and suction, achieving complete revascularization.

The day after thrombectomy, she reported right eyelid droop, binocular diplopia, and loss of peripheral vision in both eyes. On examination, near visual acuity was 20/60 in each eye. There was no anisocoria or relative afferent pupillary defect. The right eyelid had 1 mm of ptosis, and there was mild limitation of abduction and supraduction of the right eye. Anterior segment examination showed mild conjunctival chemosis OD, and dilated funduscopic examination was normal bilaterally. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits was unremarkable. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no change in the known infarct and no lesion involving the optic chiasm. MRI was not obtained because of her non-MRI–compatible pacemaker.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Bitemporal hemianopsia secondary to ischemic chiasmopathy following mechanical thrombectomy

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman with a history of childhood angioedema, episodic migraines treated with triptans, and gastroesophageal reflux presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset dyspnea. The symptoms began less than 30 minutes after an otherwise unremarkable MRI with gadolinium contrast. On examination, her oxygen saturation was 87% on room air, heart rate 106/min, blood pressure normal, and temperature 37.5 °C.
