Lung auscultation revealed bilateral crackles; there were no signs of heart failure or systemic rheumatologic disease.

D-dimer was elevated at 7593 ng/mL. CT pulmonary angiography showed no pulmonary embolism but demonstrated diffuse ground-glass opacities with a perihilar distribution. Hemoglobin was 15.2 g/dL, leukocytes 4.0 G/L (neutrophils 3.2 G/L), and creatinine 77 μmol/L. Multiplex PCR for respiratory viruses and atypical bacteria was negative, and urine antigens for Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae were negative. Cardiac evaluation revealed a normal troponin level (<3 ng/L), NT-proBNP 380 ng/L, unremarkable ECG, and echocardiography with LVEF 56% and no pulmonary hypertension. Serologic testing for ANCA, ANA, rheumatoid factor, and anti–citrullinated peptide antibodies was negative; protein electrophoresis and serum calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D levels were normal. In light of diffuse ground-glass opacities without an identified cause, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed.
title: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage after gadolinium injection during a MRI

case_prompt: A 22-year-old man presented with one month of mid–thoracic back pain and progressive difficulty walking. Over 48 hours in the hospital, he developed spasticity in both lower extremities and worsening weakness to grade 2–3, consistent with paraplegia. He had no history of trauma or prior neurologic disease. Vital signs were normal, and routine hematologic studies were within normal limits. MRI and CT of the thoracic spine revealed a well-defined, lytic, expansile mass measuring approximately 25 × 18 × 33 mm arising from the posterior elements of the T7 vertebra, including the left facet joint, invading the transverse process and lamina, and protruding into the spinal canal with compression of the cord. Intravenous contrast produced homogeneous enhancement of the lesion.
title: Pigmented Villonodular Synovitis of the Thoracic Vertebra Presenting with Progressive Spastic Paraparesis

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in January 2023. One week after graft, she was neutropenic and febrile (up to 40 °C) despite meropenem. Chest CT was negative; head and sinus CT showed acute inflammation of the maxillary, ethmoidal, and sphenoidal sinuses without bone erosion. She received meropenem, vancomycin, and voriconazole without improvement; symptoms transiently improved and she was discharged.

Two months later, she returned with persistent sinus symptoms, worsening mental status (drowsiness), and new left eye pain and swelling worsened by eye movement, with tearing and redness. On exam, she was alert but had left eyelid edema with purulent discharge, proptosis, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia, and a nonreactive left pupil; the right eye was normal. Lab studies showed WBC 4000/mm3, absolute neutrophils 90 × 103/µL, hemoglobin 10 g/dL, platelets 25 × 109/L, and elevated LDH.

Contrast-enhanced brain CT revealed a cortico-subcortical hypodense area in the left frontal white matter without hemorrhage; left proptosis, orbital cellulitis, mild globe tenting, and ongoing left maxillary, ethmoidal, and sphenoidal sinusitis; demineralization of ethmoid septae, conchae, septum, turbinates, and medial maxillary walls. Multiphasic CT angiography showed absent opacification of the left ophthalmic and facial artery and vein; intracranial vessels were otherwise normal. 

Subsequent brain MRI with contrast demonstrated bilateral fronto-basal and left temporo-polar cortico-subcortical restricted diffusion (more extensive on the left), swelling of adjacent gyri, T2 hypersignal, multiple hypointensities on SWI, ischemic signal along the left optic nerve with orbital soft tissue edema and proptosis. Post-contrast images showed minimal pachymeningeal thickening and extensive leptomeningeal enhancement in the left frontal and temporal regions; no intra-axial nodular enhancement. The left cavernous sinus lacked enhancement, consistent with cavernous sinus thrombosis.
title: Cerebritis, optic ischemia, and cavernous sinus thrombosis arising from sinonasal mucormycosis

case_prompt:
A male infant was born vaginally at 38 weeks’ gestation to a 36-year-old gravida 1, para 1 mother with blood type A RhD negative. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and routine anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis (300 µg) was administered at 30 weeks. Shortly after birth, the infant desaturated to 24% on pulse oximetry and required nasal continuous positive airway pressure with 100% FiO2 for 6 hours. 

At 2 hours of age, plasma glucose was 0.5 mmol/L (reference > 2.5 mmol/L), and hemoglobin was 4.5 mmol/L (reference 9.4–14.4 mmol/L); he received an umbilical vein glucose infusion and a blood transfusion. At 6 hours, he developed jaundice with a total bilirubin level of 144 µmol/L, and phototherapy was initiated. He was transferred to a tertiary care center, where a peripheral blood film showed leukoerythroblastosis and mild thrombocytopenia. 

On day 2, abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly with a normal gallbladder. A direct antiglobulin test (DAT) was strongly positive. Laboratory studies showed lactate dehydrogenase 66 µkat/L (reference 2.17–12.5 µkat/L), reticulocytes 246×10^9/L (reference 79–222×10^9/L), ferritin 528 µg/L (reference 10–400 µg/L), haptoglobin < 0.1 g/L, and lactate 6.3 mmol/L (reference 0.5–2.5 mmol/L). 

On day 4, total bilirubin peaked at 462 µmol/L, with unconjugated bilirubin 167 µmol/L and conjugated bilirubin 295 µmol/L (64% of total); ursodeoxycholic acid was started. Liver enzymes and international normalized ratio were within normal limits, but a persistently high intravenous glucose requirement prompted a hypoglycemia test on day 5. Plasma glucose fell to 1.0 mmol/L with insulin 51 pmol/L (reference 10–125 pmol/L) and C-peptide 1870 pmol/L (reference 379–1630 pmol/L), consistent with hyperinsulinism. Diazoxide (10 mg/kg/day) and glucagon (2.5 µg/kg/hour) were initiated, reducing but not eliminating the need for intravenous glucose.
title: Transient congenital hyperinsulinism and hemolytic disease of a newborn despite rhesus D prophylaxis: a case report

case_prompt: An 11-year-old boy presented with a history of recurrent respiratory tract infections and known tuberculosis exposure in the family. On examination, he appeared in good health with no abnormal lung or heart sounds. Tuberculin skin testing was positive. Chest radiography revealed a heterogeneous consolidation in the left lower lobe. A subsequent non-contrast CT scan showed a heterogeneous consolidation with cystic masses containing mixed fluid and air in the posterior segment of the left lower lobe, with no communication to the bronchial tree. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography demonstrated an artery originating from the descending thoracic aorta that divided into two 1.2-cm branches supplying this dysplastic area. These findings suggested intralobar pulmonary sequestration with associated bronchial atresia, superinfection, and contiguous parenchymal trapping.
title: Intralobar pulmonary sequestration with bronchial atresia and a systemic artery feeding a normal contralateral lung

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old woman with extensive‐disease small-cell lung cancer presented with 5 days of back pain. Two months earlier she had been diagnosed with stage IVB ED-SCLC and received first-cycle carboplatin, etoposide, and atezolizumab, complicated by febrile neutropenia. The second cycle was given at a reduced dose, and pegfilgrastim was administered 15 days before presentation. 

On admission she was afebrile (36.8°C) with blood pressure 168/74 mmHg, heart rate 68/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed WBC 21,000/μL (neutrophils 87%), CRP 23.99 mg/dL, and IL-6 83.6 pg/mL (normal <4.0 pg/mL). Serologic tests were negative for ANA, PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, and rheumatoid factor. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed soft-tissue thickening around the descending aorta and brachiocephalic artery without dissection.
title: Large‐vessel vasculitis induced by pegfilgrastim and immune checkpoint inhibitor in a patient with small‐cell lung cancer

case_prompt: A 26-year-old man with no history of hypertension or heart disease presented with a 3-day history of upper abdominal pain. He reported epigastric tenderness with rebound and a positive Murphy’s sign. He was afebrile. Laboratory tests showed mild jaundice and a mildly elevated leukocyte count; procalcitonin and C-reactive protein levels were normal. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a hyperdense gallbladder, mild gallbladder wall swelling, and fluid collections in the chest, pericardial sac, and abdomen. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment depression with T-wave inversion in V1–4 and a prolonged QT interval. The patient was taken to the operating room for an emergency laparotomy; intraoperatively, there was no evidence of bowel perforation, gallbladder enlargement, or cholangitis, but there was ascites and bowel wall edema. Approximately 1000 mL of peritoneal fluid was drained, and the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit.
title: Heart failure misdiagnosed as acute cholecystitis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old man with poorly controlled asthma, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension presented with a 1-week history of productive cough, worsening dyspnea, and chest pain. The chest pain was constant, worse when supine, and relieved by leaning forward. He had been hospitalized for SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia one month earlier. 

On examination, he was afebrile; blood pressure was 176/105 mmHg, heart rate 117 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 87% on room air. Findings included jugular venous distention, bilateral lower extremity pitting edema, tachypnea, and bilateral expiratory wheezing.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 26.6 × 10^3/μL with 32% eosinophils (8,512 cells/μL) and a troponin I level of 1.45 ng/mL (reference 0.00–0.05 ng/mL). Electrocardiography revealed subtle ST-segment depressions in the anterolateral leads. He was started on a heparin infusion for presumed non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and coronary angiography demonstrated nonobstructive coronary artery disease. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60–64% with severely increased wall thickness, normal diastolic and right ventricular function, and a small pericardial effusion. A computed tomographic angiogram of the chest showed no pulmonary embolism but scattered ground-glass opacities.

The initial working diagnosis was myopericarditis, possibly related to recent SARS-CoV-2 infection. He was treated with aspirin 325 mg three times daily, intravenous methylprednisolone 40 mg twice daily, bronchodilators, and empiric cefepime. By hospital day 5, his absolute eosinophil count had risen to 18,150 cells/μL (55%), prompting evaluation for autoimmune, fungal, parasitic, and other infectious causes.
title: Rapid effect of benralizumab in fulminant eosinophilic myocarditis in the setting of uncontrolled eosinophilic asthma

case_prompt:
A 10-year-old boy was referred for non-resolving redness and photophobia in both eyes. Symptoms began one day after accidental exposure to a herbal insecticide spray; he also developed flu-like symptoms and received oral acetaminophen and cefuroxime for 3 days. One week later, topical moxifloxacin-difluprednate and homatropine were started without improvement.

On presentation, he had extreme photophobia and ocular pain. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in both eyes; intraocular pressure was normal by digital palpation. Slit-lamp examination revealed diffuse palpebral and bulbar conjunctival congestion, superficial punctate keratopathy in the interpalpebral cornea, and pigment dispersion in the anterior chamber without inflammatory cells. There was pigment deposition on the inferior corneal endothelium. Pupils were round and slightly dilated (on homatropine). The iris showed diffuse stromal atrophy with a granular appearance in the mid and peripheral zones, sparing the peripupillary region, and no transillumination defects.

Gonioscopy demonstrated wide open angles with heavy pigment deposition and regular iris insertion. Anterior-segment OCT confirmed a flat (non-concave) iris contour. Fundus examination and specular microscopy were normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a normal haemogram, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 28 mm/hour, and no elevation of IgM levels for CMV, HSV-1, HSV-2, or VZV.
title: Bilateral acute depigmentation of the iris in a child following exposure to insecticide spray

case_prompt: A 28-year-old normotensive woman reported a 2-year history of paresthesia over the left side of her chest. Over the past 8 months, she noted partial ptosis of her left eyelid and anhidrosis of the left face. On neurologic examination, the left pupil was dilated and nonreactive to light, consistent with Horner’s syndrome. Sensory testing revealed hyperesthesia in the left D2 and D3 dermatomes; the remainder of the neurologic examination was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervicodorsal spine demonstrated, at the D1–D2 level on the left, a large paravertebral extrapulmonary mass that was heterogeneously enhancing on short-T1 inversion recovery images, extended into the neural foramen, and compressed the thecal sac. T2-weighted images showed multiple flow voids within the lesion and heterogeneous signal intensity.
title: Silent stellate ganglion paraganglioma masquerading as schwannoma: A surgical nightmare

case_prompt:
A 79-year-old woman was admitted for a prolonged episode of confusion. Over the past months, she had recurrent episodes of confusion, disorientation, dysphasia, and fluctuating levels of consciousness; nonconvulsive seizures and status epilepticus had been considered, and antiseizure drugs including levetiracetam and gabapentin were ineffective. Intravenous valproic acid led to severe stupor that resolved after withdrawal. Her medical history included marginal zone lymphoma in remission (previous rituximab and bendamustine) and a pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy 5 years earlier for intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm.

On examination, she was disoriented and dysphasic without focal motor or sensory deficits. Electroencephalography showed generalized, irregular delta-theta activity with triphasic waves. Laboratory testing revealed a serum ammonia concentration of 121 μg/dl (reference 19–55 μg/dl) despite normal liver and kidney function. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and brain MRI were unremarkable. Hyperammonemic encephalopathy was suspected, and lactulose, rifaximin, and daily enemas were initiated. Serum ammonia levels decreased, and her clinical status improved under this regimen. Abdominal ultrasound with elastography and abdominal MRI showed only minor signs of chronic liver disease, without evidence of cirrhosis or significant portal hypertension.
title:
Extrahepatic portosystemic shunts as an unusual but treatable cause
of hyperammonemic encephalopathy in a noncirrhotic patient – a case
report

case_prompt: A 69-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism, degenerative joint disease, and restless legs syndrome presented with a 2½-year history of intermittent abdominal pain, diarrhea, fatigue, and weight loss. One year earlier, an upper endoscopy showed patchy duodenal erythema and biopsies revealed villous blunting; celiac serologies were negative. Three months later, she was hospitalized for diarrhea, abdominal pain, and dizziness. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated small-bowel ulcerations, and an anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody (ASCA) was positive. She was treated for presumed Crohn’s disease with mesalamine and budesonide, later switched to adalimumab, without symptom improvement. Five months later, she was readmitted with weakness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and weight loss. CT imaging revealed abdominal lymphadenopathy; a CT-guided lymph‐node biopsy showed granulomata with rare fungal‐like organisms, and she received brief antifungal and corticosteroid therapy. Her last dose of adalimumab was one month before transfer. On examination at our hospital, she was cachectic (BMI 16.2), hypotensive at 96/56 mmHg, and afebrile. The abdomen was distended with minimal tenderness and hypoactive bowel sounds. Laboratory studies showed hypoalbuminemia (1.4 g/dL) and metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 12 mmol/L). Noncontrast CT of the abdomen revealed colonic distention with air-fluid levels and mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. A contrast CT 19 hours later showed bulky adenopathy, diffuse small-bowel wall thickening from duodenum to terminal ileum, and pneumatosis intestinalis. Emergent laparotomy revealed intact bowel covered with a pasty exudate. A mesenteric lymph node was excised; intraoperative brushings and frozen sections demonstrated granulomatous disease. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and Grocott’s methenamine silver (GMS) stains on the tissue were negative for organisms. Based on her history, the infectious disease service requested a periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stain on lymph node tissue…
title: Nearly Fatal Case of Whipple's Disease in a Patient Mistakenly on Anti-TNF Therapy

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old Southeast Asian woman presented with a 2-month history of pruritic blisters and bullae initially on her hands that gradually involved her face and trunk. She also reported weight loss, myalgia, fatigue, intermittent fever, self-limiting epistaxis, and hair loss. She denied dyspnea, hematuria, decreased urine output, muscle weakness, joint pain, or new medications.

On examination, temperature and respiratory rate were normal; pulse was 112 beats per minute; blood pressure was 80/60 mmHg; oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Findings included non-cicatricial hair loss, pallor, a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, and discoid lesions on the ears. Numerous tense, clear vesicles and bullae on an erythematous base involved her face, nape of neck, trunk, and hands. Superficial erosions were noted on the buccal mucosa, hard palate, and lips. The Nikolsky sign and bulla spread sign were positive; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 2600/mm³, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 194 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 53 U/L, albumin 2.9 g/L, active urinary sediments with white cells and albumin, and proteinuria of 0.42 g/24 h. Peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia with pencil and teardrop cells. Antinuclear antibody testing was positive; erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 18 mm/h; C-reactive protein was 1.8 mg/L (normal 0–4.8); and complement levels were slightly decreased.
title: A case of bullous systemic lupus erythematosus: Diagnostic challenges and clinical implications

case_prompt: A 17-year-old male presented with several hours of right lower quadrant abdominal pain associated with nausea and subjective fevers. He had a heart rate of 106 beats per minute, blood pressure of 130/90 mm Hg, and was afebrile. He appeared comfortable at rest. On abdominal examination, he had normal bowel sounds and isolated right lower quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed a normal white blood cell count, normal C-reactive protein level, and normal creatinine. A point-of-care ultrasound of the right lower quadrant was performed to evaluate for appendicitis and revealed a hyperechoic circular focus with acoustic shadowing within a hypoechoic, non-peristalsing, non-compressible, tubular structure adjacent to the iliac vessels. There was no surrounding mesenteric fat stranding, free fluid, or hyperemia, and the walls of the structure were thinner and lacked the alternating layered appearance typical of intestinal structures.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Ureteral Stone Mimics Appendicitis: A Point-of-care Ultrasound Case Report

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man presented with progressive respiratory distress. He was a heavy smoker. On admission, CT of the chest showed a 55 mm mass in the right upper lobe extending into the anterior mediastinum, with multiple enlarged regional lymph nodes. An ultrasound-guided lymph node biopsy was performed, and the initial pathological diagnosis was poorly differentiated non–small-cell lung carcinoma, adenocarcinoma type. Despite systemic chemotherapy, the tumor was refractory, and the patient died six months after admission. 
At autopsy, the thoracic mass measured 10 cm and extended from the right upper lobe to the anterior mediastinum, with widespread lymph node metastases. On gross examination, the tumor was solid, opalescent, and necrotic. Microscopically, it showed sheets of monotonous epithelial-like cells with loose intercellular connections, distinct nucleoli, rhabdoid-like cells, frequent mitoses, and areas of necrosis. 
Immunohistochemical staining showed the tumor cells were negative for desmin, S100P, TTF-1, p40, CK7, CK20, SMARCA4, and SMARCA2, and positive for SOX2, CD34, p53, and AE1/AE3. Molecular testing for EGFR mutations and ALK and ROS1 rearrangements was negative.
title: Thorahcic SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated tumors with ganglioneuroma and enchondroma: implications for SLC7A11 and ARID1A expression: a case report

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-week history of progressive weakness, exertional dyspnea, dry cough, anorexia, and a 5-lb weight loss. His medical history included mitral valve repair followed by bioprosthetic valve replacement for culture-negative endocarditis, a cerebrovascular accident, atrial flutter, and tobacco and alcohol use. On admission, his oxygen saturation fell to 85% on room air, necessitating bilevel positive airway pressure and transfer to the ICU for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure; he subsequently developed daily fevers.

Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, hematocrit 27.4%, platelets 42×10^3/µL, triglycerides 383 mg/dL, ferritin 9335 ng/mL, haptoglobin <8 mg/dL, LDH 1179 U/L, creatinine 1.78 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), ALT 80 U/L, AST 234 U/L, fibrinogen 73 mg/dL, PTT 45.1 s, PT 18.2 s, and soluble IL-2 receptor (CD25) 15,504 U/mL. The direct Coombs test was negative. A peripheral smear showed schistocytes, toxic-appearing neutrophils, large platelets, anisopoikilocytosis, and teardrop cells. Blood cultures were negative, and tests for ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, dsDNA, EBV, and CMV were unremarkable.

Chest radiography demonstrated multifocal pneumonia. CT of the chest revealed diffuse emphysematous changes, ground-glass infiltrates, and a 1.6-cm left upper lobe nodule. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Transesophageal echocardiography identified a 1.5×0.9-cm mobile echodensity on the anterior mitral leaflet.
title: An Unusual Case of Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis Associated with Mycobacterium chimaera or Large-Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma

case_prompt:
A 53‐year‐old man who has sex with men presented in August 2018 with rectal tenesmus, small‐volume frequent bowel movements, hematochezia, and mucous discharge. He denied dysuria, pollakiuria, or urethral discharge. He reported recent homosexual contact with a partner of Chinese descent. He had no relevant travel history.  
On examination, external ano‐genital inspection was normal. Vital signs were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed negative HIV, viral hepatitis, and Treponema pallidum serologies. Urethral and anal swabs were negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Trichomonas vaginalis. Serology for Chlamydia trachomatis was positive (IgG >200.0 AU/ml, IgA =58.8 AU/ml).  
Stool culture was positive for Brachypsira aalborgii. A 7‐day course of metronidazole led to transient symptom relief for three weeks.  
Proctoscopy revealed ulcerative proctitis with vulnerable mucosa. Confocal endomicroscopy showed mucosal edema, capillary leakage, and focal enterocyte destruction. Histopathology demonstrated mild active inflammation with polarized crypts and increased eosinophils; no malignancy. PCR of rectal biopsy was positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus I/II.  
A 7‐day course of doxycycline (100 mg bid) resulted in improvement but not full resolution. After symptom recurrence, an additional 21‐day doxycycline course, single‐dose ceftriaxone, and two‐week metronidazole courses provided no sustained benefit. Follow‐up STI testing remained negative.  
By June 2020, with persistent ulcerative proctitis refractory to antibiotics, mesalazine and budesonide enemas were initiated and the patient was referred for further evaluation of suspected inflammatory bowel disease. Colonoscopy showed ulcerations in the rectum, cecum, ileocecal valve, and terminal ileum with a discontinuous distribution. Histopathology was nonspecific but compatible with IBD, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of Crohn’s disease.  
Hydro‐magnetic resonance tomography demonstrated contrast enhancement in the rectum and cecal region without fistula, stenosis, or additional small‐intestinal involvement; there was also increased prostate enhancement.  
Screening for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, hepatitis B, and Clostridioides difficile was negative. The patient received systemic glucocorticoids, then anti‐TNF‐α therapy (adalimumab), and subsequently anti‐IL‐12/23 therapy (ustekinumab) over 11 months, but clinical symptoms and elevated fecal calprotectin persisted.
title: Entamoeba histolytica‐associated proctitis and ileitis mimicking Crohn's disease—A case report

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman with a 3-year history of non–insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes and inconsistent metformin use presented with 2 days of involuntary “jerking” movements of her left arm and leg. She reported increased urination and a 14-kg weight loss over the prior month. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, peripheral vascular disease, bronchiectasis, resolved hepatitis C, and steatohepatitis without cirrhosis. She smoked 20 pack-years, consumed about 10 alcoholic drinks per week, and had a remote history of intranasal cocaine use. 

On examination, her temperature was 98.1 °F, blood pressure 159/64 mmHg, heart rate 54 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and BMI 23.6 kg/m2. She was alert and oriented. Neurologic examination demonstrated nonrhythmic, circular, writhing movements of the left upper and lower extremity with intermittent ballistic jerks, consistent with chorea.

Laboratory testing showed: blood glucose 776 mg/dL, HbA1c 15.8%, venous pH 7.37, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, anion gap 13, BUN 16 mg/dL, creatinine 1.48 mg/dL, ALT 17 U/L, AST 20 U/L. A noncontrast head CT revealed asymmetric hyperattenuation of the right lentiform nucleus with sparing of the internal capsule. She was admitted and glucose was controlled with insulin; within 48 hours, the movements were suppressible with concentration. MRI performed 4 days later showed only chronic microvascular ischemic changes without focal basal ganglia abnormalities.

One month later she returned with increased frequency of left-sided chorea and ambulatory dysfunction. Blood glucose was 62 mg/dL and HbA1c 9.9%. She was treated with alprazolam, tizanidine, and haloperidol without improvement. Antinuclear antibody and paraneoplastic autoantibody tests were negative. Ceruloplasmin and copper levels were normal. It was noted that the chorea dissipated when she was not observed, and she was diagnosed with a conversion disorder.

Within 24 hours she returned with persistent chorea (blood glucose 200 mg/dL) and was diagnosed with diabetic hemichorea hemiballismus. Two days later her blood glucose was 40 mg/dL, and repeat MRI showed hyperintensity of the right lentiform and caudate nuclei with corresponding intrinsic T1 hyperintensity.
title: A Case of Diabetic Hemichorea Hemiballismus Exacerbated by Hypoglycemia

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute lightheadedness, diaphoresis, and palpitations in the evening after a 7-hour fast. He had experienced recurrent episodes of dizziness for 2 months without weight change. Point-of-care blood glucose was 1.5 mmol/L, and his symptoms resolved after IV dextrose.

He had no family history of insulinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Vital signs were normal. On abdominal examination, there was a large, firm, palpable mass in the left upper quadrant.

Serum testing during hypoglycemia showed an inappropriately elevated insulin level of 13.34 μU/mL (normal <3 μU/mL) and a C-peptide level of 2.2 ng/mL (normal <0.6 ng/mL). Serum intact parathyroid hormone, calcium, and prolactin levels were all within reference ranges.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined, lobulated, hypervascular mass measuring 12 cm in the pancreatic tail with areas of low attenuation and calcifications. There was no pancreatic duct dilatation, no hepatic lesions, and no significant lymphadenopathy.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Giant insulinoma in a 15-year-old man: A case report

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old Japanese woman with a history of Wilson disease and orthotopic liver transplantation at age 21 presented in January 2018 with several months of insomnia followed by persecutory delusions (“I am being watched”) and auditory hallucinations (“I hear a voice telling me what to do”). She exhibited bizarre behaviors, such as attempting to strip her parents because she believed they were infected. In early March 2018, she was involuntarily hospitalized for psychomotor agitation and psychotic symptoms.

On examination, she had jaundice and bilateral lower-limb edema. Laboratory tests showed WBC 3650/µL, hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, hematocrit 26.1%, platelets 76 000/µL, prothrombin time 19.7 seconds, albumin 2.7 g/dL, total bilirubin 10.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL, AST 56 U/L, ALT 54 U/L, ALP 1193 U/L, cholinesterase 85 U/L, BUN 20.8 mg/dL, CRP 0.90 mg/dL, serum copper 47 µg/dL (normal 68–128), ceruloplasmin 13 mg/dL (normal 21–37), tacrolimus level <2.0 ng/mL, and mycophenolate mofetil level <0.4 µg/mL. Chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly.

Acute graft rejection due to nonadherence with tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil was diagnosed, and she received two days of methylprednisolone. A psychiatric liaison team administered risperidone up to 4 mg/day orally and intravenous haloperidol for agitation.

Brain MRI showed only a small high-intensity focus in the corpus callosum; there was no evidence of pathological copper deposition. There was no abnormality in copper metabolism, and tacrolimus trough levels had not increased prior to symptom onset and remained low thereafter. No other medical condition or substance use disorder was identified.

Therefore, schizophrenia was suspected, although the duration of psychotic symptoms had not yet met DSM-5 criteria.
title: Graft Loss Following Onset of Schizophrenia Long After Liver Transplantation

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old boy presented after awakening with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis, lightheadedness, and approximately one minute of eye fluttering with unresponsiveness but no tonic–clonic movements or incontinence. Post-ictally, he had headache, photophobia, and vision changes. He had intermittent morning vomiting for one month but no fevers, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or prior seizures. Family history was notable for brain tumors in maternal relatives. 

On exam, blood pressure was 161/102 mm Hg, heart rate 90–110 beats/min, temperature 37.9 °C, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. He was neurologically intact with bilateral upgoing toes. Abdominal exam revealed suprapubic distension without tenderness or organomegaly.

Noncontrast head CT showed a left‐hemisphere hypodense region with artifact. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral parieto-occipital subcortical T2 prolongation and gyral swelling consistent with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. EEG captured subclinical seizures from bilateral occipital regions, which resolved with lorazepam, levetiracetam, and fosphenytoin.

Initial laboratory studies showed WBC 29.7×10^6/mL, hemoglobin 12 g/dL, platelets 265×10^6/mL, BUN 16 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed 30 mg/dL protein without blood. Lumbar puncture yielded 0 nucleated cells, 0 red blood cells, protein 43 mg/dL, and glucose 69 mg/dL. Renal ultrasound revealed bilaterally enlarged (11.6 cm) echogenic kidneys without Doppler abnormalities and a distended bladder. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal without left ventricular hypertrophy. Despite blood pressure control with intravenous nicardipine transitioned to oral agents, the etiology of his hypertension and renal enlargement remained unclear.
title: A rare cause of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive upper‐quadrant pain and postprandial vomiting. The pain became continuous, worsened after meals, and was relieved only by vomiting. She reported a 5-kg weight loss. There was no history of alcohol abuse. On examination, she had severe epigastric tenderness without abdominal distension. Laboratory tests showed an amylase level of 156 U/l (reference ≤100) and a CA 19-9 level of 52 U/ml (reference ≤37); complete blood counts were normal. 

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed normal abdominal parenchyma, a normal gallbladder, and no common bile duct dilation. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was unremarkable. 

Multidetector CT (portal phase) demonstrated cystic lesions encircling the second portion of the duodenum with circumferential duodenal wall thickening, and a soft‐tissue component in the pancreaticoduodenal groove abutting the pancreatic head; the pancreatic head and pancreatic duct appeared normal. Signs of inflammatory change, including fat stranding and fluid, surrounded the groove area. 

Contrast‐enhanced MRI confirmed intramural fluid‐signal lesions within the thickened duodenal wall and sheet‐like tissue in the groove with enhancement patterns similar to the pancreas. MR cholangiopancreatography showed a normal gallbladder and no dilation of the common bile duct or pancreatic duct.
title: Cystic dystrophy of the duodenal wall in heterotopic pancreas: an atypical case in non-alcoholic female

case_prompt: A 63-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of right-sided chest pain that had gradually worsened. He reported mild chest congestion with a mild cough but denied haemoptysis, dyspnoea, or fever. On presentation, his arterial oxygen tension was 84 mmHg and oxygen saturation was 95% on room air. Electrocardiography showed a left anterior fascicular block. A noncontrast CT of the chest demonstrated a suspicious filling defect in the right pulmonary artery. Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA) revealed filling defects in the right pulmonary artery and its upper branch, with possible focal pulmonary infarction. Laboratory studies showed a D-dimer level of 0.49 mg/L (reference range 0.02–0.80 mg/L), with normal complete blood count, hepatic and renal function tests, serum electrolytes, cardiac biomarkers, autoantibodies, and coagulation parameters; there was no evidence of internal bleeding. The patient was treated with low-molecular-weight heparin for 2 weeks. On transfer to the respiratory department, the D-dimer level remained normal. Autoantibody testing, tumour markers, mycological examination, and T-spot were all normal. Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities showed no deep vein thrombosis. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 66%, normal chamber sizes, normal pulmonary-artery pressures, and no visible thrombus in the main or branch pulmonary arteries. Considering these atypical clinical and imaging features, (18)F-PET/CT was suggested.
title: An intimal sarcoma of pulmonary artery mimicking pulmonary embolism: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 15-year-old spayed female domestic shorthair cat was examined for a routine checkup. Physical examination, complete blood count, and serum biochemistry were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 9 × 7 mm heterogeneous hypoechoic nodule at the periphery of the quadrate liver lobe. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology showed numerous grouped epithelial cells with moderate to marked anisocytosis and anisokaryosis, round nuclei with reticular to coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and poorly basophilic cytoplasm. A presumptive diagnosis of epithelial neoplasia (carcinoma) was made, and metastatic disease was considered. Serial monitoring showed progressive growth of the nodule to 1.73 × 1.34 cm over 4 months, with a transient rise in AST and ALT. Laparoscopic liver biopsy was then performed; histopathology suggested lymphocytic cholangitis, and symptomatic treatment normalized transaminases, but the nodule continued to enlarge. Whole-body CT showed a diffuse heterogeneous liver parenchyma, especially in the quadrate lobe, without any other abnormalities. A partial lobectomy of the quadrate lobe was performed. Histopathology of the excised mass revealed multilobulated epithelial cells forming follicular structures containing dense eosinophilic, colloid-like material, merging into tubular and solid proliferations with nuclear crowding and mitotic figures. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse cytoplasmic positivity for thyroglobulin in most neoplastic cells. Thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentrations were within reference intervals. Re-evaluation of the CT images revealed no abnormalities in the orthotopic thyroid gland and no nodular lesions elsewhere.
title: Adenocarcinoma originating from presumed liver ectopic thyroid in a cat

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man with a 5-year history of adult‐onset Still’s disease, maintained on anakinra (100 mg/day) and prednisolone (5 mg/day), presented to an outside hospital with a 3-day history of high-spiking fevers, sore throat, and arthralgias. He developed acute kidney injury and liver dysfunction and was transferred to the ICU with suspected sepsis. His immunosuppressive therapy was stopped, and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics were started. 

Laboratory studies showed:
- Anemia and thrombocytopenia  
- Markedly elevated ferritin and C-reactive protein levels  
- Hypertriglyceridemia and hypofibrinogenemia  
- Elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor level  
- Splenomegaly on imaging  

A bone marrow biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytosis, and treatment with etoposide and dexamethasone (HLH-94 protocol) was initiated. After one week, he redeveloped high fevers, pancytopenia, and rising inflammatory markers. On transfer to our hospital, examination revealed cervical lymphadenopathy and severe tonsillopharyngitis. Abdominal CT showed hepatosplenomegaly and cervical and mesenteric lymphadenopathy.
title: Combination Immunosuppressive Therapy Including Rituximab for Epstein-Barr Virus-Associated Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis in Adult-Onset Still's Disease

case_prompt: A 55-year-old Japanese man with a six-month history of left hilar lung cancer (suspected squamous cell carcinoma based on sputum cytology and tumor markers) treated with radiotherapy and chemotherapy presented one year after diagnosis with fever and chest pain. On admission (day 1), he was hypotensive (BP 69/58 mmHg), tachycardic (146/min), tachypneic (24/min), and had an altered mental state. Chest CT showed a left hilar mass invading the left atrium and left main bronchus, with small low-density areas within the tumor and around the intestinal membrane. Echocardiography confirmed tumor invasion into the left atrium without vegetations. Blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus. He received noradrenaline and broad-spectrum antibiotics. On day 2, he developed acute difficulty speaking, left-sided weakness, and left unilateral spatial neglect, with an NIHSS score of 7. Head CT revealed multiple small low-density areas in the right cortex and bilateral subcortex interpreted as air emboli. Brain MRI showed faint hyperintensity along the right parietal cortex, subcortex, and left frontal cortex on diffusion-weighted images and small dot-like low signals in the right frontal cortex and left parietal subcortex on susceptibility-weighted images.
title: Electroencephalographic findings after convulsive seizures due to cerebral arterial air embolism secondary to lung cancer: a case report

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old man with a 23-year history of Crohn’s disease presented with 36 hours of myalgias, fatigue, headache, and epigastric pain. He denied any change in bowel habits and had no respiratory symptoms prior to admission. Two weeks earlier, ustekinumab therapy had been restarted for active Crohn’s disease; he had previously discontinued it after 5 months of therapy two years prior.

On presentation, temperature was 39.6 °C, heart rate 120 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, blood pressure 117/83 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination was notable only for epigastric tenderness; lung auscultation was clear. Initial chest radiography showed no acute airspace disease.

On hospital day 1, he developed cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia, requiring 5 L/min of nasal cannula to maintain oxygen saturation > 90%. On hospital day 2, he was transferred to the ICU for high-flow nasal cannula at 75% FiO₂. Repeat chest radiography showed diffuse reticular infiltrates. Chest CT with contrast demonstrated bilateral consolidations and ground-glass opacities without pulmonary embolism. Laboratory testing revealed a white blood cell count of 16.3 × 10⁹/L (92% neutrophils) and C-reactive protein of 296.8 mg/L. Infectious workup—including blood cultures, respiratory pathogen panel, and bronchoalveolar lavage cultures—was negative. Serologic testing for connective tissue disease–associated interstitial lung disease was also negative.
title: Stelara struck: a case of noninfectious pneumonitis secondary to ustekinumab

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old woman, 20 days postpartum after a cesarean delivery at 35.6 weeks’ gestation, presented with a 2-day history of fever (up to 38.5°C), body aches, sore throat, and a mild cough. On admission, her temperature was 39.8°C, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and blood pressure 104/68 mmHg. A complete blood count showed a white-cell count of 9.3×10^9/L with 78.3% neutrophils. She was treated with oseltamivir and paracetamol. 

On the third day of fever, she developed generalized convulsions and an altered mental state. Neurologic examination revealed dysarthria, nystagmus, and ataxia of the trunk and all extremities. Meningeal signs were absent.

On hospital day 4, brain MRI demonstrated well-defined lesions in the bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles and the splenium of the corpus callosum that were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging with low apparent diffusion coefficient values. There was no contrast enhancement. MR angiography and venography were normal.

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 29 white cells per mm^3; Gram stain was negative, and tests for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and VDRL were negative. Electroencephalography revealed diffuse slow waves with focal spike waves.
title: Lesions more than cerebellum in a puerpera of acute cerebellitis: concurrent encephalitis, not a subtype of ADEM

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man noticed a slowly enlarging, firm mass in his right upper thigh over four months. He denied systemic symptoms such as flushing, diarrhea, or wheezing. Physical examination revealed a 3×3 cm firm mass involving the right sartorius muscle. The mass was excised en bloc.

Histopathology showed skeletal muscle and subcutaneous tissue infiltrated by polygonal cells arranged in packets separated by fine fibrovascular stroma. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated strong, diffuse positivity for synaptophysin, chromogranin, cytokeratin, Bcl-2 protein, and neuron-specific enolase, and negativity for S100, desmin, and epithelial membrane antigen. Electron microscopy revealed polygonal cells with deeply indented nuclei and abundant neurosecretory granules in the cytoplasm. A 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid level was elevated at 92 nmol (reference range 9–31 nmol/24 h). Metaiodobenzylguanidine and octreotide scans showed no abnormal uptake outside the surgical site, and contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable.
title: Neuroendocrine carcinoma arising in soft tissue: three case reports and literature review

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic mitral stenosis status post percutaneous mitral valvotomy in 2012, hypertension, persistent atrial fibrillation, and prior amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity underwent successful radiofrequency pulmonary vein isolation for symptomatic atrial fibrillation and was discharged off antiarrhythmics. Two days later, she was admitted in atrial fibrillation, converted to sinus rhythm with 360 J, and started on flecainide 100 mg every 12 hours. 

Approximately five hours after the first dose of flecainide, she developed fever (38.7 °C), chills, and a dry cough, and her oxygen requirement increased from 2 L/min by nasal cannula to high-flow nasal cannula. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocytosis of 12 000 cells/mm3. Portable chest radiography showed increased interstitial markings compared with baseline. She received 20 mg intravenous furosemide, and her symptoms initially improved.

Three hours after the second 100 mg dose of flecainide, fever recurred with worsening dyspnea, and her oxygen support escalated to bilevel positive airway pressure. Leukocytosis rose to 16 000 cells/mm3. Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities predominantly in the upper lobes, multifocal perilobular consolidation in the lower lobes, and mild traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65–70%, no mitral valve stenosis, and a small, collapsed inferior vena cava; serum brain natriuretic peptide was 186 pg/mL. Flecainide was discontinued.
title: Drug-induced acute pneumonitis following initiation of flecainide therapy after pulmonary vein isolation ablation in a patient with mitral stenosis and previous chronic amiodarone use

case_prompt: A 43-year-old Japanese man noted a gradually enlarging soft tissue mass in his right thigh since January 2015. He had no significant personal or family history. On examination, a hard, elastic, non-tender, non-pulsatile mass measuring approximately 30 cm in diameter was palpated in the right thigh without overlying skin changes. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Plain radiography showed a large soft tissue mass without calcification, periosteal reaction, or femoral involvement. MRI revealed that the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with peripheral, septal gadolinium enhancement. CT imaging confirmed the absence of calcification and no obvious cortical invasion of the femur. Differential diagnoses included malignant myxoid soft tissue tumors such as myxoid liposarcoma, myxofibrosarcoma, and metastatic carcinomas (myoepithelial or neuroendocrine). An incisional biopsy demonstrated a lobulated tumor with a myxoid matrix and atypical spindle-shaped cells forming eosinophilic cord-like structures. Immunohistochemical staining showed S-100 positivity; synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and pan-keratin (AE1/AE3) were negative; Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 10%.
title: Diagnosis of extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma in the thigh using EWSR1-NR4A3 gene fusion: a case report

case_prompt:
A 10-month-old girl born at 29 weeks’ gestation with trisomy 21 and chronic lung disease of prematurity was transferred for otolaryngologic evaluation of persistent stridor. Ten days earlier she had developed a 4-day history of cough, rhinorrhea, tactile fever, and increased work of breathing. At the community hospital she was febrile to 102°F, respiratory rate 60/min, had wheezing, and an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Chest radiography showed consolidation in the left upper and right lower lobes, and she was treated with nebulized albuterol/ipratropium, intravenous corticosteroids, and ceftriaxone; clindamycin was later added. Blood and viral cultures were negative. On hospital day 3, she developed stridor, received nebulized racemic epinephrine, and her supplemental oxygen requirement was increased. 

On transfer, a chest radiograph showed an opacity in the left superior mediastinum (possibly due to patient rotation), a right retrocardiac opacity, and hyperinflation. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest demonstrated diffuse peripheral, paraseptal, and subpleural cysts tracking along the fissures (maximum diameter 9.5 mm), predominating in the upper lobes (left > right), bilateral narrowing of peripheral bronchi, and multiple areas of patchy atelectasis or consolidation.
title: Cystic Lung Disease in Down Syndrome: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of acute onset shortness of breath and productive cough, associated with fever, chills, generalized body aches, and pleuritic chest pain. She is a lifetime non-smoker with no alcohol use. Her medical history is notable for hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, asthma, osteoporosis, and multiple hospital admissions for recurrent pneumonia since childhood, including infections with Nocardia and Moraxella and one episode of Mycobacterium avium‐intracellulare in the past five years. She has no history of pulmonary tuberculosis or known tuberculosis contacts; her father had emphysema.

On examination, her temperature was 38.1 °C, pulse 112 beats/min, blood pressure 112/56 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 91% on room air. She was in mild respiratory distress with expiratory wheezes; examination of other systems was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13,500/µl with immature granulocytosis and no eosinophilia; the basic metabolic panel was normal. A respiratory viral PCR panel and blood and urine cultures were negative.

Chest radiographs demonstrated hyperexpansion of the lungs, bronchiectasis in the right suprahilar region and left lung base, and a right-sided aortic arch. An inspiratory noncontrast CT scan of the chest showed hyperinflation of both lungs and multiple ballooning cystic bronchiectasis distal to the third-generation bronchi bilaterally. End-expiratory CT images revealed collapse of these bronchiectatic airways. Coronal minimal-intensity-projection images in inspiration confirmed cystic bronchiectasis in the fourth- to sixth-order bronchi in the right upper and left lower lobes, with calcified hilar lymph nodes and a right-sided aortic arch; expiratory coronal images again demonstrated airway collapse. An oblique volume-rendered reconstruction showed cystic bronchiectasis in the left lower lobe.

Pulmonary-function testing revealed an obstructive pattern with progression to fixed airway obstruction and no reversibility after bronchodilator administration. Quantitative immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE), serum α-1 antitrypsin levels, and sweat chloride were all within normal limits. Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and fungal cultures were negative. Anti–nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and Aspergillus‐specific immunoglobulins were negative.
title: Williams–Campbell syndrome: an unusual presentation in an adult patient

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old woman presented with several weeks of peri-umbilical and epigastric discomfort, anorexia, 10-pound unintentional weight loss, and night sweats. Her medical history included treated hypothyroidism, hypertension, chronic hepatitis C infection (genotype 1a), and a low-grade rectal neuroendocrine tumor resected in 2012 with negative re-excision margins in 2017. Physical examination revealed mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without palpable masses or hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests showed elevated serum chromogranin A at 450 ng/mL (normal < 93 ng/mL), α-fetoprotein (AFP) of 2198 ng/mL (normal 10–20 ng/mL), and AFP-L3% at 86.6%. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated (AST 72 U/L, ALT 86 U/L). 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed two hepatic lesions: a 2.2 × 2.1 cm peripherally enhancing mass with central hypodensity in segment 4, and a 1.4 × 1.0 cm low-density lesion in segment 7, with prominent portacaval lymph nodes. MRI with gadolinium confirmed a 2.7 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm T2-hyperintense lesion in segment 4 with peripheral rim arterial phase enhancement and persistent venous phase enhancement; the smaller lesion was too small for enhancement characterization. FDG-PET showed avidity in the segment 4 mass (SUV 6.6) only. Gallium-68 dotatate PET showed no uptake in the liver or lymph nodes. 

A CT-guided core biopsy of the segment 4 lesion demonstrated a high-grade malignant tumor with neuroendocrine morphology and synaptophysin positivity; Ki-67 index was 30%. Non-cirrhotic liver parenchyma was confirmed on biopsy. No extrahepatic disease was found on chest CT. The main differential diagnoses considered at this point were metastatic neuroendocrine tumor versus a primary hepatic malignancy, most likely hepatocellular carcinoma.
title: Hepatocellular carcinoma with biliary and neuroendocrine differentiation: A case report

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man with a 35-year history of back pain, stiffness, and hip pain was evaluated for persistent symptoms despite previous treatments.  
• At age 29, he was diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis based on progressive back pain, stiffness, hip pain, joint-space narrowing, and a history of ankle surgery for enthesopathy at age 19.  
• Imaging showed diffuse spinal and Achilles enthesophytes, interspinous ligament calcification, bilateral sacroiliac joint fusion (“severe AS”), and he had undergone bilateral hip arthroplasties.  
• He reported ongoing pain managed with hydrocodone and had derived no benefit from indomethacin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; he had also failed adalimumab therapy.  
• Atypical features included bilateral bowing of the proximal femoral shafts with subtrochanteric lateral proximal insufficiency fractures and progressive hearing loss since age 9.  
• A 20-year dental record review revealed chronic poor dentition with multiple abscesses, dental fractures, and extractions.  
• Laboratory studies showed inorganic phosphate 1.9 mg/dL (2.5–4.5), alkaline phosphatase 148 U/L (40–129), creatinine 0.74 mg/dL (0.7–1.3), spot urine creatinine 76 mg/dL (20–320), parathyroid hormone 115 pg/mL (16–77), 1,25(OH)₂ vitamin D 49.9 pg/mL (19.7–79.3), and serum calcium 9.8 mg/dL (8.4–10.5).  
• A 24-hour urine phosphate was 1300 mg (226–1797), inappropriately normal in the setting of hypophosphatemia.  
• HLA-B27 testing was negative.
title: Rare Causes of Musculoskeletal Pain: Thinking beyond Common Rheumatologic Diseases

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of persistent headache. Seven months earlier, she underwent right frontal craniotomy for a transitional (WHO Grade I) falx meningioma, which was completely excised (Simpson Grade I). Preoperatively, she received antihistamines and corticosteroids for poliallergic asthma. Hemostasis was achieved by filling the surgical cavity with absorbable hemostatic agents (bovine-derived gelatine with human-derived thrombin matrix and oxidized regenerated cellulose), and a dural graft was placed. Her postoperative course was uneventful. Early CT and MRI scans confirmed complete tumor removal. Blood tests showed elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (72.9 mg/L; normal <5 mg/L) but no fever, leukocytosis, or procalcitonin elevation. She was discharged on schedule.

On presentation, the surgical wound was fully healed. There was no fever, and hs-CRP remained slightly elevated (59.4 mg/L). Lumbar puncture yielded normal CSF both chemically and microbiologically. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a 2.5 cm irregular, contrast-enhancing lesion along the right frontal falx, with surrounding edema and mass effect. MRI demonstrated that the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and FLAIR sequences. A relapse of meningioma was suspected, and surgical re-exploration was planned.
title: Postoperative Aseptic Intracranial Granuloma: The Possible Influence of Fluid Hemostatics

case_prompt: A 9-year-old boy with no significant medical history presented for dental evaluation of carious teeth and a two-month history of painless swelling in the right posterior maxilla. On examination there was a non-tender, expansile swelling of the right maxillary posterior region associated with carious primary maxillary canine and first and second molars. Panoramic radiograph showed a well-corticated, unilocular radiolucent lesion measuring approximately 4 × 3 cm from the distal aspect of the permanent right lateral incisor to the mesial aspect of the permanent right second premolar. Aspiration of the cystic cavity yielded golden-yellow fluid. Based on the patient’s age, lesion location, and radiographic appearance, both an inflammatory dentigerous cyst and unicystic ameloblastoma were considered in the preoperative differential.
title: Conservative management of unicystic ameloblastoma in a young child: Report of two cases

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of wheezing and productive cough, initially diagnosed as late-onset asthma. Despite standard asthma therapy, her symptoms worsened, with new episodes of left chest pain and dyspnea. She had no relevant past medical or family history. On examination, breath sounds were bilaterally vesicular but decreased at the left lung base. A chest radiograph showed marked volume reduction of the left lung. Computed tomography of the chest revealed a rounded lesion at the carinal region, partially obstructing the ostium of the left main bronchus.  

Rigid bronchoscopy demonstrated a mobile polypoid lesion with a smooth, shiny, non-friable surface that obstructed the left main bronchus; the lesion was removed endoscopically. Grossly, the oval, encapsulated mass measured 2.3 × 1.7 × 1.5 cm, had a fibroelastic consistency, and a smooth, homogeneous brownish cut surface.  

Microscopic examination showed a low-grade mesenchymal neoplasm composed of spindle cells in small, loose fascicles, with alternating hypercellular and hypocellular areas. Hypocellular regions contained dense collagen bands and focal myxoid change. Focal aggregates of mature adipose tissue were present. Blood vessels were irregular with a “staghorn” configuration. Mitotic activity was 2 per 10 high-power fields.  

Immunohistochemical stains revealed that the neoplastic cells were negative for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), S100 protein, smooth muscle actin, and desmin, and were positive for CD34, CD99, and BCL2.
title: Endobronchial solitary fibrous tumor

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old man presented with progressive confusion and long-standing blindness of the left eye. His medical history included type II diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolemia; he had no urological complaints. On examination, he was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and neurologically nonfocal except for left-eye amaurosis. 

An axial contrast-enhanced brain CT demonstrated an irregular infiltrative hyperdense mass in the left temporal region with necrotic components, extensive osseous destruction, and extension into the orbit, sinuses, and adjacent musculature; there was left-sided exophthalmos, vasogenic edema, and a mild midline shift. T2-weighted MRI confirmed a hyperintense lesion in the left temporal lobe with osseous involvement. 

Serum PSA was 194 ng/mL.
title: Exophthalmos as the initial presentation of metastatic prostate cancer

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with 10 days of progressive nausea, slurred speech, and unsteady gait, beginning approximately 2 weeks after her first dose of the Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine. She denied headache, focal weakness, vision changes, fever, respiratory or chest symptoms, and had no known COVID-19 contacts. Vital signs were normal. On examination, she was alert and oriented; there was dysarthria, left-sided dysmetria on finger–nose testing, impaired rapid alternating movements, horizontal nystagmus to the left, and marked appendicular and truncal ataxia with inability to stand unassisted. Motor strength was 5/5 throughout, and there were no meningeal signs.

Initial laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, urinalysis, and urine drug screen, were all within normal limits. Brain MRI with and without contrast demonstrated bilateral hyperintense lesions in the cerebellar hemispheres, most prominent in the left middle cerebellar peduncle, with faint enhancement; there was no cervical spinal cord involvement. Lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid protein of 90 mg/dL, 10 white cells per mm3 with 80% lymphocytes, and negative Gram stain and culture. CSF PCR was positive for SARS-CoV-2 and negative for varicella zoster virus, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, cytomegalovirus, and enterovirus. Oligoclonal bands were absent.
title: Acute cerebellitis following COVID‐19 vaccination: A case report

case_prompt: A 40‐year‐old woman with asthma, hypertension, and a 20‐year history of psoriatic arthritis involving both temporomandibular joints presented with a 4‐month history of a hard, tender swelling (1.5×2.0 cm) in the left preauricular region. Her prior TMJ interventions included bilateral discectomy and synovectomy 14 years earlier, right‐side arthroplasty with synovectomy 3 years ago, and left‐side arthroplasty with dermis‐fat interpositional graft 1 year ago, during which surgeons noted and removed whitish “chalky” material. A year later, examination showed a well‐defined, tender preauricular nodule with normal overlying skin. An initial MRI demonstrated a well‐defined encapsulated lesion adjacent to the TMJ, and fine‐needle aspiration cytology was nondiagnostic. A dedicated TMJ MRI showed progressive bilateral calcification around both TMJs. Subsequent CT scans revealed extensive calcification with deformation and arthrosis of both TMJs, and a well‐circumscribed calcified nodule caudal to the left TMJ.
title: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease: A case report with bilateral involvement of the temporomandibular joints and concurrence of psoriatic arthritis

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of a confluent red macular rash on his face, neck, and upper chest, associated with sore throat, nausea, palpitations, fever, and malaise. He had fever to 38.7 °C, tachycardia to 130 bpm with a systolic murmur, and left hypochondrial pain. Examination revealed multiple tender head-and-neck lymph nodes. The rash, which began on the neck, spread to the face and back; it was blanching and mildly pruritic, with less pronounced involvement of the arms, legs, and abdomen.  
One month earlier, he had developed right-knee monoarthritis with elevated ESR (65 mm/h), CRP (92 mg/L), and synovitis on arthrocentesis; ANA and ANCA were negative. Sulfasalazine (500 mg five times daily) was initiated but stopped by the patient after 23 days when fever and rash appeared. He had no other chronic medications or allergies.  
Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL; AST 78 U/L, ALT 224 U/L, LDH 533 U/L, GGT 132 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 145 U/L; albumin 29.4 g/L; direct bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL; ferritin 1325 µg/L; INR 1.4; CRP 78 mg/L; WBC 10.3×10^3/mm^3 with eosinophils 4.5%. He was immune to EBV, influenza, measles, rubella, hepatitis A and B; hepatitis C and E, HIV, and paracetamol toxicity were excluded. Group A strep testing was negative. Echocardiography showed pericardial effusion without endocarditis; abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable.  
A presumptive diagnosis of delayed-onset sulfasalazine toxicity was made, with consideration of Kawasaki disease, Hodgkin lymphoma, adult Still’s disease, hypereosinophilic syndrome, and various infections. He met all seven RegiSCAR criteria for DRESS syndrome. Despite withdrawal of sulfasalazine and supportive care, he developed facial and pharyngeal swelling, hypoxia, and leukocytosis (17.1×10^3/mm^3 with 11% eosinophils); hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and pleural effusion ensued.  
CT of the chest and abdomen revealed extensive bilateral lymphadenopathy in the mediastinum, pulmonary hila, axillae, and abdomen, hepatosplenomegaly, right pleural effusion, and massive ascites. FDG-PET CT demonstrated multiple intensely hypermetabolic lymph nodes in the head, neck, and axillary regions.
title: A diagnostic dilemma: distinguishing a sulfasalazine induced DRESS hypersensitivity syndrome from a CD30 + lymphoma in a young patient

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old woman presented with a 6-year history of a painless swelling of the lower jaw, initially 1 cm in diameter on the left, which gradually enlarged to involve both sides of the face. She reported only difficulty in chewing. On examination, there was gross facial asymmetry with fullness of the cheeks and lower lip and obliteration of the mentolabial sulcus and nasolabial folds. A well-demarcated, hard, lobulated, nontender swelling measured approximately 8×6×5 cm over the left cheek and a diffuse hard, lobulated, nontender swelling extended from the left mandibular ramus to the right mandibular body, obliterating the inferior border. No cervical lymphadenopathy was present.

Intraorally, a diffuse, hard, lobulated swelling extended from the left to the right retromolar regions, with bilateral buccal, labial, and lingual cortical expansion and intact mucosa. A provisional diagnosis of a benign fibro-osseous lesion of the mandible was made, and the differential diagnoses included fibrous dysplasia, ossifying/cementifying fibroma, and central giant cell granuloma (non-aggressive).

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, serum protein, calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase levels, were within normal limits.

Panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined mixed radiopaque and radiolucent lesion from the left ramus to the right angle of the mandible, measuring about 11×7 cm, with a “cotton-wool” pattern of calcification, concentric growth producing a ball-like outline, and bowing—but no erosion—of the inferior mandibular border. Occlusal radiograph revealed buccal and lingual cortical plate expansion with lingual displacement of teeth. Posterior–anterior mandible view confirmed a mixed radiopaque–radiolucent expansile lesion extending from the left ramus to the right mandibular angle. Axial and 3D CT scans demonstrated a large (11.8×7.0×7.3 cm) expansile lesion of the right and left mandibular bodies and left ramus, with mixed sclerotic and lucent areas and central low-density foci.
journal: Journal of Natural Science, Biology, and Medicine
title: Giant cemento-ossifying fibroma of the mandible

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man with a history of low-risk prostate cancer managed by active surveillance was referred for restaging when his prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level rose to 26.6 μg/L in 2022. He had no significant comorbidities aside from prior cholecystectomy. Initial prostate biopsy in 2013 showed high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia at a PSA of 6.2 μg/L. A repeat biopsy in 2015 revealed Gleason 3+3 adenocarcinoma in 1 of 14 cores; digital rectal examination was unremarkable, and the cancer was staged as T1c. Surveillance over the next eight years included biennial biopsies that were negative for malignancy. 

When his PSA increased to 26.6 μg/L, a 3-Tesla multiparametric MRI of the prostate identified two PI-RADS 4 lesions (12 mm in the right transition zone and 6 mm in the right peripheral zone). Repeat biopsy detected Gleason 3+3 adenocarcinoma in 2 of 15 cores without perineural invasion, and his prostate volume was estimated at 86 mL. He experienced postbiopsy urinary retention and developed a left lower-limb deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, which were treated with apixaban. He otherwise had no symptoms of metastatic disease.

For staging, CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no nodal or visceral metastases. A 99m-Tc bone scan demonstrated moderate focal uptake in the right frontal calvarium. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a 2.5 cm sclerotic lesion in the right frontal bone corresponding to the area of uptake, suspicious for a solitary sclerotic metastasis.
title: Case report of a patient with an intraosseous meningioma presenting as possible metastasis from prostate cancer: Diagnostic dilemma and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 33 4/7-week, 2.22-kg female neonate was born after spontaneous vaginal delivery following premature rupture of membranes. She had an unremarkable physical examination at birth and passed meconium within 24 hours. Maternal breast milk feeds were initiated by gavage on day 1 of life. 

On day 4, after episodes of bilious emesis, she was made nil per os. Examination showed a distended, tender abdomen without rebound and normoactive bowel sounds; the remainder of her exam, including genitourinary assessment, was normal. Laboratory studies on day 4 revealed a white-cell count of 21.1×10^9/L with 14% eosinophils. 

By day 5, she developed frank bloody stools. Serial abdominal radiographs showed nonspecific bowel gas fullness without pneumatosis. An upper gastrointestinal series ruled out malrotation. Although abdominal distention resolved by day 6, leukocytosis, eosinophilia, and hematochezia persisted. Family history was notable for a sister with milk-protein intolerance who developed hematochezia after milk exposure. 

Broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin and cefepime) were started on day 5. On day 7, ampicillin was replaced with vancomycin after an abdominal ultrasound was performed to evaluate for ischemia, intussusception, and colitis; the ultrasound showed several subcentimeter hypoechoic, hypovascular liver lesions characterized as microabscesses, scattered loops of thick-walled bowel with minimal ascites, a sludge-filled gallbladder, and no biliary ductal dilatation. There was no pneumatosis, pneumoperitoneum, portal venous gas, or complex ascites. 

On day 8, a contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed irregular hypodensities in the anterior right hepatic lobe consistent with microabscesses and demonstrated mild mucosal hyperenhancement and bowel-wall thickening of the rectosigmoid.
title: Liver Microabscesses in a Premature Neonate With Eosinophilic Colitis

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man with a nine-month history of Raynaud’s phenomenon and positive ANA (1:5120, speckled pattern) and anti-U1-RNP antibody (1:256) but no other symptoms presented with a three-day history of fever and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Initial laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 9,000/μL (lymphocytes 19.7%) and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 4.31 mg/dL; urinalysis was normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated diffuse perihepatic capsular enhancement. He was treated with cefozopran and levofloxacin for presumed perihepatitis due to Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, but his symptoms persisted, and he was transferred for further evaluation.

On transfer, he denied any sexual activity. Physical examination revealed a positive Murphy’s sign. Laboratory values were: leukocytes 6.4×10^3/μL (lymphocytes 1.0×10^3/μL), hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, platelets 185×10^3/μL, CRP 9.21 mg/dL, normal liver enzymes, IgG 1244 mg/dL, complement C3 147 mg/dL, C4 28 mg/dL, ANA 1:2560 (speckled), anti–double-stranded DNA antibody 20.6 IU/mL, anti-U1-RNP 1:256, anti-SS-A negative, anti-Sm negative. Repeated urinalyses remained normal. Serologic tests for Chlamydia trachomatis (IgG, IgA) and urinary RNA tests for C. trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae were negative. A further week of ceftriaxone and minocycline produced no improvement.

During hospitalization, he developed facial erythema and the abdominal pain extended into the left upper quadrant. Repeat contrast-enhanced CT three weeks later showed persistent perihepatic capsular enhancement, bilateral pleural effusions (right-sided predominance), and a small pelvic ascites.
title: Perihepatitis as an Initial Manifestation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of progressive, continuous epigastric and right upper quadrant pain radiating to both flanks and aggravated by eating. She also had multiple episodes of nausea and nonbloody vomiting. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension; she denied tobacco or alcohol use and had a remote cesarean delivery.

On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant, a positive Murphy’s sign, and normal bowel sounds. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with T-wave inversions in leads III and V3. Serial troponin levels were 0.017 ng/mL at presentation, 0.031 ng/mL at 2 hours, and 0.056 ng/mL at 10 hours; coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries.

Laboratory studies showed normal serum amylase, lipase, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin levels. Aspartate aminotransferase was 61 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 81 U/L, and gamma-glutamyl transferase 94 IU/L. The white-cell count was 15.8×10^3/µL, and the C-reactive protein level was 232 mg/dL.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed diffuse reactionary gallbladder wall thickening (up to 9 mm) without gallstones, a thickened falciform ligament, and a normal extrahepatic and intrahepatic biliary tree. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a heterogeneous, hypodense soft-tissue mass in the fissure of the falciform ligament containing fat-attenuation areas and surrounding fat-stranding, with a normal pancreas and mild gallbladder wall thickening but no gallstones.
title: Focal necrosis of the falciform ligament as a rare cause of abdominal pain: A case report

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old woman was admitted for evaluation of progressive forgetfulness that had been present for five years. She reported difficulty preparing meals, repetitive conversations, and repeated purchasing of identical items. Neuropsychological testing showed an MMSE score of 19/30, an HDS-R score of 20/30, and a Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale–Revised total IQ of 87 (verbal IQ 83, performance IQ 92).

Her past medical history included uterine myoma at age 42 and cerebral aneurysm clipping at age 58. She graduated from junior high school and had worked in agriculture, construction, and food service. There was a family history of brain calcification: one brother had mental retardation with documented calcifications and another brother had alcoholism; her parents were asymptomatic.

On examination, there were no pyramidal or extrapyramidal signs, and the Albright sign was negative. Laboratory studies showed normal levels of thyroid hormones, parathyroid hormone, serum calcium, serum phosphate, and cerebrospinal fluid constituents. A treponemal hemagglutination assay was negative.

Noncontrast cranial CT revealed symmetric calcifications in the globus pallidus, pulvinar thalami, right frontal subcortical white matter, and the occipital cortex–white matter junction. T1-weighted MRI showed small patchy hyperintensities in the globus pallidus and pulvinar thalami, and T2-weighted MRI demonstrated corresponding hypointensities in the globus pallidus. Brain perfusion SPECT demonstrated decreased perfusion in the bilateral basal ganglia, thalamus, and right frontal lobe.
title: Longitudinal observation of ten family members with idiopathic basal ganglia calcification: A case report

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old man with a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and poor glycemic control presented four years ago with involuntary, irregular movements of the right upper and lower limbs two weeks after a fall. At that time, his blood glucose level was 712 mg/dL. A noncontrast CT scan of the brain showed no acute abnormalities. Brain MRI on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences demonstrated a tiny hyperintense lesion in the left basal ganglion. His hemichorea resolved spontaneously the next day, and he had no residual neurologic deficits.

Four years later, he returned with a two-week history of involuntary movements involving his right upper limb and jaw, which abated during sleep. Neurologic examination revealed normal strength and sensation in all extremities. Laboratory studies showed a blood glucose level of 671 mg/dL without ketoacidosis, a normal serum creatinine concentration, and an HbA1c of 17.3%. A CT scan of the brain demonstrated increased density in the left basal ganglia. Subsequent MRI revealed increased signal intensity in the left basal ganglion on T1-weighted imaging.
title: Recurrent hemichorea with different etiologies in one patient

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old woman presented with a painless, pigmented growth on the left anterior maxillary gingiva for 3 months. The lesion began as a pinpoint spot and gradually enlarged, extending to the palatal gingiva. She reported no systemic illness or head and neck trauma. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Extraoral examination revealed a tender, firm left submandibular lymph node fixed to the mandible and a separate 3 × 3 cm firm, non-tender, mobile right cervical lymph node. Intraoral examination showed a 2 × 3 cm sessile, rough-surfaced, black pigmented lesion on the left maxillary attached gingiva near the central and lateral incisors, extending to the hard-palate rugae and causing displacement of those teeth.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, biochemical tests, and urinalysis, were within normal limits. Intraoral periapical and panoramic radiographs demonstrated a radiolucent area with displacement of the left central and lateral incisors. Neck ultrasonography revealed a highly vascular mass with a low-velocity waveform indenting major vessels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing hypodense nodule in the left premaxillary region without bony erosion, and a 34 × 32 mm necrotic left level II cervical lymphadenopathy compressing the internal jugular vein.
title: Oral malignant melanoma: A case report with review of literature

case_prompt: A woman in her late forties presented with a 1.5-week history of gradually worsening pain and stiffness in both thighs, limiting her ability to walk. Her history was notable for childhood-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus complicated by retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, and end-stage renal disease; she also had hypertension. She denied trauma, rash, joint symptoms, or respiratory complaints. On examination, she had reduced strength in ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion and hallux extension and flexion bilaterally. Her temperature was 37.9 °C. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 203 mg/l, creatine kinase of 700 IU/l, and myoglobin of 1011 μg/l.
