Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria and pyuria, and a urine culture grew Escherichia coli in the absence of urinary symptoms. An MRI of the lower limbs demonstrated extensive, symmetric edema in muscles of the hips, thighs, shins, and calves, without significant muscle atrophy or fatty replacement. Serologic testing was unremarkable: antinuclear antibodies, myositis-associated and myositis-specific antibodies (including anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP), and viral hepatitis serologies were all negative.
title: Diabetic myonecrosis complicated by emphysematous pyomyositis and abscess caused by Escherichia coli: a case report

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old previously healthy man presented with 5 days of intermittent, nonradiating epigastric pain and occasional nausea. He then noted jaundice and dark urine. He denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, decreased appetite, prior tuberculosis, sick contacts, or recent travel. He emigrated from the Philippines at age 33 and had childhood BCG vaccination.  
On examination: temperature 38°C; vital signs otherwise normal; icteric sclera; epigastric tenderness without guarding, rigidity, or palpable mass.  
Laboratory data showed normocytic anemia (Hb 12.3 g/dL), total bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL, AST 167 U/L, ALT 443 U/L, ALP 424 U/L; serum lipase and amylase were normal. Chest radiograph was normal.  
Abdominal CT revealed a 3.8×2.7 cm solid mass posterolateral to the pancreatic head, suggestive of peripancreatic lymphadenopathy. MRCP showed a 4.1×2.6 cm mass in the pancreatic head encasing the portal vein with central nonenhancement, a 1.5 cm narrowing of the mid–common bile duct, mild intrahepatic ductal dilation, and no pancreatic duct dilation. The initial differential diagnosis included malignant pancreatic tumor, autoimmune pancreatitis, neuroendocrine tumor, and gastrointestinal stromal tumor.  
Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration demonstrated a heterogeneous hyperechoic lesion in the pancreatic head. Histopathological examination revealed areas of coagulation necrosis, lymphocytes, and epithelioid histiocytes suggestive of granulomatous inflammation.
title: Isolated Pancreatic Tuberculosis Mimicking Pancreatic Cancer: A Diagnostic Challenge

case_prompt: A 53-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of headache and vertigo. She was alert and oriented, with mild truncal ataxia and gait unsteadiness; nystagmus was absent. Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated a hyperdense 30 × 31 × 36 mm mass in the anteromedial cerebellar hemispheres adjacent to the medial tentorium cerebelli, with mild ventriculomegaly. Contrast-enhanced CT showed the lesion abutting the lower surface of the medial tentorium between the vein of the cerebellomesencephalic fissure and the declival vein and compressing the dorsal brainstem, causing aqueductal stenosis. With a presumptive diagnosis of tentorial meningioma, she was scheduled for MRI 10 days later. By that time, her symptoms had worsened, and she required assistance to walk. MRI revealed an extra-axial tumor with broad attachment to the medial tentorium, hypointense on T1-weighted images, mixed intensity on T2- and diffusion-weighted images with corresponding hypointensity on the ADC map, extensive perilesional edema, and intense gadolinium enhancement measuring 40 × 41 × 46 mm. Cerebral angiography showed no obvious feeding vessels or tumor blush from the internal carotid, external carotid, or vertebrobasilar systems. The serum level of soluble interleukin-2 receptor was 470 U/mL (normal range, 157–474 U/mL).
title: Dural-based large B-cell lymphoma masquerading as a tentorial meningioma

case_prompt: A 49-year-old man presented with vague pain in the left mandibular area and lower-lip paresthesia of several weeks’ duration and occasional low-grade fevers. He was edentulous. On examination, there was a firm mass of the left edentulous mandibular ridge covered by intact mucosa. Cone-beam CT showed an ill-defined radiolucent lesion extending from the left alveolar crest to the inferior alveolar canal, with buccal cortical plate invasion. An incisional biopsy yielded tan, soft to elastic tissue fragments. Histologically, the lesion consisted of sheets of malignant small to medium-sized round cells with hyperchromatic, occasionally clefted nuclei, prominent nucleoli, scant cytoplasm, frequent mitoses, perineural invasion, and crush artifact. Immunohistochemistry revealed tumor cells positive for CD45, CD20, C-MYC, CD10, and BCL-6; scattered CD3 positivity; and negative staining for CD5, BCL-2, Cyclin D1, CD19, TdT, and MPO. The Ki-67 proliferation index was >95%, and in situ hybridization for Epstein–Barr virus was negative.
title: Mandibular sporadic Burkitt lymphoma in an adult patient: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old man was referred for evaluation of newly diagnosed, asymptomatic left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction discovered after premature ventricular contractions were noted on a pre-sports electrocardiogram. His history was notable for cutaneous and pulmonary sarcoidosis diagnosed at age 25 and in remission since 2017 after corticosteroid therapy. He had no known cardiovascular disease, no relevant family history, and took no regular medications. Physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed NT-proBNP 110 pg/mL, high-sensitivity troponin T 20 ng/dL, soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2287 pg/mL (normal 458–1997), and angiotensin-converting enzyme 155 U/L (normal 8–52). A 24-hour Holter monitor revealed sinus rhythm with 9 polymorphic PVCs per hour. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a severely dilated LV (indexed end-diastolic volume 112 mL/m²), basal thinning (“scooping”) of the anterior septum, and moderate systolic dysfunction (LVEF 41%, global longitudinal strain –15.4%). The right ventricle was slightly dilated but had normal systolic function. No valvular abnormalities or pericardial effusion were noted.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed diffuse myocardial edema (T2 mapping 51 ± 6 ms; institutional cut-off 50 ms) in anterior, anterolateral, and inferolateral walls, and extensive LGE (26% of LV mass) with intramural septal and subepicardial anterior, inferior, and lateral involvement, forming a “ring-like” pattern. Coronary CT angiography was normal. A presumptive diagnosis of cardiac sarcoidosis was made based on imaging. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT revealed diffuse myocardial uptake without extracardiac involvement. Right ventricular endomyocardial biopsy was negative for granulomas.

The patient was started on prednisolone, methotrexate, ramipril, bisoprolol, and dapagliflozin. At three months, CMR showed normalization of T2 values (49 ms) and recovery of LVEF to 52%, but the LGE pattern persisted. A six-month 18F-FDG PET/CT scan demonstrated resolution of myocardial uptake.
title: Inflammation clashing onto myocardial susceptibility: a tale of two rare diseases—a case report

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old man was brought to the emergency department with generalized shaking, tremors, clonus, and altered level of consciousness. He had been seen normal nine hours earlier by his spouse. His medical history included type 2 diabetes and remote traumatic brain injury (subdural frontal and temporal hemorrhage) from a fall 3 years ago; he had no history of seizures.  

Home medications were divalproex sodium 250 mg twice daily, quetiapine 25 mg twice daily, venlafaxine 37.5 mg twice daily, trazodone 50 mg as needed, donepezil 10 mg daily, insulin glargine 15 U daily, melatonin 3 mg nightly, magnesium oxide 400 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, pravastatin 20 mg nightly, and tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly.  

On arrival, his temperature was 39.7 °C, heart rate 120 beats/min, blood pressure 188/84 mmHg, and respiratory rate 23 breaths/min. Laboratory studies showed an elevated creatine kinase level of 6.34 mg/dL and a serum calcium level of 6.8 mg/dL. Examination revealed tremors, 3+ hyperreflexia in the lower limbs, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3. He was intubated and transferred to the medical ICU. His hyperthermia persisted despite antipyretics and cooling blankets.  

“Several etiologies for encephalopathy—hepatic, endocrine, metabolic, Wernicke's, seizures—were ruled out through laboratory, diagnostic, and microbiological testing.” “Viral and bacterial encephalopathy remained in the differential diagnosis, but was of low suspicion due to an unremarkable cerebrospinal fluid analysis.” Although he was at risk for seizures from his prior brain injury, “the neurology team conveyed a low level of suspicion for seizures due to a negative electroencephalogram (EEG) and a lack of tonic or clonic activity.”
title: Clinical Relevance of Pharmacogenetics in Serotonin Syndrome

case_prompt: A 14-year-old boy presented with headache and nausea. On examination he was alert, oriented, and had no focal neurologic deficits. He had no significant medical, family, or medication history. Serum α-fetoprotein and β–human chorionic gonadotropin levels were within normal limits. Brain MRI showed extensive T2 hyperintense edema in the left frontal lobe without a hypointense rim. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed two irregular ring-enhancing lesions adjacent to the anterior horn of the left lateral ventricle—one involving the globus pallidus and the other in the frontal white matter—with no midline involvement. Arterial spin labeling and MR perfusion demonstrated increased blood flow only in the merged lesion area, not centrally. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed peripheral diffusion restriction. Susceptibility-weighted imaging and contrast-enhanced CT identified engorged veins traversing the centers of the lesions. Lumbar puncture yielded cerebrospinal fluid with an opening pressure of 255 mmH₂O, protein 105 mg/dL, normal cell count and IgG index, and five unique oligoclonal bands.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Difficult differential diagnosis of ectopic germinoma from multiple sclerosis: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old woman underwent revision total hip arthroplasty (THA) for recurrent dislocation after an initial THA for idiopathic osteonecrosis. She had no personal or family history of bleeding and preoperative coagulation studies were normal (APTT 29.8 s, PT-INR 0.98). No unusual bleeding was seen intraoperatively.

On postoperative day 21, she developed sudden right thigh pain and swelling. Laboratory testing showed C-reactive protein 495 nmol/L, white cells 10.9 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 80 g/L, and normal coagulation (APTT 28.2 s, PT-INR 1.11). An emergency operation evacuated a large hematoma; tissue cultures were sterile.

Ten days later, the wound again discharged bloody fluid. Contrast CT demonstrated a mass extending from the right hip to the proximal femur; angiography showed no active bleeding. Hemoglobin had fallen to 67 g/L, and routine coagulation studies, including von Willebrand factor, remained normal.
title: Recurrent Hematomas following a Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty in Acquired Coagulation Factor XIII Deficiency

case_prompt: A 55-year-old man presented with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and constipation, with milder similar episodes in preceding weeks. His history was notable for obesity, prediabetes, and a 30-pack-year smoking history. On examination, he was tachycardic; the abdomen was diffusely distended, mildly tender, without rebound tenderness, and had overactive bowel sounds. Blood tests, including liver and renal function, lipase, and calcium, were normal; white blood cell count was 14.9×10^9/L and C-reactive protein was 15 mg/L. Stool tests for occult blood and calprotectin, as well as QuantiFERON-TB Gold, were negative. Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed fecalization of the small bowel, dilated proximal segments, and irregular wall thickening of a distal ileal segment with partial luminal narrowing. Upper and lower endoscopies were unremarkable, and the patient improved with conservative management. Follow-up MR enterography demonstrated asymmetrical small bowel wall thickening and adjacent mesenteric lymphadenopathy, with no significant mechanical cause for intestinal obstruction. In light of a possible systemic pathology, contrast CT of the chest was obtained and showed a solid infiltrative right hilar soft tissue density mass invading the mediastinum.
title: Small cell lung cancer associated small bowel obstruction, a diagnostic conundrum: A case report

case_prompt: A 72-year-old man with a history of stage IIIA non–small cell lung cancer (cT4N0M0) treated 13 months earlier with concurrent cisplatin/docetaxel and radiotherapy followed by 1 year of durvalumab presented for evaluation of an incidental pelvic nodule. Surveillance CT showed a 15-mm, round, contrast-enhancing lesion adjacent to mesorectal vessels. FDG PET/CT revealed solitary uptake in this lesion with an SUVmax of 10.3. There was no other abnormal uptake. Laboratory tests demonstrated normal carcinoembryonic antigen, sialyl Lewis X, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, neuron-specific enolase, cytokeratin fragment, progastrin-releasing peptide, and normal coagulation studies. Total colonoscopy revealed no neoplastic lesions, and urinary cytology showed only nonmalignant urothelial cells. Endoscopic or CT-guided biopsy was deemed infeasible due to anatomical restrictions and risk of complications.
title: Mesorectal thromboembolism with increased 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake during positron emission tomography/computed tomography in a patient with non-small cell lung cancer

case_prompt: A 48-year-old man with no prior comorbidities was transferred to the ICU after emergent craniotomy and intracranial pressure monitoring for traumatic epidural hematoma and subarachnoid bleeding. He had a 3–4-day history of fever and nonproductive cough following contact with a person known to have COVID-19; SARS-CoV-2 PCR on admission was positive. Seventy-two hours after ICU admission and decompressive craniectomy, he developed a maculopapular erythematous exanthem predominantly on the trunk and extremities, with sparing of mucosae, palms, and soles. Over the next 24–48 hours, the rash evolved into a papulovesicular eruption. Concurrently, he became hypotensive requiring high-dose vasopressors and developed progressive respiratory failure with rising oxygen requirements. Routine laboratory tests showed mildly elevated inflammatory markers and lymphopenia. Arterial blood gas on FiO2 0.55 revealed an oxygenation index of 490. Initial chest CT showed no infiltrates; on day 5, repeat CT demonstrated patchy ground-glass opacities and consolidations typical of COVID-19 affecting 23% of lung volume, along with small bilateral pleural effusions. At that time, his oxygenation index had fallen to 97.
title: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, primary varicella zoster virus coinfection, and a polymicrobial ventilator-associated tracheobronchitis in an adult immunocompetent male: a case report

case_prompt:
An 88-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and stage III chronic kidney disease was admitted with one week of severe weakness, anorexia, and jaundice. He was diagnosed with prostate cancer 8 months before admission, with an initial PSA level of 4280 ng/mL, skeletal and lung metastases, and no liver metastases on contrast CT. He began androgen-deprivation therapy with bicalutamide and leuprolide, but his PSA rose rapidly from 357 ng/mL to 3030 ng/mL over several months. One week before admission, bicalutamide was stopped and enzalutamide was initiated. Other medications included leuprolide, finasteride, doxazosin, metoprolol, omeprazole, ferrous gluconate, multivitamin, psyllium, and a nutritional supplement. He denied transfusions, travel, alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drug use and had no personal or family history of liver disease.

On admission, he was afebrile, pulse 91/min, blood pressure 105/47 mm Hg (MAP 66), and visibly jaundiced without hepatosplenomegaly or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 654 IU/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 988 IU/L, albumin 4 g/dL, and INR 1.2. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed nonobstructing cholelithiasis without cholecystitis or biliary ductal dilatation, with normal portal and hepatic vasculature and no lymphadenopathy. Because of his renal impairment, contrast CT was deferred. Noncontrast MRI and MRCP demonstrated normal liver parenchyma with mild reactive hepatic hilar lymphadenopathy, small benign liver cysts/hemangiomas, nonobstructing pancreatic cysts, and no biliary obstruction or metastatic lesions.
title: A rare case of idiopathic cholestasis: Clinical conundrums complicating enzalutamide therapy in metastatic prostate cancer

case_prompt:
An 81-year-old Korean man was seen urgently for a 2-month history of a temporal C-shaped scotoma in his left eye. He had a 3-year history of neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) treated with anti-VEGF in the right eye (last injection 9 months prior) and controlled nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes. Other medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, and extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (T2b/3, N3, M1a) diagnosed 5 months earlier. He had received five cycles of durvalumab (1,500 mg every 3 weeks). Before cancer treatment, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left; intraocular pressures were normal. 

On presentation, visual acuity was 20/200 OD and 20/25 OS. The anterior segments were unremarkable. Fundus examination showed an atrophic macula in the right eye from prior nAMD and only mild pigmentary changes in the left eye. Fundus autofluorescence revealed broad C-shaped hypoautofluorescent areas with hyperfluorescent margins in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated loss of the peripapillary ellipsoid zone in the left eye corresponding to the visual field defect. Fluorescein angiography showed normal vascular perfusion.

Routine laboratory tests, including a CBC and renal function, were normal except for mildly elevated AST and ALT. Abdominal ultrasound showed moderate fatty liver. Thyroid function tests indicated subclinical hypothyroidism. Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, and HIV were negative. F-FDG PET/CT revealed pleural seeding and multiple lymph node metastases. Brain MRI noted a left superior frontal gyrus metastasis, but these findings did not explain the patient’s visual field defects.
title: Sight-Threatening Immune Retinopathy Developing Secondary to Durvalumab Treatment of Small-Cell Lung Cancer: A Case Report

case_prompt: An 8-year-old autistic boy presented with severe bilateral leg pain and difficulty walking of recent onset. He also had gum swelling and bleeding, a low-grade fever, and a maculopapular rash on both upper and lower extremities. Routine blood tests, tick titers, and an autoimmune workup were all normal. A whole-body bone scintigraphy examination showed increased radiotracer activity in the bilateral shoulders, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles, most severe in the knees. Radiographs of these areas were normal. Differential considerations included infiltrative processes such as leukemia, neuroblastoma metastases, and multifocal osteomyelitis; multifocal fractures were felt to be unlikely. Contrast-enhanced MRI of both femurs demonstrated intense metaphyseal signal abnormality and enhancement in the bilateral proximal and distal femurs and proximal tibiae, as well as subperiosteal signal abnormality and enhancement along the metaphyses.
title: Scurvy in an autistic child: early disease on MRI and bone scintigraphy can mimic an infiltrative process

case_prompt: An 86-year-old man presented with acute shortness of breath and several months of unexplained weight loss. He reported recent high-impact falls, having undergone right hip hemiarthroplasty for a femoral fracture. On examination he was hypoxic with peripheral edema but had no fever, night sweats, or other constitutional symptoms. Laboratory studies showed elevated alkaline phosphatase and D-dimer levels; hemoglobin was chronically low without an acute drop, and the white-cell count, neutrophil count, and C-reactive protein were normal. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 13 × 12 × 24 cm heterogeneous complex cystic hypoenhancing lesion in the left retroperitoneum posterior to the left kidney, with attenuation values of 9–32 Hounsfield units, displacing the kidney, encasing the renal vasculature and collecting system, and causing mild hydronephrosis. MRI showed heterogeneous T2-weighted hyperintensity with multicystic areas; multiple T1-weighted hyperintense foci consistent with hemorrhage; chemical shift imaging demonstrated microscopic lipid content by signal loss on out-of-phase images in the superior portion of the cystic component; there was diffusion restriction in the peripheral solid regions; and post-contrast fat-saturated T1 images revealed avid enhancement of the thick peripheral walls and internal septations.
title: Cystic retroperitoneal dedifferentiated liposarcoma: A case report

case_prompt: A 40-year-old man presented with a four-week history of a rapidly growing nodule at the site of a scratched surgical scar on his right elbow. His oncologic history included a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor of the right forearm in 2003 treated with surgery (negative margins), radiation, and chemotherapy, and a recurrence over the biceps in 2015 treated with resection (positive margins) and additional radiotherapy. He had no personal or family history of neurofibromatosis. On examination, there was a 2.0 cm violaceous nodule with a 1 cm red, friable papulonodule centrally located on the previous surgical scar. Histopathologic examination of the nodule showed mixed hypercellular and hypocellular areas composed of atypical spindled and epithelioid cells in a myxoid stroma. The Ki-67 proliferation index was high, PHH3 staining revealed more than 30 mitoses per high-powered field, and S-100 immunostaining was focally positive. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the right forearm demonstrated a complex, dumbbell-shaped soft-tissue mass measuring approximately 5.4 × 4.3 × 3.5 cm that displaced the ulnar nerve medially and splayed the flexor muscles and tendons, with no evidence of distant metastases.
title: Recurrent malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor as a friable nodule within a scar

case_prompt: A 44-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a one‐month history of transient numbness of her right face and arm. She also reported intermittent episodes of left‐arm weakness over several years previously attributed to psychosomatic causes. On neurologic exam, plantar responses were indifferent bilaterally, and deep‐tendon reflexes were brisk. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple T2 and FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter and periventricular regions, with mild linear cortical enhancement in the left parietal lobe. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and laboratory studies for inflammatory or autoimmune disease were unremarkable. A detailed review of the MRI revealed that the lesions were predominantly located in the watershed zone between the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery territories, without restricted diffusion. Given this watershed distribution, magnetic resonance angiography of the brain was recommended to exclude a cerebrovascular etiology.
title: Moyamoya Disease May Mimic Multiple Sclerosis?

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old male presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging mass over the left lower back and pain in the right pelvic region and bilateral lower back that worsened with activity and radiated into the lower limbs. He had no history of trauma or surgery.

On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, soft, compressible subcutaneous swelling over the left lower back and two vague masses palpable in the bilateral iliac regions.

Ultrasonography of the lower back and abdomen demonstrated sizable multiseptated cystic lesions containing echogenic fluid within both psoas muscles, extending into the subcutaneous tissues and abutting the inferior poles of both kidneys.

Noncontrast CT of the abdomen showed a large multilocular cystic mass involving the bilateral psoas muscles, the left extensor muscles, and the left posterolateral abdominal wall, with attenuation values of +20 to +27 HU and calcifications in the walls and septa but no fatty components. Multiple sharply marginated osteolytic lesions were noted in the lumbar and sacral vertebrae.

MRI revealed multiloculated lesions in both psoas muscles extending to the left extensor muscle and posterolateral abdominal wall, with low signal on T1-weighted images, high signal on T2-weighted images, no restricted diffusion on DWI, and peripheral capsular and septal enhancement after gadolinium administration. Lesions extended into the lumbosacral spinal canal and intervertebral foramina, compressing the cauda equina nerve roots.

Chest CT demonstrated interstitial thickening with nodules in the lung fields, no pleural effusion or mediastinal adenopathy, and well-circumscribed osteolytic lesions in the thoracic vertebrae.
title: Generalized lymphangiomatosis—A rare manifestation of lymphatic malformation

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department with severe right upper‐quadrant abdominal pain, moderate epigastric pain, and chest pain. He reported a COVID-19 infection 14 days earlier, after which he developed mild right upper‐quadrant discomfort that progressed over 3 days to severe pain aggravated by eating and unrelieved by changes in position. The chest pain was described as atypical for cardiac origin and was accompanied by nausea and vomiting. He denied alcohol use, trauma, and had no known chronic diseases; family history was notable for cholecystectomy in his mother and sisters.

On arrival, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, pulse 80/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure without peripheral edema, normal abdominal percussion, and a liver span of 14.5 cm at the midclavicular line.

Electrocardiogram showed bradyarrhythmia, T-wave inversion in lead V1, and ST‐segment elevation in leads V2 through V6. Chest and abdominal radiographs were unremarkable, with no evidence of pneumonia, air under the diaphragm, or biliary air; gallbladder sludge was noted. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated trivial mitral regurgitation and an ejection fraction of 55%.

Laboratory tests revealed elevated high-sensitivity troponin (0 h: 1547.6 pg/ml; 6 h: 1342.8 pg/ml), amylase 2420 U/L, lipase 987 U/L, AST 800 IU/L, ALT 760 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 361 IU/L, total bilirubin 3.27 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 2.37 mg/dl, blood sugar 203 mg/dl, and urea 68 mg/dl.
title: Elevated troponin level and nonspecific ST‐segment and T‐wave changes in a suspected acute pancreatitis patient, post‐SARS‐Cov‐2 infection: A case report

case_prompt: A 70-year-old man presented with 2 weeks of abdominal pain, headache, and new melena after a family-physician trial of NSAIDs and a mucosal protectant. On arrival, he was hypotensive (80/56 mmHg), tachycardic (100 bpm), and severely anemic (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL). After blood-transfusion stabilization, esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) showed atypical esophagitis lesions in the lower esophagus and shallow ulcers and erosions throughout the stomach and duodenum. Colonoscopy (CS) revealed extensive, map-like shallow ulcers with well-defined margins and islands of residual mucosa in the terminal ileum; biopsy showed moderate lymphocytic infiltration without malignancy or cytomegalovirus. Biopsy of endoscopically normal ileal mucosa showed only mild lymphocytic infiltration. A proton‐pump inhibitor was started, and upper GI lesions healed on follow-up EGD one month later. Capsule endoscopy had previously demonstrated multiple small aphtha-like erosions in the ileum. Stool cultures were negative. The patient’s gastrin level was 100 pg/mL (normal <200 pg/mL). Serum MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA, and antinuclear antibodies were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable. Follow-up CS one month after presentation showed that the terminal ileal ulcers and erosions remained unchanged despite discontinuation of NSAIDs.
title: Immunoglobulin G4‐related disease accompanying a small intestinal ulcer: A case

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old man presented with facial swelling. A chest radiograph showed a large mass projecting over the right lung field. CT of the chest demonstrated an enormous anterior mediastinal mass contiguous with the posterior sternum and right ribs, occluding the superior vena cava and compressing the heart. Routine blood tests, tumor markers, and acetylcholine receptor antibodies were all normal or negative. Bronchoscopic biopsy revealed features of a carcinoid tumor. 

He underwent en bloc excision of the mass, including resection of the superior vena cava with graft insertion, resection of the right phrenic nerve, and diaphragm plication. Histologic examination identified an atypical carcinoid of the thymus (intermediate-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma), with invasion into fat, pleura, lung lymphatics, and metastases in a hilar node and a cervical thymic node.

One month postoperatively, chest CT showed poststernotomy changes, a right basal fluid-filled cyst, bilateral atelectasis, and pleural thickening. An I-123 MIBG scan was negative for residual or recurrent disease. One year later, follow-up CT revealed no mediastinal recurrence, persistent linear atelectasis in both lower lobes, and elevated right hemidiaphragm. A bone scan showed increased uptake in the posterior arch of the right eighth rib. 

To further evaluate his status, a somatostatin receptor scintigraphy with In-111-DTPA-D-Phe^1-pentetreotide was performed. The scan demonstrated an area of abnormally increased radiotracer concentration in the mediastinum, raising the question of residual tumor, recurrence, or an inflammatory process.
journal: International seminars in surgical oncology : ISSO
title: Interpretation of the post-surgical Somatostatin Receptor Scintigram of a Primary Neuroendocrine Tumor of the Thymus: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
An 84-year-old woman was admitted with a  one-day history of left lower abdominal pain and nausea without fever. She had a history of hysterectomy, femoral neck fracture repair, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Her body mass index was 18.2 kg/m2; vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, there was tenderness in the left lower abdomen without peritoneal signs and no Murphy sign. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, liver function tests, and biliary enzymes, were all within normal limits. 
A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen at admission showed an enlarged gallbladder with wall thickening but no gallstones, along with prominent small-bowel gas, mild intestinal dilatation, and slight wall thickening. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed an enlarged, thick-walled gallbladder without stones. She was diagnosed with acute enterocolitis or subileus and managed conservatively with bowel rest and intravenous fluids.
Six hours later, she developed sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and vomiting unresponsive to analgesics or antiemetics. A repeat CT scan demonstrated that the gallbladder had become more distended and thickened, had rotated approximately 180°, and had shifted toward the midline; the cystic duct was now located on the right side of the gallbladder.
title: Complete gallbladder torsion diagnosed with sequential computed tomography scans: a case report

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old Sudanese girl presented with a 2-day history of colicky abdominal pain, absolute constipation, and vomiting of all ingested food. Since age 5, she had recurrent nocturnal abdominal pain exacerbated by spicy foods, frequent yellowish diarrhea, dyspepsia, and daily loud audible bowel sounds. She is the seventh of 10 siblings, with two of her siblings and four nephews having died in early childhood. 

On examination, she appeared ill, in pain, and tachypneic, with a low-grade fever. Her abdomen was distended and tender. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits. 

Supine abdominal radiography showed a tubular gas-filled structure originating in the right iliac fossa, crossing obliquely upward to the left hypochondrium. Erect abdominal radiography revealed multiple air-fluid levels. A diagnosis of acute intestinal obstruction was made, and the patient was taken for emergency exploratory laparotomy.
title: 54‐cm enteric duplication cyst in a 13‐year‐old female

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman with primary open-angle glaucoma and poor adherence to topical therapy was referred for surgical management. She had a history of severe obesity (BMI 37 kg/m2) and well-controlled insulin-dependent diabetes. Preoperative best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Untreated IOPs were consistently in the mid-30s mmHg; with tafluprost, her IOPs were 18 mmHg OD and 16 mmHg OS. Optic discs showed a temporal notch OD and were otherwise unremarkable.  

She underwent an uneventful mitomycin C–augmented trabeculectomy in the right eye. On postoperative day 1, her IOP was 8 mmHg, the bleb was functioning, and the anterior chamber was well formed; fundus examination was normal.  

Two weeks later, she complained of blurred vision in the right eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/32, and IOP was 10 mmHg off medications. Fundoscopy revealed multiple superficial, flame-shaped hemorrhages radiating from the optic disc with disc edema and no choroidal effusion. Optical coherence tomography showed macular folding with a small neurosensory detachment. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated macular microaneurysms with dye leakage, peripapillary hemorrhages, and late optic disc leakage without areas of nonperfusion or neovascularization.
title: Consecutive bilateral decompression retinopathy after mitomycin C trabeculectomy: a case report

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old Japanese woman presented with a one-month history of slightly pruritic, tender subcutaneous nodules in both temporal areas. She denied systemic symptoms, including fever, weight loss, visual changes, or musculoskeletal stiffness. Her medical history was unremarkable for allergic disease or asthma; she was a 20–30 pack-year smoker. Family history was notable only for neurofibromatosis in her son.

On examination, her temperature was 35.7°C, pulse 61/min, and blood pressure 131/71 mmHg. The nodules corresponded to enlargement of the superficial temporal arteries with reduced pulsation. Cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were normal; there was no peripheral edema.

Ultrasound of the temporal arteries showed hypoechogenic wall thickening and luminal stenosis. Initial laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 10,300/μL with 5.4% eosinophils (556/μL); ESR and CRP were within normal limits. Serologic tests including ANA, RF, ANCA, complement levels, and hepatitis serologies were unremarkable. Stool examinations were negative for parasites. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed no ischemic changes.

Over the next three months, her absolute eosinophil count rose to 1,954/μL. She developed coolness and cyanosis of the fingertips and small pruritic nodules on the sides of her fingers. CT of the chest and echocardiography were normal. Color duplex ultrasonography of the hands revealed occlusion of the ulnar arteries and a corkscrew pattern of the digital arteries. Angiography confirmed occlusion of the ulnar artery, palmar arch, and proper digital arteries.
title: Development of Eosinophilic Temporal Arteritis and Digital Ischemia in a Patient with Hypereosinophilic Syndrome

case_prompt:
A 4-month-old male infant presented with fresh blood-stained stools, sometimes loose but not frankly diarrhoeic, without fever or vomiting. He had been exclusively breastfed until 3 months of age, after which fresh cow’s milk was added. At 4 months (weight 6.0 kg), stool microscopy at a local clinic reportedly showed Entamoeba histolytica, and he received metronidazole. Over the next two months, he again had blood-stained stools despite two more courses of antiparasitic and antibiotic therapy (metronidazole, cotrimoxazole, tinidazole, chloroquine), with repeat stool microscopy each time reporting E. histolytica. He remained in good general condition, continued to gain weight, and had no diarrhoea, fever, or vomiting.

On referral to the paediatrician at age 6 months (weight 7.5 kg), the history of ongoing cow’s milk supplementation was elicited. Physical examination was unremarkable with no abdominal or perianal lesions. Abdominal ultrasound was normal. Laboratory facilities for immunoglobulin assays, specific antibodies, or skin testing were unavailable. A preliminary diagnosis of cow’s milk protein allergy was made. The antibiotics and antimalarials were discontinued, and a dietary trial was initiated. Cow’s milk was excluded from the infant’s diet, and exclusive breastfeeding was resumed.
title: Diagnosing possible infantile cow’s milk protein allergy in rural Africa, when history and physical examination are the only tools: a case report

case_prompt: A 78-year-old woman presented with five days of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and intermittent fevers. She had undergone a difficult laparoscopic subtotal cholecystectomy one month earlier for chronic cholecystitis, with placement and subsequent removal of a Jackson-Pratt drain. Her past medical history was notable for hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux. On examination, she was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had minimal right upper quadrant tenderness without jaundice. Laboratory studies showed elevated liver-function tests with a normal white-blood-cell count and lipase. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated no collection in the gallbladder fossa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed central intrahepatic biliary ductal dilation and dilation of the common hepatic duct to 1.2 cm. Based on this presentation, the decision was made to perform an endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography.
title: Combined Endoscopic and Laparoscopic Management of Postcholecystectomy Mirizzi Syndrome from a Remnant Cystic Duct Stone: Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old Samoan man was referred for evaluation of a 2-month history of persistent productive cough and worsening exertional dyspnea. Over the preceding 3 months he had noted subjective fevers and a 5-kg weight loss. He had chronic sinusitis and had been diagnosed with asthma in adolescence; treatment with inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators yielded no improvement. He was a lifelong non-smoker, worked in a mattress factory, and had no known risk factors for tuberculosis or immunosuppression.

On examination, he was afebrile, with an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Auscultation revealed coarse crackles predominantly at the lung bases, without wheezing; there were no signs of right heart failure.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral nodular interstitial infiltrates in the mid and lower lung zones. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest showed extensive tree-in-bud nodularity in all lobes, most pronounced in the lower lobes, along with bronchial wall thickening and early bronchiectasis. Spirometry revealed a fixed moderately severe airflow obstruction (FEV₁ 55% predicted, FEV₁/FVC 63%).

Sputum cultures grew Haemophilus influenzae; mycobacterial cultures were negative. An autoimmune panel, including rheumatoid factor and cold agglutinins, was within normal limits.
title: Diffuse panbronchiolitis in a Samoan man

case_prompt:
A man in his 70s was admitted with a 1-week history of abdominal fullness, jaundice, and anorexia. His medical history was notable for cutaneous melanoma diagnosed in 2017 (stage IIIc, SOX10 and S100 positive) treated with local excision and 1 year of adjuvant nivolumab, and multiple myeloma diagnosed in 2021 treated with bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone. One month before admission, he was found to have inguinal lymphadenopathy and recurrent melanoma, for which he was started on temozolomide.

Two months before admission, an abdominal CT scan showed multiple sub-centimeter hypoattenuating hepatic foci. Two weeks before admission, liver function tests were mildly elevated, and an abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an increase in size and number of the previously noted hepatic cysts. On admission, liver tests were: alanine aminotransferase 427 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 323 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 568 U/L, total bilirubin 9.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.5 mg/dL, and γ-glutamyl transferase 339 U/L.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed innumerable, mildly complex cystic liver lesions markedly increased in size and number compared with prior imaging. The lesions demonstrated diffusion restriction, internal fluid-fluid levels, and thin septations; they were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed no enhancement on postcontrast sequences.
title: Metastatic melanoma presenting as rapidly enlarging hepatic cysts

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old Indonesian man presented with a 1-year history of exertional dyspnea.  
He had been diagnosed with bronchiectasis in 2008 based on chronic productive cough and chest radiography. He denied childhood severe respiratory infections, was a never-smoker, had no environmental tobacco or biomass exposure, and worked as an engineer without dust or fume exposures. He had no cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, wheezing, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, limb swelling, fevers, night sweats, anorexia, weight loss, skin, or joint complaints.  
Vital signs were normal. Examination showed a centrally located trachea and reduced breath sounds with dullness over the left upper chest; no clubbing.  
Chest radiograph revealed increased lucency in the upper half of the left hemithorax. Chest CT showed bronchiectatic changes in the left lower lobe, a few small cysts, and several bullae occupying almost the entire left hemithorax.  
Extensive blood tests, including immunoglobulins, connective tissue disease screen, and α₁-antitrypsin level, were unremarkable.  
Pulmonary function tests: FEV₁/FVC 0.83, FVC 2.56 L (59% predicted), FEV₁ 2.13 L (59% predicted); TLC by nitrogen washout 3.43 L (56% predicted) and by plethysmography 5.33 L (88% predicted); residual volume 2.65 L (156% predicted); DLCO 77% predicted.  
Bronchoscopy was grossly normal; malacia was seen in a segment of the left upper lobe; BAL cultures were negative; endobronchial biopsies showed acute inflammation without granulomas or malignancy.
title: A breath from Houdini – A case of giant bullous emphysema

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old woman, nonsmoker, nondiabetic, and nonhypertensive, presented with a 2-month history of insidious, progressive weakness of all four limbs, accompanied by decreased sensation in the lower limbs and tingling in all extremities. Over the past 4 days she developed urinary retention. Two months earlier, she experienced a one-week history of low-grade fever that resolved spontaneously, after which she noted persistent dull neck pain and gradually worsening quadriparesis. She denied anorexia, weight loss, cough, hemoptysis, or palpable lumps elsewhere.

On examination, mild pallor was present. Neurologic exam revealed spastic quadriparesis (grade 4/5 upper limbs; grade 3/5 lower limbs), hyperreflexia in all limbs, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and hypoesthesia in the lower limbs without a clear sensory level. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL; white blood cell count 8,000/mm3; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm in the first hour; blood glucose, renal function, and liver function tests normal; HIV negative.

Chest radiograph showed an expansile lesion of the right fourth rib. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated altered marrow signal and erosion of C5 to T1 vertebrae, intraspinal extension elevating the posterior longitudinal ligament between C5 and T1, compression of the thecal sac and spinal cord, with preserved intervertebral disc height and signal. MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine revealed multifocal vertebral marrow signal abnormalities involving T6, T7, T9, T10, L2–L5, and the sacrum, with pedicle involvement at T10 and L5, intraspinal extension at T6 and sacral levels, and large pre- and paravertebral soft tissue masses.

At this stage, the differential diagnosis included metastatic disease versus an infectious etiology such as tuberculosis.

On reexamination, a small, firm, painless, mobile mass was palpated in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Ultrasonography of the right breast showed a 3.5 × 2.3 cm hypoechoic, heterogeneous lesion with internal echogenic foci and several enlarged right axillary lymph nodes; the left breast was normal.
title: Multifocal Tubercular Osteomyelitis with Tubercular Breast Abscess: An Atypical Presentation of Tuberculosis

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman presented with a several-day history of cough and fever up to 38 °C. Over the same period, she noted changing sputum color, back pain, limb weakness, dysphagia, hemoptysis, wheezing, chest pain, and alterations in bowel habits. She denied weight loss or facial changes. Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable. Vital signs were normal. Examination revealed clear lungs, normal heart sounds, and no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

Chest CT showed a 5.5 cm × 5 cm × 1.8 cm solid mass in the anterior mediastinum with adhesion to but no definite invasion of the pericardium (Masaoka IIb). The mass was completely resected thoracoscopically. Grossly, it was encapsulated, grayish-white to grayish-brown, and had an ill-defined border against surrounding adipose tissue. 

Microscopic examination of hematoxylin–eosin–stained sections revealed multiple epithelial micronodules separated by abundant lymphoid stroma forming lymphoid follicles. No necrosis was seen. Tumor cells infiltrated surrounding adipose tissue at the periphery. Residual thymic tissue lay adjacent to the lesion. The neoplastic epithelial cells exhibited marked pleomorphism with visible nucleoli and mitotic figures ranging from 1 to 9 per 10 high-power fields.
final_diagnosis_raw: Micronodular thymic carcinoma with lymphoid hyperplasia
title: Micronodular thymic tumor with lymphoid stroma: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 37-year-old Caucasian man presented with five days of redness in the right eye, three days of photophobia, ocular pain, and slight blurriness. He denied ocular trauma, recent illness, or cold sores. His ophthalmic history included uncomplicated bilateral small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) six months earlier. He had begun nighttime continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy two weeks prior for newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnea and noted increased right-eye dryness on awakening. On examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed inferonasal conjunctival injection with sectoral ciliary flush and limbitis. At the 4 o’clock position, small peripheral corneal infiltrates were visible without epithelial defect or corneal staining. Diffuse lamellar keratitis (grade I) was noted beneath the SMILE cap margin, corresponding to the area of limbitis. Examination of the left eye revealed mild superficial punctate keratopathy. Both eyes showed inspissated Meibomian glands and posterior marginal telangiectasias.
title: Marginal Keratitis with Secondary Diffuse Lamellar Keratitis After Small Incision Lenticule Extraction (SMILE) After Initiation of Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) Therapy

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of discomfort and a gradually enlarging lump at the base of her right thumb and thenar eminence. Her medical history included osteoarthritis of the right thumb, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia; she was an ex-smoker with moderate alcohol use. Family history was noncontributory.

On examination, there was a mildly tender, circumferential mass extending from the thumb base to the proximal phalanx with no movement at the metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joints; neurovascular function was intact.

A radiograph of the right thumb showed soft-tissue swelling over the dorsolateral aspect without bony scalloping or erosion and degenerative changes at the metacarpophalangeal joint. Ultrasound revealed a multilobulated hypoechoic lesion up to 6 cm surrounding the flexor pollicis longus tendon. MRI demonstrated a 4.6 × 2.9 × 6.7 cm multilobulated mass encasing the flexor pollicis longus tendon and surrounding the first proximal phalanx, metacarpophalangeal joint, and first metacarpal, with intermediate T1 signal, T2 hyperintensity, and heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement.

An ultrasound-guided biopsy showed an atypical cartilaginous lesion with mild-to-moderate cytological atypia abutting bone but without bony infiltration; high-grade malignant features were not identified.
title: Tenosynovial chondromatosis of the flexor pollicis longus tendon: A subtype of primary synovial chondromatosis

case_prompt: A 49-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of headache. Physical, neurologic, and ophthalmologic examinations, including visual acuity, fundoscopy, and visual fields, were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a sellar cystic lesion measuring 18 × 14 × 14 mm that extended from the suprasellar cistern through the diaphragma sellae to the dorsum sellae and compressed the optic chiasm. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images; in contrast studies, rim-like peripheral enhancement was noted. The normal pituitary gland and stalk enhanced typically and were displaced laterally to the right by the lesion. Computed tomography of the sellar region showed a hypodense cystic lesion with no contrast enhancement. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, routine biochemistry, pituitary hormone levels, and urinalysis, were within normal limits.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Intrasellar arachnoid cyst: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old Sri Lankan shopkeeper with diet‐controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with three weeks of generalized malaise, nightly “feverishness,” evening sweats, anorexia, and 3-kg weight loss. He denied cough, hemoptysis, or tuberculosis contacts. There was nausea without vomiting or abdominal pain and no features of autoimmune disease. He had no significant environmental or travel exposures and no history of recurrent infections.

On examination he was afebrile, mildly pale, with mild nontender hepatomegaly but no lymphadenopathy, rashes, or splenomegaly. Blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg without postural drop. Initial labs showed pancytopenia (WBC 3.0×10^9/L, platelets 120×10^6/L, hemoglobin 10 g/dL), CRP 8 mg/L, ESR 60 mm/h, normal liver and renal profiles, and HbA1c 6.5%. Chest radiograph and echocardiogram were normal. Blood and urine cultures, Mantoux test, and bone marrow biopsy (including fungal and tuberculosis studies) were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatosplenomegaly, para‐aortic lymphadenopathy, and bilateral hypoechoic adrenal masses.

One week later he returned with three days of severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and postural dizziness. He was hypotensive (90/60 mmHg with a 30 mmHg postural drop), tachycardic (100 bpm), and dehydrated. Despite fluids his blood pressure remained low. Labs showed hyponatremia (114 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (5.0 mmol/L), random cortisol 1.3 µg/L, and improved blood counts. An ACTH stimulation test showed persistently low cortisol (<1 µg/L). CT of the chest and abdomen revealed bilateral, well‐defined, homogeneously enhancing adrenal masses (left 6.9×3.7×5.0 cm; right 5.3×3.4×5.4 cm), mild hepatosplenomegaly, and patchy para‐aortic lymphadenopathy.

Ultrasound‐guided adrenal biopsy showed necrosis with plasma cells, lymphocytes, and histiocytes. Gomori–Grocott methenamine silver staining demonstrated numerous fungal spores morphologically similar to Histoplasma.
title: A Rare Presentation of Possible Disseminated Histoplasmosis with Adrenal Insufficiency Leading to Adrenal Crisis in an Immunocompetent Adult: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man with a history of dyslipidemia presented with chronic headaches without vomiting or perceived visual changes. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a suprasellar mass measuring 12.5 mm. MRI revealed a 15 × 17 × 12 mm pituitary lesion that was T1-hyperintense, T2-hyperintense, intensely enhanced with gadolinium, elevated the optic chiasm and stalk, and infiltrated both cavernous sinuses. Automated perimetry demonstrated bitemporal hemianopsia.

On review of systems, he reported longstanding fatigue, cold intolerance, hoarseness, constipation, and weight gain. Vital signs showed a pulse of 55/min. BMI was 30.5 kg/m2. Examination revealed dry skin, a pale puffy face with periorbital edema, thinning of the lateral eyebrows, and macroglossia. The thyroid gland was not palpable.

Laboratory studies showed free T4 of 0 ng/dL (NR, 0.61–1.12), free T3 of 1.88 pg/mL (NR, 2.50–3.90), and TSH > 100 µUI/mL (NR, 0.34–5.60). Prolactin was 22.5 ng/mL (NR, 2.64–13.13), testosterone was 2.04 ng/mL (NR, 2–10), LH was 2.8 UI/L (NR, 1.24–8.62), and FSH was 5.1 UI/L (NR, 1.27–19.26). Anti–thyroid peroxidase antibodies were elevated at 56.9 UI/mL (NR, 0.25–9), and thyroid ultrasound showed an atrophic, hypoechoic gland consistent with autoimmune thyroiditis.
title: An Unusual Pituitary Mass Revealing a Primary Hypothyroidism!

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old boy noted a progressively enlarging lump at his posterior left knee over one year. MRI revealed a 13 cm mass in the left posteroinferior thigh, centered in the semitendinosus muscle and extending to the biceps femoris. Fine-needle aspiration showed a heterogeneous population of ovoid to tapered spindle cells with densely eosinophilic cytoplasm and occasional multinucleated cells; no lipogenic differentiation was seen. Immunohistochemistry was positive for desmin and myogenin and negative for CD68, keratin, S-100, SOX-10, HMB-45, and Melan-A. FISH for a FOXO1 13q14 rearrangement was negative. A diagnosis of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma was made, and the patient received 10 weeks of vincristine/irinotecan chemotherapy per protocol ARST0531. 

The tumor was then completely excised. Grossly, it was a mixed cystic and solid mass with a thin white capsule. H&E sections revealed diffuse sheets of round cells with eosinophilic rhabdomyoblastic cytoplasm and large nuclei. Throughout the tumor, a subset of cells exhibited a spectrum of cytoplasmic vacuolation, from small vacuoles to multiple vacuoles indenting the nucleus, resembling adipocytes or lipoblasts. These vacuolated cells were positive for adipophilin, Oil Red O, and S-100 protein; the vacuoles were negative with periodic acid–Schiff stain, with or without diastase. Immunostaining for desmin was positive in the vacuolated cells, whereas myogenin was negative in their nuclei. There was cystic change, scattered histiocytes, extracellular hemosiderin, low mitotic activity (1 mf/10 hpf), and no coagulative necrosis.
title: Adipocyte-Like Differentiation in a Posttreatment Embryonal Rhabdomyosarcoma

case_prompt: A 14-year-old boy was referred for failure to gain weight and restrictive eating behaviors since early childhood. Parents described early breastfeeding difficulties and persistent aversions to certain textures and smells. His diet was limited to very plain and smoothly textured foods (for example, burgers without toppings, purees) and a narrow list of items (for example, Cheerios, chicken nuggets). He displayed rigid routines (insisting on the same seat at dinner, folding clothes in a particular way) and marked distress when routines were disrupted. He was anxious, with worsening anxiety after parental separation at age 5, and had inattention affecting school. His weight had tracked along the 3rd percentile until age 5, then plateaued for 8 years; bone age was delayed by one year. He was seen 2 months earlier by a pediatric endocrinologist, with no clear endocrine diagnosis. One month before admission, a psychiatrist’s formulation included sensory integration disorder, communication and other learning disorders, eating disorder, and autism spectrum disorder. Occupational therapy and psychoeducational assessments were recommended but not completed. On admission, weight was 24.4 kg (<0.01 percentile), height 143.5 cm (0.39 percentile), BMI 11.8 kg/m2 (≈68% of ideal weight). Laboratory studies showed no electrolyte abnormalities. The gastroenterology service did not find an organic cause for his failure to thrive.
title: Delayed diagnosis of avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder and autism spectrum disorder in a 14‐year‐old boy

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old man presented with lower urinary tract symptoms characterized by hesitancy, poor urinary stream, and urgency. He denied flank pain, colicky pain, haematuria, weight loss, or constitutional symptoms. His medical history was unremarkable, and he had no prior genitourinary disease. He was afebrile, with stable vital signs, and a physical examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a serum prostate-specific antigen level of 5.1 ng/ml and a serum creatinine concentration of 86 μmol/l. Urine microscopy demonstrated no haematuria or atypical cells. Transrectal ultrasound–guided prostate biopsies revealed benign prostatic hyperplasia.

An abdominal ultrasound performed to evaluate his lower urinary tract symptoms incidentally revealed an exophytic lesion in the right kidney measuring approximately 3.0 × 3.2 × 4.2 cm. The lesion was homogeneous and hypoechoic with a well-defined margin, located at the lateral border of the ventral mid-zone of the kidney. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed a soft-tissue mass in the same location, measuring up to 2.17 cm in maximum diameter, with a small area of calcification; the lesion was exophytic and situated away from the renal hilum.
title: Perirenal schwannoma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old woman presented with a 1.5-year history of progressive weakness in her left upper extremity that had impaired her work as a hairstylist. She had a background of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) and cervical intervertebral disc degeneration. Ten weeks earlier, she underwent left carpal tunnel release without symptomatic improvement.

Initial EMG/NCS (October 2020) showed moderate-to-severe left CTS, mild right CTS, and mild cervical radiculopathy. On examination, she had bilateral hyperreflexia in upper and lower extremities (3+ biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, patellar, Achilles), bilateral positive Hoffman signs, and weakness more pronounced on the left (deltoid 3/5 bilaterally; biceps 4/5 right, 3/5 left; triceps 4/5 right, 3/5 left; wrist extensors/flexors 4/5 left; hand intrinsics 3/5 left). Lower extremity strength was 4/5 in tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus bilaterally. Sensation was intact.

Cervical MRI revealed degenerative disc disease at C5–C6 and C6–C7 with a small C6–C7 disc herniation causing moderate bilateral foraminal stenosis, worse on the left, but no central canal stenosis.

Given the combination of marked bilateral weakness (left > right), hyperreflexia, positive Hoffman signs, and fasciculations, she was referred to neurology for repeat EMG/NCS and to a neurosurgeon for surgical consideration.
title: Preventing Unnecessary Surgery in Patients Presenting for Orthopedic Spine Surgery: Literature Review and Case Series

case_prompt:
A man in his 60s presented with 3 days of weakness in both lower limbs. He had visited a hot spring 5 days before presentation. His medical history included spontaneous pneumothoraces and untreated hypertension. He was a 40 pack-year smoker, drank alcohol daily, and took no regular medications. On examination, his temperature was 39.1°C, blood pressure 198/94 mm Hg, heart rate 115 bpm (irregular, atrial fibrillation), respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Neurologically, he had mild disturbance of consciousness (Japan Coma Scale I-1, Glasgow Coma Scale E4V4M6), dysarthria, kinetic tremor in both hands, and an unsteady gait. He was inattentive, mildly hyperactive, and occasionally removed his oxygen mask.  
Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (WBC 13.7×10^9/L, neutrophils 91.4%), CRP 33.83 mg/dL, elevated liver enzymes (AST 91 U/L, ALT 63 U/L), hyponatraemia (Na 131 mmol/L), and CK 1551 U/L. Legionella pneumophila urinary antigen was positive; sputum culture was negative. Chest X-ray and CT revealed consolidation in the right lower lobe and bilateral emphysema. Head CT was normal. Brain MRI on admission showed a focal hyperintense lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum on diffusion-weighted imaging, with corresponding mild T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity; MR angiography was unremarkable. No cerebrospinal fluid examination or EEG was performed.
title: Case of clinically mild encephalitis/encephalopathy with a reversible splenial lesion (MERS) due to Legionella pneumonia

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old woman was referred to the Movement Disorders Clinic with a 4-month history of vertigo and bradykinesia and a 3-month history of right-hand tremor. She reported several episodes of falling, insomnia, memory decline, depression, and urinary retention and frequency over the past few months. She also described self-mutilating behavior for 2 years, consisting of skin scratching around the umbilical area without pruritus; she felt relaxed after viewing her blood. She denied hallucinations, obsessive-compulsive behaviors, other psychiatric disorders, and REM sleep behavior disorder.

Her medical history included diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hypertension, bariatric surgery 7 years earlier, and cholecystectomy 2 years earlier. Medications were metformin, insulin, metoprolol, levothyroxine, and fluoxetine. Family history was unremarkable.

On examination, she had bradykinesia, bilateral jerky resting and postural tremor of the hands, rigidity, a wide-based gait, stooped posture, Pisa syndrome, and a positive pull test. Her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 22. Distal extremities were cold and pale, and blood pressure fell from baseline by 30 mm Hg systolic and 20 mm Hg diastolic after 3 minutes of standing. There was no minipolymyoclonus, dystonia, chorea, or pyramidal signs. Brain MRI showed nonspecific white matter lesions without cerebellar or pontine atrophy.
title: Atypical parkinsonism and self‐mutilation: A new lens on the old concept

case_prompt: A 29-year-old morbidly obese woman presented with a 6-month history of left anterior knee pain localized to the patellar region. She reported no systemic symptoms. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination of the knee revealed mild tenderness over the patella without swelling or joint effusion. Vital signs were within normal limits. A complete blood count and knee ultrasound were normal. Conventional radiographs of the knee showed no abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee identified an 8 mm well-defined round lesion in the superior aspect of the patella with an edematous-type signal: hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on fat-saturated sequences. At that time, the differential diagnoses were chondroblastoma and osteoblastoma, which may overlap in their radiological appearance.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A lesion of the patella: An unexpected location of Rosai-Dorfman disease: A case report

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old farmer presented with a two-month history of multiple shiny, nonpruritic papules, nodules, and plaques over the trunk, lower back, buttocks, arms, legs, face, chest wall, elbows, and knees, numbering approximately 42. The lesions were flat-topped, nonscaly, flesh-colored to erythematous, soft to firm in consistency, and ranged in size from 0.3 × 0.3 cm to 10.0 × 5.5 cm; they had been painful for the past 15 days. Lesions spared the scalp, ears, oral cavity, palms, soles, and genitalia. He reported a 15-day history of low-grade fever, ocular redness with pain and discharge, and nasal stuffiness; the nasal bridge appeared normal. Examination revealed no nerve thickening or lymphadenopathy and intact pain, touch, and temperature sensation. There was no history of epistaxis, insect bite, trauma, or long-term drug intake, and the family history was noncontributory. Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis, and HIV ELISA was negative.  
The clinical considerations included infective diseases (Kala azar and other granulomatous lesions), sarcoidosis, and acute febrile neutrophilic dermatoses.
title: De Novo Histoid Leprosy in an Elderly: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old immunocompetent man with diabetes, morbid obesity, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation presented with several months of new-onset headache and tremor. On examination, he had a left homonymous hemianopsia. 

Noncontrast head CT showed a mass-like lesion in the right parietal–occipital region with extensive surrounding edema in the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes, causing mass effect on the right occipital horn without midline shift. 

MRI of the brain with and without IV contrast revealed a 4.2 × 3.2 × 3.2 cm ring-enhancing mass in the right occipital lobe, with surrounding edema extending into the right parietal and temporal lobes and mass effect on the occipital horn, but no midline shift. The ADC map demonstrated a hypointense signal centrally, indicating low diffusivity. There were scattered findings of chronic small-vessel ischemic disease and a chronic cortical infarct in the right frontal lobe. 

Staging CT scans of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis and a bone marrow aspirate failed to identify a primary lesion or metastatic disease elsewhere. 

The imaging-based differential diagnosis included glioblastoma IDH-wild type, metastasis, abscess, and lymphoma. Ring enhancement in lymphoma is typically seen in immunocompromised patients. Neurosurgery was consulted for potential biopsy or resection.
title: Primary CNS ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman with essential thrombocythemia diagnosed at age 36 (JAK2 V617F–positive) was treated with hydroxyurea until 1994 and then with pyrimethamine. In February 2012, she noted a 3-month history of intermittent fevers, unintentional weight loss, and lethargy. She also developed discomfort and brownish discoloration of her left leg, initially managed as venous insufficiency. Peripheral blood film showed leukoerythroblastic changes. A bone marrow biopsy again demonstrated megakaryocytic hyperplasia consistent with essential thrombocythemia, without fibrosis or leukemic transformation.

While hospitalized for atypical pneumonia, she observed multiple nodular lesions on her left lower leg. On examination, there were numerous firm nodules from mid-shin to ankle without ulceration, bleeding, discharge, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. A punch biopsy of one lesion revealed a diffuse dermal infiltrate of large pleomorphic cells with both plasmacytic and immunoblastic features. Immunohistochemistry showed negativity for CD20 and positivity for CD138, Bcl-2, CD45, and weak CD79a, with a Ki-67 proliferation index of approximately 50%. Staining was negative for pan-cytokeratins, S-100, Melan-A, CD2, CD56, CD30, Bcl-6, and TdT. In situ hybridization for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV EBER-ISH) revealed positive nuclear staining.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left leg confirmed subcutaneous nodules with adjacent tibialis anterior myositis but no bone involvement. MRI of the spine showed a known T8 compression fracture and no new lesions. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated mild splenomegaly (16.2 cm) and no other disease sites. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 106 g/L, platelets 123 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.7 × 10^9/L, lactate dehydrogenase 1151 IU/L, β2-microglobulin 6.51 mg/L, an IgA kappa monoclonal protein of 7 g/L, and IgG kappa < 1 g/L. Serologic tests were negative for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV; there was evidence of past EBV and CMV exposure.
title: Cutaneous Plasmablastic Lymphoma in an Immunocompetent Patient with Long-Term Pyrimethamine Use for Essential Thrombocythemia: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman underwent a first-trimester ultrasound that revealed a septated fetal cystic hygroma, which had resolved by 20 weeks. Placental villous sampling showed a normal male karyotype (46, XY), and tests for congenital viral infections were negative. At 20 weeks, Doppler interrogation of the ductus venosus demonstrated a reversed a-wave during atrial contraction; this normalized later in gestation. 

The infant was born at 39+4 weeks’ gestation, weighing 4385 g, with a head circumference +3.4 SD above the mean. He required supplemental oxygen for several hours after delivery, then remained clinically stable. Physical examination revealed no dysmorphic features or cardiac murmurs. Electrocardiography and chest radiography were unremarkable.

Because of the prenatal hygroma, transthoracic echocardiography was performed on day 5 of life. Cardiac structure and function were normal except that neither the right nor left superior vena cava was visualized. Instead, a venous structure coursed posterior to the heart and drained into a markedly dilated inferior vena cava, which connected normally to the right atrium. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen confirmed absence of both superior vena cavae, with head and upper-limb venous return via a plexus draining into the inferior vena cava.

Since 1 month of age, the infant experienced persistent wheezing, worsening with respiratory infections. At 8 months, magnetic resonance angiography of the chest and abdomen reconfirmed total absence of the superior vena cava: the right arm and right head drained into the azygos vein, the left side drained into the hemiazygos vein, which joined the azygos below the carina and formed a loop beneath the diaphragm to the inferior vena cava. No vascular structures compressed the trachea. 

At 1 year, abdominal ultrasonography showed no portal hypertension. Genetic testing for CATCH 22 syndrome, Sotos syndrome, and Prader-Willi syndrome was negative.
title: Bilateral Absence of the Superior Vena Cava

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old woman, at 12 weeks’ gestation, was referred with a cystic liver-hilum mass. Six weeks earlier she had presented with jaundice (total bilirubin 12 mg/dL) and left upper-quadrant pain radiating to the left shoulder; bilirubin improved to 3 mg/dL over one week. On transfer she was mildly jaundiced and had a soft, tender mass in her left upper abdomen.

Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL (normal 0.2–1.2), alkaline phosphatase 194 U/L (normal 38–126), γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 117 U/L (normal 7–50); aminotransferases and pancreatic enzymes were normal. Serum CA 19-9 and CEA were normal; AFP was 16 ng/mL (normal <7). Hydatid serologies were negative.

An MRI in October showed a 37×40 mm multilocular cystic lesion between segments 3 and 4, with dilatation of the left hepatic duct (12 mm) and common hepatic duct (15 mm); the right hepatic duct and common bile duct were normal. On admission, MRI demonstrated a 19×17×10 cm fluid collection anterior and inferior to the left lobe, with apparent communication between the cystic lesion and intrahepatic ducts of segments 2 and 3. Percutaneous drainage yielded bile-stained fluid (fluid bilirubin 18 mg/dL vs serum 2 mg/dL) and CA 19-9 of 52 652 IU/mL (serum <34). Daily external bile output was 1000–1500 mL for nine days, then ceased.

At 14 weeks’ gestation, contrast MRI showed enhancing internal septations within the cystic liver mass.
final_diagnosis_raw: mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver
title: Spontaneous rupture of a mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver resulting in a huge biloma in a pregnant woman: A case report

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department approximately 1 hour after intentionally ingesting unknown amounts of tizanidine, hydrocodone, prednisone, enalapril, and a combination sleeping aid (Alteril). On arrival, she was minimally responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale score 12) and had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Postictally, she was lethargic with fixed, dilated pupils (left slightly larger than right). Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed normal liver biochemistries and renal function; acetaminophen, salicylate, and ethanol levels were undetectable.

On hospital day 1, she developed a wide-complex ventricular tachycardia with associated hypotension and a second seizure. She was intubated and started on vasopressor support. Repeat laboratory studies on hospital day 2 revealed: alanine aminotransferase 3,116 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase 2,710 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 48 U/L; total bilirubin 3.7 mg/dL; and international normalized ratio 2.0. Intravenous N-acetylcysteine and vitamin K were administered. Urine toxicology was positive for phencyclidine; HIV, hepatitis, and autoimmune serologies were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal liver parenchyma, patent hepatic vasculature, no cholelithiasis, and no biliary ductal dilation. Serum creatine kinase was 1,562 U/L. She developed acute tubular necrosis with acidosis and oliguria requiring continuous renal replacement therapy.

Given a poor prognosis for transplant-free survival, she underwent an expedited evaluation for liver transplantation on hospital day 2. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 19% with severe akinesis of the midanterior and distal anterior septum, apex, midinferior and distal inferior walls, and midinferoseptal segment.
title: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy Causing Induced Acute Liver Failure

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old African American man with end-stage renal disease due to hypertensive nephrosclerosis underwent a four–antigen–mismatch, flow–crossmatch–negative deceased donor kidney transplant. He received basiliximab induction and maintenance immunosuppression with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Donor CMV status was positive and recipient negative; he received trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and valganciclovir prophylaxis.

Postoperatively, he had slow graft function, with a serum creatinine level >3.0 mg/dL on day 5 without dialysis. By day 19, the creatinine fell to 2.33 mg/dL (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m^2). On day 22, the creatinine rose to 2.81 mg/dL (eGFR 30) and urinalysis showed 10–100 RBCs/μL and a few atypical epithelial cells but no decoy cells. Tacrolimus trough levels were 8–10 ng/mL, and volume status was adequate. On day 24, renal ultrasound showed increased parenchymal echogenicity with poor corticomedullary differentiation and normal perfusion and resistive indices.

A renal allograft biopsy revealed diffuse severe interstitial inflammation with macrophages, neutrophils, lymphocytes, and noncaseating granulomas; extensive necrosis; and basophilic, hyperchromatic, smudgy intranuclear inclusion bodies in tubular epithelial cells. There was widespread tubular basement membrane disruption, minimal tubulitis, and no glomerular inflammation or vasculitis. Immunostains for polyoma (BK virus) and CMV were negative. Immunofluorescence for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, fibrinogen, κ, λ, and C4d were negative. Periodic acid–Schiff and Jones stains were negative for bacteria or fungi. Blood and urine cultures, routine viral cultures, and PCR assays for Epstein–Barr virus, CMV, and BK virus were all negative. Electron microscopy demonstrated viral particles of varying densities in the nuclei of tubular epithelial cells.
title: Severe Necrotizing Adenovirus Tubulointerstitial Nephritis in a Kidney Transplant Recipient

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old woman presented with occasional dull pain below the xiphoid. Her medical history was notable for resection of a symptomatic ovarian teratoma 10 years earlier. She had no family history of thyroid or hepatic disease. Physical examination was unremarkable. Liver function tests and serum tumor markers were within normal limits.

Abdominal CT revealed:
• A lobulated 1.2 × 2.9 × 2.8 cm lesion in the hemidiaphragm (60–70 HU on noncontrast imaging) with heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast images.  
• A 4.2 × 3.9 × 3.9 cm solid lesion in segment VI of the liver (60–70 HU on noncontrast imaging) showing heterogeneous enhancement post-contrast.

MRI demonstrated that the lesions were slightly low signal on T1-weighted imaging, equal signal on T2-weighted imaging, and showed a diffusion-weighted signal increase (b = 800) without restricted diffusion. There was no uptake of hepatobiliary-specific contrast on delayed imaging.

Based on these examinations, a working diagnosis of a benign hepatic adenoma with hemorrhage was made.
title: Multiple ectopic goiter in the retroperitoneum, abdominal wall, liver, and diaphragm: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old woman presented with gradually worsening dyspnea at rest and fatigue over several weeks, accompanied by nausea, poor appetite, and palpitations. She had a 10-year history of controlled asthma on inhaled corticosteroids. On examination, blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, heart rate 103 bpm, respiratory rate 30/min, temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Jugular venous pressure was elevated. Cardiac auscultation revealed a systolic murmur at the lower left sternal border and apex. Breath sounds were diminished at lung bases, and there was bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, platelets 109 × 10^9/L, and a white-cell count of 13.5 × 10^9/L with 31% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 4.2 × 10^9/L). Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions. Analysis of pleural fluid yielded a transudative profile. Spirometry revealed mixed obstructive and restrictive patterns. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 55%, marked thickening of the ventricular side of the mitral valve leaflets extending into the basal ventricular endocardium with a 20 mm mass, severe functional mitral stenosis (mean gradient 16 mm Hg) and mitral regurgitation, sparing of the left-ventricular apex with slight right-ventricular apical obliteration, thickened tricuspid leaflets with severe tricuspid regurgitation, a dilated inferior vena cava with reduced collapse, and pulmonary arterial pressure of 43 mm Hg.
