To evaluate the cause of eosinophilia, peripheral smear was unremarkable except for elevated eosinophils. Vitamin B12, renal and hepatic panels were normal. Serologic tests were negative: ANA 0.2, C-ANCA 0.6 U/mL, P-ANCA 0.5 U/mL, and interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis. Abdominal ultrasound was normal aside from mild to moderate ascites. Stool examination showed no parasitic ova or larvae. Bone marrow biopsy showed no malignancy or myeloproliferative disorder, and tests for BCR/ABL and ETV6-PDGFRB translocations were negative.
title: Hyepereosiniphilic syndrome and COVID-19: 2 case reports

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old Hispanic woman, 5 days postpartum after a term vaginal delivery complicated by possible chorioamnionitis, initially presented with 2 days of fever to 38.9 °C and chills. She was hemodynamically stable; blood and urine cultures were negative, and she completed 2 days of IV antibiotics.

Six days later she was readmitted with fever to 40.3 °C, chills, progressive fatigue, malaise, nausea, vomiting, diffuse pain, and headache. She denied abdominal or breast pain, noted minor vaginal bleeding, and reported receiving a second dose of the Pfizer COVID‐19 vaccine 1 week before delivery. Her history was notable for gestational diabetes, hyperlipidemia, three prior spontaneous miscarriages, an ectopic pregnancy, and a molar pregnancy; there was no family history of autoimmune disease or malignancy.

On examination: temperature 39.0 °C; pulse 110 /min; blood pressure 100/67 mmHg; respirations 14 /min; O₂ saturation 98% on room air. She appeared diaphoretic and tachycardic, with palpable hepatosplenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed a normal leukocyte count, mild normocytic anemia, elevated AST, ALT, and lactate dehydrogenase; coagulation studies were within normal limits. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated focal hepatic steatosis without uterine or pelvic infection; MRCP showed no biliary obstruction. On hospital day 6, a percutaneous liver biopsy revealed mild macrovesicular, small‐droplet, and focal microvesicular steatosis (~10%) with portal and lobular inflammatory infiltrates of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and plasma cells. Extensive infectious work-up (including SARS-CoV-2 PCR) and autoimmune serologies were negative. Empiric antibiotics were discontinued.
title: An Interesting Case of Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis in a Postpartum Female With Recent COVID-19 Vaccination

case_prompt: A 50-year-old healthy man, a lifelong gardener, sustained a blow to his left zygomatic region from a projected object while using a grass trimmer eight years ago. He noted a small skin lesion, mild burning pain, and ipsilateral rhinorrhea with minimal bleeding but did not seek care. In September 2010, a dental examination revealed a metal‐appearing opacity in the left facial skeleton and “absence of areas of apical/radicular osteolysis affecting the teeth,” despite no history of dental implants or surgery. He was advised to see an otolaryngologist but declined until 2015, when he developed left facial pain. Fiberoptic nasolaryngoscopy was normal except for a deviated nasal septum. A noncontrast CT scan of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated “the presence of a metal foreign body with thread-like shape located in the region of the left maxillary sinus, which determined intense inflammatory reaction of the sinonasal mucosa interesting the same maxillary sinus. Additionally, the ipsilateral anterior ethmoidal air cells were partially involved. Radiological findings of minor importance were the presence of left concha bullosa and nasal septum deviation, while the other paranasal sinuses were within normal limits.”
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: An unusual case of unilateral sinus disease may reveal the presence of a retained foreign body

case_prompt: A 3-month-old female infant, first child born at 40 weeks’ gestation without complications, was evaluated for persistent vomiting, diarrhea, and failure to thrive since birth despite antiemetic therapy and formula feeding. On examination, she appeared dehydrated with sunken cheeks and had a cough with abnormal lung sounds. Vital signs were notable for a blood pressure of 85/45 mmHg; other parameters were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, white-cell count 1200 cells/μL (neutrophils 44%, lymphocytes 47%), platelet count 1220×10^9/L, reticulocyte count 23%, and a negative CRP. Serum electrolytes revealed sodium 124 mmol/L, potassium 2.5 mmol/L, chloride 82 mmol/L, and calcium 2.4 mmol/L; ALT was 24 IU/L and creatinine 0.5 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.60 and bicarbonate 27 mEq/L. Urinalysis revealed 13–18 WBCs and 46 RBCs per high-power field. Stool studies were unremarkable. Ultrasound examinations of the kidneys, liver, spleen, and pancreas were normal.
title: Bartter syndrome in a female infant: A rare case report from Syria

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old girl presented with tingling pain in her left leg and continuous involuntary movements of her left great toe for one month. These movements—extension and flexion of the great toe—occurred when she was awake and in early sleep and could not be suppressed voluntarily. Walking, sitting, or straining did not exacerbate the pain.

At birth, she had a sacral dimple at the S2–3 level. Four years earlier, she had voiding difficulty and underwent untethering surgery for a lipomeningomyelocele at the S2 level of the conus medullaris. A nerve conduction velocity study showed polyradiculopathy at the left L5 level and below with axonal involvement. A needle electromyogram revealed abnormal spontaneous activities in the left gastrocnemius medial head, abductor hallucis, and tibialis anterior and posterior. She did not report any movement symptoms at that time. She also underwent plantar fasciotomy for equinovarus deformity of both feet.

Five months later, voiding difficulty recurred, and she underwent a second untethering surgery. Postoperatively, she developed fever and meningeal irritation. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a red blood cell count of 60,000/mm3, a white blood cell count of 150/mm3 (69% polymorphonucleocytes), a protein level of 274 mg/dL, and a glucose level of 39 mg/dL. No organisms were cultured. Her fever and meningeal signs resolved after intravenous teicoplanin, which was later discontinued due to neutropenia.

One month after surgery, the left leg pain and involuntary movements of the left great toe began. On examination, deep tendon reflexes were increased at both knees, and the Babinski sign was negative. Brain computed tomography and electroencephalography showed no pathologic findings. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine revealed reactive inflammatory changes in the operative scar and decreased reactive meningeal enhancement compared to the previous study. Repeat nerve conduction studies showed no significant change, and needle electromyography again demonstrated abnormal spontaneous activities in the same left lower-extremity muscles with no interval change.
final_diagnosis_raw: Painful legs and moving toes syndrome
title: Painful legs and moving toes syndrome in a 16-year-old girl

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman with a 7-year history of post-tuberculosis cystic bronchiectasis presented with a 7-day history of worsening cough and dyspnea. Her dyspnea progressed to MMRC grade 4 at rest. She used inhaled salmeterol–fluticasone and tiotropium. On admission, SpO2 was 86% on room air, 96% on 4 L O2; blood pressure was 90/50 mm Hg, and other vital signs were normal. Lung examination revealed bilateral coarse crepitations; cardiac examination was unremarkable. She was treated for an acute exacerbation of bronchiectasis.

On hospital day 2, she developed sudden central crushing chest pain without radiation. Only limb leads were obtained, showing ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, with ST depression in aVR. Initial troponin I was 0.1 ng/mL, rising to 3.36 ng/mL; CPK-MB rose from 6 U/L to 25 U/L. A provisional diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction was made.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated ballooning of the left ventricular mid- and apical segments, with akinesis of the apical and mid-anterior and mid-anteroseptal walls; the remaining mid-ventricular segments were hyperkinetic, and the basal segments were hyperkinetic. The left ventricular ejection fraction was 30–35%, and the outflow tract gradient was 8 mm Hg. Given her recent bronchiectasis exacerbation, these findings raised suspicion for Takotsubo syndrome; however, the regional wall motion abnormality was more pronounced in the LAD territory, creating diagnostic uncertainty.
title: Acute myocardial infarction or Takotsubo syndrome in a patient with stunned myocardium due to myocardial bridging? A case report of diagnostic dilemma clarified after serial workup

case_prompt:
A male neonate (birth weight 3.3 kg) was delivered at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery. He had abdominal distention noted at birth and developed jaundice on day 2 of life, associated with clay-colored stools. On day 7, he was referred for further evaluation. 

Examination revealed icterus, a distended abdomen with an everted umbilicus, dilated abdominal veins, and a firm, irregular mass (approximately 15 × 10 cm) occupying the entire abdomen. 

Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 9.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.2 mg/dL, AST 78 U/L, ALT 69 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 423.6 U/L; other routine blood tests and serum alpha-fetoprotein and β-hCG levels were normal. 

Abdominal radiography demonstrated three separate areas of multiple radiodensities. Ultrasound revealed an encapsulated sac containing three malformed fetiform structures. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a well-encapsulated anterior pararenal sac containing three malformed fetuses located in the right hypochondrium, right lower pelvis, and left hypochondrium; the mass displaced the duodenum anteriorly, compressed the common bile duct (resulting in intrahepatic biliary dilation) and right kidney (causing hydronephrosis), and shifted bowel loops to the left.
journal: Journal of Indian Association of Pediatric Surgeons
title: Fetus-in-Fetu: A Tale of the Trapped Triplets

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old woman with morbid obesity (BMI 42) presented with fatigue, nosebleeds, and easy bruising.  
Initial laboratory evaluation showed:  
• WBC 5.34 K/μL, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 13 K/μL  
• Peripheral smear with 19% promyelocytes, 9% granulated blasts, and Auer rods  
• Coagulation studies: PT/INR 18.3 s/1.5, PTT 30.2 s, D-dimer 8115 ng/mL, fibrinogen 77 ng/mL  
Renal function was at baseline (creatinine 0.8 mg/dL). Cytogenetics revealed t(15;17) and trisomy 8, with PCR confirming a PML-RARA fusion, establishing acute promyelocytic leukemia.  

She began induction therapy with oral all-trans retinoic acid 45 mg/m2 twice daily on admission and intravenous arsenic trioxide 0.15 mg/kg daily starting on day 5. On day 8, she developed dyspnea, headache, and edema consistent with differentiation syndrome, which resolved with dexamethasone.  

Between days 19 and 30, she experienced intermittent loose stools progressing to fever (102°F) on day 30. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were administered briefly; blood cultures, SARS-CoV-2 PCR, and stool studies for bacterial pathogens, Clostridioides difficile, ova and parasites, adenovirus, rotavirus, and norovirus were all negative.  

By day 32, she developed nonbloody, rice-water diarrhea producing 3–6 L/day unaltered by fasting, accompanied by crampy abdominal pain. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed diffuse ileus without focal colonic lesions. On day 34, colonoscopy revealed grossly normal mucosa; random biopsies demonstrated atrophic crypts and scattered neutrophilic crypt microabscesses, with negative CMV staining.  

Concurrently, she reported epigastric pain and nausea; serum lipase was 428 U/L (ULN 60 U/L), and abdominal CT showed acute edematous pancreatitis.
title: Arsenic toxicity manifesting as profuse watery diarrhea during induction therapy for acute promyelocytic leukemia

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old woman presented with 2–3 days of severe right upper-quadrant colicky pain and biliary vomiting. She reported a history of intense dieting and minimal water intake. On arrival, she was afebrile, normotensive (120/80 mmHg), with a heart rate of 90 beats/min, respiratory rate of 16/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. She was conscious but not fully oriented. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the right hypochondrium without pallor, icterus, cyanosis, or edema. Laboratory studies showed:  
• CBC: Hb 11 g/dL, WBC 6600/mm3, platelets 171 000/mm3  
• LFTs and alkaline phosphatase: within normal limits  
• Serum creatinine: 0.8 mg/dL  
• Serum amylase: 60 U/L; lipase: 17 U/L  
• Viral hepatitis markers: nonreactive  

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple gallbladder calculi, a distended gallbladder with a 12-mm calculus at the neck, and a mildly fusiformly dilated common bile duct measuring 11–12 mm with prominent hepatic ducts; no ductal stones were visualized. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography confirmed multiple gallstones, persistent common bile duct dilation (11 mm), and ruled out choledocholithiasis.
title: Choledochal cyst mimicking as choledocholithiasis: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 27-year-old woman with a history of a marginal excision of a hidradenoma from the sole of her right foot in 2015 noted in August 2019 a 1 cm, nonmobile lump at the same site. It grew slowly over months, causing discomfort on walking, and occasionally discharged a small amount of serous fluid. In early 2020 she developed a painless right inguinal lymph node enlargement. Vital signs were normal. On exam, a firm right inguinal lymph node was palpable; the foot mass was noninflamed. Plain radiographs of the right foot showed no bone involvement. MRI revealed a 24 × 11 × 17 mm cutaneous and subcutaneous soft-tissue lesion in the central sole with a spiculated contour abutting the plantar fascia and flexor digitorum brevis; it was hypointense on T1, heterogeneously intermediate on T2, and showed significant peripheral post-contrast enhancement. No adjacent nerve or vascular invasion was seen.
title: Hidradenocarcinoma over a Surgically Excised Hidradenoma of the Foot. A Case Report of a Very Rare Presentation of a Rare Tumor

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old man, previously healthy and physically active, presented with sharp, non-radiating low back pain of 1 week’s duration after minor weight lifting. He denied fever, chills, or recent travel. He had no radicular symptoms. Physical examination showed localized tenderness over the lower lumbar spine. Neurologic examination was normal with intact strength, sensation, and reflexes in both legs. Laboratory studies, including CBC, CRP, and Brucella serology, were sent.

Given persistent pain despite NSAIDs and absence of neurologic deficits, an MRI of the lumbar spine was obtained. On post-contrast MRI, there was a 2.5 × 2 × 2 cm nodular lesion within the right psoas muscle at the L3–L4 level, surrounded by moderate edema and demonstrating rim enhancement, raising concern for a psoas abscess.

Seven days later, CT-guided aspiration was performed; no material was obtained, and cultures of lavage fluid showed no growth. CBC and CRP remained within normal limits. The patient continued NSAIDs with close clinical monitoring.
title: Psoas muscle sequestered disc mimicking an intramuscular abscess: A rare case report

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old Bulgarian man was evaluated for an 18-month history of progressive attention and memory impairment, apathy, anxiety, and irritability. His brother first noted confusion and forgetfulness that interfered with his work as a construction worker. The patient had limited formal education but had been fully independent in activities of daily living until symptom onset.

On examination, he was not fully oriented to time but was relatively oriented to place. Neuropsychological testing showed mild to moderate dementia (MMSE score 16/30), severe verbal learning impairment (immediate recall 4/10 words; delayed recall 1/10; recognition 0/10), difficulty recalling personal information, mild anomia, poor categorical fluency (10 animals/min), and a severe dysexecutive syndrome (coding score 8 with two mistakes; letter fluency 1 “M”-word/min). 

Neurological examination revealed preserved pupillary light and accommodation reflexes without signs of Argyll-Robertson pupils, but pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, dysarthria, and impaired coordination were present. Routine blood tests (CBC, electrolytes, glucose, liver and renal function, thyroid function, B12, folate) were normal.

Cerebrospinal fluid was clear, with 1×10^6/L erythrocytes, 39×10^6/L leukocytes (82% lymphocytes), protein 0.88 g/L, and positive oligoclonal bands. Serum VDRL titer was 1:128 and TPHA 1:2560; CSF VDRL was 1:64 and TPHA 1:640. HIV testing was negative.

MRI of the brain demonstrated moderate cortical atrophy and marked bilateral hippocampal atrophy on FLAIR and T1-weighted images, without focal areas of increased signal intensity.
title: Neurosyphilis with dementia and bilateral hippocampal atrophy on brain magnetic resonance imaging

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man of Pakistani origin was referred for a new-onset pruritic bullous eruption. His medical history was notable for past hepatitis B infection and chronic pruritic plaques on his legs treated intermittently with topical corticosteroids. He was taking no medications or supplements, and review of systems was negative, including for weight loss or constitutional symptoms. 

On examination, tense bullae and vesicles clustered in an annular “string-of-pearls” arrangement on an erythematous base were noted on both forearms. Lichenified erythematous plaques with overlying vesicles and some bullae were present on the dorsal hands and feet. Mucous membranes were normal. 

Given the patient’s age and the annular configuration of lesions, linear IgA bullous dermatosis and pemphigus herpetiformis were initially suspected. A skin biopsy and direct immunofluorescence study were obtained, and the patient was started on prednisone 20 mg daily. 

Laboratory studies showed an eosinophil count of 1.0 × 10^9 g/L; the remainder of the complete blood count and metabolic panel were within normal limits.
title: Annular bullous pemphigoid: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 21-month-old full-term boy with known lactose intolerance was referred for evaluation of an incidentally discovered left renal mass. His mother noted progressive abdominal distension accompanied by polyuria, polydipsia, and constipation. The parents are consanguineous; two healthy brothers and ten sisters, two of whom died in childhood. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Height and weight were at the 25th percentile. The abdomen was distended, soft, and lax without palpable masses or ascites. There were clinical signs of active rickets. Genital examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed serum creatinine 37 µmol/L, phosphorus 0.81 mmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 2178 U/L, vitamin D 16.8 ng/mL, blood glucose 8.9 mmol/L with HbA1c 5.5%, and LDH 186 U/L. CBC revealed polycythemia (Hb 18.1 g/dL, Hct 52.6%). Urinalysis demonstrated glucosuria and aminoaciduria. Genetic testing identified a homozygous c.474A>C p.(Arg158Ser) variant in SLC2A2, confirming Fanconi–Bickel syndrome.

Renal ultrasound showed a sharply marginated peripheral hypoechoic hypovascular mass at the upper pole of the left kidney measuring approximately 2.0 × 1.8 × 2.0 cm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a solitary, partially exophytic, homogeneously enhancing mass at the left upper pole measuring 1.8 × 1.9 × 2.0 cm. The kidneys were mildly enlarged, and there were radiographic signs of rickets in the ribs and femurs.
title: Pediatric metanephric adenoma with Fanconi–Bickel syndrome: a case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 46-year-old Iraqi woman with familial lens subluxation had prior right‐eye anterior chamber lens implantation and vitrectomy, resulting in poor vision in that eye. Her left eye had a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment treated with a scleral buckle; severe scleral thinning was noted. She then underwent phacoemulsification with implantation of a hydrophilic acrylic posterior chamber intraocular lens in the bag but with zonular dehiscence. Postoperatively, her left‐eye visual acuity was 6/9 with mild lens decentration. She was referred for scleral fixation of the lens, but because of scleral thinning and detachment risk, an iris suture fixation was performed. The night‐time surgery lasted 75 minutes, required multiple injections of viscoelastic, and an inferior suture was removed intraoperatively due to lens tilt. Ten hours after surgery, her vision had dropped to finger counting at 10 cm, and examination revealed a fibrinous panuveitis. B‐scan ultrasonography showed dense vitreous echoes.
title: Fulminant Panuveitis following Iris Suture Fixation of Posterior Chamber Intraocular Lens

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old Filipino man presented with a one-week history of hemorrhagic swelling in the right mandibular region. He denied pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss, tobacco use, or alcohol use. His history included hypertension (on amlodipine) and chronic kidney disease, with planned hemodialysis.

Intraoral examination revealed an exophytic, hemorrhagic, ulcerated mass (~3 cm) surrounding the buccal and lingual gingiva of the right mandibular premolars, extending posteriorly to the edentulous alveolar mucosa. The adjacent teeth showed terminal mobility, 1 cm pocket depths, and bleeding on probing. Additional gingival enlargement was noted in the left posterior mandibular buccal gingiva and the left posterior maxillary palatal gingiva. Extraoral examination found a painful, nearly fixed right submandibular lymph node.

Panoramic radiograph demonstrated alveolar bone loss near the right mandibular premolars. Cone-beam computed tomography revealed superficial resorption of the alveolar ridge and buccal cortex measuring ~7 mm by 3 mm.

The differential diagnosis included hematologic malignancies (e.g., lymphoma, leukemic infiltrate), sarcomas, squamous cell carcinoma, calcium-channel blocker–induced gingival enlargement with pyogenic granuloma–like lesions, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and brown tumor of secondary hyperparathyroidism. Incisional biopsies of all gingival lesions were performed.
title: Lymphoepithelial Subtype of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Report of an EBV-Negative Case and Literature Review

case_prompt:
An 85-year-old man presented with a 9-month history of a tender, violaceous subcutaneous nodule over the right upper quadrant at the site of his ventriculoperitoneal shunt, inserted 9 months earlier for normal-pressure hydrocephalus. He also reported malaise, reduced appetite, and a 5-kg weight loss over 5 months but denied rectal bleeding or melena. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL (normal 13–17 g/dL). On examination, multiple smaller subcutaneous nodules without epidermal changes were noted tracking along the shunt, including a prominent lesion near the right clavicle.

A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis performed 2 months before admission had attributed the right upper quadrant lesion to scar tissue of indeterminate significance. Ultrasonography of the abdominal and sternal nodules demonstrated echogenic soft-tissue masses surrounding the shunt. A biopsy of the main abdominal lesion was performed. Histologic examination revealed an intradermal malignant neoplasm with features of adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for CK cocktail, CK19, EMA, CDX2, and mCEA, and negativity for CK5/6 and D2-40. Serum tumor markers were elevated: CA 19-9 at 1545 kU/L (normal ≤37), CA 125 at 181 kU/L (0–35), and CEA at 19.1 μg/L (0–3.0).
title: Cutaneous presentation of gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma

case_prompt: A 68-year-old woman with end-stage renal failure secondary to nephrosclerosis and aplastic anemia for 23 years, maintained on hemodialysis and treated with anabolic steroids and prednisolone, presented during hemodialysis with epigastric pain and back pain. She had no history of trauma or oral antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy. On examination, temperature was 36.8 °C, pulse 66 beats/min, blood pressure 190/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There were no electrocardiographic changes. Abdominal examination revealed localized tenderness in the right hypochondrium and a positive Murphy’s sign. Laboratory studies showed elevated alkaline phosphatase (139 U/L) and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (173 U/L) but no leukocytosis, no elevated inflammatory markers, and normal bilirubin levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a distended gallbladder containing slightly hyperdense material and active extravasation into the lumen, without gallstones, cystic artery aneurysm, extrahepatic bile duct dilation, or ascites; severe arterial calcifications were noted in the aorta and peripheral vessels.
title: Successful laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallbladder hemorrhage from a Dieulafoy lesion in a patient on hemodialysis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman noted a swelling of her right lower leg 8 years ago that had been stable until 6 months ago, when it enlarged and became painful on walking more than 10 m. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, 15 × 6 × 3 cm mass continuous with the anterior border of the right tibia; the overlying skin was pinchable and without warmth.  
Plain radiographs of the leg showed an eccentric, expansile, lytic lesion in the distal third of the right tibial diaphysis with scalloping and anterolateral cortical breach; a similar small lesion was noted in the distal fibula.  
MRI demonstrated an irregular, eccentric, expansile lesion of the anterior cortex of the distal tibia measuring 6.5 × 2.2 × 5.8 cm, with a narrow zone of transition; the lesion was isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2 and STIR sequences, showed homogeneous post-contrast enhancement, and extended into the intramuscular and subcutaneous planes. A separate 7 × 2 mm lesion was seen in the lower third of the right fibular diaphysis.  
Tru-cut biopsy revealed a high-grade spindle-cell neoplasm with areas of round blue-cell rests and sarcomatous dedifferentiation. Immunohistochemistry was positive for Ki-67 (30–40%), cytokeratin, p53, and CD99. Cytogenetic analysis demonstrated a t(11;22)(q23;q12) translocation, and FISH confirmed EWSR1 gene rearrangement in 32% of cells.
title: A Rare Case of Ewing’s-like Adamantinoma of Tibia Managed by Limb Salvage Surgery Using Long Segment Ilizarov Bone Transport: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old man presented with a few days of intermittent gross hematuria. He denied systemic symptoms. He quit smoking 21 years ago and has used smokeless tobacco for 16 years. Cystoscopy at the referring institution revealed a bladder tumor. Biopsy showed high-grade urothelial carcinoma with >80% clear cell differentiation, severe necrosis, and invasion into the muscularis propria. Renal ultrasound demonstrated a large bladder mass without extravesical disease and mild right hydronephrosis. Serum creatinine was 1.6 mg/dL; chemotherapy was deferred, and the patient underwent radical cystoprostatectomy. 

Gross examination revealed a 5.5 × 5.0 × 2.3 cm fungated hemorrhagic mass arising from the right lateral wall, nearly obliterating the right ureteral orifice, and invading through the detrusor into perivesical fat. 

Microscopically, the tumor consisted of sheets and nodules of rounded to polygonal malignant cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant clear cytoplasm (>90% clear cell differentiation). No glandular differentiation or hobnail cells were seen. The tumor invaded through the full thickness of the muscularis propria into perivesical adipose tissue, with extensive necrosis, acute inflammation, lymphovascular invasion, and focal carcinoma in situ in adjacent urothelium.
title: Clear cell urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old woman with chronic hypertension was brought to the emergency department by her family after suddenly losing consciousness at home approximately 1 hour earlier. On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was E1V1M4. She had bilaterally dilated, nonreactive pupils (7 mm on the right, 5 mm on the left). She was intubated for airway protection. Initial vital signs were blood pressure 130/90 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, oxygen saturation 85% on room air, and random blood glucose 158 mg/dL.

Neurologic examination revealed left-sided hemiplegia and left facial droop. The left plantar response was upgoing; the right was mute. Motor strength was 1/5 in the left upper and lower limbs and 2/5 on the right. There were no meningeal signs. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

A noncontrast head CT scan was obtained within 30 minutes of arrival.
title: Bilateral thalamic infarct involving artery of Percheron: a case report

case_prompt: A 56-year-old man with follicular non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma underwent allogeneic HSCT in 2006 complicated by acute and chronic GVHD, and subsequently developed antiphospholipid syndrome manifesting as pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis. He was maintained on warfarin. In 2015, he developed 2 days of rhinorrhea, cough, sore throat, right upper abdominal pain relieved by sitting upright, nausea, and anorexia. He was afebrile; blood pressure was 135/58 mmHg. Examination showed mild upper-abdominal tenderness without rash or petechiae. On day 3, platelet count was 128×10^3/μL, PT/INR 1.97, aPTT 98.5 seconds, and a mixing test remained positive for lupus anticoagulant. By day 5, he was hypotensive (95/64 mmHg), sodium was 119 mmol/L, CRP 11.75 mg/dL, and aPTT 112.7 seconds. Blood cultures and fungal, mycobacterial, and viral antigen tests were negative. CT on day 3 was unremarkable; repeat CT on day 5 showed bilateral adrenal enlargement with hemorrhagic features. T2-weighted MRI confirmed low-signal regions in both adrenal glands. Endocrine studies showed cortisol 1.9 μg/mL (normal 4–19.3), ACTH 108 pg/mL (normal 7.2–63.3), with normal aldosterone and catecholamines.
title: Bilateral Adrenal Hemorrhage in a Patient with Antiphospholipid Syndrome during Chronic Graft-versus-host Disease

case_prompt: A 53-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of sudden-onset left chest pain radiating to his left back. The pain was intermittent over 48 hours, non–exertional, not localized, and partially relieved by NSAIDs and rest. He had a 30–pack-year smoking history, illicit drug use, and hypertension controlled by lifestyle measures, with no prior end-organ damage. On admission, blood pressure was 100/78 mmHg. Review of systems and examination revealed no paresthesias, numbness, weakness, or ataxia; cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurologic exams were normal. He received nitroglycerin and fentanyl with relief of pain. Because of his risk factors and presentation, a chest X-ray, electrocardiogram, and blood tests including troponin I and D-dimer were performed and were normal. To evaluate for pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection, a CT angiogram of the chest was obtained, which showed a 4.4 × 2.0 × 2.1 cm soft-tissue mass compressing the spinal cord at T8–T9. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a heterogeneous intradural extramedullary mass at left T8 that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1-weighted images, with a “dumbbell-shaped” configuration at the T8 foramen.
title: Hemorrhagic spinal melanotic schwannoma presenting as acute chest pain: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old man presented with 12 days of cyclical fevers and vague abdominal discomfort. He described the pain as an “L” shape extending from the right upper quadrant to both lower quadrants. His fevers recurred every 12 hours, reaching 101–103.4ºF, initially responsive to acetaminophen and ibuprofen but later refractory. He also noted an initial headache, myalgias, anorexia, and profound fatigue that limited his work as a personal trainer.

Three days into his illness, his primary care evaluation revealed no leukocytosis, no abdominal tenderness or guarding, and normal vital signs; testing for Lyme disease, anaplasma, babesia, ehrlichiosis, and influenza was negative. After six days of fevers, an urgent‐care visit again showed no leukocytosis, diffuse arthralgias, negative blood smear for parasites, and persistent elevations in alanine aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase. 

On arrival in the emergency department, his temperature was 99.2ºF, blood pressure 149/80 mmHg, heart rate 107 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination showed an alert man with normal strength and sensation, no meningismus, and a non-tender abdomen. Laboratory studies demonstrated a hemoglobin drop from 13.3 to 11.0 mg/dL, a leukocyte count of 12,000/μL with 84% neutrophils, normal electrolytes and lactate, an AST of 66 IU/L, an ALP of 275 IU/L, and a urinalysis without evidence of infection. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. A contrast‐enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple liver abscesses and septic thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system in hepatic segments six and eight.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Rare Complications of Acute Appendicitis: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old man with a 21-year history of Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia, previously treated with fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange, was enrolled in a trial and received zanubrutinib 160 mg twice daily for relapsed disease. He also took aciclovir and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. He had a history of mild psoriasis, a BMI of 30, weekly alcohol intake of 300 g, and a 10 pack-year smoking history. He had no other regular medications and no recent new drug exposures.

After 28 months of zanubrutinib, routine labs showed an asymptomatic rise in transaminases and total bilirubin. Eight weeks later he developed pale stools, dark urine, pruritus, and jaundice and was admitted. On examination, he was jaundiced but had no signs of liver failure. Admission labs were: ALT 2474 IU/L (ULN 45), AST 1257 IU/L (ULN 35), ALP 114 IU/L (ULN 130), total bilirubin 141 µmol/L (ULN 21), and prothrombin time 14 s (ULN 12). 

Ultrasound of the liver showed a normal biliary tree and an echogenic liver consistent with fatty changes. A comprehensive serologic liver screen—including viral hepatitis markers and autoimmune liver antibodies—was entirely negative.
title: Zanubrutinib-induced liver injury: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 51-year-old man presented for evaluation of a recently dislodged porcelain-fused-to-metal crown on the right maxillary first molar; the crown had been placed 5 years earlier. His medical and social histories were noncontributory. On routine oral examination, a well-defined submucosal mass was observed in the mucobuccal fold near the lower right second premolar. Retraction of the cheek revealed a 5 mm × 3 mm yellowish-white nodule. The lesion was soft to rubbery-firm, minimally compressible, with well-defined margins, mobile on palpation, and asymptomatic; the patient was unaware of its duration. An intraoral periapical radiograph was obtained, and vitality testing of the adjacent teeth was inconclusive. Based on clinical and radiographic findings, the differential diagnosis included lipoma, granulation tissue, scarred parulis, fibroma, leiomyoma, neuroma, schwannoma, and foreign body granuloma. The decision was made to perform excisional biopsy under local anesthesia for definitive diagnosis.
title: Foreign Body in the Oral Cavity Mimicking a Benign Connective Tissue Tumor

case_prompt: A 63‐year‐old woman with no prior medical history was diagnosed with COVID-19 and treated with azithromycin, zinc, and vitamin C. On day 15 after symptom onset, she developed painless, mildly pruritic, erythematous maculopapular lesions with atypical targetoid morphology on the trunk and lower limbs. There was no mucosal involvement. She denied any recent herpes infection, had no similar eruptions in her past, and no family history of similar lesions. Complete blood count, biochemical parameters, and serological tests—including Herpes simplex virus IgM and IgG, Epstein–Barr virus IgM and IgG, Cytomegalovirus IgM and IgG, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti–hepatitis C virus—were within normal limits.
title: Erythema multiforme eruption due to SARS-COV 2: Case report

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis presented with a 6-month history of a pruritic rash and a painful oral sore. The rash appeared within weeks after he began nintedanib (150 mg twice daily) for his pulmonary fibrosis. He was initially treated in urgent care with permethrin 5% cream, without improvement, and later with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment for one week, with only transient relief. He also reported mild nausea and gastrointestinal upset on nintedanib. His other medications included omeprazole (for 2½ years) and atorvastatin (for 1 year, with a dose increase 2 months before presentation). His medical history was notable for gastroesophageal reflux disease, coronary artery disease, prior herpes simplex virus infection, and a remote history of smoking.

On dermatologic examination, there were a few intact vesicles and pustules on the forehead and numerous scattered 1–2 mm crusted papules with erythematous bases on the forehead, scalp, face, upper chest, and both knees. Examination of the oral mucosa revealed a linear ulcer. Vital signs were within normal limits, and no other abnormalities were noted.
title: Bullous pemphigoid associated with nintedanib

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old white woman was referred for a second opinion on chronic cystoid macular edema of the left eye. She had a 10-year history of chronic intermediate uveitis in both eyes managed with prednisolone drops. Initial macular edema improved after a sub-Tenon triamcinolone injection but recurred 18 months earlier and failed to respond to intravitreal bevacizumab. She had no other medical history but was undergoing evaluation for possible breast cancer after routine screening mammography detected new right axillary lymphadenopathy with calcifications, which was confirmed on diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound. A chest CT performed five weeks later showed no axillary lymphadenopathy or pulmonary nodules. 

On ophthalmic examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 bilaterally. There was no anterior chamber inflammation; vitreous haze was trace with 1+ vitreous cells in both eyes. The right eye exhibited a mild nuclear sclerotic cataract; the left eye was pseudophakic. Fundus examination showed small patches of perifoveal atrophy. Optical coherence tomography confirmed bilateral cystoid macular edema, more pronounced in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography revealed optic disc leakage and diffuse peripheral leakage in both eyes without vasculitis. There were no cutaneous lesions, pulmonary symptoms, or other systemic complaints. 

Laboratory studies demonstrated HLA-B8 positivity and an angiotensin-converting enzyme level of 67 U/L (reference 12–68). Tests for syphilis, Lyme disease, and tuberculosis were negative. The uveitis was initially labeled idiopathic, although sarcoidosis was suspected. Methotrexate was considered but contraindicated due to alcohol use; mycophenolate mofetil was recommended, but the patient chose to await the results of her breast workup.
title: A Case of Sarcoid Uveitis Diagnosed With Mammography Two Months After Normal Chest Imaging

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of a slowly enlarging mass in the thenar eminence of his right hand. He denied trauma, systemic symptoms, or weight loss. His medical and social history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 3.0 × 1.5 cm mobile, pulseless, ovular soft-tissue mass in the right thenar eminence; the overlying skin was normal, the mass was non-tender, and there were no sensory deficits or regional lymphadenopathy. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count, serum biochemistry, inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP), electrolytes, tumour markers, coagulation, liver and renal function, were all within normal limits.  
Ultrasound showed a well-defined, encapsulated, hypoechoic 2.8 × 0.8 cm lesion with intralesional calcifications and marked hypervascularity on color Doppler. The sonographer noted an intravascular tumour of equivocal interpretation, possibly a hemangiopericytoma.  
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 2.7 × 1.7 × 0.9 cm encapsulated, ovular soft-tissue mass abutting but not invading adjacent muscles. On T1-weighted images, it was heterogeneous and nearly isointense to muscle with a central markedly hypointense area; on STIR and T2 sequences, it was heterogeneously hyperintense without fat and contained an internal low-signal septation consistent with calcification. The radiologist again favored hemangiopericytoma and recommended surgical removal.
title: An intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia of the hand radiologically mimicking a hemangiopericytoma: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 3-week-old female neonate was referred for evaluation of lower-extremity weakness. She was born at term (3.145 kg) via cesarean delivery for breech presentation; maternal history was notable only for enoxaparin use for antiphospholipid syndrome. On examination, she had a prolapsed anus, a midline lumbar dimple, absent deep-tendon reflexes, preserved primitive reflexes, flaccid distal paresis of the right leg, proximal and distal paresis of the left leg, and lax anal sphincter tone.

MRI of the brain and spine revealed a large infiltrative, avidly enhancing lesion occupying the spinal canal from T10 to S1 (8.3 cm craniocaudal), with bilateral dumbbell‐shaped extraspinal components through expanded neural foramina, abutting the psoas muscles and involving adjacent paraspinal musculature. The mass was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on T1-weighted images, and exhibited extensive flow voids; there was no fat signal, and T2 hyperintensity in both psoas muscles suggested possible denervation edema. The spinal cord was obliterated at the level of the lesion; the remainder of the cord was normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a high-attenuation mass expanding the spinal canal and neural foramina, without calcifications. Non-fusion of the posterior elements from L4 caudally was noted, consistent with spina bifida.

An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the lesion demonstrated hypoechoic protruding masses with high vascularity on Doppler imaging. Histologic examination showed lobular proliferation of capillary-sized vascular spaces lined by bland endothelial cells, with areas of focal intravascular thrombosis.
title: Massive spinal epidural infantile hemangioma, image findings, and treatment: a case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 7-month-old indoor, vaccinated, intact female Maine Coon was evaluated for acute vomiting, which began after a diet change. Initial treatment with omeprazole led to transient improvement; vomiting recurred after discontinuation, and intermittent hiccups developed. On reassessment, complete blood count and chemistry were unremarkable except for a mild non-regenerative, normocytic, normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 84 g/l; RI 98–162 g/l). Pancreatic lipase was normal; folate and cobalamin were high. Thoracic and abdominal radiographs showed marked enlargement of the cardiac silhouette with confluent margins between the heart and diaphragm. Abdominal ultrasound revealed displacement of multiple liver lobes and gallbladder through the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity, a small pericardial effusion, and a segment of gastric wall around the lower oesophageal sphincter that was thickened, hypoechoic, and lost normal layering. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a midline defect of the ventral diaphragm with continuity to the pericardial sac (peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia) and herniation of left liver lobes. A 3 cm diameter broad-based, circumferential mass arising from the gastric cardia and protruding into the lumen demonstrated heterogeneous contrast enhancement.
title: Surgical treatment of a circumferential oesophagogastric mass associated with a peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia in a Maine Coon cat

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old woman presented with a five-month history of auditory and visual hallucinations, a delusional atmosphere, suicidal ideation, and depressive symptoms including insomnia, lack of appetite, and slowed thought processes. On admission she also reported a headache. Neurologic examination revealed only mild dysdiadochokinesia and moderate hirsutism; all other findings were normal. This was her first psychiatric episode. She described a prior transient gait disorder after short-term hallucinogenic mushroom use and occasional low-dose cannabis but had remained abstinent for months before presentation. There was no personal history of cancer; her grandmother had breast cancer at age 30. 

Serum and CSF immunoblots showed weak but reproducible anti-Yo reactivity in both compartments without evidence of intrathecal synthesis; a weak anti-Ma2 reactivity was detected in serum only. No other onconeural or neuronal surface antibodies were found. Serum autoimmune and infectious serologies were negative; CSF cell count and chemistry were normal. EEG was normal. Brain MRI showed discrete frontoparietal and cerebellar atrophy for her age and a small left temporopolar arachnoidal cyst. FDG-PET demonstrated mild cerebellar hypometabolism and no mesiotemporal hypermetabolism. A comprehensive search for an underlying tumor, including whole-body imaging and breast ultrasound, was unrevealing. Polycystic ovary syndrome was incidentally diagnosed.
title: Case report: low-titre anti-Yo reactivity in a female patient with psychotic syndrome and frontoparieto-cerebellar atrophy

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old man was referred for evaluation of episodic cutaneous flushing—more prominent on the face—with profuse sweating after every meal, and intermittent bouts of diarrhea ongoing for at least one year. He denied abdominal pain, weight loss, or bloody stools. His history included unexplained chest pain, lower extremity edema attributed to venous insufficiency, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnea treated with CPAP. He reported no palpitations or headache but noted a marked reduction in energy (2/10), significantly decreased libido, erectile dysfunction with loss of early-morning erections, excessive daytime sleepiness, and depression managed by a psychiatrist. His medications were aripiprazole, amphetamine/dextroamphetamine, amlodipine, lisinopril, spironolactone, and furosemide.

He had been evaluated twice for possible carcinoid syndrome; urinary 5-HIAA excretion was marginally elevated (9.7 and 7 mg/24 h; reference <6). A colonoscopy revealed benign polyps without a tumor. He had no history of diabetes or testicular trauma, was allergic to CT contrast dye, and had been obese since childhood. He was married without children.

On examination, he weighed 133.8 kg (BMI 43.6 kg/m2), appeared depressed, and had blood pressure 135/85 mm Hg. His sense of smell was intact, with no gynecomastia or external genital abnormalities. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score was 20/24 and Swiss Narcolepsy Scale was −34, consistent with narcolepsy.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, electrolytes, albumin, creatinine, and eGFR. Morning cortisol, IGF-1, and prolactin were normal. Alanine aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase were mildly elevated. Plasma testosterone was low at 181 ng/dL; LH was subnormal at 3.8 mIU/mL and FSH low-normal at 1.3 mIU/mL. Plasma dopamine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine concentrations were marginally elevated but deemed not clinically significant.
title: Narcolepsy, depression, and severe flushing in an obese man

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of chronic abdominal pain. She described spasmodic epigastric pain radiating to the back, intermittent over 1 year, without relationship to food intake. The pain was severe enough to prompt occasional emergency visits for intravenous analgesia. She also reported dyspepsia and early postprandial satiety but denied acid reflux or dysphagia. Her medical history included asthma, dermatomycosis, and endometriosis. 

On examination, the abdomen was soft and nondistended, with no palpable masses or hernias and no signs of acute abdomen. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed cholelithiasis without evidence of cholecystitis or choledocholithiasis and incidentally revealed a lesion in the posterior wall of the stomach. 

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated multiple radiolucent gallstones and an isolated well-circumscribed submucosal lesion in the posterior gastric wall, with no lymphadenopathy. The differential diagnosis for the gastric lesion included leiomyoma and gastrointestinal stromal tumour. Percutaneous biopsy was deemed infeasible, and an MRI was scheduled for further characterization.
title: A rare case report of pigment gallstones and a concomitant gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumour

case_prompt: A 68-year-old woman was evaluated for worsening joint pain and morning stiffness in both hands. She had seronegative rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed at age 32, previously treated with penicillamine and sulfasalazine, and had been off all DMARDs for 7 years in remission. Her medical history included hypertension and a gastric ulcer, treated with losartan and ranitidine; she used paracetamol and codeine as needed. She did not smoke and consumed 35 units of alcohol weekly. On examination, she had a bronzed skin tone without stigmata of chronic liver disease and active synovitis of the left wrist and second metacarpophalangeal joint. Before initiating methotrexate, liver tests showed an ALT of 156 IU/L with normal bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and coagulation studies; prior liver tests 2 years earlier were normal. Screening revealed a serum ferritin >2000 μg/L and transferrin saturation of 92%. Abdominal ultrasound was normal. Transient elastography measured liver stiffness at 4.6 kPa, indicating no significant fibrosis.
title: Abnormal liver function tests in inflammatory arthritis: think beyond the DMARDs

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old man with metastatic small bowel carcinoid tumor and severe tricuspid regurgitation was referred for surgical valve replacement. Over the preceding 4 months, he received lanreotide depot, with serum serotonin levels decreasing from 2100 to 1200 ng/mL (normal 56–244 ng/mL) and chromogranin levels decreasing from 215 to 22 ng/mL (<15 ng/mL). Despite improved energy and diarrhea, he had persistent New York Heart Association class II symptoms, including exertional dyspnea and lower extremity edema.

Preoperative transthoracic echocardiography showed moderate tricuspid stenosis and severe tricuspid regurgitation with restricted leaflet motion and a dilated annulus, no pulmonary valve disease, a mildly dilated right ventricle with preserved systolic function, and normal left ventricular function. He underwent an uncomplicated tricuspid valve replacement with a 29 mm porcine bioprosthetic valve. Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography before cardiopulmonary bypass confirmed a dilated right ventricle with normal systolic function and retracted tricuspid leaflets with severe regurgitation; after bypass, the prosthesis was well seated with no regurgitation or stenosis and a mean gradient of 2 mmHg.

Over the next 24 hours, he could not be weaned from supplemental oxygen and inotropic support. Although carcinoid crisis was considered, his monthly lanreotide regimen was unchanged and a postoperative serum serotonin level was 171 ng/mL (within normal range). On postoperative day 2, transthoracic echocardiography showed a well-seated valve with a mean gradient of 5 mmHg. He remained unable to wean from vasoactive medications over several days; serial echocardiograms demonstrated preserved right and left ventricular function, no pericardial effusion, and no signs of hypovolemia. A repeat study then revealed tricuspid stenosis with a mean gradient of 10 mmHg.
title: Bioprosthetic Valve Thrombosis in Carcinoid Heart Disease

case_prompt: A 23-year-old nulliparous woman with no prior medical history presents to the gynecology emergency department with sudden-onset, intense right pelvic pain that began 2 hours earlier. She reports similar but milder episodes over the past year without any vaginal bleeding. Vital signs are normal. On examination, there is right lower-quadrant tenderness; pelvic examination shows a tender right adnexal mass without uterine bleeding. Laboratory tests reveal hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, leukocyte count 15 000/mm³, normal C-reactive protein, and a negative pregnancy test (hCG <5 mIU/mL). Transabdominal ultrasound shows a 65 mm hypoechoic, heterogeneous right ovary with peripherally displaced follicles and decreased Doppler flow. Adjacent to the ovary is a 10 cm cystic adnexal mass. The left ovary appears normal.
title: Hydrosalpinx with adnexal torsion in an adult patient–A case report

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old Thai woman presented with a 5-year history of pain and swelling over the dorsum of her left foot, worsening over the past month despite medication. The pain was aggravated by walking or standing, particularly over long distances. On musculoskeletal examination, there was mild swelling and a tender, firm mass over the 2nd and 3rd metatarsal bones. Vascular, neurologic, and dermatologic examinations of the lower extremity were normal.  
Plain radiographs of the foot showed bone destruction at the bases of the 2nd and 3rd metatarsals and cuneiforms, surrounded by soft-tissue calcifications and phleboliths.  
Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 4×3×3 cm lobulated mass in the midfoot involving the middle and lateral cuneiforms and bases of the 2nd and 3rd metatarsal bones, with tortuous blood vessels and dark foci characteristic of phleboliths. The lesion was bright on T2-weighted images and enhanced in parallel with blood vessels on postcontrast imaging, with insinuation into surrounding muscle.  
Routine laboratory tests were normal.
title: Spindle Cell Hemangioma of the Midfoot: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A woman in her early 20s, gravida 1 para 1, with a history of type 1 von Willebrand disease, underwent an uncomplicated primary caesarean delivery at term for arrest of descent and cephalopelvic disproportion. She was managed by hematology throughout pregnancy, received Humate-P prior to delivery and Amicar postpartum, and had an estimated blood loss of 850 mL. Her hemoglobin level was 112 g/L preoperatively and 95 g/L on postoperative day 2.

On postoperative day 35 she presented to the obstetric emergency room with heavy vaginal bleeding, nausea, diarrhea, and both periumbilical and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. She was afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal examination showed a well-healing incision without erythema or warmth and mild tenderness in the bilateral lower quadrants; the uterine fundus was palpated 3 cm below the umbilicus and was moderately tender without guarding or rebound. Pelvic examination revealed bright red blood in the vaginal vault. Her hemoglobin on admission was 101 g/L, white cell count 7.9 × 10^9/L, and a urine pregnancy test was negative. Based on these findings, there was a low suspicion for the more common causes of delayed postpartum hemorrhage.
title: Case of postpartum uterine artery pseudoaneurysm associated with von Willebrand disease

case_prompt: A 9-year-old Mongolian girl was referred with a 2-week history of frequent adherence of a small amount of blood to her underwear. Her past medical and birth history were unremarkable. On examination, there was a sessile, smooth-margined, clearly demarcated, elastic, soft red tumor encircling the urethral meatus. The lesion was hemorrhagic but the patient reported no pain and had no difficulty with urination. There were no other abnormalities on physical examination. Complete blood count and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Given her age, urethral prolapse was suspected and she was treated with topical steroid ointment for 3 weeks without clinical response. To exclude malignancy, enhanced computed tomography of the pelvis was obtained, which showed no invasion of the muscle layer and no evidence of distant metastases.
title: Urethral caruncle in a 9-year-old girl: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 62-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of progressive swelling at the left angle of her mouth, associated with pain on pressure and numbness of the left lower lip and chin. She had longstanding hypertension and diabetes. On examination, there was a hard, ill-defined, tender distension at the left mouth angle with overlying skin pigmentation; sensation in the left lower lip and chin was decreased. Intraorally, there was a poorly defined, firm, tender, sessile nodule measuring 1.5 cm in diameter on the buccal mucosa adjacent to the first and second left mandibular premolars; the teeth were intact and not mobile. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Cone-beam CT imaging demonstrated an enlarged left mandibular canal and markedly distended mental foramen. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a localized widening of the left mandibular canal with a slightly enhancing soft-tissue density mass occupying the canal.
title: A Case Report of Granular Cell Tumor of the Left Mandibular Canal

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive dyspnea accompanied by night sweats, fever, and weight loss. He was an electrician with no history of dust inhalation, drug use, or exposure to pet birds. He had smoked 20 cigarettes daily from age 20 until 3 months earlier, when he switched to an e-cig pen, which he used until the day before presentation.  
On examination, he appeared pale; temperature was 37.1°C. Chest auscultation revealed mild fine crackles bilaterally; heart sounds were normal.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 15,200/mm3 (77.5% neutrophils, 11.5% lymphocytes, 4.0% eosinophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 11.81 mg/dL. Krebs von den Lungen-6 was elevated at 1841 U/mL. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pH 7.504, PaCO2 29.0 Torr, PaO2 52.6 Torr, and HCO3– 22.7 mmol/L.  
Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a restrictive pattern with a vital capacity of 50.6% of predicted.  
Chest radiography showed extensive ground-glass opacities in the bilateral upper lung fields, predominantly in the lateral segments. Chest CT revealed ground-glass opacities with traction bronchiectasis throughout both upper lobes and nonsegmental ground-glass opacities with curvilinear shadows in the middle lobe, lingula, and lower lobes.
title: Lung injury associated with electronic cigarettes inhalation diagnosed by transbronchial lung biopsy

case_prompt: A 5-week-old male infant was referred for evaluation of an aortic arch anomaly. He had been born at term (3.07 kg), and after 3 weeks developed poor weight gain and respiratory distress with feeding. On admission, his weight was 3.65 kg (<3rd centile), heart rate 170 beats/min, respiratory rate elevated, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Blood pressure in the right arm and lower limbs was equal (80/40 mmHg). Examination revealed a grade III continuous “machinery” murmur, loudest in systole at the left infraclavicular area, fine wheezing bilaterally, and mild hepatomegaly; femoral pulses were normal. ECG showed sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy. Chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal intracardiac anatomy, left‐sided volume overload with moderate functional mitral regurgitation, preserved biventricular function, and a large aberrant vascular connection between the inferior aspect of the aortic arch and the pulmonary artery, causing a significant left-to-right shunt. To clarify the anatomy, cardiac catheterization and aortography were performed: these showed a short, large vessel arising from the inferior concave surface of the aortic arch just below the brachiocephalic artery and connecting to the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, with a 20% oxygen saturation step‐up from the right atrium to the pulmonary artery and equal systemic and pulmonary pressures.
title: Isolated persistence of the fifth aortic arch in an infant presenting with congestive heart failure

case_prompt:
A 28‐year‐old woman, gravida 2 para 1 at 35 weeks and 2 days of gestation, presented with a 1‐week history of severe hypertension. She had a prior history of moderately elevated blood pressure noted at 25 weeks’ gestation that required no therapy. One week before presentation, she complained of headache and right flank pain; her blood pressure was 165/110 mmHg. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, liver enzymes, and a random urine protein-to-creatinine ratio—were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with pregnancy‐induced hypertension and started on labetalol 200 mg twice daily. Obstetrical ultrasound and umbilical artery Doppler showed no fetal growth restriction. Her management plan included twice-daily blood pressure monitoring, twice-weekly antenatal visits, and planned delivery at 38 weeks.

Despite labetalol, her blood pressure remained labile and the right flank pain persisted. An abdominal ultrasound, performed to evaluate for renal pathology, unexpectedly revealed a heterogeneous right suprarenal solid mass measuring 6 × 4.5 cm. On transfer to our center, her blood pressure fluctuated between 200/120 mmHg and 110/80 mmHg. Repeat laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, liver panel, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine, remained normal. Twenty-four-hour urinary protein was 165 mg, making the diagnosis of preeclampsia unlikely.
title: Intrapartum adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma presenting in pregnancy: A case report

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old woman presented with involuntary movements of her right arm and leg that began 4 weeks earlier and progressively worsened, causing difficulty holding objects and walking. She had no rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthralgias, Raynaud’s phenomenon, sicca symptoms, oral contraceptive use, weight loss, headache, loss of consciousness, or seizures. There was no family history of rheumatic or neurologic disease. She was a nonsmoker and nondrinker, with two prior uncomplicated pregnancies.

On examination, there were jerky, purposeless, intermittent, and irregular choreic movements of the right hand and foot. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, blood chemistry, and liver function tests. The coagulation profile revealed a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time of 68.8 seconds (reference, 25–36.5). Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:1280; anti–double-stranded DNA was 70.5 IU (reference, <25 IU); anti–Smith antibody was positive; complement C3 was low; C4 was normal. Lupus anticoagulant was positive; anticardiolipin IgG was borderline positive at 18.5 GPL (reference, <15 GPL); anticardiolipin IgM and anti–β2-glycoprotein-1 were negative. Antistreptolysin O titer was 157 IU/mL (reference, <200 IU/mL). Thyroid function tests were normal.

Brain MRI demonstrated tiny foci of high-intensity signal on FLAIR and T2-weighted images in the bilateral basal ganglia and occipital periventricular white matter. Magnetic resonance angiography showed normal cerebral arterial caliber without stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm.
title: Chorea as the First and Only Manifestation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive pain and swelling of the right wrist extending onto the dorsal hand, associated with difficulty in wrist motion. He denied trauma, fever, or systemic symptoms, and the swelling did not respond to analgesics. On examination, there was tenderness over the wrist and carpometacarpal joints, a restricted range of motion of the wrist, and multiple lobulated swellings on the dorsal aspect of the wrist without overlying erythema.

A plain radiograph of the wrist showed a destructive, ill-defined lytic lesion of the distal radius and additional lytic lesions at the bases of the second and third metacarpals. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 2.5 × 2.4 cm osteolytic lesion of the distal radius with subarticular extension and an extraosseous soft-tissue component breaching the volar cortex; multiple lytic lesions of the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and bases of the second and third metacarpals with marrow edema; and an enhancing 2.9 × 2.1 cm soft-tissue mass abutting the carpal bones. Whole-body PET-CT revealed increased FDG uptake (SUVmax 5.0) in the distal radius lesion with soft-tissue extension and involvement of multiple carpal bones.
title: Multifocal Epitheloid Hemangioma of the Bone – A Rare Entity

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old previously healthy man was referred with a 3-week history of visible, painless, total hematuria. He also reported urinary frequency, straining, and significant weight loss and anorexia. Vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Digital rectal examination revealed a lobulated extraluminal mass at the anterior rectal wall; the upper limit could not be reached. Laboratory studies showed neutrophil leukocytosis; all other results were within normal limits.  
Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a large echogenic mass in the retrovesical area measuring approximately 69 × 69 mm that appeared to invade the posterior bladder wall. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-defined hypodense mass measuring 79 × 73 mm between the bladder and rectum, with slight post-contrast enhancement and no enlarged lymph nodes. The radiologist’s impression was a pelvic tumor, “lymphoma probably NHL,” with a differential diagnosis of teratoma.  
Because imaging was inconclusive, a multidisciplinary team performed cystoscopy, revealing a large solid tumor (approximately 80 × 80 mm) occupying the bladder neck and trigone, obscuring the ureteral orifices. Transurethral resection of the tumor was undertaken for diagnostic purposes.
title: Neuroblastoma involving urinary bladder: A rare type of tumor with diagnostic ambiguity

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old Asian man presented with five months of mild dysphagia to solid foods without chest pain, nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. His history was notable for Billroth II gastrectomy six years earlier for gastric cancer, exploratory laparotomy with adhesiolysis and inguinal hernia repair two years earlier, and eight cycles of XELOX chemotherapy. He had hypertension treated with nifedipine. He did not smoke or drink and had no relevant family history.

On examination, temperature was 36.1 °C, heart rate 61 bpm, respiratory rate 17 breaths/min, blood pressure 153/84 mmHg; lung and abdominal examinations were normal, and there was no peripheral edema.

Laboratory tests showed elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies, glycosylated hemoglobin 7.1%, total bilirubin 21.2 μmol/L, indirect bilirubin 14.2 μmol/L, and CYFRA21-1 40 ng/mL; all other laboratory values were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 55 × 35 × 29 mm round lesion in the middle and upper esophagus with homogeneous enhancement and luminal stenosis. Upper endoscopy revealed a smooth, elevated lesion 25–30 cm from the incisors with intact mucosa. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic, homogeneous mass approximately 41 mm in diameter arising from the muscularis propria, and it was provisionally diagnosed as a stromal tumor.
title: Total removal of a large esophageal schwannoma by submucosal tunneling endoscopic resection: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 65-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of absolute constipation, non-projectile vomiting of recently eaten food, low-grade fever, progressive abdominal distension, and sharp, fixed umbilical pain worsened by feeding. She had no history of abdominal surgery, peritonitis, or trauma. On examination, she appeared dehydrated, moderately anemic, and cachectic. Vital signs were stable. The abdomen was uniformly distended, tender with guarding, and bowel sounds were reduced; other system examinations were unremarkable. A supine abdominal radiograph showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with prominent valvulae conniventes; erect films demonstrated multiple air-fluid levels. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin level of 12.4 g/dL, leukocytosis (17.5 × 10^9/L), negative HIV and hepatitis panels, and normal renal and liver function. She was resuscitated with intravenous fluids, had nasogastric decompression and urinary catheterization, and was scheduled for an emergency laparotomy.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Geriatric spontaneous trans-mesenteric herniation leading to death. Case report

case_prompt: A 42-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presents with a two-month history of unintentional 6-kg weight loss and two weeks of epigastric pain accompanied by new-onset jaundice. She denies prior biliary disease. On examination, she is icteric but afebrile, and there is no palpable abdominal mass. Laboratory studies reveal cholestasis with a total bilirubin of 9.3 mg/dL. Abdominal CT and MRCP demonstrate cholelithiasis, asymmetric malignant-appearing thickening of the gallbladder wall, and a contiguous mass at the hepatic hilum infiltrating segment IVb and the common and bilateral hepatic ducts, with upstream intrahepatic biliary dilatation. There is extensive contact between the mass and the right portal vein without a clear plane of separation; no lymphadenopathy is noted. Given these findings suggestive of a resectable biliary tract malignancy, the surgical team plans a radical resection.
title: Infiltrative xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis mimicking aggressive gallbladder carcinoma: A diagnostic and therapeutic dilemma

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old healthy boy had been diagnosed in 2016 with severe left-eye uveitis complicated by central retinal vein occlusion and iris rubeosis. Initial workup—including chest radiography and laboratory evaluations—found no infectious, granulomatous, or systemic autoimmune cause. He was managed with immunomodulators and topical steroids, with complete resolution of vein occlusion and rubeosis. His last mild left anterior uveitis occurred in November 2020, treated with a 5-week taper of topical steroids. He remained quiescent at quarterly visits through spring 2021, with best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/16 in both eyes.

In June 2021, he received his first dose of the BNT162b2 (BioNTech-Pfizer) COVID-19 vaccine. The next day, he noted sudden vision loss in the left eye and presented to the ophthalmology clinic. On examination, BCVA was 20/16 in the right eye and 20/500 in the left eye. Findings in the left eye included corneal precipitates; 50 cells per slit in the anterior chamber with fibrin formation; widespread iris rubeosis; 16–25 vitreous cells per slit; and cystoid macular edema on optical coherence tomography.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Severe panuveitis with iridis rubeosis activation and cystoid macular edema after BioNTech-Pfizer COVID-19 vaccination in a 17-year-old

case_prompt: A 44-year-old man with a 13-year history of untreated HIV infection presented with a 3-week history of persistent, dull bilateral back pain, fever, fatigue, and weight loss. He declined antiretroviral therapy and on admission had a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count of 6 cells/µL and an HIV RNA load of 10 001 391 copies/mL. Physical examination was notable only for costovertebral angle tenderness. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 103 g/L), elevated aspartate transaminase (79 U/L) and γ-glutamyltransferase (207 U/L), and hypoalbuminemia (30.7 g/L). There was no serologic or microbiologic evidence of cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, fungi, or tuberculosis. Renin, angiotensin, aldosterone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, and catecholamine levels were within normal limits. Unenhanced abdominal computed tomography revealed two large (67 × 38 mm on the left, 56 × 58 mm on the right), heterogeneous, hypodense masses adjacent to both adrenal glands. Contrast enhancement was moderate and heterogeneous, with associated retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy compressing the adrenals. Given the imaging appearance and the patient’s profound immunodeficiency, lymphoma was initially suspected; adrenal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma were also considered. A CT-guided core-needle biopsy of the right-sided lesion was performed.
title: HIV-related bilateral inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors of the adrenal gland: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A full-term male infant was born by cesarean section after prenatal identification of VACTERL association, including multiple vertebral anomalies, tetralogy of Fallot with hypoplastic pulmonary valve, and unilateral renal agenesis. The patient was macrocephalic without hydrocephalus. At birth, he required mechanical ventilation for respiratory distress due to significant chest wall deformity. He had hypocalcemia and hypoparathyroidism managed with parenteral and enteral calcium supplementation. Cardiac interventions included pulmonary valvuloplasty and patent ductus arteriosus stenting.

Newborn screening for severe combined immunodeficiency showed a T-cell receptor excision circle cycle threshold of 45 (abnormal ≥40). At age 2 weeks, flow cytometry revealed absent CD3+ T cells (13 cells/mm3) and CD4+CD45RA+ naive T cells (13 cells/mm3), with normal CD19+ B cells (588 cells/mm3) and CD56+ natural killer cells (175 cells/mm3). Chest radiography demonstrated an absent thymic shadow. The mother had gestational diabetes treated with insulin; there was no reported exposure to teratogens and no parental consanguinity.

Genetic evaluation included a normal whole-genome chromosomal microarray and a primary immunodeficiency panel of 407 genes (including TBX1, CHD7, and FOXN1), all of which were normal. A clinical diagnosis of complete DiGeorge syndrome in the setting of VACTERL association was made, and the patient received immunoglobulin replacement and prophylactic antibiotics.

At age 8 months, he developed a diffuse scaly erythrodermic rash with generalized alopecia, as well as lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. By age 10 months, his absolute eosinophil count was 6116 cells/mm3 (reference 0–400), and his serum IgE level was 5096 IU/mL (reference 3–15). Repeat flow cytometry showed CD3+ T cells of 705 cells/mm3 and CD4+CD45RO+ memory T cells of 172 cells/mm3. TCR-Vβ spectratyping demonstrated an oligoclonal T-cell population. Studies for maternal engraftment were negative.
journal: The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: Global
title: Omenn syndrome in a 10-month-old male with athymia and VACTERL association

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old woman with well-controlled HIV infection (CD4 560 cells/mm3; undetectable viral load) presented with a 5-month history of an asymptomatic rash on her bilateral lower legs. On examination, there were indurated, hyperpigmented papules and nodules coalescing into plaques on both thighs. Initial clinical differential diagnoses included morphea, deep fungal infection, and atypical mycobacterial infection. Tissue cultures for bacteria, fungi, and acid-fast bacilli were negative. 

Punch biopsy showed an alternating light and dark appearance at low magnification from histiocytic and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates spanning the dermis and lobules of the subcutis, with fibrosis, lobular panniculitis with fat necrosis, and edema. There was no obliterative phlebitis. Numerous dense lymphoplasmacytic aggregates with Russell bodies were present. Lipidized mononuclear cells comprised most of the histiocytic infiltrate. Fite-Faraco, Ziehl-Neelsen, Grocott methenamine silver, periodic acid–Schiff, Von Kossa, human herpesvirus 8, and Gram stains were negative. Kappa and lambda in situ hybridization showed a polytypic plasmacytoid population. Immunostaining revealed an IgG4/IgG ratio of 50 percent with 80 IgG4-positive cells per high-power field, and the histiocytic infiltrate was diffusely CD68-positive and CD1a-negative.
title: Xanthomatous cutaneous Rosai-Dorfman disease with overlapping features of IgG4-related disease

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of fatigue, jaundice, pale stools, and right upper quadrant pain. Eighteen months earlier, he underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for fulminant autoimmune hepatitis, complicated by primary graft nonfunction and a second transplant one week later. One month before this presentation, he reported similar symptoms; his local hepatologist attributed them to late graft rejection in the setting of self-reported immunosuppression disruption and elevated liver enzymes, and he was started on high-dose oral glucocorticoids in addition to tacrolimus and mycophenolate.

On admission, laboratory studies showed: total bilirubin 6.9 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 1465 U/L, AST 109 U/L, ALT 86 U/L, CA 19-9 419 U/mL, and an EBV viral load of 1075 IU/mL. Liver ultrasound revealed an ill-defined, heterogeneously hypoechoic mass along the inferior margin of the left lobe with vascular involvement. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 7.3 cm infiltrative mass in segments II, III, and the caudate lobe, causing intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation and features concerning for high-grade stenosis.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography was consistent with a benign post-transplant biliary anastomotic stricture. Following balloon dilation, a fully covered metal stent was placed. Brush cytology of the stricture was negative for cholangiocarcinoma in situ.
final_diagnosis_raw: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder
title: A Post-transplant Immunosuppression Complication: Epstein-Barr Virus-Positive Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma Post-transplant Lymphoproliferative Disorder

case_prompt:
An 81-year-old man was referred for evaluation of lung nodules. Four months earlier, routine chest CT had shown multiple small nodules in both lungs. He was asymptomatic, received a short course of oral antibiotics, and did not follow up. Two months later he developed paroxysmal cough with scant white sputum and progressive dyspnea without fever, chills, chest pain, or hemoptysis. Repeat chest CT showed progression to multiple patchy and nodular high-density shadows, suggestive of an infectious or inflammatory etiology. 

On admission to a community hospital, he was afebrile with pH 7.46, pCO2 36.7 mmHg, pO2 63.5 mmHg on room air.
