Laboratory studies showed WBC 7.6×10^9/L, neutrophils 68.7%, hemoglobin 123 g/L, platelets 225×10^9/L, and CRP 16.5 mg/L. Immunological tests, D-dimer, liver and kidney function, ESR, CEA, CA19-9, AFP, and rheumatologic panels were normal. Sputum AFB smear and bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. T-SPOT.TB and antinuclear antibodies were nonreactive. 

Bronchoscopy was unremarkable. Brush cytology from the right lower lobe showed no malignancy. mNGS of BALF detected no pathogens. BALF β-D-glucan and galactomannan tests were negative. With no pathogens identified and imaging findings, a presumptive diagnosis of secondary organizing pneumonia was made, and methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily was started. Within 3 days, cough and dyspnea improved. A follow-up CT one month later showed partial resolution of opacities. He was discharged on oral methylprednisolone 20 mg daily.

Four weeks after discharge, cough and dyspnea recurred. Repeat CT showed increased patchy shadows and nodules in both lungs compared to prior imaging. He was readmitted with a preliminary diagnosis of pneumonia. He was afebrile, heart rate 63, respiratory rate 21, blood pressure 139/88 mmHg, and mildly labored respirations. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds without crackles or wheezes. Laboratory tests showed WBC 9.7×10^9/L, neutrophils 6.1×10^9/L, and LDH 378.9 U/L. Enhanced CT of the chest confirmed multiple patchy shadows and nodules plus hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Superficial lymph node ultrasound was normal.
final_diagnosis_raw: Primary pulmonary diffuse large B cell lymphoma
title: Primary pulmonary diffuse large B cell lymphoma presenting with features of organizing pneumonia: a case report

case_prompt: A 13-year-old boy presented with a 2–3-month history of a slowly enlarging hole in the anterior hard palate, associated with difficulty eating and a nasal quality to his speech. On examination, there was a 1-cm perforation in the anterior hard palate; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 11 700/mm3 (57% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, 13% eosinophils), and a platelet count of 294 000/mm3; other biochemical tests were within normal limits. A chest radiograph was normal, and a Mantoux test was negative. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was unremarkable. A skeletal survey showed no periosteal lesions or perichondritis. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis was normal. No Hutchinson’s teeth or other orofacial stigmata were noted, and an ophthalmic examination including fundoscopy was normal. There were no neurologic symptoms.
title: Congenital syphilis, still a reality in 21st century: a case report

case_prompt: A 69‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of macular degeneration. Her visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes, intraocular pressure was normal, and blood pressure was 132/72 mm Hg. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable. Funduscopic evaluation revealed intermediate drusen and pigment mottling in the macula of both eyes. During acquisition of spectral‐domain OCT images, dramatic choroidal pulsations in the macula of the right eye were noted on the B‐scan, corresponding to the patient’s heartbeat and dampening with gentle pressure on the eye. SD‐OCT revealed greater subfoveal choroidal thickness in the right eye during systole that thinned during diastole. Fluorescein angiography was unremarkable, while indocyanine green angiography revealed engorgement of the choroidal vasculature of the right eye. Investigational OCT angiography showed subtle tortuosity of the superficial vascular complex and engorgement of the deep vascular complex in the right eye compared to the left. B‐scan ultrasonography demonstrated subtle orbital pulsations of the right orbit without a detectable mass. The patient denied any history of trauma or orbital surgery. Magnetic resonance imaging, venography, and angiography of the orbits were unrevealing apart from slight enhancement of the right orbital soft tissue and symmetric, normal caliber of the superior ophthalmic veins.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Orbital arteriovenous fistula presenting with choroidal pulsations on optical coherence tomography

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old man was referred for evaluation of erythrocytosis discovered during follow‐up for cerebral arteriosclerosis. He appeared sanguineous; his oxygen saturation on room air was 96%. He had a history of hypertension and cerebral arteriosclerosis treated with aspirin and atorvastatin. He denied dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, smoking, high-altitude residence, and there was no family history of polycythemia or myeloproliferative disorders.

Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 175 g/L, hematocrit 54.7%, mean corpuscular volume 101 fL, lactate dehydrogenase normal, blood urea nitrogen 10.05 mmol/L, creatinine 143.2 µmol/L. Serum erythropoietin level was 53.9 mIU/mL (reference 1.48–31.88). Mutation analysis for JAK2 (V617F and exons 12–15), MPL, CALR, and CSF3R was negative. BCR::ABL1 transcripts were negative. Serum protein studies revealed a monoclonal IgA-λ spike of 5.65 g/L; IgA was elevated at 7.63 g/L (normal 0.82–4.53 g/L), with normal IgG and IgM levels. Abdominal ultrasound showed no masses or organomegaly, and spinal MRI showed no bone lesions.
title: Secondary Polycythemia May Be an Early Clinical Manifestation of Multiple Myeloma: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old postmenopausal multiparous woman noted a firm, slightly raised nodule on her right labium majus four months earlier; it progressively enlarged to about 3 cm. PET–CT performed externally showed multiple hypermetabolic foci suggesting malignancy. Cystoscopy revealed masses in the bladder trigone and near the left ureteral orifice; biopsy confirmed invasive carcinoma. Colposcopy showed invasive carcinoma involving the cervix and vaginal wall, suggesting cervical malignancy.

On examination, there were firm, non-tender, immobile bilateral inguinal lymph nodes (up to 2.5 cm), more prominent on the left. A 30 mm irregular, hard, fixed subcutaneous mass was present in the right vulva near the symphysis pubis. The vagina was patent but the anterior and lateral walls up to one-third were stiff with contact bleeding. Bartholin, Skene, and vestibular glands were unremarkable. The uterus was small and anteverted; adnexa were normal; anal exam was unremarkable.

A vulvar mass was excised. Histologic examination showed infiltrating adenocarcinoma in the dermis and subcutis without epidermal connection, arranged in nests and cords with pleomorphic cells, prominent nucleoli, 15 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, and lymphovascular invasion. All margins were free. Initial immunohistochemical results: tumor cells were diffusely positive for CK7, E-cadherin, and P53; negative for ER, PR, WT1, PAX8, CDX2, GATA3, P40, HMB45, and S100; Ki-67 index was 80%. The lesion was diagnosed as poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma.
final_diagnosis_raw: Vulvar adenocarcinoma of mammary gland type
title: A Rare Case Report: Primary Vulvar Adenocarcinoma of Mammary Gland Type

case_prompt: A 6-year-old boy from Bihar, India, presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging, non-painful swelling in the superolateral aspect of the right upper eyelid, associated with intermittent nocturnal fevers, chills, sweating, anorexia, and weight loss. There was no visual disturbance, trauma, or symptoms suggestive of pulmonary disease. He was fully immunized and had no known TB contacts. On examination, he was afebrile, alert, and underweight (15 kg, <–2 Z score). There was a diffuse, fluctuant, non-tender soft swelling (6 cm × 3 cm) involving the right lateral upper eyelid and temporal region, causing mild mechanical ptosis and an S-shaped eyelid deformity. Hertel exophthalmometry showed non-axial inferomedial proptosis (right 14 mm, left 12 mm). Right ocular motility was restricted in superolateral, lateral, and inferolateral gazes. Anterior segment and fundus examinations were normal in both eyes. Laboratory studies revealed mild lymphocytosis, an ESR of 15 mm/hr, and a reactive Mantoux test (10 mm). Liver function tests, chest radiograph, and abdominal ultrasound were normal. A CT scan of the orbits demonstrated a peripherally enhancing collection in the superolateral right orbit, with erosion of the superolateral wall and roof extending into subcutaneous and intracranial spaces, suggestive of osteomyelitis with abscess formation.
journal: JNMA: Journal of the Nepal Medical Association
title: Primary Orbital Tuberculosis with Cold Abscess: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of nasal obstruction, chronic rhinorrhea, and frequent epistaxis. Six months before presentation he developed fever and lower extremity edema. A primary hospital detected renal dysfunction with hematuria, and he was referred for investigation of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. On admission, his temperature was 37.8 °C, blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg, and heart rate 88 beats/min. Physical examination was notable for bilateral lower extremity edema; the remainder was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed: hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, creatinine 3.05 mg/dL (6 months earlier 0.76 mg/dL), blood urea nitrogen 28.3 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 1.16 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed proteinuria (1.28 g/gCr), occult blood 3+, 50–99 red cells per high-power field, and red-cell casts. Serology was positive for PR3-ANCA (28.5 U/mL) and negative for MPO-ANCA, anti-GBM antibody, and antinuclear antibodies. Complement levels were within the reference range. Chest radiography and computed tomography showed no abnormalities. Renal ultrasonography revealed mildly enlarged kidneys (11 cm longitudinally).
title: Extranodal NK/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type Accompanied by PR3-ANCA-associated Glomerulonephritis

case_prompt: A 70-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of cough and fever. His blood pressure was 120/74 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 38.2 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on 2 L/min of supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula. Laboratory studies showed: WBC 7.41 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 132 g/L, platelets 387 × 10^9/L, ESR 72 mm/h, CRP > 150 mg/L, IL-6 88.19 pg/mL, and procalcitonin 0.244 ng/mL. Arterial blood gas analysis, hepatic and renal function, electrolytes, respiratory virus panel, and fungal tests were all within normal limits. Blood cultures showed no growth; sputum cultures grew normal flora; three consecutive acid-fast bacilli smears were negative. There was no other identifiable source of infection. Autoimmune studies (ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor) were negative. A chest CT scan showed right upper lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, patchy infiltrates, and ground-glass opacities in the right lower lobe. The patient was treated empirically for community-acquired pneumonia with broad-spectrum antibiotics, but his symptoms did not improve. A repeat CT scan 10 days after initiation of antibiotics demonstrated progression of consolidation and increased density of the lung lesions.
title: Acute fibrinous and organizing pneumonia: two case reports and literature review

case_prompt: A 40-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of chronic abdominal pain accompanied by diarrhea and generalized weakness. An abdominal ultrasonogram showed an inflamed appendix. On examination, there was localized tenderness and rebound in the right iliac fossa at McBurney’s point. The total leukocyte count was elevated at 16,000/mm^3, and other routine biochemical and hematological tests were within normal limits. A clinical diagnosis of chronic appendicitis was made, and the patient underwent an appendectomy. Intraoperatively, the appendix appeared inflamed and was studded with several small tubercles on the serosal surface and adjacent periappendiceal fat. The appendix and a mesenteric lymph node were submitted for histopathological examination.
title: An Uncommon Case of Chronic Tubercular Appendicitis

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of a chronic, pruritic, occasionally tender rash affecting both ears. Six years earlier, he was diagnosed with eczematous dermatitis and treated with clobetasol 0.05% cream; three years later, he received triamcinolone 0.025% cream for a similar diagnosis. He noted mild relief of itching with topical steroids but recurrent flares within two weeks of discontinuation. He denied contact with irritants or allergens, worsening of symptoms at night, immunosuppression, or systemic symptoms. Personal and family histories were negative for connective tissue disorders, including relapsing polychondritis. 

On examination, there was confluent erythema, fine white scaling, and scattered pustules on the helices and antihelices of both ears, with relative sparing of the lobules and no involvement of the scalp or face. Dermoscopic evaluation of the right antihelix revealed background telangiectasias and follicular, cone-shaped, fine, translucent white scales.
title: Demodectic frost of the ears: Diagnostic dermoscopic features

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old Moroccan man presented with one month of vague left flank pain without radiation and one day of nausea and vomiting. He denied fevers, digestive or urinary symptoms, and any contact with dogs or sheep. His medical history was notable for new-onset hypertension over the past year, treated with bisoprolol and amlodipine. On examination he was afebrile and vital signs were stable; the physical examination was unremarkable. A standing abdominal radiograph was normal.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large 10.4 cm hypoechoic mass with an internal cystic component adjacent to the superior pole of the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 14.5 × 7.2 cm hypoattenuated cystic mass in the region of the left adrenal gland, containing multiple daughter cysts with a honeycomb appearance and exerting a mass effect on surrounding structures. No other lesions were seen in the liver, lungs, or elsewhere in the abdomen.  
Laboratory studies showed a mild leukocytosis (11 × 10^3 cells/mm^3) with eosinophilia (7%). Serum chemistries, renin, aldosterone, and 24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid and metanephrine levels were all within normal limits. A serologic test for hydatid cyst was negative.
title: Giant primary adrenal hydatid cyst presenting with arterial hypertension: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old boy was evaluated after two brief episodes of transient loss of consciousness, each preceded by warmth, light-headedness, and chest discomfort. There was no fever, vomiting, abnormal movements, frothing, incontinence, or postictal confusion. On examination, pulse was 100 bpm, regular, with synchronous peripheral pulses and no radiofemoral delay. Blood pressure was 210/140 mm Hg. Cardiovascular examination revealed a heaving apex, a normal first heart sound, a widely split second heart sound, and a short systolic murmur at the apex. 

Baseline blood tests were normal except for a serum potassium level of 2.8 mmol/L. Electrocardiography showed a prolonged QT interval of 0.47 seconds. Echocardiography demonstrated concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Renal Doppler ultrasonography revealed normal renal vessels with a normal flow pattern. Abdominal ultrasonography identified an 8 × 8 cm mass at the hilum of the left kidney with grade II hydronephrosis. Serum cortisol and 24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels were within normal limits. 

At laparotomy, an 8 × 8 cm mass was found at the left renal hilum, necessitating nephrectomy for complete excision; a single enlarged para-aortic lymph node was also removed. A presumptive diagnosis of Wilms tumor was made, and left nephrectomy with excision biopsy of the lymph node was performed.
journal: Journal of Indian Association of Pediatric Surgeons
title: Recurrent malignant juxtaglomerular cell tumor: A rare cause of malignant hypertension in a child

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old man from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with a history of occupational TB exposure in Rwanda and a positive Quantiferon Gold test in 2014 (without treatment), presented with 5 days of exertional dyspnea, midepigastric pain, fevers up to 101.9 °F, and fatigue. He denied cough, night sweats, or weight loss. 

CT chest without contrast showed diffuse ground-glass opacities and a moderate right pleural effusion; MRI abdomen confirmed a 33×30×23 mm pancreatic pseudocyst. Lipase was 216 U/L. Right thoracentesis yielded 350 mL of exudative fluid (serum protein 6.8 g/dL, fluid protein 5.7 g/dL; serum LDH 129 U/L, fluid LDH 315 U/L); pleural fluid cytology, AFB smear, and culture were negative. HIV testing was negative. He was discharged with a presumptive diagnosis of pancreatitis-induced pleural effusion.

Two months later, he developed a recurrent right pleural effusion requiring repeat exudative thoracentesis (ADA 7.6 U/L). One month thereafter he was admitted with dyspnea, tested positive for SARS-CoV-2, received dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 7 days, and underwent thoracentesis yielding 1650 mL of green-yellow exudative fluid; flow cytometry and pleural chemistries were unremarkable. 

One month after discharge, he returned febrile (102.4 °F) with left-sided pleuritic chest pain. CT angiography revealed a large left pleural effusion. He underwent left VATS with pleurectomy, pleurodesis, and biopsy. Intraoperative findings included green serous fluid and diffuse studding of the pleura and diaphragm. Pathology demonstrated organizing fibrous tissue with fibrinous exudate and multiple necrotizing granulomas; special stains for acid-fast and fungal organisms were negative.
journal: Journal of Community Hospital Internal Medicine Perspectives
title: A Case of Pleural Tuberculosis vs Latent Tuberculosis Reactivation as a Result of COVID-19 Infection and Treatment

case_prompt: A 65-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a rapidly enlarging nodule on the left preauricular cheek. Her history was notable for type II diabetes, hypertension, and immunosuppression following renal transplantation 8 years earlier. Two years prior, she had a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in situ on her left third finger treated with Mohs micrographic surgery. On examination, there was a 1.5 cm eroded, erythematous nodule on the left preauricular cheek. A shave biopsy revealed an ulcerated neoplasm throughout the dermis comprised of irregular islands of atypical cells that stained uniformly with antibodies to pan keratin and uniformly negative with antibodies to S100 protein, leading to a diagnosis of poorly differentiated carcinoma. The lesion was excised by Mohs surgery in one stage with negative frozen-section margins, resulting in a 3.5 × 2.3 cm defect. Permanent sections showed a deeply infiltrating undifferentiated carcinoma extending into subcutaneous fat without keratinization but with foci of duct formation; the neoplasm was connected to and continuous with the epidermis, suggesting undifferentiated squamous cell carcinoma, while the presence of ducts raised consideration of eccrine carcinoma.
title: Aggressive Extraocular Sebaceous Carcinoma Recurring after Mohs Micrographic Surgery

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman presented during a routine annual gynecologic examination with a painful abdominal wall mass. Her history included appendectomy, two births, a cesarean section 15 years earlier, and excision of an endometriotic mass from the cesarean scar at that time. She reported that the mass had increased in size over several months and that the pain was cyclical, correlating with her menstrual periods, similar to her previous lesion. Prior gynecologic examinations were normal, and no abdominal nodule had been noted.

On physical examination, there was a 6 cm × 6 cm tender mass in the midline of the abdominal wall, 3 cm above the Pfannenstiel scar; the mass was painful on movement and Fothergill sign positive. The rest of the gynecologic examination was unremarkable. Mammography and pelvic ultrasound were normal. Soft-tissue ultrasound of the abdominal wall showed a 70 × 60 mm lesion in the mesogastrium caudal to the umbilicus, described as “compatible with fibrous soft tissue tumor (desmoid tumor).” Given her history, endometriotic implants could not be ruled out. Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed a benign process compatible with endometriosis. Serum tumor markers were: CA-125, 243 U/mL (elevated); CEA, < 0.5 ng/mL. A provisional diagnosis of abdominal wall endometriosis was made, and surgery was scheduled for removal of the mass with exploration of the abdominal cavity.
title: Malignant transformation of abdominal wall endometriosis with lymph node metastasis☆

case_prompt: A 51-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a pruritic eruption involving her trunk and upper extremities that was recalcitrant to topical triamcinolone ointment. She took no prescription medications but reported beginning flaxseed oil supplementation a few weeks before the eruption’s onset. On examination, there were erythematous patches and thin plaques on the trunk and upper extremities. A skin biopsy showed an atypical superficial interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate extending into the reticular dermis with lymphocyte exocytosis of small lymphocytes, some of which had clear halos. The lymphocytes stained positive for CD3, and the CD4:CD8 ratio of the epidermal lymphocytes was approximately 1:4. The biopsy was reported as suspicious for CD8+ cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, mycosis fungoides–type. At the initial visit with a cutaneous oncology specialist, she had discontinued all supplements for 3 weeks, including flaxseed oil, with slight improvement of her skin findings. She had no systemic symptoms, no new tattoos, vaccinations, piercings, or sick contacts, and no recent travel. The clinical–pathologic differential diagnosis included mycosis fungoides and cutaneous pseudolymphoma. It was recommended that she continue to withhold the supplements, apply a medium-potency topical steroid ointment to affected areas twice daily for 2 weeks, and return in 2 months for possible molecular testing.
title: Cutaneous pseudolymphomatous drug eruption secondary to supplemental flaxseed oil

case_prompt:
A 64‐year‐old woman presented with daily fevers up to 102 °F for one month, associated with night sweats, muscle aches, dry cough, headache, fatigue, and an 8-pound weight loss.  
Her medical history included hypertension and anxiety; she denied smoking, alcohol use, recent travel, or pet exposure. Family history was notable for cardiovascular disease in her parents and breast cancer in her twin sister.  

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14 000/mm³ (neutrophils 10 000/mm³), hematocrit 33.5%, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate >120 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 238 mg/L. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 1.19 µIU/mL. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis showed no monoclonal spike.  

Blood and urine cultures were negative, and tests for Lyme antibody, Bartonella IgG/IgM, Anaplasma PCR, and Babesia PCR were negative.  

Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed a 3.8 × 2.9 × 5.0 cm heterogeneous, enhancing lesion in the left adrenal gland; the right adrenal gland appeared normal. A random urine normetanephrine was elevated at 2917 µg per gram of creatinine (reference, 108–524).  

Further evaluation showed serum free normetanephrine 344 pg/mL (≤148) and serum free metanephrine <25 pg/mL (≤57). Twenty-four-hour urine studies revealed normetanephrine 1915 µg (122–676), metanephrine 139 µg (90–315), norepinephrine 133 µg (15–100), dopamine 148 µg (52–480), and a normal urinary free cortisol of 27.4 µg (4–50). MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 3.4 × 4.0 × 4.7 cm mass in the left adrenal gland with heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity and T1 isointensity.
title: Fever of Unknown Origin: Could It Be a Pheochromocytoma? A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old woman with no family history of thyroid disease or malignancy was admitted with heat intolerance, increased sweating, palpitations, and polyphagia of one month’s duration. Initial evaluation revealed suppressed TSH, markedly elevated FT3 and FT4, and a TRAb level of 31.07 U/L (normal 0–1.58 U/L). Thyroid ultrasonography showed diffuse enlargement with abundant blood flow, and 99mTc thyroid scan confirmed diffuse uptake without parathyroid lesions. Methimazole and metoprolol were begun but methimazole was discontinued after 4 days due to elevated ALT (107 U/L).

On transfer, she was treated with liver-protective agents, propranolol, and a reduced dose of methimazole once liver function normalized. Four weeks later, she developed nausea and vomiting. Serum calcium was 3.22 mmol/L (normal 2.11–2.52 mmol/L) with a low PTH of 3.16 ng/L (normal 15–65 pg/mL). A 99mTc-MIBI scan showed no parathyroid or ectopic uptake. Renal function, immunofixation electrophoresis, lymph node ultrasound, and tumor markers were all normal. Bone turnover markers were elevated (osteocalcin 51.46 ng/mL; β-CTX 2105 ng/L), and BMD showed osteoporosis (L1–4 Z –2.8). Chest CT revealed a 1963.58 mm² anterior-superior mediastinal mass; PET-CT confirmed this lesion.
title: The coexistence of hypercalcemia, osteoporosis and thymic enlargement in graves’ disease: a case report

case_prompt: A 44-year-old surgeon underwent uneventful bilateral phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation for high myopia. Three months later, she developed progressive blurred vision in both eyes. Ultrasonography showed severe vitreitis with intense flare cells and dense membranes, and visual acuity declined to 20/200 OU. Slit-lamp examination revealed mild anterior-segment inflammation, well-positioned lenses, and dense vitreitis; intraocular pressure was 18 mmHg in both eyes. A comprehensive workup for uveitis was unremarkable. Despite repeated topical, subconjunctival, and sub-Tenon steroid injections, oral prednisone (1 g/kg/day), and later cyclosporine A, her vision worsened to light perception, and intraocular pressures rose to 35 mmHg OD and 50 mmHg OS. Antiglaucomatous therapy and cessation of systemic steroids produced no improvement. She then underwent pars plana vitrectomy and trabeculectomy OS without visual gain, as dense anterior-chamber inflammation recurred and IOP relapsed. Subsequent immunosuppression with prednisone and methotrexate also failed to help. By 12 months after symptom onset, her vision was light perception OU, IOP remained elevated despite therapy, and she exhibited personality changes. One day she fainted and was taken to the emergency department.
title: Masquerade Syndrome of Multicentre Primary Central Nervous System Lymphoma

case_prompt: A 34-year-old man presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging, painful swelling in the lower anterior mandible associated with pus-like discharge. He reported a similar episode three months earlier that resolved after spontaneous discharge. His history included facial trauma 18 years prior, root canal therapy on teeth 31, 41, and 42, and a crown on tooth 11. On examination, there was a 3 × 2.5 cm firm, tender, oval swelling from teeth 33 to 43 on the labial aspect, with a lingual bulge at tooth 41. Vertical percussion elicited tenderness in teeth 31, 32, 41, and 42. Electric pulp testing revealed a response level of “3” in teeth 32, 33, 34, 43, and 44. Aspiration produced straw-colored fluid tinged with blood. A panoramic radiograph showed a mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion extending from the distal aspect of tooth 32 to the distal aspect of tooth 43, containing an irregular radiopaque mass suggestive of extruded root canal filling material. Clinically, a radicular cyst was diagnosed, with a calcifying odontogenic cyst in the differential. An incisional biopsy was performed, and the specimen was sent for histopathological examination.
title: Histopathological Insight of a Case of Adenoid Ameloblastoma: A Rare Odontogenic Tumor

case_prompt: A 6‐year‐old girl with known congenital hepatic fibrosis presented with recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding from esophagogastric varices. She was deemed a candidate for liver transplantation. Preoperative laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL, platelet count 6.9×10^4/μL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, bilirubin 0.67 mg/dL, AST 43 U/L, and ALT 39 U/L. The only available living donor was her 38‐year‐old mother, who was asymptomatic. The donor’s liver function tests were within normal limits (total bilirubin 0.33 mg/dL; AST 12 U/L; ALT 11 U/L), and she had no known cystic disease in any other organ. Magnetic resonance imaging of the donor’s liver showed multiple 3–5 mm nodules with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Contrast‐enhanced CT revealed multiple 3–5 mm low‐attenuation areas throughout both lobes of the liver, with attenuation values higher than water.
title: Pediatric living donor liver transplantation for congenital hepatic fibrosis using a mother’s graft with von Meyenburg complex: A case report

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman undergoing routine breast screening had an ultrasound that detected a 1.2-cm lesion in the lower outer quadrant of her left breast, although she felt no palpable mass. She had a history of laser treatment for cervical dysplasia but no breast surgery or trauma. Family history was notable for a sister with breast cancer and a father with gastric cancer. On examination there was no palpable breast mass or axillary lymphadenopathy.  
Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein concentration of 0.16 mg/dL (reference 0.00–0.14 mg/dL), normal carcinoembryonic antigen and cancer antigen 15-3 levels, and a normal serum interleukin-6 concentration.  
Mammography revealed a focal asymmetric density in the lower outer left breast. Ultrasonography showed a smoothly marginated, relatively hypoechoic 1.2-cm mass with scant internal vascularity and partial cystic change. MRI demonstrated a 1.2-cm lesion with mildly high T2 signal, diffusion restriction, and early contrast enhancement with a plateau on delayed imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a solitary heterogeneously enhancing mass without lymphadenopathy or distant lesions.  
A core needle biopsy of the mass showed a fibrosing lesion with proliferation of fibroblastic cells in a storiform pattern accompanied by chronic inflammatory and histiocytic cells. No epithelial neoplasm was observed. Immunohistochemical staining of the spindle cells was diffusely positive for ALK-1 and negative for IgG4.
title: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase-positive inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor of the breast: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a 3-month history of abdominal discomfort predominantly in the upper quadrants. He denied other gastrointestinal or systemic symptoms. His medical history was notable only for hypertension for more than four years. On physical examination, vital signs were normal, the abdomen was soft, and no masses were palpable. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and liver function tests, were within normal limits.  

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic mass with a clear boundary and regular shape in the second hilar region; the lesion contained hyperintense echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing, suggestive of dense calcifications, and no internal blood flow signal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-circumscribed, round solid lesion with punctate central calcification and no enhancement on venous-phase imaging. On T1- and T2-weighted MRI, the mass appeared distinctly hypointense—comparable to muscle—and failed to enhance after gadolinium administration.
title: Peritoneal loose body presenting as a hepatic mass: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
An 84-year-old man presented with two weeks of right upper-quadrant abdominal pain associated with non-projectile coffee-ground vomiting, melena, and weight loss. He denied fever, abdominal distention, or constipation. An initial ultrasound suggested an intrahepatic mass. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C and HIV were negative.

On examination, the patient was weak, emaciated, pale, and icteric, with bilateral lower-limb edema. He had a history of moderate alcohol use but no known tuberculosis exposure or prior TB infection. Vital signs were within normal limits. The abdomen was soft with tenderness in the right upper quadrant; there was no hepatosplenomegaly and normal bowel sounds.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 110 mm/h, hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL, total bilirubin 108 μmol/L (direct bilirubin 34.8 μmol/L), ALT 44 I/U, and AST 81 I/U. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed mildly dilated intrahepatic bile ducts, common hepatic duct, and common bile duct (1.3 cm) with an abrupt cutoff at the ampulla of Vater, suggestive of ampullary vs. peri-ampullary obstruction. The gallbladder was dilated with asymmetrical wall thickening and a contained anterior wall perforation; no gallstones were seen.

These findings were interpreted as mild biliary obstruction secondary to ampullary obstruction with contained perforated acalculous cholecystitis. A presumptive diagnosis of gallbladder or cholangiocarcinoma was made, and the patient was taken to surgery. Intraoperatively, the gallbladder and surrounding tissues were grossly inflamed; the fundus and body of the gallbladder appeared necrotic with marked wall edema. No mass was palpable at the pancreatic head. A subtotal cholecystectomy sparing the neck was performed, and reconstruction was via a Roux-en-Y cholecystojejunostomy. The excised gallbladder tissue was submitted for histopathological examination.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Isolated gallbladder tuberculosis in an 84-year old man: A rare case report

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old man presented with 1 week of high-grade fever, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia of both knees and ankles. On day 4 of illness, he developed redness and pain in both eyes without vision loss or neurologic symptoms. He denied recent travel, unpasteurized milk consumption, or similar illnesses in contacts; he did have a pet dog.

On examination, temperature was 102°F, pulse 112/min, and discrete non-tender axillary lymph nodes were palpable bilaterally. A purpuric rash involved the trunk and distal extremities including palms and soles. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral non-granulomatous anterior uveitis. Funduscopic findings included multiple hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, Roth’s spots, and disc edema in both eyes. There was no eschar, murmur, or neck stiffness.

Initial laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 66×10^3/μL and elevated liver transaminases (AST 267 IU/L, ALT 316 IU/L). Workup for infective endocarditis—including multiple blood cultures and transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography—was negative. Malarial smears, dengue serology, scrub typhus serology, leptospira serology, and HIV ELISA were all negative.
journal: Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care
title: Spotted fever rickettsiosis presenting with bilateral anterior uveitis and retinitis: A case report

case_prompt: A 26-year-old man presented with a one-year history of constant pain in his left hindfoot after an ankle injury. Initially managed with oral analgesics, he experienced only transient relief. Over the past year, he noted progressive pain and swelling localized to the left calcaneal region. MRI of the left ankle showed high STIR signal within the calcaneus consistent with marrow edema, minimal surrounding soft-tissue edema, and no associated mass, periosteal reaction, or fluid collection; the findings were interpreted as inflammatory change. He was diagnosed with atypical rheumatoid arthritis and treated with steroids and analgesics, but his symptoms remained unremitting, and he continued to limp with pain. On examination, there was local swelling with mild to moderate tenderness over the calcaneus, without overlying skin discoloration, and full ankle joint motion.
journal: JNMA: Journal of the Nepal Medical Association
title: Solitary Plasmacytoma of the Calcaneum: A Case Report

case_prompt:
An 8-day-old full-term neonate presented with increased respiratory rate and bluish discoloration of the nails and lips. Antenatal scans had revealed a right atrial mass. There was no family history of congenital heart disease or atrial myxoma, and no maternal drug exposures other than routine supplementation.

On day 2 of life, transthoracic echocardiography showed a heterogeneous, pedunculated right atrial mass (10 × 8 mm) attached to the interatrial septum, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and a peak right ventricular systolic pressure of 61 mmHg (suggestive of severe pulmonary hypertension). Echocardiographic screening of family members was normal.

On day 8, the neonate was tachypneic and mildly cyanotic (SpO₂ 84% on room air). Cardiovascular examination revealed an ejection systolic murmur and a loud P₂. Chest radiography showed pulmonary plethora and mild cardiomegaly. Repeat transthoracic echocardiography identified a 10 × 9 mm right atrial mass attached at the atrioventricular junction of the interatrial septum, a restrictive atrial septal defect with right-to-left shunt, dilated pulmonary arteries, and severe pulmonary hypertension. Two right-sided pulmonary veins formed a common chamber draining into the superior vena cava, and one right pulmonary vein drained directly into the superior vena cava. 

Computed tomography confirmed that the right superior and right inferior pulmonary veins formed a common chamber draining to the superior vena cava, and that the left pulmonary veins joined to form a common vein that coursed infradiaphragmatically to the portal vein. A diagnosis of right atrial mass with mixed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection and severe pulmonary hypertension was made, and surgical intervention was planned.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Case Report-Right atrial myxoma with total anomalous pulmonary venous connection in neonate

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of holocranial, throbbing headache that was nearly continuous and worsened with coughing, disturbing his sleep. Over the preceding month, he noted progressive unsteadiness of gait without falls, and during the week before presentation he had recurrent vomiting. He denied visual obscurations or diplopia and had no upper-limb incoordination. He had a remote history of childhood febrile seizures without recurrence and no other medical history of note.

On examination, he was afebrile. Fundoscopic evaluation revealed early papilledema. Extraocular movements were full. Coordination testing showed bilateral finger–nose and heel–knee incoordination with dysdiadochokinesia. His gait was spastic–ataxic. Strength, sensation, and reflexes were otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver and renal function tests, serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, chest radiography, and abdominal ultrasound, were all within normal limits. HIV-1 and HIV-2 serological tests were negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated multiple bilateral cerebral cystic lesions and a large right cerebellar cyst exerting mass effect on the fourth ventricle and brainstem. Diffuse T2-weighted hyperintense lesions were present in the subcortical and cerebellar white matter. The cystic lesions showed contrast enhancement without evidence of hemorrhage.

Lumbar puncture yielded slightly xanthochromic cerebrospinal fluid containing 26 leukocytes (45% polymorphonuclear, 55% lymphocytes), protein of 106 mg/dL, and glucose of 149 mg/dL. CSF cryptococcal antigen was negative.
journal: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology
title: Leukoencephalopathy with intracranial calcifications and cysts in an adult: Case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 42-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of asthenia. She denied fever or lymphadenopathy. On examination, she had hepatosplenomegaly without other abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 16 g/dL, platelets 480 000/µL, AST 55 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, total bilirubin 2 mg/dL, and LDH 300 U/L; serum electrolytes were normal. A bone marrow biopsy revealed a myeloproliferative disorder. An abdominal ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly and portal vein thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a mass encircling the common bile duct and compressing it, with enhancement only during the portal venous phase; hepatosplenomegaly, a portosystemic shunt, and a hepatic perfusion defect were also noted. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed a sleeve of tissue around the common bile duct at the hepatic pedicle with intermediate T2 signal, no arterial enhancement, and intense, homogeneous portal-phase enhancement causing compression of the duct.
title: Pseudotumoral portal cavernoma: A rare case that challenges diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman with a history of severe alcoholic hepatitis complicated by grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy was readmitted less than 24 hours after discharge following a witnessed tonic–clonic seizure. She had no prior history of seizures and reported strict abstinence from alcohol and nonprescription drugs since her last hospitalization, with documented compliance with lactulose and rifaximin. 

On arrival, her temperature was 97.2°F, pulse 95/min, respiratory rate 8/min, and blood pressure 114/78 mmHg. Off sedation, she had no focal neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, INR 1.79, creatinine 0.3 mg/dL, total bilirubin 10.8 mg/dL, ALT 54 IU/L, AST 112 IU/L, bicarbonate 15.5 mmol/L, anion gap 21 mEq/L, unchanged from prior discharge. Urine toxicology was negative, and blood alcohol level was undetectable.

A brain MRI performed while the patient remained postictal showed high signal intensity in the subcortical and periventricular white matter of the bilateral temporal and parietal lobes on FLAIR images, similar in distribution to a limited prior study. A 60-minute EEG revealed high focal epileptogenic potential in the same temporal-parietal regions.
title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in alcoholic hepatitis: Hepatic encephalopathy a common theme

case_prompt: A 50-year-old multiparous, postmenopausal woman presented with a one-month history of burning micturition. Her blood pressure was 140/96 mmHg and pulse 76 beats/minute. Vaginal examination revealed an 8 cm × 8 cm cystic mass in the anterior fornix. Urinalysis showed pus cells; other laboratory studies were unremarkable. Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined, thick-walled cystic mass measuring 7.6 cm × 6.8 cm in the left adnexa with a few incomplete septa; the left ovary was not seen separately, and no free fluid was present. The findings were interpreted as suggesting an ovarian neoplastic mass. At exploratory laparotomy, the uterus and both ovaries were atrophic; an 8 cm × 6 cm cystic mass was identified in the left broad ligament and excised. Frozen section revealed a cyst wall lined by sheets of tumor cells with eccentric vesicular nuclei and moderate eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, and a diagnosis of sex cord–stromal tumor was rendered. Complete excision of the lesion was performed, and omental biopsy and peritoneal fluid were obtained.
title: An Unusual Case of Paraganglioma of the Broad Ligament Presenting as Cystic Mass

case_prompt: A 41-year-old woman with a history of asthma and gastroesophageal reflux disease presented with 2–3 days of a choking sensation and shortness of breath and 4 months of gradually worsening voice changes with aspiration of thin liquids. She had no history of tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she had inspiratory stridor but normal oxygen saturation on room air. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy revealed a large, pink, pedunculated ball-valving polypoid lesion arising from the anterior glottic commissure, obstructing approximately 75% of the airway. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck demonstrated a well-defined, partially enhancing 1.5-cm soft-tissue mass at the anterior commissure with moderate compromise of the laryngeal lumen. The patient was admitted for continuous respiratory and pulse oximetry monitoring, and definitive management was planned.
title: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor of the larynx: Case report

case_prompt: A 53-year-old man was referred after an asymptomatic radiolucent lesion was noted in the right maxilla during routine dental planning. He had normal overlying mucosa and slight buccal cortical plate swelling in the edentulous region of the upper right premolars. The upper right canine, premolars, and molars had been extracted about 10 years earlier, and a partial removable appliance was in place. Panoramic and periapical radiographs revealed a 1.0 cm well-defined, round, unilocular radiolucency in the edentulous premolar area, adjacent to the superficial cortical bone. The lesion was at the level of the apical third of the remaining upper right lateral incisor, with areas suggestive of cortical fenestration due to ridge resorption. Provisional clinical diagnoses included a residual cyst and an odontogenic keratocyst, and the patient was scheduled for surgical removal of the lesion.
journal: Journal of Clinical and Experimental Dentistry
title: Lateral periodontal cyst: A rare clinicopathological presentation mimicking a residual cyst

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old Asian woman with a history of stage IIB right upper lobe lung adenocarcinoma underwent video-assisted thoracic surgery, followed by adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy complicated by neutropenia and dysesthesia. Ten weeks after completing platinum-based chemotherapy, she began adjuvant atezolizumab. There was no personal or family history of cardiac disease; baseline cardiac function was normal.

She was observed inpatient during the first cycle of atezolizumab (day 1–8) without issues. On day 9 she developed persistent fever (to 38 °C) and by day 13 she presented with a temperature of 40.3 °C, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, pulse 116 bpm, WBC 4300/µL (lymphocytes 18.5%), AST 23 U/L, ALT 27 U/L, and CRP 4.76 mg/dL. Chest radiography was normal. CT of the neck showed an enlarged, tender right cervical lymph node, and subacute necrotizing lymphadenitis was diagnosed.

On day 16 she developed dyspnea on exertion, progressing to dyspnea at rest on day 17. Chest radiograph then demonstrated pulmonary congestion. Systolic blood pressure fell below 90 mmHg, consistent with shock, and she was admitted to the ICU. Laboratory tests showed AST 86 U/L, ALT 53 U/L, LDH 566 U/L, and troponin I 538.8 pg/mL. Electrocardiography revealed a sinus tachycardia at 125 bpm. Transthoracic echocardiography showed circumferential wall hypokinesia and pericardial effusion. Right‐ and left‐sided cardiac catheterization revealed a cardiac index of 2.05 L/min/m2 and right ventricular pressure of 35 mmHg. Coronary angiography was performed.
title: Fulminant myocarditis during postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy for lung cancer with atezolizumab: a case report

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old white man with a history of severe Parkinson’s disease with profound motor impairment and mild cognitive impairment was referred by neurology and psychiatry for progressive vision loss that interfered with his daily activities.

He reported daily visual phenomena, including seeing a little girl playing with blocks, a cat at his window, and men dismantling his neighbor’s roof, which he recognized as unreal. These experiences were distressing and impaired his ability to perform household tasks and engage with family.

Despite recent pharmacologic adjustments for presumed Parkinson’s disease–related psychosis—including titration of quetiapine to 300 mg twice daily over 3 weeks, addition of pimavanserin 34 mg daily for 3 weeks, reduction of carbidopa–levodopa dosage, and initiation of clozapine (increased to 150 mg twice daily over 3 weeks)—his visual disturbances persisted.

On ophthalmic examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination showed mild corneal guttae bilaterally, well–positioned posterior chamber intraocular lenses bilaterally, and visually significant posterior capsular opacification in both eyes. The anterior and posterior segments were otherwise unremarkable.
title: Charles Bonnet Syndrome in a Patient with Parkinson’s Disease and Bilateral Posterior Capsule Opacification

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old Bangladeshi woman with a 2-month history of polyarthralgia, photosensitive rash, intermittent fever, oral ulcers, and alopecia presented with sudden, progressive, painless vision loss in both eyes and progressive weakness of both lower limbs over 48 hours. She denied headaches, seizures, bowel or bladder dysfunction, Raynaud’s phenomenon, or trauma. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. She had a malar rash, oral ulceration, alopecia, and swollen tender wrist joints. Visual acuity was reduced to hand movements bilaterally; light projection was intact, the direct pupillary reflex was sluggish, and the consensual reflex was normal. Intraocular pressure was 15 mmHg in both eyes. Fundoscopy showed bilateral pale, swollen optic discs with a superotemporal flame-shaped hemorrhage in the right optic disc. 

Neurologic examination revealed bilateral upper motor neuron–type weakness in the lower limbs (muscle power reduced with brisk knee and ankle reflexes and extensor plantar responses) and sensory loss to pain, temperature, and joint position up to the T8 level. Other systemic findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normocytic normochromic anemia, strongly positive ANA (homogeneous), high-titer anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, low complement levels (C3, C4), and positive anti–aquaporin-4 IgG antibody. Cerebrospinal fluid was normal, with absent oligoclonal bands. 

MRI of the spine with contrast revealed multiple enhancing T2-weighted hyperintense lesions in the cervical and dorsal cord extending over more than three vertebral segments with diffuse cord edema; MRI of the brain and orbits was unremarkable.
title: Systemic lupus erythematosus with acute ischemic optic neuropathy complicated with neuromyelitis optica: a case report

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man presented with 2 months of progressive left hip pain and, over the preceding 2 weeks, increasing difficulty with mobilization. His general practitioner obtained a noncontrast CT of the pelvis, which revealed a cystic lesion within the left psoas muscle containing areas of coarse calcification; the findings were thought to be suspicious for a tumor, likely a teratoma. A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed that the lesion in the left psoas muscle extended from a heavily calcified pancreas, coursing over the anterior aspects of the aorta and inferior vena cava before reaching the psoas muscle. Multiple other cystic areas were noted in the pancreatic parenchyma and peripancreatic tissues.

On examination in the emergency department, the patient lay supine with his left hip externally rotated and left knee moderately flexed. He had an antalgic gait and pain on weight bearing and active movement of the left hip, especially resisted hip flexion. There was no abdominal tenderness. 

Blood tests, including inflammatory markers and serum lipase, were within normal limits, with no evidence of acute pancreatitis. His medical history was notable for a single episode of alcohol-induced acute pancreatitis 10 years earlier and occasional mild postprandial epigastric pain. He consumed 6–8 standard drinks of alcohol per day.
title: A case of pancreatic pseudocyst as a rare cause of a cystic lesion within the psoas muscle

case_prompt: A 32-year-old man noted a right mid-abdominal mass for 1 month, associated with intermittent pain but no fever, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. He presented after sudden severe abdominal pain. On examination, vital signs were stable; the abdomen was soft without palpable lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Abdominal CT revealed an 8.5×7.4×4 cm mass at the jejunoileal junction involving the adjacent intestinal wall and mesenteric fat; the colon and rectum were normal, and there was no enlargement of mesenteric or mediastinal lymph nodes; the liver and spleen appeared normal. Laboratory studies showed negative serum tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA125, SCC antigen, CA19-9) and a normal complete blood count, including white cells (5.42×10^9/L), lymphocytes (1.5×10^9/L), hemoglobin (142 g/L), and platelets (350×10^9/L).
title: Primary rare anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK positive in small intestine: case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 55-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, seizures, and hypertension was admitted after a witnessed seizure and fall, during which she lay immobile on the floor for several hours. Her outpatient medications were valproic acid, aspirin, amlodipine, metformin, and a multivitamin. On examination she appeared frail; cardiac and neurologic findings were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a creatine kinase level of 22 000 U/L, a serum creatinine level of 5 mg/dL, and a hemoglobin level of 9.8 g/dL. She was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure, anemia, and uncontrolled epilepsy, and was treated with intravenous hydration, with gradual improvement in renal and muscle markers. On hospital day 10, she developed dysphagia and odynophagia to solids and liquids, accompanied by upper chest pain and discomfort. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed plaque-like whitish material with linear streaking throughout the esophagus, without strictures, ulcers, or masses. Biopsy specimens showed an intraepithelial vesicular area, raising the possibility of esophageal pemphigus.
journal: International Journal of Biomedical Science : IJBS
title: Sloughing Esophagitis: A Not So Common Entity

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old Caucasian man was admitted to a psychiatric ward for severe depression and alcohol misuse. He had abstained from alcohol for 2 weeks prior, was a non-smoker with no recreational drug use, and had no past medical history. Seven weeks before admission, he had started sertraline 100 mg daily; he took no other regular medications. Twelve days into his admission, he developed a dry cough, dyspnea, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. He was hypoxic (SpO₂ 85% on room air, falling to 76% on exertion), tachycardic (106 bpm), and febrile (38.1 °C); blood pressure and respiratory rate were normal. Auscultation revealed reduced air entry bilaterally with bibasal crepitations. 

An urgent chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral air-space opacification. Intravenous antibiotics were started, but there was no clinical improvement over 48 hours. Screening for infection—including blood cultures, sputum culture, urinary Legionella and pneumococcal antigens, and respiratory PCR tests (including SARS-CoV-2)—was negative. Viral serologies and immunologic tests (immunoglobulins, ANA, avian and Aspergillus precipitins) were unremarkable. 

A CT pulmonary angiogram revealed no pulmonary embolism but showed bilateral widespread ground-glass attenuation, interlobular septal thickening, small pleural effusions, and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy.
title: Sertraline as a rare cause of interstitial lung disease

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old primigravida at 37 weeks’ gestation was referred for evaluation of a placental mass noted on prenatal sonography. First-trimester aneuploidy screening was low-risk with normal nuchal translucency; maternal PAPPA was 0.99 MoM and beta-hCG 1.46 MoM. She had been briefly treated for mild diastolic blood-pressure elevations with methyldopa and aspirin but self-reported normal pressures thereafter. 

At the mid-trimester anatomy scan, a 54-mm cystic placental lesion with multiple septations and internal echoes was reported; the patient then missed follow-up until 33 weeks, when ultrasound showed a 70×76-mm cystic structure with septations and calcifications on the fetal surface near the cord insertion (no Doppler assessment documented). Fetal echocardiography revealed septal hypertrophy >6 mm and mild ventricular discrepancy.

At 37 weeks, ultrasound estimated fetal weight at 2930 g, amniotic-fluid index 10 cm, and the complex placental mass measured 91×87 mm. Color Doppler revealed a small feeding vessel with low-resistance, pulsatile indices. Middle cerebral-artery peak systolic velocity was 68.9 cm/s (1–1.3 MoM); umbilical-artery Dopplers were normal; fetal four-chamber view again showed mild septal hypertrophy. 

According to the characteristics of the tumor on sonography, two main differential diagnoses were chorioangioma and, less probably, placental teratoma, and not just a simple placental cyst.
title: A giant early second‐trimester placental chorioangioma associated with isolated proteinuria and histopathologically confirmed placental insufficiency, a novel association: A case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman presented with a 7-month history of intermittent bright red rectal bleeding associated with constipation and perianal pain. She had no weight loss or abdominal pain and no significant medical history. Family history was notable only for a benign colonic polyp in her mother and various cancers in grandparents. Physical examination was unremarkable, and flexible sigmoidoscopy revealed a sessile malignant‐appearing polyp in the lower rectum. Pelvic MRI staged the lesion as T3 N0 M0, and biopsy confirmed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. She received long-course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy with oral capecitabine, with only transient angina-like chest pain. Restaging MRI showed tumor downstaging to T2, and she underwent laparoscopic ultra–low anterior resection with defunctioning loop ileostomy; pathology demonstrated a complete response (pT0 pN0 R0). 

At 3 months postoperatively, surveillance CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis identified four new subcapsular wedge‐shaped low‐attenuation lesions in the liver, reported as suspicious for metastases. Liver‐specific contrast–enhanced MRI (Primovist) showed four corresponding foci of low T1 signal, none of which were of high T2 signal or exhibited hepatic steatosis; postcontrast images demonstrated minimal arterial enhancement, no rim enhancement, and low signal on the delayed hepatobiliary phase. A subsequent PET–CT scan showed no FDG‐avid liver lesions or extrahepatic disease. The lesions were not visible on ultrasound, and the multidisciplinary team agreed to perform a CT‐guided core biopsy of the most accessible lesion.
title: Capecitabine‐related liver lesions: sinusoidal dilatation mimicking liver metastasis

case_prompt: A 54-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of fever, dry cough, and fatigue unresponsive to outpatient antibiotics. On admission, crepitant rales were heard in both lungs. Laboratory tests revealed anemia, thrombocytopenia, and a peripheral smear showing 50–60% myeloid blasts. Bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry confirmed acute myeloid leukemia arising from myelodysplastic syndrome. Her history included treated left breast cancer and type 2 diabetes. A PET/CT scan showed a heterogeneous, FDG-avid mass in the left upper-lobe apicoposterior segment, measuring 72 × 63 mm. Given the radiographic appearance, tuberculosis was initially favored but primary lung malignancy could not be excluded. A tru-cut biopsy of the lesion was obtained. Microbiologic studies for tuberculosis, including culture and adenosine deaminase, were negative. Six days after biopsy, a throat swab tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR. Repeat CT demonstrated partial regression of the mass-like lesion in the left upper lobe and new multifocal ground-glass opacities and irregular nodular consolidations with air bronchograms in the bilateral lower lobes. These radiologic findings were interpreted as progression of COVID-19 pneumonia.
title: Granulomatous inflammation in pulmonary pathology of 2019 novel coronavirus pneumonia: case report with a literature review

case_prompt: A 35-year-old woman with a history of chronic constipation was referred for evaluation of intermittent rectal bleeding and anemia. On digital rectal examination, a rectal mass was palpated. Ileocolonoscopy showed multiple polypoid lesions in the middle and lower rectum and several large polyps at the anorectal junction prolapsing through the anal canal. Biopsies of these lesions demonstrated inflammatory pseudopolyps, absence of malignancy, and a focal positive immunohistochemical stain for cytomegalovirus (CMV). Serologic testing revealed CMV IgG positivity and IgM negativity. She received intravenous ganciclovir without symptomatic improvement. Laboratory studies showed severe anemia and hypoalbuminemia; electrolytes, liver enzymes, immunoglobulins, complement levels, autoantibodies, fecal calprotectin, inflammatory markers, and tumor markers were all within reference ranges. Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, HIV, Treponema pallidum, and hepatitis B and C was negative. An abdominal and pelvic CT scan revealed only a thickened rectal wall. Upper endoscopy was normal, but gastric biopsies were positive for Helicobacter pylori; eradication therapy was given and a subsequent urea breath test was negative. Four months later, repeat colonoscopy showed ulcerated proctitis without malignancy or evidence of CMV or other pathogens. The patient’s condition worsened with frequent rectal bleeding, ongoing anemia requiring transfusion, and persistent hypoalbuminemia. It was then decided to perform endoscopic mucosectomy of the rectal polyps and transanal excision of the anal canal lesions.
title: Cap Polyposis—A Rare Cause of Rectal Bleeding in a Young Woman

case_prompt: A 50-year-old man presented with a one-week history of progressive visual loss in his right eye. He had no significant medical or infectious history. On examination, visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Pupils were round and reactive bilaterally, and extraocular movements were full. Optical coherence tomography of the macula was normal in both eyes. Intraocular pressure measured by tonometry was 27 mm Hg in the right eye and 19 mm Hg in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a yellowish mass involving the iris and covering the iridocorneal angle between the 5 o’clock and 6 o’clock positions; there was prominent tumor vascularization, cells and fibrin in the anterior chamber, and a mild hyposphagma. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated infiltration of the iris by the lesion, with no extension into the vitreous cavity.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Intraocular juvenile xanthogranuloma of the iris in an adult patient

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of a solitary small red swelling below her right lower eyelid that had been gradually increasing in size. She reported occasional throbbing pain and sweating over the lesion, both of which were aggravated by physical exertion and emotional stress. She denied any history of trauma, systemic symptoms, or similar family illnesses. 

On examination, there was a solitary, irregular, erythematous, soft, slightly elevated plaque measuring approximately 3 × 2 cm just below the right lower eyelid. The surface was smooth and moist. The lesion was mildly tender on palpation. Beaded drops of sweat were observed on the surface with mild stroking and after physical exertion. No pulsation or bruit was noted. 

Color Doppler ultrasonography of the lesion showed mild to moderate vascularization in the deep dermis.
title: Eccrine Angiomatous Hamartoma: Late Onset Facial Presentation

case_prompt:
A man in his early 60s presented with a 1.5-month history of a painful ulcer on the left edge of his tongue that had not responded to topical steroids. His medical history included type 2 diabetes managed with ipragliflozin, and he had a 37-year history of heavy cigarette smoking, now switched to e-cigarettes. He did not consume alcohol. 

On examination, he was well-nourished. Facial asymmetry was noted due to left submental swelling without facial nerve deficits. Palpation revealed multiple elastic, firm, mobile lymph nodes in the left submandibular region (one ~tip-of-index-finger size, tender; two ~soybean size, non-tender) and a tender node of similar size in the right submental area. The tongue lesion measured 23 × 14 mm on the ventral surface near the floor of the mouth, with indurated and hemorrhagic surrounding tissue.

Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 122 g/L), elevated γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (142 U/L), hyperglycemia (blood glucose 8.6 mmol/L), elevated C-reactive protein (50.1 mg/L), and HbA₁c of 68 mmol/mol.

Panoramic radiography demonstrated vertical bone resorption mesial to the left mandibular second molar and multiple dental caries without other bony lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT showed no destructive change in the tongue or mandible, but bilateral submandibular and upper internal jugular lymphadenopathy (minor axis 2–19 mm) without rim enhancement. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed an enhancing area from the left tongue margin to the mylohyoid muscle, with variably swollen lymph nodes exhibiting heterogeneous interiors and rim enhancement. ¹⁸F-FDG PET showed mild uptake in the left tongue margin (SUVmax 3.6) and bilateral submandibular nodes (SUVmax 2.8–5.2) with no other abnormal foci.

Based on these clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings, the tongue lesion was thought to be tongue cancer with cervical lymph node metastases (T2N2cM0).
journal: The Journal of International Medical Research
title:
Primary syphilis with a tongue ulcer mimicking tongue cancer: a case
report

case_prompt:
A 2-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department with convulsions and an abnormal, high-pitched cry. His mother reported three days of non-bloody diarrhoea without vomiting, fever, rash, cough, or respiratory distress. He was exclusively breastfed and feeding well until the diarrhoea began. Earlier that morning (~2 hours before arrival), a community practitioner had administered single doses of simethicone and nalidixic acid suspension, prescribed at 55 mg/kg/day (undivided).

The infant was born at term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery and had normal development. There was no family history of seizures.

On examination, he was mildly dehydrated with tachypnoea, grunting, and signs of acidotic breathing. The anterior fontanelle was subtly bulging. He was somnolent, with gaze deviated to the left, pupils 1 mm and sluggish, intermittent lip puckering, rhythmic jerking of the right arm and leg, and periodic stiffening of all limbs. Intravenous diazepam (0.2 mg/kg) terminated two successive seizures.

Initial laboratory studies revealed a mixed anion-gap and non–anion-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis on venous blood gas and an elevated white-cell count.
title: Seizure activity and anion gap metabolic acidosis secondary to adverse effect of nalidixic acid—a case report

case_prompt: A 55-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a three-week history of productive cough, dyspnea, chest pain, and unintentional weight loss. Her medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, dyslipidemia, chronic renal failure, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and chronic anemia. She had a 30 pack-year smoking history. Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed a large subcarinal mass. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a 6.2 × 5.0 cm well-circumscribed lesion in the subcarinal space. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy demonstrated suspicious malignant cells without definitive classification. A positron-emission tomography scan showed a hypermetabolic subcarinal mass with a standardized uptake value of 14.3. The differential diagnosis included an infected bronchogenic cyst, an esophageal duplication cyst, and a malignant subcarinal lymph node. Thoracoscopic surgical resection was planned for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Preoperative esophagoscopy and bronchoscopy confirmed the absence of any communication between the mass and the esophagus or airways.
title: Rare case of subcarinal thymic carcinoma in the middle mediastinum

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old man presented with right flank pain that progressed over two days to severe back pain, bilateral flank pain, scrotal pain, and bilateral thigh pain. He had no significant medical history. Analgesics administered at a local health center relieved his back pain, but his testicular and thigh pain worsened.  
On examination, blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, pulse 130 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and temperature 37°C. The leg-raising test was negative, and the neurovascular status of both legs was intact. Scrotal examination was unremarkable; both the cremasteric reflex and Prehn's sign were negative. There was no edema or swelling of the lower limbs.  
Laboratory studies showed a D-dimer level of 17 mg/L (normal, 0–0.49 mg/L), creatinine 124 µmol/L (normal, 64–110 µmol/L), white blood cell count 10×10^3/L (normal, 4–10×10^3/L), and C-reactive protein 5 mg/L (normal, 0–5 mg/L). Prothrombin time was 13.8 seconds (normal, 9.4–12.5 seconds), with normal APTT (28.4 seconds) and INR (1.1). Urinalysis was positive for blood.  
Bedside abdominal ultrasound showed no significant abnormalities. Doppler ultrasound of both legs revealed deep vein thrombosis extending from the external iliac veins to the distal veins of both legs. Computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a large thrombus in the distal inferior vena cava extending to the renal artery and both external and internal iliac veins, with no evidence of renal calculi or other abdominal pathology.
title: Inferior Vena Cava Thrombosis in a Patient with Factor V Leiden Syndrome Presenting with Scrotal Pain

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left breast mass that had enlarged progressively. She first noted a 20 mm mass in her left breast at age 21, which was diagnosed as benign and observed for 6 years. During her pregnancy at age 28, the mass grew rapidly to approximately 70 mm. On examination, a circumscribed, painless 70 mm mass was palpated in the left upper outer quadrant without overlying skin changes or dimpling. She had no medications, allergies, or family history of breast disease; she did not smoke and drank alcohol only occasionally.

Mammography demonstrated a 62 × 42 mm, equal-density, lobular mass in the upper-outer quadrant of the left breast. Ultrasonography showed a circumscribed, hypoechoic lobular mass with cystic regions measuring 61 × 57 × 34 mm in the same location. Breast MRI revealed an approximately 65 mm mass with both solid and cystic components and contrast enhancement in the upper-outer left breast.

Because of concern for malignancy, a core needle biopsy was performed, and the lesion was diagnosed as adenosis. The patient discontinued breastfeeding and was treated with cabergoline for two months; however, the mass did not decrease in size. Although the biopsy showed adenosis, the sample represented only a portion of the mass, and malignancy could not be ruled out completely.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Surgical excision of a lactating adenoma with rapid enlargement: A case report

case_prompt: A 35-year-old man presented for follow-up with a complaint of a sensation of something moving in the anterior aspect of his right knee. He had no pain or swelling. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, mobile mass palpable medial to the patellar ligament on the anterior knee. Standard radiographs of the knee showed two radio-opaque loose bodies: one immediately anterior to the patellar ligament and another within the suprapatellar pouch. Four years earlier, he had undergone extended curettage and polymethylmethacrylate cementing for a Campanacci grade 1 giant cell tumor of the right distal femur. He had an uneventful recovery, returned to full activity, and had no clinical or radiological evidence of tumor recurrence at the distal femur.
title: Giant Cell Tumor as a Rare Cause of Loose Bodies in the Knee Joint – A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old previously healthy Caucasian female presented with 20 days of left pleuritic chest pain. She reported fever to 38 °C at symptom onset but denied weight loss, night sweats, cough, or other systemic symptoms. She was treated sequentially with clarithromycin plus levofloxacin and then amoxicillin–clavulanate; fever resolved but pain persisted. 

On admission, she appeared well and was afebrile. Vital signs were normal. Examination revealed decreased breath sounds at the left base and percussion dullness in Traube’s space; there was no lymphadenopathy, edema, or palpable organomegaly. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits; HIV and hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. 

Chest radiography showed a well-circumscribed homogeneous round opacity with a broad pleural base in the left lower lobe. Thoracic CT confirmed a heterogeneous-attenuation nodular lesion in the left lower lobe and also demonstrated splenomegaly. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable, and bronchoalveolar lavage did not demonstrate acid-fast bacilli, fungi, or bacteria.
title: Pulmonary cryptococcoma: a rare and challenging diagnosis in immunocompetent patients

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old man presented in 2017 with recurrent episodes of dry, painful swelling of the right eye. CT imaging showed enlargement of the right lacrimal gland and increased size of the right lateral rectus muscle. He underwent right orbitotomy, posterior lateral rectus muscle biopsy, dacryoadenectomy, and temporal tarsorrhaphy. Grossly, the lacrimal gland was firm. Histopathology demonstrated intraglandular follicular lymphoid hyperplasia and intramuscular follicular lymphoid hyperplasia, with no phenotypically abnormal lymphocytes on flow cytometric analysis. 

His medical history included eosinophilic esophagitis and malignant hypertension managed with multiple antihypertensive agents. He denied weight loss, night sweats, or fevers. Over the subsequent two years, he received multiple courses of oral steroids of varying doses and durations, which were poorly tolerated due to his hypertension. 

In 2019, he experienced worsening flares with 10/10 ocular pain, new-onset diplopia, and severe palpebral edema (“so bad I can’t open my eye”). Examination revealed mild right proptosis, right ptosis, evoked diplopia with inability to fully medialize the right globe, and incomplete conjugate gaze at extreme fields; visual acuity remained normal. Repeat CT did not show new findings. Blood tests were negative for EBV, HIV, and CMV, and quantitative immunoglobulins (G, M, A) were within normal limits. 

Given this constellation of findings and history, a request was made for IgG4 immunostaining of the previous orbital biopsy specimens.
title: Image-Guided Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy for IgG4-Related Ophthalmic Disease

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of dull left chest pain and progressive dyspnea (MRC Grade III). He also reported a productive cough without hemoptysis. He was a non-smoker with no known environmental or occupational exposures.

On examination, his body mass index was 20 kg/m2. There was no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Chest-wall excursion and breath sounds were diminished over the left hemithorax.

A chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity in the lower left hemithorax obliterating the left cardiac border with rightward mediastinal shift. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a large, well-defined, heterogeneous mass in the anterior mediastinum with central areas of necrosis, abutting but not infiltrating the chest wall, and without mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Routine blood tests, including serum cortisol, were within normal limits. Fibreoptic bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial lesions. Bronchial washings, brushings and transbronchial needle aspiration were non-diagnostic. A CT-guided transthoracic tru-cut biopsy showed small round tumor cells, but a definitive histologic diagnosis could not be made.
journal: Nigerian Medical Journal : Journal of the Nigeria Medical Association
title: Primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of the thymus

case_prompt: An 82-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a progressive rash. She had been admitted two months earlier for acute pancreatitis; during treatment, erythema appeared over her trunk and extremities. Although her pancreatitis resolved, the rash worsened. On examination, there were multiple erythematous blisters and erosions on the extremities and trunk. Laboratory studies showed no inflammatory response; tumor markers and collagen‐disease markers, including antinuclear antibodies, were within normal limits. Trace elements (zinc) and essential fatty acids were normal, and glucagon levels were normal. Two skin biopsies were performed; autoimmune bullous diseases, such as pemphigus, were negative, and the subcutaneous adipose tissue showed no abnormalities. No source of infection was found, and infectious, drug‐related, and collagen‐disease causes were ruled out. Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated dilatation of the main pancreatic duct and a multifocal cystic mass in the pancreatic body. MRI confirmed main duct dilatation and a septated cystic lesion in the head–body region. Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a 6-mm mural nodule in the main pancreatic duct with contrast enhancement, suggestive of a mixed-type intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm with high-risk stigmata. Despite topical therapies, systemic steroids, immunosuppressants, nutritional supplementation, and immunoglobulin therapy, the rash continued to worsen, and oral involvement impaired intake, causing fatigue and weight loss.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Total pancreatectomy in a patient with a dermadrome caused by intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm: A case report

case_prompt:
A 2-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of an anechoic formation in the right lower abdomen detected on prenatal ultrasound. There was no history of acute illness or trauma. On admission, vital signs were normal and the patient was afebrile. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests, were within reference ranges. 

Postnatal abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 34×23 mm cystic formation in the right lower quadrant with parietal stratification of three alternating hyper- and hypoechoic layers (“gut sign”) and an internal septum separating a round from a tubular component.

To further characterize the lesion and aid in surgical planning, an abdominal MRI was obtained under sedation. MRI showed a 50×34×30 mm cystic lesion in the right lower abdomen with simple fluid signal (hyperintense on T2, hypointense on T1), an internal septum between tubular and round portions, and no obvious communication with the gastrointestinal tract. There were no vertebral or other anomalies.
