title: An ileal duplication cyst case report: From diagnosis to treatment

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old girl was evaluated for several weeks of dry cough that failed to improve with over-the-counter cold remedies, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and azithromycin. Two years earlier she had been treated for lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis without a clear diagnosis; at that time, physical examination, blood chemistry, bone marrow biopsy, and abdominal ultrasound were normal, but peripheral blood flow cytometry showed more than 85% mature T-lymphocytes. Hydroxyurea was discontinued after 18 months because of lack of efficacy.

On examination now, she weighed 14 kg (−3 SD) and measured 110 cm (−1 SD). Heart and lung sounds were absent over the left hemithorax; percussion was dull on the left and resonant on the right. The left chest was visibly bulging. There was no respiratory distress or cyanosis. Vital signs: respiratory rate 32/min, heart rate 93/min, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 92% on room air.

Complete blood count again demonstrated severe lymphocytosis, and peripheral blood immunophenotyping confirmed that 80% of circulating cells were mature T lymphocytes.

A chest radiograph revealed diffuse opacification of the left hemithorax with a shift of the mediastinum to the right. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a 130 × 160 × 160 mm heterogeneous, fat-containing soft-tissue mass arising in the anterior mediastinum, causing complete collapse of the left lung and contralateral mediastinal shift, with no invasion of adjacent structures.
title: Thymolipoma associated with lymphocytosis in a 6-year-old girl: A case report

case_prompt: A 22-year-old Asian man presented with bilateral facial swelling. The larger left‐sided mass, over the parotid region, had been present for 7 years after trauma, was firm, nontender, 4×5 cm, with normal overlying skin and intact facial nerve function. The right cheek swelling, of 1 year’s duration, measured 2×2.5 cm, was also firm and nontender. He denied fever, weight loss, salivary changes, or systemic symptoms. Examination revealed bilateral submandibular and upper cervical lymphadenopathy; no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 155 g/L, white blood cell count 8×10^9/L, and absolute eosinophil count 1.5×10^9/L (normal 0.0–0.4×10^9/L); serum IgE was not determined. Contrast-enhanced CT showed enlargement of both superficial and deep lobes of the left parotid gland, a well‐defined right buccal‐space lesion (3.3×2.4 cm), and enlarged level IB, III, and V lymph nodes. Fine-needle aspiration cytology from the left parotid and lymph nodes, and from the right cheek, suggested chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis and myoepithelial sialadenitis. Incisional biopsies were obtained from both lesions. Histopathology demonstrated preserved lymph node architecture with florid follicular hyperplasia; germinal centers contained eosinophilic proteinaceous deposits and folliculolysis. The interfollicular areas were richly infiltrated by eosinophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells, with eosinophilic microabscesses. Numerous thin-walled vessels with flattened endothelial lining—and no epithelioid or vacuolated cells—were present.
journal: Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology : JOMFP
title: Kimura's disease - An unusual presentation involving subcutaneous tissue, parotid gland and lymph node

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old white woman from a rural area of Espírito Santo, Brazil, presented with a 4-year history of slowly progressive erythematous lesions on her forehead. She was otherwise healthy and a non-smoker. Initially diagnosed with leprosy at another center, she received rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine for 2 years without improvement. Subsequently, she was treated for rosacea with topical metronidazole gel and oral doxycycline for 1 year, also without response. A skin biopsy had shown a diffuse lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with granulomas. Tuberculin skin test and sputum bacilloscopy were negative.

On admission, multiple erythematous infiltrated plaques were noted on the forehead, cheeks, chin, and left earlobe, and a 3-mm ulcer was observed near the right labial commissure. Oral examination revealed multiple mulberry-like gingival ulcers with hemorrhagic dots. Posterior cervical and submandibular lymph nodes were enlarged (1.5–2 cm). There was no fever, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or respiratory symptoms. Chest CT showed residual calcified granulomas in the right middle lobe. Cervical CT revealed enlarged lymph nodes in the jugular, submandibular, intraparotid, and posterior cervical chains.
title: A case of paracoccidioidomycosis due to Paracoccidioides lutzii presenting sarcoid-like form

case_prompt:
An 82-year-old woman with hypertension presented with fever, cough, and dyspnea over several days. She was a non-smoker. On admission, her peripheral oxygen saturation was 84% on room air and her respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed type 1 respiratory failure with a PaO₂ of 41 mm Hg and a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio <200. Laboratory studies showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 7.8 mg/dL and lymphopenia (470 cells/mm³). Lung ultrasound and chest CT demonstrated moderate-to-severe interstitial involvement, more pronounced at the lung bases (lung ultrasound score 18/36; CT severity score 11/20).

She was treated with CPAP (initial PEEP 7 cm H₂O, titrated to 9 cm H₂O) in a semi-sitting supine position, alternating with high-flow nasal oxygen, along with prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin and dexamethasone (6 mg/day). There was no significant improvement over the first two days.

On hospital day 3, she developed sudden hypoxia (SpO₂ <80%) and tachypnea (RR >35/min) despite escalating oxygen supplementation and conversion to pressure-support ventilation with increasing pressures. Bedside lung ultrasound revealed no pneumothorax or pleural effusion, and echocardiography showed no hypokinesia or right heart overload. The PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio dropped to around 46, with stable hemodynamics. Orotracheal intubation was planned, and she was placed supine for preparation. Soon after, there was a rapid and spontaneous improvement in peripheral oxygenation, with SpO₂ rising by more than 30% and the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio improving to 150 on a Venturi mask (FiO₂ 40%). This allowed deferral and ultimate avoidance of intubation and continuation of noninvasive respiratory support in the supine position.
title: Platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome in SARS-CoV-2 related ARDS: a case report

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, breast cancer, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (status post pulmonary vein and cavo-tricuspid isolation), and recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding on rivaroxaban was admitted for left atrial appendage closure.

Postoperatively, she received one dose of lisinopril, which led to profound hypotension requiring intravenous fluids and a low-dose vasopressor. She had a transient troponin elevation thought to be due to demand ischemia.

Further history revealed that one of her sons died suddenly in his early 50s (reported as a “heart attack”). The patient also endorsed many years of exertional dyspnea, fatigue, lower extremity edema, chest tightness, and orthopnea, with recurrent episodes of orthostatic hypotension.

A transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated:
  • Left ventricular ejection fraction 67%  
  • LV internal diastolic diameter 4.4 cm (normal 3.5–6.5 cm)  
  • Right ventricular systolic pressure 40 mm Hg (normal <36 mm Hg)  
  • LV outflow tract gradient <30 mm Hg  
  • Global longitudinal strain −15% with reduced antero-septal strain

Left and right heart catheterization showed no obstructive coronary artery disease. Hemodynamic measurements were:
  • Pulmonary arterial wedge pressure 36 mm Hg  
  • Mean pulmonary arterial pressure 45 mm Hg  
  • Right ventricular systolic pressure 62 mm Hg  
  • Right atrial pressure 12 mm Hg
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy in the Elderly: A Case Identified With Genetic Screening

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old G1P0A0 woman was referred for a routine second-trimester (20-week) ultrasound. Her first-trimester scan had shown a viable twin A with normal heart rate and crown–rump length; an adjacent abnormal structure was noted but not interpreted.  

On repeat sonography at 20 weeks 6 days by Hadlock criteria, two intrauterine fetuses shared a single placenta, sonographically monochorionic. Twin A had a two-vessel cord, all four cardiac chambers appeared normal, and M-mode fetal heart rate was 153 bpm. Estimated fetal weight was 375 g. Amniotic fluid volume measured approximately 8 cm (borderline high).  

Twin B was grossly abnormal: on grayscale imaging, no limbs were identified; the skull appeared small for gestational age with ossified calvarium but no definitive brain tissue; sagittal spine was only partially visualized; large fluid collections filled the thoracic and abdominal cavities; cine clips showed three rudimentary cardiac chambers beating synchronously; no distinct cord insertion was seen. The sonographer could not identify an intertwin membrane and initially classified the pregnancy as monochorionic-monoamniotic.  

Later that same day in the fetal assessment unit, Twin A had a middle cerebral artery velocity of 36–42 cm/sec and normal umbilical artery Doppler. Ductus venosus Doppler showed reversed “a”-wave flow. Twin B’s head measurements corresponded to a 13-week fetus; its chest and abdomen were distended with fluid and soft-tissue edema. Fetal heart rate in twin B was 110 bpm.
title: Twin reversed arterial perfusion (TRAP) sequence: A case report and a brief literature review

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman presented with a pruritic eruption on her scalp that began several days after having glued-on hair pieces applied at a hair restoration center. She had a history of diffuse hair thinning over several years without itching or flaking. The central scalp was shaved and a glued-on hair piece was applied three times over three months, each time followed within days by a pruritic rash that tracked the U-shaped adhesive pattern. Physical examination showed pink plaques with crusting and excoriations in the adhesive distribution. A clinical diagnosis of contact dermatitis was made and treated with topical betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% lotion twice daily, resulting in rapid resolution within two weeks. Treatment was discontinued, and new hair growth was noted without scarring alopecia.

One month later, she returned with severe scalp pain and “pimples.” Examination revealed erythema, erosions, crusts, follicular pustules, and peripheral alopecia around the eruption. A scalp biopsy showed epidermal atrophy, focal erosions, and a mixed neutrophilic, lymphocytic, and plasmacytic infiltrate. Fungal stains were negative, and bacterial cultures from pustules were negative. She was treated with oral prednisone (60 mg daily, tapered to 10 mg over two weeks) and topical betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% lotion, but three weeks later had increased crusting, pustules, hair loss, and atrophy, with new involvement of the central scalp and posterior neck. Repeat biopsies were similar, and direct immunofluorescence was negative for immunoglobulin and complement deposition.
final_diagnosis_raw: Erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp
title: Erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp after contact dermatitis from a prosthetic hair piece

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman with an 18-year history of asthma presented with a 2-week history of distal bilateral lower limb paresthesias that rapidly progressed to weakness preventing her from standing or walking. On examination, she was alert and cooperative; she had bilaterally symmetric lower limb weakness (2/5 strength in both distal and proximal segments), hyporeflexia, and hypoesthesia. She reported distal upper limb paresthesias, but upper-limb strength and reflexes were normal. She had purpuric lesions on the anterior aspects of both lower limbs. Oxygen saturation was normal, and she had no dyspnea, fever, or meningeal signs.

Chest radiography was normal. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count with marked eosinophilia (13,200 cells per μL, 53%; normal range, 0–7%) and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 49 mm/h (normal range, 0–20). Renal function and urinalysis were normal. A head MRI demonstrated pansinusitis. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 10 leukocytes with normal glucose and protein concentrations. Nerve conduction studies revealed bilateral peroneal, tibial, and sural conduction blocks with absent F-waves, as well as a left median nerve conduction block; the remaining upper-extremity nerves were unaffected.
title: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis Presenting as Acute Polyneuropathy Mimicking Guillain-Barre Syndrome

case_prompt:
An 80‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of a 2‐week history of fever and posterior neck pain with marked rotational restriction. On the day she underwent a 1‐hour dental procedure for periodontal disease requiring neck extension and prolonged mouth opening, she developed fever and neck pain. Acetaminophen controlled the fever, but neck pain and movement restriction persisted.  
Her medical history included chronic heart failure, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. She had no prior musculoskeletal neck disorders.  
She consulted her cardiologist, who noted elevated C‐reactive protein (CRP) levels but no other abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac vegetations, and blood cultures were negative. Dental examination showed no oral pathology to explain systemic inflammation.  
On admission, temperature was 35.7°C (on acetaminophen), blood pressure 134/43 mmHg, heart rate 81 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She was alert and oriented. Oral and neck inspection was unremarkable; there were no neurological deficits or meningeal signs. She reported posterior neck pain, especially with lateral movement, and had localized tenderness over the upper cervical spine.  
Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory therapy was initiated with partial relief. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9.19×10^3/μL, CRP 10.94 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 122 mm/h. Further immunologic and endocrine studies were unremarkable. Rheumatology consultation indicated a low likelihood of giant cell arteritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or polymyalgia rheumatica. Cervical radiography showed no abnormalities.
title: Crowned Dens Syndrome Triggered by Dental Treatment

case_prompt: An 18-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a third episode in three months of painful, prolonged erections unrelated to sexual stimulation. Previous episodes resolved with cold showers; at the first ED visit he received pseudoephedrine and ice, and at the second he received terbutaline without success. During the second visit, a corporal blood gas showed pH 7.12, PCO2 30 mmHg, and PO2 43 mmHg, suggestive of ischemic priapism; the hemoglobin level on that blood gas was reported as “results incalculable.” On his third presentation he had symptoms for at least six hours. He was not taking any medications and had no other symptoms. Urology performed penile aspiration and irrigation, and emergency physicians obtained laboratory studies. A complete blood count revealed a white blood cell count of 588 × 10^3/µL with differential showing marked neutrophilia (264.6 × 10^3/µL), lymphocytosis (17.64 × 10^3/µL), monocytosis (11.76 × 10^3/µL), eosinophilia (11.76 × 10^3/µL), basophilia (5.88 × 10^3/µL), myelocytes (164.64 × 10^3/µL), metamyelocytes (35.28 × 10^3/µL), promyelocytes (64.68 × 10^3/µL), and peripheral blasts (11.76 × 10^3/µL). Hemoglobin was 7.3 g/dL and platelet count was 109 × 10^3/µL. He was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit and started on hydroxyurea pending further evaluation.
title: The Semantics of Priapism and the First Sign of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old gravida 3 para 2 woman at 29 weeks of gestation was referred for evaluation of a vaginal mass. The lesion was first noted at 24 weeks during routine prenatal care; she had sensed perineal discomfort prior to pregnancy but its origin was unclear. She had no significant past medical history. Family history was notable only for gastric cancer in a grandmother and lung cancer in a grandfather. 

On pelvic examination, there was an elliptical, nontender, approximately 5 cm mass arising from the posterior vaginal wall, projecting into the vaginal canal; it was easily palpable and mobile. Rectal examination revealed intact mucosa. 

Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 51.7 × 32.5 mm hypervascular mass. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 52 × 37 × 35 mm lesion in the rectovaginal septum, isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with well-defined borders and no apparent invasion of the rectum or vaginal mucosa. No metastatic lesions were identified.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: An Extragastrointestinal Tumor Diagnosed as a Vaginal Mass during Pregnancy

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old woman presented with gradually bilateral decreased vision. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.50 logMAR in the right eye and 1.0 logMAR in the left eye. Ocular motility and alignment were normal without proptosis. Both eyes were aphakic from prior cataract surgery. Fundus examination was unremarkable in the right eye. In the left eye, there was a dome-shaped orange mass beneath the superotemporal vascular arcade in the macular area.  

An orbital CT scan demonstrated bilateral calcification of the dural optic nerve sheaths and posterior globe walls, as well as calcifications in the trochlear apparatus and the brain. B-scan ultrasonography revealed a highly reflective echogenic lesion with posterior acoustic shadowing. Spectral-domain OCT showed that the mass was located within the sclera, causing marked elevation that displaced the choroid and retina inward, associated with thinning of the outer nuclear layer, absence of the external limiting membrane and inner segment–outer segment junction, and no subretinal fluid.  

The patient was referred for systemic evaluation. All metabolic investigations, including serum calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, vitamin D, thyroid-stimulating hormone, calcitonin, and parathyroid hormone levels, were within normal limits.
title: Idiopathic Dural Optic Nerve Sheath Calcification Associated with Sclerochoroidal Calcification: Case Report and Review of Literatures

case_prompt: A 60-year-old man presented with 3 months of progressive pain in the right axilla and posteromedial right upper extremity, rated 10/10. He had undergone C5–6 anterior fusion for cervical spondylosis 5 years earlier and had no intervening trauma. He worked as a taxi driver. On examination, there was no sensory disturbance, no abnormal tendon-jerk reflexes, and no muscle weakness. He had known cervicothoracic scoliosis diagnosed before his cervical fusion. Frontal cervical radiographs showed a right cervicothoracic curvature with a Cobb angle of 17° before fusion and 19° at presentation. CT of the cervical spine revealed bone spurs on the C6–7 facets, and MRI showed decreased intervertebral height but preserved C6–7 nerve root canals. Further CT imaging demonstrated osteophytes of the superior costal facet and articular process at the right T2–3 level, and MRI showed a protruded disc at T2–3. Measurements on CT revealed that the right T2 nerve root canal width and height were reduced compared to the left side and to normal ranges. Blood tests, electrocardiogram, electromyogram, somatosensory evoked potentials, and head MRI were all normal.
title: A case of T2 radiculopathy after anterior C5–6 fusion

case_prompt: A 2.5-month-old male infant was brought with a 1-week history of severe pallor, hematemesis, and melena. The vomiting of blood occurred up to four times daily, always after breastfeeding; weight gain remained normal. There was progressive pallor, and laboratory testing before transfusion revealed a hemoglobin level of 3 g/dL, prompting blood transfusion. The infant weighed 5.5 kg, measured 58 cm in length, and had a head circumference of 38 cm. His mother had recovered from COVID-19 one month earlier and, during breastfeeding, had taken aspirin and unspecified NSAIDs for approximately one month without medical supervision. On examination, the infant was pale, with a pulse of 140 bpm and capillary refill of less than 3 seconds; other findings were normal. Post-transfusion laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 6.3 g/dL, a white-cell count of 11,600/µL with 76% neutrophils, platelets of 437,000/µL, an INR of 1.0, and normal liver, kidney, and electrolyte tests. Stool testing demonstrated white and red blood cells, and stool culture was negative. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a bleeding gastric ulcer on the greater curvature.
title: A case report of a gastric ulcer in a 2.5-month-old infant in Syria: Helicobacter pylori and Aspirin as possible causes

case_prompt:
A 9-month-old Caucasian girl was admitted with a 3-week history of persistent erythematous skin rash and redness of the eyes. Her past history was notable for mild atopic dermatitis since 6 months of age. She had no fever before or during admission. 

On examination, she had an erythematous rash over the trunk and limbs, fissured lips, erythema of the oral mucosa, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, and enlarged laterocervical lymph nodes. Respiratory and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Cardiac examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds.

Laboratory evaluation showed a white-cell count of 8500/mm3 with a normal differential, hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, platelet count 376 000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 35 mm/hour, C-reactive protein 1.5 mg/dL, albumin 2.8 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 59 U/L, direct bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, IgG 589 mg/dL, and IgA 34 mg/dL. Serum-specific IgE against cow’s milk proteins was elevated at 12.5 kU/L (normal, 0–0.35 kU/L). Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Serologic tests for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, measles, rubella, parvovirus, and adenovirus were negative. Antistreptolysin O titers were normal. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. 

Echocardiography demonstrated mild pericardial effusion and perivascular brightness of the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery.
title: Echocardiographic alterations in a child with cow’s milk allergy: a case report

case_prompt: A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with 2 months of lower abdominal pain. Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable. On physical examination, her abdomen was soft and non-tender. Ultrasonography revealed a solid left ovarian mass measuring 38 × 40 × 46 mm with significant enhancement; the right ovary measured 14 × 16 mm. Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a solid, enhancing left ovarian mass and noted small lymph nodes in the mesentery and bilateral external and internal iliac regions. Serum CA-125 was elevated at 327 IU/mL and CEA at 0.85 ng/mL. A staging laparotomy was performed, and frozen-section analysis of the left ovarian mass showed atypical cells with moderate pleomorphism and anisonucleosis without mitoses or necrosis, suggesting a stromal tumor.
title: Ovarian hemangioma: A rare encounter

case_prompt: A 52-year-old woman with a childhood diagnosis of biopsy-confirmed pityriasis rubra pilaris presented with poorly controlled, psoriasiform plaques on her upper and lower extremities. She had failed multiple systemic immunomodulators (isotretinoin, methotrexate, cyclosporine, adalimumab, secukinumab, ustekinumab). She denied muscle pain, weakness, dysphonia, or dyspnea. On examination, she had well-demarcated, salmon-colored plaques over the bilateral extensor forearms, elbows, and thighs. She also had subtle violaceous discoloration of the eyelids (heliotrope sign), erythema of the upper chest in a V-distribution, and erythema over the knuckles. Laboratory studies revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320, positive anti-signal recognition particle and anti-PM/Scl-100 antibodies, a low-titer anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and normal creatine kinase and aldolase levels. Skin biopsy showed psoriasiform dermatitis with confluent parakeratosis and orthokeratosis in a checkerboard pattern without epidermal atrophy or interface change. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated intravascular deposition of C3 and C5b-9, while direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgA, IgG, and IgM.
title: Wong-type dermatomyositis with interstitial lung disease and anti-SRP and -PM/Scl antibodies treated with intravenous immunoglobulin

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old Japanese man was referred after routine urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria and proteinuria. He had a history of recurrent intensely pruritic blistering eruptions on the trunk and extremities since age 25; a skin biopsy at that time led to a diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis, and he responded well to dapsone. On examination, blood pressure was 138/76 mm Hg, pulse 66 beats per minute, and the skin was tanned and free of vesicles. Urinalysis showed 2+ protein and 1+ blood on dipstick, 10–19 red blood cells per high-power field, and a urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio of 1.2 g/gCr. Serum creatinine was 0.68 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 12.1 mg/dL, and estimated GFR 99.2 mL/min/1.73 m2. Hematologic, liver-function, and cholesterol levels were normal. Serologic tests were negative for syphilis, hepatitis B and C viruses, ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, and anti-GBM antibodies. Complement C3 and C4 levels were within normal ranges. Chest and abdominal imaging showed no evidence of malignancy.

Ultrasound-guided renal biopsy yielded three cores. Light microscopy showed 30 glomeruli, three globally sclerosed, with moderate mesangial widening, capillary-wall thickening, lobular accentuation, segmental nodular formation, and double contours. Immunofluorescence revealed strong granular deposits of IgG, C3, and C1q along capillary walls and mesangium; IgA, IgM, and fibrinogen were weak or negative. Electron microscopy demonstrated effaced podocyte foot processes and massive electron-dense deposits in mesangial, subendothelial, subepithelial, and basement-membrane locations with segmental GBM duplication. These findings were consistent with the Burkholder variant of MPGN type 3. Staining for IgG subclasses was positive for IgG1 and IgG2 and negative for IgG3 and IgG4. Immunohistochemistry showed both κ and λ light chains in glomerular deposits, indicating polyclonal IgG deposition.
journal: Case Reports in Nephrology and Dialysis
title: MPGN Type 3 Associated with Pemphigus Herpetiformis Mimicking PGNMID and Dermatitis Herpetiformis

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a gradually enlarging, asymptomatic swelling of the lower left jaw and intermittent pus discharge from the lower left posterior teeth region. Ten to twelve years earlier, he had undergone extraction of a lower left molar, leaving an unhealed socket that had been unsuccessfully treated by multiple practitioners. The patient was otherwise healthy and alert. 

On extraoral examination, there was a 7 × 5 cm ill-defined, noncompressible, nonfluctuant swelling over the left angle of the mandible, fixed to underlying structures; a soft, fluctuant notch was noted in the body of the mandible 3 cm anterior to the angle, and the jaw deviated toward the right on opening. Intraorally, there was buccal cortical expansion from tooth 35 to the angle, egg-shell crackling near tooth 37, lingual plate expansion at teeth 37–38, and yellow discharge from the socket of tooth 38 and the root stump of tooth 36. Tooth 37 was nonvital on pulp testing. 

A provisional clinical diagnosis was ameloblastoma of the left mandible, with a differential that included residual cyst, dentigerous cyst, keratocystic odontogenic tumour, central giant cell granuloma, and radicular cyst. Intraoral periapical radiography showed a radiolucency extending beyond the film margins. A panoramic radiograph revealed a multilocular radiolucency with scalloped, hyperostotic borders, extending from the posterior body of the mandible through the angle, ramus, coronoid process, and condyle, with downward expansion of the inferior mandibular border, a 3 × 2.5 cm radiolucent “window” below tooth 37, and resorption of the mesial and distal roots of tooth 37. 

CT imaging confirmed involvement of the coronoid process, condyle, ramus, and body of the left mandible, and demonstrated medial deflection of the left lateral pterygoid plate and of the left maxillary posterior alveolar arch.
title: Atypical CT Findings in Plexiform Ameloblastoma

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old woman presented with 2 days of acute suprapubic pain. She denied fever, diarrhea, or vomiting but reported cyclical pain over several months. Her history was notable for two cesarean sections and known pelvic endometriosis. She took no regular medications, using only NSAIDs and co-dydramol as needed. On admission, vital signs were stable. Laboratory tests, including a serum β-hCG, were normal. On examination, there was exquisite tenderness in the midline suprapubic region without rebound tenderness. 

Transabdominal ultrasound was normal except for an irregular hypoechoic focus underlying the cesarean-section scar. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined soft tissue nodule with postcontrast enhancement in the anterior abdominal wall extending from the rectus muscle with surrounding streakiness.
title: Scar endometriosis: a mimic of acute abdominal emergencies

case_prompt: A previously healthy Japanese boy, born at term (3040 g) after a 40-week gestation complicated by meconium aspiration and prolonged neonatal jaundice, attained normal early developmental milestones. Beginning at age 9, he experienced peer bullying (pushing, hitting, verbal taunts, social exclusion), followed by depressed affect, social withdrawal, declining grades, difficulty sustaining attention to detail, and clumsiness that interfered with handwriting and activities such as riding a bicycle and playing catch. At age 10, he was diagnosed with developmental coordination disorder and managed supportively. By 11 years old, his clumsiness and school performance had further deteriorated despite ongoing support. Examination revealed hepatomegaly; he was alert and oriented but had slurred speech with impaired pronunciation, mild facial dyskinesia, slight dysarthria and dysphasia, and hyperactive deep tendon reflexes in all extremities. The finger-to-nose test was performed correctly but was slow and slightly awkward. Guided and voluntary eye movements were normal, but he was unable to perform downward saccadic eye movements. His full-scale IQ was 63 on the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-III. Routine laboratory tests, including blood counts, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, plasma amino acids, and urine organic acids, were normal. Cerebral magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormality.
title: Niemann-Pick Disease Type C Presenting as a Developmental Coordination Disorder with Bullying by Peers in a School-Age Child

case_prompt: A 55-year-old woman presented on January 26, 2011, with a 2-day history of crampy abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, progressive abdominal distention, and 1 day of absolute constipation. She denied prior abdominal surgery or any symptoms suggestive of a hernia. On examination, she appeared dehydrated and in distress; pulse was 120 bpm and feeble, blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate 32/min, temperature 36.5°C, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. The tongue and buccal mucosa were dry. The abdomen was grossly distended with generalized tenderness, guarding, and hypoactive bowel sounds. Rectal examination revealed an empty rectum without blood. Laboratory studies showed a normal hematocrit and a white-cell count of 10.6×10^3/mm^3. A plain abdominal radiograph demonstrated dilated loops of small bowel with multiple air–fluid levels and absence of rectal gas. With the impression of gangrenous small-bowel obstruction secondary to small-bowel volvulus, she was resuscitated and prepared for urgent exploratory laparotomy.
title: Ileo-ileal knotting as an uncommon cause of acute intestinal obstruction

case_prompt:
A 10-year-old Mexican boy, the only child of healthy, unrelated parents, was referred for management of refractory epilepsy and insomnia. He was born at 38 weeks by cesarean delivery (birth weight 3200 g, length 52 cm, Apgar 9 and 9), and on day 1 developed perioral cyanosis prompting NICU admission for suspected neonatal sepsis. A patent ductus arteriosus was noted but closed spontaneously. He had recurrent pulmonary infections from birth, severe gastroesophageal reflux with intolerance to feeds, and underwent Nissen fundoplication with gastrostomy at 6 months.

Since 7 months of age, he has had atonic seizures and infantile spasms that proved difficult to control; trials of valproic acid, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, and multiple other agents were limited by adverse effects or persistent seizures, and he is currently maintained on lacosamide, clobazam, brivaracetam, and acetazolamide with approximately five seizures per month. Growth parameters (weight, height, head circumference) have remained below the 3rd percentile since infancy. At 18 months, subclinical hypothyroidism, selective IgG and IgA immunodeficiency, and nephrocalcinosis were identified; he receives levothyroxine and monthly immunoglobulin infusions.

Physical examination shows microcephaly; elongated palpebral fissures with lower‐lid eversion; arched, broad eyebrows; depressed nasal tip with short columella; small, spaced teeth; micrognathia; large, low‐set, cup‐shaped ears with bilateral retroauricular pits; right‐hand and left‐foot polydactyly (surgically corrected); bilateral aberrant palmar creases; and a sacral dimple. He has never walked and is nonverbal, emitting only sounds and following simple commands. 

This clinical picture fulfilled the findings of a suspected diagnosis of Kabuki syndrome (OMIM 147920); however, sequencing of the KMT2D gene—the most commonly associated—ruled out the diagnosis. Since this diagnostic possibility was excluded, exome sequencing was performed.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Comparison of Genetic Variants and Manifestations of OTUD6B-Related Disorder: The First Mexican Case

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old Saudi woman presented for routine follow-up with a 2-month history of intermittent epigastric pain and indigestion that had become more frequent over the past 2 weeks. She had been taking antispasmodics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with minimal relief. Her medical history included hypertension and diabetes mellitus for 20 years, both well controlled, and a total thyroidectomy with neck dissection for follicular-variant papillary thyroid carcinoma (pathologic stage pT2N1cM0) in 2002, followed by two radioactive iodine ablations for rising serum thyroglobulin levels.

On examination, her vital signs were stable. Abdominal palpation revealed deep tenderness in the epigastrium without masses or organomegaly. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. The clinical differential diagnosis included chronic pancreatitis, primary pancreatic adenocarcinoma, or metastatic disease.

Laboratory tests showed normal hematological, renal, and liver function tests, normal serum electrolytes, normal thyroid-stimulating hormone and thyroxine levels, and a negative tuberculin test. Serum tumor markers carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and cancer antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) were within normal limits, but the thyroglobulin level was elevated at 672.8 ng/mL (reference range 5–25 ng/mL).

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated decreased enhancement of the neck, body, and tail of the pancreas, with a normal-appearing pancreatic head, and also revealed bilateral multiple pulmonary nodules. Whole-body iodine scintigraphy was nondiagnostic due to lack of iodine avidity. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed a 1.8 × 1.5 cm hypovascular lesion in the neck of the pancreas, with low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, no arterial enhancement, and faint delayed enhancement; the lesion abutted and narrowed the superior mesenteric vein below its confluence with the splenic vein, whereas the superior mesenteric artery was unremarkable.
title: Pancreas as Delayed Site of Metastasis from Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old African-American man with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with sudden onset of pain and swelling in his left thigh. His medical history included stage IV chronic kidney disease, background retinopathy, peripheral vascular disease with a prior below-the-knee amputation of the left lower extremity, severe peripheral neuropathy, uncontrolled hypertension, and tobacco use. He denied trauma or insulin injections into the left thigh. 

On admission, laboratory studies revealed a creatine kinase level of 1670 U/L (reference range, 32–294) and severe anemia requiring transfusion of 4 units of packed red blood cells. Cardiac markers were within normal limits (CK-MB, 0.31 ng/mL; troponin, 0.02 ng/mL), and an electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ST-T changes. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics for suspected necrotizing fasciitis without clinical improvement. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left thigh without contrast demonstrated diffuse edema in the anterior compartment and subcutaneous edema in the anterior and lateral aspects of the thigh.
title: Diabetic Muscle Infarction: A Rare Complication of Long-Standing and Poorly Controlled Diabetes Mellitus

case_prompt: A 56-year-old woman with no prior medical conditions suffered an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. She had complained of right calf pain after a long-distance flight. Emergency crews found pulseless electrical activity and administered tenecteplase (100 mg) for presumed pulmonary embolism. Spontaneous circulation returned, and she was transferred intubated and unresponsive (GCS 3) with hemodynamic shock (MAP 92 mm Hg, HR 133 beats/min) requiring epinephrine (5.5 µg/kg/min) and norepinephrine (4.5 µg/kg/min). A CT scan showed no pulmonary embolism. Soon after, hemoglobin dropped markedly; repeat CT revealed a hemoperitoneum from a traumatic liver rupture. She underwent emergency laparotomy, hepatic repair, and abdominal packing, during which she received massive transfusion (packed red blood cells, fresh-frozen plasma, platelets) and procoagulant factors (fibrinogen, antithrombin, four-factor PCC). The next day she developed abdominal compartment syndrome, acute liver failure, and progressive lung failure. She was transferred to an ECMO center, where veno-venous ECMO was initiated and then escalated to veno-venoarterial ECMO for right-heart failure. Anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin targeted an aPTT above 60 seconds. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed two pronounced hyperdense masses on both mitral-valve leaflets; the anterior mass measured 0.9 × 1.0 cm and caused systolic obstruction of the left-ventricular outflow tract. Continuous-wave Doppler showed a peak velocity of 3.52 m/s (peak gradient ~50 mm Hg). A moderate mitral regurgitation was also noted (vena contracta 0.6 cm).
title: Dynamic thromboembolic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction after aggressive procoagulant treatment in hemorrhagic shock: a case report

case_prompt: A 69-year-old woman, never smoker, with a history of hysterectomy for benign uterine fibroids 20 years earlier, presented with back pain. A chest radiograph revealed two pulmonary lesions. Chest CT with contrast showed a well-demarcated right lower lobe mass measuring 4.2×3.8 cm and a left lower lobe nodule measuring 2.8×2.6 cm extending to the left upper lobe; both were hypervascular and caused mild extrinsic compression of the adjacent bronchovascular bundles. The patient denied respiratory symptoms; spirometry showed an FEV1 of 106% predicted and a DLCO of 103% predicted. Abdominal CT revealed a 1.4×1.9 cm slowly growing hypervascular mass in the left adnexa separate from the ovary. She was on estrogen replacement therapy. An image-guided biopsy of the right lung lesion revealed a cellular spindle neoplasm with immunohistochemical findings supportive of a benign smooth muscle neoplasm.
title:
Benign Metastasizing Leiomyoma in the Lung Presenting in a Phyllodes-Like
Pattern Mimicking a Biphasic Tumor: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of a painless swelling involving the submental region and right angle of the mandible. The mass first appeared intraorally and gradually increased in size, occasionally discharging a thick creamy fluid. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. He had a long history of tobacco and cigarette use but no history of dental trauma. 

On examination, there was a solitary, hard, non-tender, 4 × 4 cm swelling extending from the submental area to the right mandibular angle above an anterior edentulous alveolar ridge. Intraorally, the buccal vestibule was elevated. The mass was fixed to underlying structures and there was numbness of the right lower lip. Oral hygiene was poor. There was no lymphadenopathy or increased local temperature.

Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Orthopantomogram showed a multilocular radiolucent lesion in the right mandible with a mixed honeycomb and soap-bubble appearance. Contrast-enhanced CT of the mandible revealed a well-defined expansile mixed-density cystic lesion measuring 3.6 × 3.9 cm; enhancing areas corresponded to solid components, and non-enhancing areas corresponded to cystic components. The right mental foramen was not visualized.
journal: JNMA: Journal of the Nepal Medical Association
title: Unicystic Ameloblastoma of Mandible: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a four-week history of cough productive of mucous-purulent sputum and progressive dyspnea. She was a lifelong nonsmoker, had no recent travel or animal exposures, and no known contact with substances associated with lipoid pneumonia. Her medical history included atrial fibrillation treated with amiodarone (200 mg daily) for 30 years, hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism.

On examination, her vital signs were normal (pulse 69 /min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, SpO2 95% on room air). Lung auscultation revealed bibasal crackles; there was no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Routine blood tests were within normal limits.

Pulmonary function testing showed a moderate restrictive defect (FVC 90% predicted, FEV1 65% predicted, FEV1/FVC 96%) and a marked reduction in diffusing capacity (DLCO 55% predicted). There was no bronchodilator response.

Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral infiltrates, prompting high-resolution CT, which revealed ground-glass opacities and air-space consolidations predominant in both lower lobes. 

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage yielded 287 500 cells/mL (macrophages 64%, lymphocytes 31%, neutrophils 3%, eosinophils 2%). Smears and cultures for bacteria, fungi, and acid-fast bacilli were negative, and cytology showed no malignant cells.
title: A rare case of lipoid pneumonia attributed to amiodarone

case_prompt:
A 79-year-old man presented with sudden loss of vision in both eyes. His ocular history was unremarkable, and he denied any recent trauma. He also reported nausea and upper abdominal pain of recent onset. His medical history included irritable bowel syndrome and chronic gastritis managed with ranitidine and omeprazole. Family history was notable for a father who had pancreatic cancer.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. Anterior segments, intraocular pressures, and pupillary reactions were normal. Funduscopic examination revealed multiple large yellow-white spots and superficial retinal hemorrhages surrounding the optic discs in both eyes. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated early hypofluorescence corresponding to the yellow-white patches and late hyperfluorescence in the same regions.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 100 U/L (normal 0–48), alkaline phosphatase 240 U/L (20–125), lactate dehydrogenase 840 U/L (50–240), and gamma-glutamyl transferase 160 U/L (10–50). Serum amylase and lipase were within normal limits.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: An unusual association between pancreatic cancer and Purtscher-like retinopathy: Presentation of a unique case

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old man with a 3-year history of rheumatoid arthritis treated sequentially with methylprednisolone, tocilizumab, adalimumab, and rituximab presented with abdominal pain and distension for 2 months and progressive difficulty in swallowing, coughing, hoarseness, and dysphonia for 1 week. He had recurrent partial small-bowel obstruction of unknown origin treated at multiple hospitals. As his condition worsened, he developed petechiae and bulbar palsy. Electromyography showed peripheral nerve axonal damage; high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin was ineffective, and plasmapheresis was planned. He also had poorly controlled diabetes managed with insulin. 

On examination, he was cachectic but hemodynamically stable, with hoarseness, dysarthria, wet rales bilaterally, weak bowel sounds, grade-3 muscle strength in all limbs, and diminished tendon reflexes. Laboratory testing revealed K 3.4 mmol/L, Na 129 mmol/L, Ca 1.88 mmol/L, and albumin 25 g/L. Chest CT showed bilateral infiltrates consistent with pneumonia, and echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 42% with impaired left ventricular movement.
title: Disseminated strongyloidiasis in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis: A case report

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation refractory to drugs underwent radiofrequency catheter ablation with pulmonary vein isolation, roof and bottom lines in the left atrium, and cavo-tricuspid isthmus ablation. Preprocedure CT angiography of the pulmonary veins was normal. Baseline echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 56%, left atrial diameter 40 mm, a calcified aortic valve, and mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation.

He was discharged on rivaroxaban and remained in sinus rhythm. On postablation day 5 he developed progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea without fever. Heart rate was < 110 bpm. Examination revealed a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border and decreased breath sounds at the lung bases.

Labs showed normal leukocyte and neutrophil counts but 79.6% neutrophils, ESR 18 mm/h (0–15), CRP 13.8 mg/L (0–6), IL-6 126.6 pg/mL (0–7), NT-proBNP 2200 ng/L (0–125), and negative high-sensitivity troponin T. Oxygen saturation was normal.

ECG in sinus rhythm demonstrated increased P-wave amplitude in V1–V4, PR-segment depression, and ST-segment elevation. CT angiography revealed no pulmonary embolism and no pulmonary vein stenosis; chest CT showed bilateral patchy flocculent densities in the right lower lobe, small pleural effusions, and localized pericardial thickening. Echocardiography revealed EF 53%, severe TR (max gradient 75 mmHg), severe PAH (est. 85 mmHg), and mild pericardial effusion. Tuberculosis spot test and autoimmune panel were negative.

Tumor, tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary vein stenosis, and pulmonary embolism were excluded. He was treated for acute heart failure with diuretics, vasodilators, and anticoagulation, but symptoms and severe PAH with TR persisted, and the cause remained unexplained.
title: Postcardiac injury syndrome caused by radiofrequency catheter ablation of persistent atrial fibrillation: severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with severe tricuspid regurgitation: a rare case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 78-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of a slow-onset, moderate-intensity, stabbing pain in the right inguinal area and an associated bulge without overlying skin changes. Her medical history was notable for a 15-year history of insulin-treated type 2 diabetes and a 7-year history of hypertension managed with amlodipine. On examination, a right groin bulge was palpable and tender to touch. There were no systemic signs of sepsis. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Clinical suspicion was for an incarcerated inguinal hernia, and the patient was referred for ultrasonographic evaluation.

Ultrasonography of the right groin using a 9 MHz linear transducer demonstrated a well-defined cystic mass containing a central tubular structure terminating in a blind end on longitudinal imaging and a target appearance on cross-sectional imaging. The tubular structure measured 0.63 mm in one axis and 0.72 mm in the perpendicular axis, with focal hypoechoic thickening of the mucosal layer. Color Doppler imaging showed increased flow at the tip and in adjacent soft tissues. The patient experienced focal tenderness when the transducer was pressed over the lesion, and the surrounding fat exhibited increased echogenicity consistent with inflammation. The preoperative surgical diagnosis was a strangulated inguinofemoral hernia.
title: Acute appendicitis in Amyand’s hernia: ultrasound findings and histopathology correlation. A case report

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old woman with a history of scleroderma, previously treated with azathioprine and low-dose steroids, presented with frequent urination. Two months after transurethral resection of a Grade 3 pT1 plus pTis urothelial carcinoma, she underwent intravesical administration of 80 mg BCG (Tokyo 172 strain) after discontinuing azathioprine 2 months and steroids 2 days earlier due to stable scleroderma (baseline KL-6 level, 651 U/mL).

The day after BCG instillation, she noted urinary frequency, gross hematuria, low-grade fever, and oxygen desaturation. Five days later, she developed dyspnea at rest. Chest CT showed scattered frosted-glass opacities centered on the pulmonary hila in the upper lung fields, along with known interstitial changes in the lower lung fields attributed to scleroderma.

On day 7 after BCG, her respiratory status worsened: SpO2 fell below 90% on 15 L/min of oxygen, arterial blood gas analysis revealed a PaO2 of 55.6 mmHg and PaCO2 of 34.0 mmHg, and KL-6 remained at 621 U/mL. She was intubated with a working diagnosis of drug-induced interstitial pneumonia.
title: Drug‐induced interstitial pneumonia after intravesical Bacillus Calmette‐Guerin administration for bladder cancer with scleroderma

case_prompt: A 61-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented to the emergency department six days after discharge from a hospitalization for severe COVID-19 pneumonia. He had two days of worsening cough productive of blood-tinged sputum, dyspnea, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, and poor oral intake. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable but tachypneic with an oxygen saturation of 84% on room air; coarse bilateral crackles were heard on lung auscultation. He required 15 L of supplemental oxygen via nonrebreather mask to maintain oxygenation. Chest radiograph showed a marked bilateral interval increase in interstitial and airspace opacities with near-complete consolidation at the lingula compared to prior imaging. An initial nasopharyngeal RT-PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 was negative but was repeated the next day and returned positive. Laboratory studies showed a ferritin level of 2010 mcg/L (prior admission peak 4157 mcg/L), a C-reactive protein of 31 mg/L (prior peak 193.1 mg/L), an interleukin-6 of 7.2 pg/mL (prior peak 67.0 pg/mL), and a serum SARS-CoV-2 IgG index of 3.58.
title: The Dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 (RT-PCR) Testing
Prostate cancer metastasis mimicking appendicitis—A rare but important differential diagnosis in PET/CT imaging

case_prompt: A 73-year-old woman was referred for mild breathlessness on exertion. She denied chest pain, fluid retention, orthopnoea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Her past history was significant for infra-renal abdominal aortic aneurysm repair 15 years earlier. On examination, she was in atrial fibrillation at 64 bpm, normotensive, and without pedal edema. Cardiovascular examination revealed a significantly elevated jugular venous pressure with systolic V waves, a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge, and a systolic flow murmur in the pulmonary area. Lung fields were clear. A continuous loud bruit was auscultated over the lower abdomen. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anaemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL) with normal liver and renal function tests. The electrocardiogram confirmed rate-controlled atrial fibrillation without ischaemic changes. A chest radiograph demonstrated massive cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic and diastolic function, severe biatrial and biventricular dilatation, moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation, mild pulmonary hypertension, and no evidence of intracardiac shunting. The cardiac output was 9.8 L/min with a cardiac index of 6.0 L/min/m2.
title: High output heart failure caused by a large pelvic arteriovenous malformation

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old primigravida at 28 weeks’ gestation was referred after a peripheral centre performed an exploratory laparotomy that revealed gangrenous small bowel. Two days before presentation, she developed sudden sharp supra-umbilical pain, rapidly progressive abdominal distension, constipation, and two episodes of nonbilious vomiting. She denied hematemesis, melaena, fever, or urinary symptoms and had no history of abdominal surgery, trauma, or hernias. Her pregnancy had been uneventful.

On arrival she appeared acutely ill and pale. Vital signs were: temperature 36.8 °C, pulse 160/min, blood pressure 97/61 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Chest examination was normal. Abdominal examination revealed distension, a midline laparotomy scar closed with nylon sutures, and generalized tenderness worst in the left hypochondrial, left lumbar, and umbilical regions; bowel sounds were absent. Pelvic examination showed a posterior, firm cervix 3 cm long with a closed os and no vaginal discharge. Fetal heart tones were absent. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable.

She was diagnosed with an acute abdomen with suspected gangrenous bowel and intrauterine fetal demise. Management included nasogastric decompression (bilious effluent), urinary catheterization, nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, antibiotics, analgesics, and transfusion of two units of whole blood. Initial laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, packed cell volume 29%, white-cell count 44.1×10^9/L (74% neutrophils), platelets 286×10^9/L, serum sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, urea 4.1 mmol/L, and creatinine 216 μmol/L. Obstetric ultrasound confirmed intrauterine fetal death. After 36 hours, vital signs stabilized (pulse 130/min, blood pressure 121/74 mmHg) and repeat labs showed white-cell count 19.3×10^9/L, platelets 142×10^9/L, urea 12.9 mmol/L, and creatinine 319 μmol/L. She was then scheduled for exploratory laparotomy.
journal: Journal of the West African College of Surgeons
title: Congenital Peritoneal Encapsulation in A Pregnant Woman: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old previously healthy, nonsmoking man underwent routine screening colonoscopy, which revealed two sessile, smooth, firm, yellowish polyps in the sigmoid colon measuring 0.2 cm and 0.3 cm. Fifteen months later, a second colonoscopy demonstrated two histologically confirmed hyperplastic polyps in the sigmoid colon. Twenty-eight months after the initial examination, a third colonoscopy identified a 0.5 cm submucosal, infiltrated, and ulcerated polyp in the cecum adjacent to the appendiceal orifice; the sigmoid colon appeared normal. The patient remained asymptomatic throughout. Cross-sectional imaging showed no evidence of extracolonic involvement.

Histologic examination of all lesions revealed submucosal nodules composed of sheets of large cells with indistinct borders and abundant lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. The nuclei were reniform to oval, with fine vesicular chromatin, nuclear grooves, and single inconspicuous nucleoli. Central necrosis was present, and the cecal lesion demonstrated focal mucosal infiltration and ulceration. No giant cells, mitotic figures, or enlarged nucleoli were identified. Immunohistochemical staining showed strong, diffuse positivity for CD1a and CD207, with weak, multifocal staining for S100 and CD68.
title: Adult Langerhans cell histiocytosis presenting as metachronous colonic polyps

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old Caucasian man presented in late June with a 5-day history of nightly fevers, nausea, and hematuria. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout, and hypothyroidism. 

Five days earlier, he had been evaluated for hematuria and nausea; he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Labs showed creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, WBC 6.9 × 10^9/L, bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, ALT 42 U/L, AST 38 U/L, and ALP 70 U/L. He was discharged with outpatient follow-up.

He returned with persistent fevers. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed diverticulosis, a 5-mm right lower lobe lung nodule, hiatal hernia, small umbilical hernia, and enlarged prostate. Repeat labs showed creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, ALT 84 U/L, and sodium 132 mmol/L. He was again discharged.

Outpatient labs days later demonstrated worsening renal and liver function: creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, AST 128 U/L, ALT 166 U/L, and total bilirubin 3.9 mg/dL; ESR was 58 mm/h. He was referred back to the emergency department.

On admission, he was febrile to 38.8 °C and otherwise stable. Laboratory evaluation revealed:
• Creatinine 2.2 mg/dL  
• WBC 11 × 10^9/L; hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL; platelets 96 × 10^9/L  
• ALT 186 U/L; AST 148 U/L; total bilirubin 6.6 mg/dL; γ-GT 310 U/L; ALP 298 U/L  
• Ferritin 5130 ng/mL
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Severe Human Granulocytic Anaplasmosis With Significantly Elevated Ferritin Levels in an Immunocompetent Host in Pennsylvania: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 41-year-old Japanese man, previously healthy and with no travel to tropical areas in the past 10 years, presented with a 2-month history of cough, wheezing, low-grade fever, and headache. On examination, his temperature was 37.2°C, oxygen saturation was 98% on room air, and an expiratory wheeze was audible over the left lung field. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, including negative tests for HIV antibody and human T-cell lymphotropic virus type I antibody. Chest radiography and computed tomography revealed a mass in the left lower lung field, multiple mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and stenosis of the left main bronchus. Brain magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium enhancement showed numerous small enhancing lesions. Bronchoscopy demonstrated aggregated white nodules causing compressive stenosis of the left main bronchus.
title: Endobronchial cryptococcosis induced by Cryptococcus gattii mimicking metastatic lung cancer

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old Russian woman presented with fatigue, chest pain, joint pain, and dyspnea. One year and ten months before her first Pfizer SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, she was hospitalized for three days with presyncope, palpitations, and a high burden of premature ventricular contractions (PVCs). Three weeks after her second vaccination, she redeveloped lightheadedness, fatigue, frequent presyncope, shortness of breath, and chest pain and was admitted with a high PVC burden. Cardiac magnetic resonance showed borderline cardiomegaly with left ventricular enlargement but no infarct, fibrosis, or amyloidosis; the ejection fraction was 62.3%. She underwent catheter ablation on two consecutive days, after which symptoms improved. Transthoracic echocardiography then showed trace mitral and tricuspid regurgitation and a small pericardial effusion. Two months later, she was treated with ibuprofen for pericarditis. Three weeks after that, she tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 and subsequently developed recurrent chest pain with movement and breathing, joint pain, and dermatitis that persisted for six months.  
Genetic analysis revealed mutations in six CVD/diabetes susceptibility loci (including APOC1 and CETP) and no variants in immune-system–related genes. Her family history was notable for diabetes, hypertension, and cardiac cirrhosis. The differential diagnosis included long COVID-19, arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus.  
Laboratory investigations showed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:80 with a nuclear homogeneous pattern. A double-stranded DNA antibody test was negative. Liver enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase) were within normal limits. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase) were negative. Additional autoantibodies, including cyclic citrullinated peptide (IgG), complements C3 and C4, antiphospholipid antibodies, Sjögren syndrome antigens, and Smith/RNP antibodies, were not detected. Blood tests showed normal hormone and white-cell counts, an LDL cholesterol of 112 mg/dL, and an HDL cholesterol that declined from 79 to 65 mg/dL over the year prior to symptom exacerbation.
title: Autoimmune Reaction Associated With Long COVID Syndrome and Cardiovascular Disease

case_prompt: An 85-year-old Caucasian man presented on day 2 of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection with a dry cough and localized right posterolateral chest pain. His medical history included asthma, COPD, Crohn’s disease, hypertension, and obesity; he was an ex-smoker (13 pack‐years) with no prior thoracic surgery. His COVID-19 was treated with inhaled budesonide and a 5-day course of ritonavir/nirmatrelvir. He described extreme stabbing pain over the right lateral chest wall when coughing, with mild discomfort at rest, unchanged by deep inspiration or expiration. On examination, he was exquisitely tender to palpation over ribs 8–10 on the right side. Vital signs and blood tests were unremarkable. Initial chest X‐ray showed no acute changes, with long-standing hyperexpansion of the lung fields. The initial impression was musculoskeletal pain, with a differential diagnosis of hepatobiliary pathology or pneumonia. He was admitted for analgesia, but despite oral and subcutaneous opioids and an erector spinae plane nerve block, his pain remained extreme on coughing. On hospital day 4, he developed an extensive flank haematoma inferior to the site of his pain, and clinical examination demonstrated significant bulging of the chest wall on deep breathing and coughing.
title: Spontaneous pulmonary herniation in COVID‐19

case_prompt: A 30-year-old primigravida at 31 weeks 2 days of gestation presented with her first episode of third-trimester vaginal bleeding. Her antenatal course had been unremarkable; a 20-week ultrasound showed a normal fetus and a posterior mid-section placenta with no cervical involvement. On admission, her blood pressure was 119/78 mmHg, heart rate 109 bpm. Speculum exam revealed ~500 mL of fresh blood in the vagina; the cervical os was closed without obvious lesions. Transabdominal ultrasound showed a single viable fetus (estimated 1429 g) in vertex presentation, a low-posterior placenta, and normal amniotic fluid. Doppler studies were not obtained. Thirty minutes later, she had continuous vaginal bleeding of 300 mL, her blood pressure fell to 60/30 mmHg, and external fetal monitoring showed a NICHD category III tracing. An emergency cesarean section was performed. A low transverse uterine incision delivered a 1310 g infant (Apgars 1 and 3). The posterior placenta was removed intact. In the endocervical region, a whitish tubular structure measuring 3 × 3 cm exhibited pulsatile bleeding. Figure-of-eight suture ligation slowed but did not stop the hemorrhage. A Bakri balloon inserted through the uterine incision and inflated with 150 mL of saline achieved hemostasis. Estimated blood loss was 1200 mL; she received four units of packed red blood cells. The Bakri balloon was left in place for 24 hours without recurrent bleeding, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 3. For diagnostic clarification, a biopsy was taken before the Bakri balloon insertion.
title: Successful management of intraoperative cesarean section bleeding due to cervical arteriovenous malformation: A case report

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old man presented to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain. His temperature was 36.4°C, heart rate 84/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and blood pressure 130/90 mmHg. The abdomen was rigid with diffuse tenderness. Laboratory studies showed WBC 7,220/mm3 (57.5% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, platelets 299,000/mm3, AST 25 IU/L, ALT 21 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.81 mg/dL, total protein 6.4 g/dL, albumin 3.5 g/dL, BUN 8 mg/dL, creatinine 0.65 mg/dL, glucose 97 mg/dL, LDH 580 IU/L, ESR 41 mm/hr, and CRP 6.84 mg/L.  
He had been diagnosed with HIV in 2010; in November 2014 his CD4+ count was 355 cells/mm3 and viral load 156,000 copies/mL. He started HAART (abacavir/lamivudine/darunavir/ritonavir) in April 2015. One week before this admission he had mild abdominal pain; endoscopy at that time showed an acute gastric ulcer and biopsy was performed. Over the next week, pain persisted and he returned to the ED.  
A plain abdominal radiograph showed multiple air–fluid levels and dilated small-bowel loops consistent with obstruction. Abdominopelvic CT revealed multiple “bowel-within-bowel” configurations in the jejunum, indicating several sites of intussusception.
title: A Case of Jejunal Intussusception caused by Burkitt Lymphoma in an Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome Patient

case_prompt: A 93-year-old woman with a history of biliary pancreatitis presented with epigastric pain, nausea, and emesis. Two weeks earlier, she had acute cholecystitis and moderately severe biliary pancreatitis; ERCP was unsuccessful due to papillary edema, and she declined cholecystectomy. On examination, she had mild scleral icterus, right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy’s sign, and no jaundice. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 25×10^9/L, alanine transaminase 179 U/L, aspartate transaminase 390 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 173 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasound revealed intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary dilatation, a common bile duct diameter of 15 mm, a positive sonographic Murphy’s sign, gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and gallbladder distension. The patient was diagnosed with ascending cholangitis, placed on intravenous antibiotics, and taken for same-day ERCP. During ERCP, an edematous major papilla was seen with bilious and purulent discharge from above the papillary orifice, which was identified as the site of a fistulous communication.
title: Stone-Induced Purulent Choledocoduodenal Fistula Presenting with Ascending Cholangitis

case_prompt: A 63-year-old Ecuadorian man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a 3-year history of adult-onset Still’s disease treated with etanercept, corticosteroids, and methotrexate was admitted for chronic daily fevers and fatigue. On examination he had moon facies, subcutaneous nodules on the left hypochondrium and left forearm, and no respiratory symptoms. Chest CT showed a right upper-lobe consolidation with central cavitation. Sputum and fiberoptic bronchoscopy for tuberculosis were negative. He was started on piperacillin/tazobactam and a fluoroquinolone. Within 24 hours, he became lethargic and developed left-sided hemiparesis. Brain CT revealed hypodense lesions in the right internal capsule and lenticular nucleus. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple rounded cortical, subcortical, and cerebellar T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions with perilesional edema and ring enhancement. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed ADA 11 U/L, protein 110 g/dL, glucose 82 mg/dL, LDH 35 U/L, and negative cultures. Contrast MRI spectroscopy revealed low choline and creatine levels with a small choline/creatine ratio.
title: Brain abscess due to Nocardia asiatica in a 63‐year‐old patient with adult‐onset still disease: A case report

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old woman was found unconscious at home by her parents after reportedly ingesting twenty 25-mg tablets of baclofen in a suicide attempt. She has a history of posttraumatic stress disorder and depression, treated with venlafaxine and clomipramine. On arrival, she was afebrile, oxygen saturation was 70% on room air, and her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 4. She was intubated emergently and transferred to the intensive care unit.

On examination, jugular venous distention was noted, bilateral crackles were present, and breath sounds were decreased at the left lung base. Pupils were reactive without anisocoria. There was no evidence of subcutaneous emphysema, trauma, or deformity of the neck or chest wall.

Chest radiography and computed tomography revealed pneumomediastinum, atelectasis of the left lower lobe, and leftward mediastinal shift. Electrocardiography was unremarkable, and echocardiography could not visualize the heart due to extensive mediastinal air. A brain CT and MRI showed no intracranial abnormalities.

A left-sided chest tube was placed, immediately releasing air, and it was removed on hospital day 4 without recurrent air leak.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Pneumomediastinum: A case report of baclofen toxicity

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman presented with multiple nontender palpable lumps in both breasts and diplopia of the left eye. Thirteen months earlier, she had been diagnosed with primary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the epidural soft tissue at the C6–T1 level and of the stomach; at that time, bone marrow biopsy showed normocellular marrow with 6.2% plasma cells, no bone lesions, no end-organ damage, and no monoclonal protein. She received 12 cycles of melphalan and prednisolone and localized radiotherapy, with no recurrence on surveillance MRI and CT for one year. 

Breast ultrasonography revealed multiple well-defined, oval, markedly hypoechoic masses in both breasts. Mammography showed multiple circumscribed or obscured, oval or round, hyperdense masses bilaterally. Breast MRI demonstrated multiple well-defined, oval or round, strongly enhancing masses with iso- to high signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images; diffusion-weighted imaging showed high signal intensity with low apparent diffusion coefficient values, indicating restricted diffusion. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI revealed massive (780%) initial enhancement with a delayed washout kinetic curve, suggestive of malignancy.
title: Imaging Findings of Plasmacytoma of Both Breasts as a Preceding Manifestation of Multiple Myeloma

case_prompt: A 6-year-old boy born to a second-degree consanguineous couple presented with speech regression, poor social interaction, and aggressive behavior. He had delayed cry at birth and was hospitalized for diarrhea at 9 months. At age 2.5 years, he lost previously acquired speech. At age 4 years, he was treated for tuberculosis. He was referred for suspected syndromic autism spectrum disorder. An EEG showed intractable epileptiform activity originating in the left occipital hemisphere with spread and diffuse right-hemisphere damage. Brain MRI revealed mild thinning of the posterior body of the corpus callosum without cerebral or cerebellar atrophy. On examination, he was nonverbal, restless, and had ichthyosis over his legs, back, and abdomen; there was no facial dysmorphism. Primary investigations, including karyotype and Fragile-X testing, were normal. Leukocyte enzyme assays showed low arylsulfatase-A activity (0.08 nmol/hr/mg protein; reference 0.6–4.99) and low arylsulfatase-B activity (0.23 nmol/hr/mg protein; reference 0.61–9.6), with normal beta-galactosidase activity.
title: Late infantile form of multiple sulfatase deficiency with a novel missense variant in the SUMF1 gene: case report and review

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman, a high-risk BRCA gene carrier with a history of left breast cancer treated 5 years ago (wide local excision and radiotherapy), underwent her annual screening MRI. On MRI, there was a 12 × 7 mm lesion in the lower central aspect of the right breast with Type 3 enhancement, classified as MRI 4 (BI-RADS 4B). No abnormal axillary lymph nodes were seen.

She was recalled for further assessment. A screening mammogram revealed a new 14 mm asymmetric density in the lower central right breast that persisted on tomosynthesis (M4, BI-RADS 4B). 

Ultrasound of the right breast showed an 8 × 7 mm necrotic hypoechoic lesion with irregular contours in the 6A position (U5, BI-RADS 5) and an unchanged benign fibroadenoma at 3 o’clock. Ultrasound also identified right axillary lymph nodes with eccentrically thickened cortices up to 5 mm (above the institution’s normal of 2.3 mm), measuring 9 × 19 mm; the fatty hilum was preserved and there was no increased cortical vascularity.

On directed questioning, she reported receipt of her first dose of the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine in her right arm 3 days before this assessment (after the MRI).
title:
Axillary lymphadenopathy in a high-risk breast screening patient
following the COVID-19 vaccine: a diagnostic conundrum

case_prompt:
An 80-year-old woman with a remote central facial fracture in childhood presented in May 2014 with progressive right eye bulging and epiphora. She had previously undergone partial resection of a right orbital/nasal bridge/sinus bony tumor in 1999 and again in 2010. Histopathology from 2010 reportedly showed “dense hyalinized and myxoid fibrous tissue associated with cartilage and bone, consistent with fibroma of the cortex of the orbital bone, and was not suspicious of malignancy.” 

On examination in 2014, she had 3 mm of right axial globe proptosis, 2 mm of right hypoglobus, complete right nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and a palpable bony prominence spanning the right medial orbit across the nasal root to the left medial orbit. Visual acuity was 20/25 bilaterally; intraocular pressures were 21 mm Hg (right) and 22 mm Hg (left). 

Non-contrast CT of the orbits demonstrated a well-circumscribed 20 × 36 mm lobular ossified mass extending from the right ethmoid sinus and medial orbital wall to the left nasal bone. In October 2014, she underwent partial resection, restoring normal bony contours and alleviating proptosis. Histology showed “cartilage with endochondral ossification with mature trabeculae of bone and osteoid without mitotic activity,” consistent with benign sino-orbital osteochondroma.

In June 2015, tumor progression caused diplopia and difficulty wearing spectacles. The patient elected repeat debulking, and histology again demonstrated benign osteochondroma. She remained asymptomatic until May 2018, when she returned with renewed diplopia. Vision was 20/40 bilaterally with full motility. Repeat CT showed a 42 × 39 × 25 mm bony lesion involving the right orbit, ethmoid sinus, frontal sinus, and floor of the anterior cranial fossa.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Sino-orbital osteochondroma with malignant transformation to osteosarcoma

case_prompt: A 1½-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of high-grade fever without chills, continuous abdominal pain, and abdominal distension. He had several episodes of non-bilious, non-projectile vomiting. His medical and surgical histories were unremarkable. On examination, temperature was 101°F, pulse 100/min, and respiratory rate 30/min. The abdomen exhibited generalized rigidity and guarding; bowel sounds were audible and no palpable masses were noted. A clinical diagnosis of acute peritonitis was made. Plain abdominal radiography was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 4 cm × 5 cm cystic structure in the left hypochondrium and epigastrium. After initial stabilization, an urgent laparotomy was planned.
title: Gastric Duplication Cyst Presenting as Acute Abdomen: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man presented to the emergency department with diffuse body pain of 2 hours’ duration. He described severe (10/10) abdominal pain, worsening at his usual sites of metastasis—including the jaw, bilateral scapulae, chest wall, and left inguinal region—and unrelieved by his home analgesics. His medical history was notable for hypothyroidism and metastatic melanoma (brain, lung, liver, and bone); he had completed seven cycles of carboplatin–paclitaxel several months earlier, with recent disease progression.  

Home medications included temozolomide, esomeprazole, acetylcysteine, atorvastatin, dexamethasone, gabapentin, levetiracetam, levothyroxine, magnesium lactate–pyridoxine, metoclopramide, ondansetron, oxycodone, and sitagliptin–metformin.  

On examination, he appeared ill and in pain but was alert and oriented. Vital signs were: temperature 37.3°C, blood pressure 126/96 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats per minute, and SpO2 95% on room air. Cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse tenderness without peritoneal signs.  

Initial laboratory tests showed a WBC count of 8824/mm3 (64% neutrophils), RBC count 2.84 million/mm3, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL (down from 12.5 g/dL one month earlier), hematocrit 25%, MCV 89.7 fl, and platelets 107,000/mm3. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated left-shifted granulocytes, polychromasia, many spherocytes, rare target cells, elliptocytes, schistocytes, and multiple dehemoglobinized “ghost cells”; the direct antiglobulin test was negative.  

Chemistry results included creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, BUN 37 mg/dL, total bilirubin 5.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 235 IU/L, AST 662 IU/L, ALT 24 IU/L, and lipase <3 U/L. Coagulation studies showed an aPTT of 42 seconds, PT 25.7 seconds, and INR 2.1. Serum lactate was 11.6 mmol/L.  

A Foley catheter yielded dark red/black urine, and venous blood samples were repeatedly grossly hemolyzed and dark in color. An arterial blood gas showed pH 7.20, PaCO2 34.8 mmHg, PaO2 87.1 mmHg, bicarbonate 13 mmol/L, SaO2 99%, carboxyhemoglobin 4.4%, methemoglobin 4.9%, hemoglobin 6.1 g/dL, and lactate 10.9 mmol/L.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed new metastatic hepatic lesions, peritoneal and lymph node disease, but no intraabdominal collections or hemorrhage.
title: Black Urine and Methemoglobinemia in the Setting of Sepsis Due to Clostridium Perfringens

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman with no known medical history presented with 4 hours of continuous right lower quadrant abdominal pain. She described the pain as dull, deep, 9/10 in severity, without gastrointestinal or genitourinary symptoms. She smokes at least 10 cigarettes per day and takes occasional NSAIDs for tension headaches.
