On examination, her blood pressure was 200/104 mm Hg. She had severe right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding.  

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 16×10^9/L (predominantly granulocytic) and a serum creatinine of 1.23 mg/dL (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m^2). Complete blood count, liver function tests, coagulation studies, and lipase were otherwise normal.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a right renal extracapsular hematoma measuring approximately 4.5×9.0×15.3 cm with an area of hypodensity concerning for active extravasation. The right kidney measured 10.4 cm in length; the left measured 10.9 cm.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Renal Artery Rupture in Association With Fibromuscular Dysplasia

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old male presented with a slowly enlarging swelling over the volar aspect of his left hand. The lesion began as a peanut-sized nodule and progressively involved the palm—from the distal forearm at the wrist to the thenar eminence and the bases of the second, third, and fourth digits—over an unspecified period. He reported periodic episodes of tingling and paresthesia in those same fingers. There was no history of trauma. On examination, there was an irregular fusiform swelling extending from the ulnar aspect of the left wrist to the thenar eminence and base of the second through fourth digits. The consistency was softer over the ulnar side and firmer over the third and fourth metacarpals. The overlying skin was pinchable and nonadherent. Neurologic examination revealed no motor weakness or sensory loss. Wrist motion demonstrated terminal restriction of palmar and dorsiflexion. No other lesions were present.

Noncontrast MRI of the left hand showed gross thickening of the median nerve. There was diffuse lipomatous tissue—hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and hypointense on SPAIR—interdigitating between prominent thickened nerve fascicles (hypointense on T1 and T2) in a coaxial cable–like pattern. This involvement extended from the distal forearm through the distal metacarpal regions of the second to fourth digits, with compression and displacement of flexor tendons and convex deformation of the carpal tunnel retinacular sheath. Lipomatous tissue tracked into the second and third intermetacarpal spaces. There were no focal osseous lesions, and the tendons appeared normal in signal intensity.
title: Fibrolipomatous Hamartoma of Median Nerve – A Diagnostic Challenge

case_prompt: A 59-year-old man presented with acute onset of chest pain. Two years earlier, he had undergone complete resection and postoperative radiotherapy for tongue cancer, with no recurrence over the past three years. He had no history of diabetes, hypertension, or cardiovascular disease. On arrival, he was in no distress. Vital signs were: blood pressure 130/75 mmHg, pulse 75 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm with ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V6, findings compatible with acute anterior wall myocardial infarction. He underwent immediate coronary angiography, which revealed only noncritical stenoses in the coronary arteries. A chest radiograph showed clear lung fields and a mildly dilated cardiac silhouette.
title: Electrocardiographic changes in right ventricular metastatic cardiac tumor mimicking acute ST elevation myocardial infarction: A case of misdiagnosis

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old woman presented with a tender 2-week history of a right upper neck lump. She reported a mild fever but denied appetite or weight loss, night sweats, cough, chest pain, nasal obstruction or otologic symptoms, and had no known tuberculosis exposure. She had been treated empirically with amoxicillin for presumed cervical lymphadenitis without improvement.

On examination, there was a firm, mildly tender 1.5 × 1.0 cm right upper cervical lymph node. Nasal endoscopy revealed an irregular mass with yellowish secretions, nearly obliterating both fossae of Rosenmüller; the remainder of the ear, nose and throat examination was normal.

Ultrasound of the neck showed multiple hypoechoic lymph nodes bilaterally with distortion of the fatty hilum. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the neck node demonstrated atypical cells with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei and irregular nuclear membranes in a background of abundant lymphoid cells and red blood cells; Ziehl–Neelsen staining was negative for acid-fast bacilli.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the nasopharynx and neck showed a heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass (2.0 × 1.4 × 3.9 cm) obliterating both fossae of Rosenmüller and extending into the upper oropharynx, along with multiple homogenously enhancing cervical nodes bilaterally. The apical lung fields showed minimal consolidation and centrilobular nodules with a tree-in-bud pattern.
title:
Diagnostic dilemma in a patient with nasopharyngeal tuberculosis: A
case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old Caucasian woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, resistant hypertension, and diastolic congestive heart failure with preserved ejection fraction presented to nephrology with acute kidney injury. Five years earlier, she had a pacemaker placed for sick sinus syndrome. Three months before presentation, she was diagnosed with recurrent atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and was started on amiodarone and chlorthalidone.

Her baseline serum creatinine had ranged from 1.2 to 1.7 mg/dL; on presentation it was 3.88 mg/dL. She noted a new pruritic rash on her chest, arms, and legs that began three months after initiation of the two drugs. She had a prior rash with hydrochlorothiazide and reacted similarly to chlorthalidone.

Her home medications included apixaban, atorvastatin, cholecalciferol, clonidine, fexofenadine, insulin glargine, labetalol, latanoprost eye drops, nifedipine, and topical triamcinolone for the rash. Blood pressure had improved from 159/66 mmHg at drug initiation to 120–140/80 mmHg.

Laboratory evaluation showed:  
• Liver enzymes normal (ALT 22, AST 25, ALP 67, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL).  
• Thyroid studies: TSH 8.1 μIU/mL, free T3 283 pg/dL, free T4 1.6 ng/dL (subclinical hypothyroidism).  
• Serologies: ANA 1:160 homogeneous; anti–double-stranded DNA 874 IU/mL; anti-histone 2.0 units; anti–smooth muscle antibody 1:160; negative anti-RNP, anti-Smith, SSA, SSB, rheumatoid factor, scleroderma antibodies, Jo-1, anti-CCP, thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and ANCA; borderline anticardiolipin IgG 16 GPL.  
• Urinalysis: moderate baseline proteinuria (0.6 g protein/g creatinine, unchanged), red blood cells increased from 1 to 9 per high-power field, white blood cells increased from 4 to 13 per high-power field, no urinary or peripheral eosinophils.
title:
Acute interstitial nephritis and drug-induced systemic lupus
erythematosus due to chlorthalidone and amiodarone: A case
report

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old man with no significant medical or family history underwent curative proximal sigmoidectomy for tubular adenocarcinoma (stage T3N0M0, Stage IIA). Postoperative CEA normalized from 11.0 to 3.3 ng/mL, and no adjuvant chemotherapy was given.  
Twelve months after surgery, CEA rose to 9.0 ng/mL; CT and colonoscopy showed no recurrence. Three months later, CEA further increased to 17.2 ng/mL. PET-CT revealed abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the rectum.  
Repeat colonoscopy showed a submucosal tumor–like lesion 10–15 cm from the anal verge; biopsy revealed tubular adenocarcinoma. CT and PET-CT identified no lymph node or distant metastases.  
Under the differential diagnosis of an atypical primary rectal cancer versus a rare intramural recurrence, the patient underwent curative low anterior resection with tumor-specific mesorectal excision and a 3 cm distal margin.
title: Intramural cancer recurrence in the rectum after curative surgery for proximal sigmoid colon cancer: a case report

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old man was referred with 20 days of progressive dyspnea and generalized edema. He was hemodynamically stable (heart rate 72 beats/min, sinus rhythm), well perfused, with jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, a systolic murmur at the tricuspid area, voluminous ascites, and marked peripheral edema. His BMI was 27.8 kg/m2. On admission, transthoracic echocardiography showed right ventricular systolic dysfunction (fractional area change 33%), severe tricuspid regurgitation (vena contracta 14 mm), preserved left ventricular function, a normally functioning aortic bioprosthesis, and a cardiac index of 8.0 L/min/m2. A TTE 9 months earlier had been normal. His history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, chronic alcoholism, low meat intake with weight loss over 6 months, aortic valve bioprosthesis, and coronary bypass grafting. 

Investigations included 3D transesophageal echocardiography, which confirmed severe tricuspid regurgitation (effective regurgitant orifice area 0.94 cm2, regurgitant volume 59 mL) and tricuspid annular dilation (44 mm) with hepatic vein flow reversal. Pulmonary scintigraphy was performed; cardiac magnetic resonance excluded myocarditis and myocardial ischemia by showing an unspecific nonischemic delayed enhancement pattern. Right and left heart catheterization demonstrated grafts with normal flow, no obstructive lesions, pulmonary artery pressure 55/13 mm Hg (mean 27), and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 13 mm Hg. Laboratory tests revealed acute kidney injury (KDIGO stage 2), lactate 1.0 mmol/L, normal thyroid function, serum thiamine 34.2 μg/L (reference 32–82 μg/L), and ascitic fluid with a serum–ascites albumin gradient ≥1.1.
title: Reversible Tricuspid Regurgitation Due to Beriberi

case_prompt: A 36‐year‐old man presented to the emergency department with multiple fluid‐filled blisters over his body for more than one month. The first blister appeared in his mouth, causing dysphagia, and subsequently the lesions spread extensively to his scalp, face, neck, chest, arms (including axillae), back, groin, genitals, and lower limbs. He reported a 4–5‐year history of persistent silvery, scaly, pruritic lesions on his scalp, which he treated as dandruff without improvement. On examination, he appeared cachectic; vital signs were within normal limits. Most blisters were ruptured, some were bleeding or had a putrid pustular discharge, and many were smeared with a foul‐smelling greenish‐brown paste. Unruptured blisters exhibited a positive Nikolsky's sign. The patient admitted applying cow dung, urine, and local herbs to his wounds for nine days. Laboratory testing showed a moderately elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and mild anemia; total leukocyte count, PT/INR, liver and renal function tests, and blood glucose were within normal ranges. The patient declined skin biopsy.
title: Delayed diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris in rural Nepal due to healthcare inaccessibility and harmful traditional practices: A case report

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 3 days of intermittent epigastric and central abdominal pain radiating to the back, worse after eating, associated with one episode of vomiting. She appeared well, alert, and oriented; vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination showed a non-distended, soft abdomen with mild epigastric tenderness. Initial laboratory tests revealed white cells 16.7×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 2 mg/L, hemoglobin 132 g/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, amylase 62 IU/L, and platelets 139×10^9/L (baseline 175×10^9/L). Lactate peaked at 7 mmol/L but normalized with fluids. She had no prior thromboembolism or heparin exposure and no family history of clotting disorders; she did report five previous spontaneous pregnancy losses that were not further investigated.  
Urgent CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed equivocal duodenitis and minimal peripancreatic fat stranding. Empirical IV piperacillin–tazobactam, gentamicin, omeprazole, and analgesics were started. On hospital day 1, oesophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed mild duodenitis in D1; duodenal biopsies were normal. Over the next 5 days, the platelet count fell to 11×10^9/L. Fibrinogen was 4.2 g/L, and there was no splenomegaly on imaging. It then emerged that she had received the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine 8 days before presentation; her D-dimer was 24,000 mcg/L.
title: Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage with renal infarction after ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 AstraZeneca vaccination

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a sensation of pelvic heaviness. She had no relevant medical or family history, and her menstrual cycles were regular. On physical examination, no abnormalities were noted.

Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated an oval, lobulated, well-demarcated mass of mixed echogenicity. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed a moderately enhancing pelvic mass.

At laparotomy, the mass was pseudo-encapsulated, regular in shape, and showed no invasion into surrounding tissues. A complete local resection was performed. On gross examination, the tumor measured 15 cm in its longest axis, was well demarcated without a true capsule, and had a yellowish-white, homogeneous cut surface without hemorrhage or necrosis.

Microscopic examination revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with alternating hypercellular and hypocellular edematous areas containing abundant thin-walled blood vessels. The tumor cells were spindle-shaped with fine chromatin, and no mitotic figures were identified.
title: Pelvic angiomyofibroblastoma: an unusual case report

case_prompt:
An 80-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after an episode of syncope and dizziness; he had awakened on the floor earlier that morning. He denied headache or neck pain but reported dysphagia.  
His medical history included atrial fibrillation on sotalol (warfarin stopped 2 weeks earlier), two-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting, hyperlipidemia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and a known 4.8-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm under surveillance.  
On examination, temperature was 97.7°F, blood pressure 160/94 mmHg, heart rate 65 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He had a small left forehead abrasion and contusion, appeared awake and coherent, and had prominent soft tissue fullness in the anterior neck. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable, and coagulation studies were normal.  
Over the next 10–15 minutes, his dysphagia worsened, and the left anterior neck swelling progressed. Within 30 minutes, he developed increasing fullness on the left side of his neck and anterior chest wall without crepitus, became hoarse, and assumed a “sniff” position. Due to airway compromise, endotracheal intubation was performed without difficulty.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a large retropharyngeal hematoma posterior to the thyroid gland with active arterial extravasation thought to arise from the thyrocervical trunk. The hematoma measured 6.7 cm transversely by 3.2 cm anteroposteriorly, extended from the lower nasopharynx to the posterior mediastinum (total length, 25 cm), deviated the larynx anteriorly, and compressed the esophagus.
title: Life-Threatening Retropharyngeal Hemorrhage Secondary to Rupture of the Inferior Thyroid Artery

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of horizontal diplopia when looking to the right and a severe headache. One month earlier he had developed right-sided otorrhea and headache; the otorrhea transiently improved with empirical systemic and otic antibiotics, but the headache persisted. Five days before presentation his headache worsened, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Three days before presentation he noted binocular diplopia in primary gaze, worse on right gaze. The headache was constant, located in the right frontal and retro-orbital area, and radiated throughout the head. 

His medical history was significant only for a right radical mastoidectomy 30 years earlier; he remained lost to follow-up with persistent right ear discharge. On examination, otoscopy of the right ear showed mucoid discharge and granulation tissue in an inflamed mastoid cavity with a high facial ridge. The left ear was normal. Neurologic examination revealed an isolated right abducens nerve palsy; all other findings were normal.

Laboratory studies showed elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein, and leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance. Audiometry demonstrated moderate right mixed-type hearing loss. Ear swab cultures were negative for microorganisms, and a biopsy of the right external ear and mastoid cavity revealed only chronic inflammation.

A thin-slice, noncontrast CT scan of the temporal bones demonstrated partial opacification of the right middle ear and residual mastoid air cells consistent with chronic otomastoiditis, a defect in the anterolateral mastoid wall from prior surgery, and poor pneumatization of the right petrous apex filled with fatty marrow.
title: Gradenigo’s syndrome secondary to chronic otitis media on a background of previous radical mastoidectomy: a case report

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman presented with four months of mild lower abdominal pain, cramping, and bloating located primarily in the left upper quadrant, with occasional spread to the entire abdomen. The pain provided only temporary relief with defecation. One month after onset, she noted alternating constipation and diarrhea (diarrhea predominant), a sensation of incomplete evacuation, and changes in bowel-movement frequency. She denied bleeding, fever, weight loss, stress or specific food triggers. Physical examination and vital signs were normal. 

Her medical history included hypertension (on telmisartan), hypothyroidism (on L-thyroxine), hypercholesterolemia (on atorvastatin), and other chronic minor bowel and gastric disorders. There was no surgical history or family history of colorectal cancer. 

An initial diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome was made based on Rome III criteria. She received dietary advice per NICE guidelines and mebeverine hydrochloride 135 mg three times daily for three weeks. Laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal C-reactive protein, and normal stool studies. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable for the gallbladder, biliary tree, pancreas, spleen, and right kidney; the lower left kidney was poorly visualized due to overlying bowel gas. Because her symptoms persisted despite treatment, colonoscopy was ordered.
title: Foreign body ingestion mimicking irritable bowel syndrome: a case report

case_prompt: A 3-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of a whitish, clouded left cornea and vision loss for 1 week. There was no history of trauma, pain, systemic infection, or known genetic disorder. His development and systemic examination were unremarkable. The parents, of Turkish origin, were consanguineous. Under general anesthesia the sclera in both eyes appeared blue. Intraocular pressures were 8 mmHg (left) and 10 mmHg (right). B-scan ultrasonography showed a normal posterior segment without retinal detachment. Axial lengths were 22.1 mm (left) and 21.7 mm (right). Cycloplegic retinoscopy of the right eye disclosed –4.0 diopters of myopia and –4.5 diopters of astigmatism at 168 degrees; retinoscopy of the left eye was not possible. The left cornea exhibited full-thickness stromal edema with bullous epithelial changes; central pachymetry was 745 μm and peripheral was 550 μm. The right cornea was abnormally thin (central, 212 μm; peripheral, 308 μm) with topographic astigmatism (–4.5 D at 169 degrees) and an inferoparacentral stromal scar. Funduscopic views were normal. The combination of decreased central thickness with stromal scarring in one eye and acute corneal edema in the other suggested bilateral keratoconus with acute hydrops on the left, and raised suspicion for an underlying connective-tissue disorder.
title: Brittle Cornea Syndrome: Case Report with Novel Mutation in the PRDM5 Gene and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man underwent elective revision lumbar fusion for adjacent segment instability at L2/3. The intraoperative course was uneventful. In the recovery room, he developed a rapid decline in vigilance. He remained hemodynamically stable with normal oxygenation. Naloxone and benzodiazepines were administered without improvement. He was intubated for airway protection.

A noncontrast cranial CT scan showed effaced sulcal relief and hypodense regions in the basal ganglia, suggesting hypoxic brain injury. He was admitted to the ICU, remained cardiopulmonary stable, but did not awaken after sedation cessation. A cranial MRI demonstrated basal subarachnoid hemorrhage, significant cerebellar vasogenic edema, swelling of the posterior cranial fossa, tonsillar descent, and ventricular compression.
title: Pseudohypoxic brain swelling following cerebrospinal fluid leakage: a case report on rapid identification and multidisciplinary management

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a mass on her left frontoparietal skull that had enlarged over 2–3 months and caused radiating pain down the left side of her face. She reported no history of trauma. Her past medical history included arthritis, depression, and hypertension; surgical history was notable only for tonsillectomy and partial hysterectomy. She had a 60–pack-year smoking history. 

The lesion was nonmobile, tender to palpation, and measured approximately 3.3 cm in diameter. Primary care management had presumed a subcutaneous or sebaceous cyst and treated her with a 10-day course of levofloxacin without relief. 

Noncontrast CT of the maxillofacial region and brain, along with plain skull films, revealed a lytic lesion in the left frontoparietal skull. The patient was referred to oncology. On initial workup, the oncologist considered metastatic neoplasm versus multiple myeloma. A contrast CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a spiculated right hilar lung nodule measuring 2.4 × 2.4 cm and no other sites of metastatic disease. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation studies were negative. 

Neurosurgical evaluation demonstrated intact cranial nerves, normal motor strength, and preserved sensation in all extremities. MRI of the brain revealed a 2.8-cm lesion extending through the outer and inner tables of the left frontal bone with slight dural encroachment and minimal mass effect.
title: Lung cancer metastasis presenting as a solitary skull mass

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive peripheral edema, heavy proteinuria, and worsening dyspnea. One year earlier, a renal biopsy had shown nodular glomerulosclerosis, and she was treated with valsartan for 3 months without improvement. During this interval, serum creatinine increased from 0.8 to 1.7 mg/dL and 24-hour urinary protein rose from 1.51 to 2.19 g. 

On admission, blood pressure was 169/97 mmHg, heart rate 62/min, and BMI 22 kg/m2. Examination revealed bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs; there was no jaundice, rash, or lymphadenopathy. 

Laboratory studies showed BUN 23.25 mg/dL, creatinine 1.92 mg/dL, eGFR 29.5 mL/min/1.73 m2, albumin 27.9 g/L, and 24-hour proteinuria 4.71 g. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ protein, 40–60 RBCs/high-power field, and 40 WBCs/high-power field without RBC casts. Complement levels were decreased (C3 0.4 g/L [0.7–1.4], C4 0.04 g/L [0.1–0.4], C1q 121.6 mg/L [160–230]). Serologic tests for ANA, anti-ENA, ANCA, and anti-GBM antibodies were negative. NT-proBNP was elevated at 1304 pg/mL (normal <125) and high-sensitivity troponin T was 16.24 ng/L (normal 0–14). Tests for hepatitis B, C, HIV, and syphilis were negative.

Both kidneys were normal size on imaging. ECG showed sinus bradycardia and low-voltage QRS complexes in the limb leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, mild pulmonary hypertension, mild tricuspid and aortic regurgitation, diastolic dysfunction (E/e′ 15.3, E/A 1.7), a left ventricular ejection fraction of 53%, interatrial septal thickening, and a small pericardial effusion.
title: Long‐term renal survival of γ3‐heavy‐chain deposition disease complicated by heart failure: A case report

case_prompt: A 4-year-old boy presented with 2 days of central, colicky abdominal pain, 4 days of vomiting, decreased oral intake, and fevers up to 38.5°C. His surgical history included an uncomplicated appendectomy. On examination, his temperature was 38.5°C, heart rate 105 BPM, blood pressure 111/66 mm Hg, SpO₂ 100%. He had tenderness and guarding in the left hypochondriac and left iliac regions. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 3.2 cm mass in the left upper quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 3 × 2.5 cm cystic mass with thick enhancing walls in the mesenteric fat between colon and small bowel, homogeneous fluid content, and surrounding inflammatory fat stranding. A provisional diagnosis of abscess with an infected cyst or bowel duplication cyst was made.
title: A rare case of gastric duplication cyst in a male paediatric Caucasian patient: a case report

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old white man presented with a 3-week history of left flank pain radiating to the groin, accompanied by dark urine. His medical history included hypercholesterolemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and an episode of pancreatitis 20 months earlier, suspected to be related to statin use. He denied fevers, weight loss, and other urinary symptoms. 

On examination, his blood pressure was 177/89 mm Hg and heart rate 65 bpm. His abdomen was soft, with tenderness in the lower abdomen and both flanks; no skin or subcutaneous lesions were noted. Laboratory tests showed a normal full blood count and normal renal and liver function, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 82 mm/h, a C-reactive protein level of 36 mg/L, and an elevated serum IgG4 level of 3.26 g/L (reference, 0.08–1.65 g/L). Tests for rheumatoid factor, antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, PR3/myeloperoxidase antibodies, hepatitis B and C, HIV, syphilis, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were all negative.

A CT angiogram demonstrated extensive para-aortic soft-tissue changes around the abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries, causing left ureteral obstruction and moderate hydronephrosis of the left kidney. At this stage, an inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm was strongly suspected, with a differential diagnosis of aortitis versus retroperitoneal fibrosis. Also considered in the differential diagnosis were idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis, IgG4-related disease, malignancy, Rosai–Dorfman Destombes disease, and Erdheim–Chester disease.
journal: Journal of Vascular Surgery Cases, Innovations and Techniques
title: A case of IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis with significant involvement of the abdominal aorta—a clinical and diagnostic challenge

case_prompt: A 54-year-old man with a 14-year history of Parkinson’s disease (PD) was admitted for bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (DBS). His regimen consisted of levodopa 600 mg/day, carbidopa 125 mg/day, entacapone 1200 mg/day, and pramipexole 0.54 mg/day, all of which were discontinued 18 hours before surgery to optimize intraoperative testing. The DBS electrodes were placed uneventfully. Three hours postoperatively, he developed tremor, muscle rigidity, and a fever unresponsive to acetaminophen. Clinicians initially attributed these findings to PD and administered levodopa 200 mg three times daily via a nasogastric tube. Systemic and central nervous system infection were considered, but cerebrospinal fluid analysis, chest radiography, and blood and urine cultures were normal. Brain MRI showed no intracranial pathology and confirmed optimal lead placement. Twelve hours after surgery, he exhibited severe axial and appendicular rigidity, a coarse resting tremor, prolonged spasms of the extremities, a temperature of 40 °C, and blood pressure of 165/94 mmHg. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 19.4 × 10^9/L with left shift, a creatine kinase level of 1500 U/L with a normal CK-MB fraction, and normal cardiac troponin levels.
title: Malignant neuroleptic syndrome following deep brain stimulation surgery: a case report

case_prompt:
A 79-year-old woman with a history of atrial fibrillation (status post–left atrial appendage closure) was admitted for elective mitral valve replacement for asymptomatic severe primary mitral regurgitation due to anterior leaflet prolapse. One month earlier, echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 56% with normal chamber dimensions, and preoperative CT angiography revealed no coronary lesions. Her only home medication was acetylsalicylic acid. 

The patient underwent implantation of a biological mitral valve without intraoperative complications; intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography confirmed normal prosthetic function, and low-dose noradrenaline (0.05 μg/kg/min) was required after cardiopulmonary bypass. 

On arrival to the intensive care unit, she developed cardiogenic shock with cold extremities, oliguria, systolic blood pressure of 80 mmHg, metabolic acidosis, and elevated lactate. Vasoactive support with noradrenaline (0.1 μg/kg/min) and dobutamine (5 μg/kg/min) was initiated. An electrocardiogram showed atrial flutter at 150 bpm, which was electrically cardioverted; a subsequent ECG demonstrated inverted T waves in the precordial leads. Chest radiography revealed pulmonary congestion. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe LV dysfunction (LVEF 20%) with mid to distal diffuse hypokinesis, most pronounced in the anterior and septal walls, with relatively preserved basal segment contractility; the mitral prosthesis functioned normally. Urgent coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries. Troponin I was mildly elevated at 0.12 ng/mL (normal <0.08).
title: Takotsubo syndrome after mitral valve surgery: a case report

case_prompt:
A 9-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a right lower-thigh mass. Over the past 6 months, he had noticed a slow-growing, painless swelling on the anteromedial aspect of his right thigh. He had no history of trauma, pain, functional limitation, prior interventions, or significant family or medication history.

On examination, there was an approximately 10 cm × 6 cm oval, elastic, immobile, non-tender mass on the anteromedial lower thigh; the overlying skin was normal and sensation was intact. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the right lower thigh showed a poorly defined area of soft-tissue prominence along the anteromedial cortex of the distal femur without mineralization. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the right thigh revealed a 10 cm × 6 cm × 8 cm well-defined, lobulated lesion abutting the distal femoral cortex on the anteromedial side. The mass was heterointense but predominantly had the signal characteristics of fat on all pulse sequences, and it did not enhance after contrast administration. The lesion was sharply demarcated from the surrounding musculature.
title: Unraveling the Mystery of Parosteal Lipoma of the Distal Femur: A Rare Case Report

case_prompt:
A 33‐year‐old Gx patient was referred at 21 weeks for monochorionic twin pregnancy complicated by twin‐to‐twin transfusion syndrome. Her obstetric history included HELLP syndrome, intrauterine growth restriction, and a cesarean delivery at 31+2 weeks.  

At 21+5 weeks, she became anxious and hypotensive (BP 60/30 mm Hg; pulse 105 beats/min). On palpation, the uterus was tense without signs of contractions. Ultrasonography showed two viable fetuses with a normally implanted adjacent placenta and free intraperitoneal fluid. Vaginal examination revealed no bleeding and 1 cm cervical dilation. She received 2 L of crystalloid. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL (previously 9.1), prothrombin time 16.1 s, and fibrinogen 3.3 g/L. The initial differential diagnosis included threatening labor, uterine rupture, and placental abruption.

After placement of an epidural, cervical dilation progressed to 2 cm, but she remained hemodynamically compromised (BP 100/60 mm Hg; pulse 120 beats/min) despite a total of 4.5 L of fluids; GCS was 15. She then developed fever (38.1 °C) and was started on antibiotics. The differential diagnosis broadened to include uterine rupture, infected hematoma, and intrauterine infection. A CT scan of the abdomen was planned.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Uterine Rupture at 21 Weeks in Twin Pregnancy with TTTS and Previous C-Section

case_prompt:
A 21-day-old female infant, born at 38 weeks’ gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery (Apgar scores 9 and 10), was discharged home on day 2 of life. There was no family history of genetic disease and no prenatal abnormalities. The mother noted frequent post-feed vomiting that was initially milky but progressed to bilious vomitus despite anti-reflux positioning and medication. At 3 kg and 21 days of age, the infant was brought to the hospital with dehydration, jaundice, irritability, and marked abdominal distension. A nasogastric tube immediately returned large volumes of bilious fluid.  
Plain abdominal radiography demonstrated distended small-bowel loops. A contrast study showed complete failure of contrast progression beyond the proximal jejunum, suggesting a type I jejunal atresia (in membrane). After correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances, the infant underwent a supraumbilical transverse laparotomy. Intraoperatively, the only abnormality was a stenotic segment of proximal jejunum with a purplish hue; the remainder of the small intestine and colon appeared normal without additional areas of stenosis. A 7 cm segment, located 15 cm distal to the ligament of Treitz, was resected, and an end-to-end anastomosis was performed, along with placement of a post-pyloric jejunostomy tube.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Kaposiform hemangioma of jejunum in a newborn: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 35-year-old G2P1 woman presented 7 days postpartum with a 1-day history of right groin swelling extending from the inguinal canal to the right vulva. On examination, there was an ~8-cm longitudinal right groin mass with ill-defined borders, erythema, and tenderness; the mass was irreducible, and a cough impulse was absent. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a hyperdense, mildly enhancing serpentine tubular structure extending from the right adnexa through the inguinal canal to the labia majora, with surrounding fat stranding. Supplementary ultrasound of the right inguinal region revealed multiple hypoechoic serpentine structures with a “bag of worm appearance”; these structures were noncompressible, and no flow signal was detected on color Doppler, with no change in size on Valsalva maneuver or positional change.
title: Round Ligament Varicosity Thrombosis Presenting as an Irreducible Inguinal Mass in a Postpartum Woman

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old Mediterranean man presented with a 7-month history of recurrent headaches, left eye pain, blurred vision, and left-sided facial weakness. Over this period he lost 15 kg and experienced recurrent strokes characterized by right-sided weakness, dysarthria, and confusion.

On examination, he had left eye exophthalmos and a mass occupying the left nasal cavity. Neurologic findings included horizontal nystagmus on rightward gaze, an absent gag reflex, right-sided extremity weakness with hypertonia, and a positive Babinski sign.

High-resolution CT of the head demonstrated bilateral basal ganglia hypodense areas suggestive of chronic ischemia and a separate hypodense region in the left basal ganglia indicative of subacute ischemia. A coronal CT scan revealed an iso-dense expansile soft tissue lesion with internal calcifications centered in the anterior left ethmoid sinus, protruding into the left orbital apex, displacing the medial rectus muscle laterally, and obliterating the left frontal sinus.

Brain MRI with FLAIR sequence showed an abnormal hyperintense signal in the left cavernous sinus and a mass in the left ethmoid sinus extending toward the cavernous sinus.

An extensive vasculitis work-up was inconclusive.
title: Synovial sarcoma of the ethmoid sinus with extension to the cavernous sinus: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old man presented with a 9-year history of a right chest wall swelling. He first noted the mass as a small, painless bulge that gradually increased in size. There were no constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, fevers, or night sweats. He denied prior trauma, surgery, or family history of similar conditions.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. The right lower anterior chest wall contained a 5-cm, firm, nonmobile, non-tender mass without overlying skin changes. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal function, liver function, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were all within normal limits.

A chest radiograph at a local center showed a densely calcified lesion centered on the right ninth rib. Subsequent noncontrast chest CT revealed a large expansile, lytic lesion of the right ninth rib with radiating (“sunburst”) internal calcification and cortical destruction. He was referred with a working diagnosis of chondrosarcoma for confirmation and management.
title: Cavernous hemangioma of the rib mimicking malignant bone tumor: A case report

case_prompt: A 47-year-old man presented with two painless masses on the plantar aspect of the lateral side of his right great toe. The larger proximal mass had been present for 5 years and measured approximately 13 cm × 8 cm; the smaller distal mass appeared 1 year prior and measured about 2.5 cm in diameter. Both masses had grown gradually and now affected his gait and prevented him from wearing shoes. Examination showed the masses to be globular, tense but soft, free from the skin and underlying tissues, and transilluminated positively. Application of pressure caused the distal mass to slip under the edge of the proximal mass and nearly reduce into it. There were no other masses or abnormal skin findings, neurovascular examination of the toe was normal, and inguinal lymph nodes were not enlarged. Plain radiographs of the foot revealed soft tissue shadows without bony involvement. MRI was not available.
title: Solitary massive lipoma in the planter aspect of great toe presenting as two masses

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman with a 20-year history of relapsing polychondritis presented with acute shortness of breath and wheezing that began during a long-distance flight. In her 30s, she had been diagnosed based on bilateral auricular chondritis, nasal chondritis, ocular inflammation, and respiratory tract involvement. Her disease had been stable for several years on prednisone 5 mg daily and methotrexate 20 mg weekly; previous tapering of immunosuppression precipitated flares requiring high‐dose steroids. Her baseline exercise tolerance was good (MRC dyspnea scale grade 1).  

On examination, heart rate was 130 beats/min (regular), blood pressure 160/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. She had a prominent saddle-nose deformity, loss of cartilage integrity in both ears, and expiratory wheeze audible throughout both lung fields and over the larynx.  

A CT pulmonary angiogram showed smooth thickening of the cartilaginous portions of the trachea and bronchi with sparing of the posterior membranes; no pulmonary embolus was detected. Nasopharyngeal aspirate was positive for parainfluenza virus 3 RNA. Antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were both negative. Kidney function was normal (eGFR > 90 mL/min/1.73 m2), and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 13 mm/hr.
title: Relapsing polychondritis with large airway involvement

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman with hypertension and no history of hypoglycemic medication use presented with a one-month history of recurrent, non-comatose hypoglycemia relieved by oral glucose. Physical examination and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. During a supervised fast, her blood glucose fell below 50 mg/dL, accompanied by sweating and mental confusion. 

Endoscopic ultrasound identified a nodular lesion near the tail of the pancreas, suggestive of an insulinoma. Pancreatic MRI showed a small, well-defined, round mass contiguous with the pancreatic tail, with intermediate T1 and T2 signals, unrestricted diffusion, intense arterial-phase enhancement, and homogenization in the portal phase. 

Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a hypervascular nodule adjacent to the pancreatic tail that followed the same enhancement pattern as the spleen and demonstrated its own vascular pedicle.
title: Intra pancreatic accessory spleen mimicking pancreatic insulinoma: a case report

case_prompt: A 64-year-old woman with a history of left invasive lobular breast carcinoma (pT1cN3, ER 90%, PgR 80%, HER2-negative), treated with wide excision, axillary dissection, adjuvant chemotherapy and aromatase inhibitor therapy, presented for routine follow-up. She reported no thyroid-related symptoms. Physical examination revealed bilaterally enlarged, multinodular thyroid lobes. Thyroid function tests were normal. Neck ultrasound showed an enlarged gland with retrosternal extension; the right lobe was finely inhomogeneous, and the left lobe was entirely occupied by a large nodule with mixed echogenicity, cystic and colloid degeneration, and calcifications. Fine-needle aspiration of both lobes was performed. Smears from the right lobe showed only colloid and benign thyrocytes. Smears from the left lobe revealed two cell populations in a colloidal background: benign thyrocytes and a second population of small cells, dispersed or in loose aggregates, with a plasmacytoid appearance and occasional vacuoles.
title: It is no longer the time to disregard thyroid metastases from breast cancer: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old Iranian man with a 24-year history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus presented in January 2022 with a 3-month history of a large right-foot ulcer overlying the Achilles tendon. His medical history included heart failure with an ejection fraction of 30%, prior coronary angiography, and pacemaker insertion. He had been self-administering metformin 500 mg twice daily for the past 7 years and had scars from multiple previously healed foot ulcers.

On examination, he had a Wagner grade II, non-infected ulcer measuring 10 cm in length and 4.2 cm in width, with 9.5 cm of the Achilles tendon exposed beyond the sheath. The ulcer had minimal granulation tissue at its edges, and most of the wound surface was occupied by the tendon. An ankle-brachial index was 0.7, indicating poor perfusion. The patient had been using dry sterile gauze dressings, and the tendon was at risk of dehydration and necrosis. Surgical repair was considered but deemed unsuitable because of his cardiovascular comorbidities.
title: Successful treatment of a high‐risk diabetic foot ulcer by ozone therapy and collagen powder: A case report

case_prompt: A 54-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension presented with a mass in the anterior left thigh that had been slowly enlarging over 10 years. He recently noted a sensation of heaviness during walking and difficulty fitting clothing over the area. He denied pain, paresthesia, pruritus, or discharge and had no history of trauma, surgery, or radiation to the thigh. On examination, there was a large, dome-shaped, firm, nontender, nonpulsatile mass measuring approximately 24 cm × 15 cm, occupying most of the anterior thigh. The overlying skin was normal, and there was no regional lymphadenopathy. Distal pulses, sensation, and motor function were intact. MRI of the left thigh showed a well-circumscribed lesion measuring 90 mm × 150 mm × 215 mm arising from the anterior surface of the femur, extending from the inguinal region to the femoral condyles. The mass displaced but did not invade adjacent muscles. It was homogeneously hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images, contained focal internal calcifications, and there was no peri-lesional vascular proliferation, cortical bone erosion, or marrow invasion.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Giant parosteal lipoma of thigh: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old male presents with a 4-year history of a nonhealing, painful ulcer over the medial malleolus of the left leg. Over the past 8 months he has experienced pain and swelling of bilateral wrists, elbows, and knees with morning stiffness, and during the past 3 months he has had weight loss and yellowish discoloration of the eyes and urine. He reports intermittent fevers for 1 month. He denies rash, oral ulcers, photosensitivity, or bleeding from other sites. Two years ago he received blood transfusions and previously had a similar ulcer on the right leg that healed after repeated dressings.

On examination he is pale, icteric, and cachectic with a Marfanoid habitus and generalized lymphadenopathy; vital signs are stable. A single large ulcer with well-defined indurated margins and surrounding hyperpigmentation is present over the left medial malleolus, with lipodermatosclerotic change of adjacent skin. Multiple joints are swollen with a flexion deformity of the left knee, resulting in a painful gait. Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly are noted; peripheral pulses are intact and there is no sensory or motor deficit.

Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 50 g/L, total bilirubin 78.7 μmol/L (indirect 65 μmol/L), total protein 82 g/L, albumin 35 g/L, positive ANA, anticardiolipin antibody (36 arbitrary units), and lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 12 weeks apart; rheumatoid factor is negative, C-reactive protein is 44.6 mg/L, HIV and hepatitis B and C serologies are negative, reticulocyte count is 0.4%, Coombs tests are negative, and hemoglobin electrophoresis indicates β-thalassemia trait. Fine-needle aspiration of an axillary lymph node shows reactive hyperplasia. Radiographs show juxta-articular osteopenia of the wrists and bilateral sacroiliitis. Synovial fluid is inflammatory (5318 cells/μL, 90% neutrophils) with negative culture.

Based on this profile, an initial diagnosis of a venous ulcer and a differential diagnosis of a vasculitic ulcer were made; however, color Doppler ultrasonography of the lower limbs and abdomen is normal with no evidence of arteriovenous fistula or venous insufficiency.
title: Nonhealing Ulcer: Acroangiodermatitis of Mali

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old man presented with a painless, progressively enlarging swelling over the right upper back and shoulder. He first noticed the mass incidentally; it was painless at rest, with only mild discomfort during shoulder flexion and extension. He denied numbness, paresthesia, trauma, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, mobile, non-tender subcutaneous swelling without overlying skin changes, superficial to the trapezius muscle.

Noncontrast MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a lobulated subcutaneous lesion with fatty components. The soft-tissue portion was predominantly hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1-weighted images, with no aggressive features. The lesion was thought to represent a slow-flow vascular malformation, such as a hemangioma, and a vascular surgery consultation with contrast-enhanced MRI was recommended. 

Three months later, a postgadolinium MRI showed an avidly enhancing soft-tissue mass with non-enhancing fatty and septal components and no invasion of surrounding structures. The radiologic interpretation remained that of a slow-flow vascular malformation (hemangioma).
title: Dendritic fibromyxolipoma with intramuscular involvement: A case mimicking slow flow vascular malformation on imaging

case_prompt: A 49-year-old woman presented with a left lower neck mass of one year’s duration, noting rapid enlargement over the preceding two weeks. She denied symptoms of thyroid dysfunction. She reported new-onset pain radiating to the back of her left ear and dysphagia. She had no history of tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, the left thyroid lobe was enlarged (3 cm × 3 cm), and a level IV cervical lymph node was palpable. Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid mass reportedly showed papillary carcinoma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a soft-tissue–density mass arising from the inferior aspect of the left thyroid lobe, extending to the thoracic inlet and across midline to the right, with compression of the esophagus. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy was normal. The patient was scheduled for total thyroidectomy and left radical neck dissection.
title: Primary Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Thyroid: A Rare Entity

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman, 12 days after cesarean delivery for her first pregnancy, presented with a 3-day history of progressive shortness of breath, leg swelling, and orthopnea. Her prenatal course had been uncomplicated, and she had no known cardiac history. On examination, her pulse was 115 beats per minute, blood pressure 140/98 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and she appeared pale. Cardiopulmonary auscultation was normal. Abdominal examination revealed a Pfannenstiel scar with serosanguineous drainage; the uterine fundus was palpable below the umbilicus. There was grade II pitting edema of the lower extremities; the neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, hematocrit 28%, white-cell count 11,370/mm3, platelet count 645,000/mm3, and D-dimer 4722 μg/dL; prothrombin time and thrombin clotting time were normal. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia with repolarization abnormalities. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Clinically, she was diagnosed with gestational hypertension, postoperative anemia, and an intermediate pretest probability of pulmonary embolism; she received two units of packed red blood cells. A computed tomographic pulmonary angiogram showed no pulmonary embolism but revealed bilateral pleural effusions, mild cardiomegaly, and signs of pulmonary venous hypertension. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation, mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 47% and lateral wall hypokinesis, mild tricuspid regurgitation, severe pulmonary hypertension (PASP 68 mm Hg), and right atrial enlargement.
title: Reversion of Severe Mitral Insufficiency in Peripartum Cardiomyopathy Using Levosimendan

case_prompt: A 6-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of progressive, bilateral neck swelling. Six months earlier, a lymph node biopsy at a peripheral hospital had shown a lymphoproliferative process, and he had been treated with prednisolone (30 mg daily for 5 months) without improvement. On presentation, he was in fair general condition and denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, or other systemic symptoms. Examination revealed multiple firm, mobile, non-tender cervical and submandibular lymph nodes bilaterally, the largest measuring 8 × 10 cm, with biopsy scars and limited neck mobility; there was no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, white-cell count 17 700/mm3 (87% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes, 2% eosinophils, 2% monocytes), platelet count 548 000/mm3, sodium 129.2 mmol/L, magnesium 1.7 mg/dL, calcium 7.9 mg/dL, ALT 5 U/L, and normal values for random blood glucose, urea, creatinine, lactate dehydrogenase, alkaline phosphatase, coagulation tests, and serologies for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and SARS-CoV-2. Ultrasound of the neck revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes bilaterally, the largest measuring 46 × 26 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes at cervical levels IB through VI, bilateral supraclavicular and mediastinal regions, bilateral axillae, and retroperitoneum.
title: Rosai‐Dorfman disease in 6‐year‐old child: Presentation, diagnosis, and treatment

case_prompt: A 60-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and sarcoidosis fell at home and lay immobilized on the floor for 2 days before being found. On arrival she was tachycardic and hypotensive. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis of 39.44 K/μL, lactate 3.4 mmol/L, creatinine 2.65 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 55 mmol/L, and creatine kinase 527 IU/L. She was treated empirically for sepsis with vancomycin and ceftriaxone, received copious IV fluids for presumed rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury, and blood and urine cultures remained negative. Over the next several days she developed generalized edema. Seven days after admission she noted superficial skin sloughing beginning on the lower extremities, which progressed to involve the trunk, upper extremities, and head and neck. Physical examination revealed superficial desquamation of nearly the entire body with one focal erosion on the forearm, sloughing of the facial skin and oral mucosa, and bilateral conjunctival injection. Nikolsky sign was negative, and the patient reported pain of the skin and mucosa.
title: Among the mimickers of Stevens-Johnson syndrome: A case of anasarca-induced skin desquamation

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old Italian man presented with an 8-month history of persistent hoarseness and throat discomfort. He was a former heavy smoker with a 20-year history of COPD (never treated with corticosteroids) and hypertension; he denied travel outside Europe and had no known immunodeficiency. On examination, there were no skin lesions, hepatosplenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies, including HIV serology, were unremarkable.  

Five months into his symptoms, a flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy and biopsy revealed only mucosal inflammation and hyperplasia; he was treated empirically with amoxicillin without improvement. At re-evaluation, laryngostroboscopy demonstrated two well-defined, firm, whitish lesions on the true vocal cords with marked hyperadduction and a defect in the mucosal wave. A second biopsy of both vocal cords was obtained for further analysis.
title: Isolated Laryngeal Leishmaniasis in Immunocompetent Patients: An Underdiagnosed Disease

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman at 37 weeks’ gestation presented with a 4-day history of fever. On day 5 she became irritable, somnolent, and aggressive, and subsequently unresponsive to commands. Examination revealed T 38.5 °C, anicteric sclerae, no pallor, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9 (E2 V2 M5). Respiratory, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. There was no neck stiffness; Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs were negative. Cranial nerves were intact, and there were no pyramidal or extrapyramidal signs. Fundoscopy showed no papilledema.

Laboratory studies on admission:
- White cell count 9,000 cells/mm3; hemoglobin 10 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume 85 fL; platelet count 60,000 cells/mm3, falling to 8,000 cells/mm3; hematocrit 33%.  
- ESR 20 mm/h; C-reactive protein 4 mg/dL; LDH < 200 U/L.  
- Peripheral blood film: thrombocytopenia without microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.  
- Urinalysis: no proteinuria or hematuria.  
- Aspartate aminotransferase 25 U/L rising to 250 U/L; alanine aminotransferase 20 U/L rising to 250 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 300 U/L; total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL.  
- Renal function and serum electrolytes were normal.  
- Coagulation profile: PT 10 s, APTT 38 s, INR 1.2, fibrin-degradation products < 0.2 U/L.  
- Ultrasound scan: no pleural effusions or ascites.  
- Dengue NS1 antigen was positive on illness day 4; dengue IgM antibodies were high in titer by day 6.
title: A rare case of dengue encephalopathy complicating a term pregnancy

case_prompt: A 66-year-old man was transferred with intense abdominal pain and acute renal failure (blood urea nitrogen 178 mg/dL, creatinine 7.92 mg/dL) after receiving an estimated 3 mg/kg of amphotericin B deoxycholate for a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of nasal leishmaniasis. He had been HIV-positive for more than 10 years but was nonadherent to antiretroviral therapy; his most recent viral load was 92 494 copies/mL and CD4 count was 5 cells/mm3 (CD4/CD8 ratio 0.08). His only other history was gastroesophageal reflux disease; he was a former smoker. On admission, he was pancytopenic (hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, leukocytes 1620 cells/µL, lymphocytes 142 cells/µL, platelets 64 000 cells/µL). He was afebrile but emaciated, with a severe ulcer in the hard palate and an extensive necrotic lesion of the left nasal ala and septum; his voice was dysphonic. Chest CT showed bilateral pulmonary consolidation and small pleural effusions. Hemodialysis was initiated because of worsening renal failure. He received amphotericin B deoxycholate 5 mg/kg/day for 3 days, then liposomal amphotericin B 4 mg/kg/day for a total of 16 days. On day +16, he developed acute respiratory distress due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa sepsis, melena, and worsening blood dyscrasia, and was admitted to the ICU. A right scrotal ultrasound revealed a 3.2 × 2.5 cm thick-walled, multiseptate fluid collection contiguous with the epididymis. A diagnostic orchiectomy showed a swollen testicle with necrotic areas and fluid accumulation. He had an unfavorable clinical course and died a few days later.
title: Epididymo-orchitis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum

case_prompt: A 70-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 1-day history of memory deficits and personality changes. Her history included stage IV duodenal adenocarcinoma with liver metastases diagnosed one year earlier, complicated at that time by a right-sided pulmonary embolism and renal and splenic infarctions attributed to paraneoplastic coagulopathy. She was receiving palliative chemotherapy (fluorouracil, folinic acid, irinotecan, aflibercept) and anticoagulation with apixaban. On examination, she was afebrile, with normal vital signs. Neurologic testing revealed a left homonymous hemianopia; there were no cardiac murmurs or peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. Laboratory studies showed thrombocytopenia (62 G/l), elevated C-reactive protein (68 mg/l), hyponatremia, acute renal failure (creatinine 134 µmol/l), and troponin T elevation (627 ng/l); the ECG was normal. CT of the head revealed a solitary right parietal lesion without hemorrhage. Diffusion-weighted MRI showed multi-territorial bihemispheric cerebral infarctions, including a left occipital ischemic stroke corresponding to her visual deficit. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated thickened mitral valve leaflets with partial destruction of the posterior leaflet and an 11×6 mm mobile vegetation associated with severe mitral regurgitation. Blood cultures were obtained, and empiric amoxicillin–clavulanic acid was initiated. After 10 days of incubation, all blood cultures remained negative.
title: Systemic embolization due to non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis: An autopsy case report and mini review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old man presented with 2 days of nausea, recurrent bilious emesis, nonradiating epigastric pain, and upper abdominal fullness that worsened after meals. He noted mild postprandial discomfort for a week and endorsed a 12-lb weight loss over the preceding 3 weeks during Ramadan fasting. He denied prior emesis, postprandial pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer disease, or NSAID use. Bowel movements were normal.  
On examination, blood pressure was 103/62 mm Hg, heart rate 94 beats/min, respiratory rate 17 cycles/min, and temperature 36.8 °C. BMI was 18.2 kg/m2. There was mild epigastric tenderness with diffuse fullness; no peritoneal signs.  
Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 10,200 cells/µL, neutrophils 75.9%, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, hematocrit 45.0%, platelets 201,000/µL, and lipase 200 U/L; liver function tests, lipid panel, electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine were normal.  
Noncontrast abdominal CT revealed a massively dilated stomach and proximal duodenum with a transition point around the region of the superior mesenteric artery, an estimated aortomesenteric angle of 20° and distance of 6 mm, no free intraperitoneal gas, and no features suggestive of pancreatic inflammation.  
A barium upper gastrointestinal series with small-bowel follow-through demonstrated a markedly distended stomach and proximal duodenal dilation with a sharp transition point between the second and third parts of the duodenum near the midline in the region of the SMA.  
He was started on maintenance IV fluids and underwent nasogastric decompression, yielding 800 mL of bilious contents.
title: Diurnal Fasting During Ramadan Leading to Superior Mesenteric Artery Syndrome

case_prompt: A 76-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of fatigue, intermittent abdominal cramps, swelling in the left lower quadrant, and a 5-kg weight loss. Physical examination showed pallid mucous membranes and no palpable lymphadenopathy; her performance status was ECOG 1. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, hematocrit 24.6%, and a white-cell count of 9300/µL (72% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes); other blood chemistries, lactate dehydrogenase, and HIV serology were normal. A myelogram was normal. Colonoscopy demonstrated multiple polyps in the rectum, sigmoid colon, descending colon, and both colic flexures. A rectal biopsy showed lymphomatous infiltration of the intestinal wall, and the pathologic diagnosis was primary colorectal lymphoma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed no extraintestinal disease and normal liver and spleen. Thoracic CT was unremarkable. Gastroduodenoscopy showed no significant abnormalities. Owing to the large size of the polypoid masses narrowing the colonic lumen, the patient developed acute intestinal obstruction and was referred for laparotomy.
title: Extensive colorectal lymphomatous polyposis complicated by acute intestinal obstruction: a case report

case_prompt: A 58‐year‐old man presented with a 1‐month history of diarrhea, fever, weight loss, and pruritus. He had a history of orthotopic liver transplantation 12 years earlier and type 2 diabetes managed with tacrolimus and oral hypoglycemic agents. On examination, he was icteric and emaciated. Laboratory studies showed a total bilirubin of 15.9 mg/dL (direct 8.3, indirect 7.6), an alkaline phosphatase level of 2052 U/L, and mildly elevated gamma‐glutamyltransferase and aminotransferases. Viral serologies were negative. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated marked dilatation of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts and occlusion of the hepatic artery. MR imaging confirmed the arterial occlusion and showed peripheral hepatic infarcts. He underwent biliary drainage and received antibiotics for cholangiolitic abscesses, with transient improvement, but continued to have impaired liver function and recurrent episodes of cholangitis.
title: Very late hepatic arterial thrombosis manifesting as central biliary necrosis: A rare presentation

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman with polysubstance abuse history and generalized anxiety disorder presented with sudden onset of abdominal pain for 1 day. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 12.5 cm heterogenous, enhancing mass in the left adrenal gland with mild to moderate hyperdense fluid throughout the abdomen, consistent with prior hemorrhage. The patient was hemodynamically stable; heart rate was 112 bpm, blood pressure 114/92 mmHg, temperature 98.6 °F, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She denied histories of hypertension or diaphoresis but reported occasional headaches, palpitations, and an unintentional 10–15 lb weight loss over 4 months. She initially denied current substance use and was taking suboxone and bupropion; there was no family history of endocrine disorders.

On examination, she had abdominal distention, diffuse tenderness, and anasarca without cushingoid features. Initial biochemical tests revealed plasma cortisol six times the upper limit of normal, plasma metanephrines 25–30 times the upper limit of normal, and urine metanephrines 30–100 times the upper limit of normal. A urine toxicology screen was positive for amphetamines, and she then admitted to amphetamine use one week before admission. After two weeks drug washout, plasma cortisol declined by more than 50%, and urine metanephrines remained elevated at 20–40 times the upper limit of normal.
title: Giant Pheochromocytoma Diagnosis Confounded by Amphetamine Use

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 1, at 38 weeks and 6 days of gestation was referred for a planned Cesarean delivery because of persistent breech presentation. Her pregnancy was complicated by HIV infection, treated since the first trimester with emtricitabine, tenofovir, and raltegravir, and by depression managed with citalopram. Routine obstetric ultrasound examinations at 12, 20, and 30 weeks showed no fetal anomalies. At 36 weeks, a scan revealed mild unilateral pyelectasis (renal pelvic diameter 9 mm) and amniotic fluid at the upper normal limit (deepest pocket 7.5 cm).

At 38 weeks 6 days, a sonographic assessment to confirm fetal presentation showed:
– A 4.0 × 3.5 cm mass in the right scrotum that was mainly solid, with a regular wall, a complex echotexture, and a few small echo-free cystic areas.  
– No detectable blood-flow signal on color Doppler and no visible peristaltic movements within the mass.  
– No evidence of intraabdominal bowel dilatation.  
– The right testis was not identified; the left scrotum contained a mild hydrocele.  
– Breech presentation persisted; moderate polyhydramnios was noted (deepest pocket 12 cm).

Based on its rapid onset and the imaging features, a scrotal tumor versus hemorrhage from testicular torsion was considered, with torsion initially favored.
title: Inguinoscrotal Hernia, a Possible Cause of Rapidly Developing Fetal Scrotal Mass: Case Report and Literature Update

case_prompt: A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 10-year history of vulvar pruritus, burning, soreness, stinging, vaginal dryness, and introital dyspareunia. She had been repeatedly treated for presumed vulvar mycosis with topical antifungals without relief. Her medical history included arterial hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and two pregnancies delivered with episiotomy. On examination, the vulvar mucosa was pale and atrophic, with a glistening, u-shaped erythematous halo of the introitus extending from the lower right labia minora to the lower left labia minora, almost encircling the urethral meatus. There was no bleeding, fissuring, excoriation, exudation, or regional lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and urinalysis, were within normal limits. Clinical differential diagnoses included erosive lichen planus, genital psoriasis, lichen sclerosus et atrophicus, and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia III). A skin biopsy was obtained from the erythematous area for histopathological evaluation.
journal: Journal of Lower Genital Tract Disease
title: Zoon Vulvitis Treated Successfully With Platelet-Rich Plasma: First Case Reported

case_prompt: A 54-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction and mild epistaxis. She denied smoking, toxic exposures, and had no family history of neoplasms. On nasofibroscopy, there was an irregular vascular lesion occupying most of the right nasal cavity. A computed tomography scan showed a heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing mass displacing the nasal septum toward the left side. Under endoscopic guidance, the lesion arising from the nasal septum was completely resected; the ipsilateral septal mucosa and cartilage were removed as surgical margins, and the contralateral mucosa was preserved. The resected specimen consisted of multiple brown tissue fragments measuring 6.0 × 3.0 × 1.0 cm in aggregate, which were submitted for pathological examination.
title: Myoepithelioma of the Nasal Septum: A Rare Case of Extrasalivary Gland Involvement

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a two-day history of bleeding from her left breast. She reported a slowly enlarging growth on the left nipple–areolar complex over two years, which recently became ulcerated with serous discharge. She denied weight loss, fever, systemic symptoms, or risk factors such as excessive sun exposure, radiation, arsenic, or immunosuppression. 

Vital signs were within normal limits except for blood pressure of 164/85 mm Hg. On examination, there was a >10 cm fungating ulcerative mass occupying most of the mid and outer left breast with distortion of the nipple–areolar complex, open bleeding wounds, foul odor, surrounding erythema, and palpable left axillary lymph nodes. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a large heterogeneous enhancing mass in the left breast and mildly enlarged left axillary lymph nodes, with no evidence of distant metastasis. Brain MRI and bone scintigraphy were negative for metastatic disease. A core-needle (Tru-cut) biopsy of the mass was performed.
title: Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Female Breast Masquerading as Invasive Primary Breast Carcinoma: An Uncommon Presentation Site

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old Filipino man presented with a 6-month history of painless blurred vision and a white subretinal lesion centered on the optic nerve head in his right eye. He had been treated elsewhere with oral prednisone and five intravitreal bevacizumab injections for presumed inflammatory choroidal neovascular membrane, resulting in temporary resolution of subretinal fluid but not the mass; fluid recurred when steroids were tapered. His past history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, steatohepatitis, prior gastric sleeve surgery, and remote herpes zoster ophthalmicus without ocular involvement. 

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS; intraocular pressures were 9 mmHg OD and 10 mmHg OS. There were no signs of anterior uveitis, vitritis, or retinal vasculitis. Fundus examination OD showed a large white subretinal lesion peripapillary with speckled autofluorescence. EDI-OCT revealed a hyperreflective subretinal mass without choroidal thickening or macular edema. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated optic nerve hyperfluorescence, staining of the lesion, and blocked fluorescence at its margin without retinal vasculitis. ICG angiography showed absolute blockage by the lesion and multiple small hypofluorescent satellite spots. B-scan ultrasonography revealed an echodense lesion at the optic nerve head. Visual field testing OD showed an inferotemporal scotoma.

Laboratory tests including CBC, ESR, QuantiFERON Gold, autoimmune screen, syphilis, Toxoplasma, and Bartonella serologies were normal or negative. Serum ACE was 55 U/L initially and 82 U/L on repeat. MRI of the brain and orbits showed increased intraneural signal in the right optic nerve without optic nerve sheath tumour or glioma. CT chest revealed no hilar lymphadenopathy. PET scan identified metabolically active lymph nodes in the pulmonary hila, para-aortic, iliac, and inguinal regions and lesions in bone, heart, and liver. A core biopsy of a right deep inguinal lymph node showed non-necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis.

Three months later, vision in the right eye declined to 20/100 with new subfoveal fluid on OCT. Given persistent diagnostic uncertainty, the team elected to perform a 27-gauge pars plana vitrectomy and subretinal biopsy of the peripapillary lesion.
journal: International Journal of Retina and Vitreous
title: Subretinal peripapillary biopsy-proven sarcoidosis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man presented with four weeks of progressive dyspnea—initially on exertion, later at rest—and two weeks of pleuritic chest pain. He had a remote history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis but no prior cardiac disease. On arrival, blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, heart rate 114 bpm, respiratory rate 27/min, and oxygen saturation 84% on room air. Cardiac examination showed a regular rhythm, a diminished second heart sound, and a grade III holosystolic murmur best heard at the left upper sternal border. Lung bases had crackles; there was no peripheral edema or jugular venous distension. SARS-CoV-2 antigen test was negative. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 14.9×10^9/L, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm, complete right bundle branch block, and signs of right ventricular systolic overload. 

A noncontrast CT of the chest demonstrated fibroatelectatic tracts, traction bronchiectasis and pleural thickening, and a hypodense mass in the right ventricle attached to the interventricular septum. CT pulmonary angiography ruled out pulmonary embolism and instead confirmed a pedunculated intracardiac mass in the right ventricle. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a heterogeneous echogenic mass in the right ventricle. Transesophageal echocardiography showed a 36×46 mm heterogeneous mass with regular borders attached to the basal interventricular septum, causing dynamic obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and right ventricular dilation. A contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal and pelvic CT scan showed no other abnormalities.
title: From dyspnea to diagnosis, unmasking undifferentiated cardiac sarcoma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old woman underwent breast cancer screening during which she detected a left axillary, fingertip-sized palpable mass. She reported no breast masses or cervical lymphadenopathy. Her height was 147 cm and weight was 45 kg. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count and normal C-reactive protein level.

Screening mammography of both breasts was unremarkable. Ultrasound of the left axilla revealed multiple, markedly hypoechoic ovoid lymph nodes, some containing coarse calcifications. Targeted mammography of the left axillary tail demonstrated irregularly shaped macrocalcifications and dense tissue nodes.

Noncontrast CT of the chest showed a cluster of 12 well-circumscribed dense nodes measuring up to 3.0 × 2.8 × 1.7 cm, distributed around vessels in the left deep axilla, supraclavicular, and infraclavicular regions. Some nodes contained large and dotted calcifications; noncalcified areas measured 54–62 HU. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated homogeneous enhancement of these nodes to 98–102 HU. CT also revealed calcification in a right parabronchial lymph node and small pulmonary nodules at the right lung apex consistent with a primary tuberculous complex.
title: CT Findings of Axillary Tuberculosis Lymphadenitis: A Case Detected by Breast Cancer Screening Examination

case_prompt: A 5-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of a 2-month history of gradually increasing upper abdominal distension without pain or gastrointestinal or genitourinary symptoms. Her birth history was uneventful, and there was no maternal illness, radiation exposure, or drug intake during pregnancy. On examination, a firm focal bulge was palpable in the left hypochondrium and epigastrium. Abdominal radiography demonstrated a faint curvilinear bony structure traversing the midline, resembling an axial skeleton. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large heterogeneous solid-cystic mass in the upper abdomen with predominantly echogenic (fatty) content, linear echogenic structures casting posterior acoustic shadowing suggestive of calcification, and an encapsulated eccentric cystic component. A suspicion of infantile teratoma was given with differential diagnosis of fetus in fetu.
title: Infantile fetiform abdominal mass: Teratoma or fetus in fetu? A case report with insights into radiological diagnosis and surgical management

case_prompt:
An 80-year-old man presented with a swelling on the dorsal surface of the tongue that had recurred several months after superficial removal by a dentist. He reported intermittent bleeding from the lesion over the preceding five months. His medical history was notable only for hypertension, and he denied any other similar lesions elsewhere. 

On intraoral examination, there was a 1×1 cm oval, reddish, sessile, slightly indurated, and painless swelling in the midline of the dorsal tongue. A biopsy was performed. 

Grossly, the specimen was an oval, creamy-to-brownish, elastic soft tissue mass covered by epithelium, measuring 10×7×5 mm. 

Microscopic examination showed a relatively well-circumscribed nodular proliferation of mostly clear cells beneath the parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The cells were arranged in nests separated by fibrous septa and featured pleomorphic vesicular to hyperchromatic eccentrically located nuclei, clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm, sharp cell membranes, and a rich capillary network. 

Special stains showed negative mucicarmine staining and PAS staining that was highly focal. Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 7 was negative.
title: Metastatic Renal cell Carcinoma Presenting as a clear-cell Tumor in Tongue: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old woman (gravida 2, para 0, abortus 1) presented with a 12-hour history of diffuse pelvic pain and abnormal uterine bleeding. She reported six weeks of amenorrhea and a positive qualitative β-hCG test. One year earlier, she had undergone evacuation of a partial molar pregnancy, with an uneventful follow-up.

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. Pelvic examination revealed dark vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix. Laboratory tests showed a quantitative β-hCG of 15,000 mIU/mL, hemoglobin of 13 g/dL, and a normal coagulation profile. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a gestational sac with a yolk sac and a crown–rump length of 5 mm without cardiac activity, and a 12 mm area of trophoblastic detachment. The right adnexa contained a corpus luteum. She was discharged with plans for follow-up ultrasound.

She returned 24 hours later with heavy vaginal bleeding. Bedside ultrasonography suggested an ongoing hemorrhagic abortion and showed abnormal Doppler flow. A quantitative β-hCG level had risen to 25,000 mIU/mL. She underwent endometrial aspiration; the product appeared normal macroscopically. Five days after the procedure, she had moderate vaginal bleeding, a β-hCG level of 10,000 mIU/mL, and remained hemodynamically stable. Transvaginal Doppler ultrasonography revealed no retained products of conception but demonstrated a focal area of hypervascularity in the anterior myometrium with a mosaic pattern of multidirectional high-velocity flow (peak systolic velocity, 55 cm/s) and an empty endometrial cavity.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Uterine arteriovenous malformations as a rare differential diagnosis of abnormal uterine bleeding: A case report

case_prompt:
A 23‐year‐old woman with no relevant past history presented with a 3‐week history of daily fevers up to 39.4°C, profound fatigue, odynophagia, loss of appetite, and polyarthralgia involving the elbows, wrists, hands, knees, and ankles.
