She reported no photosensitivity, malar rash, muscle weakness, chest pain, or palpitations at that time. On examination, she was febrile (39.4°C) with mild swelling and tenderness of the wrists and interphalangeal joints. There was a diffuse, nonpruritic macular erythematous eruption appearing with fever spikes on the neck, trunk, and upper limbs. Initial ECG was normal. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (30,350/μl with 95% neutrophils), hemoglobin of 9.3 g/dl, CRP of 286 mg/L, ESR of 150 mm, and ferritin of 18,000 ng/ml. Liver function tests were normal. ANA, rheumatoid factor, and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody were negative, as were parvovirus B19 IgM, CMV, HIV, and hepatitis B and C serologies. Chest radiograph, abdominal ultrasound, and transthoracic echocardiography were unremarkable. She fulfilled Yamaguchi’s criteria for adult‐onset Still’s disease and was started on prednisone with resolution of her symptoms.

Two months later, off treatment, she redeveloped high spiking fevers, recurrent arthralgia, odynophagia, and a 3‐day history of persistent substernal chest pain and palpitations. On examination, she was febrile (39.4°C) with tenderness of the wrists, hands, knees, and ankles without synovitis. Blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg, pulse 96 beats/min, and cardiopulmonary auscultation was normal. There was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Skin examination showed the same macular fever‐related eruption plus fixed linear erythematous streaks in a flagellate pattern on the trunk, lower back, and abdomen. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm at 90 beats/min with a new complete right bundle branch block. Repeat blood tests showed leukocytosis (20,260/μl with 19,900/μl neutrophils), CRP 480 mg/L, platelet count 1,328,000/μL, and elevated high‐sensitivity troponin I of 849 nmol/ml. Cardiac MRI was normal. Chest CT angiography showed only minimal bilateral pleural effusion, without pulmonary embolism. An infectious etiology was excluded. Coronary angiography was normal. Serologies for parvovirus B19 IgM, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were negative.
title: Flagellate dermatitis: An atypical skin finding in adult‐onset Still's disease

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of disseminated, mildly pruritic papules that had progressively increased in number and distribution without regression. An earlier skin biopsy by an outside dermatologist demonstrated granulomas, and he was treated for presumed sarcoidosis with topical steroids and hydroxychloroquine without improvement. His medical history included lumbar spinal stenosis treated surgically and complicated by Pseudomonas osteomyelitis, for which he remains on lifelong ciprofloxacin, and remote bladder cancer treated with intravesical BCG. 

On examination, there were numerous, firm, nontender, erythematous papules 0.5–0.7 cm in diameter on the face, neck, trunk, and extremities. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. A repeat punch biopsy of a chest lesion showed a diffuse, nodular, nonepidermotropic dermal infiltrate composed of crowded histiocytoid cells with a minor inflammatory component of lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells, and rare eosinophils. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the lesional cells were positive for CD1a and S100 but negative for langerin (CD207).
title: Generalized indeterminate cell histiocytosis successfully treated with methotrexate

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on maintenance dialysis was admitted in January 2017 for living-donor kidney transplantation. Two days before the planned surgery he developed fever. Blood and urine cultures were repeatedly negative, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) and vasculitis markers were negative; C-reactive protein was initially normal. Ultrasonography showed bilaterally contracted kidneys without hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or ascites. Chest radiograph and whole-body PET-CT did not identify any focus of infection or malignancy. Because he also complained of severe back pain, magnetic resonance imaging of the spine was performed and showed discitis; transpedicular disc biopsy grew Staphylococcus aureus but was negative for tuberculosis. His fever resolved with six weeks of intravenous flucloxacillin and four weeks of oral rifampicin. 

When he was re-evaluated in August 2017, chest CT showed bilateral mild pleural effusions (left greater than right), moderately enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, left axillary lymph nodes, and small bilateral supraclavicular nodes. Repeat PET-CT showed mediastinal nodes with poor FDG uptake; both erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein remained elevated, and he had severe anemia. Excision of an axillary lymph node revealed vascular transformation of sinuses without evidence of infection or malignancy. Video-assisted thoracoscopic excision of a mediastinal node showed areas of suppuration, but all cultures were negative. He received eight weeks of intravenous antibiotics followed by six weeks of oral antibiotics. His persistent left pleural effusion was exudative but tested negative for tuberculosis and malignancy. He was treated empirically with antitubercular therapy until February 2018 without improvement, and left pleurodesis was planned.
title: Successful Renal Transplant in Castleman Disease - First Case Report from India

case_prompt: A 76-year-old woman underwent mastectomy for a low-grade ductal adenocarcinoma of the breast (stage T1 N0). Three months after surgery she noted visual deterioration in her right eye. Fundoscopy by her oncologist revealed a choroidal lesion that was presumed to be metastatic disease, and she received palliative external beam radiotherapy (20 Gy in five fractions) to the right orbit. Eighteen months later she was referred to ophthalmology for further evaluation. Corrected visual acuity in the right eye was 6/18. Dilated fundus examination showed an 11 × 10 mm elevated choroidal mass in the peripheral fundus, mainly yellow in color with some intrinsic pigmentation and no associated sub-retinal fluid. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated a mushroom-shaped lesion with choroidal excavation through Bruch’s membrane and low internal reflectivity. Fluorescein angiography revealed a “double circulation,” with intrinsic tumor vasculature and overlying retinal vessels. Examination of the left eye was unremarkable.
title: Concomitant primary breast carcinoma and primary choroidal melanoma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old woman with a 9-year history of Behçet disease presented in January 2024 with a 2-week history of progressive shortness of breath, palpitations, fever, and dry cough that began after a dental extraction. She has experienced exertional dyspnea for the past year and recurrent oral and genital ulcers. In 2021, she was admitted for hemoptysis and recurrent oral ulcers; CT pulmonary angiography revealed a right pulmonary artery aneurysm and a left subsegmental pulmonary embolism. She was treated with intravenous infliximab and low-molecular-weight heparin, with resolution of symptoms. At that time, CT angiography also showed a 2.0 × 1.8 cm filling defect in the right atrium, which was asymptomatic and managed with surveillance.

In 2022, she had a similar presentation; treatment was repeated, and CT angiography showed the right atrial filling defect had grown to 3.0 × 2.0 cm. In 2024, echocardiography revealed a mobile right atrial mass measuring 4.0 × 3.0 cm that appeared soft, irregular, and echogenic. A follow-up CT pulmonary and cardiac angiogram showed a decrease in size of the right interlobar pulmonary artery aneurysm but an increase in the filling defect in the right atrium to 5.1 × 2.7 cm. The lesion’s progressive growth prompted consideration of surgical removal.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Enigmatic odyssey: A case of Behcet disease with atypical thrombotic complications

case_prompt: An 88-year-old woman was admitted for hypoxemia from community-acquired pneumonia and COPD exacerbation. Medical history included COPD and remote tobacco use; she had no prior surgeries. She received antibiotics and pulmonary toilet; her WBC count fell from 18.3 K/µL on admission to 9.9 K/µL by hospital day 9, and her respiratory status improved. Late on day 9, she developed sudden right lower quadrant abdominal pain. On hospital day 10, she reported four bowel movements (one loose) with some improvement in pain. Physical examination revealed tenderness to light and deep palpation in the right lower quadrant over McBurney’s point. An abdominal X-ray was unremarkable. Repeat CBC showed WBC 16.4 K/µL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an 8.2 cm × 4.8 cm heterogeneous fluid collection in the right lower quadrant; the appendix appeared normal, but an intra-abdominal abscess or acute cholecystitis could not be ruled out.
title: Gallbladder Volvulus Presenting as Acute Appendicitis

case_prompt: A 65-year-old woman presented with 6 months of diffuse abdominal pain, weakness, and occasional vomiting of ingested material. She had undergone abdominal surgery at an outside hospital 6 months earlier, and the biopsy performed then was reported as suggestive of gastrointestinal stromal tumor. She denied abnormal uterine bleeding, oral contraceptive use, or gynecologic surgery. On examination, she appeared chronically ill, was emaciated and slightly pale, and had a long midline abdominal scar; there was mild generalized abdominal tenderness on deep palpation. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL, a white-cell count of 6900/μL, normal liver and renal function studies, and a normal chest radiograph. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed innumerable hypoechoic masses of varying sizes throughout the peritoneal cavity and a large hypoechoic lesion measuring 7.5×4.7 cm in the right lobe of the liver. At laparotomy, there were innumerable globular masses arising from the mesentery and the walls of the small bowel (some pedunculated, most sessile), a large mass in the right hepatic lobe approximately 8×10 cm, and a grossly normal pelvis. Multiple biopsies were obtained from the mesenteric and superficial small intestinal lesions; the liver mass was left untouched to avoid bleeding.
title: Leiomyomatosis peritonealis disseminata in postmenopausal women: a case report with review of literature

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man (BMI 24.8; heavy smoker) with asthma since age 19 and a history of hepatitis A 3 months earlier presented with one week of colicky periumbilical pain radiating to the lower abdomen and thighs, progressive abdominal distension, fatigue, fever (39.1 °C), anorexia, and 10 kg unintentional weight loss over one month. He also noted worsening dyspnea, lower-limb swelling, and severe pain with numbness in his upper back and both hands. He denied trauma, gastrointestinal bleeding, or diarrhoea.  

Past surgical history included adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy at age 2 and grade 4 nasal polyposis. He is allergic to NSAIDs and penicillin. At age 19 he was admitted to the ICU for exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and edema, diagnosed as pneumonia with atelectasis.  

On examination: barrel-shaped chest with diminished expansion and faint wheezes; hepatomegaly (liver span 20 cm); firm, rounded, nontender cervical and inguinal lymph nodes (1–2 cm); audible bowel sounds; marked bilateral exophthalmos; bilateral Raynaud’s phenomenon of the hands with bluish discoloration; absent right radial pulse and weak left radial pulse; normal lower-limb exam without blood-pressure discrepancies.  

Laboratory studies showed anemia; elevated serum IgE and IgG levels; raised inflammatory markers; elevated creatinine; positive rheumatoid factor and antismooth muscle antibodies; normal electrolytes, liver enzymes, thyroid function, serologies, thrombophilia studies, albumin, and tumour markers (PSA, CEA, AFP).  

A CT pan-scan revealed mild bronchial wall thickening with centrilobular opacities; hepatomegaly with a mottled enhancement pattern; small mediastinal, hilar, para-aortic (<6 mm), and inguinal lymph nodes (<12 mm). Sinus CT showed a paranasal sinus mucocele.  

Three months later, he developed 3+ proteinuria with creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Echocardiography showed a dilated left ventricle (6 cm), reduced systolic function (EF 40%), mild LV hypertrophy, mildly dilated chambers, and moderate aortic regurgitation. Heart-failure therapy with enalapril, spironolactone, and carvedilol was initiated.
title: Atypical Presentation of Kimura's Disease in a Male Patient: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old college student presented with a 3-month history of vague lower abdominal pain, generalized weakness, and a 1-month history of passage of stool per vagina. Two days before presentation, she noted a bulging mass in her vagina while straining, which ruptured and released purulent fluid followed by fecal matter. She denied any history of instrumentation, pelvic radiation, anorectal surgery, fever, cough, changes in bowel habits, weight loss, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Her menstrual history was unremarkable. She had undergone a failed fistula repair at another hospital, after which the fistula enlarged.

On examination, she was alert, afebrile, moderately pale, and in no distress. Vital signs were normal. There was no lymphadenopathy. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and without palpable masses. On rectovaginal examination, there was a single 2.0 × 1.5 cm fistulous opening in the mid-vaginal wall with surrounding granulation tissue; the margins were firm and fixed, and fecal discharge was evident. Anal sphincter tone was normal, and the rectal mucosa appeared intact. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L (52% neutrophils, 32% lymphocytes, 16% eosinophils). HIV-1 and HIV-2 tests were negative. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. She received parenteral hematinics, and under anesthesia a biopsy of the fistula margins and surrounding mucosa was obtained.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Rectovaginal fistula due to undiagnosed rectal tuberculosis in a nulliparous young woman: A case report

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old right-handed man was admitted with a five-week history of dull, global headache that was worse when supine and aggravated by Valsalva maneuvers, accompanied by nausea and frequent early-morning vomiting. He reported lethargy and a 5-kg weight loss over four months. He denied visual changes or other focal symptoms initially but soon experienced several transient episodes of sudden onset right upper-limb weakness and numbness lasting up to 15 minutes without loss of consciousness. 

His past history included right-sided uveitis six years earlier and childhood epilepsy treated with sodium valproate. Eighteen months prior, he developed renal impairment attributed to interstitial nephritis on valproate; this was managed with levetiracetam, prednisolone (weaned off weeks before this admission), and lisinopril. 

On examination, vital signs showed blood pressure 150/107 mmHg. The chest was clear and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic examination was normal except for brisk reflexes and bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy. Multiple diffuse, non-tender cervical and axillary lymph nodes were palpable. 

Laboratory studies revealed mild normocytic anaemia (Hb 11.6 g/dL), normal white-cell count, ESR, CRP, liver function tests, and serum electrolytes (including calcium). Blood urea was 7.1 mmol/L and creatinine 282 μmol/L. Tests for HIV, VDRL, dsDNA, ANA, ANCA, serum ACE, extractable nuclear antigen antibodies (anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-Sm, anti-RNP, anti-Scl, anti-Jo1), and tuberculosis (Quantiferon, Mantoux) were normal or negative. Serologies for HSV, CMV, EBV, and VZV were negative. 

A chest radiograph and CT of the brain were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed an opening pressure of 36 cm H2O, protein 0.74 g/L, glucose 2.9 mmol/L, 9 lymphocytes/μL, 72 erythrocytes/μL; it was sterile and had no oligoclonal bands. 

Brain MRI demonstrated multiple small T2-weighted hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter of both hemispheres and the right pons. Susceptibility-weighted imaging showed microhaemorrhages, and diffusion-weighted imaging revealed a small acute infarct in the left centrum semiovale. Repeat MRI revealed new linear T2 hyperintensities with postcontrast enhancement extending from periventricular regions into the centrum semiovale bilaterally. 

CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed multiple axillary lymph nodes up to 14 mm, as well as mediastinal and left para-aortic lymphadenopathy. 

A differential diagnosis of cerebral vasculitis, a neoplastic process, or granulomatous disease was considered.
title: Systemic Sarcoidosis Presenting with Headache and Stroke-Like Episodes

case_prompt:
An 82-year-old woman presented with symptomatic hypoglycemia (blood glucose 2.4 mmol/L), corrected to 6.8 mmol/L with IV dextrose. She had a three-year history of fasting episodes marked by dizziness, hunger, confusion, and visual changes, all relieved by glucose intake. She had no history of diabetes, other endocrinopathies, or gastric surgery. Medications: simvastatin and esomeprazole.  
On examination: blood pressure 130/60 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm, O₂ saturation 98% on room air. Abdominal exam: tenderness in the right upper quadrant but soft elsewhere without masses; cardiac, respiratory, and neurologic exams were unremarkable.  
A 72-hour fast produced a hypoglycemic episode (1.7 mmol/L) with elevated insulin (12 mU/L [<3 mU/L]) and C-peptide (1.31 pmol/mL [≤0.20 pmol/mL]). Sulfonylurea screen and insulin antibodies were negative. Cortisol peak during a short Synacthen test was 749 nmol/L (normal), and TSH and growth hormone were normal.  
Triple-phase CT of the pancreas showed a bulky body but no discrete mass. 68Ga-DOTA-octreotate PET/CT was negative. 68Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 (GLP-1R) PET/CT showed diffuse pancreatic uptake (SUVmax 6.3), “suggestive of nesidioblastosis in this clinical context.” Persistent hypoglycemia required dexamethasone, frequent meals, and dextrose infusions.  
Given ongoing fasting hypoglycemia, a selective arterial calcium stimulation test with hepatic venous sampling was performed. It demonstrated a >2-fold rise in insulin in the proximal and distal splenic arteries and gastroduodenal artery, “suggesting the presence of a hyperfunctional lesion in the body and/or tail region of the pancreas.”
title: Diagnostic challenges in a patient with an occult insulinoma:68 Ga‐DOTA‐exendin‐4 PET/CT and 68Ga‐DOTATATE PET/CT

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old girl was brought for evaluation of progressively restricted mouth opening and facial asymmetry. According to her parents, she was born with a normal facial appearance and adequate mouth opening. From age 2, they noted deviation of her mouth and gradual reduction in opening. There was no history of pain or confirmed trauma.

On examination, the lower third of her face was asymmetric: fullness on the right and a shallow groove on the left cheek extending from the angle of the mandible toward the ramus. On mouth opening, the chin deviated to the left. Bilateral preauricular skin tags were present (left more prominent). Intraorally, the dental midline was shifted left, with an overjet of 15 mm, and maximum interincisal opening was 2 cm. Palpation of the left upper buccal vestibule revealed a bony hard mass in the posterosuperior region, extending toward the infratemporal fossa.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the facial bones showed a roughly conical bony structure (3 cm × 1.5 cm) in the left infratemporal region, located anterior to the condyle and overlying the coronoid process; its apex extended medial to the zygomatic arch. The mass was not attached to adjacent bone. There was asymmetric development of the maxilla and mandible, with reduced anteroposterior growth and a smaller coronoid process on the left; the condyle appeared normal.

On the basis of the clinical and radiological findings, a provisional diagnosis of heterotopic ossification was made.
title: Heterotopic Ossification: An Unusual Presentation

case_prompt: A healthy male infant was noted at birth to have a congenital mass of the left lower eyelid. On examination at 37 weeks’ gestation (cesarean delivery), there was a 5 mm subcutaneous pedunculated lesion immediately inferior to the punctum of the left lower eyelid, with occasional mild epiphora and discharge. The lesion extended 3 mm above the lid margin, raising concern for amblyopia. A partially mucosalized demarcation line was seen on its superior surface. The remainder of the eyelid structures—including the punctum and medial canthus—were intact. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive; there was no afferent pupillary defect. The cornea was clear, the sclera and conjunctiva were normal, and extraocular movements were full with symmetric orbits. The fundus and the contralateral eye were unremarkable. Intraoral and general physical examinations were normal. Six weeks later, the mass remained unchanged, and the parents reported episodic tearing and discharge. To address lacrimal obstruction, prevent amblyopia, and improve cosmesis, the decision was made to excise the lesion and explore the nasolacrimal system.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Congenital tooth-bearing tumor of the eyelid leading to lacrimal system obstruction

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old Indian man with a history of defaulting on treatment for tuberculous peritonitis presented with acute onset of left ptosis and down-and-out deviation of the left eye. He had headache and meningismus. On examination, he had a complete left oculomotor nerve palsy. 

Laboratory studies showed cerebrospinal fluid with lymphocytic pleocytosis, a glucose level of 18 mg/dl (normal 45–80), an adenosine deaminase level of 23.3 IU/l (normal 1–9), and polymerase chain reaction positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. HIV serology was negative. Serologic testing for cysticercosis IgG was negative.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain at presentation demonstrated multiple small nodular enhancing lesions at the gray–white junction in both cerebral hemispheres with mild surrounding edema, involvement of the midbrain and pons, and leptomeningeal enhancement consistent with tuberculous meningitis and parenchymal tuberculomas. The patient was restarted on first-line antitubercular therapy with adjunctive corticosteroids, and the oculomotor palsy resolved.

One month later, MRI showed resolution of most parenchymal lesions but persistent basal meningeal enhancement; the patient reported ongoing headaches. He completed a 9-month course of therapy. Four months after treatment completion, he developed urinary incontinence over 2 months and had a single generalized tonic–clonic seizure.

Repeat MRI now showed multiple rounded lesions that were mildly T1 hyperintense and T2 hypointense relative to cortex, with ring enhancement and perilesional edema. These lesions were distributed in a racemose pattern in the bilateral insular cortices and sylvian fissures, and there were additional ring-enhancing lesions in the cavernous sinuses, pituitary region, suprasellar cistern, floor of the third ventricle, perimesencephalic cisterns, and quadrigeminal cistern, with parasellar meningeal enhancement.
title: A case report of racemose pattern of intracranial tuberculoma with brain stem and hypophyseal involvement developing paradoxically during treatment.

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old man with no history of skin or autoimmune disease presented with a six-month history of an intermittently itchy rash. The lesions began as light-colored macules on his wrists and gradually spread up his arms. He had applied triamcinolone 0.05% cream twice daily for several weeks without improvement. He denied any other medications or supplements.

On examination, there were porcelain-white, hypopigmented, atrophic macules coalescing into patches on the bilateral volar forearms, extending onto the dorsal forearms, and a solitary patch on the sacrum. Many of the macules contained central hair follicles and keratotic plugs resembling open comedones. Dermoscopic evaluation of the forearm lesions revealed hypopigmented macules with central keratotic plugs.

The differential diagnosis included lichen sclerosus, morphea, discoid lupus erythematosus, lichen planus, and anetoderma.
title: A folliculocentric variant of extragenital lichen sclerosus presenting in a 29-year-old man

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old woman presented with intermittent left-sided headache of >1 year’s duration. The pain lasted minutes to an hour, was sometimes accompanied by nausea and vomiting, and improved with rest. There was no history of dizziness, visual disturbance, seizures, sensory changes, or focal neurologic deficits, and the physical examination was unremarkable. 

Brain MRI revealed a dural-based soft-tissue mass in the right frontal lobe. The lesion was surgically excised. On gross examination, the formalin-fixed specimen measured 2.0 × 2.0 × 0.8 cm, was gray-white, smooth, and attached to the dura mater.

Microscopic examination showed a network of dense small vessels and thick-walled larger vessels, most with marked hyalinization, interwoven throughout the lesion. In focal areas, a faint “whirlpool-like” arrangement of tumor cells was noted. Scattered cells exhibited bizarre, large, hyperchromatic, and irregularly distributed nuclei. No mitotic figures were identified.

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the tumor cells were strongly positive for Vimentin and SSTR2A, with focal positivity for EMA and partial positivity for progesterone receptor. CD34 and ERG highlighted only the vascular endothelium, with no staining in tumor cells. GFAP, Olig-2, and HMB45 were negative. The MIB-1 (Ki-67) labeling index was less than 3%.
title: Angiomatous meningioma with bizarre nuclei: A case report

case_prompt: A 47-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of neck pain, 2 days of shoulder pain, right-sided chest numbness, and weakness of the upper limbs. He denied weight loss, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, or alcohol use. Neurological examination showed mild left facial weakness, hypoaesthesia below T4 on the right, normal muscle tone, upper-limb strength 4–/5, lower-limb strength 5/5, normal tendon reflexes, negative Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs, positive bilateral Babinski signs, and a left Hoffmann sign. Tests for viral antibodies, syphilis serology, and HIV antibodies were negative. Lumbar puncture revealed normal opening pressure; CSF had 10 red cells/µL, 220 nuclear cells/µL, protein 91 mg/dL, normal chloride and glucose, no oligoclonal bands, and no tumor cells. Flow cytometry of CSF showed no abnormal cell differentiation. Serum antinuclear antibodies, extractable nuclear antigen, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were all negative. Serum cytokines showed slightly elevated IL-6 and TNF-α; IL-2, IL-10, IL-17, and IFN-γ were normal. Serum anti-AQP4 antibodies were positive at a titer of 1:10. MRI of the cervical spinal cord revealed multiple T2-hyperintense, enhancing lesions from C2 to T1 with cord enlargement and brain-stem involvement. Brain MRI showed FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral thalami, periventricular regions, basal ganglia, and cerebral peduncles. The working diagnosis was neuromyelitis optica, and the patient received high-dose methylprednisolone and immunoglobulin, with progressive symptomatic improvement.
title: A Case of Primary Central Nervous System Lymphoma Mimic Neuromyelitis Optica

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old asymptomatic woman was referred for suspected age-related macular degeneration. Her history was unremarkable except for well-controlled hypertension. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes, and intraocular pressures were normal. Slit-lamp examination showed unremarkable anterior segments. Funduscopic examination revealed an epiretinal membrane with retinal folds in the right eye. In the left eye, thick choroidal vessels were visible at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) from the fovea to the temporal macula, and there was an area of pigmentary alteration inferotemporal to the macula. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the left eye showed RPE elevation without intra- or subretinal fluid or hemorrhage. Fluorescein angiography and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated anomalous choroidal vessels in the arterial phase; late fluorescein angiography showed background hyperfluorescence corresponding to the area of pigmentary alteration. The patient was observed without intervention.  

Five years later, she noted decreased vision (20/40) and metamorphopsia in the left eye. Examination showed an epiretinal membrane with macular thickening and a thick choroidal vascular network throughout the macula. Optical coherence tomography again demonstrated RPE elevations with a double-layer sign corresponding to the anomalous vessels, without intra- or subretinal fluid. She underwent vitrectomy, membrane and internal limiting membrane peeling, and cataract surgery, with postoperative improvement to 20/16.  

Over the next four years, the anomalous choroidal vessels continued to extend, and an orange polypoidal lesion appeared at the temporal edge of the pigment alteration, but there were no exudative changes or visual symptoms.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Visual impairment associated with choroidal macroaneurysm in a patient with presumed anomalous short posterior ciliary artery

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old Vietnamese man living in Switzerland for 3 years presented with unremitting pain in his right knee. Two months earlier he had sustained a right knee contusion. Since that injury he reported occasional night sweats with chills and a weight loss of 5 kg. He was otherwise in good health, did not smoke, and took no medications.

On examination there was a painful, red, nonulcerating induration measuring 3 × 4 cm over the right fibular head. The lesion was fluctuating and appeared adherent to the deep subcutaneous tissues. Right knee range of motion was preserved, and the neurovascular examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 76 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 61 fl), no leukocytosis, and a C-reactive protein level of 4 mg/L. Plain radiography of the knee revealed a 1 × 1 cm lytic lesion with an ill-defined margin in the proximal right fibula, breaking through the outer cortex. MRI demonstrated a T2 hyperintense lesion at the fibular head with cortical disruption and an adjacent soft-tissue abscess, findings thought to be consistent with focal osteomyelitis rather than a bone tumor.

Surgical debridement was performed, and tissue fragments were sent for bacteriologic culture and pathology, with a special request to evaluate for tuberculosis. Empiric intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate was initiated. Pathologic examination revealed acid-alcohol resistant bacilli within an inflammatory process, but standard cultures were noncontributive. A tuberculin skin test was negative at 72 hours.
title: Atypical Focal Osteomyelitis as Initial Manifestation of AIDS

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old Greek woman was referred for persistent numbness and weakness of the left hand. Over the past three years she had undergone two carpal tunnel releases elsewhere without relief, and her symptoms had progressively worsened. She now reported tingling in both the median and ulnar nerve distributions and noted a slowly enlarging mass in the left palm and thenar eminence.

On examination, there was a soft tissue mass in the palm that was slightly tender to palpation. Wrist extension was limited to 40° and flexion to 60°. She was unable to flex the distal phalanx of the thumb. Thenar muscle strength was decreased, and sensation was diminished in the median and ulnar territories.

Plain radiographs of the hand showed a soft tissue opacity overlying the palm. MRI demonstrated an 8.0 × 4.0 × 3.75 cm well-defined lesion in the deep palmar space, extending between the tendons and metacarpals with preservation of the periosteum. The lesion was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and showed low signal on fat-suppressed sequences, suggesting a lipomatous tumor.

A nerve conduction study revealed prolonged latencies and reduced amplitudes of both the median and ulnar nerves consistent with compressive neuropathy.
title: Complications arising from a misdiagnosed giant lipoma of the hand and palm: a case report

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man came to the emergency department with sudden weakness of all four limbs that began 3 hours earlier. He denied facial or respiratory weakness, sensory changes, or autonomic symptoms. He recalled mild muscle soreness after exercising the previous day and a heavy intake of bread at dinner. His weakness began in the hands and feet and progressed proximally to involve the arms and legs. He had no paresthesia, breathlessness, dysphagia, or medications (including herbal supplements). He had no known thyroid disease, no family history of similar episodes, and no other chronic illnesses. He did report occasional, transient leg weakness after exercise since his early twenties.

On examination, blood pressure was 134/78 mm Hg, heart rate 84 beats/min, and body mass index 19.9 kg/m2. There was no goiter, lymphadenopathy, or jugular venous distension. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams were unremarkable. Neurologically, he had flaccid paralysis (motor grade 1/5) in all extremities with intact sensation.

An ECG showed a heart rate of 78 beats/min, flat T waves, and prolonged QT/QTc of 542/621 ms. Initial blood tests (available 1.5 hours after arrival) revealed a serum potassium level of 1.50 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0) and arterial blood gas showing metabolic acidosis. Intravenous potassium infusion was started, during which his blood pressure briefly dropped to 80/50 mm Hg and ECG showed bradycardia, ST-segment depression, and U waves; cardiac enzymes were normal, and repeat potassium was 1.35 mmol/L. The infusion rate was increased, and oxygen was administered. After 20 minutes, his blood pressure rose to 110/60 mm Hg, heart rate to 67/min, but chest discomfort persisted. He was admitted to the intensive care unit. Twelve hours later, ECG normalized and QRS duration returned to normal. Muscle strength began to improve four hours after presentation and fully recovered by 24 hours, by which time potassium was 3.4 mmol/L without further infusion.

To evaluate the cause of hypokalemia, urine sodium and potassium and serum aldosterone and renin levels were measured and were within normal limits. Thyroid function tests were normal. After potassium normalized, levels remained stable off infusion. A long exercise test to assess for inherited neuromuscular disease showed no abnormalities.
title: Confirming Genetic Abnormalities of Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis Using Next-Generation Sequencing: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old woman with a history of anorexia nervosa since adolescence was admitted to a psychiatric service for psychotic behavior and self-neglect. She had minimal food intake for two months and isolation for the prior two weeks. She was transferred 24 hours later to the internal medicine service. 

On arrival at the emergency room she was cachectic (BMI 13 kg/m2), hypothermic (32.6°C), and obtunded (RLS 2). She had signs of severe dehydration and muscle atrophy. Respiratory rate was 30 breaths per minute with shallow breathing; blood pressure 110/60 mmHg; pulse 77 bpm. She denied alcohol or substance use. 

Initial arterial blood gas showed pH 6.895, pCO2 0.93 kPa, pO2 22 kPa, and plasma glucose 40.6 mmol/L. There were no signs of infection, and serum electrolytes were within normal limits.
title: Severe diabetic ketoacidosis in combination with starvation and anorexia nervosa at onset of type 1 diabetes: A case report

case_prompt: A 5-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of swelling in the left lower jaw. She had no difficulty swallowing or breathing, facial pain, neural changes, or history of trauma; medical and family histories were unremarkable. Laboratory studies were normal except for a low mean corpuscular volume attributed to iron deficiency. Examination revealed a solitary, fixed, firm, non-tender 4×5 cm mass in the left submandibular region, normal overlying skin, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and normal mouth opening. Intraoral mucosa was intact; bilateral primary first molar caries were present. The initial clinical impression was an inflammatory lesion of the left primary molar despite lack of inflammatory signs; given the rapid growth, malignant mesenchymal tumors were also considered. Panoramic radiograph showed a poorly defined radiolucency in the left mandibular body with spicules of bone from the inferior border and absence of the left second premolar crypt. Cone-beam CT revealed destruction of lingual alveolar bone, diffuse periosteal bone spicules on buccal and lingual cortices, and an overlying soft-tissue mass.
title: Aggressive fibromatosis in the submandibular region of a child

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old man was admitted with one month of progressive dyspnea, cough, and fever. He initially had mild fever, dry cough, and night sweats without treatment. Two weeks later he developed shortness of breath and yellow sputum. A bronchoscopy at a local hospital showed negative bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) for acid-fast bacilli and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR. He was treated for community-acquired pneumonia with antibiotics for 10 days without improvement and was transferred.

On arrival, temperature was 37°C, pulse 84/min, respirations 28/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, and he required 10 L/min of oxygen by bag-valve mask. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.38, PaO2 70 mmHg, PaCO2 32.7 mmHg, HCO3– 19.4 mmol/L. Examination revealed dullness to percussion, fine crackles, and decreased breath sounds at the right lower lung field. Laboratory tests showed WBC 8.84 G/L (77.5% neutrophils, 13.3% lymphocytes), hematocrit 38.2%, C-reactive protein 78.4 mg/L, mildly elevated liver transaminases, and negative HIV testing. Chest radiograph demonstrated consolidation in the right lower hemithorax. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed consolidation with small necrotizing cavities.

He was treated with meropenem, ciprofloxacin, and vancomycin for four days without defervescence. Intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg daily) was then started, resulting in rapid clinical and radiologic improvement. On hospital day 14, however, fever recurred, and repeat CT showed significant regression of the consolidation.
title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis-Associated Necrotizing Pneumonia With Adjunctive Corticosteroid Therapy

case_prompt: A 62-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department with a 3-month history of progressive cognitive decline, including ataxia, memory loss, and disorientation. She had no prior neurologic illness. On examination, she was alert but disoriented to time and place, with impaired short-term memory and a broad-based gait. Vital signs were normal. Noncontrast CT of the head and CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of malignancy, infarction, or hemorrhage. Laboratory evaluations—including metabolic panels, infectious and autoimmune encephalitis panels, and toxicology screens—were unremarkable. Brain MRI revealed diffusion restriction and T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral caudate nuclei, putamen, thalami, hippocampi, and in a gyriform pattern in the bilateral frontal and temporal cortices, without contrast enhancement or mass effect.
title: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease: A case report

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman with hypertension, prior coronary bypass graft, and laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 3 years earlier presented with 3 days of intermittent abdominal pain. The pain began in the right lower quadrant, became diffuse, and radiated to her back. She noted dark, loose stools with transient relief after defecation. On the morning of presentation, her pain turned constant and was accompanied by several episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. 

In the emergency department, she was afebrile with blood pressure 181/88 mmHg, heart rate 86, and weight loss from 108 kg (BMI 37.6) pre–bypass to 72.1 kg (BMI 24.9) now. Abdominal examination revealed poorly localized tenderness. Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 10.1 mg/dL (baseline 11.6), leukocyte count 21 × 10^9/L, and lactate 1.0 mmol/L. She denied daily NSAID use (two ibuprofen doses this week), smoking, or prior GI bleeding. She remained on aspirin but had stopped clopidogrel over a year earlier; her last EGD and colonoscopy 3 years prior were unremarkable.

While awaiting evaluation, she had an episode of dark-red hematemesis. Gastroenterology was consulted; she was started on a pantoprazole drip and scheduled for EGD the next morning, with initial suspicion of Mallory-Weiss tear. 

A CT angiogram of the abdomen demonstrated dilated loops of small bowel with surrounding inflammatory changes and decreased wall enhancement, findings concerning for bowel ischemia secondary to intussusception versus internal hernia. There was no active contrast extravasation or free air. After surgical evaluation, the patient was taken to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy and intraoperative EGD.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Case report: Concurrent intussusception and bleeding marginal ulcer in a patient with gastric bypass

case_prompt: A 45-year-old Moroccan man living in Spain, who frequently traveled to Morocco, presented with progressive skin lesions on the trunk and extremities for 5 years. The lesions were intensely pruritic and did not improve with topical corticosteroids or oral antihistamines. Three years earlier, two skin biopsies showed superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal dermatitis, prompting suspicion of lupus tumidus and granuloma annulare; laboratory and serologic tests were unremarkable. On examination, multiple dome-shaped, erythematous to skin-colored infiltrated papules and nodules were present on the upper and lower extremities and to a lesser extent on the trunk. Dermoscopy (10× polarized contact mode) of several lesions demonstrated crown vessels, linear branching vessels, yellowish-orange structureless areas, shiny white structures, and peripheral hyperpigmentation. The initial differential diagnosis included sarcoidosis and mycobacterial infection.
title: Crown vessels and shiny white structures in dermoscopy of histoid leprosy

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a pruritic truncal rash in the setting of systemic immunotherapy and for numerous eruptive lower‐extremity lesions. His medical history was notable for hypertension, coronary artery disease, and a 4-mm well‐differentiated cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) treated with Mohs surgery 6 years earlier. Ten months prior, he had an SCC excised from his right lower leg; subsequently, he developed multiple exophytic papules and plaques on both lower extremities, six of which were biopsied and read as well-differentiated SCC.

An initial positron-emission tomography (PET) scan showed multifocal cutaneous lesions and nonspecific pelvic lymphadenopathy suspicious for metastatic disease, and he was started on cemiplimab. Three months later, repeat PET demonstrated progression of the skin lesions and new bilateral inguinal and external iliac hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy. He then entered a clinical trial of an LILRB2 antagonist plus a PD-1 inhibitor, received four cycles of therapy, and underwent palliative radiation to the affected extremities.

He subsequently presented with diffuse pruritus and a minimally scaly red papular rash on the trunk, which was refractory to hydroxyzine and topical triamcinolone. Biopsy of the truncal rash showed spongiotic dermatitis with eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence was negative, and an immunobullous disease antibody panel was unremarkable. The differential diagnosis included an id reaction, medication hypersensitivity, and contact dermatitis. Given the multifocal eruption on both legs, consistently well‐differentiated histology, and no other high‐risk factors for aggressive SCC, the diagnosis of unresectable metastatic cutaneous SCC was questioned. An inguinal lymph node biopsy was performed and showed a benign reactive lymph node.
title: Diffuse eruptive squamous atypia, also known as eruptive keratoacanthoma: Unique case presentation

case_prompt:
Ms. A is a 42-year-old Caucasian woman, divorced and in a stable relationship, employed full-time as a school cleaner, who was admitted for the fourth time with acute confusion, psychomotor hypo-motility, altered behavior, and psychotic features.

Medical history: hypothyroidism diagnosed in December 2003 with elevated antithyroid peroxidase antibodies; thyroid replacement gradually increased to 175 µg thyroxine by July 2009. No past psychiatric history, no substance or alcohol misuse, and no family history of mental illness.

Episode 1 (August 2006): Within hours of returning from holiday, she developed confusion, hyperpyrexia, agitation, inability to walk, and possible seizure. On the medical ward, laboratory studies, CSF analysis, CT and MRI brain, and EEG were normal except for elevated free T4. She reported nihilistic delusions (“her body was dead and rotting,” she was “Satan”), olfactory and tactile disturbances, and thought-insertion/suspiciousness. Mood was euthymic. Treated with olanzapine 10 mg daily and sodium valproate 200 mg twice daily, with full recovery in two weeks. Olanzapine stopped after 6 months; valproate continued until just before episode 2.

Episode 2 (September 2007): Again following holiday, rapid onset of motionlessness, paucity of speech, fixed belief “I think I might be dead,” and nihilistic delusions. No eyewitness seizures. Treated at home with olanzapine and valproate; recovered fully in two weeks. Three outpatient EEGs showed no ictal events. Olanzapine later stopped; valproate continued.

Episode 3 (October 2008): Similar pattern after holiday; confusion, vagueness, negative urine drug screen, no seizures on video-EEG. Treated with olanzapine and valproate; recovered within weeks. Valproate switched to levetiracetam in January 2009 due to weight gain.

Episode 4 (July 2009): Three days before planned holiday, acute confusion with monosyllabic replies, perplexity, delusions of surveillance (“cameras in her flat,” part of a TV serial), nihilistic and homicidal delusions, and an attempted hanging in hospital. Laboratory studies normal. EEG three days after admission was normal. Brain MRI showed several tiny non-specific hyperintense foci in subcortical and deep white matter, unchanged since 2006. Anti-NMDA receptor and antineutrophil antibodies were negative. Mini-Mental State Examination five days after admission was normal.
title: Cycloid Psychosis: Perris Criteria Revisited

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old woman from Madagascar, living in Germany for two years, presented to the psychiatric emergency department with acute auditory hallucinations of seven days’ duration and visual hallucinations beginning on the day of admission. She reported hearing a repetitive voice telling her to “go to the sea” and seeing an old, faceless woman—the presumed source of the voice. She had no prior psychiatric history and denied altered consciousness or orientation; she was notably frightened by the hallucinations. She also experienced episodic severe headaches that intensified the hallucinations. One week before onset of psychiatric symptoms, she had several days of severe diarrhea while working as an elderly care nurse in a retirement home experiencing an outbreak of diarrhea.

On examination, her vital signs were normal; there was no fever or neck stiffness. Neurologic and internal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including C-reactive protein and lymphocyte counts, were within normal limits. Cranial MRI and EEG showed no abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a normal cell count (1.0 cells/µl), normal blood–CSF barrier function (albumin ratio, 6.64; total protein, 474 mg/l), no intrathecal IgG, IgA, or IgM synthesis, and no CSF-specific oligoclonal bands. Tests for antineuronal and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies in serum and CSF were negative. PCR assays and antibody-specific indices for cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, and varicella–zoster virus were negative.
title: Acute Enterovirus Encephalitis as a Cause for Isolated Visual and Auditory Hallucinations in a 22-Year-Old Patient

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman with a 12-year history of hypertension and 4 years of chronic kidney disease, on maintenance hemodialysis for 2 years (thrice weekly for the past year), presented with an 8-month history of progressive, painless abdominal distension, anorexia, and weight loss. She denied abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, fever, jaundice, edema, prior abdominal surgery, tuberculosis, or peritoneal dialysis. Medications included antihypertensives, calcium carbonate, erythropoietin, iron, and multivitamins.

On examination, blood pressure was 180/120 mm Hg, pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 20/min; she was afebrile and pale. The abdomen was symmetrically distended with a fluid thrill; there were no stigmata of chronic liver disease or hernias. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, leukocyte count 10 400/mm3, normal platelets and coagulation, urea 197 mg/dL, creatinine 9.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL, normal liver enzymes, and intact parathyroid hormone 347 pg/mL. Viral serologies were negative.

Diagnostic paracentesis yielded hemorrhagic fluid with 70 cells/mm3 (70% neutrophils), protein 3.8 g/dL, sugar 83 mg/dL, ADA 32 IU/L, and a serum–ascites albumin gradient of 0.8. Ziehl–Neelsen and Gram stains, cultures (including Mycobacterium tuberculosis), TB PCR, malignant cytology, and cancer markers (CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA) were all negative. 

Echocardiography revealed mild mitral regurgitation and normal systolic and diastolic function. Abdominal ultrasound showed gross ascites, contracted kidneys, and cholelithiasis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated gross ascites with peritoneal enhancement and hyperdensities within the fluid, contracted kidneys, and cholelithiasis. Despite daily hemodialysis and repeated therapeutic paracenteses, the ascites persisted.
title: An unusual case of cocoon abdomen in a patient on hemodialysis

case_prompt: A 14-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of short stature and delayed puberty. She was prepubertal, with a height of 120 cm (−6.12 SDS) and weight of 21.6 kg (−5.58 SDS). Neurologic examination, visual fields, and other systemic examinations were normal. Laboratory evaluation showed severe growth hormone deficiency (IGF-1 <25 ng/mL; peak GH 0.47 ng/mL on insulin tolerance test), hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (LH <0.2 mU/mL; FSH 2.7 mU/mL), and dyslipidemia (total cholesterol 7.9 mmol/L; LDL 6.3 mmol/L; HDL 1.9 mmol/L; triglyceride 0.81 mmol/L). Peak cortisol from the insulin tolerance test was 800 nmol/L. Thyroid function tests, prolactin level, complete blood count, liver and renal function, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, karyotype, antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, thyroid antibodies, complement levels (C3, C4), erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and tumor markers (β-hCG, α-fetoprotein) were all normal. Bone age was delayed at 9 years. MRI of the brain revealed a homogeneously contrast-enhancing lobulated mass measuring 0.6 × 1.3 × 1.7 cm arising from the pituitary stalk, extending into the sellar and suprasellar regions, and abutting the optic chiasm. She was started on pubertal induction and pravastatin; growth hormone therapy was withheld in view of the MRI findings.
title: Xanthomatous Hypophysitis Presenting in an Adolescent Girl: A Long-Term Follow-Up of a Rare Case and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 36-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a left breast mass without systemic symptoms. On examination, the left breast was replaced by a 20 × 20 cm ulcerative lesion in the outer quadrants, and ipsilateral axillary nodes appeared inflammatory and measured 1 cm in diameter. The right breast and axilla were normal. Chest CT showed a necrotic mass occupying the entire left breast with infiltration of the skin and pectoral muscle and ipsilateral pectoral and axillary lymphadenopathy. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans showed no distant metastases. Core-needle biopsy of the lesion demonstrated a high-grade malignant spindle cell neoplasm with an osteochondral component, extensive necrosis, and negative cytokeratin staining, raising consideration of a phyllodes tumor versus a primary breast sarcoma.
title: Peripheral Neural Sheath Breast Sarcoma: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 23-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, presented with a severe, continuous frontal headache and neck stiffness immediately after a difficult epidural analgesia for vaginal delivery (four attempts). On postpartum day 1, an anesthesiology consultation led to an epidural blood patch despite headache lacking positional characteristics; the pain remained unchanged. Neurology evaluation the same day listed tension-type headache and post–dural puncture headache as leading differentials, and she was discharged after a modest pain reduction with conservative measures. Two days later, she was readmitted with a hypertensive emergency, severe frontal headache, and laboratory abnormalities including elevated lactate dehydrogenase, elevated uric acid, and proteinuria. She was diagnosed with postpartum preeclampsia and treated with 24 hours of magnesium sulfate. Her headache persisted despite antihypertensive therapy and multiple analgesics (Fioricet, Toradol, Compazine, Neurontin, caffeine, methylprednisolone), and neurologic examination remained intact. A noncontrast head CT showed possible sphenoid sinusitis, slight prominence of the pituitary gland, intraventricular air, and tentorial dural calcification. The headache improved after blood pressure control, and she was discharged. On postpartum day 10, she returned with worsening frontal headache, neck pain, and low-grade fever; her neurologic examination remained unchanged, and a CT venogram was requested.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: CVT in the Peripartum Period: A Diagnostic Dilemma

case_prompt: A 76-year-old man presented with a several-month history of pain, difficulty chewing, and swallowing. He noted a firm, internal nodule on the tongue. On examination, there was a free, well-defined, rounded nodule, approximately 1 cm in diameter, on the central region of the dorsum of the tongue; the mucosal color was normal. He did not recall any preceding trauma or foreign-body sensation. To further evaluate, an ultrasound examination of the tongue was performed using a 12 MHz linear probe. The ultrasound revealed a 1.2 × 0.7 cm lesion with a 5 mm hyperechoic linear structure at its center, located in the left lateral border of the distal third of the tongue, 0.1 cm from the surface, with surrounding tissue changes consistent with granuloma formation. At a follow-up visit, the patient recalled that he had eaten pequi fruit some time before but could not specify when.
title: Foreign Body Granuloma in the Tongue by a Pequi Spine

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old Brazilian man with no past medical history, employed as airline crew, returned from South Africa and presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever and new-onset abdominal pain. Over the prior 24 hours, he became progressively drowsy but had no focal neurologic deficits. On arrival: temperature elevated, blood pressure and heart rate consistent with systemic inflammatory response; he was drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale score <11. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, lymphocytosis, and evidence of multiorgan dysfunction. Serologic testing was positive for Plasmodium falciparum. The patient had not received adequate antimalarial prophylaxis. Within 24 hours, his level of consciousness and vital signs worsened, necessitating intubation and ICU admission. Head CT showed no acute intracranial hemorrhage. Brain MRI demonstrated:
- T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences: swelling and heterogeneous hyperintense signal in the bilateral globus pallidus and corpus callosum.
- Susceptibility-weighted imaging: diffuse punctate microhemorrhagic foci in bilateral basal ganglia, corpus callosum, and both superficial and deep white matter.
- Diffusion-weighted imaging with corresponding low ADC signal: restricted diffusion in the basal ganglia, corpus callosum, hippocampi, and parasagittal frontoparietal gyri.
title: Imaging features of fulminant cerebral malaria: A case report

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of loose upper front teeth and bleeding gums of two years’ duration.  
Her medical history was notable for recurrent skin rashes and keratotic patches on the elbows, knees, and soles since age 4, worsening in winter.  Dental history included premature exfoliation of a primary tooth.  Family history revealed consanguineous parents and an elder sibling with similar but milder skin lesions; pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable.

On examination, there were well-demarcated yellowish hyperkeratotic plaques on the palms and soles extending onto the dorsal surfaces, with peeling skin and underlying erythema; similar lesions were present on both knees.  Intraoral examination showed 28 teeth with proclination and spacing of the upper incisors, rotations of premolars, a diffuse gingival swelling around the lower left molars, and increased mobility with apical migration of the gingival margin around the upper and lower incisors.  

Periodontal assessment revealed generalized bleeding on probing and deep pockets particularly around teeth 11, 21, 36, 37, 41, and 46.  Orthopantomograph and full-mouth intraoral periapical radiographs demonstrated vertical bone loss in those same regions.
title: Papillion-Lefèvre Syndrome: Periodontists' Perspective

case_prompt: A 12-year-old girl with no history of menarche and no prior medical problems presented to the emergency department with severe acute pelvic pain of sudden onset. She had no vomiting, diarrhea, or fever. On examination, she had tenderness in the lower abdomen and right flank. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed a slight leukocytosis with mild neutrophilia and a slight decrease in hematocrit; liver and kidney function and inflammatory markers were within normal limits. Given her primary amenorrhea and acute pelvic pain, ovarian torsion was initially suspected. A suprapubic abdominal ultrasound was performed. The ovaries had normal echotexture and size, but there was marked distension of the cervix and upper vagina by an ovoid collection with heterogeneous, layered echogenicity consistent with hemorrhage in various stages. No free fluid was seen in the pouch of Douglas.
title: Hidden obstruction: A rare case of hematometrocolpos in a young adolescent with vaginal atresia

case_prompt:
A 43‐year‐old man with a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, asthma, and smoking presented with a 3-year history of intermittent pain over the posterolateral aspect of his left elbow. The pain did not limit his range of motion, was not related to activity or time of day, and he denied any tenderness to palpation over the lateral elbow. He reported that exposure to cold temperatures or cold water worsened the pain. There were no sensory or motor deficits, no palpable mass, and no overlying skin changes or signs of inflammation.

Ultrasonography of the left elbow revealed a small (0.6 × 0.2 cm) oval hypoechoic lesion in the subcutaneous tissue of the dorsal aspect, with posterior acoustic enhancement and no detectable vascularity on color Doppler. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 0.44 × 1 × 0.8 cm subcutaneous oval lesion at the posterolateral elbow. The lesion was hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences, was not suppressed on fat-saturated sequences, and showed no definite enhancement.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Diagnosis of glomus tumor of the elbow: A case report

case_prompt:
A 3-week-old female infant was referred for evaluation of an annular rash on her face and trunk that was initially thought to be tinea corporis. The lesions first appeared at 2 weeks of age and increased in size over the following week. She was feeding well and gaining weight appropriately. The baby was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy to a 26-year-old healthy mother (gravida 2, para 1) with a history of one previous spontaneous abortion. Prenatal laboratory studies and fetal ultrasonography were normal. Delivery was spontaneous vaginal; birth weight was 3060 g, length 50 cm, and Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. In the nursery, she received antibiotics for a presumed nonspecific neonatal infection and was discharged on day 5 with mild thrombocytopenia deemed transient.

On examination at 3 weeks, the infant appeared well but was pale. Multiple discrete and confluent annular lesions measuring 1–3 cm with central hypopigmentation were present on the face, anterior chest, and abdomen. There was no erythema, scale, or discharge. Heart rate was 150 beats/min with a regular rhythm and no murmurs. The abdomen was soft without hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 90 g/L, red-cell count 2.88 × 10^12/L, platelet count 58 × 10^9/L, aspartate aminotransferase 216 U/L (normal 15–59), and alanine aminotransferase 136 U/L (normal 9–72). Serum electrolytes, proteins, albumin, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine were within normal limits.
title: Neonatal lupus erythematosus—a rare syndrome of transient autoimmunity

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old primipara was transferred on her fourth postpartum day for management of uncontrolled hypertension and intractable vomiting. At her first antenatal visit (8 weeks’ gestation), she was noted to have systemic hypertension (180/100 mm Hg) and was treated with amlodipine and methyldopa throughout pregnancy. The pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated until 37 weeks, when her blood pressure rose to 220/120 mm Hg, accompanied by headache and multiple episodes of vomiting despite intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulfate. She underwent an emergency cesarean section for failure to progress; intraoperative blood‐pressure spikes were managed with nitroprusside. A healthy female infant was delivered.

During the postpartum period, her blood pressure remained markedly elevated. On arrival at our center she appeared in fair general condition. Temperature was 99°F; blood pressure, 230/130 mm Hg bilaterally; pulse, 120 beats/min; oxygen saturation, 92% on room air. She had no pallor, icterus, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration, but there was 3+ bilateral pedal edema. The breasts and thyroid examination were normal. The abdomen was distended and tender, with a positive fluid thrill, and bowel sounds were normal. Respiratory examination showed decreased air entry at both lung bases.

Laboratory studies revealed a slightly low hemoglobin, significant leukocytosis, and a serum potassium of 2.5 mmol/L; other routine hematologic and biochemical parameters were within normal limits.
title: Pheochromocytoma disguised as gestational hypertensive disease during pregnancy: A case report

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 3-month history of chronic cough, chest pain, and purulent sputum, accompanied by fatigue, intermittent fever, and night sweats. On examination, he had enlarged bilateral cervical lymph nodes. Chest CT showed multifocal patchy consolidations with multiple nodules in both lungs and necrotic lymphadenopathy in the cervical, paratracheal, and hilar regions. A cervical lymph-node biopsy demonstrated epithelioid cell granulomas with giant cells and caseating necrosis. Tuberculin skin testing was positive (11 mm). He was started on rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

After 5 months of directly observed therapy, he returned with persistent and enlarging cervical nodes, erythematous papular skin lesions over the nodes, diffuse abdominal pain, and further weight loss. Examination revealed multiple painless, voluminous cervical lymphadenopathies causing drooping of the right corner of the mouth, confluent erythematous papules overlying these nodes, bilateral axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathies, a tender abdominal mass, and splenomegaly. Abdominal CT showed multiple confluent enlarged lymph nodes forming lobulated masses with heterogeneous enhancement and an enlarged spleen. FDG-PET revealed extensive hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy (SUV 9.8–12.1), hypermetabolic costodiaphragmatic lesions, splenomegaly (SUV 3), focal liver uptake (SUV 4.17), and bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory studies showed a normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL), elevated LDH (806 U/L), elevated CRP (221 mg/L), and hypoalbuminemia (20 g/L).
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Association of multifocal Hodgkin's lymphoma and tuberculosis infection: A challenging entity

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old woman with hypertension presented with a 1-year history of intermittent difficulty swallowing liquids—especially with large boluses—and occasional dysphagia when eating rice. Symptoms occurred about once monthly and were associated with a mild loss of appetite. She denied odynophagia, globus sensation, weight loss, abdominal pain, hematochezia, and dyspepsia. Physical examination was unremarkable.

A lateral neck radiograph showed multilevel moderate anterior cervical spine osteophytes without displacement of the anterior prevertebral soft tissues, and no radiopaque foreign body was seen. Double-contrast barium esophagography revealed a smooth anterior compression of the lower esophageal lumen with well-defined margins that persisted during barium ingestion; no other strictures or mucosal defects were identified. Decreased primary peristalsis was also noted.

Upper endoscopy demonstrated a non-obstructive Schatzki ring 2 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction; the endoscope passed into the stomach without difficulty, indicating a lumen diameter greater than 12 mm. The ring produced minimal luminal narrowing and was not apparent on the esophagogram.

A contrast-enhanced chest CT scan was ordered for further evaluation of the esophageal compression.
title: Esophageal compression by a common left pulmonary venous trunk

case_prompt: A 29-year-old man with grade I obesity presented with new-onset sclero-tegumentary jaundice, pruritus, and epigastric pain. A prior CT scan revealed cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis. Laboratory evaluation showed cholestatic liver test abnormalities and mild hepatocellular injury without leukocytosis or anemia. Endoscopic ultrasonography followed by ERCP with papillosphincterotomy was performed; two biliary stones were extracted and a 10 Fr/7 cm biliary stent placed. During ERCP, a subtle, slightly elevated lesion adjacent to the major papilla with normal overlying mucosa was noted. Repeat EUS demonstrated a well-delineated 14 × 7 mm homogeneous hypoechoic submucosal mass in the periampullary region of the second portion of the duodenum, with Doppler flow and a mixed elastographic pattern. EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy (22G Franseen needle, three passes) yielded tissue showing monomorphic ovoid cells with mild nuclear atypia, low mitotic activity, and no necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and CD56; focally positive for pan-cytokeratin AE1/AE3; and negative for S100, CD34, and muscle-specific actin; Ki67 index was 1%. The lesion was classified as a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (NET grade 1). Cross-sectional CT and MRI demonstrated no local invasion or distant metastases and confirmed that the lesion was amenable to resection.
title: Duodenal Gangliocytic Paragangliomas—Case Series and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old male presented with multiple skin lesions on the bilateral lower limbs for 7 months. The lesions began as painless vesicles with clear fluid, later drained pus, and resolved spontaneously. One month before presentation, he had 10–14 episodes per day of small-volume loose stool with mucus for 14 days, without fever, abdominal pain, or vomiting. Subsequently, he developed sharp, nonradiating pain at the tip of the left second toe progressing to dry gangrene of half the phalanx. He also noted bilateral lower limb swelling and facial puffiness that subsided by evening. He had a productive cough with streaky hemoptysis but no chest pain or dyspnea. He reported fatigue, anorexia, and significant weight loss. He denied hair loss, ear discharge, joint pain, rash, photosensitivity, mucosal ulcers, lymphadenopathy, and muscle weakness. There was no drug use.

On examination, he was pale. Pulses were absent in both dorsalis pedis and the left posterior tibial artery. Dry gangrene with a sharp line of demarcation was present on the left second toe. Patchy hair loss over both toes and multiple hyper- and hypopigmented lesions were noted on the lower limbs. Chest examination revealed diminished movement on the left side, a woody dull percussion note, and decreased breath sounds.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL; leukocyte count 28 560/mm3 with 36% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 10 288/mm3); ESR 73 mm/hr; hs-CRP 10 680 ng/mL; aPTT 37.7 s (control 29 s). Urinalysis revealed 1+ protein; 24-hour urine protein was 3.17 g/day. Peripheral smear showed elevated corrected reticulocyte count and LDH, with a positive direct Coombs test. ANA was positive (homogeneous pattern, 3+); ANA immunoblot was negative. Anti-dsDNA was elevated. Lupus anticoagulant was borderline elevated; anticardiolipin and anti–β2 glycoprotein I antibodies were normal. C3 and C4 levels were normal.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT and pulmonary angiography revealed multiple intermediate-walled cavitary lesions in both lower lobes; biopsy of one lesion showed necrotic tissue. Mantoux test and sputum for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, HIV, and leptospirosis were negative. Repeated examinations of blood, urine, sputum, and stool for bacterial and parasitic infection were unremarkable; stool microscopy revealed no parasites.
title: An Unusual Case of Eosinophilia with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 69-year-old Asian man with end-stage renal disease underwent a living-donor kidney transplant nine years earlier and has been maintained on mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and low-dose prednisone. He presented with acute encephalopathy and respiratory failure immediately after a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure. Over the preceding month he had episodes of confusion, right-sided twitching, and intermittent speech disturbance described as possible aphasia. One month earlier, he had a fall with a witnessed seizure; head CT was unremarkable but brain MRI demonstrated multiple lesions, and CSF studies were positive for Epstein-Barr virus. On admission, he was afebrile, blood pressure was 130/71 mmHg, pulse 66/min, and respirations 20/min. Lung and cardiac examinations were normal. Neurologic examination after sedation revealed no movement of the right extremities in response to pain. Repeat head imaging showed multifocal parenchymal hemorrhages with surrounding edema and a 5 mm midline shift. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and antivirals were started. A whole-body PET scan demonstrated hypermetabolic lesions confined to the central nervous system. Over the next several days, he developed worsening confusion, apraxia, gaze deviation, and right flaccid hemiparesis. Given this progression in an immunosuppressed transplant recipient, the leading considerations were vasculitis, infection, and central nervous system lymphoma.
title: A Rare Presentation of Isolated CNS Posttransplantation Lymphoproliferative Disorder

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old woman with chronic sinusitis was referred for evaluation of asymptomatic neutropenia. She denied weight loss, fevers, infections, recent travel, or new medications. She had no family history of hematologic disorders. Medications included fluticasone nasal spray, and she had recently discontinued an oral contraceptive after 7 years.  
Routine labs showed a white blood cell count of 3300/μL (normal 4000–10 500/μL) and an absolute neutrophil count of 1500/μL (normal 1500–6500/μL). Review of the prior four years revealed persistently normal counts. On evaluation, her WBC count was 3600/μL, hemoglobin 15.7 g/dL, platelet count 219 000/μL, and ANC 1100/μL, which later normalized. The liver and spleen were not palpable. Peripheral-blood flow cytometry was normal.  
A peripheral-blood smear demonstrated numerous neutrophils with bilobed “pince-nez” nuclei consistent with Pelger–Huet–type morphology; other cell lines appeared normal.
title: Young Woman with Unexplained Neutropenia and Neutrophils with Bilobed Nuclei: Marrow Findings

case_prompt: A 4-kg, 1.5-month-old female with no prior medical history was scheduled for an elective unilateral inguinal hernia repair under combined general endotracheal and caudal anesthesia. On arrival to the operating room her heart rate was 135 bpm, blood pressure 105/60 mmHg, and she was calm. Anesthesia was induced with sevoflurane, mivacurium (0.5 mg), and dexamethasone (0.5 mg), and the trachea was intubated. Immediately after intubation, her heart rate dropped to 90 bpm. Atropine (20 μg/kg) was administered twice and epinephrine (10 μg/kg) once, without improvement in heart rate. Displacement of the endotracheal tube and pneumothorax were excluded by lung auscultation, and ventilation parameters were appropriate for her age and weight. Congenital cardiovascular disease was considered, but her history and pre-anesthesia condition showed no signs or symptoms suggestive of a structural heart defect.
title: Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity Following Inadvertent Intravenous Levobupivacaine Infusion in Infants: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 53-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal distention and worsening early satiety, accompanied by an increase in abdominal circumference and limb thinning. She denied pain, fever, nausea, or vomiting. She had been postmenopausal for 5 years with no vaginal bleeding. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension on loxone; she had no history of diabetes, coronary disease, or malignancy and had not had a physical examination in over 10 years. On examination, her BMI was 23.3. A giant rubbery abdominal mass extended to the xiphisternum; it was non-tender, with no rebound tenderness and normal bowel sounds. Laboratory studies, including liver and renal function tests, fecal occult blood, coagulation profile, electrolytes, and tumor markers, were all within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 30 cm × 17 cm well-defined hyperechoic mass with internal septations and minimal blood flow. Non-contrast CT showed a 16.6 cm × 28.6 cm homogeneous fat-containing mass with thin septa displacing the bowel loops and uterus to the right.
title: Giant retroperitoneal lipoma presenting with abdominal distention: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man presented with a large mass in the upper back. He reported that the lesion began as an “itchy bump” 9 years earlier and had approximately doubled in size each year. He sought care when the mass began bleeding and developing purulent discharge.  
On evaluation, vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia with an RBC count of 3.29 M/μL (reference 4.7–6.1) and an MCV of 82.1 fL (80.0–94.0), consistent with anemia of chronic disease. The white-cell count was 14.5 × 10^3/μL (4.5–11.0) but normalized after a brief course of antibiotics.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a large, heterogeneously enhancing, partially calcified, centrally necrotic soft-tissue mass in the subcutaneous tissues of the thoracolumbar back region, located immediately deep to the skin without involvement of deeper musculature. A chest radiograph showed a double-density opacity overlying the cardiac silhouette on the PA view that was extrinsic to the bony thorax on the lateral view.
title: Giant Pilomatrixoma Presenting in the Posterior Thorax, a Rare Location and the Largest Described

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old Arab woman was referred for evaluation of upper gastrointestinal bleeding after endoscopy at an outside hospital revealed a gastric antral submucosal mass. Three months earlier, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 2.5×3.5×3 cm soft-tissue mass in the gastric antrum with heterogeneous arterial-phase enhancement and intense venous-phase enhancement with a small central necrotic area; there was no lymphadenopathy or metastasis.

Over the preceding four months, she had epigastric pain radiating to the back, constipation, and multiple episodes of melena, along with headaches, fatigue, and dizziness. She denied weight loss. Her only medical history was hypothalamic hypogonadism; she took no medications and had no family history of cancer.

On examination she appeared pale; vital signs were stable, and the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, hematocrit 23.2%); other laboratory tests were within normal limits.

On hospital day 4, esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed an ulcerated antral submucosal mass with an actively bleeding vessel, which was clipped. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a 34×32 mm well-defined isoechoic mass arising from the muscularis propria of the gastric antrum. Fine-needle biopsy of the lesion demonstrated a cluster of monomorphic cells with plasmacytoid features and bland nuclei with salt-and-pepper chromatin, findings described as mostly consistent with a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor.
title: Gastric glomus tumor with a rare presentation: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a four-day history of intermittent non-specific chest pain, on a background of progressive exertional dyspnea over several months and recent loss of appetite. She denied fever, cough, hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, or upper respiratory symptoms. She had no significant past medical history, was not diabetic, and took no medications. She smoked 30 pack‐years. She lived in Darwin, Northern Territory, and was an avid gardener who often walked barefoot and used large amounts of potting mix. She had no known tuberculosis exposures, no relevant travel or occupational history, and no alcohol or drug misuse.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable; there was no clubbing, edema, cyanosis, or lymphadenopathy. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 11.5×10^9/L with neutrophilia of 7.9×10^9/L and a C-reactive protein of 15 mg/L.
