Serial troponins, liver and renal function, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Quantiferon Gold testing was negative. Pulmonary function tests were near normal (FVC 97% predicted, FEV1 92% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.787, DLCO 77%, TLC 89% predicted).

Chest radiography demonstrated an opacity in the right mid-zone. Contrast CT of the chest showed a 36×22 mm mass in the right lower lobe without endoluminal bronchial lesions or mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. PET-CT revealed mild to moderate FDG uptake in the right lower lobe mass and no FDG-avid nodal or distant lesions. Flexible bronchoscopy showed no endobronchial abnormality. Using radial EBUS with a guide sheath, a heterogeneous peripheral lesion was localized in the posterior segment of the right lower lobe. Brushings, biopsies, washings, and a transbronchial cryobiopsy were obtained from the targeted site.
title: Chronic Pulmonary Melioidosis Masquerading as lung malignancy diagnosed by EBUS guided sheath technique

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old man was referred for evaluation of recurrent neck swelling occurring after computed tomography (CT) scans with iodinated contrast. His medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, small-bowel angiodysplasia, papillary urothelial carcinoma, adrenal adenoma, and an abdominal aortic aneurysm under annual surveillance with CT. He denied allergies and had normal renal function.

He experienced two episodes, each approximately 16 hours after receiving 100 mL of iopromide (769 mg/mL), of bilateral, symmetric submandibular swelling with mild discomfort but no itching, respiratory symptoms, fever, or other systemic signs. Both episodes resolved spontaneously over 2–3 days without intervention. Between episodes he had no neck swelling.

At an immunoallergology appointment, his examination and laboratory tests, including markers of infection, were unremarkable. Skin-prick and intradermal tests with iopromide were negative at 20 minutes and at 48 hours. Despite premedication with methylprednisolone and clemastine, a third CT with 100 mL of iopromide again produced symmetric neck swelling approximately 12 hours later, resolving in 48 hours.

A salivary-gland ultrasound performed immediately before the last CT was normal. Twenty-four hours after contrast administration, on re-examination he had obvious submandibular swelling and ultrasound showed bilaterally enlarged submandibular glands with increased parenchymal echogenicity and ductal dilation.
title: Recurrent neck swelling after iodinated contrast media administration

case_prompt: A 28-year-old man presented 10 days after liposuction performed abroad with increasing abdominal discomfort, nausea, fevers, and chills. He had lost 20 kg and weighed 63 kg; he had no prior intra-abdominal pathology or surgery. He became septic from an abdominal collection. On examination, he was febrile to 38.5 °C, heart rate 104 bpm, blood pressure 137/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. His abdomen was distended by a large, fluctuant mass with generalized tenderness and maximal guarding in the left iliac fossa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed three subcutaneous cystic collections in the left flank (12.5 × 3.5 × 10.7 cm), right flank (5.9 × 1.2 × 7 cm), and left rectus muscle (1.2 × 1.8 × 2 cm), and a large cystic intra-abdominal mass displacing the bladder to the right, measuring 18 × 14 × 7.6 cm. He was treated with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and percutaneous drainage of the subcutaneous collections, then discharged for preoperative optimization prior to planned surgical resection of the intra-abdominal lesion.
title: Benign cyst with xanthogranulomatous inflammation involving the transverse colon and the common iliac artery

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old African American man with a 2-year history of hypertension, heart failure, and diabetes mellitus presented with progressive dyspnea and edema. He had episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. An echocardiogram showed dilated left-sided chambers with moderate global hypokinesis and an ejection fraction of 35–40%. He was treated, stabilized, and transferred for consideration of an implantable defibrillator. Further history revealed a 20-lb weight loss, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and breast development over 1–2 years. 

On examination, vital signs were stable (blood pressure 122/66 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats/min, regular) and BMI was 23. There were no rales, S3 gallop, or peripheral edema. He had gynecomastia, a hyperdynamic precordium, and a firm mass in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen. Testes were soft, 20 mL bilaterally. 

Chest radiograph showed an elevated left hemidiaphragm. CT of the abdomen revealed a 12 × 11 × 17 cm mass in the left upper quadrant displacing the left kidney, likely arising from the left adrenal gland. 

Laboratory studies showed a serum estradiol level of 3853 pg/mL (normal < 52 pg/mL in males), confirmed on repeat assay. Low-dose dexamethasone testing failed to suppress cortisol, 24-hour urine free cortisol was mildly elevated, DHEA-S and androstenedione were elevated, and plasma ACTH was suppressed. 

A 12-lead ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with a prolonged corrected QT interval of 477 msec and nonspecific anterior T-wave abnormalities. Chest CT, abdominal MRI, and bone scan showed no evidence of metastatic disease.
title: Feminizing Adrenal Carcinoma Presenting with Heart Failure and Ventricular Tachycardia

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man with no significant medical history except smoking presented with sudden severe left lumbar pain while jogging. Within minutes he noted weakness of the left lower limb and paresthesia below the umbilical level extending into the right lower limb, along with urinary retention. On examination, the left leg had a motor strength of 2/5 with mildly increased tone; the left patellar reflex was hyperactive. There was loss of superficial sensation below the T10 dermatome on the right. Upper limbs were normal. This pattern suggested a partial Brown-Séquard syndrome. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable. Twenty-four hours after symptom onset, MRI of the thoracic spine showed a posteromedial disc extrusion at T5–T6, slightly left‐lateralized, with 18 mm of craniocaudal migration abutting the anterior spinal cord but with no signal abnormality. A subsequent CT of the spine confirmed a calcified disc extrusion continuous with a calcified disc at T5–T6. Brain MRI was normal.
title: Spinal cord ischemia revealed by a Brown-Sequard syndrome and caused by a calcified thoracic disc extrusion with spontaneous regression: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman presented with a painless, gross hematuria of three months’ duration. Her medical history was notable for a hysterectomy 24 years earlier for uterine cancer. She also reported urinary frequency, a sensation of residual urine, nocturia, and left leg edema.

On pelvic ultrasonography, there was a 3.8 × 4.3 cm solid mass in the urethra bulging against the bladder wall, with a clear bladder lumen. Computed tomographic urography demonstrated a 4 cm low-attenuation mass with a cystic component adjacent to the vaginal stump, and multiple enlarged paraaortic and pelvic lymph nodes up to 3 cm in diameter.

Voided urine cytology showed moderate cellularity with small clusters of globular or papillary cells in an inflammatory background. Necrotic debris and inflammatory cells were present within some clusters. Tumor cells were enlarged and had abundant clear or granular cytoplasm with cytoplasmic vacuoles; some clusters exhibited hobnail features. The nuclei were round with folded, irregular membranes, vesicular chromatin, and prominent nucleoli, with moderate pleomorphism. Small hyaline bodies were noted in cell clusters, and benign urothelial cells were rare.
title: Cytologic Findings of Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma of the Urethra: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 73‐year‐old man presented with 1 day of sudden‐onset right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. His history included pulmonary emboli (on apixaban), COPD, ischemic stroke, hypertension, chronic kidney disease (eGFR 35 ml/min), gastroesophageal reflux, heavy smoking, and alcohol excess. On examination he was afebrile, hypertensive, normocardic; his abdomen was soft with tenderness in the right upper quadrant, a negative Murphy’s sign, and no peritonism. Laboratory studies showed normal hemoglobin, normal inflammatory markers, normal liver function tests, normal lipase, and chronic, unchanged renal impairment. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen revealed hyperdense nodular soft tissue filling the gallbladder lumen with a non‐thickened but prominent gallbladder wall, biliary dilatation, and extensive fat stranding and fluid around the gallbladder neck and porta hepatis. The radiologist’s differential diagnoses included malignancy or haemorrhagic cholecystitis, and an MRI with gadolinium contrast was advised. MRI showed no convincing features of malignancy; the gallbladder was distended with heterogeneous, predominantly low T1 and T2 content and demonstrated no internal enhancement, suggesting sludge and/or luminal blood clot. A subsequent ultrasound confirmed cholecystitis with no evidence of cholelithiasis.
title: Surgical case report—acalculous hemorrhagic cholecystitis

case_prompt: A 5-year-old girl presented with a progressively enlarging abdominal mass over 7 months without pain, fever, hematuria, or vomiting. On examination, there was a large right-sided abdominal mass extending from the right lumbar region to the right iliac fossa and into the umbilical and hypogastric areas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen revealed a 16 × 13 × 13 cm minimally enhancing solid mass replacing the right kidney and subcentimetric peripheral nodules in the left lung, with no extension into the adrenal gland, renal vein, or inferior vena cava. A tru-cut biopsy suggested a mesenchymal variant of Wilms’ tumour versus cellular mesoblastic nephroma. A provisional diagnosis of stage IV Wilms’ tumour was made, and the patient received six cycles of AVD-regimen chemotherapy. Post-chemotherapy CT showed resolution of the lung nodules but no significant change in the renal mass. A right nephroureterectomy with lymph node sampling was planned.
title: Metanephric Adenofibroma Masquerading as Wilms’ Tumor

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old man first presented in September 1991 with back pain managed conservatively. In April 1992, he developed sudden paraplegia. Myelography and post-myelography CT revealed three tumors at L1–L3; all were resected via laminectomy. Histology at that time was reported as “atypical ependymoma,” and his paraplegia, saddle anesthesia, sphincter disturbance, and leg weakness persisted. In December 1992, two new tumors at L5–S1 were excised, again labeled as atypical ependymoma. His neurologic deficits remained stable thereafter.

In December 2006, he noted numbness and pain radiating into his upper body and arms. Spinal MRI showed space-occupying lesions at C7–T1 and T8–T9. The C7–T1 lesion, intradural extramedullary and contacting the left T1 root, was fully resected via laminectomy without new deficits. In March 2007, the T8–T9 lesion—also extramedullary, arising from a cauda equina nerve root—was removed uneventfully.

Because of recurrent “ependymomas,” a cranial MRI was obtained, revealing a contrast-enhancing mass in the third ventricle. The patient was asymptomatic from the intracerebral lesion, with no visual field or hormonal abnormalities. He declined surgery. Follow-up MRIs in 2010 and 2012 showed no new lesions or growth of the third-ventricle mass.
title: Atypical Central Neurocytoma with Recurrent Spinal Dissemination over a Period of 20 Years: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old woman with a history of LASIK performed 4 years earlier presented 3 hours after removal of eyelash extensions and permanent eyeliner tattooing with acute bilateral eyelid swelling, redness, photophobia, and blurred vision. An experienced cosmetic technician had applied a cyanoacrylate-dissolving gel remover to the lashes while the patient’s eyes were closed, prompting an immediate burning sensation; the technician then flushed her eyes with saline. The technician proceeded with permanent eyeliner tattooing, applying several topical anesthetics (40% lidocaine/60% tetracaine followed by lidocaine with epinephrine) while instructing the patient to keep her eyes open throughout. Upon completion, the technician noted marked conjunctival redness and drove the patient to the emergency department.

In the ED, both eyes were irrigated with saline for 15–20 minutes. A provisional diagnosis of chemical conjunctivitis was made without slit-lamp examination, and the patient received a 5-day course of erythromycin ointment. Seventy-two hours later, she reported bilateral eyelid pain, photophobia, blurred vision, and tearing. Her uncorrected distance visual acuity was 20/100 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral eyelid edema, conjunctival injection, and a 6 × 6 mm epithelial defect overlying each LASIK flap. Topical moxifloxacin and loteprednol were started, erythromycin was discontinued, and bandage contact lenses were placed.

Two days later, the right epithelial defect had healed completely and the left was 1 × 1 mm; eyelid edema and injection had improved. Loteprednol was stopped, and combination tobramycin-dexamethasone drops were started. One week after injury, both epithelial defects had healed but there was significant superficial punctate keratopathy bilaterally. The visual acuities were 20/25 OD and 20/50 OS. She was switched to prednisolone acetate drops. Three weeks after injury, her visual acuity remained suboptimal; slit-lamp examination revealed anterior basement membrane changes with significant corneal staining, and she was referred for tertiary care.

At the initial tertiary evaluation four weeks after the injury, she complained of ocular pain, photophobia, dry eyes, and daily headaches. She denied a prior history of dry eyes. Uncorrected distance visual acuities were 20/30 OD and 20/40 OS with no improvement on refraction. Extraocular movements and visual fields were full. Slit-lamp examination revealed a healed epithelial defect over each LASIK flap, significant confluent superficial punctate keratitis (worse in the left eye), and trace corneal interface haze in both eyes. The remainder of the anterior and posterior segment examinations was normal.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Chemical conjunctivitis and diffuse lamellar keratitis after removal of eyelash extensions

case_prompt:
A 5-year-old girl, born to consanguineous parents with unremarkable prenatal and perinatal history, presented with gradual vision loss. Her development had been normal until age 2, when her parents noted progressive visual decline. By age 5, she was nearly blind in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed diffuse retinal degeneration with prominent macular atrophy consistent with cone–rod dystrophy. Optical coherence tomography showed diffuse retinal thinning, particularly at the center of the macula, with significant destruction of the outer retinal layer and attenuation of photoreceptors; the optic discs were normal.

At 4½ years of age, she began having monthly epileptic seizures characterized by cyanosis and lateral gaze deviation. Over the past year, her parents also observed gradual cognitive impairment and psychosocial regression. Neurologic examination confirmed developmental regression. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed mild, diffuse cerebral atrophy and periventricular white-matter hyperintensities on T2-weighted images.
title: Cone‐Rod Dystrophy and Progressive Visual Loss as the First Manifestation of Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis Type 7: A Case Report

case_prompt: An 80-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of pain and swelling of the left lower face. She had no prior awareness of the swelling. Two years earlier, her impacted left mandibular third molar had been extracted. On extraoral examination, there was an ill-defined, irregular swelling (approximately 2×3 cm) over the left lower face. Intraoral palpation revealed obliteration of the left mandibular ramus. An orthopantomograph showed a multilocular radiolucent lesion in the left angle and ramus of the mandible. Aspiration of the lesion yielded straw-colored fluid. The initial differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, ameloblastoma, and dentigerous cyst. An incisional biopsy demonstrated a non-keratinizing cystic lining epithelium with mucous cell metaplasia and a connective tissue wall. Correlating the history with the clinical, radiographic, and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of a long-standing dentigerous cyst with mucous metaplasia was made.
title: Predominantly Cystic Central Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma Developing from a Previously Diagnosed Dentigerous Cyst: Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 19‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of dental and orofacial abnormalities. She was born at term to healthy nonconsanguineous parents after an uneventful pregnancy, with an Apgar score of 8. Immediately after birth, three subdural hematomas were noted; she was hypotonic but had no feeding or breathing disorders. Her growth parameters remained between the 25th and 50th percentiles, but she exhibited delayed developmental milestones. At age 1 year, genetic evaluation was initiated because of persistent hypotonia and developmental delay.

On examination, there was no facial or neck asymmetry, and lymph nodes were not palpable. Temporomandibular joint examination revealed no crepitus, but mouth opening was limited with slight left deviation. Palpation suggested bruxism. The lips showed an excessive lower vermilion and a cupid-bow upper vermilion. Oral mucosa was normal; tonsils had been removed. The tongue was enlarged (macroglossia) and moist, with absence of lingual and inferior labial frenula; the superior labial frenulum caused a large diastema between the upper central incisors. Saliva was thick and sticky. There was an anterior open bite and mandibular prognathism. Generalized moderate gingival enlargement and heavy plaque were noted. Several molars had extensive carious lesions. Panoramic and periapical radiographs demonstrated taurodontism, supernumerary roots in premolars, and root resorption of first mandibular molars.
title: Kleefstra Syndrome—Dental Manifestations and Needs: A Case Report with a Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man presented after a road traffic accident that followed a syncopal episode 15 minutes after a bee sting. He had a history of large local reactions to bee stings but no prior anaphylaxis. His medical history included avocado oral allergy and a transient ischemic attack for which he was taking aspirin. The episode resolved rapidly after intramuscular adrenaline (500 μg). Baseline serum mast cell tryptase (MCT) was elevated at 19.2 μg/L (normal <14.0 μg/L), and total IgE was 344 kU/L (normal <111 kU/L). Bee venom–specific IgE was very high at 60.5 kU/L (very high >17.5 kU/L). 

He began bee venom subcutaneous immunotherapy. Six months later, on maintenance dosing, he developed rapid-onset visual changes, malaise, light-headedness, and a sensation of impending collapse, which resolved after adrenaline. Two years into therapy, he again experienced hypotension, light-headedness, and prolonged symptoms requiring two doses of adrenaline, IV hydrocortisone, and fluids. One week later, he was admitted with persistent light-headedness and impending collapse and was started on prednisolone and antihistamines. During admission, he had a postural blood pressure drop of 40 mmHg and a transient episode of severe lower abdominal pain. Repeat MCT was 18.0 μg/L. 

Hypoglycemia, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, and infection were excluded (normal glucose, troponin, CK, d-dimer, CRP). Tests for pheochromocytoma (serum fractionated catecholamines and metanephrines) and carcinoid syndrome (urinary 5-HIAA) were negative. Dermatological examination found no cutaneous mastocytoma. Bone marrow aspirate showed normal trilineage hematopoiesis with no increase in mast cells. Molecular testing for c-KIT D816V in marrow and serum was negative, and trephine staining for CD2 and CD117 did not demonstrate a significant mast cell population. Serum protein electrophoresis was negative for monoclonal immunoglobulins, full-body PET scan showed no abnormal uptake, and bone mineral density T score was –1.5 at the spine.
final_diagnosis_raw: Idiopathic non‐clonal mast cell activation syndrome
title: Successful treatment of idiopathic mast cell activation syndrome with low‐dose Omalizumab

case_prompt: A 50-year-old man with chronic glomerulonephritis underwent a living-donor renal transplant in 1998. He received prednisolone, cyclosporine (withdrawn after 1 year), and azathioprine, developing posttransplant diabetes mellitus but no rejection episodes. In 2007, nine years post-transplant, he noted 12 days of progressive left-eye protrusion associated with pain, redness, and diminished vision. He denied fever, weight loss, headache, vomiting, or focal neurologic symptoms. On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, with no lymphadenopathy. The left eye showed proptosis, conjunctival redness, hemorrhagic chemosis, and lid edema; the right eye was normal. Visual acuity was limited to light perception with inaccurate light projection; ocular movements were restricted in all directions. Intraocular pressure was 24 mm Hg. Fundoscopy revealed blurred disc margins, ischemia of the superior nasal retina, and macular chorioretinal folds. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 2.5 × 1.6 × 2 cm, mildly irregular, isointense lesion in the superior left orbit, predominantly extraconal with intraconal extension, abutting and partially encasing the optic nerve, displacing extraocular muscles, and with areas of bony erosion. Radiologists considered possibilities of lymphoma, metastasis, or orbital pseudotumor.
title: NK/T-cell lymphoma in a renal transplant recipient and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman with no history of cardiovascular disease underwent craniotomy for recurrent IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted grade 3 oligodendroglioma, followed by vincristine, nimustine, carboplatin, interferon-β chemotherapy and radiotherapy. On postoperative day 72, she experienced acute chest pain and, en route to the emergency department, developed ventricular fibrillation requiring immediate resuscitation.  
An electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation in lead aVR and ST-segment depression in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated akinesis of the anterior, lateral, and posterior walls and a left ventricular ejection fraction of approximately 10%. Cardiac enzymes measured just before the arrest were within normal limits. Because of refractory ventricular fibrillation, venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and an intra-aortic balloon pump were initiated.  
Urgent coronary angiography revealed patent coronary arteries without stenosis or occlusion. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan showed a mass on the left coronary cusp of the aortic valve. Subsequent transesophageal echocardiography identified a 10 × 10 × 8 mm mobile mass at the same location, intermittently obstructing the left coronary artery ostium. Laboratory studies showed no fever or inflammatory signs; blood cultures were negative. Tests for antinuclear antibodies were negative and protein C and S levels were normal.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?
title: Myocardial infarction due to non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis in a patient with oligodendroglioma: an unusual presentation and diagnostic challenge—a case report

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old boy with a 6-year history of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus was brought to the emergency department for evaluation of right upper-quadrant abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting of one day’s duration. He denied changes in urine or stool, melena, anorexia, weight loss, pruritus, jaundice, fever, or bleeding. His diabetes had been complicated by several prior episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis, and he admitted to intermittent insulin noncompliance. He took no new medications and denied alcohol or over-the-counter drug use.

On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 109 beats/min, blood pressure 109/60 mm Hg, BMI 15.8 kg/m2. The abdomen was mildly distended with tenderness in the right upper quadrant; the liver edge was palpable 6 cm below the costal margin without rebound or guarding, and there was no splenomegaly or ascites.

Laboratory evaluation on admission showed: blood glucose 480 mg/dL; arterial pH 7.25, PCO2 30 mm Hg; anion gap 21; BUN 29 mg/dL; creatinine 0.6 mg/dL. Liver tests were abnormal: ALT 262 U/L, AST 205 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 139 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 122 U/L, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL. Lactate was 3.2 mmol/L. Amylase, lipase, and acetaminophen level were normal. Complete blood count, coagulation studies, and chest radiograph were unremarkable. Urinalysis showed ketones.

He was admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis and treated with insulin infusion and IV fluids. His anion gap closed by hospital day 2, and glycemic control stabilized on his home insulin regimen, but his right upper-quadrant pain persisted. Over the next several days, his ALT and AST rose further, and lactate transiently increased before normalizing by day 7.

To evaluate persistent hepatomegaly and transaminase elevation, we obtained abdominal ultrasonography and extended laboratory studies. Ultrasonography showed a diffusely enlarged liver (24 cm) with normal echogenicity; the gallbladder, spleen, and kidneys were normal. Serum iron studies, lipid panel, HbA1c, hepatitis A, B, and C serologies, EBV and CMV serologies, antimitochondrial and anti-smooth muscle antibodies, ceruloplasmin, α₁-antitrypsin level, and thyroid function tests were all within normal limits or negative. At this point, the etiology of his hepatomegaly and elevated liver enzymes remained unclear.
title: Young Man with Hepatomegaly: A Case of Glycogenic Hepatopathy

case_prompt: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-year history of progressively worsening intermittent dysphagia and vomiting. One year earlier, barium esophagography at another clinic led to a diagnosis of gastro-esophageal reflux disease, and he received antireflux medication without improvement. On presentation, he had no remarkable findings on physical examination, and routine blood tests were normal. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed narrowing of the middle esophagus with a small area of mucosal erosion; insufflation of air did not relieve the narrowing, and the endoscope could not be advanced. Contrast esophagography demonstrated a 1.6-cm segment of esophageal narrowing at the level of the carina with mild passage disturbance. To evaluate for a possible vascular ring and other structural abnormalities, computed tomography angiography of the thoracic aorta was performed, revealing a 25-mm mass involving the esophageal or periesophageal region posterior to the paratracheal segment of the esophagus.
title: Granular cell tumor of the esophagus in an adolescent

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old G2P2 woman with a history of endometriosis presented with dull pelvic pain, worse on the left, and low-grade fever for several days. Vital signs were within normal limits. Urinalysis was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed no leukocytosis, but a neutrophil percentage of 73.5% (reference range, 40–70%) and an elevated C-reactive protein level of 64.7 mg/L (reference range, 0–5 mg/L). She was admitted with a presumed diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease.

Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a right adnexal lesion consistent with an endometrioma and a complex cystic lesion with thick walls and septations on the left. Pelvic MRI with intravenous contrast was performed to evaluate for a possible tubo-ovarian abscess. Compared with imaging six months earlier, the left adnexal endometrioma (previously T1 hyperintense) had enlarged and become T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense, with peripheral and septal contrast enhancement but no discrete solid mural nodule. In the medial portion of the right-sided endometrioma, a new focal area of T1 hypointensity corresponded to T2 hyperintensity; this area showed no contrast enhancement.

The patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics (sulbactam/ampicillin, clindamycin, and gentamicin) and underwent testing for tumor markers, which revealed a mildly elevated CA-125 of 87.1 U/mL (reference range, 0–35 U/mL); other tumor markers were within normal limits. Blood cultures were sterile.

On hospital day 3, she developed fever, worsening pelvic pain, signs of peritonitis, a rise in C-reactive protein to 299.5 mg/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 95 mm/h, leukocytosis (12 × 10^3/mm^3), and neutrophils 91.4%. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed extensive pelvic fat-stranding, peritoneal thickening, diffuse intra-abdominal fluid, and bilateral adnexal cystic lesions with thick, enhancing walls. Antibiotics were changed to meropenem and vancomycin.

By hospital day 10, her clinical status improved: leukocyte count normalized, neutrophils were 72%, and C-reactive protein decreased to 46.75 mg/L. Follow-up ultrasonography demonstrated regression of the left tubo-ovarian abscess and resolution of free fluid, while the right adnexal cyst remained, with low-level internal echoes and mildly thickened walls.

On hospital day 11, she acutely developed high fever and marked suprapubic tenderness despite continuing broad-spectrum antibiotics. Repeat pelvic MRI showed that the left lesion had largely regressed, but the right adnexal lesion had increased in volume by 50%, with a progressive increase in the T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense nonenhancing component and extensive T2 hyperintensities in the pelvic fat consistent with inflammation.
title: Multimodality imaging findings of infected endometriomas: “T1 signal reversal” as a potential diagnostic sign?

case_prompt:
A 77-year-old man with metastatic Merkel cell carcinoma involving iliac, inguinal lymph nodes and bone presented for evaluation. His medical history was notable for sarcoidosis diagnosed 10 years earlier by mediastinal biopsy after an episode of hypercalcemia; remission was achieved with glucocorticoids, although calcified mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy persisted. 

He completed six cycles of carboplatin and etoposide over six months, with a partial response: most inguinal lymphadenopathy resolved, and existing pulmonary, hilar, and calcified mediastinal nodes remained unchanged. He was then started on avelumab.

After three doses of avelumab, routine labs revealed a serum calcium concentration of 2.81 mmol/L and a creatinine clearance of 0.70 mL/s/m^2. The hypercalcemia was presumed to be malignancy-related and managed with intravenous zoledronic acid and fluids; avelumab was continued. Two weeks later, his serum calcium rose to 3.07 mmol/L, and creatinine clearance fell to 0.52 mL/s/m^2, prompting hospital admission for additional intravenous fluids and a second dose of zoledronic acid.

Further laboratory evaluation showed:  
• Serum parathyroid hormone level, 5 ng/L (reference range, 15–68)  
• Serum 25-hydroxy-vitamin D, 66 nmol/L (RR, 50–140)  
• Serum 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D, 280 pmol/L (RR, 60–210)  
• Urinary calcium excretion, 8.1 mmol/day (RR, 2.5–7.2)  
• Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level, 2,200 nkat/L (RR, 483–1,866)

Restaging investigations showed no progression of Merkel cell carcinoma compared to pre–avelumab studies.
title: Hypercalcaemia due to Sarcoidosis during Treatment with Avelumab for Metastatic Merkel Cell Carcinoma

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman was evaluated for a 5-year history of secondary amenorrhoea and infertility.  
Past medical history:  
• Beta-thalassaemia major since childhood on periodic blood transfusions.  
• Restrictive cardiomyopathy (diagnosed at age 10; on digoxin), liver fibrosis with siderosis, and pancreatic fibrosis.  
• Allogeneic HLA-identical brother bone marrow transplantation at age 19 after 15 days of conditioning (fludarabine, busulfan, cyclophosphamide).  
Menstrual history: Menarche at 13 with regular cycles until age 15; cycles ceased at age 33. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea was suspected; eating disorders, excessive exercise, and stress were ruled out.  
Laboratory studies:  
• FSH 1.06 IU/L, LH <0.3 IU/L, estradiol >18.4 pmol/L, AMH <0.007 pmol/L  
• GnRH stimulation: baseline FSH 1.03 IU/L & LH <0.3 IU/L; 30-min FSH 1.15 IU/L & LH 0.57 IU/L (subnormal pituitary response)  
• Human menopausal gonadotropin stimulation: no detectable response  
• Insulin tolerance test: peak GH 11.6 ng/mL; cortisol 26.3 μg/dL  
Pituitary MRI: decreased signal intensity on T2-weighted images and reduced gland size
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Association of Beta-Thalassaemia and Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old Asian woman presented with a rapidly progressive, diffuse lump in her left breast. She first noted bluish-purple skin discoloration in July 2021, initially attributed to trauma. From January to March 2022 her left breast enlarged significantly. She had no history of breast surgery, breast irradiation, chronic or genetic diseases, smoking, or drug use. Menarche was at age 13; she has had two live births and no oral contraceptive use.

On examination, the upper outer quadrant of the left breast contained a firm, slightly tender 8 cm × 5 cm mass with poor mobility, overlying bluish-purple discoloration, and a local rise in temperature. There was no nipple retraction, skin dimpling, dilated veins, or palpable axillary lymph nodes.

On March 26, 2022, routine blood tests and tumor markers (CA125, CA15-3, CEA) were within normal limits. Mammography showed an ill-defined, non-calcified area, suspected to be an inflammatory lesion. Ultrasonography (USG) revealed a large area of uneven echogenicity, highly suspicious for granulomatous mastitis. A subsequent USG demonstrated several possibly abnormal lymph nodes in the left axilla, the largest measuring 1 cm × 0.7 cm; an ultrasound-guided axillary lymph node biopsy showed no tumor cells. PET-CT revealed a hypermetabolic thickened tissue in the left upper breast with an SUV max of 3.5 and small axillary lymph nodes with an SUV max of 1.3, suspected to be inflammatory; no distant organ metastasis was seen.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Primary angiosarcoma of breast: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman was referred with suspected infective endocarditis after an ischemic stroke of the left middle cerebral artery nine days earlier. ECG showed no atrial fibrillation. Initial transesophageal echocardiography revealed vegetations on a port catheter and the aortic valve, and empiric ampicillin–gentamicin therapy was started. A CT pulmonary angiogram, prompted by respiratory distress, showed bilateral pulmonary emboli. Her history was notable for FIGO stage IVA clear cell cervical carcinoma diagnosed one year prior (treated with lymphadenectomy and platinum-based chemoradiotherapy, now on Navelbine for lymphogenic progression) and a prior pulmonary embolism managed with edoxaban. 

On admission she was hypotensive, tachycardic, afebrile, and required high-flow oxygen. Laboratory tests showed CRP 137 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.5 ng/mL, leukocytes 9.43 ×10^9/L, platelets 115 ×10^9/L, hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, D-dimer 15 mg/L, troponin I 11 462 pg/mL, and BNP 2624 pg/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography suggested large vegetations on the aortic valve. Urgent transesophageal echocardiography confirmed large vegetations on the aortic, mitral, tricuspid, and pulmonary valves and on the right side of the atrial septum, without valve destruction and with only moderate regurgitation, and impaired left ventricular systolic function. 

Therapy was extended to cover endocarditis according to guidelines, unfractionated heparin anticoagulation was started, and blood cultures, next-generation sequencing for pathogens, and thrombophilia testing were initiated.
title: Quadrivalvular nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis in a patient with clear cell cervical cancer

case_prompt: A 5‐year‐old spayed female Chinchilla cat was referred for evaluation of a 4-week history of weight loss and inappetence. On examination, the cat was bright and alert with a body‐condition score of 2/9. Palpation revealed a 1.5 cm intestinal mass in the mid‐abdomen; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Hematology and serum biochemistry were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 14 mm eccentric intramural mass in a small intestinal loop; the mass was hypoechoic, heterogeneous, and appeared to arise from the muscularis layer, causing focal distortion of wall layering but no obstructive pattern. The remainder of the abdomen was unremarkable, aside from globally altered small intestinal wall layering. Fine‐needle aspiration of the mass on two occasions yielded poorly cellular, nondiagnostic samples. An exploratory coeliotomy was performed; intraoperatively, diffuse ileal thickening and a 1.5 cm mass on the antimesenteric border of the distal jejunum were identified and resected with margins. Enlarged mesenteric and ileocecocolic lymph nodes were also biopsied. All specimens were submitted for histopathological examination.
title: Small intestinal peripheral nerve sheath tumour in a cat

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an abnormal radiolucency in the right mandible detected on a routine panoramic radiograph. She reported intermittent pain in the right mandibular region. Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable, and she denied any history of trauma. On extraoral examination, there was no swelling, facial asymmetry, cutaneous changes, or lymphadenopathy; motor and sensory functions were intact. Intraorally, there was buccal cortical expansion of the right mandible from the canine to the anterior border of the ramus; the area was bony-hard and non-tender, with margins blending into surrounding bone and intact overlying mucosa. All teeth in the involved region responded normally to vitality testing.

A panoramic radiograph at presentation showed a well-defined multilocular radiolucent lesion in the right mandibular body and ramus, with coarse radiopaque septa and preservation of the inferior alveolar canal; no tooth resorption or displacement was seen. Review of a panoramic radiograph taken five years earlier revealed a dome-shaped radiolucency in the retromolar area, “ground-glass” radiopacity of the ramus and posterior body, and a mixed radiodensity anteriorly from the first premolar to the second molar.

An incisional biopsy under local anesthesia revealed a thin buccal cortical plate; aspiration yielded yellowish fluid. The specimen comprised a mixture of brittle hemorrhagic-appearing tissue and fibro-osseous tissue. Microscopic examination of the solid component showed dense fibroblastic proliferation of spindle-shaped mononuclear cells without atypia or mitotic figures, interspersed with numerous bone trabeculae and cementum-like calcified spans that were often confluent and lined by regular osteoblastic cells. Smears of the aspirated fluid demonstrated a discretely hematic background with polymorphic inflammatory cells and histiocytes, without any abnormal or neoplastic cells.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Cystic degeneration in cemento-ossifying fibroma: Diagnosis challenge and conservative management - Case report

case_prompt: A 64-year-old woman with a history of orthotopic heart transplantation and end-stage renal failure on hemodialysis presented with six weeks of progressive dyspnea, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and a 5-kg weight loss. An outpatient chest radiograph showed a left upper-lobe infiltrate. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 16.5 Gpt/l and a C-reactive protein level of 245 mg/l. She was treated sequentially with oral amoxicillin and then ciprofloxacin without clinical or radiographic improvement. On hospital admission, her white-cell count was 18.2 Gpt/l and C-reactive protein was 278 mg/l. Chest computed tomography demonstrated an 8 × 8 cm mass in the left upper lobe. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy and bronchoalveolar lavage showed no evidence of malignancy on histology, yet lung cancer remained the leading diagnosis. She was transferred for further evaluation. At this point, the microbiologic results of the bronchoalveolar lavage were still incomplete.
title: Nocardiosis mimicking lung cancer in a heart transplant patient with end-stage renal disease

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman presented with a 9-month history of gradual swelling and stiffness of her right thumb, which extended to her hand and wrist after returning from Jamaica. She had no fever, and laboratory markers were within normal limits. Over this period, she was diagnosed sequentially with idiopathic carpal tunnel syndrome, De Quervain’s tenosynovitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and complex regional pain syndrome type II, and received NSAIDs, sulfasalazine, local and systemic corticosteroids without improvement. She denied major trauma but performed gardening and sometimes had minor unnoticed injuries. Tests for HIV and diabetes were negative.

Ultrasound of the hand revealed marked diffuse synovitis with low vascular flow and tenosynovitis of the common flexor tendons extending into the thumb and the fifth finger’s flexor tendon sheath. She underwent drainage of a collection in the fifth finger and limited debridement of the flexor tendon sheath. Histopathological analysis of synovial tissue disclosed intense chronic inflammation with both necrotizing and non-necrotizing granulomas. Cultures from perioperative samples grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, and mycobacterial liquid culture became positive after eight days. Ziehl–Neelsen staining showed acid-fast bacilli. She was diagnosed with chronic nontuberculous mycobacterial flexor tenosynovitis complicated by MSSA cellulitis.
journal: Journal of Clinical Tuberculosis and Other Mycobacterial Diseases
title: Mycobacterium heraklionense: An emerging cause of hand tenosynovitis

case_prompt: A 67-year-old woman with a history of right-sided colon adenocarcinoma underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic-assisted extended right hemicolectomy and was discharged on postoperative day 5. On postoperative day 10, she returned with diffuse abdominal pain, hematemesis, and subjective fevers. Abdominal CT showed free intraperitoneal fluid and pneumoperitoneum; broad-spectrum antibiotics were started, and she underwent an exploratory laparotomy. A small anastomotic leak was found and resected; an end ileostomy was created. Intraoperative vital signs were stable except for a low-grade tachycardia. She was extubated after surgery but remained obtunded. Her oxygen saturation stayed above 95% on supplemental oxygen with airway adjuncts, yet she failed to regain consciousness and developed apnea requiring bag-valve-mask ventilation. Naloxone, glycopyrrolate, and neostigmine were administered without improvement. Blood glucose was normal. Arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.03, PCO2 107 mm Hg, and PaO2 375 mm Hg. She was re-intubated for hypercapnic respiratory failure, and sedating medications were held. Given persistent unresponsiveness, a noncontrast head CT was obtained, showing diffuse cerebral edema with tonsillar herniation and hydrocephalus, most pronounced in the parietal and occipital regions. An external ventricular drain was placed, and measures to control intracranial pressure—including hypertonic saline, head elevation, normotension, and seizure prophylaxis—were initiated.
title: An unusual presentation of a rare disease: posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome following abdominal sepsis

case_prompt: A 33-year-old man presented 15 months after multi-ligament reconstruction of his right knee with a two-month history of anterolateral leg bulging. Fifteen months earlier, he had sustained a knee dislocation in a motor vehicle accident, which was reduced and immobilized. Examination revealed positive posterior and anterior drawer tests, increased posterolateral rotation, and varus stress laxity, and he was diagnosed with PCL, posterolateral complex, and ACL injuries. Two months after injury, he underwent inlay PCL reconstruction with an Achilles-tendon allograft and posterolateral corner reconstruction (including lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon, and popliteofibular ligament) using two posterior tibial allografts. Interference-screw fixations in all tunnels except the tibial PCL inlay were performed with PDLLA absorbable screws, and an articulated external fixator was applied. Six weeks later the fixator was removed. He returned to pre-injury activity by eight months post-operatively and was asymptomatic until 15 months post-surgery, when he noted a painless bulge in the anterolateral leg. Four weeks later, he observed protrusion of part of one of the screws and presented for evaluation. On examination, a fragment of a screw was visible through the skin over the anterolateral aspect of his knee; the surrounding skin appeared intact with no signs of acute inflammation. Vitals were normal.
title: Extra-articular and transcutaneous migration of the poly-l/d-lactide interference screw after popliteal tendon reconstruction☆

case_prompt: A 43-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 4-month history of a giant, painless mass on the right side of the vulva associated with ulceration and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She had no fever, regular menstrual cycles, and a history of psoriasis. On examination, she appeared pale without jaundice. Dermatologic findings included scaly, pruritic patches on her hands and feet. Genitourinary examination revealed an ulcerated, pedunculated mass measuring approximately 17×7×17 cm on the right labia majora. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, sodium 129 mEq/L, and calcium 1.28 mg/dL. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a normal uterus containing an intrauterine device, a normal left adnexa, and an enlarged right ovary. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed an oval cyst measuring 4×7 cm in the right uterine adnexa, a gallstone, a 15×7×17 cm irregular mass with central necrosis on the right labia majora, and right iliac lymphadenopathy.
title: A Rapidly Growing Giant Vulvar Fibroma on the Right Labia Majora: A Rare Case Report

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman with no prior medical or psychiatric history presented with a 6-week history of intermittent severe headaches, blurred vision, and left-hand numbness. She also endorsed night sweats, fatigue, and neck and back muscle pain. One month before referral, she developed acute agitation, shouting, confusion, disorientation, and inappropriate speech. 

She first went to an emergency department, where CT of the head, brain MRI, ECG, and CBC were normal; she was diagnosed with anxiety and discharged. When her symptoms persisted, she was admitted to psychiatry for an acute confusional state; repeat CT, MRI, MR venography, and MR angiography were all unremarkable. She was treated with quetiapine, citalopram, and mirtazapine, improved temporarily, and was discharged with a diagnosis of conversion disorder, although she had amnesia for the admission period.

Ten days later, she was evaluated in a neurology clinic. She denied fever, travel, raw meat or unpasteurized dairy ingestion, and animal contact. On examination, she was afebrile, alert, and oriented with a normal neurologic examination. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 6.4×10^3/μL, hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL (microcytic hypochromic), platelets 281×10^3/μL, CRP 4.7 mg/L. Autoimmune screening (ANA, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin) was negative. Brain CT, MRI, and MRV were normal. 

CSF analysis revealed 27 leukocytes/μL (100% lymphocytes), protein 24 mg/dL, glucose 95 mg/dL, Gram stain negative, culture negative, cytology negative. FilmArray meningitis/encephalitis panel was negative.
title: Unusual presentation of neurobrucellosis in Jeddah, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressively painful swelling in the right preauricular region. She had no history of trauma. One year earlier, she had undergone excision of a cutaneous malignant melanoma (pT1a, cN0, cM0) from the left knee. Her medical history was otherwise notable only for hypertension and allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

On extraoral examination, there was marked facial asymmetry with deviation of the chin to the left and a firm, bony swelling over the right condylar region. Mouth opening was possible without pronounced clicking or crepitus. Intraorally, she wore partial dentures; five teeth remained in the maxilla and nine in the mandible. Occlusion was Angle Class I.

An orthopantomogram showed similar size and form of both condyles. Ultrasonography of the right preauricular area revealed unsharp, circumscribed, possibly calcified lesions cranial to the mandibular condyle, without increased vascularization; both TMJs showed symmetric degenerative changes. A computed tomography scan demonstrated multiple loose calcified bodies within and outside the right joint capsule, forming a medial sacculation. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a well-circumscribed, cystic, high-intensity lesion on T2-weighted images surrounding the right TMJ and enhanced contrast uptake on T1-weighted images.

The radiologic differential diagnosis included an ectopic parotid adenoma or a sacculation of the joint capsule with calcifications. No imaging evidence of malignancy was identified. Therefore, no further imaging was performed.
title: Intra- and extracapsular synovial chondromatosis of the temporomandibular joint: Rare case and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 45-year-old woman presented with 6 months of increasing abdominal cramping and marked distention despite a 35-pound intentional weight loss. She denied other systemic or gastrointestinal symptoms. Her history was notable only for in vitro fertilization resulting in twin pregnancy 7 years earlier; she was otherwise healthy, with a body-mass index of 27 and no medications. On examination, her abdomen was firm and distended, with a palpable large mass; there was no lower-extremity edema. Laboratory studies, including serum hCG, were normal. CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 27×20×13 cm heterogeneous, hypodense intra-abdominal mass with irregular central solid-enhancing components, distinct from the uterus and without ascites or lymphadenopathy. An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy showed an admixture of mature adipocytes and spindle cells. Immunohistochemical staining was diffusely positive for smooth muscle actin, desmin, and estrogen receptor, but negative for HMB-45.
title: Large intraperitoneal lipoleiomyoma in a pre-menopausal woman: a case report

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man with a body-mass index of 28.4 presented with a 2-week history of chest tightness and nausea. He had no history of thoracic or abdominal trauma. A chest radiograph showed a double contour along the right hemidiaphragm. Chest computed tomography revealed a well-circumscribed mass in the right posterior thoracic cavity measuring 28 cm × 9 cm × 10 cm that compressed the right lower lobe. The mass consisted predominantly of fatty tissue, contained no intestinal loops or other organs, and appeared to be continuous with retroperitoneal fat. Routine blood chemistry, including tumor markers, was within normal limits.

Differential diagnoses included lipoma, liposarcoma, and diaphragmatic hernia.
title: Right-sided Bochdalek hernia containing retroperitoneal fat in the elderly: report of a case

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman presented to the emergency department after a presyncopal episode. At home she had sudden nausea and one episode of nonbloody, nonbilious emesis. On standing, she became lightheaded and nearly fainted. She denied chest pain, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, or recent illness. 

On arrival she was tachycardic but normotensive and without hypoxia. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed no abnormalities. Electrocardiography showed a new right bundle-branch block. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated right ventricular free-wall akinesis with apical sparing. 

While in the emergency department, she developed hypoxia, requiring 3 L of oxygen by nasal cannula, and hypotension that did not improve after 2 L of normal saline, prompting initiation of norepinephrine. 

Her medical history was notable for stage IV gastric adenocarcinoma with peritoneal metastases. 

Computed tomography with pulmonary angiography revealed a large saddle embolus at the right mainstem bronchus with extension into the left mainstem bronchus without obstruction.
title: Use of Ultrasound-Assisted, Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis in a Patient With High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism

case_prompt: A 48-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and psoriasis presented with a 2-day history of acute diffuse abdominal pain. On arrival, she was tachycardic (heart rate 130/min), hypotensive (blood pressure 78/45 mm Hg), afebrile, and fully oriented. She received intravenous fluids with improvement in blood pressure and heart rate. Initial laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 8.3 × 10^3/µL, arterial pH of 7.29, and lactate of 3.5 mmol/L. An acute abdominal radiograph demonstrated free air beneath the right hemidiaphragm. Examination of the abdomen showed distension, tenderness, guarding, and signs of peritonitis. Because her vital signs stabilized after resuscitation, a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan was obtained to localize the source of the pneumoperitoneum.
title: Pneumoperitoneum as a result of a ruptured splenic abscess

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old man presented with epigastric and right upper quadrant pain. On examination, there was no remarkable tenderness; vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, with other hematologic and biochemical tests normal. 

An abdominal ultrasonogram revealed a normal gallbladder containing multiple gallstones and a fusiform cystic structure adjacent to it (no biliary-tract dilatation; gallbladder wall normal in thickness and echogenicity). 

To further delineate biliary anatomy, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography was performed, demonstrating a normal gallbladder with multiple intraluminal stones and a second adjacent gallbladder; both structures drained via a common cystic duct entering the common hepatic duct. The common hepatic duct and common bile duct were otherwise normal without intraluminal filling defects.
title: Duplication of the gallbladder: Case report of a rare biliary malformation

case_prompt: A 53-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of multiple pruritic, burning, blanching erythematous macules on his trunk and bilateral upper extremities. He had a history of hypertension and a left-sided ischemic stroke 7 days earlier, after which he was discharged on aspirin 75 mg once daily, enalapril 10 mg once daily, atorvastatin 20 mg once daily, and omeprazole 20 mg twice daily. He denied any new foods, environmental exposures, pet contacts, or family history of allergic skin disease. He had no angioedema, respiratory symptoms, or prior allergic reactions. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 12,000 cells/mm3 with an eosinophil count of 550 cells/mL; other blood counts and chemistry panels were unremarkable. Because angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors can cause drug rashes, enalapril was replaced with amlodipine 5 mg once daily, and he was started on an H1-antihistamine for symptomatic relief, but the rash and pruritus did not improve.
title: Aspirin‐induced urticaria in a recently diagnosed ischemic stroke patient: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old previously healthy female presented with a 3-day history of tender, red nodules on both lower legs that had enlarged and become increasingly painful. She denied trauma, fevers, recent infections, ill contacts, or similar lesions in others. Three weeks earlier, she had received her second dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine and experienced only one day of malaise afterward. She had no side effects after the first dose. She denied recent streptococcal pharyngitis or new medications. Her medical history was negative for systemic infections or inflammatory conditions, including tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and inflammatory bowel disease. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Multiple tender, warm, erythematous nodules measuring 2–3 cm were noted on the anterior tibial surfaces bilaterally, and a single similar lesion was present on her left forearm. No other abnormalities were found.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 37 mm/hr (normal <25 mm/hr) and a C-reactive protein level of 1.7 mg/dL (normal <0.8 mg/dL). Complete blood count with differential was within normal limits. Antistreptolysin-O titers were not elevated, and an interferon-gamma release assay was negative. Given the clinical appearance, a biopsy was deferred.
title: Erythema nodosum after COVID-19 vaccination in a pediatric patient

case_prompt: A 61-year-old man (weight, 50 kg) with a history of chronic alcoholism and 50 h of abstinence was scheduled for open reduction and internal fixation of a left intertrochanteric femur fracture under regional anesthesia. Physical examination was unremarkable; laboratory studies showed mild elevation of liver enzymes. He received aspiration prophylaxis, prophylactic intravenous multivitamins, and oral lorazepam (2 mg at bedtime and 2 h before surgery). In the block room, standard monitors were applied and a left fascia iliaca compartmental block was performed with 30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine via landmark technique. Thirty minutes later, spinal anesthesia was administered with 2.5 mL of 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine and fentanyl (20 µg). After positioning on the operating table, midazolam (2 mg IV) was given. Twenty minutes after the surgical incision, he became agitated, was talking irrelevantly, and was noted to be confused and disoriented; he developed tachycardia, hypertension, and tremors. Airway patency was maintained, and oxygen was administered by face mask. Boluses of midazolam (total, 10 mg) were given, and an esmolol infusion was started for hypertension and tachycardia. Because of persistent agitation, propofol infusion was initiated and maintained at 50 µg/kg/min, after which the patient became sedated with stable vital signs, and the surgery was continued.
title: Intraoperative Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome: A Coincidence or Precipitation?

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 1-month history of epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting of gastric contents. She had no fever or diarrhea. Initial evaluation at a local hospital showed a blood lipase level of 216.2 U/L (normal < 60 U/L), normal amylase levels, and abdominal CT and ultrasound demonstrating inflammation and fluid collections consistent with pancreatitis and peritoneal effusion. She was diagnosed with cholecystitis and pancreatitis, treated with IV fluids, pancreatic‐rest measures, and somatostatin, which normalized pancreatic enzymes, but her epigastric pain and anorexia persisted. A repeat abdominal CT showed mild pancreatic swelling.  

Over the ensuing days, she developed peripheral edema, cough, and pain in the right upper limb; ultrasound revealed thrombosis of the right axillary and subclavian veins. Chest CT demonstrated focal pulmonary opacities and bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory studies revealed:  
• White-cell count 2.18 × 10^9/L (3–9.5), hemoglobin 91 g/L (115–150), platelets 33 × 10^9/L (125–350)  
• Urinalysis: 1+ protein, 1+ blood; 24-h protein excretion 7.9 g  
• Bone marrow biopsy: active hyperplasia, normal megakaryocyte count with rare platelets, megaloblastic granulocytes  
• ANA titer 1:1280; anti–double-stranded DNA and anti-SSA positive; anti–Smith, anti-RNP, and anti-SSB negative  
• IgG 24.3 g/L (7–16), IgG4 0.409 g/L (0.03–2.01)  
• C3 0.56 g/L (0.9–1.8), C4 0.06 g/L (0.1–0.4)  
• ESR 82 mm/h (0–20), CRP < 10 mg/L (0–10), procalcitonin 0.066 mg/L (< 0.064)  
• Anticardiolipin antibody and lupus anticoagulant positive  
Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure 119/71 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, pulse 86/min. Her abdomen was soft with epigastric tenderness; skin, joints, and neurologic exams were unremarkable.
title: Acute pancreatitis as an initial presentation of systemic lupus erythematosus: a case report

case_prompt: A 7-month-old previously healthy Caucasian male was referred for evaluation of a suspected right diaphragmatic hernia identified at 4 months of age during an episode of cough, cyanosis, and respiratory distress that resolved with antibiotic therapy. Since then he has been asymptomatic and thriving without recurrence of respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms. On examination, he was well-appearing with normal vital signs; abdominal and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Complete blood count and serum biochemistry values were within normal limits. A three-dimensional contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed a dilated bowel loop (hepatic flexure) interposed between the right hemidiaphragm and liver, with minimal superolateral displacement of the heart, normal liver anatomy, and no radiographic defect in the hemidiaphragm. Fluoroscopic imaging demonstrated normal diaphragmatic movement during inspiration and expiration.
title: Congenital partial diaphragmatic eventration presenting with Chilaiditi’s sign: a case report

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old premenopausal nulliparous woman presented with a longstanding history of severe constipation and intermittent abdominal pain since childhood. She reported bowel movements every 7 to 10 days, often requiring laxatives. One year earlier, she underwent exploratory laparotomy for ileus; the report noted extensive dilation and elongation of the colon with massive fecal impactions that were removed without other findings.

On current evaluation, laboratory tests and tumor markers were within normal limits. Anal manometry demonstrated basal waves and a normal rectosphincteric reflex. A barium enema revealed dilation of the entire colon, and colonic transit time was prolonged. Colonoscopy showed normal mucosal structure, and defecography was unremarkable.

Because of refractory chronic constipation, she underwent a subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis. Intraoperatively, the colon was markedly elongated and dilated. Gross examination of the resected distal ileum, cecum, ascending, transverse, and sigmoid colon revealed multiple hard, elastic nodular and polypoid formations in the mesenteric adipose tissue, up to 10 × 4 × 2.5 cm in size, either spherical-ovoid or irregularly shaped, connected to the bowel wall by thin fibrous bands. Cut surfaces were gray-white and fibrous. The colonic mucosa appeared normal, but the bowel wall was hardened and partially thickened (approximately 1.5 cm). The parietal and pelvic peritoneum, small-intestinal mesentery, uterus, and ovaries were grossly normal.
title: Disseminated peritoneal leiomyomatosis with chronic constipation: a case report

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old man was admitted with a 20-day history of left knee swelling and deformity. He denied any trauma. The knee was mildly painful; he could flex and extend but could not bear weight. An earlier local X-ray reportedly showed a displaced fracture of the left tibial plateau.

His medical history was notable only for a positive serum Treponema pallidum antibody. He had no known diabetes or other systemic illness.

On examination, vital signs were stable. There was no spinal deformity or limitation of spinal movement. Upper limbs had normal strength and sensation. Left knee inspection showed swelling and varus deformity. There was a positive floating patella test, mild tenderness, and percussion pain. Range of motion was 120° of flexion to 20° of extension. Left lower-extremity muscle strength was graded 4/5; right was 5/5. The American Knee Society clinical score was 45; functional score, 30. There was hyperpigmentation of the left leg, shallow hypoesthesia over the lateral plantar surface, and absence of the left great toe. Distal pulses were intact; Babinski and Hoffmann signs were negative.

Laboratory studies showed normal liver and renal function, electrolytes, blood glucose, hemoglobin A1c, and tumor markers; elevated platelet count, mildly increased high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

Imaging of the left knee included X-rays and CT scans, which demonstrated a comminuted medial tibial plateau fracture with articular surface fragmentation, collapse, displacement with bone resorption, and surrounding soft-tissue calcification. MRI of the left knee revealed tears of the medial and lateral patellar retinacula, anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, and medial collateral ligament; medial meniscus injury; and bone contusions.

MRI of the cervical and lumbar spine showed no evidence of syringomyelia. CT venography of the left lower extremity showed stenosis of the popliteal vein at the level of the fracture without filling defects and mild femoral vein stenosis. Electromyography revealed severe damage to the left tibial and sural nerves and mild delay in right sural nerve conduction.
journal: The Journal of International Medical Research
title:
Rotation-hinged knee prosthesis for the treatment of Charcot
arthropathy: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 6-year-old girl was evaluated for left-sided limb weakness of approximately 1 year’s duration. One year earlier she had begun to experience right ear discharge with a rancid, yellowish fluid and a history of recurrent fever; she denied seizures, prolonged cough, prior tuberculosis, or known TB exposure. Chest radiography demonstrated infiltrates in the right perihilar-paracardiac and left suprahilar regions without the typical features of pulmonary tuberculosis. A contrast-enhanced MRI of the head showed pachymeningeal enhancement in the right temporo-parieto-occipital region, enhancement in the left cisterna basalis, and a rim-enhancing cortical-subcortical lesion in the right occipital lobe. Additional axial T1 and T2 images revealed multiple cystic lesions in the subcortical right parieto-occipital lobe, consistent with encephalomalacia cysts, and communicating hydrocephalus of the lateral ventricles. Based on these imaging features, the patient was referred for neurosurgical open biopsy and wide excision of the mass.
title: Giant cerebral tuberculoma mimicking tumor in a pediatric patient: A case report

case_prompt:
Chief complaint: progressive upper thoracic back pain and lower limb weakness.  
History of present illness: A 39-year-old man with no history of trauma or constitutional symptoms reported dull upper thoracic back pain for 8 months. The pain was gradually progressive, not posture related, and initially responsive to NSAIDs. Over the 4 days before presentation, the pain intensity increased markedly, and he developed inability to walk and urinary incontinence.  
Vital signs: afebrile; stable hemodynamics.  
Physical examination: motor strength 3/5 in all lower-limb muscle groups; sensory level at the nipples (T4); tenderness over T1–T2 spinous processes; remainder of examination unremarkable.  
Investigations: CT and MRI of the thoracic spine revealed an osteolytic, expansile lesion eroding the T1 and T2 vertebral bodies, extending into the spinal canal, with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement.
title: Surgical treatment of giant cell tumor of the cervicothoracic spine with combined anterior and posterior approaches

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old boy was admitted with a 3-day history of diffuse abdominal pain, subjective fever, and vomiting, followed by an inability to pass feces or gas. His medical history was notable only for orchiopexy two years earlier. On examination, he was pale but hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and had localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa without peritoneal signs.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 15.7 × 10^9/L with 84.9% neutrophils and a C-reactive protein level of 16 mg/L. Abdominal radiography suggested small-bowel intussusception, and ultrasonography confirmed the “target sign” of intussusception along with findings concerning for appendicitis.

The patient underwent laparotomy. Exploration revealed an ileo-ileal intussusception approximately 70 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve. After reduction, a segmental enlargement of the ileum with a focal depression in the mesentery was noted, and a firm, sessile intraluminal mass was palpated. The affected bowel segment and the appendix were resected.
title: Mesenteric inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor as a rare cause of small intestinal intussusception

case_prompt: A 72-year-old woman presented after a bicycle accident with an effusion and pain primarily over the lateral joint space of her right knee. She had no palpable masses and an otherwise unremarkable medical history. Radiographs of the knee were initially read as normal, though in retrospect they show a subtle low-density structure adjacent to the lateral joint space suggestive of a fat-containing lesion. MRI demonstrated a tear of the medial meniscus posterior horn and body, and also revealed a well-circumscribed soft-tissue lesion with fatty consistency located beneath the lateral collateral ligament and the popliteus tendon. On MRI, the mass was slightly inhomogeneous, showing subtle intralesional foci of intermediate signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images.
title: Intra-articular synovial lipoma of the knee joint

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old man presented with sudden onset of pain in the left lower chest and upper abdomen, persisting at rest and worsened by coughing or rolling over. His history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, chronic renal insufficiency, renal stones, obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP, peripheral arterial disease, diverticulosis, colon polyps, and benign prostatic hypertrophy. He smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years and consumed about 21 beers per week. Medications included metformin, enalapril, amlodipine, simvastatin, and aspirin. He had childhood asbestos exposure and worked repairing telephone equipment. He denied fevers, sweats, or weight loss. Examination showed tenderness over the left lower ribs but clear lung fields and no lymphadenopathy.

An ECG was normal. Chest radiograph revealed a loculated mass in the right upper lobe. Chest CT showed a 6-cm apical mass with central cystic areas, adjacent ground-glass opacities, and a 0.2-cm noncalcified nodule; there was no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. PET-CT demonstrated moderate uptake in the mass. Over the next month, his chest pain resolved but he developed a productive whitish cough and mild exertional dyspnea. On follow-up, breath sounds were diffusely diminished without crackles or wheezes. A percutaneous needle biopsy of the lung mass was planned under CT guidance.
title: Cavitary lung lesion suspicious for malignancy reveals Mycobacterium xenopi

case_prompt: An 8-year-old Chinese girl was referred for evaluation of a cardiac murmur. She was asymptomatic, denied dyspnea, diaphoresis, or cyanosis, but had frequent upper respiratory infections and reduced exercise tolerance. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac examination revealed a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border; S1 and S2 were normal. ECG showed sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated right coronary artery with aneurysmal change and a fistulous connection to the right ventricle, extensive intercoronary collateral vessels, severe mitral regurgitation, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 61%, and fractional shortening of 33%. There was no shunt across the interventricular septum.
final_diagnosis_raw: anomalous origin of left coronary artery from pulmonary artery
title: Diagnosis of Anomalous Origin of the Left Coronary Artery from the Pulmonary Artery with Echocardiography and Digital Subtraction Angiography

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of recurrent right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back and right shoulder, worsened by fatty meals. She had no history of smoking, alcohol use, prior surgery, or drug allergies. On examination, she was afebrile, with tenderness in the right upper quadrant and a positive Murphy’s sign. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, WBC 5.1×10^3/mm^3, serum amylase 74 U/L (reference 40–140), blood glucose 85 mg/dL, and normal liver and renal function tests. Abdominal ultrasound revealed gallbladder wall thickening and multiple gallstones, the largest measuring 4.7 mm. The patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for presumed chronic calculous cholecystitis. 

On gross examination, the gallbladder measured 7 cm in length with a wall thickness of approximately 0.5 cm. A firm, well-circumscribed, yellow, lobulated nodule measuring 1.2 cm surrounded the cystic duct; a second similar nodule, 0.5 cm in diameter, was present in the serosa of the gallbladder neck. The mucosa was intact and unremarkable.
title: Heterotopic pancreatic tissue in the gall bladder neck and lymph node surrounding cystic duct identified during cholecystectomy for chronic calculous cholecystitis: a rare case report from Syria

case_prompt: A 4-year-old girl presented with 2 days of fever and emesis and was initially treated with amoxicillin for presumed strep throat. Fever persisted, and on day 5 she developed a rash, hand puffiness, and bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis and received a 3-day course of corticosteroids with transient defervescence. Fever recurred 10 days after onset. On admission, laboratory tests showed ESR 53 mm/hr, CRP 3.9 mg/dL, WBC 23.4 × 10^3 cells/µL, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 393 × 10^3 cells/µL, sodium 132 mEq/L, and multiple negative SARS-CoV-2 antibody and PCR tests. Echocardiography was normal. On day 11 she was treated with IVIG (2 g/kg) and high-dose aspirin for presumed incomplete Kawasaki disease and defervesced. She was discharged on day 13 but had low-grade fevers and elevated inflammatory markers 3 days later, prompting readmission; a second IVIG dose was given with persistence of fever, so oral corticosteroids were started. On day 17 echocardiography revealed a new small saccular aneurysm of the left anterior descending coronary artery (max diameter 2.9 mm, z-score 3.27). She met incomplete Kawasaki disease criteria and received a second IVIG dose, but fever persisted and steroids were continued. Outpatient follow-up showed progressive enlargement of the left anterior descending aneurysm to 4.5 mm (z-score 9.0) and a right coronary artery aneurysm of 3.5 mm (z-score 4.2). Steroids were weaned over 3 weeks but she developed recurrent fever and elevated CRP on day 37, with mild systemic hypertension. Echocardiogram and CT on day 38 demonstrated further enlargement of the coronary aneurysms, and she was treated with cyclophosphamide and steroids for presumed refractory Kawasaki disease. Given her prolonged and atypical course of presumed Kawasaki disease with relapsing inflammation on steroid taper, alternative forms of vasculitis were considered.
title: Coronary artery aneurysms in children is not always Kawasaki disease: a case report on Takayasu arteritis

case_prompt:
A 21-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to brachio-oto-renal syndrome underwent a deceased-donor kidney transplant five years ago. He was admitted with acute graft failure due to biopsy-proven T-cell and antibody-mediated rejection. He reported five days of worsening nausea and vomiting.  
On presentation, his serum creatinine was 27 mg/dL (previously normal), and his serum phosphate was 6.9 mg/dL. He received thymoglobulin, rituximab, bortezomib, and plasmapheresis. Over the next days, his phosphate rose to 8.9 mg/dL, and he was started on oral lanthanum carbonate, titrated to 1000 mg three times daily with meals.  
During hospitalization, a renal ultrasound suggested a “foreign body” near the transplant. A plain abdominal radiograph showed multiple radiopacities scattered throughout the abdomen. A CT scan confirmed radiopaque material within the colon, consistent with ingested material. Repeat radiographs demonstrated these densities moving along the gastrointestinal tract.  
Gastroenterology and surgery teams recommended serial abdominal imaging; the patient remained asymptomatic without signs of obstruction or perforation. Stool was collected for inspection, but no foreign objects were identified. A psychiatric consultation found no evidence of intentional ingestion. Serial radiographs continued to show an increased number of radiopaque densities throughout the abdomen.
title: Lanthanum-Induced Radiopaque Intestinal Precipitates: A Potential Cause of Intestinal Foreign Bodies

case_prompt: A 48-year-old mixed-ethnicity woman presented with a mass extruding from her vaginal orifice, associated with bleeding and pain for several hours. She brought the mass in a container. She denied any history of menstrual delay or medication use. A recent ultrasound had shown an endometrial nodule with a vascular pedicle measuring 20 × 12 cm², suggestive of a polyp or submucous myoma. On admission, she appeared calm, with only abdominal tenderness on palpation. Speculum examination revealed a closed cervix and a moderate amount of bleeding. On bimanual examination, the uterus was fibroelastic in consistency and tender. The team then dissected the extruded structure, initially thinking it was a clot; however, it was found to be very hard—a long mass that was difficult to diagnose.
title: Spontaneous expulsion of a submucosal uterine fibroid without embolization in a pre-menopausal woman

case_prompt: An 11-year-old girl was admitted with a one-month history of postprandial vomiting. Her past medical history was unremarkable, and she had no abnormal eating behaviors. Over the preceding weeks, her general condition had declined slightly. On admission, her vital signs were normal for age, and laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver function tests, and renal function tests, were within normal limits. A barium upper gastrointestinal series demonstrated narrowing at the level of the gastric outlet. Differential diagnoses included gastric outlet obstruction due to foreign body, bezoar, antral web, or diaphragm. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a normal esophagus and a stomach filled with undigested food, with severe narrowing at the pylorus through which the endoscope could not advance.
