No ulcers were observed, and due to the severe stenosis, endoscopic removal of the suspected membrane was not possible.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Gastric outlet obstruction in an 11-year-old girl due to a pyloric diaphragm – A case report and a systematic literature review

case_prompt: A 41-year-old man presented with dyspnea and hemoptysis for 2 days. He had been diagnosed with hypertension 5 years earlier but received no treatment. On admission, his blood pressure was 233/159 mmHg, heart rate 135 bpm, temperature 37.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Physical examination revealed coarse crackles in both lower lung fields and jugular venous distention; there was no rash, joint swelling, or peripheral edema. Fundoscopy showed bilateral retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots without papilledema. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, platelet count 86 × 10^3/µL, reticulocyte count 13.4 × 10^4/µL, schistocytes 3 per 1 000 red cells, lactate dehydrogenase 749 U/L, haptoglobin <10 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 84.6 mg/dL, creatinine 11.7 mg/dL (eGFR 5 mL/min/1.73 m^2), serum potassium 2.6 mmol/L, and ADAMTS13 activity 67%. Urinalysis showed 2+ protein and 1+ blood (1–4 RBCs/HPF). Immunological studies including antinuclear antibody, ANCA, and anti–glomerular basement membrane antibody were negative. Chest radiography showed extensive bilateral alveolar shadowing and cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 60%) without pleural effusions. High-resolution chest CT demonstrated diffuse perihilar ground-glass attenuation with consolidation along bronchovascular bundles. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was macroscopically hemorrhagic, and numerous hemosiderin-laden macrophages were identified. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed eccentric left ventricular hypertrophy with diffuse severe hypokinesis and an ejection fraction of 25%. Coronary angiography showed no significant stenoses.
title: Hypertensive emergency presenting with diffuse alveolar hemorrhaging and thrombotic microangiopathy: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, diabetes mellitus, and peripheral vascular disease was admitted with acute onset of altered mental status, agitation, and confusion. His temperature was 97.8 °F, blood pressure 114/55 mm Hg, heart rate 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On examination, he was alert but disoriented to time, place, and person, and was agitated and uncooperative. Laboratory studies revealed a blood glucose level of 989 mg/dL; arterial blood gas showed pH 7.2, PCO2 22.2 mm Hg, HCO3 9.8 mEq/L, PO2 90.7 mm Hg, and an anion gap of 30. Serum acetones were positive; urinary ketones were 15 mg/dL, and urinary glucose exceeded 1000 mg/dL, consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis. CT scans of the head, abdomen, and pelvis, as well as a chest radiograph, were unremarkable. He was started on an insulin infusion and supportive care.

On hospital day 3, he developed coffee-ground emesis, tested positive for fecal occult blood, and passed melena. His hemoglobin dropped from 10.5 g/dL to 7.9 g/dL. Gastroenterology was consulted, and an emergent esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated black, circumferential necrosis of the mucosa of the cervical esophagus without active bleeding. The endoscope was withdrawn immediately; biopsies were deferred. He was kept nil per os and was started on intravenous fluids, proton-pump inhibitor therapy, antibiotics, and steroids, with nasogastric tube placement deferred due to concern for perforation.
title: “Black Esophagus” or Gurvits Syndrome: A Rare Complication of Diabetic Ketoacidosis

case_prompt: A 65-year-old man with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease and hiatal hernia presented with progressive dysphagia and a 20-lb weight loss. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a distal esophageal mass; biopsy showed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Staging PET/CT demonstrated distal esophageal wall thickening with uptake extending into the proximal stomach but no brain lesions. He received neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by en bloc esophagectomy with cervical esophagostomy, pyloroplasty, and feeding-tube placement. On admission to the acute rehabilitation unit, he was found to have new left homonymous hemianopsia and confusion with decreased initiation. An MRI of the brain disclosed a 5.2×3.8×5 cm mass in the right parietal–occipital lobe. According to the radiology department report, the lesion was “likely a primary brain neoplasm, such as a neural or glial tumor, or lymphoma, but less likely a focus of metastatic disease, given its appearance.” However, according to the oncology department evaluation, the lesion was “more consistent with a metastatic tumor than a primary brain lesion.”
title: Recognized homonymous hemianopsia and delirium during the admission examination leading to diagnosis and appropriate treatment of a new stroke

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the right side of her palate and a 1-month history of intermittent dull pain in the area. Her past medical and dental histories were unremarkable. Family history was notable for similar palatal swellings and multiple cutaneous nodules in her father and newly developing nodules in her 17-year-old daughter. 

On general examination, diffuse brownish-black pigmented nodular masses of varying sizes were noted over the body; these nodules were noninflammatory and ranged from soft to firm on palpation. Ophthalmologic examination revealed Lisch nodules and early-onset cataract without glaucoma. A 1 × 1 cm right submandibular lymph node was palpable, mobile, nontender, and firm. 

Intraoral examination showed a solitary, oval, well-defined pedunculated swelling on the upper right palate, extending from the attached gingiva of teeth 11 and 12 to the distal region of tooth 16, approximately 1 cm from the midpalatal suture. The lesion measured about 2 × 3 cm, was irregular in shape, pink, non-tender, nonfluctuant, and of variable consistency. Differential diagnoses included lipoma, fibroma, schwannoma, and hemangioma. 

Panoramic and posterior–anterior skull radiographs showed no bone involvement. Based on the diffuse pigmented skin nodules, Lisch nodules, intraoral tumor, and a positive family history, a provisional diagnosis of neurofibroma associated with neurofibromatosis type I was made.
title: Neurofibroma of the Palate

case_prompt: A 17-year-old female presented with a 4-week history of evening fevers with temperatures between 37.7°C and 38.8°C. She reported no cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, prior tuberculosis, or known TB exposure. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 39 mg/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 56 U/L, and hemoglobin 11 g/dL with slight microcytosis; other hematological tests were normal. Serologic and microbiologic testing for typhoid, malaria, leptospira, rickettsial infection, urine analysis, blood and sputum cultures, and HIV were negative. A chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were normal. An ^18F-FDG PET–CT scan demonstrated multiple focal areas of increased FDG uptake within the spleen, with no corresponding lesions on non-contrast or contrast-enhanced CT and no abnormal FDG-avid lesions elsewhere. MRI of the abdomen, including diffusion-weighted imaging, did not reveal any splenic nodules.
title: Isolated splenic tuberculosis detected only on FDG-PET

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of sudden-onset sharp abdominal pain located in the umbilical and suprapubic regions, associated with a low-grade fever. She was gravida 6, para 6, with menopause 20 years earlier and no significant medical or surgical history. On examination, her temperature was 37.8 °C, pulse rate 107 beats/min, blood pressure 107/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Urinalysis showed a trace of leukocytes and protein but was otherwise unremarkable. The abdomen was soft, with rebound tenderness over the lower quadrants. Initial differential diagnoses included gastroenteritis, diverticulitis, urinary tract infection, or an ovarian cyst with possible intermittent torsion or malignancy. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 155 mg/L and a white blood cell count of 13.3×10^9/L with a neutrophil count of 11.8×10^9/L. 

Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 7.4×5.6×5.9 cm mixed-density lesion in the right adnexa containing calcifications and fat and fluid density areas; there was no perilesional fat stranding, free fluid, or bowel abnormality. Pelvic ultrasound showed a 10×3.2×6 cm well-circumscribed complex mixed solid–cystic mass in the right adnexa with a hyperechoic component, posterior shadowing, ground-glass internal echoes, and no increased vascularity. Serum CA125 was 29 U/mL. The patient was discharged with analgesia and scheduled for laparoscopic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy eight days later.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Spontaneously Ruptured Dermoid Cysts and Their Potential Complications: A Review of the Literature with a Case Report

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old previously healthy Caucasian boy was admitted with a 5-day history of fever, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. On the day of admission, he developed a diffuse skin rash and bilateral conjunctivitis. He had no personal or family history of cardiovascular disease. On examination, temperature was 38.3 °C, blood pressure was low, heart rate 112 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated N-terminal pro–brain natriuretic peptide, troponin, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, D-dimer, fibrinogen, and hyponatremia. A SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal swab was negative, but anti–SARS-CoV-2 IgG was positive. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated biventricular dilatation, global hypokinesia, and an ejection fraction of 30%. 

Electrocardiography in standard leads showed sinus rhythm, normal ventricular conduction, and diffuse repolarization abnormalities. Modified precordial-lead ECG revealed sinus rhythm with QRS fragmentation in lead D3 and saddleback ST-segment elevation.
title: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children Unmasking Brugada Type 1 Pattern

case_prompt: A 5-month-old entire male domestic shorthair kitten was referred for investigation of a month-long history of stranguria, pollakiuria, and urinary incontinence. One month earlier, the kitten had presented with stranguria and pollakiuria; examination revealed a large, firm bladder that could not be expressed, and urethral catheterisation was achieved easily without evidence of a plug, sediment, or urolith. Penile conformation and the urethral opening were normal. In-house urine sediment examination revealed bacteriuria, and urine culture was negative. The kitten received meloxicam, prazosin, and potentiated amoxicillin–clavulanate, which prevented further obstructive episodes but did not resolve stranguria, pollakiuria, or incontinence, and excessive perineal grooming was observed. On referral, clinical examination was unremarkable, with a small soft bladder. Haematology was unremarkable. Biochemistry showed a moderate increase in creatine kinase (794 IU/l [RI 33–168]), borderline high urea (10.9 mmol/l [RI 5.4–10.7]), and age-related elevations in phosphate (2.56 mmol/l [RI 0.9–2.1]) and alkaline phosphatase (135 IU/l [RI 10–93]). Abdominal radiographs revealed a normally positioned, full bladder with a smooth, rounded border. Abdominal ultrasound showed a thickened bladder wall (0.37 cm) with a hyperechoic mucosal layer and slightly irregular luminal border; no other abnormalities were noted. Cystocentesis yielded inadequately concentrated urine (specific gravity 1.010), bacteriuria, and proteinuria; culture grew sparse pure Escherichia coli resistant to cephalexin. The kitten was anesthetized for a retrograde urethrocystogram, which revealed an outpouching of the intrapelvic urethra.
title: Urinary incontinence secondary to a suspected congenital urethral deformity in a kitten

case_prompt: A 31-year-old primigravida was referred at 11 weeks’ gestation for increased nuchal translucency of 3.2 mm. Chorionic villus sampling showed a normal male 46,XY karyotype; FISH analysis, Noonan’s panel, and microarray were normal. A fetal echocardiogram at 15+5 weeks was unremarkable. At 20+1 weeks, ultrasound revealed fetal ascites and a small pleural effusion but no pericardial effusion; the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity was elevated at 1.95 MoM, suggesting anemia. Maternal serologic testing for herpes simplex virus, parvovirus, toxoplasmosis, and cytomegalovirus was performed, and PCR panels on amniotic fluid were sent. At 20+2 weeks, follow-up ultrasound showed scalp edema, worsening pleural effusion and ascites, new pericardial effusion, and persistent elevated MCA PSV at 75 cm/second.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Maternal Parvovirus B19 Infection Causing First-Trimester Increased Nuchal Translucency and Fetal Hydrops

case_prompt:
An 18-month-old Egyptian boy was referred for evaluation of generalized hyperpigmentation associated with weakness, vomiting, and recurrent convulsions. He was born to consanguineous parents after an uneventful pregnancy. One sibling had died at nine months with similar hyperpigmentation and convulsions, while other siblings are healthy. The parents noted hyperpigmentation in the first weeks of life, darker than his siblings. At 10 and 11 months, he had two brief febrile generalized tonic-clonic convulsions; no evaluation was performed at that time.

On examination, he spoke only a few words and walked with support. Weight was at the 5th percentile; length and head circumference at the 50th percentile. Blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg. He had generalized symmetric deep hyperpigmentation, especially of the elbows, knees, hands, feet, and buccal mucosa, and hypotonia. No dysmorphic features. External genitalia were normal, with bilaterally palpable testes. There were no signs of alacrima or achalasia. Other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:
• Glucose 48 mg/dL  
• Sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4 mmol/L, chloride 109 mmol/L  
• ALT 28 IU/mL, AST 30 IU/mL  
• Complete blood count normal  
• Cortisol 0.6 μg/dL (normal 2.8–23)  
• ACTH 708 pg/mL (normal 6–48)  
• No rise in cortisol after ACTH stimulation  
• 17-OH progesterone 0.01 ng/mL (normal 0.03–0.9)  
• Androstenedione 0.01 ng/mL (normal 0.1–0.17)  
• DHEA 3 ng/mL (normal 50–480)  
• Plasma renin activity 57 ng/mL/hour (normal 2.35–37)  
• Aldosterone 801 pg/mL (normal 50–900)

Bone age by left hand radiograph was two years (chronologic age 18 months). Adrenal ultrasonography showed small adrenal glands (6 × 8 mm on the left, 7 × 8 mm on the right). Brain CT was normal.
title: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency presenting with generalized hyperpigmentation in an Egyptian child: a case report

case_prompt: An 8-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of a 3-month history of swelling and pain on the medial aspect of his left ankle. The swelling had been first noted in infancy and had gradually increased in size; it was initially painless but recently became painful and aggravated by wearing shoes, leading to impingement and skin redness, causing the child to refuse school. There was no history of trauma. On examination, there was a 2 × 1.5 cm tender swelling over the medial ankle. Ankle flexion and internal and external rotation were limited, whereas extension, abduction, and adduction were normal. There was no limb-length discrepancy or muscle wasting. Radiographs revealed a 1.5 × 1 cm irregular, thickened bony mass arising from the talus near the ankle joint, with mild secondary osteoarthritic changes in the tibio-talar joint. CT scan showed symmetrical bony overgrowth of the medial distal tibial epiphysis with talar bony projections, with secondary osteoarthritis. MRI demonstrated bony fragments arising from the talar dome and anterior medial malleolus with no periosseous soft tissue or periosteal reaction.
title: A Symptomatic Swollen Ankle in an 8-year-old Male Child – A Rare Case Report of Dysplasia Epiphysealis Hemimelica

case_prompt: A 9-year-old girl from a rural area presented with a 2-week history of severe itching over a reddish, granular polypoidal lesion on the left palpebral conjunctiva. The lesion measured 5 mm × 5 mm and tended to bleed on touch. She had normal vision and no systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, a white-cell count of 9000 cells/mm3 with 65% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, and 5% eosinophils. A stool examination was negative for ova or parasites. She reported regular bathing in village ponds. Clinically, a differential diagnosis of conjunctival papilloma, foreign-body granuloma, and oculosporidiosis was considered. The lesion was completely excised with electrocautery and sent for histopathologic examination.
title: Oculosporidial polyp infected secondarily by Enterobius vermicularis

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man with a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a one-week history of difficulty urinating, characterized by incomplete emptying, dribbling, and increased urinary frequency. He denied lower back pain, chills, fever, weight loss, rash, fatigue, or dry mouth. He was taking metformin 1 g twice daily and glipizide 10 mg once daily; fasting blood glucose on admission was 8.43 mmol/L.

On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Digital rectal examination revealed a smooth, soft, nontender prostate without palpable nodules and a shallow central sulcus.

Laboratory studies showed elevated inflammatory markers on complete blood count, procalcitonin 0.080 ng/mL, and prostate-specific antigen 1.66 μg/L. Urinalysis revealed glucose 1+, occult blood 3+, protein trace, and leukocytes 2+. Quantitative urine sediment analysis showed 115 red blood cells/μL, 118 white blood cells/μL, and 7 white blood cell clumps/μL; urine culture showed no growth. Bladder ultrasound demonstrated a postvoid residual volume of approximately 655 mL. Transabdominal ultrasound of the urinary tract showed prostate enlargement with calcifications measuring 5.0 × 3.6 × 3.8 cm. Abdominal CT scan indicated prostate hyperplasia, with prostate MRI recommended if deemed necessary. In the emergency department, he had undergone urinary catheterization for acute urinary retention. Given the presumed diagnosis of benign prostatic hyperplasia causing urinary retention, he was scheduled for transurethral resection of the prostate.
title: Report of a prostate abscess mistakenly diagnosed as benign prostatic hyperplasia

case_prompt:
A 30‐year‐old female farmer presented with a midline swelling at the suprasternal notch that she reported since birth but noted an increase in size over the past two years. She described mild discomfort and dyspnea but denied symptoms of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. She had no prior surgeries or relevant family history. 

On examination, there was a 6 cm, round, non‐tender, cystic mass at the suprasternal notch that did not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count. Neck ultrasonography demonstrated a 5.2 × 4.8 cm well‐defined cystic lesion inferior to the left thyroid lobe with internal echogenic foci, high‐level echo‐debris, and peripheral color flow; the thyroid gland was multinodular but in its normal position. Fine‐needle aspiration cytology yielded a benign cyst, likely a thyroid cyst. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits. 

Given the patient’s symptoms, imaging findings, and location of the lesion, surgical excision of the cyst was planned.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Thyroglossal duct cyst on the suprasternal region: An extremely unusual location

case_prompt: A 14-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of an incidental finding of asymptomatic hyperCKemia (26,372 IU/L). He had no family history of neuromuscular disease, no parental consanguinity, and no exposure to myotoxic medications. He had been active in high-performance sports (3 h daily) without myalgia, cramps, or pigmenturia, but CK levels remained above 20,000 IU/L after cessation of exercise. Neuromuscular and systemic examinations were normal. Initial electromyography and nerve conduction studies were normal. Cardiac and respiratory assessments were unremarkable. Myositis-specific (Mi2, TIF1γ, MDA5, NXP2, SAE1, Jo1, SRP, PL7, PL12, EJ, OJ), myositis-associated (Ku, PM-Scl75/100, Ro52), and antinuclear antibodies were negative, and thyroid-stimulating hormone was normal. Given his sex and CK elevation, an X-linked dystrophinopathy was considered, but multiplex polymerase chain reaction and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification analyses detected no DMD deletions. Six months later, a right quadriceps muscle biopsy showed muscle fiber necrosis with endomysial and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, without fibrosis or fatty infiltration. A repeat electromyography revealed a myopathic pattern. These findings were felt to be consistent with polymyositis.
title: Dysferlinopathy misdiagnosed with juvenile polymyositis in the pre-symptomatic stage of hyperCKemia: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old boy presented with a 4-month history of swelling in the upper left anterior maxillary region. He reported no pain or systemic symptoms. On extraoral inspection, there was swelling of the left upper lip and slight protrusion of the left nasal ala. Intraorally, a non-tender, firm mucosal swelling extended from the primary left central incisor (61) to the primary left canine (63), obliterating the buccal vestibule; a minor palatal swelling with normal mucosa and a fistula near the root of 63 were noted. Tooth 61 was geminated. Vitality tests were inconclusive, and there was no sensory disturbance.

Panoramic and CT imaging revealed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion measuring approximately 2 × 3 cm in the left anterior maxilla. The lesion extended from the midline to the mesial root of the left first deciduous molar, encompassed the crowns of the unerupted permanent left central (21) and lateral (22) incisors, and had displaced them superiorly and posteriorly.

Based on the patient’s age, lesion location, and its association with an impacted tooth, an initial diagnosis of a dentigerous cyst involving tooth 21 was made. Marsupialization under local anesthesia was attempted but was not well tolerated. The team proceeded with enucleation of the cystic lesion under general anesthesia. Teeth 61 and 62 were extracted, the cystic lining was removed in toto along with the impacted central incisor (21), and that tooth was immediately reimplanted into the bony cavity. The surgical specimen was sent for pathological examination.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Unicystic ameloblastoma: Diagnostic challenges and uncommon treatment strategy: Case report

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presented with two weeks of throbbing right-sided neck pain radiating to her jaw, acutely worse for two days, along with transient nonspecific visual changes and bilateral upper-extremity paresthesia. An outpatient carotid Doppler ultrasound showed 50–69% stenosis of the right carotid artery. Clinic laboratories revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 67 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein level of 2.7 mg/dL. She was started on methylprednisolone 125 mg every six hours and admitted for further evaluation.

Her history included anxiety (on escitalopram), hyperlipidemia (on atorvastatin), and a prior massive transfusion for placental abruption. She denied fevers, chills, chest pain, abdominal pain, headaches, or limb claudication.

On examination, temperature was 36.6 °C, pulse 81/min, blood pressure 109/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, and SpO₂ 100% on room air. She was alert and without distress. The neck was supple but exquisitely tender to light palpation over the right carotid distribution without erythema, induration, lymphadenopathy, or bruits. Cardiopulmonary and neurologic examinations were normal; peripheral pulses were 2+ bilaterally.

Laboratory studies showed ESR 36 mm/hr and high-sensitivity CRP 0.71 mg/dL; complete blood count, metabolic panel, and autoimmune markers (rheumatoid factor; ANA; anti-DNA; and anti-ENA subtypes) were unremarkable. Carotid CT angiography revealed 0% stenosis of the extracranial internal carotid arteries, no dissections, and no pseudoaneurysms. Head CT angiography showed no intracranial vascular abnormalities. Chest magnetic resonance angiography demonstrated normal caliber and patency of the aorta and its major branches without evidence of inflammation.

Given persistent carotidynia and elevated acute-phase reactants despite unremarkable imaging, an early large-vessel vasculitis was considered, and corticosteroid therapy was continued.
title: New-Onset Ulcerative Colitis in a Young Caucasian Woman with Unclassified Arteritis

case_prompt: A 78-year-old man with diabetes mellitus type II, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and recurrent urinary tract infections presented with fatigue, left upper abdominal pain, urinary frequency for 1 week, and an unintentional 10-kg weight loss over 3 months. On examination, vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL with a normocytic normochromic anemia on peripheral smear, normal white-cell count, lactate dehydrogenase 1266 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 434 IU/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a mildly enlarged liver with normal attenuation and hypodense, wedge-shaped splenic lesions suggestive of infarcts. For evaluation of possible neoplasm, a whole-body FDG PET-CT was performed and showed diffusely increased FDG uptake in the liver (SUVmax, 4.5) with no significant FDG uptake in the splenic lesions or elsewhere.
title: Detection of Diffuse Infiltrative Primary Hepatic Lymphoma on FDG PET-CT: Hallmarks of Hepatic Superscan

case_prompt: An 8-year-old boy presented with a swelling in the anterolateral aspect of the right lower thigh of 1 year’s duration. The mass had gradually increased in size and had become painful over the past 2 months. There was no history of trauma, no constitutional symptoms, and no bleeding tendencies. Physical examination revealed an asymmetric, boggy, non-compressible, non-pulsatile swelling in the anteromedial right lower thigh measuring approximately 10 cm × 7 cm. The overlying skin was normal without discoloration, venous engorgement, or inflammatory signs. There was fullness of the medial para-patellar fossa without joint effusion, tenderness over the quadriceps (more anteromedial), no distal neurovascular deficit or bruit, equal limb lengths, and full knee range of motion. Initial differential diagnoses included lipoma, cold abscess, suprapatellar bursitis, synovitis, sarcoma, fibroma, or other extra-articular soft tissue tumors. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thigh showed a soft tissue mass measuring about 14 cm × 5 cm within the vastus medialis and intermedius that was of high-signal intensity on T1-, T2-, and proton-density FAT-SAT–weighted images.
title: Intramuscular Arteriovenous Hemangioma of Thigh: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 56‐year‐old man presented with a 6‐month history of recurrent headaches, vertigo, diplopia, impaired hearing, and gait imbalance. His medical history was notable only for well‐controlled Graves’ disease. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT ruled out acute intracranial pathology, including hydrocephalus. MRI of the brain and spine revealed:  
• A small cystic lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere.  
• Diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement of the cerebellum, brainstem, and cervical spinal cord with nodular thickening along the entire neuraxis.  
• Multiple punctate subcortical cerebellar lesions.  

Electrophysiologic studies showed evidence of demyelination in the optic and sensory pathways of the right arm and lower extremities. CSF analysis demonstrated markedly elevated protein (3032 mg/dL) and the presence of CD56‐positive cells; cytology was negative for S100, Melan A, and CD138. Genetic testing for common BRAF single‐nucleotide variants and indels was wild‐type. A repeat CSF assay was negative for Listeria and Whipple’s disease. Comprehensive infectious work‐up, including HIV, tuberculosis, Epstein‐Barr virus, syphilis, and echinococcal serologies, was negative. Full‐body imaging showed benign hepatic lesions but no evidence of systemic malignancy. Dermatologic evaluation revealed no cutaneous neoplasms. The patient was referred for a surgical biopsy to obtain a definitive histopathological diagnosis.
title: Diffuse Leptomeningeal Glioneuronal Tumor in Adults: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 20-year-old man presented with a 24-hour history of right iliac fossa pain and vomiting. One month earlier, he had similar pain for seven days; laboratory tests and plain radiographs were unremarkable, and he declined laparoscopy. His only medication was lymecycline for acne. On readmission, temperature was 39.6°C, pulse 93/min, respirations 19/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and Glasgow Coma Score normal. Abdominal examination showed diffuse tenderness with generalized guarding, absent bowel sounds, and no distension. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 16.7 g/dL, white-cell count 13.6 × 10^9/L, normal renal function, and normal C-reactive protein. A plain abdominal film was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated what appeared to be a 50 cm multiseptated collection occupying much of the abdominal and pelvic cavities, containing air pockets, with a small amount of free fluid around the liver and in both paracolic gutters; the appendix was not visualized.
title: Small Bowel Hamartoma: A Huge Diverticulum of Small Bowel

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old boy presented with a 5-month history of left ankle swelling and progressive pain on walking, with inability to bear full weight. He had a history of atrial septal defect but no trauma. On examination, there was marked swelling on the anteromedial and posteromedial aspects of the left ankle, with palpable bony prominences just medial to the tibialis anterior tendon and on the medial aspect of the Achilles tendon distal to the joint line; these sites were tender. Range of motion was 0° of dorsiflexion and 15° of plantar flexion. Neurovascular examination was normal. 
Plain radiographs (anteroposterior and lateral) showed irregularity of the talar articular surface with exuberant calcifications in the anterior joint compartment and on the posterior aspect of the talus. MRI demonstrated bone marrow edema adjacent to the bony protuberances, synovitis around the lesions, and some joint effusion. CT defined the exact size and location of bony masses in the anterior and posterior ankle compartments. The preoperative American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society hindfoot score was 68/100.
title: Combined Anterior and Posterior Ankle Arthroscopy for Dysplasia Epiphysealis Hemimelica of the Ankle in a Child: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man was referred for evaluation of pain in his right mandible. He was in good general health, a 10-pack-year smoker, with no significant systemic disease. On intraoral examination, oral hygiene was fair. Multiple teeth were missing, and there was a firm, nonfluctuant swelling with crepitus in the region corresponding to tooth sites 4.4–4.7 and the edentulous area of sites 4.5–4.6.  

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated:  
• Three well-defined, round, unilocular radiopaque lesions each surrounded by a thin radiolucent rim—two in the right posterior mandible adjacent to edentulous sites 3.6 and 4.6, and one in intimate contact with the roots of tooth 4.7.  
• A separate rounded radiolucent lesion with a sclerotic border at the apex of tooth 4.4.  

Thermal pulp testing of teeth 4.4 and 4.7 was nonresponsive. To further characterize the posterior mandibular lesions, a CT scan of the mandible was obtained, confirming three well-circumscribed, round, unilocular radiopaque masses with thin radiolucent margins; one mass was in close contact with the roots of the lower right second molar.
title: Multiple Cementoblastoma: A Rare Case Report

case_prompt: A 62-year-old woman presented with two weeks of intermittent vaginal bleeding. Her medical history was unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous 4.6 cm longitudinal mass in the uterine myometrium and a hard, whitish 2.0 cm mass arising from the anterior vaginal wall. A punch biopsy of the vaginal mass revealed a malignant tumor that was immunoreactive for smooth muscle actin but negative for HMB-45, findings reported as suggestive of leiomyosarcoma. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 4.6 × 5.5 cm heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing mass in the uterine myometrium and a 2.1 × 1.1 cm indistinct, heterogeneous, enhancing lesion in the lower vagina. Chest CT revealed multiple pulmonary nodules consistent with metastatic disease. The patient was taken for exploratory laparotomy and surgical staging.
title: Two cases of perivascular epithelioid cell tumor of the uterus: clinical, radiological and pathological diagnostic challenge

case_prompt: A 74-year-old farmer presented with a 1-year history of episodic left-sided chest pain, productive cough, and a gradually progressive swelling over the lower left chest wall. He had no history of trauma, surgery, or known comorbidities. On examination, a tender, 7 × 5 cm bulge was palpable over the left lower chest wall. A chest radiograph showed mild haziness in the left lower zone. A CT scan of the thorax demonstrated consolidation in the left lower lobe and a fluid collection with air extending through the seventh intercostal space into the chest wall, findings interpreted as suggestive of empyema necessitans requiring drainage. Routine blood tests were reported as normal. The patient was referred for ultrasound-guided aspiration of the presumed abscess. On preaspiration thoracic ultrasound, in end-inspiratory and end-expiratory views, tissue consistent with lung parenchyma was seen protruding through a widened seventh intercostal space, measuring approximately 6 × 2 cm.
title: Spontaneous lung herniation: A rare ultrasound diagnosis

case_prompt: A 79-year-old man presented with several weeks of progressive abdominal distension and pain, worsening shortness of breath, and inability to sleep. He denied any urinary symptoms. On examination, there was a large palpable mass in the right hypochondrium, extending to the hypogastrium; the abdomen was generally tender but without peritoneal signs. Chest examination was unremarkable. An urgent CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a massive homogeneous cystic lesion measuring approximately 38×17×25 cm in the right abdomen, extending from the pelvis to compress the liver and elevate the right hemidiaphragm. The lesion had a thin, regular, smooth wall, and there was bilateral hydronephrosis with normal renal cortical enhancement. At a multidisciplinary meeting, radiologists noted that the mass could represent a markedly distended bladder and recommended urinary catheterization to determine whether the lesion would decompress.
title: Unusual case of a gigantic bladder mimicking a large pelvic cystic mass

case_prompt: A 47-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis secondary to alcohol excess and multiple pancreatic pseudocysts presented with acute epigastric abdominal pain. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 3.8 cm expansile lesion at the pancreatic tail with peripheral low density and a centrally enhancing component of 1.3 cm; this component was slightly hypodense to the splenic artery in the arterial phase and slightly hyperdense on delayed phase images, raising the suspicion of a splenic artery pseudoaneurysm. He was transferred for angiography, which demonstrated no evidence of pseudoaneurysm or active hemorrhage. The patient was discharged with plans for repeat imaging in one month. On re-admission, triple-phase CT showed that the lesion had increased to 5.3 cm with the central component now measuring 2.6 cm; it remained hypodense relative to the splenic artery on arterial phase images and isodense to the portal vein on delayed phase images. Given the prior negative angiography, this finding created diagnostic uncertainty: the venous-phase enhancement suggested either a splenic vein aneurysm or a narrow-necked splenic artery pseudoaneurysm with delayed filling.
title: Splenic artery pseudoaneurysm: Challenges of non-invasive and endovascular diagnosis and management

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman with no known comorbidities was diagnosed with dengue fever after a positive NS1 antigen test and managed with as-needed oral paracetamol. Five days after the onset of fever, she developed urinary retention and was discharged with a Foley catheter in situ. Two days later, she presented with an inability to stand or walk, bilateral lower-limb weakness, and tingling sensations. She also noted a chronic burning sensation over the dorsal aspect of the right foot for three years. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. Higher mental functions were intact, and there were no signs of meningeal irritation. Muscle strength was normal in the upper limbs and reduced in both lower limbs. Fine and crude touch were preserved, but vibration and joint-position sense were diminished in the lower limbs, abdomen, and chest below the T2 level. Superficial abdominal reflexes were absent, knee and ankle reflexes were absent bilaterally, and plantar responses were upgoing. Examination of the cranial nerves, cerebellum, and upper limbs was normal. Ophthalmological evaluation was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed normal complete blood counts, negative blood cultures, nonreactive HIV serology, and normal blood glucose, electrolytes, renal function, and vitamin levels. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and an autoimmune panel were unremarkable. Anti–aquaporin 4 antibody testing was not performed because the clinical profile did not suggest neuromyelitis optica. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was normal. MRI of the spine showed a mild disc bulge at L4/L5 and L5/S1 with mild bilateral neural foraminal stenosis and lumbar spondylosis-like changes, without any findings to explain sensory deficits at the T2 level.
title: An unusual case of transverse myelitis in dengue fever: A case report from Nepal

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old woman presented with a 15-year history of a painless swelling in the left anterior maxilla. Fifteen years earlier, she sustained trauma to this area, resulting in loss of the upper left anterior teeth and subsequent bridge restoration in that region. On intraoral examination, a firm, non-tender lesion was noted on the left anterior maxillary ridge.

A cone-beam CT scan of the maxilla (9 × 14 cm FOV) was obtained. On the panoramic view, teeth 18, 21, 22, and 28 were missing. Tooth 12 demonstrated a radiopaque crown filling extending to the pulp and widened periodontal ligament space apically. Tooth 11 had undergone root-canal treatment. A radiopaque crown-and-bridge unit spanned teeth 11–23. Adjacent to this, in the left anterior maxilla (region 21–23), there was an ovoid radiolucent lesion containing internal radiopaque septa; its borders were partially well-defined and partially ill-defined with rough, destructive cortical bone edges.

Coronal reformatted images showed a mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion measuring approximately 21 × 17 × 18 mm in the edentulous ridge of teeth 21–22, mesial to tooth 23. Its borders were partially well-defined and partially ill-defined with rough, partially destroyed bone margins. Internally, it appeared semi-multilocular with septations and had a density of 129.8–252.9 gray values (consistent with fluid or soft tissue). The labial cortical plate was expanded and partially disrupted, while the palatal plate remained intact.

Sagittal and axial views revealed that the lesion contacted the apex of tooth 23, causing distal displacement without root resorption, and abutted the nasopalatine canal without wall discontinuity. It lay inferior to the nasal cavity and maxillary sinus, neither of which was involved.
title: Cone-beam computed tomography imaging of benign odontogenic lesions in the maxilla: A report of 2 cases

case_prompt: A 56-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis (valve area 0.81 cm2; mean gradient 54 mmHg), an STS score > 8, moderate COPD (FEV1 1.9 L, 53% predicted), Crohn’s disease on immunosuppression, hypertension, and nonobstructive coronary artery disease underwent TAVR under monitored anesthesia care. Preoperative echocardiography and invasive hemodynamics showed symmetric concentric left ventricular hypertrophy without an LVOT gradient. His initial intraoperative course was unremarkable. After successful valve deployment and cessation of rapid ventricular pacing at 180 beats/min, he became hypotensive, tachycardic, and dyspneic. Despite escalating doses of phenylephrine, ephedrine, vasopressin, norepinephrine, and epinephrine, he remained profoundly hypotensive and developed acute pulmonary edema requiring rapid sequence intubation. Given the timing of collapse and poor response to inotropes, LVOT obstruction was suspected, but other etiologies were also entertained. Inotropic agents were discontinued, and esmolol with phenylephrine infusion were administered, resulting in marked improvement in hemodynamics and symptoms.
title: Undiagnosed hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy during transcatheter aortic valve replacement: a case report

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old previously healthy girl presented with a 3-month history of progressive abdominal distention and rapid weight gain. She was noted to have hoarseness, marked hirsutism, cliteromegaly, and a rounded “moon face” with facial flushing. Over the same interval, her weight had increased by 3.8 kg, whereas her height increased by only 2.0 cm, and bone age was approximately 3 years greater than her chronological age.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an 80 × 50 × 50 mm right ovarian mass. CT and MRI demonstrated a fat-containing, bimodal pelvic mass, and PET-CT showed no metastatic lesions.  
Laboratory studies showed a serum testosterone level of 242.3 ng/dL, a daytime cortisol concentration of 21.5 μg/dL, an adrenocorticotropic hormone level suppressed to 1.4 pg/mL, and normal aldosterone, luteinizing hormone, and follicle-stimulating hormone levels. Tumor-marker evaluation revealed a lactate dehydrogenase level of 364 U/L and a neuron-specific enolase level of 36.6 ng/mL; other tumor markers were within normal limits.
final_diagnosis_raw: steroid cell tumor not otherwise specified
title: Malignant Ovarian Steroid Cell Tumor, Not Otherwise Specified, Causes Virilization in a 4-Year-Old Girl: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 67-year-old woman noted a slowly enlarging swelling beneath her left mandible over 12 months, associated with mild pain but no fever, weight loss, dysphonia or cough. On examination, there was a firm, well-circumscribed mass adjacent to the left submandibular gland. Laboratory studies, including thyroid function tests, were normal. Neck ultrasonography showed a normally located thyroid gland with two small nodules in the right lobe and, separately, a 28.7 × 26.8 mm vascularized, iso- to hypoechoic solid lesion with anechoic areas behind the left submandibular gland. Because of its location and sonographic appearance, an MRI of the neck was obtained, which demonstrated a 25 × 19 × 23 mm ovular prestyloid mass with irregular T1 signal, a slightly hyperintense central area on T2, and a peripheral component not clearly separable from the submandibular gland. These findings were thought to represent a prestyloid space lesion—exophytic pleomorphic adenoma, neurogenic tumor, or lymphadenopathy—and FNAC was planned.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Follicular adenoma in ectopic thyroid. A case-report

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension and hypothyroidism presented with sudden-onset dyspnea and palpitations. On arrival, her blood pressure was 60/40 mmHg, pulse 160 beats per minute, and she was cyanosed. Respiratory examination was unremarkable. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia, a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur. 

An electrocardiogram revealed supraventricular tachycardia, which was terminated by synchronized electrical cardioversion. The post-conversion ECG demonstrated right-axis deviation, an S₁Q₃T₃ pattern, a qR pattern in lead V₁, T-wave inversion in leads V₂–V₄, and p-pulmonale. 

She was started on low-molecular-weight heparin and intravenous amiodarone, and admitted to the intensive care unit. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a dilated right ventricle with severe tricuspid regurgitation and an estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 120 mmHg; the left atrium and ventricle were normal with an ejection fraction of 73%. Pulmonary‐function testing revealed a diffusion capacity of 45% with normal FEV₁, FVC, and FEV₁/FVC ratio. 

Given her supraventricular tachycardia and marked pulmonary hypertension, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension was initially suspected. Chest radiography showed oligemia and reduced volume of the right lung field with an empty right hilum, and compensatory hyperinflation and plethoric left lung field with an enlarged left pulmonary artery. A ventilation–perfusion scan demonstrated absent perfusion in the right lung field with preserved ventilation.
title: Unilateral absent pulmonary artery in an adult - A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge

case_prompt: A 36-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia on nilotinib presented with a 1-week history of progressive upper back pain and an unsteady gait, limiting him to only a few steps of ambulation. On neurologic examination, lower-limb strength was markedly reduced with hip and knee flexion graded 1/5 and ankle and toe movements graded 4/5 (MRC scale). Hyperactive knee and ankle reflexes were noted bilaterally. MRI of the thoracic spine showed extradural soft-tissue lesions from D5 to D9 on the right side, displacing the cord to the left; T1-weighted images were hypointense and STIR sequences showed hyperintense lesions in the dorsal and lumbar vertebrae, pelvis, and proximal femora. To exclude an epidural infection such as tuberculosis, a needle biopsy was performed and showed no evidence of infection.
title: Chloroma – A Rare Case of Metastatic Tumor to Dorsal Spine in Patient of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia Causing Acute Paraparesis

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old African American woman with nonischemic cardiomyopathy and an implanted HeartWare HVAD as a bridge to transplantation (UNOS status 1B) presented with gastrointestinal bleeding. She had a hemoglobin of 7.9 g/dL (baseline 10.4 g/dL), LDH 219 U/L, and haptoglobin 64 mg/dL. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy were unrevealing; capsule endoscopy localized bleeding to the jejunum, and push enteroscopy with argon plasma coagulation and clipping of an arteriovenous malformation achieved hemostasis. 

After transfer to the ward in stable condition, she acutely became hypoxic and her HVAD alarmed for low flow with decreased waveform pulsatility. Her heart rate rose into the 120s, mean arterial pressure fell into the 50s mm Hg, and she was transferred to the cardiovascular ICU for intubation. She was started on a heparin infusion, vasopressors, and inotropes. 

Right-heart catheterization showed RA pressure 13 mm Hg, RV 52/13 mm Hg, PA 53/28/40 mm Hg, PCWP 28 mm Hg, and a cardiac index of 1.6 L/min/m². Repeat LDH and haptoglobin were 165 U/L and 48 mg/dL. 

Before the GI procedure, the HVAD parameters were flow 4.0 L/min, speed 2460 rpm, power 2.8 W, MAP 68 mm Hg, with normal pulsatility. Afterward, flow was 2.1 L/min, speed 2400 rpm, and power 2.1 W. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a severely enlarged left ventricle with EF 10–20% and moderate right ventricular systolic dysfunction. No inflow cannula thrombus or pericardial effusion was seen. Inflow cannula velocities were normal; outflow cannula velocities were low (<1 m/s).
title: A Rare Complication of HVAD Outflow Thrombosis and the Importance of HVAD Waveform Analysis

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old perimenopausal woman presented after a syncopal episode. She reported three days of progressively worsening bruising over her right lower abdomen. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension, and she had undergone a cesarean section 18 years earlier, complicated postoperatively by a persistent incision-site mass thought to be a seroma, which had remained unchanged.  

On presentation, CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 6.5 cm lobulated soft-tissue mass in the right anterior abdominal wall, associated 4–5 cm masses along the right pelvic sidewall, and a 3.4 cm enhancing mass in the right inguinal region; no other pelvic or abdominal organ abnormalities were noted. A PET scan confirmed high FDG uptake in these lesions (SUV max 3.3–21.4) without identifying a clear primary site. Tumor markers were within normal limits (CA125 17.2 U/mL, CEA 2.0 ng/mL, CA19-9 26.9 U/mL).  

A percutaneous biopsy of the anterior abdominal wall lesion demonstrated malignant cells positive for CK7, PAX-8, WT-1, p53 (strong and diffuse), ER, and PR; morphology and immunoprofile were read as “high-grade adenocarcinoma, favor high-grade serous carcinoma of ovarian, fallopian tube, primary peritoneal origin, or endometrial serous carcinoma.”
title: Incisional carcinoma of Mullerian Origin: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 44-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of hypertension and preeclampsia who had taken oral contraceptive pills for 15 years presented with two weeks of intractable colicky abdominal pain that worsened with oral intake and was associated with diarrhea and nonbilious vomiting. The diarrhea was sometimes watery and hemoccult positive; gastroccult testing of vomitus was negative. On examination, she had stage III hypertension out of proportion to her risk factors and diffuse periumbilical tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16.1×10^9/L with 91% neutrophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 79 mm/hr, and a C-reactive protein level of 100 mg/L. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated nonspecific colitis. She received intravenous metronidazole and ciprofloxacin, but all microbial cultures, including three for Clostridium difficile, were negative. Urinalysis revealed nephritic-range proteinuria. Tests for P-ANCA, C-ANCA, ASCA, ANA, celiac serologies, lactate, CA-125, and TSH were all negative. Colonoscopy showed diffuse colonic lymphoid reactive hyperplasia; a small-bowel series and indium scan were unremarkable. Contrast CT scans of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, head, and a transvaginal ultrasound showed no evidence of malignancy. Although she remained normotensive off oral contraceptives, mesenteric ischemia was considered, and magnetic resonance angiography of the abdomen revealed proximal superior mesenteric artery stenosis, which was confirmed by CT angiography to be severe in both the proximal and distal segments.
title: A rare cause of chronic mesenteric ischemia from fibromuscular dysplasia: a case report

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old Caucasian man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia, recurrent prostatitis, and multiple negative transrectal ultrasound–guided prostate biopsies presented for evaluation of a persistently rising serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA). Over five years, his PSA had ranged from 8 to 10 ng/mL despite two 12-core biopsies and a 42-core saturation biopsy, all showing no malignancy. He reported 1–2 years of intermittent night sweats without fevers or chills. 

Multiparametric pelvic MRI was performed to evaluate his prostate and revealed suspicious intraprostatic lesions suitable for targeted biopsy, as well as left iliac chain and perivesical lymphadenopathy. MRI-ultrasound fusion–guided prostate biopsy yielded two cores of Gleason 3 + 3=6 prostate adenocarcinoma (5% involvement each) and was otherwise negative. Active surveillance was discussed.

To further characterize the pelvic lymphadenopathy, a ferumoxytol-enhanced MRI was obtained. This showed bilateral pelvic nodes with iron uptake but a left perivesical lymph node without significant uptake. Given the uncertain etiology and concern for malignancy versus other causes, an 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT scan was performed, demonstrating only mild metabolic activity in the left perivesical node.
title: Perivesical unicentric Castleman disease initially suspected to be metastatic prostate cancer

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old female was referred for evaluation of recurrent hypoglycemia. She was born at term (birth weight 2980 g, length 50 cm) after a pregnancy complicated by hypertension; Apgar scores were 8 and 9. There were no neonatal complications or developmental delays. At age 13, she lost consciousness; a glucometer reading after recovery was 1.87 mmol/L (33.7 mg/dL). There were no reports of tremor, sweating, palpitations, or seizures. She was not evaluated again until age 14, when routine labs for community-acquired pneumonia revealed hypoglycemia.

On referral at age 15, she had no acute symptoms. Laboratory results showed:
• Glycated hemoglobin: 3.4% (reference 4–6%)  
• Serum glucose: 1.94 mmol/L (34.9 mg/dL) (reference 3.3–6.1 mmol/L)  
• Insulin: 30.29 μU/mL (reference 2.6–24.9 μU/mL)  
• C-peptide: 4.81 ng/mL (reference 1.1–4.4 ng/mL)  
• Anti-insulin antibodies: 2.54 U/mL (reference 0–10 U/mL)  
• No detectable sulfonylureas in serum.

Endoscopic ultrasound, CT, and MRI of the abdomen showed no pancreatic mass. Continuous glucose monitoring revealed persistent asymptomatic hypoglycemia (2.8–3.2 mmol/L) on a complex-carbohydrate diet, with further drops immediately after fast-carbohydrate ingestion. The patient’s father had normal blood glucose; her mother’s fasting glucose was 3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL).
title: Mild Congenital Hyperinsulinism Caused by Mutation in Human Glucokinase Gene

case_prompt: A 54-year-old man was referred after two brief episodes of memory loss over the past year. During both episodes, he abruptly became unable to orient himself to the time and date and could not retain new information. The first episode occurred at home while working at his computer; he wandered about searching for the date, which he could not remember, and gradually recovered after approximately three hours. The second episode occurred while he was alone in his office, lasted about 20 minutes, and was witnessed by coworkers, who reported that he repeatedly asked the same questions about the time and date. During both episodes, he remained fully alert, with no staring spells, automatisms, or focal neurologic deficits. He experienced a mild headache in the week preceding the second episode. His medical history was notable for well-controlled hypertension treated with metoprolol and prior surgery for obstructive sleep apnea. Neurologic examination between episodes was normal. A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed no abnormalities, and cardiac evaluation, including assessment for arrhythmia, was unremarkable.
title: Two attacks of transient global amnesia within a year: a case report

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman presented with a slow-growing nodule beneath the skin of an umbilical surgical scar, accompanied by periodic pain worsening during menstruation. Four years earlier, she noted multiple nodules at the site of a previous laparoscopic cannula incision at the lower edge of the umbilicus; these lesions grew from approximately 0.5 cm to 1.5 cm in diameter. Six years ago, she underwent laparoscopic ovarian cyst removal (pathology showed an endometrial cyst) and bilateral salpingoplasty. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal palpation revealed no tenderness or rebound. At the inferior umbilical incision, three firm brown nodules (up to 1.5 cm) with clear borders were visible; there was no overlying erythema or ulceration. 

Laboratory studies showed a CA 19-9 level of 39.1 U/mL and a CA 12-5 level of 19.7 U/mL. Transvaginal Doppler ultrasound demonstrated an uneven endometrial echo with a slightly strong signal (endometrial polyp not excluded) and bilateral ovarian cysts measuring 1.5–2.9 cm, suggestive of endometriomas.
title: Laparoscopic umbilical trocar port site endometriosis: A case report

case_prompt:
A man in his 70s was admitted after routine laboratory tests showed a serum creatinine level of 4.0 mg/dL, elevated from a baseline of 1.3–1.5 mg/dL one year earlier. His history included 4 years of microscopic hematuria and a 3-year history of stage 3 chronic kidney disease with trace proteinuria. Prior urologic evaluation with multiple cystoscopies was unremarkable. One year earlier, a nephrologist deferred kidney biopsy for minimal proteinuria.  

On admission, he was asymptomatic, took only occasional ibuprofen, and had trace bilateral lower-extremity edema. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria, a urinary protein–creatinine ratio of 7.07 g/g creatinine, and dysmorphic red blood cells on phase-contrast microscopy. Laboratory studies showed a serum potassium level of 5.2 mEq/L and hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL.  

Given concern for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, he received a 3-day course of pulse-dose steroids, and an urgent kidney biopsy was planned. A full serologic and urine workup was obtained:  
• ANA titer, speckled 1:80  
• Complement C3 100 mg/dL (75–170), C4 27 mg/dL (10–40)  
• Cytoplasmic ANCA <1:40; perinuclear ANCA <1:40  
• Anti–GBM IgG <1.0 (reference <1.0)  
• Rheumatoid factor <10 IU/mL; hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, syphilis, and cryoglobulin negative  
• Serum protein electrophoresis: no restricted bands in the γ region; immunofixation: possible monoclonal free λ light chain  
• Random urinary protein electrophoresis: total protein 353 mg/dL, albumin 223.5 mg/dL; immunofixation: monoclonal free λ light chain  
• Serum free light chains: κ 3.47 mg/dL (0.33–1.94), λ 17.1 mg/dL (0.57–2.63), κ:λ ratio 0.20 (0.26–1.65)
title: AL Amyloidosis Presenting With Crescentic Glomerulonephritis

case_prompt: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of right elbow pain and swelling. He denied trauma; he had fevers during the first 3 days only. There was no weight loss, anorexia, cough, or prior surgery. On examination, there was a slightly tender, fluctuant swelling over the right elbow, with normal overlying skin temperature and no wounds, scars, or sinuses. Elbow movement was painful and limited. A plain radiograph of the right elbow showed a well-defined cavitary osteolytic lesion in the distal humerus, surrounded by a rim of sclerosis, with cortical expansion and periosteal reaction. Initial considerations included tubercular abscess and eosinophilic granuloma. MRI was unavailable. A CT scan demonstrated a 1.5 × 1 cm radiolucent lesion in the distal humeral metaphysis with cortical thickening and mild joint effusion. Laboratory studies revealed a normal white-cell count, a C-reactive protein level of 15 mg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/h.
title: Brodie’s Abscess of the Humeral Paddle in a Child: A case Report

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man with a history of coronary stent placement and living-donor kidney transplantation (on prednisolone 5 mg daily and mycophenolate mofetil 360 mg twice daily) presented with a 2-week history of positional vertigo and a 3-day history of tinnitus, ear pressure, and left-ear hearing loss. He denied other neurologic complaints.  

On neurologic examination, Weber lateralized to the right, there was bilateral nasolabial-fold blunting, and truncal ataxia; other cranial nerves, motor, sensory, cerebellar testing, and otoscopic examination were unremarkable. The initial impression was multiple cranial nerve palsy.  

Brain MRI showed bilateral facial nerve enhancement (left > right) and subtle FLAIR hyperintensity with T1 hypointensity in the left temporal white matter. He was admitted with an initial diagnosis of Ramsay–Hunt syndrome and received intravenous dexamethasone, oral methylprednisolone, famciclovir, and intratympanic dexamethasone, which aggravated bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. He was then referred to neurology with the impression of encephalitis of infectious or autoimmune etiology.  

CSF examination showed 8 leukocytes/µL (75% lymphocytes), a normal protein level (39 mg/dL), and negative Gram stain, bacterial culture, and cryptococcal antigen. CSF PCR was positive for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and negative for mycobacteria, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus (VZV), and John Cunningham virus (JCV). Serum JCV PCR was positive. EBV viral capsid antigen IgG was positive, but IgM was negative.  

After 2 weeks of antiviral treatment, follow-up brain MRI demonstrated FLAIR hyperintensity and T1 hypointensity in the subcortical white matter of the left temporal lobe and dorsal pons, suggesting lymphoproliferative disease or progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Whole-body PET revealed no abnormal hypermetabolism. An initial workup including ganglioside antibodies, antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, aquaporin-4 IgG, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG, vitamin B12, and folate levels was normal.
title: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy successfully treated with mefloquine and literature review

case_prompt: A 3-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a 2-month history of umbilical discharge. The umbilicus appeared slightly inflamed, with intermittent yellowish drainage. His medical history was significant for right inguinal hernia repair performed in infancy; a well-healed scar was visible in the right groin crease. Vital signs were normal. Urinalysis and blood biochemistry results were within normal limits. Abdominal radiography and ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. During follow-up, a firm swelling developed at the previous groin incision site. Approximately one week later, purulent material again discharged from the umbilicus, and the groin swelling was incised and drained under general anesthesia.
title: Acquired Umbilico-Inguinal Fistula with Persistent Discharge due to Suture Reaction: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old woman with a history of stage II mucinous adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon (treated by colectomy and 12 cycles of FOLFOX two years earlier) presented with a 3-day history of left upper-quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea, chills, and anorexia without fever, diarrhea, or constipation. Physical examination was notable only for tenderness in the left hypochondrium. 

Laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level of 6.33 ng/mL and a hemoglobin concentration of 10.1 g/dL with a hematocrit of 30.7%; other biochemical tests were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 9.3 × 14 cm well-defined cystic mass in the left adrenal gland. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed the adrenal cystic mass with associated grade 2 hydronephrosis and an 8 mm nodule in the left breast; no other abnormalities were seen.

Because of the patient’s symptoms and the size of the adrenal lesion, she underwent left adrenalectomy. Unexpectedly, multiple palpable 1 cm nodules were noted in both breasts during surgical preparation, prompting delayed investigation of the breast nodules. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry of the adrenal specimen revealed mucinous adenocarcinoma of colonic origin.

After recovery, breast examination confirmed a 1 cm nodule at 9 o’clock in the right breast and three similar nodules in the left breast (3 o’clock, 1 o’clock, and the axillary tail). Breast ultrasound demonstrated multiple hypoechoic oval bilateral masses, mostly well-defined, though three had irregular margins with central necrotic changes. Mammography showed multiple round masses without spiculations, calcifications, or skin thickening; three masses were lobulated with irregular margins (BI-RADS 4A). A core-needle biopsy was obtained from the largest lesion.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A case report of multiple bilateral breast metastases after colorectal cancer

case_prompt: A 68-year-old woman with a history of acinar cell carcinoma of the left parotid gland treated 30 months earlier with surgery and adjuvant neutron beam radiation (16 fractions of 1.15 nGy/fraction, total 18.4 nGy) presented with progressive dysnomia, memory impairment, expressive aphasia, and personality changes over several weeks. Neurologic examination confirmed expressive aphasia and mild cognitive deficits; vital signs were within normal limits. Brain MRI revealed a heterogeneous, irregular, ring-enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe in the region of the prior radiation field. She was started on high-dose dexamethasone with some symptomatic improvement but remained steroid-dependent. Given persistent symptoms and the surgical accessibility of the lesion, resection was recommended.
title: Delayed Cerebral Radiation Necrosis after Neutron Beam Radiation of a Parotid Adenocarcinoma: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A female infant was born by elective cesarean delivery at 36 weeks of gestation to a 42-year-old mother, with a birth weight of 2090 g, length of 42 cm, and Apgar scores of 8 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes. Prenatal ultrasonography had suggested Dandy-Walker syndrome, but no family history of congenital disease was reported. On day 15 of life, the infant developed episodes of stiffening of the arms and legs with hyperextension of the neck, occurring 12–20 times per day. On examination, she was alert with preserved primitive reflexes. Notable findings included bilateral iris colobomas resembling a “cat’s eye,” mild thoracic scoliosis, and absence of ribs 7–9. Brain MRI showed complete agenesis of the corpus callosum, a multiseptated interhemispheric cyst communicating with the ventricular system, and bilateral coloboma cysts.
title: Diagnostic approach to Aicardi syndrome: A case report☆

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old woman was referred for intermittent, atypical chest pain. She had no significant past medical history except for remote smoking. On examination, blood pressure was 130/67 mmHg, heart rate 70 bpm, and a 3/6 holosystolic murmur was heard over the precordium. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm, normal QRS duration, and no ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. Routine blood tests were normal.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated right coronary artery arising from the right sinus of Valsalva and an aneurysmal left main artery arising from a dilated pulmonary artery. Doppler imaging showed diastolic flow from the right coronary artery filling the left coronary arteries via epicardial collaterals. Biventricular ejection fraction was normal, and the mitral valve was myxomatous with mild to moderate regurgitation.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a mildly dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 60% and showed subtle mid-wall fibrosis of the basal septum on late gadolinium enhancement, with no infarction. The pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (Qp:Qs) was 1.8:1.

Multidetector computed tomography demonstrated an anomalous origin of the left main coronary artery from the pulmonary artery, a markedly dilated right coronary artery arising normally from the aorta, and large collateral vessels connecting the right and left coronary systems. The coronary arteries were free of atherosclerosis.
final_diagnosis_raw: anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery
title: Case report of asymptomatic very late presentation of ALCAPA syndrome: review of the literature since pathophysiology until treatment

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old man presented with palpitations. His pulse was 85 beats/min with an irregular rhythm; blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg, and he was afebrile. Cardiac examination revealed a loud first heart sound and a soft mid-diastolic rumbling murmur (grade 2/6) at the mitral area without signs of heart failure. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, renal and liver function, and urinalysis, were normal.

Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with a mitral valve area of approximately 0.9 cm2, a peak gradient of 14 mm Hg, and a mean gradient of 9 mm Hg. Both atria were dilated, and spontaneous echocardiographic contrast was present in the left atrium. A large, mobile, homogeneous round mass measuring 40 × 35 mm was seen in the right atrium. A similar large left atrial mass adherent to the interatrial septum protruded into the left ventricle; no discrete stalk was identified. The left atrial appendage was free of thrombus. Mild tricuspid regurgitation with estimated pulmonary systolic pressure of 26 mm Hg and an ejection fraction of 45 % were noted. The inferior vena cava was not dilated and was collapsible with respiration, with no thrombus.
title: Biatrial thrombi resembling myxoma regressed after prolonged anticoagulation in a patient with mitral stenosis: a case report

case_prompt: A 10-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a mass in the distal left forearm that limited pronation and supination. Two years earlier, he had sustained a distal radius fracture; follow-up radiographs after healing then had shown no abnormalities. On current evaluation, radiographs demonstrated a 6.5-cm lesion in the distal syndesmosis arising from the radius, with pressure erosions on the distal radius and ulna and slight splaying of the bones. A triple-phase bone scan revealed moderately increased radiotracer uptake in the distal shafts of the left radius and ulna and in the distal radial physis. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a large mass at the distal radial and ulnar metadiaphyses measuring approximately 6 cm craniocaudad, 3.7 cm anteroposterior, and 3 cm transverse; it was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and had overall increased signal intensity on T2-weighted images with a central area of decreased signal.
title: Desmoplastic fibroma of the distal radius: an interesting case and a review of the literature and therapeutic implications

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old girl presented with a 1½-year history of dull, intermittent pain in the anterolateral aspect of her mid-left leg, aggravated by walking and relieved by analgesics. She reported a fall one year prior, after which the pain increased in intensity, especially at night, and a gradually enlarging swelling appeared in the same region. She now ambulated with a crutch. There were no fevers, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms.

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Local inspection of the left tibia revealed a 6 × 7 cm firm, tender, ill-defined swelling on the anterolateral mid-diaphysis, warm to touch, fixed to underlying structures but mobile overlying skin, with intact distal neurovascular status and no lymphadenopathy. Knee and ankle range of motion were full.

Laboratory studies showed Hb 12.6 g/dL, WBC 13 630/mm³, CRP 2.16 mg/L, PTH 120 pg/mL, calcium 9.6 mg/dL, phosphate 2.5 mg/dL, TSH 1.22 μIU/mL, LDH 198 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 86 U/L; Mantoux test was negative. Chest radiograph was normal.

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the left tibia demonstrated an osteolytic, expansile, eccentric lesion with a sclerotic margin in the diaphysis, suggesting osteofibrous dysplasia. Bone scintigraphy showed an osteoblastic mid-shaft lesion. MRI of the left tibia revealed a mixed-signal, expansile lobulated cortical lesion of the lower diaphysis, hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2/STIR with internal fluid levels, and heterogeneous contrast enhancement; surrounding soft tissues were normal. These MRI findings were thought to be suggestive of an adamantinoma of the tibial diaphysis.

A core-needle biopsy of the lesion was performed and sent for histopathological examination.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A 15 year-old-girl with persistent leg pain diagnosed as a giant cell tumor of the tibial diaphysis: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
An 81-year-old man from northeast Thailand presented with a 1-month history of progressive shortness of breath, nonproductive cough, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, and decreased appetite. He denied fever or hemoptysis. His medical history was notable only for hypertension; he had no history of tuberculosis, no high-risk exposures, was a lifelong nonsmoker, and had no family history of lung cancer.

On examination, he was afebrile, with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute and an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Percussion of the left hemithorax revealed dullness, breath sounds were decreased, and egophony was present over the left lower lung field. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 10.9 g/dL; other hematologic and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis yielded 1.2 L of bloody pleural fluid. Analysis of the fluid revealed a pH of 7.439, glucose 104 mg/dL, protein 4.4 g/dL, LDH 1606 U/L, red blood cells 930 000/μL, and white blood cells 2730/μL (51% lymphocytes, 25% eosinophils, 24% neutrophils). The adenosine deaminase level was 24.7 U/L. Cytologic examination of the fluid was negative for malignancy. A closed Abrams needle biopsy of the parietal pleura demonstrated chronic pleuritis without evidence of granuloma or malignancy.
title: First case report of isolated pleural cysticercosis demonstrating pleuroscopic findings

case_prompt: An 18-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of right knee pain and a sensation of instability. He denied any significant trauma. On examination, there was localized tenderness over the medial femoral condyle near the medial epicondyle. Tests for the knee ligaments were normal, and there was no joint effusion. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the knee were within normal limits. Laboratory studies, including serum calcium, vitamin D3, and alkaline phosphatase, were all normal. He was advised to rest and was prescribed nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs. One week later, he returned with persistent pain and instability and was referred for magnetic resonance imaging of the knee.
title: Medial femoral Condyle Stress Fracture: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 4½-year-old boy was referred for bilateral undescended testes and short stature. He was born at term with a birth weight of 2.5 kg and had delayed motor and mental milestones. His parents noted that he remained shorter than peers (his 2-year-younger sister is taller). There was no history of systemic disease, neonatal seizures, prolonged jaundice, or signs of raised intracranial pressure. On examination, his height was 84 cm (<3rd percentile; standard deviation score –4), upper-to-lower segment ratio 0.9, weight 13 kg, and head circumference 51 cm. He had frontal bossing, doll-like facies, central obesity, and a micropenis (stretched penile length 2 cm). Both gonads were palpable in the suprascrotal region with a poorly developed empty scrotal sac. Vitals and the remainder of the systemic examination were normal. Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 13.6 g/dl (11–15), total lymphocyte count 5600/mm^3 (4–11 000), ESR 15 mm/h (5–20), random blood glucose 94 mg/dl (90–130), creatinine 0.8 mg/dl (0.6–1.5), free T4 0.9 ng/ml (0.93–1.7), TSH 7.27 mIU/ml (0.3–5.5), bone age 1 year, basal cortisol 13.76 μg/dl (8–20), FSH 0.63 mIU/ml (1.5–10.2), LH 0.1 mIU/ml (1.9–12), basal testosterone 0.025 ng/ml (3–6.5), stimulated testosterone after hCG 0.68 ng/ml (suggestive of normally functioning testes), and undetectable IGF-1. Scrotal ultrasound confirmed bilateral suprascrotal testes. Brain MRI demonstrated a 3.8 × 3.6 cm suprasellar cystic lesion compressing the pituitary gland; the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images.
title: An interesting case of Rathke's cleft cyst presenting as bilateral cryptorchidism

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old boy with a history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), including two relapses and a cord blood transplant 18 months earlier, presented with a 2-month history of intermittent right flank pain that acutely worsened over 24 hours. Three months before presentation, he had vague right flank discomfort attributed to posture; an abdominal radiograph was negative. He denied hematuria and had no history of nephrolithiasis.  

On examination, he was afebrile, with normal vital signs. He had mild right paraspinal tenderness but was otherwise unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies showed microhematuria without pyuria on urinalysis, negative urine culture, and normal blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels.  

A renal ultrasound one year earlier demonstrated mild right hydronephrosis. In the emergency department, repeat renal ultrasound revealed marked right hydronephrosis with a long segment of the distal right ureter replaced by a mass-like lesion that exhibited internal blood flow on Doppler imaging. Differential considerations at that time included relapse of ALL, an infiltrating tumor, and an atypical presentation of BK virus; the appearance did not suggest edema from recent passage of a ureteral stone.  

Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed right-sided hydronephrosis and proximal hydroureter with an abrupt transition in the mid-right ureter and demonstrated segmental wall thickening and contrast enhancement of the mid- and distal ureter.
title: Nephrogenic adenoma of the ureter in a teenager with history of leukemia

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old man with no history of immunosuppression or known malignancy presented with 3–4 weeks of lethargy, reduced exercise tolerance, anorexia, and a 4-kg weight loss. He was an ex-smoker (50 pack-years) and consumed 50–70 g of alcohol daily. His brother had pancreatic cancer. He denied fever, and examination showed no jaundice, stigmata of chronic liver disease, organomegaly, or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests revealed mild transaminase elevations, normal bilirubin, low albumin, normal APTT, and an INR of 1.4. To screen for occult malignancy, contrast-enhanced CT of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed. The head and chest were unremarkable. Abdominal images showed: 
- A 7.5 × 6.3 × 8.0 cm ill-defined, heterogeneous low-density mass in hepatic segments 5 and 6 extending toward the hilum  
- A wedge-shaped heterogeneous low-density lesion in segment 8  
- Marked intrahepatic biliary duct dilatation without extrahepatic dilatation  
- Thrombi in both right and left portal veins  
- Mild to moderate ascites
