- No pathologically enlarged lymph nodes or extrahepatic malignancy  
Tumor markers showed normal alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen, with a mildly elevated CA 19-9 of 51 IU/mL (reference < 37).
title: A rare case of cytomegalovirus hepatitis mimicking malignancy in an immunocompetent adult

case_prompt:
A 21-year-old previously healthy man was involved in a motorcycle collision. Upon transfer to a trauma center and ATLS evaluation, he was hemodynamically stable but had an open left femur fracture and comminuted fractures of the left humerus and left tibia. A whole-body CT scan ruled out cranial, thoracic, abdominal, and spinal injuries. Fourteen hours after the injury, he underwent debridement and external fixation of the open femur fracture and stabilization of the other fractures.

Twelve hours postoperatively, in the orthopedic ward, he developed hypoxia, tachypnea, fever, and tachycardia; there were no neurologic deficits or skin findings. Oxygen was given by nasal cannula, intravenous fluids were administered, blood cultures were obtained, and ceftriaxone was started. An initial chest CT angiogram showed no pulmonary embolism and only discrete bilateral consolidations at the lung bases. Tests for bacterial and viral pathogens, including COVID-19, were negative.

He was transferred to the trauma ICU for escalating respiratory support, progressed to face-mask oxygen, then required intubation 48 hours after symptom onset. He was extubated after two days and placed on high-flow nasal oxygen for five days. Despite antibiotics and diuretics, there was no clinical improvement. A repeat chest CT five days after the first study revealed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities.
title: Atypical presentation of fat embolism syndrome: A case report

case_prompt: A 42‐year‐old man fell from a height of 3.5 m and presented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 11, right‐sided chest injury with subcutaneous emphysema, and head injury. He desaturated to an SaO2 of 82% and required rapid sequence intubation, after which his SaO2 fell further to 63%. Prehospital critical care paramedics performed a DOPES assessment to evaluate the desaturation, suspected bilateral pneumothoraces, and inserted 14‐gauge, 3.25‐inch angiocaths in the midclavicular line at the second intercostal space on both sides, observing an initial rush of air that soon ceased. Persistent desaturation prompted a second needle on the left in the same space and then a third needle at the fifth intercostal space anterior to the mid‐axillary line, with minimal effect. On arrival at the trauma bay, his saturation and blood pressure worsened. Extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST) demonstrated bilateral pneumothoraces. Bilateral chest tubes were placed without removing the needles, leading to marked improvement in oxygenation and blood pressure. Shortly thereafter, the left anterior catheter began draining dark blood, his blood pressure dropped again, and a repeat eFAST showed pericardial fluid with signs of tamponade.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Needle Decompression Causing Pericardial and Pulmonary Artery Injuries in Patients With Blunt Trauma: Two Case Reports and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 5 years and poor insulin compliance presented with a 5-day history of altered sensorium, abnormal behavior, and four generalized seizures. The first seizure occurred with jerking of all limbs, eye-rolling, frothing at the mouth, and 10-minute unconsciousness, followed by persistent drowsiness. A second seizure the next day resulted in 40 hours of unconsciousness and admission to a local hospital. On day 4 he awoke confused and had two further seizures. He also had three nonprojectile episodes of vomiting with nausea. 

At the local hospital, he received intravenous insulin, potassium supplements, sodium valproate, levetiracetam, and ceftriaxone. He denied alcohol use, malnutrition, liver disease, or prior electrolyte correction. He had missed insulin doses for 1½ months.

On transfer, he was alert (GCS 15) with mild slurring of speech and an action tremor of both hands. Limb bulk and tone were normal; power was 4+/5 throughout. Sensation was intact. Reflexes were brisk, with bilateral extensor plantar responses. He ambulated slowly.

Laboratory studies showed that over the first 3 days at the local hospital, his serum sodium rose from 140 to 152 mEq/L. On admission, random blood glucose was 16 mmol/L, sodium 156 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, creatinine 118 μmol/L, and vitamin D < 8 ng/mL; other values were within reference ranges. Noncontrast CT of the brain was unremarkable. On hospital day 3, brain MRI demonstrated symmetric hyperintense lesions in the central pons and the right crus of the midbrain on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences.
title:
Occurrence of osmotic demyelination syndrome in diabetes mellitus: A
case report and literature review of various etiologies for osmotic
demyelination syndrome

case_prompt: A 48-year-old man presented with sudden-onset seizures affecting his left lower limb. He had no prior seizures or history of neurofibromatosis. On admission, vital signs were stable, and both physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable, with no cutaneous stigmata of neurofibromatosis. Brain MRI revealed a well-defined mass in the right parieto-frontal convexity that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, and demonstrated homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. Curvilinear enhancement was observed beneath the parietal bone but was considered unlikely to represent a “dural tail sign.” T2-weighted images also showed perilesional edema. Digital subtraction angiography demonstrated feeding arteries from branches of the right middle cerebral artery, right anterior cerebral artery, and right middle meningeal artery. Preoperative embolization of the middle meningeal artery branch was performed. A whole-body evaluation revealed no evidence of malignancy. Based on these findings, an extra-axial tumor such as convexity meningioma was suspected.
title: Supratentorial convexity schwannoma unrelated to cranial nerves: Case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of progressive headache, vomiting, vertigo, and gait instability. Neurologic examination revealed subtle bradypsychia; there were no focal motor or sensory deficits.  
Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated a large right parietal extra-axial–appearing mass with internal calcifications and a subtle hyperostotic spicule on the inner table of the skull.  
Brain MRI revealed a lobulated right parietal mass with mild adjacent edema. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was hypointense; on T2-weighted images, it was predominantly hyperintense with punctate areas of low signal. A partial cerebrospinal fluid cleft separated the lesion from the cortex. Post-gadolinium T1-weighted images showed heterogeneous “honeycomb” enhancement. Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion imaging demonstrated strikingly low cerebral blood volume within the tumor. There was no diffusion restriction.  
MR spectroscopy did not reveal any specific biomarkers: there was no alanine peak, no elevated myo-inositol, and no high mobile lipid signal.
title: Primary extraosseous dural chondrosarcoma: a case report

case_prompt: A 46-year-old man presented to the ENT emergency department with a 7-day history of painful tongue swelling and difficulty swallowing. One week earlier, a general practitioner had diagnosed tongue edema and prescribed oral steroids and antihistamines without improvement. He reported no fever, trauma to the mouth, or recent upper respiratory infection. Medical history was notable for schizophrenia treated with olanzapine; dental hygiene was poor. On examination, the tongue was swollen but the airway remained patent; the remainder of the head and neck examination was unremarkable. Because of concern for a possible suppurative process and the patient’s limited communication, a CT scan of the head and neck was obtained.
title: Lingual Abscess in a Psychiatric Patient: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old man was referred after advanced gastric cancer was detected on an annual health examination. Fifteen years earlier, he had undergone splenectomy and left nephrectomy after a traffic accident. He had no abdominal symptoms. On examination, he had only a left paramedian surgical scar. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and chemistry panel, were within normal limits; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Carcinoembryonic antigen was 0.87 ng/mL, and CA 19-9 was 34.0 U/mL. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a Borrmann type 2 lesion at the gastric angle extending into the muscularis propria. Biopsy confirmed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma (cT2). For staging, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated gastric wall thickening in the antrum, perigastric lymphadenopathy (cN1), a gallstone, and a 3.5 × 1.5 cm mass of splenic tissue in the left subdiaphragmatic area without a vascular pedicle. There was no detectable liver lesion on CT, and PET-CT showed no abnormal uptake in the stomach or liver. 

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a new 2.5 × 1.7 cm nodular, heterogeneous, hypoechoic lesion with clear margins in segment II of the liver. Superparamagnetic iron oxide–enhanced liver MRI identified a 2.0 × 1.5 cm nodule in segment II that was slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging, hypointense on T1-weighted imaging, and remained hyperintense on the SPIO-enhanced T2-weighted sequence.
title: Intrahepatic Splenosis Mimicking Liver Metastasis in a Patient with Gastric Cancer

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old man with no history of diabetes, uveitis, or retinal disease underwent standard phacoemulsification with acrylic posterior-chamber intraocular lens implantation under topical anesthesia. Preoperative best-corrected visual acuity was 0.1 in the right eye and 1.0 in the left eye; intraocular pressure in both eyes was 16 mmHg. Preoperative OCT of the right macula was unremarkable, and the vitreous was attached. At the end of surgery, 0.1 mL of a 10 mg/mL intracameral cefuroxime solution was administered.

On postoperative day 1, the patient complained of painless vision loss and a central scotoma in the right eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.02; intraocular pressure was 15 mmHg. Slit-lamp examination showed a clear anterior chamber without inflammation. Dilated fundus examination revealed diffuse macular edema without retinal hemorrhages or cotton-wool spots. Swept-source OCT demonstrated a serous macular detachment with subretinal fluid predominantly in the foveal area and intraretinal edema in the outer nuclear layer; the central macular thickness was 697 µm. There was no posterior vitreous detachment or vitreomacular traction. Fluorescein angiography showed an early nonfluorescent zone adjacent to the optic disc surrounded by an irregular fluorescent band, late diffuse leakage into the optic disc area, multiple nonfluorescent spots corresponding to RPE changes, and a parafoveal hyperfluorescent spot; the foveal avascular zone was normal.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Acute macular edema and serous detachment on the first day after phacoemulsification surgery: A case report

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old Caucasian man with no significant medical history presented with a 6-month history of lower chest and left upper quadrant discomfort. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed a 7.8 × 7.3 cm irregular, partially cystic mass in the body and tail of the pancreas and two hepatic lesions consistent with metastases. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a 4.9 × 3.7 cm irregular, hypoechoic, heterogeneous, lobulated, multicystic, septated mass in the pancreatic body and tail, as well as two masses in the left hepatic lobe (1.9 × 1.5 cm) and the perihilar region (2.2 × 2.2 cm). EUS-guided FNA of the left-lobe hepatic lesion was performed via a transgastric approach with three passes of a 22-gauge needle under on-site cytopathologist assessment.

Diff-Quik and Papanicolaou-stained smears were hypercellular, showing abundant malignant epithelial cells arranged singly, in sheets, and in loosely cohesive clusters with vaguely acinar and trabecular formations. The cells had pleomorphic nuclei (round, oval, or carrot-shaped), fine granular chromatin, occasional small to prominent nucleoli, and scant to moderate cytoplasm; scattered large tumor cells with giant nuclei were also present. Cell-block sections showed tumor cells in solid sheets, thick trabeculae, and poorly formed glandular or acinar patterns, with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, centrally located nuclei, small to conspicuous nucleoli, brisk abnormal mitoses, and necrosis. A metastatic pancreatic endocrine tumor was initially suspected.
title: Liver metastases of pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma with marked nuclear atypia and pleomorphism diagnosed by EUS FNA cytology: a case report with emphasis on FNA cytological findings

case_prompt: A 65-year-old man presented with acute-onset atraumatic bilateral knee pain and swelling. Four weeks earlier he had undergone revision of a bicuspid aortic valve replacement, and 4 days before presentation he was diagnosed with a sternal surgical wound infection that was treated with oral clarithromycin. The wound appeared to be responding, but his left knee symptoms worsened, and 12 hours before presentation he developed acute right knee pain and swelling with generalized fatigue. In the emergency department, his temperature was 39°C and heart rate 100 beats per minute. Both knees were diffusely swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender, with no range of motion. Hip and ankle joints were normal, and there were no signs of cellulitis. Chest and urinary sources of infection were excluded. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 15.9×10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 288 mg/L. Knee radiographs revealed no bony abnormalities.
title: Bilateral knee septic arthritis: Was it from sternal wound?

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman, 36 weeks pregnant, presented with a 2-week history of worsening peri-alar dermatitis that initially responded to topical hydrocortisone 2.5% cream. Despite continued hydrocortisone use, she developed papules and pustules localized to the perioral area, without comedones, leading to a diagnosis of perioral dermatitis. Topical steroids were discontinued, and sequential therapies with a calcineurin inhibitor, ketoconazole, azelaic acid, and metronidazole were instituted, but her eruption continued to worsen. Tetracycline antibiotics were avoided because of pregnancy. 

At a follow-up visit 2 weeks later, several days after the delivery of a healthy full-term infant, she had perioral and lip erythema, swelling, confluent pustules, and scaling, accompanied by pronounced pruritus and burning. The rest of her face and neck were spared. Vitals were within normal limits, and she had no history of new cosmetic products or habitual lip licking.
title: Perioral Demodex folliculitis masquerading as perioral dermatitis in the peripartum period

case_prompt: A 49-year-old man presented with a several-month history of bilateral hypochondrial and epigastric nonspecific abdominal pain, occasionally accompanied by nausea and vomiting. He had been hospitalized for a motor-vehicle accident 18 months earlier but had no ongoing health issues. On examination, vital signs were normal and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and biochemical panel, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an 8-mm gallstone with a normal gallbladder wall and an 8-cm heterogeneous complex mass at the inferior pole of the spleen. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed an 80-mm splenic lesion that was heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, heterogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted sequences, and exhibited heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration, with regular margins. The lesion’s nature—benign or malignant—remained indeterminate.
title: Splenic Hematoma Mimicking Angiosarcoma: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old man presented for a routine ocular examination. He had no history of ocular or systemic disease, trauma, or surgery. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye; intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg bilaterally by Goldmann applanation tonometry. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye after full dilation revealed posterior capsular haze with surface vascularization of the temporal half of the posterior capsule extending from the 6- to 12-o’clock positions. There were no cells or flare in the anterior chamber or anterior vitreous, and gonioscopic evaluation of the angles was unremarkable in both eyes. Fundus examination of the right eye by slit-lamp biomicroscopy and indirect ophthalmoscopy was normal; the left eye examination was normal throughout.

B-scan ultrasonography of the right eye showed a normal retinochoroidal complex and optic nerve head, with a few medium-reflective dot echoes in the vitreous cavity. The axial length was 22.17 mm in the right eye. Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the right eye was unremarkable. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated a thickened intact posterior capsule centrally adhered to another thickened membrane posteriorly (interpreted as neovascular tissue), with separation of the two layers peripherally, and hyperreflective signals behind the ciliary body in the quadrant corresponding to the vascularization.

The patient had an allergic reaction to a test dose of sodium fluorescein, precluding fundus fluorescein angiography. Routine blood tests, including antinuclear antibody titers and a tuberculin skin test, and carotid Doppler ultrasonography were all within normal limits. A cardiovascular evaluation was unremarkable. Given the excellent visual acuity and the asymptomatic, nonprogressive nature of the lesion, biopsy was deferred and the patient was followed closely.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Idiopathic lenticular surface neovascularization: An unusual presentation

case_prompt: A 73-year-old woman with a history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast (stage IIB, hormone receptor–positive, HER2-positive) treated 4 months earlier with surgery, trastuzumab, and aromatase inhibitor presented after an acute gait disturbance. Two months before, she had transient hand weakness and nocturnal urinary incontinence; a noncontrast head CT was normal, and she was treated for presumed symptomatic epilepsy. On the morning of admission, she was unable to advance her legs while standing. Noncontrast head CT showed multiple cerebral hemorrhages: a  high-attenuation area deep near the posterior horn of the left lateral ventricle with surrounding edema, and a faint high-attenuation focus in the right frontal operculum sulcus. She was alert, with no focal motor deficits or asymmetric pupils. Laboratory studies showed no inflammation and normal tumor markers. She received conservative management with hemostatic agents. On the next day, contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated T1 hyperintense lesions in the anterior left frontal lobe and lateral floor of the left temporal lobe with surrounding edema; corresponding areas were hypointense on T2. A few minimal hemosiderin deposits were seen on T2* sequences. The pia mater showed slight contrast enhancement but no parenchymal enhancement.
title: Cerebral hemorrhage due to amyloid angiopathy that was difficult to differentiate from breast cancer metastasis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old, 68-kg man with multiple endocrine neoplasia type IIb—manifested by metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytomas—presented for excision of a vocal cord neuroma. He had no cardiac history and reported good exercise tolerance. Surgical history included bilateral adrenalectomies five years earlier and total thyroidectomy. Medications were hydrocortisone 15 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the evening, fludrocortisone 0.05 mg daily, and levothyroxine 137 µg daily; he took his usual thyroid and steroid replacement on the morning of surgery. Preoperative vital signs showed a heart rate of 106 bpm and blood pressure of 115/68 mmHg; other vitals and laboratory results were within normal limits.

After placement of standard monitors, anesthesia was induced with propofol 120 mg, rocuronium 50 mg, and fentanyl 75 µg. A 5.5-mm laser endotracheal tube was inserted under C-MAC guidance to avoid trauma to mucosal neuromas. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV was administered for prophylaxis against airway edema and postoperative nausea. Ten minutes after incision, the patient developed persistent hypotension—systolic blood pressure < 70 mmHg and mean arterial pressure < 50 mmHg for approximately 15 minutes—despite a 500-mL bolus of 5% albumin and multiple doses of ephedrine, phenylephrine, calcium, norepinephrine, and vasopressin. The end-tidal concentration of desflurane never exceeded 4.4%. Physical examination revealed no rash or urticaria and no increase in airway pressures.
title: Perioperative Severe Hypotension in a Patient with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type IIb and Bilateral Adrenalectomies: Time to Review the Evidence for Stress Dose Steroids

case_prompt: A 73-year-old woman undergoing routine surveillance CT for a history of pulmonary MALT lymphoma was found to have a 2.0 cm × 1.1 cm peripancreatic lymph node adjacent to the pancreatic head. She denied abdominal pain, weight loss, nausea, or vomiting. Her medical history was notable for breast cancer, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and MALT lymphoma. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including fractionated metanephrines, chromogranin A, and gastrin levels, were within normal limits. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a 19 mm × 11.5 mm hypoechoic lesion near the pancreatic head. Two transduodenal EUS-FNA passes were performed. Direct smears showed tumor cells with neuroendocrine features. Initial immunoperoxidase stains on a cell block were positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin. The pathologist was informed that the lesion was peripancreatic without a definite pancreatic parenchymal mass.
title: Pancreatic paraganglioma diagnosed by endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 9-year-old boy was referred to a pediatric dentistry clinic for evaluation of a “ball of gingiva” noted by his mother, with three months of progressive growth. His medical history was unremarkable, and he was not taking any medications. Both he and his mother reported a habit of picking his teeth and “poking” the gingiva. On intraoral examination, there was an asymptomatic, rounded, pink, smooth-surfaced soft-tissue lesion with fibrous consistency, approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, located on the attached gingiva between the upper left permanent lateral incisor and the primary canine. The patient was in mixed dentition, had active carious lesions, and demonstrated poor oral hygiene. A radiograph showed no bone involvement or other abnormalities. Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, the presumptive diagnosis was pyogenic granuloma.
title: Peripheral Giant Cell Granuloma in a Child Associated with Ectopic Eruption and Traumatic Habit with Control of Four Years

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old African American woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive left nasal obstruction and intermittent epistaxis. Her medical history included well-controlled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and coronary artery disease; she had no history of immunosuppression, neurofibromatosis, or prior malignancy. On examination, a left nasal cavity mass was suspected. 

A CT scan of the sinuses demonstrated a left nasal mass measuring 3.4 × 3.1 × 2.4 cm with thinning of the medial orbital wall, nasal septum, and medial wall of the maxillary sinus. A subsequent MRI of the brain revealed a 2.1 × 1.7 × 3.5 cm avidly enhancing lesion in the superior left nasal cavity without perineural, intracranial, or cavernous sinus extension. A CT scan of the chest showed no evidence of metastatic disease.
title: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor of nasal cavity and paranasal sinus with 13 years of follow‐up—A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 47-year-old woman presented with chronic low back pain and right L5 radiculopathy. MRI of the lumbar spine (T1 and T2 weighted) showed multiple mass-like lesions in the right paraspinal soft tissues, including one at the right L5–S1 neuroforamen; all lesions had low signal intensity on both T1 and T2 sequences, and one posterior paravertebral muscle lesion demonstrated a fluid–fluid level. Noncontrast CT of the lumbar spine confirmed calcified mass-like paraspinal lesions without contrast enhancement. Incidental images of the lung bases suggested interstitial lung disease, and a dedicated chest CT showed bilateral pulmonary fibrosis with a craniocaudal gradient and oesophageal dilatation with an air–fluid level. The patient also reported dyspnea, generalized weakness, arthralgia, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
title: Tumoral calcinosis in the lumbar spine secondary to systemic sclerosis: a rare cause of radiculopathy in an adult with advanced disease

case_prompt:
A 10-month-old boy, previously healthy, was noted by his parents to have a gradually enlarging mass in the anterior aspect of his right thigh for three months. He had no fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender mass in the right anterior thigh.

Magnetic resonance imaging of both thighs (axial, sagittal, and coronal T1-weighted, PD, and PDFS sequences) demonstrated several fusiform intramuscular and intermuscular lesions measuring up to 15 × 14 mm in each thigh, more prominent on the right; the bone and bone marrow appeared normal, without lytic or sclerotic changes. The radiologic impression was that of neurofibroma.

One week later, the patient underwent radical excision of the right thigh mass. Grossly, the specimen was a 3 × 2 cm grayish tumor with areas of hemorrhage. Histologic examination showed nests of small, dark, round cells with scant cytoplasm and pseudorosette formations, together with foci of hemorrhage.
title: Neuroblastoma Soft Tissue Metastasis in a 10-Month-Old Infant with a Right Thigh Mass

case_prompt: A 67-year-old Filipino man with hypertension presented with upper abdominal pain and bloating. He underwent a routine colonoscopy that showed diverticulosis, and subsequently an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) that revealed a gastric cardia/fundus mass. At our center, EGD with endoscopic ultrasound showed a 3.5 cm subepithelial hypoechoic gastric mass arising from the muscularis propria with central umbilication and ulceration; the remainder of the stomach, duodenum, and esophagus was unremarkable. Fine-needle aspiration demonstrated groups and single enlarged atypical cells with anisonucleosis, pleomorphism, and prominent nucleoli consistent with adenocarcinoma. Immunostains on the cytologic specimen were positive for CK7, Villin, and CDX2 and negative for CK20, CD117, and CD56, indicating an upper gastrointestinal or pancreatobiliary primary adenocarcinoma. A PET/CT scan showed increased hypermetabolic activity confined to the gastric mass with no evidence of metastases or lymph node involvement.
title: Gastric Medullary Carcinoma with Sporadic Mismatch Repair Deficiency and a TP53 R273C Mutation: An Unusual Case with Wild-Type BRAF

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man with a history of obesity, hypertension, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, type II diabetes mellitus, congestive heart failure, and coronary artery disease (recent stent placement and dual antiplatelet therapy started 3 weeks earlier) presented with two weeks of progressive anterograde amnesia, intermittent confusion, one episode of urinary incontinence, and worsening ataxic gait. On examination, he was alert and oriented except for impaired word recall; there were no focal neurologic deficits.

Noncontrast head CT revealed a heterogeneously hyperdense, lobulated mass measuring 2.8 cm in diameter in the region of the posterior septum pellucidum without ventriculomegaly. MRI of the brain showed a hemorrhagic mass within the cavum vergae, posterior to the columns of the fornix and foramen of Monro, displacing the internal cerebral veins laterally. The lesion had an irregular contour with asymmetric posterior and inferior extension, producing bilateral thalamic mass effect.
title: Hemorrhagic cavum vergae colloid cyst: A presentation of anterograde amnesia without hydrocephalus

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of dry cough and occasional dyspnea on exertion, unintentional weight loss of 10 kg, fatigue, and lack of energy. He also reported occasional left flank and lower back pain over the preceding weeks and a 2-week history of fever about 6 weeks earlier. He denied night sweats, hemoptysis, or sick contacts and had stopped smoking 2 months prior. He had no significant medical history and took no regular medications.

On examination, he appeared mildly pale and ill, coughing continuously. Vital signs were within normal limits. Cardiovascular exam was unremarkable. Respiratory examination revealed decreased air entry in the left lower lung lobe. Abdominal exam showed tenderness in the left hypochondriac region without palpable masses.

Laboratory studies showed mild hypochromic microcytic anemia, C-reactive protein 139 mg/L, ferritin 149 ng/mL, and adrenocorticotropic hormone 67.9 pg/mL. Cortisol and aldosterone levels were normal. Electrolytes, liver, and renal function tests were normal. A Quantiferon test was negative, and stool occult blood testing was negative.

Chest radiographs demonstrated elevation of the left hemidiaphragm with visible bowel loops on both anterior–posterior and lateral views. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed a well-defined cystic lesion measuring 14.2 × 13.5 × 13.1 cm in the left suprarenal region, with a thin wall, areas of rim calcification, and proteinaceous/hemorrhagic contents. The left adrenal gland was not visualized separately. There was eventration of the left diaphragmatic dome and atelectasis of the left lower lung lobe. No lymphadenopathy or pleural/pericardial effusions were seen.
title: A huge haemorrhagic suprarenal pseudocyst: an unusual presentation of a rare condition

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old man presented with a three-month history of a left flank mass. The mass was initially non-painful but had become mildly painful over the preceding weeks. He denied fever, chills, trauma, or dermatologic conditions. On examination, there was a palpable, non-erythematous, non-warm, subcutaneous mass in the left flank. Vital signs were within normal limits.

An abdominal and pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a 7-cm subcutaneous cystic lesion on the left flank with an estimated volume of 70 cc; no other intra-abdominal cysts were identified. A chest radiograph and chest CT scan were unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and liver function tests, were normal. An ELISA for echinococcal antigens was negative. Abdominal CT scan oriented to the viscera showed no additional abnormalities, though the superficial cyst was not well visualized on this study.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Primary subcutaneous hydatid cyst in the left flank: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old Brazilian man with a history of presumed rheumatoid arthritis presented with several months of severe occipital headache and neck pain radiating to the left arm. He had been diagnosed 10 years earlier with polyarthritis of large and small joints, morning stiffness, subcutaneous nodules on extensor surfaces, and hand and foot deformities, and was maintained on methotrexate and low-dose prednisone. He also had hypertension treated with captopril, propranolol, and hydrochlorothiazide. 

On examination, blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg. He had swan-neck deformities of the fingers, camel-back deformities of the wrists, fixed deformities of the feet and knees with severely limited range of motion, and multiple subcutaneous nodules over the elbows. Neurologic examination revealed mild (4/5) left brachial paresis, shoulder muscle hypertrophy, and hyperreflexia (3/4) in the upper limbs, with preserved sensation but signs of autonomic dysfunction. 

Laboratory studies showed a serum uric acid of 8.6 mg/dL, triglycerides elevated, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, and negative rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies. Cervical MRI demonstrated a destructive lesion of the odontoid process, and CT of the upper cervical spine showed hyperdense foci within C1 suggestive of microcrystal deposition. Radiographs of the knees, feet, ankles, and hands revealed periarticular soft-tissue swelling, extensive bone erosions, joint-space narrowing, and normal bone density.
title: Gout Initially Mimicking Rheumatoid Arthritis and Later Cervical Spine Involvement

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive hoarseness. His medical history included hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and asthma treated for over 10 years with inhaled corticosteroids, a long-acting β₂-agonist, and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist. He had also received mepolizumab for 8 months without improvement and was switched to omalizumab three months before symptom onset. He was a former smoker (60 cigarettes per day for 34 years, quit 15 years ago) and did not consume alcohol. Current medications included lansoprazole, torasemide, amlodipine, loratadine, montelukast, atorvastatin, dextromethorphan, fluticasone/formoterol inhaler (500 μg/day), tiotropium, and omalizumab.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral wheezing; the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory tests, including HIV and HTLV-1 antibodies, were within normal limits. Chest radiography and CT scans showed no abnormalities. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated a vital capacity of 100.8% predicted and an FEV₁/FVC ratio of 0.69 (85.1% predicted FEV₁).

Flexible laryngoscopy showed an elevated red lesion on the right true vocal fold, with a normal left fold. Bronchoscopy revealed multiple white, flat, elevated lesions extending from the trachea to the left upper lobe bronchus. Biopsies from the vocal fold, trachea, and bronchus demonstrated squamous cell metaplasia, neutrophilic inflammation, and histiocyte-like cells with foamy cytoplasm beneath the epithelium.
title: Cryptococcosis in the Vocal Cords, Trachea, and Bronchi

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old girl with autism spectrum disorder was hospitalized for evaluation of fever and progressively poor oral intake. Her height was 91.5 cm, weight 14.5 kg, and she was nonverbal with limited social interaction. Three months earlier, she had been diagnosed with right corneal ulceration, left chalazion, and night blindness due to vitamin A deficiency, and was using cephem-type antimicrobial and hyaluronic acid eye drops. On admission, her temperature was 38.7 °C, blood pressure 100/77 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory testing showed a leukocyte count of 21,600 cells/µL, hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, and C-reactive protein 6.57 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed cloudy urine with bacteria, and she was started on piperacillin for a presumed urinary tract infection.

On hospital day 9, she developed swelling of both labia majora, more pronounced on the left side. Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated a subcutaneous fluid collection in the labia majora. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed bilateral labial fluid accumulation with peripheral enhancement.
title: Bilateral bartholin’s gland abscesses in a 4-year-old girl with vitamin a deficiency: a case report

case_prompt: A 37-year-old man presented after a 7-cm stab wound to the right paravertebral region at the third intercostal space. On arrival he was hemodynamically stable, with no signs of airway, breathing, or circulation compromise on primary survey. A portable chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. The wound was not sucking and had no subcutaneous emphysema; it was irrigated and closed with interrupted polypropylene sutures. Laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis (leukocytes, 1642 × 10^3/µl) with neutrophilia (neutrophils, 10.93 × 10^3/µl) and otherwise normal cell lines. The patient was observed for 6 hours and then re-evaluated. He reported worsening pain and developed respiratory distress, with oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. A repeat chest radiograph showed a new opacity in the left lung base without evidence of pneumothorax or hemothorax on the right. A chest CT scan was performed, which revealed a left pleural effusion with associated air and fluid consistent with haemopneumothorax, subcutaneous hematoma in the right hemithorax, and emphysema in the left paravertebral musculature, suggesting an oblique wound tract from right to left and from cephalad to caudad.
title: Contralateral Traumatic Hemopneumothorax

case_prompt: A 57-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a right mandibular margin mass that had recently increased in size. Her medical history was notable for bilateral metachronous breast cancer, treated surgically between 10 and 17 years earlier. On examination, there was a 15-mm, painless, nonpitting, indurated mass at the right mandibular margin. Oral mucosa was unremarkable, and the lesion was difficult to palpate intraorally because of the buccal frenulum. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed 15-mm nodule at the right mandibular margin with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Computed tomography showed a 15-mm low-density nodule without calcification, bone invasion, or lymphadenopathy. The lesion was radiologically diagnosed as an epidermoid cyst. The differential diagnoses included schwannoma, neurofibromatosis, pleomorphic adenoma, and a powdery mass.
title: Peripheral facial nerve schwannoma at the inferior mandibular margin: a case report

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old boy presented with a chief complaint of a missing left eye and decreased vision in the right eye. He was the first child of healthy, nonconsanguineous parents; there was no family history of congenital defects. His mother had a bacterial infection during pregnancy, and he was born prematurely at 30 weeks’ gestation. At birth, an ectopic left eye was surgically removed, and he required resuscitation for respiratory distress. He has since undergone eight surgeries for correction of intraoral, extraoral, and limb defects.

On examination, the left orbit was anophthalmic with signs of postenucleation socket syndrome, including superior sulcus deepening and lower lid laxity. The right eye had a coloboma and multiple scar marks. He had a surgically repaired bilateral oblique facial cleft, bilateral maxillary cleft lip and palate with a floating premaxilla, and extensive forearm pigmentation from constriction‐band lesion correction. Radiographs showed hypoplastic maxillary antra without clefting and funneling of the orbital floor. Intraorally, bilateral fibrous bands extended from the lips to the canine region and palate, with proclined anterior teeth giving a “goldfish” appearance.
title: Orbital Prosthetic Rehabilitation in “ADAM Complex” Multiple Orofacial-Cleft Disruption Syndrome

case_prompt: A 15-year-old boy with salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia diagnosed in childhood and maintained on glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement presented with progressive, painless enlargement of both testes. On examination, he was of normal stature (BMI 21.2 kg/m2). There was a firm, painless 8 cm mass in the right testis and a 10 cm mass in the left testis. Semen analysis showed azoospermia. Laboratory studies demonstrated elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone at 24.1 nmol/L (reference 1.5–6.4 nmol/L). Serum tumor markers were not elevated: α-fetoprotein 1 ng/mL (0–44), β-human chorionic gonadotropin <12 IU/L (<5). Scrotal ultrasonography revealed bilateral, hyperechogenic, hypervascular lesions measuring 8.6×3.5 cm on the right and 8.4×5.5 cm on the left. Given concern for malignant testicular neoplasm, bilateral incisional biopsies were performed. Frozen sections showed complete replacement of normal testicular parenchyma by sheets and nests of large round to polygonal cells with well-defined borders, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, round central nuclei, and intervening dense fibrous stroma. Reinke crystals were not identified. At this point, the differential diagnosis included Leydig cell tumor or mass-forming testicular adrenal rest tumor.
title: Testicular adrenal rest “tumor” or Leydig cell tumor? A report of a challenging case with literature review

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old man returned to the UK after three months of travel through Southeast Asia, including Thailand, Nepal, and India, with a non-healing ulcer on his left lower leg. He recalled an insect bite just above the lateral malleolus in Thailand that became erythematous, then enlarged and ulcerated. Despite surgical debridement in Nepal and India and multiple courses of oral antibiotics, the lesion failed to heal, and two new adjacent ulcers appeared. He remained systemically well without fever, lymphadenopathy, or organ dysfunction.

On examination, there were three undermined ulcers on the distal left leg with violaceous edges; there was no surrounding cellulitis. Laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count, urea, electrolytes, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein. Serologic studies for HIV, Schistosoma, Strongyloides, Mycoplasma, and Leishmania were negative. Antinuclear antibody was weakly positive (1:80, nucleolar), and double-stranded DNA was negative. MRI of the left leg revealed no tendinopathy or osteomyelitis.

An incisional skin biopsy demonstrated ulceration with overlying acanthotic epithelium and a deep dermal infiltrate of neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes, and plasma cells; there was no granuloma, vasculitis, malignancy, or viral inclusions. Special stains (Gram, DPAS, Grocott, Giemsa, Ziehl-Neelsen, and Wade-Fite) were negative. Tissue bacterial and fungal cultures produced no significant growth, and Leishmania PCR was negative.
title: Leg ulceration due to cutaneous melioidosis in a returning traveller

case_prompt: A 6-year-old boy presented with a 3-day history of a painless, rapidly growing swelling in the right axilla. There was no history of trauma, infection, discharge, erythema, discoloration, fever, dilated veins, or sinus tracts. On examination, he was well and alert. A 7×5 cm, globular, soft, non-tender mass was palpable in the right axilla; it was movable with arm elevation, not fixed to the skin, and there was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed: WBC 9.2 K/µL, neutrophils 56%, RBC 4.31×10^6/µL, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, hematocrit 34.3%, MCV 79.5 µm^3, MCH 26.9 pg, MCHC 33.8%, RDW 12.8%. Ultrasonography of the right axilla revealed a unilocular cystic mass measuring 6×5.5×4 cm anterior to the axillary vessels, with no septae, no calcifications or soft-tissue component, no enlarged lymph nodes, and no abnormal flow.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Rapidly enlarging axillary cystic hygroma in a 6-year-old male patient: A case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 19-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless mass in the right ischioanal fossa. He denied bleeding per rectum or changes in bowel habits. Prior perianal Doppler ultrasound identified a solid lesion with abundant blood flow, leading to a diagnosis of haemangioma. On examination, there was a 5 cm × 3 cm multilobulated, cystic-solid mass that was ductile, elastic, non-tender, movable, and smooth; no fistula, lymphadenopathy, or skin lesions were noted. Rectal examination was normal. Routine laboratory tests and CT scans of the chest and abdomen were unremarkable. Pelvic MRI revealed a well-circumscribed, lobulated subcutaneous mass surrounded by a thin complete capsule; the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated homogeneous intense enhancement of multiple nodules separated by intratumoral nonenhancing fibrous capsules. A neurogenic tumor was suggested by the radiologist.
title: Magnetic resonance imaging findings for differential diagnosis of perianal plexiform schwannoma: Case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 56-year-old man with a two-year history of progressive erythema and pruritus presented with erythroderma and generalized lymphadenopathy. Initial biopsy showed an atypical lymphoid infiltrate, and flow cytometry revealed lymphocytosis with 93% CD4+CD26– clonal T cells (absolute lymphocyte count, 11 865/μL), consistent with high–burden Sézary syndrome. Therapy with romidepsin failed, and he was transitioned to mogamulizumab. After five cycles, peripheral-blood flow cytometry showed no phenotypically aberrant T cells. Several weeks after a course of cefadroxil for Staphylococcus cellulitis, he developed a single episode of angioedema and a progressive, pruritic, grade 3 rash over the chest, axillae, and groin. Mogamulizumab was discontinued. Workup for acquired and hereditary angioedema was negative. Differential diagnoses included progression of Sézary syndrome, symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema, pityriasis rubra pilaris–like drug reaction, and drug-provoked autoimmune disorders. Extensive serologic testing (antinuclear antibodies, extractable nuclear antigens, myomarker and necrotizing myopathy panels) was negative. A punch biopsy of the chest revealed interface dermatitis with a CD8-predominant phenotype.
title: Mogamulizumab-induced interface dermatitis drug rash treated successfully with methotrexate and extracorporeal photopheresis in a patient with Sézary syndrome

case_prompt: A 42-year-old woman in otherwise good health with no personal or family history of psoriasis or systemic disease first noted nontender circinate erosions and vesicles on her soft and hard palate approximately 10 years ago. Over the next several months, similar lesions developed on the tongue, buccal mucosa, gingiva, vermilion border, and oropharynx. Five years ago, an oral surgeon documented erosive loss of lingual papillae; the lesions then became painful, causing ageusia and preventing her from eating most foods. Three years ago, she developed severely painful sterile pustules on the distal fingertips, accompanied by edema, erythema, calor, pain, erosions, and paresthesia, as well as separation and pitting of nail plates. She sought care from emergency departments, infectious-disease specialists, surgeons, and dermatologists in three states. Initial differential diagnoses included bacterial and fungal paronychia, pyoderma, herpetic whitlow, and cellulitis. Lesional swabs and blood cultures confirmed lack of pathologic organisms. She then underwent multiple failed topical and systemic therapies, including clobetasol, calcipotriol, tazarotene, tacrolimus, mupirocin, clotrimazole, terbinafine, intralesional triamcinolone, cephalexin, doxycycline, linezolid, prednisone, valacyclovir, and apremilast, and no sulfa-based agents were given because of anaphylaxis. Treatments for her oral lesions—including dexamethasone oral solution, chlorhexidine, tacrolimus, fluconazole lozenges, and valacyclovir—also failed. Interim palliative care consisted of incision and drainage of pustules and petrolatum with occlusion. Her body-mass index fell below 18, and during apremilast therapy she had prolonged nausea, vomiting, and anorexia requiring sublingual ondansetron and liquid nutritional supplements.
title: Acrodermatitis of Hallopeau and erosive oral mucositis successfully treated with secukinumab

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old woman was evaluated for persistent left hip pain and suspected prosthetic joint infection three years after the onset of hip pain and 16 months after total left hip replacement. Preoperative tests had shown an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (94 mm/hour) but normal chest radiograph and blood tests. Sixteen months postoperatively, she developed pain, movement limitation, and mild irregular fever. Hip CT showed a suspected iliopsoas abscess, confirmed on scintigraphy. Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration yielded cloudy fluid, but aerobic and anaerobic cultures remained negative despite empiric linezolid therapy and subsequent surgical debridement with teicoplanin, gentamicin, and ciprofloxacin. Histopathology revealed fibrous tissue with acute and chronic inflammation and nonspecific granulomatous features. Twenty days later, a fluctuant nodule along the surgical scar was drained; cultures again were negative. A 5-cm cutaneous fistula produced greenish, odorless secretion without surrounding inflammation.

On admission, vital signs were normal. She appeared in poor general health with diffuse brown hyperpigmentation of the skin, nails, and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed ESR of 89 mm/hour and C-reactive protein of 75 mg/L. Tuberculin skin test was positive; QuantiFERON-TB Gold was 3.08 IU/mL. At 8 a.m., serum cortisol was 9.5 μg/dL and adrenocorticotropic hormone was 2300 pg/mL; anti-cortex antibodies were negative. A second cortisol/ACTH pair was 5.5 μg/dL and 1490 pg/mL. An interferon-γ release assay based on RD1 peptides was positive. CT of the adrenal glands showed slight bilateral enlargement with calcifications.
title: Total hip replacement infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis complicated by Addison disease and psoas muscle abscess: a case report

case_prompt:
A female infant was born at 35 weeks of gestation to first-degree cousin parents after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios. Antenatal ultrasound had shown intrauterine growth retardation, polysyndactyly, and complex cardiac malformations. At birth, her weight was 1.6 kg, length 40 cm, and head circumference 29 cm (all <3rd centile); Apgar scores were 7 and 10. Physical examination revealed arched eyebrows, depressed nasal bridge, hypertelorism, low-set ears with simple helix, and hirsutism. Ophthalmic findings included microphthalmia, cataract, and vitreous hemorrhage. Limb anomalies comprised broad, proximally inserted thumbs; cutaneous syndactyly of the second to fourth fingers bilaterally; postaxial polydactyly of both hands; broad big toes; and syndactyly of the second to fourth toes bilaterally. She had central cyanosis, a soft systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border, and an oxygen saturation of 80% on 30% FiO₂.  

Laboratory and imaging studies showed:
• Electrocardiography: right ventricular hypertrophy  
• Chest radiograph: cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings  
• Karyotype: 46,XX  
• Babygram: normal ribs, vertebrae, and phalanges  
• Abdominal and cranial ultrasound: no cysts  
• Echocardiography: D-transposition of the great arteries, a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect, a moderate secundum atrial septal defect, a large patent ductus arteriosus with left-to-right shunt, and moderate pulmonary valve stenosis  

She was managed medically but died at 16 days of age from cardiac failure.
journal: Saudi Journal of Medicine & Medical Sciences
title: An Extremely Rare Case of Bonneau Syndrome with Novel Cardiac and Eye Manifestations

case_prompt: A 28-year-old multiparous woman was referred at 24 weeks of gestation after a routine ultrasound at 22 weeks showed a large cystic mass in the fetal pelvis. Ultrasound confirmed a persistently enlarged fetal bladder with a maximum diameter of 5.1 cm in an appropriately grown female fetus. Mild bilateral hydronephrosis was noted, and the amniotic fluid volume was normal. The parents declined prenatal genetic testing. Monthly follow-up ultrasounds demonstrated no progression of hydronephrosis, but the amniotic fluid gradually increased, with an amniotic fluid index of 32 at 36 weeks. In the third trimester, the fetal bowel appeared dilated on ultrasound. Fetal growth and Doppler studies remained normal. Delivery was planned by cesarean section at term.
title: Ultrasound prenatal diagnosis of typical megacystis, microcolon, intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old man with long-standing, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 10.1%) presented to the emergency department after three consecutive generalized tonic-clonic seizures and a postictal state. He reported 24 hours of nocturia, polyuria, and polydipsia. He was hemodynamically stable (BP 130/80 mmHg; HR 85 bpm; RR 20/min; T 36.5°C; SpO2 98% on room air) and had dry mucous membranes. His BMI was 32.2. He was lethargic (GCS 11/15), with muscle strength 4/5 in the lower extremities and diminished deep tendon reflexes; cranial nerves and sensation were normal. Finger-stick glucose could not register; venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, PCO2 42 mmHg, PO2 32 mmHg, lactate 1.2 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 23.7 mEq/L. Urinary and plasma ketones were negative.

Initial laboratory studies:
• Plasma glucose 838 mg/dL; blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (eGFR 71 mL/min)  
• Serum sodium 133 mmol/L; chloride 89 mmol/L; calcium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium normal  
• Serum albumin 2.1 g/dL; alkaline phosphatase 192 U/L; ALT 19 U/L; AST 21 U/L; total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL  
• Calculated serum osmolality 320 mOsm/kg  

Head CT, ECG, and chest X-ray were unremarkable. He was started on IV normal saline at 500 mL/h and insulin infusion at 0.14 U/kg/h. After 24 hours, despite gradual glucose reduction (30–40 mg/dL/hr; glucose now 200–300 mg/dL), he remained lethargic and developed worsening paraparesis (strength 3/5). Serum osmolality had decreased to 305 mOsm/kg; sodium remained within normal limits throughout admission.

Brain MRI performed 24 hours after admission demonstrated increased T2/FLAIR signal intensity with restricted diffusion in the central pons and medulla, with sparing of the thalami, mamillary bodies, and cerebral hemispheres. Lumbar puncture results were normal; EEG showed nonspecific slowing; toxicology screens were negative.
title: Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome as the Initial Manifestation of a Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State

case_prompt: A 42-year-old woman, G1P0 at 34 2/7 weeks of gestation, was admitted with preeclampsia with severe features (blood pressure 205/112 mmHg and 3+ proteinuria). She was initially asymptomatic, with normal fetal movement and no signs of distress. She received magnesium sulfate and corticosteroids. After 24 hours, induction was unsuccessful due to multiple uterine fibroids, and cesarean delivery was performed under spinal anesthesia (hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.75% 15 mg, fentanyl 15 mcg, preservative-free morphine 0.2 mg), achieving a T6 sensory level. The low transverse incision revealed clear amniotic fluid, and external uterine pressure was used to facilitate vacuum suction delivery. During delayed cord clamping, the patient became unresponsive, hypoxic, and hypotensive (noninvasive blood pressure 48/25 mmHg) and was promptly intubated. She then decompensated into pulseless electrical activity arrest. Advanced cardiac life support was initiated, and after multiple rounds of CPR and epinephrine, return of spontaneous circulation was achieved. Central venous and arterial lines were placed, and infusions of norepinephrine and vasopressin were started to maintain organ perfusion. Intraoperative transthoracic echocardiography showed right ventricular dilation with a large pericardial effusion.
title: Amniotic Fluid Embolism Treated with Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation

case_prompt: A 51-year-old Asian man with no prior abdominal surgery or significant medical history presented with sudden onset of left abdominal pain. On examination, there was a tender, mobile mass the size of an infant’s head in the left abdomen. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a smooth, solid intra-abdominal mass approximately 19 cm in diameter containing cystic components. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a well-circumscribed mass with heterogeneous internal density appearing to arise from the small intestine. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a high-signal region on T1-weighted images, suggestive of intratumoral hemorrhage, and scattered cystic areas on T2-weighted images. Small-bowel endoscopy showed ischemic mucosal changes and slight luminal narrowing 20 cm from the ileocecal valve. Based on these findings, a gastrointestinal stromal tumor was initially suspected, and surgery was planned for diagnosis and treatment.
title: Sporadic intra-abdominal desmoid tumor with a very unusual onset: two case reports

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old, female intact Black Baldy cow was presented for evaluation of a white, proliferative mass on the left cornea that had been present for approximately 2 weeks. The cow was bright, alert, and responsive, with normal mentation, and on rectal palpation was confirmed to be 45 days pregnant.

Ophthalmic examination of both eyes revealed a positive menace response, dazzle reflex, palpebral reflex, and intact direct and consensual pupillary light reflexes. Schirmer tear test results were 28 mm/60 seconds in the right eye and 27 mm/45 seconds in the left eye. Intraocular pressure by rebound tonometry was 27 mmHg in the right eye and 20 mmHg in the left eye. The right eye had faint, focal, axial, anterior stromal fibrosis.

In the left eye, there was a raised, white, exophytic mass originating from the temporal limbus extending to the medial paraxial cornea, measuring approximately 20 mm long × 10 mm wide × 8–10 mm thick, with 1–2 mm of perilesional corneal edema. Based on the ophthalmic examination, a working clinical diagnosis of suspected limbal squamous cell carcinoma of the left eye was made. Differential diagnoses included papilloma, lymphoma, parasitic infestation, and inflammatory granuloma.
title: Limbal Squamous Cell Carcinoma in a Black Baldy Cow: Case Report and Surgical Treatment

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old Kenyan man was evaluated for a 1-month history of intermittent high fevers (to 40.2 °C), night sweats, and a 3-kg weight loss over 3 months. He reported a transient productive cough early in the illness that had resolved. He denied travel to malaria-endemic regions, sick contacts, animal exposures, rashes, or significant past medical history.

An outside facility had obtained a normal chest radiograph, a negative sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli, and a negative HIV test. On transfer, he was febrile (40 °C), tachycardic, and normotensive. Physical examination was unremarkable—no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, murmurs, or focal findings.

Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (2.53 × 10^9 cells/L; neutrophils 1.87 × 10^9, lymphocytes 0.54 × 10^9), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, MCV 75 fL), and thrombocytosis (717 × 10^9/L). Inflammatory markers were elevated (CRP 138 mg/L, ESR 52 mm/h, ferritin 912 ng/mL). Renal and hepatic panels were normal. Blood, urine, and stool cultures grew no organisms. Repeat sputum Ziehl–Neelsen smears and GeneXpert for MTB were negative; chest radiograph remained normal.

Extensive workup—including serologies for HIV, hepatitis B and C, Salmonella, Brucella; malaria smears and antigen tests; fungal blood cultures; transthoracic echocardiogram; and connective tissue serologies—was unrevealing. Bone marrow biopsy showed a normocellular marrow with trilineage dysplasia and megakaryocytic hyperplasia, without organisms, tumor cells, or granulomas.

He then developed gradual left upper quadrant abdominal pain. Ultrasound revealed a 15.7 cm spleen with a 2.0 × 2.0 cm hypoechoic lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed multiple nonenhancing hypodense splenic nodules, up to 2.4 cm. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of a splenic nodule yielded bloody fluid with scant leukocytes and erythrocytes but no acid-fast bacilli, fungal elements, or culturable organisms.
title: Isolated splenic tuberculosis with subsequent paradoxical deterioration: a case report

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man presented with sudden onset of epigastric pain radiating to the back. Laboratory studies confirmed acute pancreatitis. He reported only a remote history of smoking and heavy alcohol use as a teenager, denied illicit drug use, and had no notable past medical history. Right upper quadrant ultrasonography and a hepatitis panel were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, a distal common bile duct stricture, and a moderately enlarged pancreatic head. His symptoms improved, and he was discharged without a definitive etiology for his pancreatitis.

Several days after discharge, he developed persistent diarrhea. Fixed sigmoidoscopy revealed a circumferential lesion suggestive of ulcerative colitis, whereas subsequent colonoscopy showed skipped lesions suggestive of Crohn’s disease; neither diagnosis was definitive, and indeterminate colitis was diagnosed. A few weeks later, endoscopic ultrasound identified a pancreatic head mass. Core biopsy of that mass revealed benign glandular cells, rare mildly atypical ductal cells, few plasma cells, few inflammatory cells, and stains for immunoglobulin G4 (IgG4) and CD138 demonstrated nonspecific staining, which were inconclusive. Background debris without malignant cells was also noted.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Autoimmune Pancreatitis Type 2: Case Report

case_prompt: A full-term, two-day-old female infant was admitted with choking, coughing, vomiting, bilious sputum, and cyanosis. Her heart rate was 100 beats per minute, temperature 37°C, respiratory rate 60 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Physical examination showed subcostal retractions and crackles in the right lung. Laboratory studies revealed a normal white blood cell count and differential. Three sterile oropharyngeal sputum cultures were negative, and respiratory syncytial virus PCR was negative. Chest radiography demonstrated opacities in both hilar regions and the right lower lobe. She was diagnosed with pneumonia and treated with ampicillin and cefotaxime. One month later, symptoms had improved but persisted, and she was treated with ciprofloxacin and imipenem for two months without resolution. Because the respiratory findings did not respond to antibiotics, congenital pulmonary or upper gastrointestinal anomalies were suspected. Upper gastrointestinal radiography showed no tracheoesophageal fistula, gastroesophageal reflux, intestinal malrotation, or bowel obstruction. Chest computed tomography then revealed an abnormal tubule extending from the carina through the diaphragm into the left hepatic biliary tract, containing gas and fluid, suggesting a bronchobiliary fistula.
title: Congenital bronchobiliary fistula: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 50-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging swelling in the left axilla. Initially small, the lesion grew to 7 cm × 5 cm. He reported intermittent fevers over the same period. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was no regional lymphadenopathy and no other abnormal findings. Local inspection revealed a 7 cm × 5 cm firm, non-tender, pedunculated mass in the left axilla; the overlying skin was inflamed and ulcerated. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. With a clinical and radiological impression of soft tissue sarcoma, the patient underwent fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC). Cytological smears were highly cellular and showed cohesive clusters of malignant cells composed of two distinct cell populations: polyhedral cells with dense basophilic cytoplasm and pale/clear cells containing glycogen. The nuclei were pleomorphic, hyperchromatic, round to oval with coarse chromatin and prominent nucleoli, and were eccentrically located within a moderate amount of basophilic cytoplasm, giving a plasmacytoid appearance. Numerous bi- and multinucleated cells were present, along with occasional squamous differentiation. In places, acinar and tubular patterns were noted, with numerous mitotic figures.
journal: International Journal of Applied and Basic Medical Research
title: Cytological features of malignant eccrine acrospiroma presenting as a soft tissue mass axilla: A rare sweat gland tumor with histologic correlation

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man with kappa light chain–restricted multiple myeloma and high-risk cytogenetics (including TP53 deletion) presented with fever, confusion, and new-onset right upper- and lower-extremity weakness one week after receiving the first step‐up dose of teclistamab (0.06 mg/kg). His history included penta-refractory disease after multiple lines of therapy, prior spinal cord compression at T6 treated with laminectomy and radiotherapy, and ongoing maintenance immunosuppression. On presentation, his temperature was 100.4 °F, blood pressure and oxygen saturation were normal, and exam revealed disorientation and worsened right-sided weakness compared with his baseline. He tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 but had no respiratory symptoms and received a 3-day course of remdesivir.

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated multiple new regions of white matter hypoattenuation without infarction or hemorrhage. On hospital day 3, brain MRI showed extensive confluent multifocal T2/FLAIR hyperintense signal abnormalities predominantly in the bilateral frontal lobes and left parietal lobe with corresponding areas of restricted diffusion, and there was no contrast enhancement. By day 4, his motor weakness and sensory deficits (proprioception and vibration) in the lower extremities had progressed. 

On day 5, lumbar puncture revealed CSF glucose 54 mg/dL, protein 80 mg/dL, 1 RBC, 2 nucleated cells (68% lymphocytes, 32% monocytes), and negative Gram stain, fungal and mycobacterial cultures. CSF PCRs for Varicella-Zoster virus, HSV-1/2, HHV-6, and CMV were negative. CSF VDRL and cryptococcal antigen were negative, and PCR for BK virus in blood and CSF was negative. A routine EEG showed diffuse slowing without seizures or epileptiform discharges.
title: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy Unmasked by Teclistamab in a Refractory Multiple Myeloma Patient

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old woman, gravida 6 para 6 at 13 weeks of gestation, presented with a 2-week history of a painful, enlarged cervical lymph node on the right side of her neck, accompanied by rigors, difficulty in moving her right arm, fatigue, and anorexia. Her medical history was notable for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (TSH 9.7 μIU/ml) for the past 6 years, and a cesarean delivery 7 years ago. Family history included a father with colon cancer and a mother with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. 

On examination, multiple enlarged posterior cervical lymph nodes were palpated lateral to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. A complete blood count and chemistry panel were within normal limits. A tuberculin skin test was negative. Serologic testing revealed an elevated anti-toxoplasma IgG titer of 112 IU/ml. 

Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated several right posterior triangle lymph nodes measuring 10–20 mm with loss of the fatty hilum. Given her pregnancy, computed tomography was deferred. Although active tuberculosis and toxoplasmic lymphadenitis were deemed unlikely, other serious conditions—including malignancies such as Hodgkin’s lymphoma—remained under consideration.
title: A pregnant women with history of hashimoto's thyroiditis diagnosed with Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease: the first case report

case_prompt: A 35-year-old male refugee from Eritrea, with no chronic illnesses, presented at a routine clinic visit one year after arriving in Switzerland with a soft, slightly painful swelling on the right buttock at the site of a prior surgical scar. He reported multiple surgeries in 2001 for recurrent abscesses in that area. Physical examination revealed a 20 cm linear scar on the lateral right buttock and, medially, deep indurated exophytic nodules with visible openings and spontaneous serosanguinous drainage. He was afebrile and had no lymphadenopathy. A punch biopsy of a nodule produced sanguinolent discharge containing conglomerates of small, firm blackish pellets, suggestive of eumycetoma. Histologic evaluation showed chronic suppurative inflammation with fungal elements. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated a pseudotumoral infiltration of cutaneous and subcutaneous tissues extending into the gluteal musculature without bone involvement.
title: Madurella mycetomatis infection of the buttock in an Eritrean refugee in Switzerland: a case report

case_prompt: A 19-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of persistent left hind-foot pain and swelling. He was a recreational tennis player with no history of trauma or systemic illness. Initial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at a community clinic showed bone-marrow edema of the calcaneus, and he was treated empirically for a stress fracture with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and physiotherapy, with no relief. Four months after symptom onset, T2-weighted MRI demonstrated persistent bone-marrow edema of the calcaneus and development of arthritis in the posterior region of the subtalar joint; no discrete bony lesion was seen, and he was diagnosed with subtalar arthritis and treated with a splint, NSAIDs, and ice, with only partial improvement. Six months after symptom onset, on referral, physical examination revealed tenderness at the tarsal sinus and pain with supination and pronation of the ankle; the patient also reported refractory night pain. Laboratory tests, including C-reactive protein and other biochemical markers, were normal, and plain radiographs of the foot and ankle were unremarkable.
title: Intra-articular osteoid osteoma of the calcaneus: a case report and review

case_prompt: A 73-year-old woman was found to have an incidental mass in the right external auditory canal during a routine examination. She had no ear-related symptoms and no history of cold-water swimming or sauna use. On otoscopic inspection, there was a 2 mm, firm, white, round mass covered by normal-appearing epithelium located at the medial portion of the anterior wall of the bony external auditory canal, just anterior to the short process of the malleus. The tympanic membrane appeared normal and was not contacted by the mass. Palpation with a Rosen needle revealed that the lesion was firm and nontender. A computed tomographic scan of the temporal bone showed a small lesion emanating from the anterior bony external auditory canal; the canal wall was flat with well-defined boundaries and showed no cortical erosion or invasion.
title: Two Cases of Cartilaginous Choristoma—Not Chondroma of the Bony External Auditory Canal

case_prompt: A 71-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of acute low back pain radiating to the left leg. The pain worsened despite conservative therapy and was not associated with trauma. She had no significant past medical history and denied anticoagulant use. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was no motor weakness (grade V) or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities; deep-tendon reflexes were intact. Spinal range of motion revealed painful limitation of rotation on the left side. Lumbar spine MRI demonstrated generalized degenerative spondyloarthropathy and a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous extradural mass adjacent to the left L2–L3 facet joint. The lesion measured approximately 2.8 × 2.5 × 0.5 cm, caused narrowing of the spinal canal, and compressed the dural sac and the left L3 nerve root.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Can acute radiculopathy be caused by upper lumbar hemorrhagic synovial cyst spinal compression in the elderly?

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with double vision and involuntary upward and lateral deviation of the eyes that began 30 minutes before presentation. Three days earlier, she had started metoclopramide, 0.5 mg/kg three times daily, for a 2-day history of vomiting. After treatment, her vomiting improved, but she developed the current eye findings.

On examination, she was alert but in severe distress. Neurologic examination showed sustained conjugate upward and lateral deviation of the eyes and neck stiffness limited to the neck muscles; no other dyskinetic movements were observed. She could briefly bring her eyes back to the primary position with extreme effort, but the deviation recurred within seconds. Ophthalmic examination revealed isocoria with intact direct and indirect light reflexes. Ocular motility and visual acuity were not assessable due to the eye deviation. Intraocular pressures, biomicroscopic, and fundoscopic findings were normal. Vital signs were within normal limits. Complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, and electrolytes were within normal values.
title: Oculogyric crisis in a patient taking metoclopramide

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old woman presented with 2 weeks of anal and vaginal suppuration without fever or other symptoms. She had two prior deliveries and a history of Bartholin’s gland abscess drainage during pregnancy. She denied intrauterine device use, recent travel, alcohol use, or relevant medical comorbidities.

On examination, an external fistulous orifice was noted in the posterior perineum near the left labium majus, and there was induration of the left anterior rectal wall; the gynecological exam was otherwise unremarkable. Pelvic CT showed no abscesses or masses. Under anesthesia, two fistulous tracts (one involving the vagina) were identified and setons were placed; rectal-wall biopsies and pus were obtained.

One month later, pelvic MRI demonstrated multiple complex fistulous tracts, including trans-sphincteric, suprasphincteric, and a rectovaginal fistula. Over the next 3 years, the patient underwent multiple abscess drainages, seton revisions, and empirical antibiotic courses without improvement. Extensive evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease—including upper endoscopy, colonoscopy with ileoscopy, small-bowel capsule endoscopy, CT enterography, and mucosal biopsies—was unremarkable, and anti–Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies were negative. Cytology and cultures of rectal and vaginal exudates and rectal biopsies were negative for neoplastic cells and microorganisms, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serologies for Chlamydia trachomatis, HIV, and syphilis were negative.
title: Actinomycosis Causing Recurrent Perianal Fistulae

case_prompt: A 44-year-old primiparous woman presented with a 4-week history of light vaginal bleeding. Four years earlier, she had undergone endometrial ablation for heavy menstrual bleeding and had been amenorrheic until this episode. On abdominal and pelvic examination, the uterus was normal in size, and no adnexal masses were palpable. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a cystic lesion near the cervix and an endometrial thickness of 1 cm. An endometrial biopsy yielded fragments of benign mature adipose tissue and scant benign smooth muscle, along with keratin debris; no malignancy or myometrial invasion was identified, although sampling was limited by her prior ablation. The patient was counseled about possible diagnoses, including uterine lipoma, lipoleiomyoma, uterine teratoma, and uterine perforation as a complication of biopsy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed a complex, cystic, fat-containing mass in the lower uterine segment measuring 2.0 × 3.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of adjacent infiltration or lymphadenopathy.
title: Uterine teratoma and the role of short-tandem repeat genotyping in understanding origins

case_prompt: A 59-year-old woman with a history of Guillain–Barré syndrome and a prior gastric ulcer, maintained on naproxen and omeprazole, presented with a 6-month history of intermittent abdominal pain accompanied by progressive postprandial nausea, vomiting, and unintentional weight loss. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies revealed iron deficiency anemia. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated circumferential mural thickening of the proximal duodenum. Upper endoscopy showed a clean-based antral ulcer extending into the duodenum and a severe obstructing duodenal stricture that precluded passage of an adult gastroscope. Biopsy specimens from the stricture site revealed acute on chronic duodenitis, and gastric biopsies were negative for Helicobacter pylori. Although peptic ulcer disease was initially suspected, the possibility of malignancy could not be excluded, and the patient underwent a Whipple procedure.
title: IgG4-related disease as a rare cause of gastric outlet obstruction: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and coronary artery disease presented with a  few weeks of malaise, weakness, and skin lesions. She had PCR-confirmed COVID-19 60 days earlier, with fever, cough, malaise, anosmia, and ageusia treated at home. Forty-five days after COVID-19, she noted periorbital erythema and edema and an intensely pruritic erythematous rash on her malar areas, which over days spread to her hands, neck, and buttocks. She then developed profound fatigue limiting daily activities.

Her medications included losartan, aspirin, metformin, levothyroxine, and doxepin. On examination, temperature was 38.5°C, pulse 90/min, blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Cutaneous findings included pink-violet papules on the knuckles, ragged cuticles, midface erythema involving the nasolabial folds, an erythematous plaque on the upper back, and multiple vesicles with erythematous bases on the upper extremities. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic examination showed proximal muscle weakness (2/5) at the shoulders and hips.

Laboratory studies showed AST 67 U/L, ALT 66 U/L (normal 5–40), aldolase 12.4 U/L (normal 1–7), creatine phosphokinase 2611 U/L (upper limit 195), LDH 517 U/L, and ESR 57 mm/h. Complete blood count and thyroid function were normal. Serologies for ANA, anti–dsDNA, anti–Smith, and a panel of myositis-specific antibodies were negative. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative; SARS-CoV-2 IgG was positive.

Electromyography demonstrated early inflammatory myopathy of proximal upper and lower limbs. Endoscopy, colonoscopy, mammography, CT of the paranasal sinuses, and ophthalmologic examination were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular, septal, and anterior wall hypokinesia, mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, and an ejection fraction of 45%. Chest CT revealed bilateral multifocal patchy consolidations with a reverse-halo sign, suggestive of the chronic phase of organizing COVID-19 pneumonia.
title: Dermatomyositis‐lupus overlap syndrome complicated with cardiomyopathy after SARS‐CoV‐2 infection: A new potential trigger for musculoskeletal autoimmune disease development

case_prompt:
