A 48-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of slurred speech, unsteadiness, and fatigue. She had a history of iron deficiency anemia and a melanoma excised 13 years earlier. One year before presentation, she experienced lethargy, intermittent headaches, nausea, diarrhea, and 16 kg of unintentional weight loss over 6 months, and was diagnosed with depression.  
On examination, she was ataxic, unable to walk heel-to-toe, and had subtle dysarthria; there was no other focal neurologic deficit. Cardiorespiratory and other examinations were unremarkable.  
Noncontrast CT of the brain revealed multifocal haemorrhagic foci in both cerebral hemispheres and the right cerebellar hemisphere, the largest measuring 3 cm. The initial differential included haemorrhagic metastases—possibly recurrent melanoma—and an atypical presentation of amyloid angiopathy.  
She was started on dexamethasone and referred for neurosurgical evaluation. A staging CT of the chest and abdomen and a stealth brain MRI were arranged. MRI confirmed multiple supra- and infratentorial lesions, haemosiderin staining in the sulci consistent with low-volume subarachnoid blood, and a 4 mm aneurysm of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery.  
Staging CT of the chest demonstrated a mass in the left atrium concerning for an atrial myxoma.
title: Heart or head?: A depression mimic delays diagnosis—oncotic cerebral aneurysms caused by atrial myxoma

case_prompt: A 29-year-old woman was referred for management of an incidentally diagnosed uterine “fibroid” found on screening ultrasonography. She was asymptomatic and had no significant medical or family history. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies were notable only for microhematuria (5–9 red blood cells per high‐power field). Ultrasonography demonstrated a 6.0 × 4.6 cm solid mass between the uterine wall and bladder. To clarify its origin, pelvic MRI was obtained. Sagittal T2-weighted images showed a 6.0 × 4.6 cm mass situated between the cervical region and the urinary bladder, protruding into the bladder lumen, with relatively increased signal intensity suggesting high cellularity.
title: Recurrent atypical leiomyoma in bladder trigone, confused with uterine fibroids: A case report

case_prompt: A 9-year-old boy presented with a 3-year history of a painless left scrotal mass that had gradually increased in size. He was otherwise well, with unremarkable early childhood development. On examination, there was a non-tender, fixed, 5 cm mass in the left hemiscrotum with intact overlying skin and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. A complete blood count showed a hemoglobin level of 12.3 g/dL and a white-cell count of 7600 cells/mm3; liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing mass (30–55 Hounsfield units) occupying the scrotal region, extending into both inguinal canals and the pelvis, with no bone erosion or evidence of abdominal metastasis. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. An ultrasound-guided Tru-Cut biopsy was performed. Histologic examination of H&E-stained sections revealed sheets of bland cells with spindle-shaped nuclei, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, and a storiform growth pattern, diffusely infiltrating underlying adipose tissue; prominent myxoid stroma with thin-walled vessels was also noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse, strong positivity for CD34.
title: Myxoid Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans of the Scrotum: Rare Tumor in an Uncommon Location

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of post-exercise palpitations, shortness of breath, and chest tightness lasting up to 45 minutes and resolving with rest. An ambulatory heart rhythm monitor showed sinus rhythm during her symptomatic episodes and, separately, episodes of second-degree (Mobitz type I) AV block as well as advanced, second-degree AV block with asymptomatic pauses up to 4.8 seconds. 

On admission, her physical examination, vital signs, and a 15-lead ECG were normal. Laboratory studies, including serum electrolytes, complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, antinuclear antibody panel, Lyme antibody panel, and streptolysin O antibodies, were all within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated normal cardiac structure and function without evidence of myocarditis.

During telemetry, she continued to have intermittent episodes of advanced second-degree AV block, particularly when startled awake. A treadmill stress test produced a peak heart rate of 206 bpm with maintained sinus rhythm and no dysrhythmia. A head-up tilt-table test reproduced her symptoms (palpitations, shortness of breath, chest tightness, dizziness, pallor, syncope) accompanied by sinus bradycardia (40 bpm) and hypotension but no ectopy or arrhythmia on ECG. A 1-mg dose of intravenous atropine produced no change in the frequency of her AV block episodes.
final_diagnosis_raw: atrioventricular junctional tachycardia with exit block
title: Atrioventricular junctional tachycardia with exit block in an adolescent

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old European woman with a history of Behçet’s disease diagnosed eight years earlier—manifesting then as oral and genital ulcers, arthritis, thrombophlebitis and treated with steroids, cyclophosphamide, and colchicine—presented with four days of fever, sore throat, and painful swallowing. Remission had been maintained off immunosuppression for one year. She had insulin-dependent diabetes and left knee osteoarthritis.

On examination, she was febrile, had inarticulate speech, left tonsillar and soft-palate swelling, and enlarged left cervical lymph nodes. A presumptive peritonsillar abscess was incised without pus. Clindamycin was started. Neck CT showed left peritonsillar tissue inflammation without abscess. A bilateral tonsillectomy revealed acute phlegmonous tonsillitis; cultures were negative.

Despite antibiotics, she remained febrile (up to 39 °C) with persistent neck swelling causing moderate dyspnea. C-reactive protein remained elevated (200–400 mg/L). On day 7, repeat CT showed diffuse pharyngeal swelling without abscess. Imipenem was added. By day 15, CT of neck, chest, and abdomen excluded superior vena cava syndrome, pulmonary embolism, and thoracic or abdominal abscess. On day 17, she developed single non-palpable petechiae on her right palm and foot. Transthoracic echocardiography was normal. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Syphilis and HIV serologies were negative. Vasculitis screening (ANAs, ANCAs, urinary sediment) was negative. On day 20, MRI of head and neck showed diffuse, predominantly left-sided inflammatory infiltration of epi- and mesopharyngeal tissues.
title: Persistent fever, neck swelling, and small vessel vasculitis following tonsillectomy in a patient with Behçet’s disease: a case report

case_prompt: A 52-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer on chemotherapy presented with a 2-week history of rapid-onset bilateral upper eyelid swelling, associated with decreased visual acuity and headaches. On examination, she had marked bilateral upper eyelid edema without erythema or tenderness. An initial non-contrast CT scan of the brain and orbits showed diffusely enlarged and infiltrated bilateral lacrimal glands with moderate post-contrast enhancement and subtle extraconal fat infiltration. There was no bony erosion. Subsequent orbital MRI revealed asymmetric enlargement of both lacrimal glands that were isointense to muscle on T1- and T2-weighted images, showed no diffusion restriction, and demonstrated intense enhancement after gadolinium administration. The extraocular muscles, globes, and bony orbits were otherwise normal.
title: Bilateral swelling of the lacrimal glands as first manifestation of systemic sarcoidosis in a patient with breast cancer

case_prompt: A 9-year-old boy presented with a several-month history of progressive, painless bilateral cheek swelling. His mother reported a history of similar jaw swelling in her own childhood that had been surgically corrected; his older brother was unaffected. On examination, there were symmetrical, bilateral, bony‐hard, non-tender swellings of the cheeks and the body and rami of the mandible. An orthopantomogram showed bilateral multilocular radiolucent lesions of the posterior mandibular bodies and rami, with sparing of the condyles. Multiple carious teeth were noted, along with delayed eruption and displacement of the mandibular second molar tooth buds. Blood chemistry was obtained to rule out primary hyperparathyroidism. Histopathologic examination of a biopsy specimen revealed numerous multinucleated giant cells resembling osteoclasts scattered within a fibrous connective tissue stroma.
title: Familial Case of Cherubism from South India: Differential Diagnosis and Report of 2 Cases

case_prompt: A 48-year-old perimenopausal woman (gravida 2, para 2) presented with 4 months of lower abdominal pain and intermenstrual bleeding. Vital signs were unremarkable. On pelvic examination, an 8 × 8 cm solid, ulcerated, necrotic mass protruded through the cervix into the vagina, obscuring the cervical body. Hemoglobin was 10.0 g/dL; other blood counts and biochemistry were normal. Transvaginal ultrasound could not be performed because of the unreducible, tender mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis showed a well-circumscribed, low-density, pedunculated mass (9 × 8 cm) in the cervical canal and vagina, attached to the posterior uterine corpus by a 5 cm stalk with slight contrast enhancement. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 9 × 8 cm lobulated mass distending the cervix and vagina, connected to the myometrium by a 4.5 cm stalk containing thin linear low-signal structures (“Broccoli sign”). The mass had heterogeneous T2 signal with peripheral hemorrhagic foci hyperintense on T1 and DWI, but no true diffusion restriction. On dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging, it showed progressive heterogeneous enhancement paralleling the uterine myometrium.
title: Benign and malignant prolapsed uterine tumors : 4 case reports of an extremely rare entities

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old right-handed man presented with recurrent left forearm and hand weakness. In July 2020, he developed sudden severe left shoulder pain followed by left finger-extension weakness and was diagnosed with posterior interosseous nerve syndrome elsewhere; the pain partially improved, but weakness persisted. In January 2021, his shoulder pain recurred and shortly thereafter he noted left finger-flexion weakness. Ten days later he was admitted. 

On examination, he had no weight loss or muscle weakness except in the left forearm. He had persistent shoulder-girdle pain without a clear dermatomal pattern. Neurologic examination showed severe weakness of muscles innervated by the left posterior interosseous nerve and mild to moderate weakness in muscles innervated by the median nerve (including the anterior interosseous branch) and ulnar nerve. There was atrophy of these muscles on the dorsal and palmar surfaces of the left forearm and hand. Deep tendon reflexes were normal and there were no sensory deficits or pathologic reflexes.

Laboratory tests, including antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, antiganglioside, and antiviral antibodies, were normal. Cervical spine MRI and brachial-plexus MR neurography were nondiagnostic. Nerve conduction studies on the left showed reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes in the median, anterior interosseous, ulnar, radial, and posterior interosseous nerves, with no conduction block in the median, ulnar, or radial nerves. Sensory nerve conduction studies were normal. Lower-extremity studies were normal.

Needle electromyography of forearm muscles innervated by the median, anterior interosseous, ulnar, and posterior interosseous nerves revealed abnormal spontaneous activity in all these distributions; recruitment and interference patterns were delayed and poor for muscles innervated by the ulnar and posterior interosseous nerves, but were normal for muscles innervated by the median and anterior interosseous nerves. EMG of proximal muscles (serratus anterior, deltoid, biceps, triceps, vastus medialis) was normal.
title: Nerve Ultrasonography for the Diagnosis and Evaluation of Neuralgic Amyotrophy

case_prompt: A 48-year-old woman presented with 6 months of amenorrhea and intermittent lower abdominal pain. The pain was colicky, moderate in intensity, radiated to the back, and was associated with nausea and vomiting. She denied any history of abnormal vaginal or intermenstrual bleeding prior to this time. Eight months earlier, she underwent surgical repair of a cystocele, during which she experienced blood loss requiring 2 units of transfused blood. She has four prior uncomplicated vaginal deliveries and has not used any contraceptive methods. Her medical history includes hypertension diagnosed 8 months ago, managed with amlodipine and candesartan; she has no history of diabetes or asthma. On examination, she appeared uncomfortable but was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, heart rate 80 bpm, and respiratory rate 24 bpm; there was no pallor or jaundice. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL (12–16), total white blood cell count 3.8 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 257 × 10^9/L (150–450), urine microscopy with 10–12 pus cells per high-power field, blood urea nitrogen 15 mmol/L (2.1–8.5), and serum creatinine 0.6 mg/dL (0.59–1.04). Viral screening was negative. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed fluid within the uterine cavity and pelvic area, with upward displacement of the uterus.
title: A rare cause of amenorrhea: Hematocolpos in a post‐cystocele repair patient

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive headaches and vision loss. He reported no fever, asthenia, or prior pituitary surgery. On examination, there was evidence of chiasmal compression; there were no signs of diabetes insipidus. Laboratory studies revealed: TSHus 0.25 mIU/L (0.5–5); FT4 0.7 ng/dL (1–2); ACTH 5 pg/mL (10–40); cortisol 3 µg/dL (10–20); FSH 0.7 IU/L (1–10); LH 0.5 IU/L (0.7–7.9); testosterone 50 ng/dL (200–900); GH 1.5 ng/mL (< 5); CRP 3 mg/L (< 3); WBC 9.7 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0 × 10^9/L).  
Brain MRI demonstrated a 3-cm sellar/suprasellar mass with mixed high and low T1- and T2-weighted signals, a cystic and hemorrhagic component, rim enhancement after gadolinium, and mild, partial central hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging.
title: Pituitary abscess: two case reports

case_prompt: A 73-year-old woman with a history of Helicobacter pylori gastritis (eradicated), coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco use presented with several months of postprandial epigastric pain. The abdomen was soft and nontender on examination without palpable masses. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests, serum lipase, and the tumor marker carbohydrate antigen 19-9, were within normal limits (CA 19-9 <3 U/mL; normal range, 0–37 U/mL). An abdominal CT scan with intravenous and oral contrast showed an ill-defined, 3.5 × 3.4 × 3.0 cm hypodense lesion in the head of the pancreas without dilation of the pancreatic duct or evidence of pancreatic atrophy. Endoscopic ultrasound identified a 40 × 46 mm lesion in the pancreatic head and neck.
title: A Novel Home for Hemangiomas: Sclerosing Hemangioma in the Pancreas

case_prompt: An 83-year-old Hispanic man with end-stage renal disease on thrice-weekly hemodialysis, hypertension, coronary artery disease with prior myocardial infarction and stent, seizure disorder, and remote colectomy with colostomy presented with bilateral lower-extremity weakness. He first noticed weakness around the knees after an early dinner at 3 PM, progressed to difficulty rising from a chair and walking, and persisted for several hours, prompting hospital presentation. Three days earlier, he had a similar episode that resolved after dialysis. Between episodes he ambulated normally. He denied fever, cough, diarrhea, trauma, or changes in bowel or bladder function. His medications included aspirin, clopidogrel, simvastatin, metoprolol, multivitamin, folic acid, calcium acetate, phenytoin, and omeprazole. He had a recent seizure requiring intubation and was discharged on phenytoin; prior potassium levels had reached 8.3 mEq/L. On examination, hip flexor strength was 2/5 bilaterally, cogwheel rigidity was noted at both knees, and sensory testing and reflexes were normal. Cranial nerves and upper extremity strength were intact. ECG showed peaked T waves, and serum potassium was 7.8 mEq/L. Chest radiograph revealed no acute infiltrates or fluid overload. His diet included rice, beans, pork chops, beef, chicken, and salad.
title: Hyperkalemic Recurrent Bilateral Lower Extremity Weakness in a Patient on Hemodialysis

case_prompt:
A female infant was born at 37 weeks’ gestation to a gravida 3 para 1 mother with no medical history and negative maternal labs. At birth, her heart rate was consistently above 200 beats per minute. APGAR scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. Physical examination was unremarkable except for a 4 cm × 4 cm blanching hemangioma on the back. 

In the neonatal ICU, ECG showed a heart rate of 235 bpm, broad QRS tachycardia with P waves following the QRS complexes, and possible delta waves. Vagal maneuvers and escalating doses of IV adenosine failed to terminate the tachycardia, so synchronized cardioversion restored sinus rhythm. The infant was started on an IV procainamide infusion and oral propranolol; procainamide was discontinued after 24 hours. 

The ECG continued to show wide‐complex tachycardia, and the initial differential included VT versus SVT with aberrant conduction. Assuming SVT, vagal maneuvers and adenosine were repeated; adenosine produced 1:1 conduction with no AV dissociation but did not terminate the tachycardia, necessitating another cardioversion. 

On day 2, multiple recurrences of wide‐complex tachycardia at ~200 bpm occurred, all resistant to adenosine and treated with cardioversion twice more. Propranolol was increased, and IV procainamide was replaced with IV amiodarone. On day 3, ECG again showed wide QRS tachycardia at 170 bpm, which resolved spontaneously on day 9 of life. Transthoracic echocardiography during admission showed no cardiomegaly or intracardiac masses.
title: Ventricular Tachyarrhythmia in a Newborn Baby

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF <25%) and NYHA class III–IV heart failure underwent implantation of a biventricular ICD (CRT-D) in a left pectoral submuscular pocket. He had first- to second-degree AV block, broad LBBB (QRS 168 ms), and echocardiographic dyssynchrony. He reported marked symptomatic improvement to NYHA I.

Four weeks later, he developed minimal redness at the implantation site without systemic signs. Eight weeks after implantation, the system was explanted, and he received a second-generation cephalosporin. Preoperative CRP was mildly elevated (28 mg/L), procalcitonin and leukocyte count were normal. An intraoperative swab grew Staphylococcus capitis, but its clinical significance was deemed questionable.

After healing, a new CRT-D was implanted in a right pectoral submuscular pocket; the generator was wrapped in an antibiotic envelope, the pocket was irrigated with vancomycin and gentamicin, and he received 3 days of IV cefazolin. The postoperative course was unremarkable until 8 weeks later, when discrete local reddening recurred. In November 2018, PET-CT showed periodontitis and increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the ICD pocket and around a 2014 knee endoprosthesis.

The ICD was explanted. Blood cultures, pocket swabs, and knee-aspirate cultures were sterile. Inflammatory markers remained minimally altered (mildly elevated CRP, normal procalcitonin and leukocyte count) and mild hypereosinophilia was noted. Arthroscopic synovial biopsy of the knee prosthesis was sterile, and the dental focus was extracted. A dermatology consult excluded pyoderma gangrenosum. A 72-hour skin patch test for titanium allergy was negative but limited by short exposure.
title: First-in-man implantation of a gold-coated biventricular defibrillator: Difficult differential diagnosis of metal hypersensitivity reaction vs chronic device infection

case_prompt: A 25-year-old healthy primigravida at 32 weeks’ gestation was referred for cardiology evaluation after routine prenatal ultrasound detected persistent fetal sinus bradycardia. Her obstetric history was unremarkable, and the first pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Fetal heart rates on serial ultrasounds ranged from 108 to 119 beats per minute, and a fetal echocardiogram at 35 weeks showed normal chamber dimensions, good ventricular function, and normal atrioventricular intervals. The mother denied use of any medications with bradycardic effects. Laboratory tests revealed negative anti-Ro/La antibodies, normal thyroid function, and normal serum electrolytes. A maternal echocardiogram was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG demonstrated a corrected QT interval of 482 ms. The father’s ECG was normal.
title: Low foetal heart rate, a potentially ominous finding: case report

case_prompt: A 25-year-old man with a 9-year history of focal seizures involving involuntary right arm tremors presented with recent aggravation of seizure activity and new right arm weakness. Neurologic examination was unremarkable at initial presentation. He had no stigmata or family history of neurofibromatosis. Initial brain MRI showed a 1.5×1.0×1.1 cm mass in the left precentral gyrus that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited intense gadolinium enhancement with surrounding edema but no cystic change or calcification. The initial radiologic differential diagnosis included pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, ganglioglioma, and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor. The patient declined surgery and remained stable on antiepileptic therapy; follow-up MRI 2 years later showed no change. Nine years after the initial MRI, he reported prolonged seizures and progressive right arm weakness with grade IV motor strength. CT and MRI at that time revealed an increase in the enhancing mass to 2.3×1.9×1.6 cm and the development of a 5.5 cm peritumoral cyst without calcification or cyst-wall enhancement.
title: Supratentorial Intracerebral Schwannoma : Its Fate and Proper Management

case_prompt: A 24-year-old man presented with painless decreased vision in his right eye and photophobia for 3 days. He had no significant medical or surgical history but reported heavy marijuana use for 2 years. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 10/20 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Pupils were round and reactive with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Extraocular movements were full. Intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg (right) and 14 mmHg (left). The anterior segments were unremarkable. Funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed multiple foci of subretinal fluid at the macula; the optic nerve head appeared normal. The left eye examination was normal. Spectral-domain OCT of the right eye confirmed multiple areas of subretinal fluid and showed choroidal thickening in both eyes. Fluorescein angiography of the right eye demonstrated multiple pinpoint leaks with pooling in subretinal spaces. Indocyanine green angiography in both eyes showed evenly distributed, round hypocyanescent dark dots and fuzzy, dilated choroidal vessels. Systemic evaluation, including a purified protein derivative test, serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level, and chest radiography, was unremarkable.
title: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease with a unilateral presentation in a patient with marijuana overuse: Role of multimodal imaging in suspected patients

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of left hemicranial headache and 10 days of associated vomiting. He also noted drooping of the left eyelid for 1 week. On examination, he had partial ptosis of the left eye and a left sixth-nerve palsy. The remainder of the neurologic and ophthalmologic examinations was normal. His past medical history was unremarkable. 

Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a homogeneous, expansile mass with lytic bone destruction involving the clivus, sphenoid sinus, sella, and nasopharynx; bone-window images demonstrated peripheral “eggshell” calcification. Contrast CT revealed uniform enhancement of the lesion. MRI of the brain demonstrated a well-defined clival and sphenoidal mass that was isointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images.
title: Clival giant cell tumor - A rare case report and review of literature with respect to current line of management

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a mass protruding from her genital region associated with urinary retention. The mass spontaneously retracted when she lay supine but increasingly required manual reduction. It protruded during urination or straining, causing pain and difficulty voiding.

On examination, vital signs were normal. A 5 × 5 cm solid, elastic, nontender mass arose from the upper vulva and appeared to originate from the urethral meatus; the hymen was intact. A prior gynecologic procedure had repositioned the mass into the urethra and placed a urinary catheter, with discharge during reduction appearing to be urine.

Abdominal ultrasound showed heterogeneous echogenic lesions on the posteroinferior bladder wall without hydronephrosis in either kidney. CT intravenous urogram demonstrated a 4.1 × 3.4 cm distal ureteral dilation with a 0.3 cm wall thickness, fluid density, and contrast filling in the delayed phase, as well as a 0.9 × 0.6 cm stone at the left vesicoureteral junction that did not cause obstruction.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Prolapsed ureterocele mimicking a vulval mass in young female with complete duplex system and ureteral stone: A case report

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old woman presented with a 12-month history of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction and tearing (epiphora), associated with a painless lump on the right lateral nose. She had a 2 pack-year smoking history and no constitutional (“B”) symptoms. Medical history included hypertension, mild angina, and hypercholesterolaemia; performance status was 0.

On examination, the right globe was proptosed and laterally displaced by a firm medial canthal mass; the tear lake was elevated. Visual acuity and extraocular movements were intact. Nasal endoscopy showed a mass in the right nasal cavity of unvisualized origin; the contralateral postnasal space was clear. There was a palpable right level 1B neck node. Fine-needle aspiration of that node showed reactive hyperplasia without dysplasia or malignancy.

Contrast CT of the sinuses revealed an extensive soft-tissue mass filling the right maxillary sinus, extending into the right nasal cavity, ethmoid and frontal sinuses, invading the nasolacrimal system, and breaching the lamina papyracea into the right orbit, abutting and displacing the globe. 

The patient underwent endoscopic sinus surgery, with biopsies taken from the right inferior turbinate, lateral nasal wall, lacrimal fossa, and maxillary sinus and preserved in formalin.
title: Unilateral nasal obstruction: a rare presentation of acute myeloid leukaemia

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old man presented with a brown plaque on his right posterior thigh that had been present for 1 year and had thickened over the last several months without symptoms. On examination, there was a 16 × 16 cm dusky red, thick plaque with scale on the right posterior thigh. Additional findings included a 1 × 1 cm scaly erythematous patch on the abdomen and scattered hypopigmented patches and thin pink plaques on the buttocks, back, and lower extremities; the hypopigmented patches had been present for many years. Total body‐surface‐area involvement was estimated at 2 % patches and 0.5 % plaques, consistent with stage IA mycosis fungoides.

A biopsy of a hypopigmented patch confirmed a paucicellular CD8+ epidermotropic infiltrate characteristic of hypopigmented MF. A biopsy of the posterior thigh plaque revealed two components: superficially, an epidermotropic, band‐like infiltrate of small‐ to intermediate‐sized cerebriform lymphocytes; and in the deeper dermis, a diffuse and nodular lymphocytic infiltrate. The deeper cells had round nuclei, small basophilic nucleoli, and an eosinophilic rim of cytoplasm with eccentric nuclei, imparting a monocytoid appearance.

Immunohistochemical studies showed that both the superficial and deeper infiltrates were CD8 positive with loss of CD5 and CD7. The superficial component expressed granzyme and TIA-1. The deeper component demonstrated a perinuclear dot-like staining pattern for CD68.
title: Collisional variant of CD8+ mycosis fungoides and indolent CD8+ lymphoid proliferation

case_prompt: A 48-year-old man with a history of left-sided renal cell carcinoma treated with radical nephrectomy and radiotherapy in 2004, who later developed adrenal, pulmonary, and mediastinal metastases treated with interferon until 2007, presented in December 2009 with a 2-month history of progressive dysphagia, alteration in his voice, and a 2–3 kg weight loss. On examination, he had a 5 × 5 cm exophytic mass in the oropharynx centered at the right base of the tongue, extending into the right tonsillar fossa and adjacent soft palate and crossing the midline. Tongue mobility was normal, and there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the face, neck, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed widespread visceral and osseous metastatic deposits, including the base-of-tongue lesion, with no cervical adenopathy.
journal: Indian Journal of Urology : IJU : Journal of the Urological Society of India
title: Palliation of dysphagia with radiotherapy for exophytic base tongue metastases in a case of renal cell carcinoma

case_prompt: A 27-year-old woman presented with a year of intermittent bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, weight loss, and anorexia. Her history included massive post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage and two siblings with albinism. On examination, she was dehydrated, malnourished, pale, had oculocutaneous albinism and horizontal nystagmus, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and swollen, ulcerated perianal skin tags. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, C-reactive protein 118 mg/L, and albumin 2.5 g/dL. Stool cultures and tuberculosis blood tests were negative. CT of the abdomen revealed inflammatory thickening of the rectum and sigmoid colon with enlarged lymph nodes. Pelvic MRI demonstrated complex anal fistulas and a small parietal abscess. Colonoscopy showed erythema, edema, and superficial ulcerations limited to the rectum and sigmoid colon. Histopathological examination of biopsy specimens revealed multiple noncaseating granulomas, active colitis features (edema, crypt abscesses), and chronic changes (crypt distortion, transmural inflammation). A PCR test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis on biopsy tissue was negative.
title: Granulomatous Colitis Due to Hermansky-Pudlak Syndrome

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling over the dorsum of her right foot, associated with progressive pain during exertion for the past 6 months. There was no history of trauma, fever, chills, weight loss, or loss of appetite. On examination, there was a firm swelling over the fourth metatarsal region with a healed scar and minimal tenderness; no sinuses or discharge were present. Weight-bearing exacerbated the pain, and distal neurovascular status was intact. 

She had undergone a biopsy elsewhere, which showed atypical osteoid proliferation, and a working diagnosis of low-grade osteosarcoma versus osteoid osteoma versus osteoblastoma was made. Baseline blood investigations were within normal limits. 

Plain radiographs of the right foot showed a well-defined eccentric lesion with a homogeneous matrix involving the distal two-thirds of the fourth metatarsal, with mild expansion into the intermetatarsal space. CT of the foot demonstrated a 4.6 × 3.2 × 3.6 cm, well-defined, exophytic, lobulated, dense sclerotic lesion with an osteoid matrix arising from the medial aspect of the distal fourth metatarsal shaft, causing mild thinning of the adjacent third metatarsal shaft. MRI revealed an expansile lesion of the fourth metatarsal with homogeneous hypointense signal on both T1- and T2-weighted images and low-signal internal areas, without any soft-tissue component.
title: A Foot in the Right Direction: Metatarsal Osteoblastoma-A Rare Case and its Management

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man with known Fine-Lubinsky syndrome presented with two weeks of dyspnea on exertion and bilateral lower extremity swelling. He reported a one-month history of a dry, nonproductive cough. He denied fever, myalgias, chest pain, recent travel, or sick contacts. A prior COVID-19 test was negative. Outpatient chest radiography showed cardiomegaly, prompting referral.

On examination, he was afebrile, breathing nonlaboriously, with blood pressure 106/74 mmHg and heart rate 106 beats/min. Jugular venous distension was noted, and auscultation revealed an S3. His abdomen was distended, and he had trace pitting edema of the lower extremities.

His past medical history was notable for Fine-Lubinsky syndrome, with cranial abnormalities, early auditory problems, intellectual disability, speech impairment, and multiple intracranial fibrous dysplasia resections. Family history included hypertension in both parents and a grandfather with early myocardial infarction and heart failure. He denied smoking, illicit drug use, alcohol use, and had no history of hypertension or diabetes.

Laboratory studies revealed a brain natriuretic peptide of 2878 pg/mL, troponin <0.02 ng/mL, normal thyroid function, ferritin 62 ng/mL, white blood cell count 9.4 × 10^3 cells/cm^3, hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL, and hemoglobin A1c 5.5%. 

Chest radiography showed pulmonary vascular cephalization and cardiomegaly. Chest CT excluded pulmonary embolism but demonstrated a moderate right pleural effusion, interstitial edema, and ascites; there were no coronary calcifications. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia without ST-segment changes.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe left ventricular dilation with an ejection fraction below 20% and global hypokinesis; the right ventricle was normal in size with severely reduced systolic function. No significant valvular abnormalities were noted.

Cardiac MRI with gadolinium showed a severely dilated left ventricle (end-diastolic volume index 166 mL/m^2) with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 11% and right ventricular ejection fraction of 22%. Left ventricular wall thickness was normal. There was no delayed enhancement to suggest scarring or infarction, no myocardial iron overload, and normal coronary arterial anatomy. A small patent foramen ovale was visualized.
title: Heart Failure in a Young Adult with a Fine-Lubinsky Syndrome: An Unknown Comorbidity

case_prompt:
An 83-year-old man presented with eight days of left-sided neck pain, sore throat, dysphagia, odynophagia, dysphonia, and worsening baseline dyspnea. His medical history included poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, a pacemaker for bradycardia, and severe coronary artery disease treated with nine stents. He had a 40–pack-year smoking history but quit 22 years earlier. He recalled a similar presentation in 2008 due to an oropharyngeal abscess requiring surgical drainage.

On examination, he was dyspneic but managing secretions. The oral cavity appeared normal; tonsils were symmetrical without edema, exudate, or erythema. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy revealed a large oropharyngeal mass with normal overlying mucosa, displacing the epiglottis to the right and obstructing 80%–90% of the airway; the epiglottis and tongue base were otherwise normal. Laboratory studies showed a mild leukocytosis of 11×10^9/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated a 3.0×2.2×2.9 cm oropharyngeal collection effacing the left vallecula and exerting mass effect on the aryepiglottic folds.
title:
Isolated oropharyngeal abscess with hypopharyngeal extension
recurring 12 years after initial surgical management: A case report
and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old woman underwent elective radical total gastrectomy and feeding jejunostomy for poorly differentiated T1 gastric carcinoma. Her history included hypertension and anaemia. Jejunostomy feeds commenced on postoperative day 1 without issue. On day 2, a routine contrast CT scan to evaluate the anastomosis showed no leak but revealed bilateral pleural effusions. 

On day 4, she developed multiple episodes of vomiting and had not opened her bowels since surgery. She was tachycardic (heart rate 140 bpm), febrile (39.4 °C), tachypnoeic (respiratory rate 27) with SpO2 96% on 6 L O2, and had mild abdominal tenderness; peripheries were cool. Laboratory studies showed pH 7.45, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, white-cell count 1.9 × 10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 456 mg/L. A septic workup was initiated, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started for a suspected aspiration pneumonia. A repeat CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was obtained.

The CT showed a markedly dilated Roux loop suggesting obstruction, a distended caecum and ascending colon suggestive of a caecal volvulus, and bilateral pleural effusions.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare case of caecal volvulus post gastrectomy for gastric cancer

case_prompt:
A 78-year-old Caucasian man with coronary artery disease (post–multivessel CABG), paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on apixaban, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (∼37%), chronic kidney disease stage III, and remote abdominal aortic aneurysm repair was admitted for gallstone pancreatitis and possible cholangitis.  
On hospital day 2, he had 50 mL of coffee-ground emesis and a transient hypotensive episode (70/50 mm Hg) responsive to 1 L IV fluids; he was treated empirically for aspiration pneumosepsis.  
MRI showed a filling defect in the common bile duct without dilation. ERCP revealed a duodenal diverticulum and erosive duodenitis, and a CBD stent was placed.  
On hospital day 4, repeat ERCP showed no CBD filling defect and persistent duodenitis.  
On hospital day 7, he complained of acute chest pain and had 200 mL of bright red emesis. Apixaban had been restarted the night before; INR was 2.5. He remained hemodynamically stable. Hemoglobin was 9.1 g/dL, hematocrit 27.4%, and WBC rose from 11 000 to 18 000/mm3.  
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated circumferential black discoloration of the esophageal mucosa from proximal to distal, old blood in the gastric cavity, no active bleeding, linear ulcers, and a sharp demarcation at the gastroesophageal junction; there was no history of toxin ingestion.
title: Acute Esophageal Necrosis in a Septic Patient with a History of Cardiovascular Disease

case_prompt: A 16-year-old male with recently diagnosed B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia was undergoing induction chemotherapy (vincristine, pirarubicin, prednisone, and pegaspargase followed by cyclophosphamide, cytarabine, and mercaptopurine). Four days after resuming chemotherapy—during which he had a mild COVID-19 infection managed conservatively—he presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of fever to 39°C, left facial swelling, severe headache, purulent rhinorrhea, and a foreign-body sensation in the left nostril. On examination the following day, there was erythema and edema of the left eyelid with limitation of ocular opening and necrotic crusts visible in both nostrils. Ophthalmology and otorhinolaryngology consultations raised concern for bacterial or fungal infection, and empiric therapy with fluconazole and cefepime was initiated. Despite this treatment, his condition deteriorated rapidly, necessitating transfer to the intensive care unit and initiation of inotropic and vasopressor support.
title: Co‐occurrence of rhino‐orbital mucormycosis and acute lymphoblastic leukemia post‐COVID‐19 infection in a young adolescent male: A case report from a low middle‐income country

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of a growing, firm mass in his left flank. He noted a sharp, constant pain rated 7/10, radiating to the abdomen and left groin. There were no gastrointestinal or genitourinary symptoms, and review of systems was otherwise unremarkable. He had no relevant family or social history. On examination, the abdomen was soft but tender around a firm, deep 5 cm ovoid mass in the left lumbar region. The mass was nonreducible; there was no organomegaly or hernia. Laboratory tests, including white cell count, hematocrit, electrolytes, and liver function, were all normal.  
Abdominal ultrasound showed a 56×28×27 mm homogenously hyperechoic mass within the abdominal wall musculature with mild internal Doppler flow. A provisional diagnosis of a fat-containing lumbar hernia was made, and a portal-venous-phase CT scan was obtained. CT demonstrated an ovoid mass within the external oblique muscle with heterogeneous attenuation, without calcification, inflammation, or invasion. The appearance was deemed inconsistent with a simple lipoma, so an MRI was performed to exclude sarcoma.  
On MRI, the lesion was well circumscribed within the external oblique muscle, hypointense to muscle on T1, hyperintense on T2, with avid enhancement, diffusion restriction, and prominent feeder vessels. Differentials of undifferentiated sarcoma, fibroma, or desmoid tumour were considered.
title: Intramuscular abdominal hibernoma: case report of a rare tumour and a review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man presented in 2011 with a 2-year history of right wrist volar pain, swelling, and erythema. He had no significant medical history. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 18 mg/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 24 mm/h, and a white-cell count of 6460×10^3/mm^3. He was diagnosed with seronegative arthritis and treated with prednisone (4 mg daily) and sulfasalazine (500 mg daily). Pain improved, but swelling and redness persisted.

In 2013, a wrist radiograph demonstrated increased soft-tissue density, soft-tissue swelling, and periarticular osteoporosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the wrist showed millimetric, nodular lesions along the flexor tendon sheath on T2-weighted images and diffuse synovitis.

On March 19, 2013, he underwent right wrist synovectomy and flexor retinaculum release. Intraoperatively, multiple rice bodies were noted around the flexor tendons. Specimens sent for aerobic and anaerobic cultures and liquid media remained sterile. His symptoms regressed after surgery.

Six months postoperatively, he again developed volar wrist pain, swelling, and redness. Laboratory studies and MRI findings were consistent with recurrent synovitis.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Tuberculosis tenosynovitis with multiple rice bodies of the flexor tendons in the wrist: A case report

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman presented with a 10-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling of the vulva. She denied fever, weight loss, appetite changes, discharge, or pigmentation. Twenty years earlier she had had a similar lesion at the same site, which was excised. A biopsy performed elsewhere had diagnosed dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.

On examination, her BMI was 25 kg/m2. Inspection revealed an 8 × 10 cm irregular lesion over the left labia majora and mons pubis, composed of multiple confluent nodules (0.5–2 cm each), crossing the midline to involve the clitoris. On palpation, the lesion was firm to hard, indurated, non-tender, and well demarcated. No inguinal or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was noted.

Ultrasonography showed a lobular solid subcutaneous tumor. Serum markers including CA-125, carcinoembryonic antigen, desmin, and epithelial membrane antigen were negative.

She underwent a wide local excision with clear margins under frozen-section control, followed by a thigh skin graft. Grossly, the resected mass was smooth and white on cross-section. Microscopic examination demonstrated patternless sheets of fibroblastic spindle cells embedded in a hyalinized collagenous stroma.
title: A rare mesenchymal neoplasm at unusual location: Solitary fibrous tumor of vulva

case_prompt: A previously healthy 4-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of loss of appetite, constipation, and marked agitation. He complained of pain on his buttocks, lower back, thorax, and face. Over that week, he developed erythematous skin lesions around the mouth, which progressed to superficial blistering after gentle rubbing of the skin (positive Nikolsky’s sign). On examination, he was afebrile, his mucous membranes were intact, and approximately 10% of his total body surface area showed erythema and superficial exfoliation. Initial laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 7.4 × 10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 3 mg/L, with no signs of systemic infection. Skin cultures and biopsies were obtained.
title: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in a 4-year-old child: a case report

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man was referred to our neurology clinic after 3.5 months of relapsing, diffuse headaches lasting several days, one episode of nausea and vomiting, a 15-minute period of diplopia, and intermittent back and shoulder pain. He denied fever but reported sporadic night sweats. His medical history was unremarkable, and neurologic examination findings were normal. 

Initial MRI showed cerebellar edema and extensive leptomeningeal enhancement. A lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 25 cm H2O, pleiocytosis (325 leukocytes/μl), and elevated protein (990 mg/L). Tests for tuberculosis (IGRA, tuberculin skin test, and CSF PCR) were negative.

He was referred with a differential of malignancy versus central nervous system infection. CT scans of the chest and abdomen, as well as a total-body PET scan, showed no evidence of malignancy. Repeat MRI demonstrated new leptomeningeal lesions with reduced cerebellar edema and focal contrast enhancement at L5–S1. A second lumbar puncture (June 2015) showed 301 cells/μl (predominantly polyclonal T-lymphocytes) and low CSF glucose (2.3 mmol/L). Serologic testing excluded HIV, Treponema pallidum, and Borrelia infection. Because his symptoms were mild and no diagnosis was reached, no empirical treatment was initiated.

At 3- and 9-month follow-up visits, he was clinically well and MRI findings had normalized. In August 2016, he returned with persistent mild headaches, disorientation, dizziness, and palpitations. Physical and neurologic examinations remained unremarkable, but MRI revealed new nodular leptomeningeal enhancement. A PET scan remained negative for focal FDG uptake, and a follow-up MRI in February 2017 showed a slight increase in meningeal contrast enhancement. In March 2017, an extended effort was made to detect malignant cells in the CSF and to further exclude infectious causes.
title: Case report: chronic relapsing cryptococcal meningitis in a patient with low mannose-binding lectin and a low naïve CD4 cell count

case_prompt: An 84-year-old man underwent right-eye phacoemulsification for cataract; the procedure was complicated by a posterior capsule rent, and an anterior-chamber intraocular lens was placed. One week later, he presented with lacrimation, corneal edema with keratic precipitates, anterior-chamber and vitreous haze, and absence of a retinal red reflex on indirect ophthalmoscopy. A vitreous tap was performed, and intravitreal vancomycin (1 mg) and ceftazidime (2 mg) were administered. The following day, lid edema, conjunctival hyperemia, corneal striae, and worsened anterior-chamber inflammation were noted. Vitreous cultures at 48 hours showed no growth. On postoperative day 11, corneal decompensation worsened; intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime were repeated, subconjunctival methylprednisolone was given, and a bandage contact lens was placed. On day 14, with no improvement, intravitreal amphotericin B and oral fluconazole were administered for presumed fungal endophthalmitis. On day 16, three-port pars plana vitrectomy was performed with repeat intravitreal vancomycin and sampling for microbiology; the next day, new grayish flocculent material reappeared in the vitreous and anterior chamber, and amphotericin B plus ceftazidime were again given without clinical improvement. On day 20, a second vitrectomy with intravitreal amikacin was performed. Vitreous cultures again showed no growth; samples were reserved for potassium hydroxide preparation and Gram stain.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Intravitreal linezolid in the management of vancomycin-resistant enterococcal endophthalmitis

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old African American woman with untreated HIV infection (CD4 396 cells/μL) and a history of discoid lupus, hepatitis C, active tobacco, alcohol, and intravenous drug use presented with three months of progressive abdominal pain, distension, and fever. She had not been hospitalized or on antiretroviral therapy, and denied sick contacts. On examination, her temperature was 39.6 °C; she had a distended abdomen with right costo-vertebral angle tenderness and track marks on the right lower extremity. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 9240/μL (71% neutrophils), hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, albumin 1.9 g/dL; chemistry, amylase, and lipase were normal. Urinalysis revealed 5–10 RBCs/hpf without WBCs; pregnancy test was negative. A urine drug screen was positive for cocaine and opiates.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 17.5 cm × 12.8 cm multicystic mass arising from the right kidney, containing multiple septations but no evidence of local invasion.
title: Expanding spectrum of illness due to community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus: a case report

case_prompt: A 52-year-old man presented with six months of progressively cloudy vision and a more rapid decline in visual acuity over the past six weeks. He denied headaches, seizures, or sexual dysfunction. He was a smoker. On ophthalmologic examination, there was bilateral temporal cloudiness and a left inferotemporal visual field defect; visual acuity was rapidly deteriorating. Routine laboratory studies, including a white blood cell count and C-reactive protein level, were within normal limits. Noncontrast CT of the sinuses and contrast-enhanced MRI of the sellar region demonstrated an intra- and suprasellar homogeneous mass with intense gadolinium enhancement and hyperintensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images. The clinical and radiologic impression was of a pituitary macroadenoma, and the patient was referred for surgical management.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Primary pituitary abscess with atypical imaging features: A rare case report

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with a four-week history of progressive speech difficulty—primarily word-finding problems with stuttering—and confusion, including failure to recognize family. Symptoms began with headache, fatigue, and vertigo, then evolved to intermittent confusion, slurred speech, and spasms of the right upper and lower extremities, causing a fall without loss of consciousness. He recently returned from a four-month stay in Mexico working in cattle manure. He had no prior neuropsychiatric history and no family history of dementia or seizures.

Ten days before admission, he had a normal neurologic exam, brain MRI, and carotid Doppler and was diagnosed with transient ischemic attack. On transfer to our emergency department, vital signs were stable; neurologic exam revealed persistent word-finding difficulty only. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Initial CSF showed mildly elevated protein (65 mg/dL) but no clear evidence of infection. He was admitted and treated for complex migraine with ketorolac, sumatriptan, and promethazine. On hospital day 2, EEG demonstrated focal seizures from the left frontal region, and levetiracetam was started. He then developed right upper extremity weakness with diminished reflexes and, on day 3, intermittent myoclonic jerks of the same limb. Metabolic panels, ammonia, liver and renal function, and toxins were normal; medications lowering seizure threshold were discontinued. Despite increasing levetiracetam, he became drowsier with worsening aphasia and cerebellar signs. MRI without contrast on day 3 showed only mild cerebral and cerebellar volume loss. By day 4, EEG still showed left hemispheric seizures; lacosamide was added, and continuous EEG initiated. On day 5, MRI with contrast revealed cytotoxic edema in left frontal and parietal lobes. Given elevated CSF protein and myoclonus, a 3-day course of high-dose steroids was given for possible autoimmune encephalitis. Antiseizure drugs were escalated and valproic acid added. CSF microbiology, oligoclonal bands, and autoimmune panels returned negative; acyclovir was briefly administered and stopped when CSF viral studies were negative. On days 9–11, he remained globally aphasic and flaccid in the right arm; repeat MRI showed persistent cortical ribboning in the left hemisphere, and EEG disclosed diffuse epileptiform discharges with continuous left frontal and bifrontal sharp spikes, concerning for nonconvulsive status epilepticus. Perampanel and phenobarbital were added without improvement.  

At this point, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease was considered among other etiologies, and CTA, paraneoplastic panels, and repeat CSF studies—including 14-3-3 protein—were planned.
title: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease Presenting as Expressive Aphasia and Nonconvulsive Status Epilepticus

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of altered sensorium, bilateral upper-limb weakness, and slurred speech. She denied any seizure activity, tongue biting, or incontinence. Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus (metformin), hypertension (amlodipine and losartan), and primary hypothyroidism (levothyroxine), all of which she had taken for 10 years. She reported stopping her antihypertensive medications 1 week earlier. She did not smoke or drink alcohol, and her family history was noncontributory.

On examination her blood pressure was 210/110 mm Hg, pulse 115 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 95% on room air, and Glasgow Coma Scale score 13/15. Her random blood glucose was 140 mg/dL. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed motor strength of 3/5 in the left upper limb and 5/5 in the right upper limb; 5/5 in the left lower limb and 4/5 in the right lower limb. No visual field deficits were noted. Fundoscopic examination showed grade 1 hypertensive retinopathy.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, triglycerides 430.7 mg/dL, TSH 9.7 IU/mL, and HbA1c 9.31%. Echocardiography revealed grade 1 left ventricular diastolic dysfunction. An immediate noncontrast head CT scan was normal, and a CT pulmonary angiogram showed no pulmonary embolism. Despite the normal initial CT, ischemic stroke and cerebral venous thrombosis remained considerations.

On hospital day 2, a repeat noncontrast CT scan of the head demonstrated bilateral symmetrical white matter hypodensities in the frontal lobes.
title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome due to nonadherence to antihypertensive treatment: A case report from Nepal

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man with a history of gout (on allopurinol 300 mg daily and colchicine 0.6 mg daily), morbid obesity, and osteoarthritis was admitted for unexplained new-onset nonischemic heart failure (ejection fraction 10–15%), cardiogenic shock, and sustained ventricular tachycardia. Dermatology was consulted for a single multinodular, asymptomatic plaque on the upper left arm present for 1 year. Examination revealed lesions covering approximately 25% of the body surface area, with multiple morphologies:
- Numerous 5–12 cm skin-colored to light brown indurated dermal/subcutaneous plaques on the arms, chest, back, and legs, many palpable but not visible.
- A slightly hyperpigmented plaque on the upper left back with multiple 5–10 mm punched-out depressions, giving a moth-eaten appearance.
- Scattered mildly erythematous plaques studded with 2–4 mm firm, rough-surfaced aggregates of whitish gritty material.
- A 2 cm superficial ulceration on the lower left leg extruding a whitish gritty substance.
Additional findings included ventral pterygia of most fingernails and bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement. There were no joint tophi or deformities, and the patient denied gout flares since the skin lesions appeared. Laboratory studies showed a serum uric acid level of 12.6 mg/dL. Hand radiographs demonstrated periarticular erosions consistent with gout arthropathy; foot radiographs were suggestive of gout. Punch biopsies were obtained from representative lesions.
title: An uncommon presentation of cutaneous dissemination of gout

case_prompt: A 48-year-old woman was referred with uncontrolled tachycardia. One year earlier, she had received an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for complete atrioventricular block and ventricular fibrillation arrest. Echocardiography, coronary angiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and blood tests showed no structural abnormalities; positron-emission tomography was unremarkable. An endomyocardial biopsy was not performed. After device implantation, a tachycardia initiated and terminated incessantly with atrioventricular dissociation. The R-R interval was completely irregular (cycle length 384–560 ms, mean 441 ms). The QRS duration during tachycardia was 74 ms, with a normal axis and no bundle-branch-block pattern. Bisoprolol, verapamil, and bepridil failed to suppress the tachycardia. Multipolar electrode catheters were placed in the high right atrium, His-bundle region, and right ventricular apex. At baseline, there was complete A-H block during sinus rhythm and no His potential identified. Ventriculoatrial conduction was absent during ventricular pacing. During tachycardia, the His-bundle catheter recorded His potentials preceding QRS onset by 34 ms. The tachycardia could not be entrained, and ventricular pacing produced a QRS morphology dissimilar to the tachycardia. Radiofrequency catheter ablation was performed under guidance of an electroanatomical mapping system.
title: Nonreentrant proximal fascicular ventricular tachycardia, with normal QRS duration and normal axis, originating from a region remote from the His bundle

case_prompt:
A 12-year-old boy was admitted with a 3-day history of fever (38.0 °C), headache, fatigue, and myalgia. He was alert, anicteric, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 100/min, respiratory rate 22/min. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.5 mmol/L, platelet count 68,000/µL, neutrophils 84%, absolute neutrophil count 6048/µL, and leukocyte count 7200/µL. A diagnosis of dengue hemorrhagic fever grade I was made, and he received supportive therapy.

On hospital day 3, fever persisted. Platelets fell to 20,000/µL, leukocyte count rose to 15,000/µL, hemoglobin fell to 5.4 mmol/L, and jaundice developed (total bilirubin 82 µmol/L). Additional testing included blood smear and Coomb’s tests for Evans syndrome, dengue NS1 and IgM antibodies, hepatitis A and C antibodies, HBsAg, and serum transaminases. All tests except aspartate and alanine aminotransferases (371 U/L and 120 U/L, respectively) were negative.
title: Case report: Weil’s disease with multiple organ failure in a child living in dengue endemic area

case_prompt: A male neonate, 15 minutes old, was delivered by emergency cesarean section at an estimated gestational age of 34 weeks for abruptio placentae, severe oligohydramnios, and breech presentation. His birth weight was 2.01 kg, and APGAR scores were 5 and 6 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively; he required 5 minutes of resuscitation. On admission to the NICU he was in respiratory distress with a pulse rate of 160 beats/min, respiratory rate of 70 breaths/min, temperature of 33.4 °C, and oxygen saturation of 60% on room air. On examination, the anterior fontanelle measured 2 × 2 cm. There was micrognathia and a short neck. Respiratory examination revealed intercostal and subcostal retractions with grunting. Cardiac examination showed normal S1 and S2 without murmurs. Musculoskeletal examination revealed bilateral markedly shortened upper limbs with hands appearing directly attached near the trunk; the right lower limb was normal in position and structure, while the left leg was internally rotated at the knee with a normal foot. Neurologically he was lethargic; muscle tone was normal in the right lower extremity and the Moro reflex was difficult to elicit. Laboratory studies showed blood group A+, C-reactive protein reactive, WBC 30,000/mm3, neutrophils 54%, lymphocytes 21.1%, hemoglobin 8 g/dL, and platelets 150,000/mm3. Radiographs demonstrated extreme shortening of the upper extremities and internal rotation of the left lower limb. Echocardiography was normal.
title: Bilateral Upper Limb Complete Phocomelia: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old previously healthy Hispanic man was referred for evaluation of progressive lower extremity weakness and sensory changes. Four months earlier, he noted paresthesia in his toes that progressed over three weeks to symmetrical ascending lower extremity weakness and unsteady gait. He also reported impotence, polyuria, polydipsia, hyperpigmentation, and hypertrichosis. 

Initial evaluation revealed albuminocytologic dissociation on cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and he was treated with a five‐day course of intravenous immunoglobulin for presumed Guillain‐Barré syndrome with minimal improvement. He was discharged to rehabilitation but relapsed four weeks later with new paresthesia in his hands. Nerve‐conduction studies showed a demyelinating pattern, and repeat lumbar puncture demonstrated oligoclonal bands. Antibodies against Hu and myelin basic protein were negative. He was treated for presumed chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy with plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulin, and a short course of intravenous steroids, again with only partial improvement.

On referral, he had profound proximal lower extremity weakness (left greater than right), dysesthesias, paresthesias, and hyporeflexia in the lower limbs; sphincter tone was preserved, and there were no cranial nerve deficits or fasciculations. He complained of persistent abdominal and left inguinal pain with exquisite point tenderness over the left hip. Repeat serum protein electrophoresis revealed a monoclonal spike, and he was admitted for further evaluation.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: An Occult Malignancy Behind a Demyelinating Disease

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old Chinese woman was referred after multiple pulmonary nodules were incidentally found on a health checkup. She was asymptomatic. Her medical history was notable for a total hysterectomy for uterine leiomyoma 14 years earlier. She was a lifelong non-smoker, with no family history of malignancy, no occupational exposures, and no recent weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including lung cancer tumor markers, were within normal limits.

High-resolution chest CT showed multiple well-circumscribed nodules in both lungs, the largest measuring 7 mm in the right lower lobe. To clarify the etiology, she underwent CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of the largest nodule, complicated by a small pneumothorax that resolved after aspiration. Cytologic smear revealed neither malignant cells nor organisms suggestive of tuberculosis.

Histologic evaluation of the biopsy showed a few spindle cells. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated Desmin(+) and SMA(+), consistent with smooth-muscle origin, and also showed Bcl-2(+), CD99(+), CD34(+), Vim(+), S-100(–), STAT-6(–), and CR(–).

Subsequent ^18F-FDG PET-CT revealed multiple pulmonary nodules with no FDG uptake and no abnormal uptake elsewhere.
title: Pulmonary benign metastasizing leiomyoma: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 48-year-old farmer with a history of hypertension presented with diaphoresis, epigastric pain, and lower-extremity edema for 2 months. He was afebrile and normotensive. Examination revealed xanthelasmas of the eyelids, muffled heart sounds, and mild peripheral edema. Chest radiography showed cardiomegaly. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia with low voltages. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved biventricular systolic function, no valvular disease, and massive pericardial effusion with hemodynamic compromise. Pericardiocentesis yielded a mononuclear exudate without malignant cells. A Quantiferon-TB Gold test was positive. Laboratory studies showed normal renal and lipid profiles and elevated acute-phase reactants. He was treated empirically for acute pericarditis with ibuprofen and colchicine. A follow-up echocardiogram showed recurrent large pericardial effusion without tamponade and possible ascending aortic dilation. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed soft-tissue encasement of the aorta from the arch through the iliac arteries (“coated aorta”) and a retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass causing right hydronephrosis and renal atrophy.
title: Curative Pericardiectomy in Interpheron-Resistant Severe Pericardial Erdheim-Chester Disease

case_prompt: A 68-year-old man with essential thrombocythemia (JAK2 V617F mutation), maintained on anagrelide with stable platelet counts >200×10^9/L, tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 on March 21. Initial symptoms (headache, dry cough, mild fever) appeared three days later and gradually worsened. On March 29, he presented to the emergency department with temperature 38.5 °C and SpO2 89% on room air; examination revealed no bleeding. Chest X-ray showed bilateral infiltrates. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 117 g/L, WBC 5.22×10^9/L, platelet count 14×10^9/L, immature platelet fraction 21.5%, C-reactive protein 141 mg/L, and d-dimer 1700 µg/L; other coagulation and biochemistry values were within normal limits. He was admitted for remdesivir and evaluation of grade IV thrombocytopenia. His only other medical history was hypothyroidism. A peripheral smear showed no schistocytes, dacrocytes, or blasts. To exclude transformation to myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia, or lymphoproliferative disorder, a bone marrow aspiration was performed, with samples sent for flow cytometry, cytological evaluation, cytogenetics, and FISH.
title: Immune thrombocytopenia in a patient with essential thrombocythemia after SARS-CoV-2 infection: A case report

case_prompt: A 69-year-old man with hypertension (on lisinopril and metoprolol), hyperlipidemia (on simvastatin), and treated prostate cancer presented with continuous right lower abdominal pain and signs of peritonitis. He had quit smoking six months earlier and had no allergies. On admission, the white-cell count was 16.2×10^9/L and C-reactive protein was 231 mg/L. Abdominal ultrasound and contrast CT scan showed a perforated appendix with two appendicoliths and two small abscesses; the abscesses were deemed too small for percutaneous drainage. Intravenous amoxicillin/clavulanic acid was started, and laparoscopic appendectomy confirmed purulent peritonitis. A free appendicolith was removed, the appendix was stapled off at the cecal base, and local irrigation performed. Postoperatively, leukocyte count and CRP declined slowly. On postoperative day 8, the CRP increased again and hemoglobin fell from 14.5 g/dL to 11.3 g/dL. CT angiography revealed a new right lower abdominal abscess and multiple aneurysmal dilatations arising from the medial colic artery, pancreaticoduodenal artery, several intrahepatic branches, and the splenic artery, all surrounded by a large infiltrating mass.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Case report of multiple mesenteric mycotic aneurysms after perforated appendicitis

case_prompt: A 43-year-old woman with an unremarkable medical history presented with a slowly enlarging, painless swelling of the left maxilla, first noted 3 years earlier. On extraoral examination there was mild asymmetry of the left paranasal area. Intraorally, a well-defined, firm, mucosa-covered nodule measuring approximately 32 × 30 mm involved the left anterior maxilla in the region of teeth 21, 22, and 25; teeth 23 and 24 were congenitally absent. CBCT of the maxilla revealed a well-defined, mixed hyperdense and hypodense lesion causing buccal cortical expansion, resorption of the roots of teeth 21 and 22, and extension into the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. Based on the clinical and radiographic appearance, the initial differential diagnosis included ossifying fibroma, calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor, calcifying cystic odontogenic tumor, complex odontoma, dentinogenic ghost cell tumor, and adenomatoid odontogenic tumor.
journal: Journal of Clinical and Experimental Dentistry
title: Ossifying odontogenic fibroma: A rare case report

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman with a history of systemic hypertension treated with atenolol presented with a 4–5 day history of progressively worsening headache, neck pain, severe anxiety, chest discomfort, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, tachypnea, dry cough, and lightheadedness. She denied fever or urinary symptoms. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated leukocytosis (22,500 leukocytes/mm3) with neutrophilia. She was started on ceftriaxone for suspected meningitis.

On arrival, she was alert and oriented, with preserved motor function. Extremities were cold and poorly perfused. Vital signs were: BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 140 bpm, RR 42 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 85% on room air (96% with 5 L/min supplemental O2). Cardiac examination was normal. Pulmonary auscultation revealed diffuse inspiratory rales bilaterally. The abdomen was distended. There was no neck stiffness or focal neurologic deficit. Pupils were equal and reactive; plantar responses were flexor; deep tendon reflexes were normal.

Noncontrast cranial CT was unremarkable, and a lumbar puncture was performed. Working diagnoses included meningitis, endocarditis, and severe sepsis secondary to pneumonia. Blood and urine cultures were obtained. Chest radiography showed bilateral infiltrates consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome. She received intravenous fluids, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin–clavulanate.

Shortly thereafter, she developed severe hypoxemia and hypotension (BP 90/60 mmHg), requiring escalating norepinephrine. She became agitated, confused, then suffered respiratory arrest followed by pulseless electrical activity; return of spontaneous circulation occurred after 15 minutes of resuscitation. She was intubated and sedated. Later, her blood pressure became undetectable despite maximum vasopressor support, and she experienced a second cardiopulmonary arrest from which she did not recover. She died approximately six hours after presentation.

Postmortem laboratory results showed persistent leukocytosis (26,680 leukocytes/mm3; neutrophils 82%), troponin I 0.9 ng/mL, and D-dimer 6,907.9 ng/mL. Blood and urine cultures and cerebrospinal fluid studies were negative.
title: Pheochromocytoma-induced shock: a case report

case_prompt: A 40-year-old woman from the Dominican Republic, living in the United States for 20 years, presented with a 6-week history of low-grade fevers (maximum, 100.2°F), night sweats, malaise, and fatigue. She denied rash, cough, dyspnea, arthralgias, weight or appetite changes, recent travel, sick contacts, or occupational exposures. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal examination revealed a palpable, non-tender spleen without other organomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, and extremity examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 15 000/μL with an absolute eosinophil count of 800/μL (normal <500/μL); other hematologic, renal, hepatic, and calcium values were normal. A chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography was nondiagnostic. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed splenomegaly measuring 16 × 7 × 6 cm with multiple hypodense lesions; the liver was normal and no lymphadenopathy was seen. A peripheral-blood smear and bone marrow biopsy were normal. PET scan demonstrated multiple hypermetabolic splenic lesions (maximum SUV, 13.0) without pathologic uptake elsewhere.
title: Sarcoidosis and Its Splenic Wonder: A Rare Case of Isolated Splenic Sarcoidosis

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old woman was transferred at 23:00 for acute-onset, severe, retrosternal squeezing chest pain and dyspnea. She had a history of bilateral peroneal neuropathy of unknown origin and a cerebral hemorrhage 6 years earlier (decompressive craniotomy). She had well-controlled hypertension on long-term diltiazem and no diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking, or family history of coronary artery disease.

An ECG from the referring hospital showed ST-segment elevation in the inferior, anterolateral, and posterior leads, and dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus ticagrelor) was started. On admission, vital signs were stable and the cardiovascular exam was unremarkable. A repeat ECG showed persistent ST-segment elevation in the same leads. Laboratory tests revealed troponin T 50 ng/l and myoglobin 89 ng/l. Complete blood count, liver and renal function, lipid profile, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal or negative. Echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 64% with segmental wall-motion abnormalities in the inferior and posterior walls.

The patient was diagnosed with acute inferior myocardial infarction. Emergency coronary angiography revealed nonobstructive coronary arteries; intracoronary nitrates relieved her chest pain. Continuous nicorandil infusion and antiplatelet therapy were continued and troponin I levels decreased.

Three days later, she developed recurrent chest pain progressing to cardiogenic shock with troponin T >2000 ng/l. She required intubation, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor support. PET-CT demonstrated diffuse elevated myocardial metabolism in the interventricular septum, lateral wall, and inferoapical regions, with patchy mild uptake in the right ventricular epicardium and increased metabolism in segments of the right coronary and left circumflex arteries. Myocardial perfusion scintigraphy showed a perfusion-metabolism mismatch in the apical and mid-inferior walls.

Since admission, she had worsening right lower limb pain. Electromyography confirmed bilateral peroneal nerve damage. Serologic testing revealed negative antinuclear antibodies and positive anti–proteinase-3 ANCA.
title: Recurrent Coronary Vasospasm in a 50-Year-Old Woman with Granulomatous Polyangiitis: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man with a 25-year history of left-sided ulcerative colitis presented with four days of fever, nausea, diarrhea, and hematochezia. Over the past year he had multiple steroid-dependent flares despite attempts to taper off prednisone, and azathioprine was added eight months ago. His home medications included prednisone and pantoprazole. 

On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 62 bpm, blood pressure 143/84 mmHg. His abdomen was soft and non-tender, without rebound or guarding, and there were no skin rashes. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, white cells 10.1×10^9/L, and a negative HIV antibody test. 

Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed sigmoid wall thickening, luminal narrowing, surrounding inflammatory stranding, and a 3-cm fluid collection consistent with an abscess. Blood cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae, and he received a 14-day course of antibiotics. 

After resolution of the diverticulitis, a colonoscopy was performed, which revealed a discrete tumor in the rectum.
title: Human herpesvirus-8 positive iatrogenic Kaposi's sarcoma in the setting of refractory ulcerative colitis

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man from a low socioeconomic background presented with left flank pain and unintentional weight loss. He had no flank tenderness on examination but had several enlarged cervical and inguinal lymph nodes.  
Laboratory studies showed albuminuria (2+), numerous leukocytes on urine dipstick, and 227 RBCs/hpf, 314 WBCs/hpf, and 239 bacteria/hpf on urine microscopy; bacterial cultures exhibited no growth, indicating sterile pyuria. A diagnosis of renal tuberculosis was considered with a differential diagnosis of chronic pyelonephritis.  
Plain CT of the abdomen revealed disproportionately dilated upper pole calyces, urothelial thickening with narrowing of the renal pelvis, papillary calcifications in the lower pole, and marked perinephric and periureteric fat stranding with locoregional lymphadenopathy.  
CT urogram demonstrated multiple filling defects within the calyceal system, papillary cavities in the upper and lower poles, calyceal distortion, infundibular-pelvic stenosis, and thickened, enhancing ureteric walls.
title: A case report of renal papillary necrosis due to tuberculosis—CT urogram and static MR urogram findings

case_prompt: An 84-year-old Chinese man with hypertension, prior stroke, and atrial fibrillation on dabigatran presented with acute urinary retention. After Foley-catheter placement, he had light hematuria. His serum creatinine was 130–150 μmol/L. Renal ultrasonography showed a 5.7 cm left renal mass with cystic spaces. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 5.2 × 5 × 6 cm enhancing mass at the upper to mid pole of the left kidney with internal cystic components, tiny calcifications, and hyperdense soft-tissue areas. These features were considered suggestive of cystic renal cell carcinoma. A 2.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue nodule was also identified in the left adrenal gland, with differential diagnoses of adenoma versus metastatic disease. The patient underwent laparoscopic left radical nephrectomy and adrenalectomy without intraoperative complications.
title: Case Report on Anastomosing Haemangioma: An Unusual Vascular Tumor in Kidney

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old primigravid woman at 9 weeks of amenorrhea presented with 1 day of mild lower abdominal pain. She denied vaginal bleeding, fever, or vomiting. Her menstrual cycles had been regular, and she conceived spontaneously. A urine pregnancy test was positive. Transabdominal ultrasonography at an outside facility was interpreted as suggestive of a tubal ectopic pregnancy, and she was referred for further management.  
On examination, she was afebrile, with mild pallor, pulse 82/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. Abdominal examination showed diffuse mild tenderness in the lower abdomen without rebound or guarding. On pelvic examination, the uterus was normal in size, cervical motion was mildly tender, and a 4 cm mass was palpable in the right fornix.
