Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 11.5 gm/dL, white cell count 10,100/µL, platelet count 191,000/µL, blood group O positive, random blood sugar 99 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 0.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis was unremarkable.  
Transabdominal ultrasound at our institution showed a uterus measuring 72 × 32 × 31 mm with a small endometrial collection and moderate free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. A right tubo-ovarian mass was noted. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a hyperechoic lesion in the right adnexal region, measuring 39 × 35 mm, suggestive of an ectopic tubal gestation.
journal: International Journal of Applied and Basic Medical Research
title: Ruptured ovarian pregnancy in a primigravida

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of a swelling in his left upper lip that had grown rapidly over the past month. He denied trauma, pain, bleeding, ulceration, or color change. On examination, the lesion was a 6.0 cm × 2.5 cm soft, pulsatile, immobile mass with well-defined borders; it was nonreducible and noncompressible, and there were no signs of inflammation (no erythema, heat, or discharge). Initial considerations included abscess and vascular tumors.  
 
Magnetic resonance imaging (axial T2-weighted) showed diffuse linear-tubular signal‐void areas in the soft tissue of the upper lip. MR angiography (coronal maximum-intensity-projection) demonstrated a vascularized mass in the upper lip with arterial supply from distal branches of the external carotid artery. MR venography (axial maximum-intensity-projection) revealed the mass draining into the venous system.
title: Arteriovenous malformation presenting as a lip swelling

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man presented after a fall with left-sided chest and upper abdominal pain. His history included hypertension and atrial fibrillation treated with ramipril, amlodipine, and apixaban. A chest radiograph showed a fracture of the seventh rib. Because of anticoagulation, a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed and revealed incidental bilateral adrenal masses measuring 6 cm on the left and 5 cm on the right with attenuation of 50 Hounsfield units on portal venous images, and mild splenomegaly (14.5 cm).  
In the endocrine clinic he reported 6 years of tiredness, palpitations, and weight gain. His blood pressure was 116/90 mm Hg, heart rate 97 beats/min, and BMI 32 kg/m2. Examination was normal with no lymphadenopathy or Cushingoid features.  
Baseline adrenal studies were normal, including plasma metanephrines (normetanephrine 830 pmol/L; metanephrine <100 pmol/L), aldosterone 270 pmol/L, random cortisol 230 nmol/L, and ACTH 29.4 ng/L. An overnight dexamethasone suppression test with 1 mg at 11 pm yielded an 8 am cortisol <28 nmol/L, excluding autonomous cortisol secretion.  
Eight days later, a dedicated adrenal CT showed reduction in adrenal masses to 4.5 cm on the left and 3.5 cm on the right, and spleen to 12.5 cm. Noncontrast, portal venous, and delayed-phase Hounsfield units were 35, 54, and 45, respectively, with an absolute washout of 47% and a relative washout of 17%, described as indeterminate adrenal lesions.
title: The Vanishing Adrenal Glands: A Transient Regression of Adrenal Lymphoma After a Single Dose of 1 mg Dexamethasone

case_prompt: A 65-year-old man presented with a two-year history of an asymptomatic swelling on the lateral aspect of his left ankle. There was no history of trauma, and the size had remained stable. On examination, a 5 × 9 cm well-defined, firm-to-hard, nonmobile, nontender mass was noted over the lateral malleolus with mild discoloration of the overlying skin but no warmth or induration. Anteroposterior radiographs of the left ankle demonstrated a sessile, well-circumscribed radiopaque lesion overlying the lateral malleolus, with a homogeneously calcified matrix, no areas of lysis, no periosteal reaction, and no pressure erosions of the underlying fibula; the ankle joint itself appeared normal. Laboratory studies showed a serum calcium level of 10 mg/dL, phosphate 4 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase 127 U/L, all within normal limits. Initial differential diagnoses included synovial chondromatosis, tophaceous gout, calcified lipoma, myositis ossificans, and malignant tumors such as synovial sarcoma, osteosarcoma, and chondrosarcoma.
title: An Unusual Case of Huge Tophaceous Pseudogout Mimicking as a Tumor-Like Lesion around the Ankle Joint: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, mild right upper–quadrant abdominal pain, and jaundice. One week earlier, she had experienced coryza and malaise lasting 4 days that resolved without treatment. She denied drug or alcohol use and had no recent travel. 

On examination, her temperature was 38.5 °C and heart rate was 110 beats/min. She had scleral and cutaneous icterus and mild right upper–quadrant tenderness without Murphy’s sign. Liver span on the midclavicular line was 110 mm, and the spleen measured 170 mm. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudate, mucosal rash, or skin rash.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a liver of normal size with increased echogenicity (grade 2 fatty change), splenomegaly (175 mm), normal portal-vein diameter and flow, a normal suprahepatic inferior vena cava, a normal gallbladder and biliary tree without evidence of cholestasis, and mild ascites.

Laboratory results were notable for WBC 16,300/μL (57% lymphocytes, 20% variant), hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, platelets 74,000/μL, AST 239 IU/L, ALT 219 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 1294 IU/L, total bilirubin 15.9 mg/dL (direct 8.9 mg/dL), albumin 2.4 g/dL, ESR 21 mm/h, CRP 39 mg/L, and negative blood cultures (two sets). Amylase, creatinine, coagulation studies, and other chemistry values were within normal limits.

Serologic and molecular tests for hepatotropic viruses and related infections showed:  
- HBsAg negative, anti-HBs 1 mIU/mL, anti-HBc total and anti-HBc IgM nonreactive, HBV PCR negative  
- Anti-HCV reactive, HCV RNA negative  
- Anti–HAV total within normal range  
- Anti–HEV nonreactive  
- Anti–HIV (1,2) nonreactive  
- CMV PCR negative
journal: Gastroenterology and Hepatology From Bed to Bench
title: Acute Epstein - Barr virus hepatitis without mononucleosis syndrome: a case report

case_prompt:
A 34‐year‐old man with no past medical history presented with a 1‐day history of sudden‐onset numbness and heaviness of the tongue, drooling of saliva, loss of taste, slurring of speech, and the inability to close both eyes completely. He denied earache, hearing changes, tinnitus, head or neck trauma, fever, flu‐like symptoms, gastrointestinal complaints, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered consciousness, or limb weakness or numbness. He had no recent travel, sick contacts, insect bites, or use of herbal supplements; he did not smoke or use alcohol or illicit drugs.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologically, visual fields and acuity were intact; pupils were equal and reactive; extraocular movements were full without diplopia. Bilateral lagophthalmos with Bell’s phenomenon was noted. He was unable to clench his teeth, blow, whistle, frown his forehead, or show his teeth; nasolabial folds were absent bilaterally. Facial sensation and jaw strength were normal. Hearing, palate movement, head rotation, and shoulder shrug were intact. Deep tendon reflexes were diminished (1/4) in all limbs with absent ankle jerks. Motor strength, tone, bulk, and sensation in the extremities were normal. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.

Routine blood counts and metabolic panel were unremarkable. Serum ANA, anti-dsDNA, and ANCA were within normal limits. PCR assays for herpes and CMV, EBV viral capsid antigen, Quantiferon TB, and serologies for HIV and Lyme disease were all negative. CSF analysis showed albuminocytological dissociation without pleocytosis or organisms. Non-contrast CT of the head was normal. MRI brain with contrast and intracranial MRA revealed no abnormalities. Chest radiograph, CT chest, and PET–CT scan were negative for lymphoma, malignancy, sarcoidosis, or paraneoplastic processes. EMG and nerve conduction studies demonstrated a demyelinating pattern of facial neuropathy, and the blink reflex study was abnormal bilaterally.
title: Isolated facial diplegia: A rare presentation of Guillain‐Barre syndrome

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman was admitted with persistent fever and pancytopenia following debridement of a right buttock abscess. Three years earlier, she had developed thrombocytopenia and anemia after treatment for H. pylori–associated gastric ulcers; a bone marrow examination then showed hypercellular marrow with a myeloid left shift, and CT revealed splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy. She was treated for presumed Evans syndrome with prednisone and azathioprine, with only partial improvement in cytopenias. 

On current presentation, her temperature was 37.7°C, blood pressure 126/68 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28/min, pulse 122/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Findings included pallor, mild jaundice, a 2/6 systolic murmur, splenomegaly, a 3×3 cm right buttock eschar, ecchymoses on the arms and flank, and 3+ lower-extremity edema. She was disoriented to time and place.

Laboratory studies showed: WBC 2.7×10^9/L, hemoglobin 73 g/L, platelets 15×10^9/L; sodium 126 mmol/L; bicarbonate 21 mmol/L; total bilirubin 46 μmol/L; AST 78 U/L; ALT 53 U/L; albumin 29 g/L; LDH 1068 U/L; triglycerides 4.2 mmol/L; ferritin 20 392 μg/L; fibrinogen <0.6 g/L; PT 22.5 s; INR 1.93; D-dimer 3.43 mg/L. Direct antiglobulin test was negative; peripheral smear showed no schistocytes. ANA was negative.

Chest CT showed bibasilar patchy consolidation, small pleural effusions, and calcified mediastinal nodes. Abdominal CT demonstrated splenomegaly with multiple low-density lesions, similar liver lesions, bilateral renal infarcts, and a left psoas hemorrhage.
title: Prolonged hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis syndrome as an initial presentation of Hodgkin lymphoma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old man with well-controlled HIV (undetectable viral load; CD4 count >200 cells/mm^3 on antiretroviral therapy) presented after an unprovoked syncopal episode. He reported a 10 lb weight loss over several months, decreased appetite, and a general sense of malaise. Family history was notable for cardiovascular-related deaths but no liver disease.  
On examination he was afebrile, blood pressure was normal, and he had mild hepatomegaly on abdominal palpation. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (11.44 × 10^3/µL) with neutrophilia, macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume 101.8 fL), elevated ferritin (1,403 µg/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (227 IU/L) and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (129 IU/L) with normal transaminases. Tumor markers and viral and autoimmune hepatitis serologies were unremarkable, apart from an elevated α1-antitrypsin level.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an 11.2 cm heterogeneous mass in the right hepatic lobe with areas of solid enhancement and central necrosis, and thrombosis of the right posterior portal vein concerning for tumor in vein. The initial differential included hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, liver abscess, metastatic disease, lymphoma, and hemangioma.  
He was started empirically on a 2-week course of metronidazole for presumed liver abscess and referred for hepatology evaluation.
title: An Evasive Liver Mass in a Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)-Positive Patient

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 6 months presented with a 2-year history of progressive, painless stiffness of both hands, characterized by tightening of the skin and limited movement of the wrists and interphalangeal joints. Her diabetes had been poorly controlled, with hemoglobin A1c levels between 10% and 12% despite multiple daily insulin injections; she had frequent hospitalizations for diabetic ketoacidosis but no clinical evidence of nephropathy or retinopathy. She denied symptoms suggestive of other endocrine disorders, celiac disease, or polyarthralgia.

On examination, she was a short-statured pubertal female with stable vital signs. Inspection of her hands revealed flexion contractures with thick, tight, waxy skin over the dorsal aspects of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. She had non-tender swelling but no erythema, warmth, or joint dislocations. The “prayer sign” was positive, and she was unable to lay her palms flat on a table (“table-top sign”). There were no signs of peripheral neuropathy or vascular disease in the feet. The remainder of her examination, including neurologic, ophthalmologic, and endocrine assessments, was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin A1c of 12.3%, normal thyroid-function tests, a urine albumin/creatinine ratio of 20 mg/g, a normal complete blood count, and normal inflammatory markers.
title: LIMITED JOINT MOBILITY IN A CHILD WITH TYPE 1 DIABETES MELLITUS.

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old woman presented with progressive numbness and tingling in both feet, sensory loss to mid-calf, and worsening balance. She also noted new red papules on her shoulders, lower abdomen, and back, and had unintentionally lost 15 lb over 6 months. She had been diagnosed with vitamin B₁₂ deficiency and received weekly B₁₂ injections without neurologic improvement.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Skin showed scattered red papules on the shoulders, abdomen, and back. Neurologic examination revealed decreased sensation to light touch and vibration in both lower extremities to the mid-calves, with mild ataxia.

Laboratory studies:
• Serum M protein: 0.1 g/dL with immunoglobulin G monoclonal protein and lambda light‐chain specificity on immunofixation  
• Serum lambda light chain: 85 mg/L  
• 24-hour urine total protein: 135.7 mg (normal)  
• Urine protein electrophoresis: normal  
• Bone marrow biopsy: hypercellular marrow (50% cellularity) with 10% plasma cells  
• HIV and HHV-8 serologies: negative  

Imaging:
• Skeletal survey: expansile lytic lesion at L3  
• PET–CT: L3 lesion (SUV 14.8) and enlarged left periaortic lymph node (SUV 9.4)  
• MRI spine: large lobulated lytic expansile mass at L3  
• Abdominal ultrasound: no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or free fluid  

Neurophysiology and CSF:
• EMG: demyelinating sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy  
• CSF: glucose 58 mg/dL, protein 81 mg/dL, RBCs 131/μL, nucleated cells 12/μL (18% neutrophils, 74% lymphocytes, 8% macrophages)  

Additional biopsies:
• Fat‐pad biopsy (two occasions): negative for Congo red staining and amyloid  
• Excisional biopsy of a shoulder papule: cherry angioma
title: Atypical B12 Deficiency with Nonresolving Paraesthesia

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man presented with sudden-onset dyspnea associated with a choking sensation that awakened him at midnight, accompanied by a nonproductive “brassy” cough. The dyspnea worsened in the supine position and progressed to inspiratory stridor. He reported six to eight similar episodes over the previous 24 months, with complete resolution between episodes. During each episode he was treated with antibiotics, oxygen, bronchodilators, nebulizers, and oral steroids without improvement. He was a lifelong nonsmoker with no alcohol use and no relevant medical or family history.

On examination, he was tachypneic with stridorous respirations that resolved when sitting and recurred when supine. There were no wheezes or rhonchi, and the remainder of the respiratory and cardiovascular examinations was unremarkable. There was no clubbing, cyanosis, or thyroid enlargement. Vital signs were stable except for tachypnea.

Spirometry showed flattening of the inspiratory limb of the flow–volume loop. Empey’s index was 11.69 (FEV1/PEF ≥8 suggests upper airway obstruction), and the ratio of flow at 50% of expiration to flow at 50% of inspiration (FEF50/FIF50) was 1.27, consistent with variable extrathoracic upper airway obstruction.
journal: Lung India : Official Organ of Indian Chest Society
title: Elongated uvula and diagnostic utility of spirometry in upper airway obstruction

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of a persistent dry cough of one year’s duration. He first noted upper airway irritation and cough after drinking homemade wine; the cough persisted throughout the day without sputum production, dyspnea, chest pain, fevers, or weight loss. His medical history included hyperlipidemia and prostatitis; he was a former smoker (5 pack-years, quit 30 years ago). Physical examination was unremarkable.

Two-view chest radiography was normal. Pulmonary function tests showed a forced vital capacity of 3.65 L (76% predicted), FEV1 of 3.16 L (86% predicted), FEV1/FVC of 0.86, total lung capacity 5.81 L (87% predicted), residual volume 2.16 L (92% predicted), and diffusion capacity 89% predicted. Methacholine challenge was negative. Chest CT showed only small nonspecific mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes and minimal lingular atelectasis.

In November and December 2015, two sputum cultures grew Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Specific antibody testing demonstrated elevated S. cerevisiae IgA of 22.2 U (normal <20 U) and IgG of 48.8 U (normal <20 U, positive >35 U). Tests for other fungal antibodies were negative. He received a 30-day prednisone taper (starting 60 mg daily) and a bronchodilator with near resolution of cough that recurred after stopping steroids. Antihistamines and a proton-pump inhibitor yielded no improvement. Repeat chest CT in May 2016 was unchanged.

Bronchoscopy with BAL in May 2016 showed a tiny polypoid lesion; cultures and cytology of BAL were negative, and no cell count was obtained. In June 2016, S. cerevisiae IgA and IgG remained elevated; total IgE was normal at 5.9 kU/L, and peripheral eosinophils were 0.9%. In September 2016, repeat bronchoscopy revealed diffuse airway erythema and the same polypoid lesion. Biopsies showed acute and chronic inflammation without eosinophils; PAS stain was negative. BAL cell differential showed 32% lymphocytes and 68% macrophages; cultures and stains for bacteria, mycobacteria, Pneumocystis jirovecii, and fungus were negative.
title: A Case of Chronic Cough in a Winemaker

case_prompt: An 8‐year‐old neutered male Boxer was referred for evaluation of a firm, ovoid mass (3–5 cm in diameter) on the ventral aspect of the neck present for 6 weeks. The primary veterinarian had drained serosanguinous fluid by needle aspiration on two occasions, but the swelling recurred within weeks. The dog had intermittent regurgitation when excited. On examination, the mass was mobile, well circumscribed, nonpainful, and located adjacent to the trachea; there was no lymphadenopathy. Cardiorespiratory and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Complete blood count and serum biochemistry, including liver enzymes, were within reference intervals except for mild hypercholesterolemia. Serum total T4 and TSH were not measured. Ultrasound showed an ovoid, thin‐walled cystic lesion in the region of the right thyroid lobe. Ultrasound‐guided aspiration yielded proteinaceous fluid with mild cell necrosis but no diagnostic cells. Measurement of thyroxine concentration in the cyst fluid was markedly elevated compared to serum reference intervals, confirming thyroidal origin. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 3.7 × 2.7 cm fluid‐attenuating structure with a thin, uniformly enhancing rim displacing but not invading the trachea or adjacent tissues; there was no lymphadenopathy or pulmonary lesions.
title: Non-functional thyroid cystadenoma in three boxer dogs

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis B was admitted with 1 week of fever (39.4 °C), headache, vomiting, and cough. Chest CT was normal. Brain MRI showed bilateral cortical and subcortical T2 FLAIR hyperintensities without abnormal enhancement or hydrocephalus. CSF analysis revealed glucose 2.52 mmol/L, protein 1.76 g/L, and white blood cells 300 × 10^6/L (80% mononuclear cells); acid-fast stain, India Ink preparation, and bacterial culture were negative. She had one seizure and received ganciclovir for 3 days. A diagnosis of possible tuberculous meningitis was made, and oral rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol were started; isoniazid and dexamethasone were administered intrathecally for 1 month. Six serial CSF samples showed persistent pleocytosis (80–394 × 10^6/L, 80–90% mononuclear cells). Ethambutol was withdrawn for blurred vision and replaced with levofloxacin. Fever and headaches improved but she developed bilateral hand tremor.

Three months later she developed back pain, leg weakness, memory loss, irritability, and confusion, progressing to inability to walk independently. Cervical MRI demonstrated patchy T2 hyperintensities from C2 to C7. Brain MRI showed linear and radial gadolinium enhancement perpendicular to the lateral ventricles. CSF analysis showed glucose 2.32 mmol/L, protein 1.09 g/L, and white blood cells 52 × 10^6/L (90% mononuclear cells). CSF Xpert MTB/RIF and culture were both negative. Anti-tuberculosis therapy was adjusted to moxifloxacin, amikacin, isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide. Intravenous immunoglobulin (25 g/day for 5 days) led to symptom improvement. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days, then 500 mg/day for 3 days) produced no further benefit.
title: Autoimmune glial fibrillary acidic protein astrocytopathy manifesting as subacute meningoencephalitis with descending myelitis: a case report

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 7-year-old boy was admitted for sudden-onset bilateral blindness. One day earlier, he had developed fever (39 °C), cough, and loss of appetite and was treated with azithromycin and antipyretics without improvement. On the day of admission he acutely became blind in both eyes and developed delirium. 

On examination he was agitated with features of encephalopathy; responsiveness was mildly impaired. He was febrile (38 °C). There were no focal neurologic deficits and no signs of meningeal irritation. Fundus examination was normal. Deep tendon reflexes were mildly increased.

Laboratory studies showed a CPK of 569 U/L, AST of 47 U/L, and sodium of 134 mEq/L; all other chemistries and urine analysis were normal. EEG demonstrated diffuse slowing. Lumbar puncture was performed and CSF studies, including PCR for neurotropic viruses, bacteria, and fungi, were negative; blood cultures and PCR were also negative. A nasal swab was positive for metapneumovirus.

Four hours after admission, brain MRI revealed a solitary lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum that was hyperintense on FLAIR, showed diffusion restriction on DWI with corresponding low ADC, and did not enhance with contrast. No other intracranial abnormalities were seen; magnetic resonance angiography was normal.
final_diagnosis_raw: mild encephalopathy with a reversible splenial lesion
title: Transient blindness due to mild reversible encephalopathy in a 7‐year‐old boy

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old man presented with a one-year history of a right-sided parotid mass and ipsilateral neck swelling. The mass was initially painless, then slowly enlarged, prompting evaluation. He had no history of radiation exposure, and his family and social history were unremarkable. On examination, there was a visible, palpable, non-tender, non-fixed swelling at the angle of the right mandible; no other lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 2.9 × 3.1 cm superficial hypo-enhancing mass in the tail of the right parotid gland with ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy in levels Ib and IIa, consistent with a primary parotid neoplasm and nodal metastases. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy was suspicious for malignancy. The patient underwent a superficial parotidectomy with modified radical neck dissection.

Gross examination revealed a single, well-circumscribed, soft to friable 2.8 cm mass within the parotid gland. Microscopic examination showed a non-encapsulated lesion with solid, microcystic, and papillary-cystic architecture. Tumor cells had clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm with foamy to bubbly intracytoplasmic secretions, and colloid-type secretions were noted within cystic spaces and glandular lumina.
title: NTRK3 mutation in secretory carcinoma of the parotid gland: A Case report

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman presented with intermittent right lower abdominal pain of 1 year’s duration, associated with constipation. Her obstetric history was notable for multiple pregnancies and a cesarean section 25 years earlier; there was no other significant medical or surgical history.

On examination, an oval swelling, 6 cm by 5 cm, was palpated in the right flank. The mass had a smooth surface, firm consistency, and was partially reducible; a cough impulse was present. Mild tenderness was elicited on palpation of the right flank; no other abdominal masses were found.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneously hyperechoic lesion measuring 55 mm × 44 mm × 11 mm with an internal linear strand in the lower right infra-umbilical abdominal wall. The lesion lay between the lateral margin of the right rectus abdominis and the medial border of the right internal oblique muscle, extending superficially toward the external oblique, with a neck measuring 11 mm × 10 mm. The lesion was partially reducible on compression. A CT scan was not feasible.
title: Giant spigelian hernia in a middle-aged female: The importance of intraoperative ultrasonography for hernia localization—Case report

case_prompt: A 62-year-old man with no smoking history was admitted with several weeks of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, arthralgia, and weakness. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable, with a pulmonary ejection murmur and an accentuated pulmonic second heart sound; heart rate was sinus tachycardia. There was no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed mild elevations in IgG (1398 mg/dL; normal 543–1360) and IgA (280 mg/dL; normal 58–259), with normal 24 h urine protein (115 mg), ESR (13 mm/h), and CRP (0.6 mg/dL). Chest radiography revealed a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, signs of pulmonary hypertension, congestion, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large right atrial mass and minimal pericardial effusion, with normal biventricular function. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a 3.2 cm × 2.8 cm right atrial myocardial mass involving the auricle and atrial septum, without lymphadenopathy or osteolytic lesions. Transesophageal echocardiography–guided fine-needle aspiration yielded a hypercellular malignant neoplasm with atypical polyhedral cells suspicious for a plasma cell tumour. Immunohistochemical staining of the aspirate was positive for CD138, kappa light chain clonality, and epithelial membrane antigen, consistent with plasmacytoma.
title: Primary Extramedullary Plasmacytoma of the Heart: A Rare Manifestation of Plasmacellular Tumor

case_prompt: An 18-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder and mild intellectual disability was referred for acute psychiatric decompensation. He had two prior episodes of confusional states, psychomotor agitation, speech impairment, hallucinations, and catatonic features at ages 13 and 15, both responding to quetiapine. At age 18, he developed disorganized thought, obsessive rumination, catatonic behaviors (asthenia, reduced mobility, hyporeactivity, limb stiffness, hypomimia, apathy, and social withdrawal). On admission, quetiapine was discontinued and aripiprazole was initiated at 2.5 mg/day, increased by 2.5 mg every 4 days up to 10 mg/day, with lorazepam supplementation. Two days after reaching 10 mg/day, he exhibited psychomotor retardation, hyperreactivity to stimuli, anorexia, and asthenia; creatine kinase (CK) was within normal limits. Seven days after starting aripiprazole, he experienced worsening obsessive thoughts, hyperthermia, and an acute rise in CK and was admitted to the emergency department; all psychotropic medications were discontinued, and he was transferred to the intensive care unit. On examination, he had limb stiffness, perioral myokymia, myoclonus, facial amimia, uncoordinated tongue movements, difficulty swallowing, polypnea, tachycardia, and arterial hypertension.
title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD): A Case Report and Brief Review of Recent Literature

case_prompt: A 76-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of intermittent colicky lower abdominal pain associated with bilious vomiting and mild abdominal distension. She had a history of left breast cancer diagnosed 18 years earlier, treated with wide local excision, radiotherapy, and 5 years of tamoxifen, and a regional recurrence with bone metastases treated palliatively 17 years after the initial diagnosis. On examination, vital signs were stable. The abdomen was mildly distended with peri-umbilical tenderness and guarding. Laboratory studies, including hematological, biochemical, inflammatory, and coagulation profiles, were within normal limits. A plain abdominal radiograph was unrevealing. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dilated small bowel loops consistent with obstruction, with two intraluminal filling defects: one in the proximal ileum suspicious for a non-calcified gallstone and a second area of narrowing in the terminal ileum. The patient was resuscitated and taken for laparotomy, which revealed a proximal impacted gallstone and a separate distal ileal stricture. The surgical team performed resection of both segments with primary end-to-end anastomoses. The intraoperative clinical impression was dual pathology, including gallstone ileus and Crohn’s disease.
title: Metastatic breast cancer presenting as a gallstone ileus

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old man with a nine-year history of celiac disease, in histologic and clinical remission on a strict gluten-free diet, presented with subacute gait ataxia, undirected dizziness, double vision, and cognitive impairment progressing over four days. His history included refractory celiac disease type II diagnosed six months earlier on the basis of ulcerative jejunitis and abnormal intraepithelial lymphocytes, for which he was on methylprednisolone and azathioprine with slight improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms.

On examination, he had a cerebellar syndrome with gait ataxia and dysdiadochokinesia; the remainder of the neurologic and systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function, inflammatory markers, and serologic tTG-IgA antibodies, were within normal limits. Fecal calprotectin was elevated. 

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showed multifocal T2-hyperintense, partially ring-enhancing lesions in cortical, subcortical, periventricular regions, basal ganglia, mesencephalon, and cerebellum. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a normal cell count, no malignant cells, no pathogens, and no oligoclonal bands. Polymerase chain reaction assays for neurotropic pathogens were negative. Electroencephalography demonstrated moderate diffuse cerebral dysfunction without epileptiform discharges. Onconeural antibodies and antibodies to neuronal surface antigens in serum and CSF were negative. 

Given rapid neurologic worsening, intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone was administered, with prompt clinical improvement, although follow-up MRI showed stable intracranial lesions in size and distribution.
title: Multiple cerebral lesions in a patient with refractory celiac disease: A case report

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old Dominican man presented with a 2-year history of progressively enlarging skin lesions on both lower extremities. He had lived in the United States for 2 years. His medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus and hypertension. He had previously received oral antibiotics for a presumed skin infection and intralesional steroids for presumed dermatitis without improvement.

On examination, temperature was 98.4 °F, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Dermatologic examination revealed a cluster of dark nodular lesions on the medial right thigh and multiple purple plaques of varying sizes below both knees. There was left lower-limb edema. A violaceous lesion was also noted on the soft palate. There was no lymphadenopathy; lungs were clear; heart sounds were normal; and the abdomen was without hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, hematocrit 42%, white blood cell count 4.9 × 10^9/L, platelet count 224 × 10^9/L, and normal renal and hepatic chemistries. Serologic tests for HIV were negative, and the CD4 count was 350 cells/mm^3 with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 1.10.
title:
A case of classic Kaposi sarcoma in an immunocompetent human immunodeficiency
virus–negative Dominican man

case_prompt: A 64-year-old woman with a history of treated left breast carcinoma presented with a new palpable mass in the inferior-internal quadrant of her right breast. Mammography demonstrated a medium-density, oval, circumscribed mass with partially indistinct margins and no calcifications. Ultrasound revealed an 8 × 5 mm solid lesion with regular contours and heterogeneous echogenicity; there were no palpable axillary lymph nodes. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed a well-circumscribed tumor composed of glandular structures lined by two cell layers: inner epithelial cells with basally located nuclei without atypia, and outer myoepithelial cells with large nuclei, fine chromatin, and a low nucleocytoplasmic ratio, all embedded in a dense fibro-hyaline stroma.
title: Breast adenomyoepithelioma diagnosed on core needle biopsy: a diagnostic challenge

case_prompt:
A 2-year-old neutered female outdoor domestic shorthair cat was evaluated for a 4-month history of progressive respiratory signs. Initially, the cat had snoring, dysphonia and an unproductive cough that later became productive. Empirical treatment with corticosteroids, nebulisation and multiple antibiotics (marbofloxacin, doxycycline, cefovecine) yielded no improvement. The cat was not regularly vaccinated but had undergone recent deworming with praziquantel and pyrantel. It lived in a multi-cat rescue household with free outdoor access near a forest; no other cats were symptomatic.

On presentation, the cat was febrile (40.0°C), tachypneic (80 breaths/min) and tachycardic (>200 beats/min). Thoracic auscultation revealed severe bilateral wheezing and crackles, increased tracheal sounds and tracheal hypersensitivity. Thoracic radiographs were unremarkable. Bronchoscopy showed laryngeal oedema, tracheal inflammation and abundant mucoid-to-mucopurulent secretions. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cytology demonstrated moderate cellularity with >90% degenerative neutrophils and intracellular coccobacilli, consistent with suppurative bronchitis.

An in-clinic ELISA for feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) and feline leukaemia virus was performed, revealing FIV infection. Complete blood count showed leukocytosis (27.3×10^9 cells/L), mature neutrophilia (23.6×10^9 cells/L) and mild monocytosis (0.8×10^9 cells/L).
title: Lungworm Eucoleus aerophilus (Capillaria aerophila) infection in a feline immunodeficiency virus-positive cat in France

case_prompt: A 60-year-old woman with newly diagnosed, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes was referred from oral surgery for evaluation of a duplication of the upper anterior ridge. She reported wearing maxillary and mandibular complete removable prostheses that were poorly designed and unstable during function, and she performed no routine oral or prosthetic hygiene. On extraoral examination, she had slightly reduced lower-face height from decreased vertical dimension of occlusion and a flat profile due to mandibular protrusion in centric relation. Intraoral examination revealed edentulous maxillary and mandibular ridges supporting the prostheses and an inflamed, hyperplastic tissue mass extending from the right premolar region across the contralateral maxillary vestibule. Inspection of the dentures showed abraded occlusal surfaces, sharp overextended edges, and an anteroposterior offset between the anterior vestibular sulcus and the maxillary prosthesis edge. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated moderate resorption of the maxillary and mandibular edentulous ridges, classified as Atwood class II, with no other abnormalities.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Inflammatory fibrous hyperplasia between surgery and tissue conditioning: A case report

case_prompt: A 55-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of headache, nausea, and mild dizziness. He had no history of medication use, cancer, infection, hematologic disorders, or trauma. On examination, he was alert, with normal cranial nerves, strength, and reflexes; tandem gait was mildly impaired. Vital signs were: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, heart rate 70 beats/minute. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, hematocrit 24.8%, white blood cell count 4600/µL, platelet count 130 000/µL, ESR 12 mm/hr, and CRP 1.447 mg/L. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Iron studies revealed total iron-binding capacity 324 µg/dL, serum iron 54 µg/dL; vitamin B12 and folate were normal. A peripheral smear demonstrated normocytic normochromic anemia with anisopoikilocytosis, consistent with iron-deficiency anemia. Brain MRI showed diffuse T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and T1 hypointensity in the right cerebellar hemisphere with compression of the fourth ventricle, multifocal petechial hemorrhages, and irregular gadolinium enhancement. Additionally, there was T2/FLAIR hyperintensity at the junction of the right transverse sinus and proximal sigmoid sinus.
title: Isolated Lateral Sinus Thrombosis Presenting as Cerebellar Infarction in a Patient with Iron Deficiency Anemia

case_prompt:
A 16-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of precocious puberty. His parents first noted pubic hair at six months of age and subsequently observed rapid linear growth. There was no exposure to exogenous androgens, and no family history of early puberty or short stature. 

On examination, his height was above the 99th percentile (midparental target 50th percentile). He had pubic hair at Tanner stage 2 and stretched penile length of 11 cm, with prepubertal testes. A bone-age radiograph obtained at 12 months of age was assessed as 12–18 months; by 21 months bone age was 6 years, and by 26 months bone age was 8 years.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate within normal limits.  
• Basal luteinizing hormone 0.7 mIU/mL (prepubertal <0.3 mIU/mL).  
• Serum testosterone 289 ng/dL (prepubertal <5 ng/dL).

An adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test ruled out congenital adrenal hyperplasia. A leuprolide stimulation test ruled out central precocious puberty. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen and pelvis was normal. Scrotal ultrasound revealed prepubertal testes with bilateral testicular microlithiasis and no masses. An initial α-fetoprotein level was elevated but normalized on repeat testing; β-hCG, insulin-like growth factor-1, and thyroid function were normal.

At 26 months of age, the leading diagnostic considerations were familial male-limited precocious puberty and McCune-Albright syndrome.
journal: Journal of Clinical Research in Pediatric Endocrinology
title: A Case of Familial Male-limited Precocious Puberty with a Novel Mutation

case_prompt: A 40-year-old man presented to the emergency department with swelling and pain in the left hemiscrotum of acute onset without a history of trauma or surgery. He had no significant medical or family history, smoked one pack-year, and did not consume alcohol. On examination, the left hemiscrotum was tender and swollen, consistent with acute epididymitis. Incidentally, a non-tender mass was palpated in the right hemiscrotum; his parents had first noted this mass when he was two years old, and it had been misdiagnosed as a hydrocele at that time. Scrotal ultrasound showed a normal left testis, an enlarged hypoechoic left epididymis with increased Doppler flow, and an oval right scrotal lump with echotexture and blood flow similar to the ipsilateral testis. Serum α-fetoprotein (1.44 IU/mL) and β-hCG (0.5 mIU/mL) levels were within reference limits.
title: A rare case of polyorchidism in a 40-year-old man. A case report

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man with a 13-year history of elevated creatine kinase levels and a 10-year history of positional tremor noted progressive right fifth-finger abduction weakness over 1 year, followed by bilateral paresthesias in all fingers and toes. Six months before admission, he developed low back pain radiating to both legs (more on the left). Two months before admission, he experienced anginal chest pain; cardiac evaluation showed only hypertension and mild left ventricular hypertrophy, and a stress test was halted at 80 W because of muscle weakness.  

On neurologic examination at admission, he had weakness of head flexion, tongue atrophy with fasciculations, bulbar speech, diffuse mild muscle weakness (M4) and wasting, hypotonia, positional tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, absent upper-limb tendon reflexes, bilateral gynecomastia, hip flexion weakness (M4–), absent lower-limb reflexes, and calf fasciculations. Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatic steatosis. Lumbar spine MRI showed canal stenosis at L4/5, osteochondrosis at L3/4 and L5/S1, spondylarthrosis L2–5, and spondylosis.  

Two months later, he was admitted after a fall due to leg weakness. Examination revealed bilateral peripheral facial palsy, tongue atrophy with fasciculations, quadruparesis (M3–4), stocking-type sensory loss, and a broad-based ataxic gait. Nerve conduction studies showed a sensorimotor polyneuropathy with conduction blocks in the median, ulnar, and left peroneal nerves. Brain CT was unremarkable. Laboratory studies found CK 1340 U/L, normal TSH, vitamin B12, immunofixation, antiganglioside antibodies, and Borrelia serologies; CSF showed 24 cells/µL with normal protein and glucose. Intravenous immunoglobulins were administered, leading to partial remission of the conduction block in the left median nerve and modest gait improvement, with no other clinical changes.
title: Bulbospinal muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease) responsive to immunoglobulins?

case_prompt:
A 12-year-old girl from a Himalayan district of Nepal presented with a 6-month history of headache and fatigue. She was born at term at home, with no family history of thyroid or autoimmune disorders. She denied menarche, visual changes, hair loss, constipation, or medication use. On examination, her height was 129 cm (<3rd percentile), weight 54 kg (>75th percentile), and BMI 32.4 kg/m^2. Blood pressure was 104/72 mm Hg, heart rate 63 beats/min, and respiratory rate 15 breaths/min. She had coarse, dry skin and looked short and obese for her age. Neurological and visual-field examinations were normal. The thyroid was markedly enlarged bilaterally. She was Tanner Stage I for breast and pubic hair development.

Initial laboratory studies revealed:
• TSH 149.6 µIU/mL (0.4–6.1 µIU/mL)  
• T4 0.2 µg/dL (4–11 µg/dL)  
• T3 11 ng/dL (69–202 ng/dL)  
• Prolactin 59.2 ng/mL (1.2–15.5 ng/mL)  
• GH 4.7 ng/mL (<10 ng/mL)  
• LH 0.26 mIU/mL; FSH 0.78 mIU/mL  
• Cortisol and ACTH within normal limits  
• Hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL; random glucose 80 mg/dL  
• LDL-C 156 mg/dL; triglycerides 193 mg/dL  
• Urinary iodine 12 µg/L (100–299 µg/L)  
• Thyroid autoantibodies negative

Noncontrast and contrast CT of the head demonstrated a 9 mm, round, symmetrically enlarged, homogeneously enhancing, hyperdense mass in the widened pituitary fossa.
title: Pituitary hyperplasia due to Himalayan endemic hypothyroidism

case_prompt: A 59-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of upper abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and intermittent vomiting. She also reported hot flushes over the preceding 3 months. Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable, and the physical examination was without focal findings. Laboratory tests showed mild to moderate anemia (hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, hematocrit 35.4%, MCV 81.5 fL, MCH 24.9 pg) and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level (378 IU/L; normal <280 IU/L). Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance enterography revealed circumferential thickening of the proximal jejunal wall with proximal bowel distention, shouldering of the lumen margins, mucosal disruption, and an enlarged lymph node along the posterior aspect of the greater curvature of the stomach. Given the evidence of partial small-bowel obstruction and concern for an underlying malignancy, the patient underwent a segmental jejunal resection with primary anastomosis, with grossly intact anastomotic integrity noted intraoperatively. A feeding jejunostomy was placed postoperatively. On gross examination, the resected jejunal segment (20 cm in length) showed a 4 × 3 × 2 cm exophytic mass invading from the mucosa through the serosa into the peri-intestinal fat; regional lymph nodes appeared free of tumor.
title: Mast Cell Sarcoma of Small Intestine, Early Diagnosis, and Good Prognosis: An Extremely Rare Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 54-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of proptosis, lid swelling, diplopia, and retro-orbital pain in her left eye. Her past medical history was significant for poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the stomach, with known metastases to the ovary, mesentery, subcutaneous tissue of the neck, and thoracic bone marrow; she had undergone multiple chemotherapy regimens and was on palliative care. On examination, external inspection showed left eyelid swelling, erythema, and proptosis. Ocular motility testing revealed an adduction deficit of –4.0 and an abduction deficit of –1.0 in the left eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, and intraocular pressures were normal in both eyes. Anterior segments were unremarkable. Pupils were equal and reactive without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopic examination of the left eye showed partial optic disc edema without choroidal masses or striae. Review of a CT scan performed 10 days before presentation demonstrated enlargement of the left medial rectus muscle; comparison with imaging from 3 months earlier showed progressive enlargement, while a scan from 6 months earlier was normal. There was no enlargement of other extraocular muscles or other orbital abnormalities.
title: Metastasis of advanced gastric cancer to the extraocular muscle: a case report

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old female student presented in March 2021 with 3 months of gradually progressive left-sided chest pain associated with cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness. The pain worsened when she lay on her left side. She denied hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, or prior tuberculosis exposure. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she did not smoke or drink alcohol.
On examination, she was comfortable, with a temperature of 36.4 °C, pulse rate 100 beats/min, blood pressure 116/79 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The trachea was deviated to the right, and air entry was reduced over the left hemithorax. Cardiovascular and other systems were normal.
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, serum creatinine 72 μmol/L, prothrombin time 11.3 s, INR 0.89, and normal electrolytes. A chest radiograph confirmed tracheal deviation to the right and a mass occupying the left hemithorax.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a large, well-circumscribed mass in the left posterior hemithorax measuring 12.3 cm (AP) × 14.4 cm (transverse) × 22.8 cm (craniocaudal), causing partial collapse of the left lung and mediastinal shift to the right; the mass abutted the descending aorta without bone destruction. These findings were read as “suggestive of pleuropulmonary blastoma vs. neurogenic tumor (ganglioneuroma).”
A CT-guided core-needle biopsy was performed.
title: Ectopic uterus? A rare presentation of a giant leiomyoma in the posterior mediastinum

case_prompt: An 84-year-old man with a history of pararectal gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) diagnosed 22 months earlier—initially metastatic to mesorectal and iliac lymph nodes and iliac bone—presented with rapidly progressive stridor, aphagia, and dysphonia. His prior therapy included 6 months of imatinib halted for Stevens-Johnson syndrome, surgical resection (ypT4 N0 MX L0 V0 Pn0 RX with 10 mitoses/50 HPF), and stereotactic radiotherapy to bone metastases. On examination he had a “hot potato” voice and position-dependent stridor. Endobuccal inspection revealed a 3-cm, round, elastic, non-pulsatile mass on the posterior wall of the lower oropharynx with normal overlying mucosa, obstructing the laryngeal inlet; the larynx was otherwise unremarkable and functional. Cervical palpation was normal. Videoendoscopy bypassed the mass and confirmed vocal cord mobility. Cervicofacial CT showed an infiltrative prevertebral lesion at C3 with partial destruction of the C2 and C3 vertebral bodies causing a mass effect on the oropharynx and hypopharynx. Cervicofacial MRI revealed a 7.2×5.2×4.8 cm mass compatible with a vertebral lesion.
title: Rapidly progressive stridor in a case of GIST

case_prompt: A 41-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressively decreased visual acuity and right peripheral facial paralysis. She had no significant past medical history and no family history of neoplasm or neurological disorders. Brain MRI demonstrated an expansile, well-defined oval lesion measuring 19 × 17 × 16 mm, located above the sella turcica. The lesion was isointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images and showed homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. It abutted the optic chiasm and the mammillary bodies, laterally displacing the optic tracts, without signal abnormality or contrast enhancement of the optic nerves. There was no calcification, and the anterior pituitary gland appeared normal. These radiological findings raised the differential diagnosis of pituicytoma versus craniopharyngioma.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Supra-sellar granular cell tumor: Report of a case with literature review

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man with a 20-year history of tachycardia and palpitations presented with worsening symptoms despite daily sotalol therapy. On admission, his pulse rate was 110–160 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, and temperature normal. Electrocardiography showed a short PR interval and a delta wave, consistent with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. He received sotalol and underwent direct-current cardioversion, but recurrent tachyarrhythmia prompted further evaluation.

Chest radiography showed an elevated cardiothoracic ratio due to marked right atrial enlargement. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 50%, normal right ventricular size but severe right ventricular systolic dysfunction, and a markedly enlarged right atrium compressing both ventricles; there was no significant valvular disease except a mildly increased tricuspid valve gradient (mean 3 mmHg, peak 8 mmHg) and a localized pericardial effusion posterior to the left ventricle measuring 21 mm. 

Spiral CT angiography demonstrated a large blood-containing structure measuring approximately 127 × 122 × 72 mm anterior to the right atrium and right ventricle without thrombus. The lesion caused displacement and compression of the right atrium, right ventricle, and tricuspid valve, and displaced the right coronary artery and its branches leftward. Both the superior and inferior vena cavae drained normally into the right atrium. Given the adjacency of the lesion to the right coronary artery and its broad muscular connection to the right atrial free wall, surgical resection was planned over catheter ablation.
title: Surgical repair of a giant congenital right atrial aneurysm concomitant with Wolff‐Parkinson‐White syndrome: A case report and literature review

case_prompt: An 11-month-old girl was referred for a one-month history of watery diarrhea (7–8 episodes per day) without blood or mucus, associated with malnutrition and marked abdominal distension. There was no vomiting or fever. She was born at 38 weeks’ gestation, with normal early growth and development. At 10 months of age, diarrhea began and persisted despite empirical outpatient trials, including a protein-hydrolysate, lactose-free formula (for presumed cow’s milk allergy) and antiparasitic therapy for unproven giardiasis. On admission, her weight was 8 kg (25th percentile), length 70 cm (5th percentile), heart rate 85/min, and blood pressure 80/55 mmHg. Examination revealed facial flushing and a distended abdomen without palpable masses. Laboratory tests showed mild metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia; blood counts and biochemistry were otherwise normal. Infectious enterocolitis, intestinal parasitosis, celiac disease, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency/mucoviscidosis, and cow’s milk protein allergy were excluded. Abdominal radiography showed dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels. Sonography and CT scan identified a 6×4 cm calcified mass anterior to the L1–L4 spine and aorta, separate from the pancreas. Endocrine evaluation revealed VIP 180 pmol/L (normal ≤30), 24-hour urinary homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid within normal limits, and elevated neuron-specific enolase.
title: Chronic Diarrhea Caused by Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide-Secreting Tumor

case_prompt: A 60-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a several‐week history of dysuria, urinary frequency, urinary urgency, and intermittent hematuria, without fever or chills. She reported a longstanding “lump” in her vulvar area. Empiric treatment with nitrofurantoin, phenazopyridine, topical ointments, and sitz baths provided no relief. On pelvic examination, there was mild uterine and cervical prolapse and a 3‐cm diameter reddish, partly necrotic-appearing lump encircling the urethral meatus. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a normal-sized uterus with thin endometrial lining, no pelvic masses, and no fluid collections. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count and serum chemistry. Urinalysis demonstrated leukocyturia and erythrocyturia, but urine culture yielded no bacterial growth.
title: Spontaneous Postmenopausal Urethral Prolapse Treated Surgically and Successfully

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 10-month history of a painful umbilical mass. She reported that each month, one week before menstruation, she developed pain and slight swelling at the umbilicus; the discomfort persisted throughout her cycle. Two years earlier, she had been diagnosed clinically with endometriosis because of worsening dysmenorrhea. She had never undergone abdominal surgery. 

On abdominal-wall ultrasound, there was a 1.15 × 1.07 cm heterogeneous hypoechoic umbilical mass containing cystic areas and hyperechoic spots, with slightly indistinct margins, without invasion of the abdominal fascia or increased angiogenesis. 

Pelvic MRI demonstrated an umbilical lesion with low signal intensity areas on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and punctate hyperintense foci on T1 and fat-suppressed T1 images consistent with hemorrhage; the lesion showed subtle enhancement after gadolinium. MRI also revealed a right hematosalpinx, a left ovarian endometrioma, adenomyosis, and thickening of the uterosacral ligaments and torus uterinus.
title: Primary umbilical endometriosis: case report and literature review of an unusual cause of catamenial umbilical pain

case_prompt: An infant boy was referred for evaluation of a congenital left neck mass. At 1 month of age, magnetic resonance imaging revealed a multicystic lesion adjacent to the pharynx and parotid gland. His history, physical examination, and MRI findings suggested a lymphatic malformation. He underwent OK-432 sclerotherapy at 2, 3, and 6 months of age, with each session resulting in the expected reduction in volume. At 3 years of age, a persistent bulge prompted a fourth sclerotherapy attempt, but aspiration could not reach the cystic component. MRI at 5 years showed that most of the lesion had become thick, wall-like tissue with only a small residual cystic component. A further attempt at sclerotherapy was abandoned because the cyst wall was judged too thick. Ultrasound at 5 years demonstrated virtually no cystic component and no fluid flow, findings interpreted as consistent with lymphatic malformation, postsclerotherapy scar, or blood clots. At 6 years of age, surgical resection was planned.
journal: Case Reports in Plastic Surgery & Hand Surgery
title: Mature teratoma treated as lymphatic malformation for 5 years: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: An 82-year-old man was referred for insidious onset of shortness of breath, episodic cough over several years, and recurrent chest infections. His medical history included two myocardial infarctions, coronary artery bypass grafting in 1996, and a 80–pack-year smoking history (quit). Family history was notable: his brother and two of his three daughters had spontaneous pneumothoraces in their 30s or 40s. On examination, breath sounds were diminished with a few crackles at the right base; multiple whitish dome-shaped papules were present on the head and neck. Spirometry showed mild obstruction with preserved lung volumes. A chest radiograph was reported as normal. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed multiple thin-walled round, elliptical, or lentiform well-defined air-filled cysts measuring 1–5 cm, predominantly in basilar and medial subpleural regions, without other parenchymal abnormalities.
title: A rare cause of cystic lung disease – Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome

case_prompt: A 47-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of vague, generalized abdominal pain that later localized to the right lower quadrant. Ten years earlier she had undergone total abdominal hysterectomy for menorrhagia and had been on estrogen patch hormone-replacement therapy since. On examination, she was afebrile but had localized peritonism in the right and upper central abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 12.1×10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 16 mg/L. Abdominal sonography demonstrated a hypoechoic, ovoid, irregular lesion with a blind end in the region of the hepatic flexure; probe-induced tenderness was noted over the lesion. Given the acute presentation and suspicion of an inflammatory or perforated colonic lesion, she underwent exploratory laparoscopy. At surgery, a firm, irregular omental mass (approximately 2 cm) was identified adjacent to the proximal transverse colon, appearing to extend from the colon; the appendix was normal, the right adnexa appeared normal, and the left adnexa could not be fully visualized owing to adhesions. A necrotic omental nodule (18×15×12 mm) was biopsied. Histologically, the lesion showed extensive hemorrhagic necrosis and residual monomorphic ovoid to spindle-shaped cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Immunohistochemical staining showed strong positivity for CD10, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor, raising the possibility of endometrial stromal sarcoma.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: An unexpected diagnosis of primary omental endometrial stromal sarcoma in a patient with acute right abdominal pain: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old woman with Stage IV diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, treated with anthracyclines, was transferred for escalating cardiogenic shock despite high-dose inotropes. She underwent surgical implantation of an Impella CP device via the left subclavian artery, with unfractionated heparin administered systemically (target anti-Xa, 0.3–0.5 IU/mL) and in the dextrose-based purge (25 IU/mL). On day 16, she developed persistent high fever and a new right-sided pleural effusion on chest X-ray; coagulation parameters had normalized off systemic heparin. A diagnostic thoracentesis was performed to exclude an empyema.  
The next night, after systemic heparin was restarted, her hemoglobin dropped significantly (BARC 3 bleeding), and chest X-ray showed marked expansion of the right pleural effusion. Vasopressor requirements increased, and a percutaneous pigtail catheter was inserted.
title: Switch to a bicarbonate-based Impella CP™ purge solution in a patient with haemothorax: a case report

case_prompt:
A 6-week-old girl was admitted with 1 day of lethargy, poor feeding, shortness of breath, and irritability on a background of progressive pallor. There was no relevant family history. Antenatal screens had shown low pregnancy-associated plasma protein A and growth restriction, but fetal karyotype and anomaly scans were normal. She was delivered by cesarean section at 37 weeks, birth weight 2465 g, and discharged healthy on day 3.

On admission at 6 weeks, she was tachycardic and lethargic without icterus or dysmorphic features. Weight was 3200 g. Laboratory values (normal range for age in brackets) included: hemoglobin 3.1 g/dL (10–18), hematocrit 9% (31–55%), MCV 106 fL (85–123), MCHC 34 g/dL (32–37), reticulocyte production index 0.0, absolute reticulocyte count 5.1 × 10^9/L (20–60 × 10^9/L). White cells 4.0 × 10^9/L (5–19.5), neutrophils 0.32 × 10^9/L (1–9), platelets 655 × 10^9/L (140–420). C-reactive protein was 7.7 mg/L (< 5). Urine culture grew Escherichia coli; other virology tests (CMV, HIV, rubella, EBV, toxoplasma, HSV-1/2, parvovirus B19) were negative.

She received leukodepleted, irradiated red cell transfusion (Hb raised to 10 g/dL), antibiotics for urosepsis, and was discharged after 6 days. Fourteen days later, she was readmitted with hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL and reticulocytopenia (7.0 × 10^9/L). After exclusion of infection, HIV, and tuberculosis, a provisional diagnosis of transient erythroblastopenia of childhood (TEC) was made.

Over the next 3 months she required three additional transfusions and persistent neutropenia. A bone marrow biopsy was performed. Histologic examination showed a normocellular marrow with normal megakaryopoiesis and granulopoiesis. Flow cytometry revealed T cells, mature B cells, and hematogones. Immunohistochemical staining for glycophorin demonstrated an absence of red cell precursors, confirming a pure red cell aplasia.
title: Diamond–Blackfan anemia RPL35A: a case report

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman presented with confusion after several generalized tonic-clonic seizures. She had a 4-year history of spinal cord glioblastoma with extension from the brainstem to the upper thoracic cord and a right temporal pole lesion. Two weeks earlier, her chemoradiation therapy had been completed; lumbar puncture was avoided because of intracranial mass effect. Three months prior, brain MRI confirmed tumor progression.  
On arrival she was drowsy; blood pressure was 125/65 mmHg, temperature 36.4 °C, pulse 100/min, respiratory rate 19/min. Intravenous levetiracetam, 1000 mg, was administered immediately, but she had another generalized tonic-clonic seizure without recovering consciousness. Two hours after the levetiracetam loading dose, video-EEG monitoring was started. At that time, she developed choreoathetoid movements of the face and all four limbs; concurrent EEG showed no epileptiform discharges.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and ammonia, were normal. Her chronic medications—solifenacin, esomeprazole, baclofen, and escitalopram—had been unchanged for >3 months; she was not receiving dopamine-blocking or antipsychotic agents. Levetiracetam was withheld; the movements persisted for approximately 30 minutes, during which she remained alert and able to communicate.
title: A case of dyskinesia after levetiracetam administration

case_prompt:
A 5-year-old boy of Middle Eastern descent, born full-term to first-cousin parents, presented with progressive skin lesions, abdominal distension, and red-colored urine.  
Birth & neonatal period: Born at 2200 g with a wide anterior fontanel; within days he developed poor feeding, reddish urine, ecchymoses, and pallor without jaundice or fever. Examination showed a soft parasternal pansystolic murmur, splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin, and hepatomegaly 2 cm below the costal margin.  
Initial investigations: Hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, PCV 20%, reticulocyte count 12%; normocytic normochromic anemia on smear; negative Coombs test; normal osmotic fragility; normal coagulation, liver, and renal function; negative TORCH screen; bone marrow aspiration without leukemia or myelofibrosis; echocardiogram revealing a perimembranous ventricular septal defect; abdominal ultrasound showing marked splenomegaly. DNA testing showed heterozygosity for α-thalassemia trait; Gaucher disease and mucopolysaccharidosis were excluded. He received regular blood transfusions and desferrioxamine chelation.  
Subsequent course: At 10 months, he developed worsening abdominal distension, brown-stained teeth, and persistent red urine. At 22 months, vesiculobullous lesions appeared on sun-exposed areas (face, hands, feet), healing with hypopigmented scars. At 30 months, transfusions were paused, but skin lesions progressed and red urine and brown teeth persisted. Urinalysis showed proteinuria, elevated urobilinogen, RBCs and WBCs with E. coli growth. Hemoglobin electrophoresis was AA.  
At 5 years, he had worsening photosensitive skin lesions, persistent red urine, and anemia and was evaluated at our center, where a clinical diagnosis of congenital erythropoietic porphyria was made and confirmatory porphyrin assays were ordered.
title: Neonatal hemolytic anemia does not always indicate thalassemia: a case report

case_prompt: A 53-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 1-year history of progressively worsening constipation, early satiety, and epigastric fullness. Her past medical history included anxiety, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, fibromyalgia, and hiatal hernia; she had undergone umbilical hernia repair and multiple prior cutaneous lipoma resections. She was a former 35–pack-year smoker who quit 1 year earlier and denied alcohol or drug use. On examination, she had mild epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding. Initial management with oral polyethylene glycol, followed by lubiprostone and then plecanatide, provided no relief. Colonoscopy with removal of three small rectal polyps did not improve her symptoms. A computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a mass obstructing approximately 75% of the duodenal lumen adjacent to an enlarged gallbladder. The differential diagnosis included duodenal lipoma, duodenal stricture, and irritable bowel syndrome. Six months later, esophagogastroduodenoscopy confirmed an intraluminal mass in the third portion of the duodenum.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Treatment of duodenal lipoma with robotic-assisted transverse duodenotomy: A case report of novel approach

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of a palpable left breast lump. Her past medical history was significant for biphenotypic acute lymphoblastic leukemia at age 7, treated to complete remission, and an anal mass diagnosed one year earlier as rhabdomyosarcoma treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy. On examination, the left breast contained a firm, round, nontender 3×3 cm mass without overlying skin changes; the right breast and both axillae were normal.  
Breast ultrasonography revealed a 2.3 cm circumscribed oval hyperechoic mass with a central hypoechoic portion. Core-needle biopsy of the breast lesion was consistent with rhabdomyosarcoma.  
Staging studies including chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT scans and 18F-FDG PET/CT showed intense FDG uptake in the left breast mass and in the retrocrural space at the level of the L1 vertebra, with no other sites of disease.
title: Breast Metastasis from Rhabdomyosarcoma of the Anus in an Adolescent Female

case_prompt: A 37-year-old man with a known unoperated secundum atrial septal defect and Eisenmenger syndrome was referred for evaluation of chest pain. Over 6 months he developed typical exertional angina, worsening over the past 2 months. He had no other medical or family history. On examination, he was cyanotic with digital clubbing and oxygen saturation of 86% on room air. He had signs of right heart congestion and cardiomegaly, a loud P2 component, and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border that increased with inspiration. Laboratory studies showed secondary erythrocytosis (hemoglobin 19.5 g/dL, hematocrit 55.5%). An ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm, right axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy, deep T-wave inversions in the inferior and anterior leads, and an incomplete right bundle branch block. A chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly with a prominent pulmonary conus and increased pulmonary vascular markings. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a secundum ASD with a predominantly right-to-left shunt, a D-shaped left ventricle, dilation of the right atrium, right ventricle, and left atrium, paradoxical septal motion, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and a markedly dilated main pulmonary artery measuring 48 mm.
title: Eisenmenger syndrome with left main compression syndrome: a case report

case_prompt: A 12‐year‐old girl was evaluated after a minor motor‐vehicle collision. She reported transient loss of consciousness, headache, and mild dizziness. On examination, she was alert (GCS 15), hemodynamically stable, with no scalp lacerations or visual deficits. Her medical history included thymoma and pollen allergy; laboratory studies were unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT showed no intracranial hemorrhage or fracture. Incidentally, bilateral pneumatization of the middle turbinates (concha bullosa) was noted. The left concha bullosa was markedly enlarged and contained high‐density material with coarse calcifications. Associated mucosal thickening, bony wall thickening with mild rarefaction, and opacification of adjacent ethmoidal air cells were present. There was no obstruction of the ipsilateral osteomeatal complex.
title: Fungal ball in concha bullosa as incidentaloma: A case report and the review of the literature

case_prompt: A 10-month-old full-term female was referred after a 4–6-month history of delayed motor milestones and progressive increase in head circumference. An external ventricular drain had been placed at an outside hospital for hydrocephalus before transfer. On neurologic examination, she had mild limitation of upgaze and moderate axial hypotonia without dysmetria. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a large posterior fossa mass. Diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient sequences showed decreased diffusivity. On T2-weighted and post-gadolinium T1-weighted sequences, the lesion displayed an extensive, nodular, grape-like appearance. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed no evidence of leptomeningeal spread.
title: Medulloblastoma with Excessive Nodularity: Radiographic Features and Pathologic Correlate

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old woman presented with several months of progressive bilateral proptosis, decreased visual acuity, retrobulbar pressure, orbital pain, temporal-region swelling, and headaches. On evaluation in the emergency department, she was hemodynamically stable and neurologically intact. Ophthalmologic examination confirmed reduced visual acuity and more pronounced right-sided exophthalmos. Brain MRI demonstrated:
• Bilateral hyperostotic changes of the greater wings of the sphenoid bone, hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences.  
• Bilateral dural thickening and enhancement in the anterior temporal regions, invading the cavernous sinuses, prechiasmatic optic nerves, and lateral rectus muscles via the superior orbital fissures, with more marked involvement on the right.  
• Postcontrast sagittal images showed thickening and enhancement of the free border of the tentorium cerebelli and the retroclival dura.
title: A rare case of bilateral en plaque meningioma presenting as a bilateral exophthalmos. A case report

case_prompt: A 23-year-old man with a history of chronic suppurative otitis media and right ear conductive hearing loss underwent cholesteatoma resection in 2006, with two subsequent radical resections for recurrent cholesteatoma in 2009 and 2012. In March 2016, a routine MRI revealed a 30 mm hyperintense, non–contrast-enhancing mass in the right parotid gland. By July 2016, the mass had become painful, and in September 2016 the patient noted right-sided facial droop corresponding to grade 2 facial nerve dysfunction on the House–Brackmann scale. In October 2016, otoscopic and tympanoscopic examination showed typical postoperative changes but was negative for recurrent cholesteatoma. MRI sequences demonstrated a lesion with low to intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images and hyperintensity on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images.
title: Parotid gland cholesteatoma in a 23-year-old male: Case report

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old Caucasian woman with a remote 10-pack-year smoking history presented with worsening dyspnea, productive cough, and wheezing. She reported a 10-day history of progressively severe symptoms, although she noted subtle dyspnea over several months. Over the past year, she had four similar presentations, each treated empirically for presumed bacterial pneumonia with antibiotics and short courses of oral steroids; symptoms improved transiently but recurred shortly after completing steroids.

On examination, she was hypoxemic (O2 saturation 62% on room air) and visibly dyspneic, with diffuse wheezing heard throughout both lung fields. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (WBC 16.34 × 10^3/mcL) with eosinophilia (14.4%, absolute 2.4 × 10^3/mcL), C-reactive protein 5.95 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 52 mm/h. Review of prior records confirmed persistent eosinophilia over several years.

A chest radiograph demonstrated patchy interstitial and alveolar opacities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed multilobar, peripherally based ground-glass opacities. History and medication review did not identify a drug cause for eosinophilic pneumonia. Infectious and vasculitis evaluations, including ANA, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, rheumatoid factor, cyclic citrullinated peptide, strongyloides antibodies, aspergillus antibodies, COVID-19 PCR, influenza PCR, and RSV PCR, were negative. Serum IgE was elevated at 643.3 IU/mL.

She was admitted for acute hypoxic respiratory failure secondary to suspected eosinophilic pneumonia.
title: Recurrent pneumonia with persistent peripheral eosinophilia: Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old otherwise healthy man presented with a 1-year history of multiple, gradually enlarging dark-colored warty growths over the scrotum and buttocks. The lesions were asymptomatic. He reported unprotected heterosexual intercourse with multiple partners. He denied any history of genital ulceration or discharge.

On examination, there were multiple hyperpigmented annular plaques 1–3 cm in diameter with a verrucous surface and prominent ridge-like borders on a background of hyperpigmented, velvety skin. Lesions involved the ventral scrotum, medial thighs, and buttocks. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory investigations were within normal limits, and viral serologies (including HIV and HPV markers) were negative.
journal: Indian Journal of Sexually Transmitted Diseases and AIDS
title: Perineal warty plaques: A case of verrucous porokeratosis

case_prompt: A 61-year-old woman was evaluated for a gradually enlarging nodule on her back. Four years earlier, she had undergone total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Two years after the thyroidectomy, a local recurrence was excised. Subsequent evaluation for thoracic pain with CT imaging revealed multifocal osteolytic lesions in the sternum and other bones, cervical, axillary, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and nodules in both lungs and both adrenal glands. Two axillary masses were excised; histology showed papillary architecture, and thyroglobulin staining confirmed thyroid origin. On current examination, there was a single, well-circumscribed, firm, nonmobile, painless soft-tissue nodule on the left paraspinal region of the back. The lesion was surgically excised and submitted for histopathological evaluation.
title: Unusual case of parietal metastasis from papillary thyroid carcinoma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman, two weeks postpartum, was admitted with fever, palpitations, erythema, inflammation, and purulent discharge around her cesarean wound. Vital signs: temperature 37.3 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse rate 89 bpm. Initial labs: RBC 4.4×10^6/µL, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, hematocrit 36%, WBC 11.6×10^3/µL (neutrophils 73%, lymphocytes 18%), platelets 213×10^3/µL. She was diagnosed with a wound infection and treated with cefazolin, gentamicin, and metronidazole. On day 5, she developed hearing loss and gentamicin was discontinued. She has a history of substance use and is on methadone maintenance.

On hospital day 9, she developed nausea, vomiting, aphasia, loss of consciousness, hearing disturbances, extreme rigidity, and gaze deviation and was transferred to a tertiary center. Repeat labs: RBC 4.7×10^6/µL, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, WBC 15.4×10^3/µL (neutrophils 92%), AST 29 IU/L, ALT 18 IU/L, Na⁺ 136 mEq/L, K⁺ 4.4 mEq/L, CRP 33 mg/L, arterial blood gas pH 7.307, PCO₂ 26.9 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 13.2 mmol/L. Viral serologies and blood cultures were negative.

CSF analysis: clear fluid, WBC 0–1/µL, RBC 2/µL, protein 202 mg/dL, glucose 99 mg/dL; Gram stain and cultures negative; oligoclonal bands negative; IgG index 0.6; albumin index 5.4. A CSF viral pathogen panel was negative for EBV, CMV, HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, HHV-6, HHV-7, parvovirus B19, and enterovirus.

Brain MRI (axial T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI; sagittal and coronal T2) showed diffuse T2 hyperintense signal changes in the bilateral periventricular white matter and the corpus callosum.
title: A case report of toxic leukoencephalopathy induced by metronidazole in a woman with surgical site infection

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin and dulaglutide), hypertension, and a total right hip arthroplasty performed over one year earlier presented with one week of lateral right hip pain, poor appetite, and several episodes of vomiting. She denied urinary symptoms, illicit drug use, and recent travel; she cares for pet animals. In the emergency department she was afebrile and normotensive. Examination revealed dehydration, distress, and tenderness over the lateral aspect of the right hip; range of motion was limited by pain, and the surgical site appeared clean. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.
