Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 16,000 cells/ml with a left shift, blood glucose of 974 mg/dl, venous blood pH 7.29 with bicarbonate of 17 mEq/l and an anion gap of 20, lactic acid 4.8 mg/dl, C-reactive protein 67.8 mg/dl, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 112 mm/hour. Hemoglobin A1c was 13.9%. Chest radiograph was clear. The initial clinical suspicion was septic arthritis, and she received fluid resuscitation, insulin infusion, and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Anteroposterior radiograph of the right hip was unremarkable. Point-of-care ultrasound suggested a joint effusion. Computed tomography of the pelvis showed subcutaneous inflammatory stranding and heterogeneous attenuation of the musculature surrounding the right hip. Serum creatine kinase was elevated above 1200 U/l. Arthrocentesis yielded clear fluid; synovial fluid analysis revealed calcium pyrophosphate crystals, and cultures of the aspirate were sterile.
title: Primary MRSA Myositis Mimicking Septic Arthritis

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old Black woman was brought to the emergency department for agitation and alcohol intoxication after her family called 911 for what they described as a “nervous breakdown.” On arrival, her blood alcohol level was 255 mg/dL, and a urine drug screen was positive for cannabinoids. She was admitted for medical management of alcohol withdrawal with the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol Scale and oral lorazepam.

Her past medical history included alcohol use disorder, nonfunctional pituitary macroadenoma, adrenal insufficiency, and hypothyroidism. She had undergone four transsphenoidal pituitary tumor resections, the most recent five months earlier, followed by postoperative radiation therapy. Two years before admission, “heavy alcohol use” was noted in her record but was not addressed. Six months before admission, “Alcohol Abuse” was added to her problem list without counseling or follow-up.

On addiction psychiatry consultation, she reported a long history of social drinking that sharply increased five months earlier—immediately after her last surgery—when she felt depressed and anxious due to ongoing postoperative medical needs and social isolation. Since then, she had been drinking one pint of vodka on most days and felt distress and guilt about her drinking. Her reported impairment from alcohol use met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition criteria for moderate alcohol use disorder, and her mood and personality changes were thought to be substance-induced from the central nervous system effects of acute alcohol intoxication superimposed on chronic excessive alcohol use. 

The differential diagnoses considered also included abnormal hormone levels status postpartial pituitary resection, medication nonadherence for hormone replacement, adjustment disorder, major depressive disorder, and substance-induced depressive disorder.
title: Occult Untreated Alcohol Use Disorder in a Patient with Recurrent Pituitary Macroadenoma

case_prompt: A 54-year-old woman was seen for repeated swelling of her left cheek over the past seven years. On examination, there was a mild swelling beneath the left zygoma that was tender to palpation. The left maxillary buttress was fluctuant, and purulent drainage was noted from the posterior maxilla, suggestive of an infected lesion eroding the lateral maxillary wall. There was no clinical or radiologic evidence of pulpal or periodontal infection. An orthopantomograph showed a unilocular, well-defined radiolucency in the region of the left maxillary sinus. Computed tomography confirmed a unilocular lesion causing expansion of the sinus boundaries into the surrounding soft tissue. Her medical history was notable for a maxillary sinus surgery performed 8 years earlier.
title: Postoperative Maxillary Cyst: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old female presented to the ENT clinic with a long-standing history of right-sided nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. She denied facial pain, anosmia, epistaxis, or headache. Her medical, surgical, family, and social histories were unremarkable. 

On anterior rhinoscopy, there was a right-sided deviated nasal septum with mucopurulent discharge. Nasal endoscopy of the right nostril revealed a white, solid mass arising from the floor of the right nasal cavity, covered in secretions; the left side and the nasopharynx were normal. Examination of the throat and neck was also unremarkable.

A noncontrast CT scan of the paranasal sinuses showed an enveloped focal soft-tissue density insinuated between the medial surface of the right inferior turbinate and the bony nasal septum.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Should we floss our nose? A case report of a tooth in the nasal cavity

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old previously healthy male was transferred for management of acute hydrocephalus and intraventricular hemorrhage. He had a 3-day history of headache responsive to paracetamol, followed on the day of transfer by severe headache, persistent vomiting, and a decreased level of consciousness. On arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 9 of 15; pupils were equal and reactive bilaterally, and there was spontaneous movement of all limbs.

Noncontrast head CT showed a well-defined, lobulated mass measuring 6.0 × 5.0 × 3.0 cm filling the frontal horn and body of the right lateral ventricle. The mass was predominantly hyperdense with heterogeneous attenuation and areas of calcification; there was no gross contrast enhancement. The lesion displaced the septum pellucidum and extended across midline by about 3 cm, causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Hyperdense blood was noted in the dependent portions of both lateral ventricles and in the third and fourth ventricles.

An external ventricular drain was placed emergently, yielding bloody cerebrospinal fluid under high pressure. Preoperative MRI of the brain revealed a heterogeneous mass approximately 40 mm in maximal diameter within the right lateral ventricle. The lesion was hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images and showed no contrast enhancement. Findings were consistent with an intraventricular tumor associated with hemorrhage, most pronounced in the right lateral ventricle.
title: Central Neurocytoma with Hemorrhagic Presentation Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man who cycles 40–60 miles continuously several times per week presented in 2014 with palpitations occurring at the end of a cycling session. He had no significant dyspnea or chest pain. An ambulatory ECG showed short runs of focal atrial tachycardia and unifocal ectopy, and no further investigation was undertaken as symptoms resolved.

In 2019, he returned with recurrent palpitations associated with exercise and mild lower-limb swelling. He denied presyncope, and exercise capacity was preserved. There was no family history of heart disease or sudden death. Resting ECG showed sinus rhythm with frequent unifocal ventricular ectopy of left bundle–branch morphology and inferior axis. A 5-day Holter monitor captured non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, sinus pauses up to 5.2 seconds, and runs of narrow-complex tachycardia, though he remained asymptomatic during monitoring.

He underwent an exercise treadmill test to 94% of target heart rate (10 minutes on Bruce protocol), during which Stage 2 provoked ventricular bigeminy with a right ventricular outflow tract pattern that persisted through recovery. In light of exercise-provoked arrhythmia, he was advised to curtail exercise.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a moderately dilated right ventricle and right atrium with moderate-to-severe central tricuspid regurgitation and annular dilatation; the valve structure was normal. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed severe right atrial dilation, moderate right ventricular dilation with normal systolic function, moderate central tricuspid regurgitation, and no septal defects.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with an ARVC protocol demonstrated further right atrial and right ventricular enlargement, septal flattening, normal biventricular systolic function, and non–ischaemic late gadolinium enhancement in basal inferolateral segments. Task Force criteria for ARVC were not met. Computed tomography of the coronary and pulmonary vasculature showed no obstructive coronary disease, no shunts, and no anomalous venous drainage.
title: Exercise-induced right ventricular cardiomyopathy in an endurance cyclist: a case report

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old man presented with asymptomatic white lesions on the upper and lower lips, first noted several years ago. The lesions began on the lower lip and spread to the upper lip over two weeks, gradually increasing in number and size without itching or pain. He is a half-pack-per-day smoker with hypertension, prediabetes, and lower back pain; he takes no medications. There is no family history of skin disease or early-onset breast or colon cancer, and he has no signs of PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome.

On examination, his skin type is Fitzpatrick II, and he appears healthy. Three white, acanthotic round papules (2–6 mm) are present on the wet-dry vermilion border of the right upper lip. Two larger papules (7–8 mm) straddle the wet-dry border of the mid-lower lip. When the lower lip is stretched, three linear 1–2 mm papules become visible on the mucosal surface. 

Given his smoking history, initial differential diagnoses included leukoplakia, mucosal squamous cell carcinoma, mucosal lichen planus, and verruca. A decision was made to perform punch biopsies of the papules on both the upper and lower lips.
title: A rare presentation of glycogenic acanthosis on the lips: A case report

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 1-year history of bilateral pustules on the soles of his feet, later developing confluent pustules on the groin and interdigital spaces. Examination revealed nodulocystic acne on the face and back, bilateral plantar pustules with onychosis and anonychia, and confluent groin pustules. He was afebrile with normal vital signs. Laboratory studies showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (60 mm/h), elevated C-reactive protein (101 mg/L), mild leukocytosis (11 × 10^9/L), a negative HLA-B27 test, and a negative rheumatoid factor (<20 U/mL).  
Pelvic CT demonstrated hyperostosis and sclerosis of the right symphysis pubis, suggestive of Paget disease. The patient then reported polyarthralgia, chest pain, and swelling of the left sternoclavicular joint. Thoracic CT showed hyperostosis of the manubrium with irregularities and sclerosis of the manubriosternal, bilateral first sternocostal, and left sternoclavicular joints.
title: The challenging diagnosis of synovitis–acne–pustulosis–hyperostosis–osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome: A rare case report

case_prompt: A 26-year-old man presented three months after a mild SARS-CoV-2 infection with a one-month history of intermittent low-grade fevers, malaise, and a nonproductive cough. He also reported exertional dyspnea and a 5-kg weight loss over three months. On examination he was afebrile, vital signs were normal, lung fields were clear without added sounds, and there was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Initial chest radiography at one month after COVID-19 showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Repeat RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated discrete and confluent nodular opacities in the bilateral perihilar regions involving peribronchovascular and subpleural areas in all lobes, ground-glass opacities with areas of crazy-paving, consolidation in the right upper and middle lobes, and mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Pulmonary function testing showed an FEV1 of 92% predicted, FVC of 99% predicted, FEV1/FVC of 97%, DLCO of 71% predicted, and PEF of 89% predicted.
title: Sarcoidosis in a young adult: A rare sequelae of COVID‐19 infection

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man presented with 2 months of progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and bilateral leg swelling. He also reported a 2-week history of cough productive of whitish, frothy sputum. There was no fever, facial swelling, or reduction in urine output, and no history of recurrent sore throats. He denied hypertension or diabetes. He consumed approximately 120 g of alcohol daily for 5 years and did not smoke.

On examination, he was dyspneic and cyanotic (respiratory rate 30/min, SpO₂ 78% on room air). Pulse was 110/min and regular; blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg. He had bilateral pitting edema to the knees and jugular venous pressure elevated to the angle of the jaw. The apex beat was heaving and displaced to the 7th left intercostal space, anterior axillary line. A left parasternal heave and palpable P₂ were present. Auscultation revealed an S₃, a grade 3/6 pansystolic murmur at both the mitral and tricuspid areas, a systolic ejection murmur in the pulmonary area, a widely split and fixed S₂, and a loud P₂. Bibasal fine crackles were heard. The abdomen showed tender, soft, pulsatile hepatomegaly with ascites. Other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies demonstrated mild elevation of total and conjugated bilirubin; liver enzymes, glucose, renal function, complete blood count, clotting profile, lipid profile, and serologies for hepatitis B, C, and HIV were normal. Chest radiography showed plethoric lung fields, a prominent pulmonary conus, and cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio of 0.80. ECG revealed left atrial enlargement, right ventricular hypertrophy, and incomplete right bundle branch block.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed:
• A large ostium secundum atrial septal defect measuring 27 mm with left-to-right shunt  
• Mild mitral stenosis (mitral valve area 3.0 cm² by planimetry and 2.4 cm² by pressure half-time; mean gradient 0.74 cm²) with thickened, partly calcified leaflets and uniformly restricted motion, plus bicommissural calcification  
• Severe mitral and tricuspid regurgitation and moderate pulmonary regurgitation  
• Pulmonary hypertension (estimated mean pulmonary arterial pressure 51 mmHg)  
• Preserved left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 67%) and impaired right ventricular systolic function (TAPSE 15 mm)  
• Biventricular diastolic dysfunction, dilated right ventricle, left and right atria, and spontaneous echo contrast in all chambers
title: Lutembacher syndrome presenting as heart failure in a young Nigerian at Obafemi Awolowo University Teaching Hospitals Complex (OAUTHC), Ile-Ife: a case report

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of multiple radio-opaque ovoid or circular lesions noted on an ankle radiograph obtained after an ankle sprain. He was asymptomatic with no history of fractures, bone pain, or other illness. His medications history was unremarkable. Family history was notable only for paternal hypertension; no bone disease was reported.

On examination, he appeared well. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was unremarkable except for a mild ocular squint; there were no skin lesions or bone tenderness.

Laboratory studies showed normal alkaline phosphatase activity, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, antinuclear antibodies, serum electrolytes, and tumor markers. The only abnormality was a mild vitamin D deficiency.

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right ankle showed multiple small, well-demarcated sclerotic lesions in the epiphysis and metaphysis of the tibia and fibula. Subsequent pelvis and bilateral hand radiographs confirmed numerous similar enostoses symmetrically distributed in the epiphyses and metaphyses. The pelvic film also demonstrated longitudinal bands of confluent sclerotic lesions extending from the epiphyses into the metaphyses.
title: Familiar osteopoikilosis: Case report with differential diagnosis and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 15-year-old girl was evaluated for recurrent episodes of transient paralysis beginning at age 1. During these episodes she remained fully conscious but had paralysis affecting half of her body—alternating sides or both sides simultaneously—and difficulty speaking. There was no associated or preceding vomiting, fever, seizures, loss of consciousness, or headache. Episodes lasted from a few hours to several days and recurred every 10–30 days without leaving any residual deficit. The paralysis always resolved after a good night’s sleep and reappeared within 30 minutes of awakening; she was dysarthric when the hemiplegia was unilateral and mute when it was bilateral. After seven years of these episodes, she developed ataxia and deterioration of cognitive function, and she lagged in developmental milestones. She was born at term after an uneventful pregnancy to nonconsanguineous parents, with no family history of similar illness or migraine. Multiple neuroimaging studies performed on different occasions were normal.
title: More Than a Decade of Misdiagnosis of Alternating Hemiplegia of Childhood with Catastrophic Outcome

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old Caucasian man was referred for a routine dental evaluation. He was asymptomatic.  
– Panoramic, occlusal, and periapical radiographs showed a unilocular radiolucent area with a well‐circumscribed sclerotic border in the anterior right maxilla.  
– All maxillary teeth except the left cuspid had been removed uneventfully over the years; the most recent extractions were 7 years earlier.  
– He had no history of trauma or surgery to the maxilla, was a non‐smoker, and reported no other illnesses.  
– On examination, the alveolus was of normal consistency with no expansion or swelling; there was no pain, tenderness, or change in the color of the overlying mucosa, and no lymphadenopathy.
title: An unusual presentation of an intraosseous epidermoid cyst of the anterior maxilla: a case report

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old Chinese Han woman presented with a 10-year history of constant left pulsatile tinnitus that had become unbearable and interfered with sleep. She had seen multiple otologists; each otoscopic exam was normal, and a temporal bone CT 9 years earlier was negative. She had been labeled as having a venous hum and received no effective treatment. Over the preceding 2 years she noted gradual hearing deterioration in the left ear. Her medical history was notable only for treated hypertension.

On examination, the pulsatile tinnitus was completely suppressed by digital pressure over the left internal jugular vein or by turning the head toward the affected side. Cranial, carotid, and chest auscultation were negative. Carotid ultrasonography, electrocardiography, thyroid function tests, and chest radiography were normal. Otoscopy revealed a vague, reddish mass behind the superior- posterior quadrant of an intact left tympanic membrane.

A pure-tone audiogram showed moderately severe conductive hearing loss in the left ear, most pronounced at low frequencies; tympanometry demonstrated a flat left tympanogram. High-resolution CT of the temporal bone revealed a slightly ill-defined soft tissue mass in the left middle ear involving the posterior mesotympanum, epitympanum, and mastoid antrum, with erosive changes of the facial fallopian canal and an indistinct margin between the lesion and the incus; the lateral semicircular canal was intact.
title: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor of the temporal bone presenting with pulsatile tinnitus: a case report

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old woman with a history of asthma (treated with formoterol and budesonide) and multiparity presented with a 7-year history of an intensely painful bulge in her left iliac fossa. The 15 cm elongated protrusion increased with exertion and Valsalva maneuvers (eg, evacuation, urination). Over time, a smaller, less painful bulge appeared on the right side. She denied weight loss, changes in appetite, or bowel habits.

On examination, her abdomen was globose without scars. There were bilateral bulges along the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, more prominent on the left. Peristalsis was normal. Both bulges were asymmetrically distended, mobile on Valsalva, and manually reducible, with no signs of entrapment or strangulation.

An abdominal CT scan demonstrated herniation of intestinal loops in the anterior lower abdominal wall to the left of the umbilical scar, containing adipose tissue, and no signs of bowel compromise. A right inguinal hernia was also noted.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Spigelian hernia diagnosis: Case report

case_prompt: A 39-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department with one month of progressive dyspnea on exertion and two syncopal episodes over the previous ten days. She also described intermittent chest pain radiating to her upper extremities and the right side of her back, and she noted bilateral lower-extremity swelling for one month. On examination, her blood pressure was 235/148 mm Hg, and an electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia without other abnormalities. A point-of-care echocardiogram revealed an abnormal soft tissue density in the right atrium, right ventricle, and inferior vena cava. A subsequent CT pulmonary angiogram showed a small subsegmental pulmonary embolism in the left lower lobe and a 4.2 cm hypoattenuating area in the right atrium suggestive of an atrial thrombus, along with relative enlargement of the inferior vena cava. A 2D Doppler echocardiogram measured a 2.4 × 2.0 cm echogenic mass, and cardiac MRI confirmed a large mass originating in the inferior vena cava that was prolapsing across the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
title: Point of care ultrasound facilitated diagnosis of right ventricular mass as the etiology of syncope; A case report of intravenous leiomyomatosis

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive dyspnea, decreased exercise tolerance, and a heavy sensation in her chest. She denied fever, weight loss, hemoptysis, or constitutional symptoms. There was no history of recent surgery or trauma. She took no medications and had no substance use.  

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Breath sounds were decreased over the right hemithorax with dullness to percussion; there was no peripheral edema, ascites, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly.  

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 5.9×10^9/L, hematocrit 44%, platelets 192×10^9/L, creatinine and liver-function tests within normal limits, albumin 42 g/L, and total protein 76 g/L.  

A chest radiograph demonstrated a large right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis revealed turbid, milky fluid. Pleural‐fluid analysis showed a triglyceride level of 79 mmol/L with chylomicrons, cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L, and lymphocyte predominance; cytology demonstrated lymphocytosis but no malignant cells, and flow cytometry of the fluid was negative for B‐cell or T‐cell lymphoma.  

A PET-CT scan revealed a PET-avid, bulky intraperitoneal mass encasing vessels around the abdominal aorta and pancreas, extending into the pelvic inlet. There were no mediastinal lymphadenopathy or suspicious pelvic lesions.
title: Rapid Decline of Follicular Lymphoma-Associated Chylothorax after Low Dose Radiotherapy to Retroperitoneal Lymphoma Localization

case_prompt: A 42-year-old Japanese man was admitted with a 4-day history of headache, nausea, and progressive gait instability. Neurologic examination revealed mild ataxia but no focal deficits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a 58-mm mass in the frontal lobe with prominent cystic components; T1-weighted post-gadolinium images showed ring enhancement, and T2-weighted images revealed only slight surrounding edema. Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy of the solid nodule showed an increased choline-to-creatine ratio and an apparent lactate peak, whereas the N-acetylaspartate peak was within background noise. On the basis of these neuroimaging findings, a primary malignant brain tumor such as glioblastoma multiforme or a metastatic brain tumor was suspected.
title: Mixed Germ Cell Tumor with Extensive Yolk Sac Tumor Elements in the Frontal Lobe of an Adult

case_prompt: A 12-year-old boy presented with a firm, bulging mass over the plantar aspect of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint that had been present for more than a year. The overlying skin was erythematous but the lesion was non-tender and there were no systemic signs of infection. Ultrasound showed a multilobulated, heterogeneous hypo- and hyperechoic mass with increased internal vascular flow along the flexor hallucis longus tendon. An initial surgical excision yielded a histopathologic diagnosis of localized tenosynovial giant cell tumor without further immunohistochemical testing. Four months later, he returned with a larger recurrent mass at the same location, now associated with throbbing pain and skin erosion. Hematologic laboratory tests were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the right foot revealed a lobulated mass measuring approximately 3.1 × 2.1 × 5.0 cm abutting the flexor hallucis longus tendon; the lesion demonstrated iso- to high signal intensity on T2/proton-density–weighted images, marked homogeneous enhancement, nonenhancing dark signal foci, and partial infiltration into adjacent muscle.
title: Histiocytic sarcoma mimicking localized tenosynovial giant cell tumor in the pediatric foot: A rare case report with MRI Findings

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man without prior medical history presented with 4 hours of severe, continuous, compressive left-sided chest pain radiating to the left hand, aggravated by exertion, relieved by nitroglycerine, and accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. He denied fever, dyspnea, palpitations, or trauma. He quit smoking 10 years ago and stopped opium 3 months ago. He arrived hypotensive (85/55 mmHg on norepinephrine), tachycardic (103 bpm), and afebrile (36.9°C), with cold lower extremities and an otherwise unremarkable chest, abdominal, heart, and lung exam.

An initial ECG showed ST depression in V5 and V6, which later resolved with T-wave inversion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal-sized left ventricle with severe systolic dysfunction (LVEF 15–20%) and global hypokinesia, an enlarged right ventricle with mild dysfunction, mild mitral regurgitation, and mild to moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Coronary angiography demonstrated significant mid–left anterior descending artery stenosis, and simultaneous aortography showed no evidence of dissection; the LAD lesion was stented.

Laboratory studies showed troponin 1.5 ng/dL (normal <2), D-dimer 280 ng/mL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 68 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 56 mg/dL, and white blood cell count 10.4×10^3/µL (92.7% neutrophils). After ruling out cardiogenic shock from acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, and pericardial tamponade based on ECG, echocardiography, angiography, and basic labs, suspicion for septic shock arose. Empirical antibiotics were initiated, and further investigations including chest CT, blood cultures, liver enzymes, urine analysis, and urine culture failed to identify a source.
title: Necrotizing fasciitis resembled acute coronary syndrome: A case report

case_prompt: A postmenopausal woman in her 60s presented with two episodes of vaginal bleeding over the past year. Cervical cytology demonstrated changes consistent with high-grade dyskaryosis and invasive squamous carcinoma. On cervical biopsy, histomorphology showed features suggestive of poorly differentiated invasive keratinizing squamous (basaloid) cell carcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor tissue revealed positive expression of chromogranin, synaptophysin, pancytokeratin, TTP1, and CEA and negative expression of p40 and estrogen receptor. A mixed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with a neuroendocrine tumor component was suggested. The tumor was staged as pT1b1pN0 (FIGO stage IB1). Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging showed a 2.7 × 1.8 × 3.2 cm mass in the lower uterine body and cervix, with an ulceroproliferative growth measuring 1.8 × 1.5 × 1.2 cm on the posterior lip of the cervix. The parametrium and pelvic walls were normal. The depth of invasion was 1.8 cm with evidence of lymphovascular emboli.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Neuroendocrine carcinoma of cervix and review literature

case_prompt: A 58-year-old woman with a history of childhood acute rheumatic fever and resultant mitral stenosis presented with palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain. On examination, she had hepatomegaly and a 3/6 systolic murmur at the mitral focus. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation in all leads. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed severe mitral stenosis, tricuspid insufficiency, and a 5-cm mass with areas of calcification on the superior wall of the left atrium; the left atrium measured 17 × 13 cm. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. The patient underwent mitral valve replacement, tricuspid De Vega annuloplasty and plication, and resection of the giant left atrium. A 5 × 1.5 × 1 cm gelatinous, soft, brown, hemorrhagic lesion was removed from the atrial wall and sent for histopathological examination.
title: Lesion of Aggregated Monocytes and Mesothelial Cells: Mesothelial/Monocytic Incidental Cardiac Lesion

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old nulligravid Caucasian woman presented with a 1-day history of transient blurry vision, apraxia, aphasia, chest tightness, and anxiety. She had a longstanding history of dry skin, abnormal menses with menorrhagia and increasing polymenorrhea, chronic diarrhea alternating with constipation, and a recent 20-lb weight gain. One month earlier she noted galactorrhea with breast enlargement and tenderness. Three weeks before presentation, her gynecologist found TSH >150 mIU/mL (0.5–5.5), free T4 0.4 ng/dL (0.61–1.82), and prolactin 29.4 ng/mL (3.34–26.72); an MRI at that time showed a 14×12 mm pituitary enlargement abutting the optic chiasm. 

On admission, she denied neck pain or swelling, recent infections, iodine exposure, and steroid use. Medications included amphetamine, nebivolol, clonazepam, citalopram, hydrochlorothiazide, polyethylene glycol, and levocetirizine. Family history was notable for a sister with hyperthyroidism but no pituitary disorders.

Vital signs: BMI 41.5 kg/m2, BP 110/89 mm Hg, HR 62 bpm, RR 14, O2 sat 96% on room air. Physical exam: obese, dry skin, no thyromegaly, normal neurologic and visual-field exam.

Laboratory studies: TSH 251.21 mIU/mL, total T4 2.07 µg/dL (4.87–11.72), free T4 0.44 ng/dL, free T3 1.5 pg/mL (2.2–4.2), prolactin 29.48 ng/mL (3.34–26.72), estradiol 20 pg/mL, LH 2.52 mIU/mL, FSH 5.03 mIU/mL, morning cortisol 8 µg/dL, ACTH 10 pg/mL (6–58), IGF-1 109 ng/mL (108–368), thyroglobulin antibody 4.9 IU/mL (0–4), thyroglobulin 159 ng/mL (1.3–31.8), microsomal antibody 1096.2 IU/mL (0–9), alpha subunit 3.4 ng/mL (<1.02).

A repeat pituitary MRI showed a 13×10.1 mm enlarged gland with slightly decreased optic chiasm involvement.
title: Pituitary Hyperplasia in Severe Primary Hypothyroidism: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: 19-year-old woman at 33 weeks’ gestation presented with 1 week of progressive dyspnea. Over the prior 3 months she had noted an 8-cm painful mass on the left side of her neck and developed dysphonia. On indirect laryngoscopy, a left hemilaryngeal tumor occupied >50% of the glottic lumen, with left vocal cord fixation and displacement of the right vocal cord. An urgent tracheotomy was performed, and labor was induced successfully the same day. Core needle biopsy of a left cervical lymph node and biopsy of the laryngeal mass revealed densely packed cells with uniform laminar invasive growth, nuclear hyperchromasia, nuclear molding, scant cytoplasm, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, necrosis, and a high mitotic rate; the overlying laryngeal epithelium showed no dysplasia. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated strong diffuse positivity for p63, synaptophysin, CD56, CD57, and p16; focal positivity for vimentin and CD99; and negativity for CD45, chromogranin, TTF-1, desmin, myogenin, p40, CK5/6, CK20, TdT, and S-100 protein. Ki-67 was 100%. Cervical CT showed a 3.5-cm mass in the left glottic and supraglottic region extending to the epiglottis and pyriform sinus, with airway narrowing, and an adenopathic conglomerate measuring 7.2 × 3.5 cm in left cervical level II. Thoracoabdominal CT and bronchoscopy revealed no additional lesions.
title: An unusual neck tumor in a young pregnant woman: challenge diagnosis and response to treatment

case_prompt: A 28-year-old African American man with a history of tobacco use presented with a 3-day history of lumbar back pain and posterior left lower extremity pain. He denied recent trauma, prolonged immobilization, prior thromboembolism, or a family history of clotting disorders. Vital signs showed a heart rate of 104 bpm. On examination, the left thigh was warm and tender, with moderate nonpitting edema of the left lower extremity. Laboratory testing revealed a white-cell count of 10.9 ×10^3/µL, platelets 743 ×10^3/µL, C-reactive protein 286 mg/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L, and a D-dimer >4.40 µg/mL. An electrocardiogram showed left ventricular hypertrophy and sinus tachycardia. Point-of-care ultrasound of the left leg demonstrated noncompressibility of the left common femoral vein, the saphenofemoral junction, the confluence of the superficial and deep femoral veins, and the popliteal vein. Computed tomography angiography of the chest was negative for pulmonary embolism. Computed tomography angiography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an occlusive thrombus in the left superficial and deep femoral veins extending into the left common femoral vein and into the left external, internal, and common iliac veins, with compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery.
title: May-Thurner Syndrome—a Rare Cause of Extensive Pelvic DVT, but Is there More to Know?

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 4 chronic kidney disease presented with four weeks of progressive dyspnoea, cough, weight loss, and new haemoptysis. He had a left brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula created 34 months earlier that had never been used for haemodialysis. Three months before presentation, he developed swelling and warmth at the fistula site; duplex ultrasound confirmed partial fistula thrombosis, and over the next month he reported pain and tenderness consistent with mild thrombophlebitis.

In respiratory clinic, he had a 60 pack-year smoking history, possible asbestos exposure, and a prominent swelling over the AVF. He was admitted with bilateral pleural effusions and severe anaemia (hemoglobin 64 g/L; baseline 110 g/L). CT of the thorax revealed bilateral pulmonary and pleural nodular and mass-like opacities with bilateral pleural and pericardial effusions. A chest drain yielded strongly blood-stained fluid; cytology showed non-specific inflammatory cells and no malignant cells.

On admission he was febrile with erythema at the AVF site, diagnosed as cellulitis and treated with intravenous flucloxacillin. He received 2 units of packed red blood cells. Coagulation studies were normal and platelet counts remained within the reference range despite aspirin use; he was not on anticoagulants. Renal surgeons assessed the arm lesion and suggested a distal fistula aneurysm with proximal haematoma. Given the lesion’s unusual appearance, a decision was made to proceed to surgery. On Day 5, the necrotic soft tissue mass and associated haematoma were excised, the thrombosed fistula ligated, and loose closure performed; tissue was sent for histological analysis.
title: Multi-system bleeding risk with a cutaneous angiosarcoma at an arteriovenous fistula site

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman presented with a five-day history of worsening abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting. On examination she was peritonitic, tachycardic, hypotensive, tachypneic, and required 4 L of supplemental oxygen. Three months earlier she had been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma with brain metastases and treated with craniotomy, CyberKnife radiotherapy, and a tapering course of oral dexamethasone (reduced to 2 mg three times daily at presentation). She was not on Pneumocystis prophylaxis.

Abdominal CT demonstrated perforation of the large bowel secondary to diverticulitis, and chest CT showed bilateral, patchy ground-glass opacities in both central and peripheral lung fields. She underwent emergency subtotal colectomy and ileostomy formation. Postoperatively, she was managed as COVID-19 pneumonia. However, five RT-PCR tests for SARS-CoV-2 (nose and throat swabs on days 1 and 10, bronchoalveolar-lavage samples on days 2 and 4, and endotracheal secretions on day 13) were negative. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, she remained febrile with persistently elevated inflammatory markers, progressive bilateral ground-glass opacities on repeat CT, and failure to wean from mechanical ventilation. On postoperative day 13, an alternative diagnosis was sought.
title: A diagnostic conundrum in the context of a pandemic of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19)

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old man was referred for evaluation of chronic perineal and pelvic pain. Thirty-five years earlier, after attending a party in a damp basement, he developed pollakisuria, dysuria, and a persistent foreign-body sensation in the prostate, anus, and perineum. He also reported a burning urethral sensation, a slightly reduced urinary stream, and nocturia. He experienced episodic increases in pain lasting weeks to months, with no identifiable triggers, and noted progressive worsening over time.

Over the years, he underwent multiple urological evaluations and received empirical antibiotic therapies, analgesics, nerve stimulation therapy, and a trial surgical removal of both seminal vesicles with extension surgery on the anus. None of these measures provided relief. He was taking gabapentin, diclofenac, oxycodone, and amitriptyline for nine years. His NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index score was 39 (pain 18, urinary symptoms 10, quality-of-life impact 11).

On examination, rectal palpation elicited pain in the lesser pelvis, but the prostate was inconspicuous. Pelvic sonography showed 50 ml of postvoid residual urine. His PSA level was 0.4 ng/ml.
title: Severe Case of Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome: Recovery after Injection of Procaine into the Vesicoprostatic Plexus—Case Report and Discussion of Pathophysiology and Mechanisms of Action

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of bleeding from the left nasal cavity and mild left eye proptosis. On examination, he had marked deviation of the nasal septum and a pinkish mass occupying the left nasal cavity.  
  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses and orbits showed a soft-tissue mass filling the left ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses, extending into the left nasal cavity, eroding the nasal septum, invading the left orbit, and extending intracranially into the basifrontal region.  
  
Endoscopic biopsy revealed a poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm composed of small to intermediate cells with scant cytoplasm and frequent mitoses. The mitotic count was 30–40 per 10 high-power fields.  
   
Immunohistochemical staining showed that the tumor cells were positive for cytokeratin, synaptophysin, and chromogranin, and negative for S-100.
title: Paranasal Sinus Neuroendocrine Carcinoma: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of the absence of menstruation. She weighed 66.8 kg and was 1.58 m tall. Physical examination showed normal breast development and normal axillary and pubic hair. Gynecologic examination revealed normal external genitalia with an intact hymen. On rectal examination, no uterus was palpable. Vaginometry with a cotton swab demonstrated a vaginal depth of approximately 8 cm.  
Segmental skeletal examination and radiographs of the hands and feet showed bilateral shortening of the fourth metacarpals, a small hallux, short and pointed distal phalanges, and clinodactyly. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a short-sized, solid-appearing uterus (14 cm3) without a visible uterine cavity; the right ovary measured 1.7 cm, and the left ovary was not visualized. Renal ultrasound showed a hypotrophic right kidney and a normal left kidney.  
Chromosomal analysis demonstrated a normal 46,XX karyotype. Plasma levels of follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, prolactin, and thyroid-stimulating hormone were within normal limits.
title: Hand-foot-genital syndrome - analysis of two cases

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 7-month-old male infant was referred for a 2-week history of intermittent fever up to 39 °C. He had received a 2-week course of oral cefotaxime-clavulanic acid for acute otitis media. Three days before presentation, he became continuously irritable and cried persistently.  
On examination, he was normoxic and breathing comfortably. A tender, mildly erythematous swelling (4 × 3 cm) was noted on the left anterior chest wall without any history of trauma.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 22,000/mm3 (neutrophils 15,000/mm3) and a C-reactive protein level of 240 mg/L.  
A chest radiograph demonstrated soft-tissue thickening over the lower left chest wall.  
Ultrasound of the mass revealed a heterogeneous fluid collection (3 cm) surrounding the middle arch of the left seventh rib, with irregular cortical lysis of the rib.
title: Staphylococcus aureus costal osteomyelitis with complicated by pleural effusion in a 7-month-old infant: A misleading clinical presentation

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 20-day history of dull, aching, nonradiating low back pain. Over the same period, he noted gradual numbness in both lower limbs and developed urinary and bowel retention. Within one week before admission, he became paraplegic.  
On examination, power in both lower limbs was grade 0 except for grade 1 plantar flexion. There was complete sensory loss below the T10 level. Muscle tone was increased with exaggerated deep tendon reflexes and clonus bilaterally. Sphincter disturbance required catheterization.  
A thoracolumbar spine radiograph was unremarkable except for slight loss of lumbar lordosis.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine revealed an irregular intramedullary lesion behind the body of L1, predominantly on the right side, displacing the cord to the left. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was hyperintense; on T2-weighted images, it was isointense relative to the normal cord. After gadolinium administration, there was only slight enhancement of the lesion’s surrounding wall.
title: Intradural Intramedullary Mixed Type Hemangioma: Optimizing the Surgical Management through Intraoperative Neurophysiological Monitoring

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old man, previously healthy, presented with a 6-month history of bilateral knee pain and a palpable mass over the left proximal fibula. He described pain with activity but denied numbness, tingling, or weakness in the peroneal nerve distribution. On examination, there was a firm, non–tender swelling at the head and neck of the left fibula; the right fibular region was not palpable. Distal motor and sensory function of the lower extremities was intact.

Plain radiographs of the left knee demonstrated an expansile, lytic lesion involving the epimetaphyseal region of the proximal fibula without periosteal reaction. Radiographs of the right knee revealed a smaller, similar-appearing lesion at the proximal fibular neck. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee showed a well-defined, expansile intramedullary lesion extending to the subchondral bone without soft-tissue invasion.
title: Bicentric Synchronous Giant cell tumor: A Rare Managed Case Report of Bilateral Fibula Neck Tumor

case_prompt: A 39-year-old woman presented with anal pain and protrusion during defecation. Her medical and family history were unremarkable. On examination, there was an approximately 1-cm, well-circumscribed, umbilicated, reddish nodule on the anus, in association with prolapsed internal hemorrhoids. Laboratory studies, including white-cell count, hemoglobin, platelet count, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate transaminase, were within normal limits. Viral markers for hepatitis B and serologic studies for immunocompromise were negative. Anoscopy confirmed multiple internal hemorrhoids. Endoanal ultrasound showed normal findings with no evidence of abscess or fistula. The patient underwent hemorrhoidectomy and excisional biopsy of the mass under caudal block.
title: Hidradenoma Papilliferum of the Anus: A Report of 2 Cases and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old previously healthy male was admitted with a 3-week history of daily emesis, constipation, and lethargy. He also reported decreased appetite, a 3 kg weight loss, vague periumbilical pain, and mood changes with low energy and social withdrawal. He denied bone or joint pain, fever, or night sweats. The family had immigrated from the Philippines one week before symptom onset. 

On examination, he appeared cachectic (weight 37 kg, BMI 14.1 kg/m²), alert and oriented. Neurological examination was normal. In the left lower quadrant, there was a large (10 × 5 cm), irregular, tender, mobile abdominal mass. 

Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• Corrected serum calcium 4.30 mmol/L (normal 2.14–2.65)  
• Phosphate 0.58 mmol/L (0.74–1.52)  
• Intact parathyroid hormone 51.7 pmol/L (1.3–6.8)  
• 25-hydroxyvitamin D 45.4 nmol/L (70–250)  

A plain abdominal radiograph revealed marked fecal loading and a well-defined lytic lesion in the left iliac wing. Contrast CT and MR imaging of the pelvis demonstrated a 13 × 5.1 × 5.8 cm lytic lesion with scalloped margins and a T2-intense soft-tissue component slightly extending beyond the anterior table of the iliac bone.
title: Severe hypercalcemia and a pelvic brown tumor in an adolescent with primary hyperparathyroidism: a case report

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old married woman was evaluated in an outpatient psychiatric clinic in February 2016, 2.5 months after the birth of her first child. Over the preceding 2 months, she had been hospitalized three times for acute episodes marked by auditory hallucinations and delusions with sexual themes and religious preoccupation, disorganized behavior, social withdrawal, anhedonia, and excessive guilt. There was no prior psychiatric history before the postpartum period. Imaging studies and laboratory tests ruled out organic neurologic causes, and a urine drug screen was negative. Upon discharge from her most recent hospitalization, she was given a working differential of postpartum psychosis, major depressive disorder with psychotic features (postpartum onset), and schizophrenia. 

Initial medications included oral paliperidone and divalproex sodium, followed by paliperidone palmitate long-acting injection. After another psychotic relapse, paliperidone was switched to risperidone with partial improvement of positive symptoms but persistent internal preoccupation and restricted affect. Side effects of fatigue, weight gain, and sedation led to poor adherence. 

Over the next year, she experienced discrete psychotic episodes both with and without prominent mood symptoms. When mood symptoms were present, they alternated between depressed affect with low energy and, less frequently, expansive affect with pressured speech and increased energy. Despite trials of multiple antipsychotic and mood-stabilizing regimens, psychotherapy, and eleven sessions of electroconvulsive therapy, she continued to have residual delusions, mood symptoms, functional impairment (inability to work, drive, or care for her child), and ultimately a suicide attempt in 2019.
title: Treatment of a resistant case of schizoaffective disorder with lumateperone: A case report

case_prompt: A 74-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus for 13 years and a history of coronary artery bypass grafting and recent percutaneous coronary intervention presented with a one-week history of fever, vomiting, and dyspnea. His temperature was 38.0°C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Auscultation revealed coarse inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. Chest radiography showed patchy bilateral lung consolidation and a pleural effusion. Influenza type B was confirmed, and aspiration pneumonia was diagnosed. Esophagogastroscopy demonstrated chronic gastritis and an esophageal ulcer. A percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube was placed for recurrent vomiting, but vomiting and aspiration persisted. He also complained of neck pain when he positioned his head up.
journal: Korean Journal of Critical Care Medicine
title: Recurrent Aspiration Pneumonia due to Anterior Cervical Osteophyte

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, headache, photophobia, fever, anorexia, abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. He is a gardener living in a rodent-infested informal settlement. He has a history of weekend binge ethanol use. There was no recent travel. On examination, he was tachycardic (128 bpm), hypotensive (69/35 mmHg), febrile (38.1 °C) and profoundly jaundiced with prominent conjunctival suffusion. Lung auscultation revealed left lower–zone crackles; the abdomen was generally tender with guarding. He received fluid resuscitation, vasopressors and empiric ceftriaxone. 
Laboratory studies showed CRP 349 mg/L, leukocytes 20.21×10^9/L, blood urea nitrogen 20.8 mmol/L, creatinine 331 μmol/L, total bilirubin 126 μmol/L (conjugated 109 μmol/L), ALT 35 U/L, AST 98 U/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, albumin 28 g/L, platelets 38×10^9/L; INR 1.23, fibrinogen 9.0 g/L, D-dimer 1.05 mg/L. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis: protein 0.41 g/L, glucose 3.7 mmol/L, 2 lymphocytes, 40 erythrocytes, no polymorphs, negative Gram stain and culture. HIV serology was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal CT revealed peri-appendiceal fluid but, on surgical review, findings were inconsistent with appendicitis.
journal: Southern African Journal of Infectious Diseases
title: Deeply jaundiced: Not so surgical after all

case_prompt: A 45‐year‐old woman presented with a 6‐month history of a progressively enlarging ulcerated mass in her right breast. She reported no prior breast trauma, radiation exposure, or family history of breast cancer. On examination, there was a large, lobulated, ulcerated mass replacing the right breast. Her hemoglobin level was 7.5 g/dL. Chest radiography and abdominal imaging showed no abnormalities. Fine‐needle aspiration cytology of the mass was reported as suggestive of carcinoma of the breast. The patient underwent a modified radical mastectomy. The surgical specimen measured 24 × 15 × 13 cm, with a 14 × 9 × 6 cm skin flap. On the skin surface, there was a large gray‐white lobulated ulcerated growth. On serial sectioning, an ill‐defined gray‐white mass measuring 18 × 15 × 12 cm was seen, extending to within 0.8 cm of the resection margin; the cut surface was solid with areas of necrosis and cystic change. Ten axillary lymph nodes were isolated and appeared grossly uninvolved.
title: Primary Stromal Sarcoma of Breast: A Rare Entity

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with nine days of high-grade fevers and chills in a diurnal pattern, associated with fatigue. Four days before admission she was treated with amoxicillin–clavulanate for presumed tonsillopharyngitis. Three days into her illness she developed nausea and multiple episodes of bilious vomiting, followed by severe, colicky right upper quadrant abdominal pain without clear aggravating or relieving factors. She had traveled from her home island to the capital two days before symptom onset.

On examination, she appeared dehydrated, jaundiced, and toxic. Temperature was 39 °C, heart rate 110 beats/min, and mean arterial pressure 73 mmHg. She had pharyngitis and palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed a positive Murphy’s sign and guarding in the right upper quadrant.

Laboratory studies showed lymphocytosis and monocytosis with normal total leukocytes and platelets, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminases, marked hyperferritinemia, and an elevated C-reactive protein level. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated gallbladder wall edema with a positive sonographic Murphy’s sign. CT of the abdomen revealed hepatosplenomegaly, and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography confirmed acute acalculous cholecystitis.

The patient was admitted and treated with intravenous fluids, cefotaxime, metronidazole, and analgesics.
title: Acalculous Cholecystitis in a Young Adult with Scrub Typhus: A Case Report and Epidemiology of Scrub Typhus in the Maldives

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old man was evaluated for a 30-year history of a gradually evolving papulonodular eruption involving the face, flexural areas, and trunk. On examination, there were multiple, well-defined, yellowish-brown papules and nodules symmetrically distributed on the upper and lower eyelids, cheeks, and perioral region. On the anterior neck, lesions were confluent, forming a diffuse plaque. Numerous red-brown papules were symmetrically present in the axillae, genitalia, popliteal fossae, and trunk, with some coalescing into plaques or tumor-like lesions. Small papules and nodules were also noted on the nasal mucosa.  

He reported no polyuria or other systemic symptoms. Urine osmolality testing was normal. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10,300 cells/mm3 (74% neutrophils), a C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (reference <0.5), a fasting cholesterol level of 148 mg/dL, and a triglyceride level of 141 mg/dL. A chest radiograph and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary gland were unremarkable.  

Skin-biopsy specimens revealed a dense, diffuse dermal infiltrate of histiocytes with intermixed inflammatory cells and giant cells, abundant foam cells, and no neural involvement. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD68 and negative for S-100 protein.
title: Xanthoma Disseminatum with Tumor-Like Lesion on Face

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old Yorkshire Terrier (3.2 kg, BCS 4/9) was evaluated for vomiting, anorexia, and abdominal discomfort of several days’ duration. On exam, the dog was mildly dehydrated and had abdominal tenderness without jaundice. CBC showed mild neutrophilic leukocytosis. Serum chemistry revealed elevated ALT (5.46 μkat/l; RR 0.17–1.96), AST (1.05 μkat/l; RR 0.23–0.75), GGT (0.25 μkat/l; RR 0–0.12), total bilirubin (20.52 μmol/l; RR 1.71–10.26), cholesterol (13.78 mmol/l; RR 3.24–6.99), amylase (33.15 μkat/l; RR 3.34–20.04), lipase (38.43 μkat/l; RR 3.34–30.06) and decreased BUN (2.14 mmol/l; RR 2.50–8.92). Canine pancreas-specific lipase was 1928 μg/l (RR < 400). Abdominal ultrasound showed no gallbladder wall thickening but a small hyperechoic nodule in the gallbladder. CT demonstrated a dilated common bile duct, mineralized foci presumed to be choleliths adherent to the gallbladder wall, and heterogeneous contrast enhancement of the pancreatic body. The dog was treated for pancreatitis with fluids, protease inhibitors, antiemetics, antibiotics, and liver support. Two weeks later labs normalized.

Four years later, the dog returned with vomiting and anorexia. Exam again showed epigastric pain without jaundice. CBC showed mild neutrophilic leukocytosis. Amylase (28.79 μkat/l) and lipase (32.48 μkat/l) remained elevated and cPL was 1521 μg/l. Liver enzymes were normal. Ultrasound revealed absence of bile in the gallbladder and visualization of an atrophic hyperechoic nodule (~5 mm). CT confirmed a trace 5 mm hyperattenuated atrophic gallbladder, a normal-sized common bile duct, and no other biliary obstruction.
title: Gallbladder atrophy associated with pancreatitis: Clinical and advanced imaging diagnosis in a dog

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of a large ulceroproliferative lesion over the left gluteal region. He reported a small nodular swelling at the same site for 10 years that had gradually increased in size and then ulcerated 15 days ago, after which the lesion grew rapidly. He also had a chronic discharging sinus on the right buttock, with purulent and occasionally bloody discharge but no rectal bleeding. There was no clinically significant lymphadenopathy. 

On systemic examination there were no abnormalities; routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Perirectal examination and sigmoidoscopy were unremarkable. 

Local examination of the left gluteal region revealed an oval ulceroproliferative lesion measuring approximately 10 × 7 cm near the natal cleft. The lesion was non-tender, not fixed to underlying muscle, had everted edges, and an indurated margin; its floor was covered with blood-stained purulent discharge. On the right buttock was a chronic discharging sinus from which purulent material could be expressed. Additionally, three to four nodular swellings each about 12 cm in diameter were noted over both buttocks.
journal: Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery
title: Malignant Change in an Epidermal Cyst Over Gluteal Region

case_prompt: A 79-year-old Black man with type 2 diabetes mellitus was referred after a routine diabetic eye exam identified a choroidal mass in the left eye. He was asymptomatic, with no history of cancer or neurofibromatosis. His visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, without a relative afferent pupillary defect or visual field deficit. Slit-lamp examination was unremarkable except for mild nuclear sclerotic cataracts. Fundus examination of the right eye showed extramacular drusen without diabetic retinopathy. In the left eye, there was a 12.0 × 11.0 × 3.9 mm pigmented choroidal lesion abutting the optic nerve from 7:00 to 1:00, with an amelanotic central portion and overlying retinal pigment epithelial hyperplasia. Standardized ocular echography (B-scan) revealed a dome-shaped choroidal lesion measuring 3.9 mm in thickness with irregular internal reflectivity and no internal vascularity. Posterior to the globe, there was a 3.8 mm thick dome-shaped area concerning for extraocular extension, also low reflective and avascular. Optical coherence tomography over the lesion showed a dome-shaped elevation with chronic-appearing cystoid intraretinal fluid and retinal pigment epithelial atrophy at the apex.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Pseudo-pigmented choroidal schwannoma with extraocular extension in an elderly patient

case_prompt: An 80-year-old woman was brought for evaluation of transient abnormal behavior. Computed tomography of the head showed a large low-density area involving the right temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes with mild midline shift. On admission, she had no focal neurologic deficits other than the prior behavioral changes. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a low-intensity area on T1-weighted images and a corresponding high-intensity area on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images, involving the cortex and white matter without gadolinium enhancement. T2*-weighted images revealed several low-signal intensity spots in the bilateral temporo-occipital regions, distinct from the main lesion. Initial impression was a low-grade glioma with associated vasogenic edema, and further imaging studies were planned. Over the next 6 days, the patient’s condition deteriorated to coma and left hemiplegia, and repeat MRI showed worsening edema without enhancement. She underwent emergent stereotactic-guided biopsy via a small occipital craniotomy. Intraoperative views revealed cortical swelling without obvious tumor. Rapid pathological examination showed no neoplastic cells.
title: Acute progression of cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation diagnosed by biopsy in an elderly patient: A case report

case_prompt: A 69-year-old Chinese woman was referred for evaluation of a 5-month history of postmenopausal vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. In May 2020, she noted intermittent episodes of vaginal bleeding lasting 4–5 days, and occasional blood in her stool without hematuria. Her last menstrual period was over 14 years ago. On gynecologic examination, the vulva appeared hypopigmented and atrophic; the vagina was smooth. The uterine cervix was mobile and had a roughly 5-cm cauliflower-like mass on the anterior lip; the cervix felt friable, and the shallow vaginal fornix was atrophic. No adnexal masses were palpated. Pelvic color Doppler ultrasound showed an enlarged cervix measuring 5.7 × 4.0 cm with heterogeneous echotexture, suggestive of cervical malignancy. A cervical cone biopsy demonstrated high-grade glands lined by columnar cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and pseudostratified nuclei, forming papillary and micropapillary structures with marked nuclear atypia. Immunohistochemical studies revealed focal positivity for progesterone receptor and estrogen receptor, and diffuse positivity for p16, p53, EMA, CK7, WT-1, and Ki-67. Stains for MUC6, CK20, vimentin, Napsin A, HNF-1β, and CEA were negative. An HPV test was negative. Pelvic MRI showed an irregular anteverted uterine cervix mass measuring 3.0 × 5.0 × 4.1 cm with mild heterogeneous diffusion signal; bilateral adnexa appeared normal, and small lymph nodes were seen adjacent to the right iliac vessels. Pathologic stage was assigned as FIGO IIA.
final_diagnosis_raw: Serous carcinoma of the uterine cervix
title: Molecular pathology and clinical treatment of independent HPV primary serous carcinoma of the uterine cervix (USCC): A case report

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of dysesthesia described as sensations of movement beneath the skin, accompanied by pruritus, erythema, burning, and pain. He believed “flies and worms” were emerging from his skin and attributed his symptoms to a parasitic infection, noting prior camping and travel—including South Carolina, South Florida, the Bahamas, Kansas, Louisiana, Texas, New York, Colorado, and Nevada—in which he felt he might have been exposed. His medical history was notable for a primary immunodeficiency of unknown etiology diagnosed 5 years earlier and treated with immunoglobulin; there was no history of diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency.

Over the course of his illness, he remained afebrile and received multiple courses of antiparasitic agents (ivermectin, albendazole, permethrin, and praziquantel), antibacterial agents (doxycycline and ciprofloxacin), and antifungal therapy without improvement. He subsequently developed nodules, erosions, and ulcers on his extremities, including a persistent ulcer on his left second finger from scratching and attempts to extract the presumed pathogen. 

Multiple skin biopsies revealed chronic spongiotic dermatitis, acute and chronic folliculitis, and panniculitis. Bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures were repeatedly negative, and serologic studies showed no evidence of infection. A duplex ultrasound of the upper extremities ruled out vascular disease. Although many lesions healed, the ulcer on the left second digit progressed to cellulitis and osteomyelitis, necessitating surgical amputation.

He presented to the dermatology clinic carrying his amputated left second finger in a glass container and requested evaluation to identify the causative organism. On examination, he had erythematous, eczematous patches on the face, chest, abdomen, back, and arms, along with excoriated papules and generalized xerosis. His left second digit showed a healing stump.
title: Delusional infestation complicated by gangrene and osteomyelitis requiring finger amputation

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old African American woman with a 6-week history of persistent dry cough, intermittent low-grade fever, night sweats, fatigue, weakness, and exertional dyspnea presented for evaluation. She denied orthopnea, PND, toxic exposures, weight loss, appetite changes, or joint pain. She was a non-smoker and social drinker.  
On admission: temperature 100.2 °F; pulse 113 beats/min; respirations 18 breaths/min; BP 150/80 mm Hg; PaO₂ 60 mm Hg on room air. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 11,600 cells/μL (82% neutrophils, 13% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, MCV 82 fL, platelets 518,000 cells/μL, ESR 117 mm/hr, CRP 7 mg/dL.  
Chest radiograph: nodular infiltrates in bilateral upper lobes and perihilar fullness. CT chest: extensive bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with perihilar and peripheral consolidation. Pulmonary function tests: mild restrictive pattern.  
Initial differential diagnosis included atypical pneumonia, tuberculosis, fungal or other opportunistic infections, sarcoidosis, interstitial lung disease, connective tissue or autoimmune disease, lymphoma, and occult malignancy.  
She received erythromycin and ceftriaxone (later changed to moxifloxacin) without improvement. Blood and sputum cultures for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi were repeatedly negative. PPD and HIV tests were negative. Serologic analyses for rheumatoid factor, ANA, and ANCA were negative. CT abdomen and pelvis were unremarkable.  
A mediastinal lymph node biopsy showed only reactive anthracosis with no granulomas or malignant cells.
title: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in a young female: a case report

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old girl was admitted with 5 days of progressive generalized abdominal distention, acute lower abdominal pain, nausea, and mild fever. She had no history of constipation or vomiting. On examination, the abdomen was distended and tender to light and deep palpation, with no palpable masses. Fresh and old bloodstains were noted in her undergarments. Her hemodynamic status was stable. Physical examination revealed breast enlargement (thelarche) without pubic hair or other signs of puberty.

Transabdominal ultrasound showed a multilocular–solid right-sided abdominal mass measuring approximately 63 × 40 mm with heterogeneous echogenicity. A contrast-enhanced pelvic CT scan demonstrated a 122 × 106 mm mixed solid-cystic mass in the pelvic cavity with a clear boundary, partly abutting the uterus.

Laboratory studies revealed:
• FSH <0.55 IU/L (normal 1.2–12.5)  
• LH <0.10 IU/L (normal 0.3–2.5)  
• Estradiol 115 pg/mL (normal <9)  
• Androstenedione 5.8 nmol/L (normal 0.0–3.0)  
• DHEAS 0.57 μmol/L (normal 0.090–3.350)  
• Testosterone 1.01 nmol/L (normal 0.0–2.2)  
• AMH 1322 pmol/L (normal 0.1–38.6)  
• AFP 12 kIU/L (normal 1–33)  
• β-hCG 0.11 IU/L (normal 0.0–5.0)  
• Inhibin A 291 pg/mL (normal <4.7)  
• Inhibin B 956 pg/mL (normal <111)
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Vaginal bleeding imitated rape in a 6-year old girl, a case report about granulosa cell tumor as a reason of peripheral precocious puberty

case_prompt:
A male infant was born at 37 weeks’ gestation to a 19-year-old G3P1001 mother with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura toward the end of pregnancy. Maternal serologies were negative for hepatitis B, HIV, and group B Streptococcus; rubella and VDRL status were unknown. Delivery was vaginal with spontaneous rupture of membranes 2 hours prior; Apgar scores were 9 and 9. Birth weight was 2499 g. 

On initial examination, a thin, yellow, shiny collodion membrane covered most of his skin. He was active, alert, and responsive. Findings were notable for incomplete eyelid closure, blanching of the eyelids, eclabium (inability to purse lips), and limited joint motion due to taut skin. Hearing was normal, and nails appeared normal without dystrophic changes.

On day 7, increased work of breathing occurred due to upper-airway obstruction from dried skin plugs. He was admitted to the NICU in a humidified incubator. At 6 hours of age, electrolytes were normal. Nasogastric feedings were started because he could not suck. Daily baths with gentle soap, frequent applications of Eucerin and Aquaphor, and Bacitracin zinc to skin fissures were implemented. Lacri-Lube was applied to the eyes, and ammonium lactate was added once peeling began. He received high-calorie formula via nasogastric tube for possible protein loss. A family pedigree was unremarkable.

During the second week, diffuse peeling occurred, especially on the face, and ectropion resolved as skin shed around the eyes. By day 27, skin markedly improved though lower-extremity edema persisted. On day 29, he was treated for anemia (hematocrit 22.8%, reticulocyte count 76 k/µL). He completed a 7-day course of nafcillin and gentamicin for abdominal wall cellulitis; vancomycin was briefly given for suspected coagulase-negative Staphylococcus sepsis, later deemed contamination. By day 31, his vital signs and skin status were stable, and he was discharged home.
title: Expedient Treatment of a Collodion Baby

case_prompt: A 78-year-old right-handed man presented with a 7-year history of soft-tissue swelling on his right wrist, recently increasing in size and accompanied by new tingling and numbness in the median-nerve distribution and progressive functional impairment. He had longstanding bilateral wrist arthritis managed with oral analgesics and intermittent steroid injections. Serial wrist radiographs over the years demonstrated bilateral radiocarpal, distal radioulnar, scapho-trapezium-trapezoid, carpo-metacarpal, and metacarpophalangeal joint degeneration with joint-space narrowing, large subarticular cysts, and chondrocalcinosis at the triangular fibrocartilage complex; these were interpreted as features of crystal arthropathy, but ultrasound-guided aspiration was negative for crystals. On examination, there was loss of wrist motion, firm nodular lumps over the radial aspect of the right wrist and triangular fibrocartilage complex, negative squeeze test, and mild tenderness at the right second metacarpophalangeal joint without warmth or erythema. Recent radiographs showed enlarging periarticular soft-tissue swelling with internal mineralization and progressive bone erosions. MRI demonstrated profuse synovial proliferation forming large periarticular soft-tissue masses. Given the neurological symptoms and functional compromise, the patient was referred for median-nerve decompression, debulking of the presumed tophaceous material, and biopsy.
title: Secondary Chondrosarcoma Arising in Synovial Chondromatosis of Wrist Joint

case_prompt: A 15-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of multiple erythematous, mildly painful subcutaneous swellings over the left side of the forehead and upper eyelid. Six years earlier she had sustained trauma to the forehead, and about two years later she noted a subcutaneous swelling at one end of the scar. Within 4–6 weeks of the initial swelling, lesions developed surface ulceration and formed sinuses that discharged seropurulent fluid. Two surgical drainages over the first year yielded no improvement. On examination, multiple erythematous subcutaneous nodules with ulceration, crusting, and seropurulent discharge were seen over the left forehead and upper eyelid. Routine hematologic parameters were within normal limits. Tests for HIV-1 and HIV-2 were negative. A Mantoux test was negative. Skull radiography showed no bony abnormalities. Based on the history and examination, the initial differential diagnoses included botryomycosis, actinomycetoma or eumycetoma, and scrofuloderma.
title: Cutaneous Botryomycosis in Immunocompetent Patients: A Case Series

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old woman was admitted with acute dyspnea and orthopnea of a few hours’ duration. She had COPD (Gold II) on home oxygen, chronic respiratory insufficiency, heart failure (NYHA III), insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, and BMI 44.1. In the emergency department, ABGs showed respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia (pH 7.349; pCO2 56.2 mmHg; pO2 65.5 mmHg; O2 sat 82%), blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, heart rate 84 bpm. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities; blood glucose was 450 mg/dL. She was diagnosed with an acute COPD exacerbation, stabilized, and transferred to pulmonology.

Over a 16-day hospitalization, her respiratory status improved. Routine urine sediment examination revealed 25–30 leukocytes and 8–10 squamous epithelial cells per field, rare bacteria, and mobile parasitic trophozoites; urine culture was negative. Microscopy identified two distinct protozoa by morphology and motility:

• Ciliates (~40 × 20 μm) that were kidney-shaped, bore short cilia, had a cystotome cleft one-third from the anterior end, a posterior contractile vacuole, an ovoid macronucleus, and multiple food vacuoles.  
• Flagellates (~15 × 10 μm) that were egg-shaped with a pointed anterior end, a centrally located spherical nucleus, a posterior spherical inclusion, and two flagella 1.5–2 times body length.

Under 40× magnification, ~20 flagellate trophozoites per field and fewer ciliates were seen. Chronologically, the first urine sample contained both protozoa, subsequent samples contained only the flagellate, and the final pre-discharge sample showed no trophozoites. No cysts were observed in any sample.
title: When a Ciliate Meets a Flagellate: A Rare Case of Colpoda spp. and Colpodella spp. Isolated from the Urine of a Human Patient. Case Report and Brief Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 20-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 2-month history of a visible mass in the left parotid region. She had no significant past medical or surgical history. Physical examination revealed a 3-cm, oval, semi–tense-elastic, painless mass adherent to deep planes, covered by intact skin, without facial nerve dysfunction. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and liver and kidney panels, were normal. Neck ultrasound demonstrated a large, solid nodular lesion with regular margins and internal areas of colliquation at the lower pole of the left parotid gland, along with reactive bilateral cervical lymph nodes. MRI of the neck revealed an oval-shaped lesion with lobulated margins, intermediate to low intensity on T1-weighted images, high intensity on T2-weighted and STIR sequences, and marked homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was not performed. On the basis of location, epidemiology, and imaging characteristics, the leading preoperative diagnosis was pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A solitary fibrous tumor of the parotid gland: Case report

case_prompt: A 25-year-old nulliparous woman with no significant medical history presented in June 2009 with acute onset of severe abdominal pain. On examination, she had a large, fixed pelvic mass measuring approximately 20 × 18 cm. Laboratory evaluation showed an inflammatory syndrome with an elevated C-reactive protein and accelerated erythrocyte sedimentation rate; serum calcium was 2.29 mmol/L (normal 2.25–2.60 mmol/L), and CA 125 was 186.8 IU/mL (approximately 5 × normal). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 24 × 18 × 15 cm heterogeneous cystic and solid mass arising from the left ovary, moderate peritoneal fluid with peritoneal thickening, and mild bilateral hydronephrosis. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed an irregular, highly vascular solid-cystic tumor of the left ovary measuring approximately 40 × 35 cm; the right ovary appeared normal. A total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and multiple peritoneal biopsies were performed.
final_diagnosis_raw: small cell carcinoma of hypercalcemic type of the ovary
title: Small Cell Carcinoma of the Ovary of Hypercalcemic Type: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 14-day-old boy was referred by his anxious parents for evaluation of a left lower-limb deformity. He was the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents (mother 32 years, father 33 years), born at term by vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2600 g. APGAR scores were 2 and 6 at one and five minutes, respectively. The antenatal history was unremarkable for rash, teratogen exposure, radiation, or fever.

On inspection, the left leg was short and thin compared with the right. The left foot appeared short due to absence of the fourth ray, and there was syndactyly between the second and third toes. There was no bowing or skin dimpling. Palpation revealed a normal left ankle joint but medial and lateral laxity of the left knee compared with the right. Examination of the right lower limb, both upper limbs, face, pelvis, and spine was normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

Radiographs of the left lower limb showed absence of the proximal tibial epiphysis, absence of the talus, and absence of the fourth ray; the tibia and fibula were shorter than on the right side. A skeletal survey of the remainder of the body was normal. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable. Peripheral blood karyotyping showed a normal 46,XY result.
title: Fibular Hypoplasia, Talar Aplasia, Absent Proximal Tibial Growth Plate and Oligosyndactyly (Variant of Fibular Aplasia, Tibial Campomelia, and Oligosyndactyly Syndrome) - Paucity of Case Reports with Evolving Definition

case_prompt: A 25-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with 3 days of high fever (up to 39 °C), left flank pain, and gross hematuria. She had left costovertebral angle tenderness on examination. Urinalysis showed 2055 red blood cells per high-power field; dipstick was negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrites and positive for albuminuria (2+). Microscopy revealed minimal pyuria (6 white blood cells per high-power field) and no bacteriuria. She had not taken antibiotics prior to presentation. Urine and blood cultures were obtained. Laboratory tests showed C-reactive protein 28 mg/dl, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 107 mm/h, creatinine 1.21 mg/dl, and blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dl. She was admitted with a provisional diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis and started on intravenous ceftriaxone. On the following day, contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a hypoenhancing region in the upper pole of the left kidney, suggestive of pyelonephritis.
title: Atypical Presentation of IgA Nephropathy Mimicking Acute Pyelonephritis

case_prompt: A 40-year-old man with a history of heavy tobacco use and HIV infection presented with a 5-day history of cough, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. On arrival, he was afebrile, with a pulse of 104 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 80/60 mm Hg. Chest radiography showed right lower lobe consolidation. Chest CT revealed right paratracheal lymphadenopathy and a 5.8 × 4.5 cm mass occluding the bronchus intermedius. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dense bilateral adrenal masses measuring 5.4 × 4.0 cm on the right and 4.8 × 2.0 cm on the left. Laboratory studies were notable for a white-cell count of 18.5 K/mm3, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, and a CD4 count of 567 cells/mm3. He was admitted for presumed sepsis, received IV fluids, and was started on vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam. Infectious studies—including serum CMV, influenza PCR, Mycoplasma and Bartonella IgG/IgM, Cryptococcus and Histoplasma serologies, and Legionella urinary antigen—were all negative.
