Persistent hypotension led to measurement of a random morning cortisol, which was 7.0 μg/dL. A cosyntropin stimulation test yielded cortisol levels of 10.1 μg/dL at 30 minutes and 10.3 μg/dL at 60 minutes, with an elevated serum ACTH level of 83.4 pg/mL. MRI of the brain revealed no pituitary lesion. He was treated with stress-dose IV hydrocortisone, resulting in resolution of hypotension and abdominal pain, and was transitioned to oral prednisone 15 mg each morning and 5 mg each evening.
title: Metastatic Small-Cell Lung Cancer Presenting as Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old male with a 2-year history of type I bipolar disorder presented with a 1-week history of persistent fever, sweating, sore throat, anorexia, weakness, lethargy, and reduced speech. Two months earlier, haloperidol and biperiden had been tapered off, leaving him on valproate 500 mg daily for the past 2 years. He reported no substance use or recent surgery. His mental state was markedly altered: he was not eating, speaking, sleeping, or leaving his room.

On examination, temperature was 38.5 °C (axillary), heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. He was confused, distractible, and exhibited extensive muscular rigidity. Mental status testing showed disorientation; affect was dysphoric, anxious, and irritable. He had visual and auditory hallucinations. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed: glucose 154 mg/dl, urea 78 mg/dl, creatinine 1.08 mg/dl, ammonium 84 μmol/L, lactate 13.1 mg/dl; Na 149 mEq/L, K 4.7 mEq/L, Cl 116 mEq/L, Ca 8.9 mg/dl; creatinine phosphokinase >4267 U/L; alanine aminotransferase 70 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase 240 U/L; gamma-glutamyl transferase 20 U/L; lactate dehydrogenase 759 U/L; myoglobin >1000 ng/ml; TSH 1.59 μIU/ml; free T4 15.34 pmol/L. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 9610/mm3, hemoglobin 15.2 g/dl, hematocrit 44.6%. Serum valproate concentration was <12.5 μg/ml (therapeutic range 50–100).

Peripheral blood, throat, and urine cultures showed no growth. Procalcitonin and C-reactive protein were within normal limits. Cranial computed tomography was normal. Arterial blood gas analysis was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid examination, urinalysis, and chest radiograph were normal. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia.
title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome Associated with Valproate in an Adolescent

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman was evaluated for recurrent episodes of left-sided “bronchopneumonia” characterized by high fever, chills, productive cough with mucopurulent sputum, left chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, and wheezing. Her medical history was notable for smoking (20 pack-years), obesity, and hypertension treated intermittently; she had been asymptomatic in childhood and early adulthood aside from a pulmonary infection at age 19 that was treated empirically for tuberculosis. Previous chest radiographs had been interpreted as left basal pleural thickening and chronic pneumopathy.  

On examination, blood pressure was 180/100 mm Hg. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with a left shift and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm/hr (first hour) and 68 mm/2 hr. Electrocardiography demonstrated a leftward axis deviation (QRS +50°), low-voltage QRS complexes, and T-wave inversions in leads V3–V6. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable.  

A posteroanterior chest radiograph revealed an opacity in the left lower pulmonary zone, hypoaeration of the left upper lobe, and leftward mediastinal shift without marked retraction of the left hemithorax. Multidetector CT of the chest showed a small left lung composed of multiple cystic spaces, hyperinflation of the right lung with herniation across the midline, and mediastinal deviation to the left. Multiplanar reconstructions demonstrated depression of the right hemidiaphragm facilitating right lung hypertrophy, with a normally positioned left hemidiaphragm. Three-dimensional volume renderings showed a disproportionate right pulmonary lobation and vascularity filling the thorax, whereas the left lung appeared as a cluster of small cysts with scant vasculature.
title: 3D Imaging in Unilateral Primary Pulmonary Hypoplasia in an Adult: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman with a 24-year history of bipolar affective disorder was admitted for a manic episode. She had 4 months of increased psychomotor activity, pressured speech, irritability, muttering to herself, decreased need for sleep, and anger outbursts, worsening over the 3 weeks before presentation. On examination she was alert, with fair hygiene, good eye contact, and oriented to person and place. Mental status examination revealed persecutory and referential delusions, second-person auditory hallucinations, irritable mood, dysphoric affect, crying spells, impaired judgment, and no insight.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL and mean corpuscular volume 76.1 fL, consistent with iron deficiency anemia; other hematological, renal, liver, and thyroid parameters were within normal limits. The patient was treated sequentially with risperidone (up to 6 mg daily, discontinued due to postural hypotension), lithium (up to 900 mg daily, with no clinical improvement), and valproate (titrated to 1500 mg daily). Because of partial response, lithium and valproate were continued in combination, and olanzapine was added at 10 mg daily and increased to 30 mg daily on hospital day 4.

On hospital day 10, she reported an “irritative sensation” in both calf muscles that improved with movement, worsened at rest, and was especially distressing at night.
title: Olanzapine-induced restless leg syndrome (Willis–Ekbom disease): A case report

case_prompt: A 41‐year‐old man presented with a mass in his right knee that had slowly enlarged over the past 15 years. He reported mild tenderness but no mechanical locking or instability. On examination there was a 2‐cm, solid, glossy, mobile swelling at the lateral upper pole of the patella, mildly tender to palpation. Routine radiographs of the knee were negative. MRI demonstrated a well‐demarcated, oval lesion measuring 1.5 cm in diameter in the soft tissues abutting the lateral upper pole of the patella. The lesion was isointense to muscle on T1‐weighted and STIR T1 sequences, slightly hyperintense on T2‐weighted and STIR T2 images, and its edge was heterogeneously enhanced on contrast‐enhanced T1‐weighted images. MRI interpretation was that the lesion represented a loose body or other benign process, and hemangioma was not excluded.
title: The diagnosis and arthroscopic treatment of angioleiomyoma presenting loose body in the knee joint: two case reports

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man with treated hypertension and diabetes mellitus presented after a first generalized tonic-clonic seizure, regaining consciousness before arrival. Two weeks earlier, he sustained a minor head injury with scalp abrasion but had no deficits. The day after discharge, he had another 5–6-minute generalized seizure with loss of consciousness and was admitted. He then experienced generalized tonic-clonic seizures twice daily and persistent right calf paresthesia that sometimes progressed to generalized seizures despite antiepileptic therapy.  
On examination, there were no signs of other organ involvement; in particular, there was no glandular enlargement or orbital disease. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and kidneys. Hemogram revealed no leukocytosis, and C-reactive protein was normal. Lumbar puncture showed a normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) glucose relative to blood glucose, no leukocytes, and CSF cytology was negative for malignant cells.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated focal thickening and enhancement of the dura near the superior sagittal sinus, with adjacent skull bone effacement and loss of normal fatty marrow signal.
title: IgG4-related intracranial hypertrophic pachymeningitis with skull hyperostosis: a case report

case_prompt: A 54-year-old man presented with a painful right supraclavicular mass of a few weeks’ duration, noted after swimming. He had hypertension treated with medication, a history of tonsillectomy in childhood, and knee arthroscopy in 2013. Ultrasonography revealed a single thin-walled cystic mass measuring 35 × 17 mm in the right supraclavicular region, superior and lateral to the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels, without associated nodular or tissue formation and without abnormal vascularization. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded small lymphocyte-like cells mixed with lymphedema-like material, but the cyst recurred rapidly after puncture. On examination, the mass was renitent, movable, and nonadherent. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a right supraclavicular cystic lesion anterosuperior to the subclavian vessels measuring 43 × 40 × 27 mm; it was thin-walled, had no fleshy component or nodular formation, and demonstrated no tissue enhancement after gadolinium administration.
title: A supraclavicular cystic lymphangioma in adult: a rare entity

case_prompt: A 61-year-old woman with diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia presented with seven months of progressive lower back pain and bilateral lower limb pain and weakness, worse proximally than distally, with decreased sensation extending to the abdomen and new fecal and urinary incontinence. She denied systemic symptoms. An MRI obtained at an outside facility showed spondylolisthesis at L5–S1 with spinal canal stenosis. She underwent spinal decompression and fusion. Two days postoperatively, she acutely worsened and presented three weeks later. On examination, upper-limb strength was 5/5 with normal reflexes, and proximal lower-limb strength was 3/5 with distal strength 4−/5; cranial nerves were intact, and gait could not be assessed. MRI of the spine showed post-laminectomy changes with fluid and edema, a diffusely swollen cord from T5 to the conus with high T2 signal and no diffusion restriction, and multilevel cervical osteophytes causing mild canal stenosis. The leading diagnosis was transverse myelitis, and she was started on steroids; malignancy and arteriovenous malformation were also considered. She declined lumbar puncture.
title: Things are not what they seem neurologically and radiologically: An apt descriptor for spinal dural arteriovenous fistula (SDAVF)

case_prompt: A 19-year-old man presented with a one-week history of epigastric and back pain, as well as a one-year history of intermittent hematuria and blood-tinged sputum. He reported a three-month history of decreased appetite and weight loss but denied fever, dyspnea, or cough. On examination, his blood pressure was 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats/min, chest auscultation was clear, and the cardiovascular examination was normal. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, non-tender mass palpable in the epigastric and left hypochondriac regions. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 11.4 g/dL, normal complete blood count, coagulation profile, serum electrolytes, and liver function tests, and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase of 1070 U/L (normal range, 100–190 U/L). HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody tests were nonreactive. A chest radiograph demonstrated a widened mediastinum and bilateral hilar enlargement. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large heteroechoic mass replacing the entire left renal parenchyma with multiple enlarged left para-aortic lymph nodes. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple conglomerate mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, deposits in the left lower lung lobe, bilateral prominent axillary lymph nodes, and a large heterogeneously enhancing mass lesion replacing the left kidney with renal vein infiltration. Multiple conglomerate celiac and retroperitoneal lymph nodes were seen, and lytic destruction of the D4 and D5 vertebral bodies, the left superior pubic ramus, and the right ischium was noted. A working diagnosis of metastatic renal cell carcinoma versus lymphoma was made.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Renal cell carcinoma with widespread metastasis in 19 years old young male – A rare case report

case_prompt: A healthy 2-month-old boy was brought for evaluation of a newly noted mass over the left cheek in the masseter region. On examination, the lesion was firm, partially mobile, cold, apparently painless, and measured approximately 2 cm in diameter. There was no restriction of neck rotation or lateral movement and no head tilt. Ultrasonography showed a fusiform, inhomogeneous, hypoechogenic mass measuring 17×15 mm within the left masseter muscle; the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle showed focal thickening to 8 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging of the facial soft tissues demonstrated a 20×15×21 mm enlargement of the left masseter muscle that was minimally hyperintense on T2-weighted images, isointense on T1-weighted images, and showed no contrast enhancement; the proximal sternocleidomastoid muscle was also thickened (13×14×31 mm). Repeat ultrasonography at 2 months showed interval growth of approximately 10 mm in the mass. In view of the growth rate, a decision was made to perform a punch biopsy.
title: Fetal-Type Rhabdomyoma of the Cheek: A Conservative Management

case_prompt:
A 60‐year‐old man with a history of childhood poliomyelitis and residual right‐sided weakness presented with a 6‐year history of left lower quadrant abdominal pain, a painful left groin mass, and left lower extremity swelling. He grew up in Montenegro and moved to the United States as a teenager. On examination, he ambulated with a cane, had a right leg limp, and asymmetric lower‐extremity size. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits. 

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large complex cystic collection in the left retroperitoneum along the iliopsoas muscle, extending into the left pelvis and thigh. The initial differential diagnosis included benign lymphatic malformation, malignancy such as myxoid liposarcoma, and multiloculated abscess; infection was considered less likely given the absence of sepsis. The patient was lost to follow‐up and returned 6 years later for repeat CT, which showed no change in the lesion’s size. 

MRI of the pelvis and left thigh, with and without intravenous contrast, demonstrated a large nonenhancing multicystic mass along the left iliopsoas muscle extending into the thigh, with multiple hyperintense cysts within and along the sartorius on STIR sequences and no enhancement post‐contrast. Incidentally, there was severe fatty atrophy of the right pelvic musculature and a shallow right acetabulum consistent with chronic poliomyelitis. The leading considerations remained lymphatic malformation and myxoid liposarcoma.
title: Primary intramuscular and intermuscular Echinococcal disease of the iliopsoas and sartorius muscles: A case report

case_prompt: A 62‐year‐old man with no prior comorbidities presented with right forearm pain after a minor bump against a table. On examination, there was swelling and tenderness over the shaft of the right radius, with both pronation and supination painfully restricted. Initial radiographs showed a lytic lesion with a pathological fracture of the radial shaft. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 375 IU/L, with normal white blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein. MRI demonstrated a 2.2 × 1.4 × 1.8 cm expansile lesion centered in the lateral cortex of the mid‐shaft of the right radius, appearing T1 isointense, T2 hyperintense, and showing moderate contrast enhancement, associated with a pathological fracture. Based on the MRI, the leading considerations were osteoblastoma and multiple myeloma.
title: A Rare Case of Xanthogranulomatous Osteomyelitis of Radius Presenting as Pathological Fracture – A Case Report

case_prompt: A 78-year-old man with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus (on oral hypoglycemics) and mild renal impairment for 3 years presented with a 2-week history of headache and drooping of the left upper eyelid. On examination, there was an isolated left pupil-involving third cranial nerve palsy. Best-corrected visual acuity was 6/9 in both eyes; intraocular pressures and fundoscopy were normal. The remainder of the cranial nerve and neurologic examination was unremarkable. Routine hematology showed thrombocytosis, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 77 mm/hour, and a C-reactive protein level of 4.7 mg/dL. There were no signs of temporal artery thickening, scalp tenderness, or jaw claudication. Magnetic resonance imaging and angiography of the brain and orbits were normal. A lumbar puncture was unremarkable, and chest radiography showed no abnormalities. The patient was started on oral steroids for pain management. A temporal artery biopsy—performed to evaluate for atypical giant cell arteritis—showed only hypertensive changes and was negative for vasculitis. On follow-up, his periorbital pain was unchanged with steroids, and involvement of the left ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve became apparent.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Diagnostic challenges in a case of an isolated third nerve palsy

case_prompt: A 25-year-old man from Uttar Pradesh presented with a painless left cheek swelling that had gradually enlarged over the past year. He noted that the mass transiently increased in size while eating and then returned to baseline after meals. On examination, there was a 2.0 × 1.5 cm, firm, non-tender, mobile, globular swelling below the left malar prominence, with normal overlying skin. The swelling became more prominent when he clenched his teeth. He was afebrile, and there was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed an absolute eosinophil count of 1100 cells/mm3; the peripheral smear was otherwise unremarkable. Ultrasonography of the cheek revealed cystic dilatation of the mid-portion of the left Stensen’s duct with minimal lobulated soft-tissue contents and mild ductal wall thickening. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-defined, hypodense cystic lesion superficial to the anterolateral aspect of the left masseter muscle, indenting its surface and communicating with a tubular hypodense structure continuous with the parotid gland, consistent with a dilated Stensen’s duct and sialocele formation.
title: Filariasis of Stensen's Duct: An Index Case

case_prompt: A 43-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 2, was referred for evaluation of a breast lesion detected on contrast-enhanced MRI performed because of a family history of breast cancer in her mother at age 50. She had no personal history of breast disease, trauma, or hormone use. Physical examination revealed no palpable masses, skin changes, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Diagnostic full-field digital mammography and bilateral breast ultrasound were unremarkable. On 1.5-T contrast-enhanced MRI, a 6-mm lesion with irregular margins was identified in the right lower inner quadrant. After gadolinium administration, the lesion demonstrated a type 3 enhancement curve, with rapid initial rise followed by washout in the delayed phase, raising suspicion for malignancy. A second-look targeted ultrasound and repeat mammography failed to visualize the lesion. Given the discordance and persistent concern, the patient consented to MRI-guided wire localization and wide local excision of the lesion.
title: Cavernous Breast Hemangioma Mimicking an Invasive Lesion on Contrast-Enhanced MRI

case_prompt: A 30-year-old Chinese woman presented with a 6-year history of painless swelling in the left submandibular region that, over the last 3 months, had begun to extend to the root of the neck. On examination, there was an approximately 12 cm × 6 cm soft, fluctuant, non-tender mass in the left anterior cervical region, with no swelling visible in the floor of the mouth. Color Doppler ultrasound showed a well-defined, anechoic, loculated fluid collection in the left superficial anterior cervical region—extending from the mandibular angle to the suprasternal fossa—measuring about 10.98 cm × 1.49 cm × 4.92 cm, with poor internal sound transmission, visible soft-tissue separations, and no obvious blood-flow signal on color-flow Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a non-enhancing cystic lesion extending from the submandibular region to the supraclavicular region. Fine-needle aspiration in clinic yielded an egg white–like liquid discharge.
title: Plunging Ranula Presenting as a Giant Anterior Cervical Cystic Mass: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 64-year-old woman noted a painless palpable lump in her left breast on self-examination. She had no family history of breast cancer, entered menopause at age 50, and took a mild beta-blocker for hypertension. Mammography showed a small (≈1 cm) irregular high-density mass with indistinct margins, few fine pleomorphic grouped calcifications, and focal architectural distortion in the left upper outer quadrant. Ultrasound revealed an approximately 1 cm oval, heterogeneous hypoechoic lesion with indistinct margins and anomalous vascularity; axillary lymph nodes appeared normal. Core needle biopsy demonstrated high-grade malignant neoplasia, non-lobulocentric, composed of epithelioid cells with anisocariotic and pleomorphic nuclei; receptor profile was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor negative, HER2 score 0, and Ki-67 index 70%, consistent with malignant mesenchymal histogenesis. Immunohistochemistry was positive for vimentin, cytokeratin AE1/AE3, p63, CK5/6, CD10, and weakly positive for HHF35 and E-cadherin. Serum tumor markers (CEA, CA 15-3, CA 125, CA 19-9) were within normal limits. Dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI confirmed an irregular 12 mm mass with type III kinetics in the left upper outer quadrant and incidentally detected a 14 mm homogeneously enhancing oval lesion in the left anterior superior mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and brain showed no other metastatic lesions and confirmed the anterior mediastinal nodule.
title: A rare case report of breast sarcoma and synchronous thymoma in a 60-year-old woman

case_prompt:
An 18-month-old boy was admitted with fever and rash. Four days earlier he had gastroenteritis and fever; shortly afterwards he developed a skin eruption on the ears and purpuric lesions on the extremities. On admission, temperature was 38.2°C. Examination showed bright-red, circular, painful purpuric lesions around the mouth and periorbital blushing. The ears were markedly edematous and purple. Tender, bright-red, slightly infiltrated papules and nodules were scattered on the trunk and extremities; the skin was otherwise intact. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 135.9 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 38 mm/hr; leukocyte and platelet counts were normal. Lumbar puncture was performed on suspicion of meningococcal disease; cerebrospinal fluid was normal. Skin biopsy was then performed.
Histologic examination showed a well-established leukocytoclastic vasculitis with marked fibrinoid necrosis and granulocyte infiltration in the vessel wall.
title: Methylprednisolone Therapy in Acute Hemorrhagic Edema of Infancy

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old woman was referred in June 2014 for chronic fingernail dystrophy. Over several years she had progressive hypoplasia and onychodystrophy leading to trachyonychia of all fingernails, diffuse erythema of the proximal and lateral nail folds, and extreme fingertip pain. Her history included rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, and anorexia nervosa. Medications were misoprostol, naproxen, and multivitamins. Family history was notable for unspecified arthritis. She had been seen in 2009 for fragile nails and digital fissures and treated with topical hydrocortisone and fluocinonide without lasting benefit. 

Between June 2014 and early 2018, she underwent multiple dermatology and rheumatology evaluations. Differential diagnoses over this period included infections, chronic dermatitis of the fingertips and nails, lichen planus, Raynaud’s disease, and Bazex syndrome. A workup for aerodigestive malignancy was negative. Two separate panels for connective tissue disease were negative. She developed repeated secondary bacterial and candidal colonization of the fingers. 

She received a prolonged course of topical therapies (calcipotriol–betamethasone, tazarotene, clobetasol, mupirocin), systemic methotrexate, ultraviolet B phototherapy, oral acitretin, fusidic acid, fluconazole with topical clotrimazole, sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim, alitretinoin (10–30 mg daily), dilute acetic‐acid soaks (intolerant), cephalexin, prednisone, and penicillin. Responses were mixed, transient, or absent; acitretin initially worsened her condition, and secondary ulcerations persisted despite fusidic acid. From March to July 2018, she continued to have violaceous, swollen distal digits, atrophic thin nails with partial regrowth, erythema, and eroded, macerated skin despite ongoing alitretinoin and intermittent antibiotics.
title: Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau successfully treated with adalimumab: A case report

case_prompt:
A male newborn, 18 hours old, third child of healthy Nigerian parents, born at 38 weeks via cesarean delivery, was noted to have abdominal distension and dysmorphic features, including brachydactyly with hypoplasia of distal fingers and nails, small dysplastic toenails, elongated palpebral fissures, and bilateral preauricular pits. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated; family history was unremarkable. TORCH screening and bacterial cultures were negative.  
Abdominal ultrasonography showed markedly distended intestinal loops with thin walls, and contrast enema revealed reduced colonic distensibility. On day 3, a low ileostomy was performed; intestinal biopsies confirmed congenital aganglionic megacolon. Due to ongoing high ostomy output, feeding intolerance, and dehydration, the infant required placement of a more proximal ileostomy, gastrostomy, and total parenteral nutrition via central venous catheter.  
Laboratory studies at admission were notable only for an elevated alkaline phosphatase level (1689 U/L; normal 140–500 U/L) and hyperphosphatasia. At 1 week of age, the neonate developed persistent tremors involving limbs, eyes, and trunk with associated desaturation. Electroencephalography showed a highly immature tracing; brainstem auditory evoked potentials were absent; brain ultrasonography was unremarkable.  
On day 12, brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated bilateral symmetric diffusion restriction in the superior cerebellar peduncles, dorsal mesencephalus, dorsal cerebral peduncles, and globi pallidi, along with corpus callosum thinning and increased T2 signal in the periventricular white matter. At 35 days of life, a repeat MRI showed progression to extensive cortical and subcortical white matter T2 hyperintensity and diffusion restriction in the parietal and temporal lobes and splenium of the corpus callosum. Genetic studies were initiated.
title: Two Different Brain Injury Patterns Associated with Compound Heterozygosis of the PIGO Gene in a Term Newborn: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging, painless swelling on the anterior hard palate with associated displacement of the maxillary central incisors. He denied trauma. On examination, there was a well-defined, firm, nontender swelling on the left side of the anterior hard palate that crossed the midline. The crown of the left central incisor was displaced labially and mesially, overlapping the right central incisor. Vitality tests of both central incisors were negative.  
Panoramic occlusal radiography revealed a well-defined, round radiolucency approximately 2.5 cm in diameter with corticated margins in the midline between the central incisors; the lesion displaced the incisor roots and extended superiorly to the floor of the nasal fossa, with deviation of the nasal septum to the right.  
CT imaging demonstrated a 2.6 × 2.8 cm well-defined radiolucency in the region of the incisive canal, displacing the central incisor roots without lateral extension beyond the roots, reaching inferiorly to the crest of interdental bone, with loss of corticulation buccally and palatally, mild elevation of the nasal fossa floor anteriorly, and rightward deviation of the nasal septum. A mucosal polyp was noted on the floor of the left maxillary sinus.  
Initial differential diagnoses included periapical (radicular) cyst, nasopalatine duct cyst, enlarged nasopalatine duct, central giant cell granuloma, root cyst of the upper centrals, supernumerary tooth follicular cyst, primordial cyst, and nasoalveolar cyst.
title: Nasopalatine Duct Cyst

case_prompt: A 68-year-old man presented with vague right flank pain and a history of nephrolithiasis. CT of the abdomen revealed a large heterogeneous left upper-quadrant mass. MRI confirmed a 16 × 9 cm lesion with cystic and solid components arising from the gastric wall, causing mass effect on the pancreas but without lymphadenopathy or metastases. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a submucosal lesion with intact mucosa. Fine-needle aspiration cytology demonstrated a paucity of bland spindle cells. On cell block, the lesional cells stained strongly for CD34 and failed to stain for DOG1 and CD117; PDGFR and succinate dehydrogenase testing could not be performed due to limited material. Despite these equivocal results, a GIST was favored based on morphology and location. Given extensive tumor necrosis, the patient began imatinib therapy rather than undergo repeat biopsy. After 4 weeks of imatinib, imaging showed no significant regression.
title: Solitary fibrous tumor of the stomach with high-grade sarcomatous dedifferentiation

case_prompt: A 48-year-old Caucasian man with a history of Graves disease treated with methimazole and propranolol presented via EMS with sudden onset of right-sided heaviness and weakness that peaked over 3–5 minutes, after which gross motor function began to return. On arrival, he had persistent mild right-sided weakness but was hemodynamically stable. He denied sensory deficits. He reported a similar episode of generalized weakness in 2017 when hyperthyroidism was diagnosed. His medications included methimazole, propranolol, telmisartan/hydrochlorothiazide, testosterone, albuterol, aspirin, and emtricitabine/tenofovir; he admitted noncompliance with his high-potassium diet and supplements. Examination showed 4/5 strength in the right upper and lower extremities and 5/5 strength on the left; both proximal and distal muscles were equally affected. Laboratory studies revealed a potassium level of 3.4 mEq/L, normal blood glucose, a TSH of 0.02 uIU/mL, and a free T4 of 2.34 ng/dL. CT of the head with and without angiography showed unchanged periventricular and subcortical white-matter densities but no intracranial hemorrhage or flow-limiting lesions. ECG demonstrated a right bundle-branch block unchanged from prior studies. Subsequent outpatient syphilis testing was negative.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Stroke Mimic: A Case of Unilateral Thyrotoxic Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis

case_prompt: A 27-year-old right-hand-dominant woman presented with a 4-week history of insidious onset, excruciating pain and swelling of the right elbow without any antecedent trauma. Examination showed supination limited to 50°, elbow flexion–extension from 20° to 130° due to pain, and full pronation. Plain radiographs revealed a well-circumscribed radiolucent lesion in the proximal radius with metaphyseal cortical thinning and a rim of epiphyseal bone. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined centric lytic lesion in the meta-diaphyseal region involving the radial tuberosity and proximal third of the radius, measuring 2.7 × 1.5 × 5 cm and located 7 mm from the articular surface. Endocrine and laboratory studies were normal.
title: Non-Vascularized Fibular Cortical Strut Graft with Intramedullary Nailing for Fibrous Dysplasia of the Proximal Radius – A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 5-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with one month of a progressively enlarging, painless, firm right facial mass, initially measuring 3 cm. There was no history of trauma.  
CT of the orbits showed a lytic, osseous-based mass arising within the right zygoma, with a nonossified component extending into the orbit and mass effect on the globe without scleral invasion.  
Systemic workup—including CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and a technetium bone scan—demonstrated no other lesions or primary malignancy.  
A fine-needle biopsy was inconclusive, revealing only compact and woven bone. Two months after symptom onset, the lesion had grown to 5 cm, and an incisional biopsy of the soft-tissue component again showed no malignant cells.  
Ophthalmic examination revealed best corrected visual acuity of 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS, 2 mm of right proptosis, normal pupils, and full extraocular motility. The remainder of the ophthalmic and general physical examination was unremarkable.  
MRI of the orbits demonstrated a 5.3 cm zygomatic mass with suggestion of intralesional vascular channels on T2-weighted and postcontrast sequences.
title: Large Orbital Pediatric Intraosseous Hemangioma

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old married woman presented with a history of primary amenorrhea and painful sexual intercourse. She reported normal breast development and pubic hair. At age 14, ultrasonography suggested absence of uterus and vagina. There was no family history of amenorrhea, and no maternal exposures during pregnancy. She was a non-smoker, non-alcoholic, with no prior surgeries or medical illnesses.

On examination, vital signs were stable. She weighed 74 kg and was 162 cm tall. Breast development was Tanner stage V. External genitalia showed normal labia majora, labia minora, pubic hair, and an external urethral meatus. There was no palpable vaginal pouch or bulging hymen.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, WBC 14,400/mm3, platelets 60,000/mm3. Hormonal levels, including LH, FSH, prolactin, progesterone, and testosterone, were within normal limits. Peripheral blood karyotype was 46,XX.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated absence of the uterus, cervix, and proximal two-thirds of the vagina, as well as absence of the left kidney.
title: Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser Syndrome: A rare case report from Nepal

case_prompt: A three-year-old boy presented with a one-month history of left submandibular swelling and a one-day history of lower back and left leg pain. His mother reported fever, decreased urine output, and constipation, and he had received antibiotics from his pediatrician without improvement of the neck swelling. On examination, he was afebrile, with a firm 3 cm × 3 cm left submandibular mass. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/h (normal 0–19 mm/h), C-reactive protein 0.665 mg/dL (normal 0–0.500 mg/dL), and hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL (normal 11.0–16.0 g/dL). Abdominal ultrasound revealed grade I left hydronephrosis. Ultrasound of the submandibular mass showed an intermediate echogenic lesion with prominent color Doppler flow. On hospital day 2, an excisional biopsy of the mass was performed. Histologic examination demonstrated small round blue cells with scant pink cytoplasm and focal neuropil structures. Immunohistochemical staining was diffusely positive for synaptophysin and ALK-1, negative for S-100, and Ki-67 exhibited a high proliferation index of 95%. Fluorescence in situ hybridization for N-MYC showed no amplification, and ALK mutation analysis was negative.
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
title: Metastatic Neuroblastoma Presenting as a Submandibular Mass with Mandibular Bone Involvement in a Three-Year-Old Child

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old man was brought to a level I trauma center after sustaining a stab wound to his left knee while intoxicated. On arrival, he was stuporous, hypothermic, and acidotic (pH 6.772; lactic acid 27 mmol/L). Computed tomography angiography showed transection of the left popliteal artery and vein. Within 3 hours of injury, he underwent surgical end-to-end anastomosis of both vessels and a prophylactic anterolateral fasciotomy. Intraoperatively, he received 14 units of packed red blood cells and 11 units of fresh frozen plasma, with systolic blood pressure maintained above 80 mmHg.

Immediately postoperatively, his blood pressure and hemoglobin were stable, but aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 712 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 612 U/L, and prothrombin time was prolonged to 44.5%, necessitating further plasma transfusion. On postoperative day 1, hemoglobin and acid–base status normalized (pH 7.368; lactic acid 2.3 mmol/L), but thrombocytopenia persisted (platelets 68×10^3/μL), prothrombin time was 32.3%, and AST/ALT rose to 1,655/1,465 U/L. The calf remained soft and well perfused, and he was given aggressive hydration and hydrocortisone.

On postoperative day 2, laboratory studies showed AST 8,600 U/L, ALT 6,690 U/L, creatine phosphokinase 26,817 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 7,398 U/L, interleukin-6 178 pg/mL, ferritin 41,079 ng/mL, C-reactive protein 3.55 mg/dL, D-dimer >20 μg/mL fibrinogen equivalent units, persistent thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy.  
  
Given the rapidly worsening organ dysfunction and inflammatory markers, a decision was made to proceed with plasmapheresis.
title: Reperfusion injury or cytokine storm? Utilizing plasmapheresis in severe trauma-induced multiorgan failure: a case report

case_prompt: A 32-year-old white man with type 1 diabetes and acne rosacea presented with a 7-mm reddish-brown papule on the left temple along the hairline that appeared suddenly and grew over several weeks. The lesion was asymptomatic, without pain, pruritus, ulceration, or bleeding. Three weeks before lesion onset, he had undergone intense pulsed light (IPL) therapy (500–670 nm for vascular lesions) for rosacea, during which he sustained several second-degree burns in the area where the papule eventually appeared. Initial clinical differential diagnoses included a follicular cyst, hemangioma, dermatofibroma, seborrheic keratosis, basal cell carcinoma, and amelanotic melanoma. The lesion was treated empirically with intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (0.5 mL of Kenalog-10) and oral doxycycline (120 mg daily) for one month, resulting in approximately 80% reduction in size but incomplete resolution; the papule recurred within a month. An incision and drainage with an 11 blade yielded no keratinaceous material. A 4-mm punch biopsy was performed to rule out a neoplastic process.
title: Eruption of solitary reticulohistiocytoma after intense pulsed light burn

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks and one day gestation was admitted for elective induction of labor. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Labor was induced with misoprostol and oxytocin. At 3 cm cervical dilation, an epidural analgesia was requested. Placement at L4–L5 in the sitting position was noted to be technically difficult, with transient tachycardia that resolved spontaneously. Analgesia with fentanyl was effective.

Eight hours after epidural catheter placement, she developed a severe frontal headache and neck pain rated 10/10, pounding in nature, nonradiating, and worsened by head movement and upright positioning. She denied visual disturbances, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, or limb weakness. Vital signs remained normal, and neurologic examination was unremarkable. The epidural infusion continued for labor analgesia.

Labor failed to progress, and she underwent an uncomplicated Cesarean section. Postoperatively, she continued to complain of persistent positional headache with waxing and waning intensity. On postoperative day 1, because of ongoing headaches, a noncontrast CT scan of the head and neck was obtained.
title: Pneumocephalus secondary to epidural analgesia: a case report

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old obese Caucasian man with a history of insomnia, bipolar disorder, and chronic headache presented with multiple episodes of brief seizures, all induced by laughter when he watched comedy shows. He had experienced several mild episodes over the past month, each lasting approximately 5–10 seconds, characterized by the onset of laughter followed by arm shaking and a sensation that “his consciousness was being vacuumed away.” He denied tongue biting or incontinence. He averaged five episodes per day. There was no family history of seizure disorder.

On examination, he was alert and hemodynamically stable. Neurologic examination was normal. Serum electrolytes and glucose were within normal limits. A sleep-deprived electroencephalogram (EEG) was normal. Brain MRI revealed an arachnoid cyst measuring 4.2 × 2.1 cm in the right anterior middle cranial fossa. He underwent two days of video EEG monitoring, which showed several bursts of generalized high-amplitude spike-and-wave activity with frontotemporal predominance, associated with staring, eye rolling, unresponsiveness, and tonic-clonic movements for 5–10 seconds, all provoked by deep, belly laughter; he reported complete lack of awareness during these episodes.
title: Laugh-induced seizure: a case report

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old woman with a history of generalized anxiety disorder presented initially with a 1-day history of retrosternal chest pain. Medications included acetylsalicylic acid, ramipril, and citalopram. In the emergency department, electrocardiography demonstrated ST-segment changes consistent with a non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Coronary angiography revealed a type 3 spontaneous coronary artery dissection with diffuse coronary ectasia and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. She was treated conservatively and discharged on aspirin 81 mg daily, ramipril 2.5 mg daily, and atorvastatin 80 mg daily.

Twenty days later, she returned with a 4-day history of fevers above 38.5 °C and bilateral flank pain that did not respond to NSAIDs. In the emergency department, the leukocyte count was 16.6 K/μL, eosinophils were 300 cells/μL, alkaline phosphatase was 365 U/L, ALT 265 U/L, GGT 185 U/L, and total bilirubin 10 mg/dL; lipase was normal. Urinalysis showed pyuria and trace ketones without nitrites. A chest radiograph and CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis were unremarkable. She received a single dose of ceftriaxone for presumed pyelonephritis and was discharged.

Two days later, she was admitted with persistent fevers, myalgias, malaise, lower-limb weakness, and abdominal pain. On admission, her temperature was 38.5 °C, heart rate 72 bpm, blood pressure 93/51 mm Hg, and SpO₂ 100% on room air. Leukocytes were 20.2 K/μL, eosinophils 500 cells/μL, alkaline phosphatase 666 U/L, ALT 236 U/L, GGT 236 U/L; lipase and urinalysis were normal. An abdominal ultrasound showed borderline gallbladder thickening but no signs of infection. Blood cultures were negative, and nasal swab for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Physical examination revealed a low jugular venous pressure; heart, lung, abdominal, skin, joint, conjunctival, and oral examinations were otherwise normal, with no lymphadenopathy.

She was started empirically on metronidazole and ceftriaxone, later broadened to piperacillin–tazobactam. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C; CMV; and EBV were negative. Autoimmune markers including ANA, rheumatoid factor, ANCA, mitochondrial antibody, and smooth muscle antibody were negative. Eosinophils rose to 1900 cells/μL, raising the question of drug reaction versus sepsis.
journal: Allergy, Asthma, and Clinical Immunology : Official Journal of the Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
title: Liver enzyme elevation and eosinophilia with atorvastatin: a case of probable DRESS without cutaneous symptoms

case_prompt:
A 21-year-old university student experienced syncope shortly after exercise. He reported no chest pain or dyspnea but had a self-limited diarrheal illness two weeks earlier. In the emergency department he was afebrile, blood pressure was 127/78 mmHg, heart rate 81 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination was unremarkable. His mother had idiopathic cardiomyopathy; his maternal grandmother died of sudden cardiac arrest.

On telemetry, he developed sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a cycle length of 220 ms, treated with intravenous metoprolol, amiodarone, and lidocaine. In the coronary care unit, he had polymorphic VT that degenerated into ventricular fibrillation; he was successfully defibrillated.

Serum chemistry was normal. Initial troponin I was 0.23 ng/mL (normal <0.04 ng/mL) and subsequently decreased. Pre-arrest ECG showed sinus rhythm with premature ventricular complexes of left bundle branch block, inferior axis morphology; there were no epsilon waves, precordial T-wave inversions, conduction delays, or QT prolongation. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 45% and severe basal-anterior hypokinesis with mild hypokinesis of adjacent segments. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated sub-epicardial late gadolinium enhancement in the basal-anterior and basal anterolateral segments and additional mid-inferior and mid-anteroseptal enhancement. The right ventricle was normal in size and function without late enhancement. An endomyocardial biopsy showed mild lymphocytic myocarditis, interstitial fibrosis, and myocyte hypertrophy.
title: Case report: DSP truncation variant p. R1951X leads to arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man presented with a dry cough and occasional hemoptysis. Chest imaging revealed two discrete lung lesions: a 2.5 cm mass in the right lower lobe and a 0.7 cm nodule in the right upper lobe. PET/CT showed mild uptake in the larger lesion and no other abnormalities. Surgical specimens included the right lower lobe lobectomy containing the dominant lesion, a wedge biopsy of the smaller nodule, and multiple mediastinal lymph nodes, which were negative for tumor.

Microscopic examination showed unencapsulated but well-circumscribed nodules with a prominent capillary network and intervening stromal cells displaying eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm with fine lipid vacuoles. Occasional solid lobules lacking vasculature demonstrated increased cytological atypia. On frozen section, the tumor appeared highly vascular with microcystic changes and epithelioid cells mimicking renal cell carcinoma.

Initial immunohistochemistry revealed nonreactivity for pancytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, synaptophysin, chromogranin, Melan-A, and CD10, findings that did not support carcinoma, melanoma, or neuroendocrine tumor. The lipid-containing cells were negative for Melan-A, inconsistent with adrenal cortical neoplasm. Further stains were negative for the histiocytic markers CD68, CD1a, CD45, and lysozyme.

Communication with the referring hospitals disclosed two prior posterior fossa surgeries for brain tumors 20 and 7 years earlier. Additional immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the stromal cells were positive for inhibin-A, neuron specific enolase (NSE), S-100, and vimentin. CD34 highlighted only the capillary vasculature; fewer than 5% of cells reacted for Ki-67, and GFAP was negative.
title: Hemangioblastoma in the Lung: Metastatic or Primary Lesions?

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old woman with high myopia (spherical equivalent −10.0 diopters in both eyes) was referred for sudden onset of decreased vision and a central scotoma in the right eye. She denied recent trauma or a Valsalva maneuver. Her medical history was notable only for panic disorder treated with alprazolam and escitalopram; routine blood tests two months earlier were normal. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/100 OD and 20/20 OS.

Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a stellate intraretinal hemorrhage in the fovea with a petaloid pattern and feathery edges, suggesting localization within Henle’s fiber layer. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the right eye showed an elevated hyperreflective lesion in the outer retina with shadowing of the underlying retinal pigment epithelium and adjacent intraretinal fluid within the outer plexiform layer.
title: Myopic Simple Hemorrhage Presenting as Radial Hemorrhage in Henle's Fiber Layer

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman presented with a sacrococcygeal mass that she first noticed 6 months earlier. Initially the size of a pigeon egg and asymptomatic, the mass gradually enlarged and was associated with a sense of lumbosacral fullness. She had no prior medical history and no family history of similar lesions. On digital rectal examination, a large, hard, fixed mass was palpated anterior to the rectal wall, with indistinct borders. Routine blood tests and tumor markers, including CEA, AFP, CA 19-9, and CA125, were all within normal limits. 

Preoperative pelvic MRI demonstrated a sharply demarcated paracervical mass measuring 9.5 × 8.1 cm with a layered appearance on T2-weighted images, displacing the uterus cephalad. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis showed a mass between the cervix and rectum with nonenhancing areas, pushing the anterior vagina and right posterior rectum. 

Transrectal ultrasonography with a biplane probe revealed an irregular left pelvic mass with an internal layered pattern of alternating hyperechoic and hypoechoic areas and a clear interface with the rectal wall. Color Doppler imaging showed scattered intratumoral vessels corresponding to the lamellar pattern. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) via the transrectal probe demonstrated a laminated distribution of contrast agent within the mass.
title: Value of contrast-enhanced ultrasound in deep angiomyxoma using a biplane transrectal probe: A case report

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old Sri Lankan woman was referred for evaluation of an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) found during workup of a febrile illness; she was asymptomatic on admission. She had a history of hypertension, dyslipidemia, bronchial asthma, and bilateral knee osteoarthritis, managed with rosuvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, glucosamine, and low-dose aspirin. Two years earlier, she had a biopsy of painful cervical lymphadenopathy showing noncaseating granulomatous inflammation; atypical mycobacteria, fungal infection, and tuberculosis were considered, and she completed 6 months of category 1 anti-tuberculous therapy.

Current evaluation revealed mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL), lymphocyte-predominant leukocytes without lymphoproliferative features, mild eosinophilia, and an ESR of 102 mm/hr with normal C-reactive protein. Liver and renal tests were normal. Chest radiography, sputum for acid-fast bacilli, urine AFB, and urine cultures were negative; serum protein electrophoresis showed polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. She was discharged.

One month later she returned with fever and recurrent cervical lymphadenopathy. Excisional biopsy again showed noncaseating granulomata; immunohistochemistry excluded hematologic malignancy and TB PCR was negative. Empirical anti-TB therapy was restarted. After 2 months of therapy she developed intermittent low-grade fever, symmetrical arthritis of hands and legs, backache, diaphoresis, vomiting, anorexia, and bilateral extremity edema; there was no rash or jaundice. On examination she was febrile and diaphoretic; joints were not inflamed. Laboratory tests showed ESR 130 mm/hr, white blood cell count 12,000/mm3 with 82% neutrophils, C-reactive protein 200 mg/L, and normal creatine phosphokinase. Serum calcium, acetylcholine esterase level, and MRI of the spine were normal; liver enzymes were mildly elevated. 

AOsD, sarcoidosis, polymyalgia rheumatica spectrum disorders, and RS3PE syndrome were considered. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal, TB PCR and cultures remained negative, purified protein derivative test was <5 mm, antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor were negative, and extractable nuclear antigen panels were unremarkable. Serial blood, urine, and CSF cultures were sterile, and PCR for bacterial or fungal DNA was negative. Serum ferritin was mildly elevated. Empirical ceftriaxone, followed by meropenem and vancomycin for 10 days, failed to resolve the fever or inflammatory markers.
title: Noncaseating suppurative granulomatous lymphadenitis in adult onset Still’s disease – a diagnostic dilemma in a tuberculosis-endemic region: a case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man presented with progressive nausea and vomiting over several weeks. He reported a history of watery diarrhea since the age of 6 months; at that time, investigations showed a stool chloride concentration >90 mmol/L, low serum and urinary chloride and potassium levels, metabolic alkalosis, and elevated serum uric acid. He had been managed with a high-salt diet and oral potassium and calcium supplements. Twelve years earlier, he developed recurrent gouty arthritis treated with multiple NSAIDs.

On examination, he was alert and oriented, with a blood pressure of 180/110 mmHg, afebrile, and a body weight of 104 kg. There was no jugular venous distension, edema, or abnormal findings on systemic examination, including the lungs.

Laboratory results revealed:  
• Hemoglobin 104 g/L, normal MCV, transferrin saturation, and vitamin B12  
• White-cell and platelet counts within normal limits  
• Serum urea 40 μmol/L, creatinine 650 μmol/L  
• Sodium 129 mmol/L, chloride 93 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, calcium 1.8 mmol/L  
• Uric acid 700 μmol/L, albumin 41 g/L  
• Normal liver tests, serum cholesterol, and TSH  
• Arterial pH 7.5, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L  
• Urinalysis: 1+ proteinuria, no hematuria or pyuria  
• Complement C3 and C4, IgA, and protein electrophoresis normal  
• Negative anti-CCP, ANA, anti–dsDNA, ANCA, anti–GBM, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti–HCV  
• Stool studies negative for ova, parasites, and occult blood; stool chloride 120 mmol/L, urine chloride and potassium undetectable  
• Chest radiograph and ECG normal  
• Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound showed bilateral small kidneys (8 cm) with thin, echogenic cortex and foci of papillary calcification, findings confirmed by CT scan
title: “Recurrent Papillary Necrosis and Nephrocalcinosis Induced by Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs for Gouty Arthritis Associated with Congenital Chloride-Losing Diarrhea: A Major Risk for Kidney Loss”

case_prompt: A 17-year-old boy presented with progressive lower abdominal pain and a left lower quadrant mass. Three months earlier, he had fallen from the fourth floor; initial examination, laboratory tests, and CT scan at that time were unremarkable, and he was discharged after 12 hours of observation. One month after the fall, he began to experience abdominal pain that gradually worsened, prompting presentation to our emergency department. On examination, he was afebrile, with extensive abdominal tenderness, involuntary muscle guarding, and a firm, tender mass in the left lower quadrant. His leukocyte count was 16 400/mm3. A plain abdominal radiograph was normal. Ultrasonography demonstrated a mass in the left lower quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a heterogeneous soft-tissue mass located between the left psoas muscle and lateral abdominal wall, partially surrounding the sigmoid colon. The radiologist interpreted these findings as consistent with an internal herniation of the intestines. Despite fluid resuscitation and administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics, signs of acute abdomen persisted, and an emergency laparotomy was planned.
title: Actinomycosis Presenting as an Abdominal Mass in a Child

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of fever, breathlessness, weight loss, anorexia, and a dull, continuous, dragging pain in the left abdomen. She had no significant past medical or trauma history. On examination, the abdomen was slightly distended, and there was a tender, firm, irregular mass palpable in the left upper quadrant, extending 6–7 cm below the left costal margin to the level of the umbilicus; no other abnormalities were noted on systemic examination.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 12,000/mm^3 with 7% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 840/mm^3) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm in the first hour. Plain abdominal and chest radiographs were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an enlarged spleen with multiple cystic areas measuring 18 × 15 × 11 cm in total. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large splenic mass (17.5 × 15 × 10 cm) with heterogeneous, predominantly low-density contents and air-fluid levels, causing elevation of the left hemidiaphragm; other abdominal organs appeared normal.
title: Giant isolated splenic hydatidosis

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old woman with a history of smoking, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and hypertension underwent an L1–S1 laminectomy and L2–L5 in situ fusion with iliac crest bone graft and bone morphogenic protein for severe multilevel lumbar stenosis and degenerative scoliosis. She had no history or symptoms of coronary artery disease or heart failure. Surgery was complicated by an incidental durotomy that was repaired without issue; estimated blood loss was 550 mL. She was extubated in the operating room and transferred to the postanesthesia care unit, where she required a brief trial of supplemental oxygen via Venturi mask but otherwise recovered uneventfully. The first two postoperative days were unremarkable.

On the evening of postoperative day three, she experienced a seven-hour episode of squeezing chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath. Initial cardiac biomarkers showed a peak troponin level of 1.3 ng/mL. Electrocardiography demonstrated diffuse T-wave inversions and T-wave flattening. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 30%–35%, a left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 4.6 cm, a left atrial diameter of 5.0 cm, and akinesis of the anteroseptal, lateral, and apical walls.
title: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy following a L2–L5 Laminectomy and Fusion In Situ with Bone Morphogenic Protein

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old girl presented with primary amenorrhea and a 6-month history of cyclical lower abdominal pain, constipation, and an episode of acute urinary retention that was temporarily relieved by catheterization. She had no prior surgeries and was self-medicating with anti-helminthics. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Secondary sexual characteristics were appropriate for age. Abdominal palpation disclosed a mobile, slightly tender midline mass extending nearly to the umbilicus. External genital examination revealed normal labia and a completely intact, bulging hymenal membrane without any canalization. On rectal examination, a mobile central pelvic mass was palpable anterior to the rectum.  
A repeat abdominal ultrasonogram showed a single ovoid, sonolucent mass in the mid-pelvis extending from the upper vaginal area to just below the umbilicus; the bladder was decompressed, and no separate uterine structures were identified.
title: Virginity-sparing management of hematocolpos with imperforate hymen: case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an incidentally detected murmur. He had a history of well-controlled hypertension and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. He denied chest pain, dyspnoea, constitutional symptoms, or any history of infections, including tuberculosis or syphilis. He had no family history of aortic disease or autoimmune disorders and reported no systemic symptoms suggestive of vasculitis or connective tissue disease.

On examination, blood pressure was 160/59 mm Hg and heart rate 59 beats per minute. There was prominent head-nodding (De Musset’s sign), a grade IV/VI diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, and bounding carotid pulsations. Lung and other cardiovascular findings were unremarkable.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a tricuspid aortic valve with severe aortic insufficiency and an enlarged ascending aorta; left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%. Contrast CT angiography confirmed a fusiform aneurysm of the ascending thoracic aorta measuring 5.7 × 6.5 cm. Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a central aortic regurgitant jet occupying 60% of the left ventricular outflow tract. Laboratory tests revealed a normal complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein. Preoperative coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries.

The patient underwent aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthesis and supracoronary replacement of the ascending aorta. Intraoperative histopathologic examination of the aortic wall demonstrated lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with some fibrosis, consistent with non-infectious ascending aortitis.
title: An unusual presentation of non-infectious ascending aortitis: a case report of an asymptomatic murmur

case_prompt: A 31-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis underwent a living nonrelated kidney transplant at age 16. He received cyclosporine A, prednisone, and azathioprine but was poorly compliant, suffered multiple acute rejection episodes, and developed severe chronic allograft damage. Eleven years posttransplant, he resumed hemodialysis; four weeks later he presented with a 3-day history of watery diarrhea, vomiting, fever with rigor, mild diffuse abdominal pain, and one episode of gross hematuria. His temperature was 37.9°C, pulse 101/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 138/93 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination revealed mild generalized abdominal and graft tenderness. Urinalysis showed WBCs 7/HPF, RBCs 1/HPF, and protein 600 mg/dL. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 143 g/L, WBC count 3.9×10^9/L, platelets 150×10^9/L, normal electrolytes, BUN 6.2 mmol/L, and creatinine 801 µmol/L. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 14.3 cm allograft with a well-defined, round, midzonal lesion measuring 1.8 cm, suspicious for malignancy; both native kidneys were atrophic without cysts or focal lesions. CT of the abdomen confirmed a 1.8 cm enhancing lesion in the middle third of the renal allograft. He was treated for presumed acute gastroenteritis with cefazolin and gentamicin, which resolved his gastrointestinal symptoms. Electively, he underwent embolization of the renal artery supplying the graft followed by graft nephrectomy.
title: Incidental Eosinophilic Chromophobe Renal Cell Carcinoma in Renal Allograft

case_prompt: A 27-year-old woman with a history of pulmonary tuberculosis and recent abdominal trauma resulting in a lumbar fracture presented with a several-month history of chronic abdominal pain and nausea. On examination, her abdomen was soft with a palpable midline mass. Laboratory studies revealed mild anemia; results of tumor markers were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 183 × 170 × 73 mm abdomino–pelvic cystic lesion with hypodense contents; the liver, spleen, and pancreas appeared normal, and an ovarian origin was initially suggested. Subsequent MRI demonstrated a well-defined peritoneal cystic mass with homogeneous hyperintensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, punctate areas of low T2 signal, and no identifiable fatty component. A dark peripheral capsule was seen on T2-weighted images. The mass displaced but did not invade adjacent bowel and other organs. Both ovaries were visualized as separate, multifollicular structures uninvolved with the lesion, and there was a small volume of peritoneal fluid.
title: Intraperitoneal chronic expanding hematoma mimicking an ovarian tumor: A case report

case_prompt:
A seven-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of a painless mass of the left wrist. His parents first noted a 4–5 mm soft tissue swelling four months earlier, which had progressively enlarged. He had an uncomplicated birth history, no trauma, vascular access, or known connective tissue or rheumatologic disorders.  
On examination, there was a 1 cm bluish, non-tender, pulsatile mass over the left radial artery. A Doppler-assisted Allen test raised concern about arterial patency.  
Arterial duplex ultrasound showed a 9 × 9 mm lesion, suspected to be a true aneurysm, with normal distal flow. Magnetic resonance angiography demonstrated a 1.1 × 0.8 × 1.0 cm mass arising from the radial artery, with retrograde filling from the superficial palmar arch and thrombosis proximal to the lesion.  
Surgical exploration revealed a multi-lobular, focally bluish arterial mass adherent to the flexor carpi radialis sheath. Trial clamping of the radial artery proximally and distally confirmed brisk distal perfusion, so the involved segment was excised without reconstruction.  
Histopathology of the specimen showed medial attenuation with large areas of complete media loss, intimal fibroplasia, and mural thrombus.
journal: Case Reports in Plastic Surgery & Hand Surgery
title: Spontaneous radial artery pseudoaneurysm in an infant due to idiopathic medial hypoplasia – a case report

case_prompt: A 40-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of dry cough and exertional dyspnea. She had no history of tuberculosis, smoking, chemical or organic dust exposure, regular medications, or prior surgery. On examination, she was afebrile with stable vital signs. Chest auscultation revealed reduced breath sounds on the right side, accompanied by wheeze and occasional crackles; cardiac pulsations were palpable on the right chest. A frontal chest radiograph showed volume loss of the right lung, ipsilateral tracheal and mediastinal shift, cardiac dextroposition, and tenting of the right hemidiaphragm. Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of right lung collapse was made. The differential diagnoses for the etiology included: (a) post-tubercular sequelae (common in this part of the world), (b) neoplastic processes, and (c) mucus plugging or a forgotten foreign body.
title: Unveiling the anomaly: Scimitar syndrome in a middle-aged female patient

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old Turkish man presented with a 6-month history of pain in the tongue and buccal mucosa and difficulty chewing and swallowing solid foods. He has had severe chronic periodontitis since age 25, untreated, leading to loss of most teeth by age 60. He smokes 1–1.5 packs per day since age 24. His only prior surgery was a tonsillectomy in childhood, and he reported no other systemic symptoms.

Vital signs were normal. Oral examination showed poor hygiene, heavy plaque, near-complete edentulism, and a diffusely enlarged, red tongue with bilateral white plaques and translucent papules that bled easily when removed. Two small flat-based ulcers with erythematous halos were on the buccal mucosa.

Laboratory studies revealed chronic renal failure with hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, leukocytosis, fibrinogen, and hs-CRP. High-resolution CT of the chest showed minimal emphysematous changes at both apices; spirometry was normal. Rectal and bone marrow biopsies, serum and urine protein electrophoresis, echocardiogram, abdominal CT, and liver function tests were unremarkable. Cultures of the oral plaques were negative. Biopsies of the tongue and buccal mucosa were obtained for histopathological evaluation.
title: Oral involvement in a case of AA amyloidosis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old man presented with 20 days of periumbilical abdominal pain, 10 days of progressive abdominal distension, and 3 days of loose stools. The pain was a dull ache around the umbilicus, becoming intermittent with bloating relieved by passage of flatus. He denied vomiting, fever, jaundice, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Outside laboratories showed an absolute eosinophil count of 11 400/μL. He had no history of allergies, atopy, new medications, or B symptoms, and no relevant family history.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs and a BMI of 22 kg/m2. Nailfold inspection revealed splinter hemorrhages; abdominal examination showed distension with shifting dullness and sluggish bowel sounds, without organomegaly. Systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory studies demonstrated a leukocyte count of 33 000/μL with an absolute eosinophil count of 25 000/μL; hemoglobin and platelet counts were normal. Renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. Total IgE was elevated at 830 kUA/L. Midnight diethylcarbamazine provocation test and multiple stool examinations were negative for parasites. Ascitic fluid analysis revealed an exudative fluid (SAAG 0.7 g/dL) with 95% eosinophils. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed septated ascites. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed diffuse bowel wall thickening with submucosal edema. Upper and lower endoscopy revealed erythematous mucosa; biopsies from the antrum, duodenum, terminal ileum, cecum, and rectum demonstrated dense eosinophilic infiltration in the lamina propria and muscularis mucosa.
journal: World Journal of Gastrointestinal Pharmacology and Therapeutics
title: Hypereosinophilic syndrome presenting as eosinophilic gastroenteritis disorder and splinter hemorrhages: A case report

case_prompt: A 14-year-old girl and competitive karate and judo athlete presented with bilateral bony prominences on the lateral aspects of her knees, first noted one year earlier without pain or functional limitation. Over the past year she developed mild pain at the prominences after sports activities, worse on the right, and was concerned about the cosmetic appearance. On examination there was no generalized ligamentous laxity (Beighton score 2/9). Both proximal fibular heads were prominent, displaced posterolaterally, and exhibited mild anteroposterior instability on manual testing. The prominences became more obvious with knee flexion and squatting. There was no tenderness at the bony prominences, and knee range of motion was normal bilaterally. Radiographs of both knees showed posterior and lateral subluxation of the fibular heads, with the ratio of lateral displacement to maximum fibular head width (Y) measuring 1.40 on the right and 1.44 on the left (normal <1). Magnetic resonance imaging of both knees revealed intact superior tibiofibular ligaments and joint capsules, normal joint spaces, and no cartilage abnormalities.
title: Bilateral Subluxation of the Proximal Tibiofibular Joint: A Rare Case Report

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus presented with a 4-day history of left periocular pain, a drooping eyelid, and limitation of left-eye movements. Two weeks earlier, she had a severe left-sided headache unresponsive to sedatives, accompanied by fatigue, a dry cough, and fever. She denied trauma or recreational drug use.

On examination, there was complete external ophthalmoplegia of the left eye, total left ptosis, and mild chemosis. The left pupil was semi-dilated and nonreactive to light. Hertel exophthalmometry showed 3 mm of proptosis on the left. Uncorrected visual acuity was 0.6 (0.18 LogMAR), intraocular pressure was 16 mmHg, and color vision was normal. She was alert and oriented. Tendon reflexes and muscle tone were normal, with no meningeal or cerebellar signs. Ear, nose, and throat examinations were unremarkable. The sensory examination was normal initially; left corneal hypoesthesia developed 2 days later.

Laboratory studies, including CBC, PT, INR, D-dimer, ferritin, urea, LDH, creatinine, liver enzymes, and electrolytes, were within normal limits. C-reactive protein was elevated at 11.4 mg/L, and blood glucose was 300 mg/dL. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive.

Brain and orbital CT and MRI were unremarkable, with no evidence of inflammation or mass.
title: A case of total ophthalmoplegia associated with a COVID-19 infection: case report

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old woman presented with a 9-month history of a progressively enlarging, painless swelling in her left breast. She noted the mass while showering; there was no nipple discharge, skin changes, or history of trauma or prior breast surgery. She had no family history of breast cancer. 

On examination, there was a 6 × 8 cm non-tender, hard mass fixed to the skin in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast; there was no erythema, ulceration, or discharge. Vital signs were normal.

Ultrasound of the breast showed an anechoic cystic mass with a double-layered wall and posterior acoustic enhancement. Fine-needle aspiration produced a crystal-clear fluid; cytologic examination revealed a few laminated, metachromatic materials without cellular atypia.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare case of hydatid cyst presenting as a breast cancer. A case report☆

case_prompt: A 3-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a 6-month history of dysphagia and repeated oral bleeding. On examination, there was a soft, painful, reddish-blue, immobilized mass measuring approximately 3 cm in its greatest dimension on the mid-dorsum of the tongue extending toward the base, without cervical lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI showed a 3.3×1.9×2.0 cm hypervascular mass obstructing the pharyngeal inlet, initially interpreted as a hemangioma. Under general anesthesia, an incisional biopsy was performed; histopathology was reported as a benign capillary hemangioma by both the treating institution and a specialized vascular anomalies center. The patient received systemic corticosteroids and interferon alpha-2a, but over the next six months the mass continued to enlarge, leading to partial airway obstruction. He underwent tracheostomy and wide local excision of the lesion; review at a pediatric tumor center again favored hemangioma.
title: Alveolar soft part sarcoma of the tongue in a 3-year-old boy: a case report

case_prompt: A 14-year-old boy from a rural region of Ethiopia presented with an 8-month history of a painless, reddish-pink, fleshy mass on the left eye, associated with foreign-body sensation and intermittent discomfort. He denied any trauma or similar lesions elsewhere. Vital signs were within normal limits. On ocular examination, there was a 20×4 mm pinkish, pedunculated, fleshy mass on the left palpebral conjunctiva, studded with multiple yellowish and white nodules on its surface; visual acuity was normal. With a clinical impression of pyogenic granuloma, the lesion was excised at its base under local anesthesia, and hemostasis was achieved. A formalin-fixed tissue fragment was submitted for histopathologic evaluation.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Conjunctival rhinosporidiosis mimicking pyogenic granuloma: A case report

case_prompt: A 54-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of left hip pain that had markedly worsened over the past 10 days, accompanied by difficulty walking and intermittent fever. She denied low back pain, radicular symptoms, trauma, abdominal pain, weight loss, or recent infections. Her medical history was notable for cervical cancer treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy 3 years earlier and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. On examination, temperature was 37.1°C, pulse 95/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. She appeared pale and mobilized with difficulty; the left hip was flexed at 50°, with pain on attempted movement and tenderness over the greater trochanter. Right hip and lumbar spine movement were full and painless; there was mild spasm of left lumbar paravertebral muscles without neurologic deficits. Distal pulses were palpable, and there was no lower-extremity edema. Laboratory studies showed leukocytes 17.9×10^3/µL, hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, ESR 110 mm/h, CRP 31.2 mg/dL, creatinine 1.56 mg/dL, negative Brucella agglutination, and urinalysis with 3+ protein and 1500 leukocytes/HPF. Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine, pelvis, and left hip were unremarkable except for mild degenerative changes. Ultrasound of the left hip and gluteal region revealed a slight amount of fluid in the trochanteric bursa. Magnetic resonance imaging of the hip was attempted but could not be performed due to severe pain. An urgent non–contrast abdominal CT scan was obtained.
title: An Easily Overlooked Presentation of Malignant Psoas Abscess: Hip Pain

case_prompt: A 50-year-old woman, previously well, presented initially with a week of flu-like symptoms and three days of purulent ear discharge, followed by vomiting, collapse, and reduced consciousness. She was diagnosed with Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis secondary to otitis media, treated with antibiotics and supportive care, and discharged 11 days later. Three days after discharge, she was readmitted after a fall with gradually increasing lower‐limb weakness and painless urinary retention. On examination, she was afebrile and fully conscious. Cranial nerves and upper limbs were normal. Lower limbs showed slightly reduced tone, pyramidal‐pattern weakness, brisk reflexes, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and a sensory level at T10. Initial blood tests showed mild neutrophilic leukocytosis; other routine results were normal. An urgent MRI of the spinal cord showed no epidural collection, no discitis, and no intrinsic cord signal abnormality. MR venography of the cerebral veins was normal. Brain MRI revealed several ill-defined high T2 signal foci in the corona radiata bilaterally. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (12 polymorphs, 96 lymphocytes per mm3), elevated protein (1.84 g/L), normal glucose, no oligoclonal bands, negative virology, and no organisms cultured.
title: Post-infective transverse myelitis following Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis with radiological features of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis: a case report

case_prompt: A 67-year-old white man with type II diabetes, hypertension, and myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts II, for which he had received two cycles of azacitidine (last cycle 2 weeks earlier), presented with a 1-week history of worsening dyspnea and a mild productive cough. He had a 15–pack-year smoking history. On presentation, his temperature was 98°F, blood pressure 120/75 mm Hg, heart rate 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 80 % on room air. Lung examination revealed bilateral basal fine inspiratory crackles. Arterial blood gases showed mild respiratory alkalosis. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, platelet count 30×10^3/mm^3, and WBC count 8.4×10^3/mm^3; coagulation parameters, BNP, renal and liver function were normal. ECG and echocardiogram were normal. Chest radiograph revealed bilateral interstitial infiltrates. He was started on levofloxacin and piperacillin-tazobactam for possible pneumonia. On hospital day 2, his oxygen requirement rose, and he was transferred to the ICU for noninvasive ventilation. Noncontrast chest CT showed multifocal bilateral pulmonary consolidations—some rounded with surrounding ground-glass opacities—and bilateral pleural effusions.
