Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and left pleural fluid sampling were performed. BAL studies were negative for aerobic and anaerobic bacterial cultures, fungal stain and culture, and HSV and CMV PCR. Pleural fluid analysis was consistent with a transudate (LDH 206 U/L [serum 390], protein 2.2 g/dL [serum 5.3], glucose 210 mg/dL) with 90 % lymphocytes; cytology was negative for malignant cells.
title: Azacitidine-induced cryptogenic organizing pneumonia: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 6-month-old female infant was referred for evaluation of a right upper-quadrant abdominal mass. She had a one-month history of fever unresponsive to antibiotics, right hypochondrial pain, and progressive abdominal enlargement without jaundice. Perinatal and developmental history were unremarkable. On examination, her liver was palpable with a span of 8 cm (normal 5–5.5 cm) with tenderness in the right hypochondrium. Laboratory tests revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 8.4 g/dl), leukocytosis (13.1×10^3/mm^3), thrombocytosis (620×10^3/mm^3), a slightly elevated alpha-fetoprotein level (26.6 ng/ml), and normal liver function tests. Abdominal ultrasound showed a well-defined heterogeneous mass in the right lobe of the liver with cystic degeneration and calcific foci, measuring 7.4×8.4 cm. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a large nonenhancing hypodense cystic lesion occupying segments V–VII of the right liver (8×8×8.3 cm), with an exophytic component encroaching on the right suprarenal region and inferior displacement of the right kidney; no enlarged abdominal lymph nodes were seen. Based on imaging, the mass was highly suggestive of a mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver, with hepatoblastoma as an alternative consideration. The patient was scheduled for surgical resection and histopathological confirmation.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Right adrenal gland neuroblastoma infiltrating the liver and mimicking mesenchymal hamartoma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with left lower extremity bruising, swelling, and pain. Two months earlier, during a softball game, she collided with another player’s cleat and was diagnosed that day with a hairline fracture of the left tibial diaphysis with an overlying hematoma. She followed up with orthopedics, completed physical therapy, and was cleared to resume sports six weeks before this presentation. Six days prior, she played two softball games, denying any significant trauma or sliding events during these games. Five days before presentation, she awoke with pain and bruising of her left lateral shin and treated her pain with ibuprofen—the first NSAID she had taken in two months. Over the next days, her pain and bruising worsened, and she noted edema of the left calf. 

On re-presentation, she required morphine for pain. Vital signs showed mild hypertension; all other vitals were normal. Examination revealed extensive bruising, edema, and pain with light palpation or weight-bearing of the left calf; no erythema, abrasions, or skin tightness; distal dorsalis pedis pulses were 2/4 and symmetric; Homan sign was negative. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, complete metabolic panel, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, creatine kinase, C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and uric acid, were within normal limits for age. 

Frontal and lateral radiographs of the left leg demonstrated anterior, medial, and lateral subcutaneous soft-tissue edema of the proximal and mid leg. An ultrasound showed a complex fluid collection in the lateral subcutaneous soft tissues, prompting further evaluation with MRI.
title: Delayed Onset of Pediatric Morel-Lavallée Lesion: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man was admitted with progressive jaundice, muscle wasting, and abdominal distension. His past history included portal hypertension attributed to cryptogenic cirrhosis diagnosed 4 years earlier on the basis of thrombocytopenia and large non-bleeding esophageal varices; no liver biopsy was performed at that time. On examination he was icteric and had tense ascites.

Laboratory studies showed an alkaline phosphatase level of 674 U/L, total bilirubin of 6.8 mg/dL, and transaminases of 60 U/L. An abdominal CT scan revealed a low‐attenuation lesion in the right hepatic lobe measuring 3.7 × 6.4 × 5.1 cm with peripheral nodular enhancement, suggestive of hemangioma. Both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts were dilated, with the common bile duct up to 1.5 cm in diameter.

MRCP demonstrated intra- and extrahepatic biliary dilatation and an irregular narrowing of the common bile duct at the porta hepatis, surrounded by an ill-defined soft-tissue lesion. Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic head region with associated distal bile duct obstruction and extensive collateral circulation. ERCP showed a localized biliary stricture with a malignant appearance, and a self-expandable metal stent was placed via sphincterotomy.

Fine-needle aspiration of the peripancreatic lesion and brush cytology of the bile duct stricture were negative for malignancy. A liver biopsy showed nodular regenerative hyperplasia with minimal fibrosis and intact bile ducts without injury. After stent placement, the patient’s jaundice, ascites, bilirubin level, and alkaline phosphatase level all improved.
title: Portal Cavernoma Mimicking Pancreatic Malignancy

case_prompt: A 27-year-old woman with a 5-month history of ileal Crohn’s disease presented with 3 days of fever, central pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and a 2-month history of intermittent right-eye visual loss. She was an active smoker with a prior splenectomy for sterile splenic abscesses. She was not taking any medications. On examination, temperature was 39.0°C, heart rate 110 b.p.m., blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg. There were no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis; heart sounds were dual without murmurs; lungs were clear; visual acuity and fundoscopic examination were normal. ECG showed sinus rhythm with inferior T-wave inversion. Chest radiograph was normal. Laboratory studies revealed WBC 21.0×10^9/L, CRP 115 mg/L, hemoglobin 106 g/L with MCV 75 fL, platelets 572×10^9/L, troponin 900 ng/L, and normal renal function. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF >50%, a markedly thickened hypokinetic basal inferolateral wall, and a mobile echodense mass on the atrial side of the posterior mitral leaflet with mild regurgitation. Blood cultures were obtained and empiric antibiotics for infective endocarditis (flucloxacillin, vancomycin, gentamicin) were started. On hospital day 7, transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated mobile echodensities on both anterior and posterior mitral valve leaflets. After 8 days, all blood cultures remained negative, and the patient continued to have fevers despite switch to a regimen for culture-negative endocarditis (ceftriaxone, flucloxacillin, high-dose vancomycin).
title: Myocarditis in Crohn’s disease: a case report

case_prompt:
A 65‐year‐old right‐handed Ethiopian man was referred to neurology for diffuse, symmetrical fat deposition. Fifteen years earlier, he noted gradual accumulation of abdominal fat, which later extended to involve his anterior chest with bilateral breast enlargement and, over time, his torso, upper arms, and thighs, sparing his face and distal limbs. During the past six months, he developed deep aching pain in both knees and ankles, and more recently low back pain, resulting in difficulty standing and walking. He had been told at a nearby clinic that his symptoms were due to excess body weight (114 kg) and was treated with oral analgesics and advised weight loss, without improvement. He denied significant alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drug use. 

He found it difficult to fit his clothing but otherwise had no dyspnea, dysphagia, abdominal pain, or distal sensory or motor symptoms. He had lost his driving job because of mobility issues. He had no family history of similar illness.

On examination, BMI was 39.6 kg/m2; vital signs were normal. There was diffuse, bilateral, symmetrical, non-tender, soft swelling of the trunk, shoulders, upper arms, thighs, and bilateral breast enlargement. Skin folds over the back and torso were thick and redundant, with large lipomatous masses sparing the neck. The forearms and shins appeared normal. Neurologic exam revealed mild lumbar tenderness; motor and sensory exams were normal. No joint swelling or crepitus was noted.

Laboratory tests showed hyperuricemia (10.6 mg/dl) but were otherwise within normal limits, including blood glucose, lipid panel, liver and thyroid function, renal function, rheumatoid factor, and HIV serology.

Sagittal T1-weighted MRI of the cervical and lumbar spine demonstrated diffuse subcutaneous fat deposition in the posterior neck and lower back, along with multilevel degenerative disc prolapse and osteophytic changes.
title: Madelung’s disease in a non-alcoholic Ethiopian male patient mistaken for obesity: a case report

case_prompt:
A 5-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of an enlarging scalp mass at the site of minor blunt trauma from a ground-level fall. One week after the fall, the mother noted a flesh-colored bump that enlarged to approximately 3.0 × 3.0 cm. The patient denied fever, pain, itching, drainage, vision changes, or hearing changes.

On examination, she was well appearing. On the left frontotemporal scalp was a 3.0 × 3.0 cm oval, circumscribed mass that was firm, nonmobile, painless, and erythematous.

Unenhanced CT of the head showed a circumscribed superficial soft-tissue mass with a small internal calcification, confined to the subcutaneous fat and skin, without underlying bony involvement, osseous destruction, fat stranding, or surrounding inflammatory changes.

Ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous solid mass with a peripheral hypoechoic rim, internal hyperechoic foci with posterior shadowing suggestive of calcification, and prominent internal flow on Doppler imaging.

MRI revealed a heterogeneous mass with patchy and reticulated areas of increased T2 signal, peripheral rim enhancement with irregular internal reticular enhancement, a few internal foci of susceptibility artifact, and no diffusion restriction.
title: Post-traumatic pilomatricoma presenting as rapidly enlarging pediatric scalp mass

case_prompt: A 66-year-old Caucasian woman with no comorbidities presented with epigastric pain. Physical examination of the abdomen was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed an elevated C-reactive protein level; all other hematological parameters were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a regular hypoechoic nodular formation at the lower pole of the spleen measuring 8 cm in maximum diameter, with an internal calcification spot. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 77 mm hypodense splenic lesion with intralesional calcifications and identified a 1 cm accessory spleen adjacent to the lower pole. MRI characterized the mass as a 6.3 cm × 8.2 cm lesion with heterogeneous signal intensity: iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images and predominantly hypointense on T2-weighted images, with centrally scattered hyperintense areas on fat-saturated precontrast sequences. On dynamic contrast imaging, there was peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase with progressive centripetal filling in a radiating pattern on delayed images.
title: Sclerosing Angiomatoid Nodular Transformation: Laparoscopic Splenectomy as Therapeutic and Diagnostic Approach at the Same Time

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man presented with a 34-day history of persistent fever, chills, weight loss, and progressive dyspnea. He reported moderate left rib‐cage pain and palpitations early in the course. Five years earlier, he had completed treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis that was resistant to isoniazid, streptomycin, and ethionamide. On day 4 of illness, a chest radiograph was interpreted as normal despite ongoing fever (38°C), chills, and leukocytosis with neutrophilia. During the ensuing month, he also noted abdominal discomfort and continued weight loss. Serologic testing for HIV 1–2 and three sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were nonreactive and negative, respectively; abdominal ultrasound and stool studies were unremarkable.

On admission to the hospital, he appeared thin and moderately dehydrated, with a heart rate of 110 bpm, blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Examination revealed abolition of vesicular breath sounds over the middle and lower third of the left hemithorax. Laboratory tests showed rising leukocyte counts, neutrophilia, and elevated C-reactive protein.

On hospital day 9 (illness day 42), thoracentesis yielded 600 mL of purulent, greenish fluid, and a left-sided thoracostomy tube was placed. Intravenous broad‐spectrum antibiotics were initiated. By hospital day 12, his fever and leukocytosis had resolved, and inflammatory markers began to decrease. A chest CT scan performed on illness day 35 demonstrated a large, thick‐walled pleural fluid collection occupying the posterior left hemithorax; repeat imaging on illness day 48 showed a marked reduction in collection size.
journal: Revista Peruana de Medicina Experimental y Salud Publica
title: Pleural empyema by Parvimonsd micra in an immunocompetent patient: a case report

case_prompt:
A 58‐year‐old man was admitted in February with acute confusion. He had a 3-day history of cough, fever, headache, decreased appetite, restlessness and agitation. His medical history was unremarkable, and he had not received influenza vaccination in the prior 6 months. On examination, his temperature was 38.1 °C. He was alert but had apraxia, global dysphasia with paraphasia, and over several hours became mute. There was no meningism or cranial-nerve dysfunction.  
Initial blood tests showed leukocytes 3.8×10^9 cells/L and platelets 118×10^9 cells/L; other values were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 2 cells/µL, protein 0.92 g/L and an IgG oligoclonal‐band pattern identical to serum; PCR and cultures for viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites were negative. Electroencephalography showed diffuse slowing without epileptiform discharges. A nasopharyngeal swab was positive for influenza virus by PCR; sputum and urine cultures were negative.  
Brain MRI demonstrated multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions in both grey and white matter, including the ventral corpus callosum, without gadolinium enhancement or diffusion restriction.
title: Acute influenza virus-associated encephalitis and encephalopathy in adults: a challenging diagnosis

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old right-handed boy from an endemic region, with a history of left pleural hydatid cysts treated with albendazole, presented with six months of moderate, nonradiating pain in the upper third of his right arm. He had no fever or weight loss. On examination, the right shoulder and elbow were without swelling, tenderness, or limitation of motion; neurovascular findings were normal. Pulmonary auscultation revealed decreased vesicular breath sounds and dullness to percussion on the left. 

Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 150 mg/L (normal <6 mg/L), a white-blood-cell count of 20,000 cells/mm3, and normal liver enzymes and alkaline phosphatase. Hydatid serology was positive.

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right humerus demonstrated a lytic metaphyseal lesion at the proximal humerus without calcification or marginal sclerosis, with cortical breakthrough and expansion (Lodwick grade 1c) and no periosteal reaction. CT of the right humerus revealed a fluid-density lesion at the proximal humerus containing thin internal septations, with cortical destruction and extension into adjacent soft tissues, abutting but not invading the deltoid muscle. Chest CT showed multiple uniloculated subpleural cysts in the left lung.
title: Hydatid cyst of the humerus presenting as a suspicious lesion: A rare case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 43-year-old man presented with a one-month history of dysuria and difficulty initiating urination. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits, and no abnormalities were noted on physical examination. Laboratory studies, including a prostate-specific antigen level and urine analysis, were normal. To relieve symptoms and obtain tissue for diagnosis, transurethral resection of the prostate was performed; the pathology report described a low-grade stromal sarcoma of the prostate. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 5.2 × 4.9 × 5.6 cm, well-demarcated, heterogeneous mass in the right prostate lobe with both cystic and solid components. There was no evidence of capsular invasion or involvement of the bladder or seminal vesicles.
title: Prostatic stromal sarcoma: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old male presented with a 2-day history of nausea and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. He denied fever, vomiting, dehydration, or anorexia. He had a similar self-limited episode of pain 3 weeks earlier. His diet was high in carbohydrates (75–80% of intake). He had no other medical history except childhood treatment for a hearing problem; his mother has diabetes mellitus.  
On examination, his vital signs were normal and findings were consistent with acute appendicitis. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 14.9×10^3/µL (reference 4–10), neutrophils 74% (50–70), lymphocytes 17.8% (20–40), C-reactive protein 148.6 mg/L (0–5), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 99 mm/hr (0–20). Other blood counts and chemistries were normal.  
Abdominal ultrasonography did not visualize the appendix separately but identified a 40×35 mm septated abscess in the right lower quadrant with surrounding mesenteric and intestinal inflammation, suggesting a retrocecal location.  
Emergency laparoscopy revealed an appendix firmly adherent to the cecum cranially, without omental wrapping. The borders between appendix and cecum were distinguishable. The appendix appeared inflamed but lacked the typical hyperemia and increased vascularity of acute bacterial appendicitis. The surrounding fluid resembled lymphatic extravasation, and the appendix measured 1.5–2 cm in thickness without a discrete phlegmon. Difficulty in mobilization prompted conversion to laparotomy.  
At open surgery, the appendix showed intense fibrotic adhesions to the cecum and was excised with difficulty. The ileum, cecum, and ascending colon appeared normal. A Penrose drain was placed, and the patient was discharged after 1 week of broad-spectrum antibiotics with an uneventful recovery.
title: Diagnosing granulomatous disease during appendectomy

case_prompt:
A 6½-year-old boy was admitted with a 12-day history of intermittent-remittent fever up to 39.3 °C, treated at home with acetaminophen. He had pharyngitis, lateral cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy, and complained of right medial proximal thigh pain and a limp on walking. On admission, C-reactive protein was 7.17 mg/dL (normal < 0.5), white blood cell count was 19 360/µL (81.4% neutrophils), and antistreptolysin O titer was 451 IU/mL (normal < 200). Intravenous ceftriaxone was begun.  
Right lower limb venous ultrasonography excluded phlebitis or phlebothrombosis. Over the next day, C-reactive protein rose to 15.90 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 51 mm/h, and neutrophilic leukocytosis increased further. Ultrasonography of the thigh and hip showed minimal fluid intrafascial thickening of the proximal adductor muscle.  
Magnetic resonance imaging with contrast demonstrated proximal thickening of the right longus and magnus adductor muscles and the ipsilateral gracilis muscle, attributable to an inflammatory process, without any involvement of the joints.
title: Pyomyositis is not only a tropical pathology: a case series

case_prompt:
A 1-year-old girl was admitted for progressive abdominal distension and irritability. She had no other symptoms, and her developmental milestones were appropriate for age. On examination, she was active and playful, with a height of 70 cm and weight of 6.5 kg. Abdominal palpation revealed hepatomegaly, with the liver edge 6 cm below the right costal margin.

Laboratory studies showed:
- Hemoglobin 8 g/dL (11.5–15.5 g/dL)
- White blood cell count 12 400/μL (4500–11 000/μL)
- Platelet count 720 × 10^3/μL (150–450 × 10^3/μL)
- AST 73 U/L (10–34 U/L), ALT 20 U/L (7–56 U/L), ALP 394 U/L (53–128 U/L), GGT 260 U/L (0–51 U/L)
- Total bilirubin, albumin, PT, and INR were within normal limits.
- Serum alpha-fetoprotein was 160 000 ng/dL (normal < 10 ng/dL).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined hypodense lesion spanning segments I, IV, V, and VII of the liver, containing punctate calcifications and without vascular invasion. Small nodular lesions were noted in the apical segment of the left lower lobe and the posterior segment of the right lower lobe.

An ultrasound-guided biopsy of the liver lesion showed scattered islands of abnormal hepatocytes and haphazardly arranged bile duct structures in a myxoid stroma, suggesting a mesenchymal hamartoma.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Mesenchymal hamartoma versus hepatoblastoma: A diagnostic dilemma

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2 at 34 weeks 5 days’ gestation with gestational diabetes mellitus treated with 6 units of insulin detemir daily, presented with a 1-week history of dyspnea, myalgia, headache, tachycardia, fatigue, and productive cough causing chest pain. Symptoms worsened over the preceding 2 days despite outpatient IV fluids.  
Her history included papillary thyroid carcinoma diagnosed by fine-needle aspiration in early pregnancy, for which surgery was deferred postpartum; she was taking levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. She had mild gestational diabetes since 20 weeks’ gestation and pre-pregnancy propranolol therapy that was stopped for pregnancy.  
On admission, blood glucose was 70 mg/dL; blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg; heart rate 120 bpm; respiratory rate 35 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She reported household exposure to COVID-19; SARS-CoV-2 PCR returned positive the next day.  
Chest CT demonstrated 40% bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltration with subpleural and ground-glass opacities. Platelet count was 70,000/µL with no schistocytes on smear.  
Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.33, PCO₂ 16.7 kPa, bicarbonate 8.2 mmol/L, with an anion gap of 21 mmol/L.  
Urinalysis revealed 3+ ketones and no glucosuria.
title: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis and COVID‐19 management in a term pregnant patient; a case report

case_prompt: A 62-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (NYHA class I–II), heart failure, hypertension, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a history of smoking underwent two coronary angiograms via left radial arterial access with a 6-Fr sheath and manual compression, the second of which included stent placement and initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy. Three weeks after the most recent procedure, she noted a tender, pulsatile, and expansile mass over the left wrist. She denied paresthesia or symptoms of hand ischemia. On examination, the mass was approximately 2 cm in diameter, painful, and had an associated bruit; distal pulses were intact. Duplex ultrasound demonstrated a 2.2-cm longitudinal lesion arising from the radial artery via a narrow neck, with turbulent bidirectional (“yin-yang”) flow within the mass.
title: Pseudoaneurysm of radial artery after coronary angiography

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old gravida 2 para 2 Japanese woman presented with a 2-month history of fever and left vulvar pain. Her past medical history included appendicitis, erythema nodosum, and hypertension; menopause occurred at age 53. Initial examination revealed a 10×6 mm firm, ulcerative mass on the inner side of the left labium minorum. A presumptive vulvar abscess was treated with antibiotics without improvement. A needle biopsy strongly suggested squamous cell carcinoma, and she was referred for further care.

On admission, the ulcerative mass had grown to 31×24 mm. Pelvic MRI showed a 31×24 mm mass of moderate-to-high intensity in the left vulvar region without involvement of the urethra or anus. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no inguinal lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. With a preoperative diagnosis of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, she underwent radical local excision and bilateral inguinal lymphadenectomy.
title: Eccrine porocarcinoma of the vulva: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: An 8-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder presented with a several-month history of limping and recurrent left knee pain localized chiefly to the back of the knee, worsened by activity and partially relieved by rest. Clinical examination was limited by the patient's cooperation; there was no swelling or joint-line tenderness. Range of motion of the left knee was slightly limited in extension compared with the right side, and flexion was painful and mildly restricted. McMurray, Lachman, and varus/valgus stress tests were negative. Plain radiographs of the knee were normal. Because of the patient’s difficulty remaining still, an MRI was performed under general anesthesia. Scans revealed a 29 mm × 16 mm × 17 mm well-defined septated cyst in the intercondylar notch between the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, abutting primarily the posterior cruciate ligament. On proton density–weighted and turbo spin echo images, the mass was homogeneous and low in signal intensity, slightly hyperintense relative to muscle, and on turbo inversion recovery magnitude images it was hyperintense.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of a Symptomatic Posterior Cruciate Ganglion Cyst in a Child with Autism

case_prompt: A 48-year-old woman presented with a 4 × 3 cm well-defined, irregular, non-ulcerated, non-erythematous, firm swelling over the left shoulder, arising from the superficial plane. Three years earlier, fine-needle aspiration cytology of a smaller lesion had led to a diagnosis of sebaceous cyst, but the patient was lost to follow-up. She now reported a rapid increase in size over the past 6 months without pain or other symptoms. Routine physical examination was otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulder revealed a solid-cystic mass lesion with hemorrhagic areas involving the superficial and deep subcutaneous planes without intramuscular or bony involvement and no evidence of regional lymphadenopathy; radiologic interpretation raised the possibility of a soft tissue sarcoma.
title: Malignant adnexal tumour of the shoulder—a rare case report

case_prompt:
A 10-year-old Caucasian girl was referred in May 2009 for lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine pain. Both parents and two siblings were healthy. She was Turner stage II with bone age concordant with chronological age. One year earlier she had sustained a compression fracture of the T10 vertebral body without trauma. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry of L1–L4 showed a z-score of –2.3. Extensive evaluation for thyroid and rheumatologic disease, osteogenesis imperfecta, hypercalcemia, vitamin D deficiency, and lysosomal storage disorders was unremarkable. Serum alkaline phosphatase, osteocalcin, and urinary hydroxyproline were within normal limits.

At age 11, she received oral alendronate, 70 mg weekly for six months, with improvement in pain. Three months after stopping therapy, a lateral thoracic spine radiograph showed decreased height of lower thoracic vertebral bodies with barely discernible ossification of anterior epiphyseal plates. A frontal pelvis radiograph demonstrated symmetric sclerotic metaphyseal lines of the proximal femurs and sclerotic contours of both acetabula. Repeat DXA at L1–L4 showed a z-score of –1.8.

At age 13 and Turner stage IV, she again reported back pain. Radiographs of the thoracic and lumbar spine revealed a classic “bone in bone” appearance. Pelvic radiographs showed three discrete parallel layers at the iliac wings and a double contour of the acetabula and ischial bones; the proximal femoral physes were closed with mild sclerotic margins and normal tubulation of the femoral shafts. MRI of the thoracolumbar spine showed unremarkable sagittal T2, STIR, and axial T2 images. Sagittal T1 images disclosed mild hypointensity of the epiphyseal plates, and T1-fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced images demonstrated a double contour of the vertebral bodies. Repeat DXA z-score at L1–L4 was –1.1.
title: Radiographic and MR Imaging Findings of the Spine after Bisphosphonate Treatment, in a Child with Idiopathic Juvenile Osteoporosis

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old woman with no personal or family history of alopecia or autoimmune disease noted an asymptomatic, erythematous papule on the posterior mid-scalp. Five months later, she developed an area of alopecia surrounding this papule and was referred for excision.

Excisional pathology showed a circumscribed neoplasm with focal, irregular infiltration into deep adipose tissue. The tumor was contiguous with the epidermis and exhibited deep trichoblastic and superficial squamous components merging together within a distinct cellular fibrous stroma. Fibromyxoid stroma with separation artifact was absent. Both components demonstrated low-grade cytologic atypia with occasional mitotic figures and apoptotic bodies, and there was a patchy, mild inflammatory reaction. The deep margin was focally involved.

Adjacent nonneoplastic skin revealed prominent features of alopecia areata, including a brisk peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate around the majority of follicles, follicular miniaturization, an increased proportion of catagen and telogen follicles, trichomalacia, abnormally thin hair shafts, lack of follicular scarring, and retained sebaceous glands.
final_diagnosis_raw: Low-grade cutaneous carcinoma with squamous and trichoblastic features
title: Paraneoplastic alopecia areata surrounding a low-grade cutaneous carcinoma with squamous and trichoblastic features

case_prompt: A 48-year-old woman presented with six months of progressive lower abdominal and pelvic pain and intermittent constipation relieved by laxatives. She had a history of lateral internal sphincterotomy for anal fissure five years earlier but denied other gastrointestinal, urinary, or neurologic symptoms. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable with no remarkable findings. Laboratory tests, including hemoglobin, leukocyte and platelet counts, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and serum tumor markers (CA 15-3, CEA, CA 125), were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 4 × 5 cm hypodense cystic lesion externally compressing the rectum in the presacral region. Pelvic MRI showed a 4 × 4 × 5 cm encapsulated, multiloculated cystic lesion posterior to the rectum without internal septations; it was hypo-intense on T2-weighted imaging, heterogeneously hyper-intense on T1-weighted imaging, and showed no significant post-contrast enhancement. A tiny T1‐ and T2-hypo-intense focus at the dome suggested calcification. The lesion’s main bulk exhibited true diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC mapping; small adjacent peripheral cysts were also noted, and the mass displaced the rectum laterally. Colonoscopy confirmed external compression of the rectal wall, and biopsies of the overlying mucosa were nondiagnostic.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A report of presacral epidermoid cyst in perimenopausal women: An extremely rare site and an unusual cause of chronic constipation

case_prompt: A 58-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with 7 days of fever, fatigue, cough, and progressive dyspnea. On arrival, his oxygen saturation was 70% on room air, and he was intubated the same day. Chest radiography showed bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates with interstitial thickening and basal consolidation. A nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2. Initial laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (WBC 2.6 × 10^3/µL, ANC 1.8 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, platelets 85 × 10^3/µL), acute kidney injury (creatinine 120 µmol/L), transaminitis (ALT 170 U/L, AST 330 U/L), and elevated LDH (857 U/L). He received hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, tocilizumab, methylprednisone, and intravenous immunoglobulin. His course was complicated by septic shock requiring vasopressors, broad-spectrum antimicrobials, and dialysis. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a normal‐sized spleen without focal lesions. Despite granulocyte colony‐stimulating factor support, by hospital day 16 his pancytopenia had worsened (WBC 0.5 × 10^3/µL, ANC 0.3 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 74 × 10^3/µL).
title: A Rare Case of Hairy Cell Leukemia with Unusual Loss of CD123 Associated with COVID-19 at the Time of Presentation

case_prompt: A 35-year-old man with a 5-year history of recurrent mucocutaneous blisters presented with intermittent flares characterized by blisters progressing to ulcers on the tongue, scrotum, elbow, and dorsal fingers. Previous workup, including multiple punch biopsies, showed subepidermal vesiculation, interface dermatitis, and mixed inflammatory infiltrates with negative direct immunofluorescence (DIF) studies. Serologic studies revealed mildly elevated bullous pemphigoid antibodies (BP180 and BP230). The differential diagnosis included erythema multiforme, fixed drug eruption, and atypical bullous pemphigoid. He failed to improve on dapsone and valacyclovir for presumed erythema multiforme and after two infusions of rituximab for presumed bullous pemphigoid. His disease was controlled on high-dose oral prednisone, but this was unsustainable long term. His maintenance regimen of mycophenolate mofetil, doxycycline, and niacinamide had been interrupted due to severe pain from tongue ulcers. He reported intermittent cigarette use and had smoked one pack one week before presentation. He was afebrile with stable vital signs. Examination revealed numerous ulcers on the tongue, scrotum, glans penis, elbow, and bilateral dorsal fingers without ocular or nasal mucosal involvement. Laboratory tests showed no leukocytosis. He was admitted for pain control and wound care and started on topical clobetasol, viscous oral lidocaine, valacyclovir, and intravenous methylprednisolone 48 mg daily. Blood and urine cultures, a respiratory viral panel, and HIV testing were negative. A shave biopsy of the right third finger showed interface dermatitis with prominent dyskeratosis and subepidermal vesiculation; DIF was negative. The biopsy also demonstrated a lichenoid interface dermatitis with prominent necrosis, full-thickness epidermal dyskeratosis, and an inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and neutrophils without significant eosinophils.
title: Nicotine-induced bullous fixed drug eruption

case_prompt: A 40-year-old Japanese man with a 9-year history of HIV-1 infection (CD4 T-cell count >500 cells/µL, plasma viral load ~1000 copies/mL, untreated) was admitted urgently with high fever, severe malaise, headache, and a diffuse tender skin rash. One month earlier he had mild sinusitis treated symptomatically. On examination: temperature 39.5°C, blood pressure 84/– mmHg, pulse 110 beats/min, mild alteration of consciousness, slight neck stiffness, diminished skin turgor, and no focal neurologic deficits or visual disturbance. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (11 600/µL), elevated C-reactive protein (12.1 mg/L), hyperproteinemia (9.6 g/dL), creatinine 1.54 mg/dL, hyponatremia (116 mEq/L), and hyperkalemia (7.3 mEq/L). CT scans revealed moderate cervical lymphadenopathy. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis: protein 66.5 mg/dL, IgG 14.6 mg/dL, 56 leukocytes/µL (98.2% monocytes), and normal glucose. Dermatology diagnosed atypical generalized zoster; high-dose acyclovir led to rapid rash resolution. Empirical cefepime and micafungin were given for a week. Persistent electrolyte disturbances prompted endocrine evaluation, which revealed panhypopituitarism. MRI of the head demonstrated inhomogeneous pituitary enlargement, loss of the normal posterior pituitary T1 bright spot, mucosal thickening of the sphenoid sinus, and an intrasellar lesion with gadolinium ring enhancement, high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging, and low signal on apparent diffusion coefficient imaging.
title: Pituitary abscess in an HIV-1-infected patient

case_prompt: A 5-year-old right-handed boy fell on the palm of his right hand with the elbow extended and hyperpronated. He presented to the emergency department with acute, painful, total functional incapacity of the right elbow. On examination, the right elbow was swollen and tender. Pronation and supination were blocked, and flexion and extension were significantly limited compared with the left side. The anatomical landmarks of the elbow were preserved, and there were no vascular or neurological deficits. Frontal and lateral radiographs of the right elbow, along with an ipsilateral forearm film, demonstrated an isolated anterior dislocation of the radial head without any fracture of the ulnar diaphysis.
title: Isolated anterior dislocation of the radial head (case report)

case_prompt:
History of Present Illness: A 33-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of a progressively enlarging, tender mass on the ulnar aspect of the right wrist. The lesion first appeared shortly after local injury with glass foreign-body debris. Tenderness has been present since onset and worsened over the past 3–4 months, prompting emergency department evaluation.

Emergency Department Evaluation: On initial ED presentation the mass was lanced, yielding mild bloody drainage without abscess. Radiographs of the right wrist showed a 2.1 × 1.7 cm rounded area of soft-tissue density along the ulnar aspect of the distal ulna, with no osseous abnormality or radiopaque foreign body.

Orthopedic Examination: The mass was soft, somewhat mobile, and very tender, with no overlying warmth or erythema. Neurovascular function was intact. A small skin incision was noted from the ED drainage attempt.

MRI of the Wrist (with contrast): A well-circumscribed, lobulated, septated subcutaneous soft-tissue mass measuring 2.1 × 1.3 × 1.6 cm was centered in the subcutaneous fat along the ulnar wrist. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated avid, relatively homogeneous postcontrast enhancement. Central areas of internal T2 hypointensity and nonenhancement likely represent blood products or internal hemorrhage. No involvement of adjacent bone, muscle, tendon, nerve, or vascular structures was seen.

Given this presentation and imaging, what is your differential diagnosis?
title: Extradigital glomus tumor: a rare etiology for wrist soft tissue mass

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old woman with no significant past medical or family history presented with a 5-day history of progressive neurologic symptoms that began after emotional stress. Initial symptoms included bradykinesia, motor stereotypies, ataxia, bruxism, mutism, dysphagia, and urinary incontinence. She was treated for presumed conversion disorder with benzodiazepines and promethazine but continued to deteriorate and had two generalized seizures.

On admission, she was hemodynamically stable with normal respiratory status but was disoriented and unable to follow commands (GCS score of 10: eye opening to pain, localizing painful stimuli, inappropriate words). Pupils were mid-sized, equal, and reactive. Examination revealed bilateral Babinski signs, spasticity of all limbs, and hyperactive deep tendon reflexes (4+ in the upper extremities, 3+ in the lower extremities). Formal cerebellar and sensory testing were not possible due to lack of cooperation.

Brain MRI showed multiple confluent high-signal lesions on FLAIR and T2 in the bilateral frontoparietal white matter and corpus callosum, with peripheral edema and diffusion restriction. Post-contrast images demonstrated nodular and partial ring enhancement of oval lesions arranged perpendicular to the lateral ventricles. Cervical spine MRI and CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were unremarkable. Toxicology screening was negative except for benzodiazepines.

Laboratory studies revealed a serum magnesium level of 1.5 mg/dL (normal 1.9–2.5) and C-reactive protein 11 mg/L (normal 0–6). HIV and hepatitis B/C serologies were negative. CSF analysis showed 12 heterologous oligoclonal bands with none in serum and evidence of intrathecal IgG synthesis. CSF cell counts, chemistry, Gram stain, culture, and HSV PCR were unremarkable. Paraneoplastic and autoimmune encephalitis antibody panels in serum and CSF were negative except for a mildly elevated cardiolipin IgM antibody. EEG demonstrated generalized background slowing without epileptiform discharges or delta brushes.
title: Fulminant multiple sclerosis versus autoimmune encephalitis: A case report

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-year history of urinary frequency, dysuria, and a bulging sensation in her vagina. She had no significant medical or surgical history. There was no abnormal vaginal discharge, weight loss, or fatigue. Her last menstruation was over eight years ago, and she reported occasional dyspareunia. She had four prior vaginal deliveries. 

On examination, a soft, bulging red mass measuring approximately 32 mm × 28 mm surrounded the urethral meatus. Palpation of the anterior vaginal wall showed no extension of the mass into the urethra or bladder neck. The initial differential diagnosis included urethral caruncle, urethral mucosal prolapse, and malignancy.

Urinalysis was normal. Under local anesthesia, a biopsy of the lesion was performed without complication. Flexible urethrocystoscopy revealed no urethral stenosis or bladder abnormalities. Human papilloma virus screening was negative.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Case report of an unusual presentation of a urethral caruncle

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old Turkish man presented with dyspnea. He had undergone orthotopic heart transplantation 10 months earlier and was maintained on cyclosporine–based immunosuppression. His medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (40 pack–year smoking history), hypercholesterolemia, hypothyroidism, gout, normocytic anemia, steroid-induced myopathy, obesity, and a recent PCR-confirmed cytomegalovirus infection. 

Initial chest CT revealed a small nodule in the left lower lobe. Bronchial lavage was non-contributive for viral, bacterial (including mycobacteria), fungal pathogens, or malignancy. Follow-up CT scans at three and four months showed three progressively enlarging nodules (up to 1.6 cm) in the left upper and lower lobes and one in the right lower lobe. There were no palpable lymph nodes and no cutaneous or mucosal lesions.

Because the lesions were not accessible bronchoscopically or thoracoscopically, an open thoracotomy was performed, and wedge resections of the left upper and lower lobe nodules were obtained for diagnosis.
title: Pulmonary Kaposi's sarcoma after heart transplantation: a case report

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old white man with severe alcohol use disorder presented repeatedly over 2 years for inpatient detoxification. Upon each admission he had symmetric purpuric rashes on his lower extremities, appearing during periods of excessive ethanol intake (>300 g/day) and beginning to resolve within one week of abstinence. He denied itching, pain, fever, arthralgias, gastrointestinal symptoms, or other systemic complaints. Examination also revealed cerebellar ataxia, affective lability, mild sensorimotor polyneuropathy of the lower limbs, and hepatomegaly.

Routine blood tests over multiple admissions showed normal platelet counts and coagulation parameters, moderately elevated transaminases, and mildly increased C-reactive protein. Abdominal ultrasound showed fatty liver without cirrhosis. Serologic tests for hepatitis, HIV, and syphilis were negative. Neuroimaging, echocardiography, angiology, and capillary microscopy revealed no evidence of vasculitis or thrombosis. 

A skin biopsy of a fresh purpuric lesion demonstrated a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with reactive endothelial changes and extravasated red blood cells; vessel walls were intact without fibrin or thrombi. Immunodiagnostic studies showed markedly increased serum IgE and IgA levels, decreased B-lymphocytes and CD4 T-cells, and an elevated ratio of activated T-lymphocytes; no circulating immune complexes or autoantibodies were detected. A provocation test with vinegar (50 ml four times daily) reproduced fresh “cayenne pepper” purpura on the lower legs 24 hours after ingestion.
title: Recurrent purpura due to alcohol-related Schamberg’s disease and its association with serum immunoglobulins: a longitudinal observation of a heavy drinker

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old Bahraini man with diabetes and hypertension presented with several months of left flank pain. He had no other significant complaints.  
Physical examination and vital signs were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed mild normochromic normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL). Urea and electrolytes, prostate-specific antigen, thyroid function tests, and autoimmune serologies were normal. Midstream urine revealed 3–5 RBCs/hpf and 2–4 WBCs/hpf; no protein, casts, crystals, or bacteria were seen. No tumor markers were measured.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 16 × 10.7 × 11.7 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass at the upper pole of the left kidney, displacing the lower pole and with mild perinephric fat stranding, interpreted as a renal neoplasm.  
Subsequent MRI demonstrated an 11 × 12 × 13 cm oval mass with heterogeneous enhancement and a nonenhancing cystic degeneration area in the anteromedial aspect of the left kidney, displacing it posteroinferiorly. The mass abutted the splenic vein and abdominal aorta and stretched the left renal vein and artery, suggesting an adrenal origin. The right kidney, liver, right adrenal gland, gallbladder, and abdominal lymph nodes were normal.  
Radiological differential diagnoses included pheochromocytoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, and leiomyosarcoma.
title: Primary Adrenal Leiomyosarcoma in an Arab Male: A Rare Case Report with Immunohistochemistry Study

case_prompt: A 2-year-old Caucasian girl was referred to pediatric dentistry for management of totally intruded lower right primary incisors. On initial exam, an asymptomatic tissue growth was noted on the lingual gingiva adjacent to the intruded incisors. The mother had not observed the lesion previously. The child was otherwise healthy. Six months later, the patient returned; oral hygiene was poor with gingivitis. On exam, a firm, nonhemorrhagic, pedunculated fibrous lesion measuring approximately 5 mm × 5 mm × 3 mm was attached to the lingual gingiva of the lower right primary central and lateral incisors. The overlying mucosa was intact and white. The adjacent primary teeth remained in their original positions. No other oral abnormalities were present. Based on its appearance, the clinical differential diagnosis included reactive and benign neoplastic lesions such as fibroma, fibrous hyperplasia, peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral odontogenic fibroma, giant cell fibroma, and odontogenic hamartoma. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia and submitted for histopathological analysis.
title: Giant Cell Fibroma in a Two-Year-Old Child

case_prompt: A 7-year-old boy with T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma was receiving induction chemotherapy with the MCP-841 protocol, including prednisolone, vincristine, and intrathecal methotrexate; L-asparaginase was discontinued after a hypersensitivity reaction to the first dose. On day 6 of induction, he had a generalized tonic–clonic seizure preceded by blurred vision and followed by altered sensorium. On examination his blood pressure was 130/100 mm Hg, and funduscopic examination revealed grade II hypertensive retinopathy. Laboratory studies showed a normal hemogram, biochemistry, and electrolytes. Workup for secondary hypertension—including cardiac echocardiography, abdominal ultrasonography, renal Doppler studies, and urinalysis—was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral frontal and parietal hypodense areas suggestive of vasogenic edema. He was started on antihypertensive and antiepileptic therapy.
journal: Indian Journal of Medical and Paediatric Oncology : Official Journal of Indian Society of Medical & Paediatric Oncology
title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in pediatric acute leukemia: Case series and literature review

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, and femoral–popliteal bypass presented with 2 months of recurrent abdominal pain, an 11-kg weight loss, nausea, and vomiting. Two weeks before transfer, an EGD at an outside hospital showed a “blue stomach,” and abdominal CT demonstrated gastric wall emphysema. He improved enough to eat minimally and was discharged to a rehabilitation facility, but his symptoms worsened and he was transferred for further evaluation.

On arrival, he complained of constant mild right upper–quadrant abdominal pain, nausea with retching, nonbloody emesis, and episodic intense epigastric pain with dysphagia around meals. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable throughout hospitalization, with no history of hypotension. Physical examination showed a soft abdomen with deep palpation tenderness in the right upper quadrant; no bruits were heard.

Laboratory tests revealed a leukocytosis of 21,500 cells/μL (73% neutrophils), normal lipase, normal liver function tests, and a normal lactate level of 1.4 mmol/L. Repeat abdominal CT with IV contrast showed resolution of prior gastric emphysema and no acute ischemia. On hospital day 2, EGD revealed a normal esophagus and duodenum; in the proximal gastric body and fundus, there were excavated lesions and a large contiguous area of pale scarring with deep central ulceration, sharply demarcated from normal mucosa in the antrum and cardia. Multiple biopsies from the scarred area and the central ulcer showed ulceration and necrosis.
title: Chronic Gastric Ischemia Leading to Gastric Perforation

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old man presented for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes found on routine health screening. He was asymptomatic. Laboratory results showed:  
• AST 410 IU/L (reference 10–45), ALT 209 IU/L (5–45)  
• Alkaline phosphatase, GGT, and total bilirubin normal  
• Prothrombin time, INR, and albumin normal  

History: He drinks 2–4 units of alcohol per week for the past 1.5 years; last binge drinking episode was 6 days before initial tests. He denies recreational drugs, is a nonsmoker, and has no family history of liver disease.  

Physical examination: Average build, normal vital signs, and no stigmata of liver disease.  

Initial investigations:  
• CBC, renal function, lipid profile, urine microscopy – within normal limits  
• Serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV – negative  
• Abdominal ultrasound – unremarkable  

He was advised to abstain from alcohol. Three days later, repeat testing showed:  
• AST 580 IU/L, ALT 277 IU/L  

He then underwent further testing:  
• Serology for hepatitis A and E, dengue – within normal limits  
• ANA, anti‐LKM antibody, anti–Smith antibody – negative  
• Thyroid function tests – normal  
• Serum ceruloplasmin – normal  

The AST and ALT remained markedly elevated with no clear hepatic etiology.
title: Strenuous Exercise-Induced Tremendously Elevated Transaminases Levels in a Healthy Adult: A Diagnostic Dilemma

case_prompt: A 67‐year‐old Asian man was referred for evaluation of a rod‐shaped, pedunculated mass at the left inner canthus, present for two months with noted rapid growth. He denied pain, discomfort, systemic symptoms, prior malignancies, or significant medical history. On examination, he appeared well. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac, pulmonary, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. The eyelid mass measured approximately 3.0 cm in length, was dark yellow with a smooth surface and longitudinal texture; the base was soft and pliable, permitting easy twisting, whereas the distal portion was stiff. Routine blood, urine, and stool tests were normal. Chest radiography, electrocardiography, and coagulation studies showed no abnormalities.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Cutaneous horn masquerading as a seborrheic keratosis

case_prompt: A 41-year-old man presented with right groin pain and apprehension. He had undergone bilateral hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement three years earlier; operative notes did not describe any capsular repair. In 2016, after a ground-level fall, he sustained an anterior dislocation of the right hip that was reduced closed in the emergency department. He recovered with physiotherapy, but 10 months later sustained a second anterior dislocation of the right hip while pivoting on a standing leg; this too was reduced closed. On examination, he ambulated with crutches, complained of groin pain and pain with hip extension, and had no neurovascular deficits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right hip demonstrated disruption of the anterior hip capsule. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction showed irregularity of the anterior-superior acetabular rim with adjacent bone fragments and a reduced center-edge angle (15.7° on the right, 25.2° on the left). MRI arthrography revealed rupture of the anterior capsule with deficiency of the anterior ligaments and leakage of contrast antero-superiorly.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Late post-arthroscopy hip instability. Diagnosis, treatment, and 5-year follow-up: A case report

case_prompt: A 30-year-old man presented with left lower abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting. His medical history was notable for aneurysms of the abdominal aorta and several of its branches, a surgically repaired pseudoaneurysm of the left subclavian artery, coil embolizations of the superior ophthalmic veins and cavernous sinuses, and a recent coil embolization of a splenic artery aneurysm. His father also had multiple aneurysms. On examination, he had tenderness and guarding in the lower abdomen. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL (normal, 12–16 g/dL) and a white-cell count of 8800 cells/mm3 (normal, 4800–10 800 cells/mm3) with 84.2% neutrophils. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed ascites and findings consistent with his prior aneurysms. A repeat CT scan demonstrated a right pleural effusion and nonspecific enteritis involving small-bowel loops in the left abdomen and descending colon. A clinical diagnosis of intestinal obstruction was made; symptoms improved after nasogastric decompression. On hospital day 7, he remained stable with normal laboratory and chemistry parameters, but abdominal radiography showed persistent dilation of the small bowel. Medical management was recommended. On hospital day 11, he developed fever, leukocytosis, and a sudden drop in hemoglobin to 6.5 g/dL. Right thoracentesis yielded hazy pleural fluid. Later that night, he developed respiratory distress and worsening abdominal pain and died.
title: Spontaneous perforation of small intestine followed by rupture of the cystic artery: the natural history of Vascular Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome

case_prompt: A 40‐year‐old Caucasian woman was found in her apartment by the fire department after her carbon monoxide detector had been beeping intermittently. She woke at 3 a.m. with a severe frontal headache, deep orbital pain, blurred vision, light‐headedness, and stabbing chest pain. On arrival, her blood pressure was 150/100 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and temperature 97.6°F. The fire department measured indoor CO levels of 60 ppm, and her carboxyhemoglobin concentration was 3.9%. She was given 100% oxygen by non‐rebreather mask during transport, after which her vital signs normalized and her mental status improved. She was discharged later that day. The following morning, she noted that the distal margins of all her fingernail beds—most prominently on the first and second fingers—were eroded with a bite‐like border. There was no separation between nail plate and nail bed, no other surface deformities, and the nail beds were pink, with redder and bluish areas at the top border. She denied any history of trauma to her nails or extremities.
title: Abnormal fingernail beds following carbon monoxide poisoning: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old woman presented with an eight-month history of painless proptosis and redness of her right eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity was counting fingers at 2 m in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. On external examination of the right eye, there was severe ptosis, marked proptosis with downward displacement of the globe, and limitation of extraocular movements in all gazes. Slit-lamp examination revealed eyelid erythema and edema, conjunctival injection, and chemosis. The left eye examination was unremarkable.

Orbital computed tomography showed a 5.2 × 2.5 cm homogeneous extraconal mass within the superior rectus–levator complex, causing globe indentation and optic nerve compression. Brain and orbital magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a hyperintense fusiform lesion occupying the superior rectus muscle throughout its length, sparing the origin and insertion, with no extension into the cranial fossa or paranasal sinuses. Systemic evaluation and imaging revealed no evidence of metastasis.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Alveolar soft part sarcoma of the superior rectus muscle: Case report and review of literature

case_prompt: An 8-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of an unaesthetic appearance of her maxillary central incisors, which were positioned behind the lower anterior teeth. Her medical and dental history was non‐contributory, and there was no family history of Class III malocclusion. On examination, the permanent maxillary right and left central incisors were both in crossbite; the maxillary lateral incisors had not yet fully erupted. She was in the early mixed dentition stage and had a bilateral Class I molar relationship, with a 2 mm overjet and 100% overbite. The maxillary dental midline was coincident with the facial midline, whereas the mandibular midline deviated 2 mm to the left. Mild spacing was present in the maxillary arch, with sufficient mesiodistal space for labial movement of the maxillary central incisors. A panoramic radiograph showed no bone or dental pathology. A lateral cephalometric radiograph showed no evidence of a basal skeletal discrepancy between the maxilla and mandible.
title: Management of anterior dental crossbite with removable appliances

case_prompt: A 32-year-old gravida 2 para 2002 presented seven days after a repeat cesarean section with severe abdominal pain. She had two prior uncomplicated full-term cesarean deliveries. On arrival she was tachycardic; hemoglobin was 6.3 mg/dL and quantitative hCG was 5 038 mIU/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple hemorrhagic pulmonary nodules, hepatic masses with a subcapsular hematoma, and a seven-centimeter uterine mass. Interventional radiology performed emergent embolization of the hepatic hematoma. Brain MRI demonstrated hemorrhagic lesions in the left middle frontal gyrus and the left parieto-occipital junction. Core needle biopsy of a liver lesion was reported as metastatic gestational choriocarcinoma. Given the large disease burden and risk of hemorrhage, low-dose induction etoposide-cisplatin chemotherapy was initiated.
title: Successful management of stage IV epithelioid trophoblastic tumor using multimodality treatment: A case report

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on apixaban and a left total knee replacement four weeks earlier, complicated by hemarthrosis and joint infection treated with intravenous daptomycin, was transferred from a rehabilitation facility for evaluation of worsening cough of one week’s duration. He reported an intermittent productive cough with one episode of hemoptysis, dyspnea, and chills.  

On examination, temperature was 100.4 °F and respiratory rate elevated; lung auscultation revealed bilateral rales from bases to mid zones. There was no lower extremity edema; his knee incision was clean with minimal drainage.  

Laboratory results: WBC 10,900/μL (4.7% eosinophils, 69.7% neutrophils), hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, ESR 22 mm/hr (normal < 15), CRP 7.23 mg/dL (normal < 1.00), sodium 129 mmol/L.  

Initial chest radiograph showed patchy infiltrates most pronounced in the right lower lobe. He was treated for presumed multifocal pneumonia with cefepime and metronidazole, then switched to levofloxacin, and continued daptomycin for septic arthritis. Despite antibiotics, his respiratory status worsened.  

On hospital day 4, CT of the chest demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities in all lobes and consolidations at both bases. Concern for daptomycin-induced eosinophilic pneumonitis prompted a switch to intravenous vancomycin. By day 7, he required 4 L/min of oxygen.  

Cardiac evaluation: echocardiogram showed LVEF 55% with no wall-motion abnormalities; BNP peaked at 486 pg/mL then fell to 179 pg/mL on day 7. Multiple diuretic trials yielded a net negative fluid balance of 12.4 L over 17 days without change in oxygen needs.  

Repeat chest imaging revealed persistent bilateral patchy infiltrates, worsened ground-glass opacities, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Infectious workup was negative: two SARS-CoV-2 NAATs, respiratory pathogen panel, blood cultures, urine Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae antigens, mycoplasma IgM, HIV antigen/antibody, and procalcitonin 0.07 ng/mL. CRP rose to 20.8 mg/dL and ESR to 38 mm/hr; WBC 14,700/μL (4.2% eosinophils).  

Rheumatologic studies, including ANCA, rheumatoid factor, myeloperoxidase and serine proteinase antibodies, dsDNA, SSA/SSB, were negative; ANA was 1:80, speckled. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis serologies for Aspergillus, Thermoactinomyces vulgaris, and Micropolyspora faeni were negative.  

On hospital day 11, bronchoalveolar lavage yielded 355 cells/mm3 (36% neutrophils, 8% lymphocytes, 16% monocytes, 3% eosinophils); cultures grew oral flora and Candida albicans (likely contaminant); cytology was negative for malignancy.  

Due to progressive respiratory failure, he was transferred to intermediate care and pulmonology was consulted.
title: A Case Report of Steroid-Resistant Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia Managed with Intravenous Immunoglobulins

case_prompt: An 8‐year‐old female Shetland sheepdog was referred for evaluation of a progressively enlarging mass in the left parotid region. The owner first noted a subcutaneous nodule measuring <1 cm 20 months earlier. The dog, weighing 12.9 kg, was not obese and had no other lipomatous lesions. On presentation, the mass measured 9.0×7.0×1.5 cm but the dog was otherwise asymptomatic. Ultrasonography demonstrated a well‐circumscribed capsule around the lesion, and skull radiographs showed no evidence of bone invasion. A Tru‐Cut biopsy performed one week before surgery was non‐diagnostic; histopathology showed “scattered serous lobules (probably of salivary gland origin) between mature lipid cells and hemorrhagic foci.” The entire left parotid gland was surgically excised. Grossly, the gland had a flat, smooth surface without distinct fibrous encapsulation, and its lobular configuration was well maintained. In formalin, the gland floated, suggesting high fat content. On microscopic examination, individual and variably sized sheets of mature adipocytes diffusely infiltrated interlobular and intralobular spaces, occupying the greater proportion of the gland, while the remaining serous acini and ducts showed little morphological change. A thin collagen fiber capsule was intermittently present around the gland, and there was no infiltration of adipocytes into adjacent tissues.
title: Lipomatosis of the canine parotid gland: case report with a literature review

case_prompt:
A 78-year-old woman with osseous and pulmonary metastatic endometrial carcinoma receiving pembrolizumab (200 mg every 3 weeks; three cycles completed, last dose 12 days before admission) presented with 10 days of bilateral but left-predominant ptosis, new dysphagia, dysarthria, and head drop due to inability to sustain neck extension. She denied fever, chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, or dizziness. Her medical history was notable for cataract surgery months earlier and a transient ischemic stroke one year before. Home medications included aspirin 100 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg.

On admission, ECG showed alternating third-degree atrioventricular block and Mobitz II second-degree block with ventricular rates of 35–55 bpm. Laboratory tests revealed TSH 12.40 μIU/mL with normal T3 and T4, creatine kinase 910 U/L, CK-MB 81.5 ng/mL, and troponin T 1.24 ng/mL. Inflammatory markers were normal; creatinine was 0.96 mg/dL (eGFR 55.9 mL/min). A panel of autoantibodies (anti-AChR, anti-SOX1, anti-LRP4, anti-VGCC) was negative.

Transthoracic echocardiography performed one day after pacemaker implantation showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 41% with apical akinesia and apical-septal, apical-inferior, and anterior hypokinesia; mild mitral regurgitation and moderate tricuspid regurgitation were also noted.
title: Immune-Related Adverse Events in a Patient Treated with Pembrolizumab: A Case Report from the Point of View of a Geriatrician

case_prompt: A 27-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks of gestation presented with a 2-day history of isolated right iliac fossa pain. She had no nausea, vomiting, urinary symptoms, or similar previous episodes. Her temperature was 38.4 °C. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness localized to the right iliac fossa without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 22 450/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 67.7 mg/L. Urinalysis was normal. Transabdominal ultrasonography confirmed a viable intrauterine pregnancy but did not visualize the appendix or reveal any other abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging was not available. Given the clinical suspicion for acute appendicitis, a planned appendectomy was undertaken.
title: Acute abdomen during pregnancy: appendicular deciduosis—a case report

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old woman from a remote area of Nepal presented with seizures on and off since childhood, with increased frequency over the past 6 months, and progressive inability to perform her daily activities. On examination, she made no eye contact, produced incoherent speech, and did not obey commands. Vital signs were within normal limits. Results of complete blood count, blood glucose, liver-function tests, and renal-function tests were normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated marked asymmetric dilation of the right lateral ventricle, involving both the occipital and temporal horns. There was dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, with preservation of the genu and anterior body but absence of the posterior body and splenium. In the right paramedian region adjacent to the posterior cingulate gyrus, there was a well-defined cyst measuring 16 × 15 mm with cerebrospinal-fluid–intensity on T1-, T2-, and FLAIR-weighted images and minimal surrounding edema.
title: Asymmetric ventriculomegaly, interhemispheric cyst, and dysgenesis of corpus callosum (AVID) - case report

case_prompt: A 5-month-old girl was admitted with a 4-week history of fever unresponsive to antibiotics, weight loss, and pallor. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and had normal growth until symptom onset. On transfer after 4 weeks of fever, laboratory studies showed anemia (hemoglobin 8 g/dL), neutropenia (white-cell count 1650/µL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 100 000/µL), elevated ferritin (13 362 ng/mL), hypertriglyceridemia (674 mg/dL), hypofibrinogenemia (fibrinogen 100 mg/dL), and an increased soluble interleukin-2 receptor (>7500 U/mL). Microscopic examination of a bone marrow aspirate demonstrated hemophagocytosis features without visible amastigotes. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed marked splenomegaly with diffuse multifocal hypoechoic nodules, most smaller than 1 cm.
title: Spleen nodules: a potential hallmark of Visceral Leishmaniasis in young children

case_prompt: A 21-year-old man with no history of alcohol, tobacco, or drug use presented with persistent jaundice since early childhood, noted first at age 5, and worsening over the past 6 months with occasional non-projectile vomiting. There was no fever, pruritus, abdominal pain, or pale stools; dark urine was reported. Birth history was unremarkable without neonatal jaundice or transfusions, and development was normal. He had tried various undocumented alternative therapies without benefit. On examination, he had visible jaundice without hepatosplenomegaly; the remainder of the physical exam was normal. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 7.5 mg/dL (direct 0.6 mg/dL), normal liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT), and normal synthetic function. A comprehensive hemolytic workup (reticulocyte count, LDH, peripheral smear, antiglobulin tests) was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal.
title: A rare case of Crigler–Najjar syndrome type 2: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 1 year, managed with metformin and gliclazide, presented with 3 months of unintentional 26 kg weight loss and bilateral burning thigh pain (VAS 5–6) worse at night, preceded by 5 months of anorexia and fatigue. Despite the pain, she could still ambulate slowly but was unable to work or perform household chores. She denied weakness, numbness, fever, or trauma. Screening for respiratory, gastrointestinal, hyperthyroid, and connective tissue disease, as well as depression, an eating disorder, and psychosocial stressors, was negative. Her HbA1c at presentation was 6.9%; there was no retinopathy or nephropathy.

On examination, she appeared cachectic (BMI 15.5) with marked subcutaneous fat loss and muscle atrophy. Random blood glucose was 7.0 mmol/L. Both quadriceps were tender without signs of inflammation. Neurologic exam showed lower-limb muscle wasting, hypotonia, hyporeflexia at knees and ankles, and grade 4/5 power in both quadriceps (other lower-limb muscles 5/5); sensation was intact. Basic hematology, biochemistry, autoimmune screening, inflammatory markers, serum CK, thyroid tests, tuberculosis workup, chest and femoral radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Repeat HbA1c was 6.2% and fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, so antidiabetic agents were withheld. She was admitted for further evaluation.

Nerve conduction studies demonstrated mild slowing of motor and sensory conduction velocities, mildly reduced peroneal CMAP amplitudes, and mild conduction block in both peroneal nerves, interpreted as possible mild or early patchy demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy, probably CIDP. She declined CSF examination, and although the NCS features did not fulfil diagnostic criteria, she was treated as having CIDP.
title: Diabetic Neuropathic Cachexia in a Young Woman

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of a painless, slow-growing swelling in the right maxillary teeth region. There was no history of trauma, pain, smoking, or other deleterious habits. His medical history was noncontributory. 

On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, firm, nontender swelling extending from the tip of the nose to 3 cm lateral to the right ala and from the ala-tragus line to the lower border of the upper lip, causing mild nasal tip deviation and obliteration of the right nasolabial fold. A single, firm, fixed, tender right submental lymph node was palpable. 

Intraoral examination revealed a 5 × 4 cm lobulated, purplish-black pigmented growth between the maxillary right central incisor and first molar, involving the marginal, attached, and interdental gingiva on the labiobuccal aspect without palatal extension. The lesion was firm, bled on probing, and the right canine and first and second premolars were missing, with slight lateral displacement of the right lateral incisor. Oral hygiene was poor. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, biochemical tests, and urinalysis, were within normal limits. A panoramic radiograph showed a partially edentulous right maxilla with an irregular radiolucent lesion with ill-defined margins from the canine to the first molar. 

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mass lesion involving the anterior wall of the right maxillary sinus and the right maxillary alveolar arch up to the second molar, with extension into the gingivobuccal sulcus, buccinator muscle, and zygomatic prominence laterally, showing heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement.
journal: Journal of International Society of Preventive & Community Dentistry
title: Oral malignant melanoma: An aggressive clinical entity - Report of a rare case with review of literature

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old man was brought to the emergency department in a comatose state (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 4). Relatives reported sudden onset of headache followed by several episodes of vomiting. On arrival, he was sedated, intubated, and unresponsive to verbal or painful stimuli; pupils were bilaterally dilated and nonreactive.  
 
An urgent noncontrast head CT revealed a large right frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage with severe surrounding edema, significant mass effect, compression of the right lateral ventricle, and evidence of tonsillar herniation.  

An external ventricular drain was placed in the left lateral ventricle, and an intraparenchymal pressure monitor was inserted in the right frontal perilesional region; intracranial pressure exceeded 40 mmHg. The patient underwent bilateral decompressive craniectomies and evacuation of the hematoma. Intraoperatively, after clot removal, a cherry-like, round, lobulated lesion was identified in the edematous right frontal lobe and was completely resected.
title: A supratentorial primitive neuroectodermal tumor presenting with intracranial hemorrhage in a 42-year-old man: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 71-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis and stress incontinence presented with worsening lower extremity spasms and new visual hallucinations. Routine laboratory tests revealed a serum creatinine of 8.18 mg/dL (baseline normal 3 months earlier). She received intravenous fluids without improvement and was transferred for nephrology evaluation. She denied fever, chills, rash, urinary symptoms, or decreased urine output. Medications included long-term amantadine and nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily, which she had continued for over 3 months after cancellation of an elective urologic procedure. On examination, she was lethargic with altered mental status; vital signs were normal and lungs were clear. Laboratory studies showed creatinine 7.6 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 60 mg/dL, bland urine microscopy (no cells or protein), negative urine cultures, urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.20 mg/mg, and an absolute eosinophil count of 1.8 × 10^3/µL. Liver tests, albumin, and complete blood count were otherwise unremarkable. Renal ultrasound showed no stones or hydronephrosis. Vasculitic screening, autoimmune panel, serum immunoglobulins, protein electrophoresis, complement levels, hepatitis B and C serologies, and parathyroid hormone level were all within normal limits.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title:
Nitrofurantoin-Associated Acute Granulomatous Interstitial
Nephritis

case_prompt: A 15-day-old female infant was referred for intraoral masses causing feeding problems. She was born at 39 weeks’ gestation (birth weight 3200 g; Apgar scores 9 and 10) by normal vaginal delivery. The lesions were first noted at birth and originated from the anterior mandibular alveolus, occupying the oral entrance and partially protruding outside the mouth. On examination, there was a 5×4 cm reddish, pedunculated, smooth, erythematous mass with surface scales attached to the anterior mandibular gingiva; two smaller, similar tumors were adjacent. Palpation revealed firm, non-compressible, non-tender lesions that prevented mouth closure but did not cause airway compromise. A nasogastric tube was placed for feeding. General physical examination and laboratory studies were otherwise normal.
title: Multiple Congenital Epulis of the Mandibular Ridge: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 33‐year‐old man with a history of percutaneous closure of a secundum atrial septal defect in 2008 was referred for evaluation of valvular heart disease. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed for a murmur was technically difficult because of mesocardia and revealed grossly normal left ventricular wall motion, moderate posteriorly directed eccentric mitral regurgitation, mild prolapse of the anterior mitral leaflet, mild aortic insufficiency, and an echogenic structure contiguous to the lateral aspect of the tricuspid annulus; the right atrium and ventricle were poorly visualized. The patient reported overall well‐being but experienced fatigue after walking 200–400 meters. An exercise stress test on a standard Bruce protocol lasted 12 minutes 26 seconds, achieving 14.2 METS and 96% of the age‐predicted maximal heart rate; he had no chest pain or ischemic ECG changes. A chest radiograph suggested possible right ventricle on the left side of the chest, raising concern for dextrocardia or congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries. Cardiac CT angiography showed normal origin and course of all coronary vessels without evidence of coronary artery disease. CT evaluation of cardiac structure demonstrated that the right ventricle received blood from the left atrium via the tricuspid valve and ejected into the aorta, while the left ventricle received blood from the right atrium via the mitral valve and ejected into the pulmonary artery; the right ventricle had concentric hypertrophy, with a mid‐septal wall thickness of 9.9 mm.
final_diagnosis_raw: congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries
title: A Case of Congenitally Corrected Transposition of the Great Arteries Discovered on Coronary Computed Tomography

case_prompt: A 26-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a growth in the floor of her mouth, with progressive alterations in speech and difficulty swallowing over the past 2 years. On extraoral examination, her neck appeared short and thick, producing a double chin appearance; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Intraoral inspection revealed a smooth, non‐tender, 3×3 cm swelling involving the submental, submandibular, and sublingual regions, adhered to deep planes and displacing the tongue upward such that the soft palate could not be visualized; the overlying mucosa and the orifices of Wharton’s ducts were normal. Upon applying pressure to the submental area, the mass was displaced upward. Ultrasonography demonstrated a cystic area with echogenic material and internal echoes and no flow on color Doppler. MRI showed an encapsulated cystic mass without calcification.
