title: Epidermoid cyst of the floor of the mouth

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old man with metastatic melanoma involving an axillary lymph node and mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy was treated with two cycles of ipilimumab and nivolumab but discontinued due to immune-related colitis and other toxicities. Four months later, a PET-CT showed progression of mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes and hypercalcemia; mediastinal lymph node biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas. He remained off ICPI therapy.

Ten months after ICPI initiation, he developed a two-week history of progressive headaches, visual changes, and word-finding difficulty. On neurologic examination, he had a right incongruent homonymous hemianopia, finger agnosia, acalculia, left-right disorientation, and alexia. Brain MRI showed subtle leptomeningeal enhancement and T2 FLAIR signal abnormality in the left occipital pole and overlying left parietal lobe. 

Lumbar puncture revealed a protein level of 75 mg/dL (reference 15–50 mg/dL), 13 white blood cells, and normal glucose; CSF cytologic examination was negative. During hospitalization, he experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure and was started on levetiracetam.
title: Neurosarcoidosis following Immune Checkpoint Inhibition

case_prompt: A 13-year-old boy with no significant medical history and no recent infections or exposures presented with a 4-day history of dysphagia and dyspnea on a background of low-grade fever and malaise. Twenty-four hours after admission, he developed descending muscle weakness that began in the fingers and hands bilaterally and subsequently progressed to involve the forearms and proximal lower limbs. On examination, he had a normal gait, bilateral upper-limb weakness (2/5) and lower-limb weakness (4/5), preserved deep-tendon reflexes, bulbar muscle involvement, and no sensory deficits. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a protein level of 0.51 g/L, 2 white cells, and sterile culture, without albuminocytological dissociation. MRI of the complete neuraxis was normal. Electromyography demonstrated an acute pure motor axonal polyneuropathy with markedly slowed conduction velocities in the upper limbs.
title: Dysphagia Revealing a Pharyngeal–cervical–brachial Variant of Guillain–Barré Syndrome in Pediatric Cases

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man presented with a central forehead swelling that had been gradually enlarging over several months. He reported no pain, headaches, epistaxis, nasal discharge, obstruction, or smell disturbances. He denied systemic symptoms such as fever or weight loss. His medical history was unremarkable, with no history of facial trauma or sinonasal disease. He was a nonsmoker and had no occupational exposures.

On examination, there was a firm, smooth, oval, 5-cm mass just superior to the medial eyebrows. The overlying skin appeared normal. The mass was mildly tender to palpation but showed no pulsations or bruits. No other head or neck abnormalities were found, and an intranasal examination was unremarkable.

A computed tomography scan of the head and paranasal sinuses demonstrated an isolated soft-tissue mass occupying the left frontal sinus. The lesion produced a locally expansile effect with partial erosion of the anteroinferior frontal sinus wall. There was no extension into the nasal cavity or ethmoid sinuses.
title: Solitary Neurofibroma of the Frontal Sinus

case_prompt: A 79-year-old woman with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, and arterial hypertension underwent successful transcatheter mitral valve repair with one MitraClip. Transthoracic echocardiography immediately and 1 day after the procedure showed no pericardial effusion. On post-procedural Day 3, she reported fatigue, malaise, and non-specific epigastric pain. Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 70 mg/L (normal <5), white blood cell count 9/nL, and procalcitonin 0.16 ng/mL (normal <0.5). Chest X-ray revealed new bilateral pleural effusions without congestion or infiltrate. Electrocardiogram was unchanged, and blood cultures remained sterile. On Day 5, TTE demonstrated a mild circular pericardial effusion (8 mm); by Day 7, this progressed to 13 mm without hemodynamic compromise. Cardiac CT showed pericardial and pleural effusions of similar low density (~10 HU), suggesting serous fluid.
title: Post-cardiac injury syndrome after transcatheter mitral valve repair using MitraClip system: a case report

case_prompt: A 65-year-old man with a history of hypothyroidism and hyperlipidemia presented with two months of recurrent lightheadedness and dizziness at rest. He denied chest pain, palpitations, diaphoresis, dyspnea, focal neurologic symptoms, exertional or positional triggers, medication use including AV-nodal blockers, or recent illness. There was no family history of heart disease or sudden death. In the emergency department, his blood pressure was 70/50 mm Hg and heart rate 30–50 beats/minute. ECG showed sinus bradycardia at 47 beats/minute, an incomplete right bundle-branch block pattern, and a PR interval of 200 ms. He remained hypotensive despite fluid resuscitation and required a dopamine infusion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 60%, mild left ventricular hypertrophy, and normal right ventricular size and function. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies were notable for sodium 121 mEq/L, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 89 fL, ferritin 856 ng/mL, TSH 5.33 mIU/L, and total T4 5.39 μg/dL. Evaluation of hyponatremia showed serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 346 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium 66 mEq/L, findings consistent with either adrenal insufficiency or SIADH. Endocrinology was consulted and a cosyntropin stimulation test was performed.
title: A case of isolated sinus bradycardia as an unusual presentation of adrenal insufficiency

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old man with a history of pan-ulcerative colitis presented with odynophagia and an inability to swallow due to significant oral ulceration and a 20–25 lb weight loss. He was diagnosed at age 20 and initially treated with prednisone and adalimumab; he remained asymptomatic for 8 months before discontinuing adalimumab. Two years later, he re-presented with one month of bloody diarrhea and weight loss during which adalimumab was re-induced along with a prednisone taper. His gastrointestinal symptoms resolved quickly; however, 7–10 days after re-induction, he developed severe oral mucosal ulcerations and a papular rash.

On admission, he was afebrile. Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 151.5 mg/L, white blood cell count 13.0×10^9/L with neutrophils 78.4%. Laryngoscopy demonstrated ulcerations along the epiglottis. On hospital day 2, he developed a fever to 38.3 °C and was noted to have erythematous, scaly papules and nodules on his face, scalp, trunk, and buttocks draining a transparent yellow discharge. Dermatology punch biopsies were obtained from both skin lesions and oral ulcers. The gingival biopsies were nonspecific; the skin biopsy showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the dermis with microabscess formation in the epidermis and superficial dermis.
title: Sweet Syndrome, Not so Sweet during an Ulcerative Colitis Flare Especially When You Cannot Eat

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old Middle Eastern girl presented with 2 days of vomiting and upper abdominal pain that began after she fell from her bed, and 2 weeks of left-sided chest pain radiating to her left shoulder, worse with deep breathing and relieved by propping herself on two pillows; she also noted gradual weight loss. Two siblings had pneumonia in the past month. 

On examination, she was tachypneic and in respiratory distress with an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air; air entry and chest movement were markedly reduced on the left side, and a small bruise was present over the left chest. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and without masses. 

An anteroposterior chest radiograph revealed an air–fluid level occupying the entire left hemithorax. A chest tube was placed on suspicion of hydropneumothorax. A subsequent chest radiograph showed the tube lying between the chest wall and the air collection and failing to drain any fluid, raising further diagnostic uncertainty.
title: Chest X-ray findings in late-onset congenital diaphragmatic hernia, a rare emergency easily misdiagnosed as hydropneumothorax: a case report

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old girl was referred with a 3-year history of ocular misalignment and a 1-year history of poor distance vision in the left eye. There was no history of head or facial trauma, diplopia, pain on eye movement, systemic symptoms, or family history of strabismus. Developmental and medical histories were unremarkable.

Unaided visual acuity was 6/24 in the right eye and counting fingers in the left eye; with refraction, acuity improved to 6/9 and 6/60, respectively, with a hypermetropic correction of +4.50 diopters in each eye. Anterior and posterior segment examinations were normal bilaterally.

Prism cover testing in primary gaze revealed a 10-prism-diopter left hypotropia without horizontal deviation or abnormal head posture. Palpebral fissures were equal in the primary position. Ocular motility testing showed marked limitation of elevation of the left eye on adduction (looking to the right), with nearly full elevation on abduction (looking to the left). Under sedation, a forced duction test demonstrated marked mechanical restriction of passive elevation of the left eye in adduction. Systemic examination was normal.
title: Brown syndrome with severe amblyopia: a case report from Africa

case_prompt:
A 62‐year‐old man was referred for evaluation of progressive respiratory failure attributed to bilateral diaphragmatic dysfunction. Over several months he had experienced low‐grade fever, neck and shoulder arthralgias, nocturnal hypoventilation, fatigue, and a ring‐shaped rash on the back of his right leg that expanded to 10 cm in diameter. He also noted transient numbness of the left side of his face. He reported dyspnea that worsened in the supine position but denied limb weakness, sensory changes in his extremities, or headache.

He was otherwise healthy. He had stopped smoking decades earlier, drank two units of alcohol daily, and took no medications.

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Upright respiratory rate was 24 breaths per minute, SpO₂ 97%. When supine for 45 seconds, his respiratory rate rose to 40 breaths per minute, paradoxical respiratory movements appeared, and SpO₂ fell to 91%. Percussion revealed an elevated left lung base. Chest radiographs showed elevation of the left hemidiaphragm. Fluoroscopic sniff testing demonstrated paradoxical motion of both hemidiaphragms. Pulmonary function testing revealed a supine vital capacity decrease of over 20% of predicted. Arterial blood gases showed pH 7.40, PaCO₂ 4.9 kPa, PaO₂ 7.8 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 24.6 mmol/L, base excess –0.2 mmol/L.

Antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens (SSA, SSB, RNP, Sm, SCL‐70, Jo‐1) and serology for Q fever were negative. Diaphragmatic ultrasonography revealed no inspiratory thickening. Polysomnography off ventilatory support showed out‐of‐phase thoracoabdominal movements and intermittent desaturation. Phrenic‐nerve conduction studies demonstrated normal distal motor latency and CMAP amplitude bilaterally; needle EMG of the right hemidiaphragm showed good recruitment without spontaneous activity, leading to the conclusion that there was no evidence of traumatic phrenic‐nerve palsy.
title:
Case Report: Bilateral diaphragmatic dysfunction due to
Borrelia Burgdorferi

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old Caucasian man was transferred to the neurology service after one month of “seizure-like” limb movements accompanied by episodes of reduced awareness and unresponsiveness. He had a recent diagnosis of eosinophilic vasculitis treated with methotrexate, which was discontinued before transfer.

During typical episodes, he described a pulsating sensation in his ears, followed by a wave of tension and pain down his limbs, facial grimacing, and tremors of the lower limbs that progressed to violent shaking. He retained awareness and could communicate throughout the episode, denied loss of consciousness, incontinence, or tongue biting, and developed transient peripheral cyanosis of the toes. Each event lasted a few seconds, followed by approximately 2 minutes of unresponsiveness during which he reported full awareness but could neither move nor speak. Most episodes occurred in the presence of staff, and his oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure remained normal during and after events. He reported palpitations with each episode. These movements were unresponsive to levetiracetam and low-dose diazepam.

His medical history included type 2 diabetes with peripheral neuropathy and prior retinal detachment. He lived alone following bereavement and managed his elderly mother. He expressed significant stress related to his vasculitis diagnosis and concerns about COVID-19 vaccination.

On examination, vital signs were stable. General and systemic examinations were unremarkable. Detailed neurological examination revealed no focal deficits. Muscle strength was normal but exhibited inconsistent “give-way” weakness on upper extremity flexion and, to a lesser extent, lower extremity movements. Sensation was intact except for known diabetic neuropathy. Coordination, reflexes, and gait were normal. Mental status testing was normal.
title: Case report on psychogenic nonepileptic seizures: A series of unfortunate events

case_prompt: An 11-year-old girl presented with sudden-onset horizontal diplopia when gazing at distant objects for 2 weeks. She had no history of head trauma, systemic illness, or psychogenic stress. Her daily near-work time was approximately 3 hours. Uncorrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Refraction was −0.50 + 0.50 × 170° in the right eye and +0.00 + 0.25 × 175° in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 19 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS. Pupils were equal and reactive, and no nystagmus was observed. Anterior segment and funduscopic examinations were unremarkable. Cover testing revealed basic esotropia of 30 prism diopters at near and 35 prism diopters at distance. Ocular ductions were full without nystagmus. Hess red-green testing showed inward displacement of both eyes, and under 45Δ base-out prism neutralization, equal field sizes confirmed comitant esotropia. As acute acquired comitant esotropia was suspected, brain MRI was performed to detect intracranial disease.
title: Two Pediatric Patients with Acute Acquired Comitant Esotropia as the First Symptom of Brainstem Tumor: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man presented with an ulcerated swelling of the right thumb. One month earlier, he had noted a small nodule on the distal phalanx of the thumb that progressively enlarged and ulcerated over the skin one week before presentation. He reported bleeding from the wound margins, tenderness, and pain on movement. His medical history was notable for stage IV non–small cell lung cancer with spinal metastasis, managed palliatively. He also reported weight loss, anorexia, and weakness. 

On examination, there was an ulcerated lesion involving the nail bed of the right thumb with necrotic slough at the ulcer floor. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (26.4 × 10^3/mm^3), hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, serum urea 170 mg/dL, creatinine 1.44 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 400 IU/L, and serum albumin 2.5 g/dL. The patient tested positive for COVID-19. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated a left pulmonary mass. Right thumb radiographs revealed complete destruction of the distal phalanx cortex with sparing of the interphalangeal joint. Contrast-enhanced CT of the right hand showed a 3 × 2 × 2 cm soft-tissue mass destroying and expanding the distal phalanx, with cortical breakdown, extension into dorsal and palmar soft tissues, increased vascularity, and invasion of tendons and muscles; the interphalangeal joint was spared. 

A biopsy of the lesion was performed. Histopathological examination of H&E-stained sections revealed partly skin-covered, partly ulcerated tissue composed of trabecular sheets of atypical basaloid cells and many multivacuolated cells; nuclei showed marked atypia and numerous (including atypical) mitoses, with areas of necrosis and involved margins. The biopsy was suggestive of a malignant adnexal tumour of the skin with sebaceous differentiation.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Rare malignant adnexal tumour of the skin involving distal phalanx of right thumb with co-existing primary lung cancer in a 72-year-old patient: A case report

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of acute right medial knee pain, difficulty walking, and reduced range of motion. The pain began after an episode of overexertion; he denied any trauma or prior knee problems. His past medical history was unremarkable, with no known crystalline arthropathy, inflammatory arthropathy, or hypercalcemia. On examination, the medial aspect of the knee was mildly inflamed, swollen, and exquisitely tender; pain worsened with knee flexion or direct pressure. His pain score was 9 of 10 on the visual analog scale.  

Plain radiographs of the knee showed a curvilinear calcification adjacent to the medial femoral condyle. Ultrasound demonstrated a 1-cm curved echogenic line with a marked posterior acoustic shadow over the internal femoral condyle. MRI revealed a linear, hypointense signal on all sequences, located along the course of the distal tendon insertion near the medial femoral condyle.
title: Calcifications of the Knee’s Medial Compartment: A Case Report and Literature Review on the Adductor Magnus Tendon as an Uncommon Location and the Role of Ultrasound-Guided Lavage

case_prompt:
An 88-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of intensely pruritic erythematous plaques on the trunk and lower limbs that were unresponsive to topical and systemic corticosteroids. On examination, there was erythroderma involving approximately 90% of the body surface area, with ill-defined erythematous and edematous plaques on the back, abdomen, and thighs, and superimposed excoriations. Results of blood chemistry, liver enzymes, electrolytes, glucose, renal function tests, lactate dehydrogenase, and beta-2 microglobulin were within normal limits. Staging ultrasound and total-body computed tomography showed generalized superficial lymphadenopathy without visceral involvement.

After a 1-month treatment washout, a skin biopsy of a thigh plaque revealed psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with compact hyperorthokeratosis, mild spongiosis, and occasional dyskeratosis. In the superficial dermis, there was a dense perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils and plasma cells, exhibiting occasional lichenoid and vaguely nodular arrangements. The infiltrate consisted of small lymphocytes intermixed with atypical medium and large neoplastic cells constituting more than 25% of the infiltrate, with easily detectable mitotic figures and a Ki-67 index of approximately 30%. Focal epidermotropism with Pautrier microabscesses was present.

Immunohistochemical studies showed that the lymphoid cells were positive for CD4 and T-cell receptor βF1, with partial loss of CD7, intact CD3, CD2, and CD5 expression, and focal CD30 positivity. A subset of neoplastic cells coexpressed the TFH markers PD-1 and CXCL13, with focal positivity for BCL6 and CD10. Epstein–Barr virus–encoded RNA was negative. T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies demonstrated a monoclonal T-cell population. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood revealed a CD4:CD8 ratio >10 and a population of clonal CD3+CD4+CD7±CD5+CD26– T cells comprising 40% of circulating lymphocytes.
title: Sézary syndrome with large cell transformation and T-follicular helper phenotype

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman in her usual state of health was incidentally found, on routine medical examination, to have a 1.2-cm nodule in the right lower lobe of the lung. She had no symptoms, her family history was noncontributory, and physical and laboratory examinations were unremarkable. A CT scan of the chest confirmed a well-circumscribed pulmonary nodule. Concurrent lumbar MRI showed a lytic lesion in the left transverse process of the fifth lumbar vertebra, confined to bone and separate from the spinal canal. Initial biopsy specimens of both lesions showed a bland spindle cell neoplasm, but were too small for definitive diagnosis. 

Over the next 5 years, both lesions increased slightly in size. The patient underwent video-assisted thoracic surgery for the pulmonary lesion and curettage of the vertebral lesion. The lung specimen was a 13-mm well-circumscribed solid lesion composed of fascicles of bland spindle or polygonal cells without necrosis or mitoses. The tumor cells contained intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen, D2-40, progesterone receptor, vimentin, and S100 antigen, and negative for alpha-smooth muscle actin; the Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 1.5%. The vertebral lesion demonstrated identical morphology and immunoprofile.
title: Extracranial meningiomas concurrently found in the lung and vertebral bone: a case report

case_prompt: A 52-year-old woman presented with 9 months of neck pain and 4 months of progressive weakness in all four limbs, beginning with right triceps then involving right and left thigh muscles and left biceps, accompanied by urinary urgency and frequency. On examination, she was quadriparetic (MRC grade 4 on the right, 3 on the left), with hyperesthesia in the C2 dermatome, hyperreflexia, bilateral extensor plantar responses, difficulty swallowing, and respiratory compromise. No stigmata of neurofibromatosis were noted, and routine blood tests were normal. Sagittal and axial MRI of the craniocervical junction showed a well-defined, purely posterior, dural-based mass at the foramen magnum measuring 2.0 × 2.5 cm that was hypo-intense on T1-weighted images, iso- to hypo-intense on T2, and demonstrated inhomogeneous enhancement after contrast administration.
title: Pure posterior chordoid foramen magnum meningioma: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of intermittent palpitations and a newly detected cardiac murmur. She had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or connective-tissue disorders, and no family history of congenital heart disease. Vital signs were: blood pressure 109/64 mm Hg, pulse 77 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 36.5 °C. Cardiac auscultation revealed a continuous grade 3/6 murmur best heard at the right second and third intercostal spaces. A chest radiograph showed normal heart size, and electrocardiography showed no ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests—including NT-proBNP, coagulation profile, anti-nuclear antibody, complete blood count, cardiac enzymes, and lipid panel—were all within normal limits. 

Transthoracic echocardiography with Doppler imaging revealed a tunnel-like structure with continuous flow signals originating from the left coronary sinus and draining into the right atrium. The pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio was 1.3 : 1. The left ventricle was of normal size, with a calculated ejection fraction of 64%, and all valves appeared normal. An exercise treadmill test produced no ischemic changes.
title: A Case of Aorta-Right Atrial Tunnel Presented with an Asymptomatic Murmur

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old previously healthy man from India presented in June with a 2-month history of worsening left elbow pain and limited motion. He recalled a fall onto the elbow 2 months earlier; an outpatient X-ray in April had shown no fracture but “unclear soft tissue calcification” and a possible osteolytic area. On examination, the skin was intact with mild swelling and tenderness over the olecranon. Range of motion was limited: flexion to 130°, extension to 30°, pronation/supination to 70°/70°. There were no systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein of 10.3 mg/L and elevated creatine kinase; other values were normal. A CT scan demonstrated an erosion at the proximal olecranon at the triceps insertion without clear osteolysis. He was discharged with NSAIDs and activity modification.

Three weeks later, he returned with worsening swelling and a perforated lesion over the olecranon. MRI revealed the known erosion with marked peripheral edema of the proximal olecranon and a joint effusion, concerning for early bone infection. He was afebrile and leukocyte count was normal; CRP was 12.3 mg/L. Given suspicion of purulent bursitis, he was admitted for bursectomy and collection of four native tissue specimens for microbiologic and histopathologic analysis.
title: Tuberculosis of the elbow joint: the complexity of diagnosis and treatment—A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 5-year-old girl was evaluated for a mass in the right parapharyngeal region present since birth. On examination, the lesion was firm, solid, non-tender, and measured 4 × 3 cm; the overlying skin was normal. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a solid, well-circumscribed lesion. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy was performed under ultrasound guidance, yielding five smears. The aspirates were moderately cellular without a fibrillar or necrotic background. Two distinct cell populations were noted: the first consisted of spindle-shaped cells with wavy nuclei; the second consisted of large oval to polygonal cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, one to three large round vesicular nuclei often eccentrically placed, and prominent nucleoli.
title: A 5-year-old girl with a congenital ganglioneuroma diagnosed by fine needle aspiration biopsy: a case report

case_prompt: A 21-year-old woman presented with a six-month history of a slow-growing, painless swelling on the left side of her lower lip. On examination, there was a 1 cm × 1 cm dome-shaped, non-tender, firm-to-soft, mobile mass with a smooth surface and well-demarcated margins. There was no sensory deficit and no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient denied any history of changes in lesion size, local trauma (including habitual lip biting), or paraesthesia. Because the lesion was thought to represent a benign fibrous overgrowth or an organizing mucocele, no imaging or preoperative biopsy was performed. Under local anesthesia, a curvilinear incision and blunt dissection were used to excise the lesion. Intraoperatively, the mass was ovoid, well-encapsulated, and easily separable from surrounding tissues, and the surgical specimen was an ovoid soft tissue mass with a thick capsule.
title: Swelling on lower lip…not always a mucocele !!!

case_prompt: A previously healthy 7-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of fever, cough, and left earache. He had normal palatal studies on prior evaluation for hypernasal speech and no other significant history. A chest radiograph at the referring hospital suggested a diaphragmatic hernia. On arrival, a repeat chest radiograph showed a large air-filled cavity at the left lung base and smaller cystic cavities medially at the left base and in the right mid to lower zone. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT revealed a large left-sided empyema with an air-fluid level, collapse of the left lower lobe with a multiloculated fluid collection suggestive of a necrotic lung abscess, a large thrombus in the left pulmonary vein extending into the left atrium, and a segmental left lower lobar pulmonary embolus; the left hemidiaphragm was intact and no abdominal source of sepsis was identified. On hospital day 2, he underwent left thoracotomy, which revealed a bronchopleural fistula at the left lung base; pleural debridement was performed and chest drains were placed. Over the next 7 days, chest radiographs demonstrated a persistent and increasing left pneumothorax with worsening consolidation. On postoperative day 8, he acutely deteriorated with reduced oxygen saturations, and imaging disclosed a new right-sided tension pneumothorax that required emergency drainage.
title: Lemierre syndrome: a diagnostic dilemma in paediatric patients

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman with a history of resection of a large uterine leiomyoma presented with sudden onset of severe back pain. She was initially treated for pneumonia with antibiotics and NSAIDs, but her symptoms persisted. One week later she was referred because of an elevated white blood cell count of 14.9 × 10^3/mL and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 18.1 mg/dL.  
On admission, repeat blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 10.4 × 10^3/mL and a CRP of 2.8 mg/dL. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was within normal limits. Oxygen saturation was 97% on room air.  
A plain chest CT scan revealed a flat mass measuring approximately 4.5 cm in maximum diameter along the left diaphragm near the T11 vertebral level, accompanied by a small left pleural effusion. One week of antibiotics and NSAIDs led to improvement in inflammatory markers, but serial chest radiographs showed a rapid increase in left pleural fluid and her back pain persisted.  
Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated increasing pleural fluid with a density of 39 Hounsfield units, raising concern for hemorrhage. The mass failed to enhance during arterial through late phases. Given these findings and ongoing severe pain, emergency surgical exploration was planned for diagnosis and treatment.
title: Extra-Lobar Lung Sequestration Infarction That Caused Sudden Back Pain: An Adult Case of Surgical Resection

case_prompt: A 3-month-old female, with an unremarkable birth history, was referred for evaluation of an enlarging right chest-wall mass that had not improved with antibiotic therapy. On examination, there was a 5-cm subcutaneous mass over the right 8th rib with overlying skin redness and tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 11,000/µl and a C-reactive protein level of 4.8 mg/dl; serum tumor markers were within reference ranges. A chest radiograph revealed an increased radiolucent lesion at the right 8th rib. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 28 × 27 mm multicystic mass with homogeneous enhancement, and three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed an osteolytic defect of the 8th rib. MRI showed a mass with a thickened septum that enhanced after gadolinium administration. These imaging features suggested mesenchymal hamartoma. However, malignant neoplasms such as Ewing sarcoma, neuroblastoma, fibrosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and chondroblastoma were also considered. During the hospital course, the mass self-destructed with serous fluid discharge and decreased markedly in size; the overlying erythema and tenderness resolved gradually. Despite this spontaneous regression suggesting a benign process, surgical resection of the mass with surrounding tissue was performed to obtain a definitive diagnosis.
title: Infantile juvenile xanthogranuloma of the chest wall mimicking mesenchymal hamartoma: report of a case

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of occasional epigastric pain, decreased food intake, and nausea. Her medical history was notable for hypertension (11 years), type 2 diabetes mellitus (11 years), hypothyroidism (38 years), a prior cholecystectomy, and hysterectomy. She had no history of alcohol or drug use, and her only allergy was to dipyrone. There was a family history of malignancy: her father died of peritoneal carcinomatosis; no familial genetic mutations were identified.  

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a serum CA 19-9 level of 25 U/mL (reference range 0–37 U/mL) and a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 2 ng/mL (reference range 0–2.5 ng/mL).  

An abdominal ultrasound revealed a retroperitoneal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an 8 cm tumor in the distal pancreas, closely abutting the splenic vessels and the renal hilum.
title: Frantz tumor in a 58 year old woman; case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old man was referred for evaluation of slowly enlarging, symmetric subcutaneous masses over 2 years, most prominently in the parotid and submandibular areas, with more rapid growth over the past 7 months. He also reported 6 months of bilateral hand joint pain with morning stiffness, dry mouth, calf rash, and nail changes. His history was significant for metabolic liver cirrhosis (Child–Turcotte–Pugh B, MELD score 9), portal hypertension, and secondary megaloblastic anemia diagnosed in 2019. He had a history of moderate alcohol intake but had abstained for over 6 months.  
On examination, he was slightly overweight (BMI 25.5 kg/m2). There were firm, painless, egg-sized subcutaneous masses in the parotid and submandibular regions, softer mobile masses over the occiput and upper forearms, and mild gynecomastia. Skin examination revealed psoriatic plaques on the calves and onychodystrophy. Hand joint palpation was tender. Schirmer’s test showed reduced tear production.  
Laboratory studies showed elevated ESR (26 mm/h), rheumatoid factor 235 U/mL, low C4 complement, normal IgG4, negative anti-CCP, and negative extractable nuclear antigen and ANCA panels. Tests supported alcohol-related cirrhosis. Viral hepatitis markers were negative. He had mild hyperglycemia and hyperuricemia.  
High-resolution ultrasound of the neck revealed well-circumscribed, homogeneous subcutaneous fat masses with parallel thin echogenic lines and minimal internal vascularity on power Doppler and superb microvascular imaging. Breast ultrasound confirmed mild bilateral gynecomastia.  
Head and neck MRI demonstrated markedly thickened subcutaneous adipose tissue in the parotid, submandibular, and upper neck regions, with homogeneous fat signal and no features suspicious for malignancy.
title: Multidisciplinary diagnostic dilemma in differentiating Madelung’s disease — the value of superb microvascular imaging technique: A case report

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 2½-year-old boy was referred for acute fever, abdominal pain, and decreased oral intake. He had also had linear splinter hemorrhages of the nails for several weeks. His past history was unremarkable except for a recent tonsillectomy.

On examination he was febrile, tachypneic (respiratory rate 36/min), tachycardic (heart rate 165/min), and hypoxemic with room-air saturations of 89–93% (improving to 97–98% on 1 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula). Blood pressure was 121/76 mmHg. Auscultation revealed decreased air entry over the left hemithorax and a pleural friction rub; hepatomegaly was present.

Laboratory studies showed: C-reactive protein 333 mg/L (normal <10), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 37 mm/h (3–13), platelet count 573 × 10^9/L (150–450), and white blood cell count 24.6 × 10^9/L (4.0–10.0) with 86.6% neutrophils and 6% immature neutrophils. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated a basal consolidation in the left lower lobe with opacification along the lateral chest wall and rightward mediastinal shift, findings consistent with pneumonia and pleural effusion; a reticulonodular pattern was also noted in the right lung and left upper lobe. Ultrasound confirmed a left pleural effusion. He was started on amoxicillin–clavulanic acid and gentamicin, and blood cultures remained negative.

After four days he redeveloped dyspnea and increased oxygen requirements. Ultrasound showed increased, organizing pleural effusion. Bacterial endocarditis was excluded by negative blood cultures and a normal cardiac ultrasound. He underwent mini-thoracotomy and decortication; pleural fluid analysis revealed an exudate (pH 6.92, glucose <0.6 mmol/L, protein 35.7 g/L, LDH 2677 U/L) with cultures negative, although 16S-PCR identified Streptococcus pneumoniae. He recovered fully over 10 days and was discharged on oral antibiotics.

Eight weeks after recovery, chest radiography continued to show a reticulonodular pattern with features of honeycombing. High-resolution CT of the thorax revealed numerous bilateral cysts of different sizes and varying wall thickness, without emphysema or bronchiectasis.
title: Langerhans cell histiocytosis presenting with complicated pneumonia, a case report

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with seizure-like activity characterized by confusion, eye fluttering, facial tics, and diffuse weakness. She reported 6 months of progressive right-sided headaches, unintended weight loss, and occasional abdominal pain. Her medical history was notable only for polycystic ovarian syndrome. On examination she was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and intermittently confused, with multiple episodes of emesis; there were no focal motor or sensory deficits after treatment with steroids and levetiracetam.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated enlarged, multiloculated, peripherally enhancing lesions involving both ovaries and fallopian tubes, scattered pelvic peritoneal thickening, and free fluid. Brain MRI revealed a single 3.2 × 2.5 cm centrally necrotic lesion in the right parieto-occipital region with thick, nodular peripheral enhancement and surrounding vasogenic edema. The lesion was centrally T2 hypointense. Diffusion-weighted imaging with apparent diffusion coefficient mapping showed a subtle rim of peripheral restricted diffusion corresponding to the region of enhancement. There was no associated hemorrhage.
title: Tuberculosis presenting with seizure and abdominal pain in a young female: A case report

case_prompt: A 37-month-old boy from Guangxi Province, China, with a history of recurrent pneumonia since infancy, presented with 3 months of intermittent right-sided abdominal pain—worse after eating—and fevers up to 40 °C. On examination he had left cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly (liver and spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margins). His abdomen was soft with normal bowel sounds. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (16.9×10^9/L) with neutrophil predominance, hemoglobin 90 g/L, hypoalbuminemia (29.0 g/L), C‐reactive protein >192 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h, and an elevated serum galactomannan index (0.826; normal <0.5). HIV and interferon-γ autoantibodies were negative. Blood and stool cultures were negative. Chest CT demonstrated patchy pulmonary exudates. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed hepatomegaly, thickening of the ascending colon wall, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy in the ileocecal region. Colonoscopy showed a cobblestone pattern with erosions, ulcers, polypoid lesions, and lumen deformation from the colon to the cecum. Crohn’s disease and intestinal tuberculosis were considered, and the patient was treated with mesalazine and thalidomide for 1 week without clinical improvement.
title: Disseminated Talaromyces marneffei infection presenting as multiple intestinal perforations and diffuse hepatic granulomatous inflammation in an infant with STAT3 mutation: a case report

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old man initially underwent excision of a 2.0 × 1.5 × 0.7 cm left gingival mass, which was diagnosed at an outside hospital as non-Hodgkin lymphoma and treated with six cycles of cyclophosphamide, adriamycin, vincristine, and prednisone. Nine months later, he presented with a painless left submandibular mass.  
On contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, there was a 3.2 × 2.5 × 2.2 cm enhancing mass with a central low-attenuation area suggestive of cystic or necrotic degeneration, and there was enlargement of cervical lymph nodes at levels IIa and IIb.  
The submandibular mass was excised. Grossly, it was tan-white, well-circumscribed, and on sectioning showed a centrally necrotic and cystic cut surface.  
Microscopic examination revealed two distinct components:  
• A central undifferentiated epithelial component with primitive malignant cells arranged in sheets, cords, nests, and trabeculae.  
• A peripheral neurogenic component composed of mature ganglion cells and Schwann cells within a neurofibrillary stroma.  
Immunohistochemical staining of the undifferentiated component demonstrated diffuse positivity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, cytokeratin 8/18, S-100 protein, and focal CD56, and was negative for synaptophysin, chromogranin, neuron-specific enolase, melan-A, GFAP, CD45, CD99, CD20, CK5/6, CK7, CK20, EMA, p63, and EBV antigen. The ganglion cells of the neural component were positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin.
journal: Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology : JOMFP
title: Cervical ganglioneuroma in collision with a metastatic undifferentiated carcinoma

case_prompt: A 32-year-old unemployed Yemeni man with a 10-year history of schizophrenia characterized by auditory hallucinations and passivity phenomena had been stable for 6 years on clozapine (400 mg daily) and olanzapine (10 mg daily). In March 2014, he developed anxiety, tremor, dizziness, and slowing of movements, and all antipsychotic medications were stopped. Four weeks later he presented to the emergency department with a sudden decline in consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale score, 5) and generalized fast-rhythm tremors of all four limbs. He was intubated and admitted to the intensive care unit. Status epilepticus with possible herpes encephalitis and neuroleptic malignant syndrome were considered. He underwent electroencephalography, lumbar puncture, and brain MRI, all of which were within normal limits. He received antiepileptic therapy and empirical antiviral therapy and was discharged on levetiracetam. Over the following months, he had multiple brief hospital admissions with recurrent altered mental status, fast-rhythm limb tremors, perseverative and echolalic speech, and odd staring. Each time, comprehensive medical evaluations including neurologic and toxicologic studies were unremarkable. On the most recent admission, a prolonged video EEG showed no ictal changes during the tremor-like movements and no interictal epileptiform discharges.
title: Severe Relapsing Clozapine-Withdrawal Catatonia

case_prompt: A 20-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of asymptomatic discoloration and thickening of both areolas. It began as a pink, scaly, eczematous plaque on the areola that gradually darkened, with notable worsening over the past 2 months. She denied atopy, bloody nipple discharge, personal or family history of breast malignancy, and was not taking any medications. On examination, there was diffuse brownish pigmentation and verrucous thickening of the entire right areola and the upper part of the left areola with overlying scale-crust. No palpable breast masses, lymphadenopathy, nipple retraction, or discharge were noted. The remainder of the skin examination was unremarkable, her body mass index was within the normal range, and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. A skin biopsy of the areolar lesion showed marked epidermal thickening with slight papillomatosis, filiform downward anastomosing rete ridges, basal-layer hyperpigmentation without melanocytic proliferation, and slight fibrosis of the upper dermis.
final_diagnosis_raw: Nevoid hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola
title: Nevoid Hyperkeratosis of the Nipple and/or Areola: Treatment with Topical Steroid

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old man presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the cervical and epigastric regions, occurring hours after an episode of vomiting. He had no significant medical history. On examination, he was anxious and agitated but hemodynamically and respiratorily stable. He had pale, sweaty skin, cold cyanotic extremities, tachypnea without added lung sounds (SpO2 98% on room air), normal heart sounds (heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg), and abdominal rigidity with antalgic contracture. EKG showed sinus rhythm without repolarization changes.  
To exclude aortic dissection, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis was performed.
The CT scan excluded aortic dissection and revealed pneumomediastinum in moderate to large quantities, predominantly in the posterior mediastinum, with visualization of a fistulous tract at the lower esophagus and thickened, edematous distal esophageal walls; after oral contrast, there was extraluminal contrast in the mediastinum at the level of the lower esophagus, along with a small right pneumothorax and a distended stomach with liquid content.
title: Early Presentation of Boerhaave Syndrome in the Emergency Department: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of 5 days of sudden-onset excessive thirst and urine output. She reported extreme craving for cold fluids, consuming approximately 10 L of mostly cold water daily, and passing large volumes of urine both day and night. She denied fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, or other neurological symptoms. Her appetite and weight had remained stable.

Her medical history was unremarkable, with no medications. There was no family history of renal, endocrine, or psychiatric disorders. Two days earlier, outpatient tests had shown normal plasma glucose and normal serum electrolytes; dipstick urinalysis was negative for glucose and protein.

On examination, she appeared well and euvolemic. Blood pressure was 105/76 mm Hg, pulse 70 beats/min, temperature 37.2 °C. Height was 154 cm (25th percentile), weight 52.3 kg (50th percentile), and BMI 22.0 kg/m2 (75th percentile). Neurologic examination—including cranial nerves, muscle tone, and reflexes—was normal.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
 Serum sodium 133 mmol/L (135–145), serum osmolality 261 mOsm/kg (275–295), urine sodium 12 mmol/L (20–40), urine osmolality 47 mOsm/kg (500–800).  
Basal endocrine studies—including ACTH, TSH, thyroxine, IGF, cortisol, and prolactin—were within normal limits. Brain MRI demonstrated a normal posterior pituitary and pituitary stalk. Renal ultrasonography was unremarkable.
title: Psychogenic polydipsia in a female adolescent without a psychiatric background: A case report

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of worsening epigastric and left upper quadrant abdominal pain. He noted unintentional weight loss of 20 lb over 6 weeks but denied pancreatitis, trauma, surgery, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or bowel or urinary symptoms. His medical history included hypertension, untreated hepatitis C infection, intravenous drug use, and smoking; he denied recent alcohol use. On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 92/min, blood pressure 150/113 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Breath sounds were diminished at the left lung base. He had tenderness in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant without peritoneal signs. 

Laboratory studies showed: WBC 18,700/mm³, hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL (baseline 14.1 g/dL), platelets 222,000/mm³, PT 14 seconds, INR 1.2; electrolytes and renal function were normal. Total bilirubin was 0.7 mg/dL; ALT 120 U/L; AST 80 U/L; ALP 71 U/L. Troponin I was 0.014 ng/mL; procalcitonin 0.11 ng/mL. Urine drug screen was positive for methamphetamine and fentanyl. Hepatitis C antibody was positive; HIV and SARS-CoV-2 were negative. 

Noncontrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a high-density left pleural effusion and fluid in the deep pelvis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated wall thickening of the mid-distal esophagus and gastric cardia with a large surrounding high-density collection consistent with hematoma, a small focus of active contrast extravasation medial to the gastric cardia, and a moderate left hemothorax. Small-volume high-density fluid in the left upper quadrant tracked along the greater curvature of the stomach, most compatible with hemoperitoneum.

A corroborating history and these imaging findings raised suspicion for possible malignancy, esophageal perforation, bleeding varix, and left-sided hemothorax.
title: Spontaneous Subdiaphragmatic Hemorrhage From an Aneurysm of Inferior Phrenic Artery

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman presented in March 2022 with a 1-month history of insidious, progressive right knee pain, aggravated by movement and relieved by rest and analgesics. She noted local warmth but no erythema. Initial examination revealed joint tenderness and limited range of motion. She was diagnosed as having synovitis and treated empirically with antibiotics and painkillers, but her pain persisted.

One week later she returned with the same knee pain plus fever. An MRI of the right knee showed a suspected meniscus tear, anterior cruciate ligament degeneration, synovitis, and joint-capsule fluid; no bone lesions or lymphadenopathy were described. She underwent arthroscopic drainage under antibiotic coverage; no tissue was sent for histology.

Over the next 3 weeks, she developed severe knee pain, marked swelling, high-grade fevers to 103°F, profound malaise, unintentional 5-kg weight loss, and near-complete loss of knee mobility. A second arthroscopy was performed 6 weeks after the first; synovial tissue was sent for histopathology, which was negative for malignancy and for Koch’s disease. She was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and steroids without improvement.

A repeat MRI showed polypoidal soft-tissue thickening throughout the knee joint, mildly enhancing post-contrast, and multiple linear T2-hyperintense fracture-like signals in the fibular head with marrow edema. Two weeks later, an ^18F-FDG PET-CT demonstrated a large, FDG-avid, peripheral enhancing soft-tissue mass around the right knee (SUV 52.4), mild cortical erosion of the medial femoral condyle, and juxta-articular osteopenia. A mildly FDG-avid right popliteal lymph node and metabolically active right external iliac and inguinal nodes were noted, though no lymphadenopathy was palpable. One week later, she underwent open debulking of the knee lesion and excisional biopsy of the popliteal node; specimens were sent for histopathology and immunophenotyping.
title: A Rare Case of Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma of the Knee Joint

case_prompt: A 50-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of intermittent colicky abdominal pain. Abdominal ultrasonography and plain radiography (KUB) showed a 1.2-cm calculus in the mid right ureter with mild hydronephrosis; the left kidney was normal in size, and both kidneys had a normal corticomedullary pattern. His renal function was within normal limits. While awaiting lithotripsy, he developed chest pain, which was diagnosed as an extensive anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. Coronary angiography revealed complete occlusion of the left anterior descending artery, and he underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with 150 mL of iodixanol contrast agent. Hemodynamic parameters remained stable throughout; he was normotensive, with a jugular venous pressure within normal limits and clear lung fields. From the onset of chest pain, he did not pass any urine, and anuria persisted despite adequate fluid resuscitation and administration of 80 mg of intravenous furosemide. His complete blood count was normal, without eosinophilia; urinalysis was unremarkable, with no urinary eosinophils; and serum complement levels were within the normal range. His serum creatinine rose steadily to 6.2 mg/dL 48 hours after the intervention. Urinary electrolytes and the fractional excretion of sodium were inconsistent with prerenal azotemia. Repeated abdominal ultrasonography with Doppler showed the known right ureteric calculus but no abnormalities in renal arterial or venous flow. Two-dimensional echocardiography demonstrated anterior wall hypokinesia with a preserved ejection fraction. Renal replacement therapy was initiated.
title: Reflex anuria following acute cardiac event

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman was referred to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of a small mass on the dorsal aspect of the right fourth finger. She reported that the lesion had been present for approximately 15 years, with a slight increase in size, but it caused no pain or functional limitation. Her medical history was significant only for a mitral valvuloplasty 20 years earlier. There was no history of trauma to the area, no family history of similar lesions, and she denied systemic symptoms.

On examination, there was a firm, round, immobile, and nontender subcutaneous mass measuring about 1 cm in diameter over the proximal interphalangeal joint of the right fourth finger. The overlying skin appeared normal, and the range of motion of the finger was intact. No other abnormalities were noted on physical examination.

Given the persistence and growth of the lesion, an excisional biopsy was performed and the specimen was sent for pathologic evaluation.
title: Plexiform Schwannoma of the Finger: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 4½-year-old boy was brought in because of constant peer harassment due to his “old man” appearance and bleeding from his upper right and left posterior teeth during brushing. His mother reported that his primary teeth had always shown abnormal color and continuous chipping of the tooth structure; he denied pain or sensitivity. He was born at term with normal developmental milestones. There was no history of bone fragility, systemic illness, or drug use. His mother has a diagnosis of Shields type II dentinogenesis imperfecta and has worn an overdenture for 6 years.

On extraoral examination, the child had an edentulous appearance with loss of vertical dimension of occlusion, decreased lower facial height, a prognathic profile, and diminished lip support. Intraorally, all deciduous teeth were attrited to the gingival level; teeth 54, 64, 81, 51, and 61 appeared as mobile root stumps. All remaining teeth were yellow-brown and translucent.

Panoramic and intraoral periapical radiographs showed bulbous crowns with marked cervical constriction of teeth 55, 65, 74, 75, 84, and 85; total obliteration of pulp chambers and root canals of 52, 62, 71, 72, and 82; partial obliteration in the other teeth; and apical resorption with periapical radiolucencies at the root stumps. Developing permanent tooth buds were present, and the dental age matched the chronological age.
journal: International Journal of Clinical Pediatric Dentistry
title: Complete Overlay Denture for Pedodontic Patient with Severe Dentinogenesis Imperfecta

case_prompt:
A 9-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of progressive lower back pain that was aggravated by bending and associated with an inability to stand upright. He denied any history of trauma or febrile illness. He also reported a focal, pin-point left chest pain. On examination, he appeared unwell and had lower limb paresthesia with reduced muscle power and bulk.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• White‐cell count 4.0×10^9/L (normal 4.0–10.0×10^9/L)  
• LDH 25 U/L (normal <40 U/L)  
• Urea 6.0 mmol/L (normal 2.5–8 mmol/L); creatinine 70 μmol/L (63–115 μmol/L)  
• Potassium 4.0 meq/L (3.5–5.5 meq/L); sodium 136 meq/L (135–155 meq/L)  
• Calcium 6.0 mg/dL (8.5–10.5 mg/dL)

Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine showed a destructive lesion at L3. CT of the chest revealed an osteolytic lesion in the left third rib, and CT of the head demonstrated an osteolytic lesion in the left calvarium. Histologic examination of the L3 lesion demonstrated cells with eccentric nuclei and prominent Golgi apparatus. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD138 and CD56, and in situ hybridization revealed a small serum monoclonal IgA spike of kappa light chain. Bone marrow evaluation was normal.
title: Plasma cell myeloma in a 9‐year‐old male: Case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with a 3-week history of a neck mass. He initially experienced a globus sensation and pain on swallowing, which resolved spontaneously after one week. Physical examination revealed a smooth, non-tender, approximately 3 cm mass in the left thyroid lobe. Thyroid function tests were normal (TSH 2.4 mU/L [0.5–5.0 mU/L]; FT4 13.7 pmol/L [12.0–22.0 pmol/L]); calcitonin and thyroglobulin levels were within normal limits.

Thyroid ultrasound showed a solid, homogeneous, hypoechoic lesion in the left lobe measuring 2.0 cm × 2.8 cm × 3.4 cm. The lesion was taller than wide, had a well-defined smooth border, and contained two macrocalcifications; Doppler signal was absent. On compression, the lesion was partially elastic without fluctuation. A left cervical lymph node of normal size lacked a fatty hilum and exhibited internal calcifications with heterogeneous echotexture.

Based on the ultrasound findings, the differential diagnosis included thyroid adenoma, thyroid carcinoma, and a thyroidal epidermal cyst.
title: Epidermal inclusion cyst of the thyroid: a rare case of a nodule-like structure at ultrasound

case_prompt: A 19-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Neurologic examination revealed cerebellar ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and bilateral papilledema. Noncontrast CT of the head showed two hypodense lesions in the right cerebellar hemisphere and the vermis, each demonstrating peripheral heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration and causing mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Cranial MRI demonstrated irregularly contoured mass lesions in contact with the fourth ventricle, heterogeneous signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images suggestive of subacute intratumoral hemorrhage with discrete surrounding edema, and lesions measuring 3×4 cm with heterogeneous ring enhancement and central necrosis.
title: Primary glioblastoma of the cerebellum in a 19-year-old woman: a case report

case_prompt: A 78-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis presented with 1 week of bilateral periorbital edema and 3 days of fever and dyspnea. His medications for rheumatoid arthritis included methotrexate, iguratimod, and prednisone. On admission, his temperature was 40.3 °C, and he required 3 L/min of nasal oxygen. Examination revealed marked bilateral eyelid swelling with blood-tinged conjunctival discharge; lung auscultation was clear. Contrast-enhanced head CT showed conjunctival thickening with enhancement, consistent with periorbital cellulitis. Chest radiography demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities, and non-contrast chest CT confirmed extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities with a focal consolidation in the left lower lobe. Urinalysis revealed occult blood and proteinuria. Laboratory tests showed a WBC count of 12,100/μL with 72.5% neutrophils, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 161,000/μL, AST 44 IU/L, ALT 23 IU/L, LDH 391 IU/L, CRP 12.2 mg/dL, KL-6 713 U/mL, and MMP-3 374.9 ng/mL. Autoimmune serologies, including ANA, RF, ANCA subtypes, and a broad panel of specific autoantibodies, were within normal limits. Infection markers for Legionella, Streptococcus pneumoniae, viruses, and fungi were negative; however, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was isolated from conjunctival and sputum cultures. The differential diagnoses included rheumatoid lung, contagious pneumonia, and drug-induced pneumonia.
title: An autopsy case of acute fibrinous and organizing pneumonia with periorbital MRSA cellulitis and rheumatoid arthritis

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 1-day history of retrosternal burning chest pain, diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fatigue. Her blood pressure was 200/100 mmHg and heart rate 88 b.p.m.; examination revealed right hypochondriac tenderness but no murmurs, no jugular venous distension, and clear lung fields. She had a history of hypertension treated intermittently with amlodipine and indapamide, and 6 months earlier had presented with similar chest pain, ST changes, mildly elevated troponin, global left ventricular hypokinesis (EF 36%), and a normal coronary angiogram; that episode was labeled “acute myocarditis.” Her mother and aunt had polycystic kidney disease.  

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 18×10^3/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm/h; electrolytes, troponin I, and renal function were normal. Electrocardiography demonstrated 1.0–2.5 mm ST depression in leads II and V2–V6 and >0.5 mm ST elevation in aVR. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple cysts in both kidneys and a multicystic mass in the right liver lobe; the adrenal glands were not visualized. Transthoracic echocardiography showed global myocardial hypokinesis.  

During her admission, she experienced several transient episodes of sweating, pallor, nausea, and vomiting accompanied by hypertensive crises with blood pressure exceeding 200/100 mmHg. Based on these recurrent sympathetic surges and her prior evaluations, the team decided to measure 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines.
title: Catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy in a patient with pheochromocytoma and polycystic kidney and liver disease: a case report

case_prompt: A 64-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious at home with “generalized shaking,” without trauma or incontinence. He recovered spontaneously, was hemodynamically stable and afebrile, and had a normal neurologic examination. Arterial blood gas testing showed normoglycemia and no acid–base or electrolyte disturbances. Laboratory studies revealed a mildly elevated serum creatine kinase level of 762 U/L (reference <145), with normal renal and hepatic function and a normal complete blood count. Noncontrast brain CT demonstrated a well-defined hyperdense lesion measuring 20.8 × 14.5 mm in the right temporal fossa, producing mass effect on the adjacent temporal lobe, without ventricular involvement, edema, structural deviation, skull fracture, or hemorrhage. An electroencephalogram showed generalized epileptiform activity arising from the right temporal lobe.
title: Enostosis-related epilepsy

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of pleuritic chest pain localized to the base of the left hemithorax. The pain was initially intermittent and variable in duration. She denied fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Her medical history included asthma and papillary thyroid carcinoma resected 8 years earlier, with no evidence of relapse. On examination, vital signs were normal, and the only notable finding was a central neck scar.

A chest radiograph demonstrated a round opacity at the base of the left lower lobe. Thoracic computed tomography confirmed a peripheral, juxtapleural lesion in the anterior segment of the left lower lobe, measuring approximately 2.5 cm in its greatest dimension.

Given her history of thyroid cancer, a neoplastic process was suspected, and the patient underwent a thoracotomy with wedge resection of the pulmonary lesion.
title: Pulmonary histoplasmoma: a disguised malady

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old boy was referred to the pediatric dentistry clinic for crowding of the lower front teeth. He was born at 34 weeks’ gestation with a birth weight of 3.3 kg after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Early developmental milestones were reported as normal.  
On examination, his body habitus was thin and marfanoid with low subcutaneous fat. Skeletal abnormalities included pectus carinatum, genu recurvatum, pes planus, camptodactyly of the toes, and joint hypermobility.  
At age 2 years, evaluation for chronic constipation led to a barium enema that suggested aganglionosis, and rectal biopsy confirmed absence of ganglion cells with increased acetylcholinesterase staining; the rectoanal inhibitory reflex was absent.  
Cardiac assessment, including echocardiography, was within normal limits for age.  
Extraoral examination revealed a dolichocephalic skull with frontal bossing, tall forehead, exophthalmos, hypertelorism, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, proptosis, bilateral blepharoptosis, low-set ears with prominent helices, and maxillary hypoplasia. Lips appeared competent, but the patient was a mouth breather.  
Intraoral examination showed a high-arched palate, micrognathia, and mixed dentition with crowding of mandibular incisors. Radiographs demonstrated taurodontism of multiple molars, gross caries of select primary and permanent teeth, and absence of the mandibular right second premolar tooth bud.
journal: Journal of Clinical and Experimental Dentistry
title: A Rare Case of Shprintzen-Goldberg craniosynostosis syndrome with Hirschsprung disorder: Dental characteristics and its Clinical Management

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old right-hand–dominant Colombian cleaner presented with a 3-week history of pain and swelling in the tip of her right thumb. She had hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine, was a non-smoker, and functionally independent. She reported a longstanding vertical midline split of the right thumbnail and felt her symptoms began after trimming this nail. A 5-day course of oral flucloxacillin prescribed by her general practitioner yielded no improvement.

On examination, the right thumb was swollen with tenderness under the nail plate but no pulp tenderness, erythema, or fluctuant collection; there were no Kanavel signs. A small area of peeled, devitalized skin was present at the tip. The digit was neurovascularly intact.

Blood tests were unremarkable. Plain radiographs of the right thumb showed a lytic lesion involving the tuft of the distal phalanx. She was admitted for presumed infection, treated with elevation and intravenous antibiotics, and underwent emergency surgical washout and debridement. Intraoperatively, no pus was found in the pulp, but the distal phalanx bone was eroded and soft. Multiple bone specimens were sent for microscopy, bacterial culture, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) culture, and histopathology.

Citrobacter freundii was isolated from bone biopsies on enrichment culture, and AFB cultures were negative. Two weeks after biopsy, the histopathology report described “fragments of a cellular spindle cell tumour with islands of osteoid, which was suspicious for a primary bone malignancy.”
title: Fibro-osseous pseudotumour of the digit—a diagnostic challenge

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old man with no history of renal disease presented 13 days after two-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting with progressive shortness of breath and orthopnea. He required supplemental oxygen.  
Computed tomography of the chest showed a left pleural effusion, a small pericardial effusion, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates concerning for pneumonia.  
Laboratory evaluation revealed a serum creatinine of 1.64 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL at discharge), a C-reactive protein level of 165 mg/L, a pro–BNP of 589 pg/mL, a white blood cell count of 22 × 10^9/L, a hemoglobin level of 7.2 g/dL, and negative blood cultures.  
He was treated with intravenous furosemide and piperacillin–tazobactam but showed no clinical or laboratory improvement.  
Given the lack of response to diuresis and antibiotics, pulmonology recommended assessment for an autoimmune process.
title: Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody Vasculitis after Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting

case_prompt: A 41-year-old Caucasian woman noticed left cheek swelling and pain in the corresponding upper premolars and molars lasting more than a week. Her medical history included a prior ischemic cerebrovascular accident treated with anticoagulants. On extraoral examination, there was a firm swelling of the left cheek without lymphadenopathy or sensory loss. Intraorally, there was severe periodontal disease, pain on percussion of the left upper premolars and molars, buccoalveolar sulcus bulging, and a floating tumefaction adjacent to the left upper molar roots. The lesion was initially managed as a dental abscess with drainage and antibiotics, and a multislice CT was requested. The patient returned three weeks later with new-onset paresthesia, severe left facial pain, and progressive cheek swelling. She was admitted, and noncontrast multislice CT showed, on axial images, a hypodense soft-tissue mass filling the left maxillary sinus with discontinuity of the anterior and lateral sinus walls extending toward the orbital floor; frontal images revealed involvement of the nasal cavity. A repeat CT scan demonstrated enlargement of the lesion, greater nasal cavity extension, and more extensive bony destruction. Routine blood counts, coagulation studies, lymphocyte immunophenotyping (CD3+/CD4+), and parathyroid hormone levels were all within normal limits.
title: Maxillary Sinus Natural Killer/T-Cell Extranodal Lymphoma Mimicking a Dentoalveolar Abscess

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of progressive swelling in the right mandibular region. He had no significant past medical or family history and a three-year history of cigarette smoking. After extraction of his right lower third molar by an oral surgeon, the extraction site failed to heal, and he reported mild facial swelling near the right mandibular angle. 

On examination, intraoral inspection revealed a nonhealing socket at the right lower third molar site with otherwise normal dentition and mucosa; there was no inferior alveolar nerve paresthesia. Extraoral examination showed adequate mouth opening, an intact mandibular border, and no cervical lymphadenopathy.

An orthopantomogram demonstrated a large, radiolucent lesion extending from the right lower second molar to the mandibular ramus without fracture. Contrast CT of the mandible revealed a 4.7 × 3.4 × 8 cm expansile, destructive lesion centered at the right mandibular angle, with extension into the ramus, coronoid, and condylar processes and areas of cortical perforation, suggesting a locally aggressive tumor.

An incisional biopsy performed at an outside facility was reported as pleomorphic adenoma.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma of mandible: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 26-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 2-month history of intermittent vomiting, headaches, and vertigo, accompanied by progressive visual deterioration. Physical examination was unremarkable without lymphadenopathy. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed bifocal hyperdense, compressive extra-axial masses with surrounding edema in the right parieto-occipital and left frontal regions, causing mass effect on the lateral ventricles and midline. Subsequent MRI confirmed dural-based lesions: T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences showed iso- to hypointense signals with vasogenic edema, diffusion-weighted imaging (b1000) revealed no restriction, and gadolinium-enhanced images demonstrated strong, homogeneous enhancement.
title: Bifocal Intracanial Rosai-Dorfman Disease Mimicking Lymphoplasmacyte-Rich Meningioma: Diagnostic Pitfalls About a Case Report

case_prompt: An 85‐year‐old Caucasian woman with diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was evaluated for a right dorsal foot lesion first noticed about 12 years earlier. She had not sought care because it was slow‐growing and asymptomatic until, over the past 3 weeks, it enlarged more rapidly and developed a foul odor. She denied pain, paresthesias, weight loss, trauma, smoking history, and significant sun exposure. On examination, there was an 8.0 × 8.0 × 0.6 cm exophytic, fungating, malodorous mass on the dorsum of the right foot that was insensate to light touch without surrounding erythema. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were palpable, and she had full range of motion. The remainder of her skin exam was unremarkable. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging showed a large soft‐tissue irregularity surrounding the second to fifth extensor tendons.
title: Large fungating basal cell carcinoma of the dorsum of the foot: A case report

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old man presented with blurred central vision and reduced visual acuity in his left eye. Three years earlier, he had been diagnosed with central serous chorioretinopathy of the left eye based on serous macular detachment on examination and OCT-confirmed subretinal fluid, and he received a single intravitreal anti-VEGF injection after 3 months of persistent fluid.

On current presentation, best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in the right eye and 0.5 in the left. Examination of the posterior poles showed a serous retinal detachment superior to the optic disc in the right eye and a well-defined serous macular detachment in the left eye. OCT confirmed subtle interpapillomacular subretinal fluid in the right eye and a significant inferotemporal subretinal fluid pocket in the left eye. Fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrated punctate hyperfluorescent pinpoint foci in the macula of both eyes in the early venous phase, with pooling of dye around the optic disc (OD) and superior and inferior to the fovea (OS) in the late phase. Notably, there were no typical leakage spots to guide laser photocoagulation.

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, p-ANCA, PR3 IgG, ANA, circulating immune complexes, Borrelia antibodies, Toxoplasma antibodies, and HIV testing, were all normal or negative. The only positive result was CMV IgG, considered incidental in this immunocompetent patient.
title: Bilateral multifocal and recurrent chorioretinopathy - case report

case_prompt: A previously healthy 3-year-old Caucasian boy presented with a 4-month history of intensely pruritic erythematous papules and plaques on the upper and central trunk and upper extremities. The lesions failed to clear after a 3-month course of topical corticosteroids. A clinical diagnosis of scabies was made 3 weeks earlier, and symptoms worsened after application of permethrin cream 5%, suggesting a hypersensitivity reaction. The rash did not improve with topical pimecrolimus cream 1%. On examination, there were erythematous papules and plaques in a V-shaped distribution on the chest and back, with papular eruptions on the upper arms and thighs, sparing the palms, axillae, soles, and lower extremities. A skin biopsy from the back showed a neutrophilic infiltrate within and surrounding the eccrine ducts, with sparing of the coiled secretory glands.
title: A case of neutrophilic superficial eccrine ductitis

case_prompt: A 15-year-old boy presented with a 4-year history of recurrent mild epistaxis, managed intermittently with silver nitrate cautery. He denied smoking, anticoagulant use, anemia, heart disease, or antihypertensive medications. His only medical history was seasonal allergies treated with antihistamines. During the last month he had daily 1-hour bilateral nosebleeds, worse on the right. Physical examination initially showed a midline septum and prominent intranasal vessels on the right. Cautery provided temporary relief. Thirteen months later, he experienced multiple 1-hour bleeds over 2 days, this time worse on the left; exam showed left septal deviation and cautery was repeated. Four months later, he reported persistent symptoms, and exam revealed left septal spurring, mucosal edema, congestion, rhinorrhea, and bilateral nasal clots. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated left septal spurring, inferior turbinate hypertrophy, polypoid swelling in the middle meatus, purulence in the right nasal floor, and soft tissue swelling obstructing the right nasopharynx. Adenoiditis was suspected, and he received doxycycline, prednisone, and saline spray. On follow-up he had continued epistaxis, intranasal clots, and right-sided nasal obstruction impacting breathing and daily activities. A noncontrast CT of the sinuses showed a right-sided soft tissue density mass causing widening of the right pterygopalatine fossa, globulation of its margins, and bowing of the posterior wall of the right maxillary sinus without aggressive bony destruction. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, nasopharyngeal polyp, and rhabdomyosarcoma were considered, and contrast-enhanced MRI was recommended.
title: The radiological perspective of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma: A case report

case_prompt: A 14-year-old female student (height 179 cm, weight 110 kg; BMI 34.3 kg/m2) presented with significant infrapatellar pain when kneeling and recurrent external patellar dislocations. She had a prior diagnosis of Osgood–Schlatter disease treated conservatively and a history of irritable bowel syndrome. There was no pain with simple knee flexion or extension. Preoperative knee scores were low (Kujala 32, Lysholm 19, KOOS pain 21.4, KOOS symptoms 58.3, KOOS ADL 41.2, KOOS sports 10, KOOS QOL 25). On examination of the left knee, there was no focal tenderness, but patellar tracking and apprehension tests were positive; rotational stress, drawer, and grinding tests were negative. Range of motion was full. Laboratory tests, including inflammatory markers, were all within normal limits. Lateral radiographs at 20° of flexion showed patellar height ratios: Caton–Deschamps 1.7, Insall–Salvati 0.8, modified Insall–Salvati 2.3, Blackburne–Peel 1.6. CT measurements revealed a TT–TG distance of 21.1 mm, patellar tilt 36.5°, femoral torsion 13.6°, tibial torsion 30.2°. MRI demonstrated a sulcus angle of 129.3° and trochlear depth of 6.4 mm without meniscal or ligament injury. The patellar morphology ratio (length of patella to articular facet) was 2.
title: Anatomical and clinical significance of the Cyrano long-nosed patella in combination with patellofemoral instability: a case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 73-year-old woman, hospitalized for unrelated medical issues, developed a continuous headache, nausea, and vertigo. Noncontrast brain CT revealed a 4 × 3 cm calcified lesion at the left cerebellopontine angle with erosion of the mastoid bone around the facial and semicircular canals. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed a rim-enhancing mass with surrounding edema and central necrosis. Diffusion-weighted imaging did not demonstrate the restricted diffusion typical of an abscess. Given her remote history of otitis media and CT evidence of a passage between the middle ear and posterior cranial fossa, a chronic brain abscess was initially suspected. The patient underwent burr‐hole trephination and attempted abscess drainage; when no purulent material was obtained, a biopsy was performed. The pathological diagnosis on that specimen was fibrous meningioma. One week later, she developed aspiration pneumonia secondary to unilateral vocal cord palsy, and MRI demonstrated indentation of the pons and medulla consistent with low cranial nerve palsies. She then underwent a lateral suboccipital craniotomy. The lesion was noted to be stony hard peripherally with a yellowish-gelatinous central core, and a subtotal resection was achieved.
title: Intracranial Inflammatory Myofibroblastic Tumor: A Rare Case Report

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman presented with three weeks of progressive abdominal distension and a single episode of self-limited diarrhea. She reported recent dietary increases in nuts and green tea use. Her medical history was notable only for recurrent allergic bronchitis.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was moderate, doughy abdominal distension without pallor, icterus, or peripheral edema.
