Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated moderate ascites without signs of portal hypertension or liver or renal disease. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed free peritoneal fluid and diffuse, circumferential thickening of small-bowel loops as well as the distal stomach and esophagus.

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 22,900/mm3 with 52% eosinophils and no immature myeloid precursors. C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and IgE levels were within normal limits. Tumor marker CA-125 was normal. Skin-prick testing for food allergens and stool studies for bacteria, ova, and parasites were negative.

Diagnostic paracentesis yielded moderately cellular fluid composed entirely of eosinophils; cultures were sterile and no malignant cells were identified. 

Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy showed only mild erythema of the gastric antrum; the esophagus, duodenum, terminal ileum, and colon appeared normal. Histologic examination of gastric and duodenal mucosal biopsies revealed a mild inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and scattered eosinophils in the lamina propria.
title: Eosinophilic ascites: A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge

case_prompt: A 74-year-old man with hypertension and a prior left PCA infarct on ecosprin presented with sudden-onset left-sided weakness; imaging confirmed a right ACA-territory infarct. Upon admission, he complained of left hip pain and was unable to bear weight. Examination showed painful left hip rotations; the right hip was normal. Plain radiographs of both hips were unremarkable. MRI of the hips demonstrated a bulky region of heterogeneous signal intensity within the left obturator internus muscle on T2-weighted fat-saturated images, an iso- to slightly hyperintense area on T1-weighted images, a heterogeneous collection on coronal T2 images, and minimal peripheral enhancement on post-contrast T1 fat-saturated axial images. Laboratory tests revealed Hb 12.5 g/dL, WBC count 7,400/µL, platelet count 295,000/µL, ESR 35 mm/h, PT-INR 1.00, and APTT 37.8 s (control 38.9 s).
title: Spontaneous Obturator Internus Hematoma–a Rare Cause of Hip Pain: Case Report

case_prompt:
An 82-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia presented with an 8-day history of oral pain and burning that made eating difficult. Eight days earlier, he had begun topical imiquimod therapy for a basal cell carcinoma on his left shoulder. He had used imiquimod in the past without incident and had no new medications or known drug allergies.

On examination, there were hemorrhagic crusts on the vermillion border, erosive gingivitis, stomatitis, and ulcers on the palate. The skin showed erosions at the application site and discrete erosions on the back involving approximately 5% of the body surface area, along with atypical target lesions on the left arm and a positive Nikolsky sign. There was no ocular, genital, or anal mucosal involvement.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, a normal chest radiograph, and a C-reactive protein level of 17.8 mg/L. The initial differential diagnosis included erythema multiforme major versus Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Empiric oral prednisone and valacyclovir were initiated but were rapidly discontinued after negative herpes simplex virus and varicella–zoster virus PCR from mucosal lesions, and negative Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae serologies.
title: Topical imiquimod adverse event: Beyond the local skin reaction—A case report

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old multiparous woman presented with an 8-month history of bilateral breast enlargement. She reported painful, swollen breasts with multiple palpable nodules and erythema. She had used a levonorgestrel implant for two years. On examination, there was bilateral, symmetrical breast enlargement, erythematous skin with peau d’orange changes, and edema. A 4-cm mass was palpable in the lower inner quadrant of the right breast; no mass was felt on the left. A right axillary lymph node was palpable. She denied any personal or family history of breast cancer.

Bilateral mammography was nondiagnostic due to extremely dense breast tissue. Breast ultrasound revealed heterogeneous echotexture with multiple circumscribed solid, hypoechoic masses in both breasts, measuring 3–8 cm in diameter, and two right axillary lymph nodes with cortical thickening. The lesions were categorized as BI-RADS 4A.

Percutaneous core needle biopsy of the right breast mass showed breast parenchyma composed of ductal–lobular units and stromal tissue containing a complex pattern of linear spaces lined by spindle cells. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong positivity for CD34, actin, and calponin, and negativity for estrogen and progesterone receptors. Fine-needle aspiration of the right axillary lymph node revealed lymphoid hyperplasia.
title: An Uncommon Case of Bilateral Breast Enlargement Diagnosed as Tumoral Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia: Imaging and Pathological Findings

case_prompt: A 69-year-old woman noted a painless, slowly enlarging mass in her right eye over 18 months. Her history included treated uterine cancer with no recurrence. Visual acuity was 20/25 OU, and intraocular pressures were normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed a dark-red, lobulated subconjunctival lesion (7 × 5 mm) on the temporal side of the right eye. The lesion was noncompressible, nonpulsatile, not reducible, and did not enlarge with Valsalva. The overlying conjunctiva was freely mobile, whereas the mass itself moved minimally along the horizontal meridian. There was no proptosis; ocular alignment and motility were normal. The rest of the anterior and posterior segments were unremarkable. Provisional diagnosis was a benign vascular tumor. Anterior-segment OCT showed multiple intralesional hyporeflective spaces filled with moderate to high reflectivity causing back-shadowing, consistent with blood‐filled vascular lumens.
title: Intramuscular Hemangioma of Lateral Rectus Muscle with Rare Presentation as an Epibulbar Mass: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 30-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a localized gingival swelling between the mandibular left canine and first premolar. The lesion had grown slowly, causing displacement of the teeth and widening of the interdental space. She recalled a similar growth in the same region 11 years earlier that had been excised, but no records were available. On examination, there was an approximately 0.8 × 1.0 cm sessile, nonlobulated mass with sharp margins, covered by mucosa of normal color and of firm, fibrotic consistency. Full-mouth periodontal examination revealed generalized 3–4 mm pockets with subgingival calculus and poor oral hygiene. A clinical diagnosis of chronic periodontitis with focal fibrous hyperplasia (irritation fibroma) was made. An intraoral periapical radiograph showed horizontal bone loss in the involved area. The lesion was removed by excisional biopsy with an internal bevel incision and open-flap debridement; healing was uneventful. Five weeks later, the surgical site appeared well healed. Microscopic examination of the excised tissue revealed a partially circumscribed lesion composed of interlacing fascicles of collagen fibers and abundant islands and strands of odontogenic epithelium; the connective tissue contained focal chronic inflammatory infiltrates (predominantly plasma cells) and occasional multinucleated giant cells. The overlying epithelium was hyperplastic, parakeratinized stratified squamous with elongated rete ridges.
journal: Journal of Indian Society of Periodontology
title: Peripheral odontogenic fibroma: A case report and review

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old woman presents with a several-week history of intermittent vaginal bleeding. On colposcopic examination, a friable, solid mass measuring approximately 5 × 5 cm is noted on the posterior lip of the uterine cervix and bleeds easily when touched. A cervicovaginal specimen is obtained using a liquid-based cytology (SurePath™) technique, and a punch biopsy of the lesion is performed.

Cytologic findings:
• Hypercellular sample composed of isolated cells and tightly cohesive, multilayered clusters of endocervical cells in a clean background  
• Presence of papillary frond-like structures with smooth contours  
• Nuclear overlapping within cell clusters  
• Individual cells with high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratios; nuclei round to oval with irregular membranes  
• Nuclei hyperchromatic with evenly distributed granular chromatin and distinct nucleoli  
• Occasional mitotic figures and apoptotic debris
title: Liquid-Based Cytology of Villoglandular Adenocarcinoma of the Cervix: A Report of 3 Cases

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old Moroccan girl presented with painful swelling of both forearms. The swelling first appeared on her left forearm and, six months later, on her right forearm. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. She reported progressive pain despite daily use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and narcotic analgesics.

On examination, she was afebrile and in good general condition. There was swelling over the upper one-third of the right forearm and the upper two-thirds of the left forearm, with inflammatory signs.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, white blood cell count 11,210/μL with 80% neutrophils, and C-reactive protein 60 mg/L.

Plain radiographs demonstrated osteolytic lesions of the upper one-third of the right ulna and the upper two-thirds of the left radius, without mineralized matrix but with cortical breakthrough and internal trabeculations.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed osteolytic masses in those locations that invaded the elbow joints, were hyposignal on T1-weighted images, hypersignal on T2-weighted and STIR images, contained septa, showed annular enhancement after gadolinium administration, crossed the physis from the diaphysis, and were associated with a soft-tissue mass and edema.
title: Langerhans cell histiocytosis presenting as eosinophilic granuloma of the bilateral forearms in an 8-year-old girl: a case report

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man presented with progressive asthenia of eye-opening and bilateral ptosis for more than one year. He denied itching, swelling, pain, or other periocular discomfort and had no visible lesions on the eyelids or face. He underwent neuroelectromyography, neostigmine test, myasthenia gravis antibody assays, thyroid-function tests, and brain imaging; all results were normal, and neurogenic and myogenic causes were excluded. He was initially diagnosed with senile blepharoptosis but declined surgery and returned when his ptosis worsened.

His medical history was notable only for well-controlled diabetes and hypertension. He denied dermatoses (rosacea, acne, erysipelas, contact dermatitis, angioedema, lupus), trauma, surgery, or periocular rash, and had no known allergen exposures. His father had a similar progressive ptosis.

On examination, moderate bilateral blepharoptosis was seen without overt edema, erythema, papules, or masses. Careful palpation revealed subtle skin infiltration and shallow glabellar wrinkles. Seven days after skin biopsy of the upper eyelid and forehead, faint erythema appeared at the biopsy sites.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, antinuclear antibody, anti‐DNA, anti‐ENA, muscle enzymes, and IgE, were all normal or negative. Repeat neuroelectromyography, neostigmine test, myasthenia gravis antibodies, and thyroid function remained normal.

Histopathological examination of eyelid and forehead skin showed dermal edema, lymphatic hyperplasia and dilatation, perivascular lymphocytic infiltration, and an increased number of mast cells (>5 per high‐power field). Craniocerebral imaging was unremarkable.
title: Morbihan disease misdiagnosed as senile blepharoptosis and successfully treated with short-term minocycline and ketotifen: A case report

case_prompt: A 37-year-old pregnant woman (gravida 2, para 1), with no systemic disease, was referred at 25 + 5 weeks of gestation for evaluation of a persistent and enlarging left adnexal mass. At 7 weeks’ gestation, routine ultrasound had demonstrated a left ovarian cyst measuring 3.4 × 2.5 cm. Follow-up sonography revealed gradually increasing moderate echogenic protrusions within the cyst. On presentation, transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound showed an 8.4 × 5.8 cm multilocular cystic mass in the left ovary, with abundant blood-flow signals in papillary projections from the capsule wall and inner wall. Serum CA-125 was 44.9 U/mL (normal, 0–35 U/mL), and CA19-9 was 41.4 U/mL (normal, 0–34 U/mL). After multidisciplinary discussion, concern for ovarian malignancy led to recommendation for laparoscopic left salpingo-oophorectomy at 26 + 1 weeks’ gestation.
title: Decidualized ovarian endometrioma mimicking malignancy in pregnancy: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A male infant was delivered at 35 2/7 weeks’ gestation via cesarean section for recurrent fetal heart rate decelerations. The pregnancy was notable for first-trimester cystic hygroma and persistent intrauterine growth restriction. Prenatal ultrasound revealed absence of the corpus callosum, high-riding third ventricle, absent cavum septum pellucidum, indented occiput, and an absent ductus venosus draining directly to the hepatic vasculature. Noninvasive prenatal testing was low risk for trisomies 13, 18, 21, and monosomy X; amniocentesis was declined.

At birth, Apgar scores were 9 and 9. Birth weight was 1510 g (1st percentile), length 38.5 cm (1st percentile), and head circumference 30 cm (8th percentile). On examination, he had short palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, low-set ears, micrognathia, flat nasal bridge, elongated philtrum, thin upper lip, anteverted nares, hirsutism, and single palmar creases. Neurologically, he was centrally hypotonic with bilateral upper-limb hyperreflexia and a sacral dimple with a hair tuft.

He remained in the NICU for 70 days. Brain MRI confirmed agenesis of the corpus callosum and septum pellucidum with parallel colpocephalic ventricles; EEG showed poorly differentiated low-voltage background and temporal sharp transients. He required prolonged noninvasive respiratory support without parenchymal lung disease. Echocardiography demonstrated a small apical VSD, moderate PDA, small secundum ASD, and left superior vena cava to coronary sinus; the PDA later closed spontaneously. He had severe feeding intolerance despite negative GI imaging and required continuous enteral feeds and total parenteral nutrition.

Genitourinary examination revealed an underdeveloped scrotum with bilateral undescended testes, incomplete foreskin, and distal penile shaft enlargement. A pinpoint coronal hypospadic meatus could not be catheterized despite multiple attempts, and manual expression of the distal penis was required for voiding. Voiding cystourethrogram showed pooling of contrast in a urethral diverticulum. The initial differential diagnosis for the genitourinary abnormality included anterior urethral valves, megalourethra, or a urethral diverticulum secondary to distal urethral atresia; the working diagnosis was a coronal hypospadias with anterior urethral valves leading to a urethral diverticulum.
title: Road to a rare diagnosis: Description of novel unbalanced translocation causing partial trisomy 17p

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old man presented for evaluation of left anterior knee discomfort. He reported a small bump over the inferior pole of the patella that had recently increased in size, with extreme sensitivity to touch and pain when kneeling directly on it. He denied systemic symptoms, and there was no history of trauma.

On examination, a 1 cm × 1 cm subcutaneous, fluid-filled mass was palpated over the anterior aspect of the left knee. There were no signs of infection or warmth. The arc of motion was painless, weight bearing was tolerated without pain, and there was no mechanical instability. 

Plain radiographs of the left knee (AP, lateral, and sunrise views) showed preserved joint spaces, no fractures or loose bodies, and a subtle anterior subcutaneous soft-tissue mass without calcification. No further imaging was obtained.

Given the size, location, and sensitivity of the lesion, the patient elected to undergo surgical excision. An open excision under local anesthesia was performed, and the specimen was sent for histopathologic evaluation.
title: Rare Occurrence of Extradigital Glomangioma in the Prepatellar Bursa of a 40-Year-Old: A Case Study

case_prompt: A 24-year-old man with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with 17 hours of abdominal pain localized to the right iliac fossa and right flank. The pain was sharp, non-radiating, and worsened with movement; there were no associated gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms. On examination, bowel sounds were decreased, percussion was tympanic, and there were positive McBurney, Blumberg, psoas, obturator, and talopercussion signs in the right lower quadrant; bilateral Giordano signs were negative. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 15.3 g/dL, hematocrit 46.7%, platelets 385 × 10^3/µL, white-cell count 11.08 × 10^3/µL with 66% neutrophils, normal coagulation studies, and a normal urinalysis. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an aperistaltic, noncompressible appendix measuring 6 mm in outer diameter with a small periappendiceal fluid collection and no other abnormalities. With a working diagnosis of acute appendicitis and 20 hours of symptoms, the decision was made to proceed with laparoscopic exploration.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Omental torsion; an unusual case of acute abdomen. Case report

case_prompt: A 47-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of epigastric pain, melena, and a sensation of epigastric fullness. Two prior upper and lower endoscopies had been reported as normal. He had no notable medication, family, or psychosocial history. On examination, he appeared pale; conjunctivae, palms, and oral mucosa were pale without jaundice or cyanosis. Blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 95 beats/min, temperature normal, and BMI 38. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, without organomegaly or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin level of 8 g/dL with normal electrolytes, liver, and renal function tests. He received two units of packed red blood cells. Repeat upper endoscopy demonstrated a large pedunculated polyp with ulceration arising from the second part of the duodenum just distal to the ampulla of Vater. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed no additional lesions or abnormalities.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Duodenal gangliocytic paraganglioma: A very rare cause for upper gastrointestinal bleeding: Case report with review of literature

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of gradual-onset periumbilical abdominal pain, nausea, and nonbloody vomiting. Her medical and surgical history was unremarkable, and she took no medications. She denied tobacco, alcohol, and illicit drug use. On examination, she was mildly tachycardic; abdominal examination revealed periumbilical tenderness without guarding or rigidity. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10.8×10^3/μL and a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL; serum lipase was normal, and a pregnancy test was negative. Contrasted CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed small-bowel wall thickening with minimal ground-glass changes in the mesentery, suggestive of enteritis. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance enterography demonstrated persistent small-bowel wall thickening with jejunal distention up to 4 cm. The patient was treated with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole and was discharged home after partial improvement.

She returned several days later with worsening abdominal pain and recurrent nausea and vomiting. Vital signs and laboratory values were unchanged. Push enteroscopy revealed a jejunal bezoar causing an almost complete small-bowel obstruction. Two months after her initial presentation, she was transferred to our facility for repeat enteroscopy and bezoar removal. On push enteroscopy at our center, multiple clean-based jejunal ulcers were seen, along with a foreign body that could not be dislodged despite multiple attempts. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 29.8 mg/dL. Based on these findings, Crohn’s disease was suspected, and methylprednisolone (30 mg intravenously twice daily) was initiated. The patient initially noted improvement in pain, tolerated a full liquid diet, and had loose bowel movements.
title: Mesenteric Venous Thrombosis Masquerading as Small Bowel Obstruction

case_prompt:
An 18-month-old Saudi girl was referred for evaluation of recurrent hypoglycemic episodes. She was born at term via cesarean section with a birth weight of 1.0 kg after a pregnancy complicated by maternal gestational diabetes and required 2 months of NICU care for respiratory distress. She met developmental milestones appropriately until age 9 months, when she developed generalized tonic–clonic seizures without fever, lasting 2–3 minutes. A 6-year-old brother has epilepsy.

At 13 months, she became lethargic, drowsy, and irritable; blood glucose measurement revealed hypoglycemia, and she was discharged on dietary recommendations. She then had another seizure and decreased consciousness; a local hospital PICU admission showed a blood glucose level of 30 mg/dL treated with intravenous fluids. On referral, she required high concentrations of dextrose (up to 25%), frequent high-dose octreotide, and glucagon.

Multiple samples during hypoglycemia demonstrated serum glucose 4.0 mmol/L, insulin 3744 pmol/L, and C-peptide 0.02 ng/mL. Physical examination revealed a swelling with needle-insertion marks on the upper lateral right thigh and bilateral deltoid needle marks; the child remained calm during needle pricks. The mother insisted on pancreatectomy. All other investigations—including genetic testing, PET imaging of the pancreas, brain MRI, and EEG—were unremarkable. All hypoglycemic episodes occurred while the mother was present, raising suspicion of an exogenous cause of hypoglycemia.
title: Munchausen syndrome by proxy: a case report

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old man with a 2-year history of Crohn’s disease in clinical remission on mesalazine and azathioprine underwent routine imaging. He denied fever, cough, dyspnea, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Vital signs were normal, and the physical examination was unremarkable.

Chest CT revealed two nodules in the right lung: a 7-mm lesion in the upper lobe and a 20-mm irregular lesion in the lower lobe. PET-CT showed marked uptake in the lower nodule (elevated SUV) and physiologic uptake in the upper nodule. A CT scan 3 months earlier had shown only old inflammatory changes in the right upper lobe.

Bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial abnormalities. Transbronchial biopsy of the right lower lobe lesion demonstrated granulomas with chronic inflammatory cells around the bronchus and non-obsolete fibrosis; no malignant cells were seen. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and lung tissue cultures were negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi.
title: Pulmonary manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease: Two case reports

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old woman was referred from dermatology for a chronic, discharging submental lesion. She reported recurrent submental swelling that had been treated as a sebaceous cyst with incision and drainage followed by antibiotics, without improvement. She was otherwise healthy. Dental history was notable for trauma 12 years earlier and two previous root canal treatments on mandibular incisors about 2 years ago. On examination there was a 40 mm nonfluctuant, nontender submental swelling with an overlying sinus tract and purulent discharge on palpation. A gutta-percha point was inserted into the sinus and a periapical radiograph was obtained.  
The intraoral periapical radiograph revealed that the gutta-percha traced to the apical regions of teeth 31 and 41 and there was a diffuse periapical radiolucency around the roots of these previously treated teeth.
title: Nonsurgical management of cutaneous sinus tract of odontogenic origin: A report of two cases

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man was referred for severe swelling of the maxilla. He had no systemic symptoms and denied any jaw pain. On examination, there was bony expansion in both the maxilla and mandible, with partially edentulous areas, several decayed roots, and malposed erupted teeth. The overlying gingiva and mucosa appeared normal. A family history revealed no similar jaw conditions.

Panoramic radiographs showed multiple, diffuse, lobular radiopaque masses throughout the edentulous regions of both jaws, along with multiple impacted teeth displaced toward the periphery of the jaws by expansile lesions. Laboratory studies revealed a normal serum alkaline phosphatase level. A scintigraphic bone scan demonstrated no increased osteoblastic activity in other skeletal sites.
title: Florid Cementoosseous Dysplasia: A Rare Case Report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old girl presented with a 3-year history of a progressively enlarging, painless swelling in the left posterior cheek overlying the masseter region, causing facial asymmetry that was more pronounced when she clenched her teeth. She denied bruxism, gum chewing, facial trauma, dental problems, or psychiatric illness. On examination, the swelling was homogeneous, soft to firm, non-tender, and there were no signs of local inflammation or occlusal abnormalities. 

The initial differential diagnosis included salivary gland pathology, lymphatic or arteriovenous malformation, muscle tumor, and lipoma. Multidisciplinary consultations (psychological, neurosurgical, dentoalveolar and maxillofacial surgery, ophthalmologic) and laboratory tests were all within normal limits.

Ultrasound of the left masseter region showed uniformly enlarged muscle fibers measuring 13 × 48 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed that the left masseter muscle was approximately twice the size of the right, with normal morphology and signal characteristics and no abnormal contrast enhancement. No intracranial abnormalities or mandibular bone changes were identified.
title: Unusual Case of Masseter Muscle Hypertrophy in Adolescence—Case Report and Literature Overview

case_prompt: A 34-year-old woman with a history of vitiligo presented with six months of episodic speech and language impairment. Her family history was notable for a sister with Sydenham chorea. Neurologic examination revealed brisk reflexes on the left side only. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral frontal subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions with a micronodular, curvilinear perivascular pattern of gadolinium enhancement. CSF analysis showed a lymphocytic pleocytosis (9 cells/mm3), normal protein and glucose levels, increased CSF IgG, and absent oligoclonal bands. Chest and abdominal CT scans were unremarkable. Serum testing, including ANA, rheumatoid factor, anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-RNP, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, ANCA, ASCA, complement levels (C3, C4), ACE, viral serologies (HBsAg, HCV, HIV, HTLV), and syphilis testing, was within normal limits. The patient received methylprednisolone, 1 g/day for 5 days, with complete clinical and radiological resolution at three months. She had no relapses during a six-month follow-up and underwent an uncomplicated pregnancy two years after onset. Six years after initial presentation, she developed new cognitive impairment and headaches. Repeat MRI revealed new nodular and linear perivascular T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the frontal subcortical and deep white matter with corresponding contrast enhancement. Considering a disease relapse, a brain biopsy was performed.
title: Supratentorial Lymphocytic Inflammation with Parenchymal Perivascular Enhancement Responsive to Steroids (SLIPPERS)—Does it Really Exist?

case_prompt:
An 81-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, prior cerebrovascular accident, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a 60 pack-year smoking history presented after a witnessed non-mechanical fall “several hours” earlier. She had new left facial droop and slurred speech without head trauma. Home medications included atorvastatin, ticagrelor, and metformin. 

On arrival, she was asymptomatic but hypotensive and tachycardic: temperature 98.5°F, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, heart rate 110/min, oxygen saturation 93% on room air. She was confused (GCS 14, best verbal response). Initial laboratory tests showed troponin 2.60 ng/ml (≤0.05) and creatinine 2.19 mg/dl (0.60–1.20). Other admission labs included mild leukocytosis and elevated BUN. 

ECG showed minimal ST-segment elevation and T-wave inversion in leads V2–V3. Non-contrast head CT revealed only chronic microvascular changes without acute pathology. She received aspirin and heparin. Repeat troponin fell to 1.98 ng/ml after 1 hour. Serial ECGs showed transient resolution of ST elevation with subsequent biphasic T-wave inversions in leads V1–V6. Brain MRI and MR angiography of head and neck were unremarkable.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mid-anteroseptal and apical akinesis with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40–45%.
title: An unusual presentation of takotsubo syndrome in an elderly patient

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old girl with no prior medical history presented with right axillary swelling. She had high fevers and evening low back pain for 4 days and axillary pain and swelling for 1 week. On examination, she had a 20×10 mm right axillary lymph node; otherwise the physical exam was normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 8800/mm3, platelet count 188 000/mm3, C-reactive protein 88.5 mg/L (normal < 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 64 mm/h (normal 0–20), procalcitonin 0.21 ng/mL (normal < 0.05), aspartate aminotransferase 65 U/L, and creatine kinase 1299 U/L. Tests for Brucella (Rose Bengal and tube agglutination), Widal, CMV IgM, Brucella abortus IgM, and Quantiferon were negative; peripheral smear showed no blasts or atypical cells; other biochemical and electrolyte analyses were unremarkable.

She reported a recent cat scratch and was started on oral azithromycin. Two days later she was readmitted with severe back pain. She had painful lumbar flexion, limited range of motion, and left-sided paravertebral muscle spasm; straight-leg raising was 50° bilaterally with no neurologic deficits. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted sagittal MRI of the lumbar spine revealed increased signal at the inferior endplate of T10 and the posterior region of L2, consistent with osteomyelitis. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Teicoplanin and cefotaxime were added.

Axillary ultrasound showed five pathologic lymph nodes. PET/CT demonstrated hypermetabolic lesions in T10, L2, the right scapular neck; conglomerated hypermetabolic lymphadenopathies in the right axilla; hypodense hypermetabolic areas in liver segments 5–6; increased focal activity in the splenic hilus; and multiple peripancreatic and gastric cardia lymphadenopathies.
title: Multifocal Osteomyelitis in an Adolescent Patient With Cat Scratch Disease

case_prompt:
An 80-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension was brought to the emergency department by ambulance for altered mental status. Her family reported a rapid onset of worsening lethargy that began shortly after she awoke. En route, emergency medical services noted tachycardia and hypotension. On arrival, she was somnolent but arousable to voice and unable to provide a history.

Vital signs: temperature 38.4 °C; heart rate 128 beats/min; blood pressure 100/64 mm Hg; respiratory rate 32 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Physical examination of the left lower extremity revealed mottled skin with intact dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses; no crepitus or bullae; the entire extremity was tender to palpation, especially in the groin and proximal calf.

Laboratory studies: white cell count 12.2×10^9/L; venous lactate 9.8 mmol/L; serum creatinine 3.05 mg/dL (baseline 1.00); sodium 140 mmol/L; glucose 167 mg/dL; venous blood gas pH 7.21, pCO2 32 mm Hg, HCO3– 13 mmol/L. Blood cultures were obtained.

Plain radiographs of the left lower leg showed mild soft-tissue edema without gas in the tissue planes.

Point-of-care ultrasonography of the left calf demonstrated thickened subcutaneous tissue with a fluid collection >4 mm superficial to the deep fascial layer in the superficial posterior compartment. Distal to the popliteal fossa, deep to the fascial layer, there was an anechoic fluid pocket with swirling on compression. The gastrocnemius muscle exhibited abnormal sonographic architecture.

Noncontrast CT of the left lower extremity revealed soft-tissue swelling, subcutaneous fatty stranding, and mildly enlarged inguinal lymph nodes with a possible small hematoma.
title: Sonographic exploration for fascial exploration (SEFE) in necrotizing fasciitis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man suddenly collapsed at mile 17 of a marathon. Bystanders initiated CPR for approximately 10 minutes until emergency medical services arrived; he regained spontaneous circulation and was intubated due to a Glasgow Coma Scale of 4. On admission, he had generalized tonic–clonic seizures that resolved with benzodiazepine.  

He had a history of anxiety-related palpitations since childhood and recurrent left shoulder dislocations but no prior chest pain, cardiac disease, or family history of sudden death. He trained 5 days per week, up to 19 miles, and had one episode of dizziness without syncope at 12 miles a month earlier. He denied smoking or drug use.  

Initial investigations included:  
- Cranial and cervical CT scans, CT angiography of cerebral arteries, spine radiographs, and brain MRI: no acute structural lesions.  
- Toxicology: negative.  
- ECG: sinus rhythm at 69 bpm, no ST–T changes.  
- Cardiac biomarkers: high-sensitivity troponin T 0.115 ng/mL (normal <0.014), CK 328 U/L (24–204), myoglobin 212 μg/L (28–72).  
- Electrolytes and metabolic panel: normal.  
- Transthoracic echocardiogram: normal systolic and diastolic function, normal chambers, no valvular or pericardial abnormalities.  

He was extubated on day 2. Continuous telemetry showed no arrhythmias. An EEG demonstrated normal baseline activity without epileptic discharges. A repeat head CT on day 10 remained normal.
journal: Journal of Cardiovascular Development and Disease
title: Myocardial Bridging Leading to Cardiac Collapse in a Marathon Runner

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with acute lower chest pain and a 3-month history of skin nodules. He reported a 5-kg weight loss over the past month. On examination, there was a 2 × 1 cm dome-shaped, indurated, erythematous-purplish nodule on the nose surrounded by atrophic, telangiectatic skin. Similar firm, homogeneously erythematous nodules were present on the forehead and left forearm. All lesions were asymptomatic. The remainder of the skin, oral cavity, and lymph nodes were unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed:  
- Leukocyte count 17,700/mm3 (3,600 lymphocytes without blasts; 12,900 neutrophils)  
- Hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL  
- Platelets 35,000/mm3  
- Lactate dehydrogenase 1,569 IU/L  

The initial diagnostic impression was cutaneous lymphoma, and a skin biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathologic examination.
title: Leukemia cutis in a patient with pre–B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia

case_prompt: A 19-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging papule on the right infraorbital region. He denied trauma, insect bites, or systemic symptoms, and had been treated with topical steroids, oral antibiotics, and attempted drainage without improvement. On examination, there was a 1.5 cm violet, dome-shaped nodule with defined edges and peripheral telangiectasias, soft to semi-solid, and painless to palpation. The frontal region showed multiple papules, pustules, and comedones; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. An incisional biopsy revealed a nonspecific chronic inflammatory process. Complete surgical excision was performed; histopathology suggested a small-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoproliferative process, prompting immunohistochemical studies.
title: Differential diagnoses of pseudolymphomatous folliculitis: considerations as regards one case

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man initially presented 15 days before current admission with epigastric pain, fever, chills, and oral intolerance; his symptoms transiently improved and he was discharged. Five days later, he developed right flank pain radiating to the testis, hypogastric discomfort, dysuria, scrotal swelling, and discolored urine, prompting referral to urology and readmission to the emergency department. 

On evaluation, he reported fever, chills, dyspnea, chest pain, and myalgia. He had no significant past medical history, drug use, allergies, smoking, or addiction. Vital signs were: temperature 37.5°C, pulse 135 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and blood pressure 70/50 mmHg. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed erythema of the right flank that was soft to palpation, tenderness in the hypogastric and right lower quadrant regions, and ecchymosis of the left scrotum without crepitus. An anaerobic odor was noted.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 20,000/mm3, hemoglobin 14 g/dL, platelets 70,000/mm3, C-reactive protein 42 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 32 mm/h, creatine phosphokinase 525 U/L, and a venous blood gas with pH 7.489, PCO2 22.1 mmHg, HCO3− 16.7 mEq/L, and O2 saturation 93.4%.

CT angiography of the chest excluded pulmonary embolism. Echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 25–30% consistent with myocarditis, and he was managed with hemodynamic support. Urology consultation raised concern for Fournier’s gangrene based on scrotal ecchymosis, anaerobic odor, and swelling.

Scrotal and abdominal ultrasound revealed inflammation of the right flank but no evidence of appendicitis. A noncontrast abdominal CT scan showed myositis and fasciitis of the soft tissues in the right flank and inguinal region, collections in the lower right abdominal area, air bubbles adjacent to the psoas muscle, and necrosis and inflammation of the right inguinal and abdominal wall.
title: Fournier's gangrene after missed acute perforated appendicitis: A case report

case_prompt: A 67-year-old Syrian woman with a history of iodine-deficiency hypothyroidism and remote angioedema presented with one month of malaise, fatigue, arthralgia, fever, night sweats, anorexia, and weight loss. On examination she was febrile (38 °C) and had mild hepatomegaly; no other abnormalities were noted. Initial laboratory results showed a white-cell count of 14.1 K/μL with 80% neutrophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 100 mm/h, and C-reactive protein of 35 mg/dL. Tests for ANA, ANCA (c and p), rheumatoid factor, interferon-gamma release assay, Widal, Wright, and malaria were negative; CMV IgG and EBV IgG were positive. She received paracetamol and NSAIDs without improvement. She then developed vague chest pain, and echocardiography revealed mild reactive pericardial effusion and pericardial thickening. Fifteen days later, she noted painful cervical lymph nodes. Physical examination showed tender, mobile, bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Cervical ultrasound demonstrated enlarged hypodense lymph nodes. CT of the neck, chest, and abdomen showed massive bilateral axillary and mild (<10 mm) retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. She underwent an excisional cervical lymph-node biopsy.
title: Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease: a case report of a multi-drug resistant, grueling disease

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old primiparous woman at 15 weeks and 5 days of gestation presented with a 1-day history of acute-onset bilateral frontotemporal headache associated with dizziness, blurred vision, and two episodes of non-projectile vomiting without blood. She then developed reduced responsiveness, impaired vocalization with incomprehensible speech, and sudden weakness in her left upper limb that progressed to her left lower limb. There was no history of head trauma, urinary incontinence, respiratory or cardiac symptoms, or vaginal bleeding. Her past medical history was unremarkable; she had one prior cesarean delivery. 

On examination, temperature was 97.2°F, pulse 102/min, blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO₂ 96% on room air, and body-mass index 18.2 kg/m². Glasgow Coma Scale was 10 (E3 V2 M5); she was disoriented with sluggish left pupil reaction and impaired speech but no facial palsy. Motor testing revealed increased tone, hyperreflexia, and bilateral upgoing plantar responses on the left, with decreased strength in the left upper and lower extremities.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (13 500/mm³; normal 4 000–11 000) with neutrophilia (81%; normal 45–75), hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL (normal 12–18), hyponatremia (128 mEq/L; normal 134–146), hypokalemia (3.5 mEq/L; normal 3.6–5.0), and elevated fibrinogen (533 mg/dL; normal 200–400). Dengue serologies and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative or within normal limits. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed acute hyperintense lesions on T2/FLAIR in the right pons and right cerebellar peduncle. Magnetic resonance angiography demonstrated occlusion of the basilar artery and obstruction of the V3 segment of the right vertebral artery. A noncontrast head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality.
title: Beyond the womb: pontine hemorrhage’s impact on maternal and fetal outcomes: a case report from Nepal

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old man with hypertension, alcohol abuse, and a history of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) treated with ABVD 4 years earlier presented with one week of worsening shortness of breath, cough, and exertional chest pain without diaphoresis or palpitations. He was afebrile, blood pressure 131/73 mm Hg, heart rate 109 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination revealed jaundice, scleral icterus, and decreased breath sounds at the left lower lung field.

Two months prior, he had two admissions for suspected HL recurrence. A mediastinoscopy with lymph node biopsy was negative for disease; flow cytometry was inconclusive. He developed transaminitis and a marked alkaline phosphatase elevation. MRCP showed no biliary obstruction, and a liver biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. He was lost to follow-up before ERCP.

On this presentation, CT of the abdomen showed a normal liver without biliary dilation but new peri-aortic and para-diaphragmatic lymphadenopathy. Complete blood count showed WBC 47,000/µL (86% neutrophils), Hb 8.8 g/dL, platelets 425,000/µL. Metabolic panel showed Na 127 mmol/L, Cl 97 mmol/L, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L. ALP was 1,876 U/L (up from 1,045 U/L), ALT and AST remained near prior levels. Total bilirubin was 28.2 mg/dL with a direct bilirubin of 23.3 mg/dL. CTA of the chest revealed bulky mediastinal and axillary lymphadenopathy, bilateral pleural effusions, and a pericardial effusion. Thoracentesis yielded exudative fluid without malignant cells.

A biopsy of a left axillary node showed CD15+, CD30+, PAX5+, consistent with recurrent classical HL. Renal function worsened (creatinine 2.7 mg/dL), attributed to bile acid nephropathy. To investigate his cholestasis, ERCP was performed, demonstrating sclerosing cholangitis and atrophy of the intrahepatic bile ducts.
title: Vanishing Bile Duct Syndrome in a Patient With Recurrent Hodgkin Lymphoma

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old Asian man presented with primary hyperparathyroidism. His parathyroid hormone level was 335.4 pmol/L (normal, 2.3–9.3), and his serum calcium was 4.11 mmol/L (normal, 2.10–2.57), despite treatment with bisphosphonates, aggressive hydration, and calcitonin. Neck ultrasound revealed a large heterogeneous hypoechoic nodule in the expected location of the right parathyroid gland. Tc-99m sestamibi scintigraphy showed intense uptake with differential washout in the right thyroid bed, and SPECT/CT localized a hypodense nodular mass posterior to the right thyroid lobe without other foci of uptake. The patient underwent parathyroidectomy, and a 3.5-cm mass weighing 10.27 g was removed; histology confirmed a giant parathyroid adenoma.

Two weeks later, he reported bone pain in the right arm and both thighs. A skeletal survey including X-ray, CT, and MRI showed multiple lytic bone lesions, a right humeral fracture, and bilateral femoral fractures. Laboratory studies revealed a serum calcium of 2.01 mmol/L (normal, 2.10–2.57), phosphate of 0.4 mmol/L (normal, 0.8–1.6), magnesium of 0.59 mmol/L (normal, 0.70–0.91), an alkaline phosphatase level of 1784 IU/L (normal, 52–171), and a 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level of 12 nmol/L (normal, 50–220).
title: Giant parathyroid adenoma and hungry bone syndrome in MEN1 syndrome: A case report

case_prompt:
An 81-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 2-week history of abdominal distension. Her medical history was notable only for a cesarean section; there was no prior malignancy. Laboratory studies, including carcinoembryonic antigen, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, and cytokeratin-19 fragment levels, were within normal limits.

Upper endoscopy revealed:  
• A mildly granular elevated lesion with slightly depressed, irregular mucosa extending along the distal esophagus.  
• A separate 10-mm superficial elevated tumor in the lower body of the stomach.

Biopsy results:  
• Gastric lesion: well-differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma.  
• Esophageal lesion: intraepithelial clusters of large clear cells with atypical nuclei and prominent nucleoli; no glandular structures or intracellular mucin. Differential diagnoses included malignant melanoma, pagetoid spread of adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma, and Paget’s disease.

Immunohistochemistry of the esophageal cells showed:  
• Diffuse positivity for CK7 and partial positivity for CK20.  
• Negative staining for S100 protein and HMB-47 (excluding melanoma).  
• Negative for mucin core proteins MUC2, MUC5AC, and HIK1083.  
• Overexpression of p53 in tumor cells.

Staging imaging with enhanced CT and ^18F-FDG PET/CT revealed no lymph node or distant metastases; FDG uptake was noted only in the gastric region correlating with prior endoscopic submucosal dissection.

How do you integrate these findings into a unifying diagnosis?
title: Paget’s disease derived in situ from reserve cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia, and squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagogastric junction: a case report

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man was referred for evaluation of progressive intermittent fevers, night sweats, and new exertional dyspnea. He had a 5-month history of fluctuating upper airway symptoms consistent with rhinosinusitis and had received multiple courses of oral antibiotics with minimal relief. Two weeks before admission, he noted increasing shortness of breath on exertion.

On examination he was afebrile. Cardiovascular exam revealed a soft pansystolic murmur at the mitral area; a cardiac resynchronization therapy-defibrillator (CRT-D) pocket was clean and non-tender. There were no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. Lung, abdominal, and skin examinations were unremarkable.

His history included dilated cardiomyopathy diagnosed 2 years earlier after cardiac arrest, for which a CRT-D was placed; he also had mitral regurgitation, hypertension, congestive heart failure, and gout. He lived at home with his wife and had no history of alcohol excess, smoking, ischemic heart disease, or familial cardiac disease.

Three sets of blood cultures drawn on admission grew Staphylococcus aureus (two of the three sets were positive). No antibiotics had been started at that time. A CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated segmental pulmonary emboli with a small pulmonary infarction. Transthoracic echocardiography did not identify any new pathology. On day 2, a working diagnosis of sub-acute bacterial endocarditis was made, and transesophageal echocardiography was planned.
title: Cardiac device-associated lead infection: a diagnosis not to be missed

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man was admitted for elective cystoscopy and perineal urethrostomy because of a 2-year history of dysuria, haematuria, and the passage of blood clots per urethra, unrelieved by multiple courses of antibiotics and anti-inflammatory agents. Initial urologic investigations included rigid cystoscopy with meatal dilatation and a CT urethrogram, followed by a urethral biopsy; these revealed a stricture of the penile urethra. He was deemed unsuitable for urethroplasty and subsequently required a long-term urinary catheter owing to intermittent urinary retention. The plan was to defunction his urethra via perineal urethrostomy to improve symptoms. 

On the current admission, cystoscopy under anaesthesia showed a rigid anterior urethra with a tight, circumferential fibrotic stricture of the penile urethra; a small piece of plastic was removed as a foreign body, and necrotic debris consistent with self-instrumentation was noted. The patient told the urology team that he believed “ticks [were] coming out from his penis” and that they had “clogged up” his urethra, causing pain and retention. The urology team requested a psychiatric evaluation to assess his mental state and capacity to consent for surgery.
title: Urethral stricture secondary to self-instrumentation due to delusional parasitosis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old African American woman with morbid obesity was referred for evaluation of a slowly enlarging left buttock mass. She noted minor discomfort and was unable to tolerate prolonged sitting. The mass had been growing over six months. She denied urinary, rectal, or gynecological symptoms and had no prior surgeries. 

On examination, there was a 25 × 14 cm soft mass in the left perineal area. Pelvic examination revealed a bulging mass on the left lateral vaginal wall without invasion; the rectal tone was normal but the left lateral rectal wall was displaced toward midline. 

Endoscopic ultrasound showed a demarcated fat plane between the rectum and the mass; in contrast, CT imaging showed no clear fat plane. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a subcutaneous mass in the left perirectal region displacing the anal canal to the right and elevating the levator ani muscle. Uterine leiomyomas and colonic diverticulosis were noted incidentally. 

MRI measured the lesion at 23 × 8 × 11 cm, with well-defined walls, no muscular or osseous invasion, and marked enhancement. The radiologist’s preliminary impression was a pedunculated leiomyoma, although a soft-tissue sarcoma could not be excluded. On the basis of imaging, a large leiomyoma was suspected, but a low-grade soft-tissue sarcoma remained in the differential.
title: Giant Perineal Leiomyoma: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman with a history of FIGO stage Ib nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the uterine cervix underwent radical hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, pelvic lymphadenectomy, and adjuvant radiotherapy in 1996. She remained disease-free on annual follow-up for 16 years until 2012, when L2–L3 vertebral metastases were treated with conformal radiotherapy and stereotactic body radiotherapy. In October 2013 and January 2014, successive spinal metastases at Th12 and L1 were similarly irradiated. 

In January 2014, she noted acute onset of right upper leg weakness accompanied by new-onset left eyelid drooping, nausea, and vomiting. On examination, strength in the right upper leg was Grade 2. Cranial nerve examination demonstrated left mydriasis, a decreased left pupillary light reflex, and impaired adduction, supraduction, and infraduction of the left eye, consistent with left oculomotor nerve palsy. Physical examination and laboratory tests revealed no evidence of infection or diabetes. Noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable. Brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrated abnormal enhancement and swelling of the left oculomotor nerve without midbrain abnormalities or diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement. MR angiography showed no intracranial aneurysm.
title: Leptomeningeal metastasis of uterine cervical cancer 17 years after primary tumor treatment

case_prompt: A 16-month-old girl was evaluated for a right posterior shoulder/low posterior neck mass that had been present since birth and was progressively enlarging. The lesion occasionally decreased or increased in size without associated erythema or tenderness. There was no significant medical or surgical history. On examination, the mass measured approximately 4–5 cm, was well circumscribed, mobile, and had a slight telangiectatic appearance of the overlying skin. An ultrasound showed a lobular cystic lesion confined to the subcutaneous tissues with internal layering and no internal vascularity. The history, physical examination, and imaging results all favored the diagnosis of a macrocystic lymphatic malformation, and the parents elected to proceed with excisional biopsy.
title: Bronchogenic cyst of the posterior neck mimicking lymphatic malformation

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of itching and redness of the vulva and a 6-month history of diffuse vulvar swelling. Examination revealed an asymmetrical, well-defined, indurated erythematous plaque (5×4 cm) over the right labia majora extending onto the mons pubis. Within this plaque were multiple papules and nodules and a central superficial ulcer (1.5×1 cm), and there was diffuse pitting edema of the entire vulvar region with bilateral firm, non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Per speculum examination could not be performed due to pain and induration. Initial clinical considerations included cutaneous tuberculosis, cutaneous Crohn’s disease, invasive squamous cell carcinoma, and amelanotic melanoma. 

Biopsy specimens were obtained from both the plaque and one of the nodules. CT of the chest demonstrated multiple metastatic nodules in the liver but showed no evidence of breast, lung, bladder, or gastrointestinal neoplasm. PET–CT revealed tracer uptake in the liver, bilateral inguinal lymph nodes, and maximal uptake in the vagina. 

Histologic examination of the plaque biopsy showed singly scattered and nested tumor cells within the epidermis; these cells had moderate to abundant clear cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei, and conspicuous nucleoli. The nodule biopsy revealed dermal nests and islands of tumor with foci of signet-ring cell differentiation without glandular or cribriform architecture. 

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated tumor-cell positivity for cytokeratin 7, carcinoembryonic antigen, HER2/neu, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, and androgen receptor; and negativity for cytokeratin 20, p40, CDX2, and estrogen receptor. Periodic acid–Schiff with Alcian blue staining highlighted intracytoplasmic mucin vacuoles in the signet-ring cells. 

Colonoscopy revealed no mass lesions; a solitary polyp was removed and found to be a hyperplastic polyp on microscopy.
title: Primary Extra Mammary Paget’s Disease of Vulva, With Apocrine Adenocarcinoma, Signet Ring Cell Differentiation and Distant Metastasis

case_prompt: A 47-year-old man presented with a one-year history of parietal and occipital headaches, retro-orbital pain, transient blurry vision, fatigue, and difficulty completing routine tasks. He denied symptoms of hyperprolactinemia. His family, medical, surgical, and medication histories were unremarkable. On examination, findings were noncontributory. Laboratory studies showed a serum prolactin level of 269 ng/mL; all other laboratory results were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the sphenoid sinus and pituitary region revealed a 2 cm mass within the clivus extending into the sphenoid sinus, with moderate enhancement and peripheral calcifications; the intrasellar pituitary gland and stalk appeared normal.
title: Clival ectopic pituitary prolactinoma was successfully managed by transsphenoidal surgery: A rare case report

case_prompt: A 42-year-old man presented with a 1½-year history of progressive abdominal discomfort and distension. He had quit smoking 4 years prior. On examination, there was a large, non-tender mass in the right hypochondrium. Testes were descended and normal. Routine blood tests and serum CA 19-9 were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated what appeared to be a unilocular cystic lesion in the right lobe of the liver, thought to represent a hydatid cyst. At an initial laparotomy, the liver was normal; instead, five cystic, multilocular masses were found in the median retroperitoneum between the inferior vena cava and aortic bifurcation. The pancreas, spleen, and kidneys were unremarkable. Three masses were excised; two were left in situ due to dense vascular adhesions. Contrast-enhanced CT showed residual hyperdense retroperitoneal masses with both cystic and solid components and no enhancement. MRI revealed multiple retroperitoneal processes from behind the pancreas to the aortic bifurcation, adherent to vessels; they were hyperintense on T1 and T2 with fat suppression (consistent with mucinous content) and exhibited slight enhancement of some solid areas after gadolinium. The pancreas was homogeneous without focal lesions. At re-exploration, four additional encapsulated, multicystic masses filled with mucinous material were removed; none was attached to any intra-abdominal organ.
title: Primary retroperitoneal mucinous cystadenocarcinoma in a male patient: a case report

case_prompt: A 60-year-old woman reported a 3-month history of discomfort in her right lower abdomen. In late November she developed nausea and anorexia. On examination, there was a mildly tender, firm, 10-cm mass in the right lower quadrant without guarding or rebound. Laboratory tests showed WBC 8040/µl, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dl, CRP 1.75 mg/dl, and normal tumor markers. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated extensive edematous wall thickening of the ileocecal region. Pelvic MRI revealed a 9.6-cm mass extending from the ileocecal area to the posterior aspect of the uterus, with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, inhomogeneous T2 signal, and an unclear border with the uterus. Based on these findings, a uterine sarcoma or an ileocecal malignancy was suspected, and the patient was taken to surgery for a laparotomy.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Intraabdominal actinomycosis resulting in a difficult to diagnose intraperitoneal mass: A case report

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of pelvic floor weakness, during which an incidental liver mass was palpated. She denied gastrointestinal symptoms, changes in bowel habits, weight loss, fevers, or night sweats. She reported drinking one bottle of wine nightly for 10 years but had no stigmata of cirrhosis and no family history of liver disease or malignancy.

Laboratory studies showed:
• Normal complete blood count and platelet count of 224×10^9/L  
• International normalized ratio 0.9  
• Plasma ammonia 32 μmol/L  
• Normal liver function tests: albumin 50 g/L, bilirubin 17 μmol/L, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase 63 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 32 U/L  
• Tumor markers (CEA, CA15-3, CA125, CA19-9) all within normal limits  
• Negative hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibodies

Contrast-enhanced CT of the liver demonstrated a large exophytic mass in segment 5/6 with multiple central hypodense areas. On arterial phase, there was hypervascular curvilinear and nodular internal enhancement with hypoenhancing components. During the portal venous phase, the hypodense areas showed gradual enhancement, and on delayed imaging the solid component was hyperenhancing relative to liver parenchyma. The biliary ducts were not dilated, and hepatic vessels appeared patent. The initial imaging differential included atypical focal nodular hyperplasia and hemangioma.

Subsequent MRI of the liver with gadoxetic acid showed:
• A heterogeneous mass with intermediate T1 and low T2 signal septations, areas of diffusion restriction, and circumscribed T2 hyperintense foci  
• No definite fat or lipid content; mild signal increase on T1 opposed-phase consistent with possible haemosiderin  
• Dynamic sequences revealed moderate peripheral arterial enhancement, minimal centripetal filling in the portal venous phase, and no washout  
• On 20-minute hepatobiliary phase imaging, there was uptake of gadoxetic acid throughout both the low and high T2 signal regions of the mass
title: A rare case of MRI of myxoid hepatocellular adenoma with gadoxetic acid uptake

case_prompt: A 65-year-old man with a 20-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented with acute onset dyspnea without cough, fever, or chest pain. His dyspnea intensified with exertion beyond his usual level. He denied weight loss or night sweats. He has a history of smoking one to two cigarettes per day and gastroesophageal reflux disease. His medications included leflunomide, prednisolone, valsartan/amlodipine, atorvastatin, quetiapine, citalopram, omeprazole, and folic acid. On examination, temperature was 36.7°C, blood pressure 115/85 mmHg, heart rate 82/min, respiratory rate 16/min; he did not appear pale or cyanotic. Musculoskeletal exam revealed synovitis of the hand joints with ulnar deviation and interphalangeal joint tenderness. Laboratory studies showed rheumatoid factor 59 IU/mL (normal 0–20), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 62 mm/h (normal ≤20), C-reactive protein 39 mg/L (normal 0–6), and normal serum angiotensin converting enzyme level; tuberculin skin test and Interferon Gamma Release Assay were negative. Viral, bacterial, and parasitic serologies were normal. Chest CT showed no pulmonary embolism but multiple cavitary pulmonary nodules, predominantly in the left lower lobe.
title: Pulmonary Nodules After Leflunomide Therapy in Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 62-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of a right palatal swelling that had gradually increased in size over the past 2 years, associated with intermittent toothache and occasional facial swelling. Initial examination showed a firm, non-tender mass over the anterior palate without buccal or lingual expansion and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Dental panoramic tomogram revealed a radiolucent lesion with a well-defined sclerotic border of the right maxilla extending into the right maxillary sinus and significant root resorption of the upper right central and lateral incisors and first molar. An excisional biopsy of the anterior palate was performed intraorally; hematoxylin and eosin sections demonstrated small epithelial tumor cell cords in a densely collagenized stroma without obvious dysplastic features. Contrast-enhanced CT scan showed an expansile, enhancing osteolytic mass of the right maxilla with marked buccal and palatal bone perforation, extension into the right inferior turbinate, and breach of the nasal septum; there was no evidence of cervical lymphatic spread.
title: Sclerosing odontogenic carcinoma of maxilla: A case report

case_prompt: A 51-year-old woman presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting for a few days. She also noted intermittent dull generalized abdominal discomfort over the past six months. She denied any history of trauma or travel. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and hyperlipidemia; her body-mass index was 37.5. She had quit smoking two years earlier and denied alcohol or illicit drug use. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs and had mild tenderness in the left upper quadrant. Complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, liver-function tests, and urinalysis were all within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 7.7-cm complex mass in the medial aspect of the spleen. Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography revealed a 10.4 × 8.2 cm hypodense cystic mass in the medial spleen with attenuation of 15 Hounsfield units and multiple foci of fat attenuation (–102 Hounsfield units).
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Epidermoid cyst of the spleen, a case report

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old girl was referred for gradual decreased vision in the right eye. Her neonatal history was unremarkable, developmental milestones were normal, and there was no history of ocular surgery, trauma, or systemic illness. On initial examination, uncorrected visual acuity was no light perception in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed a retrolental floppy membrane, retinal detachment, and pre-retinal infiltration; the left eye was normal. A clinical diagnosis of endophthalmitis was made and a vitreous tap with intravitreal cefazolin and vancomycin was performed.

Two weeks later, there was no improvement. Intraocular pressure in the right eye was 18 mm Hg. Slit-lamp examination revealed a clear cornea, deep anterior chamber, ectropion uvea, neovascularization of the iris, a dilated fixed pupil, and a complicated cataract. One week later, she developed progressive leukocoria. At our hospital, vision was light perception in the right eye and normal in the left. Intraocular pressure measured 30 mm Hg in the right eye and 15 mm Hg in the left. Motility was full bilaterally, and external adnexa appeared normal. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed inferonasal conjunctival injection, a clear cornea, deep anterior chamber with 4+ cells, a dilated nonreactive pupil, ectropion uvea, and a retrolental whitish hemorrhagic membrane. There was no fundus view. The left eye examination, including the fundus, was normal.

Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the right eye revealed a posterior cavity mass, a ruptured lens, dense vitreous opacities with an area of calcification, an open funnel-shaped retinal detachment, a subretinal cyst nasally, and mild subretinal opacities. MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass in the posterior chamber of the right globe with multiple calcific flecks, a funnel-shaped total retinal detachment with low T2 signal, increased vitreous signal on FLAIR, heterogeneous contrast enhancement, vitreous seeding, and hemorrhage behind a thinned, deformed lens. There was no optic nerve or intracranial invasion.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A case of retinoblastoma masquerading as endophthalmitis: Unusual presentation and clinicopathological correlation

case_prompt: An 18-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a slowly enlarging, firm, nontender mass over her lower back. On examination, the lesion measured approximately 25 × 12 cm, was superficial to the lumbar spine, fixed to deeper tissues, and had no overlying skin changes or regional lymphadenopathy. MRI of the lumbar spine showed a large lesion in the superficial subcutaneous tissue abutting the deep fascia, with intermediate signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images. CT-guided core biopsy of the mass revealed spindled and histiocyte-like cells that were strongly S100+ and CD163+; these cells were negative for smooth muscle actin, nuclear β-catenin, CD34, and keratin AE1/3. Additional studies showed p16 negativity, a wild-type p53 pattern, focal weak cyclin D1 expression, absence of MDM2 amplification by FISH, and a low Ki-67 index (<1%). A chronic perivascular infiltrate of CD3+ T cells and CD20+ B cells was also noted. Given the benign cytologic features and immunoprofile, a benign process was favored, and the differential diagnosis included a regressing Rosai–Dorfman lesion versus localized massive lymphedema. The patient elected to undergo surgical excision of the mass.
title: Rare Presentation of Rosai-Dorfman Disease in Soft Tissue: Diagnostic Findings and Surgical Treatment

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of polydipsia, polyuria, headache, blurry vision, and an 11.3-kg weight loss over 6 months. Her medical history included generalized anxiety disorder, depression, and chronic interstitial cystitis; medications were cyclobenzaprine and lorazepam as needed. Initial laboratory evaluation showed a serum sodium of 145 mEq/L and a glycated hemoglobin A1c of 5.1%. A 24-hour urine collection revealed a volume of 8400 mL, urine sodium of 202 mEq/24 h, and urine osmolality of 88 mOsm/kg. A water deprivation test was recommended but not pursued.

Two months later, she returned with progressive, atraumatic thoracic back pain inadequately relieved by acetaminophen, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, and ice and heat. Lumbar spine radiography showed mild rightward curvature and spondylosis without acute findings. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated prominent stenosis from T2 to T4 with a low-signal–intensity mass anterior to the cord. While awaiting neurosurgical evaluation, she developed worsening lower extremity weakness and numbness and sustained a fall. CT of the thoracic spine confirmed an unchanged stenotic lesion. She underwent emergent surgical decompression.

During the 10 hours of preoperative fasting, her serum sodium rose from 143 to 160 mEq/L, and urine osmolality was 109 mOsm/kg. After administration of 5% dextrose in water and 0.01 μg IV desmopressin, her urine osmolality increased to 689 mOsm/kg. MRI of the pituitary gland revealed mild enlargement and loss of the normal posterior pituitary bright-spot signal.
title: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency Heralding Rosai-Dorfman Disease With Neurological Manifestations

case_prompt:
A 79-year-old Japanese woman with a history of hypertension and arrhythmia suddenly developed left-sided weakness and drowsiness and was admitted to the emergency department. On examination, she was mildly obtunded, had conjugate gaze deviation to the right, mild dysarthria, left unilateral spatial neglect, left facial weakness, left arm and leg weakness, and left sensory loss. 

Laboratory studies on admission showed hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, hematocrit 39.8%, serum sodium 142 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.69 mg/dL. Electrocardiography revealed atrial fibrillation. Brain MRI demonstrated a large diffusion-weighted hyperintense lesion in the right middle- and posterior-cerebral artery territories, and MRA showed occlusion of the right internal carotid artery. Noncontrast CT showed no hemorrhage, and she was started on anti-edema therapy and a continuous heparin infusion.

Her neurological status remained stable, and follow-up CT showed improving edema. On day 14, MRA revealed recanalization of the right internal carotid artery, but new hemorrhage appeared in the right middle-cerebral-artery infarct, prompting discontinuation of heparin. On day 15, CT showed expansion of hemorrhage and edema, and her level of consciousness worsened. Concurrently, she developed marked polyuria and hyponatremia, with clinical signs of dehydration, including reduced skin turgor, collapse of the inferior vena cava, and a 4.6% loss in body weight. Despite aggressive fluid replacement (input 3410 mL vs. urine output 3710 mL on day 20), she remained in negative fluid balance.

On day 28, a water-deprivation antidiuretic hormone stimulation test was performed by administering 10 µg of intranasal desmopressin, but her urine volume did not decrease.
title: Cerebral salt-wasting syndrome due to hemorrhagic brain infarction: a case report

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman (G10P3) of African origin at 31 weeks’ gestation was referred for fever (38.7 °C), tinnitus, and emesis. Her history included chronic hypertension treated with nicardipine and labetalol, morbid obesity (BMI 41.9 kg/m2), and prior appendectomy. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, leukocytes 12 ×10^9/L, platelets 83 ×10^9/L, CRP 243 mg/L, fibrinogen >7 g/L, haptoglobin <10 mg/dL, proteinuria 3.89 g/L (P/C ratio 1.16 g/g), AST 53 IU/L, ALT 25 IU/L, bilirubin 34 µmol/L, creatinine 40 µmol/L, Na 135 mmol/L, K 3 mmol/L. Exam showed lower‐limb edema without headache or visual changes.

Peripheral smear confirmed Plasmodium falciparum (20% parasitemia); artesunate was started. Because of intense proteinuria, superimposed preeclampsia was presumed; magnesium sulfate and one unit of platelets were administered. Neurological decline (GCS 13) led to emergency Caesarean section; a 1700 g male infant was delivered.

Postoperatively, fever peaked at 38.6 °C and the abdomen became distended and painful. CT of the abdomen was read as “postoperative ileus and uterine hyperemia,” and metronidazole with meropenem was started. Over the next hours, oliguria developed and serum creatinine rose to 210 µmol/L despite saline infusion, while abdominal distension and pain persisted.
title: Ogilvie Syndrome and Acute Kidney Injury: A Rare Complication of Cesarean Section and Preeclampsia

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old man with newly diagnosed acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) was started on all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and idarubicin along with supportive transfusions. He received ATRA 45 mg/m2 orally daily (in two doses) and idarubicin 12 mg/m2 on days 3, 5, 7, and 9. He was on levofloxacin and fluconazole prophylaxis. 

On day 9, he developed fever to 38.8 °C without hypotension, weight gain, edema, dyspnea, or rash. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated. Serial central and peripheral blood cultures, urine cultures, contrast-enhanced CT scans of the sinuses, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and galactomannan assays showed no evidence of bacterial or fungal infection. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no vegetations. C-reactive protein rose to 17.6 mg/dL (reference < 0.5 mg/dL). 

On day 14, he developed burning pain while eating and was found to have necrotic gingival ulcers; these improved with photobiomodulation and antibiotics, and CRP fell temporarily. However, fever persisted. On day 20, he reported severe right calf pain. Examination revealed redness, swelling, tenderness, and pitting edema of the right calf; the left leg was normal. A lower-limb Doppler ultrasound to evaluate for deep vein thrombosis was negative. Serum creatine phosphokinase was 178 U/L (reference 39–308 U/L), normal.
title: All-trans retinoic acid-induced myositis in a 36-year-old patient with acute promyelocytic leukaemia: Case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging nodule of the right shoulder and a new axillary lump. On examination, there was a 10-cm mass in the right deltoid region with overlying skin edema and involvement. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder showed a necrotic tumor in the lower posterior deltoid and triceps, extending into the axillary region with a suspicious lymph node. 

Microscopic examination of the deltoid lesion revealed normal epidermis overlying dense fibrocollagenous tissue with few perivascular inflammatory cells. The axillary specimen, initially presumed to be a lymph node, lacked lymphoid tissue and showed extensive necrosis; nests and cords of cells with small, round nuclei, dense chromatin, scant cytoplasm, and larger eosinophilic cells forming acinar and alveolar structures; occasional signet-ring–like and plasmacytoid cells; and areas of myxoid stroma containing stellate, myoepithelial-type cells. There was perineural and muscle infiltration, and scattered PAS-positive cells. In summary, the lesion was a biphasic tumor composed of epithelial and myoepithelial elements, raising the possibility of carcinoma or a malignant mixed tumor of the skin.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Malignant chondroid syringoma in a West African cancer institute: A case report

case_prompt: A 31-year-old Caucasian man with a 7-year history of well-controlled HIV infection (normal CD4+ count; undetectable viral load) presented with a 4-month history of a solitary mass over the left mandibular area. The lesion was slightly tender and exuded pus from several openings. On examination, there was a 5 × 5 cm erythematous mass with a rough surface and multiple draining sinuses over the right mandibular region. A dental origin was ruled out by prior dental evaluation, and mandibular radiography showed no periostitis or bone destruction. Two 4-mm punch biopsies were obtained—one for histology and one for culture. Histologic examination revealed a squamous-lined cystic structure at the deep biopsy edge compatible with a sinus tract. Periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott’s methenamine silver, Ziehl–Neelsen, and Fite stains were all negative. Aerobic and anaerobic cultures grew only a few Staphylococcus aureus organisms and were negative for Actinomyces species. Tissue cultures for deep fungi, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and atypical mycobacteria were all negative.
title: Case report of hidradenitis suppurativa localized to the face in an HIV patient

case_prompt: A 91-year-old man with nonischemic cardiomyopathy status post dual-chamber implantable cardioverter–defibrillator implantation in 2010 and upgrade to a biventricular device in 2013, permanent atrial fibrillation, and essential thrombocythemia on hydroxyurea presented with 2 weeks of progressively worsening swelling and erythema over his device pocket. He denied pain, fever, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, the left anterior chest wall pocket was erythematous and swollen with overlying telangiectasias. He was afebrile, and laboratory studies showed a mild leukocytosis. Ultrasound of the pocket demonstrated an irregular fluid collection measuring 4.0 × 2.6 × 3.3 cm inferior to the generator. He was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed device infection and referred for pocket exploration. Surgical exploration revealed a solid mass with cystic components extending onto the generator, leads, and surrounding tissues, and a biopsy was obtained. Bacterial and acid-fast bacilli cultures of the pocket were negative, as were blood cultures, and antibiotics were discontinued given low clinical suspicion for infection and absence of supportive microbiologic data. Microscopic examination of the biopsy specimen showed fragments of fibrous tissue with focal chronic inflammation and fibrosis but no malignant cells.
title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma presenting as implantable cardioverter-defibrillator pocket swelling: A case report

case_prompt: A 73-year-old man presented after a fall with headaches and memory loss over the past year. His medical history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, and prostate cancer treated 22 years earlier. On examination, he was mildly confused but had no focal neurologic deficits. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a well-circumscribed, partially hemorrhagic mass in the left temporal–occipital region causing effacement of the occipital horn and atrium of the left lateral ventricle and trapping of the temporal horn. MRI of the brain demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing mass with mixed cystic and solid components. At this time, a differential diagnosis of glioblastoma multiforme or metastasis was proposed. A metastatic workup with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, however, was unremarkable. The patient and his family elected to proceed with a stereotactic biopsy for tissue diagnosis.
