title: A Pediatric Tumor Found Frequently in the Adult Population: A Case of Anaplastic Astroblastoma in an Elderly Patient and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 93-year-old Caucasian man presented in late summer with a one‐month history of fevers of unknown origin, chronic neck pain, and stiffness. One month earlier he had been hospitalized for fever and dehydration; blood cultures were negative and he was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone, then discharged on clindamycin for systemic inflammatory response syndrome of unknown cause. His medical history included hypertension, acute renal failure, osteoarthritis, and a prior episode of SIRS. He denied travel, tobacco, or alcohol use. 

On examination, temperature was 39.1°C, blood pressure 146/63 mmHg, heart rate 104/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. He had multiple oral ulcers, sinus tachycardia, a 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, left knee crepitus, and blood in the urine from a recent Foley insertion. There were no rashes or respiratory findings.

Laboratory tests showed a procalcitonin level <0.05 ng/mL and repeated blood cultures remained negative. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no evidence of endocarditis. Within 24 hours of admission he developed altered mental status, persistent fevers, nuchal rigidity, myoclonic tremors of the upper extremities, unresponsive pinpoint pupils, and positive Babinski and Brudzinski signs. Empiric therapy with intravenous vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and acyclovir was initiated.

A head and neck CT scan was normal. Lumbar puncture yielded clear cerebrospinal fluid with 530 WBC/µL (76% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes, 14% monocytes), 15 RBC/µL, glucose 91 mg/dL, and protein 154 mg/dL. CSF studies were negative for VDRL, coccidioidal IgG/IgM, HSV‐1/2 PCR, cryptococcal antigen, bacterial Gram stain and culture, and fungal cultures.
title: Fever of Unknown Origin in a Patient with Confirmed West Nile Virus Meningoencephalitis

case_prompt: An 83-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, spinal canal stenosis, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with pruritus. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 1333 U/L, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 350 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed intrahepatic bile duct dilatation. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 13-cm mass in the right hepatic lobe causing compression of the hilar bile ducts. ERCP confirmed extrinsic compression at the hepatic hilum; nasobiliary drainage improved jaundice. Biliary cytology showed disturbed architecture with variation in internuclear distances and dyskaryosis, raising suspicion for malignancy. On transfer, cholestatic enzymes had improved (total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL; direct bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase 600 U/L; γ-GTP 57 U/L) but revealed coagulopathy (platelet count 9.6×10^3/mm^3; fibrinogen 122.5 mg/dL; fibrin-fibrinogen degradation products 200 µg/mL; D-dimer 88.8 µg/mL). Repeat CT showed a well-demarcated, nonenhancing 13-cm lesion in segments IV–V with intrahepatic ductal dilation. Review of CT from 5 years earlier revealed a 28-mm low-density lesion at the same site. MRI demonstrated a 13-cm mass with low T1 and slightly high T2 signal intensity, heterogeneous appearance, and fluid–fluid levels at the margins. ERCP again showed a 2-cm common bile duct stricture from extrinsic compression, with segmental intrahepatic ductal dilation.
title: Obstructive jaundice caused by a giant liver hemangioma with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome: a case report

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old right-handed woman presented with a 2-year history of intermittent, nonradiating, achy pain in her left wrist without numbness or tingling. She denied trauma or prior surgery. On examination, there was no edema or skin changes; however, a firm, mobile, tender soft-tissue mass was palpable over the volar aspect of the left wrist. Transillumination was inconclusive, and an ultrasound was obtained.

Ultrasound examination demonstrated a 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.4 cm, well-defined, solid, oval hypoechoic soft-tissue mass in the volar lateral wrist abutting the radial artery. There was no internal calcification or necrosis, and color Doppler showed little to no intrinsic vascularity; the radial artery and veins were patent. 

Differential diagnosis included complex ganglion cyst, angioleiomyoma, schwannoma, neurofibroma, thrombosed pseudoaneurysm, nodular fasciitis, and leiomyosarcoma.
title: Angioleiomyoma in a 52-year-old female wrist: A case report

case_prompt: A 62-year-old woman with a 3-year history of stage IV grade 1 to 2 follicular B-cell lymphoma, managed with observation, presented with a mildly pruritic patch over her frontoparietal scalp and forehead of 3 months’ duration that had not changed. She had stable disease on a “watch and wait” protocol without treatment. Physical examination revealed an approximately 10 cm × 15 cm ill-defined erythematous reticular patch with blanchable telangiectasias over the frontoparietal scalp and forehead. The patient had applied clobetasol 0.05% solution twice daily for 2 weeks, which she discontinued 1 week before presentation due to lack of response, and she noted no change in the rash with steroid use. Given her medical history, cutaneous lymphoma was high on the differential, and a punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the frontal scalp.
title: Rare presentation of disseminated follicular lymphoma as an ill-defined reticular patch over the scalp and forehead

case_prompt: A 51-year-old transgender female presented with right submandibular swelling and a 1-year history of episodic enlargement, often associated with upper respiratory infections and self-limited by oral antibiotics. She reported odynophagia, dysphagia, and intermittent dyspnea but denied fever. Her medical history included well-controlled HIV and seizure disorder. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a large, well-defined, soft, non-tender swelling of the right submandibular region without erythema or warmth. Intraoral examination revealed elevation and firmness of the right floor of mouth, tongue elevation, and contralateral uvular deviation; the airway was patent. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the face demonstrated a 3.8-cm, well-defined, oval, hypodense lesion in the right submandibular space with mild rim enhancement, located above the anterior belly of the digastric muscle and inferior to the mylohyoid muscle. MRI showed the mass to be hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with thin rim enhancement, an internal septum, and dependent nonenhancing sediment. The submandibular gland was displaced dorsally by the lesion, and there was surrounding soft-tissue edema.
title: Heterotopic gastrointestinal cyst within the submandibular space in an adult: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension had a mild SARS-CoV-2 infection confirmed by PCR one month earlier. She now presents with a 3-day history of worsening generalized body aches, chills, fever, watery diarrhea, nausea, mild dry cough, mild dyspnea, and nonspecific chest pain. On admission, her blood pressure was 82/44 mmHg, heart rate 132 beats per minute, temperature 101.5°F (38.6°C), and oxygen saturation remained above 90% on 2 L nasal cannula. Cardiovascular examination revealed an S3 gallop, 2+ peripheral pulses, warm extremities, and bilateral pitting edema. Pulmonary examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed positive SARS-CoV-2 RNA by PCR, troponin-I 4.295 ng/mL, B-type natriuretic peptide 2291 pg/mL, and elevated inflammatory markers including LDH, ferritin, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and interleukin-6. Blood cultures were negative. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ST-segment changes. Chest radiograph and CT angiography of the chest were unremarkable.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 20–25%, left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 6.1 cm, and apical akinesis; there was no pericardial effusion or significant valvular abnormality.
title: COVID-19 Induced Cardiomyopathy Successfully Treated with Tocilizumab

case_prompt: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, prior ischemic stroke, alcoholic cirrhosis, and COPD was treated for L5–S1 spondylodiscitis and Bacteroides fragilis bacteremia. After surgical washout and L4–S1 fusion, he received ertapenem, then was stepped down to oral metronidazole and moxifloxacin. Eight weeks later, he returned with progressive altered mental status, decreased appetite, and generalized weakness. On examination, he had dysarthria, dysphagia, and both visual and auditory hallucinations. A delirium workup, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, and biochemistry, was unremarkable. To exclude stroke, a noncontrast head CT and CT angiogram were obtained and showed no acute ischemia or hemorrhage. Brain MRI demonstrated symmetric T2/FLAIR and diffusion hyperintensity without restriction on apparent diffusion coefficient mapping in both dentate nuclei, and symmetric T1 hyperintensity in the globi pallidi, subthalamic nuclei, and substantia nigra.
title: Metronidazole-induced encephalopathy in a patient with cirrhosis

case_prompt:
A 22‐year-old man presented with a 2-week history of intermittent fevers, nonproductive cough, night sweats, and weight loss. Born in India, he had arrived in Australia 12 months earlier for university; he had no significant past medical history and was a nonsmoker. He denied known TB contacts.  

On examination: temperature 37.8°C; heart rate 80 beats/min; blood pressure 130/70 mmHg; respiratory rate 16/min; oxygen saturation 97% on room air. No lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or skin lesions were noted, and the chest was clear.  

Laboratory studies: normal blood count, renal and liver function tests; C-reactive protein 36 mg/L; HIV serology negative; interferon gamma release assay for TB antigens positive. He was unable to produce sputum.  

Chest radiograph showed a right paratracheal opacity with otherwise clear lung fields. CT of the chest revealed multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes with endobronchial involvement and multiple micronodular changes in the right lower lobe.  

Bronchoscopy demonstrated two discrete, polypoid, friable endobronchial lesions at the carina and left main bronchus, with mildly increased vascularity and normal surrounding mucosa. Biopsy of the lesions revealed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation with lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate. AFB smear and TB-complex DNA PCR (GeneXpert MTB/RIF) on biopsy samples were negative. Bronchial washings from the right lower lobe were negative for AFB smear, TB-complex DNA PCR, and bacterial culture; no malignant cells were identified, and cellularity was insufficient for differential count.
title: Endobronchial tuberculosis polyps

case_prompt: A 70-year-old man with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes, poorly compliant with medications and glucose monitoring, presented with 2 days of severe involuntary movements of the right lower extremity. He had no ketonuria. Non-fasting plasma glucose was 9.08 mmol/L, serum osmolality 307.10 mOsm/L, and urinary ketones were negative. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed increased attenuation in the left putamen and caudate nucleus. MRI revealed heterogeneous hyperintensity in the same regions on T1-weighted images, an irregular hyperintense lesion with mild mass effect on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, and a ring-like enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging. The lesion was iso- to hypo-intense on diffusion-weighted imaging. Single-voxel short-echo time 1H magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated markedly increased lactate and lipid peaks, a slightly elevated choline peak, a slightly decreased N-acetylaspartate peak, and stable creatine, with a Cho/NAA ratio of 0.675, Cho/Cr of 1.04, NAA/Cr of 1.54, and (Lac + Lip)/Cr of 1.34.
title: Non-ketotic hyperglycaemia-induced hemichorea-hemiballism may represent glioma-like pattern on multimodal magnetic resonance imaging: can 1H spectroscopy help in the differentiation?

case_prompt: A 36-year-old white British man presented with three weeks of progressively worsening exertional central chest pain and breathlessness. He had a ten-year history of Erdheim–Chester disease, previously controlled with pegylated interferon; nine months earlier he had COVID-19 complicated by deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, for which he was taking apixaban. A recent disease flare had prompted increases in interferon and a course of prednisolone. He had no traditional cardiovascular risk factors. On admission, ECG showed sinus rhythm with <1 mm convex ST-segment elevation in V1–V6 and T-wave inversion in leads I and aVL. High-sensitivity troponin T was 51 ng/L, rising to 132 ng/L at six hours; D-dimer was 608 ng/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced gated CT coronary angiography demonstrated a zero calcium score but an ostial left anterior descending (LAD) non-calcified plaque 1.5 cm in length with positive remodelling and a low-density lipid core causing severe stenosis; a small pulmonary infarct was also seen. Invasive coronary angiography confirmed an ostial filling defect in the LAD with TIMI 3 flow; the left main stem, circumflex, and right coronary arteries were normal.
title: Paradoxical coronary embolism in Erdheim-Chester disease: invasive assessment and multidisciplinary management

case_prompt: A 46-year-old woman with HIV on stable ART (tenofovir, lamivudine, dolutegravir) for 14 years and hypertension controlled by diet presented with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. On arrival: blood pressure 210/130 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37.1 °C. Examination was notable only for elevated blood pressure; there was no abdominal tenderness and other findings were unremarkable. She received intravenous cimetidine 400 mg, followed 5 minutes later by oral nifedipine 30 mg. One hour later, she developed carpopedal spasm of the fingers, rigid plantar flexion of the feet, and could not stand. She also experienced severe retrosternal chest pain, shivering, chills, and shortness of breath. Blood pressure was 160/110 mmHg; there was no rash. She was administered intranasal oxygen, morphine 5 mg IV, and calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 30 minutes. The spasms resolved over the hour of calcium infusion, but chest pain persisted without ECG evidence of ischemia. Twelve hours later, chest pain diminished and she remained stable except for mild epigastric discomfort. Laboratory evaluation before calcium showed total serum calcium 7.1 mg/dL; two days later it was 8.8 mg/dL. Serum albumin was 5 g/L; sodium, potassium, and chloride were normal. CD4 count was 573 cells/mm³; complete blood count, renal and liver function tests were all normal. A brain CT scan showed no intracranial lesion. Tests for ionized calcium, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and phosphate were unavailable.
title: Hypocalcemic tetany associated with simultaneous administration of cimetidine and nifedipine: a case report

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old man was referred in May 2014 for evaluation of suspected duodenal lymphoma. He had a long history of chronic dyspepsia and esophagitis following laparoscopic fundoplication in 2004 and recurrent need for proton-pump inhibitors. Over the preceding 6 months he noted increasing postprandial abdominal discomfort despite regular pantoprazole. His medical history also included resolved hepatitis B (PCR negative) and moderate COPD (GOLD II). He denied recent antibiotic use.

On presentation he was asymptomatic apart from intermittent abdominal discomfort and had an ECOG performance status of 0. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts and normal renal and liver function tests. Serologic and histologic screening for Helicobacter pylori was negative. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA, thyroid antibodies, rheumatoid factors, SS-A/SS-B) were negative.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed multiple small nodules with superficial erosions in the post-bulbar duodenum and otherwise normal gastric and esophageal mucosa; gastric and esophageal biopsies showed only mild chronic gastritis and esophagitis without lymphoma. Multiple biopsies of a duodenal nodule showed a follicular lymphoid infiltrate composed of small centrocytes with fewer than 5 centroblasts per high-power field. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated CD20+, CD79a+, bcl2+, CD10+, bcl6+, and CD3–/CD5–. 

An 18F-FDG PET/CT scan showed no abnormal tracer uptake in the duodenum or elsewhere in lymph nodes or other organs.
title: Successful Clarithromycin Monotherapy in a Patient with Primary Follicular Lymphoma of the Duodenum

case_prompt: A 14-year-old girl presented with chronic recurrent pelvic pain since menarche, with monthly exacerbations during menstruation despite regular flow. She had no significant personal or family history and no prior sexual activity. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and a two-month trial of oral contraceptives provided no relief. Examination revealed normal vital signs and Tanner stage 4 pubertal development. Abdominal and external genital examinations were unremarkable; no masses were palpable. Transabdominal ultrasound showed a normal-sized uterus; a 35×30 mm heterogeneous, mostly hyperechoic mass was noted adjacent to the left ovary with internal vascularity, and a small simple cyst was seen in the right ovary. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a well-defined left pelvic mass with high T2 signal intensity, low-to-intermediate T1 signal, and significant gadolinium enhancement; it lay close to, but was not connected with, the left ovary or the uterus. There was no lymphadenopathy or ascites. Based on imaging, a paraovarian mass or a uterine myoma was suspected.
title: Pelvic Pain and Adnexal Mass: Be Aware of Accessory and Cavitated Uterine Mass

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old boy was admitted to a referral hospital in northern Democratic Republic of the Congo in December 2016 with a 3-day history of illness. On admission (day 1), he had low-grade fever (37.9°C), rhinitis, conjunctivitis, cough, and severe left-sided cervical lymphadenitis. He was alert, with a heart rate of 115 bpm and respiratory rate of 30 breaths/min. He had a non-itchy vesiculopapular rash, with lesions measuring 5–10 mm in diameter, distributed over the trunk and face. He was previously healthy, unvaccinated, and three adults in his village had experienced similar but milder symptoms. 

On day 2, he and his father were moved to an isolation unit on suspicion of chickenpox or measles. Treatment was initiated with intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanic acid, oral retinol, topical antibiotic eye drops, paracetamol, nutritional supplement (plumpynut), and intravenous maintenance fluids. Over the next 2–5 days, his fever spiked to 38.5°C, and the rash worsened: “all elements grew simultaneously penetrating 3–4 mm into his skin.” The rash then spread to the entire body surface, including palms, soles, and mucous membranes, leading to painful stomatitis. Antibiotic therapy was changed to intravenous ceftriaxone, and analgesia was intensified with morphine.

On admission day 2, a blood sample was sent to a diagnostic laboratory in Kinshasa for measles IgM and IgG testing.
title: A Case Report of Monkeypox in a 4-Year-Old Boy from the DR Congo: Challenges of Diagnosis and Management

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old woman noted a palpable, painless, hard, movable mass (~2.6×3.5 cm) in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast, with no skin changes, nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Three years earlier, she had been diagnosed with AML (M2) on the basis of nasosinal lesions, treated with six cycles of cytosine arabinoside, and attained remission. 

Mammography revealed a 2.5×2.4 cm round mass with irregular, well-defined margins and prominent vessels in the upper outer quadrant, and a second 1.4×1.1 cm mass in the lower outer quadrant; several right axillary lymph nodes measured up to 1.9 cm. Ultrasound showed a lobulated, hypoechoic 3.7×2.6 cm mass with marked vascularity (resistive index 0.60) in the upper outer quadrant and a second 1.8×1.1 cm hypoechoic lesion below the nipple; a 1.8 cm hypoechoic axillary node was also seen. 

Complete blood count, chest radiograph, and abdominopelvic CT were normal. Fine-needle aspiration of both breast lesions revealed inflammatory cell infiltration, granular calcification, and several atypical epithelial cells, suggesting possible malignancy. Bone marrow aspirate showed no evidence of leukemia. A lumpectomy was performed under local anesthesia; frozen section examination revealed a poorly differentiated malignant tumor.
title: An uncommon granulocytic sarcoma of the breast: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 27-year-old man, 6 months after deceased-donor kidney transplantation for IgA nephropathy, presented with 3 days of high-grade fever, retro-orbital pain, headache, and myalgia. His brother, a household contact, had been diagnosed with dengue fever. He was on mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus (trough 7 ng/ml), and steroids; graft function had nadir creatinine 0.8 mg/dl. He denied abdominal pain, dysuria, jaundice, arthralgia, rash, or neurologic symptoms. On exam he was dehydrated, hypotensive (90/60 mmHg), tachycardic, and otherwise unremarkable. Initial labs showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dl, WBC 2000/mm3, platelets 39 000/mm3), acute graft dysfunction (creatinine 2.1 mg/dl), hyponatremia (Na 127 mEq/L), and ECG with sinus tachycardia. Abdominal ultrasound revealed mild splenomegaly. Intravenous fluids stabilized his blood pressure; tacrolimus dose was reduced, mycophenolate was held, and stress-dose steroids were given. Dengue NS1 antigen was positive; tests for leptospirosis, malaria, and scrub typhus were negative, and blood and urine cultures were sterile. He was diagnosed with dengue fever. Over the next days, renal function and blood pressure normalized, but fever persisted, pancytopenia worsened, and hsCRP and D-dimer levels rose. He developed mucosal bleeding requiring platelet transfusion; serum ferritin was 26 250 ng/ml and LDH 665 U/L.
title: An Uncommon Complication of a Common Tropical Infection in a Kidney Transplant Recipient – A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 78-year-old Asian woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive weakness of the lower extremities culminating in inability to walk and urinary retention. Four years earlier, she had transient lower limb weakness after a fall but fully recovered. 

On examination, vital signs were normal and she was alert. Manual muscle testing revealed weakness in the iliopsoas (2/1), quadriceps (2/1), tibialis anterior (2/1), gluteus maximus (3/1), and gastrocnemius (3/3). Deep tendon reflexes of the lower limbs were increased, and plantar responses were bilaterally extensor. Sensation to light touch and proprioception was absent below the T9 dermatome. 

Laboratory studies showed:
• Viral serologies positive for anti-HBs antibody, HBc antibody, HCV antibody, and anti-HTLV-1 antibody; no other viral, bacterial, or fungal infection detected.  
• Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/hour (normal <20 mm/hour).  
• Rheumatoid factor 36.6 IU/mL (normal <20 IU/mL).  
• Immunoglobulin levels: IgG 2447 mg/dL (700–1600), IgA 787 mg/dL (70–400), IgM 95 mg/dL (40–230).  
• Autoantibodies: anti–SS-A 81.7 units, antinuclear antibody 640 units; PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, and serum IgG4 were not elevated.  

Neuroimaging revealed a normal brain MRI. Spinal MRI demonstrated a hypointense, mass-like lesion compressing the spinal cord from T2 to T10 on both T1- and T2-weighted images. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a total protein of 1882 mg/dL (normal 15–60) and 95 cells/μL (normal 0–5).
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Hypertrophic spinal pachymeningitis associated with human T-cell lymphotrophic virus-1 infection and Sjogren’s syndrome: A case report and brief literature review

case_prompt: A 26-year-old man presented with left occipital and posterior cervical pain and swelling that began 6 months after a military‐training injury. He also noted decreased hearing and a sensation of fullness in both ears. He had no prior medical history. Examination revealed ulcerations with scaling in the left occipital region and diffuse swelling extending into the posterior cervical area. Laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level that decreased on repeat testing. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated ill‐defined soft-tissue masses from the posterior cervical region to the occiput, with lytic “sponging” of bilateral mastoid and occipital bones and opacification of the left mastoid air cells and middle‐ear cavities. MRI revealed extensive cervicocranial soft-tissue thickening and edema, most pronounced posteriorly at the cervical and left occipitoparietal regions, with intracranial parenchymal and meningeal enhancement, associated vasogenic edema, mild rightward midline shift, and compression of the left lateral ventricle. No areas of restricted diffusion were seen. Initially, a malignant soft tissue process was suspected, and a scalp biopsy was recommended for histopathological confirmation.
title: Tumor mimicking cervicocranial actinomycosis with intracranial extension- a diagnosic dillema-first case report in somalia

case_prompt:
A 10-year-old boy of Iraqi descent presented with a 2-week history of lethargy, weight loss, polydipsia, and polyuria. He was born in the UK to healthy parents of Iraqi origin, had a history of nocturnal enuresis and adenotonsillectomy, and took no regular medications. On examination his weight was 56.6 kg; vital signs were normal. Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• Blood glucose, 42.9 mmol/L  
• Venous pH, 7.38; bicarbonate, 21.3 mmol/L; base deficit, 3.3 mmol/L  
• Urine ketones, negative  
• Hemoglobin, 130 g/L; WBC count, 8.1 × 10^9/L; platelets, 274 × 10^9/L  
• Serum sodium, 127 mmol/L; renal and liver function, and thyroid function, normal  
• Positive islet cell antibodies; GAD antibodies > 2000 U/mL  
• HbA1C, 116 mmol/mol  

He was diagnosed with new-onset type 1 diabetes without ketoacidosis, started on subcutaneous insulin, and discharged on day 5 on a basal–bolus regimen. Eleven days later, a home visit noted normal blood glucose but new jaundice and extreme lethargy. He was referred to hospital. On arrival, he had icteric sclera but no hepatomegaly and no stigmata of chronic liver disease; vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests revealed:  
• Hemoglobin, 81 g/L; RBC count, 2.65 × 10^12/L  
• Normal urea, electrolytes, ALP, ALT, CRP, and albumin  
• Total bilirubin, 88 μmol/L; conjugated fraction, 6 μmol/L  

Peripheral blood film showed anisocytosis, spherocytes, polychromasia, and occasional red cell fragments. Further studies showed lactate dehydrogenase 243 U/L and haptoglobin < 0.08 g/L, consistent with acute hemolysis.
title: Manifestation of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency in the wake of new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus: a case report

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old male college aviation student presented with chronic pain and a skin lesion on the left fourth toe. His symptoms began at age 7 while playing soccer, with intermittent pain when kicking. At age 15, he was diagnosed with verruca vulgaris and underwent two liquid nitrogen cryotherapy treatments without improvement. At age 20, he attempted self-excision of the lesion, noted significant bleeding, and cauterized it without resolving the lesion. He then saw a podiatrist who, during attempted wart excision, encountered bone under the skin and ordered radiographs.

On examination, there was a 3 × 5 mm ovoid, hyperkeratotic lesion with diffuse borders at the tip of the left fourth toe, immediately beneath the nail, without erythema or drainage. The toe tip appeared bulbous and was firm and nodular on palpation, eliciting sharp pain (8/10) on direct pressure. There was no tenderness on passive toe movement, and neurovascular examination was normal.

Plain radiographs of the left foot showed a pedunculated bony exostosis at the tuft of the distal phalanx with clear cortical and medullary continuity with the parent bone in a skeletally mature patient. Comparison views of the right foot were normal.
title: Pedunculated Osteochondroma Presenting as Verruca Vulgaris: A Diagnosis Requiring a High Index of Suspicion: Case Report

case_prompt: An 11-year-old girl was seen for delayed eruption of her permanent teeth. She had premature birth and no familial history of similar findings. Developmentally she was 1–2 years behind her chronological age. On examination, she had splenomegaly and lacrimal duct obstruction. Extraoral features included exophthalmos, dry eyes, facial telangiectasia, and a flattened nasal bridge. Dermatologic examination revealed macular erythematous and hyperpigmented lesions on the forearms and anterior chest, and hyperkeratotic hypopigmented areas on the palms and soles. Intraorally, her gingiva was red, edematous, and hyperplastic. Only 12 permanent teeth were present, with widespread caries and destruction of all first molars. Radiographs showed a conservative bone age of 8 years, absence of unerupted or impacted tooth germs, and normal alveolar bone, periodontal membranes, and lamina dura. Examination of the tongue revealed a well-demarcated erythematous atrophic patch on the midline dorsum consistent with median rhomboid glossitis.
title: Oral Findings of Rothmund-Thomson Syndrome

case_prompt: A 39-year-old man was admitted with low back pain and dyspnea 3 days after being caught between a motor vehicle and a wall. He had a history of ankylosing spondylitis treated with corticosteroids. On arrival, he was alert (GCS 15) with stable vital signs. Neurologic examination was normal, and he had intact light-touch sensation in all extremities; movement of the lower extremities was limited by pain. Radiographs showed fractures of three left lower ribs, hemothorax, and subcutaneous emphysema. Lumbar–sacral imaging revealed fractures of the L2, L3, and L4 vertebrae, with no cervical spine injury. CT of the thorax confirmed bilateral pleural effusions, fractures of ribs 8, 9, and 10 on the left, fractures of vertebrae L2–L4, and multiple air bubbles within the upper thoracic spinal canal.
title: Thoracic Pneumorrhachis in Patient with Lumbar Fractures; a Case Report

case_prompt: A 55-year-old man (ASA I) presented with a two-week history of a single episode of biliary colic. He had no symptoms of cholangitis, no significant past medical or surgical history, and a normal physical examination. Routine laboratory tests, including liver function tests and complete blood count, were within normal limits. A screening abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple gallbladder stones but no liver lesions. He underwent an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Intraoperatively, the gallbladder contained multiple calculi without signs of acute cholecystitis. Unexpectedly, multiple firm to hard, whitish nodules were noted on liver segments II, IVB, VI, and VIII; the remainder of the peritoneal cavity appeared normal. A standard cholecystectomy was completed, and laparoscopic wedge biopsies of the liver nodules in segments IVB and VI were obtained. The patient’s immediate postoperative recovery was uneventful.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Multiple bile duct adenomas mimicking hepatic metastases during laparoscopic cholecystectomy - A case report

case_prompt: A 77-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a generalized pruritic bullous eruption. He had eczematous and urticarial-like lesions with vesicles and tense blisters on the trunk, abdomen, and upper and lower limbs, along with postbullous erosions and crusting but no lichenoid papules. Bullae were also noted on the proximal nail folds of several fingers. On examination, the right thumbnail was severely atrophic, with a wide band of smooth skin bridging from the proximal nail fold to the nail bed; there were no longitudinal ridges, furrows, or splits. The patient recalled large periungual blisters of the thumbs that led to loss of those fingernails, and subsequent regrowth yielded only two narrow lateral nail fragments of the right thumbnail. Light microscopy of a thigh biopsy showed subepidermal blister formation with a dermal inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils and no hydropic degeneration of basal cells. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin revealed linear deposits of IgG and C3 along the epidermal basement membrane zone. By enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, circulating autoantibodies against BP180 were elevated at 37.5 U/mL (normal < 12 U/mL).
title: Pterygium in bullous pemphigoid: An unusual complication

case_prompt: A previously healthy 4-year-old girl presented to the pediatric emergency department with a few hours’ history of constant pressure–type lower-quadrant abdominal pain and an urge to urinate, following a low-energy blunt abdominal trauma while playing. On examination, she had localized tenderness of the lower abdomen without other remarkable findings. Laboratory studies showed a neutrophilic leukocytosis (white blood cells 14 810/mm3, 71% neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 122 mg/L. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a hyperechoic, inhomogeneous solid mass measuring 10×4×8 cm cranial to the bladder, with no vascular signal on color Doppler, and the left ovary was not visualized. Serum tumor markers revealed an elevated cancer antigen 125 level of 220.9 IU/mL, with beta human chorionic gonadotropin, alpha-fetoprotein, and carcinoembryonic antigen within normal limits. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy was initiated, and, suspecting an ovarian mass and/or adnexal torsion, the patient was taken for abdominal exploration through a Pfannenstiel incision.
title: Lipoblastoma as a cause of secondary omental torsion in children: report of the first case

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of undescended testes and a nodular lesion in the left inguinal region. His early history was notable for bilateral cryptorchidism and inguinal hernias at age 4; MRI had shown an intra-abdominal hypoplastic right testis and a left paramedian retrovesical structure resembling an atrophic testis. He underwent right orchidopexy; the left testis was not found.

At age 5, recurrent testicular ascent prompted MRI demonstrating a left intra-abdominal testis and a right inguinal canal testis. Laparoscopy revealed a left testis with a medial fibrous structure extending toward the right inguinal ring, resembling a rudimentary uterus. Biopsy of the left testis showed immature testicular tissue. A subsequent laparoscopy dissected and removed the fibrous structure; histopathology confirmed Müllerian tissue. Karyotype was 46,XY.

Annual ultrasounds showed progressive left testicular hypotrophy; at age 12 a left orchidectomy revealed epididymis, ductus deferens, and seminiferous tubules without gonadal tissue. The right testis remained in the scrotum.

At age 13, physical examination showed Tanner stage II, a small right testis in the scrotum, and a palpable left testis in the inguinal area. Scrotal ultrasound measured the right testis at 14×6.2 mm and the left gonadal structure at 16×8.9 mm in the superficial inguinal region. Hormonal studies revealed FSH 3.03 mIU/mL (0.4–4.6), LH 0.434 mIU/mL (0.1–7.8), and testosterone 3.12 ng/dL (Tanner 2: 2.5–432). Serum AMH and inhibin B were within normal limits for age. Tumor markers were within reference ranges (LDH 148 U/L; AFP <0.908 ng/mL; β-hCG ≤0.70 mIU/mL).
title: Persistent Müllerian Duct Syndrome with Supernumerary Testicles Due to a Novel Homozygous Variant in the AMHR2 Gene and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 5-year-old boy presents with a 6-month history of intermittent right knee pain without trauma, fever, or weight loss. On examination, there is tenderness to palpation over the proximal right tibia without swelling, erythema, warmth, or restriction of motion. Plain radiographs show a well-circumscribed metaphyseal lesion of the proximal tibia that is lytic with a thin sclerotic rim, has a mixed lytic–blastic matrix, and lacks periosteal reaction or physeal involvement. CT confirms a cystic, well-demarcated metaphyseal lesion with sclerotic margins and no periosteal reaction or physeal breach. MRI reveals a multilocular cystic lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis with well-defined margins, surrounding marrow edema, fluid–fluid levels, and heterogeneous contrast enhancement.
title: Metaphyseal chondroblastoma in a pediatric patient

case_prompt: A 20‐year‐old Hispanic man with no past medical history presented with 4 weeks of generalized weakness, 3 weeks of progressive cough productive of yellow sputum, and persistent shortness of breath; he also reported intermittent fever and chills for the preceding 3–5 days. He denied smoking, alcohol use, and illicit drugs. He was monogamous, with two lifetime sexual partners, and had not traveled outside the United States in 12 years. On examination, he appeared cachectic and tachypneic, with bilateral diffuse crackles and rhonchi. Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits. Chest CT revealed diffuse tree‐in‐bud nodularity, bronchiectasis, thick‐walled cavities in the upper lobes, and a moderate right pleural effusion. An HIV rapid ELISA was reactive. Acid‐fast bacilli were seen on sputum smear, and he was started on combination anti-tuberculosis therapy. Over the next 3 days, his symptoms improved. HIV Western blot was negative, and HIV viral load was undetectable. His CD4+ T-cell count was 124 cells/mm3, CD8+ T-cell count was 185 cells/mm3 (CD4:CD8 ratio, 0.7). Further workup, including immunoglobulin A, immunoglobulin G, and immunoglobulin M levels, urine protein electrophoresis, and serum protein electrophoresis, was unremarkable.
title: Idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia in Hispanic male: case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman with no prior comorbidities presented with a 3-week history of holocranial headache, weight loss, and anorexia, followed over 1 week by fluctuating alertness and a single episode of nonbilious, non–blood-stained projectile vomiting. She denied fever, photophobia, blurred vision, or seizures. One week before transfer she was diagnosed with HIV-1 infection at another hospital and started on tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz. 

On examination, her pulse was 136 beats/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, and respiratory rate 24/min. She was drowsy but arousable and afebrile. Neurologic findings included bilateral papilledema, restriction of upward gaze, bilateral gaze-evoked nystagmus, and neck stiffness. The remainder of her physical examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL), leukopenia (total WBC count 2 × 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 95 × 10^9/L), and a CD4+ T-cell count of 46 cells/μL. 

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed communicating hydrocephalus with periventricular hypodensities suggestive of transependymal CSF seepage. An external ventricular drain was placed, and CSF analysis showed 80 WBC/mm^3 (lymphocytic predominance), protein 108 mg/dL, glucose 2.72 mmol/L (simultaneous blood glucose 6.22 mmol/L), negative Gram stain and India ink, negative CSF Xpert® MTB/RIF, negative bacterial and fungal cultures, negative cryptococcal antigen in serum and CSF, negative toxoplasma IgM and IgG, and no abnormal cells on cytospin. CSF PCR was positive for CMV DNA.

After removal of the external drain, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated resolution of hydrocephalus and numerous periventricular high T2-signal regions with restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging, as well as faint enhancement lining the ependymal surfaces of the lateral ventricles.
title: Cytomegalovirus ventriculoencephalitis presenting with hydrocephalus in a patient with advanced HIV infection

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old man underwent colonoscopy after a positive fecal occult blood test and was found to have two distinct colorectal masses, one well-differentiated adenocarcinoma and one moderate-to-poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. His serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level was 15.1 ng/mL (normal for a healthy smoker < 5.5 ng/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 1.0-cm left adrenal nodule and a 6-cm heterogeneous, ill-defined splenic mass. On portal venous phase images, the splenic lesion measured 42 Hounsfield units (HU) and was unchanged on 4-minute delayed images. A noncontrast CT later measured the lesion at 28 HU, suggesting mild enhancement. The adrenal nodule was subsequently characterized as a benign adenoma. Assuming metastatic colorectal cancer, systemic chemotherapy was initiated; the CEA level dropped to 0.9 ng/mL, and follow-up CT showed that the splenic mass remained stable in size.  
A fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan showed no abnormal uptake in the splenic lesion. Tc-99m–labeled red blood cell scintigraphy demonstrated a photopenic region in the spleen corresponding to the mass. MRI of the abdomen with gadolinium revealed a well-defined splenic lesion with heterogeneously high T2 and low T1 signal intensity and centripetal contrast fill-in on delayed images, but without complete homogeneous enhancement. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound showed a mildly hyperechoic splenic mass with peripheral vascular flow on Doppler. Immediately after intravenous microbubble contrast, straight vessels feeding the mass were seen, with heterogeneous early enhancement and early wash-out; the enhancement pattern was not typical for either a hemangioma or a lymphangioma.
title: Unusual imaging profile of a solitary splenic lymphangioma

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 6-month history of gross hematuria. She denied dysuria, frequency, fever, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable.
  
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan showed a 6.8 cm exophytic mass arising from the anterior wall and dome of the urinary bladder, with invasion into the anterior abdominal wall.
  
Cystoscopy revealed mucosal erosion over the mass, and a bladder biopsy demonstrated enteric-type adenocarcinoma in the bladder wall, partially covered by urothelium with reactive changes.
  
To evaluate for a possible metastatic source, a thoracic CT scan and virtual colonoscopy were performed, which showed no distant metastases and no evidence of primary colonic neoplasm.
title: Urachal Tumor: A Case Report of an Extremely Rare Carcinoma

case_prompt: A 46-year-old farmer from a rural area presented with a progressive, nonpainful swelling of his left foot. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. On examination, there was diffuse swelling extending from the left big toe to the forefoot, with multiple fistulous tracts draining foul-smelling serous fluid. Plain radiographs of the foot showed soft-tissue enlargement without evidence of bone erosion. Laboratory studies were within normal limits, including a white-cell count of 6900 cells/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 1 mg/L. Initial mycological and bacteriological cultures of drainage fluid were negative for spores, yeast, or filamentous organisms. MRI of the foot demonstrated extensive infiltration of the dorsal and plantar soft tissues of the midfoot and forefoot, with increased signal intensity on T2-weighted images, decreased signal on T1-weighted images, and marked contrast enhancement of the infiltrated areas.
title: Madura foot: How MRI aids in diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old woman was referred for persistent right knee pain 8 months after a cemented cruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty without patellar resurfacing. Range-of-motion and weight-bearing exercises began on postoperative day one. One week after surgery, she developed localized pain in the right popliteal fossa associated with a catching sensation and audible click during active knee flexion.

Her medical history was notable only for a successful left TKA at age 58. She was a housewife. On examination, there was no erythema, swelling, heat, or effusion; the midline patellar incision was well healed. Deep palpation between the iliotibial tract, proximal fibular head, and biceps femoris elicited mild tenderness. A snapping was palpated over the same region during active knee flexion at 80°–90°, with pain rated 91 mm on a 100 mm visual analogue scale; the snapping did not occur with passive motion. Knee range of motion was 10°–120° without instability. Neurologic examination and routine blood work were unremarkable. The Japanese Orthopedic Association score was 65 (pain on walking 25; pain on stairs 5; range of motion 25; effusion 10).

Plain radiographs showed a standing femorotibial angle of 174° and component angles within normal limits (α 97°, β 88°, γ 6°, δ 89°). A fabella measuring 11 mm along its major axis was seen at the posterolateral femoral condyle. Serial radiographs demonstrated that the fabella pre-existed surgery and that osteophyte formation at the posterior condyle had progressed over the 5–7 months post-TKA. CT at 7 months confirmed an 11×10 mm fabella over the posterior femoral condyle, with the femoral component in 2° of internal rotation relative to the epicondylar axis and a normally aligned tibial component.
title: Fabella Syndrome as an Uncommon Cause of Posterolateral Knee Pain after Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 57-year-old man was evaluated for left renal colic and consideration of definitive treatment for nephrolithiasis. His medical history included chronic hepatitis B, hypertension, left bundle-branch block, prostate enlargement, and a splenectomy performed in childhood after a motor-vehicle accident. He reported no other symptoms. On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits and the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, showed no abnormalities. CT-urography demonstrated a 9 mm calculus in the lower calyx of the left kidney and multiple nodular lesions up to 3 cm in size along the left and right iliac axes, within pelvic peritoneal fat, and along the intestinal serosa, particularly adjacent to the sigmoid colon and cecum, findings suggestive of pathologic lymphadenopathy.
title: Splenosis mimicking lymphadenopathy

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old woman, 14 weeks pregnant, was found on routine antenatal ultrasound to have a complex cystic mass in the right kidney. MRI showed a well-defined unilocular cystic lesion with multiple mural nodules at the inferior pole, radiologically suspicious for renal cell carcinoma. There was no prior chemotherapy and all blood tests were normal. At 15 weeks’ gestation, she underwent right radical nephrectomy; the tumor was confined to the kidney. 

Grossly, the specimen revealed a 5.5 × 4.5 × 3.5-cm well-encapsulated unilocular cystic tumor with multiple friable tan-gray mural nodules up to 2.0 cm in size. Microscopically, the lesion consisted of malignant epithelial cells in papillary, trabecular, and nested/alveolar patterns. The cells had discrete borders and abundant eosinophilic or finely vacuolated clear cytoplasm, mildly enlarged nuclei with occasional prominent nucleoli (Fuhrman grade 2). The stroma contained hyaline nodules, numerous psammoma bodies, and areas of hemorrhagic necrosis with hemosiderin-laden macrophages. No lymphovascular invasion was identified, and margins were clear.
title: Xp11.2 translocation renal cell carcinoma occurring during pregnancy with a novel translocation involving chromosome 19: a case report with review of the literature

case_prompt: A 60-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive hoarseness and a 3- to 4-month history of exertional dyspnea. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years; his other medical history was unremarkable. Videolaryngoscopy revealed a 1.5 cm vascularized, pedunculated, polypoid lesion with a smooth surface, originating from the posterior half of the right vocal cord and the vocal process of the arytenoid, subtotally obstructing the endolarynx. To secure the airway, a tracheotomy was performed under general anesthesia, and the mass was excised via endolaryngeal microsurgery. At 4-month follow-up, videolaryngoscopy showed a well-healed incision with no residual or recurrent lesion.
title: A Case of Angiomyolipoma Rarely Located in the Larynx

case_prompt: A 44-year-old obese white man with end-stage renal disease secondary to childhood hemolytic-uremic syndrome underwent a deceased-donor renal transplant in 1998. He was found to have an asymptomatic rise in serum creatinine to 3.4 mg/dL from a baseline of 2.0 mg/dL. He denied any symptoms. On examination, a left inguinal hernia was palpable. Renal ultrasonography revealed moderate to severe hydronephrosis of the transplanted kidney with nonvisualization of the distal ureter and no bladder abnormalities. Despite intravenous hydration and adequate bladder emptying, his urine output remained marginal and his serum creatinine remained elevated at 3.1 mg/dL. A noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained.
title: Different Management Options for Transplant Ureteral Obstructions within an Inguinal Hernia

case_prompt: A 53-year-old man with no prior ocular history presented with redness, pain, and blurred vision in his right eye that developed one to two weeks after a course of oral azithromycin for a respiratory sinus infection. Initial evaluation documented an intraocular pressure of 46 mm Hg and iritis, and he was started on difluprednate, brimonidine, and timolol drops. Three months later, a pigmented iris lesion in the right eye was noted and he was referred for ocular oncology evaluation. On presentation, visual acuity was 20/60 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left; intraocular pressure was 24 mm Hg OD and 18 mm Hg OS. Examination of the left eye was notable only for a nuclear sclerotic cataract. In the right eye, the pupil was mid-dilated, irregular, and poorly reactive without a relative afferent pupillary defect. There were episcleral pigment deposits adjacent to conjunctival vessels, extensive pigment dusting on the iris stromal surface, and diffuse iris pigment–epithelium transillumination defects. There was no corneal infiltration, Krukenberg spindle, keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cells, or iris stromal atrophy. Gonioscopy revealed circumferential dense pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork. Dilated funduscopic examination was unremarkable. Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography showed no posterior bowing of the iris but demonstrated clumping of the pigment epithelium along the pupillary margin, focal absence of the pigment epithelium, and thickening of the adjacent iris root. Ultrasound biomicroscopy revealed thickening of the inferior anterior chamber angle structures with hyper-reflective foci suggestive of pigmented cell dispersion and effacement of the anterior chamber angle structures.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Unilateral acute iris transillumination syndrome with glaucoma and iris pigment epithelium dispersion simulating iris melanoma

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman was referred for a 2-year history of hoarseness, globus sensation, and slowly progressive noisy breathing. She denied dysphagia, odynophagia, allergies, atopy, and aspirin sensitivity. On examination, she had mild audible biphasic stridor; oropharyngeal findings were normal. Fibreoptic nasoendoscopy showed asymmetry of the glottis and a limited view of the subglottis. A chest radiograph was normal. 

Microlaryngoscopy for further airway evaluation revealed trauma to an incidental subglottic lesion during intubation. After securing the airway, biopsies were taken. 

Histologic examination under low power revealed a dense collagenous sclerosing lesion with mixed acute and chronic inflammatory cells. High-power view showed significant numbers of eosinophils in the inflammatory infiltrate surrounding vessels. Immunohistochemistry was positive for vimentin and negative for S100 and AE1/AE3. 

A CT scan demonstrated a homogeneous soft tissue mass about 1 cm in the subglottic region without bony or cartilaginous invasion. MRI confirmed a similarly confined soft tissue lesion. 

Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, biochemistry, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, coagulation parameters, antinuclear antibody, anti-PR3 (c-ANCA), and anti-MPO (p-ANCA)—were all within normal limits.
title: Eosinophilic Angiocentric Fibrosis as a Stenosing Lesion in the Subglottis

case_prompt: A 25-year-old man with a history of primary sclerosing cholangitis and ulcerative colitis (on mesalazine and ursodeoxycholic acid) presented with six days of watery diarrhea (ten stools per day), lower-abdominal cramps, and fevers up to 40 °C. He had returned from Thailand 16 days earlier without symptoms. Initial laboratories showed bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 276 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 56 U/L, lipase 501 U/L, C-reactive protein 9.2 mg/dL, and a leukocyte count of 15 000/mL. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged gallbladder (11 cm) without signs of cholecystitis or acute pancreatitis. Blood and stool cultures were obtained, and intravenous ciprofloxacin and metronidazole were started. When stool cultures grew non-typhoidal Salmonella spp., therapy was changed to ceftriaxone 2 g daily. Despite this change, his condition worsened: he developed increasing epigastric pain, continued fevers, and his diarrhea stopped. Repeat ultrasound showed a mildly enlarged pancreas with peripancreatic edema. Bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, leukocytes, and C-reactive protein continued to rise. Antibiotic therapy was then switched to imipenem 500 mg every six hours.
title: Severe infection with multidrug-resistant Salmonella choleraesuis in a young patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis

case_prompt: A 58-year-old homeless man with hypertension, type II diabetes, and a history of prior venous thromboembolism presented with 1 week of progressive weakness and fatigue. His only medications were atenolol, lisinopril, and metformin; he was not on anticoagulants. He denied hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest pain, headache, nausea, or vomiting. In the emergency department, his heart rate was 113 bpm and the remainder of his physical examination was unremarkable. He had an infrarenal inferior vena cava (IVC) filter placed 15 years earlier and was unaware of the indication. While in the ED, he suddenly became unresponsive; ACLS was initiated for 11 minutes, after which he was intubated and transferred to the ICU. Serial hemoglobin measurements revealed a drop from 12.3 gm/dL to 6.8 gm/dL. Given concern for acute blood loss, a noncontrast CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was obtained, showing a large left-sided retroperitoneal hematoma contiguous with the aorta and IVC, mass effect on the bladder, and an expansile appearance of the IVC below the filter. A subsequent CT angiogram with arterial and venous phases excluded an arterial source of bleeding and demonstrated nonocclusive thrombi in the IVC and bilateral common iliac veins extending slightly above the IVC filter. CT angiography of the chest revealed multiple subsegmental pulmonary emboli in the right lower lobe.
title: Diagnosis and Management of Spontaneous Lumbar Venous Retroperitoneal Hematoma in Setting of Deep Venous Thrombosis: A Case Report and Algorithm

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old woman presented with intermittent pus discharge at the base of her chin for the past 3 years. She denied any tooth pain or swelling. She reported facial trauma while playing at school 4–5 years earlier; a cutaneous draining lesion appeared on the chin about 2 years after the injury. She had received several courses of oral antibiotics and had been evaluated by a dermatologist and an otorhinolaryngologist without lasting improvement.  

On extraoral examination, there was a 1-cm-diameter sinus tract on the chin rimmed by erythema; palpation elicited purulent exudate. Intraoral inspection revealed a slightly discolored mandibular right central incisor without visible caries or swelling. Pulp-vitality testing was positive for all mandibular incisors except the lower right central incisor. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined, unilocular periapical radiolucency measuring approximately 2 cm × 4 cm associated with the mandibular incisors. A computed tomography scan confirmed a radiolucent lesion involving the labial cortical bone at the apex of the mandibular right central incisor.
title: Dental Infection Mimicking Dermatological Lesion: Three Case Reports of Cutaneous Fistulae and Sinus Tracts on Face

case_prompt: A 46-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presented with a 7-day history of progressive left testicular pain and swelling accompanied by dysuria and intermittent chills. He denied hematuria, urethral discharge, fever, back pain, recent trauma, or prior urinary tract infections. There was no family history of coagulopathy, and no clinical concern for malignancy. In the emergency department, he was tachycardic (heart rate 121 beats/min) and had a leukocytosis (white-cell count 26,000 per μL). Urinalysis showed nitrites, white blood cells, and moderate bacteriuria, and urine culture grew Escherichia coli (negative for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and other sexually transmitted organisms). Scrotal ultrasonography demonstrated an enlarged, hypervascular left epididymis with normal Doppler flow in both testes. Computed tomography of the abdomen suggested possible left-sided pyelonephritis. He was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and doxycycline, but his symptoms worsened. Overnight, he developed a fever of 100.8°F and escalating left testicular pain and swelling, and therapy was broadened to cefepime. A repeat scrotal ultrasound showed a hypoechoic, heterogeneous left testicle with peripheral edema and no internal Doppler flow.
title: All pain, no gain: When epididymitis drops the ball

case_prompt: A 54-year-old man presented with four months of gradually increasing abdominal distension. He denied abdominal pain, bowel or bladder symptoms, and had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or other systemic illness. On examination, large firm to hard masses were palpable in both lumbar regions; there was no lower-limb edema. Ultrasonography showed large, well-defined hypoechoic masses in the bilateral perirenal spaces with distortion of the renal outlines, no hydronephrosis, and displacement of adjacent organs. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed large, homogeneous, hypodense, minimally enhancing masses in both perirenal spaces completely encasing the kidneys and causing scalloping of the renal cortex. The residual renal parenchyma had normal enhancement and excretion, and a few tiny renal calculi were noted on the noncontrast images. No enlarged intra-abdominal lymph nodes or ascites were present. Laboratory tests showed normal renal function.
title: Bilateral perirenal space fibromatosis with renal infiltration: case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old Caucasian man presented with three weeks of feeling unwell, a nonproductive cough, and constant upper abdominal discomfort, all beginning after a tooth extraction. He denied any changes in bowel or bladder habits. His medical history included only a subarachnoid aneurysm clipping seven years earlier. 

On examination, his pulse was 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation and temperature were normal. Auscultation revealed bronchial breathing at the left lung base, and his abdomen was tender in the epigastrium without rebound or guarding. 

Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 14,000/µl and a C-reactive protein level of 88 mg/dl; other blood tests were normal. A chest radiograph demonstrated an opacity at the left lung base. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed cavitating nodules in the left lower lobe and a small infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm.
title: Wegener's granulomatosis presenting as an abdominal aortic aneurysm: a case report

case_prompt: A 37-year-old man presented with three months of right-sided, ventilatory-dependent chest pain and a progressively enlarging mass on the anterior right hemithorax. He also described facial edema and neck vein distension. He had a 10-year history of smoking (20 cigarettes per day), quitting 8 years earlier; his mother died at age 35 of metastatic breast cancer. On examination, there was a painless, erythematous, infiltrative tumor over the right anterior chest wall, facial edema, and jugular venous distension. Laboratory studies showed hypergammaglobulinemia with elevated IgM, IgA, and IgG, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 85 mm/h. Contrast-enhanced chest MRI revealed an infiltrative retrosternal lesion extending into soft tissues and intercostal muscles between the first and fourth right costal cartilages. Surgical biopsy via thoracotomy demonstrated fusiform cell proliferation in curved bundles with foamy histiocytes, plasma cells, and multinucleated cells without atypical lymphocytes, consistent with an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT). Because the lesion was unresectable, prednisone (1 mg/kg) was started. After one month, the chest wall mass regressed, but facial edema and superior vena cava syndrome worsened. A PET/CT scan showed the retrosternal lesion with heterogeneous uptake (SUV 3.8) and new mediastinal lymphadenopathy with intense uptake (SUV 19.9).
title: ALK Negative Inflammatory Myofibroblastic Tumor Synchronous with Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma

case_prompt: A 55-year-old premenopausal woman underwent routine gynecologic examination, which revealed bilateral adnexal cysts. She had three prior vaginal births and three miscarriages, with no pelvic pain or menstrual irregularity. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 7.9 × 5.9 × 4.8 cm unilocular hypoechoic cyst with thin walls and minimal peripheral blood flow adjacent to the left ovary, classified as IOTA B1; the right adnexa contained a 3.4 × 2.7 × 2.1 cm hydrosalpinx. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 7.5 × 4.4 × 4.9 cm cystic lesion posterior to the left side of the uterus with wall enhancement; the left ovary appeared normal. Serum CA-125 and HE4 levels were within normal limits. No other abnormalities were noted on examination.
title: A Rare Case of Multiple Subserous Uterine Adenomyomas Misdiagnosed as an Ovarian Cyst, Diagnosed and Treated by Laparoscopy

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of a painful mass in her left latissimus dorsi that had gradually increased in size. There was no history of trauma. Physical examination revealed a solid 4–6 cm mass on the posterior aspect of the left shoulder; the overlying skin was normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.  
Ultrasound of the mass showed a heterogeneously echogenic intramuscular lesion in the latissimus dorsi with preservation of the normal fibrillary pattern and traversing continuous muscle fibers.  
MRI demonstrated a well-defined mass in the posterior shoulder within the latissimus dorsi that was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and homogeneously hyperintense on T2- and proton-density–weighted images. Linear hypointense strands corresponding to preserved muscle fibers were seen within the lesion. There was no hemorrhage or adjacent bone abnormality. After intravenous gadolinium, the lesion showed homogeneous but ill-defined enhancement, suggesting marked edema and an inflammatory process, although a neoplasm could not be excluded.
title: Proliferative myositis: case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
An 85-year-old man presented with left buttock pain radiating to his left leg, left foot drop, and gait disturbance of 4 weeks’ duration. Two months earlier, he had undergone a left posterior iliac bone marrow biopsy for evaluation of a suspected nasopharyngeal plasmacytoma. Immediately after the biopsy, he experienced severe left buttock pain radiating to the leg, treated with oral analgesics. Four weeks later, he noted onset of left foot drop and worsened gait disturbance without improvement on gabapentinoids, oral steroids, NSAIDs, or painkillers. 

His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, COPD, type II diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease for which he was taking aspirin. On examination, he was afebrile with normal infection markers and a hemoglobin level of 12.3 g/dL. There was mild swelling and tenderness over the left buttock; the straight-leg-raising test was positive at 30°. He had hypesthesia in the sciatic distribution and severe weakness (0/5) of the left tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, and peroneal muscles. 

Given the concern for either an intraspinal or extraspinal cause of sciatic palsy, an MRI of the lumbar spine and pelvis with intravenous contrast was obtained. Spine MRI showed a moderate left L3–L4 intraforaminal disc herniation, which seemed unlikely to account for the patient’s presentation. Pelvic MRI revealed a 4.5 × 3.2 × 3.0 cm soft-tissue mass adjacent to the left piriformis muscle, compressing the sciatic nerve, which was felt to represent either a hematoma or a pseudoaneurysm in the context of the recent biopsy.
title: Sciatic Nerve Palsy due to a Superior Gluteal Artery Pseudoaneurysm PostBone Marrow Biopsy: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 4-month-old boy was referred for right leukocoria noted by his parents for 1 week. Examination under anesthesia showed intraocular pressures of 13 mm Hg in the right eye and 16 mm Hg in the left eye, with normal anterior segments bilaterally. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a white vascularized retinal tumor in the temporal macula measuring 10 × 9 × 3.6 mm. Germline testing for RB1 was negative, and a baseline MRI of the brain and orbits was normal. The patient was diagnosed with unilateral Group B retinoblastoma of the right eye. He was treated with one session of intra-arterial chemotherapy (melphalan 4.8 mg), followed by three sessions of diode laser transpupillary thermotherapy at four- to six-week intervals, after which complete clinical regression of the primary tumor was achieved.

At 45 weeks after initial treatment, a new cyst-like retinal lesion was identified at the superior margin of the regressed tumor scar. Fundus photography showed a dome-shaped, translucent lesion at the edge of the scar. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated abnormal vascularity and leakage within the lesion. Optical coherence tomography revealed an irregularly thickened floor and dome-shaped roof with effacement of the normal retinal layers. Optical coherence tomography angiography showed abnormal blood vessels located primarily within the roof of the lesion in the superficial vascular complex.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Cyst-like recurrence of retinoblastoma diagnosed by multimodal imaging

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old man presented with a painless nodule on the dorsum of his tongue, present for 1 year. His medical and dental histories were noncontributory. He reported occasional pork consumption but denied trauma, bleeding, pain, or paresthesia. 

On intraoral examination, there was a 1 cm × 1 cm firm, non-tender, non-ulcerated, well-circumscribed, mucosal-colored mass on the dorsum of the tongue. Candidiasis with loss of papillae was noted on the dorsal tongue. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Routine hematologic tests were within normal limits.

A provisional diagnosis of fibroma was made, with a differential diagnosis that included lipoma, pleomorphic adenoma, mucocele, and rhabdomyoma. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia.
title: An asymptomatic tongue nodule

case_prompt: A 17-year-old female presented with a 2-year history of severe, poorly localized, crampy abdominal pain that began about 1 hour after meals and was accompanied by vomiting. The pain did not radiate and was alleviated by lying on her left side. Over this time, her body-mass index decreased from 25.7 to 20.1 kg/m², and her symptoms interfered with weight maintenance, concentration, social life, and education. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were normal, abdominal and pelvic examinations were unremarkable, and gynecological evaluation was normal. Repeated complete blood counts, liver-function tests, electrolytes, and arterial blood gases were within normal limits, and electrocardiography showed no abnormalities. Gastroesophageal reflux disease was suspected, but esophageal function testing and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy were unremarkable. Doppler ultrasonography of the abdominal vessels showed no abnormalities. A small-bowel follow-through was not performed due to resource limitations. An abdominal computed tomography scan with contrast was then obtained.
title: Challenges and pitfalls in diagnosing superior mesenteric artery syndrome: A case report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old Albanian girl with a 4-year history of epilepsy was referred for progressive neurological deterioration. She initially presented in early adolescence with generalized tonic–clonic seizures treated with valproic acid; levetiracetam was later added due to continued seizures. Over the past year she developed visual hallucinations, emotional disturbances, and irritability, for which fluoxetine was prescribed. Subsequently, she experienced cognitive decline, behavioral changes, dysarthria, and difficulty walking.

On admission, she weighed 40 kg, was disoriented, irritable, and nonverbal, and required assistance to stand. The remainder of her neurologic and systemic examinations was notable only for unsteady gait. Routine blood tests, including hemoglobin, platelet count, ESR, CRP, liver enzymes, urea, creatinine, acid–base status, and urinalysis, were all normal. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid analyses excluded infectious and immune-mediated etiologies. Electroencephalography showed diffuse low-voltage activity initially and, on follow-up, severe epileptic paroxysms bilaterally. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was normal. Owing to progressive decline and lack of response to antiepileptic drugs, plans were made for advanced genetic testing and an axillary skin biopsy.
title: Lafora disease: a case report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old Punjabi Pakistani boy presented with a 2-month history of high-grade, continuous fever with morning and evening spikes, rigors, chills, a persistent productive cough with scanty whitish sputum, anorexia, and moderate weight loss. Two years earlier, he had been treated for a pyogenic liver abscess with antibiotics and drainage. Over the past year, he had multiple episodes of acute gastroenteritis, urinary tract infections, and respiratory infections. His parents were consanguineous; his brother and two cousins had similar histories and were edentulous.

On examination, temperature was 101 °F, pulse 116 /min, blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20 /min. He appeared pale with poor oral hygiene and diffuse transgradient hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles. The spleen was just palpable; lung auscultation revealed coarse crepitations bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, total leukocyte count 11 400/µL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 68 mm/h; liver enzymes and alkaline phosphatase were mildly elevated. Three consecutive sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Stool examination, thick and thin blood smears for malaria, typhidot IgM/IgG, bone marrow examination, and serologies for HBsAg, anti-HCV, VDRL, and HIV were all negative. Blood cultures grew Pseudomonas. Chest radiography demonstrated soft-tissue opacities throughout both lung zones. A dental orthopantomogram showed marked alveolar bone atrophy.
title: Papillon-Lèfevre syndrome with palmoplantar keratoderma and periodontitis, a rare cause of pyrexia of unknown origin: a case report

case_prompt: A 36-year-old woman, never smoker and with no significant medical history, presented with a several-month history of persistent cough, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, and intermittent small-volume haemoptysis. Physical examination was unremarkable. Chest radiography and high-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated a soft-tissue mass arising from the right lower lobe bronchus and abutting the middle lobe bronchus. Bronchoscopic and CT-guided biopsies revealed inflammation and granulation tissue with some evidence of squamous metaplasia but no malignant cells. An FDG-PET scan showed a 70 mm × 80 mm endobronchial mass with an SUV of 6.4 and a subcentimetre subcarinal lymph node with an SUV of 4.5. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated an FEV1 of 1.93 L (63% predicted), FVC of 2.43 L (69% predicted), TLCO of 4.72 mmol min–1 kPa–1 (52% predicted), and evidence of obstruction in the right lower lobe.
title: A rare solitary and endobronchial pulmonary hyalinising granuloma requiring bilobectomy

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old Trinidadian woman presented with intermittent left-sided chest pain for 3 days, worsened by exertion, and associated with shortness of breath. Over the preceding year, she had experienced headache, fatigue, a 15–20-lb weight loss, and bilateral lower extremity pain. Physical examination revealed numerous facial xanthelasmas. 

A chest radiograph showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette, possible pulmonary vascular congestion, and subcentimeter calcifications attributed to old granulomatous disease. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated small pericardial and left pleural effusions and a large left upper-lobe paramediastinal mass with extensive mediastinal and supraclavicular adenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed soft-tissue infiltration surrounding both kidneys. Noncontrast and contrast CT of the head identified enhancing lesions in the right frontal cortex and right posterior cerebellum with mild mass effect; these were confirmed on brain MRI. A whole-body bone scan showed abnormal uptake in the seventh thoracic vertebral body and intense uptake in the distal femurs and tibias bilaterally.

CT-guided biopsy of a superior mediastinal lymph node revealed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma positive for cytokeratins AE1/AE3 and TTF1, compatible with a lung primary. The patient was referred for dermatologic biopsy of a right cheek xanthelasma.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Erdheim-Chester Disease With Concurrent Lung Adenocarcinoma

case_prompt: A 50-year-old African-American woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and gastroesophageal reflux disease presented postoperatively after elective anterior lumbar interbody fusion for spinal stenosis. In the postanesthesia care unit, she developed sudden shortness of breath with mild hypoxemia but denied chest pain, palpitations, hemoptysis, wheezing, leg pain, or swelling. Temperature was 98.1°F, blood pressure 164/86 mmHg, heart rate 96 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Examination showed an obese woman in mild distress with fine inspiratory crackles at both lung bases and no jugular venous distension. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with nonspecific ST changes. Laboratory studies revealed a WBC count of 13,700/µL, hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, platelet count 293 K/mm³, creatinine 1.47 mg/dL (baseline 1.72 mg/dL), and bicarbonate 24 mg/dL. A chest radiograph demonstrated widening of the mediastinum compared with a film obtained 10 days earlier. Since aortic dissection was a major concern, a labetalol infusion was initiated and an emergent chest CTA was performed.
final_diagnosis_raw: Azygos continuation of the inferior vena cava
title: An Unusual Benign Cause of an Alarming Finding on Chest-X ray: A Case Report of Widened Mediastinum due to Rare Congenital Abnormality (Azygos Vein Continuation of Inferior Vena Cava)

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old woman with a history of multinodular goiter was seen in routine follow-up after noting a recent growth on the right side of her neck. She had no other significant personal or family history. On examination, there was a solid, partly exophytic nodule in the right thyroid lobe that was mobile with swallowing and non-tender. There was no dysphonia, dysphagia, or palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed normal TSH, free T4, and free T3; thyroglobulin, calcitonin, thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and thyroglobulin antibodies were negative. Ultrasonography and CT imaging demonstrated a 3.0-cm hypoechogenic, heterogeneous nodule in the right thyroid lobe, abutting the sternocleidomastoid muscle and internal carotid artery. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was reported as TIR 3B (indeterminate follicular lesion). The patient underwent a total thyroidectomy with central compartment (level VI) lymphadenectomy. The postoperative course was uneventful. 

Histopathologic examination revealed a 2.3-cm solid, whitish nodule with irregular margins extending into perithyroid soft tissue. Microscopically, the tumor contained two intermingled components: a mesenchymal spindle-cell proliferation comprising approximately 70% of the lesion with a fibromatosis-like (desmoid) appearance, and an epithelial component comprising approximately 30% of the lesion showing features of papillary thyroid carcinoma. The lesion was staged as pT3b N0.
final_diagnosis_raw: papillary thyroid carcinoma with fibromatosis-like stroma
title: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with fibromatosis-like stroma: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old Filipino woman presented with a three-month history of multiple bilateral tender red nodules over the distal lower limbs. She felt well overall and denied fevers, weight loss, chills, or preceding infections. She had no history of tuberculosis exposure, animal contact, smoking, alcohol use, or intravenous drug use. Her past medical history was unremarkable, and she was not taking any medications or supplements.

On examination, there were tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules on the lower legs with angular purpura and bilateral ankle effusions; no other joints were inflamed. The abdomen was soft and non-tender.

Laboratory studies showed normal urinalysis, complete blood count, metabolic panel, and creatine kinase. Inflammatory markers were elevated (ESR 44 mm/hr, CRP 10 mg/dl). Testing for antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigen, cryoglobulin, cryofibrinogen, rheumatoid factor, anticardiolipin antibody, β-2 glycoprotein antibody, lupus anticoagulant, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, hepatitis B and C, HIV, measles, mumps, rubella, and interferon-gamma release assay were all negative.
