An incisional biopsy of a nodule showed fibrinoid necrosis of an arteriole with a perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, neutrophils, histiocytes, and eosinophils extending into the subcutis. Special stains (PUTT and ABPAS) demonstrated no pathogens.

Whole-body PET-CT and CT abdominal angiography revealed no systemic vessel involvement or end-organ ischemia.
title: The spectrum of cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa. A case report of two contrasting cases and review of the literature

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old woman was admitted with a 3-day history of refusal to eat, glazed eyes, and abnormal behavior. Three days prior, she had developed sudden psychomotor changes without clear precipitant.  
She was born by cesarean delivery at 33 weeks’ gestation, weighing 3.8 kg (+1 SD), length 48 cm (–1 SD). Her anterior fontanelle closed at age 5 years. She remained markedly shorter than peers throughout childhood, with relative overweight, and experienced occasional muscle tetany and limb numbness. School performance was mildly below average. Menarche occurred at age 13 with subsequent irregular cycles (28–90 days).  
Her parents are healthy, nonconsanguineous, and she has two unaffected sisters. There is no family history of endocrine or genetic disorders.  
On examination, blood pressure was 104/78 mmHg. Height was 132 cm (–5 SD), weight 40 kg (–2 SD), and head circumference 48 cm. Distinctive facial features included cheek freckles, high anterior hairline, sparse scalp hair, prominent forehead, depressed nasal bridge, and low‐set ears. Dental exam showed partial dentition and a small mandible. Limbs were stubby with small hands and feet and bilaterally short fourth toes. There was no scoliosis or cubitus valgus. Gynecologic exam revealed Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair development. After partial correction of her metabolic disturbances, her MMSE score was 28/30.  
Laboratory studies showed AST 94 U/L, ALT 70 U/L, potassium 2.57 mmol/L, chloride 96.4 mmol/L, corrected calcium 1.06 mmol/L, magnesium 0.45 mmol/L, and phosphorus 1.86 mmol/L.  
Noncontrast cranial CT demonstrated symmetric calcifications in the cerebellar hemispheres, frontotemporal–parietal lobes, basal ganglia, and thalamus. Skeletal radiographs revealed cortical thickening and medullary narrowing of long bones, short phalanges of the little finger, and short, small fourth and fifth metatarsals and phalanges. Pelvic ultrasound showed a small anteverted uterus with uniform endometrium and normal ovaries.
title: Clinical and genetic features of Kenny-Caffey syndrome type 2 with multiple electrolyte disturbances: A case report

case_prompt: A 34-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of painful, progressive diminution of vision in both eyes, accompanied by redness and whitish corneal opacities. He had been applying topical antibiotics for 3 days. He reported a 10-year history of heavy alcohol use and multiple prior episodes of hemoptysis. On examination, he appeared severely malnourished and had multiple oral ulcers with difficulty in swallowing. Visual acuity in both eyes was light perception with accurate projection of rays in all quadrants. The eyelids and adnexa were normal. There was diffuse conjunctival congestion and mild chemosis. Corneal examination showed total corneal melt with fluorescein uptake, peripheral thinning, and adjacent limbitis in both eyes, without neovascularization. Details of the anterior chamber and fundus were obscured. B-scan ultrasonography of both eyes was unremarkable. Corneal scrapings were sent for Gram and KOH stains, as well as bacterial and fungal cultures, and tear PCR for herpes simplex virus. Blood tests, including a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide, cytoplasmic and perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, serum calcium, and ACE level; peripheral blood smear; stool examination; Mantoux test; chest radiography; and serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis were all inconclusive for a causative etiology.
title: Bilateral liquefactive corneal necrosis: a rare and devastating complication of vitamin A deficiency in the adult

case_prompt: A 46-year-old man with HIV/AIDS (CD4 count, 100 cells/μL; viral load, 38 541 copies/mL) and poor antiretroviral adherence presented with one day of binocular diplopia and a three-month history of intermittent occipital headaches. He reported occasional fevers and night sweats but denied respiratory symptoms. Six days earlier, lumbar puncture had shown mild monocytic pleocytosis, normal protein and glucose, and a negative Gram stain; brain MRI and MR angiography were unrevealing, and he received empirical ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and acyclovir. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Neurologic findings included left ptosis, exotropia, and impaired adduction of the left eye. Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC, 2.6 × 10^3/μL), neutropenia (ANC, 1.4 × 10^3/μL), normocytic anemia, and mildly elevated transaminases (ALT 63 U/L; AST 45 U/L). Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Repeat lumbar puncture showed 8 WBC/μL (88% lymphocytes), 13 RBC/μL, protein 45 mg/dL, glucose 52 mg/dL, and a negative Gram stain. Brain MRI demonstrated an acute lacunar infarct with restricted diffusion in the left paramedian midbrain at the oculomotor nucleus. Chest CT with contrast revealed innumerable tiny bilateral miliary nodules, predominantly in the upper lobes, raising concern for miliary tuberculosis versus fungal or malignant etiologies.
title: Ischemic brain infarcts and vasculitis in histoplasmosis of the central nervous system: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man with a history of a mediastinal mixed germ cell tumor treated by resection and combination chemotherapy presented 6 months after completing therapy with easy fatigability and generalized weakness. On examination, he was pale without lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 3,000/µL, and platelets 20,000/µL; the peripheral smear showed no blasts. Bone marrow aspiration was a dry tap. Trephine biopsy revealed blast infiltration; blasts were negative for myeloperoxidase and leukocyte common antigen but positive for CD61, consistent with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia. He received daunorubicin and cytarabine. Six months later, he developed a single 4×4 cm right cervical lymph node. Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the node and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination were performed.  

Microscopic examination of the FNA smears revealed numerous blasts 2–3 times the size of mature lymphocytes, with scant to moderate granular cytoplasm, fine chromatin, and single or multiple prominent nucleoli. Some blasts had nuclear notches, indentations, and folds. Cells were mostly single but formed small clumps reminiscent of marrow particles. A few larger cells exhibited moderate to abundant cytoplasm with lobated, indented, or horseshoe-shaped nuclei. Bi- to multinucleated cells reminiscent of megakaryocytes were present, along with numerous anucleate pale-blue cytoplasmic fragments.  

Cytocentrifuge preparations of the CSF showed blasts with scant to moderate granular cytoplasm, irregular nuclear margins, fine granular chromatin, and prominent nucleoli, as well as binucleate and multinucleate forms.
title: Cyto-morphological features of extramedullary acute megakaryoblastic leukemia on fine needle aspiration and cerebrospinal fluid cytology: A case report

case_prompt: A 57-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a cranial bone lesion incidentally found on brain CT during workup for a thyroid tumor. Two months earlier, he had undergone facial nerve decompression for right facial palsy. He was asymptomatic and alert. On examination, there was a hard, non-tender protuberance over the left parietal region without skin discoloration or hair changes. Laboratory tests, including blood counts and tumor markers, were within normal limits. Noncontrast brain CT showed a 3 cm iso-dense lesion involving the left parietal bone with cortical thinning and a lytic appearance. MR imaging demonstrated that the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on diffusion-weighted imaging, and showed uniform, faint enhancement after gadolinium.
title: Fibrous granulation mimicking cranial intraosseous tumor

case_prompt:
A 22-month-old Holstein–Friesian bull was referred for recurrence of fever and new neurological signs 24 days after treatment for bronchopneumonia due to Trueperella pyogenes. On examination, the bull was severely obtunded, with low head carriage, poor appetite, rectal temperature 38.2 °C, severe bradycardia (32 bpm), and a normal respiratory rate. Neurologic findings included generalized ataxia, hypersalivation, mild tongue prolapse, dropped jaw, dysphagia, a mild right head tilt, and right-sided ptosis. Plasma total protein was increased at 90 g/l and the glutaraldehyde clotting time was shortened (4 min). Venous pH was slightly decreased at 7.37; all other blood parameters were within reference ranges.  
Cerebrospinal fluid collected from the atlanto-occipital site was colourless and slightly turbid, with 2437 cells/µl (reference <10 cells/µl) showing 59% neutrophils, 26% lymphocytes, 9% eosinophils, and 6% monocytes. Protein concentration in CSF was 3.1 g/l (reference <0.75 g/l).  
Pre-contrast CT of the brain showed an enlarged hypophysis occupying the sella turcica with heterogeneous attenuation higher than surrounding parenchyma (left side: 75.6 ± 17 HU; right side: 94.2 ± 16 HU). Post-contrast images 100 s after iohexol injection revealed increased attenuation of the right hypophysis (108.1 ± 19 HU) and an irregular central cavity in the right half with low attenuation (77 ± 16 HU).  
A radiographic diagnosis of a cavitary lesion at the centre of the right side of the hypophysis was made. The most likely aetiology of the lesion was an abscess. Differential diagnoses of the cavitary lesion including a Rathke’s cleft cyst, haematoma or neoplasm were considered less likely because of the asymmetry of the lesion, the pre-contrast attenuation values and the clinical findings.
title: Computed tomographic findings and treatment of a bull with pituitary gland abscess

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old man presented with a sudden episode of hematemesis. He had no prior medical history, did not smoke or drink alcohol, and denied use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.  
On examination, his vital signs were stable. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with no organomegaly. Rectal examination was negative for melena. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 11 g/dL (baseline 13 g/dL).  
Upper endoscopy revealed a 4 cm yellowish submucosal mass in the gastric antrum with an ulcerated surface and a positive pillow sign on compression.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-circumscribed, hypodense submucosal gastric mass without lymphadenopathy.  
Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a 4 cm, homogeneous, hyperechoic lesion arising from the third layer of the gastric wall, with no perigastric lymphadenopathy.  
Mucosal biopsy of the lesion was negative.
title: Gastrointestinal bleeding as an initial manifestation of gastric lipoma: Case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: 24‐year‐old man with 2‐year history of right lateral knee snapping and recurrent discomfort. Snapping was elicited on active extension and reproducible with direct pressure over the posterolateral knee; there was no history of trauma. He retained full active range of motion; an audible and palpable snap occurred when moving from flexion to extension, but passive motion was not consistently provocative. Cabot sign was positive; other special tests were negative. Plain radiographs showed a round osseous structure in the posterolateral joint. CT and MRI revealed an ovoid bone posterior and superior to the musculo‐tendinous junction of the popliteus muscle, articulating non-cartilaginously with the lateral femoral condyle; the popliteus tendon appeared inflamed. A steroid injection at the snapping point provided no relief.
title: A symptomatic cyamella in the popliteus tendon causing snapping knee: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old man with a 10-year history of immunoglobulin G4–related disease affecting the liver, biliary tract, and pancreas (controlled with prednisone 5 mg daily) and type 2 myotonic dystrophy presented with recurrent episodes of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). His VT initially responded transiently to antiarrhythmic agents (amiodarone, sotalol, flecainide) but recurred despite multiple radiofrequency catheter ablations and a stellate ganglion block. He received a primary-prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillator; at each VT episode, transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF of 25% that normalized within 48 hours of VT termination.

Over two years, VT became refractory to medical and interventional therapies. During a recent VT episode unresponsive to defibrillation, he developed cardiac arrest requiring extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and was placed on peripheral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Initial echocardiography on ECMO showed severe biventricular failure without pericardial involvement. Endomyocardial biopsy from the right ventricle revealed areas of fibrosis but was inconclusive for myocarditis; immunohistochemical staining demonstrated only occasional IgG4-positive plasma cells.
title: Fulminant Myocarditis in Patients With Autoimmune Disease That Requires Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Support

case_prompt: A 71-year-old man with a history of prediabetes and renal insufficiency presented in early 2021 with one week of blood with wiping and anal pain. He reported three loose stools per day for two weeks, beginning three days after his first dose of the Moderna mRNA-1273 COVID-19 vaccine; his bowel habits were previously normal. On examination, an anal fissure was noted; his pain resolved with topical therapy, but he continued to have occasional rectal bleeding. Eighteen days after the first dose, he received his second vaccine and subsequently developed up to 12 watery bowel movements daily, including four at night. One week later, in the gastroenterology clinic, he denied recent antibiotic use, travel, sick contacts, or other exposures; he used NSAIDs rarely and had no family history of colon cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Laboratory tests showed a creatinine of 1.22 mg/dL (normal 0.67–1.17), a markedly elevated fecal calprotectin of 2634 mg/kg (normal <50), negative tissue transglutaminase IgA, and negative C. difficile and gastroenteritis PCR panels. Five days after that visit, an urgent colonoscopy demonstrated continuous, edematous, erythematous, granular mucosa in the sigmoid colon, with tortuosity and edema that required a smaller-diameter endoscope to reach the cecum; the terminal ileum appeared normal, and mild edema and erythema extended from the cecum to the descending colon. Biopsies were obtained throughout the colon.
title: De Novo Diagnosis of Lymphocytic Colitis After SARS-CoV-2 Vaccination

case_prompt: A 45-year-old woman presented with sudden onset of progressive weakness and numbness in both lower extremities and difficulty initiating urination. Five hours after symptom onset, she became unable to walk. She reported no back pain, fever, trauma, or chronic medication use. On initial evaluation, her heart rate was 94 beats per minute and blood pressure was 193/104 mm Hg. Neurologic examination revealed normal mental status, grade 0/5 strength in both lower limbs, and paresthesia below the umbilicus; sensation to fine touch, pain, temperature, and vibration was completely absent below the umbilical level. Deep tendon reflexes were absent at the knees and ankles, while upper-limb reflexes were normal; bilateral Babinski signs were positive. A noncontrast MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a well-demarcated, oval extramedullary lesion at the T9 level ventral to the spinal cord, isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. The lesion was initially interpreted as a possible tumoral mass, and conservative management was attempted without improvement. Twenty hours after onset, she was referred for further care, and repeat neurologic assessment confirmed flaccid paraplegia with complete sensory loss below T10. An emergency laminectomy was planned to decompress the spinal cord.
title: Spontaneous thoracic ventral spinal subdural hematoma mimicking a tumoral lesion: a case report

case_prompt: A 63‐year‐old African American woman with a history of invasive ductal breast carcinoma treated by lumpectomy in 2005 and 2008 presented in 2009 with right wrist and hand pain. Initial radiographs showed mild osteoarthritis of the interphalangeal joints, and conservative treatment yielded no improvement. Electrophysiologic evaluation suggested cubital tunnel syndrome, and surgical release was performed without symptomatic relief. She subsequently developed progressive neck pain, right upper extremity pain, and weakness. Cervical spine MRI showed degenerative spondylosis without neural compression. Dedicated MRI of the right shoulder and brachial plexus revealed a 2.4 × 3.9 × 5.5 cm soft tissue mass in the axilla and along the brachial plexus. The lesion was heterogeneously enhancing, hypointense on T1‐weighted images, and hyperintense on T2‐weighted images, displacing adjacent neurovascular structures.
title: Radiologic manifestation of the malignant peripheral nerve sheet tumor involving the brachial plexus

case_prompt: A 14-year-old adolescent male presented with a 2-week history of persistent headache, 5 days of projectile vomiting and neck stiffness, and a single episode of generalized tonic–clonic seizure lasting 10 minutes. On neurologic examination, papilledema was noted, and there was right-sided hemiparesis (power 2/5) with hyperactive deep tendon reflexes and a positive Babinski sign. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed a 6.2×5.2×4 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass centered in the left lateral ventricle, with extension into the ipsilateral parietooccipital white matter, surrounding vasogenic edema, and a 6 mm midline shift. MR spectroscopy demonstrated reduced N-acetyl-aspartate, elevated choline, and a lactate peak. There was no evidence of spinal cord involvement.
title: Choroid plexus carcinoma in an adolescent male: a case report

case_prompt: An 18-year-old boy with a 4-year history of transfusion-dependent thalassemia major presented with one month of back pain and progressive bilateral lower-limb weakness. On examination, strength was 2/5 in the knee extensors and in ankle plantar- and dorsiflexors; deep-tendon reflexes were 4+ at knees and ankles; plantar responses were extensor bilaterally; sensation and bladder function were normal. The liver was palpable, and there was a splenectomy scar. Complete blood count showed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, hematocrit 27.6%, red-cell count 3.32 × 10^6/µL, and platelets 395 × 10^3/µL. Peripheral smear revealed anisopoikilocytosis, primarily normocytic normochromic cells with occasional macrocytes, polychromasia, nucleated red cells (68% of total nucleated cells), and target cells. Chest radiography demonstrated widening of diploic spaces of the thoracic ribs with thinning of the inner table and prominent anterior rib widening. MRI of the thoracic spine revealed a large, homogeneously enhancing paravertebral epidural mass from T4 to T10 that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and caused marked obliteration of the subarachnoid space with spinal cord compression.
title: Extramedullary Hematopoiesis Presenting with Thoracic Spinal Cord Compression in a Young Adult with Thalassemia Major: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old G2P1 woman with a dichorionic twin pregnancy at 35+5 weeks was brought for an emergency cesarean section because of failure to progress. She had a 7-year history of hyperthyroidism treated with propylthiouracil 50 mg twice daily throughout pregnancy; her free T4 level had ranged from 1 to 3 ng/dL, and 6 days before surgery it was 2 ng/dL. She was diagnosed with gestational hypertension at 24 weeks, with systolic pressures rising from 145 mmHg to 175 mmHg by 35 weeks; proteinuria was absent. 

On arrival in the operating room, she reported abdominal pain and mild nausea. Vital signs were notable for heart rate 124 beats/min, blood pressure 210/117 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. During preparation for spinal anesthesia she developed dyspnea; oxygen saturation fell to 90% despite 10 L/min via mask, and arterial PaO2 was 58 mmHg. Electrolytes were within normal limits. Blood pressure acutely rose to 240/120 mmHg with heart rate 200 beats/min, and she became irritable with altered consciousness. General anesthesia was induced with propofol and succinylcholine, and a cesarean delivery was performed; two infants were delivered with 1- and 5-minute Apgar scores of 7 and 9, respectively. 

Postoperatively, she was transferred to the ICU. She developed fever, persistent tachycardia, and diarrhea. Chest radiography showed bilateral pulmonary edema, and echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with acute decompensated heart failure and a preserved ejection fraction.
title: Thyroid Storm Superimposed on Gestational Hypertension: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 74-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive bitemporal hemianopia and decreased visual acuity. She had a history of chronic arterial hypertension. On examination, visual field testing confirmed bitemporal hemianopia, and visual acuity was diminished. Routine endocrine evaluation, including thyroid‐stimulating hormone, free T3 and T4, growth hormone, insulin‐like growth factor‐1, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, prolactin, luteinizing hormone, and follicle‐stimulating hormone, revealed basal anterior pituitary hormone levels within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary region showed a well-defined, homogeneous, cystic sellar lesion measuring 30 × 15 × 17 mm, isointense with cerebrospinal fluid on all sequences, with suprasellar extension. The lesion had thin walls, no solid components or calcifications, and caused superior displacement of the optic chiasm, with the pituitary gland and stalk flattened against the dorsum sellae.
title: Endoscopic transnasal transsphenoidal management of sellar/suprasellar arachnoid cyst: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman presented with 3 months of heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea. Her medical history included asthma, depression, and anxiety; she had previously undergone a cesarean section. Family history was noncontributory. On examination, the uterus was enlarged, mobile, and otherwise unremarkable.  
Pelvic ultrasound and CT scan showed a thickened endometrium and peritoneal thickening, with no ascites, lymphadenopathy, or distant metastases. Serum CA125 was 23 kU/L (normal range).  
Hysteroscopy revealed a diffusely thickened endometrium without distinct masses, and dilation and curettage yielded predominantly benign endometrium with two small fragments of poorly preserved epithelioid tumor. These cells were arranged in trabeculae within fibrous stroma and stained positively for AE1/3, calretinin, and CD10. Based on these findings, the lesion was interpreted as a uterine tumor similar to an ovarian sex cord tumor, and the patient was scheduled for exploratory laparotomy with possible ovarian preservation.  
At laparotomy, there were opaque ascites, omental caking, and multiple small nodules studding the pelvic peritoneum; the uterus and adnexa appeared macroscopically normal. A total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingectomy, and omentectomy were performed with optimal cytoreduction.  
Histologic examination of the uterus and cervix showed patchy infiltration by an epithelioid malignancy eroding through the myometrium and endometrium, with extensive lymphovascular and perineural invasion and involvement of the fallopian tube serosa. The omental tumor measured up to 70 mm and displayed mixed tubulopapillary, trabecular, and solid architecture.  
Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated positivity for calretinin, CK5/6, D2-40, and CK7 (focally CK20), and negativity for PAX-8 and Claudin-4. There was loss of nuclear staining for BAP1.
title: Diffuse Peritoneal Malignant Mesothelioma Presenting with Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: Case Report

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with severe dorsal pain requiring morphine. He was a non-smoker, non-drinker, and had worked as a metalworker for 25 years. On examination he appeared asthenic and had right hemithoracic pain with bilateral paresthesia and dysesthesia in the C8–D1 dermatomes; otherwise the examination was unremarkable.

A chest radiograph was non-diagnostic. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a 1.5 cm nonspecific nodule in the right upper lobe, a right-sided pleural effusion, and bilateral subpleural thickening adjacent to the ninth thoracic vertebra. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 12,000/mm3 with normal eosinophils, normal renal function, and minimal cholestasis. Bronchoscopy showed inflammation of the right lower-lobe bronchus but biopsies were non-informative. 

Thoracentesis yielded a sterile exudative lymphocytic effusion (85% lymphocytes, 10% neutrophils, 5% monocytes) without malignant cells. During surgical resection of the pulmonary nodule, pleural biopsies revealed a dense perivascular inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells without definitive vasculitis. Examination of the nodule showed a central necrotic focus surrounded by palisading histiocytes; multinucleated histiocytes formed true granulomas within the wall of an adjacent pulmonary artery.
title: Wegener Granulomatosis Revealed by Pleural Effusion

case_prompt: A 12-year-old female presented with sudden-onset right shoulder pain following a traction injury to her right arm. The pain was diffuse, relieved by rest, and exacerbated by movement. Over the next two months, the pain intensified and persisted despite rest. Radiographs of the shoulder revealed a lesion in the proximal humerus without evidence of recent fracture. On outpatient examination one month later, there was increased volume of the proximal right humerus with a palpable, indurated mass. Shoulder abduction was limited to 60°, while internal and external rotation were preserved. Comparative radiographs and computed tomography of the shoulder showed a cystic lesion in the proximal humerus with sclerotic margins, cortical thinning, and internal septations; the expansile, multilobulated tumor measured approximately 5 × 3 cm. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a heterogeneous cystic lesion confined to the humeral head, measuring 4.5 × 4.1 × 5.1 cm, with thin septations, fluid-fluid levels, cortical thinning, intra-articular fluid, and surrounding soft-tissue edema. A clinical suspicion of a bone tumor was raised, and an incisional biopsy and metastatic bone survey were scheduled.
title: Chondroblastoma of the Proximal Humerus in a 12-years-old Female: A Case Report and a Review of the Literature.

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old man was referred for treatment of acute appendicitis. During his evaluation, an incidental renal mass was detected on computed tomography. The patient was asymptomatic with no clinical signs, and routine blood tests were normal. 

Plain CT demonstrated a 30 × 28 × 25 mm, homogeneously slight hyperattenuating renal mass (CT number 49 HU). Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT showed slight, gradual, and homogeneous enhancement in the mass without fat, calcification, or cystic elements. 

On MRI, the mass was located in the renal medulla and showed homogeneous low signal intensity on T2-weighted images and fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, with internal areas of mildly high signal intensity but no obvious capsular structure. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed homogeneous low signal intensity, and the apparent diffusion coefficient map showed high signal intensity. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI again demonstrated slight, gradual, and homogeneous enhancement of the mass.
title: A case of renomedullary interstitial cell tumor: Radiologic-pathologic correlation

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old boy presented with a 2-day history of a painful vesicular skin eruption accompanied by low-grade fever and sore throat. His history was notable for adrenoleukodystrophy treated 12 years earlier with two myeloablative umbilical cord transplants, resulting in durable donor engraftment and chronic eczematous graft-versus-host disease managed with topical tacrolimus and oral methylprednisolone. The family increased his hydrocortisone from 5 mg three times daily to 30 mg three times daily when the rash worsened.

On examination, vesicles involved the scalp, face, axillae, antecubital fossae, inguinal folds, penis, scrotum, buttocks, and dorsal hands, all corresponding to sites of known chronic GVHD. He was afebrile; complete blood count and metabolic panel were normal. He was started on intravenous acyclovir and continued on hydrocortisone, 30 mg three times daily.

On hospital day 2, dusky violaceous macules appeared on the palms, soles, and hard palate without targetoid lesions. A punch biopsy from the right arm revealed a prominent lymphocytic interface dermatitis with dyskeratotic keratinocytes at all levels, superficial epidermal necrosis with neutrophilic aggregates, and a superficial to mid-dermal perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells, and rare eosinophils. No herpes viral cytopathic changes were noted.

Coxsackievirus A and B serum titers, enterovirus and herpes simplex virus cultures from vesicle fluid, and direct fluorescent antibody testing for HSV and varicella zoster virus from vesicle fluid were negative.
title: A case of eczema coxsackium with erythema multiforme–like histopathology in a 14-year-old boy with chronic graft-versus-host disease

case_prompt: A 28‐year‐old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 2‐year history of left hip pain on walking, which had worsened over the past few months. She denied fever, chills, weight loss, or recent trauma. On examination, left hip range of motion was limited and painful, and there was a poorly defined, renitent, 4‐cm swelling in the left groin without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13 g/dL, eosinophils 800/µL, and C‐reactive protein 56 mg/L. A pelvic radiograph revealed a mildly expansile lytic lesion in the periacetabular region of the left iliac bone with scalloped medial wing erosion and scattered hyperdense foci suggesting intrapelvic extension; the femoral head and neck were intact. Contrast‐enhanced pelvic CT confirmed a multiloculated, expansile lytic process of the left acetabulum and ilium with a honeycomb appearance, peripheral enhancement, calcifications, cortical destruction, periosteal reaction, adjacent muscle infiltration, and a communicating subcutaneous collection; the sacroiliac joint and femoral head were preserved. MRI demonstrated multiple small hyperintense T2‐weighted cystic areas in the iliac wing and supraacetabular soft tissues, heterogenous signal in the proximal femur without bone invasion, and no sacroiliac or sacral involvement.
title: Osseous hydatid disease: A mimic of other skeletal pathologies

case_prompt: A 12-year-old girl presented with 5 days of fever, right lateral-cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy, and frontoparietal headache. Her medical history was unremarkable; she had no pets and no recent travel. On examination, she had a 3 cm tender right lateral-cervical swelling with overlying erythema. Laboratory evaluation showed a white blood cell count of 16.2×10^3/µL (12.8×10^3/µL neutrophils) with normal C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; an oropharyngeal swab was negative. Ultrasound of the neck demonstrated multiple reactive lymph nodes without central necrosis and additional reactive nodes in the left cervical and bilateral inguinal regions. She was discharged on a 14-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate, with initial improvement in lymphadenopathy and fever. Two days after completing antibiotics, she returned with recurrent severe headache and cervical swelling and was admitted. Physical examination again revealed right cervical swelling and noted a new 2 cm left parietal-occipital scalp swelling. Repeat blood counts and inflammatory markers were normal. Because of the scalp lesion, contrast-enhanced cranial magnetic resonance imaging was performed, revealing a 10 mm area of skull erosion in the left temporoparietal region. A whole-body bone scan excluded additional sites of osteomyelitis. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 1 cm round hypoechoic lesion in the spleen consistent with a granuloma.
title: Osteomyelitis in Cat-Scratch Disease: A Never-Ending Dilemma—A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old man was referred with a 6-day history of progressive neurologic symptoms and an abnormal brain MRI. He initially noted weakness and paresthesia of the right upper extremity that gradually extended to the left arm and both lower limbs. On day 3, he experienced haziness of vision in the right eye with pain on lateral gaze and several generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

On examination he was alert and afebrile. Neurologic findings included right visual acuity of 20/200 with a central scotoma and papillitis on fundoscopy, jerk nystagmus on lateral gaze, decreased muscle strength (right 3/5, left 4/5), +1 deep-tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, and a mild ataxic gait with intact sensation. He was started on valproate.

Laboratory studies showed normal CBC, blood glucose, electrolytes, liver and kidney function tests, and urinalysis; ESR was 15 mm/h. Serologic tests for HIV, HCV, EBV, HZV, Borrelia, and Toxoplasma were negative; tuberculosis skin test and collagen-vascular workup were negative; chest radiograph was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid had 2 RBCs, 0 WBCs, protein 125 mg/dL, glucose 50 mg/dL (serum 110 mg/dL), LDH 43 U/mL, and positive oligoclonal bands. Visual-evoked potentials in the right eye and left-sided sensory-evoked potentials were prolonged. Cervical spine MRI was normal.

Brain MRI demonstrated multiple large, round lesions in the right centrum semiovale and periventricular left occipital region extending to the splenium of the corpus callosum. These had central T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, peripheral T2 hypointense rims, associated severe vasogenic edema, heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement, but no mass effect or midline shift.

Differential diagnoses included acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, multifocal glioma, metastasis, vasculitis, lymphoma, lymphoproliferative disease, and tumefactive multiple sclerosis. A stereotactic brain biopsy was recommended but was refused by the patient and his family.
title: Multiple Large Tumefactive MS Plaques in a Young Man: A Diagnostic Enigma and Therapeutic Challenge

case_prompt: An 83-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of vaginal bleeding. She had a similar bleeding episode six years earlier, when an endometrial polyp was diagnosed on biopsy. Her medical history included pulmonary emboli, hypertension, osteoarthritis, gout, and a cardiac pacemaker. On examination, there was active bleeding from the cervix. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an endometrial thickness of 13 mm with multiple cystic foci and polypoid formations; both ovaries were atrophic without masses. Diagnostic hysteroscopy with polypectomy and endometrial curettage was performed. Histologic examination revealed adenocarcinoma infiltrating the surface of an endometrial polyp, characterized by papillary and micropapillary formations and eosinophilic cytoplasm; there was no necrosis. On initial morphologic assessment, high-grade serous carcinoma and clear cell carcinoma were considered.
journal: Turkish Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Epidermal growth factor receptor-mutated lung adenocarcinoma diagnosed from endometrial polyp metastasis: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and a heavy tobacco history presented with a 3-month history of a painful mass on the left hard palate. He reported rapid growth of the lesion over this period; the pain had lessened over time. He denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. He had no known drug allergies and no significant alcohol use. His father had lung cancer; his mother had diabetes mellitus.

On intraoral examination, there was an ulcerative, exophytic, pigmented lesion with irregular margins, measuring approximately 4 × 2 × 2 cm on the left hard palate. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy, and cranial nerve examination was normal.

Maxillofacial CT (axial and coronal) demonstrated a focal bony defect in the left maxillary canine–premolar region with preservation of the inferior cortical bone and no involvement of the maxillary sinus floor. Contrast-enhanced paranasal sinus CT revealed a destructive 12 mm lesion in the left maxilla extending into the alveolar process, with an adjacent 27 mm infiltrative soft-tissue mass.

Differential diagnoses at this stage included peripheral giant cell granuloma, peripheral fibroma, and soft-tissue malignancies such as squamous cell carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and mucoepidermoid carcinoma. An incisional biopsy was performed under general anesthesia for definitive diagnosis.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Malignant melanoma of the oral cavity: A case report

case_prompt:
A 57‐year‐old woman (height 146 cm; weight 54.3 kg; BMI 25.3 kg/m2) with early gastric adenocarcinoma (cT1N0M0, stage IA) underwent laparoscopy‐assisted distal gastrectomy. She had no history of smoking, lung disease, or heart disease. Preoperative labs and chest radiograph were unremarkable, and spirometry showed a vital capacity of 2160 mL and FEV1 of 1640 mL.

Under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation (7.0 mm tube at 21 cm), the patient was positioned supine with legs apart and head‐up tilt. Pneumoperitoneum (CO2) was maintained at 10 mmHg for 214 minutes of the 309‐minute operation. Approximately 247 minutes after induction, SpO2 declined, and under bronchofiberscopic guidance the tube was withdrawn 1 cm. Total fluids administered were 2560 mL, urine output 330 mL, and blood pressure and heart rate remained stable. A chest radiograph taken in the operating room immediately after surgery showed no significant abnormalities. The patient was extubated and transferred to the ward.

One hour later she developed dyspnea and respiratory failure: SpO2 85% on 10 L O2 by mask; arterial blood gas showed pH 7.237, PaO2 56.2 mmHg, PaCO2 63.9 mmHg. Large amounts of pink, frothy sputum were noted from the airway and nasogastric tube. Chest radiography demonstrated diffuse ground‐glass attenuation and alveolar consolidation, and a clinical diagnosis of pulmonary edema was made.
title: Reexpansion Pulmonary Edema following Laparoscopy-Assisted Distal Gastrectomy for a Patient with Early Gastric Cancer: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 27-year-old man with a Crouzon syndrome phenotype presented with multiple episodes of epistaxis over several days and several months of progressive nasal obstruction. He had no other medical history. On examination, a polypoid mass was visible in the right nostril, with facial asymmetry and prominence of the right canine fossa. Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses revealed an inhomogeneous soft-tissue mass completely filling the right nasal cavity, maxillary sinus, and anterior and posterior ethmoidal cells. The mass caused extensive bone remodeling of the right maxillary sinus with loss of the anterior wall, erosion of the posterior wall extending into the pterygopalatine fossa, and erosion of the ipsilateral orbital floor and medial wall with intraconal extension. Despite its size, the lesion appeared well defined without obvious invasion of adjacent structures. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits, and odontogenic disease was excluded by maxillofacial consultation. A biopsy under local anesthesia demonstrated nonspecific inflammation.
title: A Case Report of Aggressive Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps Mimicking Sinonasal Malignancy

case_prompt: A 44-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a 10-day history of an intermittent cough and hemoptysis, sometimes accompanied by sudden shortness of breath. He had no history of tuberculosis, asthma, diabetes, or hypertension. He smoked one to two cigarettes per day, did not drink alcohol, and had an unremarkable family history. On examination, breath sounds were bilaterally symmetrical without adventitious findings. Routine laboratory tests, including a white-cell count of 7900/mm3, hemoglobin, differential leukocyte count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver and kidney function tests, and CBNAAT for tuberculosis, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph was essentially normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a smoothly marginated, well-defined 15 × 14 mm solitary nodule within the right main bronchus. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy demonstrated a 3 × 2 cm pedunculated polypoid mass in the right main bronchus.
journal: Lung India : Official Organ of Indian Chest Society
title: Endobronchial capillary hemangioma a rare cause of hemoptysis

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman with uncontrolled type II diabetes mellitus (HBA1C 11.8%), neuropathy, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, morbid obesity (BMI 43.3 kg/m2), and a 15-pack-year smoking history presented with a 4-week history of left breast swelling and associated nipple retraction. She denied pain, erythema, or tenderness and had no family history of cancer. A screening mammogram one year earlier was normal. 

On diagnostic mammography, there was a new retro-areolar mass in the left breast measuring 2.5 cm with associated nipple retraction. Complete left breast ultrasound demonstrated an irregular, complex cystic and solid mass measuring 2.7 × 2.3 × 1.3 cm at the 3:00 axis retro-areolar location; left axillary lymph nodes appeared normal. These imaging findings were highly suggestive of malignancy. 

An ultrasound-guided biopsy yielded thick, odorless, nonpurulent brown fluid.
title: The breast cancer that wasn't: Breast abscess mimicking malignancy

case_prompt:
A 19‐year‐old man with no past medical history presented with sudden‐onset chest pain for 1 day. The pain worsened with deep breathing and when supine. He had an upper respiratory infection 1 week earlier. On admission, vital signs were notable only for a sinus tachycardia; physical examination was otherwise normal. ECG showed sinus rhythm at 136 bpm, PR‐segment deviation, and diffuse upsloping ST‐segment elevation. Troponin and CK‐MB levels were normal. Echocardiogram was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 11 200/mm3 and C‐reactive protein of 24 mg/L (reference <5). He was observed for 24 hours, his chest pain resolved, and he was discharged on NSAIDs with a presumed diagnosis of viral pericarditis.

Seventy‐two hours later, he returned with worsening chest pain, fever, and generalized myalgia. He appeared acutely ill and febrile, but his hemodynamics remained stable. Heart and lung examinations were unremarkable. Repeat laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 22 000/mm3 with left‐shift, CK‐MB of 89.5 ng/mL (reference <5), CRP of 391 mg/L, and ESR of 44 mm in the first hour. Echocardiography showed pericardial thickening without effusion or tamponade. On hospital day 2, he became septic and developed clinical tamponade. He underwent surgical pericardial drainage and biopsy.
 
The procedure yielded 250 mL of pus. Histopathological examination of pericardial tissue showed acute exudate with fibrin and neutrophils, consistent with acute fibrinous pericarditis.
title: Pyopericarditis and tropical pyomyositis: unusual concomitance

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man presented with a six-month history of progressive neck swelling and sore throat. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was a 4-cm, hard mass in the right anterior neck. Thyroid function tests (T4, free T3, TSH) and other laboratory studies were within normal limits.  
   
Contrast-enhanced CT showed a heterogeneous mass at the level of the hyoid bone (35 × 47 × 38 mm) that expanded the cortical bone of the hyoid and contained a central solid component with calcification as well as a marginal cystic component; left submental lymphadenopathy was also noted. The thyroid gland appeared normal in its usual paratracheal position.  
   
MRI demonstrated that the solid portion of the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, slightly hypointense on T2-weighted images, and showed marked enhancement on contrast-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted images; the cystic areas were T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense.  
   
Fine-needle aspiration of the mass revealed papillary carcinoma.
title: Thyroglossal Duct Carcinoma Originating in the Hyoid Bone

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old woman with controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a remote history of marginal zone B-cell lymphoma presented in summer with 1–2 days of abdominal pain and watery diarrhea, body aches, and 2–3 weeks of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. She reported a 20-pound unintentional weight loss. She denied travel, sick contacts, or recent hospitalization. She smoked 3–5 cigarettes per day.  

On examination, temperature was 38.9 °C, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, heart rate 110 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air; lung auscultation revealed diffuse crackles and end-expiratory wheezes. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  

Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, hematocrit 28.9%, white blood cell count 5.5 × 10^3/μL, platelet count 311 × 10^3/μL, blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, and urinalysis with hyaline casts and epithelial cells. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus arrhythmia with a new first-degree atrioventricular block.  

Chest radiograph and computed tomography revealed pulmonary infiltrates with hyperinflated lungs, centrilobular emphysema, scattered blebs and bullae, consolidation with air bronchograms in the right upper and lower lobes, and a small right pleural effusion. She was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia and given bronchodilators.  

Despite treatment, she developed hypoxic respiratory failure, hemoptysis, and worsening infiltrates, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. Bronchoscopic bronchoalveolar lavage yielded progressively hemorrhagic fluid consistent with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.
title: An interesting case of mycoplasma pneumonia associated multisystem involvement and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old woman presented in June 2022 with a one-month history of slowly progressive central vision loss in the right eye associated with a right-sided headache since her COVID-19 infection six months earlier. Her medical history included hypertension, irritable bowel syndrome, and a pituitary adenoma resected in 1980 without chiasmal involvement. She did not smoke or drink, and there was no family history of blindness.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuities were 20/200−1 OD and 20/25−2 OS. Pupils were normal, and no afferent pupillary defect was recorded. Intraocular pressures were 12 mm Hg OD and 16 mm Hg OS. Funduscopy revealed cup-to-disc ratios of 0.9 OD and 0.7 OS with an inferior notch on the right. Automated perimetry showed superior arcuate and cecocentral defects in the right eye and an inferior nasal step in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated bilateral superior and inferior retinal-nerve-fiber-layer thinning, worse on the right.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a mildly elevated C-reactive protein (1.0 mg/dl; normal, 0.0–0.8). MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast revealed no recurrence of her pituitary adenoma and no abnormal enhancement of the optic nerves. Temporal-artery ultrasound by color Doppler was normal. She was diagnosed with normal-tension glaucoma and started on brimonidine/timolol ophthalmic drops twice daily.

One month later, she experienced new central vision loss in the left eye, with visual acuities of 20/200 in each eye. Perimetry showed worsening field loss OS, and OCT now showed increased average RNFL thickness in the left eye, indicating mild optic-nerve swelling. Concerned about an inflammatory optic neuropathy, she was hospitalized and received three days of IV methylprednisolone. Laboratory evaluations for nutritional, toxic, infectious, and autoimmune etiologies were normal. Lumbar puncture and temporal-artery biopsy were normal. A whole-body PET–CT scan and paraneoplastic antibody panel were also normal. Four days after discharge, she had further vision loss and was re-admitted for another course of IV steroids, five sessions of plasmapheresis, and intravenous immunoglobulin. Mitochondrial DNA sequencing was ordered, and results were pending.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Diagnostic dilemma: Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy in a 70-year-Old woman

case_prompt: A 5-year-old girl underwent a routine physical examination, which revealed a hard, non-tender, palpable mass in the right abdomen. She had no urinary symptoms, flank pain, hematuria, or systemic complaints. Ultrasonography identified a mass in the right kidney. Laboratory studies were notable only for an elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9 level of 128.4 U/mL (reference <25); other tumor markers and blood counts were normal. Noncontrast CT showed a well-circumscribed right renal mass with multiple internal high-density calcifications. On contrast-enhanced CT, the lesion demonstrated marked enhancement in the cortical phase and decreased enhancement in the medullary phase. MRI confirmed significant cortical enhancement with washout in the delayed phase.
title: Metanephric adenoma in children: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old morbidly obese African American woman presented with a 4-month history of a persistent dry cough. She had been treated for an upper respiratory infection with antibiotics and prednisone, but her cough persisted. She also reported malaise, dyspnea, and wheezing. 

On initial evaluation, her blood pressure was 187/93 mmHg, pulse 105 beats per minute, she was afebrile, and her peripheral oxygen saturation was 100% on room air. A chest radiograph showed a left hilar opacity. Noncontrast CT of the chest revealed an infiltrative mass in the medial aspect of the left hemithorax, measuring 11.8 cm × 2.6 cm, along with mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Bronchoscopy demonstrated yellow-tan, polypoidal endobronchial lesions in both the right and left mainstem bronchi, with significant mucosal swelling and narrowing of the left mainstem bronchus. Biopsy specimens were obtained from the endobronchial lesions and a mediastinal lymph node.  

Histopathological examination showed acute and chronic inflammation with granuloma formation. A Gomori methenamine silver stain of the endobronchial tissue highlighted a rare yeast form, from which the initial impression was histoplasmosis.
title: Endobronchial blastomycoses: A rare pathogen in a unique location

case_prompt: A 64-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive hoarseness. He was a former smoker (10 pack-years, quit 5 years earlier) and denied excessive alcohol use. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed thickening and fixation of the left true vocal fold. A roughly 3-cm mass arising from the left true vocal fold invaded the left arytenoid and occupied the ventricle. Under general anesthesia, a suspension microlaryngoscopy with biopsy was performed. Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen showed fused cells of variable dimensions with eosinophilic cytoplasm, irregular hyperchromatic features, and large or multiple nuclei. Contrast-enhanced CT scans of the neck, chest, and abdomen showed no evidence of lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. The tumor was clinically staged as T3N0M0 glottic cancer.
title: Pleomorphic Rhabdomyosarcoma Arising from True Vocal Fold of Larynx: Report of a Rare Case and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 50-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of headache and, on the day of admission, abrupt onset of dizziness, dysarthria, and aphasia while shoveling snow. Vital signs were within normal limits. Noncontrast brain CT showed a hypoattenuated lesion without enhancement in the left parietal cortex and underlying white matter. On MRI, T2-weighted images revealed a localized irregular, low-signal-intensity lesion with surrounding high T2 signal. Susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated dark signal intensity within the lesion. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images showed a thin peripheral rim of enhancement. Diffusion-weighted images and ADC maps both showed low signal intensity in the lesion and surrounding edema, indicating a lack of diffusion restriction, though this was attributed to susceptibility artifact from blood products. Perfusion MRI revealed no increase in relative cerebral blood volume at the lesion. MR spectroscopy demonstrated an increased lactate peak, decreased N-acetyl aspartate peak, and no elevation of choline. The initial differential diagnosis was between a hemorrhagic brain tumor and a hemorrhagic non-tumorous lesion. The patient underwent excisional biopsy of the lesion; minimal active bleeding was noted intraoperatively. One week later, follow-up MRI revealed multiple new lesions in both supratentorial and infratentorial regions, each showing peripheral high T2 signal, central dark SWI signal, thin rim enhancement, surrounding edema, and low signal on DWI and ADC maps. The patient tested negative for HIV and had no history of immunodeficiency.
title: Fulminant Disseminating Fatal Granulomatous Amebic Encephalitis: The First Case Report in an Immunocompetent Patient in South Korea

case_prompt: A 73-year-old cachectic Iranian man presented with a general feeling of being unwell, acute loss of vision in his left eye, and severe headache. He denied pain elsewhere. He had a history of painless, dry, mobile skin nodules on his buttocks, back, and arms. On brain magnetic resonance imaging, multiple contrast-enhancing masses with surrounding edema were noted. Chest computed tomography showed a few cavitary lesions in the upper lobes. Abdominal imaging, including computed tomography and ultrasonography, was unremarkable. A lumbar puncture was negative for tuberculosis by direct smear, polymerase chain reaction, culture, and cytologic examination. Serum tumor markers (PSA, CA125, CA19-9, AFP) were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 70 mm/hr and a highly reactive C-reactive protein level. Fine-needle aspiration of the skin lesions revealed bacterial infection but no Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A purified protein derivative skin test yielded 20-mm induration. A technetium-99m methylene diphosphonate bone scan demonstrated multiple foci of intense uptake throughout the axial and appendicular skeleton—including regions of the skull, clavicle, sternum, ribs, humerus, forearm, wrists, hands, femur, tibia, ankle, and first metatarsophalangeal joint—findings suggestive of metastatic bone disease.
title: Diagnostic role of whole body bone scintigraphy in atypical skeletal tuberculosis resembling multiple metastases: a case report

case_prompt: A 33-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a painless, well-demarcated, pink to yellowish mass with a delicate papillary surface on the right ventral tongue. The lesion measured 2.2 × 1.2 cm and had been present for at least 4 years. On palpation, the mass was soft. There were no extraoral lesions or cervical lymphadenopathy, and routine laboratory results were normal. With a provisional diagnosis of benign papillary lesions (including large squamous papilloma, verruciform xanthoma, and condyloma acuminatum), an excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. Microscopic examination revealed a papillary hyperparakeratotic acanthotic epithelium with parakeratin plugging between the papillary projections. The rete ridges were elongated to a uniform depth, and the connective tissue papillae were filled with numerous large macrophages with foamy cytoplasm (xanthoma cells).
title: Verruciform Xanthoma of the Ventral Surface of the Tongue: A Rare Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 77‐year‐old man with a 15‐year history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with iguratimod and low‐dose prednisolone and diabetes mellitus presented with a cough and sputum production. He had a 40‐year history of smoking 20 cigarettes per day. On examination, he was afebrile (37.1°C), blood pressure was 135/67 mmHg, heart rate 87 bpm, and respiratory rate 20/min. Neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C‐reactive protein level of 6.9 mg/dL (normal 0.03–0.17 mg/dL) and reduced creatinine clearance of 45.5 mL/min. Serum β‐D‐glucan, myeloperoxidase‐ANCA, proteinase‐3‐ANCA, Aspergillus antigen, interferon‐gamma release assay for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and anti–Mycobacteria antibody tests were negative. HIV antibody was negative. Chest computed tomography revealed multiple cavitary lesions in the right lower lobe. Infectious causes such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, acid‐fast bacillus infection, and staphylococcal pneumonia, follicular bronchiolitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis were considered.
title: Multiple cystic lesions after treatment for pulmonary cryptococcosis

case_prompt: A 15-year-old Indo-Aryan male presented with a sudden, painless decrease in vision in his right eye for 4 days. He had no significant ocular or family history, and review of systems was unremarkable. Best corrected visual acuity was 6/60 in the right eye and 6/6 unaided in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 15 mmHg in the right eye and 16 mmHg in the left eye. There was an afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. Slit-lamp examination of both anterior segments was normal. Dilated fundus examination showed a normal left eye. In the right eye, there was telangiectasia of the retinal vessels with subretinal lipid exudation in the superotemporal and superonasal quadrants, subretinal fluid extending into the fovea, and a single flap horseshoe tear at the 10 o’clock equatorial region without secondary changes. Complete blood counts, viral serology, chest radiograph, and Mantoux test were all normal. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the right macula demonstrated a hyporeflective space between the retinal pigment epithelium and neurosensory retina, consistent with subretinal fluid.
title: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in Coats’ disease: a case report

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old woman with hypertension and a history of right uncemented metal-on-polyethylene total hip arthroplasty 2 years earlier for osteoarthritis noted gradual enlargement of a mass over her right hip. The mass caused discomfort when sitting or lying on that side, and she developed a Trendelenburg gait to the right. Examination showed a well-healed posterolateral incision without warmth or erythema, a large palpable mass over the surgical site, painless hip range of motion, and intact distal neurovascular status. 

Plain radiographs demonstrated an uncemented total hip prosthesis with osteolysis beneath the stem collar, no radiolucencies at the implant–bone interface or eccentric polyethylene wear, and a circular soft-tissue density surrounding the joint. A three-phase technetium bone scan showed increased blood pooling in the soft tissues lateral to the prosthesis but no evidence of prosthetic loosening. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a large, well-circumscribed collection lateral to the hip joint with extension into the iliopsoas bursa, surrounded by a thin capsule, with intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images and increased signal on T2-weighted images.

What is your differential diagnosis?
title: Formation of a large rice body-containing cyst following total hip arthroplasty

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old gravida-1 nulliparous woman with an unremarkable medical history underwent a routine second-trimester anatomy ultrasound that demonstrated ventriculomegaly and possible agenesis of the corpus callosum. A fetal MRI was obtained at 21 weeks 5 days’ gestation and showed:
• Severe lateral and third ventriculomegaly (atrial diameters up to 15 mm bilaterally).  
• A dysplastic, Z-shaped brainstem.  
• Poor visualization of the cerebral aqueduct; a normal fourth ventricle.  
• Hypoplastic cerebellar vermis (5 mm craniocaudal), with normal cisterna magna and transverse cerebellar diameter for gestational age.  
• Subjectively decreased supratentorial brain parenchymal volume without definite cortical malformations.  
No additional anomalies were identified. A detailed family history revealed no birth defects or known genetic disorders.
title: Second trimester fetal MRI features in a fetus with TUBB3 gene mutation

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old African American man with a history of depression and tuberculosis presented to the gastroenterology clinic with several months of rectal pain and occasional dark-red bleeding. He described the pain as right-sided, occurring about twice weekly during bowel movements and resolving afterward. He reported one bowel movement daily with variable consistency; hard or bulky stool exacerbated his pain. He also noted a slight increase in bowel movement frequency coinciding with the onset of pain and the appearance of dark-red blood in his stool. He denied abdominal pain, changes in appetite, weight loss, dysphagia, odynophagia, skin rashes, fever, or rigors. There was no family history of colon cancer or inflammatory bowel disease.

On examination, bowel sounds were normal; the abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended, with no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. A rectal examination revealed a small external hemorrhoid but no fissures or masses. Fecal occult blood testing was negative with a positive control. The patient was scheduled for colonoscopy and started on zinc sulfate suppositories and fiber supplements for presumed hemorrhoids and constipation.

Colonoscopy with retroflexion revealed a solitary hyperpigmented lesion in the distal rectum and internal hemorrhoids.
title: Rectal Blue Nevus: Distinguishing Features of a Rare Entity

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 26-year-old woman presented with four months of progressive left-sided abdominal pain radiating to the back and left flank, associated with fatigue but without gastrointestinal, urinary, or constitutional symptoms. Physical examination was notable for normal vital signs and a firm, round mass of approximately 13 × 10 cm in the left upper and lower quadrants without tenderness. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, pregnancy test, and tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, CA 125, AFP), were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 17 × 12 × 10 cm bilobed retroperitoneal mass with cystic components displacing the pancreatic body and tail anteriorly and the upper left kidney posteriorly; the inferior part of the mass was inseparable from the third part of the duodenum, proximal jejunum, and left adrenal gland, with no clear invasion and no evidence of lymphovascular invasion. MRI confirmed a mass measuring 18.7 × 10.7 × 11.1 cm with high T2 signal and moderate T1 signal suggesting a myxoid component, central necrosis, hemorrhagic foci, and peripheral enhancement; it again was inseparable from adjacent bowel and adrenal structures and encased the inferior mesenteric vein and possibly the artery. PET/CT showed hypermetabolic activity confined to this mass without metastatic disease.  
The differential diagnosis included myxoid soft tissue sarcoma, adrenal cortical carcinoma, or, less likely, gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A case report of retroperitoneal Ewing sarcoma requiring adrenalectomy

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman with a family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with unintentional weight gain of approximately 10 kg per month over the past year, hyperpigmentation of both palms, and general fatigue. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed hyperlipidemia (LDL cholesterol 173 mg/dL [normal <100 mg/dL], HDL cholesterol 42 mg/dL [normal >65 mg/dL]) and an elevated plasma ACTH concentration of 113.0 pg/mL (normal 0.1–46.0 pg/mL). Other pituitary hormone levels were within normal limits.

An overnight dexamethasone suppression test and 24-hour urinary free cortisol excretion were incompatible with Cushing’s syndrome. ACTH stimulation and insulin tolerance tests excluded adrenal insufficiency. Stimulation tests for thyrotropin-releasing hormone and gonadotropin-releasing hormone, as well as MRI of the sellar turcica and abdominal sonography, were all normal. The patient was discharged on oral cortisone and atorvastatin but continued to gain weight, had persistent hyperlipidemia, and had persistently elevated ACTH. On readmission, her blood pressure was 126/83 mm Hg, pulse 70/min, and palmar hyperpigmentation persisted. Repeat pituitary MRI and adrenal CT scans were unremarkable. Given the unexplained isolated elevation of ACTH, retesting with an alternative ELSA-ACTH assay was advised.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title:
A Pitfall of Falsely Elevated ACTH: A Case Report and Literature
Review

case_prompt:
A 9-month-old boy with a history of mild eczema presented with a 5-day history of swelling of the dorsal left hand extending across the wrist. The swelling was tender and warm but was not associated with fever; no other joints were involved. There was a pigmented area on the left hand without itchiness, discharge, or skin breakdown. Systemic review was unremarkable. He had been admitted one month earlier for a hypocalcemic seizure and received intravenous calcium gluconate in the left hand. 

On examination, the dorsal aspect of the left hand and wrist was swollen with bluish discoloration, redness, warmth, and tenderness; there was no fluctuation, discharge, or overlying skin lesion. Hand motion was restricted, and distal pulses were intact. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 11.3 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, platelets 530 × 10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 9 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 0.36 mg/L. Serum sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine, corrected calcium (2.5 mmol/L), phosphate (1.8 mmol/L), and vitamin D (120.6 nmol/L) were all within normal limits. 

He was diagnosed with post-intravenous-line cellulitis and treated with intravenous clindamycin. A left-hand ultrasound was normal. The swelling gradually subsided, and he was discharged on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. 

At one-week follow-up, he was well, with a normal bone profile and biochemistry. Examination revealed a hard swelling over the dorsal left hand with mild restriction of motion. A left-hand radiograph was ordered.
title: Iatrogenic calcinosis cutis in 9-month-old baby boy: a case report

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man with a 5-year history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and a 32–pack-year smoking history (quit at age 51) was referred for evaluation of gradually enlarging mediastinal lymphadenopathy and ground-glass opacity in the lower lung fields on CT. He reported dry cough and mild dyspnea (mMRC grade I). Physical examination revealed fine crackles at both lung bases; no superficial lymphadenopathy was palpable. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 7400/μL, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, platelets 250 × 10^3/μL, total protein 6.4 g/dL, albumin 3.7 g/dL, creatinine 1.09 mg/dL, LDH 247 IU/L, β2-microglobulin 2.4 mg/L, soluble IL-2 receptor 469 U/mL, KL-6 805 U/mL, ACE 37.4 U/L, IgM 791 mg/dL (reference 33–183), IgG 531 mg/dL (861–1747), and IgA 52 mg/dL (93–393). Urinalysis detected kappa-type Bence-Jones proteins. 

Pulmonary function testing showed obstructive impairment (FEV1/FVC 61%). ECG and echocardiography were normal. Enhanced chest CT demonstrated upper-zone emphysema, lower-zone ground-glass opacities with septal thickening, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and a paravertebral soft tissue shadow. FDG-PET revealed SUVmax 2.5 in mediastinal soft tissue and 2.4 in retroperitoneal soft tissue. 

Bronchoalveolar lavage was unremarkable. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed lymphocytes and plasma cells in alveolar walls. Given elevated IgM, urinary Bence-Jones protein, and lymphadenopathy, the initial differential included lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, MALT lymphoma with plasma cell differentiation, and multiple myeloma. 

Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy revealed normocellular marrow with kappa-predominant lymphocytes and plasma cells; the smear showed 24.2% lymphocytes, 3.0% plasma cells, and some atypical cells. Flow cytometry demonstrated kappa-predominant B cells. These findings supported the diagnosis of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma but were not definitive.
title: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving the mediastinum and the lung, followed by amyloidosis: A surgically and genetically proven case

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man was evaluated after two episodes of generalized convulsive seizures. He has no personal or family history of febrile convulsions or epilepsy. He reports playing Mahjong almost daily for 12 years.

First event: While playing Mahjong for over 24 consecutive hours and smoking (no alcohol), he experienced a generalized convulsion. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed no abnormalities, and video-EEG showed no definitive interictal epileptiform discharges or photoparoxysmal responses. No antiseizure medication was prescribed.

Seven months later, he again had a generalized convulsion while playing Mahjong all night. Repeat EEG and MRI again showed no abnormalities. He reports no seizures in any other context, including other games or spontaneously, between these two events.
title: A Single-center Analysis of Three Japanese Patients with Mahjong-related Seizures

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of dull, aching abdominal pain that began insidiously in the right hypochondrium and gradually worsened, radiating to the left hypochondrium, with intermittent vomiting but no clear triggers. He also noted a swelling in the left inguinal region over the same period. His medical history was notable for transurethral resection of a low-grade bladder papillary urothelial carcinoma followed by intravesical BCG. He had no history of diabetes, tuberculosis, asthma, or hypertension and had ceased alcohol use one year earlier.

On examination, he appeared well nourished and in no distress. Abdominal palpation elicited mild tenderness in the right hypochondrium without organomegaly or peritoneal signs. In the left inguinal region there was a 3 × 2 cm soft, non-tender, non-reducible swelling with a positive cough impulse. The testes were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple 9–10 mm calcified nodules in the left diaphragm, bilateral intercostal muscles, left erector spinae, right psoas, and bilateral gluteal and thigh muscles. A 12 × 8 mm hypodense splenic lesion was also noted; all other abdominal organs were normal. An AP X-ray of the upper thighs showed multiple radiopaque soft-tissue lesions in the gluteal and thigh muscles.
title: A rare case of muscular cysticercosis: Incidental discovery in a patient presenting with inguinal swelling

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old previously healthy woman presented with sudden onset of severe left hip pain. The pain began one day earlier and nine days after testing positive for SARS-CoV-2; she was otherwise asymptomatic from COVID-19. She was unable to bear weight. On examination, the hip was held in 15° of flexion and 20° of external rotation; there was no warmth or erythema, but groin tenderness on palpation and with leg rotation, and she could not perform a straight-leg raise. Neurologic and vascular exams were normal. She denied trauma. Her history included endometriosis resected three months earlier; she had no rheumatologic conditions.

Initial blood tests showed a white-cell count and C-reactive protein (values not specified). Vital signs were within normal limits. Pelvic radiographs were unremarkable. MRI of the left hip revealed a large intra-articular fluid collection without other abnormalities. Under sedation, 8 mL of yellowish synovial fluid was aspirated and sent for microbiology and sensitivities.
title: Acute COVID-Related Hip Arthritis. Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 48-year-old woman presented with a 20-month history of right-sided orofacial pain. She described severe, paroxysmal burning sensations deep in the posterior wall of the right external auditory canal, the pinna, the jaw, and the adjacent retromastoid area. Attacks were triggered by chewing, light touch, or contact with warm water, lasted seconds to 1–2 minutes, and were rated 10/10 in intensity. She denied odynophagia. Trials of carbamazepine (up to 1200 mg/day), sertraline, amitriptyline, and pregabalin provided no significant relief. Otoscopic examination was normal bilaterally, and there was no facial weakness, sensory deficit, or other neurologic abnormality. MRI with angiography, including 3D T2-weighted fast spin echo and CISS sequences, demonstrated a loop of the right posterior inferior cerebellar artery crossing the cerebellopontine cistern in close contact with the right facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves near the internal auditory canal.
title: Microvascular decompression of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery for intermediate nerve neuralgia

case_prompt:
A 10-month-old South Asian boy was brought for evaluation of a limp in his right leg when walking with support. The parents denied any history of trauma. His birth and perinatal course were uneventful, and developmental milestones were normal. Vaccinations were up to date. Family history was unremarkable. 

On examination, he was afebrile and appeared well. There were no bruises, café-au-lait spots, or other dermatologic findings. Systemic examination was normal. In the right leg, there was no overt swelling, tenderness, deformity, or ulceration, but a bony hard lump was palpable over the mid-tibia and fibula with tibia vara and internal rotation. 

Plain radiography of the right leg showed a callus from a previous stress fracture and multiple expansile lytic lesions of the tibia with cortical erosions and sclerotic areas in adjacent bone; a pathological fracture was seen in the fibula. Laboratory studies—including serum alkaline phosphatase, calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, and 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol levels—were all within normal limits. 

Given the unexplained long-bone lesions and fracture in a non-ambulant infant, the possibility of child abuse was considered, and the child was referred for further assessment.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Bone pathology mimicking non-accidental injury in a child – Bewildered by bones, case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 54-year-old man was diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 infection during the first wave of the pandemic. He reported a mildly elevated temperature (37.5 °C) without need for antipyretics, incomplete loss of taste and smell, and no cardiac or pulmonary involvement; he was managed as an outpatient. His medical history was notable only for type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin, and he had no personal or family history of psychiatric illness. He had a stable social situation, supportive family, and no recent psychosocial stressors or concerns about his prognosis. The patient was prescribed hydroxychloroquine (200 mg twice daily). After five days of treatment, he developed sudden depressive symptoms with melancholic features and severe suicidal ideation. He attempted to jump from his balcony but was interrupted by his son. He was admitted to a COVID-19 unit under constant surveillance and psychiatric consultation and was started on sertraline 50 mg/day and olanzapine 5 mg/day.
title: Chloroquine/Hydroxychloroquine Use and Suicide Risk: Hypotheses for Confluent Etiopathogenetic Mechanisms?

case_prompt: A 45-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of intense frontal headache, nausea, and temporal and spatial disorientation. Over the same period, he developed inappropriate behavior. On arrival he was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 170/100 mm Hg. Neurologic examination showed spontaneous eye opening but reduced blink rate; lack of spontaneous movements; mutism; waxy flexibility; negativism; and catalepsy. There was no cranial-nerve palsy, and deep tendon reflexes were normal. He manifested repetitive stereotypic perioral movements and clonic jerks of the right upper limb lasting for more than five minutes, interpreted as continuous partial motor status with impaired consciousness. After intravenous phenytoin (20 mg/kg), he had improvement in interaction and complete remission of the abnormal movements but remained mute and unable to speak, though he could follow commands (motor aphasia). Laboratory studies revealed no signs of infection or metabolic disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed six cells/mL, glucose 56 mg/dL, total protein 27 mg/dL, and negative bacterial and fungal cultures. Noncontrast head CT disclosed a hypodense area in the left temporal region with small hyperdense spots. On hospital day 2, EEG revealed diffuse disorganization of cerebral activity with predominantly slow delta waves in the left posterior–medial temporal region and no epileptiform discharges.
title: Catatonia, beyond a psychiatric syndrome

case_prompt: A 38-year-old woman with morbid obesity and chronic hypertension, at 36 weeks of gestation, presented with a 1-week history of mild headache, nausea, epigastric and right upper quadrant pain, and dark urine. On examination, she was jaundiced with hepatomegaly; the neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory values showed a leukocyte count of 12.0 × 10^9/L, platelet count of 450 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL (direct 5.0 mg/dL), AST 83 U/L, ALT 87 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 319 U/L, glucose 66 mg/dL, LDH 679 U/L, uric acid 4.2 mg/dL, and total serum bile acids 71 μmol/L. Coagulation studies showed a prothrombin time of 17 seconds (INR 1.4). Viral hepatitis serologies, autoimmune markers, and ceruloplasmin level were unremarkable. A 24-hour urine protein was elevated at 1300 mg (baseline 180 mg prior to pregnancy). Ultrasonography revealed marked hepatomegaly (≈27 cm), fatty infiltration of the liver, a right hepatic hypoechoic 2.8 cm lesion, and heterogenous echotexture with areas of nodular contour.
