title: Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma Masquerading as Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless mass in the left submandibular region that had been present for 1 year. She had a history only of dyslipidemia, with no prior surgeries, smoking, or alcohol use. On examination, the mass measured approximately 20 mm, had slightly limited mobility, and was nontender; the remainder of the head and neck examination was unremarkable.  

Neck ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous, well-circumscribed mass measuring 21 × 20 × 16 mm posterior to the left submandibular gland, with low internal echogenicity and mixed papillary hyperechogenic foci at its margins. The submandibular gland itself appeared normal. The thyroid gland was in its usual location and contained multiple 10–20 mm cystic and hypoechoic nodules, consistent with an adenomatous goiter.  

Contrast-enhanced cervical CT revealed a well-defined mass behind the left submandibular gland. On noncontrast images, the mass was mostly hyperdense with areas of lower density; it showed minimal enhancement after contrast administration. The thyroid gland was confirmed to lie in its normal cervical position.  

Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass yielded a bloody specimen with foamy cells but no epithelial cells, and was nondiagnostic.
title: Follicular adenoma with a papillary architecture originating from an ectopic thyroid gland: a case report

case_prompt: A 74-year-old man was referred for repair of a presumed left inguinal hernia after he noticed a gradually enlarging mass over 10 years. On examination, there was an elastic, hard, slightly mobile mass in the left inguinal region that could not be reduced, even after analgesia. No skin changes were observed. Ultrasonography revealed a 9 cm × 4 cm, rigid, inhomogeneous structure originating in the left inguinal space beneath the skin without extension into the hemiscrotum. Doppler sonography demonstrated prominent, rich vascularity. Noncontrast CT of the scrotum showed a 13 cm, round, inhomogeneous lesion within the anterior abdominal wall fat at the level of the left spermatic cord, displacing the left testis.
title: Angiofibroma of the spermatic cord: a case report and a review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old girl was brought to the emergency department after two hours of rightward eye deviation, altered consciousness, and unresponsiveness, followed by urinary incontinence and right-sided focal convulsions that became bilateral tonic-clonic but remained more intense on the right. She had no fever but complained of frontal headache and foaming at the mouth. In the ED she received IV phenytoin 15 mg/kg, which controlled the seizures after 20 minutes, and was started on maintenance phenytoin, vancomycin, and ceftazidime. 

Her history was notable for otalgia 3 weeks earlier diagnosed as acute otitis media treated with inadequate antibiotics. There was no prior surgery or congenital disease, but her parents were fourth-degree consanguineous. On arrival, vital signs were normal, Glasgow coma scale was 11/15 after 90 minutes, pupils were equal and reactive, and there were no meningeal signs. On hospital day 2 she was alert, but had upper extremity hypotonia more pronounced on the left. 

Laboratory studies showed: CRP 30 mg/dL, WBC 16,300/mm3, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, platelets 676 × 10^9/L, creatinine 0.37 mg/dL, and urea 18 mg/dL. Noncontrast head CT showed cerebral edema with a low-density area in the left temporal lobe. MRI demonstrated a 24 mm left temporal lobe mass with low T1 and high T2-FLAIR signal, a hyperintense rim on diffusion-weighted imaging, and smooth circumferential enhancement. Imaging also revealed left mastoiditis.
title: Conservative management of a large brain abscess in a child with severe manifestations: A case report from Syria

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of diffuse dull abdominal pain aggravated at night and relieved when prone, accompanied by difficulty in passing stools and passage of mucus. Over the past 6 months, he noted loss of appetite, early satiety, and occasional nausea without fever, vomiting, melena, or weight loss. He had previously been treated for irritable bowel syndrome. On examination, there was a well-defined, firm, tender 10 × 10 cm mass in the left lumbar and umbilical regions, freely mobile perpendicular to the mesentery, with a nodular surface, no respiratory excursion, and impaired resonance on percussion. Rectal examination was normal.  
Ultrasonography of the abdomen demonstrated a lobulated hypoechoic intra-abdominal mass lesion with areas of vascularity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an 8.6 × 9.7 × 9.0 cm neoplasm arising from the small-bowel mesentery, displacing adjacent intestine without invasion, and no evidence of liver metastases or lymphadenopathy.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Leiomyosarcoma of the mesentry, a rare mesentric tumour

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with an 8-month history of progressive bilateral leg weakness and paresthesias following a mechanical fall onto her lower back while dancing. Her Oswestry Disability Index score was 68%. On neurologic examination, lower extremity strength was graded 3/5 bilaterally, with leg apraxia, paresthesias below the T7 dermatome, and symmetric hyperreflexia in the lower extremities. 

An initial thoracic spine MRI demonstrated multiple flow voids at the midthoracic level, most prominent at T8, concerning for dural arteriovenous fistula, but a subsequent spinal angiogram was negative. Two additional spinal MRIs and a CT myelogram were interpreted as normal. On retrospective review of the most recent MRI, the thoracic spinal cord was displaced ventrally, with evidence of thoracic stenosis and turbulent adjacent cerebrospinal fluid flow, but without extrinsic cord compression, neural foraminal narrowing, syrinx formation, or the scalpel sign. Retrospectively, similar flow abnormalities were noted on the prior MRIs and serpiginous CSF filling defects were seen on CT myelogram, all of which had been deemed artifactual initially.

In the setting of her long-term symptoms and radiographic evidence of spinal cord stenosis with surrounding flow abnormalities, surgical exploration was planned.
title: Scalpellum occulta: A rare case of dorsal spinal arachnoid web without the scalpel sign

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old African American woman was referred for a 6-month history of left lower quadrant abdominal pain and a soft-tissue mass at the same site. The pain was sharp, cramping, nonradiating, positional, and worsened during menstruation. Her medical history included three cesarean deliveries and obesity (BMI, 38.66). She took a combined oral contraceptive (norgestimate-ethinyl estradiol).

On examination, there was a non-tender, palpable mass beneath the lateral aspect of her prior cesarean scar in the left lower quadrant.  
Ultrasound showed a 19 × 19 × 9 mm extra-fascial macrolobular hypoechoic mass with internal color flow at the anterior margin of the left rectus muscle.  
CT of the abdomen revealed a poorly delineated ∼2.5 cm mass just medial to the left anterior superior iliac spine, lying superficially over the fascia.  
An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was attempted, but Interventional Radiology was unable to perform it due to her body habitus.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Abdominal wall endometriomas. Should the approach vary based on its relationship to the fascia? A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old girl with severe developmental delay and presumed epilepsy—on levetiracetam despite multiple normal EEGs—was admitted in a postictal state with slight dehydration. She was hemodynamically stable (HR 99 bpm, normal blood pressure, SpO2 99%).  
Laboratory studies showed marked rhabdomyolysis (CPK 6640 U/L, later rising to >42 670 U/L) with elevated troponin I (1156 ng/L) and transaminases (AST 187 U/L, ALT 65 U/L); serum electrolytes were normal. The initial ECG demonstrated a normal QTc interval.  
Levetiracetam was discontinued, and she was transferred to a pediatric center, where repeat ECG revealed QTc prolongation (570 ms), prompting initiation of oral propranolol (1 mg/kg/day). Over the next days, she developed hypotension and hydro-electrolyte disturbances and was admitted to the PICU.  
She then experienced non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (HR ~200 bpm) treated with intravenous magnesium (50 mg/kg) and lidocaine bolus followed by infusion (35 µg/kg/min). Echocardiography showed no structural or functional abnormalities.  
Upon transfer to the cardiac ICU, she was managed as presumed congenital long QT syndrome with maintenance of normal plasma potassium, calcium, and magnesium while on lidocaine. After a brief return to sinus rhythm, frequent polymorphic ventricular premature beats in short–long–short sequences triggered torsades de pointes and ventricular fibrillation requiring defibrillation.  
A temporary pacemaker was placed for ventricular pacing, and esmolol infusion (25 µg/kg/min) was added to ongoing lidocaine, resulting in transient rhythm stabilization. Despite this, two further episodes of torsades de pointes occurred, each requiring defibrillation, concurrent with worsening rhabdomyolysis and a drop in LVEF to 40%.
title: The TANGO2 disease and the therapeutic challenge of acute arrhythmia management: a case report

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of intermittent visual distortions. She reported difficulty focusing on details when reading or watching television and noted that objects appeared distorted in both eyes. She denied headache, trauma, fever, cough, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, ocular motility and color vision were normal; pupils were equal and reactive; fundoscopic examination was unremarkable. She was alert, oriented, and cooperative. Vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologic examination showed no motor deficits, a negative Babinski response, and no tremor or dyskinesia.

Routine laboratory studies including complete blood count, blood glucose, electrolytes, and liver and kidney function tests were all normal. Serologic and immunologic tests, including Brucella agglutination, anti-double-stranded DNA, anti-SSA, anti-SSB, antinuclear antibody, PCR for cytomegalovirus, p-ANCA, and c-ANCA, were negative. A screening RT-PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 was positive in the absence of respiratory or other viral symptoms.

Brain MRI demonstrated a focal lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, and showed restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging. MR angiography revealed discontinuity of the terminal branches of the right posterior cerebral artery. Carotid and vertebral Doppler ultrasonography showed no evidence of atherosclerosis, thrombus, stenosis, or occlusion.
title: Imaging findings of two patients with isolated infarction of the splenium during COVID-19

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old man with no significant medical history was evaluated for abdominal pain and mild elevations in liver enzymes. Initial ultrasonography revealed multiple hypoechoic lesions in the liver. CT of the abdomen showed multiple low-attenuation areas within the hepatic parenchyma. Following CT-guided liver biopsy, the patient’s hemoglobin dropped from 14 to 10.2 g/dL, and he received packed red-cell transfusions. He was transferred for further management.

On arrival, he complained of right upper quadrant discomfort without nausea, vomiting, fever, or chills. Vital signs: blood pressure 80/30 mm Hg, pulse 110 beats/min; respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable. The abdomen was soft, with tenderness in the right upper quadrant but no guarding or rigidity.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL (13–18)  
• Hematocrit 28% (40–53)  
• Platelets 139 × 10^9/L (150–400)  
• AST 30 IU/L (5–30), ALT 19 IU/L (5–30)  
• GGT 153 U/L (6–50), ALP 195 U/L (50–100)  
• Total bilirubin 5 mg/dL, ammonia 60 µg/dL  
• PT 12.5 s (11–14), INR 1.14, aPTT 44.3 s (20–40), fibrinogen 420 mg/dL (180–400)

He was managed conservatively in the ICU with stable hemoglobin and no further transfusions. After transfer to the surgical ward, contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a heterogeneous 10.6 × 11.4 cm mass in hepatic segments VI and VII, with high-density fluid in the right paracolic gutter suggestive of hemoperitoneum. MRI of the liver showed innumerable T2-hyperintense nodules throughout the liver with delayed enhancement and a large T2-hyperintense lesion in segments VI and VII containing multiple smaller lesions with delayed enhancement.
title: A Fatal Case of Intra-Abdominal Hemorrhage Following Diagnostic Blind Percutaneous Liver Biopsy in a Patient With Peliosis Hepatis

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old man with cystic fibrosis, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and CF-associated liver disease presented with a 5-week history of intermittent spasmodic abdominal pain, increased frequency of nonbloody stools, and symptoms worsened by stress. Physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies—including CBC, ESR, CRP, electrolytes, amylase, lipase, and fecal occult blood—were within normal limits; a liver panel showed mild transaminase elevations consistent with his known liver disease. He was initially treated for functional abdominal pain with antispasmodics. 

Because of refractory symptoms, he underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and colonoscopy. EGD was visually normal; colonoscopy showed mild scattered colonic exudates and a normal terminal ileum. Biopsies demonstrated chronic active eosinophilic ileitis and colitis, leading to initiation of sulfasalazine and oral budesonide. 

Despite adherence, symptoms persisted. He was admitted for presumed distal intestinal obstruction syndrome (DIOS) based on radiologic evidence of organized contents in the distal small bowel and treated with polyethylene glycol and N-acetylcysteine. On follow-up, he reported continued pain. Repeat EGD and colonoscopy showed resolution of colitis but revealed a protruding intraluminal mass with a smooth surface and normal overlying mucosa in the terminal ileum; biopsies, including from the mass, were normal. 

Small-bowel capsule endoscopy was normal. Magnetic resonance enterography showed thickening of the ileocecal valve but no discrete mass, polyp, or external compression. Repeat CBC remained normal. He was readmitted for recurrent bowel obstruction; repeat colonoscopy confirmed a nonocclusive mass in the terminal ileum but was otherwise visually unremarkable. Biopsies again showed small-bowel and colonic mucosal eosinophilia. Given normal biopsy histology, laboratory and imaging results, the mass was presumed benign, and recurrent obstruction was thought secondary to DIOS.
title: Small Bowel Hemolymphangioma Treated by Polypectomy in a Pediatric Patient with Cystic Fibrosis

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old woman presented with progressive right leg pain localizing to the lateral hip and radiating down the side of her right leg, accompanied by low back pain and an abnormal gait. She also noted bilateral palpable masses in the anterior thighs that limited her range of motion.

Her medical history included hypertension, anxiety, chronic pain syndrome, a right total hip arthroplasty (with later revision for leg-length discrepancy), and a right total knee arthroplasty. In her forties, she participated in heavy-weight bodybuilding and recalled feeling a tearing sensation in both thighs while squatting.

On examination, her right leg appeared slightly longer than her left, and she had lumbar hyperlordosis. She was tender over the right greater trochanter and iliotibial band. Symmetric masses were palpable in the anterior thighs along the rectus femoris muscles. The right knee hyperextended 2° and flexed to 120° with the hip flexed, but only to 30° with the hip extended; ligaments were stable. The right hip was stable with minimal discomfort, and she had an equivocal straight-leg raise on the right. Sensation was reduced over the right lateral thigh. The left leg was neurovascularly intact and non-tender, with an identical knee flexion pattern.

Radiographs of the right knee showed a stable implant and linear calcifications in the anterior thigh compartment. CT of the right leg demonstrated a fusiform calcified mass with peripheral plaque-like calcifications tracking the rectus femoris muscle and an avulsion of the anterior inferior iliac spine. MRI of both legs revealed heterogeneous lesions that were dark on all sequences, replacing the entire rectus femoris muscles. No mechanical issues were identified with the hip or knee implants.
title: Bilateral Lower Extremity Calcific Myonecrosis: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 17-year-old boy was referred with a one-month history of progressive shortness of breath, intermittent nonproductive cough of eight months’ duration, fever, and a 6-kg weight loss. He had no prior medical history. On examination, right-sided fremitus was decreased, dullness was noted over the upper and mid–right lung fields, and breath sounds were diminished in the same area. Routine laboratory tests, including leukocyte count and C-reactive protein level, were normal. Tumor markers (AFP, CEA, LDH, and β-HCG) were within reference ranges. Pulmonary function tests revealed an FEV₁ of 3.5 L (94% predicted) and an FVC of 4.5 L (97% predicted). A chest radiograph showed a mass in the right paratracheal and parahilar mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a semicystic, septate mass in the right lateral to anterior superior mediastinum. “With this imaging appearance, a provisional diagnosis of lung cancer was made.” Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated stenosis of the distal trachea and both main bronchi from external compression. “Bronchial lavage cytology showed negative malignant epithelial cells.” Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery was recommended for further evaluation.
title: Diagnostic challenges in differentiating mediastinal tuberculosis from mediastinal tumors: A case report

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a right hip limp and mild activity-related pain (3/10). There was no history of trauma. She had been diagnosed elsewhere with bilateral Perthes disease and treated with physical therapy, analgesics, and activity restriction. 

Family history was negative for orthopedic or storage diseases; parents were nonconsanguineous. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her only surgery was repair of a patent urachal canal in infancy. 

On examination, weight was 24.3 kg (50th percentile), height 116 cm (10th percentile). Facial features included a mildly depressed nasal bridge, wide mouth, and thick lips. Cervical spine mobility was normal. There was increased lumbar lordosis and a correctable dorso-lumbar kyphosis on trunk flexion. Upper extremity joints had slight widening of the wrists and interphalangeal joints but full range of motion. Hip examination showed mild pain at end-range right abduction; knee valgus was 12° bilaterally with 30 mm intermalleolar distance. Foot arches were normal. 

Her 8-year-old brother, asymptomatic, was evaluated because of similar habits. He weighed 22.9 kg (10th percentile) and measured 119 cm (1st percentile); sitting/standing height ratio was below the 3rd percentile. He had the same facial features, mild anterior chest prominence, and 12° knee valgus with 40 mm intermalleolar distance. 

Radiographs in both siblings showed platyspondyly and kyphosis at the thoraco-lumbar junction. Pelvic films revealed acetabular dysplasia and flattened, irregular femoral heads with fragmented epiphyses. Hand radiographs demonstrated triangular distal phalanges. These combined findings were noted to be compatible with spondylo-epiphyseal dysplasia.
title: Bilateral Perthes Masking Morquio Disease

case_prompt: An 80-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a right upper abdominal encapsulated fluid collection. Two weeks earlier, he presented with abdominal pain and nausea. Abdominal ultrasonography and computed tomography in the emergency department showed a large fluid collection in the right upper abdominal cavity and gallbladder stones. He had no past history of abdominal surgery or trauma. On admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed slight tenderness and a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory tests showed albumin 2.3 g/dL (3.5–5.0), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 82 mm/h, C-reactive protein 5.2 mg/dL (0.00–0.80), and calcium 7.7 mg/dL (8.6–10.2); viral hepatitis markers were negative. A repeat CT scan demonstrated an 18.9-cm right hepatic subcapsular fluid collection. Abdominal MRI revealed multiple common bile duct stones with biliary dilatation and a large subcapsular fluid collection along the lower margin of the right hepatic lobe without any direct communication with the biliary system.
title: Spontaneous biloma managed with endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and percutaneous drainage: a case report

case_prompt: A 46-year-old North-African man with well-controlled hypertension and hereditary spherocytosis presented after 12 days of fever, cough, and progressive dyspnea when he developed visual loss in his left eye. He was admitted to the ICU for respiratory failure and unilateral visual impairment. Chest radiograph showed bilateral peripheral airspace opacities, and SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by RT-PCR; bacterial co-infection was excluded. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, normal platelet and leukocyte counts, total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL (mostly indirect), lactate dehydrogenase 690 U/L (normal 230–460), and haptoglobin 244 mg/dL (normal 34–200). Peripheral blood smear demonstrated erythrocyte agglutinates (confirmed with direct antiglobulin test), spherocytes, polychromasia, and circulating erythroblasts; G6PD levels were normal. Ophthalmic evaluation showed visual acuity 20/20 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left. Fundus examination revealed bilateral retinal hemorrhages with right parafoveal and left foveal involvement. Anterior segment examination, pupillary responses, and intraocular pressure were normal. Optical coherence tomography identified hemorrhages beneath the internal limiting membrane in both eyes, obliterating the foveal depression in the left eye. Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated bilateral blockage corresponding to areas of hemorrhage in the context of normal retinal and choroidal circulation, excluding vascular occlusion, hypertensive retinopathy, and vasculitis.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Bilateral macular hemorrhage in a patient with COVID-19

case_prompt: A 26-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of persistent fever with occasional high peaks, and 2 months of loose stools and vomiting. He also noted bilateral upper-limb numbness and burning in both lower limbs, resulting in difficulty walking, along with loss of appetite and weight loss. Examination showed hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal lymphadenopathy, and impaired sensation to the groin on the right, mid-thigh on the left, and in the fingers of both hands. Laboratory studies revealed HIV seropositivity (CD4 count, 38 cells/mm3) and normal biochemical parameters. He received empirical antitubercular therapy for transaminitis at an outside hospital without clinical improvement. Cytomegalovirus PCR was positive. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated intense tracer uptake in abdominal lymph nodes and bilateral bulky adrenal glands, with hepatosplenomegaly.
title: 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging and PET-guided biopsy in evaluation and treatment decision in adrenal histoplasmosis

case_prompt:
A 41‐year‐old woman was admitted for progressive shortness of breath and productive cough of 3 months’ duration. She had a history of myasthenia gravis secondary to thymoma, previously resected twice, treated with mycophenolate mofetil, pyridostigmine, and intermittent prednisone; prior exacerbations were managed with IVIg, rituximab, and tacrolimus. On admission, her cough and dyspnea had not improved with oral and intravenous antibiotics. 

On hospital day 3, she developed a mixed petechial and morbilliform rash on the extremities with malar erythema. A skin biopsy of the left forearm showed spongiotic and interface dermatitis without eosinophilia, favoring a viral exanthem. Over the next week, the rash evolved into violaceous, scaly, hyperkeratotic plaques on the bilateral acral surfaces. A repeat biopsy revealed vacuolar interface dermatitis with dyskeratosis; direct immunofluorescence was negative.

Chest CT demonstrated a 2.2-cm pleural‐based nodularity along the right lung base. Video‐assisted thoracoscopic surgery with bronchoscopy identified a 4.5-cm invasive thymoma in the left upper lobe. She was discharged on topical steroids, with plans to restart her immunosuppressive regimen and to proceed with surgical resection and radiotherapy of the thoracic mass.
title: Thymoma-associated multiorgan autoimmunity treated with multimodal therapy including extracorporeal photopheresis

case_prompt: A 17-year-old male high-school athlete presented with a one-year history of bilateral, symmetrical swelling of the second, third, and fourth proximal interphalangeal joints. He first noticed painless nodules three months before evaluation. He denied pain, redness, or limitation of his usual activities, including sports. Physical examination showed non-tender, symmetric swelling of the PIP joints with preserved active and passive range of motion. Laboratory evaluation, including serologic testing for inflammatory and connective-tissue diseases, was negative. Plain radiographs of both hands demonstrated soft-tissue swelling around the PIP joints with normal bone and joint architecture. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed no evidence of inflammation in the synovium, ligaments, tendons, or subcutaneous tissues and no osseous or soft-tissue mass.
title: Pachydermodactyly – A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 77-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of an enlarging, erythematous-to-brownish indurated lesion on the left thigh. The lesion was mildly tender and had expanded centrifugally without any preceding trauma or infection. Her medical history included hip replacement surgery, cataracts, and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine; thyroid-stimulating hormone levels were normal. On examination, there was a large annular plaque with an erythematous mildly tender border on the medial left thigh and no ulceration. Initial differential diagnoses included eosinophilic cellulitis, necrobiosis lipoidica, and morphea. A punch biopsy was inconclusive. At follow-up, the lesion had migrated distally to the left lower limb. A second punch biopsy from the new tender area revealed a mild lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with vascular proliferation in the superficial and deep dermis, and septal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with slight thickening in the subcutaneous tissue; no neutrophilic infiltrate or well-formed granulomas were seen, consistent with septal panniculitis with vascular proliferation. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 mm/h (normal, 2–30 mm/h) and a neutrophil count of 8.5 × 10^9/L (normal, 2.0–7.5 × 10^9/L); all other tests, including antinuclear antibody, α-1 antitrypsin, serum amylase, and serum lipase, were within the normal range.
title: An unusual presentation of Vilanova disease (erythema nodosum migrans) with superficial histologic changes

case_prompt: A six-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of one month of progressive abdominal distension and pain. Her weight was 5.5 kg. On examination, her abdomen was markedly distended; palpation revealed a firm, tender, irregular mass occupying the entire left lumbar and pelvic regions that moved with respiration. Liver and renal function tests and complete blood counts were all within normal limits. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a left pelvic kidney measuring 18 cm in diameter with marked dilation of the collecting system and mixed internal cystic and solid components. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed a mass arising from the left kidney containing low-density areas; the right kidney was normal, and no other masses were identified. Given that congenital mesoblastic nephroma is the most frequent neonatal renal tumor and that ectopic kidneys have a heightened risk for Wilms’ tumor, the leading preoperative considerations were congenital mesoblastic nephroma versus Wilms’ tumor arising in an ectopic kidney. The patient was taken for exploratory laparotomy and left renal mass excision. After an uneventful postoperative course, the specimen was sent for histopathological examination.
title: Primary renal teratoma: a rare entity

case_prompt: A 47-year-old gravida 3 para 3 premenopausal woman with no significant medical history presented with a four-month history of a mass protruding through the vagina, accompanied by intermittent vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain. On examination, she had diffuse abdominal distension and pelvic tenderness. Gynecologic evaluation revealed a 30 cm mass protruding from the vaginal introitus with areas of necrosis; the cervix was not visualized. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 28.4 %, and white-cell count 12 100/mm3. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large, heterogeneous anterior mass arising from the cervix measuring 30 cm, prolapsed into the vagina; the urinary bladder was displaced superiorly and there was right-sided hydronephrosis due to mass effect.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A huge prolapsed cervical leiomyoma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old man presented with a one-day history of increasing fatigue and malaise, preceded by nausea, vomiting, myalgia, and arthralgia. This was his sixth similar presentation over six months. His past medical history included mild obstructive sleep apnea, prior intracranial hemorrhage, and two hospital admissions for undefined “septic shock.” He took aspirin and vitamin B12, had no allergies, was a nonsmoker, and reported a long history of heavy alcohol use. Family history was notable for a brother with lymphoma.  

On examination, he was tachycardic at 103 bpm and had an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air; other vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 224 g/L, red-cell count 6.66×10^12/L, hematocrit 64%, albumin 34 g/L, white-cell count 19.7×10^9/L, and evidence of acute kidney injury (creatinine 121 µmol/L, eGFR 59 mL/min/1.73 m^2). A 130-mL venesection was performed, and the patient was admitted.  

Despite aggressive fluid resuscitation, his blood pressure fell to 83/41 mmHg, and he was transferred to the ICU. After further fluids, blood pressure normalized but urine output remained low (26 mL/h). He developed pitting edema to the knees, mild bilateral basal crackles, and sacral edema. Mixed metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate was noted. Blood and urine cultures were negative.  

Within 24 hours in the ICU his urine output increased to 200–500 mL/h, his hemoglobin normalized, and he left by his own request. Twelve hours later he returned with dyspnea; he was tachypneic and hypoxic and had pulmonary edema. He received intravenous furosemide and improved rapidly.
title: Recurrent undifferentiated shock: Idiopathic Systemic Capillary Leak Syndrome

case_prompt: A 46-year-old woman with a 5-year history of hypertension and hypothyroidism presented for preoperative assessment after the diagnosis of a left breast mass on screening mammography. She reported progressive shortness of breath and dry cough for 2 years, with orthopnea developing over the past 6 months. She denied palpitations, syncope, hemoptysis, chest trauma, or prior thoracic surgery. Her medications included levothyroxine and metoprolol; she was a nonsmoker without known allergies. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac examination revealed regular rhythm and normal heart sounds; physical examination was otherwise unremarkable except for grade 2 bilateral lower-limb edema. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm. A preoperative chest radiograph demonstrated a well-defined, oval opacity at the right cardiophrenic angle. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a homogeneous mass measuring 7.2 × 9.1 cm in the right lower thorax, most consistent with a pericardial cyst, although a bronchogenic cyst could not be ruled out. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a 7.5 × 7 cm cystic structure adjacent to the right atrium, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%. Complete blood count, liver function tests, serum creatinine, and electrolytes were within normal limits. An ELISA test for hydatid disease was negative. Urinalysis showed no microscopic hematuria, and abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated normal kidneys.
title: Anesthetic and surgical considerations of giant pericardial cyst: Case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain. Physical examination was unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 1.6 cm hyperechoic mass at the lower pole of the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 1.7 × 1.4 × 1.7 cm hypodense, enhancing, mainly endophytic lesion in the left lower pole without perinephric fat invasion or renal vein involvement; the RENAL nephrometry score was 7.  
She underwent robotic-assisted laparoscopic left partial nephrectomy with selective clamping of the lower-pole artery; the warm ischemic time was 25 minutes without complication.  
Gross examination revealed a 2.2 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm pinkish nodule weighing 3.8 g, with no necrosis.  
Microscopically, the tumor was partly covered by a thin fibrous capsule and rim of renal tissue. It consisted of tightly packed tubules and occasional elongated tubular structures set in a myxoid stroma with extracellular mucin highlighted by Alcian Blue. Tumor cells ranged from cuboidal cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm to bland spindle cells; mitotic figures and necrosis were absent.  
Immunohistochemical studies showed positivity for EMA, AMACR, CK7, PAX8, and CD56; the MIB-1 proliferation index was less than 1%.
final_diagnosis_raw: Mucinous tubular and spindle cell carcinoma
journal: Journal of Kidney Cancer and VHL
title: Mucinous Tubular and Spindle Cell Carcinoma: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old male was referred for evaluation of bilateral impalpable testes. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, he appeared as a normally developed adult male; the scrotum was hypoplastic and empty, and no gonads were palpable in the inguinal or paragenital regions. Ultrasonography did not detect any gonadal structures in the scrotum, inguinal canals, pelvis, or abdomen. Laboratory evaluation revealed azoospermia, normal luteinizing hormone, normal testosterone, and mildly elevated follicle-stimulating hormone. 

With informed consent for possible gonadectomy, the patient underwent laparoscopic exploration. On the right side, a 35 mm abdominal testis with normal vas deferens, epididymis, and vessels was found at a high iliac position and was successfully mobilized and fixed into the right hemiscrotum. Intraoperative biopsy confirmed arterial flow.

On the left side, a smaller 20 mm gonad was found in the pelvis, completely disconnected from hypoplastic vasoepididymal structures and supplied only by the internal spermatic vessels. During mobilization along the spermatic vascular bundle, a second off-white ovoid structure resembling a “third testis” appeared, and further dissection revealed a third identical ovoid structure. The three tandem structures were connected proximally by a cord-like band.
title: “Rosary of Testes”: Splenogonadal Fusion in Association with Bilateral Abdominal Testes Presenting as Polyorchidism

case_prompt: A 51-year-old man presented with progressive right facial fullness over 4 years, accompanied by recent facial pain and serosanguinous drainage. He denied fever, fatigue, weight loss, or facial weakness and had no history of trauma or radiation. On examination, there was a palpable, firm, 4-cm mass in the right parotid region; cranial nerve VII function was intact, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 3.3 × 2.8 × 3.2 cm, well-defined, cystic and solid mass with peripheral enhancement and internal septations in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland. The patient underwent a right superficial parotidectomy with selective level II and III neck dissection. Grossly, the specimen was a well-circumscribed, unilocular cystic mass with a surrounding solid component. Histologically, the lesion consisted of a large cyst lined by either papillary projections or a single layer of cuboidal cells with mild to moderate nuclear atypia, and adjacent solid tumor nests exhibiting a focal cribriform growth pattern; there was no overt mitotic activity or necrosis.
title: High-grade Features of Papillary Cystadenocarcinoma of the Parotid Gland

case_prompt: A 3-year-old girl presented with a one-month history of non-productive cough and recurrent bronchial infections despite symptomatic treatment and antibiotics. There was no significant family history or underlying medical illness. On examination, she appeared unwell; oxygen saturation was 87% on room air, and breath sounds were absent at the left lung base. She was afebrile with no focal neurological deficits. A chest radiograph showed an opaque mass occupying the left hemithorax with contralateral mediastinal deviation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a large, well-defined mass filling nearly the entire left hemithorax, with heterogeneous enhancement, associated pleural effusion, and no evidence of costal erosion or diaphragmatic invasion. A scan-guided needle biopsy was performed, and histological analysis suggested rhabdomyosarcoma. Staging studies ruled out other tumor localizations.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Type II pleuropulmonary blastoma mistaken for rhabdomyosarcoma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman presented with acute left-sided, ibuprofen-resistant neck pain localized over the left common carotid artery. The pain began 3 weeks earlier and worsened over the past 8 days; she had no focal neurologic deficits. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and dyslipidemia, and she had received her second mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccination (elasomeran, mRNA-1273) in the left arm 7 days before symptom onset. An outpatient carotid ultrasound showed wall thickening of the left common carotid artery, prompting referral.

On admission, CT angiography demonstrated a semilunar hypodense thickening of the left common carotid artery with slight luminal narrowing. MRI showed periarterial STIR-signal enhancement in the middle third of the left common carotid artery on postcontrast T1-weighted Dixon sequences, along with a membranous structure within the artery and ventrally accentuated circumjacent contrast enhancement. High-resolution ultrasound revealed a 30 mm long, medially located focal eccentric wall thickening of the middle third of the left common carotid artery with a multilayered appearance and a minor, hemodynamically irrelevant stenosis; no intraluminal thrombus or dissection membrane was seen. Initial laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated C-reactive protein (16 mg/L); vasculitis and sarcoidosis laboratory screenings were negative.
title: Relapsing TIPIC Syndrome after Administration of an mRNA-Based COVID-19 Vaccine

case_prompt: A 39‐year‐old Hispanic woman presented with a one‐day history of severe colicky, non‐radiating lower abdominal pain, nausea, several episodes of vomiting, and constipation. She reported 3 kg of unintentional weight loss over the prior five months and a five‐month history of undiagnosed, intermittent abdominal pain that recurred approximately every two weeks and then resolved spontaneously; this episode of pain persisted. She had no past medical or surgical history, took no regular medications, and had regular menstrual cycles without menorrhagia or dysmenorrhea. She was hemodynamically stable on arrival. On examination, her abdomen was distended with tenderness in the lower quadrants; digital rectal examination revealed an empty rectum. Routine biochemical and hematological tests, including tumor markers, were within normal limits. A plain abdominal radiograph showed multiple air‐fluid levels and dilated bowel loops with no air in the rectum. Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated focal dilation of the distal ileum and a 3.4 × 3.1 × 2.8 cm polypoid lesion, with adjacent free fluid and prominent ileocolic lymph nodes; the large bowel, ovaries, and uterus appeared unremarkable. Colonoscopy was performed and revealed no intraluminal lesion. The patient underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, which revealed a right ovarian hemorrhagic cyst, prominent small‐bowel dilation, and a transition point in the distal ileum where the appendix was tethered to the ileum, forming a mass. A right hemicolectomy with end‐to‐side anastomosis was performed.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Beyond borders: A case report of small bowel obstruction secondary to undiagnosed florid endometriosis

case_prompt:
A 10-month-old girl was brought with four episodes of bloody vomiting and melena. She also had fever and clinical dehydration.  
Her neonatal history included sepsis at 3 days of life treated with exchange transfusions via an umbilical catheter, meningitis, and bouts of abdominal distention requiring incubator care before switching to bottle feeding. Parents are consanguineous; there is no known family history of bleeding or clotting disorders.  
On examination, temperature was 39 °C; she had sunken eyes, mild jaundice, abdominal distention with a navel bulge, bilateral inguinal hernias, and a spleen palpable 4–5 cm below the left costal margin without hepatomegaly.  
Laboratory studies showed WBC 41 300/mm3, CRP 16.5 mg/l, platelets 37 × 10³/µl, hemoglobin 6.8 g/dl, albumin 2.7 g/dl, BUN 74 mg/dl, and potassium 3.1 mEq/l.  
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed multiple esophageal ulcers causing constriction, grade IV esophageal varices, and congestive gastritis.  
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated approximately 3 L of ascites, homogeneous splenomegaly, and absence of a visible portal vein in the hepatic hilum.  
Doppler ultrasonography showed prior splenic vein thrombosis, varices in the gastric antrum and splenic hilum, fibrosis, and impaired blood flow in the portal vein.
title: Portal vein thrombosis in a 10-month-old infant as a complication of neonatal umbilical catheterization: a case report

case_prompt: A 36-year-old man with bipolar disorder, prior alcohol abuse (last drink 2 years ago), hypertension, recent-onset diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia presented with a 1-week history of left upper quadrant and epigastric pain. Six weeks before admission, he began sertraline 200 mg daily, buspirone 15 mg three times daily, and olanzapine 20 mg at bedtime. He was compliant with a fibrate for mild hypertriglyceridemia, but his last lipid panel was 5 years earlier. On examination, his BMI was 40 kg/m2, he was tachycardic, and his temperature was 102.1 °F. Laboratory studies showed a lipase level of 1322 U/L, a glucose level of 290 mg/dL with a hemoglobin A1c of 11.4%, a triglyceride level of 5185 mg/dL, total cholesterol of 677 mg/dL, and an HDL of 16 mg/dL. Abdominal and pelvic CT with contrast demonstrated findings consistent with acute pancreatitis, no necrosis or hemorrhage, and a normal-appearing gallbladder without cholelithiasis. He was diagnosed with acute pancreatitis secondary to hypertriglyceridemia and transferred for plasmapheresis.
title: Olanzapine-Induced Hypertriglyceridemia Resulting in Necrotizing Pancreatitis

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old white woman presented with a 7-year history of recurrent episodes of severe vulvar swelling associated with itching, prominent hyperemia, white vaginal discharge, low-grade fever (up to 38.5°C), heaviness in the genital area, and dyspareunia. Each flare began with itching, followed within hours by edema and erythema of the vulva and perianal region, and then fever. Initially flares recurred every 6 months but later shortened to 2–3 months despite local and systemic antibiotics and glucocorticoids. Between flares she noted persistent mild hypertrophy and induration of the labia majora and minora. Past gynecologic history included recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis, uterine leiomyomas, and endometrial polyp.

On examination, there was bilateral asymmetric enlargement and indurative edema of the labia majora (right > left) with fissures exuding clear fluid, crusted in places. The labia minora were dense, hypertrophic, protruding beyond the majora, with papilliform vegetations. In the perianal area there were cone-shaped vegetations resembling condylomata. Bimanual and pelvic examinations were otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normal total IgE, elevated antistreptolysin O (562 IU/mL; reference <200), C-reactive protein 2.4 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L), positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA titer 4.0 ++, SS-A positive), and slightly elevated anti–Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA 21.31 rel μ/mL; reference <20 rel μ/mL). Tests for Treponema pallidum, HIV, hepatitis B and C viruses, and protozoan infections were negative. Annual cervical and vaginal swabs for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma, Ureaplasma, Trichomonas vaginalis, Gardnerella vaginalis, Candida albicans, HPV, HSV, and CMV by microscopy, culture, and PCR were consistently negative. Molecular assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Candida spp., and Actinomyces DNA from the lesion were negative.

Colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed no significant structural or endoscopic pathology. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans showed no fistulas, abscesses, or masses.
title: Crohn's disease of the vulva: A tough diagnosis (a case report of a 47 y.o. patient)

case_prompt: A 17-year-old healthy woman presented with a 9-month history of right groin pain. The pain initially occurred with long-distance walking, without any history of trauma, and gradually progressed to occur at night; it was associated with a palpable swelling in the same region. She denied fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was a mildly tender, firm, localized swelling over the right pubic area without overlying skin changes or pulsations. The range of motion of the right hip was full and painless. A pelvic radiograph showed an expansile lytic lesion of the right superior pubic ramus. Pelvic MRI demonstrated an expansile multicystic bony lesion measuring 6.8 × 3.3 × 4.5 cm with multiple fluid–fluid levels in the right pubic ramus. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, kidney function, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and alkaline phosphatase, were all within normal limits.
title: Surgical Management of Aneurysmal Bone Cyst of the Pubis: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 50-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department at 7 a.m. by her family, who were unable to awaken her after an evening of alcohol consumption. On admission, she was somnolent, with moderate dysarthria, horizontal gaze-directed nystagmus, trunk ataxia, and incoordination. Laboratory testing showed a blood ethanol concentration of 2.3 ‰. At 8:00 a.m., noncontrast head CT and CT angiography were negative for acute ischemia or hemorrhage. She was treated with forced diuresis and underwent hourly neurologic assessments. By late morning, her level of consciousness improved and dysarthria and ataxia resolved. However, at 2 p.m., she developed worsening somnolence, severe horizontal nystagmus, diplopia, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Repeat head CT remained negative. Carotid and vertebral duplex ultrasonography showed no stenosis, but transcranial Doppler revealed a high pulsatility index and low flow velocity in the basilar artery.
title: Acute alcohol intoxication may cause delay in stroke treatment – case reports

case_prompt:
A 12‐year‐old boy with a history of congenital hypothyroidism treated since birth presented at age 12 years 5 months with a generalized tonic‐clonic seizure. His growth and development had been delayed compared with peers, though academic performance was normal. On examination, he had a round face, short stature, brachydactyly of the third and fourth digits, and palpable subcutaneous calcifications. The right ankle was held in fixed plantar flexion with hyperextension at the ankle and popliteal fossa, and a tendon contracture prevented the heel from touching the ground. Neurologic and cardiovascular examinations were otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed: corrected serum calcium 1.03 mmol/L (2.1–2.7), phosphorus 2.45 mmol/L (0.83–1.48), magnesium 0.76 mmol/L (0.70–1.15), parathyroid hormone (PTH) 249.4 pg/mL (12–65), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 17.74 ng/mL (30–100), TSH 7.408 μIU/mL (0.35–4.94), FT4 10.17 pmol/L (9.01–19.05), alkaline phosphatase 351.3 U/L (34–121), white blood cell count 2.4 ×10^9/µL (4–10), and creatine kinase 921.7 U/L (22–269). ECG showed sinus rhythm with a prolonged corrected QT interval of 482 ms.

Plain radiography of the left hand confirmed brachydactyly of the third and fourth digits. CT of the right lower limb demonstrated ectopic calcification extending from the gastrocnemius region to behind the knee joint. Head CT showed calcifications in the basal ganglia, subscalp soft tissues, and frontal lobes.
title: A novel GNAS mutation in pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a with articular flexion deformity: A case report

case_prompt:
Two men with end‐stage renal disease—aged 57 and 39 years—received deceased‐donor renal transplants. Underlying diseases were Alport syndrome (57‐year‐old) and chronic glomerulonephritis (39‐year‐old). Both had been on hemodialysis for 7 and 8.5 years and had hypertension. The donor was a 62‐year‐old man with hypoxic brain injury after a 10‐minute cardiac arrest during an asthma attack, a history of smoking, insulin therapy in the ICU, an estimated GFR of 42.4 ml/min/1.73 m2, and atherosclerotic renal arteries.

After arterial end‐to‐side anastomosis to the external iliac artery, neither graft had primary function. Both patients experienced DGF—requiring 6 and 10 hemodialysis sessions, respectively. After recovery, the GFR stabilized at 26 and 23.9 ml/min/1.73 m2 by discharge and remained at that reduced level on follow‐up. Doppler ultrasound repeatedly demonstrated homogeneous perfusion of both grafts, with resistance indices between 0.67 and 0.76.

Warm ischemia times were 46 and 65 minutes; cold ischemia times were 11 hours 40 minutes and 19 hours 6 minutes. Immunosuppression included a calcineurin inhibitor, prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, and IL‐2–receptor–antagonist induction. One patient required re‐exploration for postoperative bleeding (6 units of packed red cells); the other had CMV reactivation on day 18, treated successfully with ganciclovir and valganciclovir prophylaxis. Hypertension worsened with immunosuppression.

Physical examination revealed no livedo racemosa or purple toes. Laboratory studies showed elevated serum creatinine consistent with DGF, but C‐reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, leukocyte count, and eosinophil count were normal.
title: Cholesterol-crystal embolism presenting with delayed graft function and impaired long-term function in renal transplant recipients: two case reports

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old man from central Iran noted a small pimple on his right upper eyelid 4 months before presentation. Over time, it slowly enlarged into a well-defined, firm, nontender, subcutaneous, skin-colored nodule measuring 1 cm × 1 cm, with slightly erythematous raised borders, crusting, and no pain or systemic symptoms.  
On examination, vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including CBC, ESR, CRP, and blood chemistries, were within normal limits. A culture of lesion fluid grew Staphylococcus aureus. The patient underwent sequential courses of cephalexin, cloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and a brief course of systemic steroids—each for 10 days—with no improvement.  
Given his residence in an area endemic for cutaneous leishmaniasis and the lesion’s lack of response to therapy, cutaneous leishmaniasis versus basal cell carcinoma was proposed as the leading diagnostic considerations.
title: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis of the Eyelid: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 48-year-old South Asian man presented with sudden onset of slurred speech, episodes of vomiting, and complete motor aphasia of 10 hours’ duration, which had begun to improve over the preceding hour. He had experienced a similar self-limited episode 5 months earlier. He had no history of hypertension or diabetes. On examination, he was afebrile; blood pressure was 106/74 mm Hg; heart rate, 104 beats per minute with a regular rhythm; and all distal pulses were palpable. Cardiac examination revealed a faint, short mid-diastolic murmur. Neurologic examination showed motor aphasia without peripheral deficits. Computed tomography of the brain demonstrated multiple infarcts in the left parietal lobe, right occipital lobe, right caudate nucleus, left internal capsule, left thalamus, and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed multiple foci of high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging in the right corona radiata, left thalamus, and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, consistent with acute infarction. These findings suggested a cardio-embolic source, although the patient had no known cardiac history.
title: A case report of left atrial myxoma presenting as embolic stroke

case_prompt: A 72-year-old man experienced an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest while asleep. Emergency medical services found a non-shockable rhythm, performed 22 minutes of CPR, and intubated him, achieving ROSC immediately after intubation. He regained full consciousness and was weaned off mechanical ventilation after a successful spontaneous breathing trial. During the admission, he had a second cardiac arrest after falling asleep; prompt intubation again restored circulation. Arterial blood gas analysis showed profound hypercapnia with a PaCO2 up to 101.5 mmHg. On pressure-controlled ventilation, reducing the respiratory rate to 0.5 breaths per minute reproducibly induced apnea, whereas he had no apnea when awake. Neurologic examination revealed normal muscle strength, intact cranial nerves, and no sensory deficits. He reported one month of progressive oropharyngeal dysphagia. Brain MRI showed no structural lesions in the pons or medulla. Chest CT demonstrated a 3.2-cm middle mediastinal mass.
title: Central sleep apnea as an initial presentation of small cell lung carcinoma with anti‐Hu antibody‐related paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome

case_prompt: A 68-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension presented with 2 weeks of progressively decreasing vision in her right eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/66 OD and 20/28 OS. Anterior-segment examination showed 1+ nuclear sclerosis bilaterally. Funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed a 2.3-mm yellowish-red intraretinal mass at the superior temporal arcade, surrounded by hard exudates and retinal hemorrhages. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated a prominent intraretinal mass with an overlying epiretinal membrane and subretinal fluid extending to the subfoveal area. Fluorescein angiography revealed early hyperfluorescence with tortuous, telangiectatic vessels within the lesion and slight late leakage, with no dilated or tortuous feeder vessels.
title: Retinal vasoproliferative tumor regression after intravitreal aflibercept

case_prompt: A 63-year-old man with a history of orthotopic liver transplantation in 2010 for hepatitis C–related cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma presented with an 8-month history of nonbloody diarrhea, occurring more than six times per day, accompanied by bloating, cramping, and a 15-pound weight loss. He denied fevers or night sweats. Three months earlier, MRI performed for mild elevations in liver enzymes showed stable prominent mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest measuring 11 mm. His medications included mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, cyclosporine 100 mg twice daily, and ursodiol; he reported taking only half the prescribed immunosuppressive doses. On examination, the abdomen was soft without tenderness or organomegaly. Laboratory studies revealed an AST of 37 IU/L and ALT of 75 IU/L. No stool studies were obtained because the diarrhea was attributed to noninfectious causes, and bulking agents led to symptomatic improvement. Upper endoscopy showed duodenal inflammation; colonoscopy revealed continuous mild erythema in the rectosigmoid colon up to 30 cm from the anal verge. Biopsies from the duodenum and colon demonstrated a prominent infiltrate of small atypical lymphocytes with round to irregular nuclei, mature chromatin, and scant clear cytoplasm. There was no evidence of intraepithelial lymphocytes or villous atrophy to suggest celiac disease. Immunostaining of the biopsies was negative for cytomegalovirus.
title: Mantle Cell Lymphoma Presenting as Diarrhea in a Liver Transplant Recipient

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of left facial asymmetry and a scar at the left mandibular angle, resulting from a fall and laceration. His chief complaint was an enlarging left-sided facial “growth” without pain. He had no systemic illness.

On extraoral examination, there was a unilateral swelling centered over the left mandibular angle. Palpation revealed that the tissue was of normal tone and nontender. Mandibular movements were within normal limits. When asked to clench his teeth, the swelling became more prominent and firm. The patient reported preferential use of the left side when chewing. There was no temporomandibular joint clicking and no family history of similar findings.

Intraoral examination revealed bilaterally distoangularly impacted mandibular third molars. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a prominent left mandibular angle without evidence of osseous lesion.
title: Management of Unilateral Masseter Hypertrophy and Hypertrophic Scar—A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old woman (G4 L4) with menopause 12 years earlier presented with a 2-month history of vaginal bleeding. Her medical history was notable for right mastectomy for breast cancer 8 years earlier followed by chemotherapy and ongoing tamoxifen 10 mg twice daily since that time; she also had hypertension managed with telmisartan. She denied postmenopausal estrogen therapy and had no family history of cancer. 

On examination, she appeared anemic. The abdomen was soft, with mild lower-quadrant tenderness and no organomegaly or ascites. Pelvic and speculum examinations were unremarkable; bimanual exam showed an anteverted, irregular, soft, and enlarged uterus with free adnexal areas. Other systemic findings were normal.

Laboratory studies revealed microcytic, hypochromic anemia; normal renal and liver function; and negative infectious serologies. Chest radiograph was normal. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an irregular, heterogeneous endometrium measuring 22.2 mm in thickness. A Pap smear was negative for dysplasia or malignancy.

Fractional curettage yielded multiple soft gray-brown fragments measuring 2 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm. Microscopic examination demonstrated a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma with predominant papillary and glandular patterns. Tumor cells were tall, columnar, mildly to moderately pleomorphic, with small vesicular uniform nuclei and fine chromatin. The cytoplasm was clear with marked supranuclear and subnuclear vacuolization. The mitotic rate was 2–3 per high-power field with atypical forms, and there was stromal invasion.

A diastase-sensitive Periodic Acid–Schiff stain revealed eosinophilic fine granular material in the vacuolated cells, while mucin stains were negative. Immunohistochemical studies showed strong nuclear positivity for estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor, high p53 expression, and a Ki-67 proliferation index of 60%.
title: Secretory Endometrial Adenocarcinoma: A Rare Sequelae in a Postmenopausal Woman Following Tamoxifen Therapy for Breast Cancer

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old Caucasian woman presented to the emergency department with a 4-week history of amenorrhea and lower abdominal pain. She had been treated for primary hypothyroidism with levothyroxine 200 mcg daily but had discontinued the medication one month earlier. Menarche occurred at age 11; her menstrual cycles were irregular. She denied use of any contraception, had no history of in vitro fertilization or known gynecologic pathology, and reported one prior spontaneous pregnancy complicated by severe sepsis at age 18.

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation revealed bilateral, mobile adnexal masses. Laboratory evaluation showed:
- Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH): 515 IU/mL (reference 0.4–4)  
- Free thyroxine (fT4): undetectable (reference 0.7–1.8 ng/dL)  
- Cancer antigen-125 (CA-125): 1,045 U/mL (reference 0–10)  
- Elevated hematocrit and hypoproteinemia  
- Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia  
- Mildly elevated liver enzymes and creatinine  

Transvaginal ultrasound identified a single intrauterine fetus with regular cardiac activity, consistent with 9 weeks 2 days of gestation; both ovaries were massively enlarged (right 15 × 14 × 16.6 cm; left 15 × 8.2 × 18.3 cm) with extensive multilocular cysts and moderate ascites. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mild mitral valve prolapse and a circumferential pericardial effusion without hemodynamic compromise.
title: Severe primary hypothyroidism and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in a spontaneous pregnancy: a case report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old previously healthy boy presented with a 6-month history of progressive blurring of distance vision. Initial examination at a local clinic revealed degenerative lesions in the macular area, raising suspicion for Stargardt’s disease. On referral, best-corrected visual acuity was 0.9 in each eye (1.0 with minor astigmatic correction). Static perimetry (24-2) showed subtle central depression (RE MD −2.36 dB; LE MD −2.55 dB, both p < 5%). Anterior segment examination, intraocular pressures (16.5 mmHg RE; 17.2 mmHg LE), Ishihara color testing, and Farnsworth D-15 were normal.

Funduscopic examination with indirect ophthalmoscopy and a Volk lens revealed symmetrical, bilateral circular foci of RPE rearrangement around the optic disc and hypertrophic hyperpigmentation encircling the macula, extending peripherally into a reticular “fishing-net” pattern. Retinal vessels appeared normal. Macular OCT showed no structural anomalies (central thickness 282 μm RE; 279 μm LE). Autofluorescence imaging demonstrated numerous patchy, mosaic areas of hypofluorescence corresponding to the pigmented lesions. Fluorescein angiography revealed blocked choroidal fluorescence in the same reticular distribution.

Multifocal ERG was abnormal in the right eye—with increased P1 implicit times in rings R1–R3—but normal in the left eye. Pattern ERG responses were normal bilaterally. Electro-oculography showed Arden ratios of 3.3 in the right eye and 1.8 in the left eye, indicating significant interocular asymmetry and a near-lower-limit value in the left eye. Flash ERG revealed only slight increases in a- and b-wave implicit times of the rod-cone response, effectively excluding cone and cone-rod dystrophies.

Next-generation sequencing of 317 genes associated with retinal diseases (RetNet panel) detected no pathogenic variants in known retinal dystrophy genes; it identified a C2 gene variant (c.841_849+19del, rs9332736) not previously linked to retinal pathology.
title: Observations for Sjögren’s Pigment Epithelial Reticular Dystrophy in a 16-Year-Old Boy—An Extremely Rare Retinal Case Report

case_prompt: A 14-year-old girl from eastern Nepal presented with a one-year history of massive, gradually progressive enlargement of both breasts, causing chest discomfort, pressure sores in the inframammary folds, and grooving of the shoulders from bra straps. She felt embarrassed and limited her school attendance and social activities. On examination, both breasts were markedly pendulous and firm, without discrete masses or tenderness; the areolae were widened, and there were areas of pressure necrosis. Axillary lymph nodes were not enlarged. Her BMI was 23.15 kg/m2. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, thyroid function tests, follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, estradiol, progesterone, and prolactin, were all within normal limits.
title: Virginal breast hypertrophy in a 14‐year‐old girl: A case report

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old previously healthy Afro-asiatic man presented with a 3-month history of headache and one generalized tonic–clonic seizure. He had no other symptoms. On examination he was afebrile, alert (GCS 15), and oriented. Neurologically, power was 4+ in the right upper and lower limbs; tone and reflexes were normal. General physical and systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including stool and urine tests, were normal. 
Noncontrast head CT showed a focal area of high density in the left parietal region. MRI of the brain revealed a fairly well-defined 1.8 × 1.0 cm lobulated, cortical-based intra-axial lesion in the left posterior parietal region with homogeneous enhancement, moderate perilesional vasogenic edema, and mild localized mass effect; no other lesions were identified. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated a choline peak suggestive of cell membrane turnover seen in conditions such as neoplasms, demyelination, inflammation, and gliosis; given the patient’s age and history, an inflammatory lesion was thought to be more likely. 
A preliminary differential diagnosis included granulomatous lesion, lymphoma, primary glial neoplasm, and less likely meningioma.
title: Surgical management outcome of cerebral schistosomiasis: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 53-year-old man with untreated gallbladder stones presented with progressively worsening right-sided hemiparesis and difficulty speaking. He had no fever, chest pain, or dyspnea. On examination, his temperature was normal, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg. He had mild jaundice, a grade 3 systolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex, and hepatomegaly. Neurologic evaluation showed motor dysphasia and right hemiparesis (muscle strength 3/5). Brain MRI revealed a left periventricular infarction with hemorrhagic transformation in the left temporal lobe. Routine transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 10.7 × 13.8 mm homogenous, slightly hypoechoic mass attached to the edge of the right coronary and noncoronary cusps of the aortic valve, with mild aortic regurgitation; an 11 × 4.4 mm mass on the atrial side of the posterior mitral leaflet with mild mitral regurgitation; and a 43 × 11 mm right ventricular mobile lesion of similar echogenicity. Transesophageal and 3D echocardiography confirmed additional masses on the left coronary cusp and better characterized their motion. Cardiac MSCT showed homogenous, non–contrast-enhancing lesions on all three aortic valve leaflets with minimal motion. Free-breathing cardiac MRI demonstrated the right ventricular lesion as a band-shaped hypointense signal without gadolinium enhancement. Three sets of blood cultures and PCR for typical bacterial and fungal pathogens were negative. Protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III levels were normal; D-dimer was elevated at >7.65 mg/L; PT was 21.8 s and APTT 42.5 s. Anti–double-stranded DNA and ANA antibodies were negative.
title: Multimodality Imaging Supports Cardiac Lesion Diagnosis in Patient With Liver Carcinoma: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 33‐year‐old G2P1 woman at 19 weeks’ gestation presented with several days of dyspnea on exertion. She denied alcohol, tobacco, and drug use. Examination was notable only for mild jaundice; blood pressure and other vital signs were within normal limits for pregnancy.

Laboratory studies on admission:
- WBC 86.5 k/µL (82% blasts), hemoglobin 5.5 g/dL, platelets 18 k/µL  
- ALT 33 U/L, AST 21 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 215 U/L, INR 1.1  

Bone marrow biopsy confirmed AML with inv(16). She received hydroxyurea for cytoreduction and then induction chemotherapy with cytarabine (100 mg/m2 days 1–7) and daunorubicin (60 mg/m2 days 1–3).

On cycle 1 day 5, total bilirubin rose to 2.7 mg/dL (direct 1.0 mg/dL) while AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and INR remained normal. By day 15, total bilirubin peaked at 13.4 mg/dL (direct 8.5 mg/dL) without transaminase elevations. There was no clinical or laboratory evidence of hemolysis.

Imaging and serologic studies:
- RUQ ultrasound on day 5: cholelithiasis without ductal dilation or cholecystitis  
- MRCP without contrast: no biliary ductal dilation  
- Hepatitis A, B, and C serologies and CMV and EBV PCR: undetectable  
- Autoimmune hepatitis panel (ANA, AMA, ASMA, total Ig): negative
title: Cytarabine-Induced Hyperbilirubinemia in a Pregnant Patient With Acute Myeloid Leukemia

case_prompt: A 45-year-old man with no significant medical or surgical history presented with an asymptomatic, slowly growing, palpable right inguinal mass. On examination, there was a hard, multinodular, mobile mass along the right spermatic cord near the upper pole of the testis, and the testis itself appeared uninvolved. Scrotal ultrasound showed normal testicles and a 3.5 cm paratesticular heterogeneous hyperechoic lesion along the right spermatic cord, cranial to the testicle, without tunica albuginea involvement. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a diffuse-proliferated nodular mass with iso- and low-intensity signal on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and minimal contrast enhancement. Laboratory investigations revealed negative lactate dehydrogenase, alpha-fetoprotein, and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin. The patient underwent inguinal surgical exploration; intraoperative frozen-section assessment was reported as benign, and a testis-sparing enucleation of the mass was performed.
title: Paratesticular fibrous pseudotumor with histological features of IgG4-related disease: two case reports and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 14-year-old boy presented with progressive enlargement of the second through fifth toes of the right foot, noted since birth and worsening over time. At age 7, he developed inability to wear shoes; one month before presentation he began to experience forefoot pain and difficulty walking. He had no other anomalies, no family history of similar conditions, and an uneventful past medical history. On examination, vital signs were normal. The right foot showed enlarged second through fifth toes without tenderness; the neurovascular examination was intact. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, with hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, hematocrit 33.1%, MCV 78 fL, potassium 3.96 mmol/L, sodium 138.3 mmol/L. Plain radiographs of the right foot demonstrated enlargement of the phalanges—especially the distal phalanges—with soft-tissue overgrowth, “no fracture, sclerotic or osteolytic changes,” no bone erosion, and preserved joint spaces and ankle alignment, “features suggestive of macrodactyly.”
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Megadactyly with syndactyly of the right toes, a rare case report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old right-handed male high-school rugby player sustained severe right-sided neck and shoulder pain while tackling an opponent. The pain improved with rest, and he returned to play, but intermittent shoulder pain recurred, resolving after brief rest periods. He was initially diagnosed with shoulder muscle strain and underwent 4 weeks of physical therapy without improvement; persistent pain progressed to noticeable shoulder weakness by 6 weeks. Two months after the injury, his chief complaint was limited right shoulder elevation. He had no remarkable past medical or family history.

On examination, active elevation of the right shoulder in the scapular plane was limited to 50° (left normal). Medial scapular winging was observed on wall push-up and during active elevation (right > left). Rotator cuff and impingement tests were negative in the right shoulder. Manual testing showed normal strength of the biceps, triceps, and hand grip. Plain radiographs were unremarkable. MRI of the shoulder revealed atrophy of the right serratus anterior and subclavius muscles without intrinsic joint or cervical spine pathology. Laboratory tests showed mildly elevated muscle enzymes (creatine kinase 870 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 526 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 370 U/L, aldolase 10.9 U/L). Further history revealed lifelong difficulty sucking high-viscosity drinks and subtle orbicularis oculi weakness on facial examination.

Initially, neuralgic amyotrophy or a long thoracic nerve injury was suspected. However, given the facial muscle weakness, further diagnostic evaluation was pursued before electromyography.
title: Scapular Winging following Sports-Related Injury in a Rugby Player

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 5-month history of gradually enlarging, painful bilateral vulvar masses. She also reported increased thirst and polyuria (>5 L/day). Her past history was notable for an isolated right maxillofacial lesion diagnosed in October 2021 as Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), treated with local excision; immunohistochemistry at that time was positive for CD1α, Langerin, S100, and CD21. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with NovoMix 30.

On gynecological examination, the right vulvar mass measured 3.0×3.0×2.0 cm with a 0.5×0.5 cm superficial vesicular area and yellowish discharge; the left mass measured 3.0×3.0×3.0 cm with intact overlying skin. The vagina, cervix, uterus, and adnexa were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed low triiodothyronine and thyroxine with elevated TSH, hyperglycemia (fasting 10–13.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 10.7%), reduced lymphocyte subsets, and negative viral serologies; routine blood counts, liver and kidney function, and coagulation were normal.

PET/CT revealed a hypermetabolic soft-tissue mass in the left neck (7.7×3.4 cm, SUVmax 14.5), bilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle thickening (SUVmax 12.7), and striated nodular soft-tissue shadows in the perineal area with a “figure-of-eight” pattern (SUVmax 9.6) involving the bilateral vulva and obturator internus muscles. Pelvic MRI demonstrated bilateral pelvic floor involvement along the obturator internus muscles and perineal region, with striated T2 slightly hyperintense signals, unclear margins, and significant enhancement (thickness ~2.5 cm). Enhanced MRI of the saddle region was normal.

A biopsy of the right vulvar mass showed clusters of medium-sized cells with dense eosinophil infiltration. Immunohistochemistry revealed: “Langerin positive, CD1a positive, CD68 partially positive, CD163 partially positive, CD45 positive, vimentin positive, and Ki-67 (hotspot area approximately 40% positive).”
title: Recurrent multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving the female genitalia: A case report

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-week history of low-grade fever, night sweats, and progressive dyspnea. Chest imaging showed bilateral ground-glass opacities, and brain MRI revealed a subacute infarct in the right corona radiata. On 5 L/min oxygen, her temperature was 37.1 °C, blood pressure 126/71 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 91%. Lung auscultation revealed slight expiratory crackles; cardiac exam showed a soft pansystolic murmur at the apex. Neurologic exam demonstrated mild left-sided dysmetria on finger–nose testing.

Initial laboratory studies demonstrated:
• LDH 1027 U/L (normal 120–220)  
• sIL-2R 1180 U/L (145–519)  
• CRP 3.49 mg/dL (0–0.35)  
• ANA ×1280 (<40) and anticentromere antibody ×1280 (<40)  
• Other serologies, cultures, and markers of infection were negative

Community-acquired pneumonia was suspected, but her hypoxia worsened despite treatment. Given the high-titer anticentromere antibody, rapid renal dysfunction with hematuria and proteinuria, and lung findings, interstitial pneumonia related to systemic scleroderma was diagnosed, and she received methylprednisolone pulse therapy and plasma exchange. Subsequent chest imaging showed improvement of the ground-glass opacities but new bilateral pleural effusions.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: A Case of Intravascular Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma Initially Suspected as Interstitial Pneumonia Associated With Systemic Scleroderma

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old farmer presented in January 2011 with a 6-year history of a progressively enlarging plantar lesion on the right heel. He first noted a 1 cm superficial wound in May 2003 and underwent multiple local treatments elsewhere, including excisions, superficial biopsies, and parenteral antibiotics. A culture grew Proteus mirabilis, and earlier histological examinations demonstrated only epithelial hyperplasia without malignancy. Despite topical agents for verruca vulgaris and antibiotic courses, the lesion slowly enlarged and became ulcerated.

His medical history was notable for spinal trauma 30 years earlier, treated with vertebral fixation, resulting in permanent urinary catheterization but otherwise healed fractures. On examination, there was a large ulcerated, verrucous plaque over the calcaneus of the right foot; no other lesions were present. Laboratory studies remained nondiagnostic. The patient underwent aggressive debridement with marginal excision and multiple deep biopsies.

High-quality radiographs and CT scan of the right foot showed extension of the lesion into the soft periosteal tissues and expansion beneath the calcaneus, suggesting bone invasion.
title: Verrucous Carcinoma of the Foot with Bone Invasion: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old woman presented with vague epigastric pain and dyspepsia of one week’s duration. She had no history of liver disease, pancreatitis, trauma, or prior abdominal surgery. Her abdomen was soft and nontender, and there were no stigmata of portal hypertension. She had well-controlled diabetes treated with oral hypoglycemic agents. Complete blood count and liver and pancreatic function tests were normal.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 2.5 cm anechoic lesion in direct continuity with the main portal vein. Color Doppler demonstrated a monophasic, nonpulsatile venous flow pattern within the lesion, and there was no evidence of intraluminal thrombus. Other abdominal organs appeared normal.
