To further evaluate her persistent pain and to characterize the lesion, a triple-phase CT scan of the abdomen was obtained. In the portal venous phase, there was a focal, well-defined, smoothly marginated, homogenously enhancing mass near the hepatic hilum in direct continuity with the portal vein, with enhancement identical to that of the portal vein. There was no evidence of intraluminal thrombus, liver cirrhosis, or portal hypertension.
title: Radiological evaluation of extrahepatic and intrahepatic portal vein aneurysms: A report of two cases

case_prompt: A 72-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department with sudden onset of posterior neck discomfort that spread to both shoulders, after which she became unable to move her neck. She had no history of trauma, no history of anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and no relevant family history. Her medical history was notable only for dyslipidemia and past appendicitis. On arrival, her temperature was 37.5°C, pulse 87 beats per minute, respiratory rate 21 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 182/88 mmHg. Neurologic examination revealed full strength and sensation in all extremities without signs of paralysis. Noncontrast cervical CT at the referring hospital demonstrated a high-density mass in the right posterior epidural space. Sagittal T2-weighted cervical MRI showed a heterogeneous high-signal epidural mass posterior to the spinal cord extending from C2 to C5.
title: Conservative management of spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma: A case report with favorable prognosis

case_prompt:
An 8-month-old Japanese boy was brought to the emergency department after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He was born at 39 weeks’ gestation (birth weight 3708 g) and was exclusively breast-fed; rice paste and vegetables were introduced at 5 months. His intake was poor, with a marked preference for bread. From 5 months of age he had persistent muddy diarrhea and failure to thrive, falling below weight milestones.

On arrival, he was alert without focal neurologic deficits. His height was 64.3 cm (–2.0 SD) and weight was 6.3 kg (Kaup index 15.2). Laboratory studies showed serum calcium 4.9 mg/dL (ionized calcium 0.745 mmol/L), prolonged prothrombin time (PT-INR 7.8), hypolipidemia, and low levels of vitamins A, D, E, and K. Sudan staining of stool revealed excess lipid droplets. A wrist radiograph demonstrated metaphyseal cupping and flaring consistent with rickets. Serum biochemical analysis and abdominal CT scan showed no evidence of biliary atresia, cystic fibrosis, congenital apolipoprotein abnormalities, or intestinal lymphangiectasia.

He was diagnosed with multiple vitamin malabsorption resulting in severe hypocalcemia, rickets, subclinical vitamin K deficiency, and hypolipidemia, and was started on intravenous calcium, vitamin D, A, E, and K supplementation. His chronic diarrhea persisted.
title:
A Japanese infant presenting with hypocalcemic seizures resulting from
hypovitaminosis D induced by non-celiac gluten sensitivity

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old woman presented with three months of progressive weakness in all four limbs, beginning in the lower extremities and extending to the upper extremities over the last month. She also noted right calf pain one month before weakness onset, but denied numbness, sphincter dysfunction, trauma, headache, fever, or seizures. Her developmental history was significant for delayed ambulation until age 4, with no prior surgery or family history of neurologic disease. 

On examination, there were no cutaneous stigmata of dysraphism. Muscle strength was graded 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs. Reflexes were normal in the upper extremities and hyperactive in the lower extremities, with positive Babinski and Chaddock signs bilaterally and myoclonus of the lower limbs. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervicothoracic spine revealed an intradural tumor extending from C5 to T4 that was hyperintense on T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences and hypointense on STIR images. The leading diagnostic considerations at this stage were intratumoral bleeding, dermoid cyst, and a cervicothoracic subpial lipoma.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Adult cervicothoracic subpial fibrolipoma without dysraphism: An extremely rare case report

case_prompt: A 32-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with two months of intermittent, mild discomfort below the left costal margin without nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed no tenderness, guarding, or palpable mass. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 13.7 g/dL and a normal white-cell count of 5.4×10^9/L; other serum chemistries, including pancreatic enzymes, were within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen revealed an 18 mm focal lesion at the junction of the body and tail of the pancreas, without invasion of surrounding vascular structures or communication with the main pancreatic duct. Serum tumor markers were within reference ranges. On multidisciplinary review, the differential diagnosis included a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, a pseudotumor, and an intrapancreatic splenunculum.
final_diagnosis_raw: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
title: Laparoscopic enucleation of Frantz's tumor of the pancreas: Case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman with a history of primary mediastinal non-Hodgkin lymphoma in 1992 and multiple relapses of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma treated with chemotherapy, autologous and allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, CAR T-cell therapy, and cranial and ocular radiation presented with new painless vision loss in her left eye.

On initial examination, left eye visual acuity was 20/150 with a central scotoma, color plates 1/10, and an afferent pupillary defect. The anterior chamber was quiet. Fundus examination revealed optic disc swelling with splinter hemorrhages, possible early retinitis-like lesions inferior to the fovea, and perivascular infiltrates. MRI of the orbits with and without contrast demonstrated focal enhancement of the left optic nerve head without other lesions.

Six weeks later, her visual acuity had deteriorated to counting fingers at 2 feet. Examination showed 1+ anterior chamber cell, 1+ vitreous cell, diffuse pallid disc swelling and infiltration, and translucent perivascular sheathing consistent with frosted branch angiitis in the left eye.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Vitreoretinal lymphoma presenting as frosted branch angiitis in a patient with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old girl was referred for asymptomatic skin-colored papules and nodules on the left labium majus and perineal area that had rapidly increased in size over one month. At birth, she had five café au lait macules (>5 mm) overlying the perineal lesions. On examination, the left buttock was larger than the right, with the perineal nodules felt as a “bag of worms.” There was no axillary freckling, no other medical history, and no family history of neurocutaneous disease.

Pelvic MRI showed extensive, multifocal, conglomerated enhancing nodular lesions involving both labia majora, vestibular fossa, obturator internus, ischiocavernosus, urethral orifice, ischioanal fossa, and extending into the left gluteal muscle and external anal sphincter, with atrophy of the left gluteus maximus.

A skin biopsy from a nodule demonstrated an intraneural tumor confined by thickened perineurium, with tortuous plexiform bundles. Schwann cell fascicles followed the nerve’s long axis, and the endoneurial space was widened and mucinous, containing loosely spaced rounded endoneurial cells. Tumor cells were S-100 positive on immunohistochemistry.
title: Giant Plexiform Neurofibroma of the Perineum and Pelvic Cavity Manifesting as Segmental Neurofibromatosis

case_prompt:
An 84-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for a second opinion on glaucoma management. She was asymptomatic and had no vision complaints. Her medical history was notable only for systemic hypertension; there was no history of trauma, intraocular inflammation, renal disease, or parathyroid disorder. She had undergone bilateral cataract surgery 4 years earlier and was pseudophakic in both eyes. Current medications included timolol 0.5% twice daily; intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg in each eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes.

On dilated fundus examination, the optic discs had cup-to-disc ratios of 0.7 bilaterally. In each eye there was a well-demarcated, yellowish-white lesion located superotemporally, away from the macula, measuring approximately 8.5 mm × 5 mm × 2 mm in the right eye and 7 mm × 4 mm × 2 mm in the left eye. No choroidal neovascularization or subretinal hemorrhage was observed. Fundus autofluorescence showed corresponding hypoautofluorescent areas. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated a subtle elevation of the retina with slight retinal thinning and underlying choroidal thickening with some large choroidal vessels. Automated perimetry (24-2 SITA Standard) revealed a diffuse mild sensitivity reduction in the right eye and a superior arcuate defect in the left eye.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
title: Bilateral Choroidal Osteomas in an Elderly Woman: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman presented with one month of persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back, worsening over time and unrelated to meals. She reported poor appetite, early satiety, and postprandial nausea without changes in bowel habits or systemic symptoms. Her medical history was significant only for uterine fibroids; second-degree relatives had pancreatic and gastric adenocarcinomas. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs and had mild to moderate epigastric tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed a microcytic, hypochromic iron-deficiency anemia (Hb 11.2 g/dL) and otherwise normal ESR, renal and liver function, pancreatic enzymes, coagulation tests, bilirubin, and tumor markers (CA19-9, AFP, CEA). 

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 48 × 40 mm heterogeneous hypo- and hyperechoic lesion at the pancreatic head adjacent to the liver hilum. Contrast CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined 45 × 46 mm hypodense mass near the celiac trunk abutting the left gastric artery, with engorged mesenteric vessels, mild gastric wall thickening, and subcentimeter porta hepatis lymph nodes. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a 43 × 45 mm hypoechoic lesion posterior to the stomach, encasing the left gastric artery and a short segment of the celiac trunk without ductal dilation; elastography strain ratio was 22. EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration was performed but yielded indeterminate results.
title: Retroperitoneal lymphangioma as the final diagnosis of a middle-aged woman with abdominal pain: a case report

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 1-week history of dry cough and dyspnea on exertion. She denied fever or chills but reported a 20-lb weight loss and anorexia over 2 months. She immigrated from Nigeria 2 years earlier, is a lifelong nonsmoker, and takes no medications. 

On examination she was in mild respiratory distress. Temperature was 99 °F, pulse 152 beats/min, blood pressure 116/83 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She had hepatomegaly; the remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelets 94 000/µL, AST 664 U/L, ALT 1703 U/L, LDH 3462 U/L, and CPK 2742 U/L. A rapid HIV test was positive; CD4 count was 8 cells/µL and HIV viral load exceeded 10 million copies/mL. Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody were positive, with a viral load >17 million IU/L.

Chest radiography revealed bilateral homogeneous ground-glass opacities. Chest CT showed lower-lobe predominant bilateral ground-glass opacities and atelectasis.

Differential diagnosis included Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, atypical bacterial pneumonia, and viral infections. The patient was started empirically on intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (220 mg trimethoprim component every 6 hours) plus oral prednisone 40 mg daily for presumed PJP, and on ceftriaxone with azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia. 

Over the next 48 hours her respiratory distress worsened, and she required endotracheal intubation. Arterial blood gas analysis on 100% FiO2 showed a PaO2 of 157 mm Hg with an alveolar–arterial gradient of 506 mm Hg. She subsequently underwent flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial lung biopsy because of poor response to standard therapy.
title: Pulmonary Toxoplasmosis Diagnosed on Transbronchial Lung Biopsy in a Mechanically Ventilated Patient

case_prompt: A 19-year-old woman presented with recurrent nonspecific upper abdominal pain of several weeks’ duration. She had no jaundice, no palpable abdominal mass, and normal laboratory studies. Ultrasonography demonstrated a hypoechogenic, nearly spherical, homogeneous formation with a smooth contour in direct contact with the underside of the liver and no intervening tissue layer, suggestive of a large hepatic cyst. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-demarcated, hypodense, homogeneous structure measuring 11 cm in transverse diameter, located adjacent to segment 5 of the liver, anterior to the right kidney, and posterior to the gallbladder. A second, similar-appearing hypodense structure of 3 cm was noted on a lower CT slice. Serologic testing excluded cystic echinococcosis. On the basis of these findings, both lesions were interpreted as congenital hepatic cysts. Because of persistent pain, laparoscopic fenestration of the larger cyst was recommended.
title: Choledochal cyst as a diagnostic pitfall: a case report

case_prompt: A 58-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidemia, peripheral arterial disease, and a 40-pack-year smoking history presented with persistent exertional dyspnea. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 56. He previously underwent surgery for a pituitary adenoma. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a round, oval, mobile tumor (approximately 11 mm in diameter) attached to the pulmonary valve on the right cusp, with an estimated ejection fraction of 55%, no segmental wall-motion abnormalities, and no signs of pulmonary thromboembolism. Coronary angiography demonstrated chronic occlusion of the circumflex artery, severe distal right coronary artery stenosis, and severe stenosis of the intermediate branch. To further characterize the mass, cardiac MRI was performed and showed a 1.1 × 0.8 cm lesion that was iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images, mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and displayed peripheral enhancement without central enhancement on delayed post-contrast sequences.
title: Pulmonary Valve Fibroelastoma, Still a Very Rare Cardiac Tumor: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 14-year-old previously healthy boy presented with 5 days of fever, headache, generalized body aches, and retro-orbital pain. On day 3 of illness, dengue NS1 antigen was positive; a complete blood count showed a platelet count of 170 × 10^3/µL and a white blood cell count of 5.7 × 10^3/µL. He received outpatient supportive care with oral fluids. On day 5, his platelet count fell to 98 × 10^3/µL and white blood cell count to 4.2 × 10^3/µL, and he was admitted for observation. Admission vital signs: pulse 140/min, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, capillary refill <2 s; hematocrit rose from a baseline of 36% to 42%. Over 24 h, he developed vomiting and abdominal pain without bleeding. Exam showed generalized flushing, right hypochondrial tenderness, and 3 cm hepatomegaly; bedside ultrasound revealed a mild pleural effusion and gallbladder wall thickening. Lab tests demonstrated leukopenia (2.2 × 10^3/µL), thrombocytopenia (68 × 10^3/µL), and mild transaminitis (ALT 88 U/L, AST 124 U/L). He was managed in a high‐dependency unit for dengue hemorrhagic fever; platelets nadired at 6 × 10^3/µL on day 7, and dengue IgM and IgG were positive. He clinically recovered by day 11; at discharge, white blood cells were 7.5 × 10^3/µL and platelets 52 × 10^3/µL. Follow-up at 2 weeks showed platelets of 47 × 10^3/µL and at 1 month 100 × 10^3/µL. He then defaulted from follow-up, and over the next year his platelets ranged from 30 to 45 × 10^3/µL. One year after discharge, he re-presented with a one-week history of multiple purpuric lesions and documented persistent thrombocytopenia.
title: Dengue hemorrhagic fever as a rare cause of chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura—a pediatric case report

case_prompt:
A five-month-old female Border Collie was evaluated for a one-month history of a severe wound on digit II and III of the left hind limb. The owner reported intense licking, chewing, and biting of the feet leading to self-mutilation. Previous topical treatments with povidone–iodine and a healing ointment produced no improvement. 

On examination, large ulcerative lesions were present on the lateral aspects of digits II and III of the left hind limb; the areas appeared insensitive to painful stimulus. General and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable. 

A differential diagnosis of vascular disease (arteriovenous fistula/shunt), traumatic injury, or genetic defect such as acral mutilation syndrome (AMS) was made. Cytologic impression smears of the lesion showed neutrophils and extracellular bacteria consistent with oral contamination. A genetic test for AMS (GDNF gene mutation) was performed. Pending the result, the dog was treated with lidocaine/prilocaine cream and pregabalin (2.6 mg/kg twice daily). 

The AMS genetic test returned homozygous normal. One month later, new ulcerative and necrotic lesions developed on digits of all four limbs. The dog exhibited intense licking and biting of all extremities. On neurologic re-examination, gait remained normal, but postural reactions were reduced on both hind limbs and the right forelimb; the withdrawal reflex was absent on all limbs, and nociception was severely reduced to absent.
final_diagnosis_raw: inherited sensory and autonomic neuropathy of the Border Collie
title: Inherited Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy in a Border Collie, Interest of Oclacitinib for the Control of Self-Mutilation

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man with no significant medical history was found unconscious outdoors after an evening of heavy alcohol consumption. Emergency Medical Services performed CPR and intubated him on scene because of decreased respiratory effort and a low Glasgow Coma Scale score. On arrival at the hospital he remained mechanically ventilated, unresponsive, and hemodynamically stable.

Initial noncontrast head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality. Echocardiography was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed normal cell counts without xanthochromia. Electroencephalography demonstrated paroxysmal epileptiform activity, and repeat studies documented ongoing epileptiform discharges despite anticonvulsant therapy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain on hospital day 1, including T2, FLAIR, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) sequences, showed no abnormalities.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, electrolytes (sodium 144 mmol/L), renal function, and C-reactive protein level, were noncontributory. Arterial lactate was 1.7 mmol/L and pH was 7.35. Liver tests were mildly elevated (ALT 153 IU/L, AST 122 IU/L, GGT 305 IU/L). Viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Troponin was 0.31 μg/mL without ECG evidence of myocardial infarction. Toxicology screening revealed a blood alcohol level of 48.8 mmol/L and benzodiazepines; opiates and amphetamines were negative.

On hospital day 6, repeat MRI of the brain demonstrated new areas of increased signal on DWI with corresponding low signal on ADC mapping, symmetrically involving the white matter of the centrum semiovale and posterior parietal regions. Conventional T2 and FLAIR sequences remained normal.
title: Delayed post-hypoxic leukoencephalopathy following alcohol consumption and cardiopulmonary arrest

case_prompt: A 16-year-old boy with a 6-year history of treated hypothyroidism presented with a 3-month history of progressive tightening and swelling of both forearms, morning stiffness of the wrists, and a 17-kg weight loss despite a normal appetite. The tightening began a few days after an intense period of gym workouts. He denied fever, Raynaud’s phenomenon, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, sicca symptoms, dysphagia, or changes in bowel or bladder function. On examination, there was woody induration of the forearm skin with sparing of the hands and face, and pitting edema of the legs; there was no sclerodactyly, skin or oral lesions, or other systemic findings. Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL; white-cell count 11,900/mm3 with 41% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 4900/mm3); platelet count 370,000/mm3; ESR 24 mm/h; CRP 39.9 mg/L; creatine phosphokinase 29 U/L; lactate dehydrogenase 72 U/L; TSH 37.82 mIU/L with free T4 normal; and serum calcium 12.2 mg/dL.
journal: Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care
title: A rarer association of eosinophilic fasciitis

case_prompt: A 63-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-month history of severe, persistent, gradually worsening sharp pain over her left distal fibula. The pain interfered with sleep and did not improve with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. She denied fevers, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was extreme tenderness to palpation over the lateral distal fibula and a soft-tissue prominence over the mid to lower third of the fibula. Radiographs of the left lower leg demonstrated two ill-defined osteolytic destructive lesions measuring 29 mm and 37 mm in the fibular diaphysis, with a pathologic fracture through the distal lesion. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy showed avid radiopharmaceutical uptake in both fibular lesions. Laboratory evaluation, including serum protein electrophoresis, alkaline phosphatase, and basic metabolic profile, was unremarkable. CT scans of the chest and abdomen revealed no evidence of primary malignancy or metastatic disease.
title: The debate is still open; benign or malignant: a case report of a multifocal epithelioid haemangioma of fibula

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old man with a 5–pack-year smoking history presented with progressive exertional dyspnoea over several years. He had worked from age 18 to 55 removing asbestos lagging from ship pipes with minimal respiratory protection. His medical history included rheumatoid arthritis treated in the past with methotrexate, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and obesity.

On examination, his BMI was 40.2. He was afebrile, normotensive, with an RR of 24 breaths per minute and an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. There was no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Fine crackles were heard in the mid and lower lung zones bilaterally; cardiac auscultation was unremarkable, and there were no signs of pulmonary hypertension.

Pulmonary function tests showed FEV1 2.09 L (82.4% predicted), FVC 2.75 L (82.7% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.76, TLC 4.46 L (72.2% predicted), and DLCO 12.95 mL/min/mm Hg (57.1% predicted), consistent with a restrictive ventilatory defect and reduced gas transfer.

High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated bilateral calcified pleural plaques predominantly in the lower zones and increased subpleural reticular markings at the lung bases with relative sparing of the upper zones. There was no obvious honeycombing.
title: Transbronchial lung cryobiopsy: a novel confirmatory tool to diagnose asbestos‐related pulmonary fibrosis

case_prompt:
A six-month-old girl, born to second-degree consanguineous parents, was brought for evaluation of scant scalp hair growth over the past three months. At birth, only a few tufts of scalp hair were present; eyebrows and eyelashes were completely absent from birth. There was no family history of hypertension, atopy, hair loss, or autoimmune disorders. The infant had been otherwise healthy, with normal developmental milestones, up-to-date vaccinations, and normal sweating and body temperature regulation. There was no history of seizures, and her two-year-old sibling was healthy.

On examination, there was complete loss of hair on the occipital and bilateral temporal scalp regions, with only sparse terminal hairs on the frontal and parietal regions. Superciliary and ciliary hairs were absent, and no hair was noted on the rest of the body. The hair‐pull test was negative. There were no signs of follicular inflammation or hypopigmented streaks. Mucous membranes and nails were normal. An asymptomatic erythematous-to-pink, blanchable patch with a well-defined border (3 × 4 cm) was noted on the occipital scalp.

Trichoscopy demonstrated remaining terminal hairs of moderate thickness with patent follicular openings and no perifollicular pigmentation or inflammation. Microscopic examination of the hair shaft and bulb was normal. Laboratory studies showed normal levels of vitamin D3, serum calcium, and immunoglobulin E. A scalp biopsy was not performed due to lack of parental consent.
title: Congenital atrichia associated with nevus flammeus: A rare association

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old Caucasian man presented with a several-month history of recurrent left lower quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss, and progressive asthenia. He reported occasional diarrheic stools without visible blood. He had no significant medical history. On examination, he appeared pale and had tenderness in the left lower quadrant without palpable masses, ascites, or peripheral edema. Laboratory studies revealed mild iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dl; serum iron 33 μg/dl) and an inflammatory syndrome (positive C-reactive protein; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm/h). 

In the prior month, he underwent upper endoscopy, which found no lesions, and two unsuccessful colonoscopy attempts that failed to pass the sigmoid colon. A barium enema demonstrated diverticulosis, and his symptoms were managed as diverticulitis with anti-diarrheics, spasmolytics, and a fluoroquinolone, yielding only partial and temporary relief. He was referred for further evaluation.

Colon capsule endoscopy (Pillcam Colon2) was performed, revealing multiple diverticula without surrounding mucosal inflammation and a submucosal mass approximately 3 cm in diameter in the sigmoid colon. Subsequent CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple colonic diverticula and a 5 cm soft-tissue mass in the sigmoid colon with a necrotic center, increased sigmoid wall thickness, indistinct margins relative to the urinary bladder, and densification of the perisigmoid fat.
title: Colon capsule endoscopy leading to gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) diagnosis after colonoscopy failure

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man presented with a 9-month history of gradually progressive intermittent dysphagia and significant weight loss but no hematemesis or melena. His medical history was unremarkable, and physical examination was normal.

A barium oesophagogram showed dilation of the entire oesophagus, multiple air bubbles with a mottled appearance, and contrast-filling defects extending from the cervical oesophagus to the upper body of the stomach. 

Computed tomography of the chest revealed a relatively smooth, sausage-shaped intraluminal mass with a bulbous distal tip, extending from the cervical oesophagus to the upper body of the stomach, and containing soft-tissue densities with a central area of fat attenuation.

Endoscopy demonstrated a smooth submucosal mass occluding the oesophageal lumen. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded benign fibro-fatty elements on cytological examination.
title: Giant fibrovascular polyp of the oesophagus: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old woman presented in January with a 2-month history of a burning, minimally pruritic rash in her axillae and inframammary folds. She had no fevers, systemic symptoms, or oral lesions. Her medical history was notable for obesity (BMI 36.5 kg/m2) and nephrolithiasis. Medications included multivitamins, fish oil, and a levonorgestrel intrauterine device (unchanged for >1 year) and compounded semaglutide, initiated weekly in late October. She denied new skincare products or detergents. 

Prior treatments—topical clotrimazole-betamethasone, ketoconazole, hydrocortisone, and oral fluconazole—provided minimal relief. On examination, there were ill-defined erythematous patches with fine scale in the axillary and inframammary folds, without vesicles, pustules, satellite lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucosal involvement. A KOH preparation was deferred. Initial differential diagnoses included contact dermatitis, symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema, and erythema annulare centrifugum. She was treated with topical hydrocortisone and a prednisone taper, but the rash progressed.

After missing two doses of semaglutide, she noted partial improvement; however, the rash recurred rapidly three days after her most recent injection. Examination now showed annular erythematous patches with prominent trailing scale in the axillary and inframammary folds. A punch biopsy from the left axilla revealed subcorneal pustular dermatosis with parakeratosis, mild acanthosis, mild spongiosis, and a superficial lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrate; periodic acid–Schiff staining was negative.
title: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis sine pustules following semaglutide injection

case_prompt: A 33-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of cough and sputum production. She had no fever but reported progressive dyspnea. Initial peripheral blood counts showed leukocytosis; chest radiographs were unremarkable, and she was treated empirically for allergic bronchitis without lasting benefit. On return, laboratory studies again demonstrated leukocytosis (white cell count elevated) with a normal absolute eosinophil count, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, negative autoantibodies, carcinoembryonic antigen below reference range, and a weakly positive tuberculin skin test. Chest radiography and computed tomography revealed a 5.0×4.8 cm mass in the right upper lobe with associated atelectasis and no mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Bronchial mucosal biopsy and CT-guided percutaneous needle aspiration showed extensive eosinophil infiltration but no definitive malignant cells. A positron-emission tomography scan and bone marrow biopsy were normal. Repeated sputum cultures, parasite antigen testing, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid smears for acid-fast bacilli, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA assays were all negative. The lesion was provisionally diagnosed as eosinophilic granuloma, and a trial of systemic glucocorticoids led to symptomatic relief. However, follow-up CT showed enlargement of the mass, and a repeat lung biopsy was undertaken; bone marrow biopsy remained normal and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate stayed elevated.
final_diagnosis_raw: T cell histiocyte rich large B cell lymphoma
title: Diagnosis of primary pulmonary T- cell/histiocyte-rich large B cell lymphoma with tissue eosinophilia via clinicopathological observation and molecular assay

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 4-month history of fever, weight loss, and fatigue. His medical history was notable for ulcerative colitis on azathioprine and a Bentall–De Bono surgical procedure with implantation of a prosthetic aortic valve and tube in 2014; he also had a cardiac resynchronization therapy defibrillator.  
In October 2018, fever and fatigue began, and empiric amoxicillin–clavulanate produced no improvement; colonoscopy excluded ulcerative colitis exacerbation. Two months later, at a community hospital, CT of the chest and abdomen was unrevealing, and transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed hyperechoic material around the aortic valve and tube, findings interpreted as post-surgical fibrosis; steroids were prescribed.  
In February 2019, on transfer to our center, he remained febrile with fatigue. On examination, he had a mild systolic murmur; blood pressure was 125/75 mmHg, heart rate 86 bpm, and oxygen saturation 98%. Laboratory studies showed mildly elevated C-reactive protein; blood cultures and broad serologic tests (including for toxoplasmosis, syphilis, brucellosis, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungal markers, pneumococcal and legionella antigens, viral serologies, and autoimmune screens) were negative. Repeat TEE confirmed a 10-mm layer of echoic irregular material between the native aortic root and the prosthetic valve and tube, but could not distinguish postoperative changes from infection.  
According to Duke’s criteria, he met one minor criterion and was classified as having possible infective endocarditis, prompting an 18F-FDG PET/CT scan. The scan revealed two hypermetabolic foci: one around the prosthetic tube in the aortic bulb (maximum standardized uptake value [SUV] 8.0) and another adjacent to the prosthetic aortic valve (SUV 6.9). Empirical treatment with daptomycin was initiated.
title: 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography as a diagnostic and follow-up tool in Coxiella burnetii endocarditis of prosthetic valve and aortic valved tube: a case report

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman with a 20-year history of cigarette smoking and a family history of lung cancer presented with symptoms of bronchitis. A chest radiograph followed by CT scanning revealed an incidental 2.0 cm mass in the posterior mediastinum abutting the T9 vertebral body. The lesion was clinically and radiologically most consistent with schwannoma. A minimally invasive resection showed no pleural thickening or multifocal nodules, and the mass was completely excised.

On gross examination, the lesion was an ovoid, tan-white, completely encapsulated, rubbery mass measuring 2.3 × 2.2 × 1.7 cm. Frozen-section microscopy demonstrated cytologically bland epithelioid cells arranged in cords and luminal configurations. On permanent sections, the neoplasm was confined to a fibrous pseudocapsule and composed of epithelioid cells forming cords and gland-like lumina, with areas of hypercellularity and focal hypocellularity. The cells exhibited mildly pleomorphic nuclei with vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and vacuolated eosinophilic cytoplasm. No mitotic figures were seen, the Ki-67 proliferative index was <2%, and there was no evidence of infiltration.

Immunohistochemical studies showed strong, diffuse positivity for pancytokeratin, calretinin, and nuclear WT1, and negativity for TTF-1, CD31, CD34, PAX8, p53, and chromogranin.
title: Posterior Mediastinal Adenomatoid Tumor: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 6-year-old African boy was evaluated for a 6-month history of dull, aching abdominal pain and a progressively enlarging abdominal mass, which worsened over the month before presentation. He had no past medical or surgical history and no family history of similar illness. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation revealed an ill-defined, smooth-surface, fixed, nontender intra-abdominal mass centered in the abdomen and extending into the left upper quadrant, measuring approximately 8 cm × 10 cm. Laboratory tests, including liver and renal function, pancreatic enzymes, and tumor markers, were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed multiple adjacent, non-communicating cystic masses, the largest measuring 8 cm × 7.5 cm × 9.5 cm, lying adjacent to the head of the pancreas without a clear plane between the lesion and pancreatic tissue. The initial radiology report listed pseudocyst and duodenal duplication among the possibilities, whereas a senior radiologist raised the possibility of a lymphatic origin for the lesion.
title: Cystic pancreatic lymphangioma: a case report

case_prompt: A 71-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of right-sided abdominal pain unresponsive to acetaminophen. On evaluation her blood pressure was 144/78 mmHg, temperature 37.7 °C, and she had mild right abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed WBC 5800/µL and CRP 20.16 mg/dL; HIV test was negative. Tumor markers revealed an elevated neuron-specific enolase of 44.6 ng/mL. All hormonal studies—including plasma cortisol, ACTH, DHEAS, aldosterone, renin activity, catecholamines, and 24-hour urine cortisol, aldosterone, metanephrines, normetanephrines, and 17-ketosteroids—were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a poorly enhancing, heterogeneous 10 × 6 × 11 cm right adrenal mass with a normal adrenal gland visible dorsally, an infiltration shadow at the base of the right lung, mediastinal and inguinal lymphadenopathy, and obstruction of the inferior vena cava. MRI showed the 11 cm heterogeneous adrenal lesion without signal drop on out-of-phase imaging and T1-weighted hyperintensity in the IVC extending into the iliac veins, consistent with venous thrombosis. An ^131I-MIBG scan was negative.
title: Challenges in the diagnosis of the enigmatic primary adrenal leiomyosarcoma: two case reports and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 26‐year‐old woman, gravida 2 para 1 at 31 weeks of gestation, developed sudden, severe abdominal pain just before boarding a three‐hour flight. She reported a similar brief episode of pain that morning, localized to the left upper quadrant. On arrival at the emergency department, she appeared pale. Vital signs were: respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 100% on room air, blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, and pulse 93 beats per minute. She had diffuse abdominal pain, but palpation of the uterus did not elicit additional tenderness.  
Obstetrical ultrasound showed a fetal heart rate of 115 BPM and no sonographic evidence of placental abruption. Cardiotocography revealed no tachycardia, normal beat‐to‐beat variability, and accelerations without decelerations.  
A bedside ultrasound of the maternal abdomen demonstrated free intra‐abdominal fluid. Laboratory testing revealed a plasma hemoglobin level of 6.4 mmol/L. Ultrasound‐guided aspiration of the fluid yielded blood. At that moment, the differential diagnosis included rupture of a splenic artery aneurysm, rupture of a uterine artery, uterine rupture, or partial placental abruption.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Saved from a fatal flight: A ruptured splenic artery aneurysm in a pregnant woman

case_prompt: A 38-year-old woman presented to the periodontology clinic with a painless swelling of the gingiva between her maxillary right canine and first premolar. She was systemically healthy, not taking any medications, and not pregnant. Intraoral examination revealed a 0.7×0.6×0.4 cm fibrotic, sessile, smooth-surfaced gingival overgrowth interdentally between teeth #13 and #14, with slight plaque accumulation, mild gingival inflammation, and edema. The adjacent teeth were vital, nonmobile, and non-tender to percussion. Periapical radiographs showed no abnormalities. Full-mouth periodontal indices were: mean plaque index 1.09, gingival index 1.11, and mean probing depth 2.92 mm. The patient received oral hygiene instruction and scaling/root planing, but the lesion persisted with minimal change.
title: Soft Tissue Reconstruction with Free Gingival Graft Technique following Excision of a Fibroma

case_prompt: A 27-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of loss of appetite, mild abdominal distension, and a sense of fullness in the right upper quadrant. She had no significant medical history and a 1–pack-year smoking history. On examination, there was no jaundice. The right upper quadrant was mildly distended, and palpation revealed a tender, smooth-surfaced mass in the region of the liver. Routine blood tests were within normal limits except for a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 6.5 ng/mL. Beta human chorionic gonadotropin and echinococcus serology were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an ill-defined, contrast-enhancing, multilobulated cystic lesion measuring 19 × 15 × 10 cm in liver segments II, III, VI, and VIII, containing adipose tissue with calcifications and multiple septations.
title: Rare giant: mature cystic teratoma in the liver

case_prompt: A 4-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with painful left hip and fever. She had no prior medical history. On examination, she walked with a limp; movements of the left hip, especially external rotation, were painful but not restricted. A single cervical lymph node was palpable. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, a normal white‐cell count, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 123 mm/h, and a C‐reactive protein level of 149.7 mg/L. A pelvic radiograph was normal. Ultrasound of the left hip revealed a small effusion and synovitis. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the hip joint yielded fluid that was macroscopically compatible with reactive arthritis, and samples were sent for general and bacteriological analysis.
title: Irritable Hip as the Inaugural Symptom for Neuroblastoma

case_prompt: A 33-year-old man, a member of a local soccer team, presented with a 2-week history of unilateral redness, foreign-body sensation, and gradually worsening vision in the left eye. He had been treated empirically with topical antivirals for presumed viral conjunctivitis without improvement. He was otherwise healthy, with no systemic diseases. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 0.5 in the left eye and 1.2 in the right eye. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the left cornea revealed diffuse, multifocal, coarse punctate epithelial lesions that stained positively with fluorescein. There was mild conjunctival injection with no significant anterior chamber reaction. Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography showed hyperreflective spots at the level of the corneal epithelium with subtle anterior stromal infiltration and diffuse stromal edema.
title: Microsporidial keratoconjunctivitis – first outbreak in Japan

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old Caucasian woman presented with two days of diffuse abdominal pain and discomfort, nausea, and vomiting. Her medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus and hypertension, managed with medication. She had no relevant family history and denied tobacco or alcohol use.

On examination, she appeared tachycardic and demonstrated signs of an acute abdomen, with a palpable, tender mass in the left abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13,000 cells/mm3. Chest and abdominal radiographs were unremarkable.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a complex cystic mass with internal septa and no increased vascularity; the organ of origin could not be identified. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed an 18.7 × 13.2 × 22 cm, well-defined, hypodense intra-peritoneal mass in the upper left abdomen—between the greater curvature of the stomach, spleen, and tail of the pancreas—and extending to the upper pelvis, compressing adjacent organs. The lesion had no internal septa on CT, no enhancement after intravenous contrast, and there was no abnormal lymphadenopathy.
title: Benign multicystic peritoneal mesothelioma: a case report

case_prompt: A 31-year-old Japanese man presented with a 3-week history of fever and headache. Three weeks earlier, he noted fever (37–38°C) and headache and received antibiotics and NSAIDs without improvement; his temperature then rose to 39°C. His only past medical history was aseptic meningitis accompanied by axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy 5 months before, which resolved with NSAIDs. On examination, he was alert and oriented; temperature 38.5°C, blood pressure 128/60 mmHg, pulse 72/min, respiratory rate 20/min. Neurologic findings, including meningeal signs, were unremarkable. Multiple tender bilateral cervical lymph nodes were palpated. Laboratory studies showed WBC 3,200/µL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 15 U/L, CRP 1.77 mg/dL, and ANA negative. CSF analysis revealed 57 cells/µL (96% mononuclear), protein 96 mg/dL, and glucose 38 mg/dL (serum glucose 99 mg/dL; CSF/serum glucose ratio 0.38). CSF cultures for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungus were negative. PCR assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, HSV-1/2, HHV-6, EBV, CMV, and VZV were all negative. No Mollaret cells were detected in the CSF. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed multiple bilateral cervical lymphadenopathies and splenomegaly.
title: Recurrent Aseptic Meningitis Associated with Kikuchi's Disease (Histiocytic Necrotizing Lymphadenitis): A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A healthy 23-year-old woman (secunda gravida) was referred at 20 3/7 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of fetal tachycardia and hydrops fetalis. Ultrasound showed a fetal heart rate of 175–180 bpm, a structurally normal heart, normal systolic function, and a regular rhythm with 1:1 atrioventricular conduction but minimal heart-rate variability. Spectral Doppler demonstrated increased retrograde flow during atrial systole in the ductus venosus and hepatic and pulmonary veins, and monophasic ventricular filling. Ascites and a small pericardial effusion were present. Maternal antithyroglobulin and anti-SSA/SSB antibodies were negative; fetal anemia and infection were excluded. A fetal magnetocardiogram at 21 5/7 weeks’ gestation demonstrated an incessant narrow QRS tachycardia with a cycle length of 333 ms (181 bpm), predominantly 1:1 retrograde ventriculoatrial conduction (VA = 77 ms), and brief episodes of VA dissociation with sinus capture beats.
title: Prenatal diagnosis and management of junctional ectopic tachycardia

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old Japanese man with hyperuricemia and bronchitis presented with sudden urinary retention and fever. Three days after symptom onset, he was treated with levofloxacin and silodosin without improvement, and a urethral catheter was placed. He was admitted for persistent symptoms. 

Medications: febuxostat, theophylline, ambroxol, long-acting β-agonist/inhaled corticosteroid. No prior urinary symptoms.  
On examination: blood pressure 139/75 mmHg, pulse 85 bpm, temperature 37.5 °C. Skin: erythematous nodules on face and extremities. Eyes: misty vision; diagnosed with uveitis. 

Laboratory studies: 
• Serum creatinine 1.09 mg/dL (eGFR 51 mL/min/1.73 m²).  
• C-reactive protein 14.0 mg/dL; calcium 9.4 mEq/L; PSA 16.3 ng/mL.  
• Urinalysis: dipstick proteinuria (1+), no pyuria or casts; transient microscopic hematuria.  
• Blood and urine cultures: negative.  
• Urinary β2-microglobulin 38,952 µg/L; proteinuria 0.45 g/gCr; no hematuria on repeat.  
• Serum soluble IL-2 receptor 3010 U/mL; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D 85 pg/mL; PTH 47.0 pg/mL; ACE 10.1 U/L.  
• MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA, and anti-GBM antibodies: negative.  
• Workup negative for neoplasia; autoimmune disorders; eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; Behçet’s disease; cryoglobulinemic vasculitis; fungal and Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

Imaging:  
• Contrast CT: lymphadenopathy in hilar, mediastinal, inguinal, and other nodes.  
• FDG-PET/CT: uptake in those lymph nodes, subcutaneous tissue, spleen, mild diffuse renal uptake, and prostate.

Procedures:  
• Skin biopsy of nodules: erythema nodosum.  
• Transbronchoscopic lymph node biopsy: epithelioid cell granulomas; diagnosed as systemic sarcoidosis.  

During hospitalization, renal function worsened (SCr 2.2 mg/dL, eGFR 22.4 mL/min/1.73 m²) despite catheter drainage. After nephrology consultation, kidney and prostate biopsies were performed to clarify the cause of acute kidney injury and urinary retention.
title: Systemic sarcoidosis presenting as a rare combination of interstitial nephritis with necrotizing vasculitis and urinary retention due to prostate involvement: a case report

case_prompt: A one‐month‐old girl was referred with a 2‐day history of intermittent fever and a progressively enlarging oral ulcer. She was alert, feeding well, and had stable vital signs. On examination, there was a unilateral, round, 2 × 2 cm ulcer at the junction of the hard and soft palate with a yellowish floor and erythematous margin, without exudate or cervical lymphadenopathy. Initial hematologic studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis and a marginally elevated C‐reactive protein level. Swab, blood, and urine cultures were negative. The infant was started on empirical intravenous antibiotics, but low‐grade fever persisted despite escalation of therapy. To evaluate possible central nervous system involvement, a noncontrast brain computed tomography scan was performed and showed no abnormalities.
title: Spontaneously Regressing Neonatal Oral Aphthous Ulceration of the Palate

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old Hispanic woman, G3P1011, at 9 weeks 4 days of gestation by last menstrual period, presented with two days of vaginal spotting, lower abdominal pain, and nausea. She denied fluid leakage, urinary symptoms, fever, or dizziness. Her obstetric history was notable for pelvic inflammatory disease with an intrauterine device in situ seven years earlier; cultures then grew Actinomyces, Streptococcus viridans, and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, and the IUD was removed. She had no other significant medical, surgical, or family history.

On examination she appeared pale. Her abdomen was mildly distended and tender, more on the right than the left. Pelvic examination showed a closed, long, posterior cervix with cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness; no adnexal mass was palpated. 

Laboratory studies revealed blood type A Rh positive, β-hCG 146 864 mIU/mL, progesterone 28.52 ng/mL, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL with a steady decline to 7.6 g/dL over serial measurements, and hematocrit from 30.6% to 22.8%. 

Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a single live intrauterine pregnancy corresponding to 8 weeks 4 days with a fetal heart rate of 188 bpm and a large amount of free intraperitoneal fluid.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Spontaneous Heterotopic Pregnancy: Dual Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 39-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a two-year history of epigastric pain radiating to the right hypochondrium and late postprandial vomiting. She weighed 58 kg and was 159 cm tall, with no significant past medical history. She underwent multiple hospitalizations during which gastroscopy and colonoscopy were unremarkable; she was discharged with a diagnosis of functional gastropathy and treated with levosulpiride. A radiographic study of food transit demonstrated slow gastric emptying. Over this period, she lost 18 kg, reaching a BMI of 15.8. Acute intermittent porphyria, infectious etiologies, and other non-surgical causes were excluded. Upon admission, conservative therapy with parenteral and enteral nutrition was initiated. An abdominal CT scan showed marked gastric ptosis extending to the pelvis, delayed gastric emptying, dilation of the duodenum, and an aortomesenteric angle of 25°.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: An unusual cause of abdominal pain: Case report of a Superior Mesenteric Artery syndrome

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old African-American man with a history of nephrolithiasis and prostate adenocarcinoma treated 20 years earlier (external-beam radiation and bilateral orchiectomy) presented with acute renal failure and bilateral hydronephrosis. He had undergone transurethral bladder resection and bilateral ureteral stent placement at an outside hospital, where biopsy showed bladder adenocarcinoma invading the muscularis propria. 

On referral for possible cystoprostatectomy, preoperative colonoscopy revealed only a tubular adenoma. Serum PSA was <0.01 ng/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated: 
• Multiple pulmonary nodules up to 0.6 cm in both upper lobes and the lingula  
• Retroperitoneal adenopathy (para-aortic and aortocaval lymph nodes up to 1.9 cm)  
• Bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter  
• Diffuse bladder wall thickening with perivesical stranding  
• Multiple filling defects within the bladder lumen consistent with invasive tumor  

FDG-PET showed no uptake in the pulmonary or retroperitoneal lesions but revealed FDG avidity in a left cervical lymph node and a 1 cm nodule within the left flank abdominal wall musculature. An attempted fine-needle aspiration of the cervical node was nondiagnostic. CT-guided core biopsy of the abdominal wall mass yielded: 

Cytology: Crowded clusters of tumor cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios and prominent small nucleoli.  
Histology: Malignant glands lined by intestinal-type columnar cells with occasional goblet cells, necrotic debris in the lumina, infiltrating skeletal muscle, and a desmoplastic stroma.  
Immunohistochemistry: Tumor cells were positive for CK7, membranous/cytoplasmic β-catenin, CDX2, and AMACR, and negative for CK20, p63, PSA, and PSAP.
title: Urinary Bladder Adenocarcinoma Metastatic to the Abdominal Wall: Report of a Case with Cytohistologic Correlation

case_prompt: A 51-year-old man with multiple hereditary exostoses, allergic rhinitis, and recent nasal repair for a fracture presented with sinus pain, pressure, low back pain, and fevers up to 100.8°F, predominantly at night. Postoperatively he received cyclobenzaprine and amoxicillin–clavulanate for presumed sinusitis, but fevers persisted and he was admitted for presumed sepsis. On admission, his qSOFA score was 0; laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (WBC 16.8→19.4 K/μl), elevated glucose, and mild AST elevation. CT of the sinuses demonstrated opacification of the frontal and ethmoid sinuses with polypoid soft-tissue densities. MRI of the lumbar spine revealed slight enhancement of the cauda equina, consistent with arachnoiditis. Venous duplex imaging was negative. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy revealed hemorrhagic sinus drainage; the fluid was sent for culture. A broad microbial cell-free DNA panel was negative, but gram stain of the sinus fluid showed budding yeast, and micafungin was started. Point-of-care ultrasound of the right lung base showed a small pleural effusion. PET-CT of the skull base demonstrated no significant FDG uptake. Autoimmune evaluation revealed a positive ANA titer (1:40 speckled) but negative dsDNA and anti–Smith antibodies; rheumatology favored an infectious etiology given the acute postoperative onset, elevated WBC count, and improvement with antimicrobial therapy.
title: Mucosal infection with Tsukamurella species following nasal septum procedure: a rare case report

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of right shoulder discomfort related to a dorsal scapular mass. He described pain when lying on his back, which sometimes disturbed his sleep, and mild weakness when using his right arm below shoulder level. His history was notable for a solitary kidney and nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma treated with chemotherapy and mantle-field radiotherapy 12 years earlier, with no recurrence.

On examination, there was a nonmobile, hard, tender mass measuring approximately 3 cm transversely by 3 cm anteroposteriorly by 2 cm craniocaudally at the posterior superomedial angle of the right scapula. Muscle bulk was symmetrical. The right shoulder had a full range of motion, but there was pain and weakness with active elevation and abduction. 

A shoulder radiograph (AP, lateral, and Neer views) was reported as normal. A thoracic CT scan demonstrated a 2.6 cm × 2.6 cm × 2.2 cm solid, well‐defined bony mass on the posterior aspect of the superomedial angle of the scapula, without cortical destruction or adjacent soft-tissue mass. 

MRI of the right shoulder showed that the lesion’s medullary cavity was continuous with that of the scapula, the cartilage cap was thin, and there were no features suggestive of malignancy; the spinal accessory nerve was compressed between the lesion and the deep layer of the trapezius, but there was no muscle atrophy.
title: Osteochondroma of the Scapula with Accessory Nerve (XI) Compression

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man presented with one week of left-sided chest pain. The pain began after a vigorous coughing episode and was described as a tearing sensation in the left hemithorax. It worsened with movements that increased intrathoracic pressure (coughing, sneezing, deep inspiration) and was accompanied by shortness of breath and a persistent dry cough.

His medical history was notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity (BMI 37.0), and a 10-pack-year smoking history. He had no diagnosis of COPD, no history of chest wall trauma or thoracic surgery, and no chronic steroid use.

On admission, vital signs were: blood pressure 176/102 mm Hg, heart rate 107 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 96 % on room air. Chest‐wall inspection showed no ecchymosis, bruising, or visible bulge. Palpation revealed tenderness over the left anterior and lateral chest wall and splaying of the left eighth and ninth ribs; there was no crepitus or detectable intercostal bulge. Lung auscultation demonstrated decreased breath sounds at the left base.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 12.9 k/μL, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, platelets 413 k/μL, normal creatinine, and normal lactic acid. 

Chest radiograph demonstrated blunting of the left costophrenic angle. CT of the chest revealed a moderate left pleural effusion with compressive atelectasis; the initial report noted no rib fractures, masses, rib separation, or pleural-fluid herniation.

He was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for suspected community-acquired pneumonia, with concurrent concern for an underlying pulmonary malignancy given his smoking history. Left thoracentesis removed 1.5 L of serosanguinous fluid. The effusion was exudative by Light’s criteria (protein 4.2 g/dL; LDH 606 U/L; pH 7.40; glucose 107 mg/dL). Fluid cell count was 5,344 cells/μL (68 % neutrophils, 30 % lymphocytes, 2 % monocytes). Gram stain, cultures, and cytology were negative. His symptoms improved and he was discharged on oral antibiotics with plans for an outpatient chest CT.

Two weeks later, outpatient CT again showed a large left pleural effusion and demonstrated separation of the left eighth and ninth ribs with herniation of pleural fluid through that intercostal space; no rib fractures or masses were seen.
title: Spontaneous intercostal herniation of lung and pleural fluid

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old Norwegian woman presented in November 2006 with a low-grade fever and severe left-sided chest pain, felt to be pericardial in nature. Her history included Raynaud’s phenomenon and seronegative Sjögren’s syndrome. Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, and an enterovirus antibody titer of 128 (normal <20); viral pericarditis was diagnosed.

One month later she developed generalized body pain with fasciculations, painful cramps, burning sensations, and hyperalgesia so severe that she could not tolerate tight clothing or a watch. She reported painful swallowing, and marked purplish discoloration over the extensor surfaces of the knees and elbows without joint swelling. Proximal thigh weakness ensued, and she became bed-bound. Antinuclear antibody testing was negative; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and creatine kinase levels were normal. No neurophysiologic studies were performed. Treatment with prednisone 40 mg daily was tapered over six months without significant benefit; her symptoms were attributed to a viral-triggered immunologic myopathy. She slowly improved over three years.

In autumn 2009 she noted weight loss, anxiety, difficulty lifting her arms, and an inability to drive. In spring 2010 she developed tonic–dystonic shoulder posturing, severe insomnia, and facial flushing with rosacea. A benzodiazepine triggered a six-week manic psychotic episode with singing and distractibility, leading to psychiatric hospitalization and a diagnosis of somatoform disorder.

Within a week after discharge, she developed torticollis-like head movements, myoclonic jerks in the right arm and leg, fluctuating elbow contractures, dyspnea from laryngospasm and chest muscle stiffness, and purplish discoloration of the hands and feet. Over subsequent weeks she developed total-body stiffness, palmar flexion contractures of the wrists and fingers, and fixed plantar flexion of the ankles and toes. Admission to neurology revealed a normal needle EMG and nerve conduction studies showing F-wave hyperexcitability in the tibial nerve that was misinterpreted as normal; repetitive nerve stimulation was not performed. A deltoid muscle biopsy showed nonspecific inflammation and atrophy; repeat ANA and ribonucleoprotein tests were positive. She was again diagnosed with a somatoform disorder.

Over the next years she remained bed-bound. By 2014 she could walk several kilometers but relapsed into severe stiffness and pain after exertion. In May 2015 her serum VGKC antibody titer was 100 pmol/L. She remained ANA and ribonucleoprotein positive, with transient SS-B positivity. Paraneoplastic panels and tests for antiglutamate, anti-GABA, glycine-receptor, Caspr2, and LGI1 antibodies were negative. Brain MRI and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal.
title: A Patient with Double-Negative VGKC, Peripheral Nerve Hyperexcitability, and Central Nervous System Symptoms: A Postinfectious Autoimmune Disease

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old black African man presented with 12 hours of ongoing chest pain. On admission, his blood pressure was 130/70 mm Hg and his heart rate was 100 beats/min. An electrocardiogram showed anterior ST-segment elevation. He received 500 mg of acetylsalicylic acid and 180 mg of ticagrelor, then underwent emergency coronary angiography. Point-of-care transthoracic echocardiography revealed akinesia of the apical segments, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%, and a large thrombus in the apical inferolateral wall. Initial differential diagnoses included myocardial infarction, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, and herpes zoster. 

Coronary angiography demonstrated a large intracoronary thrombus in the proximal left anterior descending artery with total occlusion in its mid segment. A floppy wire was advanced distally without restoration of flow. Intravascular ultrasonography confirmed a large thrombus burden in the proximal segment but showed no evidence of endothelial destruction. 

Intravenous tirofiban was initiated, and multiple manual thrombus aspirations with an Export Advance catheter failed to restore distal flow. Subsequent aspiration through a Finecross microcatheter improved flow to TIMI grade 2 and confirmed intraluminal guidewire position. The patient remained hemodynamically stable, received tirofiban for 18 hours followed by low-molecular-weight heparin for 48 hours, and experienced symptom resolution. His peak high-sensitivity troponin level exceeded 50,000 pg/mL on day 1. Repeat angiography on day 2 showed TIMI grade 3 flow throughout the vessel with no residual thrombus.
title: Diffuse LAD and LV Thrombus as Possible Manifestation of Protein-S Deficiency in a Young Patient

case_prompt: A man in his 60s, a former smoker, was treated and declared cured for sputum-positive pulmonary tuberculosis 4 years ago. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus on oral agents. For the past 3 years, he has had streaky hemoptysis treated intermittently with tranexamic acid. He presented with two episodes of large-volume hemoptysis 10 days earlier and reported a 12-kg weight loss over 3 months. Vital signs were stable, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 14 400/mm3, hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, a glycated hemoglobin level of 12.2%, normal platelet count, normal renal function, and normal coagulation indices. Three sputum specimens were negative for acid-fast bacilli on microscopy and culture, and an Xpert MTB/RIF assay did not detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a thick-walled fibrocavitatory lesion with surrounding consolidation in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe; the posterior segment bronchus appeared to lead directly into the cavity. A separate nodular consolidation was noted in the left upper lobe, and no hypertrophied bronchial arteries were seen. Due to persistent symptoms and negative sputum studies, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was planned to exclude reinfection or reactivation of tuberculosis or infection with other bacterial or fungal organisms.
title: Bronchoscopic view of post-tuberculosis lung cavity: A case report

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old Japanese woman presented with low back and right buttock pain since November 2019 that progressed to bilateral leg pain and intermittent claudication. In June 2020, she underwent elective L2–S1 decompression and interbody fusion for lumbar spinal stenosis. Her medical history included right distal radius fracture repair, carpal tunnel release, dyslipidemia treated with rosuvastatin, and pregabalin for numbness; she smoked 20 cigarettes per day.  

Preoperative radiographs showed spondylotic changes with L2–L3 instability and disc narrowing at L3–L4 and L4–L5; MRI confirmed L2–S1 spinal canal stenosis. Myelography revealed dural canal narrowing at L2–S1. Pulmonary function tests showed mild obstruction; baseline blood counts, serum biochemistry, chest radiograph, ECG, and echocardiography were normal.  

General anesthesia was induced with propofol, fentanyl, and rocuronium and maintained with sevoflurane, fentanyl, oxygen, and air. Tranexamic acid 1000 mg was given intravenously at surgery start and 2000 mg immediately postoperatively. The 291-minute surgery had 850 mL blood loss, 250 mL urine output, and 400 mL autologous blood returned.  

Upon awakening in the supine position, she experienced a 1-minute generalized tonic–clonic seizure; seizures briefly abated after propofol but then recurred multiple times. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.10, PaCO2 15.3 mmHg, and HCO3– 13.9 mEq/L. Serum glucose was 105 mg/dL; sodium 142 mmol/L; potassium 4.0 mmol/L; chloride 110 mmol/L; calcium 8.9 mg/dL. Head CT showed no hemorrhage or intracranial lesion. By ICU transfer, she had a total of 10 seizures treated with diazepam.
title: Generalized Tonic-clonic Seizure Caused by Tranexamic Acid Administration in Spinal Surgery: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 51‐year‐old never‐smoker dentist presented with 15 days of left chest pain, mild exertional dyspnea, dry cough, evening fevers up to 38.5 °C, and 5 days of diffuse arthralgias. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On admission she was febrile (39.2 °C) and tachypneic (25 breaths/min). Chest examination revealed decreased expansion, dullness to percussion, and reduced vesicular sounds at both lung bases. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.44, PaO₂ 67 mmHg, PaCO₂ 29 mmHg. Laboratory studies: WBC 12 000/µL, hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, ESR 33 mm/h. Chest radiograph demonstrated a left pleural effusion, and empiric ampicillin–sulbactam with azithromycin was started. Thoracentesis yielded 5000 WBC/mm³ (38% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, 20% eosinophils). Blood, urine, and sputum cultures, stains and cultures of bronchial wash, and tuberculin skin testing were all negative. CT of the chest and abdomen, abdominal ultrasound, mammography, and fiberoptic bronchoscopy ruled out malignancy. CT pulmonary angiography showed no pulmonary embolism but revealed a small right‐sided effusion. Rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, ANCA, and anti-CCP antibodies were negative. She denied chest trauma, travel, parasitic symptoms, and use of any drugs known to cause EPE. On hospital day 5, fevers recurred to 39.4 °C with worsening dyspnea; chest radiograph showed an increased right pleural effusion, and 1 L of exudative fluid (22% eosinophils) was removed via chest tube (stains, cultures, and cytology negative). She continued to report arthralgias, and exam revealed arthritis of the small joints of the hands and feet and the knees, with no evidence of connective‐tissue disease, systemic vasculitis, or other chronic inflammatory disease.
title: Adult Onset Still's Disease: A Case Report with a Rare Clinical Manifestation and Pathophysiological Correlations

case_prompt: A 43-year-old woman was admitted for recurrent falls and confusion. Her history was notable for congenital bicuspid aortic valve disease, for which she underwent mechanical aortic valve replacement and tricuspid annuloplasty in 2011. In April 2021, she had a second aortic valve replacement with an On-X valve, complicated intraoperatively by the development of an aorto–right ventricular fistula and severe tricuspid regurgitation. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. She was obese and had slowed mentation with slurred speech. Cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm, a III/VI holosystolic murmur at the upper right sternal border radiating to the carotids, a mechanical S2 with near-obliteration of S1, and no jugular venous distension. Neurologic exam showed bilateral asterixis. There was no peripheral edema, organomegaly, or labored breathing. Laboratory evaluation revealed an elevated serum ammonia level of 122 µmol/L (normal 13–40), an alkaline phosphatase of 411 U/L (35–104), an AST of 40 U/L (10–35), and an ALT of 22 U/L (10–35). A liver ultrasound demonstrated dilated hepatic veins and bidirectional flow in the main portal vein. Contrast CT of the abdomen showed hepatomegaly, hepatic steatosis, and features consistent with congestive hepatopathy.
title: Hepatic encephalopathy due to aorto-right ventricular fistula responsive to percutaneous repair: a case report

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old Togolese student presented with an 8-month history of a chronic, nonhealing ulcer of the glans penis. Two weeks before presentation, he noted dysuria and burning on urination. The ulcer began as painless erythematous nodules (≈1 × 1 cm) on the glans that evolved into multiple enlarging ulcers around the urethral meatus. He denied trauma, surgery, weight loss, fever, cough, or other constitutional symptoms. He had received BCG vaccination at birth and had tried various herbal treatments without benefit.

On examination, he appeared in good general condition with well-colored conjunctivae. Genitourinary exam revealed a circumferential ulcer of the glans measuring 6 × 4 × 3 cm with irregular margins, a dirty, hemorrhagic, and necrotic base, and a poorly defined urethral meatus. Bilateral inguinal lymph nodes (0.5–2 cm) were firm and mobile. The remainder of the genital exam and systemic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (54 mm/hr), normal blood glucose, urea, and creatinine levels, and negative HIV and VDRL serologies. Microscopic examination and cultures of urine showed no abnormalities; no acid‐fast bacilli were seen in ulcer scrapings, urine, or sputum. Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder was normal, and a chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. A biopsy of the lesion was obtained and sent for histopathologic evaluation.
title: African histoplasmosis of the penis

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old woman was referred at two weeks’ gestation in her second pregnancy for evaluation after surviving an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest four months after delivering her first child. At that time, she underwent implantation of an ICD for secondary prevention following a working diagnosis of peripartum or dilated cardiomyopathy versus primary electrical disease. Initial transthoracic echocardiography and cardiac MRI revealed only mild myxomatous mitral valve prolapse with mild regurgitation, a mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, and no other abnormalities. 

When seen in our center, she was asymptomatic. Blood pressure was 112/76 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98%, and an apical mild systolic murmur was noted without signs of heart failure. A 12-lead ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with frequent premature ventricular complexes showing a right bundle-branch block morphology. Exercise testing reproduced regular PVCs without ischemic changes and yielded 81% of predicted workload. Echocardiography confirmed myxomatous mitral valve prolapse with mild to moderate regurgitation, and normal left and right ventricular dimensions and function. 

Her pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated, and she remained in hospital for rhythm observation for 3 days without events. However, four weeks postpartum, she experienced sudden syncope at home. ICD interrogation revealed primary ventricular fibrillation terminated by an appropriate shock. No reversible causes, including ventricular dysfunction or electrolyte imbalance, were identified. Repeat echocardiography showed unchanged findings. Review of serial ECGs demonstrated persistent PVCs with a right bundle-branch block pattern and superior axis, consistent with an origin in the inferolateral basal left ventricle.
title: Repetitive out of hospital cardiac arrests following pregnancy: a case report of an unfortunate presentation of mitral annular disjunction

case_prompt: A 7-year-old girl of Spanish descent was referred for evaluation of recurrent unexplained fevers and multiple bone injuries. She was born to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. She displayed no response to painful stimuli and had evidence of self-inflicted skin lesions. Developmental assessment revealed cognitive delay. On examination, her skin was warm and dry with an absence of sweating, and there was marked thickening of the palms and soles. Lower-limb edema was noted. Skeletal radiographs demonstrated avascular necrosis, generalized osteopenia, extensive osseous destruction, and, following a midshaft fracture of the right tibia sustained four months earlier, features of hypertrophic pseudoarthrosis.
final_diagnosis_raw: congenital insensitivity to pain and anhidrosis
title: Update Review and Clinical Presentation in Congenital Insensitivity to Pain and Anhidrosis

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman with a history of regular narrow-complex tachycardia presented for an elective electrophysiology study. Two weeks earlier, her tachycardia had not responded to adenosine administered by paramedics and terminated spontaneously in the emergency department. The recorded tachycardia had a narrow QRS complex, a cycle length of 330 ms, and no evident retrograde P waves.

On presentation in the EP laboratory, she was in sinus rhythm. Quadripolar catheters were placed in the right ventricular apex, His position, and right atrium; a decapolar catheter was positioned in the coronary sinus. At a sinus cycle length of 820 ms, the AH and HV intervals were 83 ms and 42 ms, respectively. Ventricular pacing showed concentric and decremental retrograde conduction. During programmed atrial stimulation, dual AV nodal physiology was evident, and a nonsustained 1:1 narrow-complex tachycardia with cycle lengths of 280–350 ms was easily induced.

During tachycardia, the atrial activation was concentric with a septal VA time of 20 ms. On two occasions, tachycardia was induced after a 2-for-1 response. The tachycardia terminated spontaneously with the atrial electrogram consistently last. His‐synchronous premature ventricular contractions did not advance or delay the atrial electrogram or the tachycardia. Entrainment from the right ventricular apex at 10–20 ms shorter than the tachycardia cycle length yielded a V-A-V response with a post-pacing interval minus tachycardia cycle length of 170 ms and a stimulus‐atrial minus VA difference of 115 ms. Atrial pacing at 260 ms during tachycardia dissociated the atrium without affecting the tachycardia cycle length.

During sustained tachycardia, there were intermittent loss of atrial depolarizations and periods of Wenckebach and 2:1–3:1 VA periodicity with fixed VA intervals. Further ventricular pacing entrainment resulted in complete VA dissociation, with the ventricular rate unchanged and stable QRS morphology and HV interval. Ventricular pacing at a rate faster than the tachycardia had no effect, and intravenous adenosine (6 mg followed by 12 mg) failed to terminate the tachycardia.
title: The existence of upper common pathway: Evidence from concomitant atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia and atrial fibrillation

case_prompt: A 6-year-old girl was brought to a rural primary-care emergency center in Bangladesh with vaginal bleeding of 2 hours’ duration. The child’s mother reported that the bleeding began mildly but increased over time; there were no other bleeding sites, and no history of trauma or sexual abuse. The girl had no significant past medical history and was fully immunized. On arrival she was pale and anxious. Vital signs: blood pressure 95/65 mm Hg, pulse 118 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min. Her weight and height were age-appropriate. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Perineal packing revealed active bleeding from the external genitalia; the hymen was intact and there were no signs of injury to external structures. After fluid resuscitation, she was taken to the operating room and placed under deep sedation. A thorough perineal inspection again showed no lacerations or trauma. Bright red blood and clots were noted at the vaginal introitus. Clots were removed, and bleeding from within the vagina was confirmed. Further history elicited that she had swum in a nearby pond just before the onset of bleeding.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: A Case Report on Prepubertal Vaginal Bleeding due to Leech Bite: History Is Very Important

case_prompt: A 37-year-old G3P2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries presented with persistent vaginal bleeding three weeks after attempted termination of an early failed pregnancy. Initial ultrasound had shown a 13-week embryo without cardiac activity in the lower uterine segment, with an anterior placenta obscured by intracavitary clots. After misoprostol and suction curettage for presumed missed abortion, the patient had heavy intraoperative bleeding, a 5.0 g/dL hemoglobin drop requiring transfusion, and an ultrasound showing heterogeneous remnants (14 × 38 mm) in the lower uterine segment with focal myometrial thinning. One week later she returned with continued bleeding; repeat ultrasound revealed a large, ill-defined, hetero-echoic area (52 × 45 × 58 mm; 72 cc) in the endometrial cavity extending into the anterior myometrium at the prior cesarean scar, with significant peripheral vascularity. Serum β-hCG levels remained low (70–80 mIU/mL). On referral, color Doppler ultrasound demonstrated an 80 × 50 mm heterogeneous cystic myometrial mass with high vascularity. CT of the pelvis showed a 60 × 68 × 60 mm heterogeneous uterine mass with multiple tortuous internal vessels on the right uterine body and prominent parametrial vessels, and no clear fat plane between the mass and posterior bladder wall, suggesting bladder involvement.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Placenta increta mimicking placental site trophoblastic tumor: A rare case report
