case_prompt: An 18-year-old man presented with insidious onset of weakness in his right hand and forearm, progressing over the past year, and difficulty with fine tasks such as writing and buttoning. He denied neck pain, paresthesias, gait disturbance, dysphagia, or bowel/bladder dysfunction, and had no history of trauma or other medical conditions. On examination, neck movement was painless. There was marked wasting of right hand muscles with weakness of handgrip, and finger abduction and adduction were reduced. Wrist flexion was Medical Research Council grade 3 on the right; strength was grade 5 elsewhere in the upper limbs and in both lower limbs. No involuntary movements, sensory deficits, cerebellar signs, or cranial-nerve abnormalities were noted; bowel and bladder function were intact. Routine blood tests were unremarkable. Cervical spine radiographs showed loss of cervical lordosis. MRI in the neutral position demonstrated a subtle intramedullary T2-weighted hyperintensity in the lower cervical cord. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography revealed chronic motor axon denervation with likely localization to the anterior horn cells.
title: Surgical Management of Hirayama Disease: A Rare Entity with Unusual Clinical Features

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old G1P1 woman at 38 weeks’ gestation, with no comorbidities, was admitted for labor. Four days before delivery she tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR but remained asymptomatic. She delivered a female infant vaginally; Apgar scores were 10 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes. Birth weight was 2670 g.

At 11 minutes of life the neonate developed tachypnea, nasal flaring, chest retractions, grunting, and an oxygen saturation of 90%, requiring noninvasive ventilation. The Silverman score was 3. Heart sounds were normal and peripheral perfusion was intact. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.30, PCO₂ 60 mmHg, PO₂ 65 mmHg, and bicarbonate 20 mmol/L. At 30 minutes a nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2; IgM and IgG were negative. The infant was isolated and transferred to the NICU for continued noninvasive ventilation.

A chest radiograph at 30 minutes showed bilateral opacities consistent with respiratory distress syndrome. Intravenous penicillin and gentamicin were started. After 5 days, blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures remained negative and C-reactive protein levels were low; antibiotics were discontinued. On day 6 of life, respiratory distress persisted. A chest CT scan showed bilateral parenchymal ground-glass lesions involving 10–20% of lung volume. Laboratory tests at that time revealed elevated liver enzymes (ALT 60 IU/L, AST 540 IU/L), elevated LDH, and a pro-BNP level >350 ng/L; echocardiography showed no coronary dilation.
title: Prenatal transmission of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, resulting in neonatal severe acute pneumonia, from an asymptomatic mother: a case report

case_prompt:
A 1-day-old boy was brought in with a large neck mass and difficulty breathing. He required urgent endotracheal intubation and was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit. The mass had not been detected in utero, although gestational ultrasonography had noted polyhydramnios. The pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated. 

On examination, a large, irregularly lobulated mass extended from the auricles to the clavicles bilaterally. Chest radiography, abdominal ultrasound, and echocardiography were unremarkable. Neck ultrasonography showed a mass with hypoechoic, cystic areas measuring approximately 80 × 55 mm in the middle and left side of the neck. 

A neck MRI revealed a well-defined, multiloculated complex mass with solid components of intermediate T1 and T2 signal intensity and cystic components of high T2 and low T1 signal intensity, displacing the esophagus and airway.
title: Successful surgıcal management of a giant neck teratoma in a newborn Baby: A case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 0, with known tuberous sclerosis and polycystic ovarian syndrome on metformin, was admitted for management of a persistent left pneumothorax and had a chest tube in place. On the day of planned pleurodesis, a routine urine pregnancy test was positive. She denied abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding and reported a last menstrual period 6.6 weeks prior. Her obstetric history included one first-trimester termination without dilation and curettage.

On hospital day 7, her serum beta-hCG was 2578 mIU/mL. A transvaginal ultrasound on day 8 did not identify an intrauterine gestational sac, and she was labeled as having a pregnancy of unknown location. A repeat beta-hCG 48 hours later rose to 5028 mIU/mL (95% increase). Transvaginal ultrasound at that time again showed no intrauterine sac but demonstrated a 1.64 × 1.32 cm hypoechoic lesion in the fundal myometrium just left of the midline with surrounding vascularity.

The patient remained asymptomatic, and, given her desire for the pregnancy, the plan was for another interval beta-hCG and ultrasound. Forty-eight hours later, her beta-hCG rose to 9335 mIU/mL (19% increase), and transvaginal ultrasound was unchanged except for a small amount of pelvic free fluid. The fundal hypoechoic lesion was once again seen and was now classified as a fibroid versus an interstitial ectopic pregnancy. The patient continued to deny pain or bleeding, and her abdominal examination remained benign. She was counseled on the likelihood of interstitial versus cornual ectopic pregnancy and the need for medical versus surgical intervention.
title: Ectopic pregnancy of the fundal myometrium in a patient with tuberous sclerosis

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1 at 24 weeks’ gestation, presented with a 1-week history of gradually worsening, generalized crampy abdominal pain, constipation, and nonbilious vomiting of food material. She denied fever, trauma, or vaginal discharge but noted decreased fetal movements. Her obstetric history was notable for a prior cesarean delivery via Pfannenstiel incision for preeclampsia; current pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated. 

On examination, she appeared ill, was mildly pale and dehydrated, and had a temperature of 38.0 °C, pulse 136 beats/min, and blood pressure 112/81 mmHg. A nasogastric tube drained fecal material. The abdomen was symmetrically distended, tense, and diffusely tender with hyper-tympany on percussion and absent bowel sounds. Rectal and pelvic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9.17 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, platelet count 441 × 10^9/L, and serum potassium 2.52 mmol/L (corrected with IV potassium). Obstetric ultrasound revealed a viable 24-week fetus and extensive gaseous distension of the maternal bowel. A supine abdominal radiograph demonstrated multiple high air–fluid levels and a distended gastric bubble, findings consistent with intestinal obstruction and raising the possibility of a perforated hollow viscus. She was kept nil per os, received IV fluids and electrolyte correction, and was consented for emergency laparotomy.
title: Sigmoid volvulus in pregnancy: a case report

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of progressive generalized body pain and weakness. She also reported chronic nasal obstruction with occasional moderate epistaxis. Treatments with analgesics, decongestants, and antidepressants provided little relief, and she became wheelchair-bound after multiple falls due to incapacitating pain.

On examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. Musculoskeletal examination revealed diffuse bone tenderness and proximal muscle weakness; neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable. Examination of the nasal passages showed bilateral obstruction without a visible mass.

Pelvic radiographs demonstrated diffuse loss of bone mineral density with bilateral comminuted proximal femoral fractures (subcapital and subtrochanteric) and bilateral superior and inferior pubic rami fractures. Radiographs of the hands showed marked cortical thinning, prominent trabeculae, and multiple metacarpal and phalangeal fractures.

Biochemical studies revealed an inorganic phosphate level of 0.57 mmol/L (reference range 0.78–1.42), an alkaline phosphatase level of 420 U/L (42–98), and a parathyroid hormone level of 5.1 pmol/L (1.5–7.6). Urinary studies showed a fractional excretion of phosphate of 56% and decreased tubular reabsorption of phosphate; serum calcium was normal.

These findings led to the conclusion that the hypophosphatemia was secondary to fibroblast growth factor 23 abnormalities.
title: Advanced tumour-induced osteomalacia secondary to sinonasal phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive pain and swelling over the left thenar eminence and proximal thumb. She denied any preceding trauma, constitutional symptoms (no fever, weight loss, or night sweats), or history of tuberculosis exposure. On examination, there was a tender, firm swelling over the first carpometacarpal area with painful thumb movement; she was afebrile and otherwise hemodynamically stable.

A plain radiograph of the hand demonstrated a lytic lesion at the base of the first metacarpal with a pathological fracture and surrounding soft-tissue haziness. Ultrasound confirmed a fluid collection consistent with an abscess. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a large heterogeneous lesion at the first carpometacarpal joint space with joint widening, findings interpreted as most consistent with an infectious abscess and less likely a neoplastic process. 

Based on these findings, the initial differential diagnoses included pyogenic osteomyelitis, tuberculous osteomyelitis, soft-tissue swelling (eg, post-traumatic), and malignancy.
title: Excision Arthroplasty for First CMC Joint Tuberculous Osteomyelitis

case_prompt: A 33-year-old nulliparous woman with a body‐mass index of 19.4 kg/m2 and no significant medical or family history underwent a routine gynecologic examination. She was asymptomatic and her physical examination was unremarkable. A transvaginal ultrasound revealed a multilocular solid mass measuring 20 × 20 × 16 mm adjacent to the left ovary, with an internal solid component 13 mm in diameter and 7 mm in height. Color Doppler showed no blood flow in the solid component, although one septation demonstrated vascularity. Serum CA-125 was 13.3 U/mL and other laboratory tests were within normal limits. An International Ovarian Tumor Analysis (IOTA) risk assessment using the ADNEX model yielded a 9.1% risk of malignancy. Pelvic MRI showed a cystic mass of uncertain origin adjacent to the left ovary, measuring 18 × 15 × 20 mm, with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images and low signal on T1-weighted images; a nodular solid element was present, and postcontrast images demonstrated enhancement of the cyst wall. The uterus and right adnexa appeared normal.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Adenomatoid tumor of the fallopian tube: A case report and a review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man with a 27-year history of intermittent palpitations and no structural heart disease underwent evaluation. His baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram in sinus rhythm showed no delta waves. During episodes of palpitation, surface ECG demonstrated a regular supraventricular tachycardia at 205 beats per minute with negative P waves in the inferior leads. 

An electrophysiologic study was performed with multipolar catheters in the high right atrium, His bundle region, right ventricular apex, and coronary sinus. At baseline, programmed RV pacing revealed concentric, nondecremental ventriculoatrial conduction, and atrial pacing maneuvers did not induce sustained tachycardia. After isoproterenol infusion, atrial pacing provoked a sustained supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) with a cycle length of 240 ms and a concentric atrial activation sequence. 

With constant RV apical pacing at a cycle length of 600 ms in sinus rhythm, three paced stimuli conducted retrogradely over an accessory pathway and induced an SVT with a cycle length of 270 ms. Notably, the VA interval during SVT was 70 ms, which was 20 ms longer than the VA interval of 50 ms during RV pacing.

A premature stimulus delivered to the RV apex immediately after the His bundle electrogram terminated the tachycardia. During RV overdrive pacing at a cycle length slightly faster than the tachycardia (230 ms versus 255 ms), the first stimulus captured atrium prematurely without altering the ventricular cycle length or atrial activation sequence and did not terminate the tachycardia.
title: Novel analysis of ventriculoatrial interval prolongation during a narrow QRS tachycardia using a right atrial nondecremental-midseptal accessory pathway

case_prompt: A 73-year-old Caucasian man with a history of a left orchiectomy at age 59 for a 4.2 cm encapsulated testicular Leydig cell tumor without lymphovascular invasion or extratesticular involvement presented with two months of progressive lower back pain. MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine demonstrated lesions at the L1 and L5 vertebral levels concerning for osseous metastatic disease. An L5 vertebral body biopsy showed a lesion composed of polygonal, plump cells with abundant cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical studies revealed that the tumor cells were positive for calretinin, α-inhibin, synaptophysin, melan-A, chromogranin, and vimentin, with a Ki-67 proliferative index of 7%, and were negative for CK AE 1/3, AFB, CK 20, CK 7, EMA, S100, WT1, arginase-1, SALL-4, and SOX10.
title: An insight into metastatic Leydig cell tumors: A case report

case_prompt: A 37-year-old man presented with high fever, severe frontal headache, left retrobulbar and hemifacial pain, and nasal obstruction. He had no history of facial trauma, dental treatment, sinus surgery, or chronic illness. On examination, he had diplopia and absence of motility on left lateral gaze, consistent with an abducens nerve palsy; other cranial nerves were intact, and visual acuity and pupillary reflexes were normal. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (22.6 × 10^3/µL) and a C-reactive protein level of 14.06 mg/dL. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated polypoid neoformations occupying both nasal cavities. Maxillofacial CT revealed a voluminous expansile lesion in the left parasellar region involving the ipsilateral cavernous sinus and all paranasal sinuses, with osteostructural rearrangement of the posterolateral wall of the left sphenoid sinus lacking a well-defined bony outline. MRI of the brain, orbits, and paranasal sinuses confirmed a large expansile process in the left sphenoid sinus extending into the infratemporal fossa and pterygoid muscles, compressing the temporal lobe and involving the cavernous sinus but without evidence of thrombosis of the internal carotid artery. Because the radiological features were nonspecific, a neoplasm could not be excluded. The patient was therefore submitted to endoscopic sinus surgery with the goal of reducing mechanical compression on the cavernous sinus and obtaining a definitive histopathological diagnosis.
title: Intracranial Complication of Rhinosinusitis from Actinomycosis of the Paranasal Sinuses: A Rare Case of Abducens Nerve Palsy

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a two-month history of diffuse abdominal pain and postprandial vomiting. He reported significant weight loss and appeared in poor general condition. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed elevated blood urea with a satisfactory hemoglobin level. 

An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a markedly distended stomach filled with retained food; the prepyloric region could not be traversed. Multiple blind biopsy specimens showed chronic gastritis without dysplasia or malignancy. A barium upper gastrointestinal series demonstrated a distended stomach and markedly delayed passage of contrast through a stenotic zone in the prepyloric region. 

Abdominal computed tomography showed asymmetric, contrast-enhancing wall thickening of the prepyloric region measuring 71 × 35 mm, resulting in significant gastric distension. Numerous calcifications were noted throughout the pancreas. No focal hepatic lesions or adenopathy were identified.
title: A disconcerting false gastric diverticulum mimicking malignancy

case_prompt: A 72-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of chest pain localized near the sternum. Over the preceding month he had developed progressive exertional dyspnoea but remained well at rest, with no fever or peripheral oedema. He had no history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, or other comorbidities. On arrival, vital signs were stable (blood pressure 110/65 mmHg; pulse 70 b.p.m.; respiratory rate 20 breaths/min). Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, low‐amplitude QRS complexes in the limb leads, and a right bundle branch block. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular thickening, biatrial enlargement, a small pericardial effusion adjacent to the right atrium, and a preserved ejection fraction with predominant basal hypokinesis. Serial measurements of high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin T were elevated (388 pg/mL on admission and 467 pg/mL at 3 h; normal ≤24.9 pg/mL), whereas creatine kinase–MB levels remained within normal limits. Given the concern for acute coronary syndrome, urgent coronary angiography was performed and showed non-obstructive coronary arteries.
title: Cardiac amyloidosis mimicking acute coronary syndrome: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation and prior cerebral infarction presented with 38 hours of progressive left testicular pain without trauma. Physical examination findings were not detailed in the report. Emergency scrotal ultrasound was performed:

• 2D gray-scale ultrasonography showed a well-defined, heterogeneous hypoechoic area measuring approximately 16 × 11 × 10 mm within the left testis; the surrounding parenchyma appeared homogeneous.  
• Color Doppler flow imaging and color Doppler energy detected no blood flow or energy signal within the lesion, with normal signals in the remainder of the testis.  
• Contrast-enhanced ultrasound revealed a 20 × 15 mm patchy area of no enhancement in the left testicular parenchyma during the arterial, venous, and delayed phases; contrast filled the surrounding tissue starting at 45 seconds, peaked at 60 seconds, and faded by 80 seconds.  
• Quantitative CEUS parameters comparing the lesion to adjacent normal tissue showed delayed time to peak (29.32 s vs. 18.42 s), shorter rise time (5.67 s vs. 11.67 s), and reduced maximum intensity (61.9% vs. 100%), consistent with hypoperfusion.  
• Laboratory studies revealed mildly elevated C-reactive protein and leukocyte count; testicular tumor markers were negative.
title: A case report of staged testicular infarction

case_prompt: A 39‐year‐old woman presented with a 4-year history of a progressively enlarging mass in the left temporal scalp region. She reported left‐sided facial pain and weakness, difficulty opening her mouth and chewing, and hearing loss in the left ear. Previous symptomatic treatments provided no relief. On examination, she appeared ill and cachectic, with trismus grade 2 and left facial nerve palsy grade 3. A non‐tender, soft, warm scalp mass measuring 15 cm by 20 cm occupied the left temporal and parotid regions; the inferolateral skin was tense and shiny, and the left external auditory canal was obliterated. She was otherwise healthy, with no personal or family history of cancer; she neither smoked nor drank alcohol. Contrast CT and MRI of the head and neck demonstrated a destructive mass eroding the temporal bone with intracranial extension. CT scans of the chest and abdomen–pelvis showed no evidence of distant metastases. A working impression of a malignant scalp tumor was made, and an incisional biopsy was performed, yielding a diagnosis “suggestive of basal cell carcinoma.”
title: Giant pilomatrix carcinoma of the scalp with intracranial extension: A case report

case_prompt: A 28-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presented with fever, chills, hypotension, and tachypnea. On admission, blood cultures were positive for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated right-heart failure with moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation and two vegetations on the anterior tricuspid leaflet measuring 1.6 × 1.0 cm and 0.8 × 0.6 cm. Computed tomography of the chest revealed multiple bilateral peripheral wedge-shaped opacities; multiple peripheral pulmonary nodules with central cavitation, some showing a feeding‐vessel sign; reactive hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy; and a small right-sided pleural effusion.
title: Computed tomography findings in septic pulmonary embolism: A case report and literature review☆

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging swelling over the right thigh. The overlying skin showed puckering. On palpation the mass was nontender and hard. Systemic examination was unremarkable. 
Magnetic resonance imaging of the right thigh demonstrated a 3.0 × 2.5 × 1.5 cm T1- and T2-hypointense mass in the posterolateral upper third of the thigh, with significant postcontrast enhancement and extension into the vastus lateralis; there was no bone erosion. A provisional diagnosis of soft tissue sarcoma was made, and fine‐needle aspiration (FNA) was performed. 
Cytologic smears were cellular and showed a bimodal population: clusters of spindle cells with bland, ovoid nuclei separated by fibrovascular septae, and scattered multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells whose oval nuclei resembled those of the spindle cells. The background was hemorrhagic, and mitotic figures were absent.
final_diagnosis_raw: giant cell tumor of soft tissue
journal: Journal of Cytology / Indian Academy of Cytologists
title: Giant cell tumor of soft tissues of low malignant potential: A rare diagnosis on fine needle aspiration cytology

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old lean Pakistani man presented with lifelong photosensitivity, skin discoloration, painful burning on sun exposure, nail dystrophy, ocular irritation with tearing and redness, oral ulcers, and one year of urinary difficulty marked by frequency, hesitancy, burning, and incomplete voiding without hematuria or pyuria.

He was born of a consanguineous marriage; parents and four siblings are healthy, but a maternal nephew has a similar skin condition. At 5 months, he began developing itchy, painful, hemorrhagic blisters on his feet that spread over the body; the lesions ceased by age 5, leaving pigmented, easily sunburned skin and nail distortion.

On examination, there was generalized hypo- and hyperpigmentation with areas of skin atrophy and telangiectasias on the face, neck, and arms; palmoplantar keratoderma; loss of dermatoglyphics; absent cuticles; and rough, distorted nails. Mild ectropion with misdirected lashes and conjunctivitis was noted. Oral examination revealed angular cheilitis, restricted mouth opening, and loss of all teeth except three premolars.

Baseline blood tests, chest and pelvic radiographs were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a thick-walled bladder suggestive of outlet obstruction. Two urine cultures, one month apart, grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa then E. coli. A urethrogram demonstrated bladder sacculations and diverticulae with significant postvoid residual, plus an irregular narrow-caliber penile and bulbar urethra with partial stricture at the bulbomembranous junction. Antinuclear and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies were negative.
title: Battling a rarity: A case of kindler syndrome from a developing country

case_prompt: A 66-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 1-year history of low-grade fever and productive cough, despite two hospitalizations for pneumonia in the past year. She had a history of hypopharyngeal cancer treated with radiation 20 years earlier. She was a non-smoker with no alcohol use; her younger brother had pulmonary tuberculosis. On admission, temperature was 37.3°C, heart rate 72 bpm, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg. She appeared underweight (BMI 14.2 kg/m2). Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 1.6 mg/dL; arterial oxygen tension was 85 mmHg. On auscultation, coarse crackles were heard bilaterally in the lower lung fields. A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral infiltrates and micronodular changes in the lower lobes. Chest CT revealed diffuse centrilobular micronodules and areas of consolidation in the left lower lobe and right middle lobe, with bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe. On hospital day 6, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) was performed. BAL fluid showed a total cell count of 2.1 × 10^6/mL with 90% neutrophils; cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii; tests for mycobacteria were negative. TBLB specimens from the right lower lobe revealed inflammatory infiltrates and giant cells within the bronchioles; there was no evidence of malignancy.
title: A case of diffuse aspiration bronchiolitis due to oesophageal stenosis after radiation therapy

case_prompt: A 45-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of progressively worsening headaches, right-sided weakness, and speech difficulties, and one generalized tonic-clonic seizure. On examination he had papilledema, expressive aphasia, and right hemiparesis (MRC grade 4/5). He had no history of intravenous drug use, radiation exposure, or other comorbidities. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits, and serologic tests were negative for HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and Epstein–Barr virus. Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced head CT showed a heterogeneously enhancing left temporo-parietal mass extending into the basal ganglia, with extensive perilesional edema and midline shift. Brain MRI revealed a 5.9 × 4.4 × 5.2 cm heterogeneous solid and cystic lesion that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement, with massive surrounding edema and mass effect. Preoperative chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were normal. The differential diagnosis included high-grade glioma or atypical meningioma.
title: Primary intracranial leiomyosarcoma presenting with massive peritumoral edema and mass effect: Case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old premenopausal woman (G2P2) presented with a 1-day history of dull, gradual-onset right lower-quadrant abdominal pain and mild nausea. She also described a 1-year history of abdominal distension, anorexia, and early satiety, and noted irregular menstrual bleeding for 6 months. She denied vaginal bleeding or discharge. Her medical history included hypertension and peptic ulcer disease treated with medication, and she used combined oral contraceptive pills. There was no personal or family history of ovarian, uterine, bowel, or breast cancer.

On examination, her blood pressure was 160/83 mmHg; other vital signs and blood glucose were normal. The abdomen was distended, rigid, and tender in the right lower quadrant; a smooth, firm pelvic mass was palpable. Bowel sounds were not clearly audible. Vaginal examination revealed full fornices and a normal-appearing cervix. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated CA-125 and CEA levels; β-hCG and α-fetoprotein were normal. Complete blood count, liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. ECG and echocardiography were normal.

Pelvic MRI demonstrated a well-defined septated cystic lesion measuring 15 × 26 × 27 cm arising from the right adnexa, without enhancing solid components. The uterus was bulky with multiple intramural and subserosal leiomyomas.

An exploratory midline laparotomy revealed a 20 × 20 × 19 cm smooth cystic mass of the right ovary, without obvious solid areas and with minimal ascitic fluid. The uterus was bulky with fibroids. A total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed, and the mass was sent for histopathological evaluation.
title: Management of a Borderline Brenner Tumor of the Ovary in a Premenopausal Woman in Northern Tanzania. A Rare Case Report and Review of the Current Literature

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old woman, G1P1001, presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by poor appetite and weight loss. Her menses were regular without dysmenorrhea or pelvic pain at presentation. Six years earlier, she had chronic pelvic pain treated empirically with injectable progestin. One year prior, a CT scan at another hospital showed large ascites, peritoneal nodules, and pleural effusion; paracentesis and pleural tapping yielded exudative fluid without malignant cells. A subsequent CT scan suggested circumferential mid‐ to upper‐rectal wall thickening “suggesting rectal cancer” plus ascites and right pleural effusion, but colonoscopic biopsy revealed only acute colitis without malignancy. 

On examination at our institution, she appeared chronically ill and emaciated (BMI 14.9 kg/m2). Her abdomen was markedly distended without tenderness or palpable masses. Vaginal examination showed anterior vaginal‐wall bulging from ascites but no adnexal masses. 

Laboratory tests showed a CA-125 level of 112 IU/mL; CA 19-9 and CEA were normal. A CT scan revealed massive loculated ascites with internal septation and infiltrative enhancing lesions in the cul-de-sac and perirectal region; the uterus and ovaries appeared unremarkable. Chest X-ray demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions and lower‐lobe atelectasis. 

Repeat abdominal paracentesis produced clear yellowish fluid; cytologic examination indicated inflammation without malignant cells. Ascites fluid was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis by PCR and acid-fast bacilli staining. An exploratory laparotomy was scheduled for tissue diagnosis.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Endometriosis-Associated Massive Ascites in an Asian Woman: A Case Report of a Rare Clinical Entity

case_prompt: A 53-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a sensation of a foreign body in the back of her throat, which had worsened over the past 2 weeks. She denied hoarseness, dysphagia, odynophagia, or systemic symptoms. Examination revealed no thyroid enlargement or palpable cervical lymphadenopathy; systemic examination was unremarkable. Indirect laryngoscopy showed a soft tissue lesion in the posterior pharynx with medialization of the right vocal cord. Routine blood tests and thyroid function were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a right supraglottic enhancing mass within the pyriform fossa measuring 2.0 × 1.8 × 2.2 cm and two small thyroid nodules (0.2 × 1.0 cm on the right and 1.3 × 1.3 cm on the left). Neck ultrasonography reported a right ACR-TIRADS 1 nodule (0.5 × 0.8 × 1.0 cm), a left ACR-TIRADS 2 nodule (0.4 × 0.5 × 0.6 cm), and normal-appearing subcentimeter cervical lymph nodes. An initial biopsy of the posterior pharyngeal mass showed benign mucosal tissue.
title: Ectopic Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma of the Posterior Pharynx

case_prompt: A 22-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of lower left abdominal pain without urinary or bowel symptoms. She had no significant medical or surgical history. On bimanual pelvic examination, there was a well-circumscribed, firm, slightly movable, spherical lesion noted on the left vaginal wall. Urinalysis was normal. Pelvic ultrasonography showed a relatively irregular, heterogeneous mass in the left posterior wall of the bladder. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 3.2 × 2.5 cm soft-tissue mass with mild enhancement near the left posterior bladder wall, protruding into the bladder lumen. Cystoscopy revealed a hemispherical mass on the left bladder wall near the internal urethral orifice with intact urothelium, suggesting an intramural or extravesical lesion. A transurethral resection deep biopsy was performed, which showed normal tissue.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Transvaginal Resection of a Bladder Leiomyoma Misdiagnosed with a Vaginal Mass: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 37-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 5-year history of intermittent right knee pain aggravated by strenuous activity. He denied instability, locking, systemic symptoms, or weight loss. On examination, flexion was limited to 110° with moderate pain on further flexion. There was no swelling, effusion, or palpable mass. Routine blood tests were normal. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the knee were unremarkable. MRI revealed a 16×15 mm encapsulated nodular lesion within the infrapatellar Hoffa’s fat pad, medially located. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, showed a discrete hyperintense signal on T2-weighted images interrupted by hypointense punctuations, and demonstrated intense homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. Bone and patellar tendon were uninvolved.
title: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour in Hoffa fat pad: a case report

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old man presented on March 14, 2020, with a 3-day history of fever, dry cough, headache, and limb aches. He was previously healthy and had completed a half marathon one week before presentation. On arrival at a nearby hospital, he reported progressive shortness of breath and had a reduced general condition. Physical examination revealed crackles in the right upper lung field. His medical, family, and psychosocial history was unremarkable.

Because of concern for SARS-CoV-2 infection, he was admitted directly to the ICU. Initial therapy included piperacillin/tazobactam (4.5 g three times daily i.v.) and clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily i.v.). Polymerase chain–reaction tests for SARS-CoV-2, influenza virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Legionella species were all negative. Two days later, because of persistent fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and further respiratory deterioration, broadening antimicrobial coverage to meropenem (1 g three times daily i.v.), linezolid (600 mg twice daily i.v.), and fosfomycin (3 g i.v.) was undertaken, while the working diagnosis of COVID-19–related ARDS was maintained.

Chest imaging (X-ray and CT) demonstrated a diffuse interstitial reticular pattern, multilobular patchy ground-glass opacification, and consolidation of the right upper lobe. After one week of high-flow oxygen, the patient’s oxygenation index (PaO2/FiO2) fell to 130 mm Hg, necessitating endotracheal intubation. Despite prone positioning, he developed worsening hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis, and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 108 mm Hg with escalating vasopressor requirements. On March 22, an ECMO team was mobilized for transfer under COVID-19 precautions. After review of ventilator settings, imaging, and laboratory data, on-site ECMO was deferred, and the patient was moved under full COVID-19 PPE protocols.

Upon arrival, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed, and repeat naso- and oropharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 were obtained. A new chest X-ray showed predominantly right-sided pneumonia, felt to be “not typical for COVID-19,” and the working diagnosis was revised to an atypical pneumonia. Meropenem was continued, and clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily i.v.) was reintroduced. Laboratory studies revealed hemolysis with elevated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, and macrocytic hyperregenerative anemia (hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL, mixed-venous oxygen saturation 67%). A direct Coombs’ test was positive for cold agglutinins.
title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae Misinterpreted as SARS-CoV-2 Infection

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old Caucasian man underwent routine screening colonoscopy. He was asymptomatic and denied bleeding, pain, weight loss, fevers, or chills. He had no significant medical or surgical history and took no medications. Family history was unremarkable for cancer. On examination, vital signs were normal and the abdomen was soft, non-tender, with no palpable masses. Skin examination revealed no pigmented lesions. Laboratory tests including CBC, metabolic panel, liver function, coagulation studies, and hepatic serologies were all within normal limits.  
Colonoscopy showed a 3 cm submucosal pedunculated polyp 15 cm from the anal verge. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 2.3 cm × 1.4 cm submucosal lesion without adenopathy. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a 2.8 cm × 1.52 cm avascular, mixed-echogenicity lesion confined to the submucosa with no involvement of the muscularis mucosa or propria.  
Fine-needle biopsy of the lesion showed a bland spindle cell proliferation in a uniform fascicular pattern with edematous stroma. The cells were elongated with oval, wavy nuclei; no mitotic figures, necrosis, or hemorrhage were seen. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated strong, diffuse S100 positivity with rare penetrating axons, negative staining for c-kit and desmin, and a low Ki-67 index.
title: Isolated colonic neurofibroma, a rare tumor: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 41-year-old woman first presented with a left fifth metatarsal base fracture after an inversion sprain; the fracture healed with conservative treatment. Eight months later, she had sudden left forefoot pain without trauma, and radiographs showed a fracture of the left second metatarsal with callus formation. One year after the initial fracture, she returned with spontaneous left fourth toe pain; radiographs demonstrated old fractures of the bases of both fifth metatarsals and proximal phalanges of both third toes, with callus formation of the left second metatarsal and a crack fracture of the proximal phalanx of the left fourth toe. She was newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, but there was no sensory or neurological deficit of the feet. A dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan showed a T-score of –3.0 at L2–L4. She was premenopausal. To investigate secondary osteoporosis, an overnight dexamethasone suppression test showed a cortisol level of 660 nmol/L (not suppressed), 24-hour urine cortisol was 605 nmol/day, and a low-dose short synacthen test produced a peak serum cortisol of 699 nmol/L; plasma ACTH was <1.6 pmol/L. Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed bilateral adrenal adenomas.
title: Bilateral Adrenal Adenoma Presented As Multiple Metatarsal And Phalangeal Fractures

case_prompt: A 38-year-old Afro-Trinidadian woman with known endometriosis, intermittently adherent to oral contraceptive pills, presented with 2 days of acute dyspnea. Her blood pressure was 142/?, heart rate 112/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. On examination, jugular venous pressure was mildly elevated to 10 cm H2O; the right chest was stony dull to percussion; there was no peripheral edema; and she was actively menstruating. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia with an incomplete right bundle branch block, right ventricular hypertrophy, and subtle secondary ST-T changes. Chest radiography revealed a large right pleural effusion with mild perihilar vascular congestion. Laboratory studies showed a D-dimer of 208 ng/dL (normal ≤500), pro–BNP 323 pg/mL (normal ≤300), troponin I 0.08 ng/mL (normal 0.0–0.15), and arterial blood gas consistent with mild hypoxia and an alveolar–arterial gradient of 14 mm Hg on 24% FiO2. CT-guided thoracentesis yielded a hemorrhagic exudative effusion that recurred within 48 hours. Video-assisted thoracoscopic pleural biopsy revealed endometrial tissue, consistent with catamenial pleural effusions. The patient reported dyspnea that often coincided with her menses. During hospitalization, she developed persistent shortness of breath and an episode of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Transthoracic echocardiography showed preserved left ventricular function with moderate right heart enlargement, septal flattening, and an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 45 mm Hg. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated an intact interatrial septum with an agitated saline “bubble” study but incompletely visualized pulmonary veins.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Partial Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection: A Great Imitator?

case_prompt: A 23-year-old man, previously healthy army personnel, presented with intermittent postprandial vomiting and leg cramps for one month, which worsened over two days to about ten episodes per day. He denied loin pain or hematuria. On examination, he was alert, not pale, not jaundiced, and without cachexia; vital signs were: blood pressure 130/73 mmHg, pulse 92 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Initial laboratory studies revealed severe metabolic alkalosis (venous pH 7.56, bicarbonate 62 mmol/L), hypokalemia (K⁺ 1.6 mmol/L), hyponatremia (Na⁺ 126 mmol/L), and acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 218.3 μmol/L, eGFR 35.5 mL/min/1.73 m²); corrected calcium was 2.04 mmol/L. Shortly after arrival, he had a generalized tonic seizure followed by pulseless electrical activity cardiac arrest; return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after 70 minutes of CPR and 14 defibrillation shocks. He was intubated, required inotropic support, and became anuric, necessitating renal replacement therapy. A nasogastric tube drained approximately 2 L of gastric contents, but he remained intolerant of feeding. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed a markedly distended, elongated stomach with an air–fluid level; no lesion or compression at the pylorus or gastric antrum; significant narrowing of the third part of the duodenum in the precaval and preaortic region with loss of intervening fat; an aortomesenteric angle of 21° (normal 25–60°) and a distance of 8 mm (normal 10–28 mm).
title: Acute Kidney Injury Caused by Superior Mesenteric Artery Syndrome

case_prompt: A 58-year-old woman presented with a painless mass in her left thigh of 3 years’ duration. She had no history of trauma. On examination, a firm 3×4 cm mass was palpated in the anterior aspect of the left thigh. A lateral plain radiograph of the thigh showed irregular mineralization within the soft tissue. Axial MRI revealed a well-circumscribed intramuscular mass in the rectus femoris muscle that was predominantly high in signal intensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images, with interspersed areas of intermediate signal intensity. The medial border of the lesion was poorly defined, and no enhancement was seen after administration of gadolinium-DTPA. On sagittal images, the lesion showed irregular intermediate-signal areas surrounding regions of high signal intensity on T1-weighted sequences, and on T2-weighted sequences it was heterogeneous, with both high and intermediate signal intensities.
title: Ossifying chondrolipoma of the thigh: radiographic pathologic correlation

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 10-year-old girl was evaluated for a 4-year history of dyspnea on exertion and progressive spinal deformity. She had no fever or other respiratory symptoms. On examination, she was not in respiratory distress; breath sounds were diminished in the left lung field, especially at the base, with dullness to percussion. 

Chest radiography showed a large opacity occupying the left hemithorax, containing amorphous calcifications and causing a rightward shift of the cardiomediastinal silhouette. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography revealed a giant, well-defined, encapsulated mass in the anterior mediastinum measuring 135 × 150 × 197 mm. The lesion had areas of soft-tissue density, cystic change, and calcification, with heterogeneous enhancement, extended beyond the midline into the retrocardiac space, displaced and compressed the left lung (rendering it hypoplastic), and shifted the thymus to the right. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and biochemical profile, and negative levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (B-HCG).
title: Unusual presentation of giant mature mediastinal teratoma in a young child: A case report

case_prompt: A 69-year-old man presented with two months of rectal bleeding and pain. He had a history of chronic anal fissures and a remote basal cell carcinoma of the face, along with morbid obesity (BMI 33), hypertension, and a prior anti-reflux procedure. He denied tobacco use and had no family history of colorectal cancer. On examination, there was a large, ulcerated, fungating mass in the posterior midline of the anal canal. Laboratory evaluation showed a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 3.7 ng/mL (normal). Colonoscopy identified four tubular adenomas in the colon and confirmed a fixed, posterior midline fungating lesion extending into the anal canal. Staging MRI of the pelvis (rectal cancer protocol) demonstrated a 4.8 × 3.1 × 1.3 cm mass involving the internal and external anal sphincters without lymphadenopathy. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no distant metastases.
title: A case report of the rarest anal cancer: Basal cell carcinoma

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old non-smoking woman was referred for management of an extensive lesion affecting the maxillary right lateral incisor. She reported mild discomfort at that tooth and a history of a fall 10 years earlier, after which the tooth was asymptomatic. Several years ago, caries had been removed from its proximal surfaces, and an external cervical resorption (ECR) lesion was diagnosed at a private clinic. Discomfort gradually increased as radiographic translucency enlarged. She had no relevant medical history, no history of orthodontics or parafunctional habits, and her oral hygiene was good.  

On examination, there was no mobility of the affected or adjacent teeth, no tenderness to palpation, and slight pain on vertical percussion. Pulp sensibility tests elicited no response to cold or electrical stimulation, in contrast to adjacent teeth. Periodontal probing depths were <3 mm on the buccal side and 4 mm with bleeding and slight pus exudate on the distal palatal aspect. Root caries was ruled out as no infected dentine was detected.  

Periapical radiography demonstrated a large radiolucent defect extending from the distal to proximal surfaces without periapical pathology. Cone-beam computed tomography revealed that the lesion had reached the pulp tissue along one-third to one-half of the root in the axial plane, and horizontally involved approximately 180° of the palatal root surface. On the basis of these findings, the lesion was classified as Class III by Heithersay’s criteria and Class 2Bp by Patel’s criteria.
title: Repair of an Extensive External Cervical Resorption Lesion Using Intentional Replantation with Crown Rotation

case_prompt: A 32‐year‐old man presented with two asymptomatic facial lesions present unchanged in size for 12 months. He denied other skin eruptions, mucosal involvement, photosensitivity, and there was no relevant past medical, occupational, or family history. On examination, there were two erythematous macules, each about 5 mm in diameter, on the right cheek and forehead. Initial clinical differential diagnoses included discoid lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, granuloma annulare, and seborrheic dermatitis. A skin biopsy of the cheek lesion revealed prominent changes in the superficial epidermis with acantholysis primarily within the stratum granulosum, and in the dermis a predominantly superficial lymphocytic infiltrate with scattered scarce eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin showed intercellular deposits of IgG and C3 within the epidermis.
title: Two asymptomatic facial erythematous macules in an adult male

case_prompt: A 13-year-old boy with global developmental delay and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome presented with a 3-week history of progressive lower-limb bruising, pain, swelling, poor feeding, irritability, and recent loss of ambulation. Three weeks earlier, an intraoral mass on the right mandible had been noted. He had a similar presentation a year before, with bilateral lower-limb purpura, arthritis, severe anemia (hemoglobin 5.9 g/dL), normal platelet count, elevated C-reactive protein (80 mg/L), and elevated serum IgA; at that time he was diagnosed with IgA vasculitis. A second episode occurred one year later with purpura, arthritis, moderate anemia, raised acute-phase reactants, and proteinuria; he was again treated presumptively for IgA vasculitis. His medical history included epilepsy managed with phenobarbitone, valproic acid, risperidone, and lamotrigine. He was nonverbal, required full assistance for feeding, and ate mainly porridge, noodles, cabbage, and bananas. On admission, he was underweight (below the 5th percentile), irritable, and lying flexed. Blood pressure was 103/70 mmHg and heart rate 110 bpm. Examination revealed a fungating right mandibular intraoral mass without active bleeding, petechiae and ecchymoses on the extremities, pitting edema of the lower limbs, and painful, limited motion of ankles, knees, and the right wrist. Laboratory studies showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 4.0 g/dL), leukopenia (1.8 ×10^9/L), elevated CRP (89 mg/L), elevated ESR (42 mm/hr), and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio that had normalized. Autoantibodies (ANA, PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA) were negative; complement levels were normal. A noncontrast CT scan of the mandible demonstrated an inflammatory mass or abscess without bony destruction. During surgical consultation, gingival friability with hypertrophy, bleeding, deep periodontal pockets, and loose maxillary and mandibular teeth were noted. All deciduous teeth were extracted, gingival tissue was debrided, and biopsies were obtained from the intraoral lesion and from skin on the upper and lower limbs.
title: Scurvy masquerading as IgA vasculitis

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old man with a one-year history of asymptomatic skin lesions presented for evaluation. The lesions began on his upper limbs and gradually increased in number and size. He is a house builder who works outdoors without a shirt and has a history of diabetes mellitus, with glycemic control unchanged during the course of the rash. There is no family history of similar skin changes.

On dermatological examination, there were multiple asymmetric erythematous papules and atrophic plaques with slightly elevated borders arranged in annular configurations on the neck, trunk, arms, and forearms. No mucosal or nail abnormalities were noted.

Initial differential diagnoses included granuloma annulare and leprosy. Direct mycological examination and anti-HIV tests were negative. A punch biopsy from a forearm lesion revealed fragmentation of elastic fibers in multinucleated giant cells and the superficial dermis, along with granulomas centered by necrobiosis and multinucleated giant cells with apparent palisading.
title: Hybrid Clinical and Histopathological Pattern in Annular Lesions: An Overlap between Annular Elastolytic Giant Cell Granuloma and Granuloma Annulare?

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus presented with a 1-month history of a painful ulcerative lesion on the tip of his left middle finger. The lesion began as a small blister at the distal fingertip, then ruptured and became ulcerated with serous, nonfoul-smelling discharge. He had sustained a cat bite to that finger one month before the lesion appeared. He received multiple courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics, including oral amoxicillin–clavulanate, and underwent daily wound dressings for presumed diabetic ulcer care, but the lesion continued to enlarge, extending to the interphalangeal joint area, causing pain.

On examination, vital signs were normal and capillary blood glucose was 7.9 mmol/L. The left middle finger showed an approximately 2×2 cm ulcer with irregular margins, serous and bloody discharge, and tender palpation; the surrounding skin was normal without erythema. There were no palpable nodules on the dorsum of the hand or forearm and no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, white-cell count 6.0×10^9/L, platelet count 165×10^9/L, normal liver and renal function tests, and hemoglobin A1c 7.9%.

A skin biopsy from the lesion showed irregular epidermal hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis, inflammatory-cell infiltration within the epidermis, and marked acute and chronic inflammatory-cell infiltrates with histiocytes in the dermis.
title: A Diabetic Elderly Man with Finger Ulcer

case_prompt: A 76-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history presented with 4 days of fever, cough, and purulent sputum. He had worked as a farmer and had a remote inguinal hernia repair; his history also included diverticular disease and microscopic anemia. On admission, temperature was 38.2°C; other vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests showed a mild hypochromic anemia (Hct 38%), moderate neutrophilic leukocytosis, and elevated C-reactive protein (18.9 mg/L). A chest radiograph demonstrated an irregular, elongated shadow in the right upper‐lobe zone. Contrast CT of the chest confirmed an elongated irregular opacity with air-bronchogram stripes. To exclude malignancy, fiberoptic bronchoscopy was performed. The upper airways and trachea appeared normal, but the right main bronchus mucosa was roughened by multiple, variably sized white nodules without mucosal infiltration along its entire length; all more distal airways appeared normal. Bronchial washings and brushings were obtained from the apical segment of the right upper lobe, and multiple biopsies were taken from the nodules in the right main bronchus. The patient received intravenous cefuroxime for 5 days followed by oral cefuroxime axetil for 5 days, with near‐complete radiographic clearance of the right upper‐lobe shadow. Biopsy specimens were sent for histopathological evaluation.
title: Right Upper Lobe Shadow and Tracheobronchopathia Osteochondroplastica Confined to Right Main Bronchus: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
An 80-year-old woman with hypothyroidism, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and hypertension presented with progressive low back pain and acute left lower-extremity numbness leading to a fall. One year earlier, she had a mechanical fall down stairs causing back pain that initially improved with conservative measures. Six months ago, intermittent low back pain developed radiating to the left buttock; she was treated briefly with tramadol. One month before presentation, bilateral lower-extremity radiculopathy emerged, and she self-medicated with aspirin and acetaminophen. On the day of admission, she experienced severe left leg numbness and fell. She denied fevers, chills, incontinence, weight loss, and other systemic symptoms.

On examination, she was afebrile (36.4 °C), blood pressure 104/65 mmHg, pulse 54 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, BMI 32.1 kg/m2. She appeared uncomfortable but in no acute distress. Lumbar spine had mild point tenderness without overlying erythema or skin changes. Neurologic exam was intact: strength, sensation, reflexes, and rectal tone were normal. She had chronic-appearing abdominal fold and bilateral groin skin breakdown.

Laboratory studies revealed blood urea nitrogen 32 mg/dL, creatinine 1.23 mg/dL, corrected calcium 11.1 mg/dL, and white blood cell count 11.8 K/µL; other labs were within normal limits. A CT scan of the spine showed advanced degenerative joint disease with severe L4–L5 spinal stenosis. Intravenous dexamethasone was administered, and on hospital day 2 an MRI of the spine demonstrated vertebral body edema and enhancement most evident at L4–L5, with paravertebral soft-tissue thickening at L5–S1 concerning for osteomyelitis/discitis, along with severe central canal stenosis at L4–L5. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated.
title: Trauma Induced Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease of the Lumbar Spine

case_prompt: A 39-year-old man with acute B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation 6 weeks earlier. He presented with a 1-week history of nonproductive cough and fevers. Vital signs were stable, with an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Pulmonary examination revealed faint crackles at the right lung apex. Laboratory studies showed a normal white-blood-cell count and differential. A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral airspace opacities. Chest CT revealed widespread, multifocal patchy opacities most prominent in the apices and scattered bibasilar opacities. On hospital day 2, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (right upper lobe) yielded 605 WBC/mL (76% histiocytes, 19% neutrophils, 6% lymphocytes); cultures for bacteria, fungi, viruses, and acid-fast bacilli were negative. Transbronchial biopsy of the right lower lobe was nondiagnostic. The patient was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals, but over the next week he had worsening cough, progressive dyspnea, and hypoxemia.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Acute Fibrinous and Organizing Pneumonia Associated With Allogenic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant Successfully Treated With Corticosteroids

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman with a 30-year history of HIV infection presented with a 3-month history of a mildly pruritic, widespread rash accompanied by fevers, night sweats, headaches, cough, and dyspnea. Originally from Zimbabwe, she immigrated to Canada 7 years earlier and had since discontinued antiretroviral therapy. Over the preceding year, she and her family noted weight loss and progressive functional and cognitive decline. 

On admission, her CD4+ cell count was 1 cell/μL, and her HIV viral load was 5.28 log10 copies/mL. Dermatologic examination revealed diffusely infiltrated, scaly, verrucous, hyperpigmented thick plaques on the face producing a leonine facies. On the torso and extremities, there were non-blanching, violaceous-to-brown papules and plaques of varying sizes, each surrounded by a blanchable, erythematous halo.

A computed tomography scan of the chest showed calcified granulomata in both upper lobes and bulky mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain identified a small lesion in the right parietal lobe.

A lesional skin biopsy, stained with hematoxylin and eosin, demonstrated a dermal infiltrate of histiocytes containing numerous ovoid, yeast-like organisms. These organisms were more clearly defined using periodic acid–Schiff and Grocott’s methenamine silver stains, supporting a fungal etiology.
title: An immigrant with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome presenting with a rash: A case report

case_prompt: A 51-year-old Indian woman presented with a sudden-onset, severe bilateral occipital headache that began three days earlier without prodrome or visual aura. The continuous pain was exacerbated by coughing, relieved when recumbent, and radiated over the vertex to the temporal regions; it was also associated with nausea and mild photophobia. She had no prior headaches, no significant medical history, and no regular medications. There was no family history of headache or sudden death. On examination, she was alert with normal vital signs. The neurologic examination was unremarkable: Kernig’s sign was negative, there was no neck stiffness or rash, and fundoscopy showed no papilledema. Initial labs showed mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia; erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture revealed no red cells, an opening pressure of 11 cm H2O, and no xanthochromia. A magnetic resonance angiogram of the head was normal. With symptomatic improvement on bed rest and weak opioid analgesia, she was given a tentative diagnosis of migraine and discharged.
title: Intracranial hypotension secondary to spinal arachnoid cyst rupture presenting with acute severe headache: a case report

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and prostate cancer was referred for cataract evaluation of the right eye. He reported no photophobia, eye pain, discharge, contact-lens use, ocular trauma, or prior ocular procedures, and no personal or family history of metabolic disorders or corneal dystrophies. Medications included atorvastatin, chlorthalidone, clopidogrel, metformin, primidone, topiramate, tamsulosin, and propranolol. 

Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left. Pupillary reactions and intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. Corneal pachymetry measured 549 µm centrally and 681 µm peripherally in the right eye, and 547 µm centrally and 673 µm peripherally in the left. 

Slit-lamp examination revealed symmetric bilateral circular mid-peripheral full-thickness stromal white rings (7–8 mm in diameter). Corneal sensation was intact; there was no vascularization, fibrosis, thinning, or fluorescein staining. Gonioscopy showed open angles without a thickened Schwalbe’s line or iris processes. Posterior-segment examination was unremarkable bilaterally.

Laboratory studies—including basic metabolic panel, complete blood count, lactate dehydrogenase, beta-2 microglobulin, and serum protein electrophoresis—were within normal limits. Lipid profile showed slightly reduced high-density cholesterol. Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated highly reflective material throughout the entire corneal stroma.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Bilateral idiopathic corneal opacity: A report of Ascher ring and a review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman noted a left breast mass and was referred for evaluation. On examination, there was a 2.0-cm, well-defined, mobile, elastic-hard mass in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast; no axillary lymphadenopathy was palpable. 

Mammography demonstrated a 2.0-cm micro-lobulated, high-density mass with internal polymorphic calcifications. Breast ultrasonography showed a 1.3×1.0×1.1-cm irregular hypoechoic mass with angular margins and calcifications. MRI revealed a 1.9×1.8×1.7-cm irregular tumor with early contrast enhancement and washout in the late phase, with heterogeneous internal enhancement.

A 16-gauge core needle biopsy showed fibrosis in all specimens, with duct components and squamous-epithelium–like cells in some samples; spindle cells had low mitotic activity and low nuclear grade, and AE1/AE3 was negative. A subsequent 10-gauge vacuum-assisted biopsy again demonstrated fibrosis and inflammatory cell infiltration without malignant features. 

Three months later, ultrasound showed growth of the mass to 1.8×1.7×1.5 cm. A repeat 16-gauge core needle biopsy revealed proliferation of fibroblast-like spindle cells and clusters of squamous-like cells with low-grade atypia in all specimens. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated positivity for CK5/6 and AE1/AE3 in both spindle cells and squamous cells; CK14, p63, and p40 were also positive, and CAM5.2 was partially positive in squamous cells but negative in spindle cells.
title: A difficult-to-diagnose fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma of the breast: a case report

case_prompt: A 76-year-old man with type 1 diabetes since age 7 underwent simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplantation 19 years ago for end-stage renal disease attributed to diabetic nephropathy. His posttransplant course was uncomplicated with no rejection episodes. Maintenance immunosuppression includes tacrolimus (levels 6.5–10 ng/mL), mycophenolic acid, and prednisone. He has been insulin-independent with fasting glucose 90–94 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 5.2–5.8% without glucose-lowering therapy. Lipase and amylase levels were within normal limits. His baseline serum creatinine is 1.0–1.2 mg/dL (eGFR 58–68 mL/min/1.73 m2). On routine evaluation, urinalysis showed 2+ proteinuria without hematuria. Urine protein-creatinine ratios ranged from 3.0 to 4.3 g/g, confirmed by a 24-hour collection (3.5 g/day). Blood pressure is well controlled on amlodipine and metoprolol; losartan was added. Physical examination revealed trace pedal edema. Body mass index is 20.5 kg/m2. There are no donor-specific antibodies. Due to new-onset nephrotic-range proteinuria, a kidney allograft biopsy was performed.
title: Mesangial sclerosis in a patient with type 1 diabetes following simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplantation despite maintenance of normoglycemia: a case report

case_prompt: A 66-year-old woman presented with isolated uterine bleeding for 6 months. Examination revealed a cervical tumor, confirmed by biopsy as well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. As part of staging, a thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT scan showed a large right‐sided retroperitoneal abdominal-pelvic cystic mass that displaced the right kidney anteriorly. The mass had well-defined, regular contours with a thin wall, multiple thin septa, and dense fluid content that enhanced faintly after contrast administration. Delayed CT acquisitions at 15 minutes and 2 hours demonstrated slow, progressive, and partial filling of the mass by contrast medium. Ultrasonography revealed an anechoic cystic mass with multiple fine septa in a fishnet pattern, displacing the kidney anteriorly. In addition, there was bilateral ureterohydronephrosis, with a 17-mm pelvicalyceal dilation on the left and a 51-mm dilation on the right. Laboratory tests showed elevated urea and creatinine, an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 11 mL/min, mild hyperkalemia without ECG changes, and leukocytosis.
title: Imaging of an exceptional urinoma complicating a cervical cancer and leading to death: A case report

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old man who works as a gym instructor and trains five times per week was evaluated for one month of gradually worsening neck pain with a feeling of heaviness in the head. The pain began during weightlifting (bench press, shoulder press, squats) and treadmill use, was aggravated by lower-body training, and reached a worst intensity of 8/10 on a numeric rating scale. He noted stiffness and limited rotation of the neck bilaterally, worse with cold exposure, and morning stiffness that improved over hours but left persistent head heaviness. He had no history of trauma, night pain, or dizziness, and he self-treated with foam rolling. Medical history included adolescent-onset hyperreflexia and dysmetria of the left arm, testicular torsion repair in 1982, and left shoulder arthroplasty in 2018. Both he and his brother had lifelong thrombocytopenia and leukopenia; his father had hypertension.  

On examination, there was bilateral trapezius spasm, painful restricted neck rotation (8/10), and neck extension that increased head heaviness. Temperature was normal. Oxygen saturation was 99%, resting heart rate 68 bpm, and resting blood pressure averaging 130/80 mmHg. To assess exercise response, BP, heart rate, and rate of perceived exertion were measured every 3 minutes during treadmill walking at 5 km/h with a 2% incline, with the left arm relaxed. At minute 3, BP was 145/85 mmHg (HR 91 bpm, RPE 0); at minute 6, BP 160/95 mmHg (HR 96 bpm, RPE 5) with recurrence of his usual neck pain; at minute 9, BP 190/100 mmHg (RPE 8) with sharp worsening of neck pain and an unsteady gait, prompting test termination. After exercise, left blepharoptosis was noted.
title: Physiotherapy Screening for Referral of a Patient with Patent Foramen Ovale Presenting with Neck Pain as Primary Complaint: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 63-year-old woman presented with recurrent microhematuria. She denied flank pain, episodes of gross hematuria, hypertension, renal trauma, or prior renal instrumentation. On examination, her blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg without abdominal bruit, and the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Urinalysis was negative for infection but positive for erythrocytes. Renal ultrasonography revealed a discrete hypoechogenicity in the left upper renal pole. Intravenous pyelography demonstrated an irregular configuration of the upper pole collecting system, which was confirmed on retrograde ureteropyelography. Cystoscopy and ureterorenoscopy showed blood clots in the upper calyceal group but no apparent mass; biopsy of the pericalyceal tissue revealed no malignant cells on cytology or histology. A ureteral stent was placed, and the patient was discharged. Four days later, she was readmitted with hemodynamically significant gross hematuria and a hemoglobin concentration of 70 g/L, requiring transurethral clot evacuation. Duplex sonography and computed tomography angiography revealed multiple arteriovenous fistulas with erosions into the calyceal system.
title: Congenital intrarenal arteriovenous malformation presenting with gross hematuria after endoscopic intervention: a case report

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old man presented with a 2½-year history of intermittent scleral icterus. His total bilirubin measurements ranged from 1.8 to 7.2 mg/dL, with an isolated elevation of the indirect fraction. He denied abdominal pain, swelling, bleeding, fever, chills, neurologic symptoms, or any precipitating factors. He took no medications or supplements, used no tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs, and had no significant birth or neonatal history.

On examination, vital signs were normal, and there was no jaundice beyond mild scleral icterus. Abdominal and systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normal ceruloplasmin, peripheral blood smear, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, acetaminophen level, and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Acute viral hepatitis serologies were negative for hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B core IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a liver of normal size and echogenicity without intrahepatic biliary dilatation; the gallbladder was normal without stones or pericholecystic fluid.

Given the patient’s asymptomatic indirect hyperbilirubinemia, the differential diagnosis included Crigler–Najjar syndrome type 2 versus Gilbert syndrome, and targeted mutation analysis of the UGT1A1 gene was sent.
title: A Rare Presentation of Indirect Hyperbilirubinemia: Coexistence of Multiple UGT1A1 Gene Variants

case_prompt:
A 12-year-old otherwise healthy boy was referred from an urgent care center to the emergency department for fever and back pain. According to the referring clinician, he had several days of leg pain and lumbar spine pain and was febrile to 102°F; during a rectal examination there, he became incontinent of “bloody-brown stool.” 

On arrival he was in no acute distress. He reported bilateral lower leg pain for one week, beginning in his left hip, achy, radiating to the lower legs (not the feet), worse with movement and better with rest. His mother noted an abnormal gait. By the day of evaluation, he had developed focal low back pain described as achy and sometimes sharp, worse with movement and sitting, better when supine. He had no urinary retention but did have the above-mentioned bowel incontinence, and he did not sense either the rectal exam or the incontinence until it was pointed out. He stated that his leg pain almost completely resolved after the digital rectal examination, and his back pain improved but persisted. He also had some loose stools over the prior two days.

Initial vital signs were temperature 37.1°C, heart rate 95 beats/min, blood pressure 103/57 mm Hg, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. The patient appeared well and thin. Head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat examination was normal; there was no neck stiffness or meningismus. Cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations were normal. The abdomen was soft and nontender. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness, but he complained of midline low back tenderness to palpation. Arm and leg examinations revealed no acute abnormalities, and the skin was without lesions. Neurologic examination showed increased tone in both quadriceps, although the patient was able to relax with coaching. Cranial nerves were intact; gait was normal; toe and heel walking were normal; motor strength was 5/5 throughout; sensation to light touch was normal; speech was normal; and there was no dysmetria.

When he was rolled to his side for a digital rectal examination, copious thick, brownish-red, malodorous fluid resembling stool oozed from his anus. The external perianal region appeared normal after cleaning. A digital rectal examination revealed no mass, and the patient could bear down, but he could not sense either the finger or the fluid. Stool was sampled and guaiac positive. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis of 13,000 cells/mm³ without a left shift and a normal metabolic panel. Urine studies were normal, with a postvoid residual volume under 100 cc. An MRI of the lumbar spine was then obtained.
title: Perirectal Abscess Masquerading as Cauda Equina Syndrome in an Otherwise Healthy 12-Year-Old Child

case_prompt: A 14-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of localized swelling and pain over the proximal lateral aspect of her left fibula. The pain was insidious in onset, most severe at night, and was not related to physical activity. There were no systemic symptoms such as fever or weight loss. On examination, there was focal tenderness and mild soft-tissue swelling over the proximal fibular shaft; distal neurovascular findings were normal. Plain radiographs of the left leg demonstrated a small, well-circumscribed lucent focus in the proximal lateral fibula, surrounded by a zone of reactive sclerosis. A trial of acetylsalicylic acid led to immediate pain relief; however, her symptoms recurred within days of stopping the medication.
title: Osteoid Osteoma of the Proximal Fibula: An Uncommon Location with the Indication for Open Surgery

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man presented with painful sores on the upper and lower lips, worsened by eating and talking. Four days earlier, he noted “canker sores” in the oral cavity, and two days later similar lesions appeared on the lips. He had had a fever about one week before the onset of the oral lesions. He initially applied petroleum jelly without relief, then used triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% in orabase once daily, with partial improvement of the intraoral ulcers but persistence of the lip lesions. He denied use of other medications, allergies, systemic disease, alcohol use, or smoking, but reported frequent lip licking and poor nutrition. No lesions were present on other parts of the body.

On examination, vital signs were normal and no lymphadenopathy was noted. The lips bore serosanguineous crusts that were tender and bled easily. Intraoral examination showed erythematous, irregular lesions with diffuse borders on the upper and lower labial mucosa. A white hyperkeratotic plaque that could not be scraped off was present on the left buccal mucosa. A removable yellowish-white plaque was seen on the dorsal tongue without underlying erythema, and there were scalloped lateral tongue margins. A painless 2×1×0.5 cm hard nodule lay midline on the hard palate. Oral hygiene was poor with multiple carious, endodontic, and edentulous sites.

Psychological assessment (DASS-21) was normal. Based on history and clinical examination, the working diagnosis was suspected herpes-associated erythema multiforme (HAEM). The differential diagnosis for the lip lesions included exfoliative cheilitis, which lacks herpes virus involvement. Serological testing for anti–HSV-1 IgG was indicated to confirm the diagnosis.
title: Evaluation of Oral Health-Related Quality of Life in Patient with Herpes-Associated Erythema Multiforme: A Unique Case Report

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old right-handed woman with no prior medical history presented with one week of right lower extremity numbness from toes to hip and three days of progressive left lower extremity weakness, resulting in use of crutches. She reported a minor fall onto an air mattress three days before the onset of weakness but denied significant trauma or other injuries. She had no fevers, chills, upper extremity symptoms, facial or visual changes, speech or swallowing difficulties.
On examination, she was alert and afebrile with normal cranial nerve function. Upper extremity strength and sensation were intact. In the lower extremities, left hip flexion was 3/5, knee extension 4/5, foot dorsiflexion 3/5, and plantarflexion 5/5; right lower extremity strength was 5/5 throughout. Sensory testing showed decreased pinprick and temperature on the right up to the T11–T12 dermatomes, and reduced proprioception and vibration in the left from mid-shin downward. Left patellar clonus was present with 6–7 beats; ankle jerks were symmetric, and Babinski and Hoffman signs were equivocal.
MRI of the spine demonstrated multifocal T2‐hyperintense lesions with contrast enhancement, suspicious for an inflammatory or demyelinating process, without space-occupying lesions. Brain MRI showed periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial gadolinium-enhancing lesions. An axial T2‐weighted image at L1 revealed a high-signal lesion hemisecting the spinal cord.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Newly Diagnosed Multiple Sclerosis Presenting as Brown-Séquard Syndrome: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old girl was brought to the hospital with intermittent fever for 4 days, generalized edema and oliguria for 2 days, and an erythematous macular rash on her trunk and limbs for 1 day. She also had two episodes of vomiting. There was no history of jaundice or previous similar illness.

On examination, she was febrile, tachycardic (heart rate 134/min), and hypotensive (blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg) with poor peripheral perfusion. She had anasarca, a blanching macular erythematous rash over her trunk, hands, and legs, and multiple nontender, nonmatted cervical lymph nodes (largest 1.5 × 1.5 cm). Her lips were erythematous and cheilotic, but she had no strawberry tongue or conjunctival injection. Abdominal examination revealed tender hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, white cells 10,000/μL (72% neutrophils), platelets 430,000/μL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 4 mm in the first hour. Blood cultures were negative and peripheral smear showed no malarial parasites. Liver tests were notable for ALT 155 IU/L, total protein 4.8 g/dL, and albumin 2.0 g/dL. Tests for dengue IgM and leptospira IgM were negative. Cardiac monitoring was normal, and serum creatinine and creatine phosphokinase were within reference ranges.

She was treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone and saline boluses; because hypotension persisted, dopamine was started. Fever continued, and on hospital day 3 she developed red lips and a strawberry tongue, although her rash resolved over the next 2 days. Dopamine was discontinued on day 4. On day 5, repeat studies showed a platelet count of 477,000/μL and an ESR of 135 mm in the first hour.
title: Kawasaki's disease: An unusual presentation

case_prompt:
