A 25-year-old woman presented in 1994 with sustained episodes of flashes in both eyes and transient visual-acuity drops that normalized over days. She was morbidly obese (140 kg) and a smoker. She also reported monthly right-sided headaches with photophobia lasting less than 24 hours, episodes of blurred vision, and paresthesias in the left jaw, arm, and leg. Examination, including optic discs and neurologic assessment, was normal. Multiple sclerosis was considered but deemed unlikely, and she was diagnosed with complicated migraine.

In 1998, she re-presented with intermittent tingling bilaterally, a sensation of imbalance, and short-lasting visual obscurations. Neurologic examination remained normal. An MRI could not be performed due to body habitus.

In 2002, she developed bilateral granulomatous uveitis and multifocal retinal periphlebitis; the optic discs were healthy, with no cystoid macular oedema. Laboratory tests showed a normal ANA, antiphospholipid screen, full blood count, an ESR of 28 mm/hour, and an atypical ANCA. A brain MRI demonstrated lesions involving the deep white matter. Visual evoked potentials were normal; lumbar puncture was not performed.

Between 2002 and 2004, she experienced episodes of vitritis, hypopyon, and macular oedema requiring high-dose oral prednisolone. There was debate about a demyelinating process versus vasculitis, and she received six cycles of intravenous cyclophosphamide followed by mycophenolate mofetil. 

In 2005, despite treatment, she had a posterior circulation transient ischaemic attack and retinal haemorrhage. Repeat MRI showed progression of white matter lesions with multifocal deep grey matter and brain stem involvement. She was treated with aspirin, a β-blocker, and a statin. 

From 2004 to 2010, she continued to have uveitis and retinal bleeds treated with high-dose prednisolone. A follow-up MRI demonstrated progressive, multifocal small-vessel disease. The unusual distribution of the lesions and ongoing clinical progression sparked the search for alternative diagnoses.
title: Pattern recognition is a sequential process—accurate diagnosis and treatment 20 years after presentation

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old man with a 12-year history of relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis had been treated with interferon until June 2009 and then started on natalizumab because of worsening gait dysfunction. In December 2011, he noted progressive memory and concentration deficits and experienced episodes of verbal aggression, mood changes, and suicidal thoughts. He was admitted for evaluation.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was performed on a 3.0-T scanner, including T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, diffusion-weighted imaging, post-gadolinium T1, and single- and multivoxel proton spectroscopy. Imaging showed a large, irregular subcortical lesion in the semioval center beneath the left frontal lobe with minimal involvement of subcortical white matter of the right hemisphere and the anterior commissure. The lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, hypointense on T1-weighted images, showed no contrast enhancement after gadolinium administration, and no restricted diffusion. Proton spectroscopy demonstrated elevated lactate and myoinositol levels and an increased choline peak with reduction of creatine and N-acetyl-aspartate in both mono- and multivoxel spectra.

On the basis of these findings, natalizumab was discontinued and a lumbar puncture was planned.
title: Early Magnetic Resonance Detection of Natalizumab-Related Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy in a Patient with Multiple Sclerosis

case_prompt: A 10-year-old boy with a history of prematurity and a sister who died in infancy from presumed vitamin K–related intracranial bleeding was referred for sudden onset of a scalp mass and fever. There was no history of head trauma, although he had massaged his scalp the day before admission. On examination, his temperature was 38.8°C and he was clinically stable. A 5×5-cm soft, non‐tender mass was noted over the right temporal scalp without signs of inflammation. Petechial rashes were present on the oral mucosa, trunk, and limbs, and new petechiae appeared readily at the site of tourniquet compression. Laboratory studies showed a normal platelet count and normal prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen level; a white-cell count of 2900/mm3 with relative lymphocytosis; and a C-reactive protein level of 3.26 mg/dl. Head computed tomography revealed subcutaneous hemorrhage without skull fracture or intracranial bleeding. The presumptive diagnosis was Henoch–Schönlein purpura, although the rashes were non‐palpable and had an atypical distribution. Further testing, including bleeding time, protein C and S levels, and screening for collagen‐vascular diseases, was unremarkable. No additional bleeding occurred, and his symptoms resolved spontaneously over several days; he was discharged on hospital day 6.
title: Cephalhematoma and petechial rashes associated with acute parvovirus B19 infection: a case report

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a conjunctival nodule in the right eye. His parents first noted the lesion three months earlier; it had not changed in size, and he reported no pain, visual disturbance, or other ocular symptoms. There was no history of trauma, ocular surgery, or systemic disease.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes, and intraocular pressures were within normal limits. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a pale-yellow, firm nodule approximately 5 mm in diameter beneath the bulbar conjunctiva in the superotemporal quadrant. The lesion had clear borders, was immobile, mildly congested, and non-tender. There was no proptosis, and extraocular movements were full. Funduscopic examination of the right eye showed a normal posterior segment.

Computed tomography of the right orbit demonstrated a crescent-shaped calcified nodule on the temporal scleral surface without involvement of the extraocular muscles. To exclude systemic causes of tissue calcification, laboratory studies were obtained: serum calcium, phosphate, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were all within normal limits.
title: Epibulbar osseous choristoma

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of heavy menstrual bleeding, requiring pad changes every 3–4 hours. She reported working long hours without rest and had taken excess acetaminophen for body pain over the preceding 4 months. She had no personal or family history of bleeding disorders, no gynecological abnormalities, and no weight loss. On examination, she was pale; the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, leukocytes 5.4×10^3/µL, and platelets 268×10^3/µL. Bleeding time was prolonged at 9 minutes 11 seconds (Ivy method). Coagulation studies revealed a partial thromboplastin time of 59.2 seconds and a prothrombin time of 33.1 seconds (INR 5.97), both of which corrected on a mixing test without incubation. von Willebrand factor antigen and activity and fibrinogen were normal; factor X activity was 8%. She was started on iron and folic acid and acetaminophen was discontinued. Two weeks later, bleeding time normalized but PT and PTT remained prolonged.

She then developed acute severe dizziness with gait instability and was admitted. Repeat studies showed PTT 38.5 seconds and PT 21.2 seconds (INR 2.51), with normal liver-function tests. A full coagulation factor assay demonstrated factor II 41%, factor VII 3%, factor IX 24%, and factor X 52%; no inhibitors were detected. On further history, she disclosed six months of consuming primarily high-energy drinks with inadequate nutritional intake.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Acquired Vitamin K Deficiency as Unusual Cause of Bleeding Tendency in Adults: A Case Report of a Nonhospitalized Student Presenting with Severe Menorrhagia

case_prompt: A 46-year-old woman presented to dermatology with a 3-month history of nonpruritic, nontender, hyperkeratotic papules and plaques on her upper and lower extremities. Her medical history was notable for de novo metastatic hormone receptor–positive breast cancer (involving the brain, liver, bones, and lymph nodes) and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. She was being treated with dexamethasone, whole-brain radiation, tamoxifen, leuprolide, and insulin, with good control of her cancer and glycemia. She was referred by her oncologist to rule out disseminated zoster because of significant lymphopenia from prolonged steroid use. On examination, there were discrete, erythematous, umbilicated papules and plaques with central adherent hyperkeratotic cores measuring 1 to 2 cm on the extensor surfaces of her arms and legs; Koebnerization was noted on the forearms. Laboratory studies showed a creatinine level of 0.48 mg/dL, a glucose level of 217 mg/dL, and a hemoglobin A1c of 11.5%.
title: Giant acquired reactive perforating collagenosis in a patient with diabetes mellitus and metastatic breast carcinoma

case_prompt: An 87-year-old man presented with a two-week history of edema and erythema of the distal phalanx of the left fourth digit. He had received oral antibiotics followed by intravenous antibiotics for presumed infection without improvement. On examination, the fingertip was erythematous, edematous, and tender. Radiographs of the left hand showed no bony abnormalities. An incisional biopsy of the soft tissue was performed. Histologic examination revealed small lobules, cords, and single epithelial cells set within a desmoplastic stroma. Immunohistochemical stains were strongly positive for cytokeratins CK7 and CK AE1/3, and negative for cytokeratins CK20, TTF-1, prostate-specific antigen, synaptophysin, chromogranin, p63, and S-100. To evaluate for a possible metastatic source, MRI of the left upper extremity and computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were obtained. Imaging demonstrated a 5.1 × 4.2 cm solid heterogeneous right upper lobe hilar mass with irregular margins, an enlarged right axillary lymph node, multiple mediastinal lymph nodes, and an enlarged right paratracheal lymph node. A chest radiograph obtained one year earlier had been normal.
title: Aggressive Digital Papillary Adenocarcinoma of the Hand Presenting as a Felon

case_prompt:
A 16-month-old girl, born at term, presented with a 3-day history of cough, upper respiratory infection symptoms, and fever. She had had recurrent admissions since 10 months of age for presumed asthma exacerbations with viral or bacterial pneumonia, all showing persistent or worsening right-sided infiltrates on chest X-ray every 2 months. On examination, her temperature was 38.5°C, pulse 167/min, respiratory rate 75/min, blood pressure 115/53 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 96% on 2 L nasal cannula. She appeared alert but in moderate respiratory distress. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral crackles and rhonchi, more pronounced on the right. The cardiovascular exam was normal. Laboratory tests showed hypochromic microcytic anemia, CRP 54 mg/L, and a venous pH 7.43 with pO2 62 mmHg, pCO2 24 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L. A respiratory viral panel was positive for rhinovirus; blood cultures were negative. Chest radiographs demonstrated bilateral infiltrates, predominantly right middle lobe. Pulmonology was consulted, and an ECG was obtained.
ECG findings: left-axis deviation, peaked P waves, and incomplete right bundle branch block.
title: Uncovering the Hidden Cause of Recurrent Chest Infections in a Child: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 77-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of a painless, soft mass on the left lateral border of the tongue. Her medical history was notable for hypertension; she had no tobacco or alcohol use and no family history of tumors. On examination, the lesion was movable, 15 mm in diameter, with an intact surface; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an 18×12×8 mm, well-circumscribed mass in the tongue, slightly hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, without vascular or muscular invasion. A clinical diagnosis of lipoma was made, and the lesion was excised. Grossly, the specimen was a 13-mm, yellow, partially encapsulated nodular lesion with a soft texture. Microscopic examination revealed relatively uniform spindle cells separated by mature adipocytes in a collagenous stroma; the spindle cells exhibited minimal cytonuclear atypia, lipoblasts, necrosis, and mitoses were absent, and the lesion showed infiltrative growth at the margins. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated diffuse CD34 positivity in spindle cells, negativity for smooth muscle actin and S-100 protein, and focal MDM2 positivity in adipocytes.
title: Atypical spindle cell lipomatous tumor of the tongue: A rare entity arising in an unusual location

case_prompt: A 45-year-old Caucasian woman with stage IVB cervical cancer treated 8 months earlier with six courses of combined radiochemotherapy and brachytherapy presented with 5 months of progressive dysuria, pollakisuria, and lower-abdominal cramps. She had a 45 pack-year smoking history and remote history of cocaine and heroin use. Her surgical history included gastric banding, abdominoplasty, and recurrent breast abscess excision. On examination, vital signs were stable; pelvic examination was unremarkable. Urinalysis showed sterile leukocyturia. Cystoscopy revealed three small nonspecific mucosal lesions and one ulceration compatible with postradiation changes. To exclude cancer recurrence and investigate her symptoms, a CT scan of the thorax, abdominal wall, and pelvis was performed, which demonstrated multiple bilateral micronodular and cystic lung lesions and diffuse hypodense lesions in the liver. An ELISPOT assay for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an HIV screening test, and ANA/ANCA testing were all negative.
title: Spontaneous Remission of Severe Systemic Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis with Bladder Involvement: A Case Study

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of a right parietal region mass that began enlarging after her pregnancy in 2010. She denied trauma, pain, seizures, visual symptoms, or motor or coordination deficits, but reported altered sensation over the lesion. Her past history included surgically repaired pulmonary artery stenosis and medically managed irritable bowel syndrome. She did not use tobacco, alcohol, illicit drugs, or hormonal contraception.

On examination, she was well-nourished and in no distress. Cranial nerves were intact without visual field deficits or papilledema. Strength, reflexes, coordination, and gait were all normal. Sensation was intact except for mild hypesthesia over the right parietal region.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed a 6.4 × 6.4 × 4.0 cm right parietal calvarial mass expanding the diploic space with mass effect on the underlying parietal lobe but no evidence of cortical destruction. MRI revealed a lesion centered in the right parietal bone, extending into the extra-axial space over the right posterior-frontal and parietal lobes, causing cerebral compression. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2, did not enhance with gadolinium, and there was no parenchymal edema or other lesions identified.
title: Giant calvarial intraosseous angiolipoma: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old Caucasian woman underwent right superficial parotidectomy and neck dissection two years ago for a slow‐growing right parotid mass. Histopathology at that time showed a low‐grade carcinoma with tubular and cribriform architecture and eosinophilic colloid‐like material; the tumor was positive for mammaglobin and S100 protein. Margins were negative, and there was no lymphovascular invasion or nodal metastasis.

She presented two years later with new onset of back and left flank pain. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple hepatic lesions, the largest measuring 5.4 cm in the left lobe. A core‐needle biopsy of the largest lesion was performed.

Microscopic examination of the liver biopsy showed a carcinoma with a cribriform pattern and eosinophilic proteinaceous secretions in the centers of cystic spaces. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong positivity for mammaglobin and S100 protein.
title: A Cribriform Cancer Metastatic to Liver: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 42-year-old Thai male ophthalmologist with well-controlled dyslipidemia received his second dose of CoronaVac vaccine at 12:50 pm. Thirty minutes of post-vaccination observation were uneventful, but ten minutes later he noted blurred, foggy central vision that expanded over minutes to obscure the entire left visual field without darkening. There was no headache, weakness, or other neurologic symptoms. He presented to ophthalmology 10 minutes after onset. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Anterior segments and fundi were normal. There was no intraocular inflammation or relative afferent pupillary defect. Macular OCT was unremarkable. Automated perimetry (24-2) demonstrated a left congruous homonymous hemianopia respecting the vertical midline. Stroke evaluation was initiated; neurologic examination was normal except for a blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg. Brain MRI with DWI showed no evidence of acute infarction, hemorrhage, significant stenosis, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm. Approximately two hours after onset his vision returned to normal and repeat perimetry was normal.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Transient visual field loss after COVID-19 vaccination: Experienced by ophthalmologist, case report

case_prompt: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hypothyroidism presented with acute-onset nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. He denied fevers or chills and had no prior gastrointestinal procedures. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the right upper and lower quadrants without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated no evidence of bowel obstruction, ischemia, or abscess; however, there was an extensive amount of gas in the portal venous system. Given his stable presentation and lack of alarming findings, he was managed conservatively with intravenous fluids and bowel rest.
title: A case of hepatic portal venous gas due to viral gastroenteritis

case_prompt: A 7-year-old girl presented with one week of abdominal pain localized to the left iliac fossa and right lumbar region. She had no fever, anorexia, vomiting, hematochezia, or diarrhea, and had slight relief with analgesics. There was no relevant family history. On examination, she was well appearing; vital signs were normal. Her abdomen was soft without guarding, but a palpable mass was noted in the right iliac fossa extending into the corresponding lumbar region, which was tender on palpation, without signs of peritoneal irritation. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 13,000/mm3, and platelet count 487,000/mm3. All tumor markers, including CEA, CA 125, CA 19-9, AFP, and β-hCG, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large cyst filling the cecum and ascending colon without connection to the liver or right kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large cystic mass lateral and superior to the cecum and ascending colon, also without evidence of connection to adjacent organs.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare case of enteric duplication cyst in the cecum of a 7-year-old child: Case report

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman with morbid obesity (BMI 43), a 17-year history of insulin-treated type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia presented with a severe pulmonary infection. She had no flank pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, or gross haematuria, but she had a longstanding elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and recent microscopic haematuria on urinalysis. Urine culture was negative. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anaemia (hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL), mild leukocytosis (white-cell count 10.1×10^9/L), hyponatraemia (Na+ 130 mmol/L), and normal levels of CEA, CA19-9, CA125, and CA15-3.  

Renal ultrasonography revealed a large round hypoechoic solid-appearing mass in the lower pole of the right kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 10×8 cm heterogeneous soft-tissue mass in the lower pole with faint enhancement, adjacent fatty stranding, pararenal fascial thickening, and a bear’s paw sign due to calyceal dilation. There was no renal calculi.  

Chest CT demonstrated bilateral irregular nodules (<2 cm), a 3.5×2.5 cm cavitating lesion in the right upper lobe, a wedge-shaped consolidation in the right lower lobe, right pleural effusion, and right hilar adenopathy. On the basis of these findings, a complex cystic renal mass or renal malignancy with pulmonary metastases was suspected.
title: Focal Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis with Pulmonary Lesions on the Background of Type Two Diabetes Mellitus

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old obese man presented with sudden-onset, pressure-like chest pain and lightheadedness lasting one hour. This was his first episode of chest pain and was not exertional. He had a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation diagnosed one year earlier, but was not on anticoagulation because his CHA2DS2-VASc score was 0. He was a lifelong nonsmoker and had no notable family history. 

On admission, vital signs were stable. Physical examination showed an irregularly irregular rhythm with a borderline tachycardic rate and normal heart sounds without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. An electrocardiogram revealed coarse atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate and premature ventricular contractions. Chest radiography was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed mild thrombocytopenia, normal coagulation tests, mild hyperglycemia, and sequential troponin T levels of 0.02, 0.03, and 0.80 ng/ml (upper limit of normal, 0.10 ng/ml). ProBNP was 1104 pg/ml. Thyroid testing revealed an undetectable TSH, FT4 of 3.79 ng/dl, and FT3 of 6.9 pg/ml. Hemoglobin A1c was 5.6% and LDL cholesterol was 58 mg/dl.

Transthoracic echocardiography with contrast showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45–50%, apical wall akinesis, normal right ventricular function, mild biatrial dilation, mild-to-moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, and moderate pulmonary hypertension.

He was treated with aspirin, a statin, a beta blocker, and a heparin infusion. A left heart catheterization revealed a thrombotic occlusion of the distal left anterior descending artery without any evidence of obstructive epicardial atherosclerotic coronary disease.
title: Coronary Embolism despite CHA₂DS₂-VASc Score of Zero: Should We Reconsider Anticoagulation?

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma, hypertension, prior deep-vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism (with an IVC filter) received her second dose of ipilimumab and nivolumab shortly before presentation. She arrived at the emergency department with altered mental status, hypotension, and fever.

Two weeks earlier, she had undergone prophylactic right femur nailing with excision of a metastatic lesion and then developed fever, hypotension, and acute tubular necrosis; she completed a course of vancomycin, aztreonam, and metronidazole for presumed sepsis, with all cultures negative, and was discharged to rehabilitation. Four days after discharge, she returned with fever and hypotension.

On arrival, temperature was 98.4 °F, blood pressure 75/40 mm Hg, heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. She was ill‐appearing, in moderate respiratory distress, with altered mental status and bilateral lower‐extremity edema.

Laboratory studies before fluid resuscitation showed hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, WBC 13.9 K/µL, platelets 164 K/µL, sodium 133 mEq/L, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, chloride 110 mEq/L, bicarbonate 1 mEq/L, BUN 23 mg/dL, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL, AST 737 U/L, ALT 399 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 99 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, calcium 7.3 mg/dL, magnesium 1.5 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.5 mg/dL, procalcitonin 59.11 ng/mL, lactic acid 1.7 mmol/L, INR 1.46, and a venous blood gas with pH 7.24 and PCO2 24 mm Hg.

An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with occasional premature ventricular contractions. Chest radiograph showed no consolidation or effusion. CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast revealed perinephric stranding and cholestasis. CT of the head without contrast was unremarkable.

Urinalysis showed few white blood cells and red blood cells, no casts, a urine pH of 7.5, urine anion gap of 40 mEq/L, and a fractional excretion of sodium of 0.6%.
title: A Rare Presentation of Checkpoint Inhibitor Induced Distal RTA

case_prompt: An 18‐year‐old unmarried woman presented with intermittent low‐grade fever and a perineal swelling of two years’ duration that had slowly increased in size. She was a migrant from Azamgarh, Uttar Pradesh. On examination, she was afebrile with no lymphadenopathy. Local inspection revealed a 5 × 6 cm soft, polypoidal growth arising from the left labium minus with rugose overlying skin. A clinical diagnosis of fibrolipoma was made. Fine‐needle aspiration of the lesion yielded hypocellular smears with occasional lymphocytes in a proteinaceous background. The lesion was then excised. Grossly, it measured 5.2 × 3.4 × 2.2 cm, was polypoidal and firm, and on section was gray-white to gray-yellow. Microscopic examination showed a polypoidal lesion covered by acanthotic epidermis; the dermis and subcutis had dense collagenization with numerous dilated lymphatics. In the deep dermis there were a few noncaseating granulomas and foreign-body giant cells. A patchy infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils was present. Ziehl–Neelsen, Grocott's methenamine silver, and periodic acid–Schiff stains were negative for organisms, and examination of a buffy‐coat preparation showed no microfilariae.
title: Vulval Elephantiasis: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 26-day-old male neonate weighing 2.9 kg presented with a 4-day history of increasing abdominal distention. He was born at term without complications. On examination, he was alert and active, with marked abdominal distention and palpable masses in both upper quadrants. Laboratory studies, including clotting tests, renal function, and urinalysis, were within normal limits. Urinary vanilmandelic acid, homovanillic acid, and catecholamine levels were normal.  
Gray-scale ultrasonography of the abdomen showed bilateral suprarenal cystic masses containing internal echoes and debris, measuring 7.9 × 4.3 cm on the right and 4.4 × 4.6 cm on the left. Color and power Doppler imaging confirmed that the masses were avascular. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated well-defined bilateral suprarenal cystic lesions that were hypointense on T1-weighted images and markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted images.
journal: Indian Journal of Urology : IJU : Journal of the Urological Society of India
title: Nonsurgical management of bilateral adrenal abscess in newborn with therapeutic aspiration under ultrasonographic guidance

case_prompt: A 25-year-old African woman presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging gingival mass in the anterior mandible. She was in good general health with unremarkable extra-oral findings. Intraorally, there was a solitary, well-defined, roughly oval swelling arising from the attached and free labial gingiva overlying teeth 33 and 34. The lesion measured 2 × 2 cm, was firm, non-tender, had a smooth surface, intact mucosa of normal color, and there were no symptoms of pain, bleeding, discharge, or numbness. Oral hygiene was inadequate. A periapical radiograph demonstrated minor arc-shaped bone loss adjacent to teeth 33 and 34. Based on these clinical and radiographic findings, a diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made, with a differential that included peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and fibrous epulis; rare considerations were benign connective tissue tumors and peripheral odontogenic neoplasms. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia and submitted for histopathological examination.
title: Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor in a cloak of an epulis: report of a rare case

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old Caucasian man with relapsed follicular lymphoma (t(14;18)), previously treated with rituximab, lenalidomide, and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, was started 7 weeks earlier on rituximab and copanlisib. He presented with fever, shortness of breath, and a  generalized rash. On examination, there were scattered faint pink papules on his back, pink papules and atypical targetoid macules on his upper and lower extremities (including dorsal hands and palms), and significant cervical lymphadenopathy; there were no oral or mucosal lesions. Topical triamcinolone was initiated, and punch biopsies were obtained from the left arm and left leg. 

Low-power hematoxylin–eosin staining revealed nodular aggregates of cells within the dermis. Higher-power views showed non-necrotizing granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells. Within some giant cells, degenerated elastic fibers were seen. Verhoeff–Van Gieson staining confirmed elastolysis in the dermis and elastophagocytosis within the giant cells. Alcian blue staining was negative for mucin within the granulomas.
title: Rare presentation of the generalized papular variant of elastolytic giant cell granuloma associated with follicular lymphoma

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman was admitted with acute confusion, progressive muscle weakness, and worsening hypertension. She had a 2-year history of well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine, but over the past 3 months her blood pressure increased despite escalation to amlodipine 10 mg and addition of hydrochlorothiazide, then replacement with lisinopril because of lower extremity edema. One month prior, she presented with rapid-onset weakness and profound hypokalemia (<1.9 mEq/L), attributed to diuretic use; despite potassium supplementation, spironolactone, and losartan, her hypertension and hypokalemia (2.8 mEq/L) persisted. 

On admission, blood pressure was 161/103 mm Hg; weight 54.4 kg (baseline 57.2 kg), BMI 17.2 kg/m². Physical examination showed thin extremities, ecchymoses over arms and abdomen, focal superficial skin breakdown, and oral thrush. On further review, she had muscle wasting, facial and supraclavicular fullness, and disproportionate abdominal adiposity without skin hyperpigmentation. 

Laboratory studies revealed potassium 2.6 mEq/L, bicarbonate 35 mEq/L, creatinine 0.56 mg/dL; normal blood count; thyroid-stimulating hormone 1.7 µIU/mL, free thyroxine 1.2 ng/dL, total triiodothyronine 32 ng/dL. Primary hyperaldosteronism was excluded after plasma renin activity was 0.34 ng/mL/h and serum aldosterone was undetectable (<1 ng/dL). 

Computed tomography of the head and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain were unremarkable, with a normal-appearing pituitary gland. Chest CT showed a 2.9 × 2.3 × 3.8 cm mass in the right lower lobe with mild right hilar and subcarinal adenopathy; abdomen CT showed bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Endocrine studies revealed morning cortisol >50 µg/dL, ACTH 308 pg/mL, and 24-hour urine cortisol 8369 µg. Adrenal androgen testing showed DHEAS 48 µg/dL and total testosterone 11 ng/dL (both normal), whereas androstenedione was markedly elevated at 398 ng/dL (20–75 ng/dL). 

Fluorodeoxyglucose–PET scanning identified a 3.1-cm hypermetabolic right lower lobe lung mass with hypermetabolic right hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes and no evidence of distant metastases.
title: Elevated Serum Androstenedione Level in a Patient With Ectopic Adrenocorticotropic Hormone Syndrome

case_prompt:
A 25‐year‐old man presented with one day of high‐grade fever without localized symptoms. He had no significant medical history and denied alcohol, herbal, or illicit drug use. On examination, his temperature was 39.5°C, and he had non‐tender hepatomegaly (liver span, 14 cm) without jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly, or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Initial laboratory tests showed AST 303 U/L (normal 5–34), ALT 374 U/L (normal 0–55), and otherwise normal bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, complete blood count, and coagulation profile. A hepatitis panel was positive for hepatitis A IgM; all other viral, bacterial, and autoimmune markers (including hepatitis B, C, E, dengue, EBV, HIV, and ANA) were negative. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatomegaly without focal lesions or biliary abnormalities. He was diagnosed with acute hepatitis A. 

Over the next several days, he remained febrile (39–39.5°C) with worsening liver biochemistry: AST and ALT rose to more than twenty‐fold the upper limit of normal, total bilirubin increased, and the INR prolonged. Serial tests revealed mild thrombocytopenia, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, and markedly increased ferritin levels.
title: Acute hepatitis A infection‐associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in adult presenting as impending acute liver failure: A case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 36-year-old nonalcoholic woman with a 15-year smoking history presented with epigastric pain radiating to her back that was not relieved by NSAIDs. She also reported multiple episodes of nonbilious vomiting, nausea, and intermittent nonbloody diarrhea. On examination, a palpable mass was noted in the epigastric region. Laboratory studies were normal except for mild anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/dL). Abdominal ultrasound and noncontrast CT scan showed a unilocular cystic lesion measuring 8 cm in the tail of the pancreas, adherent to the spleen. She underwent distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy; three regional lymph nodes were removed. Grossly, there was an 8 cm cystic mass in the distal pancreas adherent to the spleen, with no other solid component. Microscopic examination of the cyst wall revealed nests of neoplastic histiocyte-like cells embedded in a fibrovascular stroma; the cells had clear to granular cytoplasm and uniform round to oval nuclei without mitoses or vascular invasion. Margins, lymph nodes, and spleen were free of tumor. Initial immunohistochemical stains showed tumor-cell positivity for CD56 and cyclin D1, weak positivity for neuron-specific enolase, and negativity for CK7, CK20, panCK, chromogranin A, synaptophysin, CD68, S100, vimentin, EMA, and SMA.
title: Diagnostic challenge of a cystic solid pseudopapillary tumor in pancreas: A case report

case_prompt: A 13-year-old boy presented with a 1-year history of right ankle pain and swelling. The pain was insidious in onset, dull, nonradiating, worse at night, and partially relieved by NSAIDs. The swelling was diffuse over the anteromedial aspect of the ankle and had progressively increased over 6 months. He denied trauma, fever, weight loss, or other joint involvement. On examination, there was a soft, ill-defined swelling anterior and inferior to the medial malleolus, with tenderness but no warmth or skin changes. Ankle dorsiflexion was limited to 20° and plantar flexion to 40°, both movements eliciting pain; subtalar inversion and eversion were full and painless. Anteroposterior radiographs were normal, but the lateral view showed a solitary, osteolytic, circular lesion in the neck of the talus with a homogeneous matrix, sclerotic rim, and narrow zone of transition, without periosteal reaction or soft-tissue abnormality. MRI T2-weighted images demonstrated a small hyperintense lesion in the dorsal talar neck surrounded by diffuse bone marrow edema.
title: Osteoid Osteoma of Talus – A Rare Occurrence Mimicking Ankle Arthritis: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man from Ghana presented with 7 days of altered mental status, weight loss, neck pain, cough, fever, nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. He reported greenish sputum with streaks of blood and an approximately 20-lb weight loss over the past month. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, diarrhea, or skin rash. His medical history was notable only for intermittent asthma and migraines. He smoked 10 cigarettes daily, drank alcohol occasionally, and denied illicit drug use except for marijuana. He last traveled to Ghana 6 months earlier. He was sexually active with multiple partners.

On examination, he appeared cachectic and lethargic but was oriented to person, place, and time. Vital signs: temperature 98°F, heart rate 102 bpm, blood pressure 108/69 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. His BMI was 19.2 kg/m2. He had no lymphadenopathy, clear bilateral breath sounds, and unremarkable cardiovascular and abdominal exams. Neurologic examination revealed neck stiffness.

Laboratory testing on admission revealed HIV infection with a CD4 count <20 cells/mm3 and a high viral load. A lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 23 cm H2O, CSF white blood cell count 2 cells/mm3, red blood cell count 57 cells/mm3, protein 102 mg/dL, glucose 25 mg/dL, and negative Gram stain and bacterial antigen tests. He was treated empirically for bacterial meningitis and started on quadruple antitubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide).

A chest radiograph demonstrated numerous small nodular opacities throughout both lungs, suggestive of a miliary pattern. A noncontrast chest CT scan confirmed diffuse micronodular infiltrates. Despite a negative quantiFERON-TB test, antitubercular therapy was continued. Over the next days, the patient had four negative sputum acid-fast bacilli smears and a negative M. tuberculosis PCR assay. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy was planned to obtain tissue for diagnosis.
title: Atypical Radiographic Presentation of Cryptococcus Pneumonia in a Newly Diagnosed HIV Patient

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old G4P3013 woman with a recent pregnancy of unknown location initially managed with two doses of methotrexate in April 2018 had a slow decline of β-hCG to normal levels. In June 2018 she was found to have a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation and underwent coil embolization. She was followed with weekly β-hCG levels until they were undetectable in July 2018, then was lost to follow-up.

In October 2018 she presented with right shoulder pain, abdominal pain, and shortness of breath. On examination she had abdominal tenderness with rebound. Her quantitative β-hCG level was 1011 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound showed free pelvic fluid, and liver enzymes were elevated (AST 193 U/L, ALT 270 U/L). Because of concern for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, she underwent emergent laparotomy. At surgery there was 650 cc of hemoperitoneum, but both fallopian tubes appeared normal; the bleeding source was a ruptured subcapsular hepatic hematoma without active bleeding at that time.

Postoperatively, CT of the abdomen revealed multiple foci of active contrast extravasation in both hepatic lobes, concerning for hepatic arteriovenous malformations. A head CT angiogram showed a left parietal subarachnoid hemorrhage, and cerebral angiography identified a left parietal micro–arteriovenous malformation. Daily β-hCG levels over the next several days were 1011 → 748 → 861 → 1185 mIU/mL.
title: Pulmonary arterial venous malformations as primary manifestation of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia

case_prompt: A 6-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of intensely pruritic pustular lesions on the trunk and extremities. One month earlier, he had been diagnosed with generalized pustular psoriasis and treated with oral corticosteroids and topical calcipotriol without improvement. He denied fever or constitutional symptoms. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and there was no family history of dermatologic or rheumatologic disease. On examination, there were multiple scaly pustular eruptions forming annular or serpiginous patterns distributed across the face, neck, trunk, and extremities; the palms, soles, and mucous membranes were spared. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, normal serum biochemistry, and normal serum protein electrophoresis.
title: Subcorneal pustular dermatosis as a cause of pityriasis amiantacea in a young child

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old retired civil servant was referred with an FNAC report of a benign salivary gland tumor. He had a one-year history of gradually progressive, bilateral submandibular swellings with no size change on feeding. Initially painless, he later developed a burning sensation in the head and neck. Concurrently, he noted progressive tongue enlargement that nearly filled his oral cavity and impaired speech. He denied purulent discharge, halitosis, dry mouth or eyes, eyelid swelling, weight loss, abdominal discomfort, or musculoskeletal symptoms.  

On examination, he appeared anxious, with an open-mouth posture and “hot potato” speech. The skin of the head and neck was thickened. He had massive, moist, pink macroglossia with a depapillated surface, obscuring the oropharynx. Bilateral submandibular glands measured 4×3 cm, were bosselated, firm to hard, and fixed to skin. There was no lacrimal gland swelling or slanting of the palpebral fissures.  

A provisional diagnosis of multiple myeloma with amyloidosis was made, with Mikulicz disease as a differential. Laboratory tests showed a PCV of 38%, WBC 6,400/cmm (neutrophils 42% [low], lymphocytes 46% [slightly high], monocytes 7%), and platelets 123,000/cmm. Electrolytes, urea, creatinine, and urinalysis were normal. HIV-1/2 testing was nonreactive. Neck ultrasound showed a normal thyroid gland and diffusely enlarged submandibular glands without stones, cysts, or lymphadenopathy.  

An open biopsy of the left submandibular gland provoked a torrential bleed, suggesting major arterial injury, but no discrete vessel was found; hemostasis was achieved with mass suturing. Approximately 250–500 mL of blood was lost. He was discharged after 48 hours with a clinical diagnosis of submandibular haemangioma. He rebled spontaneously on postoperative days 25 and 29. The submandibular swelling had become massive and was nearly compromising the airway, making further neck exploration hazardous.
title: Amyloid angiopathy of the floor of the mouth: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 44-year-old man presented with his first episode of a hemodynamically unstable sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) with a cycle length of 250 ms, which required two electrical cardioversions by emergency medical services. He reported sudden palpitations, fatigue, and mild dyspnea while cycling; no chest pain. His medical history was remarkable only for a self-inflicted thoracic gunshot wound at age 16, with emergency cardiac surgery documenting a bullet perforation of the pericardium and contact with the anterolateral left ventricular surface. He had recovered fully, with no ongoing medications or illicit drug use, and maintained regular exercise. On admission, he was asymptomatic in stable sinus rhythm. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed elevated troponin I (187 pg/mL; normal <14 pg/mL) with normal creatine kinase. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with flattened or inverted T waves in leads I, II, aVL, and V5–V6. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal biventricular function. Coronary angiography showed no coronary artery disease. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging identified a localized transmural myocardial scar with regional thinning in the mid–left ventricular free wall without any T2-weighted signal enhancement. Other differential diagnoses, including cardiac sarcoidosis, were considered but deemed unlikely based on the patient’s history and imaging findings.
title: Bullet-associated ventricular tachycardia: a case report

case_prompt: A 48-year-old man presents with a several–year history of a recurrent, pruritic right‐sided papular eruption. The lesions first developed after an injury during military service in Afghanistan and flare with stress, during which they appear vesicular, erythematous, painful, and intensely pruritic. Between flares, he has a baseline erythematous, mildly pruritic rash lasting 4–5 months post-flare. On examination, he has Fitzpatrick phototype II skin and erosive pink papules forming curvilinear plaques that strictly follow the lines of Blaschko on the right anterior shoulder, chest, abdomen, and posterior upper back. There is no mucosal, acral, or palmoplantar involvement. His medical history includes celiac disease, hemochromatosis (on regular phlebotomies), and degenerative disc disease. He takes medical cannabis, nortriptyline, and trazodone. He is a former smoker (10 pack‐year) and does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. There is no family history of similar rashes or autoimmune disease. He was previously diagnosed with refractory herpes zoster and treated with topical betamethasone valerate 0.1% without improvement.
title: Segmental Darier’s disease: A case report

case_prompt: A 34-year-old woman with no family history presented with one month of epigastric pain, dyspepsia, and postprandial abdominal distension. She had known uterine leiomyomatosis and denied estrogen–progestin use or abdominal trauma. On palpation, a mass was felt in the left upper quadrant. Abdominal ultrasound showed a bulky, solid mass with irregular margins that was homogeneously hypoechoic with anechoic areas of necrosis, located lateral to the tail of the pancreas and medial to the upper pole of the left kidney and the lower splenic pole. Laboratory tests revealed normal cancer markers (AFP 1.3 ng/mL, CEA <0.50 ng/mL, TPS 38.8 ng/mL, CA 19-9 <2 U/mL, CA 125 4.5 U/mL, CA 15-3 15.8 U/mL), a modest elevation of ALP (141 U/L), ALT (70 U/L), and LDH (614 U/L), and neutrophilic leukocytosis (12.36×10^3/mL) with a normal platelet count. A percutaneous ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy of the mass was interpreted as adenocarcinoma (stage II). The patient was admitted for surgical resection.
final_diagnosis_raw: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
title: Solid and papillary neoplasm of the pancreas (SPNP): a case report

case_prompt: A 54-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a painless, palpable lump in her right breast, noticed for one year. On examination, there was a soft, deep-seated mass measuring 4.5 × 4.0 cm in the upper inner quadrant, without skin changes, nipple discharge, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Her history included diabetes mellitus and nonobstructive coronary heart disease with a pacemaker. Mammography and ultrasound showed a well-marginated oval lesion measuring 4.1 × 2.9 × 2.7 cm at the same location, with an inhomogeneous isoechoic-hyperechoic signal, a small hypoechoic halo, and minimal peripheral vascularity (BI-RADS 4). A core-needle biopsy was performed. Histologically, the lesion consisted of short fascicles of bland fusiform cells in a patternless architecture around branching vascular spaces within a fibrous stroma with wispy collagen and scattered mast cells; the stroma contained mature adipose tissue without atypia or lipoblasts. No ductal epithelial component was observed. On immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells were negative for pancytokeratins (CKAE1/AE3, CK5/6, CK7, CK19), EMA, p63, SMA, desmin, and S100-P; they were strongly positive for vimentin, CD34, and nuclear STAT6.
title: Lipomatous (Fat-Forming) Solitary Fibrous Tumor of the Breast: A Case Report of an Uncommon Variant of a Rare Clinical Entity

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman (G3P3) was referred for evaluation of an abnormal lesion on the vulva. She first noticed a small wart-like lesion 10 months earlier that continued to grow and eventually resembled a small cauliflower. She denied pain but reported discomfort and occasional bleeding. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and hyperthyroidism, both controlled with medication. 

On gynecologic examination, there was a 2 cm lobulated, reddish mass on the upper part of the right labia majora, parallel to the clitoris, with ulceration at its distal end. Vaginal and cervical examinations were normal. 

During the office visit, a decision was made to perform a wide local excision under local anesthesia, and the entire lesion was removed and sent for histopathological examination.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Vulvar Lobular Capillary Hemangioma: A Rare Location for a Frequent Entity

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old man, non-smoker with no prior medical history, presented in May 2020 with 3 days of fever (up to 38°C), cough, and worsening shortness of breath. On examination he was febrile, working at a respiratory rate of 24 breaths/min, and had bilateral wheezing. He denied asthma, chronic sinusitis, nasal polyps, new drug use, vaping, occupational exposures, or second-hand smoke.  
Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (14.45×10^3/μL) with eosinophilia (1.8×10^3/μL; 12.5% of leukocytes), neutrophils 61.6%, lymphocytes 17.7%, monocytes 7.6%, basophils 0.6%. C-reactive protein was 1.53 mg/dL, procalcitonin negative, lactate dehydrogenase 384 U/L, interleukin-6 12.4 pg/mL, D-dimer 230 ng/mL. Arterial blood gas on 35% FiO2 showed pH 7.39, PaO2 59 mmHg, PaCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L (PaO2/FiO2 = 168).  
High-resolution chest CT demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities in the left upper lobe (lingular segment) and right lower lobe. Nasopharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 were negative on two occasions, and SARS-CoV-2 serology was negative. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) were negative. Over the next 24 hours his dyspnea worsened (respiratory rate 25 breaths/min), requiring high-flow oxygen at 60% FiO2. Inhaled formoterol/beclomethasone was initiated with partial improvement. Due to persistent respiratory failure and peripheral eosinophilia, flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed: 150 mL instilled, 70 mL of clear fluid recovered with no visible blood. BAL cell count showed 40% eosinophils; bacterial and viral studies were negative.
title: May 2020: Is It Always COVID-19 No Matter What?

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old previously healthy white man presented on June 22, 2020, with 3 days of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and more than ten episodes of vomiting, initially gastric contents then bilious, without blood. Four days before the abdominal symptoms began, he had tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by nasopharyngeal RT-PCR as part of surveillance screening; he had no respiratory symptoms. He denied smoking, alcohol, or drug use except occasional paracetamol. He had no history of similar attacks, trauma, or family history of pancreatitis.

On examination, blood pressure was 94/50 mmHg, pulse 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 27 breaths/min, temperature 37.5 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Abdominal examination revealed marked epigastric tenderness without distension; neurologic examination was normal. A repeat SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR on admission remained positive.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 17,700/mm3, neutrophils 13,140/mm3, lymphocytes 2,850/mm3, platelets 386,000/mm3; ALT 176 U/L, AST 158 U/L, total bilirubin 1 mg/dl; serum amylase 773 U/L, lipase 286 U/L; triglycerides 119 mg/dl; CRP 38 mg/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV serologies negative. Abdominal X-ray was unremarkable. Abdominal–pelvic ultrasound revealed mild diffuse enlargement of the pancreatic head with a normal gallbladder and biliary tract. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed mild diffuse enlargement of the pancreas.
title: Acute pancreatitis associated with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 infection: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
An 80-year-old woman presented with 2 weeks of worsening back pain, 5 days of dyspnea on exertion, and fever. Two days before admission, she had transient unconsciousness and a temperature of 40°C. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes; she was a passive smoker on oral antidiabetic therapy and had no prior autoimmune or hematologic disorders.

On examination, she was alert but dyspneic without chest pain. Temperature was 38.2°C; blood pressure, 106/72 mmHg; pulse, 110 bpm; oxygen saturation, 90% on room air. Findings included bilateral pulmonary crackles, a II/VI systolic apical murmur, jugular venous distension, jaundice, and petechiae and purpura on the toes. Neurologic exam was nonfocal.

Laboratory studies showed platelet count 13 × 10^3/μL, estimated glomerular filtration rate 22 mL/min/1.73 m^2, total bilirubin 7.3 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 812 IU/L, brain natriuretic peptide 1306 pg/mL, creatine kinase 411 IU/L, CK-MB 40 IU/L, and troponin I 19 966 pg/mL. Haptoglobin was undetectable; D-dimer was 33.9 μg/mL; coagulation studies were near normal.

Chest radiograph revealed bilateral congestion. ECG showed ST-segment depression in leads V5 and V6 with sinus tachycardia at 105 bpm. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50% with inferior-posterior wall hypokinesis. Chest CT demonstrated pulmonary congestion without focal infection. Brain CT and MRI showed no intracranial hemorrhage or infarction.
title: Evaluations of coronary microvascular dysfunction in a patient with thrombotic microangiopathy and cardiac troponin elevation: a case report

case_prompt:
An 11-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a midline frontal, non-tender scalp swelling that had recently grown rapidly. She also had recurrent headaches, giddiness, mild behavioral changes, epiphora, diplopia, and blurring of vision. Fundoscopic examination revealed bilateral papilledema; no focal neurologic deficits were detected.

Non-contrast CT of the head showed a 7.0 × 5.0 × 5.0 cm, densely calcified, mushroom-shaped, parasagittal hyperdense mass arising from the anterior falx. The non-calcified portion of the lesion enhanced markedly with intravenous contrast. There was destruction of both the inner and outer tables of the overlying calvarium with transcalvarial–subgaleal extension and extensive perilesional vasogenic white-matter edema.

On MRI, the mass was predominantly hypointense on T1-weighted images with internal hyperintense foci corresponding to calcifications and was heterogeneously isohyperintense on T2-weighted images. Diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC mapping showed no areas of restricted diffusion. Post-gadolinium T1-weighted images demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement. MR angiography revealed extensive neovascularity with splaying and posterolateral displacement of both anterior cerebral arteries. MR venography showed nonvisualization of the anterior one-third of the superior sagittal sinus, consistent with thrombosis or invasion. MR spectroscopy was noninformative due to the calcification and high vascularity. MRI of the spine and thoracoabdominal CT scans were negative for additional lesions.
journal: The Indian Journal of Radiology & Imaging
title: Case Report: Intracranial peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor – Ewing's sarcoma of dura with transcalvarial–subgaleal extension: An unusual radiological presentation

case_prompt:
A woman in her early 40s presented with lower abdominal pain and fever for several days. Her temperature was 37.6 °C, and she had tenderness in the right lower abdomen. Obstetric history was gravida 3, para 2 with two normal vaginal deliveries 13 and 11 years earlier; there was no history of gynecologic abnormalities, abdominal surgery, or trauma. Menstrual cycles were regular, and her last menstrual period was 2 weeks earlier. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 11 210/µL, a C-reactive protein level of 1.54 mg/dL, and normal serum levels of carcinoembryonic antigen, CA19-9, and CA125. 

Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a 132 × 120 × 155 mm cystic lesion with an 80 × 37 mm solid component on the ventral side of a retroflexed uterus; a 43 × 34 mm posterior subserosal leiomyoma was also noted. Magnetic resonance imaging showed that the cystic lesion had high signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images without fat suppression, suggesting bloody or protein-rich contents. A dorsal sediment was consistent with old clots. The cyst wall measured up to 5 mm and was isointense to normal myometrium. Diffusion-weighted images demonstrated some diffusion restriction within the cyst. The lesion appeared contiguous with the right ovary. An intramural leiomyoma was present on the dorsal cervix. No congenital uterine, renal, or urinary tract malformations were identified. 

Based on these imaging findings, an infected endometriotic cyst of the right ovary was initially diagnosed.
title: Uterine diverticulum mimicking endometriotic cyst of the ovary

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old woman with suboptimal oral hygiene underwent extraoral submental silicone-based genioplasty for retrognathia without perioperative complications. One month later she noted a small chin nodule. On examination she was afebrile with normal vital signs. The 4 × 5 mm dark red, hypertrophic nodule at the surgical site was asymptomatic, without pain or discharge, and there were no signs of active infection.

The initial differential diagnoses included suture granuloma, abscess, or a cutaneous fistula. The patient declined implant removal and elected observation. After three weeks with no improvement, she underwent operative drainage and fistulectomy with implant preservation; a swab was sent for culture (result negative), and the pocket was irrigated with antibiotic solution. Two weeks later, an identical lesion recurred. The patient then agreed to implant removal. Three weeks after explantation, another lesion appeared at the edge of the surgical incision.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Radicular cysts and Chin implants; An unexpected complication prompting explantation – Case report

case_prompt: A 61‐year‐old man was referred for sudden loss of vision in his left eye for 6 days. He had a 1‐year history of non–insulin‐dependent diabetes and was found to have a blood pressure of 180/100 mm Hg on presentation, prompting initiation of antihypertensive therapy. His visual acuity was counting fingers at close range in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg in the right eye and 16 mm Hg in the left eye, and gonioscopy showed open angles bilaterally. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable in both eyes, except for a dense nuclear and posterior subcapsular cataract in the right eye; the left eye was pseudophakic. Fundus examination of the right eye was limited by cataract but showed a cup:disc ratio of 0.8:1. Examination of the left eye revealed a cup:disc ratio of 0.8:1, dilated arterioles with arteriovenous crossing changes, cotton‐wool spots, and multilayered preretinal and subretinal haemorrhage around the optic disc and macula. Fluorescein angiography of the left eye demonstrated blocked retinal and choroidal fluorescence from the overlying haemorrhage and a discrete “light‐bulb” hyperfluorescent focus at the centre of the optic nerve head in the mid and late phases.
title: Optic nerve head retinal artery macroaneurysm: Report of a case

case_prompt: A 13-year-old boy presented with a painless, progressively enlarging mass in his left inguinal region, first noted 2 months earlier. His past history included spinal surgery 6 years previously, resulting in paraplegia and chronic decubitus ulcers on his left foot. On examination, the inguinal mass measured approximately 3.5 × 2.4 cm, was mobile over deeper structures and the overlying skin, nontender, and without erythema or warmth. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 119 mm/hr; results of a complete blood count, liver-function tests, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, and lactate dehydrogenase were all within age-appropriate reference ranges. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated enlarged lymph nodes inferior to the inguinal ligament (largest, 3.5 × 2.4 cm) with no other lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.
title: Challenging diagnosis: unusual presentation of Unicentric Castleman disease—a case report

case_prompt: A 13-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of intense anterior left knee pain, localized to the anterosuperior aspect. The pain was continuous (VAS score 3 at rest), increased to 7 during sports, and over the last month had worsened at night (VAS 8) without daytime exacerbation. Six months earlier she had been diagnosed with patellofemoral malalignment and completed a course of physical therapy without relief. She had no history of trauma, no fever, and no systemic symptoms. On examination, the Q-angle was normal, range of motion was full and painless, and there was focal tenderness at the superior patella at the quadriceps insertion. Patellar crepitus was absent and the patellar apprehension test was negative. Laboratory studies (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and basic biochemistry) were normal. A standard knee radiograph in two projections was interpreted as negative. Because her pain was predominantly nocturnal, she was given one aspirin nightly for 10 days, after which she reported significant pain reduction whenever she took the medication.
title: Patellar Osteoid Osteoma as a Cause of Anterior Knee Pain in Adolescents: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 5-year history of a slowly growing, painless, spherical nodule over the right temporal scalp. The 1.5 × 1 cm mass was subcutaneous, tethered to the skin but mobile over the skull, firm, noncompressible, nonpulsatile, without central punctum. There was no pain, secretion, redness, or regional lymphadenopathy. She had undergone regular screening for breast and colorectal malignancies, with no abnormalities detected. An excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia without complications, and the wound was closed primarily.

Histopathological examination showed hair-bearing skin with underlying lakes of mucin separated by delicate fibrous septae. Floating within these mucinous lakes were nests, clusters, and cords of predominantly uniform round to cuboidal epithelial cells with mild to moderate nuclear variability, focal duct formation, and occasional cribriform proliferation. There was no connection to the overlying epidermis or adnexal structures. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated strong positivity for cytokeratin 7, estrogen receptors, and progesterone receptors, with negativity for cytokeratin 20 and Her-2-neu. The morphologic and immunohistochemical features were consistent with mucinous adenocarcinoma. Because histopathological distinction between a primary eccrine mucinous adenocarcinoma and metastatic mucinous adenocarcinoma is almost impossible, a complete extracutaneous work-up—especially to exclude a breast primary—was recommended.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Primary mucinous adenocarcinoma of the scalp: A case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 55-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history notable for a malignant melanoma of the right thigh (1.05 mm thickness, Clark level IV, no ulceration, negative sentinel node) treated with wide excision. She had been asymptomatic until she developed new-onset back pain and generalized fatigue, followed shortly by painless gross hematuria. Urinalysis confirmed hematuria without infection. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple hepatic and splenic lesions, bilateral subcentimeter pulmonary nodules suspicious for metastatic disease, and several intraluminal bladder masses, the largest measuring 1.9 cm. On cystoscopy, three polypoid, spherical, stalked lesions were identified (two ~2 cm on the left anterior bladder dome; one ~1 cm on the left lateral wall), without any gross discoloration. The tumors were excised by monopolar loop electrocautery, and the bases were fulgurated.
title: Metastasis of Malignant Melanoma to Urinary Bladder: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A woman in her late 40s (parity 1) with a history of grade 1 endometrioid ovarian carcinoma (FIGO stage IC2), treated 4 years earlier with total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, peritoneal washings, and five cycles of carboplatin/paclitaxel (sixth omitted for toxicity), was referred for suspected recurrence. Her medical history also included asthma and obesity (BMI 37). Routine follow-up included appointments every four months for two years, then every six months. 

Three years after surgery she reported mild abdominal discomfort and intermittent lower back pain. CA 125 was 42 kU/L. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a complex pelvic mass measuring approximately 7 cm. Diagnostic laparoscopy with biopsy showed tissue “in keeping with an atypical endometrioma,” and she received 6 months of GnRH analogue therapy with serial imaging.

On reevaluation, a CT abdomen and pelvis now demonstrated a 12 cm pelvic mass with wall thickening “in keeping with malignant change.” MRI of the pelvis revealed a part-cystic, part-solid mass with restricted diffusion. PET-CT showed high FDG avidity in the mass. Imaging also described adhesions between the pelvic mass and bowel, without lymph node involvement or distant metastases. The right ureter was obstructed by the mass, producing hydronephrosis and marked right renal atrophy. A DMSA scan confirmed minimal right kidney function. 

An MDT recommended a two-stage surgical approach: exploratory laparoscopy to assess resectability with intent to achieve R0 resection, followed by radical exenterative surgery if feasible.
title: Radical total pelvic exenteration with concomitant right nephrectomy in the management of recurrent endometrioid ovarian adenocarcinoma: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old Chinese man presented with an 8-month history of progressively worsening back pain, which acutely intensified over the 5 days before admission, accompanied by bilateral lower-limb numbness and weakness. He denied trauma, urinary or bowel dysfunction, and had resorted to a walking stick for ambulation. On examination, he had an unsteady gait, pain on spinal movement, paravertebral tenderness from T5 to T10, decreased sensation in both lower limbs, and bilateral lower-limb paraparesis (grade 2/5). There was no saddle anesthesia, and anal tone was intact; upper-limb neurologic examination was normal.
Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and electrolytes. Thoracolumbar spine radiographs demonstrated slight loss of the T6 anterior vertebral height, sclerosis of the T5–T6 endplates, and mild disc-space narrowing at T5–T6 without fracture or spondylolisthesis. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the spine revealed a 1.6 × 1.0 × 1.2 cm enhancing lesion at the T9 level, predominantly intradural and extramedullary, causing compression of the thoracic cord with extensive cord edema from T1 to the conus, and suggestion of intramedullary invasion.
title: Hemangiopericytoma of the thoracic spine: a case report

case_prompt: An 18-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of low back pain and progressive weakness of both lower extremities, with new onset of bowel and bladder dysfunction over the past week. On examination, there was tenderness over the lower back, flaccid paraplegia (0/5 strength) of both lower limbs, and approximately 90% sensory loss to all modalities without sacral sparing. MRI of the spine showed an intramedullary lesion extending from T11 to L2 that was predominantly isointense on T1-weighted images, demonstrated homogeneous contrast enhancement, and contained interspersed cystic or necrotic areas. A differential diagnosis of intramedullary ependymoma (myxopapillary variant), paraganglioma, other glial neoplasms, metastases, or inflammatory pathology was considered. The patient underwent laminectomy and tumor decompression.
title: Primary spinal intramedullary primitive neuroectodermal tumor

case_prompt: A 49-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging, mildly tender lump in her left lower abdominal wall. She had no significant medical or gynecologic history and reported no weight loss. She had undergone a cesarean delivery 15 years earlier. Recent pelvic ultrasonography was normal. On examination, a firm, 5 cm mass was palpated in the left lower quadrant, approximately 3 cm below the umbilicus, with tenderness only on deep palpation. Routine laboratory tests, including tumor markers, were within normal limits. Abdominal CT and MRI showed a 6.7 × 4.9 × 3.5 cm mass within the left rectus abdominis muscle and no other intra-abdominal abnormalities. The mass was excised with clear margins; intraoperative inspection revealed both ovaries of normal size and no ascites or peritoneal lesions. Histologic examination demonstrated a high-grade carcinoma with strong cytokeratin 7 and CA-125 positivity and weaker estrogen receptor staining.
title: Primary solitary peritoneal tumor of the abdominal wall—report of a rare case and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old woman with no history of diabetes, tuberculosis, smoking, alcohol abuse, or leprosy presented 8 months after beginning intravesical BCG therapy for high-grade non-invasive papillary urothelial carcinoma. Bone scintigraphy showed increased uptake in the right clavicle, right knee, and left ankle. Radiographs of the right knee revealed narrowing of the medial tibiofemoral compartment and suprapatellar bursa opacification without calcifications or bone texture changes. MRI of the right knee confirmed joint effusion and synovitis. She reported dactylitis and intense, asymmetric pain in the affected joints. 

Concurrent symptoms included fever up to 38.2 °C and purulent urethral discharge. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 98.6 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 97 mm/h. Complete blood count, renal function, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Immunologic tests—including rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, complement levels, and immunoglobulins—were normal. Serologic tests for Chlamydia, Salmonella, HIV, and hepatitis B and C were negative, and the urethral discharge culture showed no growth. HLA typing revealed A24/AX, B44, B27, BW4/BW4, DQ7, and DQ5. A purified protein derivative skin test measured 18 mm.
title: Poncet’s disease after the intravesical instillation of Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG): a case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman presented with acute eruptions that had appeared 4 days earlier on her face and trunk and then spread to her extremities. She reported taking a single dose of bupropion for smoking cessation 1 day before the onset of the eruptions and noted a fever for the past 4 days. She had no personal or family history of psoriasis or prior drug allergies, and she denied use of any other prescription or over-the-counter medications, supplements, herbal remedies, or new topical products. 

On examination, numerous small pustules were present on erythematous skin over the face, trunk, and legs; the erythematous areas tended to coalesce and were not limited to hair follicles. There were no mucosal lesions, and examination of other organ systems was unremarkable. Her temperature was 38.2°C. 

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12.90 × 10^9 per L with 88.8% neutrophils, an elevated C-reactive protein level, and no eosinophilia. Liver enzymes, serum protein and albumin levels, and electrolytes were within normal limits.
title: An Uncommon Side Effect of Bupropion: A Case of Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulosis

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old man was referred for evaluation of mild swelling and intermittent pus drainage in the anterior lower jaw. Six years earlier, he had blunt trauma to his mandibular incisors (teeth 31 and 41) while playing soccer; both had received composite restorations and endodontic therapy elsewhere. Medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, the incisal edges of teeth 31 and 41 were restored with composite and showed dark discoloration. There was mild labial mucosal swelling and an inflamed gingival margin on tooth 41 with spontaneous purulence. A bony defect was palpable both lingually and vestibularly. Thermal sensitivity testing was negative on teeth 31 and 41 and normal on adjacent anterior teeth. There was no increased mobility, though teeth 31 and 41 were mildly tender to percussion.

Cone-beam CT revealed:
• Inadequate root-canal fillings—root perforation or untreated canal on tooth 41 and insufficient working length on tooth 31  
• Internal resorption in the lower third of the root of tooth 41 (0.9 mm diameter)  
• A continuous, ellipsoid, periapical radiolucent lesion (volume 2.67 cm^3; 16 mm height × 21 mm width × 8 mm depth) spanning teeth 32 to 42  
• Incidental retained mesiodens in the maxilla and impacted third molars

After consultation and patient consent, combined endodontic and surgical intervention was planned for tooth preservation.
title: Tunnel Fenestration of the Mandibula after Unsuccessful Post Traumatic Treatment: A Case Report of the One Year Follow-Up

case_prompt: A 47-year-old man with a 5-year history of untreated type 2 diabetes mellitus (hemoglobin A1c 13% on admission) presented with a 4-day history of fever and dyspnea. Two days before admission, he tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR. He denied known contact with COVID-19 cases. On admission, temperature was 38.3°C, heart rate 90/min, blood pressure 132/83 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min, and SpO2 93% on room air. Chest CT showed bilateral ground-glass opacities and patchy shadows consistent with COVID-19 pneumonia. On hospital day 2, his respiratory status worsened, and he was intubated and transferred to the ICU. From hospital days 6 to 8, he had remittent fevers of 37.5°C to 40.4°C. On day 9, the patient developed sustained fever of 40°C to 41°C unresponsive to acetaminophen, accompanied by marked disturbance of consciousness and hypotension with systolic pressures <70 mm Hg, consistent with warm shock. His PaO2/FiO2 ratio declined from 202 to 140 mm Hg. He received large-volume fluid resuscitation, vasopressors (norepinephrine, vasopressin, and epinephrine), hydrocortisone, and was started on venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) on the night of day 9. Laboratory testing revealed lactic acidosis, acute kidney injury, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hepatic dysfunction, and profound rhabdomyolysis (creatine kinase peaking at 255 870 U/L). After VA-ECMO initiation, his sustained fever rapidly abated and multiorgan failure began to improve.
title: Heatstroke‐like symptoms in a patient with coronavirus disease pneumonia

case_prompt:
A 21‐year‐old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 4‐month history of a pulsatile mass over the dorsal aspect of the right hallux. She reported that the lesion appeared after a moderate trauma and then rapidly increased in size, with intermittent pain. On examination, there was a mildly tender, firm, 3×3 cm pulsatile, angiomatous mass on the right hallux, with areas of hemorrhagic crusting and superficial venous dilatation. No lymphadenopathy was palpable. Routine laboratory tests were normal.  
Doppler ultrasonography showed a high‐flow vascular lesion with arteriovenous shunting. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well‐circumscribed, 3 cm vascular mass over the distal phalanx characterized by a tangled mesh of dilated arteries and veins connected by focal shunts and no discrete soft‐tissue mass signal. T2‐weighted gradient‐echo sequences demonstrated hyperintense fast‐flow vessel networks.
title: Cutaneous leiomyosarcoma mimicking arteriovenous malformation

case_prompt: A 33‐year‐old man with a history of heavy alcohol use presented with 24 hours of epigastric pain and progressive abdominal distention. He reported drinking 3 L of cane alcohol daily over the past week and had six prior hospitalizations for alcohol‐related acute pancreatitis in the past two years. He noted steatorrhea, worsening ascites, and a 10-kg weight loss over the past year. On examination, he was tender throughout the abdomen, had tense ascites, and was oliguric. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 16 g/dL, white blood cell count 11 × 10^9/L, platelets 262 × 10^9/L, INR 1.4, AST 42 IU/L, ALT 19 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 111 U/L, lipase 1270 U/L, amylase 442 U/L, triglycerides 140 mg/dL, creatinine 6 mg/dL, and albumin 2 g/dL. Hepatitis and HIV serologies were negative. Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed pancreatic necrosis with atrophy, no biliary tract abnormality, and free intraperitoneal fluid. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded 4.4 L of opaque black fluid. Ascitic fluid analysis showed 2–3 red cells/μL, 30 white cells/μL, total protein 3.3 g/dL, amylase 2769 U/L, and albumin 1.6 g/dL; the serum–ascites albumin gradient was 0.4. Fluid cytology was negative for malignant cells, tests for tuberculosis were negative, and bacterial and fungal cultures showed no growth.
title: Black ascitic fluid in a patient with history of alcohol abuse: report of an unusual case and literature review

case_prompt: A 50-year-old man presented with a more than one-year history of recurrent left lumbar pain. He had no significant medical, surgical, or family history. The pain was initially relieved by self-administration of paracetamol but later became more intense and prolonged, with diminishing relief from analgesics. On examination in primary care, vital signs were normal, and abdominal and flank examinations were unremarkable; a urine dipstick test was negative. Laboratory studies showed preserved renal function. Renal ultrasonography suggested a cystic lesion at the superior pole of the left kidney with exophytic extension. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined, lobulated, unilocular cystic mass measuring 110×50×30 mm in the left perirenal space, with bumpy contours and no enhancement after iodinated contrast, abutting the posterior-superior aspect of the left kidney but preserving the renal capsule. No additional lesions were identified in the contralateral kidney or intraperitoneal cavity.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Perirenal cystic lymphangioma mimicking a renal cyst in an elderly patient: Case report

case_prompt:
A 2-month-old African American female infant was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, with birth weight 2890 g and Apgar scores of 7 and 9. In the newborn nursery her exam was normal, no murmur was noted, and her pre- and postductal oxygen saturations were 100% on day two. She was discharged on day two with planned pediatric follow-up. At home the mother noted mild “darkness” of the hands and feet but was reassured this was acrocyanosis. Two routine pediatric visits noted no murmur or other abnormalities.

Three days before presentation, the infant developed cough, congestion, and rhinorrhea. At her scheduled 2-month well-child visit, her weight was 4.3 kg (10th percentile).
