The pediatrician noted visible acrocyanosis and documented an oxygen saturation of 80% on room air. She was referred to the emergency department.

In the ED she was hypoxic (oxygen saturations 20–30%) and hypothermic (32°C), with no murmurs on exam. Peripheral access was obtained, and she received a normal-saline bolus. A blood culture was drawn (which remained negative), and a dose of ceftriaxone was given. She underwent rapid-sequence intubation without complication. Despite increasing FiO₂ to 100%, her oxygen saturation peaked at 80%. Initial laboratory studies showed blood glucose 95 mg/dL, white blood cell count 7 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 22 g/dL, hematocrit 68%, and lactate 5.5 mmol/L. Chest radiography could not visualize the aortic knob or descending aorta clearly and could not rule out a right-sided aortic arch. Given the severity of her hypoxia and these findings, she was transferred to a tertiary pediatric center for further evaluation.
title: Delayed Presentation of Tetralogy of Fallot with Isolated Cyanosis

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of right upper eyelid swelling and temporal pain. Her ocular history included nasal pterygia and chronic dry eye. On examination, there was tenderness over the lacrimal gland and erythema on eversion of the right upper eyelid. An initial differential diagnosis included infectious or allergic periorbital edema. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal, and she was treated with oral azithromycin.

Three weeks later, her right periorbital edema had worsened despite antibiotics, and she had new-onset right lacrimal gland tenderness. Computed tomography of the orbits demonstrated right lacrimal gland inflammation and periorbital soft-tissue swelling. She was started on prednisone, 60 mg daily.

Two weeks after that, she had persistent symptoms and new-onset conjunctival injection of the right eye. The right conjunctiva blanched with topical phenylephrine. A diagnosis of dacryoadenitis and episcleritis was made, and she was prescribed clindamycin, 300 mg three times daily for 10 days, while continuing a prednisone taper.

Two months later, she returned with worsening periorbital edema and a sudden eruption of erythematous, smooth, indurated plaques on her right upper eyelid, right cheek, right chest, and right calf. A skin biopsy from one lesion showed a superficial and deep dermal perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with increased dermal mucin.

Over the following week, the rash rapidly progressed to involve the chest, back, and upper extremities and became tender and pruritic. Repeat skin biopsies of cheek and calf lesions revealed vacuolar interface alterations with superficial and deep perivascular and perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrates and increased reticular dermal mucin. 

Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, metabolic panel, urinalysis, antinuclear antibody, anti–double‐stranded DNA, extractable nuclear antigen panel, complement levels (C3, C4), creatine kinase, aldolase, and rheumatoid factor—were all within normal limits.
title: Periorbital swelling and episcleritis may be a sign of cutaneous lupus erythematosus

case_prompt:
A 37‐year‐old G3P3 woman was referred for evaluation of a subcutaneous mass in her lower abdominal wall. Her obstetrical history included three lower‐segment cesarean deliveries—two elective at term without complications and one emergent at 32 weeks for placenta previa hemorrhage with a healthy infant. Seven months after the last cesarean, she noted a slowly enlarging mass beneath the transverse scar, associated with mild pain and occasional brown leakage that coincided with her menses. 

On examination during menstruation, vital signs were normal. Palpation revealed a tender, oval, subcutaneous mass measuring approximately 80 × 35 mm directly beneath the cesarean scar. At the center of the mass was a 2‐mm diameter skin orifice. When the skin on either side of the orifice was compressed, thick brown fluid was expressed. 

A sonographic examination of the abdominal wall showed a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass with scattered echogenic spots and a few small arterial vessels surrounding it on Doppler imaging. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography of the anterior abdominal wall demonstrated a thin fistulous tract between the mass and the overlying skin, tracking through the subcutaneous tissue without involvement of deeper structures.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Cesarean Scar Endometriosis: An Uncommon Surgical Complication on the Rise? Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 9‐year‐old boy was referred for bilateral leukocoria. He was born at term, had no history of prematurity or oxygen supplementation, and had no family history of ocular disease; both parents’ ophthalmologic exams were normal. On exam, he could fix and follow with each eye but had reduced direct and consensual pupillary responses and nystagmus without a null point. Best‐corrected visual acuity was 1.3 logMAR in each eye. Horizontal corneal diameters measured 11.8 mm OD and 11.9 mm OS. The lenses were clear except for localized posterior capsular opacifications. Fundus examination showed bilateral fibrovascular stalks connecting the optic disc to the posterior lens capsule and dragging of retinal vessels. Under anesthesia, RetCam imaging confirmed fibrovascular stalks: in the right eye the stalk ran temporally from the optic disc to the posterior lens, causing opacification; in the left eye it ran inferotemporally, stretching the capsule peripherally. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated patent vessels along the stalks branching on the posterior lens capsule, fine capillary arborization with bridging fibrous material, inclusion and stretching of the macula within the folds, absence of a foveal avascular zone, patchy perivascular hyperfluorescence, ischemic areas in the vascularized retina, and peripheral nonperfusion without exudation. OCT showed diffuse internal limiting membrane hyperreflectivity, no foveal depression, and abrupt interruption of retinal layers with cone‐shaped fibrous tissue arising from the optic nerve head.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Familial exudative retinopathy TSPAN12 positive presenting as bilateral retinal stalks: late structural and functional findings

case_prompt:
A 72‐year‐old man with hypertension and reflux esophagitis presented with three years of progressive dysphagia. In June 2022, he developed respiratory distress in the left lateral decubitus position. Fiberscopic examination showed a pedunculated mass arising from the right aryepiglottic fold that swung pendulum‐like during phonation and breathing, nearly obscuring the glottis. Narrow‐band imaging revealed no mucosal abnormalities. Contrast‐enhanced CT demonstrated a 25×12×25 mm homogeneous, oval soft‐tissue mass bordering the right lamina propria with enhancement similar to pharyngeal mucosa. Contrast‐enhanced MRI showed uniform early enhancement. The preoperative differential diagnosis included cancer, lymphoma, soft‐tissue tumour, and amyloidosis. A tracheotomy was performed under local anaesthesia, and the mass was completely excised via direct laryngoscopy. 

Histologic examination revealed diffuse proliferation of plasma cells in the submucosal stroma with germinal centres. Immunohistochemistry showed CD138 positivity, IgG+, IgA–, IgM–, and focal CD20+ cells. In situ hybridization demonstrated kappa light‐chain restriction. DFS staining was negative for amyloid, and AE1/AE3 cytokeratin staining was negative. Flow cytometry of the tumour cells was CD19+, CD10–, and CD56–. Bone marrow biopsy showed no tumour infiltration. Serum levels of IgG, IgA, IgM, and the κ/λ ratio were within normal limits. Cytogenetic analysis of the lesion revealed a normal karyotype.
title: Primary lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma of the larynx mimicking extramedullary plasmacytoma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 25‐year‐old Indian man presented with three months of fatigue, night sweats, fevers, a nonproductive cough, and 30 lb weight loss, plus ten days of worsening low back pain radiating to the thighs. He immigrated from India 2½ years earlier, with no known TB exposures. On admission he was febrile (103.1 °F), tachycardic (160 bpm), normotensive, and had an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. Exam showed decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right middle and lower lung zones and mild digital clubbing; the remainder was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies revealed a mild normocytic anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, hyponatremia (127 mmol/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (201 IU/L), and hypoalbuminemia. Chest imaging showed a large right loculated pleural effusion, right upper‐lobe density with compressive atelectasis, multiple bilateral subcentimeter pulmonary nodules, and a 1.5 cm right hepatic lesion. MRI of the lumbar spine identified multiple poorly defined enhancing lesions in the vertebral bodies and posterior elements, concerning for metastatic disease. Testicular ultrasound demonstrated bilateral intratesticular masses suspicious for metastases; serum α-fetoprotein and β-hCG were within normal limits. 

Thoracentesis yielded a lymphocyte‐predominant exudative effusion with normal adenosine deaminase; cultures were negative for acid-fast bacilli. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy showed necrotizing granulomas, with negative stains for mycobacteria and fungi; culture remained negative at six weeks. Subsequent pleural biopsy also grew no mycobacteria but revealed focal granulomatous inflammation.
title: A case of disseminated tuberculosis mimicking metastatic cancer

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old man was referred for evaluation of recurrent kidney stones. He had his first episode at age 20 while drinking parsley infusions and continued to have multiple recurrences, particularly in the right kidney, despite extracorporeal lithotripsy and surgery. His father also had urolithiasis; there was no history of significant dairy intake or other medications.

On examination, his blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg; height, 196 cm; weight, 74 kg; BMI, 19.2 kg/m2. Urine dipstick was negative for protein, blood, and glucose. There were no extrarenal abnormalities.

Analysis of a right coral-shaped stone removed at age 30 showed Weddellite (50%), carbapatite (40%), anhydrous ammonium acid urate (5%), carbonated amorphous calcium phosphate (1%), and whewellite (1%). 

A 24-hour urine collection revealed calcium 5.52 mmol/24 h (normal 2.5–7.5 mmol/24 h), phosphate 24 mmol/24 h (7–32 mmol/24 h), and low-molecular-weight proteinuria of 3 g/24 h (normal <0.3 g/24 h). Serum studies showed calcium 2.77 mmol/L (2.25–2.60 mmol/L), creatinine 200 µmol/L, albumin 53 g/L, and estimated GFR 36.4 mL/min/1.73 m2. Parathyroid hormone was 19.1 pg/mL (26.5–96 pg/mL). Autoimmune tests, protein electrophoresis, and urine cultures were normal or negative.

Renal ultrasound demonstrated a small right kidney (9.0 cm), enlarged left kidney (11.5 cm), and medullary nephrocalcinosis without vesicoureteral reflux.
title: Decoding Hypercalcemia and Renal Stones in a Young Adult: Could it be Dent’s Disease?

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old man with no significant medical history was brought to the emergency department after a high-speed, rear-end motor vehicle collision with rapid deceleration and airbag deployment. He reported exposure to a white powder fume inside the closed cabin and shortly thereafter developed a cough productive of scant mucoid sputum. He denied dyspnea, fever, chest pain, or palpitations.

On examination, he was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. There were no cutaneous signs of trauma and no tenderness of the ribs or sternum. Auscultation revealed crackles over the left lower lung field.

Laboratory studies showed no significant electrolyte abnormalities. Chest radiography demonstrated an infiltrate in the left lower lobe and retocardiac region. Noncontrast chest CT revealed tree-in-bud opacities in the right middle lobe and left lingula, with ground-glass opacity in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe. Sputum Gram stain, sputum culture, and blood culture were noncontributory. A respiratory viral PCR panel, including influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and parainfluenza types 1–3, was negative.
title: Airbag Pneumonitis

case_prompt: A 22-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left cervical mass noted on routine examination. She reported no symptoms of chest pain, dyspnea, cough, fever, or weight loss. Her medical history was unremarkable. On physical examination, vital signs were normal. A soft, non-tender mass was palpable in the left supraclavicular area; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, electrolytes, and thyroid function tests, were within normal limits. Cervical ultrasound demonstrated a 2.4×3.8 cm hypoechoic lesion in the left supraclavicular region. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed two adjacent cystic lesions: one measuring 3.8×2.3×5.1 cm in the lower anterior neck and another measuring 2.7×2.2×1.8 cm in the anterior mediastinum abutting the left common carotid artery; both had smooth, mildly enhancing walls and a small calcification at the rim. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded inflammatory cells without malignant features or a specific diagnosis.
title: Ectopic pancreatic pseudocyst and cyst presenting as a cervical and mediastinal mass - case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A male child presented in infancy with joint pain and swelling of the wrists, knees, ankles, and feet and was diagnosed with rheumatoid factor–negative, CCP–negative polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. By age 4, while receiving methotrexate and adalimumab, examination revealed high-arched feet with minimal midfoot motion. Laboratory studies showed a CRP <1 mg/L and an ESR of 20 mm/h. Foot radiographs demonstrated bilateral erosive changes of the tarsal and navicular bones with marked cavovarus deformity. Over the next 6 years, he had ongoing foot stiffness and discomfort treated with steroid injections and a pulse of methylprednisolone; etanercept was added at age 11. Despite extensive navicular destruction, his distal phalanges and metatarsals remained intact, and serial inflammatory markers remained low (CRP 1–6 mg/L, ESR 2–6 mm/h), with only a transient rise during a viral illness. At age 12, tocilizumab was initiated for significant wrist pain and restriction, and imaging revealed destructive changes of the carpal bones and proximal metacarpals. Ophthalmologic evaluation identified corneal clouding and a unilateral cataract.
title: Monogenic disorders as mimics of juvenile idiopathic arthritis

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old journalist presented with a one-month history of sudden-onset left-sided tinnitus, hearing loss, and general dizziness without true vertigo. He had been treated empirically by an ENT physician with oral prednisolone, betahistine, magnesium, and flunarizine for presumed “acute idiopathic vestibulocochlear loss,” with no improvement in hearing but resolution of dizziness. He also noted a pressure sensation in the left ear. His only notable medication was aspirin 100 mg daily for borderline elevated hematocrit. Otoscopic examination was normal bilaterally. There was no spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus; the head impulse test was inconclusive. Head-shaking elicited a right-beating nystagmus. Pure-tone audiometry revealed a marked left-sided sensorineural hearing loss. Video head impulse testing showed complete loss of left semicircular canal function; dynamic visual acuity was highly pathological on the left. Cervical VEMPs were borderline on the left, and ocular VEMPs showed 100% left-sided loss. Caloric testing demonstrated a 77% left-sided weakness.  
An MRI of the petrous bones demonstrated normal anatomy but unenhanced T1 images showed high-intensity signal in the left cochlea and vestibule.
title: Partial Recovery of Audiological, Vestibular, and Radiological Findings following Spontaneous Intralabyrinthine Haemorrhage

case_prompt:
An 8-day-old full-term girl was referred for evaluation of fetal and neonatal bradycardia. Generalized jaundice was noted on day 1 of life. There was no fever, vomiting, diarrhea, respiratory distress, or change in urine color; stools were well pigmented. The infant was born via cesarean delivery for fetal bradycardia to an otherwise healthy mother with no history of infections, cholestasis, rheumatologic or autoimmune disease. Birth weight was 2700 g; Apgar scores were 8 and 9. The infant required positive-pressure ventilation and was intubated for a heart rate in the 60s; she remained on isoproterenol until transfer on day 8.

On examination, heart rate remained in the 60s, generalized icterus was present, and the liver edge was palpated 2 cm below the costal margin. Growth parameters were at the 25th percentile, with normal tone, no dysmorphism, and no rash. 

Laboratory studies showed transient thrombocytopenia that resolved, a chemistry panel within normal limits aside from liver tests demonstrating cholestasis: total protein 49 g/L (57–82), albumin 29.5 g/L (40.2–47.6), ALP 173 U/L (46–116), GGT 61 U/L (<73), ALT 44 U/L (10–49), AST 42 U/L (34–118), total bilirubin 331 µmol/L (5–21), direct bilirubin 245 µmol/L (0–5). The highest INR was 1.38, which corrected with vitamin K. 

Serologies for toxoplasma, HSV, CMV, syphilis, HIV, blood and urine cultures, thyroid function, and newborn screening were unremarkable. Ferritin was elevated at 2772 ng/mL (13–150) and triglycerides were 3.42 mmol/L (<1.7). Cardiac echocardiography and liver ultrasound were normal. Electrocardiography confirmed third-degree atrioventricular block.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
title: Neonatal Lupus presenting with neonatal hemochromatosis-like liver disease that responded to steroids: a case report

case_prompt: A 65-year-old Japanese man with a 17-year history of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) maintained on prednisolone and cyclophosphamide was evaluated after a new right lower lobe nodule was detected on chest imaging at age 64. His GPA had been diagnosed at age 47 on the basis of positive PR3-ANCA serology and biopsies showing necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in the nasal mucosa, lung, and kidney. At age 64, a chest radiograph confirmed a nodular shadow in the right lower field. He had a smoking history of 56 pack-years. Laboratory studies showed renal dysfunction, an elevated C-reactive protein level, and positive C-ANCA without an increase from prior levels. Prednisolone was increased because of suspected relapse, but the nodule did not change in size. Serum tumor markers rose: squamous cell carcinoma antigen from 3.2 to 6.2 ng/mL. On examination, breath sounds were decreased in the right middle and lower lung fields. Repeat chest radiography revealed an irregular opacity with lobar collapse in the right lower field. PET/CT showed FDG uptake in the right lower lung nodule, mediastinal lymph nodes, thoracic wall, right iliac bone, and right retroperitoneum. He was admitted for diagnostic bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration.
title: Lung cancer development in the patient with granulomatosis with polyangiitis during long term treatment with cyclophosphamide: first documented case

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man was referred to the sleep clinic for a 3-month history of snoring, witnessed apnea, poor sleep quality, and excessive daytime sleepiness. He also reported a 4-year history of occipital headache, present most of the day and worst on awakening, aggravated by Valsalva maneuvers and neck flexion, without photophobia, phonophobia, visual scotoma, nausea, vomiting, or Lhermitte’s sign. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or substance abuse and lived at 1189 m above sea level. 

On examination, his BMI was 29.4 kg/m2, neck circumference 40 cm, and he had a short neck. STOP-BANG score was 5 and Epworth Sleepiness Scale score was 15. Mallampati score and tonsil grade were both 2. Neurologic examination showed normal mental status, cranial nerves, fundoscopic exam, motor strength, plantar responses, and sensory, cerebellar, and gait testing. Deep tendon reflexes were increased, with a positive Hoffman sign and non-sustained clonus.

Overnight polysomnography (AASM 2015) showed a total sleep time of 440 min, sleep efficiency 95.7%, and apnea-hypopnea index of 82.4/h, with 423 central apneas, 26 obstructive apneas, 88 mixed apneas, 68 obstructive hypopneas, and no central or mixed hypopneas. Mean oxygen saturation during sleep was 89.1%, with a nadir of 73%.

He was diagnosed with central sleep apnea. Cardiac evaluation revealed a normal ejection fraction of 65%. Fasting blood glucose, thyroid function, and renal function tests were all normal. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.44, PCO2 34 mmHg, and HCO3– 23.1 mEq/L. According to his neurologic signs, brain and cervical MRI was performed.
title: Treatment emergent obstructive sleep apnea after Chiari surgery: A case report

case_prompt: A 39-year-old woman presented with dull upper abdominal pain and fever up to 38 °C lasting 5 days. Her history was significant only for Graves’ disease. On admission, blood pressure was 145/54 mmHg, heart rate 87 bpm, temperature 38.8 °C. The abdomen was soft with upper abdominal tenderness; no palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level of 5.9 mg/dL; all other hematologic and endocrine tests were normal. Plain abdominal CT revealed a 95×80 mm cyst in the left adrenal gland displacing the kidney caudally; the cyst interior was almost homogeneous with high water density. On MRI, the cyst contents were hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted images; a septum and a 52 mm solid component were noted within the cyst. Adrenal cyst was diagnosed, but primary malignancy could not be ruled out, so surgical resection was planned.
title: Giant adrenal pseudocyst removed using robot‐assisted surgery

case_prompt:
An 18-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of multiple firm, nonpitting indurations of her back and shoulders. At 12 months of age, she fell from bed and developed swelling of her face, neck, and shoulder with restricted movement; the swelling regressed with ibuprofen, leaving some residual stiffness. By 15 months, multiple painful hard swellings appeared on her upper back. Radiographs and bleeding studies at that time were reportedly normal. 

On examination, she was well-nourished (height 79.5 cm, 25–50th percentile; weight 11 kg, 50th percentile) but had sparse scalp hair, limited neck and trunk mobility, a clumsy gait, and multiple firm masses on the thoracic cage and back (older lesions were painless, newer ones painful). She had marked bilateral shortening and sharpening of the proximal phalanges of both great toes with hallux valgus deformities present since birth; there was no family history of similar findings. No bruising, cutaneous discoloration, or evidence of bleeding diathesis was noted.

Laboratory studies showed microcytic, hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL), normal serum calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase, and normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Bleeding and clotting times, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time were all within normal limits. 

A skeletal survey at 15 months confirmed bilateral hallux valgus (hallux valgus angle 65°, intermetatarsal angle 20°), small deformed middle phalanges of the little fingers, and clinodactyly, without evidence of soft-tissue or skeletal calcification. Ultrasonography of the neck and upper chest demonstrated marked thickening of soft tissues and muscle swelling without discrete masses. Initial contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and upper chest mirrored the sonographic findings, showing soft-tissue thickening but no calcifications.
title: Sporadic Fibrodysplasia Ossificans Progressiva in an Egyptian Infant with c.617G > A Mutation in ACVR1 Gene: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 71-year-old woman was admitted with sudden faintness and bilateral leg weakness. Her history included hypertension, osteoporosis, and coronary heart disease treated in 2011 with a DES in the LAD. On admission, troponin I was 189 ng/l (normal <45), rising to 7510 ng/l on hospital day 2, consistent with a NSTEMI treated by PTCA and placement of a DES in the right coronary artery. Dual antiplatelet therapy was started. Initial labs also showed serum calcium 3.35 mmol/l (normal 2.15–2.55), phosphate 0.36 mmol/l (0.81–1.62), vitamin D 47 nmol/l (50–250), and PTH 1156 ng/l (18.4–72). She reported polydipsia, polyuria, and mild dysphagia but denied nephrolithiasis, bone pain, or dyspepsia. Examination revealed a firm, nonmobile right-sided neck node. Neck ultrasound identified a 5 cm right thyroidal mass classified as TIRADS 5. Fine-needle aspiration showed a monomorphic, partially follicular cell population with focal weak PTH immunopositivity. CT and MRI demonstrated a 5 cm tumor at the right caudal thyroid pole compressing the trachea by ~50% without clear extrathyroidal invasion. A 99mTc-sestamibi scan was halted early for pain, but early images revealed nodal uptake at the right tracheal side, suggesting a parathyroid origin. Cinacalcet was started, lowering calcium to near normal over 8 weeks while PTH remained elevated.
title: Coronary Heart Disease and an Incidental Parathyroid Carcinoma

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old Pakistani sailor presented with a 1-year history of generalized, vague abdominal pain that was insidious in onset and aggravated by squatting. One month after the onset of pain he noted bilateral dependent pedal edema. He had occasional nausea but no vomiting, changes in bowel habits, fever, or weight loss. 
Earlier evaluation at another hospital revealed a palpable epigastric–umbilical mass. An abdominal CT scan showed a fat-density mass in the retroperitoneum, and a presumptive diagnosis of liposarcoma was made. At laparotomy, there was a vaguely defined thickening in the small-bowel mesentery; complete excision was limited by its proximity to the gut loops. The peritoneal cavity and bowel loops appeared otherwise unremarkable, and no lymphadenopathy was seen. Histologic examination of the excised tissue showed benign adipose tissue with nonspecific inflammatory infiltrates, without distortion of the tissue architecture or vascular invasion. Recovery was unremarkable.
Nine months after the laparotomy, his abdominal pain and pedal edema persisted, his weight was stable, and he denied constitutional symptoms. On examination there was a healed midline laparotomy scar, generalized moderate abdominal tenderness, a firm ill-defined epigastric–umbilical mass, and bilateral pitting pedal edema. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, peripheral blood film, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, amylase, lipase, liver-function tests, and autoimmune markers, were all normal. Review of the preoperative CT scan demonstrated diffuse stranding and thickening of the mesentery, a soft-tissue density encircling the mesenteric vessels, a “misty mesentery,” and whorling/stranding of the mesentery. There was no bowel obstruction, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly.
title: Mesenteric panniculitis with pedal edema in a 33-year-old Pakistani man: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 22‐year‐old woman presented with pain in her right shoulder. Radiographs of the proximal humerus showed a poorly defined, irregular osteolytic lesion. MRI demonstrated low signal intensity on T1‐weighted images and heterogeneous low- to high-signal intensity on T2‐weighted images. An open biopsy established the diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma. Routine laboratory studies were unremarkable except for a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level of 0.83 mg/mL; serum albumin remained normal, and her weight was maintained during treatment. She underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy with vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide, followed by surgical resection and joint replacement. Total cumulative doses included doxorubicin 375 mg/m², cyclophosphamide 10 800 mg/m², vincristine 1.8 mg/body, ifosfamide 72 000 mg/m², and etoposide 4000 mg/m². At the completion of chemotherapy, a routine chest CT revealed a new 5-mm solitary nodule in the right upper lobe, which had not been present on initial staging CT. A follow-up CT six weeks later showed persistence of the solitary nodule. Given the high metastatic potential of Ewing sarcoma, surgical resection of the lung lesion was undertaken.
title: Pulmonary cryptococcosis mimicking a metastasis in a patient with Ewing sarcoma

case_prompt:
A 12-year-old girl presented with a one-month history of eczematous changes of the left areola and bloody nipple discharge. Topical treatment had not improved her symptoms. She had no prior breast trauma, no significant medical history, and no family history of breast cancer. On examination, the left areola showed eczematous changes with adherent blood clots. A firm, movable, non-tender mass was palpated beneath the left nipple, and gentle compression revealed bloody discharge from a single duct orifice. There was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. 

Breast ultrasound with a 15-MHz linear transducer showed a 3.6 cm, oval, circumscribed mass in the left subareolar region that was mostly solid, with heterogeneous internal echoes (hyperechoic and hypoechoic areas) and small anechoic foci at the periphery. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated mildly increased internal vascularity. Shear wave elastography revealed intermediate elasticity. No dilated ductal structures were identified around the lesion. The right breast had normal fibro-glandular tissue without focal lesions. Based on these findings, the lesion was assigned BI-RADS category 4a.
title: Bloody nipple discharge caused by an intraductal papilloma of the breast in an adolescent girl: A case report

case_prompt: An 81-year-old Japanese woman presented with chest pain at rest for one month. She had a history of papillary thyroid carcinoma treated surgically 30 years earlier and was followed for psychiatric problems and hypothyroidism. On admission, blood pressure was 125/81 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Physical examination revealed no heart murmurs, jugular venous distention, or pedal edema. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with an incomplete right bundle branch block. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a heterogeneous, irregular mass–like lesion measuring approximately 45×40 mm on the right ventricular free wall, contacting the tricuspid valve in diastole, with a small pericardial effusion. Transesophageal echocardiography showed part of the mass was mobile. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a 51 mm lobular mass involving the right ventricle and pericardium with heterogeneous enhancement. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed the mass to be isointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images. 18-Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography demonstrated increased uptake in the anterior lower wall of the right ventricle without evidence of metastasis. Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries and an arterial branch supplying the mass.
title: Cardiac angiosarcoma in the right ventricle treated by surgical resection

case_prompt:
A woman in her 20s was referred for vision loss in her right eye. Her medical history was notable for stage IV T-cell lymphoma in infancy treated with chemotherapy and bone marrow transplantation; subsequent cerebral cavernous haemangioma; primary ovarian insufficiency; type 1 diabetes with growth hormone deficiency; gout; hypertension; fatty liver disease; diabetic retinopathy; and an autonomously functioning thyroid nodule. She had no significant family history.

On examination, corrected visual acuity was 20/600 in the right eye and 20/22 in the left eye. Funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed vitreous hemorrhage from proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and the left eye showed severe diabetic retinopathy with a yellowish-white, elevated lesion measuring approximately two optic disc diameters in the temporal periphery. The right eye underwent vitrectomy with cataract extraction, and panretinal photocoagulation was performed in both eyes.

One year later, visual acuity in the left eye declined to 20/600 due to macular hemorrhage, and the temporal lesion had enlarged. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated a 3.5–4.0 mm ciliary body mass. Given concern for malignancy, total excision of the ciliary tumour combined with vitrectomy, silicone oil tamponade, and cataract extraction was planned in the left eye.
title: Granular cell tumour in the ciliary body

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old man presented to the emergency department with dyspnea at rest and right loin pain eight weeks after augmentation of an ileal neobladder. His past medical history included polycystic kidney disease, and he was receiving oral antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection. He had undergone radical cystoprostatectomy and Studer pouch reconstruction one year earlier and neobladder augmentation cystoplasty three months before presentation.

On examination, he appeared cachectic with dry mucous membranes. His respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute, heart rate 108 beats per minute, and blood pressure 92/64 mmHg. Cardiorespiratory and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable, and his surgical incision was well healed.

Initial blood tests showed a leukocyte count of 14.1 × 10^3/μL and a C-reactive protein of 23.3 mg/dL. Biochemistry revealed a potassium of 3.3 mmol/L, creatinine of 304 μmol/L (baseline 98 μmol/L), and urea of 33.1 mmol/L; all other electrolytes were within normal limits. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated an uncompensated metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap of 12.1 mEq/L. Urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria and sterile pyuria. The ECG revealed sinus tachycardia and the chest radiograph was normal.

The patient was admitted with a presumed diagnosis of severe urosepsis and acute kidney injury and was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, urinary catheterization, and crystalloid resuscitation. Over the next 48 hours, he became increasingly confused and dyspneic. A repeat arterial blood gas showed a worsening hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: An unrecognised case of metabolic acidosis following neobladder augmentation cystoplasty

case_prompt: A 19-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of non-projectile, greenish vomiting (2–3 times daily) and periumbilical pain. He also reported long-standing (since age 6) intermittent constipation, generalized weakness, and significant weight loss, with partial relief on a liquid diet. He denied abdominal distension or fever. On examination, he appeared undernourished, mildly dehydrated, blood pressure was 102/55 mmHg, pulse 98 bpm, respirations 17 bpm, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and BMI 16 kg/m^2. Abdominal exam showed a scaphoid abdomen, positive succussion splash, periumbilical tenderness, normal bowel sounds, and no organomegaly. Laboratory studies revealed normal white blood cell count, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, sodium 122.4 mmol/L, potassium 2.57 mmol/L, and normal renal and liver function. An abdominal ultrasound was normal. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed normal mucosa and 2 L of bilious fluid in the stomach but no intrinsic obstruction. Abdominal CT showed severe dilation of the duodenum with a transition point at the superior mesenteric artery and twisting of the mesentery around the artery, producing a “whirlpool sign.”
title: Late presentation of midgut malrotation in a young adult

case_prompt: A 34-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of white nipple discharge from her left breast. On examination, there was a 3-cm palpable mass in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast, approximately 4 cm from the nipple. Bilateral breast ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 16.5×7.5 mm lobulated fluid collection in the left breast at 5 o’clock, 2 cm from the nipple, and a 23.5×10 mm heterogeneous, inflamed parenchymal area without clear borders at 4 cm from the nipple. An atypical left axillary lymph node measuring 28.5×14.5 mm, with cortical thickening of 7.5 mm and a preserved fatty hilum, was also identified. The radiological evaluation was considered compatible with an abscess. Cytological evaluation of the nipple discharge and abscess drainage was performed, and tetracycline was administered; the patient’s symptoms regressed, and cytology was consistent with an abscess. During follow-up, the discharge became bloody, the breast mass enlarged, and overlying skin changes suggested invasion. A core-needle biopsy of the lesion was then planned.
title: Primary Mucinous Cystadenocarcinoma of the Breast: Clinicopathological Analysis of a Case and Difficulties Encountered in a Biopsy

case_prompt: A 54-year-old woman with a 15-pack-year smoking history presented with 7 months of NYHA class III exertional dyspnea without cough, wheezing, chest tightness, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or peripheral edema. She had no rashes, arthralgias, myalgias, travel, or exposure history. Oxygen saturation was 91% on 3 L/min oxygen; blood pressure 115/76 mm Hg; heart rate 82 beats/min. Pulmonary examination revealed normal breath sounds without wheezes, crackles, or pleural rubs. Cardiac examination showed normal S1 and S2 and an early-peaking grade II/VI crescendo–decrescendo murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids. No stigmata of chronic liver disease were present. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction > 60% and mild to moderate subaortic stenosis without other valvular abnormalities or shunts on color Doppler. Transesophageal echocardiography with agitated saline injection revealed more than 20 bubbles in the left atrium after the fourth cardiac cycle, consistent with an extracardiac right-to-left shunt. Computed tomography of the chest showed no interstitial lung disease or large pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.
title: The Role of TEE in Diagnosing Hepatopulmonary Syndrome and Cryptogenic Cirrhosis

case_prompt:
A 25‐year‐old man presented with a 1‐year history of right‐eye blurred vision, headache, and a 30‐kg weight loss. On examination, his body‐mass index was 28 kg/m2, and perimetry revealed visual‐field defects in the right eye. Initial magnetic resonance imaging showed a lightly spotted heterogeneous suprasellar mass measuring 19×16×19 mm, abutting but not invading the pituitary gland. Endocrine studies demonstrated secondary hypogonadism (low follicle‐stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, and testosterone) with intact thyrotroph and lactotroph axes. An ACTH stimulation test yielded a subnormal cortisol response (30‐min cortisol, 248 nmol/L; reference, > 420 nmol/L) with low plasma ACTH, consistent with secondary adrenal insufficiency; hydrocortisone therapy was initiated. The somatotroph axis was not evaluated.  
The mass was presumed to be a craniopharyngioma, and the patient underwent craniotomy. Intraoperatively, the lesion appeared gray‐reddish, capsulated, fragile, and prone to bleeding—features atypical for craniopharyngioma. The tumor was partially resected, leaving a small capsule remnant beneath the optic chiasm. Perioperative frozen‐section histology described lymphocytic infiltration, raising suspicion for malignant lymphoma.  
After surgery, the patient continued to have headaches and visual deficits. Repeat MRI showed regression of the mass to 9×6×8 mm, with residual tissue below the optic chiasm. He was found to have pan–anterior‐pituitary hormone deficiencies and central diabetes insipidus and was started on hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, testosterone, growth hormone, and desmopressin. Endocrine evaluation did not support a hormone‐producing adenoma. Workup for immunodeficiency, infectious and rheumatologic diseases, and drug‐induced pituitary infiltration was unremarkable.
title: Recurrent autoimmune hypophysitis treated with rituximab: a case report

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to obstructive nephropathy presented with 2 months of swelling of the left side of his neck, face, and left upper limb. He denied recent trauma, fever, or chills. His medications included amlodipine, pantoprazole, carvedilol, calcium carbonate, and calcitriol. He had been on hemodialysis for 1½ years via a left internal jugular catheter. After failure of a left radiocephalic arteriovenous fistula, a left brachiocephalic fistula was created, after which he developed severe venous hypertension of the left arm.

He denied chest pain, night sweats, or weight loss. On examination, he was afebrile with a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg. There was diffuse edema over the left face, neck, chest, and left upper limb. The arteriovenous fistula showed no signs of infection. There was no thyroid enlargement or lymphadenopathy. Jugular veins were not distended, cardiac auscultation was normal, and lung fields were clear.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, white-cell count 8400 cells/mm3, normal liver function tests, and normal bleeding and clotting times. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, T3, and T4 levels were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph demonstrated increased density and soft-tissue swelling over the left neck, chest, and arm, with a massive left-sided pleural effusion. Doppler ultrasonography of the neck revealed decreased flow in the left subclavian vein. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal biventricular function with an ejection fraction of 62%. Computed tomography of the thorax confirmed a large left pleural effusion without evidence of malignancy or lymphadenopathy. A conventional angiogram revealed total occlusion of the left innominate vein. Percutaneous angioplasty of the left innominate vein was performed, after which his facial and upper-limb swelling markedly improved.
title: A Case of Chylothorax in a Hemodialysis Patient with Left Innominate Venous Stenosis

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man was referred for brain MRI after experiencing multiple generalized seizures over the past five years. He was the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents, born at term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery with normal birth weight and no neonatal issues. Early development was unremarkable, with no delays in feeding or milestones. 

Physical examination revealed hypertelorism. High-resolution karyotyping and a screening cardiac ultrasound were normal. At age 20, he developed erratic sleep patterns, constipation, irritability, and increasingly frequent seizure episodes. Routine biochemical and hematological tests, including electrolytes and liver function, were all within normal limits.

Brain MRI demonstrated:
• Nonfusion of the bilateral thalami with an interthalamic adhesion  
• Marked dilation of the lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle  
• Partial fusion of the frontal and occipital horns of the lateral ventricles, with gross hydrocephalus  
• Absence of the cavum septum pellucidum and wide communication between the lateral ventricles and the third ventricle  
• A subependymal nodule  
• Thinning of the corpus callosum (genu and body) with nonvisualization of the splenium  
• Inferior displacement of the cerebellum without tonsillar herniation  
• A bone defect in the right posterior parietal bone with herniation of cerebrospinal fluid and meninges into the extracalvarial region  
• Hypoplastic optic chiasm  
• Preservation of the falx, pituitary fossa, infundibulum, brainstem, and basal cisterns
title: Lobar holoprosencephaly with associated meningocele: A rare case report of a 25-year-old patient with multiple seizures

case_prompt: A 16-year-old female with autism spectrum disorder presented with 4 days of inability to pass stool or flatus and episodic screaming abdominal pain. Parents reported multiple episodes of bilious vomiting over the preceding day. There was no fever or reported abdominal distension. On examination, she was alert, hemodynamically stable, and afebrile. Her abdomen was non-distended, tender in the umbilical region, with present bowel sounds. Rectal examination revealed a collapsed rectum with stool staining the examining finger. Laboratory tests including complete blood count, renal and liver function, and C-reactive protein were all within normal limits. Supine and erect abdominal x-rays showed dilated small-bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels and a well-defined oval, peripherally radio-opaque lesion with central lucency in the pelvis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an oval, well-defined soft-tissue density structure with a hyperdense rim measuring about 4.4 × 3.4 × 3.3 cm in the proximal ileum at the transition point, with proximal jejunal dilatation and air-fluid levels.
title: Acute intestinal obstruction secondary to ingested foreign body in an adult with autism spectrum disorder: A rare case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A woman in her 50s presented with a 1-week history of worsening right-sided abdominal pain.  
Her medical history included chronic back pain managed with methadone and hepatitis C treated 9 years earlier; she had no known vascular disease. She reported longstanding abdominal discomfort, bloating, and frequent flatulence and was taking lactulose 50 mL once daily for constipation related to methadone use. She was an ex-smoker and former IV drug user.  
On examination, she appeared in some distress, vital signs were normal, and abdominal examination revealed localized peritonism in the right abdomen.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6.2 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 2.8 × 10^9/L, and a C-reactive protein level of 6 mg/L.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple subserosal and submucosal gas locules in the caecum and ascending colon and a small volume of free intraperitoneal air; there was no free fluid, no evidence of ischaemia, and no diverticulosis.
title: Pneumatosis coli secondary to lactulose use masquerading as an acute abdomen

case_prompt: A 45-year-old woman, gravida 2 with two prior cesarean deliveries, presented with a 1-year history of lower abdominal heaviness, abnormal uterine bleeding, and severe dysmenorrhea. On speculum examination, only a small portion of the anterior cervical lip was visible and appeared normal. Bimanual examination revealed a bulging, tense, cystic lesion arising from the posterior cervical lip, extending supravaginally to fill the posterior fornix; the mass felt like bulging membranes at full cervical dilation but had a tense cystic rather than fibroid consistency. Transvaginal ultrasonography suggested a right ovarian cyst. Because of the discrepancy between imaging and clinical findings, magnetic resonance imaging was performed, which demonstrated a 15 cm × 10 cm cystic lesion arising from the cervix. Cancer antigen-125 levels were within normal limits. Cervical cytology was negative for malignancy, and endometrial sampling showed proliferative-phase endometrium.
title: Giant Nabothian Cyst Mimicking a Huge Cervical Fibroid: Challenging Aspects in Laparoscopic Hysterectomy

case_prompt: A 37-year-old man presented with swelling in the lower anterior jaw for one year. He had undergone excision of a previous lesion in the same area. He denied pain or trauma. On extraoral examination there was no facial asymmetry. Both right and left submandibular lymph nodes were palpable, approximately 1.5 × 2 cm, soft to firm, mobile, and non-tender. Intraorally, there was an oval growth on the gingiva buccally and lingually from the lower right canine to first molar, measuring 4 × 2 cm, pinkish white, with diffuse margins, a smooth surface, soft to firm consistency, non-tender, and not fixed. The clinical differential diagnosis included pyogenic granuloma and malignancy of the lingual alveolar mucosa in the 41–46 region. An orthopantomogram showed an ill-defined radiolucent lesion extending from the lower right canine to the distal of the first molar. CT of the mandible demonstrated an ill-defined, intensely enhancing mass lesion in the right buccal mucosa near the alveolar ridge and adjacent to the tongue, measuring 4.5 × 2.2 cm, with bilateral submandibular lymphadenopathy (largest 1 × 0.6 cm). Ultrasound of the neck was unremarkable. A biopsy was performed.
journal: Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology : JOMFP
title: Malignant fibrous histiocytoma of the mandible: A rare case report with diagnostic challenge and treatment approach

case_prompt: A 33-year-old man with a 5-year history of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis treated with steroids and immunosuppressants (later discontinued) was admitted for severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) associated with fatigue and dyspnea on minimal exertion. His baseline renal function had slowly declined over the past year (creatinine 2.5 mg/dL; proteinuria ~1.8 g/24 h). On admission, laboratory studies showed: hematocrit 18%, reticulocytes 4.25%, white cells 6.1×10^3/µL; haptoglobin <7.5 mg/dL, LDH 300 U/L, normal bilirubin; negative direct and indirect Coombs tests; normal G6PD activity. Autoimmune tests were unremarkable except for C3 72 mg/dL (normal C4 24 mg/dL); anticardiolipin IgG and IgM were 0; ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, P-ANCA, and C-ANCA were negative. Infectious serologies and cultures were negative. He received red-cell transfusion with transient improvement in hemoglobin. On hospital day 3, he developed new cough and radiography showed bilateral bronchopneumonic opacities in the middle lobes. On day 4 he had hemoptysis with bright-red blood. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral multilobar ground-glass opacities with intralobular and intra-acinar involvement and septal thickening, sparing subpleural zones. Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide was elevated at 157% of predicted with reduced alveolar volume.
title: A Case of Rare Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 16‐year‐old Hispanic male was booked into a juvenile detention facility reporting 4 days of persistent intractable epigastric pain, pleuritic chest pain, multiple episodes of vomiting, dysphagia, and odynophagia. He denied prior medical problems or foreign‐body ingestion but admitted to daily marijuana smoking. Initial treatment with ondansetron, aluminum hydroxide/magnesium hydroxide, and simethicone relieved nausea but not chest pain. An electrocardiogram was interpreted as suspicious for acute pericarditis, prompting transfer to a local emergency department. There, he was normotensive, mildly tachycardic, and had moderate epigastric tenderness; vomiting had improved but dysphagia persisted. Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated pericholecystic fluid, distal esophageal edema and dilation with questionable air in the esophageal wall, and possible hiatal hernia. A repeat electrocardiogram confirmed diffuse ST elevations. Chest radiography revealed a questionable infiltrate. Right upper quadrant ultrasound showed gallbladder wall thickening near the fundus without gallstones. Further labs revealed elevated WBC count (12.5 × 10^9/L), ESR (28 mm/h), CRP (21.77 mg/dL), and procalcitonin (11.02 ng/mL); troponin and metabolic panel were normal. He received IV fluids, antiemetics, hydrocodone/acetaminophen, famotidine, a GI “cocktail,” ceftazidime, and azithromycin, and continued to deny foreign‐body ingestion. He was then transferred to a pediatric specialty center, where he remained tachycardic but afebrile, received piperacillin–tazobactam, famotidine, and ondansetron IV, and underwent an esophagram with water‐soluble contrast that revealed a filling defect in the distal esophagus.
title: Body stuffing during apprehension resulting in distal esophageal impaction: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 40-year-old man presented with chronic fatigue and anemia of 2 years’ duration. Workplace medical examinations revealed progressive anemia; 3 months before evaluation his hemoglobin was 8.1 g/dL and mean corpuscular volume 82.9 fL. On examination, he was pale but otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, MCV 82.6 fL, aspartate aminotransferase 81 IU/L, and alanine aminotransferase 103 IU/L; plasma electrolytes, ferrum, ferritin, and thyroid function were normal. A peripheral blood smear showed no abnormalities. Fecal and urinary occult blood tests were negative. Upper and lower endoscopy, small-intestinal capsule examination, and whole-body contrast-enhanced CT failed to identify a bleeding source. Tumor markers, immunoglobulins, protein electrophoresis, viral serologies, antinuclear antibodies, zinc, and copper levels were unremarkable. Because a diagnosis remained elusive, a bone marrow biopsy was performed: chromosomal analysis and leukocyte surface markers were normal, iron staining showed no ring sideroblasts, but the marrow smear revealed basophilic stippling of erythrocytes.
journal: The Journal of International Medical Research
title:
Basophilic stippling in red blood cells in the bone marrow:
indication for lead poisoning diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of severe headache, vomiting, and progressive confusion. On examination, he was alert but disoriented, with no focal motor deficits. An urgent CT scan demonstrated triventricular hydrocephalus and a solitary hemorrhagic lesion centered in the septum pellucidum. An external ventricular drain was placed, relieving his symptoms. MRI of the brain revealed an inhomogeneous intraventricular mass, hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images, with strong gadolinium enhancement and extension into the third ventricle causing stenosis of the foramina of Monro. The patient underwent right frontal craniotomy and transcallosal gross total excision of the bleeding tumor, followed by a septostomy. A postoperative total-body CT scan showed no extracranial lesions. Two months later, the patient’s neurologic status declined, and he died. No autopsy was performed.  
Histologic examination of the surgical specimen revealed an extensively necrotic and hemorrhagic neoplasm composed of large, pleomorphic, round to polygonal epithelioid cells with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. The cells were arranged in sheets and nests, with occasional tubular structures and irregular thick-walled vessels lined by atypical epithelioid cells. Mitotic figures were numerous, including atypical forms, and the Ki-67 labeling index was very high.
title: Epithelioid Angiosarcoma of the Septum Pellucidum

case_prompt: A 14-day-old male infant presented with a 24-hour history of right cheek swelling and redness. He was born at 38 weeks’ gestation as a twin via cesarean delivery without complications and had been feeding and gaining weight appropriately. The parents noted fussiness and crying between feeds but denied fever, rash, or sick contacts. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. His right preauricular area was erythematous and swollen; palpation elicited crying. The left side was normal. The right tympanic membrane could not be visualized due to edema. The oral mucosa appeared normal, but purulent material was visible in the mouth. Gentle massage of the right parotid gland expressed additional purulent drainage from the opening of the right Stensen’s duct. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel except for elevated total and direct bilirubin. A respiratory viral panel was negative. Point-of-care ultrasonography of the right parotid gland demonstrated a swollen, hypervascular gland without ductal dilation, calcifications, or abscess formation. Consultations with otolaryngology and infectious diseases agreed with acute parotitis as the presumptive diagnosis.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Neonatal Parotitis: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old active-duty service member first presented in 2007 with progressive dyspnea on exertion. He denied recurrent sino-pulmonary infections but had a history of seasonal allergies. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed mild microcytic anemia with normal iron studies and mild hypoproteinemia. Chest radiography was normal. Spirometry demonstrated an FVC of 100% of predicted, FEV₁ of 92% of predicted, and FEV₁/FVC of 80% of predicted; methacholine challenge testing was negative. Despite these findings, he was diagnosed with asthma and treated with inhaled corticosteroids, bronchodilators, courses of azithromycin for presumed infections, and repeated oral corticosteroids—with minimal improvement.

Over the next decade, he continued to have exertional dyspnea that limited his military fitness, and allergen testing, repeat spirometry, treatment for gastroesophageal reflux, and an initial high-resolution chest CT scan were unrevealing. In 2016, chart review noted a CT scan of the abdomen done for appendicitis that showed numerous ground-glass nodules. A dedicated noncontrast CT of the chest subsequently revealed innumerable ground-glass and consolidative nodules with mediastinal, supraclavicular, and axillary lymphadenopathy. A PET–CT scan confirmed multiple hypermetabolic thoracic and abdominal lymph nodes and mild splenic uptake. Given concern for malignancy, an excisional biopsy of a right axillary lymph node was performed; pathology demonstrated reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with scattered granulomas, and “there was no evidence of malignancy on histology or flow cytometry.”
title: An unusual mimicker of asthma in an active duty army physician: Common variable immunodeficiency presenting as granulomatous lymphocytic interstitial lung disease

case_prompt:
A 4-month-old Saudi girl was brought with 7 days of acute pallor, jaundice, and poor feeding. She was born at term without perinatal complications; family history was negative for hematologic or autoimmune disorders, and she was taking only vitamin D. On examination she was pale and jaundiced but afebrile, with no hepatosplenomegaly or bleeding signs; growth parameters were appropriate.

Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 5.4 g/dL, MCV 111.4 fL, reticulocytes 18.7%, platelet count initially reported “in clumps” then measured 72×10^3/µL falling to 62×10^3/µL, WBC 20×10^3/µL with normal differential, total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dL (direct normal), LDH 1477 U/L. Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test was positive only for IgG. Peripheral smear showed anemia, thrombocytopenia, increased reticulocytes, occasional normoblasts, and no schistocytes. Blood groups of mother and infant were both A, Rh+.

Hemoglobin electrophoresis was normal for age. Folate, vitamin B12, and antinuclear antibodies were within normal limits. IgM against CMV, EBV, and HIV were negative. A bone marrow aspirate showed normal cellularity, brisk erythroid hyperplasia (76% of cells), normal numbers of megakaryocytes with proper platelet separation, occasional hemophagocytes, and no dysplastic cells.
journal: Saudi Journal of Medicine & Medical Sciences
title: Early-onset Evans Syndrome in a 4-Month-Old Infant: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman with stage IV non–small cell lung cancer (T2a, N2, M1b), status post right adrenalectomy for oligometastatic disease, received concurrent cisplatin–etoposide chemotherapy and thoracic radiotherapy (60 Gy) completed in August 2012. Restaging CT at that time showed regression of her primary tumor and no interstitial lung disease. Fifty-six days after radiotherapy, she began maintenance pemetrexed (500 mg/m2 every 21 days) with vitamin B12 and folic acid supplementation. 

Thirteen days after her second dose of pemetrexed, she presented with fever, cough, lethargy, and resting dyspnea of several days’ duration. She had no chest pain or peripheral edema. On examination, temperature was 38 °C, respiratory rate 30 bpm, and oxygen saturation 78% on room air. Arterial blood gas on 8 L/min oxygen revealed pH 7.47, PO2 73 mm Hg, and PCO2 32 mm Hg. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 4 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 3.5 × 10^9/L), hemoglobin 101 g/L, normal renal and liver function, and C-reactive protein 170 mg/L. Chest radiograph demonstrated diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities in the upper lobes. Chest CT revealed widespread interstitial opacities with interlobular and intralobular septal thickening, fine nodularity, and ground-glass attenuation diffusely throughout both lungs, including areas outside the prior radiation field. CT pulmonary angiography showed no pulmonary embolus. 

Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics were initiated, and repeated blood cultures and induced sputum samples were obtained.
title: Pemetrexed-Induced Interstitial Pneumonitis: A Case Study and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old man, previously healthy and active, noted a 4-month history of gradual weight gain despite daily aerobic exercise and no change in diet. Three months before presentation, he observed progressive abdominal distension, describing it as feeling “like a large ball in my belly.” He subsequently developed intermittent abdominal discomfort that increased in intensity and frequency, constipation, and severe gastroesophageal reflux, for which he began taking laxatives and a proton-pump inhibitor. 

He underwent contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen, which revealed a large unilocular retroperitoneal cystic mass measuring 32 cm by 25 cm. The mass did not communicate with the pleural space or any other abdominal viscera, displaced the entire bowel to the left, spanned from the pelvis inferiorly to the liver hilum superiorly, and compressed the liver and stomach. 

He had no history of asbestos exposure or other occupational risks (silica, cadmium), no family history of malignancy, no significant alcohol or tobacco use, and no history of trauma.
title: Mesothelioma as a rapidly developing Giant Abdominal Cyst

case_prompt:
A 13‐year‐old boy with no prior medical or ocular history presented after a BB gun injury to his left eye. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye. There was a full‐thickness corneal laceration of the left eye, and CT of the orbits showed a retained BB pellet. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye was normal. The patient underwent emergent repair of the left open‐globe injury without complication, and repeat exam of the right eye under anesthesia remained normal. He remained hospitalized for left eyelid edema and chemosis, which improved conservatively. 

On hospital day 5, before discharge, the right eye remained 20/20 with no visual complaints. Dilated examination revealed mild vitreous haze and white condensation in the mid‐vitreous overlying the inferonasal macula; there was no anterior chamber inflammation, snowbanking, or serous detachment. Spectral‐domain OCT demonstrated fine hyper‐reflective material in the vitreous, focal areas of hypotransmission due to vitreous opacity, and possible mild choroidal thickening. Fluorescein angiography showed inferior vascular staining with mild leakage, mild optic disc leakage, and blockage effects over the posterior pole.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Sympathetic ophthalmia presenting 5 days after penetrating injury

case_prompt: A 14-year-old boy with no personal or family history presented with a lesion on his middle back that had been present for several months and became painful and swollen during the week before his visit. On examination, there was a large subcutaneous tumor measuring 6 × 4 cm with two overlying protruding, crusted, erythematous nodules, each with umbilicus-like openings and noted discharge. An inflamed follicular cyst was diagnosed initially. Multiple incisions and drainages were performed; bacterial culture grew Staphylococcus aureus. Over the following months, he received oral antibiotics (cephalexin, doxycycline, clindamycin) and topical antibiotics (gentamicin cream, spersin ointment), with gradual improvement in swelling and pain. Total excision of the tumor was arranged six months after the first visit.
title: Panfolliculoma: Report of the Youngest Case and Literature Review of Its Histopathologic Variants

case_prompt: A 95-year-old woman noticed a mass in her left breast and was referred for suspected breast cancer. On examination, the 2-cm mass was well defined, mobile, with normal overlying skin and nipple–areola; axillary lymph nodes were not palpable. She had no café-au-lait spots, no family history of breast cancer, and no comorbidities. Mammography showed a round, well-defined, hyperdense mass without calcification in the mid-lateral left breast. Ultrasonography revealed a 16 × 16 × 15 mm round lesion with circumscribed margins, posterior acoustic enhancement, mixed hypoechoic and heterogeneous hyperechoic areas, no internal blood flow on Doppler, and a Tsukuba elasticity score of 4. Tumor markers (CEA, CA 15-3) were within normal limits. Core needle biopsy showed a spindle cell lesion with no malignant features. Two months later, ultrasound showed the mass had increased to 27 × 26 × 19 mm, but repeat biopsy was similarly non-diagnostic. Because of its growth and persistent uncertainty regarding malignancy, the decision was made to resect the tumor.
title: Neurofibroma with adenosis in the mammary gland: a case report

case_prompt:
A 5-year-old Saudi girl presented to dermatology with asymptomatic skin lesions on the left hand and left foot that had been present since birth and were spreading gradually. Her parents noted exclusive hyperhidrosis of the left hand and foot. There was no history of excessive sun exposure, trauma, or similar lesions in the family. She had previously used topical calcipotriol without improvement. 

On examination, multiple yellowish hyperkeratotic papules coalescing into verrucous plaques were arranged in a linear distribution along the marginal surfaces of the left hand and foot. On the palm, lesions extended from the thenar eminence to the proximal aspect of the fourth finger; on the foot, lesions involved the lateral side and fifth toe. A 4-mm punch biopsy was obtained from a foot papule.
title: A sporadic case of unilateral acrokeratoelastoidosis in Saudi Arabia: a case report

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old recreational male trail runner (∼5 hours per week) presented with several months of palpitations at rest and during exercise. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, dizziness, syncope, stimulant use (including caffeine), illicit drugs, supplements, or recent infection. His medical history was unremarkable; he had no hypertension, diabetes, or smoking history. Family history included a mother who died suddenly at 72 (no autopsy) and a father who died at 60 of chronic illness. 

On examination, blood pressure was 124/81 mm Hg, heart rate 66 beats/min; cardiac and pulmonary exams were normal. Laboratory tests were within normal limits, with no elevation of creatine kinase or troponin. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm, normal atrioventricular and intraventricular conduction, and low QRS voltage (<0.5 mV in limb leads). 

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated nondilated ventricles and atria, preserved systolic and diastolic function, and no valvular disease. On exercise stress testing (Bruce protocol), he achieved 107% of maximum predicted heart rate, with isolated infrequent polymorphic PVCs suggesting both LV and RV origins, three ventricular couplets, and one monomorphic triplet; no PVCs occurred during recovery. 

A 24-hour Holter monitor recorded frequent PVCs (419 total, 0.5% of all beats), frequent couplets, and one 5-beat run of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia; the predominant PVC morphology was negative in both leads, with other morphologies also noted.
title: Critical role of cardiac magnetic resonance in the diagnosis of left-dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy: A paradigmatic case in a recreational middle-aged athlete

case_prompt: A 2-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of noisy breathing. She was born at term, with an uncomplicated delivery and birth weight of 2.8 kg. She has been fed by both breast and bottle. Over the prior 15 days, her noisy breathing worsened during feeding. She weighed 3.5 kg at presentation (below the 3rd percentile) but was afebrile with normal vital signs and maintained an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Examination revealed inspiratory stridor with suprasternal and intercostal retraction. Flexible upper endoscopy demonstrated a 1 cm cystic lesion in the vallecula pushing the epiglottis backward and partially compromising the airway. A same-day CT scan of the neck showed a well-defined, rounded, nonenhancing hypodense cystic lesion measuring 9 mm, projecting into the oropharynx, with no soft tissue component. A provisional differential diagnosis of thyroglossal or retention cyst was suggested. Thyroid function tests were normal.
title: Congenital Vallecular Cyst Causing Airway Compromise in a 2-Month-Old Girl

case_prompt: An man in his 80s (height 148 cm, weight 50 kg) with hypertension and a history of asymptomatic cerebral infarction (on aspirin) underwent surgical excision of extramammary Paget's disease under general anesthesia. Preoperative ECG showed complete right bundle branch block; routine labs were unremarkable. Anesthesia was induced with propofol, fentanyl, remifentanil, and rocuronium, and maintained with sevoflurane, remifentanil, and intermittent rocuronium. Intraoperative hemodynamics and oxygenation remained stable. Surgery lasted 2 h 49 min. After discontinuation of anesthetics, the patient opened his eyes at an end‐tidal sevoflurane concentration of 0.1%–0.2%, received sugammadex, and was extubated. Minutes later, his level of consciousness declined to a Glasgow Coma Scale score of E1V1M1, with stable respiratory status. Naloxone was given without improvement. Body temperature was 37.0 °C. Blood gas analysis showed normal pH and electrolytes, and blood glucose was 110 mg/dL. New right conjugate eye deviation was noted. Head CT and MRI revealed no new infarction or hemorrhage. There were no respiratory or circulatory abnormalities, and he was transferred urgently to the ICU for close observation.
title: Presumed first episode of nonconvulsive status epilepticus as the cause of postoperative disorder of consciousness following the completion of general anesthesia: A case report

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old Indian woman presented with a 2-week history of a non-tender mass on her left upper eyelid. She had noted a small erythematous lesion that increased in size despite warm compresses. She denied visual changes, trauma, or constitutional symptoms. Her medical history was notable only for iron deficiency anemia. On examination, visual acuity was 6/9.5 bilaterally, intraocular pressures were normal, and extraocular movements were full without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Eversion of the left upper eyelid revealed a smooth, homogeneous, firm, rubbery mass measuring approximately 1 cm × 1 cm. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable, and vital signs were within normal limits.

The lesion was treated as a presumed pyogenic granuloma with intralesional triamcinolone. One month later, after slight initial improvement, swelling recurred with intermittent pain and blurred vision; visual acuity was 6/12 bilaterally. Because the lesion persisted, an incisional biopsy was performed with repeat intralesional triamcinolone.

Histopathologic examination showed a mass composed predominantly of histiocytic cells, including epithelioid histiocytes and Touton-type multinucleated giant cells, with admixed lymphocytes, plasma cells, and polymorphonuclear cells. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated lesional cells positive for CD163 and CD68 and negative for S100, CD1A, and Langerin. The lesion extended to the peripheral and deep margins of the specimen.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Adult onset xanthogranuloma of the eyelid

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man with no prior surgeries presented with one day of colicky epigastric pain and several episodes of low‐volume, non-bilious vomiting. He had no significant alcohol or tobacco history. On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed epigastric tenderness without peritonism or distension. Initial blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 12 × 10^9/L and a normal C-reactive protein, liver function tests, and lactate. Chest and abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. 

Because of ongoing pain, a contrasted CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis and an abdominal ultrasound were performed to exclude gallstone pathology; both studies were reported as normal. The patient was admitted for conservative management. Over the next 2 days, inflammatory markers remained stable, but on day 4 he developed worsening pain, intractable vomiting, and had not passed flatus or stool. Physical examination now showed upper abdominal distension and localized tenderness in the left hypochondrium. A nasogastric tube returned feculent material. A chest radiograph showed dilated small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels in the upper abdomen. A repeat CT scan demonstrated dilated jejunal loops with a transition point on the left side of the abdomen, in keeping with mechanical small-bowel obstruction and a suspected obstructing band, with no evidence of ischemia or perforation.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Rare cause of small bowel obstruction secondary to epiploic appendagitis: Diagnostic dilemma and role of minimal invasive surgery

case_prompt: A 53-year-old man with hypertension, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, pulmonary embolism, and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with increasing dyspnea, malaise, low-grade fever, and signs of heart failure. Blood pressure was 123/71 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats/min, and peripheral oxygen saturation 97%. He was afebrile and had no cutaneous signs of endocarditis or skin infection. Electrocardiogram showed an anterior myocardial infarction of indeterminate age with abnormal ST-segment and T-wave changes suggesting lateral ischemia. Chest radiograph revealed a right pleural effusion, cardiomegaly, and interstitial edema. White blood cell count was 5,200 ×10^9/L (normal 4.5–11), C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (normal <0.3), and procalcitonin 0.09 µg/mL. Complete blood count, creatinine, and cardiac enzymes were normal. Blood cultures were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% with apical and anterolateral akinesia and pleuro-pericardial effusions. Coronary angiography revealed a large aneurysm of the left anterior descending artery with a fistula draining into both ventricles. Positron emission tomography indicated an inflammatory process in the anterolateral right ventricle with a hypodense central zone concerning for abscess. Cardiac computed tomography demonstrated multiple pseudoaneurysms in the left anterior descending and right coronary arteries, the largest arising from the distal left anterior descending artery with a biventricular fistula communicating with both the right and left ventricles.
title: Mycotic Coronary Aneurysm Associated With Biventricular Fistula

case_prompt: A 39-year-old man with a 20–pack-year smoking history presented with a several-day history of painful oral ulcers that did not respond to fluconazole or valacyclovir. He denied fever, chills, night sweats, anorexia, or weight loss. Ten days later, he developed diffuse bullous and erosive skin lesions on the chest, abdomen, and arms. Initial blood tests showed isolated neutropenia. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed an 18 × 8.9 cm necrotic, irregular mesenteric mass without lymphadenopathy. A percutaneous core biopsy was nondiagnostic. On transfer, he had febrile neutropenia (WBC 900/mm3), persistent oral ulcers, and widespread cutaneous lesions. Viral serologies (HBV, HCV, HIV) and EBV PCR were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed 80% cellularity with left-shifted granulopoiesis, mild dysmegakaryopoiesis, and reactive plasmacytosis, but “no evidence of an epithelial or mesenchymal tumor, lymphoproliferative disorder, or acute leukemia.” A repeat core biopsy of the abdominal mass showed a cellular proliferation of mildly to moderately atypical oval-to-spindle-shaped cells in fascicular to vaguely storiform arrangements with a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated tumor cells positive for vimentin, CD21, and CD68, weakly positive for CD45, focally positive for S100 protein, CD34, and SMA, and negative for ALK, CD117, DOG-1, CD3, CD20, CD23, and EBER.
title: Paraneoplastic Pemphigus as a First Manifestation of an Intra-Abdominal Follicular Dendritic Cell Sarcoma: Rare Case and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 9-year-old boy presented with right-sided sciatica and a gradually enlarging swelling in the right buttock of 6 months’ duration. His pain was constant and unrelated to activity, with no constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was a mildly tender, firm-to-hard, fixed mass measuring 8.5 × 7.5 cm in the outer upper part of the right buttock; no other lesions were noted. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. MRI of the right gluteal region showed a relatively well-defined mass measuring 5.5 × 7.5 × 8.5 cm involving the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus muscles and infiltrating the piriformis; the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense with marked heterogeneity on T2-weighted images, abutting but not eroding the iliac blade. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was reported as a benign spindle cell lesion with a differential diagnosis of proliferative fasciomyositis and desmoid tumor.
title: Desmoid Tumor of the Buttock in a Preadolescent Child

case_prompt: A 59-year-old man presented with acute urinary retention. He reported a 6-month history of chronic hypogastric pain, lower urinary tract symptoms, and constipation. On examination, the bladder was distended, requiring transurethral catheterization. Digital rectal examination revealed a bulging pelvic mass; the prostate itself was not palpable. Laboratory studies showed a serum creatinine of 123 μmol/L, leukocytosis, a normal prostate-specific antigen level, and a sterile urine culture. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT revealed a 13×10×9 cm multilocular heterogeneous cystic mass in the rectovesical and supravesical spaces, compressing the bladder and ureters, with bilateral upper-tract dilation; there were no nodular solid components or lymphadenopathy. Hydatic cyst was suspected, but hydatic serology was negative on two occasions. Urethrocystography demonstrated a 12-cm mass projecting over the bladder area.
