Pelvic MRI showed a 13×10 cm supra-rectal, retro-vesical multilocular cystic lesion of heterogeneous signal with fluid levels, areas of T1 hyperintensity and T2 hypointensity, and thin-walled septa mildly enhancing after gadolinium, findings “evoking a hemorrhagic cystic retro-peritoneal mesothelioma or cystic lymphangioma.”
title: Prostatic cystadenoma presenting as a large multilocular pelvic male mass

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman presented with a 6-day history of bilateral painful, severe vision loss and right leg paresthesia. One month earlier, she had a two-week flu-like illness with nausea, diarrhea, cough (without dyspnea), anosmia, and ageusia; anosmia and ageusia persisted. Her medical history included vitiligo, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance.

On examination, visual acuity was hand motion in both eyes; pupils were sluggish without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Extraocular movements were full but elicited pain in all gazes. Static perimetry revealed severe bilateral visual field defects; color testing was not possible. Slit-lamp and funduscopic examination, including the optic nerves, and optical coherence tomography were unremarkable.

Neurologic examination showed anosmia, ageusia, irritability, headache, and a sensory-motor thoracic spinal syndrome with left lower-limb hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign, and right-sided sensory impairment.

Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 51 mm/h (normal 0–20), positive anti–SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid IgG, and a negative nasal swab PCR for SARS-CoV-2. MRI of the brain and spine demonstrated bilateral optic nerve enhancement, multiple post-gadolinium T1-weighted brain lesions, and a T2-hyperintense D7–D8 spinal cord lesion. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (22 cells/mm3, 95% CD3+ T cells), a CD4:CD8 ratio of 7:1 (reference 1.2–2:1), mild hyperproteinorrachia (452 mg/L; normal 150–450 mg/L), and a positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR. Serum and CSF were negative for anti–aquaporin-4 and anti–myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Bilateral optic neuritis as the presenting sign of post SARS-CoV-2 acute disseminated encephalomyelitis

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman presented with a three-year history of painless anterior neck swelling. Her medical history included hypertension and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine; she had no prior head or neck surgery, radiation, or family history of thyroid disease. She reported mild dysphagia and episodes of nocturnal dyspnea but no pain or systemic symptoms.

On examination, there was a 5-cm, smooth, non-tender, mobile mass confined to the right thyroid lobe; the lower pole of the mass was not palpable. The left lobe was normal, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Indirect laryngoscopy showed normal vocal cords and movement.

Routine blood tests, including thyroid-stimulating hormone and anti-thyroperoxidase antibodies, were within normal limits. Chest radiography demonstrated leftward deviation of the cervical trachea. Cervical ultrasound revealed a right multinodular heterogeneous goiter with a solitary well-defined cyst measuring 7 cm in diameter; no lymph nodes were seen. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck confirmed a thin-walled, homogeneous fluid-density cyst located within the right thyroid lobe that extended retrosternally into the anterior mediastinum, causing deviation and mild compression of the trachea.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesion indicated the presence of normal-appearing squamous cells.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Intrathyroid thyroglossal duct cyst: A case report

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old Japanese man, an apple farmer with no significant medical history, was admitted with difficulty moving and a several-day history of right inguinal swelling.  
CT imaging showed a right inguinal incarcerated hernia without signs of bowel obstruction. Manual reduction failed, and he underwent inguinal hernia repair with ileal resection.  
Postoperatively, he was admitted to the ICU for acute kidney injury and tachycardic atrial fibrillation attributed to dehydration; both improved after blood transfusion, and he was transferred to the general ward on postoperative day (POD) 1.  
He developed prolonged ileus managed with fluids and ileus-tube decompression. On POD 8, psychological disturbance prompted a presumptive diagnosis of delirium; mild spasm-like movements were noted but he remained alert with no focal neurologic deficits.  
On the night of POD 9, he was readmitted to the ICU for hypoxemia and difficulty clearing sputum. His respiratory status improved after bronchoscopy, but he then exhibited marked muscle rigidity throughout his body in response to minimal stimuli.  
At ICU readmission, arterial blood gas under 6 L/min O2 showed pH 7.32, PaO2 139 Torr, PaCO2 45 Torr, and base excess –2 mmol/L. He was in sinus tachycardia at 110–120 beats/min.  
Shortly after starting tazobactam–piperacillin, he developed sudden hypotension (systolic blood pressure 40 mmHg), desaturation (SpO2 50%), and a diffuse rash, leading to a diagnosis of anaphylactic shock requiring intubation and continuous intravenous adrenaline (up to 0.15 μg/kg/min).  
On POD 10, adrenaline was weaned, but muscle rigidity worsened with tapering of propofol (2–3 mg/kg/h) and dexmedetomidine (0.4 μg/kg/h), hindering ventilator weaning.  
Blood cultures, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and electroencephalography were negative. His irritability increased, tidal volumes dropped from 8 to 3 mL/kg, and respiratory rate rose above 25 breaths/min during awakenings.  
He developed labile blood pressure with systolic peaks of 180 mmHg on awakening, managed with noradrenaline (0.1 μg/kg/min). Despite severe rigidity, he remained able to communicate and reported intense pain from muscle stiffness, necessitating repeated propofol boluses.
title: Difficult diagnosis of tetanus in a sedated patient after ileal resection

case_prompt: A 17‐day‐old female neonate, born at 38 weeks’ gestation by cesarean delivery (birth weight 3100 g), had an uncomplicated prenatal course. From day 7 of life she developed stridor, tachypnea, and respiratory distress. She was admitted to a local NICU, where an AP chest radiograph showed opacity in the right upper lobe consistent with collapse consolidation and atelectasis. She received ampicillin, cefotaxime, oxygen by oxyhood, inhaled Pulmicort, and salbutamol without clinical or radiographic improvement and was transferred to our NICU. Repeat chest radiography showed persistent right upper‐lobe opacity. Given concern for tracheoesophageal fistula or other obstructive lesion, an upper gastrointestinal study with thin barium was performed. The study showed no evidence of tracheoesophageal fistula but demonstrated esophageal regurgitation during contrast ingestion and a 35 × 34 mm mass adjacent to the upper intrathoracic esophagus with mild mass effect. On hospital day 3 she developed respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. After relative stabilization, a contrast‐enhanced thoracic CT scan was planned for further evaluation.
title: Neonatal neuroblastoma presented with respiratory distress, a case report

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman was referred for extraction of a right impacted mandibular third molar. She was in good general health, with no history of trauma, systemic disease, or medication use. Extraoral and intraoral examinations were unremarkable. A panoramic radiograph showed no clear lesion or root resorption around the third molar. Under local anesthesia, the tooth was extracted without complication. On inspection of the surgical site, the dentist noted a yellowish, soft mass measuring 12 × 10 × 6 mm that was not attached to the crown or root of the extracted tooth and without signs of infection.  
Dentigerous cyst was excluded because the lesion was not associated with a tooth crown. Odontogenic keratocyst was excluded due to its non-cystic appearance.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Intraosseous lipoma of the jaws: Review of the literature and rare case report

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 1-day history of severe dysuria, urgency, frequency, fever, and chills. He denied hematuria or flank pain and had never experienced similar symptoms. He was a heavy smoker. On examination, he appeared ill, was febrile to 39.3 °C, and had normal blood pressure. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis with a left shift. Urinalysis showed numerous white blood cells, 1–2 red blood cells per high-power field, and bacteria.  
A renal and bladder ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined lobulated heterogeneous isoechoic mass with possible mural calcification and internal blood flow at the right anterolateral bladder wall; the kidneys were normal without hydronephrosis. A contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed a 5.5 × 4.3 cm oval mass on the right bladder wall with mild dilation of the right distal ureter.  
He was admitted with a diagnosis of febrile urinary tract infection and started on intravenous imipenem–cilastatin and supportive care. Four days later, he improved clinically. Urine culture grew Escherichia coli resistant to most antibiotics except imipenem and ertapenem. Urine cytology was negative for malignancy.  
Under general anesthesia, cystoscopy revealed a large bulging mass arising from the right lateral bladder wall with intact, smooth overlying mucosa. Examination under anesthesia confirmed a mobile lower abdominal mass. A transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed, and tissue was sent for histopathologic analysis.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Leiomyoma of Urinary Bladder Presenting with Febrile Urinary Tract Infection: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 68-year-old woman presented six years after implantation of a cemented endoprosthetic hinge total knee arthroplasty for conversion of a long-standing knee fusion. For the past five months she noted mild distal thigh and knee pain while walking. On examination, the knee was cool, stable, with a range of motion of 0–80° of flexion and no extensor lag. Radiographs of the femur showed a radiolucent line in the distal diaphyseal cement mantle, a periosteal erosion, and an adjacent soft-tissue mass surrounding the distal femoral diaphysis. A CT scan demonstrated an eccentric lytic lesion of the medial cortex of the distal femoral diaphysis with an adjacent soft-tissue mass measuring approximately 7 cm in length and 2–3 cm in breadth, with septations and a peripheral calcific border. Knee aspiration yielded 259 white cells (71% neutrophils) and was negative for bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast cultures; alpha-defensin and Synovasure tests were negative. Serum C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal. Evaluation for metastatic disease was negative.
title: Periosteal pseudotumor in complex total knee arthroplasty resembling a neoplastic process

case_prompt:
A 2-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of fever and abdominal distension. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His only prior significant infection was at 6 months of age, when he developed a methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus lymphadenitis near the left ear that recurred once but resolved after two drainages and antibiotic therapy.

At 28 months of age, he had daily fevers up to 39.4°C for nearly 1 month, with intermittent dysuria and mildly loose stools. There was no travel history or family history of immunologic, hematologic, or oncologic disease. His weight percentile declined from the 36th to the 7th over the preceding year. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed:
- Albumin 2.8 g/dL (3.8–5.4)  
- Alkaline phosphatase 509 IU/L (<290)  
- C-reactive protein 10.69 mg/dL (0.08–1.2)  
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 131 mm/hr (0–20)  
- Ferritin 178.1 ng/mL (10–60)  
- Hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL (11.5–13.5)  
- Hematocrit 30.5% (34–40)  
- Lactate dehydrogenase 258 IU/L (<171)  
- Platelets 399 × 10^9/L (156–369)  
- Neutrophils 57% (12–34)  

Other laboratory results were within normal limits. Initial differential diagnoses included Kawasaki disease, hematologic malignancy, early juvenile idiopathic arthritis or other rheumatologic disease, and intestinal infection; Lyme disease, toxoplasmosis, Bartonella, cytomegalovirus, and tuberculosis were also considered. Subsequent testing excluded these entities, and he defervesced on empiric therapy.

One month later, he returned with persistent fever and abdominal distension. Examination revealed a fluid wave. Repeat studies showed:
- Platelets 457 × 10^9/L  
- ESR 74 mm/hr  
- Ferritin 79.2 ng/mL  
- Hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL  
- Persistently low albumin; prealbumin 5.6 mg/dL  
- Proteinuria negative; alpha-1-antitrypsin normal  

Abdominal CT revealed ascites, contour irregularity of the colon, diffuse peritoneal enhancement, and fat stranding consistent with peritonitis. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded purulent fluid with numerous neutrophils and macrophages but no malignant cells; bacterial and fungal cultures were sterile. The serum-to-ascites albumin gradient was 1 g/L. Gastrointestinal evaluation with esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy, including duodenal, terminal ileal, and colonic biopsies, was unremarkable. A bone marrow biopsy was also unremarkable, and a tagged white-blood-cell scan showed no focal uptake.
title: Chronic Granulomatous Disease Presenting as Aseptic Ascites in a 2-Year-Old Child

case_prompt: A 51-year-old woman with fibromyalgia, right-sided sciatica, DVT, asthma, nephrolithiasis, vertigo, and oral/genital herpes returned from the Dominican Republic with a 10-day history of progressive lower extremity sensory changes and weakness. She had transient bilateral arm pain with neck and head pressure before onset of leg symptoms. She reported one day of urinary hesitancy and described “leg heaviness,” worse on the right, causing a fall without loss of consciousness. Vital signs were normal. Examination showed bilateral knee flexor/extensor strength 3/5, dysesthesia to touch and pinprick from mid-thigh distally, absent knee reflexes, and bilateral Babinski signs without clonus. A bladder scan excluded significant retention. MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine was performed. Laboratory studies showed WBC 5.1×10^3 cells/mL, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 371×10^3 cells/mL, eosinophils 5.7%, normal metabolic panel, vitamin B12 290 pg/mL, ESR 30.9 mm/h, CRP 5.9 mg/L; CPK, aldolase, methylmalonic acid, Lyme titers, copper level, and SSA/SSB were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture yielded CSF with WBC 360 cells/mL (100% lymphocytes), protein 182 mg/dL, and no albumin-cytologic dissociation. An initial EMG study during the first week was unremarkable.
title: Elsberg syndrome in HSV-2 infection

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with fever up to 41°C, vomiting, diarrhea, and severe pain in the distal parts of her fingers and toes. She had undergone splenectomy at age 18 for immune thrombocytopenic purpura; pneumococcal vaccination had lapsed more than 5 years earlier. On examination, temperature was 36.3°C, heart rate 94/min, blood pressure 111/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Both fingers and toes were symmetrically cyanotic and extremely tender.

Laboratory studies showed: CRP 291 mg/L; hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; white blood cell count 17.8×10^3/μL; platelet count 63×10^3/μL; INR 1.99; fibrinogen 82 mg/dL; D-dimer >35 000 ng/mL; von Willebrand factor antigen 200%; ADAMTS13 activity 17%; serum creatinine 2.55 mg/dL; LDH 783 IU/L; total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL; schistocytes <1%; direct Coombs test negative; haptoglobin 1.76 g/L; complement C3 0.92 g/L; C4 0.32 g/L; ANCA, anticardiolipin antibodies, and cryoglobulins negative. Urinalysis revealed 5 RBCs/hpf, 8 WBCs/hpf, proteinuria of 0.83 g/g creatinine, and albuminuria of 316 mg/g creatinine.

Blood cultures drawn on admission grew Streptococcus pneumoniae (serogroup 24) after 9 hours of incubation.
title: Streptococcus Pneumoniae Bacteremia with Acute Kidney Injury and Transient ADAMTS13 Deficiency

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman, gravida 7, para 3, postmenopausal for 10 years, presented with 2 months of vaginal bleeding. Physical examination was unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a mass-like submucous degenerated myoma nodule in the uterine cavity. An endometrial biopsy performed elsewhere was reported as endometrial hyperplasia with cellular atypia; a Papanicolaou smear was normal. The patient underwent laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. 

Gross examination revealed a 4.0 × 2.5-cm polypoid mass in the lower left lateral uterine segment, pressing on the myometrium. Histologic examination showed a diffuse proliferation of relatively uniform small neoplastic cells with scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, frequent mitoses, numerous apoptotic bodies, and large areas of necrosis. The tumor had fully penetrated the uterine wall, with histologic evidence of lymphovascular and cervical invasion. There was no associated endometrial lesion in the hysterectomy specimen.
journal: Turkish Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Primitive uterine neuroectodermal tumours: Two case reports

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and psoriasis presented with three days of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. On admission, temperature was elevated; blood pressure 115/52 mm Hg; heart rate 75 b/min; respiratory rate 20 b/min; oxygen saturation 93% on room air; BMI 29 kg/m2. Physical examination showed bilateral chest crackles; cardiovascular examination was normal. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block and left axis deviation. Chest radiography revealed patchy peripheral ground-glass opacities in both lungs and soft consolidations in the right middle lobe. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive. Laboratory studies showed WBC 5.9 × 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 10 g/dL, CRP 146 mg/L, ferritin 2619 μg/L, creatinine 190 μmol/L, and D-dimer 2.3 mg/L FEU. He became severely hypoxic shortly after admission and was managed with nasal-cannula oxygen, then CPAP in the ICU to maintain SpO2 95%.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal biventricular size and function, mild pulmonary hypertension (estimated RVSP 48 mm Hg), and two right atrial masses: an echodense mass on the right atrial roof in the four-chamber view and an echolucent mass protruding into the tricuspid annulus on the RV inflow view. A TTE one month earlier had shown no intracardiac mass.  
Because of the patient’s severe COVID-19 and elevated D-dimer, the right atrial masses were presumed to be thrombi, and he was anticoagulated with heparin followed by warfarin (INR target 2–3). Repeat TTE after two weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation showed no change in the masses. A transesophageal echocardiogram was deferred due to respiratory instability, and a cardiac MRI was planned for further evaluation.
final_diagnosis_raw: Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum
title: Right atrial mass in a patient with COVID‐19 pneumonia: A case report

case_prompt:
A 3-day-old full-term male, born appropriate for gestational age (birth weight 3065 g) after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, presented with three apneic episodes on day of life 3. The episodes, each lasting about 10 seconds, were characterized by turning ruddy, limp tone, and eye-rolling; the infant returned to baseline after stimulation. Pregnancy was notable for maternal polycystic ovarian syndrome treated with metformin in the first trimester and treated Group B Streptococcal colonization; there was concern for borderline gestational diabetes but a normal 3-h glucose tolerance test.

After difficulty breastfeeding and poor milk production, feeds were supplemented with formula from day 2. In the ED, vital signs were stable, and a point-of-care glucose was undetectable. He received D10% boluses and was started on a D10% infusion. A repeat glucose of 18 mg/dL prompted another bolus and escalation to a glucose infusion rate of 13.85 mg/kg/min. A sepsis evaluation, including blood and urine cultures, was initiated; chest X-ray was normal, and COVID-19 testing was negative.

Forty-eight hours later, cultures remained negative, and antibiotics were discontinued. The infant, still requiring a high glucose infusion, was transferred to the NICU. On arrival, his glucose was 66 mg/dL on D12.5% at 13.85 mg/kg/min. Physical examination showed duplicated earlobes but was otherwise unremarkable. After 12 h of stable glucose levels, the infusion was weaned to 12 mg/kg/min.

During a hypoglycemic episode (glucose 40 mg/dL), critical laboratory values were obtained: serum insulin 6.0 µIU/mL, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.2 mmol/L, cortisol 5.8 µg/dL, growth hormone 13.7 ng/mL, and ammonia 70 µmol/L. A low-dose ACTH stimulation test demonstrated a robust cortisol response. Diazoxide and chlorothiazide were initiated for presumed hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.
title: Congenital hyperinsulinism in a newborn presenting with poor feeding

case_prompt: A 52-year-old woman with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, hiatal hernia, and hypertension presented with intermittent chest and neck pain ongoing for 10 days. Ten days before admission, she had experienced severe chest and left shoulder pain with temporary loss of left arm function; during that episode her entire arm turned gray and dusky. Those arm symptoms resolved, but her neck and chest pain persisted. On presentation, her physical examination was normal. To evaluate for compressive neuropathy, a cervical spine MRI was obtained, which demonstrated an abnormal lack of flow void in the left vertebral artery. CT angiography of the head, neck, and chest showed hyperdensity and thickening of the ascending aortic wall and proximal arch, with extension into the origins of the great vessels resulting in near-complete occlusion of the left vertebral artery. The descending thoracic aorta, the abdominal aorta, and all major branch vessels were widely patent, and abdominal organs including the pancreas were normal.
title: The great imitator: IgG4 periaortitis masquerading as an acute aortic syndrome on computed tomographic angiography

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old African-American woman was seen for a 4-year history of right eye proptosis associated with excessive tearing. She also reported generalized headaches diagnosed as migraine, without improvement on topiramate. On review of systems, she noted pain triggered by chewing, speaking, and brushing her teeth, along with numbness, burning, and tingling in the V1 and V2 distributions of the right trigeminal nerve. She described intermittent right-sided facial muscle spasms and hyperesthesia to external stimuli. She denied any periorbital lesions, herpetic keratitis, head trauma, or infection. Her medical history was negative for diabetes, thyroid disease, cancer, oral herpes, recent infection, or head trauma; her family history was noncontributory.

On examination, pupils were equal, round, and reactive; extraocular movements were intact; and funduscopic exam was normal. The right eye was actively tearing and proptotic, with a Hertel measurement of 25 mm on the right versus 21 mm on the left. There was mild right upper-eyelid ptosis and right eyelid closure weakness. No other neurologic or systemic abnormalities were noted.

Screening tests for diabetes and thyroid disease were within normal limits, and HIV testing was negative. MRI of the orbits, face, and neck with and without contrast demonstrated enlargement and enhancement of the right trigeminal nerve from the cavernous sinus through the superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, and foramen ovale, with a 17 × 16 mm well-circumscribed solid and cystic mass arising from the V2 division in the right pterygopalatine space, causing anterior displacement of the globe. Nasal endoscopy revealed only a left mid-septal deviation without other abnormalities.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Trigeminal hypertrophic interstitial neuropathy presenting as unilateral proptosis, ptosis, tearing, and facial neuralgia

case_prompt: A 70-year-old woman from a rural village presented with a 6-month history of more than 10 watery diarrheal stools per day and an 18-kg weight loss. Laboratory studies showed normal hemoglobin; white-cell count with differential; C-reactive protein; serum albumin; immunoglobulin levels; iron studies; vitamin B12; and folate; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 40 mm/hr. Chest radiograph was normal. Two stool examinations for occult blood, leukocytes, parasites, and bacterial pathogens were negative. Colonoscopy with biopsies was unremarkable, and duodenal biopsies showed only mild, non-diagnostic villous changes. Serologic tests for tissue transglutaminase antibodies, endomysial antibodies, chromogranin-A, and HIV were negative. A small-bowel videocapsule endoscopy demonstrated mucosal areas of denuded villi and prominent submucosal vessels in the jejunum, as well as multiple linear whitish lesions surrounded by reddish mucosa in the ileum.
title: Possible Strongyloides stercoralis infection diagnosed by videocapsule endoscopy in an immunocompetent patient with devastating diarrhea

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man presented with multiple erythematous to violaceous papules and excoriations on both lower extremities for two weeks. The lesions began as pea-sized papules on the ankles and spread over the entire lower extremities; excoriations occasionally bled and were macerated. Empiric oral steroids and antibiotics produced no improvement. He had no prior medical conditions, family history of skin cancer, or systemic symptoms. 

On examination, vital signs were stable, and numerous non-tender 1–2 cm papules overlying erythema with pitting edema were noted on both legs. 

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (63,500/mm^3), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (41 mm/h), elevated C-reactive protein (24.3 mg/L), alkaline phosphatase (458 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (1,067 U/L). Abdominal CT revealed splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. 

Peripheral blood smear demonstrated >90% segmented neutrophils and 4.6% neutrophilic precursors including promyelocytes, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes. Bone marrow biopsy was hypercellular with abundant neutrophils and scant erythroid cells and megakaryocytes. 

Skin biopsy of a new lesion showed diffuse dermal infiltration by inhomogeneous neutrophils with pustules; higher magnification revealed mature and immature neutrophils with nuclear atypia, mitotic figures, and bizarre segmented bands. Myeloperoxidase staining of the infiltrate was strongly positive.
title: Leukemia Cutis in Chronic Neutrophilic Leukemia Associated with Colony Stimulating Factor 3 Receptor Mutation: Clinical Severity Paralleled with Hematologic Abnormality

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man presented with several weeks of persistent epigastric abdominal pain that was nonradiating and not associated with nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel habits, or weight loss. He denied jaundice, postprandial vomiting, or early satiety. His medical history was unremarkable, with no prior abdominal surgery, trauma, infections, or congenital disorders. On examination, the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and without masses or tenderness.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver function tests, serum amylase, and lipase, were all within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound showed no biliary pathology. Gastroscopy revealed normal gastric and duodenal mucosa without ulcers or masses.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a well-defined, nonenhancing 36 × 30 mm soft-tissue lesion in the aortocaval (retroduodenal) region with punctate calcifications; there was no lymphadenopathy or ascites. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed an isoechoic 36 × 30 mm mass between the inferior vena cava and aorta; fine-needle biopsy was deferred because of bleeding risk.

To exclude a paraganglioma, 24-hour urine collections for normetanephrine and metanephrine were obtained and were within normal limits. Gallium-68 PET/CT showed no increased tracer uptake in the lesion. The patient was referred for surgical evaluation.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Retroduodenal lymphangiomyoma: A rare cause of abdominal pain – A case report

case_prompt:
A 70‐year‐old man with a history of multivessel coronary artery disease, multiple prior stents, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted electively for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Over the preceding three months, he had progressive chest pain and exertional dyspnea. A nuclear stress test demonstrated anterior and anterolateral reversible defects with a drop in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) from 47% at rest to 31% on stress and a blood pressure decrease from 125/77 to 106/44 mmHg. A limited echocardiogram showed an LVEF of 40%–45% with anterior and lateral wall hypokinesis.

On admission, he was afebrile, blood pressure 130/84 mmHg, heart rate 87 beats/min, and in sinus rhythm. Physical examination was unremarkable. An initial electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with frequent premature ventricular contractions and an atypical left bundle branch block.

He underwent triple‐vessel CABG (LAD, OM1, RPL1) with cardiopulmonary bypass, systemic cooling to 34°C, and cardioplegia every 15–20 minutes. Postoperatively, he was transferred to the cardiac ICU with temporary epicardial pacing wires and brief norepinephrine support. Routine chest tube removal occurred on postoperative day 1.

On postoperative day 1, telemetry recorded a 4‐second run of high‐grade atrioventricular block with ventricular standstill. The patient remained fully alert and asymptomatic without syncope. Over postoperative day 2, multiple additional 3–5 second episodes of ventricular standstill were noted, all asymptomatic and without capture by the epicardial pacer wires. Serum electrolytes were within normal limits (potassium 3.6–4.1 mEq/L; magnesium 2.1–2.5 mg/dL; calcium 7.8–8.4 mg/dL; sodium 134–140 mEq/L). On postoperative day 3, a rhythm strip showed atrial flutter with loss of capture from the epicardial pacemaker; the patient remained asymptomatic.
title: Asymptomatic paroxysmal ventricular standstill in an elderly male following revascularization of multivessel coronary disease: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of intermittent, bilateral bloody tearing. Her menarche began at age 13, with regular menstrual cycles and no correlation between episodes of bloody tearing and menses. She had no history of trauma, bleeding diathesis, or hematologic disorders, and there was no relevant family history.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Findings on slit-lamp examination, intraocular pressures, and funduscopy were normal. Pupils were equal and reactive. There were no foreign bodies, vascular lesions, or lacerations on the eyelids, conjunctiva, cornea, or in the punctal region. The lacrimal glands were neither enlarged nor tender, and compression of the nasolacrimal ducts did not produce a blood-stained discharge. Nasolacrimal passages were patent.

Dacryocystography and gradient-echo magnetic resonance imaging of the nasolacrimal canals showed no abnormalities. Intranasal endoscopic evaluation was normal.

Two samples of the bloody tears were sent for pathological examination; analysis revealed numerous squamous cells and dysplastic cells but no endometrial tissue. Hematologic workup, including platelet count, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, bleeding time, and a full coagulation panel, was within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 1–2 cm ovarian cyst. Further investigations for systemic or ocular causes were unrevealing.
title: Idiopathic Bilateral Bloody Tearing

case_prompt:
A 12-year-old boy was referred with a 1-week history of bloody diarrhea (8–10 times per day) and a 2-week history of vomiting (initially clear, then bilious, 3–5 times per day), high-grade intermittent fever with chills and rigors, arthralgias, and unquantified weight loss. He had swum in a pond and experienced a transient pruritic skin rash. At a local health center, he was treated with metronidazole, ceftriaxone, cimetidine, vitamin B complex, and vitamin K for presumed fulminant viral hepatitis, schistosomiasis, and acute kidney injury and then referred for further evaluation.

On examination, he appeared acutely ill. Temperature was 37.8 °C; other vital signs were normal. Abdominal palpation revealed epigastric tenderness and hepatomegaly (liver span 11 cm); the rectal examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Negative serologies for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody.  
• Total bilirubin 2.33 mg/dL (subsequently 1.84 mg/dL); direct bilirubin 1.69 mg/dL (later 1.53 mg/dL).  
• AST 137 U/L (subsequently 35 U/L); ALT 110 U/L (subsequently 41 U/L).  
• Coagulation: PTT 68.2 s, PT 21.1 s, INR 2.41 (PT later 16.4 s, INR 1.17).  
• Renal: BUN 85 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL (BUN/Cr 26.5).  
• CBC: WBC 12,000/mm3 (neutrophils 67.8%, lymphocytes 22.5%, eosinophils 9.7%), platelets 92,000/mm3.  
• Stool microscopy: Schistosoma mansoni ova and Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites; H. pylori antigen negative.  
• Fecal calprotectin normal.  
• Abdominal ultrasound: hepatomegaly with hypodense hepatic nodules and marked colonic and small-bowel wall thickening and edema consistent with enterocolitis.  
• Urinalysis: leukocytes +1, WBCs 7–10/HPF, protein +2, ketones +1.  
• Electrolytes and blood glucose were normal.

Video pan-colonoscopy to the cecum showed diffuse colonic mucosal inflammation, intense rectal involvement, extensive ulceration, exudates, and loss of vascular pattern. A rectal biopsy was obtained with the clinical impression of ulcerative colitis versus inflammatory bowel disease.
title: Fulminant Hepatitis and Ulcerative Colitis: Case Report of Ethiopian Child with Schistosomiasis and Amebiasis Co-Infection

case_prompt: A 44-year-old woman with a history of possible inflammatory arthritis presented with abdominal fullness and early satiety. She had no family history or stigmata of connective tissue disease. Laboratory testing showed mildly elevated alanine aminotransferase (89 U/L; reference, 14–54 U/L). An abdominal ultrasound performed to evaluate possible gallbladder disease disclosed a mass in the neck of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT imaging confirmed two well-circumscribed pancreatic nodules measuring approximately 1.4 cm and 0.6 cm in diameter; there was no lymphadenopathy or hepatic lesions. The patient also reported periodic diaphoresis and tremulousness; home glucose measurements during these episodes were as low as 60 mg/dL, with symptom resolution after oral glucose. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed at least one hypoechoic pancreatic lesion, and fine-needle aspiration was nondiagnostic. The patient underwent a 72-hour supervised fast during which multiple serum glucose levels measured 40 mg/dL (reference, 70–125 mg/dL), but insulin was 9 mcIU/mL (reference, <18 mcIU/mL) and C-peptide was 0.2 ng/mL (reference, 1.0–7.6 ng/mL), findings felt to be inconsistent with an insulinoma.
title: Nodular Elastosis of the Pancreas

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman with stage IV clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (liver and lung metastases) underwent left nephrectomy in June and then received three cycles of ipilimumab (1 mg/kg) plus nivolumab (240 mg) in August. Her history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, asthma, and treated early colon cancer. In October she developed immune-related liver dysfunction treated with prednisolone (60 mg tapered to 30 mg). On day –5 she had a 5-day sore throat and nasal discharge; EBV titers suggested past infection and CMV antigen was negative. 

On day 0 she developed anorexia, fatigue, and erythema on her face and trunk. By day 3 she was hypotensive (89/55 mmHg) and hypoxic (SpO₂ 92% on 5 L/min oxygen). Chest CT showed bilateral ground-glass opacities sparing the periphery, bilateral pleural effusions, and interlobular septal thickening. Abdominal CT revealed ascites without adrenal abnormality. Laboratory tests demonstrated elevated C-reactive protein, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, eosinophilia, and stable liver enzymes. ECG was normal; echocardiography showed no wall motion or valvular abnormalities and a collapsed central vein (5 mm diameter). Despite ongoing prednisolone 30 mg, hypotension worsened (74/52 mmHg) and hypoxia progressed (SpO₂ 96% on 12 L/min). Concerned for immune-related adverse event or severe infection, the patient was started on methylprednisolone pulse therapy (500–1000 mg daily) and meropenem.
title: Cytokine Release Syndrome with Relative Adrenal Insufficiency Induced by Ipilimumab and Nivolumab Combination Therapy for Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old woman underwent routine screening mammography, which revealed a nonpalpable mass in the left breast. Her medical history was notable only for controlled hypertension and mild osteoarthritic changes. She had three pregnancies, two deliveries, and breastfed for a total of 30 months. She denied any breast pain, nipple discharge, skin changes, or prior breast surgery or biopsy. A mammogram two years earlier was normal.

On physical examination, there was no palpable mass, skin erythema or dimpling, nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy.

Diagnostic imaging:  
• Mammography demonstrated an isodense, circumscribed, oval mass, 1.8 × 1.0 cm, at the junction of the upper quadrants of the left breast.  
• Ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic, homogeneous, oval lesion measuring 1.4 × 0.7 cm, parallel to the skin, with two lobulations, circumscribed margins, and no posterior acoustic shadowing or hyperechoic halo.  

The lesion was classified as BI-RADS category 4.
title: Leiomyoma of the breast parenchyma: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 1-week history of worsening central vision in his left eye. He had a history of recurrent tonsillitis treated empirically with amoxicillin but no other medical issues, travel, or tick exposures. He had no prior ocular history.

On examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. Pupils were equal and reactive; intraocular pressures were normal. The anterior chambers and vitreous cavities were quiet bilaterally. Dilated fundus examination of the left eye revealed a whitish sub-retinal lesion temporal to the fovea with a small associated hemorrhage; the right eye was unremarkable.

Optical coherence tomography of the left macula showed a hyperreflective sub-retinal elevation with a small pocket of fluid. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated focal late-phase hyperfluorescence temporal to the fovea. Indocyanine green angiography revealed early blockage with mild late leakage and isolated focal hypocyanescent areas. OCT angiography showed a coralliform vascular complex originating in the choroid and traversing the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch’s membrane into the sub-retinal space.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts and chemistries. Rapid plasma reagin, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, antinuclear antibody profile, and toxoplasmosis titers were nonreactive. Chest radiography demonstrated a calcified nodule in the right upper lung field. 

He was treated with an intravitreal bevacizumab injection in the left eye.
title: Inflammatory choroidal neovascularization associated with immunoglobulin G4-related disease: a case report

case_prompt:
An 80-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-year history of a gradually enlarging mass on the left side of her neck. She reported mild dysphagia but denied any dysphonia or dyspnea. On examination, there was a firm, smooth, pulsatile left laterocervical swelling measuring 6 × 5 cm with regular margins; no cranial-nerve palsies were noted.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck demonstrated a 3.7 × 3.0 × 5.7 cm hypodense, heterogeneous mass that did not enhance, displacing the common, external, and internal carotid arteries anteriorly and the internal jugular vein anterolaterally. On MRI, the lesion was low in signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high in signal intensity on T2-weighted images. These radiological findings aligned most closely with a diagnosis of vagal nerve schwannoma, although cervical sympathetic chain schwannoma could not be excluded.
title: Cervical sympathetic chain schwannoma masquerading as a vagus nerve: a case report

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman with a five-year history of essential thrombocythemia presented after detection of a palpable mass in her left flank. She reported no weight loss, fever, or abdominal pain. On examination, the liver and spleen were both enlarged and palpable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.7 g/dL, platelet count 73 × 10^3/µL, and leukocyte count 24 010/µL. Serum α-fetoprotein was <3 ng/mL, and serologic tests for hepatitis B, C, and A were negative. A recent bone marrow biopsy demonstrated transformation of essential thrombocythemia into idiopathic myelofibrosis.

Noncontrast CT of the abdomen revealed a 2-cm, well-defined, homogeneously low-attenuation mass in segment VI of the liver, with diffuse hepatosplenomegaly. On portal-venous-phase contrast-enhanced CT, the lesion showed intense homogeneous enhancement; no other focal lesions were identified. On MRI, the mass was homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on fat-saturated T2-weighted images, with no signal change on in- and opposed-phase T1 sequences. After administration of gadolinium contrast, the lesion enhanced homogeneously and intensely in the arterial phase and remained enhanced at five minutes. Ten minutes after intravenous superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) administration, there was no signal drop in the lesion on T2*-weighted images.

Considering her history of anabolic steroid use for thrombocythemia and the appearance of a well-defined hypervascular lesion, the leading radiologic diagnosis was hepatocellular adenoma. Differential considerations also included focal nodular hyperplasia, hepatocellular carcinoma, angiomyolipoma, and a solitary hypervascular metastasis.
title: Intrahepatic Extramedullary Hematopoiesis Mimicking a Hypervascular Hepatic Neoplasm on Dynamic- and SPIO-Enhanced MRI

case_prompt: A 16-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of sore throat, progressive dyspnea, and spiking fevers. On arrival, his temperature was 103 °F and SpO₂ was 89% on room air; other physical findings were unremarkable. Initial laboratory tests showed a normal white cell count, normal liver function and coagulation tests, but mild anemia, mildly elevated bilirubin, and increased LDH. Notable abnormalities included a creatinine of 277 μmol/L, urea of 94 mg/dL, and D-dimers of 13 970 µg/L. A chest radiograph was initially normal. He was admitted with a working differential of sepsis-induced acute kidney injury, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and pulmonary-renal syndrome. Over the next 48 hours, he deteriorated with worsening dyspnea, hypoxia (SpO₂ 70% despite supplemental oxygen), and a leukocytosis to 24 × 10⁹/L. Repeat chest radiography demonstrated extensive bilateral consolidation, and a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest revealed right-sided extensive consolidation with a parapneumonic effusion. An extensive diagnostic workup including ANA, anti-GBM antibodies, tests for infectious mononucleosis, pneumococcal and Legionella antigens, influenza A and B, and respiratory syncytial virus was negative. Thoracentesis yielded exudative pleural fluid; both Gram and Ziehl–Neelsen stains were negative.
title: Human Infection with Fusobacterium necrophorum without Jugular Venous Thrombosis: A Varied Presentation of Lemierre's Syndrome

case_prompt: A 55-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass on the left palate, accompanied by left-sided nasal blockage, facial pain, and intermittent epistaxis. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 18 years and denied alcohol use. On examination, he had left-sided facial swelling and palpable left cervical lymphadenopathy. Nasal endoscopy revealed a frail, vascular mass nearly filling the left nasal cavity, with extension into the left palate. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a heterogeneous mass of the left maxillary sinus and nasal cavity with destructive extension through the hard palate into the retromaxillary and premaxillary spaces; there was no intracranial or intraorbital spread. Multiple necrotic lymph nodes were noted in the left upper deep cervical, submental, and submandibular regions. Biopsies of the nasal mass and a cervical lymph node were reported as undifferentiated carcinoma.
title: INI-1-Deficient Sinonasal Carcinoma: Case Report with Emphasis on Differential Diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman underwent cementless ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty through a straight lateral approach for a displaced femoral neck fracture. She was immunocompetent, non-diabetic, a light smoker, and had an uneventful early postoperative course: afebrile by postoperative day 2, dry wound without inflammation, halving of CRP every 2 days, and resumed mobility and pain-free hip function. She was discharged on day 8. Skin staples were removed on day 14, and at 5 weeks postoperative her radiographs and clinical exam were excellent.

In the ninth postoperative week, she developed tenderness, warmth, and redness around the surgical scar. Examination revealed a small draining sinus with minimal seropurulent discharge. Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level of 1.4 mg/dL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/h; the white blood cell count was normal. Ultrasonography demonstrated an abscess in the deep layer of the hypodermis with multiple sinus tracts toward the surface. Given the local signs, imaging findings, and elevated CRP, the team scheduled prompt surgical irrigation and debridement.
journal: Journal of Orthopaedics and Traumatology : Official Journal of the Italian Society of Orthopaedics and Traumatology
title: Suture-related pseudoinfection after total hip arthroplasty

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old Hispanic man with a 1-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (diagnosed on renal biopsy) and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, progressive shortness of breath, and bilateral lower extremity edema. He also reported leg pain. He underwent emergent hemodialysis for hyperkalemia, uremia, and hypervolemia, but his abdominal symptoms persisted. 

On examination, he was icteric with significant right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies on admission showed:  
– AST 2365 µ/L, ALT 1315 µ/L (peaking at 3594 µ/L and 1705 µ/L on hospital day 1)  
– Total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL  
– Albumin 2.2 g/dL  
– INR 1.9 (no anticoagulation)  

Initial evaluation for acute liver failure revealed immunity to hepatitis A and B, false-positive hepatitis C serology but negative RNA titers, and a negative toxicology screen for acetaminophen. Right upper quadrant ultrasound with Doppler flow was normal, excluding venous thrombosis, cirrhosis, steatosis, or mass. There was no history of hypotension to suggest ischemic hepatitis, and no clinical evidence of metabolic liver disease. Autoimmune hepatitis markers were negative, including anti–mitochondrial and anti–smooth muscle antibodies. Complement levels were low at C3 23.6 mg/dL (normal 80–150) and C4 3.8 mg/dL (normal 15–40).
title: Acute Hepatic Failure and Epididymitis in a Hispanic Patient With Active Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

case_prompt: A 35-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of bilateral frontal, episodic headaches and secondary amenorrhea. Six months before referral, evaluation revealed a prolactin level of 125 ng/mL (reference, 4.8–23.3 ng/mL) and a pituitary MRI reported as a 13×10×12 mm macroadenoma. Cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly was started, but after 6 months her amenorrhea persisted and gonadotropin levels remained low. She had no personal or family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, vital signs were normal and visual fields were full. Laboratory testing demonstrated panhypopituitarism. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the sella showed a 13×11×12 mm lesion with heterogeneous intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images, diffuse enhancement extending toward the infundibulum and dura, and no optic-chiasm compression. These findings were interpreted as suggestive of a complicated cyst, cystic adenoma, hemorrhage, or hypophysitis. Hydrocortisone and levothyroxine were initiated, and transsphenoidal surgery was planned for tissue diagnosis and decompression.
title: Xanthomatous Hypophysitis Secondary to a Ruptured Rathke’s Cleft Cyst: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A male infant was delivered at 35 5/7 weeks’ gestation via induced vaginal delivery after partial placental abruption. The mother, of European descent with hypothyroidism, had an unremarkable pregnancy until a 19-week anatomy scan that demonstrated a small intracranial cyst. A follow-up fetal MRI at 25 weeks showed a large, posterior midline, extra-axial vascular structure—a giant venous lake at the torcular herophili and posterior superior sagittal sinus—with evidence of partial thrombus, mass effect on adjacent cerebral and cerebellar parenchyma, noncommunicating hydrocephalus, and effacement of the prepontine cistern.

At birth, the infant was macrocephalic and minimally responsive but was hemodynamically stable, fed by mouth, and breathed room air. On day 1, brain MRI revealed a 5.8 × 5 × 8.8 cm posterior midline extra-axial structure with restricted diffusion, hydrocephalus without transependymal flow, and cerebellar tonsillar herniation 9 mm below the foramen magnum. Given the size of the lesion and herniation, the family was counseled regarding palliative care versus intervention. The infant’s stable vital signs and feeding led to a decision to discharge home for close follow-up.
title: The Case of the Rare Malformation and Rare Variant: An Infant with a Self-Embolized Torcular Dural Sinus Malformation and a Concomitant Prothrombin Variant

case_prompt: A 55-year-old Asian Indian woman presented with a several-month history of menorrhagia, abdominal discomfort, and pain. On examination, a non-tender, fixed mass was palpable in the lower abdomen. Ultrasound revealed an abdominopelvic mass and ascites. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a lobulated, calcified mass measuring 17 × 15 × 16 cm in the abdominopelvic cavity. Cytologic examination of ascitic fluid was positive for malignant cells. At exploratory laparotomy, both ovaries were enlarged with intact capsules. A total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed; no pelvic or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy or peritoneal nodules were identified. Grossly, the left ovary measured 24 × 20 × 20 cm with a smooth, lobulated surface; on sectioning it was solid, gray-white, gritty, and granular without necrosis. The right ovary measured 7 × 6 × 2 cm and showed small cysts filled with clear fluid.
title: Psammocarcinoma of ovary with serous cystadenofibroma of contralateral ovary: a case report

case_prompt: A 64-year-old woman with diabetes, hypertension, and hypothyroidism presented with a 3-week history of violaceous, edematous, vegetative, ulcerated plaques on the forehead, nose, and chin (sparing the nasal bridge) and a few erythematous, smooth, umbilicated papules and nodules on the left arm. The rash was refractory to oral and topical antibiotics. She reported facial pain and a mild cough but denied fevers at presentation, new medications, recent travel, or excess ultraviolet exposure. Laboratory testing showed elevated inflammatory markers; infectious and autoimmune panels were otherwise unremarkable, and antidesmoglein antibody titers were negative. Tissue cultures were negative. An initial skin biopsy demonstrated ulcerated skin with mixed dermal inflammation. A repeat biopsy revealed marked papillary dermal edema with superficial and deep perivascular and interstitial lymphohistiocytic inflammation; immunohistochemical staining for myeloperoxidase (MPO) and Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA were both negative. Correlating the clinical and histologic findings, the working diagnosis was atypical polymorphous light eruption versus discoid lupus. She completed a 21-day systemic corticosteroid taper but returned with fevers, malaise, and recrudescence of the umbilicated nodules.
title: An atypical facial eruption in skin of color: A rare presentation of histiocytoid Sweet syndrome

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old woman with a history of sick sinus syndrome diagnosed 9 years earlier presented with progressive shortness of breath and a decline from New York Heart Association functional class I to II. A Holter electrocardiogram revealed a total heart rate of approximately 55 000 beats per day. Chest radiography showed an increased cardiothoracic ratio, and stress echocardiography demonstrated an impaired heart rate response to exercise. The patient was scheduled for permanent pacemaker implantation. 

On admission, her blood pressure was 109/66 mmHg, heart rate 37 bpm, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed clear lung sounds, no heart murmurs, and no lower extremity edema. Her medical history included diabetes mellitus and a treated submucous uterine myoma. Laboratory studies showed an N-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide level of 132 pg/mL (normal <55 pg/mL), with normal creatinine and electrolytes. 

Chest radiography revealed no lung infiltration and a cardiothoracic ratio of 55%. Electrocardiography showed sinus bradycardia at 43 bpm. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a dilated coronary sinus and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 71% without significant valvular disease. Preprocedural cardiac multidetector computed tomography revealed a persistent left superior vena cava with an absent right superior vena cava and showed no significant coronary artery stenosis.
title: Pacemaker implantation in a patient with isolated persistent left superior vena cava using a delivery catheter: a case report

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old woman was evaluated for an incidentally discovered distal pancreatic mass. Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration revealed adenocarcinoma. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. She underwent distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and adrenalectomy for vascular involvement, and a right internal jugular venous port was placed intraoperatively.

On postoperative day 5, she developed fever. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a peripancreatic fluid collection, which was drained under ultrasound guidance; cultures were negative, and she remained on antibiotics with persistent low-grade fever. By day 21, she had high-grade drenching fevers and respiratory distress. Chest CT angiography demonstrated partial thrombosis of the superior vena cava with air bubbles, suspicious for an infected thrombus. The port was removed; cultures of the port grew Candida species on two occasions, while three sets of simultaneous blood cultures were negative. A follow-up abdominal CT scan was normal. Laboratory studies were nonspecific, and a full sepsis workup was nondiagnostic. Physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Caspofungin was added, and she defervesced by postoperative day 30; she was discharged on caspofungin.

Two weeks later, she presented with severe weakness, new low back pain, and low-grade fever. Conservative management was initiated, and an abdominal CT scan remained normal. Despite this, her symptoms—weakness, back pain, and intermittent low-grade fever—persisted for three months. A thoracoabdominal CT scan was then performed and revealed destruction of the T6 and T7 vertebral bodies. Neurologic examination remained normal, and she had no ambulatory difficulties aside from profound weakness. Thoracic MRI confirmed destruction and collapse of the T6 and T7 vertebral bodies.
title: Fever of unknown origin as the first presentation of candida vertebral osteomyelitis: A case report

case_prompt: A 45-year-old man presented with a 2–3 month history of recurrent, self-limited left-sided epistaxis, each episode lasting up to 10 minutes. He also noted intermittent dull pain over the left side of his nose and a sensation of a slowly enlarging intranasal mass, without nasal obstruction or facial numbness. An attempt at excision under local anesthesia was aborted because of brisk bleeding, and he was referred to our clinic. On arrival, bleeding had ceased. Medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension; there was no tobacco, alcohol, or drug use, and no family history of cancer. Examination revealed a healthy, obese man with marginally elevated blood pressure. Nasal inspection, after removal of a nosepad and suction, showed a well-circumscribed 10 mm mass on the anterior face of the left inferior turbinate; the surface had several incision marks from the prior procedure. Anterior and posterior rhinoscopy otherwise were unremarkable. External examination revealed a slight palpable swelling between the lateral cartilage and nasal bone on the left. Contrast-enhanced CT of the nasal cavity demonstrated a 24 mm lesion of the inferior turbinate with only marginal enhancement, no bony erosion, and uncertain involvement of the adjacent lateral nasal cartilage. Subsequent MRI showed a 9 × 11 × 8 mm nodular, contrast-enhancing lesion arising from the lateral nasal wall at the level of the piriform aperture without any sign of infiltrative growth.
title: A Rare Differential Diagnosis of a Nasal Tumor: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman presented with 40 days of intermittent low-grade fever, cough, hemoptysis, and dyspnea. She had no systemic symptoms, no smoking or alcohol history, and no significant past illnesses. Initial chest radiographs and CT scans showed diffuse bilateral thick-walled cavitating nodules of varying sizes, consolidation in the right lower lobe, and a small right pleural effusion; mediastinal lymph nodes and vasculature appeared normal. Echocardiography demonstrated trivial tricuspid regurgitation without vegetations and normal left ventricular function. 

On examination she was pale and tachycardic (pulse 160/min), hypotensive (90/60 mm Hg), tachypneic (30/min), and afebrile. Respiratory auscultation revealed diffuse crackles and occasional rhonchi in the right mid and lower lung fields. Other systems were unremarkable. 

Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 11 370/mm3 (90% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, and platelets 248 000/mm3. Sputum cultures were negative for pyogenic bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi. She received broad-spectrum antibiotics without improvement; hemoglobin later fell to 7.1 g/dL despite transfusion, and she continued to have cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss. Repeat workup included negative blood cultures and Mantoux skin test, normal abdominal ultrasound, and serologies negative for ACE, ANA, RF, C-ANCA, anti-GBM, and anti-aspergillus antibodies, but positive CRP and intermittent P-ANCA by indirect immunofluorescence. 

Bronchoscopy revealed normal airway architecture but active bleeding from the right lower lobe bronchus that could not be controlled endoscopically.
journal: Lung India : Official Organ of Indian Chest Society
title: Isolated pauci-immune pulmonary capillaritis

case_prompt: A 76-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease secondary to chronic glomerulonephritis has been on peritoneal dialysis for two months. She was admitted for persistent fever (37–38°C) of three months’ duration and, more recently, mucous and bloody stools. Two months earlier, at the initiation of dialysis, physical examination and imaging were unrevealing; tuberculin skin testing and interferon-γ release assays were positive, and she received isoniazid, streptomycin, and rifampicin without resolution of fever. On transfer, her temperature was 39.1°C, blood pressure 134/66 mmHg, heart rate 72/min, and respiratory rate 12/min. Examination showed anemic conjunctivae, diffusely increased bowel sounds, abdominal tenderness, moderate bilateral pretibial pitting edema, and a peritoneal catheter exit site without signs of infection. Laboratory results were notable for leukocytes 4,810/μL (neutrophils 2,732/μL), hemoglobin 85 g/L, platelets 300,000/μL, C-reactive protein 161 nmol/L, albumin 21 g/L, BUN 10.35 mmol/L, creatinine 499.5 μmol/L; urinalysis showed 1+ proteinuria and 1+ hematuria; stool was guaiac-positive. Abdominal radiography revealed loss of haustral markings throughout the descending colon. Contrast-enhanced CT showed extensive circumferential wall thickening from the ascending colon to the rectum without abscess formation.
title: Ulcerative Colitis Presented as Fever and Bloody Diarrhea at Initiation of Dialysis in an Elderly Patient with End-Stage Kidney Disease

case_prompt: A 25-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of dull, aching pain in the right groin that was insidious in onset, gradually progressive, nonradiating, aggravated by walking and squatting, and relieved by rest and medications. He noted an abduction gait and progressive restriction of right hip motion. There was no history of trauma. On examination, the skin over the medial right groin was unremarkable, and no sinus, scar, or swelling was present. A firm mass was palpable in the right perineal region. Active adduction of the right hip was limited to 20°, external rotation to 25°, internal rotation to 10°, and extension to 5°. Thigh muscle circumference on the right was decreased by 2 cm compared with the left. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, and alkaline phosphatase, were within normal limits. An anteroposterior pelvis radiograph showed a well-corticated bony protuberance arising from the right ischium and extending toward the lesser trochanter, with no evidence of joint degeneration. Computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed a 5.2 × 2.0 cm bone formation between the right ischial tuberosity and lesser trochanter. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated surrounding marrow edema but no cartilage cap.
title: A Rare Symptomatic Pelvic Rib – A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man presented with a one-month history of a right-sided abdominal swelling that became painful and irreducible over the past day. He reported multiple episodes of vomiting and no passage of stool or flatus for several hours. He denied any history of trauma, surgery, or activities raising intra-abdominal pressure. His medical history was notable for right undescended testis diagnosed at age 6 without subsequent treatment and azoospermia noted on two occasions; no hormonal workup had been performed. He had no major comorbidities and was a non-smoker; his BMI was 26.4 kg/m2.  

On examination, there was a firm, tender, 7 × 7 cm swelling in the right lumbar region in the midclavicular line. The swelling was non-pulsatile, non-fluctuant, irreducible, and had no cough impulse; the overlying skin was normal. Palpation of the scrotum revealed an empty right hemiscrotum, with the left testis palpable and normal. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (12.6 × 109/L) with granulocytosis, elevated creatine phosphokinase (689 U/L), and elevated CK-MB (59 U/L). Abdominal radiography demonstrated distended small-bowel loops with multiple air–fluid levels, consistent with small-bowel obstruction. Ultrasonography revealed mild small-bowel dilation with increased peristalsis and confirmed an empty right scrotum; the right testis was visualized lateral to the rectus abdominis muscle. The imaging studies suggested a small abdominal wall hernia causing obstruction and ipsilateral cryptorchidism, but the precise location of the hernial defect was unclear.  

Given these findings, a right-sided hernia with cryptorchidism was suspected, and open hernial repair was planned.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: An unusual presentation of cryptorchidism: A case report of Spigelian-cryptorchidism syndrome☆☆☆

case_prompt: A 28-year-old woman presented with a 14-day history of epigastric pain partially relieved by mild analgesics. She also reported diffuse pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. Examination showed a well-appearing but jaundiced patient with a firm, palpable mass in the epigastric and right hypochondrial regions. Laboratory studies revealed a cholestatic pattern of liver‐function tests; CEA and CA19-9 levels were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a large (approximately 13 × 9 × 13 cm), heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass with internal cystic areas located between the left hepatic lobe and pancreas, with dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts and proximal common bile duct. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined, 12.8 × 12.1 × 10.9 cm lesion centered in the pancreatic head and body, with mixed solid and cystic components, intense enhancement, displacement but no invasion of adjacent structures, and marked dilation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.
title: Primitive Neuroectodermal Tumor of the Pancreas: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 39-year-old healthy man on HIV preexposure prophylaxis presented with a 4-day history of painless papules in the genital region and  painful erythema and edema of the left groin. He had been traveling in Europe and reported unprotected sexual activity with multiple male partners 10 days before presentation. On return to Israel, he obtained a new tattoo on his left arm. He was afebrile. Examination showed 4 discrete umbilicated papules with adherent brown crust at the base of the penile shaft and suprapubic area. Dermoscopy revealed white radiating peripheral lines and a central reddish-brown structureless zone. The left groin had a tender, warm, erythematous mass. Complete blood count and basic metabolic panel were normal; C-reactive protein was 46 mg/dL. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Blood and throat cultures were unrevealing. Serologic tests for syphilis (TPHA, VDRL), hepatitis A, B, and C, and HIV were negative.
title: Sexually transmitted monkeypox with pseudo-koebnerization within a tattoo

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old male farmer presented with a 2-year history of an ulcer in the right inguinal–scrotal region associated with hemorrhagic points at the scrotal–inguinal junction, which eventually progressed to the contralateral side. He also reported a 9-kg weight loss over 6 months but denied fever, cough, dyspnea, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a 1 × 10 cm ulcerated lesion with a granulomatous base and hemorrhagic points at the transition between the scrotum and the right inguinal area, extending slightly to the opposite side. 

An incisional biopsy was performed. Histopathological analysis showed non-specific chronic dermatitis with intraepidermal microabscesses, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and numerous yeast cells of varying sizes amidst scattered giant cells. Fungal culture and direct microscopic examination of the tissue specimen were negative.

Chest computed tomography revealed a confluent ground-glass opacity in the right middle lobe without mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Serologic tests for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. Sputum studies for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and fungal elements were also negative.
title: Genital cutaneous ulcer as a manifestation of systemic mycosis: A rare presentation

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of bilateral lower-extremity radiculopathy and neurogenic claudication with a walking distance of approximately 300 m. She reported intermittent low back pain but denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, or a history of tuberculosis.  
On examination, she was afebrile, and there was no paraspinal tenderness, muscle spasm, or local warmth. Neurologic examination was unremarkable except for mild bilateral lower-extremity paresthesias.  
Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine showed hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum and a posterior soft-tissue mass causing significant spinal-canal narrowing.  
Computed tomography of the lumbar spine demonstrated a lytic lesion in the right lamina of the second lumbar vertebra.  
Laboratory studies revealed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.
title: Unusual Presentation of Koch’s Spine Involving Posterior Elements of Vertebra– A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old woman with no prior thyroid disease presented with progressive anterior neck pain, headache, asthenia, insomnia, hand tremor, hyperhidrosis, diarrhea, weight loss of 8 kg, and palpitations. These symptoms began 14 days after a mild SARS-CoV-2 infection confirmed by PCR one month earlier and had initially regressed with symptomatic therapy. She had delivered a child one year ago and denied recent iodine exposure. On examination, palpation of the neck was painful without discrete nodules; the thyroid gland was slightly enlarged and tender. The skin was warm and moist, and a fine finger tremor was noted. Laboratory studies showed:  
• TSH 0.005 mIU/L (reference 0.27–4.20),  
• fT3 15.5 pmol/L (3.1–6.8),  
• fT4 51.8 pmol/L (12–22),  
• ESR 98 mm/h,  
• CRP 78 mg/L (≤ 5).  
Thyroid ultrasonography revealed a 50 ml gland with an inhomogeneous, predominantly hypoechogenic structure and mild hyperperfusion throughout the organ.
title: Subacute Thyroiditis Complicating COVID-19 Infection

case_prompt: An 87-year-old man on oral anticoagulation presented with one week of right lower-quadrant abdominal pain and noted a tender mass with overlying erythema. He denied prior lower abdominal surgery. On examination he was febrile, and laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein and white blood cell count. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a large fluid collection in the right lower abdominal wall, which was interpreted as a superinfected hematoma. Incision and drainage were performed, yielding large amounts of pus, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated. Over the next several days, purulent wound discharge persisted, and he developed clinical signs of sepsis. A decision was made to obtain repeat imaging.
title: Incarcerated peri-inguinal hernia containing the appendix: a case report

case_prompt: A 4-month-old female infant was brought for evaluation of an upper-lip mass noted since birth. On examination, the lesion measured approximately 2×2 cm, was smooth, nonpulsatile, and mobile, occupied the midline and left upper lip with slight extension to the right, and caused deformation of the columella with superior displacement of the left alar. There was no respiratory distress. The mass did not transilluminate and did not change in size with crying. The remainder of the head, neck, and systemic examinations was unremarkable. Ultrasonography with color Doppler revealed a solid lesion without evidence of increased vascularity. Magnetic resonance imaging was planned to assess for an intracranial connection.
journal: Indian Journal of Plastic Surgery : Official Publication of the Association of Plastic Surgeons of India
title: Glial heterotopia of the lip: A rare presentation

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old woman with early-stage breast cancer presented with 2 days of weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and watery nonbloody diarrhea following a restaurant meal. In the emergency department, temperature was 37.4°C, heart rate 156 beats/min, and blood pressure 95/63 mm Hg; she was alert and oriented. Laboratory studies showed WBC 21 430/μL, hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, platelets 227 000/μL, potassium 3.5 mEq/L, lactate 8.68 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, BUN 37 mg/dL, and creatine kinase 10 846 U/L. She was diagnosed with hypovolemic shock and acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis, received aggressive IV fluids and empiric antibiotics, and was admitted to the ICU.

Over the next five days, she became anuric and transitioned from continuous renal replacement therapy to hemodialysis. She developed severe thrombocytopenia (nadir 50 ×10^3/μL) and anemia (hemoglobin nadir 5.0 g/dL). A peripheral blood smear showed numerous schistocytes and reticulocytosis, and laboratory tests confirmed hemolysis. Cold agglutinin, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria markers, antinuclear antibody, and direct antiglobulin tests were negative. Fecal pathogen PCR was positive for enteropathogenic Escherichia coli. ADAMTS13 activity was 32% (normal > 67%) with a PLASMIC score of 2 (low risk for TTP). Complement levels were low in the acute setting. An atypical HUS genetic panel was negative, and CH50 and C1 esterase inhibitor levels were normal. Other etiologies—including DIC, HELLP syndrome, severe hypertension, medication interactions, autoimmune disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, dialysis-related mechanical hemolysis, and occult malignancy—were ruled out. Urinalysis revealed 3+ hemoglobin without myoglobin, 15 RBCs/HPF, and nephrotic-range proteinuria (2 g/day).
title: A unique case of hemolytic‐uremic syndrome secondary to enteropathogenic E Coli

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old South Asian woman with systemic lupus erythematosus complicated by class IV lupus nephritis and hypertension, in clinical remission on prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine, and antihypertensives, received her first dose of intravenous rituximab (375 mg/m2). Ten days later, she presented with one day of spontaneous oral and nasal bleeding and new patchy ecchymoses on her trunk and extremities. She had no other complaints.  
On examination, she had oozing blood from the gums, two blood-filled blisters on the hard palate, blood on the alar nares without crusting, and multiple ecchymotic patches. The spleen tip was palpable. The rest of the examination was unremarkable.  
Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• Platelet count 5 × 10^9/L (150–450)  
• Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL (11–15)  
• White-cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L (4–11)  
• Serum creatinine 98 μmol/L (44–97)  
• Serum albumin 4.03 g/dL  
• INR 0.92 (<1.0)  
• C-reactive protein 0.6 mg/dL (<5.0)  
• Direct Coombs test negative  
Blood smear confirmed severe thrombocytopenia without schistocytes or abnormal cells.
title: Rituximab induced acute thrombocytopenia in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus: a case report

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of vague left lower abdominal and back pain, abdominal fullness, lethargy, and a non-ballotable lump in the left lumbar and iliac region. She denied genitourinary, gastrointestinal, or gynecological symptoms. Laboratory tests showed microcytic hypochromic anemia, an ESR of 92 mm/hr, and a CRP of 24 mg/L. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed no monoclonal bands. Renal and liver function, 9 AM cortisol, testosterone level, 24-hour urine metanephrine, and vanillylmandelic acid were all within normal limits. Pan endoscopy was unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasound identified a 12 × 12 cm solid mass in the left suprarenal area. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 17.5 × 11.5 cm enhancing lesion replacing the left adrenal gland with peripheral coarse calcification, inferior displacement of the left kidney, and no lymphadenopathy; the contralateral adrenal gland and other intra-abdominal organs were normal. Comprehensive screening for extra-adrenal primary malignancies was negative.  
On this basis, a non-secreting left pheochromocytoma was considered, and elective laparoscopic left adrenalectomy was planned.
title: Pleomorphic spindle cell sarcoma of the adrenal gland: an extremely rare cause of a large abdominal mass and a challenging diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 78-year-old woman with palliative pancreatic head cancer presented initially with mild fever (37.6°C), upper abdominal pain, and jaundice. She had undergone chemotherapy and had a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, deep vein thrombosis (on rivaroxaban), and chemotherapy‐induced peripheral neuropathy. Contrast‐enhanced CT showed a dilated common bile duct and an enlarged gallbladder with wall thickening, suggestive of cholecystitis; no pseudoaneurysms were seen. ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy and nasobiliary drainage was performed, and two days later a fully covered self‐expandable metal stent was placed uneventfully. Her fever and jaundice resolved, and she was discharged 7 days after stent placement.

Seven days after stent placement, she returned with two episodes of copious hematochezia accompanied by mild upper abdominal pain and fever. On examination, her temperature was 37.0°C, heart rate 87 bpm, blood pressure 137/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and SpO₂ 95% on room air. She was jaundiced but had no abdominal tenderness or Murphy’s sign. Laboratory tests demonstrated anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and elevated liver enzymes.
title: Ruptured cystic artery pseudoaneurysm after self‐expandable metal stent placement for malignant biliary obstruction

case_prompt: A 63-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia presented with a 2-week history of nonbloody, nonmucoid, watery diarrhea occurring more than 20 times daily, intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, and an 8-kg weight loss. He had been taking atorvastatin (20 mg daily) and olmesartan (20 mg daily) since 2019. He had no prior surgeries. Initial empirical treatment with nitazoxanide (3 days) and ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily for 7 days) yielded no improvement. There was no fever, and physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation revealed a white-cell count of 7420 cells/µL, hemoglobin of 14.4 g/dL, platelets of 174 × 10^3/µL, sodium 138 meq/L, potassium 3.8 meq/L, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, creatinine 1.05 mg/dL, ALT 65 U/L, and AST 51 U/L. Stool studies including culture, Clostridium difficile assay, leukocytes, ova and parasites, and fecal calprotectin were negative; fecal occult blood was initially positive. Serologic tests including tissue transglutaminase IgA, perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies were normal; TSH, C-reactive protein, and COVID-19 serologies were unremarkable. Colonoscopy with serial biopsies was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed gallbladder wall thickening, echogenic bile, hydrops, acalculous cholecystitis, and mild steatohepatitis. Gastroscopy demonstrated a small hiatal hernia, erythematous gastritis with mucosal erosions, and in the second part of the duodenum mucosal atrophy with loss of folds. Biopsies of the second portion of the duodenum revealed a severe atrophic mucosa with complete loss of villi and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.
