title: Olmesartan-Induced Enteropathy: A Rare Case of Chronic Diarrhea

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man with a 2-year history of late‐onset asthma presented with a 4-day history of shortness of breath and cough, beginning 4 days after receiving an influenza vaccine. He was initially treated for presumed pneumonia with ceftriaxone and levofloxacin, with some improvement in pulmonary symptoms. One week later, he developed palpable petechiae, purpura, and hemorrhagic bullae on the lower limbs that progressed to the face, accompanied by pain, stiffness, and swelling of both ankles, the left knee, and the left elbow. 

On hospital admission, vital signs were normal. Examination revealed widespread palpable petechiae and purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, and signs of arthritis in the affected joints. On hospital day 2, he reported tingling in the upper limbs and developed right wrist drop and left foot drop.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (13.64×10^3/µL) with 47% eosinophils, an ESR of 85 mm/h, CRP of 75 mg/L, and P-ANCA of 300 IU/mL (normal 0–15). ANA, anti-dsDNA, complements, rheumatoid factor, and serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were all within normal limits or negative. Spirometry demonstrated severe lower airway obstruction. Electrocardiogram and echocardiography were normal. Chest CT showed a mosaic parenchymal pattern with scattered subpleural opacities and pulmonary nodules. EMG-NCV revealed low-amplitude or absent sensory and motor potentials, consistent with moderate to severe axonal motor-dominant peripheral polyneuropathy and mononeuritis multiplex.  

A punch biopsy of a forearm skin lesion showed leukocytoclastic vasculitis with necrotic keratinocytes, subepidermal bullae, and eosinophils highlighted on Congo red staining.
title: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis following flu guard influenza vaccination: A case report

case_prompt: A 46‐year‐old male marathon runner presented with one week of localized right lower quadrant pain. The pain was excruciating when seated or upright, worsened with movement, and was relieved only in the supine position; he also experienced nausea. His only surgical history was orchidopexy in childhood. On examination, there was guarding and rigidity at McBurney’s point, rebound tenderness, and a positive psoas sign; the Rovsing sign was negative. No masses or cutaneous lesions were palpable. Hip flexion beyond 90° elicited pain, but internal and external rotation were pain‐free. Neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory studies were within normal limits except for a mildly elevated C‐reactive protein level of 12.5 mg/L; the Alvarado score was 4. A contrast‐enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed no abnormalities and excluded the classic causes of right lower quadrant pain. The patient was admitted for monitoring and NSAID pain management, but symptoms persisted despite stable laboratory values. Given the movement‐dependent pain, an MRI of the lumbar spine and neurologic evaluation were performed, revealing no pathology.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Abdominal Mondor disease mimicking acute appendicitis

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman, gravid 2 para 1, at 38 weeks’ gestation was admitted with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and decreased fetal movements. Her obstetrical history was notable for a Cesarean delivery in 2016 and, on antenatal ultrasound, velamentous cord insertion detected at 20 weeks and fetal growth restriction noted at 33 weeks. On admission, she was hemodynamically stable: heart rate 90/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. The uterine fundal height was 29 cm, and the fetal heart rate by Doppler was 150/min. Vaginal examination revealed a cervix 2 cm dilated, 60 % effaced, posterior.  
Ultrasound showed a single cephalic fetus with a biparietal diameter of 89 mm, femur length 67 mm, abdominal circumference 325 mm, estimated weight below the 10th percentile (2667 g), anterior Grade I placenta with velamentous cord insertion, and no free fluid in the abdomen. Continuous CTG tracing was reassuring, and routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.  
The preoperative diagnosis was second pregnancy at 38 weeks with transverse lie, intrauterine growth restriction, velamentous cord insertion, and previous Cesarean section scar.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Uterine torsion in pregnancy: A case report

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old healthy woman was referred to gynecology for a livid-colored umbilical nodule that had gradually increased in size over the past three years. She reported severe dysmenorrhea (NRS 10), dyspareunia (NRS 10), dyschezia (NRS 7), tenesmus, and cyclical umbilical bleeding synchronized with menstruation during withdrawal bleeding. She had irregular menses and was taking an ethinylestradiol–gestodene oral contraceptive. Her obstetric history included a cesarean delivery nine years earlier; five years ago she underwent laparoscopic appendectomy via an umbilical port, and the appendix showed histologic endometriosis. There was no family history of endometriosis.

On examination, the umbilicus contained a 1.2 cm soft, irreducible nodule with two bluish-purple dots and normal overlying skin; the lesion was painless. The rest of the abdominal exam was normal with no signs of hernia. Hormonal therapy was changed to continuous dienogest 2 mg, resulting in amenorrhea and cessation of umbilical bleeding.

Ultrasonography of the umbilical nodule revealed an image suggestive of a dermoid cyst. Pelvic CT scan demonstrated two contiguous left adnexal cystic lesions with peripheral contrast enhancement, for which the differential diagnosis included endometrioma, tubo-ovarian abscess, and serous cystadenoma. A second ultrasound of the nodule showed two superficial 2 mm cysts and a deeper 4 mm cyst with a nonspecific appearance compatible with sebaceous or dermal inclusion cysts. Pelvic MRI showed a 92 × 40 × 58 mm uterus with multiple small T2-hypointense intramural nodules consistent with leiomyomas, 6 mm endometrial thickness with findings suggestive of adenomyosis, and two left ovarian cysts (40 × 33 mm and 28 × 18 × 24 mm) with T1 hyperintensity and slight T2 hyperintensity, suggesting hemorrhagic cysts or endometriomas.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Umbilical Nodule with Cyclical Bleeding: A Case Report and Literature Review of Atypical Endometriosis

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old boy had 6 years of mucoid diarrhea, occasional rectal bleeding, and intermittent fecal incontinence.  
He had undergone colonoscopy elsewhere, which showed rectal pseudopolyps; biopsies demonstrated inflammation with granulation tissue.  
Laboratory tests revealed mild iron deficiency anemia and hypoalbuminemia.  
Several of the larger polyps were removed by endoscopic polypectomy, and he was treated with topical steroids and diphenoxylate-atropine, with minimal improvement.  
He was referred for surgical management but then evaluated by a pediatric gastroenterologist.  
Upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, and magnetic resonance enterography were performed to assess for inflammatory bowel disease.  
There was no endoscopic or radiographic evidence of inflammatory bowel disease, but colonoscopy again revealed marked, friable polyposis localized to the rectum.  
Tests for Helicobacter pylori infection were negative.
title: Cap Polyposis: An Elusive Diagnosis in a Pediatric Patient Successfully Managed With Endoscopic Treatment

case_prompt: A 21-year-old woman presented with sudden onset diffuse abdominal pain worse in the epigastrium and right lower quadrant, with associated vomiting, dysuria, and subjective fever. She denied vaginal bleeding; her last menstrual period was two months prior, and she denied any known pregnancy. She had one prior Cesarean delivery one year earlier and no history of gallstones. On exam she was afebrile, pulse 65/min, RR 24/min, BP 111/50 mm Hg. The abdomen was diffusely tender with involuntary guarding and rebound in the RUQ and RLQ. She declined a pelvic exam. Initial differential included acute pancreatitis, perforated peptic ulcer, appendicitis, cholecystitis with perforation, ovarian cyst rupture, and ectopic pregnancy. A urine pregnancy test was positive; serum β-hCG was 31 239 mIU/mL. Lipase was negative; WBC was 19.25 × 10^9/L; hemoglobin was 11.6 g/dL. A POCUS showed what appeared to be a live intrauterine pregnancy and large amounts of free fluid in the RUQ, spleen area, and RLQ. A formal ultrasound confirmed a 16-week live intrauterine pregnancy with an anterior placenta and free fluid. Obstetrics and surgery were consulted, and the working differential included appendicitis, ruptured ovarian cyst, or possibly a ruptured cervical ectopic pregnancy despite the ultrasound read. MRI of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained and was interpreted as revealing a low fetal implantation near the cervix concerning for cervical ectopic pregnancy; the majority of the uterine body lay above the fetus, and free fluid demonstrated increased T1 signal, suggesting hemoperitoneum. Hemoglobin subsequently fell to 9.7 g/dL.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Intra-abdominal Rupture of a Live Cervical Pregnancy with Placenta Accreta but Without Vaginal Bleeding

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old woman with a body mass index of 31.2 kg/m² and a history of diabetes and hypertension underwent bilateral total knee arthroplasty. Her postoperative course was unremarkable until the night before planned discharge (postoperative day 1), when she received an intramuscular injection of diclofenac in her right buttock for pain control. Immediately after the injection, she complained of intense pain at the site. On examination, the skin was swollen and diffusely erythematous with central blanching. 

The following morning, the area was exquisitely tender to palpation. Cutaneous findings included scattered erythematous macules and a livedoid, violaceous patch with dendritic extensions at the injection site. 

Initial differential diagnoses included an allergic reaction to diclofenac, acute bleeding, hematoma, and acute compartment syndrome.
title: Nicolau Syndrome in Patient Following Diclofenac Administration: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 32-year-old man with no prior medical history was referred for suspected meningitis after developing fever, headache, urinary retention, and constipation. Seven days before admission he had a sudden fever of 39 °C and received antibiotics the next day. Two days before admission he developed acute urinary retention requiring temporary catheterization. On admission, his temperature was 38 °C. Neurological examination showed nuchal rigidity; he was alert (GCS 15), cranial nerves were intact, motor and sensory exams were normal, deep tendon reflexes were intact, and Babinski signs were absent. He had a mild ataxic gait. Bladder-filling sensation was preserved but he was unable to void; anal sphincter reflex was depressed. Urodynamic studies demonstrated a noncontractile neurogenic bladder. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count and serum chemistry. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 240 mmH₂O, 127 mononuclear cells/μL, and a protein concentration of 202 mg/dL; bacterial smears and cultures were negative. CSF interleukin-6 was 18.3 pg/mL, myelin basic protein was 401.5 pg/mL, and oligoclonal bands were negative. Lumbosacral MRI performed on hospital day 4 showed no lesions in the spinal cord. Empiric intravenous acyclovir was started on admission and discontinued on hospital day 9 when CSF PCR for herpes simplex virus type 1 was negative.
title: Meningitis retention syndrome associated with complicated mild encephalitis/encephalopathy with reversible splenial lesion in a young adult patient: a case report

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old Saudi woman presented with an 8-month history of a right buttock swelling that had rapidly increased in size over the past 2 months and caused pain on sitting. She also reported lethargy but no weight loss or history of trauma. Her medical history included type 1 diabetes mellitus for 11 years and hypothyroidism for 4 years, treated with insulin and thyroxine 50 µg daily. She was a non-smoker.

On examination, vital signs were stable. In the right gluteal region there was a fixed, hard, noninflammatory mass measuring approximately 13 × 10 cm, moderately tender, with no inguinal lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the musculoskeletal and neurologic examinations was unremarkable. Neck examination revealed an enlarged, non-tender right thyroid lobe without cervical lymphadenopathy. Chest, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were normal.

Routine hematology, serum electrolytes, and liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. MRI of the pelvis demonstrated a 13 × 11.7 × 6.8 cm lobulated heterogeneous mass centered within the right gluteus medius muscle, also involving the gluteus maximus and piriformis muscles, and extending to the right iliac bone and sacroiliac joint. The anteroposterior center of the lesion lay within muscle, suggesting a primary muscular origin rather than a bone lesion.
title: Skeletal Muscle Metastasis as an Initial Presentation of Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma: A Case Report and a Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 61-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of progressively worsening tremulous movements of her hands that she could not voluntarily suppress and that interfered with daily activities. She also reported a sensation of instability when standing that immediately resolved with walking or when she touched a wall. She had no history of seizures. On examination, there were frequent, moderate-amplitude myoclonic jerks of both hands at rest that worsened with posture and action. Superimposed on these jerks was a regular oscillatory 6-Hz tremor of both hands. When she stood, there was a very low-amplitude, high-frequency tremor of her legs that was visible and palpable; this tremor abated immediately when she placed her hand on a wall or began to walk. There were no signs of parkinsonism. Brain MRI and routine EEG were unremarkable.
title: Cortical Tremor (CT) with coincident orthostatic movements

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of recurrent left mandibular swelling and trismus. He had no history of trauma, paresthesia, or skin lesions and no significant medical or family history. His dental history was notable for extraction of a carious left mandibular third molar after painful swelling, with complete resolution. Two months later, sudden swelling occurred in the left submandibular region with pain and restricted mouth opening; symptoms resolved with antibiotics but recurred after 2 months. Over the next year he experienced eight similar episodes, each with swelling and 2 weeks of restricted opening followed by gradual resolution. An early panoramic radiograph showed no infectious focus but mild mandibular sclerosis that was overlooked.

On examination, he was afebrile. There was facial asymmetry and a diffuse 7×5 cm firm, non‐tender swelling over the left masseter region. Interincisal opening was 5 mm. Intraoral examination revealed no focus of infection and all mandibular teeth responded to vitality testing. A provisional diagnosis of trismus secondary to chronic infection was made, and the differential included masseter hypertrophy and an atraumatic variant of myositis ossificans.

Intraoral periapical radiographs showed a coarse sclerotic trabecular pattern in the left premolar and molar region. Panoramic radiography revealed unilateral diffuse sclerosis of the left hemimandible with a ground-glass appearance extending from the left canine to the ipsilateral condyle and resorption of the condylar head. Multislice CT demonstrated extensive endosteal sclerosis of the left hemimandible, cortical thickening, mild periosteal new bone formation, and condylar head resorption with loss of cortical–medullary border demarcation. MRI showed the left hemimandible as hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and on postgadolinium images there was intramedullary enhancement along with enhancement of the overlying masticatory and floor-of-mouth muscles.
title: Chronic Diffuse Sclerosing Osteomyelitis of the Mandible

case_prompt: A 17-year-old female with refractory acute myeloid leukemia awaiting a second allogeneic stem cell transplantation presented with difficulty chewing and speaking because of two growths on her tongue. She had pancytopenia (platelets 54 000/mm3, erythrocytes 3.06 million/mm3, leukocytes 2170/mm3) and recent episodes of febrile neutropenia treated with broad‐spectrum antibiotics and antifungals. Intraoral examination revealed two bilateral, pedunculated, tumor-like lesions, each approximately 1 cm2 in size, with a normal mucosal color on the lateral borders of the tongue. Based on these findings, a clinical diagnostic hypothesis of fibroma was made, with pyogenic granuloma as a differential diagnosis.
title: High-power laser for oral excisional biopsy in an oncologic patient with pancytopenia

case_prompt: A 55-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 1-month history of night sweats, palpitations, asthenia, and a 7-kg weight loss. On examination, he was alert but tachycardic (113 bpm) and hypotensive (98/77 mmHg); he appeared pale without peripheral lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or hemorrhagic signs. Laboratory studies showed a normochromic, normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (72,000/mm3); other cell lines were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography suggested bilateral adrenal masses. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated large, bilaterally homogenous, polylobed adrenal masses (right: 130 × 103 × 91 mm; left: 114 × 91 × 78 mm) with mild enhancement and multiple retroperitoneal, para-aortic, and celiac-mesenteric lymphadenopathies. FDG-PET showed intensely hypermetabolic bilateral adrenal lesions (SUVmax 47 right, 50.2 left) along with hypermetabolic supra-clavicular, mediastinal, and external iliac lymph nodes.
title: Bilateral primary adrenal diffuse large B cell lymphoma: A rare presentation

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 0 at 21 weeks of gestation, presented with 5 days of sudden, severe frontoparietal headache, projectile non-bilious vomiting, right eyelid droop, and bilateral visual deterioration, with altered sensorium for 3 days. She denied fever, neck stiffness, trauma, abdominal pain, per-vaginal bleeding, or rash. Her antenatal course had been uneventful.

On arrival, she appeared ill but hemodynamically stable; Glasgow Coma Scale was 14 (E3V5M6). Neuro-ophthalmologic examination revealed that she could count fingers with the right eye and had vision of 1/60 in the left. Right ptosis was present, and the right pupil was 4 mm with a sluggish light reaction and a Grade I relative afferent pupillary defect; the left pupil was normal. Fundoscopy showed disc and macular edema in the right eye. Other cranial nerves were intact. Motor strength was 4+/5 in all limbs; reflexes and tone were normal, but plantar responses were upgoing bilaterally. The rest of the neurologic and systemic examinations were unremarkable. Obstetric examination confirmed a 20-week uterus with palpable fetal parts.

She was initially treated at a local center for impending eclampsia with intravenous magnesium sulfate and transferred for further care. Laboratory studies showed sodium 147 mmol/L, potassium 2.6 mmol/L, elevated uric acid, ALT 237 U/L, AST 142 U/L, and prolactin >200 ng/mL. Obstetric ultrasound demonstrated a single live intrauterine pregnancy of 19 weeks + 2 days with placenta previa.

Because MRI was not feasible, a non-contrast CT scan of the head was obtained, which showed sellar and suprasellar hyperdensity with a cystic hypodensity lesion, findings suggestive of pituitary apoplexy on a pituitary adenoma.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Delayed identification of massive pituitary apoplexy in pregnancy: A case report

case_prompt: A 69-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout, and former tobacco use presented to the ED with worsening shortness of breath, productive cough, and dyspnea on exertion. One day earlier, at an urgent care center, he had a normal chest radiograph and was diagnosed with bronchitis; he was started on oral steroids, antibiotics, and a metered-dose inhaler. His symptoms worsened, prompting this ED visit. He reported chronic sinusitis but felt these symptoms were similar to prior respiratory infections. On arrival, his blood pressure was 124/94 mmHg, pulse 108/min, respiratory rate 36/min, temperature 97.4°F, and oxygen saturation 87% on room air. He was placed on 2 L oxygen by nasal cannula, and his vital signs subsequently normalized.
title: Point-of-care ultrasound, anchoring bias, and acute pulmonary embolism: A cautionary tale and report

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old male without structural heart disease was referred for catheter ablation of symptomatic paroxysmal narrow QRS complex tachycardia. During tachycardia, the 12-lead ECG showed a long RP interval with negative P waves in leads II, III, and aVF. Burst and extrastimulation from the right ventricle revealed retrograde conduction with a long, decremental ventriculoatrial interval; the earliest atrial activation was at the ostium of the coronary sinus.

Atrial and ventricular extrastimulation reproducibly induced SVT1, with AH intervals of 130–150 ms and HA intervals of 278–306 ms. An activation map during SVT1 localized the earliest atrial activation at the 6 o’clock position of the coronary sinus ostium; radiofrequency ablation at that site eliminated SVT1 and retrograde conduction.

A subsequent atrial extrastimulation induced a second tachycardia (SVT2). During SVT2, AH intervals fluctuated between 110 and 122 ms and HA intervals between 306 and 336 ms. SVT2 terminated with a 2 mg bolus of adenosine triphosphate, and transient AV block occurred during tachycardia with catheter mechanical stimulation.

Right atrial mapping during SVT2 identified fragmented diastolic atrial potentials in the cavotricuspid isthmus, around the coronary sinus ostium, and in the inferior vena cava, with the earliest diastolic potential at the 6 o’clock position adjacent to the tricuspid annulus. The overall atrial activation pattern was noncentrifugal. Entrainment pacing from the right atrial appendage showed that the diastolic potentials were orthodromically captured while other atrial electrograms were antidromically captured. The difference in ventriculoatrial intervals after entrainment from the appendage versus the proximal coronary sinus was 6 ms, indicating positive VA linking.
title: Diastolic potentials manifest the extension of a slow pathway to the inferolateral right atrium during fast-slow atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia

case_prompt: A 30-year-old woman who had undergone bilateral aesthetic breast augmentation with Poly Implant Prothèse (PIP) implants in 2007 presented electively in January 2015 for removal and replacement of her implants. She was otherwise healthy, with a body-mass index of 20 kg/m2, a non-smoker, and had no clinical signs of capsular contracture; inframammary scars were inconspicuous. Under general anesthesia, both implants were removed via previous inframammary incisions. On the right, the implant was intact, with no paraprosthetic fluid and a normal capsule. On the left, approximately 50 mL of milky seroma fluid was encountered; air bubbles were visible within the shell, and "fatty" smears appeared on the gloves. Manual compression of the explanted device caused rupture of the shell. Further exploration of the left implant pocket revealed a well-demarcated yellowish mass measuring 4 × 5 cm in the central lower quadrant of the breast, overlying the fascia of the pectoralis major muscle. A malignant neoplasm was suspected, and an excisional biopsy with histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses was performed.
journal: Case Reports in Plastic Surgery & Hand Surgery
title: An unusual case of a ruptured Poly Implant Prothèse breast implant associated with xanthoma

case_prompt: A 77-year-old man presented with hematemesis associated with nausea and epigastric pain. He had a history of hypertension, bilateral hip and knee replacements, and chronic non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug and aspirin use. On arrival, his blood pressure was 104/63 mmHg, heart rate 71 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 37°C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Abdominal examination revealed a non-distended abdomen with epigastric tenderness without guarding, rebound tenderness, or palpable mass. Laboratory tests showed a lipase level of 50 U/L (reference range 0–60 U/L); bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase levels were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated inflammatory stranding around the second and third segments of the duodenum and an abnormal course of the proximal duodenum, which traveled posteriorly and superiorly before the third segment crossed the midline at an unusually high position. MRI of the abdomen was performed to exclude a pancreatic head lesion and was negative. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy confirmed duodenitis.
title: Duodenum inversum: a rare cause of nausea and epigastric pain

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old man with a 10-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (meeting ACR criteria) and secondary antiphospholipid syndrome (two prior DVTs, positive anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant) presented with 2 months of fatigue, fever, arthralgias, oral lesions, and elevated ESR. His regular medications included prednisolone 7.5 mg/day, azathioprine 100 mg/day, hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day, and warfarin.

After increasing prednisolone to 15 mg/day and azathioprine to 150 mg/day, he developed dyspnea, persistent symptoms, and new pancytopenia. Rituximab was added and azathioprine discontinued. Two weeks later, on admission he was febrile (38 °C), tachypneic (RR 30/min), mildly tachycardic (HR 100/min), with O2 saturation 89% on room air. Exam showed splenomegaly and 1–2 cm cervical lymphadenopathy. He had painless oral ulcers and bilateral wrist swelling without motion limitation.

Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (WBC 1.9 ×10^3/μL, Hb 8.7 g/dL, platelets 26 ×10^3/μL), ESR 102 mm/h, CRP 187 mg/L, anti-dsDNA 23.5 IU/mL, low C3 and C4, hypercalcemia (12 mg/dL), elevated pro-BNP (786 pg/mL), and negative blood cultures, HIV, EBV, CMV, and Coombs tests. Urinalysis showed trace protein.

Transthoracic echo revealed mild pericardial effusion. Chest CT was unremarkable; abdominal CT showed splenomegaly. He received IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days, broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed infection, and IV pamidronate for hypercalcemia. Fever and oral lesions improved, and pancytopenia converted to bicytopenia, but anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypercalcemia persisted despite treatment.
title: Concomitant manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus flare‐up and nodal marginal zone B‐cell lymphoma in a 41‐year‐old male patient: A challenging case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man with bipolar affective disorder had been stable on olanzapine 5 mg daily and sodium valproate 400 mg daily for 7 years. Three weeks before transfer, he had fever with rigors for 3–4 days that resolved with over-the-counter medications; he continued his usual medications. Two weeks later, he developed recurrent fever with rigors and was admitted to a local hospital for 4 days. While hospitalized, he experienced increased urinary frequency, loose stools, insomnia, and progressive confusion with inability to recognize relatives; he stopped oral intake by the fourth day. His antipsychotics were withheld.

On admission to our hospital, his temperature was 103 °F, pulse 122 bpm, and he was mute with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 (E3 M4 V1). Neurologic examination showed lead-pipe rigidity in all four limbs and neck, tremors in the left hand and jaw, brisk deep-tendon reflexes, and equivocal plantar responses.

Laboratory studies on admission revealed a white-cell count of 8300 cells/mm³. A blood smear and rapid test for malaria were negative. Blood urea, creatinine, electrolytes, thyroid-stimulating hormone, serum calcium, urine analysis and culture, blood cultures, and chest radiography were all normal. Serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Random blood glucose was 412 mg/dL, and liver enzymes were mildly elevated.

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed clear fluid with 6 lymphocytes/mm³, protein 67.9 mg/dL, glucose 59 mg/dL (serum glucose 112 mg/dL), and adenosine deaminase 2 U/L; Gram, fungal, and acid-fast stains were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain was normal.
journal: Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care
title: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome in a patient with stable dose of olanzapine

case_prompt:
A 7-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of one month of progressive, painless abdominal distention. His prenatal and family history were unremarkable; past history included bilateral inguinal hernia repair and thalassemia minor. Growth and development were normal. On exam, he was well-appearing; his abdomen was distended and tense, with a positive fluid thrill, but there was no organomegaly or palpable mass. There were no clinical, laboratory, or imaging signs of portal hypertension or liver disease. 

Abdominal ultrasound showed free fluid in Morison’s pouch, the left upper quadrant, and Douglas space, without septations or multicystic appearance, and no organ abnormalities. A comprehensive workup excluded hepatic, renal, cardiac, intestinal, pancreatic, inflammatory, or infectious diseases; malignancy; and congenital metabolic disorders. 

Previously, he had a mild pleuro-pericardial effusion during a febrile illness and transient hyperkalaemia, raising concern for stomatocytosis, but PIEZO1 gene testing was negative. A positive interferon-gamma (QuantiFERON®) test prompted evaluation for peritoneal tuberculosis: chest radiograph and Mantoux tests (patient and parents) were negative; gastric aspirate cultures and repeat interferon-gamma assay were negative; atypical mycobacterial infection was excluded.

Abdominal MRI confirmed an abundant fluid collection, centralization of bowel loops, and normal-appearing organs. Paracentesis yielded pale-yellow serous fluid with a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.1; triglycerides and leukocyte counts were normal (98% lymphocytes); cytology showed reactive lymphomonocytes, mesothelial cells, and foam cells without malignant cells. Fluid rapidly re-accumulated in days. 

Diuretics (spironolactone and furosemide) provided only transient relief; recurrent paracenteses were required over the following months. Repeated imaging and fluid analyses did not reveal any new diagnostic clues. Eighteen months after symptom onset, repeat ultrasound and MRI again showed free-appearing ascites without additional findings.
title: Case report: horse or zebra, ascites or pseudo-ascites? Care for pictural details!

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old female with peritoneal dialysis–dependent end-stage renal disease secondary to steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and calcineurin inhibitor toxicity was noted to be bradycardic at a routine outpatient dialysis clinic visit. Her medical history included anemia of ESRD, malnutrition requiring a gastrojejunal feeding tube, chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD), wheelchair dependence for chronic pain and deconditioning, and significant medication nonadherence in the setting of persistent depressive disorder.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated new complete atrioventricular (AV) block with a junctional escape rhythm at 50 beats per minute and a borderline prolonged QTc of 465 ms. Seventeen months earlier, an ECG had shown normal sinus rhythm with PR intervals between 130 and 160 ms; a Holter monitor 13 months earlier similarly demonstrated intact AV conduction. She denied recent fever, viral symptoms, syncope, or near-syncope; she reported mild fatigue but had limited physical activity at baseline.

On admission for further evaluation, telemetry confirmed persistent complete AV block, intermittently oscillating to high-grade second-degree block and rare first-degree block without relation to activity. Review of prior cardiac assessments revealed subaortic hypertrophy with mild dynamic outflow acceleration on echocardiography and normal systolic function with moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy on cardiovascular magnetic resonance 18 months earlier. Medication review identified aripiprazole as a potential contributor, but it had been discontinued weeks before presentation.

Laboratory studies showed a normal serum calcium level (8.9 mg/dL), normal inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, ferritin), and negative tests for COVID-19, Lyme disease, tuberculosis, anti-streptolysin O antibodies, and anti-COVID antibodies. Rheumatologic workup revealed a positive antinuclear antibody screen (1:640) but negative complement levels and specific autoantibodies (anti-dsDNA, anti-SSB, anti-RNP, anti-Sm, anti-SSA, anti-Scl-70, anti-Jo). There were no clinical features suggestive of Kearns-Sayre or Holt-Oram syndromes.

Given concerns for uncontrolled CKD-MBD, further evaluation revealed an elevated parathyroid hormone level of 726 pg/mL (upper limit of normal 80.1 pg/mL), a phosphorus level of 11.3 mg/dL (normal 2.5–5.0 mg/dL), and a calcium-phosphate product of 101.7 mg2/dL2 (normal <55 mg2/dL2). Serial echocardiograms demonstrated echo-bright papillary muscles first noted one year earlier, raising suspicion for cardiac calcium deposition.
title: Extraskeletal calcifications in a dialysis-dependent teenager: A novel cause of acquired pediatric complete heart block

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of bilateral eye pain and redness that worsened with eye movement and touch. One month earlier, he had been diagnosed with chikungunya and was under rheumatology care. He had no other comorbidities or a family history of eye disease.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy revealed bulbar conjunctival hyperemia graded 3+/4+ with 360° ciliary injection and no other anterior segment abnormalities. Intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg and 14 mmHg. A 1% phenylephrine test produced no blanching of the vessels after 10 minutes, suggesting scleritis rather than episcleritis.

One week later, the patient returned with worsening eye pain. Hyperemia increased to 4+/4+, and examination showed medial scleral elevation, more pronounced in the right eye. Intraocular pressures were 16 mmHg and 15 mmHg. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated an edematous space between layers of the sclera in both eyes.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, leukocytes 10,120/mm³, platelets 318,000/mm³, C-reactive protein 10.63 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 25 mm/h, AST 35 U/L, ALT 105 U/L, urea 35 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. Serologic tests were negative for HIV-1/2, HTLV-1/2, hepatitis B and C, and toxoplasmosis; VDRL and FTA-ABS were negative. A PPD test measured 5 mm (BCG vaccinated), and RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Dengue serology showed IgG positive, IgM negative; chikungunya serology showed both IgG and IgM positive. Rheumatologic screening (rheumatoid factor, ANA, anti-CCP, anti-DNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro, anti-La, ANCA, HLA-B27) and complement components C3 and C4 were within normal limits.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Anterior scleritis treated with systemic corticosteroids in Chikungunya infection

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a one-hour history of sudden onset left-sided weakness of both upper and lower extremities following a fall while seated. He also reported a frontal headache, slurred speech, and nonradiating, burning epigastric pain. His past medical history was notable only for recurrent left flank pain previously treated as renal colic with NSAIDs. He smoked 18 pack-years and denied alcohol or drug use.  

On examination, he was alert and oriented; blood pressure and heart rate were normal and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Neurologic examination revealed nonfluent speech with intact comprehension and repetition, preserved sensation, and marked left-sided weakness (1/5 strength in both upper and lower limbs) with a muted left Babinski sign. Cranial nerves were intact.  

Initial laboratory tests showed elevated cardiac enzymes, normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 7 g/dl), reticulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, prolonged aPTT, normal PT/INR, and evidence of intra-renal injury (BUN-to-creatinine ratio 17:1). Indirect hyperbilirubinemia and elevated inflammatory markers were present; electrolytes and haptoglobin were normal. Urinalysis revealed 2+ proteinuria and 3+ hematuria.  

An ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm, a prolonged PR interval, and diffuse ST-segment elevation. Echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% with bi-atrial dilation. Cardiac catheterization revealed nonobstructive coronary arteries consistent with microvascular thrombosis.  

Brain CT scan revealed a large acute nonhemorrhagic infarction in the right fronto-parietal–temporal lobes and multiple lacunar infarctions, which were confirmed by MRI. Magnetic resonance angiography showed total occlusion of the right middle cerebral artery.
title: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome presenting with a stroke as a first presentation: case report

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman with metastatic colon adenocarcinoma presented with new-onset left hemiparesis, left facial anesthesia, and right-hand paresthesia. Her cancer history included a pT4N1M0 primary treated with partial colectomy, followed by hepatic resection of metastases and multiple lines of chemotherapy. Most recently she had received nine cycles of bevacizumab plus FOLFOX before the neurologic symptoms appeared. 

On neurologic examination, she had reduced strength in the left upper and lower extremities, decreased sensation over the left face, and paresthesia in the right hand. Vital signs were within normal limits. Routine laboratory tests, including coagulation studies, were unremarkable.

Brain MRI showed three millimetric lesions in the right temporooccipital white matter, left pontine region, and right parietal lobe. On fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images they were hyperintense, on diffusion-weighted imaging they showed restricted diffusion, and on postgadolinium T1-weighted images there was no contrast enhancement.
title: Brain microischemic phenomena in a woman receiving bevacizumab treatment: a case report

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of epigastric pain and nausea. He was an ex-smoker and social drinker with no significant comorbidities or family history. On examination, he was jaundiced with hepatomegaly. Routine serum parameters were within normal limits; tumor markers including AFP, CEA, and β-HCG were not assessed. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a thickened posterior gastric wall at the pylorus, periaortic lymphadenopathy, and multiple hepatic and pulmonary metastases; no primary lesions were seen in the testes, mediastinum, or other sites.  

He underwent palliative gastrectomy with partial hepatic resection. The gastric specimen contained a 33×33×15 mm ulcero-vegetative mass; the liver specimen revealed a 30×20×15 mm whitish, necrotic, hemorrhagic tumor. Histologically, there was a proliferation of large, dyscohesive, pleomorphic cells from the mucosa through the muscularis with extensive hemorrhage and vascular emboli. Two cell populations were identified: (1) giant cells with lobulated, bizarre nuclei resembling syncytiotrophoblasts and (2) oval cells with pale cytoplasm resembling cytotrophoblasts.  

Immunohistochemical staining showed that both cell types were diffusely positive for cytokeratin 7, MLH-1, MSH-2, PMS-2, and c-MET. The syncytiotrophoblast-like cells were diffusely positive for inhibin and CD138, whereas the cytotrophoblast-like cells were negative for these markers. A minor adenocarcinoma component (<10% of the tumor) at one margin was diffusely positive for CDX2, cytokeratin 7, CEA, and c-MET, with focal positivity for cytokeratin 20 and CD138. The choriocarcinomatous cells were negative for CEA and CDX2 but positive for cytokeratin 7 and HCG. There was progressive loss of E-cadherin in both components; in vascular emboli, tumor cells were positive for CD138 and β-catenin but negative for inhibin. The choriocarcinomatous component was also present in hepatic metastases.
title: Primary gastric choriocarcinoma - a rare and aggressive tumor with multilineage differentiation: A case report

case_prompt: A 22-year-old woman, gravida 1 at 22 weeks’ gestation, was admitted for decreased fetal movement and transvaginal bleeding. Two weeks earlier she had intermittent spotting; over days, fetal mobility decreased. She had no significant medical history and denied smoking, alcohol, or drug use. On admission, the fetal heart rate was 130 beats per minute; uterine contractions and fetal movements were absent; speculum examination revealed bloody discharge. Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated absence of amniotic fluid. Empiric antibiotics (ampicillin and azithromycin) were initiated, and benzathine penicillin was given for a positive serum VDRL at 1:64. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, leukocyte count 7710/mm³, platelet count 217 000/mm³, C-reactive protein 31 mg/dL, and negative HIV tests. Three days later, she developed fever, abdominal pain, leukocytosis, and further elevation of C-reactive protein; chorioamnionitis was suspected, and labor was induced with misoprostol. Two days after induction, she reported mild headache, neck stiffness, and fever; retained products of conception were suspected, and sharp curettage was performed with initiation of piperacillin–tazobactam and vancomycin. Head CT showed diffuse cerebral edema and hydrocephalus. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed protein 49 mg/dL, glucose 56 mg/dL, five lymphocytes/mm³, adenosine deaminase 4.6 U/L; CSF VDRL and cryptococcal antigen were negative.
title: Disseminated hematogenous tuberculosis in puerperium—case report

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old man with gastroesophageal reflux disease and hypertension was referred for evaluation of polycythemia (hemoglobin 220 g/L), hypotension, and bilateral calf pain. Over the preceding week he noted progressive bilateral leg swelling and pain, accompanied by nausea and weakness. In the two days before presentation the calf pain intensified to “the worst pain of his life.” He had begun a treadmill exercise program five weeks earlier.

On arrival, he was alert and oriented; blood pressure was 150/99 mm Hg (previously 68/40 mm Hg at the referring hospital after 2 L of normal saline). Examination was notable only for bilateral “rock hard,” tender calves with severely limited ankle range of motion due to pain on plantar and dorsiflexion. Compartment pressures were measured at 110 mm Hg, and he underwent emergent bilateral fasciotomies. Phlebotomy of 600 mL was performed for hemoglobin of 210 g/L before surgery.

Intraoperatively and postoperatively he remained hypotensive despite 3 L of normal saline and required norepinephrine to maintain MAP > 65 mm Hg. He received a total of 6 L of crystalloid and 2.5 L of 5% albumin, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and parenteral steroids. Cardiac index measured by an esophageal device was 0.9–1.6 L/min, prompting initiation of milrinone. A CT angiogram of the lower limbs showed marked narrowing of distal arterial and venous vessels but no occlusive pathology. He developed oliguria, rising creatinine (to 135 µmol/L), and creatine kinase rising from 1 353 U/L preoperatively to 11 590 U/L by postoperative day 1, with positive urine myoglobin; continuous renal replacement therapy was started. Continued intravascular fluid extravasation led to fasciotomies of the thighs and forearms. He required ventilator support for 11 days and developed mild pulmonary edema, bilateral pleural effusions, and ascites.

Further workup showed negative JAK2 mutation, normal C3 and C4 complement levels, and serum immunofixation demonstrating a monoclonal IgG band.
title: Compartment Syndrome as a Result of Systemic Capillary Leak Syndrome

case_prompt: A previously healthy 5-year-old girl was evaluated for new-onset seizure-like activity. Over one night she had seven episodes, each beginning as left lower extremity shaking and evolving to generalized motor involvement without tongue biting, incontinence, or postictal confusion. She was discharged on levetiracetam but developed persistent left foot trembling during the day and localized pain between the left ankle and knee exacerbated by weight-bearing; range of motion remained full. Two weeks after the initial presentation, she was admitted for uncontrolled seizures. EEG showed frequent epileptiform discharges in the midline central and central–parietal regions. Brain MRI demonstrated mild cortical atrophy in the paramedian right frontal lobe at the vertex and subtle white matter signal changes extending toward the lateral ventricle. Two weeks later, she was readmitted for intractable seizures, and PET-CT revealed hypometabolism in the right paramedian frontal lobe corresponding to the MRI findings, as well as additional patchy hypometabolism in the right anterior frontal lobe.
title: Rasmussen's encephalitis in a pediatric patient with subtle early MRI changes: A case report

case_prompt:
A previously healthy six-year-old girl presented with a one-day history of severe pain in both lower limbs, extending from the knees to the feet and preventing her from standing or walking. Two days before the onset of pain, she sustained a cut to her right hand and received a tetanus toxoid injection in the deltoid muscle. She had no fever, recent infection, or trauma. Her vaccination history was up to date, with her last routine dose six months earlier.

On examination, she had swelling and tenderness of the right foot and both elbows without erythema or warmth. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Initial laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 9,000/mm3 with a normal differential, hemoglobin 12 g/dL, platelet count 260,000/mm3, C-reactive protein 5 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 8 mm/hr, complement C3 90 mg/dL, and C4 28 mg/dL. Ultrasound of the right foot revealed mild edema of the subcutaneous soft tissues over the dorsum.

On the second hospital day, she developed a nonpruritic petechial rash on both lower limbs that resolved spontaneously by the third day. By that time, she was able to walk without pain and had no remaining joint swelling or rash.
title: Serum Sickness following Tetanus Toxoid Injection

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old boy presented with a 2-year history of oral ulcers and difficulty eating. Parents first noticed small ulcerations on the tongue and buccal mucosa 2 years ago. For the past 8 months, he reported a burning sensation exacerbated by spicy and hot foods. Previous local treatments had been ineffective, and no records were available. His medical and family histories were unremarkable, and there was no history of vesicular or bullous skin eruptions.

Physical examination revealed no cutaneous, genital, scalp, or nail lesions. Oral inspection showed white interlacing striae extending from the commissures to the retromolar areas bilaterally at the occlusal plane. On the left buccal mucosa, there was a 2 cm × 3 cm erosive lesion in the retromolar region; the right buccal mucosa exhibited slender radiating white striae. The dorsum of the tongue had depapillated areas interspersed with white striae and melanin pigmentation. Lesions were flat, non-tender, non-indurated, and non-scrapable. Oral hygiene was fair; deeply carious first molars were noted bilaterally without any restorations. 

Routine hematological investigations were unremarkable.
journal: Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology : JOMFP
title: Oral lichen planus in an 8-year-old child: A case report with a brief literature review

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive nasal obstruction and frequent epistaxis. His medical history included well-controlled hypertension and diabetes. On examination, no café-au-lait spots or other cutaneous lesions were observed; HIV serology was negative.

Endoscopic evaluation demonstrated a polypoid mass extending from the midportion of the right inferior turbinate to the choana. Paranasal sinus CT showed a 2.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass filling the right nasal cavity, extending into the right choana and nasopharynx, with erosion of the nasal septal bone. MRI revealed a well-demarcated 2.5 × 1.5 cm fungating mass with gadolinium enhancement, internal hemorrhage, and increased vascularity.

The lesion was removed endoscopically in a piecemeal fashion. Grossly, the specimen was a soft, pinkish, friable mass originating from the right choana and the posteroinferior aspect of the nasal septum; the adjacent septal mucosa was resected, and the septal bone was preserved.
title: A Solitary Malignant Schwannoma in the Choana and Nasal Septum

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old man was transferred for evaluation of cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP). He had a six-week history of intermittent chills, myalgia, general weakness, and dyspnea. Chest CT suggested COP, confirmed by video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge biopsy. He developed acute respiratory distress syndrome and required six weeks of ICU care with mechanical ventilation in PEEP mode; vasopressors were not used.

Three weeks into ICU care, liver tests showed ALT 126 U/L and ALP 463 IU/L with normal total bilirubin. He had no prior hepatobiliary disease; the clinician suspected drug-induced hepatitis. Abdominal ultrasound showed slightly coarse liver parenchyma and sludge in the gallbladder but no intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilatation.

Two weeks later, ALP remained elevated and total bilirubin rose to 4.39 mg/dL. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed multifocal strictures and irregularities of both intrahepatic bile ducts, diffuse mild wall thickening, and increased intraluminal attenuation in the right main intrahepatic duct; hepatic vessels were patent. The first impression was sclerosing cholangitis with bile sludge. Immunoglobulin G4–related sclerosing disease was considered because of combined interstitial pneumonia and sclerosing cholangitis, but serum IgG and IgG4 levels were normal. A prior chest CT had shown no hepatobiliary abnormality, indicating new biliary changes.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed multiple strictures, irregularity, and a beaded appearance of both intrahepatic ducts, and an elongated intraluminal filling defect in the central intrahepatic ducts extending into the proximal common bile duct, suggestive of biliary casts.
final_diagnosis_raw: sclerosing cholangitis in critically ill patients
title: Biliary Cast Formation with Sclerosing Cholangitis in Critically Ill Patient: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of worsening blurry vision and mild headache that progressed to ataxia and difficulty ambulating. On examination, she had nystagmus, left-eye ophthalmoplegia, and diplopia; the remainder of her neurologic examination and a CT scan of the brain were normal. She was admitted to neurology for further workup to exclude multiple sclerosis. Her medical history was notable for fibromyalgia and pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta, for which she had been taking prednisone (30–50 mg/day) for 2 years and dapsone (150 mg/day). 

Three days into her admission, she developed ongoing hypoxia with pulse-oximetry saturations of 88%–92% while receiving 8 L of oxygen via Hudson mask. She complained of dyspnea and appeared tachypneic but denied cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, or any history of deep-vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, or asthma. Examination revealed mild central cyanosis of the lips and fingertips. Lung auscultation was clear, heart sounds were dual without murmurs, and there was no lower-limb swelling or tenderness. Blood pressure was 103/66 mm Hg, and heart rate was 90–105 bpm in sinus rhythm.

An arterial blood gas performed on 8 L/min of oxygen showed pH 7.56, PaO₂ 178 mm Hg, SaO₂ 98%, PCO₂ 20 mm Hg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.9 mmol/L, and hemoglobin 98 g/L. Because she had not received DVT prophylaxis for 3 days, a CT pulmonary angiogram was obtained; both pulmonary embolism and pneumonia were excluded. She was transferred to the ICU and placed on high-flow nasal prongs. Repeat arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated a marked discrepancy between the pulse-oximeter saturation (88%–90%) and the calculated arterial oxygen saturation with a PaO₂ in the normal range.
title: Dapsone‐induced methemoglobinemia—A case report

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old woman with a history of obesity was in her usual state of health until she received the first dose of the BNT162b2 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. Two days later, she developed severe headache, myalgia, and noted excessive thirst and urination. Myalgia resolved over 2 weeks, but headache, polydipsia, and polyuria persisted. She received the second vaccine dose 5 weeks later; the following day, she experienced worsening headache, fatigue, widespread joint pain, hourly urinary frequency (≈4 L per day), and an 18-kg weight loss since the first dose. She presented to the emergency department 2 months after her first vaccination with intolerable polydipsia, polyuria, headache accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and light-headedness. She denied visual changes or altered mental status and reported amenorrhea since the first vaccination (previous menses had been regular). Family history was negative for autoimmune disease.

Vital signs were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable. During an 8-hour observation, she ingested 0.4 L of fluid and produced 2.2 L of urine. Laboratory studies showed a serum sodium of 142 mmol/L (reference, 133–144 mmol/L) and a normal complete blood count. Because of persistent headache, a contrast-enhanced brain MRI was obtained and demonstrated a 4-mm, round, thickened pituitary stalk and a partially empty sella. Initial endocrine evaluation revealed a serum osmolality of 306 mOsm/kg (reference, 275–295 mOsm/kg) and a urine osmolality of 97 mOsm/kg (reference, 100–1200 mOsm/kg).
title: A Case of Hypophysitis Associated With SARS-CoV-2 Vaccination

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old girl was referred for elective hospital admission because of recent weight loss, a 2-week history of intermittent epigastric abdominal pain, iron deficiency anaemia, and a palpable epigastric/left upper quadrant mass. She had lost 1 kg in the past week despite a normal appetite, reported intermittent dark stools attributed to oral iron, and denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, or constitutional symptoms. Exercise tolerance was slightly reduced. Her past history included congenital adrenal hyperplasia, delayed puberty, and poor growth over 3 years, and she had experienced similar episodes of abdominal pain and a palpable mass over the past year. An abdominal ultrasound in June 2017 was unremarkable apart from a small left kidney. Medications were hydrocortisone, fluticasone, and oral iron.

On admission, vital signs were normal. Examination revealed a firm, non-tender mass in the epigastric and left upper quadrant regions with mild abdominal distension; the remainder of the abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no alopecia, mucosal ulceration, or skin changes. Height was 146 cm (1st percentile) and weight 34.6 kg.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 76 g/L, MCV 67 fL, albumin 32 g/L, ferritin < 5 µg/L, and ESR 25 mm/hr. Extensive urine, stool, and blood tests—including autoimmune, endocrine, infectious, and vitamin panels—were negative.

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated grossly enlarged left upper quadrant lymph nodes, free fluid in the right iliac fossa, and an atrophic left kidney with lower pole cystic changes; the report concluded these findings were atypical for mesenteric adenitis and recommended CT or MRI. A chest radiograph showed no mediastinal lymphadenopathy or other pathology.
title: Large gastric trichobezoar causing failure to thrive and iron deficiency anaemia in an adolescent girl: a case report emphasising the imaging findings and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 78‐year‐old woman presented to her general dentist with an enlarging soft‐tissue mass of several months’ duration. She was otherwise healthy, with no history of malignancy, and was not in acute distress. Intraoral examination revealed a fluctuant, exophytic lesion of the maxillary anterior gingiva, extending from the right lateral incisor to the left central incisor. The lesion measured 3.0 cm × 1.5 cm, appeared dark red with secondary tan‐gray ulceration, and the tissue collapsed under pressure from the forceps. A smaller, similar lesion was identified in the right maxillary vestibule adjacent to the labial frenum. A periapical radiograph showed no changes in bone quality or quantity and no evidence of odontogenic infection. A clinical diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made, and an incisional biopsy was performed.

Histologic examination showed stratified squamous epithelium with focal ulceration. Beneath the epithelium, tumor cells completely effaced the lamina propria. The cells were arranged in lobular aggregates separated by thin fibrous septa, some with a perivascular pattern, and the lesion exhibited a rich vascular network. On high‐power magnification, the cells displayed pink to vacuolated cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, marked nuclear pleomorphism, and brisk mitotic activity.
journal: Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology : JOMFP
title: Renal cell carcinoma metastatic to the maxillary gingiva: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 45-year-old African woman with no significant medical history presented with intermittent decreases in visual acuity and headache. Cranial MRI revealed a 2.0 × 1.5 × 1.0-cm solid sellar mass arising from the adenohypophysis, with suprasellar extension but no evidence of invasive growth, and marked contrast enhancement on T1-weighted images. Laboratory evaluation of pituitary function showed normal levels of follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, prolactin, corticotropin, and thyrotropin. A nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma was suspected, and the mass was completely resected via transsphenoidal surgery with no adjuvant therapy. Postoperatively, the patient developed panhypopituitarism that was managed with hormone replacement.
title: Spindle cell oncocytoma of the adenohypophysis in a woman: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old man was admitted for evaluation of an intense, right-sided hemicranial headache that worsened with coughing. Three weeks earlier, he developed a dry cough followed by a brief febrile upper respiratory infection treated with antibiotics; the fever resolved but the cough persisted. Two weeks before admission, he noted pulsating pain behind the right eye associated with nausea and vomiting; there were no visual changes, diplopia, or other neurologic symptoms.  
His past medical history was negative; he denied trauma, surgery, or previous headaches. He played recreational football.  
On examination, temperature was normal, other vital signs were stable. Neurologic examination was normal except for a slightly wider right rima oculi and mild neck stiffness on forward flexion; there was no conjunctival injection or proptosis.  
Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance; other inflammatory markers were normal. Noncontrast head CT was normal. Lumbar puncture yielded clear cerebrospinal fluid with normal cytobiochemical results.  
Because his cough-induced hemicranial headache did not fit criteria for a primary headache disorder and was considered a “red flag,” further evaluation was pursued.  
The patient’s examination remained otherwise unremarkable.
title: Hemicranial Cough-Induced Headache as a First Symptom of a Carotid-Cavernous Fistula-Case Report

case_prompt:
A woman in her 90s presented with a 7-day history of intermittently severe right upper quadrant pain associated with nausea and bloating. She denied vomiting, fever, or jaundice. Her medical history included a childhood appendectomy, a later laparotomy and adhesiolysis for small-bowel obstruction, and a lumbar vertebral fracture 4 months earlier. On examination, she was afebrile, anicteric, and normotensive, with a heart rate of 90 beats per minute. Abdominal examination revealed a palpable gallbladder, right upper quadrant tenderness, and a positive Murphy’s sign. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 8.1 × 10^9/L, a C-reactive protein of 0.8 mg/L, and normal liver-function tests including bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a distended gallbladder with wall thickening up to 7 mm and sludge but no definite gallstones, and no dilation of the biliary tree.  
She was admitted with a presumptive diagnosis of acute calculous cholecystitis; biliary colic was also considered less likely given the duration of symptoms and a positive Murphy’s sign. Nonoperative management with intravenous fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, and antibiotics was initiated. After 24 hours, her pain worsened, she developed vomiting and right upper quadrant guarding, and her C-reactive protein rose to 98.2 mg/L while her white-cell count remained normal. The decision was made to proceed to laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
title: Gallbladder torsion with gangrenous cholecystitis: a case report

case_prompt: A 41-year-old man presented with a swelling of the chest wall. The mass had been present since birth, had grown later in life until it burst 15 years ago, and then, three months after the rupture, had gradually enlarged to its current size. He reported no pain or overlying skin changes. His medical history included asthma and a percutaneous coronary intervention in 2019; medications were aspirin, clopidogrel, and an inhaled short-acting beta-agonist as needed. He was a non smoker. On examination, there was a 7 cm × 7 cm soft, round, slightly mobile, non-fluctuant, non-pulsatile, non-tender subcutaneous mass over the sternum. The overlying skin was of normal color and temperature. The provisional diagnosis was lipoma. No investigations were performed, and surgical excision was planned at the patient’s request.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Subcutaneous bronchogenic cyst of the chest wall: A case report with brief literature review

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man with no history of rheumatic fever presented with a 10-month history of dyspnea and palpitations. On examination, his pulse was irregular at 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and a prominent apical diastolic murmur continuing into the first heart sound was noted. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation with a right bundle-branch block. Chest radiography revealed an enlarged left atrium and pulmonary congestion.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated critical mitral stenosis (mitral valve area 0.7 cm2 by planimetry; peak/mean gradients 16/8 mmHg), mild mitral regurgitation, severe pulmonary arterial hypertension (70 mmHg), and mild functional tricuspid regurgitation. The mitral valve appeared rheumatically deformed with thickened leaflets, commissural fusion, and calcifications. The left atrium was enlarged (area 40 cm2) and contained a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous mass measuring approximately 10 cm2, adherent to the atrial wall. Transesophageal echocardiography localized this mass to the left atrial appendage, with marked spontaneous echo contrast in the atrium.

Given the severe mitral stenosis, atrial enlargement, and atrial fibrillation, the patient received four weeks of anticoagulant therapy. Follow-up echocardiography showed persistence of the mass. Cardiac computed tomography revealed a 6-cm oval tissue mass in the left atrium with regular borders. Preoperative coronary angiography showed no coronary artery stenoses but demonstrated neovascularization from a branch of the left circumflex artery with fistulous contrast entry into the left atrial cavity.
title: A Neovascularized Left Atrial Mass

case_prompt:
A 77-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, Barrett’s esophagus, and prior carotid stenting presented with progressive fatigue. Routine laboratory tests revealed a normocytic, normochromic anemia unresponsive to iron supplementation and erythropoietin. His hemoglobin was 6.0 g/dL (13.4–17.0), MCV 101 fL (82–98), reticulocytes <0.010 × 10^12/L (0.03–0.1), platelets 445 × 10^9/L (145–348), and leukocytes 6.8 × 10^9/L (3.5–11.0). Differential counts were within normal limits. 

Bone marrow biopsy showed total absence of erythropoiesis, normal megakaryocytes, normal granulocytopoiesis, and abundant iron stores; aspirate cytomorphology confirmed absence of erythroid precursors without dysplasia. 

Serologic tests for parvovirus B19, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis A, B, and C, and HIV were negative. Chest CT showed no thymoma. Bone marrow flow cytometry revealed no monoclonal B-cell or T-cell populations. Cytogenetic analysis demonstrated a deletion on the long arm of chromosome 20: 46,XY,del(20)(q11)/46,XY.
title: Pure Red Cell Aplasia with Del(20q) Sensitive for Immunosuppressive Treatment

case_prompt: A 22-year-old woman presented with an 8-day history of dull right upper quadrant abdominal pain associated with abdominal distention, anorexia, weight loss, and bilateral lower leg edema. She also reported recurrent severe headaches with occasional visual disturbances and, over the prior two weeks, new-onset eyelid ptosis and diplopia. Her medical history was notable for surgical removal of an ovarian teratoma six months earlier. She reported irregular menstruation but no known endocrine disorders. On examination, she appeared distressed and pale, with a distended abdomen, epigastric tenderness, shifting dullness, hepatomegaly, and bilateral pitting edema. An abdominal ultrasound revealed massive ascites, surface irregularity and heterogeneous echogenicity of the liver, abdominal lymphadenopathy, and suspicious hepatic nodules suggestive of metastatic disease. A head CT scan showed a 3.7 × 2.1 × 1.6 cm, lobulated, well-circumscribed suprasellar mass isodense to gray matter, with stippled internal calcifications, avid post-contrast enhancement, and small non-enhancing, fluid-attenuating areas. The optic chiasm and infundibulum were slightly displaced anterosuperiorly; the internal carotid arteries were bilaterally encased by approximately 180 degrees; the lesion abutted but did not encase the basilar artery; and there was no extension into the pituitary fossa. The brain parenchyma and ventricular system were otherwise normal. Bilateral maxillary and ethmoid sinuses were partially opacified without air-fluid levels. The right globe was internally rotated.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Craniopharyngioma in young female patient occurring after ovarian teratoma removal – A case report

case_prompt: A 12-year-old girl presented with enlargement of her right breast over 2 months. She had first noticed a small nodule near the nipple that rapidly increased in size. There was no nipple discharge. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Menarche occurred at age 11, and her menstrual cycles were normal. On physical examination, the right breast was substantially enlarged and replaced by a large lump occupying the entire breast, with diffuse tenderness and firmness on palpation. There was no skin thickening or nipple retraction. Ultrasonography of the right breast using an 8–10 MHz linear array transducer showed a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass measuring 17.3 cm in maximum diameter, with multiple cystic channels within the lesion. The right axilla contained lymph nodes with benign features. The lesion was classified as BI-RADS category 4, and ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was advised.
title: Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia of the breast: a case report of a 12-year-old girl

case_prompt: A 36-year-old woman with no significant medical or family history presented with three months of persistent dyspnea that did not limit her daily activities. Vital signs were stable, and lung auscultation was normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, blood chemistry panel, and COVID-19 PCR test, were all within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed mediastinal widening. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed an 84 × 47 mm heterogeneous lesion in the right anterior mediastinum; additional findings included a 5 mm pulmonary nodule in the lateral segment of the left lower lobe, fibrotic bands at the lower lobes, and splenomegaly, with no pleural effusion or chest wall abnormality. The lesion was reported to be suggestive of thymoma or teratoma, and biopsy was not planned because of a high risk of bleeding. Surgical excision through a median sternotomy was recommended.
title: A case report of mediastinal cavernous hemangioma

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old primiparous woman at 26 weeks of gestation was admitted with regular uterine contractions and severe upper abdominal pain. Two weeks earlier, she had been hospitalized for threatening preterm birth and discharged after symptoms resolved. Her history was notable only for first-trimester vaginal bleeding that resolved spontaneously. Prenatal care had been provided offsite, and the 12-week scan images (including adnexal assessment) were unavailable.

On admission, cervical length measured 23 mm. Betamethasone was given for fetal lung maturity, atosiban for tocolysis, and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection. Despite analgesia, her upper abdominal pain intensified and she developed dyspnea. She became hypotensive and tachycardic. Abdominal examination revealed rebound tenderness and involuntary guarding. Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrated free fluid in the abdomen.

With a working diagnosis of hemoperitoneum leading to hypovolemic shock, a surgical consultation was obtained, and the patient was taken for emergent exploratory laparotomy.
title: A unique case of diagnosis of a heterotopic pregnancy at 26 weeks – case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 77-year-old man was referred for evaluation of suspected unilateral iris rubeosis in his right eye found on routine examination before cataract surgery. He was asymptomatic. Medical history included hypertension with renal involvement, metabolic syndrome, atrial fibrillation, prostatic syndrome, moderate COPD, and longstanding childhood divergent strabismus with left‐eye amblyopia.

On examination, visual acuity was 0.5 in the right eye and 0.15 in the left eye, with divergent strabismus. Slit‐lamp biomicroscopy of the right eye revealed radial vascular engorgement of the iris at the 5–7 o’clock position, with vessels originating in the iris stroma and extending circumferentially. Gonioscopy showed a grade IV open angle and a 360° vascular racemose network in the iridocorneal angle. No sentinel episcleral vessels or iris masses were seen. Intraocular pressures were 10 mmHg in the right eye and 12 mmHg in the left eye; the left eye exam was otherwise normal.

Fundus examination of the right eye showed an oblique optic disc, myopic chorioretinitis, and no exudates, hemorrhages, or neovascularization. There were no clinical signs of diabetic retinopathy, central or branch retinal vein or artery obstruction. Indentation fundus exam with maximal mydriasis revealed no peripheral tumors (eg, choroidal melanoma, retinoblastoma, metastasis, or ciliary body lesions). Supra‐aortic Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated no hemodynamically significant carotid stenosis.

An anterior‐segment OCT demonstrated poorly defined intrastromal hyporeflective spaces corresponding to the vascular lumina. Fluorescein angiography showed normal contrast uptake without extravasation in the iris, iridocorneal angle, or retinal vessels, with early filling of the iris vessels and no diffusion of dye.
title: Iris Vascular Malformation with 360-Degree Iridocorneal Angle Affectation

case_prompt: An 85-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of epigastric and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Her medical history was notable only for mild hypertension and a squamous cell carcinoma of the right hand excised 4 years earlier. She reported a 5-kg weight loss over 2 months but denied hematemesis, hematochezia, or melena. On examination, her sclerae appeared mildly pale. Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 34%, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 113 fL, and red-cell distribution width 13.5%. The alpha‐fetoprotein level was markedly elevated at 155 000 IU/mL; other serum tumor markers were within normal limits, and tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a mass in the gastric antrum. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed a 7-cm antral mass and multiple liver lesions consistent with metastases.
title: AFP-producing hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the stomach: a case report

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old man, previously healthy, presented with progressive ascending paresthesia and weakness beginning 10 days after a flu-like illness. Within 24 hours he developed paresthesia in his upper limbs, and by day 2 he had weakness of the lower and then upper limbs, along with discrete dysphagia and frequent choking on liquids. He was admitted on day 8 of symptoms. Three days into hospitalization he developed respiratory weakness and worsening dysphagia; by day 14 he had facial diplegia. No autonomic dysfunction was noted. 

On examination, he had flaccid tetraplegia (MRC grade 3/5 in the upper limbs and 2/5 in the lower limbs), absent reflexes, glove-and-stocking hypoesthesia, a positive Romberg sign, and facial diplegia. Nerve conduction studies showed sensory and motor demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with decreased motor conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies in the ulnar, median, tibial, and peroneal nerves, prolonged F-wave latencies in all four limbs, and decreased sensory conduction velocities in the right musculocutaneous and left ulnar nerves. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed albumino-cytologic dissociation with 0 white cells and protein 0.7 mg/dL.

He was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome and received a single course of IV immunoglobulin, with progressive improvement; at discharge his strength was MRC 4+ and respiratory and bulbar signs had resolved. Two weeks later, he returned with worsening dysphagia and new sensory ataxia. Examination showed positive Romberg sign, loss of deep sensation on the right, absent reflexes, MRC grade 4+ strength, a weak gag reflex, and mild facial diplegia. He was treated with a second course of IV immunoglobulin, resulting in complete resolution of dysphagia and ataxia. After discharge he continued to improve, recovering all reflexes, with only mild proximal weakness and paresthesia treated with pregabalin.
title: Acute‐onset chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy with cranial nerves and respiratory tract involvement: A case report

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old man was referred for evaluation of isolated thrombocytopenia and suspected myelodysplastic syndrome. He reported a long-standing history of thrombocytopenia first documented at age 17 when his platelet count was 40 × 10^9/L; hemoglobin and leukocyte counts were then normal. Current laboratory testing showed a platelet count of 21 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, and white blood cell count 5.5 × 10^9/L. He described only general fatigue and denied significant bleeding. His family history was notable for multiple relatives with thrombocytopenia (almost all with platelet counts <100 × 10^9/L) and a maternal history of breast, colon, and gastric cancers. He consumed no alcohol and worked as a turkey farmer.

A bone marrow aspirate and biopsy revealed a hypercellular marrow with prominent dysmegakaryopoiesis characterized by micromegakaryocytes with hypolobated or bilobated nuclei, concerning for single-lineage myelodysplastic syndrome. Cytogenetic analysis detected an abnormal clone: 46,XY,inv(12)(p13q21)/46,XY.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Inherited Thrombocytopenia Caused by Germline ANKRD26 Mutation Should Be Considered in Young Patients With Suspected Myelodysplastic Syndrome

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old man noted a large, nonpainful left lateral–cervical mass that had gradually increased in size over several months and was initially neglected. Fifteen days before admission, he developed dyspnea. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender mass in the left lower neck extending toward the clavicle.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest showed a large (10.4 × 6.6 × 18.9 cm), well-circumscribed, nonenhancing soft-tissue density lesion in the upper and middle mediastinum with cervical extension, containing peripheral microcalcifications. The mass displaced the trachea, esophagus, and azygous vein to the right and surrounded the left subclavian and vertebral arteries without evidence of invasion; it contacted the vertebral bodies from C7 to T6 without bone erosion.

MRI demonstrated a mediastinal mass with uniformly low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and no marked enhancement after gadolinium.

The patient underwent a cervical biopsy. Histologic evaluation showed a non‐atypical myxoid spindle cell proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining suggested a low-grade myxoid spindle cell tumor, favoring either low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma or low-grade myxoid liposarcoma.
title: Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma arising in the mediastinum: Case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 46-year-old Spanish man with no significant medical history, a former smoker and nondrinker, was referred after his primary care physician identified bilateral adrenal masses on CT. He reported 4 months of evening fevers and an unintended 5-kg weight loss following a SARS-CoV-2 infection. He denied abdominal pain, had a normal appetite, and regular bowel and urinary function. On examination he was afebrile, with a heart rate of 107 bpm, blood pressure 140/70 mmHg, and respiratory rate 20/min; cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, MCV 78.5 fl, MCH 26.0 pg, INR 1.3, CRP 140 mg/L, and endocrine testing excluded hormone-producing tumors. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an 11.5 × 10.5 cm heterogeneous mass in the right adrenal gland with central calcification and a 2.5 cm lesion in the left adrenal gland without features suggestive of malignancy; there was no evidence of metastases.
