title: Recurrent fever leading to the diagnosis of an angiosarcoma of the adrenal gland: a case report

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old G3P2 woman at 22 weeks’ gestation with two prior cesarean deliveries and three live births was brought by ambulance to the emergency department with severe dyspnea and a brief syncopal episode. According to her husband, she had a short-lived crampy abdominal pain just before the syncope. She denied ongoing abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fever, or other symptoms.

On examination, she appeared pale and cool. Vital signs: pulse 72 beats/min, blood pressure 110/80 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, temperature 37.0 °C. She had intermittent drowsiness and restlessness. The gravid uterus was palpated just above the umbilicus without tenderness. A speculum exam showed no vaginal bleeding.

Despite normal blood pressure, her cool extremities and altered mental status suggested compensated shock. Initial labs (not yet available during resuscitation) later demonstrated leukocytosis (24.4 × 10^3/mm^3), hemoglobin fall from 9.8 g/dL to 7.9 g/dL, venous pH 7.295, and lactate 4 mmol/L.

A point-of-care ultrasound revealed a large amount of free fluid in the abdominal cavity and fetal bradycardia. Uncrossmatched O– negative blood was started, and obstetrics was consulted. Repeat bedside ultrasound confirmed intra-abdominal hemorrhage and absence of fetal cardiac activity but did not localize a uterine defect. The patient was taken for emergent surgical exploration.
title: Atypical presentation of hemorrhagic shock in pregnancy: a case highlighting the developing field of emergency medicine in Israel

case_prompt: A 33‐year‐old previously healthy man presented with 2 days of fever, sore throat, irritability, and an inability to drink water because of severe anxiety when he saw or thought about water. One month earlier, he had traveled to join a new job. He recalled being bitten on his right ear by an unknown animal three months before presentation; the wound had healed without medical care. On examination, he was agitated and febrile (38.3°C) with stable other vital signs. There was no nuchal rigidity or focal neurologic deficits. A healed scar was noted on the right pinna. Complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and C‐reactive protein were within normal limits. Computed tomography of the head showed no abnormalities. Lumbar puncture revealed a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid, and bacterial cultures were negative. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and acyclovir were initiated but were discontinued when CSF bacterial cultures and a viral PCR panel returned negative. Real‐time PCR for rabies virus on CSF and on a nuchal‐skin biopsy specimen was negative, and no rabies virus neutralizing antibodies were detectable in CSF or plasma.
title: Antemortem diagnosis of human rabies: A case report

case_prompt: A 45-year-old woman with a 2-year history of relapsed, refractory immunoglobulin A kappa multiple myeloma presented with a one-month history of progressive blurred vision in her left eye after an initial outside diagnosis of optic neuritis. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and hand motion in the left eye, with a left relative afferent pupillary defect; she denied diplopia or pain with eye movement. She reported bilateral frontal headaches and had a chronic 2-mm ptosis of the left eyelid. Extraocular movements were full. Confrontation visual fields were intact in the right eye but could not be assessed in the left eye. Red desaturation testing showed 100% in the right eye and 30% in the left eye. Dilated fundus examination revealed a normal right optic disc and, in the left eye, disc edema with hyperemia, superior splinter hemorrhages, and a small, lobulated elevation on the nasal aspect of the optic nerve head with blurring of the disc margin and obscuration of small vessels.
title: Optic nerve head plasmacytoma as a manifestation of multiple myeloma

case_prompt: A 51-year-old man presented to the neurology clinic with a one-week history of right-sided retrobulbar pain unrelieved by over-the-counter analgesics. One week later he awoke with constant binocular vertical diplopia that worsened on downgaze but denied changes in visual acuity, photopsias, or trauma. His medical history was negative for hypertension, diabetes, or other vascular risk factors. Examination showed mild depression and intorsion of the right eye on downward gaze consistent with isolated right fourth cranial nerve palsy; the remainder of the neurologic and ophthalmologic examination was unremarkable. Ophthalmology testing for thyroid eye disease and acetylcholine-receptor autoantibodies to evaluate for Myasthenia Gravis were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits was inconclusive. Computed tomographic angiography of the head demonstrated an enlarged vein in the anterior interhemispheric fissure draining into a prominent inferior sagittal sinus but did not suggest a specific vascular abnormality.
title: Isolated trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV) palsy in a patient with carotid-cavernous fistula

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old white man presented with 3 months of fatigue, evening fevers, night sweats, an unexplained 5-kg weight loss, worsening dyspnea, cough, and mucopurulent sputum. He was a current smoker (30 pack-years) and had worked in a stone quarry until 12 years earlier. His medical history included chronic catarrhal bronchitis, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and an intestinal polypectomy. He denied ever having spirometry or taking systemic or inhaled corticosteroids; a chest radiograph 3 years earlier showed rarefaction of the bronchovascular tree.

On examination, he was afebrile. Chest auscultation revealed reduced vesicular sounds and widespread rhonchi; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a neutrophilic leukocytosis (white-cell count, 16 500 per µL [70% neutrophils]), mild anemia (hemoglobin, 11.4 g/dL), an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (72 mm/h), and a C-reactive protein level of 20 mg/L. Plasma immunoglobulins, liver and renal function, and an HIV antibody test were normal or negative. 

Spirometry revealed a severe obstructive defect with a post–β₂ agonist forced vital capacity of 72% and a forced expiratory volume in one second of 46% of predicted. Chest radiography showed bilateral apical and subclavian sclerosis with multiple cavitary nodules. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated multiple nodular opacities with small central cavitations in both upper lobes and apical segments of the lower lobes, tree-in-bud foci, and cystic bronchiectasis in both lung apices; there was no significant mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and the findings were interpreted as “consistent with chronic TB.” 

Three sputum samples were obtained on different days and submitted for the search for Mycobacteria spp.
title: Pulmonary nocardiosis in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A new clinical challenge

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus (HBA1C 11.2%), hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, and a history of right above-ankle amputation presented with a 2-day history of two episodes of hematemesis (each 300–400 mL) accompanied by postprandial abdominal pain, melena, polyuria, polyphagia, and fatigue. He denied odynophagia, hematochezia, syncope, palpitations, NSAID use, alcohol use, or chronic liver disease. He had not been taking his insulin regularly.  
On arrival he was tachycardic (110 bpm) with blood pressure 141/77 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 bpm, temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The abdominal, chest, and cardiac examinations were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.4 g/dL, hematocrit 46%, white blood cell count 6.43 × 10^9/L, platelets 304 × 10^9/L, INR 1.6, serum glucose 316 mg/dL, blood urea 41 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, serum amylase 19 U/L, arterial blood pH 7.34, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, and anion gap 12 mmol/L. Viral serologies (HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV I & II) were negative.  
Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. He was resuscitated with IV fluids and insulin, after which a gastroenterology consultation was obtained for endoscopic evaluation of his hematemesis and melena.  
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed diffuse, circumferential patchy necrotizing esophagitis with black discoloration and ulcerations affecting the middle and distal thirds of the esophagus beginning 25 cm from the incisors; the severity increased distally and abruptly ended at the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsies were not taken due to the risk of perforation.
title: Acute Esophageal Necrosis (Gurvits Syndrome): A Rare Cause of Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding in Somalia

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old woman presented with painless loss of vision in her right eye 3 weeks after an uncomplicated phacoemulsification with posterior-chamber intraocular lens implantation. She had bilateral hyperopia (+4.25 D) but no prior ocular disease or surgery. Before cataract surgery her vision was equal in both eyes, and her general medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity in the right eye was 20/50 (−1.50 sph/–1.0 cyl × 90°). Intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg. Slit-lamp examination revealed a deep, quiet anterior chamber and a well-centered endocapsular lens; gonioscopy showed no cyclodialysis cleft. Dilated fundoscopy disclosed optic disc hyperemia, macular edema, and multiple retinal folds at the posterior pole extending into the mid periphery.

Fluorescein angiography showed optic-disc staining and focal hyperfluorescence in the superior mid periphery. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated no choroidal ischemia but confirmed the peripheral hyperfluorescent spot. Optical coherence tomography revealed cystoid macular edema, subretinal fluid at the fovea, irregular retinal pigment-epithelium elevations, and lobular choroidal thickening. B-scan ultrasonography showed uveal thickening without intraocular mass or peripheral choroidal detachment. Brain and orbit MRI excluded orbital or intracranial lesions but showed gadolinium enhancement of the retina-uvea complex.

She was initially treated with topical NSAIDs and systemic prednisolone (1 mg/kg) tapered over 20 weeks. At 4 weeks there was no change in clinical or imaging findings, and steroids were discontinued after 2 months.
title: Posterior Uveal Effusion after Cataract Surgery

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of atypical abdominal pain, intermittently associated with vomiting and hematemesis. The pain was localized to the left hypochondrium, nonradiating, and described as a feeling of heaviness. Her past medical history was notable for a splenectomy performed 18 months earlier; she reported no other health issues or systemic symptoms.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal palpation revealed mild epigastric and left hypochondrial tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, coagulation profile, blood electrolytes, liver function tests, C-reactive protein, serum lipase, fasting glucose, and tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein, CA19-9, CEA), were all within normal limits.

A plain abdominal radiograph showed a mass with internal gas bubbles in the left hypochondrium but no radiopaque marker. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 4.2-cm hypodense, spongiform-appearing mass in the splenectomy bed with a mildly enhancing wall, communication with the gastric fundus, and surrounding fat stranding. MRI revealed the lesion to be heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, uniformly hypointense on T1-weighted images, and with mild peripheral enhancement after gadolinium administration.
title: Transgastric migration of retained intraabdominal surgical sponge: Gossypiboma in the fundus

case_prompt: A 31-year-old Black woman, nulliparous and obese, presented with a history of pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an enlarged heterogeneous uterus. In May 2017, she underwent a complete hysterectomy; the specimen weighed 13.9 pounds, and pathology revealed leiomyomas without malignancy. One month later, she developed dyspnea and chest pain. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a mass presumed to be a thrombus in the right atrium. At sternotomy, the lesion was deemed unresectable; biopsy revealed “a fusocellular neoplasm, without atypia, richly vascularized, with areas of stromal fibrohyalinization, and the immunohistochemical analysis revealed angioleiomyoma.” Magnetic resonance imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis identified a vascularized lesion within the inferior vena cava extending 19 cm from the iliac confluence to the right atrium, with an external component around the right gonadal vein. MRI also showed a 2.5-cm lingular lung nodule; percutaneous biopsy of this nodule demonstrated “neoplasm with smooth muscle differentiation of gynecological/Müllerian type without criteria for malignancy.” Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a mass partially filling the IVC and projecting into the right atrium, suggestive of a tumor.
title: Symptomatic uterine leiomyomatosis with intracaval and intracardiac invasion: Video case report

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old Caucasian woman was evaluated for a few days of abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting, as well as dysphagia, cachexia, and progressive dyspnea when supine. She reported painless, progressive abdominal distension and a weight gain of over 15 kg during the past year (body-mass index, 30.5). She denied hirsutism, skin changes, or other signs of hormonal excess. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable for gynecological disease.

On examination, her abdomen was markedly distended. Office transabdominal ultrasound revealed massive ascites. Laboratory studies showed a CA 125 level of 1744.3 mUI/ml; carcinoembryonic antigen, α-fetoprotein, and CA 19-9 were within normal limits. A second-level ultrasound (transvaginal and transabdominal) identified a 20-cm mobile solid mass in the right adnexa with a smooth surface, color score 2, and acoustic shadows; there was no evidence of pelvic-structure infiltration or carcinomatosis. The uterus was of normal size, and a small uterine fibroid was noted.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed abundant peritoneal fluid and demonstrated a 17-cm abdominal mass of uncertain origin, as well as a 4.3-cm uterine fibroleiomyoma. CT of the chest showed a moderate left pleural effusion.
title: Pelvic mass, ascites, hydrothorax: a malignant or benign condition? Meigs syndrome with high levels of CA 125

case_prompt: A 25-year-old woman presented with three months of colicky epigastric pain and nausea, and over the last month she noted weight loss and intermittent rectal bleeding. On examination, her blood pressure was 104/60 mmHg, pulse 68/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and temperature 37 °C. Abdominal palpation revealed a firm, ill-defined 5 × 8 cm mass in the left epigastrium. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 12.8 × 10^9/L (reference 4–11 × 10^9/L) and albumin 21 g/L (reference 34–48 g/L); liver and renal function tests and electrolytes were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large mass in the left transverse colon with mural thickening, irregular luminal narrowing, and multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. A barium enema revealed a long irregular stricture of the distal transverse colon. Colonoscopy showed an incomplete stricture of the middle and distal transverse colon with mucosal ulceration. Biopsy specimens demonstrated chronic active colitis with extensive ulcerations.
title: Basidiobolomycosis of the Colon Masquerading as Stenotic Colon Cancer

case_prompt: A 20-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of sleeping with an open mouth, snoring, a foreign-body sensation in the throat, and difficulty swallowing. On oropharyngeal and nasal endoscopic examination, there was a medium-hard, semimobile, painless, well-circumscribed mass measuring 2 × 1 cm, originating in the nasopharynx and extending downward from the posterior soft palate. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a vascular-appearing lesion without high-flow characteristics, arising in the nasopharynx and completely filling the choanae. Computed tomography demonstrated a nonhomogeneous lesion that did not erode adjacent tissues and showed no calcifications. Ear, nose, throat, and cranial nerve examinations were otherwise normal.
title: Schwannoma Located in Nasopharyngeal Region

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old non-smoking Chinese woman presented with a 45-day history of cough, sputum production, and throat discomfort, without fever, chest pain, or congestion. Examination revealed multiple pale, dome-shaped papules on the cheeks, eyelids, axillae, and back. She first developed a right-sided pneumothorax at age 36, was treated with tube thoracostomy, and had recurrences at ages 48 and 50; at the third event, her right lung was 40% collapsed, prompting surgical resection. Intraoperatively, multiple thin-walled bullae (0.1–3.0 cm) and a >10 cm fissural bulla were resected; histology showed cysts lined by CK7-positive, TTF-1–positive pneumocytes with internal septa. 

She reported frequent illnesses during childhood. Her mother and maternal aunt both had pulmonary bullae and recurrent pneumothoraxes; her mother died of renal cancer at age 71. A 31-year-old daughter and a 69-year-old cousin had no similar findings. 

Chest CT demonstrated numerous round to oval cysts with thin, uniform walls, predominantly in the lung bases, including a dominant 8.4 × 5.1 cm cyst anterior to the heart. A new 2.8 × 2.3 cm solid lesion with irregular margins and adjacent pleural thickening was noted in the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy of this lesion revealed fibroblastic proliferation with plasma cells and lymphocytes, negative staining for CEA, IgG4, IgG, and ALK. Abdominal ultrasound showed no renal masses, and thyroid ultrasound revealed multiple nodules.
title: Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome: a literature review and case study of a Chinese woman presenting a novel FLCN mutation

case_prompt:
A 30‐year‐old Caucasian woman, gravida 2 para 0, conceived by in vitro fertilization and followed from the first trimester. At 24 weeks’ gestation, because of preterm‐birth risk, a vaginal pessary was placed. An oral glucose tolerance test showed fasting 70 mg/dL, 1 h 180 mg/dL, and 2 h 155 mg/dL, establishing gestational diabetes mellitus. The patient was managed with diet alone; third‐trimester HbA1c was 5.41%. She was enrolled in an education program for self‐monitoring of blood glucose with targets of fasting <95 mg/dL, 1 h postprandial <140 mg/dL, and 2 h postprandial <120 mg/dL. Despite counseling, her logs revealed irregular meals, periods of nausea and loss of appetite, alternating with anxiety‐driven intake of high‐glycemic snacks and beverages, resulting in marked glycemic variability. 

At the same visit, obstetric ultrasound showed an amniotic fluid index (AFI) of 27.42 cm. Four days later, repeat AFI was 18.85 cm. Serial ultrasounds until 30 weeks demonstrated oscillations in AFI that closely tracked her periods of poor versus improved glycemic control. Given that over 80% of her glucose readings met targets on diet alone, pharmacologic therapy was not initiated.
title: Transient Polyhydramnios during Pregnancy Complicated with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: Case Report and Systematic Review

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old Caucasian man presented with one week of fever (up to 39°C), general weakness, headache, dry cough, and diarrhea. He was a 20 pack‐year smoker with no other comorbidities or travel. He had been treated empirically with oral amoxicillin–clavulanate without improvement.

On admission: temperature 38.9°C; pulse 100/min; respiratory rate not recorded; oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Chest examination revealed reduced vesicular breath sounds and crackles over the left upper lung field. 

Initial laboratory studies showed WBC 2020 cells/mm3, total bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 382 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 69 U/L, and CPK 422 U/L. Serologies were negative for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. Blood cultures were negative. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated extensive consolidation of the left upper lobe without pleural effusion. The patient was started on IV piperacillin–tazobactam and oral clarithromycin. On hospital day 3, a urine antigen test was positive for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1; clarithromycin was replaced with IV levofloxacin, and piperacillin–tazobactam was continued.

By day 6, his respiratory status worsened, and rifampicin was added. On day 9, he developed respiratory distress (40 breaths/min); arterial blood gas on room air showed PaO2 50 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg, pH 7.50, and SaO2 86%. Chest CT revealed extensive left upper lobe consolidation with ground-glass opacities and pleural effusion, and patchy ground-glass areas in the right lung. On day 10, PaO2/FiO2 was 101 and he was transferred to the ICU and placed on CPAP, improving to a PaO2/FiO2 of 254.

Levofloxacin was held on day 17 for washout and resumed with IV fluconazole on day 19. On day 21, he again developed respiratory distress; CT showed increased bilateral consolidation and a left-sided pneumothorax. On day 22, he was intubated and underwent bronchoalveolar lavage, which revealed 32% macrophages, 26% lymphocytes (CD4/CD8 ratio 0.8), 40% neutrophils, and 2% eosinophils; no protozoa, fungi, or malignant cells were seen. 

On day 23, IV methylprednisolone 120 mg/day was initiated for presumed ongoing ARDS.
title: Eosinophilic infiltrate in a patient with severe Legionella pneumonia as a levofloxacin-related complication: a case report

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old man presented with a two-month history of progressively worsening dyspnea and an unintentional 10-kg weight loss. His medical history included childhood asthma, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, and coronary artery bypass grafting two years earlier. He had been empirically started on first-line antituberculous therapy 15 days before presentation by a general practitioner. He was a lifelong non-smoker with no known tuberculosis exposure.  

On examination, he had bilateral pitting pedal edema and numerous hyperpigmented nevi distributed over his body, none of which had changed in size, shape, or color. Auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds at the left lung base.  

Chest radiography showed a moderate left pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated left-sided pleural fluid with irregular, nodular pleural thickening. Thoracic ultrasound confirmed septated and loculated fluid. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis yielded black pleural fluid. Analysis of the fluid revealed an exudate with protein 3.9 g/dL, total nucleated cell count 700 cells/µL (30% neutrophils, 70% lymphocytes), and glucose 231 mg/dL. Gram stain, bacterial culture, acid-fast bacilli smear and culture, Xpert MTB/RIF assay, and fungal culture were all negative. Pleural fluid cytology showed atypical cells.
title: Black pleural effusion: an unusual presentation of metastatic melanoma diagnosed by medical thoracoscopy

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old man from Mozambique presented with a 5-year history of a massive, predominantly localized fibrous gingival enlargement with signs of inflammation and insufficient oral hygiene. He had no known pre-existing conditions, no prescribed medications, no family history of similar problems, and no history of orthodontic treatment. On examination, there was deep bite, anterior crowding, multiple carious lesions, and root remnants of teeth 16 and 25 associated with radicular cysts. A panoramic radiograph confirmed diverse carious lesions and cystic changes at roots 16 and 25. Between November 2018 and February 2019, he underwent monthly professional tooth cleaning, oral hygiene instruction, treatment of carious lesions, and extraction of root remnants. Once oral hygiene was satisfactory, a gingivectomy of the upper jaw (February 2019) and lower jaw (March 2019) was performed without complications. The excised gingiva was coarse and fibrous and was submitted for histopathological examination.

Histopathology (hematoxylin and eosin) showed stratified acanthotic squamous epithelium with slight parakeratosis and focal erosion. The underlying stromal connective tissue revealed collagen-rich fibrosis with a superficial, dense infiltrate of inflammatory cells, predominately plasma cells accompanied by a few lymphocytes. Neutrophils were absent except within the small area of surface erosion, and eosinophils were not detected. Immunostaining for kappa and lambda light chains demonstrated a polyclonal plasma cell population. Additional immunostaining for IgG and IgG4 showed an IgG4/IgG ratio value of 0.279 in a single high-power field of ten examined.
title: Interdisciplinary assessment and management of a patient with a fibrous gingival enlargement of unknown origin: A case report

case_prompt: A 30-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of right elbow pain, swelling, and stiffness. He noted partial relief with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and had been treated with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. There was no fever, nocturnal pain, history of trauma, or involvement of other joints. On examination, moderate joint effusion was present, flexion–extension ranged from 20° to 110°, pronation–supination was normal, and the elbow was stable. Plain radiographs of the elbow were unremarkable. Inflammatory markers were within normal limits. Synovial fluid analysis revealed nonspecific inflammation and sterile cultures. Computed tomography of the elbow demonstrated a 5 mm well-defined lucent nidus with a central sclerotic focus breaching the articular margins of the trochlear notch, with minimal surrounding sclerosis, periosteal reaction, and adjacent soft-tissue edema. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a hypointense central nidus on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences with minimal peripheral T2 hyperintensity and surrounding sclerosis, as well as bone marrow edema of the proximal ulna, small joint effusion, and synovial proliferation.
title: Arthroscopic Excision of an Intra-articular Osteoid Osteoma in the Trochlear Notch of Ulna – A Case Report

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of right-sided facial pain, otalgia with purulent otorrhea, and binocular diplopia, which worsened over the past 2 days. He had a fever of 38 °C and appeared fatigued. He denied recent trauma or dental procedures. Six months earlier he had an episode of acute otitis media that responded to medical therapy; he reported no intervening ear infections.

On examination, he could not completely close his left eye, and neurological assessment revealed a left abducens nerve palsy responsible for the diplopia; the remainder of the neurologic examination was normal. Otoscopy showed purulent otorrhea obscuring the tympanic membrane.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 14,000/µL (4,000–11,000/µL) and a C-reactive protein level of 45 mg/L (< 5 mg/L).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the temporal bone revealed opacification of the left middle ear, lysis of the ipsilateral petrous apex, intact ossicles, and a rim-enhancing fluid collection consistent with a retropharyngeal abscess. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated the retropharyngeal abscess, opacification of the middle ear and mastoid air cells, and enhancement extending into Meckel’s cave.
title: Gradenigo syndrome complicated by a retro-pharyngeal abscess in an 8-year-old child: A case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 72-year-old gravida 10, para 10 woman with hypertension was referred for evaluation of a pelvic mass of 2 months’ duration and progressive dyspnea. On examination, she had a palpable lower abdominal mass; the uterus was of normal size, and there was no lymphadenopathy. Chest radiography and CT scan showed a massive right pleural effusion. Pleural fluid cytology revealed inflammatory cells without malignant changes; cultures and tuberculosis smears were negative. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 53-mm multilocular cystic-solid mass of the right ovary with 6.8-mm septa and a 19-mm mural nodule; the right ovarian artery had a low-resistance flow pattern (RI = 0.61). Free intraperitoneal fluid was noted. Abdominopelvic CT with contrast revealed a 95 × 120 mm multicystic pelvic mass with irregular calcified mural nodules. Serum tumor markers were: CA125 607.4 U/ml, CA19-9 62.72 U/ml, CEA 1.92 ng/ml, and inhibin A < 0.1.
title: Struma ovarii associated with Pseudo-Meig's syndrome and high serum level of CA 125; a case report

case_prompt: An 87-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive left-sided weakness. She initially had difficulty ambulating and ascending stairs, and over time became wheelchair-bound. On neurologic examination, she had diffuse 3/5 left-sided strength, a left leg drift, and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a large confluent T2-hyperintense lesion in the right frontal lobe with multifocal nodular enhancement throughout the left cerebral hemisphere, as well as enhancement in the cerebellum and leptomeninges. The radiologic differential diagnosis included vasculitis, lymphoma, and CNS sarcoidosis as the most probable causes of the multifocal process, with glial neoplasm, demyelination, and metastases considered less likely.
title: Cerebral Amyloidoma Resulting from Central Nervous System Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old man was evaluated for recurrent pulmonary infections and possible immunodeficiency. Since June 2017 he had recurrent pneumonias and a 1½-year history of productive cough with green sputum. He also reported intermittent headaches, sinus congestion, rhinorrhea, intermittent diarrhea, fatigue, and anosmia but denied fever, chills, or night sweats. At disease onset he lost 10–11 pounds. Family history was notable for a brother with thrombocytopenia who died of a brain aneurysm.

In 2017, platelet counts ranged from 91 to 108 × 10^9/L; other CBC parameters, metabolic panel, and urinalysis were normal. Over the next year, quantitative immunoglobulins were IgG 256–308 mg/dL (reference 700–1600), IgM 9–25 (40–230), and IgA 23–33 (70–400). CT of the chest and abdomen revealed mediastinal and upper abdominal lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and multiple pulmonary nodules. Pulmonary function tests showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 59% with a normal vital capacity and moderate diffusion impairment. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and endobronchial lymph node biopsies was negative for bacterial, fungal, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, and no malignancy was identified.

He was treated with inhaled fluticasone, umeclidinium, and vilanterol, improving the FEV1/FVC ratio to 85%. After a positive serum aspergillus galactomannan assay, he received isavuconazonium sulfate for 5 weeks but discontinued it due to elevated liver enzymes, nausea, and vomiting. A repeat CT in December 2018 showed progression of multifocal pulmonary nodules with persistent mediastinal lymphadenopathy. In January 2019, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical biopsy of the right lower lobe was performed. Histologic examination showed lymphoid hyperplasia with interstitial fibrosis, patchy foci of organizing pneumonia, rare giant cells and histiocytes, acute bronchopneumonia, and occasional fibrin exudates.
journal: Allergy, Asthma, and Clinical Immunology : Official Journal of the Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
title: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) with granulomatous interstitial lung disease (GLILD) and SARS COVID-19 infection: case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 61-year-old woman who did not smoke or drink alcohol was referred for evaluation of recurrent bilateral lower-limb skin lesions. Over the preceding 2 months, she had been admitted three times with presumed lower-limb cellulitis and treated with oral and intravenous antibiotics without improvement. She had a history of schizophrenia treated with risperidone. On examination, there were multiple tender, erythematous, non-suppurative nodules on both lower limbs extending to the thighs. A skin biopsy showed striking fat necrosis in the dermis and subcutis with focal neutrophilic infiltrate; ghost outlines of fat cells were seen with focal basophilia, raising the possibility of pancreatic fat necrosis. Her serum amylase was 148 IU/L (reference range, 0–100 IU/L).
title: Pancreatic panniculitis preceding acute pancreatitis and subsequent detection of an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm: A case report

case_prompt:
An 11-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a bleeding gingival swelling that had developed gradually over 3 months. She was in orthodontic treatment, took no medications, and had no relevant medical history. There was no history of trauma, smoking, or dental infection, and her oral hygiene was excellent.

On examination, the lesion on the gingival papilla between teeth 44 and 45 measured 15 × 10 × 13 mm. It was sessile, violaceous, lobulated, and depressible, with telangiectasias and fibrinous ulcerations, and it bled easily on palpation. Over the preceding five years she had undergone six complete surgical excisions of similar lesions, with each recurrence appearing within months of excision.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were normal. Periapical radiography and cone-beam CT of the area showed no anomalies of the adjacent teeth or alveolar bone. Under local anesthesia, the lesion was excised with healthy margins, and the specimen was sent for histopathological analysis.
title: Corticosteroids as a conservative treatment for recurrent pediatric oral pyogenic granuloma: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old woman was diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 infection after two positive PCR tests (November 5 and 20, 2020) and a negative test on November 30. During the acute illness, she had low‐grade fever (maximum 37.2 °C) and severe leg pain but no cough, dyspnea, or loss of smell or taste. She received no treatment and did not undergo chest imaging. She returned to work in early December, and one week later she began having severe, brief episodes of circular dizziness when getting out of bed or turning to the right. These attacks, which lasted seconds at a time, continued for six days and were accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She also had severe occipital headaches radiating to the neck during the first few days. 

On initial evaluation by her general practitioner and subsequent neurologic consultation, her dizziness had lessened. Laboratory studies were notable only for a serum potassium level of 3.7 mmol/L. She was afebrile, normotensive, independently mobile, and breathing comfortably. Her neurologic examination was normal. She was referred to otolaryngology. She had no hearing complaints and denied tinnitus but continued to have a moderate occipital headache. 

On neurotological assessment, there was no spontaneous nystagmus, and head-impulse and skew-deviation tests were negative. The Romberg test (eyes open and closed) and the Fukuda stepping test revealed no lateralization. During the Dix–Hallpike maneuver on the right, after a latency of approximately 10 seconds she experienced dizziness and nausea, and a small vertical-torsional geotropic positional nystagmus was observed for about 5 seconds. On returning to the seated position, her vertigo and nystagmus intensified.
title: Post-COVID-19 Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo

case_prompt: A 12-year-old boy with type II diabetes mellitus presented with an 8-month history of a gradually enlarging mass on the left lateral nasal wall. He reported a history of nasal trauma approximately one year earlier. He had no nasal obstruction, epistaxis, sinus infections, olfactory changes, or snoring. There was no family history of childhood cancers. On examination, a 1.5 × 1.5 cm firm, nontender, immobile subcutaneous mass was noted over the frontal process of the maxilla without overlying skin discoloration. Limited MRI of the face was nondiagnostic due to artifact but suggested a possible nasal dermoid. Subsequent CT imaging showed a hyperdense, nonlipomatous soft-tissue mass of the left lateral nasal wall. An excisional biopsy was performed; there was no apparent intranasal extension.
title: Subcutaneous Lobular Capillary Hemangioma Presenting as a Facial Mass

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of insidious pain over the lateral aspect of his left foot and pins-and-needles sensation in the plantar surface. He denied any history of trauma. Six months earlier he had noted a small, peanut-shaped swelling behind his left knee, which gradually increased in size.

On examination, there was an oval, firm, nonpulsatile, nonfluctuant, nontransilluminating mass measuring approximately 2×3×1 cm in the left popliteal fossa. The mass was mobile in both directions and the overlying skin was pinchable. Neurologic examination revealed decreased sensation over the lateral plantar aspect of the left foot; motor strength was preserved. Distal pulses in the left popliteal and dorsalis pedis arteries were palpable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left popliteal fossa showed an encapsulated, round to oval lesion eccentrically placed within the intermuscular space posterior to the knee joint. The lesion was homogeneously isointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with focal hypointense areas suggestive of a fascicular sign. Sagittal images demonstrated continuity of the mass with the tibial nerve and a fat-split sign. The lesion measured 2×3×1 cm.
title: Tibial Nerve Schwannoma: An Unexplained Cause of Lateral Foot Pain – A Rare Case Report and Review

case_prompt:
A woman in her 50s with hypercholesterolemia, osteoporosis, mild aortic-root dilation, and recurrent atypical chest pain presented with recurrent bilateral flank pain. She had a history of occasional alcohol use and was a former smoker (20 pack-years, quit 4 years earlier). Medications included atorvastatin, ezetimibe, calcium/vitamin D, and sublingual glyceryl trinitrate as needed.

Family history was notable for her daughter’s recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces and bilateral renal cysts, and her brother’s bilateral renal cysts with mild aortic-root dilation. Her mother had emphysema; her father had lung cancer.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen showed bilateral renal cysts and an enlarged right adrenal gland. She underwent multiple percutaneous aspirations of symptomatic renal cysts. Skin lesions suggestive of fibrofolliculomas were biopsied and reported as milia. CT of the chest showed no pulmonary cysts.

Targeted next-generation sequencing of FLCN, FH, MAX, RET, SDHA, SDHAF2, SDHB, SDHC, TMEM127, and VHL genes did not identify a pathogenic variant.

Over the ensuing months she experienced episodic hypertension, anxiety, diaphoresis, and headaches. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated 24-hour urine norepinephrine level. Metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy demonstrated a 2.4-cm right adrenal lesion that was avid.
title: Phaeochromocytoma in a patient with a Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome phenotype

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old woman presented to the emergency department in March 2023 with a several-day history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, and features of intestinal obstruction. She was afebrile and had no significant past medical history. 

Abdominopelvic CT scan revealed an enlarged right adnexa containing multiple fluid-filled cysts; thickening of the left uterine wall contiguous with the left bladder wall; colonic wall thickening with hyperemia; and heterogeneous peritoneal fluid collections. 

On physical examination, the abdomen was distended and tender. Bimanual pelvic examination demonstrated indeterminate solid tissue and firm adnexal adhesions. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a thin, linear endometrium; an enlarged right ovary; and the left ovary densely adherent to the sigmoid colon.

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (white blood cell count 15.02 × 10^3/µL) and elevated C-reactive protein (40.49 mg/L). 

Given the high suspicion for a gynecologic malignancy based on clinical and imaging findings, the patient underwent a laparotomic hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, sigmoid resection with ileostomy, omentectomy, appendectomy, and peritoneal biopsies.
title: Pelvic Actinomycosis and Diagnostic Complexity: Case Report with Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man was referred for white masses in the anterior chamber of his right eye. He had undergone bilateral penetrating keratoplasty for progressive keratoconus 24 years earlier and had yearly ophthalmologic follow-up; an examination one year before referral was normal. He first noted the iris lesions in 2019.  
On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/32 (limited by cataract) and intraocular pressure was 19 mmHg. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy and gonioscopy revealed three amelanotic confluent lesions in the superior anterior chamber, adjacent to but not invading the iridocorneal angle. The lesions were transparent on transillumination and caused corectopia and uveal ectropion due to traction on the iris.  
Ultrasound biomicroscopy with a 50-MHz probe showed cystic lesions with slightly hypoechogenic mucous content. High-frequency color Doppler imaging demonstrated absence of intralesional or parietal vascularization. Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography revealed round lesions with thin hyperreflective walls and isoreflective content. These cystic lesions were adjacent to a hyperreflective transcorneal structure consistent with the penetrating keratoplasty scar.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Implantation iris cysts developing 24 years after penetrating keratoplasty

case_prompt: A 24-year-old man presented with acute urinary retention and fever. He reported 10 days of diffuse myalgia followed by painful dysesthesia in the left arm, for which he received corticosteroids. On examination, there was marked weakness of the upper extremities (worse on the left), light spastic paraparesis, and decreased pain, position, and touch sensation below the T1 level. Deep tendon reflexes were weak, Babinski signs were negative bilaterally, and gait was slightly unsteady. Abdominal palpation elicited pain in the hypogastric region. After Foley catheter placement, urinary microscopy showed a normal leukocyte count and no erythrocytes. Because of sudden gait instability and worsening neurologic status, emergency MRI of the spine was obtained. Imaging revealed a 27×8 mm intradural, extramedullary mass posterolateral to the spinal cord at the C7–T1 level, causing compression without signal changes in the cord. The lesion was homogeneously hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images and showed heterogeneous hyperintensity on STIR sequences, suggesting a highly vascularized nature.
title: Intradural extramedullary cavernous hemangioma of the cervicothoracic junction: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A man in his 60s with prostate cancer metastatic to bone and end-stage renal disease was brought by his wife for several days of decreased appetite and inability to ambulate independently. He had a history of strokes 2 years and 10 months earlier, with residual expressive aphasia, and 5 months earlier had catheter-associated sepsis (Enterobacter cloacae) from his tunneled dialysis catheter.

On presentation, he was febrile to 104°F, normotensive, heart rate 134/min, and oxygen saturation 95%. He had a right chest tunneled dialysis catheter in the right internal jugular vein and a left chest subcutaneous chemotherapy port in the left subclavian vein. Neurologic examination confirmed expressive aphasia. Empirical antibiotics were started for presumed catheter-associated sepsis.

While obtaining blood cultures from the chemotherapy port, an attempt with a large-bore needle yielded no blood return. Shortly thereafter the patient lost consciousness, developed torticollis, and had rightward gaze deviation; a stroke code was activated. Head CT showed no acute hemorrhage. The event was initially attributed to a complex seizure, so no thrombolysis was administered. Follow-up brain MRI demonstrated acute ischemic lesions in the right and left frontal lobes, and examination progressed to new right-sided weakness.

Blood cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae. On hospital day 2, the tunneled dialysis catheter was removed at the bedside, and removal of the chemotherapy port under general anesthesia was scheduled. The patient recovered from sepsis and was bridged with heparin to long-term warfarin.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Iatrogenic Paradoxical Stroke in a Patient With Catheter-Associated Thrombosis and Systemic-to-Pulmonary Venous Shunt

case_prompt: A 77-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 2-week history of generalized abdominal pain and distention. She had undergone menopause at age 50 and had a history of dysmenorrhea without prior gynecologic follow-up. On examination, mild to moderate ascites was noted. Pelvic ultrasound showed severe abdominopelvic ascites, omental thickening, and a 155 × 87 mm solid-cystic mass with internal vascularity in the right adnexal region; the left ovary appeared atrophic. MRI of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a mainly cystic mass with a large enhancing mural nodule, ascites, omental thickening, a thickened irregular right fallopian tube, and adhesion of ileal loops to the mass. Laboratory studies included WBC 9300/mm3, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 499,000/mm3, negative β-hCG, normal LDH, CA-125 740 U/mL (normal 0–35), CA19-9 78 U/mL (0–37), and HE4 262 pmol/L (<140). Laparoscopy at another center yielded only inflammation and necrosis on biopsy. At laparotomy, severe inflammation, ascites, extensive adhesions, and endometrial implants were noted. A total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, supracolic omentectomy, and partial small-bowel resection were performed. Peritoneal cytology was negative for malignancy. Grossly, the right adnexal mass infiltrated adipose tissue with extensive necrosis; no lymphovascular invasion was identified. Immunohistochemical studies of the right adnexal tumor were positive for vimentin, CD10, WT1, ER, and PR.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Ovarian adenosarcoma in a postmenopausal woman: Case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old woman with uterine leiomyomata underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingectomy via a midline vertical incision. Her preoperative workup showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL) and a normal creatinine (0.71 mg/dL). She had no prior cross-sectional abdominal imaging.

Intraoperatively, a nonmobile 18-cm leiomyomatous uterus and extensive adhesive disease were encountered; both ureters were visualized distal to the iliac bifurcation, and left ureteral peristalsis was noted. After the hysterectomy, cystoscopy showed a normal bladder and a patent left ureteral orifice with efflux of urine; the right ureteral orifice was stenotic, difficult to visualize, and had no efflux. Urology was consulted.

Repeat cystoscopy confirmed these findings. A right retrograde pyelogram demonstrated a dilated distal ureter, extravasation of contrast proximal to the iliac vessels, and no opacification of the proximal ureter or renal pelvis; a catheter could not be advanced proximally. The left retrograde pyelogram was normal. The right ureter was then dissected up to the external iliac vessel—its tissue was of poor quality, dilated distally, thinned to obliteration in the mid ureter, and showed no peristalsis.

An intraoperative intravenous pyelogram was performed. The left collecting system opacified with normal drainage; the right collecting system and ureter showed no contrast pooling.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Absent Ureteral Efflux after Hysterectomy Leads to Diagnosis of Ureteral Atresia with Renal Atrophy

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old man presented with sudden onset of dyspnea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain that began a day earlier at rest. Three weeks prior, he had undergone decompressive craniectomy for elevated intracranial pressure after a left middle cerebral artery thrombosis, which manifested as aphasia and right hemiparesis. Two years earlier, he had an acute coronary syndrome due to left anterior descending artery occlusion treated with angioplasty. He has no significant dyslipidemia, uses tobacco occasionally, and has a family history of ischemic heart disease in first-degree relatives at older ages.

On examination, he was alert, tachypneic (26 breaths/min), and tachycardic (124 beats/min) but hemodynamically stable without fever. Neurologic exam confirmed residual left-sided weakness. Lung and cardiac auscultation were normal, and healing craniectomy graft was noted on the scalp.

Initial laboratory tests including complete blood count, liver and renal function, urine analysis, electrolytes, inflammatory markers, and lipid profile were unremarkable. A pulmonary CT angiogram showed filling defects in segmental arteries of both lower lobes and a wedge-shaped infarct in the left lower lobe. A brain CT scan obtained to assess bleeding risk demonstrated no intracranial hemorrhage, only evidence of the recent craniectomy.
title: Antiphospholipid syndrome with major arterial thrombosis, presenting as pulmonary thromboembolism, cerebrovascular accident, and coronary artery disease: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 77-year-old woman with a history of asthma was admitted to the coronary care unit because of sudden onset of severe chest pain.  
On admission:  
• ECG showed slight ST-segment depression in leads V4 to V6.  
• Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild hypokinesis of the anterior wall and slight pericardial effusion.  
To rule out aortic dissection or pulmonary embolism, contrast-enhanced CT was performed after a bolus of methylprednisolone (125 mg) given prophylactically; no dissection or embolism was found.  
Initial labs in the emergency room (before steroid): eosinophils 8,555 cells/µL (58% of leukocytes). Four hours after the steroid bolus, eosinophils fell to 1,363 cells/µL (15%).  
Coronary angiography showed no significant stenosis. Left ventriculography demonstrated mild hypokinesis of the anterior midwall.  
Based on these findings, acute coronary syndrome from coronary spastic angina was diagnosed. Acetylcholine testing was not performed due to asthma. Sarcoidosis and amyloidosis were excluded because chest pain was atypical and echocardiography lacked basal thinning or hypertrophy. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy was excluded due to atypical ventriculography and absence of giant T-wave inversions on ECG.  
Symptoms improved on a calcium-channel blocker, and she was discharged.  
One month later, chest pain recurred. On readmission:  
• Troponin I level was 11,906 pg/mL.  
• Eosinophils were 15,262 cells/µL (62.5%).  
• Echocardiography again showed mild anterior wall hypokinesis and slightly increased pericardial effusion.
title: A Pitfall in the Diagnosis of Eosinophilic Myocarditis in a Patient who Received Steroid Therapy

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old woman presented with a dark-brown papule on the anterior middle third of her left leg that had appeared one year earlier and had slowly increased in size. She reported no pain, pruritus, trauma, or other preceding injury. She had severe venous insufficiency with a superficial hypertrophic and congested venous capillary network but no other relevant medical history.

On examination, the lesion was an oval, ulcerated papule measuring 30 mm in diameter. It was fixed to surrounding soft tissues, with ill-defined margins, and no palpable lymphadenopathy in the draining fields. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia; the specimen measured 30 × 20 × 12 mm.

Histologic examination of hematoxylin–eosin–stained sections showed a dermal lesion composed of a variable admixture of fibroblast-like cells and histiocytes, with more than 85% of cells exhibiting large eosinophilic cytoplasm filled with granules or microvacuoles. The stroma was loose and vascular, with a predominantly lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate and globular collagen bundles at the periphery. The lesion had defined margins with a pseudocapsule. The overlying epidermis was atrophic, with basal hyperpigmentation and melanin deposition. No mitotic figures were identified.

Immunohistochemical studies revealed diffuse CD68 positivity in the lesional cells. The lesional cells were negative for S-100 protein, CD34, Melan-A, and CD10. Ki-67 proliferation index was less than 1%.
title: Granular cell dermatofibroma: A potential diagnostic pitfall

case_prompt:
A 30‐year‐old man with no significant medical history was referred for recurrent tonsillitis. While awaiting tonsillectomy, he developed new‐onset snoring, a sense of airway obstruction relieved by neck extension, and a lump‐in‐throat sensation. He denied smoking or alcohol use.

On examination, flexible nasendoscopy showed a firm, smooth swelling arising from the left lateral pharyngeal wall, extending from the soft palate superiorly to the level of the epiglottis inferiorly. The oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, and piriform fossae appeared normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well‐defined 2.9×1.9 cm low‐signal mass on T1-weighted precontrast images, inseparable from the left longus capitis muscle, displacing well‐preserved prevertebral fat anteriorly, with no locally aggressive features. There was uniform enhancement with contrast and no diffusion restriction. Overall, the appearances were in keeping with a benign soft tissue tumor.

Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed absence of calcification or enhancement, supporting a benign process with no aggressive features. Fine‐needle aspiration of the neck and biopsy of the pharyngeal mass showed only inflammatory cells and numerous benign squamous epithelial cells with occasional macrophages.

The case was discussed at a head and neck multidisciplinary meeting, and local excision of the lesion was recommended to relieve symptoms.
title: A prevertebral desmoplastic fibroblastoma presenting with sleep‐related breathing dysfunction

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and benign thyroid nodules presented with a 5-month history of a gradually enlarging left parietal scalp lesion. She had no personal history of cancer and was up to date with screening mammography. A scoop excision of the lesion revealed a malignant dermal neoplasm extending to the margins. Initial immunohistochemical stains showed strong positivity for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and E-cadherin; focal weak positivity for cytokeratin 20; and negativity for cytokeratin 7. 

On second-opinion review, additional stains demonstrated strong positivity for GATA-3 and confirmed negativity for cytokeratin 7, cytokeratin 20, p63, and TTF-1. There was no evidence of Her2/neu amplification. Clinical breast examination was unremarkable. A 3D mammogram performed 4 weeks after the biopsy showed no abnormalities. A PET/CT scan 6 days later revealed only a mild left scalp defect consistent with recent surgery and no adenopathy or distant metastases. Four months after the biopsy, bilateral breast MRI showed no identifiable breast lesion.
title: Occult Breast Carcinoma Presenting as Scalp Metastasis

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old obese woman was evaluated for progressive dyspnea on exertion. Physical examination revealed a 3/6 crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the aortic area. Preoperative evaluation included:
• ECG: Normal sinus rhythm.  
• Echocardiogram: Severely calcified aortic valve, valve area 0.8 cm2, mean gradient 55 mmHg, preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, left ventricular wall thickness 14 mm.  
• Coronary angiography: Completely normal coronary arteries.  

She underwent aortic valve replacement via mini-sternotomy with a Sorin 23 mm mechanical prosthesis. Myocardial protection was achieved with cold antegrade and retrograde St. Thomas’ cardioplegic solution. Early postoperative recovery was unremarkable.

Twelve weeks after surgery, she reported severe chest pain on mild exertion and at rest. On admission:
• ECG: T-wave inversions in leads V2–V5 and aVL; during pain episodes, marked ST-segment depression in V2–V5.  

Coronary angiography demonstrated a 90% diameter reduction at the left coronary ostium extending into the left main stem.
title: Unstable angina early after aortic valve replacement surgery in a female patient with normal coronary arteries preoperatively – a case report

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, GERD, severe asthma, COPD, and newly diagnosed alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (PI*ZZ) developed acute shortness of breath and fatigue shortly after her first Prolastin infusion. She received a second infusion one week later with premedication. Over the next three weeks she experienced worsening dyspnea, wheezing, one episode of hemoptysis, nonspecific arthralgias, and a diffuse rash. She was treated empirically with oral steroids and amoxicillin-clavulanate at an outside hospital without improvement and was transferred for further evaluation.

On admission: T 37.0°C, BP 132/78 mm Hg, HR 73 bpm, RR 18 breaths/min, O₂ saturation 98% on 3 L nasal cannula. She appeared comfortable with a cushingoid habitus. Skin exam showed multiple palpable purpuric violaceous papules coalescing into serpiginous plaques with large adherent black eschars on the upper and lower extremities, and punched-out ulcerations with yellow fibrinous material on the bilateral thighs and buttocks. Lung auscultation revealed bibasilar crackles; the rest of the exam was normal.

Laboratory studies revealed normocytic anemia, mild leukocytosis, elevated ESR and C-reactive protein, and low serum alpha-1-antitrypsin. Urinalysis was unremarkable. Chest CT demonstrated patchy consolidative infiltrates in the left lower lobe and scattered alveolar infiltrates in both lungs. Bronchoscopy identified old blood in a right lower lobe subsegmental bronchus; bronchoalveolar lavage return was bloody but cleared. Skin punch biopsy from the left lower leg showed mild superficial dermal perivascular neutrophilic inflammation; direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, and fibrinogen.
title: Hypersensitivity Vasculitis with Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis Associated with Alpha-1-Proteinase Inhibitor

case_prompt:
A 12-month-old girl born to non-consanguineous parents was evaluated for seizures and developmental delay. She had bluish discoloration of her hands and lips and episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures involving all four limbs, with eye up-rolling and drooling. She also demonstrated global developmental delay, including lack of neck control, inability to sit unsupported, and poor grasp, in the setting of generalized hypotonia. 

On examination, she had multiple patches of bluish pigmentation over the back and gluteal region, low-set ears, coarse facial features, a depressed nasal bridge, and increased intercanthal distance. Her head circumference was 51.5 cm (>97th percentile); other anthropometric measures were normal. 

Laboratory studies showed normal bilirubin and elevated liver enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, 800 IU/L; aspartate transaminase, 165 IU/L; alanine transaminase, 42 IU/L). Electroencephalography demonstrated central epileptiform discharges. Abdominal sonography revealed hepatomegaly (liver span, 12 cm). A skeletal survey showed antero-inferior beaking of the second to fourth lumbar vertebrae. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed bilateral thalamic hyperdensity. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral bulky thalami that were hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images, along with T2 hyperintensity in the anterior limbs of the internal capsules, frontal lobar and periventricular white matter, and subcortical U fibres, with isointense T1 signals consistent with hypomyelination.
title: Imaging manifestations in infantile GM1 gangliosidosis: a rare lysosomal storage disorder: a paediatric case report

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old Syrian female was evaluated for severe cutaneous ulceration and scarring of the face and hands, accompanied by dyspigmentation. Her parents reported that symptoms began in her first year of life with skin redness and blistering in sun-exposed areas, progressing to ulcers, scarring, and deformity of the nose, hands, and fingers. There was also a history of urine discoloration in early childhood. There was no family history of similar symptoms or consanguinity. 

On physical examination, the face showed areas of dyspigmentation and hypertrichosis on the cheeks and forehead, crusted old ulcers, and a sclerodermatous appearance with linear and spotted atrophic lesions; the nose was severely deformed and scarred. The teeth exhibited reddish-brown discoloration under visible light. Eye examination revealed conjunctivitis, scleromalacia, and mild blepharitis without corneal injury. The dorsum of the hands had extensive ulcerations with sclerodermatous changes and acrolysis of the distal phalanges. The liver was palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen was not palpable. Under Wood’s lamp, there was bright red fluorescence of the teeth and bright green fluorescence in the interdigital spaces of the hands.

A 24-hour urine porphyrin profile showed markedly elevated uroporphyrins (9820 nmol/24 h; reference ≤30) and coproporphyrin I (2514 nmol/24 h; reference ≤168).
title: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Gunther disease): a case report

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman was referred to the hospital one hour after developing multiple episodes of bloody sputum (approximately 30–35 mL per expectoration, five times) accompanied by sudden dyspnea (MMRC grade IV), bilateral chest pain, and nausea. Her medical history was notable for cholecystectomy one year earlier, during which severe mitral stenosis (MS) was diagnosed, and percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy had been recommended but not performed. One month prior, she had undergone coronary angiography for left-sided chest pain and dyspnea and was found to have single-vessel coronary disease; angioplasty was deferred at her request.

On examination, blood pressure was 115/70 mmHg, pulse 150 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 84% on room air (improving to 96% with supplemental oxygen). Lung auscultation revealed diffuse crackles bilaterally. Cardiac examination disclosed a loud, delayed first heart sound with an opening snap and a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur best heard at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position. Jugular venous pressure and abdominal examination were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 8000/mm3, hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, platelets 138 000/mm3, ESR 22 mm/hr, CRP negative, D-dimer negative, Mycobacterium tuberculosis smear and cultures negative, PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza negative, and negative serologies for ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, and antiphospholipid antibodies. 

Noncontrast chest CT demonstrated bilateral central patchy consolidations with air bronchograms.
title: Pulmonary apoplexy following severe mitral valve stenosis: A case report

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of progressive dull aching throat pain, a foreign body sensation in the left oropharynx, and gradual left facial asymmetry. She denied dysphagia or dyspnea. On oropharyngeal examination, there was a diffuse swelling occupying the left tonsillar fossa and deviation of the uvula to the right. Palpation of the neck revealed a non-tender, fixed mass in the left submandibular area.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 4.0 × 4.5 × 6.0 cm, well-defined, dumbbell-shaped mass in the left post-styloid parapharyngeal space, extending into the left prevertebral area. The mass demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement with internal cystic changes and no calcifications. It was separate from the left parotid gland and displaced the left internal carotid artery laterally; there was no adjacent bony erosion.  

MRI revealed that the mass was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with multiple cystic areas. On contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images, the lesion showed homogeneous, strong enhancement.
title: Solitary fibrous tumor of the post-styloid parapharyngeal space

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidentally detected intra-abdominal mass. She reported a 20-year history of chronic constipation and intermittent abdominal discomfort without weight loss. She had no cardiopulmonary symptoms. Her past history included a total hysterectomy eight years earlier for uterine leiomyoma and a diagnosis 12 years ago of retroperitoneal sarcoma with lung metastases treated with chemotherapy; CT scans in 2005 and 2007 showed no change in disease extent.  

On examination, blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg; lungs were clear; the abdomen was soft and obese without palpable masses or organomegaly; no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 15.6 g/dL, WBC 7600/µL, platelets 205 000/µL, LDH 564 U/L, and normal CA 125, CA 19-9, and CEA.  

Abdominal CT showed multiple large, well-defined, hyperenhancing masses in the retroperitoneum and pelvis unchanged since 2005. Chest CT demonstrated multiple tiny cavitary and cystic nodules in both lungs, also stable. FDG PET/CT showed bulky retroperitoneal and pelvic masses with heterogeneous uptake (SUVmax 4.0). Pulmonary lesions were too small for biopsy, so a 12.2 × 6.3 × 4.5 cm retroperitoneal mass was resected.  

Grossly, the 283 g mass had a pale brown capsule and a whitish homogeneous cut surface. Microscopically, there was spindle cell proliferation with mild to focally moderate nuclear atypia, mitotic activity <1 per 50 HPFs, and no coagulative tumor cell necrosis. Immunohistochemistry was negative for pancytokeratin, CD117, PDGFR, and CD34; positive for actin and desmin; Ki-67 labeling index <5%; p53 negative; estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor positive.
final_diagnosis_raw: smooth muscle tumor of uncertain malignant potential
title: Retroperitoneal smooth muscle tumor of uncertain malignant potential after hysterectomy: a case report

case_prompt: A 75-year-old man presented with 1 hour of sudden‐onset, retrosternal, nonradiating chest pain and shortness of breath. His medical history was notable for 30 years of hypertension treated with nifedipine, and he had undergone transurethral resection of the prostate 1 week earlier. He denied leg swelling, fever, cough, or recent trauma. On examination, he was distressed. Blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg with narrow pulse pressure, heart rate 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86% on a non‐rebreather mask at 20 L/min. The chest examination was unremarkable. Cardiovascular examination showed elevated jugular venous pressure, normal heart sounds without murmurs or gallops, and no peripheral edema. Neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory testing revealed hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, AST 193 U/L, ALT 234 U/L, PT 23 seconds, aPTT 204 seconds, INR 1.9, D-dimer 2.53 μg/mL, and normal troponin I. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia without other abnormalities. Chest radiography demonstrated an increased cardiothoracic ratio of 70%.
title: Thrombus in transit associated with fatal pulmonary thromboembolism in an elderly Ethiopian man following a surgical procedure: A case report

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted for investigation of a transient ischaemic attack characterized by expressive dysphasia and left hemiparesis following cardiac stress testing. Her medical history included primary hypertension diagnosed at age 19, an iatrogenic left main coronary artery dissection treated with bypass grafting in 2007, an internal carotid artery dissection in 2001, and recurrent TIAs. 

While inpatient, she developed sudden severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain associated with dizziness and hyperventilation. Initial liver function tests were normal, but subsequent tests showed a mixed hepatocellular pattern: alkaline phosphatase 246 U/L (53–141), GGT 433 U/L (<38), ALT 508 U/L (<34), AST 760 U/L (<31), and total bilirubin 22 μmol/L (<20). 

Extensive evaluation for common causes of liver injury revealed:  
• Negative viral hepatic serology.  
• Paracetamol level <10 mg/L.  
• Autoimmune serologies, including ANA, ANCA, anti-smooth muscle, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies, were negative or noncontributory.  
• Unremarkable abdominal ultrasound and noncontrast CT scan.  

Her liver enzymes improved over three days and she was discharged with the presumption of statin-induced liver injury. Six days later she re-presented with severe intermittent right upper quadrant pain and worsened liver enzymes (ALT 770 U/L; AST 992 U/L; GGT 295 U/L). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed abnormal arterial wall thickening of the coeliac trunk and hepatic artery. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated mild stenosis of the hepatic artery. A contrast CT angiogram revealed dilation of the common hepatic artery with an intimal flap and perivascular fat stranding consistent with an isolated hepatic artery dissection; no coeliac trunk dissection, biliary obstruction, thrombosis, or hemorrhage was seen.
title: Spontaneous hepatic artery dissection—a rare presentation of fibromuscular dysplasia

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old Indian man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease presented with sudden visual impairment in both eyes followed minutes later by a brief generalized tonic–clonic seizure. He had no prior history of epilepsy or substance abuse, but a history of skin abscesses attributed to poor glycemic control. In the emergency department, he was postictal—agitated and drowsy—without focal deficits. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Random plasma glucose, 581 mg/dL; HbA1c, 11.4%; serum ketones, negative.  
• Serum sodium, 136 mEq/L; creatinine, 2.9 mg/dL.  
Lumbar puncture yielded normal cerebrospinal fluid, and noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Intravenous phenytoin, insulin infusion, and hydration were initiated. 

After regaining consciousness, examination revealed a complete right homonymous hemianopia. Multiple brief complex partial seizures were observed, characterized by rightward head and eye deviation, right-sided nystagmus, and impaired awareness, each lasting about 60 seconds. Brain MRI demonstrated focal hypointensity in the left occipital lobe on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences. Conventional scalp EEG recorded three seizures, each beginning with high-amplitude fast activity over the left occipital region with ipsilateral and contralateral spread, followed by gradual postictal slowing.
title: Occipital seizures and persistent homonymous hemianopia with T2 hypointensity on MRI in nonketotic hyperglycemia

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old woman presented with a 5-week history of a painless, rapidly enlarging mass on the right auricle. She first noted a small lesion on the conchal skin that, on examination, measured approximately 2.0 × 2.0 cm. The mass was fragile and bled easily with manipulation. The external auditory canal and tympanic membrane could not be visualized directly, but the lesion appeared discrete from the canal. There were no cervical lymphadenopathies, and a full skin examination revealed no other lesions. The patient denied preceding trauma or systemic symptoms.

With a preoperative impression of a pyogenic granuloma and to exclude sarcoma, a punch biopsy was performed. One week later, the lesion had increased to approximately 3.0 × 4.5 cm. Microscopic examination showed a proliferation of plump, mitotically active spindle-shaped cells with oval, pale-staining nuclei arranged in short, irregular bundles in a loosely myxoid stroma with extravasated red blood cells and multinucleated giant cells. Immunohistochemical staining revealed negative cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, and S-100 protein, with strong positivity for smooth muscle actin and vimentin.
title: Nodular Fasciitis of the Auricle: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old man presented with two months of mild, intermittent, diffuse lower abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or hematochezia. He had a history of well-controlled hypertension and a 20-year, 10–12 cigarettes/day smoking history; he denied alcohol use. Vital signs were normal. The abdominal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, liver enzymes, protein, albumin, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose, urinalysis, and stool examination—were within normal limits. Chest and abdominal radiographs and abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. Upper endoscopy revealed chronic superficial gastritis. 

After bowel preparation, colonoscopy revealed a single, 15-mm semi-pedunculated lesion in the sigmoid colon with a smooth surface. The lesion was firm (cushion sign negative) and lifted easily after submucosal injection of epinephrine/saline (lifting sign positive). A snare polypectomy was performed, and the lesion was removed without bleeding or perforation.
journal: Journal of the Korean Society of Coloproctology
title: A Case of Endoscopic Resection of a Colonic Semipedunculated Leiomyoma

case_prompt:
An 87-year-old man was referred for hiccups that persisted for a full day despite prior symptomatic treatments (esomeprazole, metoclopramide, dimethicone, prokinetic and antispasmodic herbal medicines). Over the previous 2 years, he had two similar 3-day episodes with intervening 4–7 days of relief; this was his third episode, and it had not abated with shakuyakukanzoto. He denied dysphagia, chest pain, chest discomfort, nausea, or headache. His medications included frequent esomeprazole for hiccups and chronic amlodipine and bisoprolol for hypertension; he had never used corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; there was no nuchal rigidity or cranial-nerve deficit. Laboratory studies were within normal limits, without evidence of diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression. Cranial MRI showed only chronic lacunar infarcts; no tumors or ventricular enlargement were seen. Chest CT revealed a midesophageal diverticulum projecting rightward at the level of the tracheal bifurcation; there was no lymphadenopathy or other thoracoabdominal abnormality. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated several white deposits throughout the esophagus. A midesophageal diverticulum was noted on the right wall approximately 30 cm from the incisors, with white residue at its margin that was readily flushed away; inside the diverticulum, extensive white deposits were present.
title: Intractable hiccups caused by esophageal diverticular candidiasis in an immunocompetent adult: a case report

case_prompt: A 67-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of sudden-onset, progressively worsening right lower quadrant abdominal pain. She had associated nausea and a low-grade fever but denied vomiting, prior similar episodes, or any history of abdominal surgery or other significant medical problems. On admission, her temperature was 37.8°C, BMI was 28.2, and other vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed mild right lower quadrant tenderness; McBurney’s sign was negative, and there was no marked right iliac fossa tenderness. On the following day, localized right lower quadrant tenderness with guarding and rebound developed, while the remainder of the examination remained unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 13.1 G/L with a neutrophil count of 7.8 G/L; liver and renal function tests were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography was inconclusive due to overlying bowel gas. A noncontrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated a fat-density lesion with surrounding fat stranding in the right lower quadrant and streaks of whirling in a concentric pattern (whirl sign); the appendix was visualized and appeared normal.
title: Primary omental torsion with clinical masquerading as acute appendicitis and radiological key for diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old Caucasian woman underwent wide local excision and axillary clearance for a grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, with 7 of 28 nodes positive. She received four cycles of paclitaxel (stopped for hypersensitivity) and then 40 Gy of radiotherapy in 15 fractions to the left breast and supraclavicular fossa. She had no prior dermatologic history. 

Eight weeks after completing radiotherapy, she had edema, erythema, blistering, and desquamation over the left breast and chest wall, with additional desquamation on her back in the radiotherapy exit field. She was afebrile, with normal vital signs. The skin changes began four weeks after radiotherapy and were initially confined to the radiation field. 

Differential diagnoses included radiation-induced skin changes with possible cellulitis, an autoimmune bullous disorder, or a paraneoplastic process. She was admitted and started on intravenous antibiotics and antivirals, along with a regimen of Viscopaste, Tubigrip, Hydromol, and Dermovate ointment. A superficial skin swab grew only mixed skin flora. 

Despite this treatment, her skin deteriorated, with new desquamation over the right hip. She also developed painful oral erosions.
title: Radiation-induced pemphigus in a patient with an invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast: a case report

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old Japanese man with alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A), uncontrolled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c ~14%), and a 1-year history of abstinence from heavy drinking presented with acute wet cough and altered mental status (GCS E4V2M5). He was underweight (BMI 16.6) and a long-time smoker. 

On admission: T 36.4°C; HR 106 bpm; RR 20 bpm; BP 145/92 mmHg; SpO₂ 99% on room air. Exam: dry oral mucosa, gynecomastia. 

Initial labs: WBC 12,020/μL (Neu 88.7%); BUN 41 mg/dL; Cr 1.64 mg/dL; glucose 556 mg/dL; Na 127 mEq/L; measured osm 304 mOsm/kg; ketones 369 μmol/L; NH₃ 188 μg/dL; ABG: pH 7.382, pCO₂ 25.7 mmHg, HCO₃ 15.3 mmol/L, lactate 7.1 mmol/L, anion gap 20.5. CT chest: right middle and lower lobe ground-glass opacities; liver nodularity; no ascites.

He was diagnosed with DKA, community-acquired pneumonia, lactic acidosis, and prerenal AKI. Treatment: azithromycin, IV ceftriaxone, IV Ringer’s, continuous insulin infusion, rifaximin, lactulose, and amino acids. Over the first 24 h, glucose fell to 275 mg/dL, sodium rose to 135 mEq/L, osmolarity decreased to 295 mOsm/kg.
