On hospital day 3, consciousness improved to GCS E4V4M6; insulin was switched to subcutaneous. On day 8, he re-deteriorated to GCS E4V2M5, with new dysphagia and chorea. Labs on day 8: WBC 10,440/μL (Neu 75.5%); glucose 138 mg/dL; Na 155 mEq/L. Neurologic exam revealed bilateral chorea of the head, trunk, and upper extremities; Babinski and Chaddock signs were negative; no myoclonus.
title: Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome in a Patient with Diabetic Ketoacidosis despite No Rapid Sodium Correction

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old man presented with palpitations and dyspnea on mild exertion. He had been noted to have an asymptomatic systolic murmur at age 17 but was lost to follow-up. On admission, he had dyspnea with minimal exertion and mild ankle swelling. Cardiac examination revealed an apical systolic murmur (grade 4/6) and a continuous murmur (grade 3/6) at the right parasternal border. Vital signs were: heart rate 85 bpm, blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Lung fields were clear, and the chest radiograph was unremarkable. Routine blood tests were normal except for an elevated NT-proBNP of 700 pg/mL. ECG showed sinus rhythm with premature supraventricular beats, left atrial enlargement, and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated continuous turbulent flow on color Doppler from the right coronary sinus to the roof of the right atrium and severe mitral valve prolapse with flail of the P1 scallop and prolapse of P2 and P3, resulting in severe regurgitation. The left ventricle was dilated (LVEDV 172 mL, LVESV 73 mL) with preserved ejection fraction (58%), and the left atrium was severely dilated (LAVi 85.9 mL/m^2). The right atrium and right ventricle were dilated with mild RV systolic dysfunction (fractional area change 35%), moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary hypertension (systolic PAP 51 mmHg). Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a flow velocity of 5.2 m/s at the right atrial drainage orifice.

Cardiac catheterization revealed a left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs 1.8), mean pulmonary artery pressure 25 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 15 mmHg, and PVR 1.03 Wood units. Coronary angiography showed a large tunnel originating from the right coronary sinus and draining into the right atrium; the origin of the right coronary artery was not identified. Computed tomography angiography revealed an extracardiac, anterior-type tunnel arising from the ascending aorta at the right coronary sinus, coursing anteroinferiorly, making a sharp U-turn toward the roof of the right atrium along the posterior interatrial septum, and draining into the right atrium through a restrictive opening. The distal tunnel was narrower, and the right coronary artery originated from the tunnel near its U-turn.
title: Aorta-right atrium tunnel and mitral valve prolapse complicated with flail leaflet: a case report of a multimodality approach for an accurate diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man employed at a limestone company presented with chronic chest wall pain following two occupational chest injuries. The first injury, a chest contusion by a metal bar, resulted in a dislocation of the third left costochondral joint and 55 days of work leave. The second injury, blunt trauma from someone driving a forklift, occurred at the same site and led him to seek emergency care. At that time, vital signs were stable, and examination showed only mild erythema over the anterior chest wall. Blood tests, electrocardiogram, and chest radiographs were all normal, permitting exclusion of life-threatening emergencies. He returned to work after a total of 50 days of leave.

One year later, he was referred for evaluation of persistent anterior chest pain. He described parietal sternal pain worsened by deep breathing and left arm movement, significantly limiting his work and daily activities. On physical examination, there was a marked swelling of the second left sternoclavicular joint with sharp tenderness on palpation but no warmth or erythema. Shoulder mobility was full but reproduced the chest pain on movement, and there was tenderness at the xiphoid process. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed thickening of the synovium with the presence of air in the left sternoclavicular joint space, hypertrophy and hypodense appearance of the cartilages of the first through third left costosternal joints, and retrosternal tissue edema with no detectable collection or signs suggestive of a systemic rheumatic condition.
title: Post-traumatic Tietze syndrome as an occupational accident: A case report study

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old man with Mibelli’s porokeratosis presented with an 8-month history of swelling of the left knee and recurrent joint effusions. The pain was insidious, without clear aggravating or relieving factors. Since age 15, he had experienced inflammatory polyarthralgia of the lower-limb large joints, with intermittent joint swelling and talalgia. He underwent multiple knee aspirations and received intra-articular corticosteroids and NSAIDs, with no significant improvement. 

On examination, there was a diffuse, painless suprapatellar swelling of the left knee, a positive patellar tap, and limited hip movements. Laboratory studies showed a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal rheumatoid factor, normal white-cell count, and normal uric acid level. Aspiration of the left knee yielded 60 cm3 of sterile, citrine-yellow fluid containing 3900 white cells/mm3 and no crystals.

Spine and pelvic radiographs were normal. Knee radiographs demonstrated increased density in the suprapatellar recess consistent with effusion, without bone lysis or osteosclerosis. Ultrasonography confirmed a significant suprapatellar effusion. 

MRI of the left knee showed multiple frond-like projections of the synovium into the joint. These projections exhibited high signal intensity on T1-weighted images and low signal on proton-density fat-saturated sequences, with suppression of their signal on fat-saturation sequences. After gadolinium, these villous projections did not enhance, although the overlying synovial membrane showed diffuse enhancement. Moderately abundant joint effusion was present. Sagittal GRE T2* images showed no low-signal foci to suggest hemosiderin deposition. No meniscal or ligamentous lesions were identified.
title: Lipoma arborescens of the knee: A case report

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old Tibetan woman presented with a 3-month history of mild cough and occasional hemoptysis, recently worsened by right chest pain. She had been treated empirically with oral penicillin without full resolution of symptoms. She had no history of surgery, trauma, or known infectious disease and lived in a farming region where occasional raw meat consumption is customary. 

On examination, temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 115/65 mmHg, heart rate 73 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Breath sounds were diminished over the left lung with collapse; moist rales were heard bilaterally. No rash or subcutaneous nodules were noted.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10.4 × 10^9/L with 37.2% eosinophils and elevated serum IgE (1650 IU/mL). Tumor markers (CA-125, neuron-specific enolase) were mildly elevated; other blood chemistries were unremarkable. Bone marrow aspirate was hypercellular with marked eosinophilia.

Left-sided thoracentesis yielded yellow-cloudy exudative fluid with >20,000 cells/μL, 100% multinuclear cells, and eosinophil predominance; glucose was low and LDH high. Cytology showed no malignant cells or parasites. Gram stain, acid-fast stain, fungal smear, TB-DNA, and cultures were negative.

Chest CT demonstrated a left hydropneumothorax with partial compressive atelectasis and patchy consolidation in the right lung.
title: Cutaneous myiasis with eosinophilic pleural effusion: A case report

case_prompt: A 51-year-old Asian man with a 2-year history of recurrent left auricular swelling was referred with suspected relapsing polychondritis. His medical history included hypertension and chronic eczema. He presented with pain and swelling of the left pinna sparing the lobule. He also had urticarial erythema and papules on the upper trunk. He was treated with oral cefteram pivoxil and loxoprofen for the ear inflammation, and levocetirizine plus topical betamethasone for the skin lesions, with symptomatic improvement. Approximately 3 months later, he had worsening pain and swelling of the left ear and stiffness in the postauricular area. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a diffusely enhancing soft-tissue mass in the left parotid region with enlargement of adjacent lymph nodes.
title: Recurrent auricular inflammation caused by Kimura’s disease: reminiscent of the early phase of relapsing polychondritis?

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presented with a 1½-year history of intermittent high-grade fevers, each episode lasting 7–10 days with 2–3-month symptom-free intervals, and a 15- to 20-kg unintentional weight loss. He described daily fevers up to 102°F with rigors, chills, and night sweats unresponsive to oral antipyretics. He denied rashes, arthralgia, myalgia, or other systemic complaints, reporting only intermittent constipation, a mild cough, left shoulder pain, and nonspecific headaches. He had multiple prior hospitalizations; a prior EEG and neurologic evaluation were unremarkable. Medications included metformin PRN, glargine insulin, clonazepam at bedtime, and a recent 14-day course of meropenem. He had a ceftriaxone allergy with prior rash. He used naswar and smoked 2–3 cigarettes daily. 

On examination the temperature was 102°F. A single 1×1-cm firm, nontender, fixed lymph node was palpable in the occipital region. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed mild anemia (Hb 11.6 g/dL), leukopenia (3.6×10^3/µL), normal platelets, renal and liver function, and electrolytes. Inflammatory markers were elevated (ESR 62 mm/hr; CRP 4.79 mg/L). Hemoglobin A1c was 8.5%. Malaria, dengue, and other infectious serologies were negative. Autoimmune markers (ANA, anti-dsDNA, ENA) were negative. Echocardiogram, abdominal ultrasound, and CT imaging showed no abnormalities. An ultrasound of the occipital region revealed bilateral hypoechoic lymph nodes with benign features.

Persistent fever prompted an excisional biopsy of an occipital lymph node and a bone marrow biopsy to rule out hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
title: Diagnostic challenges and management of kikuchi-fujimoto disease: a rare case report

case_prompt: A 59-year-old man was referred for evaluation of 3 months of intermittent melena, left upper-quadrant abdominal pain, and fatigue. He denied changes in bowel habits or hematochezia. He had two prior episodes of LUQ pain with tarry stools that resolved spontaneously. His medical history was unremarkable; he took no medications and had no tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. On examination he was pale, had tenderness in the left upper abdomen without rebound or masses, and digital rectal examination revealed melena. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL with a hypochromic microcytic pattern (MCV 70.2 fL, MCH 21.4 pg), serum iron 6.4 μmol/L, and ferritin 28.8 μg/L; carcinoembryonic antigen was 1.2 μg/L. Lipase, chest and abdominal radiographs, abdominal ultrasound, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy were all unremarkable. Capsule endoscopy was unavailable, so MR enterography was performed and revealed a large pedunculated polyp measuring approximately 2.5 × 2.3 cm in the mid-ileum with ulceration at its apex.
title: A case of ectopic pancreas in the ileum presenting as obscure gastrointestinal bleeding and abdominal pain

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old man was found unconscious at home with open doors and windows and brought to the emergency department. On arrival he developed ventricular fibrillation; cardiopulmonary resuscitation restored sinus rhythm after two defibrillations and cardiopulmonary bypass was used for rewarming, with total ventricular fibrillation duration under 2 minutes. His history included heavy alcohol use and 20 cigarettes per day; no medication data were available.

On examination his temperature was 24.5 °C, blood pressure 145/70 mmHg, heart rate 35 bpm, and respiratory rate 8–10 /min. He was unconscious (RLS-85 score 4) and had slight anisocoria (right pupil larger than left). Heart and lung auscultation were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed moderate electrolyte disturbances and elevated liver enzymes; drug and alcohol screens were negative.

Noncontrast head CT on admission was interpreted as normal, with no hemorrhage or acute infarction. In the ICU he was sedated and ventilated; his course was complicated by pneumothorax after CPR, pneumonia, bilateral pleural effusions, intestinal paralysis, acute pancreatitis, and ascites. Sedation was discontinued two weeks after admission. He opened his eyes to voice but was nonverbal; he withdrew his arms, moved his left foot, and grimaced to pain. He again had slight anisocoria (left pupil now larger) but symmetric pupillary reflexes. EEG showed irregular theta/delta activity without epileptiform discharges.

On hospital day 24, repeat head CT revealed bilateral ischemia in the medial thalami and a smaller ischemic area in the left pons.
title: Artery of Percheron infarction: a case report

case_prompt: A 2-month-old male infant, first of dichorionic diamniotic twins, was admitted for persistent anaemia and HIV exposure. He was born at 34 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section (birth weight 2.080 kg) to a 30-year-old Nigerian mother who arrived in Italy at 27 weeks and tested positive for HIV and CMV; antiretroviral therapy was started. At birth, the male twin’s HIV-RNA PCR was negative, and he received zidovudine prophylaxis for 6 weeks. TORCH screening and abdominal and cerebral ultrasonography were negative. One week before transfer, he was hospitalized elsewhere for severe anaemia (Hb 5.1 g/dL) and received a blood transfusion. On presentation, he was afebrile (36.5 °C), pulse 135 bpm, respirations 35/min, weight 3.910 kg. Examination was normal except for hepatomegaly (4 cm below right costal margin). Laboratory tests (one week after transfusion) showed WBC 12 000/mm3, Hb 9.1 g/dL, platelets 198 000/mm3, reticulocytes 169 000/mm3, total bilirubin 1.31 mg/dL (direct 0.64 mg/dL), LDH 945 U/L, and normal renal and hepatic function. Zidovudine‐induced myelosuppression was suspected, and folic acid and oral iron were started. Over the next days, hemoglobin fell to 6.8 g/dL despite supportive care, requiring additional transfusions. Causes of blood loss and hemolysis were investigated: direct and indirect Coombs tests and fecal occult blood were negative; hemoglobin electrophoresis was unremarkable. On repeat examination, splenomegaly was noted and confirmed by ultrasound. Malaria was then considered.
title: Challenging diagnosis of congenital malaria in non-endemic areas

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis–related bronchiectasis presented with a 3-month history of increasing dark brownish-red sputum and dyspnea. She expectorated about a cup of brownish-red sputum each morning, without fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. Over the past year she had several brief, non-hypoxemic episodes described as haemoptysis.  
Her chest CT scan showed progressive cylindrical bronchiectasis predominant in the lower lobes. Ulcerative colitis was in remission on mesalazine and low-dose prednisolone. Past history included corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis, peripheral arterial disease, and remote alcohol abuse.  
On examination she was slightly malnourished, with normal vital signs; lungs had moist crackles at both bases and no clubbing. Current medications included prednisolone 7.5 mg/day, inhaled budesonide, mesalazine, calcium, vitamin D, azithromycin (250 mg three times weekly), clopidogrel, and levetiracetam.  
Laboratory studies revealed CRP 38 mg/L and leukocytes 12.5 G/L with lymphopenia (1.3 G/L). Pulmonary-function tests showed normal volumes and a mild reduction in diffusing capacity. Chest imaging confirmed extensive bronchial wall thickening, mucus plugging, and bronchiectasis predominantly in the right lower lobe.  
Sputum cytology demonstrated many leukocytes but no erythrocytes or haemosiderophages. The initial differential diagnosis included lower respiratory bacterial infection, haemoptysis from bronchiectasis with tortuous bronchial arteries, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. The latter was ruled out by absence of asthma, normal total IgE (47 kU/L), and negative sputum cultures for Aspergillus. Other diagnoses such as pulmonary embolism or vasculitis were deemed unlikely.  
An empirical 14-day course of moxifloxacin produced no improvement. Sputum cultures for bacteria and yeast were sterile. However, mould cultures grew 34 colonies of a filamentous mould producing a red pigment.
title: Ochroconis gallopava bronchitis mimicking haemoptysis in a patient with bronchiectasis

case_prompt: An 82‐year‐old Japanese woman underwent routine upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and was found to have a protruding submucosal lesion in the middle esophagus. She had no dysphagia or other symptoms, and laboratory studies, including hemoglobin, liver and renal function tests, and tumor markers for adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, were normal. White‐light endoscopy revealed a 8 mm brownish submucosal tumor 25 cm from the incisors with mild surface reddening and a central depressed area; the lesion was elastic, mobile, and hard on forceps compression. Narrow‐band imaging with magnification showed a central brownish area with slightly dilated, non‐uniform intrapapillary capillary loops. The central depression stained only slightly with Lugol’s solution. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic, homogeneous 8.0 × 4.2 mm mass involving primarily the second and third layers of the esophageal wall, with a thickened hyperechoic submucosa and slight irregularity of the third layer. Biopsy specimens showed only esophagitis without evidence of tumor. Contrast‐enhanced CT did not demonstrate lymphadenopathy or distant lesions. With these findings, squamous cell carcinoma and gastrointestinal stromal tumor were considered.
title: Endoscopic submucosal dissection in a patient with esophageal adenoid cystic carcinoma

case_prompt:
A 7½-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of balance disturbances, incoordination of extraocular muscles during walking, dysfunctional gag reflex and swallowing, vocal tremor, monotone speech, and weakness of the masticatory muscles. His motor development had been delayed. There was no family history of laryngeal dystonia; his grandfather had late-life Parkinson’s disease. He had no history of birth asphyxia or cyanosis, and psychological evaluation revealed normal cognition.

Routine laboratory tests, including serum electrolytes, blood glucose, liver function, and kidney function, were normal. Urine and blood chromatography showed no abnormal bands or amino acid elevations. Plasma copper (90 μg/dl) and lactate (9.6 mg/dl) levels were within normal limits, with no evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction.

On examination, he was alert with normal language comprehension, naming, and repetition. Cranial nerves were intact: pupils, visual fields, and funduscopic exam were normal; Kayser–Fleischer rings were absent. He had extraocular incoordination during walking. Facial sensation and movements were normal. The palate and uvula elevated symmetrically; tongue protruded midline. Deep tendon reflexes were hyperactive with bilateral Babinski signs and persistence of a biting reflex. Cerebellar testing was normal. Masticatory muscles were weak, and the gag reflex was hypersensitive.

Brain MRI showed bilateral signal abnormalities in the globus pallidus: axial FLAIR images demonstrated hypointensity with central hyperintensity, and sagittal T2-weighted images confirmed a hyperintense medial portion. The remainder of the brain, ventricular system, brainstem, and cervical cord appeared normal. CT head showed normal gray–white matter differentiation and no lesions. Brainstem auditory evoked potentials, somatosensory evoked potentials, and flash visual evoked potentials all had normal wave morphology, amplitudes, and latencies.

Audio recording and perceptual assessment of a 10-minute speech sample revealed breathiness, roughness, vocal tremor, monotone pitch, and breathy breaks. Maximum phonation time averaged 5 seconds.
title: Childhood Laryngeal Dystonia Following Bilateral Globus Pallidus Abnormality: A Case Study and Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old man was diagnosed with Wilson’s disease in March 2021 after routine occupational tests showed elevated liver enzymes (ALT 158 U/L [<41]; AST 80 U/L [<40]). Workup revealed low ceruloplasmin (14.7 mg/dL [20–60]), elevated 24-h urinary copper excretion (60 µg/24 h [<50]), and a Kayser–Fleischer ring on slit-lamp exam. He had no neurological symptoms, and brain MRI was normal. He was started on d-penicillamine, titrated to 1000 mg/day.

After 15 months, his liver function tests normalized, but he developed double vision on downward gaze and evening ptosis of both eyelids. Neurologic examination confirmed diplopia and bilateral fatigable ptosis. Brain MRI, brain angio-MRI, and routine blood tests including thyroid function were normal. Copper metabolism studies showed 24-h urinary copper excretion of 480 µg/24 h (target 200–500 µg/24 h), serum ceruloplasmin 12 mg/dL, and serum copper 42 µg/dL (70–140 µg/dL), consistent with good compliance and excluding copper deficiency. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal, excluding neuroboreliosis. Repetitive nerve stimulation in the left orbicularis oculi and left abductor pollicis brevis, and single-fiber electromyography of the left orbicularis oculi, did not reveal signs of abnormal neuromuscular junction transmission.
title: D-Penicillamine-Induced Myasthenia Gravis—A Probable Complication of Wilson’s Disease Treatment—A Case Report and Systematic Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old, 48-kg male with idiopathic scoliosis was scheduled for posterior spinal osteotomy. He had no notable medical or family history; first- and second-degree relatives had undergone anesthesia without adverse events. Physical examination showed spinal and thoracic deformities with normal lower-limb muscle strength. Radiographs confirmed scoliosis. Preoperative serum creatine kinase was elevated at 1158.3 U/L (normal 24–195); electrocardiogram, blood counts, renal function, and coagulation studies were normal. He was classified as ASA physical status 1.

On the morning of surgery, he received penehyclidine hydrochloride and dexamethasone 30 minutes before induction. General anesthesia was induced with midazolam 3 mg, sufentanil 20 μg, cis-atracurium 10 mg, and propofol 60 mg. After endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation was set with a tidal volume of 8 mL/kg, respiratory rate 16/min, and I:E ratio of 1:2. The end-tidal CO2 (PetCO2) immediately after induction was 38 mmHg. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane, propofol, and remifentanil. Surgery began at 9:45 am.

At 9:50 am, the PetCO2 rose abruptly to 59 mmHg, heart rate increased to 100 bpm, and the surgeon noted increased muscle tension. The anesthesiologist deepened anesthesia, administered additional cis-atracurium, replaced the soda lime, and increased minute ventilation. By 10:00 am, the PetCO2 had climbed to 144 mmHg, heart rate to 135 bpm, and nasopharyngeal temperature to 38.3°C. Arterial blood gas at that time showed pH 6.748, PCO2 > 130 mmHg, K+ 6.4 mmol/L, and ionized Ca2+ 1.46 mmol/L.
title: Perioperative management of malignant hyperthermia during general anesthesia: A report of two cases

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of a progressively enlarging, mildly painful mass in the lower right jaw. On examination, a firm swelling was palpable in the body and angle of the right mandible without overlying skin changes or intraoral ulceration. 

Noncontrast CT of the nasal sinuses demonstrated a multiloculated lytic lesion in the body and angle of the right mandible, with cortical expansion and thinning. The lesion was in intimate contact with the roots of the right inferior canine, first and second premolars, and second molar. Sagittal reconstructions revealed fine septa oriented perpendicular to the lesion borders, partitioning the mass into small rectangular spaces.
title: Odontogenic myxoma: A case report of a rare tumor

case_prompt: A 48-year-old Asian woman presented with a 15-day history of headache and intermittent bleeding from her right nasal cavity. She had a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine and enalapril. Anterior rhinoscopy showed a mildly deviated nasal septum and a right-sided nasal polyp. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. A computed tomography scan revealed a low-density lesion with a few soft-tissue–density areas completely filling the right maxillary sinus and extending into the middle meatus and posterior nasal cavity, with widening of the antrum; no bony destruction was noted. The radiologic impression was an antrochoanal polyp. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. The patient underwent endoscopic polypectomy and middle meatal antrostomy. Multiple irregular gray-brown soft-tissue fragments measuring up to 3.0 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm were submitted for histopathology. Microscopic examination revealed mature adipose tissue admixed with hematopoietic cells, including myeloid, erythroid, and megakaryocytic lineages.
title: Primary myelolipoma presenting as a nasal cavity polyp: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia was brought to the emergency department by his wife for altered mental status. Two hours before arrival, he had consumed two glasses of wine and taken a nap; he was asymptomatic before the nap. On awakening, he exhibited dysarthria and extremity discoordination.

Home medications included bupropion, dutasteride, lisinopril, and tolterodine. 

Vital signs were: blood pressure 115/78 mm Hg, heart rate 83 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air.

On examination, he had waxing and waning alertness but could intermittently follow commands. Pupils were reactive but sluggish, with horizontal and vertical nystagmus. Facial symmetry was intact, the tongue was midline, and speech was dysarthric. Motor strength could not be formally assessed; he moved all extremities symmetrically. He had bilateral dysmetria on finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing and truncal ataxia when seated.

During approximately 1.5 hours in the ED, his ataxia and mental status progressively worsened. A stroke alert was activated, and a head CT angiogram was negative for hemorrhage or other abnormalities. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, coagulation studies, and urinalysis, were within normal limits. His blood alcohol concentration was 57 mg/dL. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm with a QRS duration of 108 ms and a QTc of 497 ms. Naloxone, 0.4 mg IV, produced no improvement.

Neurology evaluation yielded an NIH Stroke Scale score of 11; tissue plasminogen activator was administered for presumed posterior circulation stroke. The patient was intubated for airway protection and admitted to the intensive care unit.

In the ICU, he developed status epilepticus with three 5-minute episodes of generalized tonic–clonic seizures. He received benzodiazepines, phenytoin, and a propofol infusion, after which seizure activity ceased. Subsequent EEG showed no ongoing seizures.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain did not show evidence of acute stroke.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Clozapine Intoxication Mimicking Acute Stroke

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old man presented with pleuritic chest pain, a swollen painful right knee impairing weight bearing, and hip and back pain after a fall. He reported a 40-kg weight loss over 2 years, poor appetite, fever, night sweats, and increased infections. He has a 16-year history of untreated hepatitis C (genotype 3) and a history of intravenous heroin use. He had prior pulmonary embolism, disc prolapse, mild depression, osteomyelitis with digit amputation, and multiple fracture repairs.

On examination he was cachectic with rib and mediastinal tenderness, hepatomegaly (6 cm below costal margin), non-tender lymphadenopathy in the left jugular chain and bilateral groins, and a warm right knee effusion. Vital signs were normal. 

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 102 g/L, elevated C-reactive protein, calcium 2.57 mmol/L, albumin 23 g/L, and a transient mild elevation of free T4. Liver function, renal function, coagulation, α-fetoprotein, vasculitic screen, iron studies, B12, urate, and globulins were normal. HIV tests were negative on two assays; hepatitis C serology was positive; CMV and EBV were reactive; HHV-8 was not detected.

CT of the chest and abdomen revealed enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes and lytic lesions in T8 and T9. CT pulmonary angiogram, chest X-ray, and troponin I were normal. Knee aspiration grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and was treated as septic arthritis. Transesophageal echocardiography excluded infective endocarditis.

Further workup for suspected hematologic malignancy showed normal β2-microglobulin and LDH, no monoclonal band on serum or urine electrophoresis, and normal B- and T-cell subsets by flow cytometry. A bone scan demonstrated destructive thoracic lesions, and MRI confirmed T8–T11 osteomyelitis with epidural involvement. A bone marrow biopsy excluded lymphoma and multiple myeloma.
title: Multicentric Castleman's Disease in a Hepatitis C-Positive Intravenous Drug User: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 52-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of whitish lesions on both buccal mucosae and crusting of the lips. He initially noted oral dryness and discomfort that worsened on hot, sunny days, followed by crusting and fissuring of the lips with tenderness at the outer margin. The condition gradually progressed over time. His medical history included type 2 diabetes (on antidiabetic medications) and gastric ulcers. He worked as a clerk, was a smoker, a social drinker, and wore dentures. There was no family history of similar lesions. On examination, there were no cutaneous abnormalities. Intraoral examination revealed multiple asymptomatic, coalesced papules with a rough texture along the vermilion border; the lips appeared dry and crusted. A biopsy of the lip margin was performed. Histopathologic examination showed suprabasal splits in the epithelium with acantholytic and dyskeratotic cells observed as round and granular corpuscles.
title: A Rare Clinical Presentation of Intraoral Darier's Disease

case_prompt: A 23-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 4-year history of a painless midline neck mass that had enlarged dramatically over the past 3 months and was now causing difficulty swallowing and shortness of breath. He denied fevers, weight loss, pain, or other masses and had no family history of thyroid or neck malignancy. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a 4×5 cm hard, irregular, non-tender central neck mass that moved slightly with tongue protrusion and swallowing; there were no skin changes, no intraoral extension, and no palpable cervical lymph nodes. Laboratory studies showed normal hemoglobin, white-cell count, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin. Thyroid function, renal function, liver function, and coagulation tests were all within normal limits. Neck ultrasound revealed a 5×5 cm irregular cystic mass with a solid component and increased vascular flow; the thyroid gland appeared normal without nodules and there was no lymphadenopathy. A thyroid uptake scan showed normal uptake in both lobes and no cold nodules. MRI of the neck demonstrated a 5×5 cm mixed cystic and solid soft-tissue mass anterior to the hyoid bone, compressing the trachea, with no thyroid nodules or enlarged lymph nodes. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the solid component was performed.
title: Isolated poorly differentiated cancer (insular) in a thyroglossal cyst: a case report

case_prompt: A 25-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of a gradually enlarging right gluteal swelling associated with deep lower abdominal and pelvic pain, constipation, and increased urinary frequency. She reported difficulty ambulating and sitting. On examination, there was a 15 cm × 15 cm firm, non-tender mass in the right gluteal area displacing the perineal body contralaterally. Abdominal examination revealed a poorly defined abdomino-pelvic mass extending to the level of the umbilicus. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 9.8 mg/dl; liver and renal function tests were normal. Serum alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and carcinoembryonic antigen levels were within normal limits. Pelvic MRI revealed a 35 cm × 25 cm × 20 cm multiseptated cystic and solid sacrococcygeal mass involving the perineal area and remodeling the coccyx, with superior displacement of the vagina, uterus, and bladder. Based on these findings, the differential diagnoses of teratoma, fibrosarcoma, and neurofibroma were considered.
title: Adult case of giant sacrococcygeal teratoma: case report

case_prompt:
A 22‐year‐old Syrian man presented with a 2‐week history of recurrent fever, intermittent vomiting, aphthous ulcers, fatigue, polyuria, and polydipsia. He had no significant weight loss or anorexia. His medical history was notable for low birth weight, sparse subcutaneous tissue, short stature, high‐pitched voice, orchiopexy for undescended testes at age 10, recurrent chest and middle‐ear infections, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. His parents are first cousins; a sister has proportionate short stature and similar facial features.  

On examination, he weighed 33 kg and was 146 cm tall (BMI 15.5 kg/m2). Vital signs were normal except for a respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min and temperature 37.5 °C. He had dolichocephaly, a prominent nose, and pale conjunctivae. Ophthalmologic findings included right‐sided lateral strabismus, amblyopia, and bilateral lower‐eyelid ectropion; pupils, lenses, media, and fundi were unremarkable. A sun‐sensitive malar rash with telangiectasias, cheilitis with peeling vesicles, a missing upper incisor, café‐au‐lait spots, hypopigmented areas, and chest telangiectasias were noted. Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds; no lymphadenopathy, purpura, or petechiae were present.  

Chest radiograph, ECG, and urinalysis were normal. Laboratory studies showed glucose 237 mg/dL, hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, hematocrit 18.9%, MCV 85 fL, platelets 19 × 10^3/μL, LDH 692 IU/L, ALP 273 IU/L, CRP 145 mg/dL, and ESR 105 mm/h. White‐cell count was normal. ANA, ANCA, RF, tuberculin skin test, and QuantiFERON were negative. Spirometry showed FEV1/FVC 75%. An islet‐cell antibody test confirmed type I diabetes mellitus. Endocrine studies (GH, testosterone, FSH, LH) were normal; semen analysis revealed azoospermia.  

Peripheral smear showed hypochromic microcytic anemia with anisocytosis, spherocytes, elliptocytes, tear‐drop cells, giant platelets, and hyposegmented granulocytes. Bone‐marrow aspiration and flow cytometry demonstrated hypercellular marrow with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio, 6% myeloblasts, dysplasia in erythroid and megakaryocytic lineages, and ringed sideroblasts. These findings were consistent with myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts‐1.
title: Bloom syndrome with myelodysplastic syndrome that was converted into acute myeloid leukaemia, with new ophthalmologic manifestations: the first report from Syria

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old girl was evaluated for a slowly enlarging plaque-like lesion on the left chest wall that had been present for 2 years. Initially palpable only beneath the skin, the lesion became visible over the last several months and measured approximately 0.5 cm in diameter with a light violet color. On ultrasound examination, there was a 0.5-cm ovoid, well-demarcated lesion in the subcutaneous region with dermal involvement and without clear separation from the underlying pectoralis major muscle. The internal echotexture was heterogeneously hypoechoic with small echogenic foci and no posterior acoustic enhancement or shadowing.

Given the persistence of the lesion, a complete surgical excision was performed. Grossly, the specimen had a polypoid appearance with raised epidermis; on sectioning, a firm white-gray nodule was seen, centered in the dermis and extending focally into the subcutaneous tissue. Histologic examination showed hyperplastic epidermis with hyperkeratosis and elongated rete ridges. Within the dermis, there was a spindle‐cell proliferation in a storiform to whorled pattern; the cells had eosinophilic cytoplasm, monomorphic nuclei, and sparse mitotic activity. Tumor cells infiltrated fat lobules in a honeycomb fashion, and the stroma was collagenous. 

The differential diagnosis based on hematoxylin and eosin staining included dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans and dermatofibroma.
title: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in a child, that’s why soft tissue lesions are not always innocent in children

case_prompt: A 72‐year‐old man presented with a 4‐hour history of fever, chest tightness, and dull precordial chest pain unrelieved by rest or nitroglycerin. His temperature was 39.7 °C, pulse 136 beats/min, respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, and blood pressure 98/67 mmHg. He had a history of right upper lobectomy for stage IIB lung adenocarcinoma in 2016, adjuvant chemotherapy, nodal recurrence treated with chemotherapy in 2018, tracheal tumour involvement treated with cryotherapy and radiotherapy in early 2024, and most recently three cycles of pemetrexed, carboplatin, and bevacizumab for progressive disease. On examination, lung sounds were slightly coarse without rales; heart rate was 136/min with distant, dull heart sounds and no murmurs. Laboratory tests showed WBC 10.05×10^9/L with 93.2% neutrophils, hemoglobin 110 g/L, platelets 187×10^9/L, CRP 130 mg/L, D‐dimer 7.83 mg/L, and normal cardiac enzymes including troponin I and BNP. ECG showed sinus tachycardia, abnormal Q waves, and ST‐segment elevation (> 0.1 mV) in leads II, III, and aVF, with ST-segment changes in leads I and aVL. He received aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous nitroglycerin. Four hours later, repeat ECG still showed ST‐segment elevation without dynamic change, cardiac biomarkers remained normal, and chest pain persisted. At that time, he was taken for coronary angiography.
title: Tracheopericardial fistula in lung cancer masquerading as acute myocardial infarction: a case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman from Karachi presented with a 2-month history of productive cough with purulent sputum, generalized weakness, anorexia, weight loss, and intermittent fever up to 37.8 °C. Over the preceding 3 weeks she also had severe watery diarrhea. She had received multiple empiric antibiotics in the past and, without confirmatory testing, was started on daily Myrin-P Forte (isoniazid 225 mg, rifampin 150 mg, ethambutol 275 mg, pyrazinamide 400 mg) plus pyridoxine; she was not fully compliant. Ten days after initiating anti-tuberculosis therapy, she developed arthralgias and new rashes on her face, chest, and upper extremities. She had no other medical history except a blood transfusion during childbirth.

Vital signs were notable for heart rate 84 bpm, blood pressure 107/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and she was afebrile. Examination showed a pale erythematous malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, alopecia of the scalp, palpable bilateral cervical and axillary lymph nodes, and a linear pustular rash on the right anterior chest consistent with herpes zoster. Crackles were heard at the right lower lung field, and splenomegaly was present. Muscle strength was 5/5 in all limbs, and there was symmetric calf wasting without tenderness.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, WBC 4.3 × 10^9/L, platelets 341 × 10^9/L, ESR 58 mm/h, ALT 72 IU/L, AST 100 IU/L, ANA positive at 1:160, anti–double-stranded DNA 221.7 IU/mL, and a normal ENA panel. Sputum AFB smear, culture, and GeneXpert for TB were all negative. HIV antibody, fourth-generation enzyme immunoassay, and HIV-1 confirmatory assays were reactive.
title: Drug-Induced Lupus in an HIV-Positive Patient Treated for Tuberculosis: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of gingival overgrowth that had been present since his first tooth erupted at 6 months of age. The painless gingival enlargement progressed slowly without discomfort until age 6, when its esthetic appearance became intolerable. He had no other complaints and was systemically healthy. He was the only child of two healthy non-consanguineous parents, and there was no family history of similar findings.

Oral examination showed severe gingival enlargement involving both mandibular and maxillary arches, most prominent in the anterior regions. The gingivae had slight redness, mild edema, and absence of normal stippling. Oral hygiene was poor, with pseudopockets containing abundant dental plaque and minimal calculus; marginal gingiva was slightly inflamed. No other mucosal lesions were observed. Radiographs revealed no periodontal bone destruction.

Routine hematological and biochemical tests were unremarkable. Initial phase therapy to control gingival inflammation did not alleviate the overgrowth. A gingivectomy was performed, and healing was uneventful. Histopathological examination of gingival specimens stained with hematoxylin–eosin revealed hyperplastic epithelium, mild inflammatory cell infiltration, proliferation of the capillary layer, and increased fibrous tissue. One week after the gingivectomy, recurrence of gingival enlargement occurred.
title: Hyaline fibromatosis syndrome: a case presenting with gingival enlargement as the only clinical manifestation and a report of two new mutations in the ANTXR2 gene

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old Japanese woman was referred for evaluation of multiple abnormal opacities on her annual chest radiograph. She had no respiratory symptoms. Vital signs were: temperature 35.7 °C, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, pulse 97 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Breath sounds were normal. Her medical history was notable only for hematuria and nephritis at age 59. For the past 6–7 months, she had taken choreito (7.5 g/day) for hematuria; she also used Seihaito intermittently. She smoked one pack per day for 31 years and drank 700 mL of beer five times weekly. BMI was 29.2 kg/m2. 

Chest CT showed multiple nodules predominantly in the bilateral lower lobes and a small peribronchial ground-glass opacity in the left lingular lobe. Laboratory studies revealed a mildly elevated CRP (0.33 mg/dL) and positive ANA (1:80 speckled; 1:40 nucleolar). Tests for proteinase 3 ANCA, myeloperoxidase ANCA, T-SPOT tuberculosis, anti-Mycobacterium avium complex antibody, Aspergillus antigen, Cryptococcus neoformans antigen, β-D-glucan, tumor markers, and soluble IL-2 receptor were all negative. Complete blood count, liver function tests, and urinalysis were unremarkable except for slight hematuria. Spirometry was normal. 

Bronchoscopy revealed no visible bleeding. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) from the left B5 segment became serially and increasingly hemorrhagic. Bacterial and mycobacterial cultures of BALF were negative, and cytology showed no malignant cells; no hemosiderin-laden macrophages were seen. A transbronchial biopsy of a subpleural nodule in left S8 demonstrated alveolitis and intraluminal polypoid structures with chronic inflammatory infiltrates, consistent with organizing pneumonia.
title: Organizing Pneumonia With Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage Induced by the Kampo Medicine Choreito

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of a painful ulcerative lesion on the left lateral tongue. Initially the lesion was the size of a sorghum grain and ulcerated after 2 weeks; it subsequently enlarged steadily to about 2 cm. He had tried oral anti-inflammatory agents, topical sprays, and mouthwash without improvement. He reported no weight loss, chills, night sweats, or cough. His medical history was unremarkable; he had smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 30 years and consumed alcohol regularly.

On examination, there was a 2.0 cm round mass on the left tongue margin with a central ulcer, firm consistency, ill-defined borders, and tenderness. The tongue could be extended centrally without deviation. Palpable left submandibular lymph nodes measured up to 1.5 × 1.0 cm, were moderately mobile, and slightly tender.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; three standard infectious disease screenings were negative. Chest CT revealed diffuse patchy and nodular opacities in both lungs with areas of coalescence, visible bronchograms, and punctate calcifications in the right upper lobe, suggesting pulmonary tuberculosis.
title: A case of oral tuberculous ulcer and literature review

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset headache, right facial droop, confusion, and left-sided weakness. His blood pressure was 200/190 mm Hg; respiratory rate, 18 breaths/min; pulse, 82 bpm; and Glasgow Coma Scale score, 3. He was intubated, and head CT revealed a large right basal ganglia and temporal lobe intraparenchymal hematoma with extension into the ventricles and a 13 mm midline shift. He underwent external ventricular drainage on the left and a right craniotomy with evacuation of the hematoma; blood pressure was controlled perioperatively.

Thirty-one days after surgery, significant tongue swelling developed. An allergic reaction was suspected, and he was treated with steroids and diphenhydramine. Despite discontinuation of all potential offending medications, the swelling persisted and worsened. MRI of the tongue showed marked enlargement with prominent vascular engorgement. Laboratory studies revealed a mild increase in C1 esterase inhibitor level.
title: An idiopathic severe macroglossia in a young adult patient: a rare case

case_prompt:
A 65‐year‐old man presented with involuntary, repetitive movements of his left upper limb for 2 days. He described continuous clonic jerking of the left elbow, wrist, and fingers occurring every 2–5 hours and lasting 1–3 minutes per episode, with preserved consciousness and sphincter control. He had no prior history of seizures or epilepsy. On examination, he appeared unwell. Temperature was 37.2°C, pulse 98/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and blood pressure 100/70 mmHg. He was notably thirsty with dry lips and mouth. Neurological examination was otherwise normal.

Initial considerations included central nervous system lesions and electrolyte abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed a glucose level of 330 mg/dL (normal 70–100 mg/dL) and three-plus ketone bodies in the urine. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.24, pCO₂ 22.1 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L; normal pH 7.35–7.45, pCO₂ 35–45 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L). Serum sodium was 125 mEq/L (normal 135–145 mEq/L), calcium 8.7 mg/dL (normal 8.5–10.5 mg/dL), albumin 3.1 g/dL (normal 3.4–5.4 g/dL), and serum osmolarity 292 mOsm/L (normal 275–295 mOsm/L).

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, cerebrospinal fluid studies, and electroencephalography were all reported as normal.
title: Epilepsia Partialis continua secondary to diabetic ketoacidosis

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old White-British woman presented with intermittent swelling of the left parotid gland for 3 years, associated with tenderness and pruritus. She also reported recurrent urticarial and eczematous lesions on the trunk and limbs. Her medical history included hay fever, childhood atopic eczema, and hypothyroidism. On examination, the left parotid gland was slightly enlarged and tender; intraoral findings were normal. Urticated erythematous plaques and papules were present on the trunk and limbs. 

An external parotid biopsy showed benign lymphoid aggregates with follicular hyperplasia of intra- and peri-parotid lymph nodes. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, renal function, autoimmune screen, serum ACE, protein electrophoresis, and viral serology, were unremarkable; allergen patch testing was negative. Ultrasonography of the parotid gland indicated sialadenitis, and sialography demonstrated normal unstimulated flow. Sjögren’s syndrome was excluded. The patient received a course of co-amoxiclav and metronidazole for presumed chronic sialadenitis and was started on cetirizine for presumed chronic urticaria, but her symptoms persisted after one year. 

Sialoendoscopy with corticosteroid washout provided limited benefit. A PET scan demonstrated increased uptake in the left parotid gland and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsies of cervical lymph nodes and cutaneous lesions were non-specific, showing no obvious pathology. CT imaging revealed multifocal soft tissue abnormality in the left parotid gland with enlarged left cervical and superficial supraclavicular lymph nodes. Laboratory studies at this time showed a serum IgE level of 541 KU/L (normal 0–81) and an eosinophil count of 0.9 ×10^9/L (normal 0.0–0.4).
title: Kimura’s disease of the parotid gland with cutaneous features in a Caucasian female patient

case_prompt:
An 8-week-old male Finnish Lapphund puppy was referred for evaluation of poor mobility and limb deformities. The puppy and one male littermate had been noted at 3 weeks of age to be significantly smaller and less mobile than four healthy littermates; both had delayed eruption of deciduous teeth but were eating well and had normal elimination. At presentation the puppies weighed 1.2 kg and 1.6 kg. Physical examination revealed mild hypodontia, retrognathism, valgus deformities of both carpi, limited range of motion at the elbows and shoulders, profound muscle atrophy of all four limbs, pain on hip extension and knee flexion, and a varus deformity with contracture of one hindlimb. Neurologic evaluation found delayed proprioception in all limbs, deemed to be pain related.  

Complete blood counts showed mild anemia (hematocrit 34%), mild reticulocytosis, and a mild mature neutrophilia. Serum biochemistry showed mild panhypoproteinemia, hyperphosphatemia (5.7 and 6.5 mg/dL; reference 2.7–5.4), alkaline phosphatase within adult reference range (86 and 88 U/L; expected to be higher in puppies), and increased creatine kinase (592 and 751 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (412 and 369 U/L).  

Radiographs and CT imaging revealed diffuse osteopenia with severe cortical thinning throughout the skeleton and multiple “folding” fractures of long bones with minimal callus formation.
title: Osteogenesis Imperfecta in Two Finnish Lapphund Puppies

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man with persistent atrial tachycardia and three prior left atrial ablation procedures for atrial fibrillation presented for repeat ablation. He had no other medical history. Preprocedure echocardiography showed a structurally normal heart without regional wall motion abnormalities. The procedure was performed on uninterrupted warfarin. After induction of anesthesia and transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus, transseptal punctures were made and an electroanatomic map of the left atrium was generated. Endocardial RF energy failed to block a perimitral flutter, so epicardial RF energy was delivered within the distal coronary sinus (maximum 20 W, temperature limit 43°C, irrigation 25 mL/min) for a total of 103 seconds, achieving an average power of 16 W and temperature of 39°C. The perimitral tachycardia terminated, and subsequent arrhythmias were successfully ablated. Anticoagulation with heparin maintained an activated clotting time above 300 seconds. There were no intraprocedural complications, and postprocedure echocardiography showed no pericardial effusion. 

After extubation, the patient complained of chest discomfort described as pericardial in nature. His ECG showed an accelerated idioventricular rhythm. He received morphine and atropine, after which the rhythm reverted to sinus without obvious ischemic changes. He continued to have chest pain and developed up to 0.1 mV of ST-segment depression in leads V4 to V6 at 40 minutes after reversion to sinus rhythm. Coronary angiography was performed immediately.
title: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm after left atrial tachycardia ablation as a marker of acute coronary ischemia

case_prompt: A 22-year-old right-handed woman was referred for several weekly episodes of paroxysmal motor behaviors and a possible generalized tonic–clonic seizure. Each stereotyped episode began with tonic elevation and abduction of the right arm, sometimes followed by right leg movements. Birth, developmental, and medical histories were unremarkable, and there was no family history of epilepsy. Neurological examination was normal. Brain MRI and routine interictal EEG were interpreted as normal. Because of the suspected unprovoked tonic–clonic seizure, oxcarbazepine was started; the stereotyped movements decreased but persisted. A neurologist who witnessed an episode diagnosed psychogenic nonepileptic seizures and antiepileptic treatment was progressively withdrawn. Shortly after cessation, she experienced clusters of similar paroxysmal motor events followed by probable generalized tonic–clonic seizures and was referred to our department. On arrival, she was awake, alert, and her neurological examination remained normal.
title: Pitfalls in the diagnosis of new-onset frontal lobe seizures☆

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of jaundice and general fatigue. Two days before admission she noted yellowing of her bulbar conjunctiva and low-grade fever. She had no history of alcohol use, dietary supplements, or exposure to hepatotoxins. Her body-mass index was 24. Her older sister died in her thirties of hepatic failure of unknown cause.

On examination, she was alert, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed: total bilirubin 33.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 25.5 mg/dL, ammonia 143 μg/dL, prothrombin time 19% (INR 2.43), hemoglobin 6.1 g/dL, platelets 202 ×10^3/μL, AST 164 U/L, ALT 15 U/L, ALP 26 U/L, γ-GTP 371 U/L. Viral hepatitis serologies, antinuclear antibody, anti–mitochondrial M2 antibody, and other autoimmune markers were negative.

Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed hepatosplenomegaly without focal lesions or biliary dilation. She was diagnosed with acute hepatic failure and treated with fresh frozen plasma transfusions and plasma exchange under continuous hemofiltration.

Over the next 2 days, her hemoglobin and platelet counts declined further. Reticulocyte count rose to 175‰, haptoglobin was < 10 mg/dL, and both direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. Additional testing did not reveal viral, autoimmune, or drug-induced causes. A liver biopsy could not be performed due to coagulopathy.

On hospital day 4 she developed flapping tremor and confusion consistent with grade II hepatic encephalopathy (NH₃ 168 μg/dL). On day 5, bone marrow examination demonstrated macrophages phagocytizing blood cells, fulfilling HLH-2004 criteria.  
Based on guideline definitions, she was diagnosed with fulminant hepatitis accompanied by hemophagocytic syndrome of unknown etiology.
title: Clinically diagnosed late-onset fulminant Wilson’s disease without cirrhosis: A case report

case_prompt: A 62-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a slowly enlarging, mildly tender mass in the anterolateral aspect of her left distal forearm. She had no history of trauma, and the overlying skin was normal without adherence. She reported paresthesia and numbness over the dorsoradial aspect of the left hand, corresponding to the superficial radial nerve distribution. On examination, there was an immobile, nonpulsatile subcutaneous mass in the distal forearm. Percussion over the mass elicited radiating pain, and a positive Tinel’s sign was present in the superficial radial nerve distribution. Sensory testing confirmed hypoaesthesia in the dorsoradial hand. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies demonstrated an isolated sensory deficit of the radial nerve. Conventional radiographs of the forearm were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the distal forearm showed a multilobulated, well-circumscribed mass with homogeneous low isointensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images.
title: Superficial radial nerve compression due to fibroma of the brachioradialis tendon sheath: A case report

case_prompt: A 13-year-old boy with a 1-year history of progressively worsening exertional intolerance and dyspnea was referred for evaluation of chronic heart failure. He had no family history of heart disease or sudden death. On examination, his blood pressure was 100/64 mm Hg and pulse was 76 beats/min, and the ECG showed sinus rhythm. A chest radiograph demonstrated massive cardiomegaly and interstitial pulmonary congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normally sized but hypokinetic left ventricle (ejection fraction, 37%), and massive enlargement of both atria with spontaneous echo contrast in both ventricles. The apical portions of both ventricles had a markedly trabeculated, spongy appearance. The maximum end-systolic ratio of the noncompacted endocardial layer to the compacted myocardium was >2. Color-flow Doppler examination showed blood flow within the intertrabecular recesses. There was severe tricuspid regurgitation, and the calculated peak systolic pulmonary-artery pressure by the tricuspid-regurgitation gradient (75 mm Hg) indicated severe pulmonary hypertension. Restrictive left-ventricular inflow patterns and reduced myocardial velocities suggested a markedly elevated left-ventricular end-diastolic pressure.
title: Isolated Biventricular Noncompaction in an adult with severe pulmonary hypertension: An association reviewed

case_prompt: A 53-year-old woman was admitted to the ICU for angiocholitis complicated by septic shock. Her history included hypertension, two prior kidney transplants, end-stage renal disease, and ongoing immunosuppression (prednisolone, mycophenolate, cyclosporine). Initial empiric antibiotics were piperacillin-tazobactam plus amikacin, narrowed to ceftriaxone on day 5 after isolation of biliary Klebsiella pneumoniae. On ICU day 21, she developed a second septic shock from recurrent angiocholitis and was restarted on piperacillin-tazobactam plus amikacin; on day 23, therapy was changed to ceftriaxone and vancomycin after blood cultures grew Pantoea agglomerans and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. A third septic shock on day 26 led to addition of piperacillin-tazobactam and amikacin to ongoing vancomycin. On day 29, she developed a mild rash on her chest. Forty-eight hours later, after transient hemodynamic stability, she developed high fever and distributive shock requiring norepinephrine at 1 µg/kg/min. Procalcitonin rose to 2.98 µg/L. The rash progressed to diffuse erythroderma, and she had enlarged cervical and inguinal lymph nodes, an eosinophil count of 1.0 × 10^9/L, agranulocytosis (neutrophils 0.4 × 10^9/L), and circulating activated T lymphocytes.
title: DRESS Syndrome in the ICU: When a Patient Is Treated with Multiple Drugs

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man presented after a forced inversion injury of his left foot. He had no relevant medical or family history and was taking no medications. On examination, there was edema over the left lateral malleolus, tenderness with movement and weight bearing, no deformity, and palpable distal pulses of normal intensity and frequency.  

Plain radiographs of the left foot showed soft-tissue edema and a discrete lesion in the first metatarsal. MRI of the left foot with gadolinium demonstrated, in both sagittal and coronal planes, a heterogeneous intramedullary lesion in the base and proximal diaphysis of the first metatarsal that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with evidence of cortical injury related to the lesion.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Solitary enchondroma in a metatarsal bone, an incidental discovery

case_prompt: A 78-year-old man with a history of bladder cancer treated initially with transurethral resections and later with radical cystectomy and ileal conduit for advanced disease presented for evaluation of abnormal liver tests. Fourteen months after cystectomy, para‐aortic lymph node metastases were detected, and combination therapy with nivolumab (1 mg/kg) plus ipilimumab (3 mg/kg) was initiated. Five days before the first dose of immunotherapy, he had pyelonephritis treated successfully with doripenem. After the third dose of the checkpoint inhibitors (day 71), laboratory tests showed aspartate aminotransferase 251 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 266 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 2867 U/L, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 461 U/L, without bilirubin elevation. Serologic tests were negative for cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and hepatitis B and C viruses. Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:40, immunoglobulin G was moderately elevated, and antimitochondrial antibodies were negative. CT and abdominal ultrasonography showed no liver metastases or bile duct dilation. He was diagnosed with grade 3 immune‐related hepatitis, and treatment was started with intravenous prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day), and the doripenem infusion was discontinued.
title: Successful mycophenolate mofetil treatment of a patient with severe steroid‐refractory hepatitis evoked by nivolumab plus ipilimumab treatment for relapsed bladder cancer

case_prompt: A 76‐year‐old Syrian man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 25–30% with an implantable cardioverter–defibrillator), treated bladder cancer, hypothyroidism, and interstitial lung disease presented with a 4-month history of multiple painful skin lesions on his arms. He had recovered from a COVID-19 infection requiring a two-week hospitalization; two weeks after discharge he noticed small erythematous papules on his upper extremities. Over the next months the lesions enlarged slowly, with significant worsening over the past 15 days and tenderness but no discharge or bleeding. He was afebrile and denied trauma, insect bites, or previous similar lesions. On examination, there were multiple erythematous plaques with central hemorrhagic crustations on the extensor surfaces of both upper extremities, especially over the elbows; no other sites were involved. The initial clinical impression was an infectious process such as ecthyma (deep impetigo) versus a neoplastic etiology like cutaneous metastasis. A swab was obtained for bacterial culture and sensitivity, clinical samples were collected for smears, and a skin biopsy was performed. The patient was instructed to apply topical ketoconazole and fusidic acid ointments and to cleanse the lesions twice daily with saline until biopsy results were available.
title: Impetiginous Cutaneous Leishmaniasis after COVID-19 Infection in a Patient with Poor Cardiac Profile: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
An 86-year-old man was admitted for generalized weakness and dyspnea on exertion after noting a new nonpruritic petechial rash on both feet. Fifteen days earlier, he had undergone placement of a WATCHMAN left atrial appendage occlusion device and was converted from rivaroxaban to apixaban and aspirin, and from flecainide to amiodarone. His medical history included diverticulosis with partial bowel resection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation complicated by gastrointestinal bleeding, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage IIIb, major depressive disorder, and obstructive sleep apnea. Home medications also included trazodone, citalopram, sitagliptin, metoprolol, pravastatin, oxybutynin, and tamsulosin. He denied chemical exposures, insect bites, or prior allergic reactions.

On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, with an irregularly irregular rhythm and no respiratory distress. He had a nonblanching, nonpainful petechial rash on the feet that later spread to the thighs and arms, accompanied by diffuse myalgias. Laboratory studies revealed:  
• WBC 11.3×10^9/L with 0.3% eosinophils (0.3–5.0%)  
• Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, platelets 289×10^9/L  
• Creatinine 2.14 mg/dL (baseline 1.5)  
• ESR 63 mm/h, CRP 11.7 mg/dL  
• ANA titer 1:40 (borderline), antihistone antibody 4.4 U (strongly positive)  
• C3 147 mg/dL, C4 72 mg/dL  
• Negative double-stranded DNA, ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies  
• Negative serologies for SARS-CoV-2, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, syphilis, coxsackievirus, and ehrlichia

Apixaban was discontinued, and prednisone 30 mg twice daily was initiated. A skin biopsy of a fresh lesion demonstrated superficial and deep perivascular neutrophilic infiltration consistent with leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
title: Drug-Induced Lupus with Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis Associated with Apixaban

case_prompt:
A 21-year-old man presented with progressive right shoulder pain of several weeks’ duration. He had no history of trauma or heavy lifting and no family history of malignancy. On examination, his right shoulder was asymmetrically deformed compared with the left, and palpation of the distal third of the right clavicle elicited tenderness.  

Plain radiographs showed a well-defined osteolytic lesion with cortical thinning in the distal third of the right clavicle. MRI with contrast demonstrated an enhancing mass in the lateral third of the clavicle. Multislice CT of the chest and abdomen, plus a complete bone survey, revealed no other lesions. Based on the clinical and radiological findings, a primary benign bone lesion was suspected (Bone RADS score 1). Three days later, an open biopsy with curettage, bone grafting, and internal fixation via an anterior clavicular approach was performed.  

Microscopic examination of the curetted tissue revealed diffuse sheets of moderately sized tumor cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. Some cells had oval or eccentric nuclei with nuclear grooves. The background contained numerous eosinophils, lymphocytes, and multinucleated osteoclastic giant cells.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Isolated skeletal Langerhans cell histiocytosis in adults: A case report

case_prompt:
A 3-year-old girl was referred for 18F-FDG PET/CT to stage newly diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma.  
History:  
• Born after a complicated delivery with documented birth asphyxia  
• Congenital hypothyroidism  
• Clinical cerebral palsy, neurodevelopmental delay, cortical blindness  
• Seizures onset at age 3 months, treated with phenobarbital and primidone; no seizure on day of scan  
• No prior brain surgery or known metabolic disorder or infection; Epstein–Barr virus studies negative  
• Consanguineous parents; neonatal glucose nadir 40 mg/dL but no recurrent hypoglycemia during lymphoma treatment  

Neurologic exam:  
• Increased muscle tone in all extremities; deep-tendon reflexes reportedly normal but variably assessed due to agitation  
• No pathologic reflexes  
• Microcephaly  

Cranial CT (prior to lymphoma diagnosis):  
• Occipital volume loss and hypodensity without mass lesion or hemorrhage  

PET/CT findings:  
• Marked bilateral occipital hypometabolism  
• Uptake in known malignant lymphatic regions in the neck and abdomen  

Brain MRI:  
• Cystic area in the occipital region with surrounding gliosis  
• Bilateral occipital cortex hyperintense on axial T2-weighted images  
• Posterior parasagittal increased signal on T2 and FLAIR in both occipital lobes  
• Millimetric subcortical cystic changes and thinning of the occipital cortex on FLAIR  
• Identical, nonprogressive findings on repeat MRI one year later
title: Occipital Hypometabolism on FDG PET/CT Scan in a Child with Hodgkin's Lymphoma

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old multiparous Nigerian woman presented at 35 weeks’ gestation with premature rupture of membranes and suspected abruptio placentae. She began antenatal care at 6 weeks; booking investigations were normal. There was no history of consanguinity, diabetes, teratogen exposure, or irradiation. Her first three pregnancies were unremarkable; a fourth was terminated at 20 weeks for anencephaly. A routine ultrasound at 24 weeks showed tetraphocomelia, which had been missed on earlier scans. The mother elected to continue the pregnancy.

An emergency cesarean delivered a live female infant weighing 1.1 kg (<3rd percentile) with Apgar scores of 5 at 1 and 5 minutes. The neonate required intranasal oxygen but died 10 minutes after NICU admission. Examination revealed microbrachycephaly (OFC 24 cm), length 34 cm, oligodactyly with thumb aplasia, micrognathia, malar hypoplasia, down-slanting palpebral fissures, ocular hypertelorism, broad nose, dysplastic low-set ears, and absence of all four limbs (tetraphocomelia). Additional findings included minor omphalocele, imperforate anus, absence of external genitalia, and hemangiomas on the forehead and back. Heart sounds were faint; renal and cardiac structures could not be assessed. Autopsy and radiographs were declined, and cytogenetic testing was unavailable.
title: Roberts syndrome with tetraphocomelia: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B carrier status and a remote history of colonic interposition for childhood esophageal atresia presented with a 1-day history of dysphagia and abdominal pain. Two weeks earlier, he had been hospitalized for abdominal pain and nonbloody diarrhea; colonoscopy at that time showed linear, noncircumferential ulcerations of the right colon with moderate wall edema and loss of vascular pattern, normal transverse and descending colon, and a few sigmoid diverticuli. He received empiric antibiotics then mesalamine and was discharged.

On return, he had progressive dysphagia for solids and liquids and mild epigastric tenderness. Vital signs were normal, and laboratory studies, including electrolytes, blood counts, and liver chemistries, were within normal limits. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed only mild colonic wall thickening. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a normal native esophagus; at the esophagocolonic anastomosis 25 cm from the incisors there was circumferential ulceration and severe stricture, and the colonic conduit was diffusely erythematous with overlying exudate, mucus, and areas of ulceration; the cologastric anastomosis and stomach appeared normal. The esophagocolonic stricture was dilated to 10 mm. Biopsies from the colonic conduit showed architectural disarray with crypt distortion, Paneth cell metaplasia, acute and chronic inflammatory exudate, and granulation tissue. Infectious studies on conduit aspirate and biopsy were negative, and CT angiography showed no vascular stenosis or signs of ischemia in the conduit.
title: Ulcerative Colitis in Colonic Interposition for Esophageal Atresia

case_prompt: An 8-year-old boy was referred with a “boil” in the upper right posterior maxillary gingiva that had been enlarging over 6 months. Six months earlier, a similar lesion in the same location had been excised by a general dentist. Medical history was noncontributory. On examination, there was a sessile, reddish nodular lesion measuring 1.5 × 0.5 × 1.0 cm on the maxillary right gingiva. The lesion was fluctuant and bled easily on slight pressure but showed no blanching or purulent exudate. An intraoral periapical radiograph demonstrated a radiolucency surrounding the developing maxillary right premolar, with focal loss of the alveolar crest. Grossly carious mandibular right molars were noted to be traumatizing the area. Extraction of the lower molars to remove the irritant was considered.
journal: International Journal of Clinical Pediatric Dentistry
title: A Case of Painless Excision

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old man of Somali descent presented with intermittent upper abdominal pain. He had no history of liver disease or alcohol use; his medical history was notable for recurrent urticaria and angioedema of unknown etiology controlled with antihistamines. He had traveled to Djibouti 3 months earlier. On examination, he was obese and had mild tenderness in the epigastrium and right hypochondrium; no skin lesions were observed. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 15,710/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 6,237/µL (normal 28–273/µL; 450/µL one year earlier), C-reactive protein 6 mg/L, ALT 54 U/L, LDH 299 U/L, and normal AST, GGT, and alkaline phosphatase. Tests for viral, autoimmune, and hereditary liver disease were negative; α-fetoprotein was normal. IgE was elevated at 334 kU/L; tryptase was normal.  
Bone marrow aspiration showed 24% eosinophils but no pathological, cytogenetic, or molecular abnormalities. PET-CT demonstrated multifocal, metabolically active masses anterior to the right hypochondrium, multiple reactive mesenteric and hilar lymph nodes, and multiple metabolically active hypodense liver lesions; there was no bile duct dilation, portal vein occlusion, or splenomegaly. Upper endoscopy revealed mild Helicobacter pylori–associated gastritis without eosinophilic infiltration. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the liver showed multiple lesions in segments 5–7 that were T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense in the portovenous phase, exhibited delayed-phase enhancement, and diffusion restriction; branches of the portal vein traversed the largest lesion. Serologic testing was positive for schistosoma, Fasciola hepatica, and strongyloides.
title: Focal eosinophilic infiltration of the liver, benign or malignant?

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old man with hypertension presented with 6 months of sharp, constant lower back pain rated 7–8/10 that radiated to the posterior and lateral thighs. The pain was aggravated by increases in intra-abdominal pressure (cough, hip motion) and initially responded to over-the-counter analgesics but later became refractory. He noted a pulsatile periumbilical mass that appeared concurrently with his pain. He denied limb coldness, pallor, cyanosis, swelling, recent infection, or trauma. His medications included an oral antihypertensive; he smoked two pack-years; BMI was 27 kg/m2.  
On examination, vital signs were stable. He appeared pale. Palpation revealed a pulsatile periumbilical abdominal mass with a localized bruit; lower-limb pulses were normal. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL; infection markers were within normal limits.  
Duplex ultrasound demonstrated an infrarenal aortic aneurysm measuring 73 × 70 mm with intraluminal thrombus. A contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed an infrarenal aneurysm with a posterolateral retroperitoneal collection consistent with hematoma, infiltrating the lumbar vertebral bodies and psoas muscle. Imaging also showed smooth, well-corticated vertebral erosions with callous borders and cloudiness of the iliopsoas contours. The rest of the arterial tree was unremarkable.
final_diagnosis_raw: Chronic contained rupture of abdominal aortic aneurysm
title: Chronic contained ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with a rare presentation of lower limb neuropathic claudication: a report of two cases

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old man presented with frontal headache, fever, and somnolence for 48 hours. He had no prior medical history except for an incidentally noted lymphocytosis (44,000/μL) 10 months earlier that was not investigated further. He lived in an urban area, worked in a shoe store, and denied rural or animal exposures.

On examination he was hemodynamically stable with no focal neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies showed a lymphocyte count of 59,000/μL and a C-reactive protein level of 200 mg/L. A chest radiograph revealed a moderate left pleural effusion; thoracentesis yielded a citric, lymphocyte-predominant exudate (1,800 cells, 98% mononuclear) with unremarkable microbiology.

Contrast-enhanced head CT demonstrated a large space-occupying lesion in the sella turcica and sphenoidal region with heterogeneous density, no enhancement, expansion of the sphenoidal sinus, and erosion of adjacent bone. Brain MRI confirmed a mass centered in the sphenoidal sinus extending to the sellar and suprasellar regions, with bone thinning and features suggestive of fungal infection.

The patient underwent sphenoidectomy, during which abundant caseous material was removed, and empirical liposomal amphotericin B was started. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and mildly elevated protein; cultures were negative. Histologic examination of the sinus contents revealed necroinflammatory tissue with thin, branched hyphae at acute angles and no clear septation. PCR assays for Mucor, Aspergillus, and Fusarium on both the biopsy sample and CSF were negative.
title: Schizophyllum commune sphenoidal sinusitis as presentation of a non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old woman with hypertension and end-stage renal disease secondary to a congenitally malformed kidney was admitted for deceased-donor kidney transplantation. Preoperative evaluation, including hepatitis panel, HIV, CMV, and EBV serologies, was negative. Cardiac evaluation (ECG, echocardiogram) and both virtual and physical cross-matches were unremarkable. Baseline liver tests were normal: AST 14 U/L, ALT 9 U/L, bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, PT 10.6 s, INR 0.9. 

Induction immunosuppression included methylprednisolone and basiliximab. Anesthesia was induced with propofol, fentanyl, and rocuronium and maintained with sevoflurane (1.7% in oxygen) for a four-hour operation. Intraoperative course was uneventful: minimal blood loss, no vasopressors, heart rate 68–86 beats/min, systolic BP 110–160 mmHg. The transplanted kidney appeared well perfused at closure. 

Five hours postoperatively, the patient became increasingly somnolent with a Glasgow Coma Score of 12. Abdominal examination showed mild tenderness at the incision. Arterial blood gas revealed pH 6.8, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, lactate 10 mmol/L. Laboratory tests demonstrated acute liver injury with AST 2673 U/L, ALT 2680 U/L, ammonia 137 mcg/dL, PT 25.4 s, INR 2.2. She was transferred to the surgical intensive care unit and received bicarbonate and urgent hemodialysis.
title: Sevoflurane-Associated Acute Liver Injury in Renal Transplantation and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 38-year-old South African woman with HIV (CD4 count 132 cells/µL; viral load 136 copies/mL) on second-line ART presented with progressive, painless bilateral visual loss since March 2020 and mild intermittent headaches. She was treated for panuveitis and macular edema with topical/sub-Tenon’s steroids and bilateral bevacizumab injections, which temporarily resolved the edema. In April 2020, she began anti-TB therapy for radiographically diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis and noted worsening vision. On examination in February 2021, visual acuity was 6/60 in the right eye and 1/60 in the left, with no pinhole improvement.
