Anterior segment exam showed bilateral keratic precipitates, anterior chamber and vitreous cells, and lenticular opacities. Fundus exam revealed optic disc pallor with macular exudates, retinal striae, and extensive retinal vasculitis with non-perfused vessels. A chest radiograph was normal. Brain CT showed a small focus of nodular irregular thickening of the right retina adjacent to the optic nerve insertion, described as possibly inflammatory or non-benign. Lumbar puncture results were unremarkable, and liver ultrasound revealed no cystic lesions. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated a tractional retinal detachment in the right eye and tractional bands with a round intravitreal lesion showing a “double-walled” sign in the left eye.
title: A case and literature review of intraocular echinococcus causing bilateral visual loss in a HIV-infected patient

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of an itchy skin eruption that began on her left thigh and progressively extended. Her medical history was notable for mitral valve prolapse repaired in 2018; she had no history of cutaneous disease, asthma, or nasal polyps. Current medications included aspirin, bupropion, citalopram, and zopiclone. She worked in an office, had not traveled recently, and her cancer screenings were up to date.

On examination, she had large annular and arcuate erythematous and edematous plaques over the trunk and extremities, sparing the palms, soles, genitalia, and face. Plaques on the legs were more purpuric and annular. Vesicles were seen at the periphery of plaques on the arms. The eruption was fixed, and she reported fatigue, anorexia, and peripheral edema. She was afebrile; there was no lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

A 4-mm punch biopsy showed spongiotic dermatitis with intraepidermal vesicles and abundant eosinophils without flame figures or vasculitis. Perilesional direct immunofluorescence was negative. Laboratory studies revealed an absolute eosinophil count of 2.7×10^9/L, a slightly elevated C-reactive protein level of 12.8 mg/L, and a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Hemoglobin, platelets, renal and liver function tests, thyroid function, hemoglobin A1c, complement levels, and urinalysis were all normal. Indirect immunofluorescence for cutaneous basement membrane antibodies was negative.

She was treated with oral prednisone (50 mg daily for 5 days, then tapered by 5 mg every 5 days) and topical betamethasone. One week after starting prednisone, her eosinophil count rose to 5.3×10^9/L without lymphocytosis. A hematologic work-up was performed: serum immunoglobulins, vitamin B12, and tryptase were normal; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative; serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation showed no monoclonal spike; molecular genetic studies were all negative, including FIP1L1-PDGFRA and BCR-ABL fusion genes, JAK2 V617F and KIT D816V mutations, PDGFRB, and T-cell receptor gene rearrangements; flow cytometry revealed no monoclonal lymphocytic population; interleukin-5 level was 2.4 pg/mL; and abdominal ultrasound showed no hepatosplenomegaly.
title: Vesiculobullous eosinophilic annular erythema: A case report

case_prompt: A 58-year-old woman with a history of FIGO stage IIIC high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma had undergone primary debulking surgery and six cycles of paclitaxel-carboplatin, with complete radiographic response and normal CA 125. One year later, she presented with new axillary lymphadenopathy. On examination, there was a hard, relatively fixed 1.0 × 1.5 cm left axillary lymph node and a 1.0 × 1.0 cm right axillary lymph node. Breast and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Breast MRI showed a 10 mm left breast lesion (BIRADS 4a). CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no other abnormalities aside from the axillary nodes. Serum CA 125 was mildly elevated at 41.2 U/L. Core-needle biopsies were obtained from the left breast lesion and both axillary nodes. Histology showed a fibroadenoma in the breast lesion and metastatic carcinoma in the axillary node.
title: Recurrent ovarian cancer presenting with isolated axillary lymph node metastasis: A rare case report

case_prompt: A 36-year-old G3P3 woman with three prior cesarean deliveries was referred at 9 weeks of amenorrhea with one day of mild vaginal bleeding. She denied abdominal pain. Her vital signs were normal, and the abdomen was non-tender. Serum β-hCG was 109,754 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a viable gestational sac with a crown–rump length of 3.3 cm (10 weeks + 1 day) low in the uterine isthmus, bulging at the site of the previous lower‐segment cesarean section scar. The lower anterior uterine wall over the scar was markedly thinned (<1 mm) and stretched (1.5 cm). The placenta was low-lying, covering the internal cervical os, crossing midline, and extending anteriorly to the scar. Both ovaries appeared normal. MRI demonstrated a 6.4 × 4.3 cm gestational sac bulging at the cesarean‐section scar with only a thin layer of myometrium between the sac and the bladder. The placenta completely covered the cervical os; there was no pelvic hematoma or free fluid, and the cervix, vagina, ovaries, and bladder were unremarkable.
title: Cesarean section scar pregnancy: Challenges in choosing treatment approach

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old man was referred for evaluation of chronic hypercalcemia. Eight years earlier, he had an episode of presyncope, during which an electrocardiogram showed a shortened QTc interval; serum calcium was 11.5 mg/dL (RR, 8.5–10.5 mg/dL). One month before presentation, laboratory studies again showed a serum calcium of 11.5 mg/dL and an intact PTH level of 106 ng/L (RR, 10–65 ng/L). He denied bone pain, kidney stones, abdominal pain, or neuropsychiatric symptoms, and he had no history of lithium or hydrochlorothiazide use. Family history was notable for PTH-dependent hypercalcemia in his mother and half-brother, and his half-brother remained hypercalcemic after removal of three parathyroid glands. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Repeat labs showed serum calcium 11.6 mg/dL, ionized calcium 1.63 mmol/L (RR, 1.16–1.31 mmol/L), and PTH 144.2 ng/L. Twenty-four-hour urine calcium excretion was 91.7 mg/day (RR, 100–300 mg/day), and the fractional excretion of calcium was 0.004.
title: Two Cases of Symptomatic Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia: Treatment Response to Calcimimetic Therapy

case_prompt: A 7-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of an asymptomatic, diffuse, bony-hard swelling of the left mandible and intermittent nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps. On extraoral examination, there was a painless, hard swelling from the left mandibular body to the pre-auricular area; intraorally, there was buccolingual expansion from tooth 36 to the ascending ramus with normal overlying mucosa. Baseline blood testing showed hyponatremic, hypochloremic metabolic acidosis (Na+ 134 mmol/L; Cl− 92 mmol/L; HCO₃− 14 mmol/L; anion gap 33 mmol/L), treated with fluids and antiemetics. A panoramic radiograph revealed a poorly defined, multilocular radiolucency in the left mandibular body extending to the condylar and coronoid processes, with bowing of the inferior border and inferior displacement of an unerupted tooth. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 42×34×45 mm expansile, lytic, multilocular lesion of the left mandibular body and ramus with areas of cortical perforation. A provisional radiographic diagnosis included central giant cell granuloma, unicystic ameloblastoma, or aneurysmal bone cyst. An incisional biopsy showed mononuclear spindle to ovoid cells with numerous multinucleated osteoclastic giant cells in a loose, fibrovascular stroma, consistent with a giant cell lesion.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Lytic brown tumour of the mandible as the initial presentation of hyperparathyroidism in a 7-year old girl: A case report

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old African-American man presented with a 1‐month history of bilateral eye pain, redness, and blurry vision. He had been treated for presumed conjunctivitis without improvement and now complained of throbbing pain in both eyes. He also had a pustular rash over his face, neck, and upper chest. 

On examination, visual acuity was 20/100 uncorrected (pinhole 20/70) in the right eye and 20/150 uncorrected (pinhole 20/60) in the left eye. Slit‐lamp examination revealed multiple perilimbal stromal infiltrates with vascularization and areas of thinning superiorly and inferiorly in both eyes. In the right eye, there was an inferotemporal perilimbal ulcer. In the left eye, there was an inferotemporal perilimbal corneal perforation measuring about 4.5 × 3 mm plugged with prolapsed iris and superotemporal peripheral thinning. There was no scleral involvement, but there was significant conjunctival injection and bilateral keratitic precipitates. A dilated fundus examination was unremarkable.

Review of systems was notable only for the skin rash; he denied fevers, weight loss, arthralgias, and any history of severe acne, cold sores, or travel. He admitted to unprotected sex with multiple female partners but denied genital lesions or discharge. 

Corneal scrapings were negative for herpes simplex virus by PCR, and culture of the right cornea grew Staphylococcus aureus. Vitamin A level was normal, and a urine toxicology screen was negative.
title: Perforating Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis in Syphilis

case_prompt:
A 10-year-old boy, obese (90th percentile) and tall (75th percentile), presented with a 6-month history of recurrent generalized weakness and episodes of loss of consciousness, followed by multiple generalized tonic–clonic seizures over the past month. He had no significant past medical or family history, and his physical examination was unremarkable.

During an episode of hypoglycemia, laboratory studies revealed:
• Blood glucose: 35 mg/dL  
• Serum insulin: 35.8 mIU/L (normal < 2 mIU/L)  
• C-peptide: 8.9 ng/mL (normal 0.15–2.72 ng/mL)  
• Urine ketones: negative  
• Serum cortisol: 18.4 µg/dL (normal 7–28 µg/dL)  
• ACTH: 28.5 pg/mL (normal 10–60 pg/mL)  
• Growth hormone: 12 ng/mL (normal 0–20 ng/mL)  
• Serum prolactin: within normal limits  

Given the inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia alongside normal counterregulatory hormones, diazoxide therapy was initiated to prevent further hypoglycemic events.
title: Sporadic Insulinoma as a Rare Cause of Recurrent Hypoglycemia in Children

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman with a history of gastritis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and known hyperthyroidism (noncompliant with antithyroid therapy) presented with 2 weeks of nausea, vomiting, epigastric burning, and poor appetite. In the days before presentation, she developed persistent malaise and shortness of breath. She smokes and reported recent work stress and high coffee intake.  
On arrival: temperature 37.1 °C; respiratory rate 29 breaths/min; pulse 120 beats/min; blood pressure 123/71 mmHg; oxygen via nasal cannula at 3 L/min.  
Laboratory studies: serum potassium 1.2 mEq/L, sodium 136 mEq/L; other values notable for albumin 2.2 g/dL and antithyroid peroxidase antibody pending.  
Arterial blood gas on O₂ showed pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 22 mmHg, PaO₂ 116 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 9.6 mmol/L.  
Electrocardiogram: sinus tachycardia, T-wave flattening/inversion, ST depression, prominent U-waves, T–U fusion, prolonged QU.  
Chest radiograph: right lower lung infiltration.  
Thyroid function tests: TSH 0.021 μIU/mL; free T₄ 2.01 ng/dL.  
She was transferred to the ICU, where she developed progressive dyspnea, sudden drowsiness, and use of accessory muscles. Respiratory rate 33 breaths/min. Repeat arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.11, PaCO₂ 72 mmHg, PaO₂ 206 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22.9 mmol/L.
title: Noninvasive ventilator prevents intubation in thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis-associated respiratory failure: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old man presented with blurred vision and left eye pain. Three months earlier he acquired a kitten. Two months earlier he had been deer hunting, sustained multiple tick bites, and developed a transient rash. He denied fever, myalgias, headache, or nausea. Concurrently, he began treatment with an antibiotic for chlamydia. Two weeks before presentation he noted a “dark spot” in the left visual field and pain with eye movement, prompting urgent-care evaluation.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left eye. Confrontation visual fields showed a superior-temporal defect in the left eye. External and slit-lamp examination was unremarkable on the right; the left eye had 2+ vitreous cells. Funduscopic examination revealed normal findings in the right eye and 2+ optic disc edema with telangiectatic vessels and macular edema in the left eye.

Laboratory evaluation demonstrated normal results for Bartonella (IgM and IgG), syphilis T.ab, T-spot, a tick-borne disease PCR panel, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever IgM. Positive findings included Rocky Mountain spotted fever IgG at 1:64 (reference, 0–1:64), Toxoplasma IgM >160 IU/mL (≤7.9 AU/mL), and Toxoplasma IgG 57.9 IU/mL (≤7.1 IU/mL).
title: Toxoplasma Neuroretinitis

case_prompt: A 5-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of a painful mass on his left upper eyelid. He had been treated with a course of oral amoxicillin by a general practitioner without improvement. There were no similar lesions noted on his body or among family members. His past medical, surgical, nutritional, social, and family histories were unremarkable, and his growth and development were within normal limits. On ocular examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes; the conjunctiva was quiet, the cornea was clear, the anterior chamber was deep and quiet, the lens was clear, and the red reflex and fundus were normal. Examination of the left upper eyelid revealed a single, tender, mobile mass with a focal abscess and a 1-cm-diameter opening with granulation tissue at the margin; there was no overlying skin. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. The patient was admitted, and the decision was made to perform surgical excision and curettage of the mass with closure using absorbable suture.
title: Eyelid molluscum contagiosum presenting as a giant solitary ulcerating mass

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old Hispanic woman presented with a 3- to 4-week history of fevers, weight loss, and a pruritic rash. On examination, there were well-demarcated pink-tan to slightly violaceous edematous nodules without scale scattered on the face, trunk, and extremities. She also had bulky submandibular lymphadenopathy. 

Her medical history was unremarkable except for a urinary tract infection treated 3 weeks earlier. Laboratory studies showed a low-titer antinuclear antibody of 1:80 in a speckled pattern; other autoimmune antibodies were negative, and complement levels were normal. Infectious testing revealed positive Epstein–Barr virus viral capsid antigen IgG and two positive HIV screening tests with negative confirmatory testing, attributed to cross-reactivity with EBV.

A 4-mm punch biopsy of the skin showed focal vacuolar interface dermatitis with a papillary to mid-dermal perivascular and interstitial lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with karyorrhexis. The histiocytes were CD68+ and myeloperoxidase+. Most lymphocytes were CD3+ T cells; rare CD20+ B cells were present. Gomori methenamine-silver and acid-fast bacilli stains were negative.

An excisional lymph node biopsy revealed necrotizing lymphadenitis with an appearance similar to that of the skin biopsy. Features typical of acute EBV lymphadenitis—namely follicular and paracortical hyperplasia with Reed–Sternberg–like cells—were absent. Lymph node and bone marrow flow cytometry showed no monotypic B-cell population or aberrant or expanded T-cell population.
title: Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease diagnosed by correlating skin and lymph node biopsies

case_prompt: A 20-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of progressively increasing right knee pain, described as a constant, dull ache aggravated by walking and climbing stairs, and a 2-month history of knee swelling. He denied trauma, fever, weight loss, or appetite change. On examination, there was a 2 × 2 cm swelling over the anterior knee, more prominent in full flexion; the joint line was non-tender, there was no warmth, range of motion was full, and there was no instability or limb-length discrepancy. Laboratory studies, including blood counts, coagulation profile, and inflammatory markers, were normal. Knee radiographs were unremarkable. Ultrasonography showed a thick-walled hypoechogenic lesion (14.4 × 5 mm) inferomedial to the patella with tortuous vascular channels, and a second small lesion in the suprapatellar recess. MRI demonstrated two intra-articular lesions (one in Hoffa’s fat pad, one in the suprapatellar pouch adherent to the lateral femoral condyle) that were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and fat-suppressed sequences, and showed contrast enhancement; multiple dilated vascular channels were noted adjacent to the lesions, and there was no invasion of muscle or bone. Fine-needle aspiration yielded blood cells and synovial cells without granuloma or malignancy.
title: Two Discrete Intra-articular Synovial Hemangiomas of a Knee Joint Presenting as Chronic Knee Pain

case_prompt: A 51-year-old woman, gravida 0, with a recent diagnosis of mucinous breast carcinoma, was referred for evaluation of a right pelvic mass. She had undergone a myomectomy 10 years earlier and was receiving treatment for hypertension. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an 11.2 × 10.3 cm multiseptated cystic adnexal mass. During breast‐cancer staging, CT revealed a 12 cm abdominopelvic cystic tumor with a thick septum, located behind the bladder and anterior to the uterus. On pelvic MRI, the mass was slightly hypointense on T1 with gadolinium enhancement and markedly hyperintense on T2 with curvilinear dark signal, raising suspicion for borderline ovarian cancer. The patient was postmenopausal, asymptomatic, and on pelvic examination a firm, mobile, non-tender mass was palpated. Serum CA-125 and HE4 values corresponded to a low ROMA score for epithelial ovarian cancer. She underwent breast-conserving surgery with concurrent total laparoscopic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Intraoperatively, the multiseptated cystic tumor was found to be attached by a stalk to the anterior uterine body rather than the ovary. The mass was aspirated, resected, and sent for frozen biopsy, which reported a benign lesion.
title: Cystic Angiomyofibroblastoma of the Uterus Mimicking Ovarian Cancer

case_prompt: A 62-year-old Caucasian man with well-controlled asthma (on fluticasone–salmeterol) presented with acute chest pain and right-sided weakness. Initial studies showed a troponin-I of 0.044 ng/mL and pro-BNP of 5555 pg/mL. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral hyperinflation, congestion at the lung bases, and right lower lobe granuloma. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 2-cm bilobed thrombus in the left atrial appendage and an ejection fraction of 58%. ECG showed pathological Q waves, ST-segment depression, and inverted T waves, suggesting anterior myocardial infarction. Stroke evaluation with head CT was negative; brain MRI identified small acute nonhemorrhagic infarcts in the posterior left parietal lobe. He received IV heparin and chewable aspirin and was admitted with acute ischemic stroke and NSTEMI. Despite analgesics, nitrates, and nitroprusside, he had persistent chest pain. On hospital day 6 he developed new bilateral weakness, aphasia, decreased consciousness, skin petechiae on his lower extremities, diffuse abdominal pain, pleural and pericardial effusions on imaging, and a drop in EF to 18%. CT abdomen showed a gastric perforation requiring surgery. In the ICU he required dialysis and vasopressor support and was transferred to a tertiary center. There, laboratory evaluation revealed an absolute eosinophil count of 13 046 cells/µL, an ESR of 23 mm/h, and CRP of 16 mg/L. Review of records showed a persistent eosinophilia (absolute count 700–940 cells/µL; 11% differential) over the preceding five months. Extensive rheumatologic, clonal (including Jak2, BCR/ABL, and PDGFRα), and infectious studies (including serologies, cultures, and antigen tests) were negative.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: A Progressive Case of Eosinophilic Myocarditis Due to Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis in a Caucasian Male

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old woman was referred with a 2-month history of daily fevers and night sweats. She reported 1.5 years of intermittent interphalangeal joint pain after COVID-19 vaccination, treated with oral corticosteroids and NSAIDs, without rash or systemic symptoms at that time. She denied malar rash, photosensitivity, Raynaud phenomenon, pharyngitis until 2 weeks before referral, and had lost 10 kg over 6 months. Two weeks prior to admission, she developed fevers unresponsive to NSAIDs, salmon-colored macular rashes on the trunk, sore throat, and pain in the small joints of her hands and knees; she had no dyspnea or chest pain.  
On examination, temperature was 37.7°C. There was a nonpruritic, salmon-colored macular rash on the trunk, mild pharyngitis, and no synovitis. Cardiovascular and pulmonary exams were unremarkable.  
Initial evaluations elsewhere showed: blood and urine cultures negative; serologic tests for hepatitis B and C, HIV, anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG/IgM, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were all within normal limits. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-CCP, HLA-B27) were negative.  
Laboratory studies on admission: hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, WBC 17 × 10^3/mm^3, platelets 119 × 10^3/mm^3; LDH 1102 IU/L, ferritin 9954 ng/mL, CRP 80 mg/dL, AST 101 IU/L, ALT 76 IU/L, ALP 676 U/L.  
She was referred for further evaluation of persistent fever, rash, and cytopenias.
title: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis accompanying Still's disease: A case report

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old right-handed Caucasian woman with a history of asthma presented with recurrent episodes of left hand redness, swelling, warmth, pain, and tenderness over the dorsum, initially after puncture injury 4 days earlier. She had no respiratory symptoms. Examination consistently showed erythema and mild edema over the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints extending proximally up the forearm, full range of motion, and intact neurovascular status.  

Initial plain radiographs of the left hand were normal. Laboratory tests showed slight basophilia (3%; normal 0–1%), normal eosinophils, and two sets of blood cultures with no growth. She received cephalexin and symptomatic analgesics.  

Over the ensuing months, she returned multiple times after minor traumas (e.g., dog’s paw strike) with worsened erythema, pain, occasional fever (home measurement up to 103°F), and numbness at the radial index finger. Imaging repeatedly suggested cellulitis with lymphangitis but no abscess or osteomyelitis. Each time, cultures remained negative, and she was treated with various antibiotics (cephalexin, clindamycin, TMP-SMX) and NSAIDs, with only transient improvement.  

Eight months later, she presented with constant resting left hand pain (8–10/10), decreased range of motion, and anxiety and depression due to chronic symptoms. Vital signs were stable; radiographs again showed soft-tissue swelling without bony changes. Lab studies revealed leukocytosis (14.5×10^3/µL), neutrophils 92.8%, elevated CRP 16.4 mg/dL (0–1), and ESR 54 mm/hr (0–20).  

Given the severity of swelling, erythema, intense pain, and concern for a potentially necrotizing infection, she was scheduled for surgical incision, irrigation, and debridement with a preoperative diagnosis of left hand and forearm possible acute necrotizing fasciitis.
title: Orthopedic Considerations with Eosinophilic Fasciitis: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old woman with a history of long QT syndrome—diagnosed after a syncopal event—underwent submammary implantation of a dual-chamber ICD with a right atrial appendage lead and an RV apical dual-coil shock lead. The implant was uncomplicated, and in-hospital DFT at 16 J was successful twice. 

Four years later, a device alert indicated elevated impedance of the SVC coil. Interrogation showed high impedance on the RV-to-SVC and SVC-to-can vectors; tapping over the generator produced noise in those vectors. The SVC coil was disabled; all other parameters and fluoroscopy were satisfactory.  

Repeat DFT was performed with a 20 J shock; VF was sensed and terminated appropriately. Immediately after the shock, intermittent noise appeared on the device electrograms, on the CardioLab external rhythm monitor, and on the anesthetic ECG. The patient was moved to a different lab and reconnected to new monitors, yet the noise persisted. All lead measurements remained unchanged before and after DFT. Tachycardia therapies were disabled, and she was admitted for continuous monitoring, during which no further noise occurred and lead parameters stayed stable.
title: Defibrillation threshold testing: What is all that noise?

case_prompt: A 35-year-old man presented with sudden, severe pain in his right calf after a minor leg-extension movement one day earlier. He reported a brief, sharp pain at the time of injury that intensified overnight. On examination, he was alert but mildly distressed. There was visible swelling and bruising over the medial aspect of the proximal right calf, and he walked with an antalgic gait. Palpation revealed tenderness and swelling in the mid-calf. The Thompson test was negative. Active and passive dorsiflexion of the ankle were both restricted and reproduced pain. Pain was especially prominent with knee extension combined with ankle dorsiflexion. Neurovascular examination was normal. A preliminary diagnosis of calf muscle injury was made, and ultrasonography of the right posterior proximal calf region was advised as the initial imaging study.
title: Trivial incident leading to tennis leg managed conservatively: A case report

case_prompt: A 40-year-old woman with newly diagnosed stage IV gallbladder adenocarcinoma metastatic to the liver received four cycles of intravenous gemcitabine and cisplatin. Ten days after the fourth cycle, she presented with convulsions and altered mental status. On admission, she was normotensive; serum electrolytes were normal, and renal function tests were deranged. On hospital day 2, she developed aphasia and bilateral lower limb weakness. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense signal involving the gyri of both parieto-occipital lobes and the subcortical white matter of the right parietal lobe, with abnormal contrast enhancement and a glutamine peak on spectroscopy.
journal: Journal of Research in Pharmacy Practice
title: Gemcitabine and Cisplatin induced posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome: A case report with review of literature

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, Bell’s palsy, and nephrolithiasis presented with a 1-month history of chest pain, dyspnea, and syncope that acutely worsened. He denied fever, diarrhea, cough, or exertional symptoms. On arrival, blood pressure was 209/132 mm Hg, heart rate 93 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.9 g/dL, hematocrit 16.7%, platelets 157×10^3/mcL, PTT 37.5 seconds, BUN 252 mg/dL, creatinine 32.5 mg/dL, BNP 2816 ng/L, and troponin 225 ng/L. Arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.29, PCO2 20.2 mm Hg, PO2 98.1 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 9.6 mmol/L. Urinalysis demonstrated protein >500 mg/dL and 6–10 RBCs per high-power field. Physical examination was notable for signs of fluid overload. In the ED, he received clonidine, intravenous furosemide, potassium chloride, and one unit of packed red blood cells. 

Upon ICU admission his blood pressure remained elevated at 219/130 mm Hg, creatinine was 31.96 mg/dL, and BUN was 247 mg/dL. He was managed with a nicardipine infusion followed by oral nifedipine, carvedilol, and losartan for blood pressure control. Repeat studies revealed microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL, hematocrit 20.3%, reticulocyte count 11.5%, LDH 619 U/L, and peripheral smear showing microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes, anisopoikilocytosis, and schistocytes. Imaging showed bilateral pulmonary edema and a pericardial effusion. 

Nephrology evaluation included a renal ultrasound without evidence of artery stenosis and serologic testing (C3, C4, ANCA, ADAMTS13 activity), which returned with normal complement levels, negative ANCA, and ADAMTS13 activity of 52%. He underwent daily hemodialysis, four sessions of plasmapheresis, and empirical eculizumab. A CT-guided renal biopsy demonstrated active thrombotic microangiopathy with severe fibro-intimal thickening, mucoid intimal edema in large vessels, and onion–skin intimal changes in smaller arterioles, but was inconclusive regarding the underlying etiology. Genetic testing was initiated.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Complement-Mediated Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome Due to MCP/CD46 Mutation: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 30-year-old woman with homozygous sickle cell disease was transferred to the ICU for respiratory failure and new neurologic deterioration during an acute vaso-occlusive pain crisis. She had fever and lower-extremity pain similar to prior episodes. On admission she was lethargic; temperature 38 °C and heart rate 140 bpm. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, haptoglobin 17 mg/dL, white-cell count 23.1 × 10^3/µL (neutrophils 18.7 × 10^3/µL), CRP 215 mg/L, AST 121 U/L, ALT 64 U/L, ALP 450 U/L, LDH 3861 U/L, total bilirubin 3.9 mg/dL; renal function was normal. Arterial PO2 was 80%. A chest CT angiogram excluded pulmonary embolism and showed bilateral pulmonary consolidations. Unenhanced brain CT and CT angiography were unremarkable. SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR and serology were negative. Brain MRI showed a few punctate foci of restricted diffusion with corresponding T2 FLAIR hyperintensities and numerous punctate low-signal foci on susceptibility-weighted images in both supra- and infratentorial regions.
title: Fat emboli and critical illness-associated cerebral microbleeds (CICMs) in a patient with sickle cell disease: Do these 2 entities coexist?

case_prompt: An 11-month-old otherwise healthy boy had a 3-month history of relapsing fevers (37.7°–38.6°C) every 5–6 days, associated with irritability and a tender skin eruption. There was no lethargy, arthralgia, myalgia, edema, conjunctival injection, or recent medication use, and developmental milestones were normal. On examination, multiple fixed, somewhat indurated erythematous-to-violaceous nodules and plaques, some with dusky centers and pink patches, were scattered on the face and extremities; there was no vesiculation, bullae, pustules, lymphadenopathy, or mucosal involvement. A lesional skin biopsy showed mild papillary dermal edema and an interstitial infiltrate of CD68-positive mononuclear cells in the upper dermis. The infiltrating cells were negative for S100 and CD1a, and myeloperoxidase staining was positive in these cells.
title: Infantile histiocytoid Sweet syndrome without an underlying systemic association

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old man with a history of renal transplantation on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone presented with 5 days of intermittent fevers, generalized malaise, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. His past infections included Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia and multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections. On admission, he was diagnosed with enteroaggressive Escherichia coli colitis, carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia, and Enterococcus faecalis urinary tract infection. Because of new-onset altered mental status, a lumbar puncture was performed, and cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction testing was positive for cryptococcal antigen. 

During hospitalization, he noted an ulcer on his left eyelid, which he attributed to a pimple he had repeatedly picked over the preceding 2 months. Dermatologic examination revealed a 3-cm tender, deep, ovoid ulcer on the lateral aspect of the left upper eyelid with heaped-up borders, overlying purulence, and honey-colored crust. The differential diagnosis included localized herpes simplex virus infection, nonmelanoma skin cancer, cutaneous cryptococcosis, blastomycosis, and coccidioidomycosis. Wound cultures and polymerase chain reaction testing for herpesviruses were negative.
title: Persistent eyelid ulceration in an immunocompromised host: A cutaneous sign with the potential for early diagnosis and intervention in disseminated cryptococcosis

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old heavy ex-smoker with hyperlipidemia and hypertension presented with chest pain, sweating, nausea, and progressive dyspnea. Initial vital signs were temperature 37.5°C, blood pressure 96/70 mm Hg, pulse 95 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral crackles, more pronounced on the right. ECG showed ST-segment elevations in the precordial leads. Chest radiography demonstrated peri-hilar “bat-wing” consolidations consistent with pulmonary edema. 

Urgent coronary angiography revealed total occlusion of the left main artery; stenting of the LAD and balloon angioplasty of the ramus intermedius were performed. During and after the procedure, the patient received a total of over 1000 mg of IV amiodarone in 24 hours, IV furosemide, heparin, epinephrine infusion, and dobutamine. On hospital day 2, dyspnea improved and amiodarone (200 mg BID) and furosemide (40 mg BID) were switched to oral. Echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 20%, pulmonary artery pressure of 45 mm Hg, severe left ventricular hypertrophy, grade III diastolic dysfunction, anteroseptal and apical akinesia, and no significant valvular abnormalities.

On day 7, he developed worsening dyspnea, fever, and a nonproductive cough. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 14.8 K/μl, CRP 42.7 mg/L, negative procalcitonin, negative blood and sputum cultures, two negative COVID-19 PCR tests, negative ANA, and normal complement levels. Follow-up chest radiography showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates and a right pleural effusion. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral diffuse consolidations and ground-glass opacities. He was treated with high-dose diuretics and broad-spectrum antibiotics without improvement. Echocardiography showed unchanged left ventricular dysfunction but increased pulmonary artery pressure to 60 mm Hg. Pulmonary embolism was ruled out.
title: Early amiodarone pneumonitis: A case report

case_prompt: A 75-year-old man with an 80–pack-year smoking history presented with 6 months of progressive chest pain radiating to the back. On examination, he had sharp tenderness along the costovertebral angles; lung auscultation and neurologic examination were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function, and C-reactive protein, were normal. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity without air bronchograms above the carina, vertically oriented along the right lateral aspect of the thoracic vertebrae, with an obtuse mediastinal border and upper extent above the clavicle, suggestive of a posterior upper mediastinal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a posterior mediastinal tumor with heterogeneous enhancement and extension into the spinal canal. MRI demonstrated a well-defined oblong mass (30×20×35 mm) in the right costovertebral gutter from T1 to T3. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with interspersed areas of high signal on both sequences that suppressed on fat-saturation images, confirming a fatty component. Post-contrast fat-suppressed images showed early, intense, heterogeneous enhancement, indicating a highly vascular tumor. The mass extended through the right and left T1–T2 intervertebral foramina, widening both foramina and scalloping the posterior vertebral body and arches without cortical destruction; it filled the anterior epidural space, slightly compressing but not invading the spinal cord. These MRI features were interpreted as consistent with a nonaggressive, mixed mesenchymal, fatty, highly vascular tumor, and an angiomyolipoma was suspected.
title: Angiofibrolipoma of Posterior Mediastinum with Transforaminal Extension

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old Japanese man presented with a 2-month history of progressive fatigue and a 5-kg weight loss. His past medical history included cerebral infarction, aortic stenosis, carotid stenosis, overactive bladder, and hyperlipidemia, all well controlled on lansoprazole, carvedilol, mirabegron, and cilostazol. He smoked 14 cigarettes daily until age 45 and drank alcohol daily.  

On examination he appeared pale without rash or lymphadenopathy. Temperature was 37.5 °C, blood pressure 92/59 mmHg, heart rate 78 bpm. Cardiopulmonary exam was normal, with no rales or abnormal heart sounds; no clubbing or edema.  

Laboratory studies showed:  
- Hematology: leukocytes 1 530/µL, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, platelets 75 000/µL  
- Chemistry: albumin 2.8 g/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, AST 65 IU/L, ALT 57 IU/L, ALP 1673 IU/L, GGT 106 IU/L, LDH 517 IU/L, CRP 1.97 mg/dL  
- Sarcoid markers: ACE 34.1 U/L (8.3–21.4), lysozyme 29.8 µg/mL (5–10.2), soluble IL-2 receptor 7835 U/mL (145–519)  
- Serologies: ANA negative, ANCA negative, RF negative, interferon-γ release assay negative, viral hepatitis serologies negative, beta-glucan 0.8 pg/mL  

Chest radiograph and CT showed no lung or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Abdominal CT demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly and bilateral renal enlargement.  

A bone marrow biopsy revealed numerous non-caseating epithelioid granulomas within hematopoietic tissue.
title: A case of bone marrow involvement in sarcoidosis with crescentic glomerular lesions

case_prompt:
A term male neonate (birth weight 2.5 kg) was discharged home on day 2 of life after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. On day 3, he was treated with intensive phototherapy for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 20.6 mg/dL). By day 5, his bilirubin had decreased to 9.6 mg/dL and he was discharged. On day 9 of life, he presented with a 6-hour history of poor feeding, lethargy, and reduced activity, along with yellow discoloration of the hands and feet for 2 days. 

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable: heart rate 120 beats/min, warm extremities, capillary refill <3 s, and temperature 36.6 °C. Random blood glucose was 98 mg/dL. Icterus was noted up to knees and elbows without any signs of bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction. Neurologic examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9 (eye opening to pain, withdraws to pain, cries to pain), equal reactive pupils, a level anterior fontanelle, normal cry, generalized hypotonia, hypoactive deep tendon reflexes, and poor respiratory effort. There were no seizures, neck retractions, or cranial-nerve deficits.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.8 g/dL, white-cell count 7300 cells/mm³ (63% neutrophils), platelets 290 000/mm³, C-reactive protein 0.5 mg/L, total bilirubin 12 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.8 mEq/L, total protein 5.5 g/dL, albumin 3.5 g/dL, AST 50 U/L, ALT 36 U/L, and a normal random blood sugar. 

The patient was admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit for further evaluation.
title: Acute flaccid paralysis in a neonate: tick bite a differential?

case_prompt:
An 84-year-old Ethiopian man presented with an 8-month history of progressive right-sided weakness and headache. The weakness began in the right lower extremity and gradually extended to the right upper extremity; it was initially mild but became severe enough that he could not walk even with assistance. He reported a diffuse headache of similar duration. He denied loss of consciousness, seizures, vomiting, confusion, swallowing difficulty, lethargy, personality change, memory loss, language deficit, visual symptoms, or trauma. He had no history of bleeding diatheses, coagulopathy, systemic illness, alcohol use, or surgery.  
On examination, vital signs were normal. Chest examination was unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Score of 15, midsize reactive pupils, intact sensation, and normal deep tendon reflexes. Motor testing showed hypertonia with strength 4/5 in the right upper extremity and 3/5 in the right lower extremity; the left limbs had normal tone and strength of 5/5.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and organ function tests, were within normal limits. Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced brain CT demonstrated a right hemispheric extra-axial collection crossing suture lines with a maximum thickness of 2.3 cm, causing effacement of the right lateral ventricle and a 3 mm midline shift. The collection was heterogeneously hyperdense with diffuse thick calcification and showed no postcontrast enhancement. The remaining sulci and ventricles were prominent. No abnormal parenchymal, meningeal, or vascular enhancement was observed.
title: Symptomatic calcified chronic subdural hematoma in an elderly patient: a case report

case_prompt: A 13-year-old Caucasian girl presented with a 2-week history of purulent discharge distal to the upper right second molar, associated with a foul taste and odor. She denied swelling and had no intraoral or extraoral enlargement. Examination revealed a full maxillary dentition except for teeth #18 and #28; all present teeth were firm, vital, and noncarious. A panoramic radiograph showed an ectopic right maxillary third molar located within the right maxillary sinus and surrounded by a well-defined hyperdense lesion that obliterated the sinus cavity. Cone beam computed tomography demonstrated the unerupted third molar with incompletely formed roots in the posterosuperior aspect of the right maxillary sinus, closely approximating the orbital floor and pterygoid plates. The lesion measured 23×36×35 mm, caused mediolateral expansion of the alveolar ridge, and had eroded the sinus floor and buccal cortical plate distal to tooth #17, resulting in an oroantral communication. Differential diagnosis included dentigerous cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, and Gorlin cyst. The patient was scheduled for surgical removal of the ectopic molar and enucleation of the lesion via an intraoral Caldwell–Luc approach under general anesthesia.
title: Case Report: Ectopic third molar in the maxillary sinus with infected dentigerous cyst assessed by cone beam CT

case_prompt: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes was referred for evaluation of non-resolving pneumonia. Over three weeks he had received amoxicillin–clavulanate plus azithromycin followed by piperacillin–tazobactam without improvement. High-resolution CT of the thorax showed bilateral lower-lobe consolidation and a small pleural collection. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed bilateral pleural effusions, minimal lower-lobe infiltrates, and a paraoesophageal fluid collection with thickened oesophageal wall. On further questioning, he admitted to progressive dysphagia to solids for two months. PET-CT showed diffuse fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the oesophageal wall and at the gastro-oesophageal junction. A working diagnosis of oesophageal carcinoma with possible tracheo-oesophageal fistula was made. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrated multiple mucosal sinus tracts 3–7 mm in diameter with overlying plaques but no mass lesion or evidence of fistula.
title: Oesophageal intramural pseudodiverticulosis presenting as non‐resolving pneumonia: A sinister cause diagnosed by EUS‐B‐FNA

case_prompt: A 6-year-old Tunisian boy was brought with a chief complaint of dental caries on the primary maxillary left central incisor (#61) and lateral incisor (#62). His medical and family histories were unremarkable, with no history of trauma. He reported occasional hypersensitivity to thermal stimuli and sweets in the affected anterior teeth. Extraoral examination was noncontributory. Intraorally, he had a complete primary dentition; tooth #61 appeared enlarged with slightly deep buccal and lingual grooves and decay, and tooth #62 had extensive caries on its distal, lingual, and incisal surfaces. Functional assessment showed nasal breathing, infantile swallowing, and functional chewing. Periapical and maxillary occlusal radiographs demonstrated a single large central root canal in tooth #61 and carious lesions approaching the pulp chambers of both teeth. A panoramic radiograph revealed normally erupting permanent incisors except that the permanent upper left lateral incisor (#22) was rotated and slightly developmentally delayed compared with its contralateral counterpart.
title: Fusion or Gemination? Diagnosis and Management in Primary Teeth: A Report of Two Cases

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old previously healthy woman was admitted with a two-week history of a progressively worsening skin rash on both lower limbs. It began as a painful small vesicle on the left foot that enlarged, with new vesicles cropping up bilaterally; some evolved into 2–4 cm bullae that ruptured and healed with scarring. She reported progressive pain and numbness in both lower limbs up to the knees and numbness of the left fingers over two weeks, but no muscle weakness or gait difficulty. She noted bilateral ankle edema and frothy urine, with no hematuria or oliguria. She had low-grade fever, malaise, and a recent onset of wheezing managed with inhalers, but denied cough, sinusitis, epistaxis, joint symptoms, digital ulcers, or gastrointestinal complaints.

On examination, there was an erythematous rash with small blisters and bullae around both ankles, plus a few small hyperpigmented lesions on the left palm; no trunk, facial, or mucosal lesions. Neurologic exam showed reduced lower-limb reflexes and sensory impairment to knee level, intact vibration and joint-position sense, and no motor deficit; upper limbs were normal. Peripheral pulses were intact. Blood pressure was 160/100 mm Hg, and there was bilateral pitting ankle edema.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 27 000/mm3 with 57% eosinophils (absolute 15 500/µl), normal hemoglobin and platelets, ESR 54 mm/h, and CRP 103 µ/l. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria and 10–15 RBCs per high-power field; 24-hour protein was 1340 mg (normal <150 mg) with normal serum creatinine. Serum albumin was 30 g/l and total globulin 49 g/l. Rheumatoid factor was elevated (512 and 480 µ/l on two occasions), and qualitative cryoglobulins were repeatedly positive. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody were negative. P-ANCA (MPO) was positive; C3 was normal and C4 low-normal. Liver function tests and ANA were normal. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. 

Skin biopsy showed leukocytoclastic vasculitis with perivascular eosinophilic infiltrates and no granuloma. Renal biopsy revealed mild interstitial inflammation; immunofluorescence on skin was not performed.
title: A Rare Case of Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis Associated with Cryoglobulinemia Presenting with a Bullous Skin Eruption of the Lower Limbs

case_prompt: A 4-year-old girl was brought with heavy, fresh red vaginal bleeding over several days, without trauma or sexual assault. On examination she had short stature, short blunt hands, delayed dentition, bradycardia, and other stigmata of hypothyroidism; the thyroid gland was nonpalpable. Laboratory studies showed macrocytic anemia, a normal coagulation profile, markedly elevated TSH at 699 IU/mL (normal 0.35–4.9), low T3 (<1 pg/mL; normal 2.6–4.8), low T4 (<0.4 ng/dL), and thyroid peroxidase antibody 2152 U/mL (normal 0–60). Basal FSH was elevated, while LH and prolactin were within normal limits. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a 6.3×1.3 cm uterus with a tri-layered endometrium, a 5.7×3.7 cm septated cystic lesion in the right adnexa without internal vascularity, and a bulky left ovary with a dominant follicle. Neck ultrasound demonstrated bilaterally hypoplastic thyroid lobes with an absent isthmus. A skeletal survey showed delayed bone age (ossification of hamate and capitate consistent with 3–4 months; distal radial epiphysis consistent with 1 year; no triquetral or lunate ossification), multiple Wormian bones, an enlarged sella, and cortical thickening of the proximal femoral diaphyses. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the pituitary gland revealed homogeneous enlargement of the anterior pituitary compatible with hyperplasia; the posterior pituitary bright spot was preserved.
title: Imaging in Van Wyk Grumbach syndrome: An uncommon presentation of hypothyroidism

case_prompt: A 42-year-old woman presented with 3 months of abnormal vaginal bleeding. She had one prior vaginal delivery and one induced abortion, and was not on any medications, including hormonal therapy. On pelvic examination, there was a tender, smooth-surfaced mass on the anterior vaginal wall. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a well-circumscribed vaginal mass. MRI revealed a round, well-circumscribed 22×22×32 mm tumor in the vagina with heterogeneous high signal on T2-weighted images, intermediate signal on T1-weighted and fat-suppressed T1-weighted images, and a cord-like structure of markedly low signal on both T1 and T2 sequences extending from the anterior vaginal wall to the mass. The lesion showed high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging (b=1000) and on ADC maps (ADC 1.8–1.9×10^−3 mm^2/s), consistent with T2 shine-through. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated heterogeneous strong enhancement of the tumor, with the low-signal region on T2WI showing more intense enhancement than the high-signal area. No malignant lesions were identified in the pelvis or elsewhere.
title: Superficial myofibroblastoma of the vagina with a stalk: case report of a rare vaginal tumor with notable radiological findings

case_prompt: A 56-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of headache, nausea, and appetite loss. She had no history of malignancy. On admission, vital signs were stable and the neurologic and general examinations were normal. Laboratory studies showed an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 435 U/L and a soluble interleukin-2 receptor level of 1850 U/mL; coagulation parameters were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a protein concentration of 220 mg/dL and a cell count of 18 mature lymphocytes, with normal cytology. A noncontrast CT scan of the head demonstrated a low-density lesion in the left cerebellum with minimal mass effect. T2-weighted and FLAIR MRI sequences showed multiple hyperintense lesions in the left cerebellum and right frontal lobe that were iso-intense on diffusion-weighted imaging. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images revealed slight enhancement of these lesions, particularly in the vermis and along the left cerebellar sulci. Some dilated vessels were noted on the cerebellar and right frontal surface.
title: Intravascular Lymphoma with an Acute Course of Cerebellar Hemorrhage: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 26-year-old man presented in February 2021 with 3 days of diaphoresis, dizziness, loose stools, and loss of taste. His medical history was notable for occasional methamphetamine and cocaine use and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. On examination, his temperature was 36°C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 131/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 6.6 × 10^9 cells/L with lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 0.3 × 10^9 cells/L); the remainder of his complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel were normal. A chest radiograph demonstrated clear lungs, and stool PCR testing for Clostridium difficile was negative. A nasopharyngeal PCR swab confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. The patient reported recently ending a long-term relationship with a female partner and then having several condomless sexual encounters. HIV screening in the emergency department yielded a reactive laboratory-based fourth-generation antigen/antibody assay and a negative HIV-1/2 differentiation test.
title: Concurrent COVID-19 and Acute HIV: A Case Report and Diagnostic Review

case_prompt: A 56-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a painless right breast lump that rapidly increased in size and developed a bluish discoloration of the overlying skin. She had no personal or family history of cancer, breast surgery, or irradiation. On examination, there was a firm, fixed, ill-defined 5 cm mass involving the upper quadrants of the right breast; the overlying skin was bluish but not ulcerated. There was no nipple retraction, axillary lymphadenopathy, or lymphedema. Mammography showed a large, homogeneous mass without spiculation or suspicious calcifications. A core needle biopsy revealed anastomosing round-to-oval vascular spaces containing erythrocytes; the lining cells had thin, elongated, hyperchromatic nuclei that protruded into lumina, and vascular channels invaded adipose tissue. Immunohistochemical stains showed membranous reactivity for CD31 and CD34. These findings were initially interpreted as a benign vascular tumor.
title: Diagnostic difficulties of primary angiosarcoma of the breast: a case report

case_prompt: A 15‐year‐old boy presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever, weight loss, and arthralgia. For the past 2 months, he also noted pain in both calves that worsened during fever episodes. On examination, temperature was 37.8 °C, pulse 90 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 16 /min. All peripheral pulses were palpable; there was no rash or erythema of the skin. Abdominal examination and 2D echocardiography were unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.96 g/dL, leukocyte count 12 600 /mm3 (71% neutrophils), serum urea and liver and renal function tests within normal limits, and ionic calcium 1.18 mmol/L. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria (6 RBCs per high-power field). ESR was 55 mm/h, CRP mildly elevated, and ACE level 55.8 mg/L (reference 12–68). Serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Cold agglutinins, ANA, and ANCA were all negative. High-resolution ultrasound of both legs demonstrated multiple ill-defined hypoechoic lesions centered around intramuscular vessels in the gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles, suggesting perivascular inflammation; Doppler ultrasound showed no thrombosis or luminal narrowing. MRI of both legs revealed multifocal patchy high signal on T2-weighted, STIR, and proton density fat-suppressed sequences in the same muscles; on postcontrast T1-weighted images there were small, ill-defined enhancing areas centered on blood vessels with a fuzzy, “cotton-wool” appearance.
title: Leg muscle involvement in polyarteritis nodosa (limited form)—A rare case report

case_prompt:
A 77-year-old woman was referred for a 2-year history of severe constipation and intermittent abdominal pain. She had no relevant medical or psychological history. Despite multiple hospitalizations for presumed bowel obstruction, no mechanical causes were identified. She was treated with various laxatives (magnesium, mosapride, pantethine, lubiprostone, daikenchuto, sodium picosulfate) without sustained relief.

Colonoscopic examination was performed to evacuate retained gas and stool; there was no mechanical obstruction or stenosis from the cecum to the rectum, although mucosal edema was noted in several segments. Abdominal radiography demonstrated massive colonic gas levels. Contrast-enhanced CT showed dilation of the cecum, ascending colon, and transverse colon proximal to the splenic flexure with no obstructing lesion. Enteroclysis revealed normal small-intestinal peristalsis without strictures or dilatation. Barium enema demonstrated a markedly dilated right colon, an abruptly collapsed descending colon to rectosigmoid, and a normally distensible rectum. Cine MRI showed weak peristalsis in the dilated colon and absent peristalsis in the collapsed segment, while defecography confirmed normal anorectal function. There was no evidence of systemic disease or relevant medication use that could cause secondary colonic dysmotility.
title: Successful surgical procedure based on careful preoperative imaging for chronic idiopathic colonic pseudo-obstruction: a case report

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of fever, vomiting, headache, sialorrhea, dysphagia, and progressive upper-limb weakness. On admission, he was afebrile, alert, and oriented. Neurologic examination showed absent deep-tendon reflexes in the upper extremities, preserved strength and reflexes in the lower extremities, and no meningeal signs. There were no seizures, hydrophobia, or aerophobia. Cardiovascular and pulmonary findings were unremarkable. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

On hospital day 2, weakness progressed to involve both lower limbs, and he developed psychomotor agitation and persecutory delirium. By day 4, he was quadriparetic and became unconscious. His medical history was notable only for scars on his hands and right forearm. Four weeks before symptom onset, he had been bitten on the hands and right forearm by a stray dog; wounds were cleaned with soap and water, he received oral antibiotics and four doses of rabies vaccine, but no immunoglobulin.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with and without contrast (performed on day 2 of admission) showed bilateral, symmetric hyperintense signals on T2-weighted and FLAIR images in the basal ganglia, thalami, and frontoparietal white matter. There were no abnormalities on T1-weighted images, no contrast enhancement, and a mild increase in apparent diffusion coefficients in the involved regions.
title: Magnetic resonance imaging in rabies encephalitis, a case report, and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 10-year-old previously healthy boy presented with gradually worsening visual acuity over 1 year, associated with fatigue, severe polyuria–polydipsia (168 cc/kg/day), and gait instability, without fever or systemic symptoms. On examination he was afebrile and normotensive, with diuresis of 7 cc/kg/h. Neurologic findings included ataxic gait, cutaneous hyperesthesia, impaired deep sensation, hyperreflexia, and vertical gaze palsy (Parinaud’s syndrome). Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed visual acuity of 3/10 (right) and 2/10 (left), decreased pupillary light reflexes, semi-mydriasis, and bilateral grade-2 papilledema. Tanner staging was I. Laboratory tests showed normal serum potassium, HbA1c, and renal function; urinary osmolality was 64 073 mosm/L. Hormonal studies demonstrated an 8-am cortisol of 1.7 µg/dL and TSH of 2320 µU/mL. CSF β-hCG was elevated at 15.54 mIU/mL; plasma β-hCG and α-fetoprotein were negative. CSF immunohistochemistry for placental alkaline phosphatase and GFAP was negative. Brain CT (noncontrast and contrast) showed a well-circumscribed 10×12 mm suprasellar lesion abutting the optic chiasm and an 8×10 mm lobulated pineal lesion with a macrocalcification; both enhanced homogeneously. MRI additionally revealed multiple small T2/FLAIR hyperintense, contrast-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia, internal capsules, cortex, nodular ependymal enhancement, and pial involvement consistent with cerebro-medullary dissemination.
title: Intracranial bifocal germinoma☆

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man with no previous medical history was admitted after being found unresponsive at home. On arrival, he was confused (GCS 11), hypotensive, mottled in the legs, and hypoperfused. Initial labs showed extreme hyperglycaemia (unrecordable), ketones 3.6 mmol/L, lactic acidosis, acute kidney injury (urea 41.3 mmol/L, creatinine 277 µmol/L, eGFR 21 mL/min), hypernatraemia (Na 172 mmol/L), elevated CRP rising from 53 to 374 mg/L over 5 days, and a normal white cell count. He tested positive for SARS-CoV-2, developed respiratory failure requiring intubation and haemofiltration, and had findings of pulmonary aspergillosis treated with voriconazole.

One month after admission, he developed acute chest pain. ECG showed anterior ST-segment elevation. Emergency coronary angiography revealed an acute occlusion of the left anterior descending artery and moderate bystander atheroma elsewhere. He underwent primary PCI with a drug-eluting stent and restored TIMI 3 flow. During the procedure he developed acute pulmonary oedema poorly responsive to IV furosemide.  
Bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated moderately impaired left ventricular systolic function with relatively preserved basal segment contraction and an echogenic mass attached to the hypokinetic anteroseptal wall.
title: Early Left Ventricular Thrombus Formation in a COVID-19 Patient with ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction

case_prompt: A 32-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of AIDS presented with a 2-month history of progressive shortness of breath and a 40-lb unintentional weight loss. Chest radiography and sputum studies confirmed Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. On hospital day 7, he developed painful stomatitis involving the upper lip, the vermilion border of the lower lip, and the middle and anterior thirds of the dorsal tongue. Examination of the oral mucosa showed numerous 3-mm painful papules clustering into vegetative plaques measuring 0.6 to 1.2 cm with defined, scalloped borders and ulcerated, bleeding surfaces on a background of a fissured tongue. The remainder of the cutaneous examination was unremarkable. Venereal disease research laboratory and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests were negative. A Tzanck smear of the lesions revealed multinucleated giant epithelial cells with basophilic and pale cytoplasm.
title: Herpetic geometric glossitis presenting as vegetative plaques in the context of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old Caucasian man noted sudden onset of a blurred central circle in his left eye while skiing at 1,800 m. He reported recent sun exposure while using a laptop on a balcony without sunglasses and denied systemic symptoms. He was otherwise healthy, with no medical or recreational drug use and no recent vaccinations. One week later, visual acuity was 85 EDTRS letters in the right eye and 45 EDTRS letters in the left. Fundus examination of the left eye showed a pale circular area surrounding the fovea. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated submacular fluid, an area of increased hyperreflectivity of the subfoveal retinal pigment epithelium corresponding to loss of the ellipsoid and interdigitation zones in the detached macula, thickening and hyperreflectivity of the detached ellipsoid, interdigitation, and outer plexiform layers, and thinning of the outer nuclear layer. The right eye was unaffected, and there were no inflammatory cells in either chamber. An initial diagnosis of central serous chorioretinopathy was made, and follow-up was arranged for four months later.

At the four-month follow-up, the patient’s symptoms and visual acuity were unchanged. Fundus examination showed a fine hypopigmented dot at the fovea. OCT revealed resolution of the submacular fluid with reduced thickness of the ellipsoid, interdigitation, and outer plexiform layers but persistent subfoveal loss of the ellipsoid and interdigitation zones and thinning of the outer nuclear layer.
title: An Unusual Case of Unilateral Maculopathy

case_prompt:
Three term infants, aged 5 to 9 weeks, were referred to neurosurgery for scalp swelling. One had a vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery after failure to progress; two were delivered via uncomplicated cesarean section. All had fetal scalp electrodes placed during labor. They were otherwise healthy and reaching developmental milestones appropriately.

On examination, each infant was awake and alert. Scalp masses were non-tender, soft, compressible, fluctuant, and crossed suture lines; palpation of the skull was normal. No other abnormalities were noted.

Skull radiographs in two patients demonstrated well-circumscribed smooth masses overlying the skull without fractures, lucency, or sclerosis; in the third patient, radiographs showed no soft-tissue abnormality despite the physical findings. Noncontrast CT scans in two patients confirmed soft-tissue swellings with Hounsfield units similar to water, normal ventricles, cisterns, and cerebrospinal fluid spaces, and no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage, fracture, or mass effect.
title: Delayed sub-aponeurotic fluid collections in infancy: Three cases and a review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old Somali woman with history of Helicobacter pylori infection, gastroesophageal reflux disease, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted for excision of a large pelvic sarcoma. Preoperative airway evaluation showed Mallampati class II, full cervical, atlanto-axial, and atlanto-occipital mobility, mouth opening of three fingerbreadths, a somewhat hypoplastic mandible, and a thyromental distance of less than three fingerbreadths. 

Premedication included midazolam. Induction was with fentanyl, lidocaine, propofol, and rocuronium. Mask ventilation was easy and direct laryngoscopy with a Miller 2 blade provided a Grade 1 view; intubation was atraumatic. A nasogastric tube was placed without difficulty. The surgery lasted 11 hours, during which bilateral ureteral stents were placed and the sarcoma was removed. 

At the end of the procedure, spontaneous respirations returned but she was slow to follow commands. She was extubated in the PACU, transferred to the SICU on supplemental oxygen, and remained somnolent overnight. A nurse noted that she was unable to close her mouth and appeared to be in severe pain. Examination by the on-call surgery resident led to a diagnosis of muscle spasm, and hydromorphone PCA was initiated. 

The following morning, the primary surgical and SICU teams re-evaluated her; she still could not close her mouth despite analgesia, and muscle spasm remained the presumed etiology.
title: Unrecognized bilateral temporomandibular joint dislocation after general anesthesia with a delay in diagnosis and management: a case report

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old man presented with an asymptomatic, slowly enlarging, exophytic, brownish nodule on the abdominal wall that showed surface telangiectasia. Four years earlier, a lesion at the same site had been resected and was misdiagnosed as dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. His general health was otherwise excellent, and systemic examination was unremarkable. The recurrent nodule, measuring 22 mm in diameter, was completely excised; on gross examination it was a firm, well-demarcated dermal nodule with dark-brown and yellow areas on cut surface.

Microscopically, the lesion was an unencapsulated dermal nodule with overlying epidermal hyperplasia and a grenz zone, extending superficially into subcutaneous tissue. At the periphery, there were hyaline, large, round collagen bundles. The tumor consisted of dense interlacing fascicles and storiform arrays of histiocyte-like and fibroblast-like spindle cells, intermingled with mononuclear and giant cells exhibiting foamy cytoplasm and large, hyperchromatic, irregular nuclei. Mitotic activity was 4 figures per 10 high-power fields; atypical mitoses and necrosis were absent. Prominent blood-filled spaces, siderophages, and hemosiderin deposits were noted.

Immunohistochemical studies showed focal positivity for CD68 and complete negativity for S100 protein, HMB45, CD34, and alpha smooth muscle actin.
title: Atypical Cutaneous Fibrous Histiocytoma: An Unusual and Misleading Variant of Fibrous Histiocytoma

case_prompt: A 63-year-old Indonesian man presented with 1 week of sudden-onset binocular horizontal diplopia, constant and worse on left gaze, and left facial muscle weakness. He denied changes in visual acuity, trauma, or prior similar episodes. His history included 10 years of hypertension on treatment and left-eye anisometropic amblyopia; he had no smoking or drug use. Vital signs were normal. Visual acuity was 0.8 in the right eye and 0.08 in the left. Primary gaze was orthotropic; red glass testing showed uncrossed diplopia. On left gaze, the right eye failed to adduct and the left eye failed to abduct; there was no nystagmus. Eyelid position, pupillary reactions, color vision, and visual fields were intact. Anterior segment was unremarkable; fundus exam showed myopic changes with sharp optic disc margins bilaterally. Neurologic exam revealed left facial nerve palsy with incomplete eyelid closure, inability to raise the left eyebrow, and forehead involvement; the remainder of the exam was normal. Blood glucose and lipid profile were within normal limits. Brain MRI (T2W FLAIR) showed hyperintense periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (“Dawson’s fingers”), multiple small round hyperintense lesions in the cortex and juxtacortical cerebellar hemispheres with post-contrast enhancement, and a small hyperintense lesion in the left paramedian pontine reticular formation in the dorsal pons with post-contrast enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated hyperintensity attributable to T2 shine through, with normal apparent diffusion coefficient maps, effectively excluding acute ischemia.
title: Horizontal Gaze Palsy and Ipsilateral Facial Nerve Palsy in Older Patient as Initial Manifestation of Very Late-Onset Multiple Sclerosis Successfully Treated with Oral Corticosteroids: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of painless outward protrusion of the left eye, progressive vision deterioration, limited upward gaze, and partial loss of vision in that eye. She had no other medical or family history of similar disorders.  

On ophthalmologic examination, the left eye showed exophthalmos, ptosis, optic nerve atrophy, senile macular degeneration, and vitreous destruction. Visual acuity was +2.75 diopter sphere bilaterally, and movement of the left eye was restricted.  

Ocular ultrasonography revealed a tissue‐type echoic mass measuring 1.3 cm × 1.4 cm behind the left eye. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated thinning of the macular retina and reduced retinal nerve fiber layer thickness in all quadrants of the left eye, consistent with ganglion cell axon loss.  

Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a 1.5 cm × 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm intraconal mass occupying most of the left orbit, with thinning and depression of the extraocular muscles.  

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits revealed a smoothly contoured retrobulbar mass extending along the left optic nerve through the prechiasmal region into the optic chiasm, measuring approximately 5.2 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.9 cm. The lesion demonstrated peripheral contrast enhancement, cystic changes, restricted diffusion on DWI (ADC value 1500 × 10^−6 mm^2/s at b = 1000 s/mm^2), and high T2 signal intensity.
title: Optic Nerve Glioblastoma with Optic Chiasm Involvement: A Case Report and a Brief Literature Review

case_prompt: A 78-year-old man and chronic smoker presented with a 6-week history of difficulty swallowing solids and pharyngeal pain. On examination, there was a 3 × 2 cm solitary pedunculated lesion on the right side of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue crossing the midline; tongue mobility was normal, and there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination of the chest, abdomen, and heart was unremarkable. A biopsy of the lesion was initially reported as a primary squamous cell carcinoma with some clear cell changes. Blood tests, including renal function, were normal. While awaiting staging MRI, he developed severe oral pain and worsening dysphagia; the tongue lesion doubled in size over two weeks and began to protrude outside the mouth. Because this behavior was unusual for a primary tongue carcinoma, the pathology was reviewed and described as infiltration by carcinoma nests with extensive clear cell changes. The differential diagnosis included squamous cell carcinoma with clear cell changes, metastatic salivary gland neoplasm, and metastases from renal cell carcinoma. An urgent CT scan was arranged, and surgical debulking of the tongue lesion was planned to improve symptoms.
title: Tongue metastasis as an initial presentation of renal cell carcinoma: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 65‐year‐old retired computer repairman and active pilot, with no significant past medical history, reported mild memory problems for one year and thrashing movements during sleep for one year, followed by new‐onset panic attacks over three months. MRI performed after these complaints revealed a fourth ventricular mass, which was resected (pathology: subependymoma). 

Immediately post‐operatively, he became markedly confused with fluctuating attention, initially attributed to post‐operative delirium and benzodiazepine withdrawal. He developed visual hallucinations, poor spatial perception, and a left-leaning gait. During inpatient rehabilitation, cognitive impairment, hallucinations, and new myoclonus persisted despite treatment with aripiprazole, divalproex, donepezil, escitalopram, quetiapine, and clonazepam.

One month after surgery, he was admitted to the neurology service. Examination revealed masked facies, a left‐hand resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, lethargy, perseveration, and halting speech with preserved repetition. He had nearly constant hallucinations and delusions.

Basic laboratory studies were unremarkable. Brain MRI showed post‐surgical changes with meningeal enhancement. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was negative for malignancy. Cerebrospinal fluid studies revealed white blood cells 86 (lymphocytes 46%, monocytes 54%), red blood cells 25, protein 124 mg/dL, glucose 40 mg/dL, findings felt to reflect post‐surgical changes versus inflammation. CSF cultures, RT‐QuIC, and a paraneoplastic autoantibody panel were negative. Electroencephalography demonstrated nonspecific slowing.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
title: Prodromal Dementia with Lewy Bodies: A Case Series of the 3 Prodromal Types from Clinical Practice

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of progressively worsening pain and swelling in the proximal left arm, accompanied by limited flexion, extension, and abduction of the left shoulder. On inspection, there was loss of the normal shoulder contour due to a diffuse swelling of the pectoral girdle, with normal overlying skin and mild venous prominence. Palpation revealed a tender, bony-hard mass approximately 6 cm by 4 cm, fixed to underlying structures. 

Plain radiographs of the left shoulder demonstrated an ill-defined, expansile osteolytic lesion of the humeral neck and proximal shaft, with a wide zone of transition, endosteal scalloping, cortical breakthrough, several specks of calcification within the lesion, and an adjacent soft-tissue component. An additional calcified nodular opacity was noted in the peripheral left lung mid zone.

A 5 mm–slice CT scan from the superior shoulder to mid-arm confirmed an osteolytic expansile lesion with endosteal scalloping, cortical thinning and multiple cortical breaches, matrix calcifications, and anterolateral soft-tissue extension displacing the deltoid muscle.

MRI of the left arm showed a well-defined lobulated lesion that was predominantly hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with low-signal septations. The glenohumeral joint space was preserved and the neurovascular bundle was uninvolved.
title: Intramedullary Chondrosarcoma of Proximal Humerus

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with six weeks of diarrhea, hematochezia, left lower-quadrant abdominal pain, and a 25-lb weight loss. She denies vomiting, diet changes, sick contacts, or travel.  
On examination, her mucous membranes are dry; abdominal tenderness is diffuse but most pronounced in the left lower quadrant; bowel sounds are sluggish.  
Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10 g/dL, white blood cell count 15 × 10^3/μL, sodium 131 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20.2 mmol/L (normal anion gap), albumin 2.1 g/dL, globulin 3.9 g/dL.  
Stool studies are negative for Clostridium difficile PCR and Giardia lamblia antigen.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrates wall thickening of the distal descending and sigmoid colon concerning for colitis.  
Colonoscopy reveals ulcerated mucosa and multiple punched-out ulcers throughout the colon.
journal: Journal of Community Hospital Internal Medicine Perspectives
title: Cytomegalovirus infection in the setting of occult ulcerative colitis: case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old Japanese woman presented in June 2002 with a chief complaint of swelling at the left nasal alar base. She reported no intranasal or intraoral discharge, pain, history of trauma, or signs of inflammation. Her medical history was notable for restrictive lung disease and a gastric cancer resection at age 60. There was no relevant family, social, or environmental history.

On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, non-tender swelling of the left nasal alar base; the left nasolabial fold was less distinct and the left ala appeared elevated. Intraorally, the left upper gingivolabial sulcus was swollen, with a normal mucosal surface and fluctuant, non-tender consistency; the right sulcus was normal.

A panoramic radiograph showed apical periodontitis of the left upper central incisor but no other abnormalities. Computed tomography demonstrated a well-circumscribed oval lesion measuring approximately 19 × 14 × 12 mm inferior to the left nasal alar base, with relatively homogeneous low density compared to muscle. There was no clear maxillary or septal bone absorption. A small high-density area was also noted adjacent to the right piriform aperture, but a definitive lesion could not be confirmed.
title: Bilateral nasolabial cysts: a case report

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of right nasal obstruction and frequent blood-tinged crusting.  Endoscopic examination revealed a soft, fungating mass resembling a nasal polyp in the right middle meatus, partially adherent to the nasal septum and measuring more than 1 cm at its greatest dimension. The surrounding mucosa was hyperemic, with scattered blood clots but no active bleeding.  

Paranasal sinus CT showed a 2.2 cm polypoid lesion in the right middle meatus with well-defined margins and heterogeneous iso-intensity; there was slight expansion and erosion of the anterior cortex of the maxilla. The mass appeared to originate from the nasal septum and occupied the middle meatus without evidence of sinusitis.  

The lesion was completely excised via endoscopic sinus surgery, removing the septal mucosa while preserving the septal bone and cartilage. Grossly, the specimen was a relatively circumscribed, pinkish soft tissue mass measuring 2.2 × 1.5 × 0.7 cm.
title: A Rare Case of Interdigitating Dendritic Cell Sarcoma in the Nasal Cavity

case_prompt:
