A 69-year-old woman with a history of hypertensive heart disease, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, gastroesophageal reflux, renal insufficiency, former smoking, obesity (BMI 39.2), and macromastia underwent double coronary artery bypass grafting using the left internal mammary artery without perioperative complications. Shortly afterward, she developed septicemia, mechanical instability of the sternum, and mediastinitis. The sternotomy was managed with vacuum-assisted closure and re-sutured successfully five weeks after surgery.  

During this period, she complained of persistent pain in her left breast. Initial ultrasonography revealed a 2 cm hyperechoic edema of the breast fat centrally, without focal masses. Seven weeks after surgery, examination showed slight erythema over one third of the breast, most pronounced centrally and in the inner quadrants, with a palpable painful lump measuring 8 × 6 cm. Laboratory tests revealed mildly elevated C-reactive protein. Given her recent wound infection, mastitis was suspected and empirical antibiotics were started.  

Two weeks later, antibiotics had no effect, and a new 2–3 cm movable lump in the left axilla raised concern for a pathologic lymph node. Ultrasonography demonstrated edema and disruption of normal glandular architecture, without well-defined masses or fluid collections. Three weeks after that, repeat ultrasound showed a poorly defined hyperechoic mass with irregular hypoechoic zones and acoustic shadowing. Clinical findings of nipple retraction and skin thickening further suggested inflammatory carcinoma. Mammography revealed asymmetric increased density of the left breast, thickened areolar skin, nipple retraction, and diffuse glandular destruction consistent with inflammatory carcinoma.
title: Focal necrosis mimicking breast cancer following coronary bypass grafting

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old man underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for hepatitis B–related cirrhosis 10 weeks earlier and was maintained on routine immunosuppression. His postoperative course was complicated by pulmonary aspergillosis, for which he underwent left lower lobe wedge resection. Three weeks after thoracic surgery, he began to experience low back pain that progressed over several weeks despite conservative therapy.  

On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Neurologic examination was normal. Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine were unremarkable.  

Lumbar spine MR imaging revealed the following:  
• T1-weighted images showed band-like to diffuse hypointense signals in vertebral bodies L2 through L5.  
• T2-weighted images showed vertebral isointensity to minimal hyperintensity.  
• In the L2–3 and L4–5 intervertebral discs, intranuclear clefts were preserved and discs lacked hyperintense T2 signal; in the L3–4 disc, the intranuclear cleft was lost.  
• Endplate irregularities were seen at involved levels, with disc space narrowing at L3–4 and L4–5.  
• Postcontrast images demonstrated band-like or diffuse enhancement of involved vertebrae and an epidural fluid collection.  
• A relatively well-defined paraspinal abnormal signal was present.  

Based on these MR findings, a diagnosis of tuberculous spondylitis was favored over pyogenic spondylitis.
title: Aspergillus Spondylitis involving the Cervico-Thoraco-Lumbar Spine in an Immunocompromised Patient: a Case Report

case_prompt:
A 10-year-old girl with Thevenards syndrome presented with a 7-month history of painless right hip swelling and progressively restricted movement. Seven months prior, she sustained a bicycle fall onto her hip. One week after the trauma, she developed functional impairment of the right lower limb. An anteroposterior pelvic radiograph showed a right hip dislocation and extensive heterotopic ossification in the soft tissues, mainly over the posterior capsule and gluteus muscles, clearly separated from bone; pelvic bones were normal without periosteal reaction. The patient was treated conservatively but was lost to follow-up.

On re-presentation, clinical examination revealed markedly reduced abduction, extension, and internal rotation of the right hip, with inability to stand or walk. A firm, well-circumscribed mass was palpable over the anterolateral aspect of the right hip.

Follow-up pelvic radiographs demonstrated persistent hip dislocation and increased ossifying masses in the soft tissues projecting over the acetabulum and right femoral head and neck; the periphery of these masses was denser than their centers. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed an extensive area of ossification within the right iliopsoas, obturator, and gluteus muscles, extending from the pelvic inlet to the lesser trochanter. There was a clear cleavage plane between the calcified mass and the adjacent iliac bone. Multiple well-defined calcific areas suggestive of mature bone were seen at various levels. In more caudal images above the lesser trochanter, a hypodense central zone was surrounded by hyperdense zones with a focal, well-defined calcification anteriorly. No significant enhancement was noted after contrast administration.
title: Pediatric myositis ossificans circumscripta following traumatic hip dislocation: A case report

case_prompt:
An 88-year-old woman presented after a mechanical fall. Her heart rate was 150 beats per minute, blood pressure 147/92 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination was notable for a regular tachycardia and mild confusion. Laboratory studies showed a B-type natriuretic peptide level of 962 ng/L and a troponin level of 9.8 ng/L (normal range, 0–53.7 ng/L). Serum potassium was 3.7 mmol/L, magnesium 2.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, and glucose 110 mg/dL. An electrocardiogram demonstrated atrial flutter with 2:1 ventricular conduction. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% to 45%, down from 65% three months earlier.

Her medical history was significant for ischemic cardiomyopathy treated with orthotopic heart transplantation 21 years earlier, an ischemic stroke six years ago without residual deficits, shoulder and hip arthropathies, and recently diagnosed dementia. She had missed doses of tacrolimus, leading to subtherapeutic levels.

A coronary angiogram showed normal epicardial coronary arteries. Right heart catheterization revealed a right atrial pressure of 3 mm Hg, pulmonary artery pressure of 21/8 (15) mm Hg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg, and a cardiac index of 1.51 by thermodilution and 2.19 L/min/m2 by the Fick method.
title: Wild-Type Transthyretin Cardiac Amyloidosis in a Transplanted Heart

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation was referred after screening for hydroxychloroquine therapy revealed bilateral multifocal pigment epithelial detachments. Her medical history included mixed connective tissue disease (positive ANA and rheumatoid factor), polycystic ovary syndrome, hypothyroidism, and a resolved dengue infection one year earlier. She had no visual symptoms.  
On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes with myopic correction; Amsler grid and color vision testing were normal. Pupils were equal and reactive with no afferent defect. Anterior segments were unremarkable, and intraocular pressures were 20 mmHg OD and 21 mmHg OS.  
Dilated fundus examination revealed multiple serous PEDs in the macula extending beyond the vascular arcades in both eyes, with no hemorrhage, exudate, drusen, or subretinal fluid. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated multiple dome-shaped serous, nonvascularized PEDs without neurosensory detachment. OCT angiography showed no choroidal neovascularization. Subfoveal choroidal thickness measured 380 µm in each eye.  
Laboratory testing showed persistently positive ANA consistent with her connective tissue disease. QuantiFERON-Gold, reactive plasma reagin, protein electrophoresis, complete blood count with differential, free kappa and lambda light chains, and chikungunya antibody testing were within normal limits.
final_diagnosis_raw: multifocal idiopathic retinal pigment epithelial detachments
title: MULTIMODAL IMAGING OF BILATERAL IDIOPATHIC MULTIFOCAL RETINAL PIGMENT EPITHELIAL DETACHMENTS IN YOUNG PATIENTS

case_prompt: A 40-year-old man with no prior medical history except postbulbar ulceration presented with 3 days of absolute constipation, acute abdominal pain, and nausea. On examination, he was tachycardic (heart rate, 106 beats/min), with abdominal distension and diffuse tenderness. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 15,320/mm³ and a C-reactive protein level of 33.5 mg/dL. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed mildly distended and thickened ileal loops clustered in the hypogastric quadrant and enclosed within a sac formed by a thickened peritoneal membrane with contrast uptake and a “cocoon-like appearance,” causing upstream small-bowel dilatation with air–fluid levels. Peritoneal fluid was noted within the sac, and perihepatic calcifications were seen in the thickened peritoneal membrane. Although an internal hernia was initially considered, it was ruled out based on the finding of a distinct peritoneal membrane encasing the ileal loops.
title: Bowel obstruction complicating an encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis: A case report

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old boy with a history of platelet-function defect, sleep apnea (post-tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy), prematurity, and developmental delays presented with 5 days of fever and abdominal pain and a known household exposure to SARS-CoV-2 2½ weeks earlier. On day of illness (DOI) 3, he had fever without other vital-sign abnormalities and an unremarkable physical examination. Laboratory tests showed modest elevations in the erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, ferritin, and prothrombin time. He was well-appearing, without focal signs of bacterial infection, and was discharged with supportive care. Later on DOI 3, he returned with pharyngeal erythema, a negative rapid streptococcal test, and improvement with acetaminophen, and he was discharged again. 

On DOI 5, he returned with persistent fever and new symptoms: four episodes of nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting, five episodes of nonbloody diarrhea, poor appetite, bilateral conjunctival injection, and a rash developing over the previous 24 hours. His temperature was normal, heart rate 150 beats per minute, respiratory rate 56 breaths per minute, blood pressure and oxygen saturation were normal. He appeared ill. Examination revealed erythematous lips, anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, tachycardia without murmur, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and a generalized erythematous macular rash most pronounced on the palms, soles, posterior thighs, and back. 

Laboratory studies on DOI 5 demonstrated anemia, hyponatremia, elevated aspartate transaminase, elevated alanine transaminase, hypoalbuminemia, elevated C-reactive protein, elevated ferritin, elevated D-dimer, elevated fibrinogen, and elevated N-terminal prohormone b-type natriuretic peptide.
title: Five days of fever and myocardial inflammation

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-week history of vaginal bleeding. Her Pap smear demonstrated high-grade cytologic atypia. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed an endometrial stripe measuring 12 mm and a diffusely inhomogeneous myometrium. Colposcopy with directed biopsies showed atypical squamous cells suspicious for carcinoma. On bimanual examination, the uterus was enlarged. 

Her past medical history was noncontributory; surgical history included four cesarean deliveries and bilateral tubal ligation. She was a former smoker with a four pack-year history. Menarche occurred at age 12 and menopause at age 50, with no prior postmenopausal bleeding.

Hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage and cervical conization were performed. Curettage specimens showed a highly atypical squamous epithelial proliferation replacing the endometrium, while the cervical cone biopsy was benign. Pathology raised three main considerations: primary squamous cell carcinoma of the endometrium, squamous metaplastic change in an endometrioid adenocarcinoma with pauci-glandular proliferation, and metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to the endometrium from a distant site or cervical extension. P16 immunohistochemical staining was negative, effectively excluding a cervical primary. Endocervical curettage also showed p16-negative atypical squamous cells.

The case was reviewed at a multidisciplinary tumor board, and surgical staging was recommended.
title: Primary endometrial squamous cell carcinoma with synchronous early stage Fallopian adenocarcinoma: A case report and review of diagnostic and treatment considerations

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old Pakistani woman presented with 6 hours of hematemesis. She had no history of GI bleeding, liver disease, peptic ulcer disease, alcohol or NSAID use, medications, or supplements. Family history was notable for only hypertension in her father. On examination she was lethargic and tachycardic (pulse 122 beats/min), with a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and temperature 37.6 °C. There was no abdominal pain or stigmata of chronic liver disease. A nasogastric aspirate was negative for blood. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 4 g/dL, MCV 77.2 fl, WBC count 9000/mm3, platelets 238 000/µL, urea 26 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, AST 32 IU/L, ALT 40 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 87 IU/L, INR 0.9, and PT 12.9 s. She received IV fluids and 4 U of packed red blood cells.  
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a swelling in the first part of the duodenum. The lesion appeared as an abnormally placed or accessory papilla with a small (<3 mm) opening suggesting a biliary or pancreatic orifice. On gentle manipulation with a catheter, blood spurted from the area and a vessel became visible.
title: Bleeding “Dieulafoy’s-like” lesion resembling the duodenal papilla: a case report

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of recurrent left-sided epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction. She had no personal or family history of tuberous sclerosis complex, hamartomas, or epilepsy, and her past medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a polypoid mass occupying the anterior part of the left nasal cavity, with deviation of the nasal septum to the right. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. 
 
A noncontrast CT scan of the sinuses showed a 1.5-cm polypoid lesion in the left nasal fossae filling the inferior meatus, with homogeneous density, preservation of the bony framework, and no evidence of bone erosion. Coronal and sagittal T1-weighted MRI after gadolinium administration demonstrated a homogeneously enhancing mass confined to the left nasal cavity, without signs of infiltration of adjacent structures.
title:
Early onset of a nasal perivascular epithelioid
cell neoplasm not related to tuberous sclerosis
complex

case_prompt: A 20-year-old HIV-negative man in Lilongwe, Malawi, presented with several weeks of weakness, dry cough, night sweats, and weight loss. His body mass index was 19.4 kg/m2. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL; alkaline phosphatase 668 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 766 U/L, AST 78 U/L, ALT 58 U/L, and total bilirubin 0.63 mg/dL. Serum creatinine was normal. A GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay on expectorated sputum was negative. Chest radiography revealed nonspecific bilateral opacities. A FASH ultrasound scan using convex and linear probes showed no pericardial or pleural effusions, no ascites, and no lymphadenopathy. On detailed ultrasound, the liver was diffusely hyperechoic compared with the kidney without focal lesions; the spleen contained innumerable 1–2 mm hypoechoic lesions in a sponge-like pattern; multiple <3 mm hypoechoic micronodules were seen in the peritoneum superficial to the liver; and the visceral-parietal pleural interface had multiple echogenic foci with vertical, comet-tail artifacts.
journal: The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene
title: Subtle Sonographic Signs of Disseminated Tuberculosis: A Case Report and Narrative Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidental low-density area on liver CT, initially suspected to represent peliosis hepatis. Her history included an acute myocardial infarction treated with percutaneous coronary intervention at age 49 and treatment of a large left internal carotid aneurysm and right middle cerebral artery aneurysm at age 45. Laboratory studies showed a normal blood count and no elevation in liver enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the liver revealed an early and persistently enhancing hypervascular nodule in segment 7, multiple small enhancing lesions consistent with telangiectases, and early opacification of the portal and hepatic veins, indicating arterioportal and arteriovenous shunts. There were no signs of portal hypertension, although the portal vein was dilated. Follow-up ultrasound showed stability of the nodule.  

One year later, she presented with anemia (hemoglobin, 6.0 g/dL). Gastrointestinal endoscopy was negative, but capsule endoscopy identified multiple angiodysplasias in the small intestine. Two years later, anemia recurred (hemoglobin, 8.9 g/dL), and gastric angiodysplasias were treated with argon plasma coagulation. Several years afterward, a chest CT incidentally revealed a small pulmonary arteriovenous fistula. Detailed history taking uncovered recurrent spontaneous epistaxis beginning in her teens. She had no visible cutaneous telangiectasia and no known family history of similar symptoms; her mother had died suddenly at age 29, and her two adult children had no history of epistaxis.
title: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia Presenting with Asymptomatic Liver Lesions and a History of Early-onset Myocardial Infarction and Multiple Intracranial Aneurysms

case_prompt: An 18-year-old man with a history of traumatic right eye enucleation five years earlier presented with headache, vomiting, and a decreased level of consciousness. Noncontrast CT of the head showed hydrocephalus and a hyperdense lesion in the right thalamus with surrounding edema, mass effect, and midline shift; a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed. On transfer, he was alert (Glasgow coma scale 15), with stable vital signs and an otherwise normal neurologic examination. MRI revealed a large right thalamic mass compressing the lateral ventricles. A stereotactic biopsy yielded insufficient tissue for immunohistochemical staining but demonstrated discohesive pleomorphic cells, reactive lymphocytes, necrosis, and vascular proliferation, leading to a provisional differential of high-grade glioma versus lymphoma. CSF cytologic examination showed benign mature lymphocytes without malignant cells, and a bone marrow biopsy revealed no evidence of lymphoma.
title: Thalamic germinoma: a challenging diagnosis, case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old Japanese man with a history of insulin-treated diabetes mellitus and prior ischemic stroke on long-term antiplatelet therapy presented with cognitive changes and new-onset seizures. One year earlier, he had been diagnosed with systemic B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (flow cytometry: CD19+, CD20+, kappa+, CD5–, CD10–) involving spleen and bone marrow and had achieved complete remission after eight courses of reduced-dose R-CHOP without CNS prophylaxis.

Three days before admission, he became unable to recognize playing cards and exhibited confusing behavior. On the day of admission, he developed prolonged generalized tonic-clonic seizures and was transferred to the emergency department.

On exam, he was febrile (40.5 °C), tachycardic (157 bpm), hypertensive (187/79 mm Hg), and in a postictal state (GCS E1V1M4) with right conjugate gaze deviation and no neck stiffness. There was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 15.1 × 10^9/L, Hb 9.9 g/dL, platelets 188 × 10^9/L, LDH 313 U/L, CRP 0.75 mg/dL, normal coagulation, renal, and liver panels, and normal glucose and electrolytes. 

Noncontrast brain CT revealed a high-density mass with surrounding edema and intratumoral hemorrhage in the left temporal lobe. MRI showed the lesion to be iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images, and to enhance heterogeneously after gadolinium. Diazepam and levetiracetam were started, and a stereotactic brain biopsy was scheduled for definitive diagnosis.
title: Secondary Central Nerve System Lymphoma With Intratumoral Hemorrhage Suggested as Intravascular Lymphoma by Autopsy: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 24-year-old woman with a history of cholecystectomy and relapsed acute promyelocytic leukemia presented with a 2-day history of nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain. One year after induction with cytarabine, daunorubicin, and ATRA, she began arsenic trioxide (17 mg IV daily, 5 days/week). On day 11 of therapy, she developed her current symptoms. Examination showed epigastric tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed an amylase of 405 U/L (normal 30–110), lipase of 4960 U/L (normal 6–75), AST 43 U/L (normal 14–36), and hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL (normal 12.3–15.3). CT of the abdomen/pelvis showed post-cholecystectomy changes. Right upper quadrant ultrasound demonstrated a normal pancreas, a common bile duct of 3.5 mm without intrahepatic ductal dilation, and no gallbladder. MRI/MRCP showed normal pancreatic morphology with no evidence of pancreas divisum. Bile aspirate was negative for microcrystalline disease. Triglycerides, antinuclear antibodies, and IgG4 levels were within normal limits. Arsenic therapy was held; she improved with intravenous fluids, pain control, and antiemetics, and her enzymes normalized by hospital day 8. One week later, arsenic was resumed at 0.1 mg/kg/day. On day 14 of therapy, she developed mental-status changes, respiratory distress, hypotension, and recurrent epigastric pain. Amylase and lipase were again elevated. CT showed pancreatic heterogeneity consistent with pancreatitis. Arsenic was held, succimer chelation was initiated, and blood and urine arsenic levels were found to be significantly elevated 25 days after cessation. EEG revealed generalized slowing consistent with toxic metabolic encephalopathy. She ultimately required tracheostomy and percutaneous gastrojejunostomy and was transferred to a long-term care facility.
title: Arsenic-Induced Pancreatitis

case_prompt: A 72-year-old woman with cT1N0M0 stage IA primary right upper lobe lung cancer and poor pulmonary function underwent stereotactic body radiotherapy (48 Gy in 4 fractions). She was a heavy smoker (Brinkman index 900). Before SBRT, serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was 14.7 ng/mL; KL-6 was 230 U/mL and SP-D was 72.8 ng/mL. Follow-up CT at 2 months showed irregular patchy consolidation in the irradiated field; at 6 and 9 months the consolidation retracted and CEA declined. At 12 months, CT demonstrated a mass-like consolidation around the treated area, and at 13 months it had increased in size; no air bronchograms were seen, and the right 3b bronchus was displaced. Serum CEA, KL-6, and SP-D were unchanged. FDG-PET showed high uptake in the consolidation (SUVmax = 5.61). CT-guided biopsy yielded class II cytology and no histologic evidence of malignancy.
title: A Case of Radiation Fibrosis Appearing as Mass-Like Consolidation after SBRT with Elevation of Serum CEA

case_prompt: A 32-year-old woman with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade III enrolled in a clinical trial of intravaginal imiquimod presented with diffuse hair loss. She had applied increasing doses of imiquimod suppositories over 16 weeks, using a cumulative dose of 250 mg. Fifteen weeks after treatment initiation, she noted progressive shedding of scalp hair. During therapy, she experienced mild-to-moderate fatigue, flu-like symptoms, headache, increased vaginal discharge, and genital itching. On examination, hair density was slightly reduced in the frontoparietal and occipital regions, with a positive hair pull test in those areas. Trichoscopy of the scalp, nails, and skin was normal. A trichogram showed an anagen-to-telogen ratio of 79:21 in the frontoparietal area and 73:27 in the occipital area. Laboratory tests were negative for acute or chronic infection, endocrinologic disease, autoimmunity, and iron or vitamin deficiencies.
title: Imiquimod-induced effluvium after intravaginal application for treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia

case_prompt: A 47-year-old man with no prior medical or surgical history and no tobacco, alcohol, or drug use presented with a 4-month history of a slowly enlarging abdominal mass in the epigastrium. He denied weight loss, fever, night sweats, changes in bowel habits, anorexia, or vomiting. He appeared well; vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, there was a firm, immobile, tender mass measuring approximately 10 cm × 5 cm in the epigastric region. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 000/µL (normal range 4000–11 000/µL) and a C-reactive protein level of 220 mg/L (normal range 0–3 mg/L). Colonoscopy revealed no abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated a large heterogeneous mass within the anterior abdominal wall, measuring 10 cm in greatest diameter, with extensive inflammatory changes in the surrounding fat and regular thickening of the transverse colon. MRI of the abdomen confirmed an infiltrative mass adherent to the posterior rectus sheath, the transverse colon, and the stomach, with no evidence of a colonic fistula. A multidisciplinary team decided to proceed with surgical resection of the mass.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Abdominal Actinomycosis Abscess Mimicking Malignancy: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 6-year-old boy presented with the sudden onset of severe back pain and marked swelling over the lumbar region. He was unable to walk because of bilateral knee pain and swelling of his right leg. There was no history of trauma. An orthopedic evaluation raised concern for a subcutaneous hematoma or bleeding diathesis.  
  
Initial laboratory studies showed normal platelet counts and normal coagulation and fibrinolytic parameters.  
   
An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a low-density, symmetrically localized fluid collection along the erector spinae muscles with a smooth, well-defined margin and a small gap between the superficial fascia and the muscle. These features were noted to differ from those of typical hematoma or abscess and from irregularly distributed edema along the superficial fascia.  

A sagittal lumbar MRI showed that the lesion in the posterior lumbar subcutaneous tissues had a low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a high signal intensity on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, consistent with soft-tissue fluid accumulation and edema.
title: Posterior lumbar subcutaneous edema as the rare sign of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura): A case of a child

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of developmental delay and sensorineural hearing impairment. She was born at term to consanguineous parents and had sparse medical follow-up until age 5, when bilateral hearing aids were fitted. Parents reported frequent balance loss in toddlerhood. By age 7, she had toe-walking with tight, almost spastic Achilles tendons; brain MRI showed a central lesion in the mesencephalon extending from the red nucleus dorsocaudally to the cerebellar peduncles. At age 12 she developed bilateral peroneal muscle weakness and absent peripheral reflexes; electrodiagnostic studies demonstrated sensorimotor polyneuropathy and chronic neurogenic changes in leg muscles. Repeat brain MRI was unchanged. At age 13, cognitive delay, impaired gross and fine motor skills, and tremor prompted consideration of a neurometabolic disorder. By age 15 there was generalized muscle weakness, hyperflexible fingers, planovalgus feet, poor balance, delayed growth (skeletal age 10.7 at chronologic 14), primary ovarian failure, and absence of pubertal signs. No retinal or optic-nerve abnormalities were noted.  
Laboratory studies at age 13 showed: moderately elevated plasma C26:0 with increased C26:0/C22:0 ratio, borderline C24:0/C22:0 ratio, markedly elevated phytanic and pristanic acids, and normal erythrocyte plasmalogen levels.  
Fibroblast studies revealed normal VLCFA concentrations and normal dihydroxyacetonephosphate-acyltransferase activity. Immunofluorescence microscopy for catalase showed normal peroxisomal staining in most cells at 37 °C but a markedly reduced number of peroxisomes in some cells. After 2 weeks at 40 °C, catalase staining became completely cytosolic, indicating a temperature-sensitive defect in peroxisome import.  
Given these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
title: Identification of a novel mutation in PEX10 in a patient with attenuated Zellweger spectrum disorder: a case report

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old man presented with chest distress and shortness of breath for more than 2 months. He reported recurrent oral and external genital ulcers for over 10 years, and a family history of recurrent oral ulcers in his mother, younger brother, and sister. He had hypertension for more than 10 years and underwent left carotid artery stent implantation in 2016 for a carotid aneurysm, and left femoral artery stent implantation later that year for a pseudoaneurysm; he has been taking aspirin since. In January 2019, he developed exertional chest distress, dyspnea, chest pain, and occasional nocturnal orthopnea without fever, cough, or expectoration. At another hospital he was diagnosed with pulmonary infection and rheumatic heart disease. 

On examination, the jugular veins were distended; a palpable thrill was present over the aortic area; heart rate was regular; a grade 4/6 systolic blowing murmur was heard at the aortic area; and grade 3/6 systolic blowing murmurs were heard at the mitral and tricuspid areas. Small ulcers were noted on the left buccal mucosa, and scattered acneiform nodules were seen on the chest and back. 

Laboratory tests: high-sensitivity troponin 0.022 ng/ml, BNP 5435 pg/ml, CRP 6.11 mg/l, ESR 15 mm/h. ECG: sinus rhythm 99 bpm, poor R-wave progression in V1–V4, ST elevation in V2–V3, and T-wave inversion in V3–V4. 

Transthoracic echocardiography showed rupture of the right aortic sinus with interventricular septal dissection, a large shunt between the aortic sinus and septum, moderate mitral regurgitation, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and enlargement of the left heart and right atrium. Enhanced aortic CTA showed an arc-shaped low-density shadow in the ascending aorta (pulsation artifact) and no definite sign of aortic dissection. Pathergy test was negative, and there were no ocular lesions.
title: Aortic sinus aneurysm invading ventricular septum and dissection caused by Behcet’s disease: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 47-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of painless upper‐lip swelling. He reported that the enlargement was initially episodic and recurrent but became persistent. His medical and family history were unremarkable. On examination, there was a homogeneous swelling of the upper lip without erythema or tongue or pharyngeal edema. In the same area, there were erythematous lesions with closely adherent scales that had appeared one year earlier. Similar smaller erythematous lesions were present on the neck, and achromic scarring lesions were noted on the shoulders. Two skin biopsies were performed. Histopathology of the swollen lip showed “upper dermis vasodilation with perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, while in the reticular dermis non‐necrotizing granulomas constituted by epithelioid cells and Langhans’ type cells were observed.” The biopsy of an erythematous lesion revealed an atrophic epidermis with hyperkeratosis, vacuolar degeneration of basal cells, a perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis, and mucin among collagen bundles. Laboratory studies, including immunological markers, were within normal limits.
title:
Cheilitis granulomatosa associated with lupus erythematosus discoid and
treated with methotrexate: report of a case*

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old Caucasian woman presented to the breast surgery clinic with a three-month history of a rapidly growing left chest wall mass and an overlying open, draining wound. Her medical history was significant for stage IIB (T2N1M0) triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast treated in 2003 with bilateral mastectomies, left axillary lymph node dissection, and adjuvant chemoradiation. Other comorbidities included atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and morbid obesity (BMI 48). She had no history of smoking or alcohol use and was BRCA 1/2 negative.

On examination, there were radiation‐induced skin changes over the left chest wall and a firm, fixed 15-cm mass with a central draining wound. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed an 8.2-cm circumscribed fluid collection in the left chest wall with a central opening and direct extension into the pectoralis muscles.

Given these findings, what should be included in your differential diagnosis and what is the most likely underlying process?
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Oncoplastic reconstruction of a large chest wall defect using dual fasciocutaneous flaps: A case report

case_prompt: A 50-year-old woman underwent preemptive living-donor kidney transplantation for diabetic end-stage kidney disease. She received induction with basiliximab and maintenance immunosuppression with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone. Before transplantation, EBV viral capsid antigen IgG titers were >750 U/mL in both donor and recipient. Because of stable graft function, tacrolimus dose was halved, mycophenolate was discontinued, and sirolimus 1 mg daily was initiated. Four months after transplantation, the EBV viral load rose to 652,111 copies/mL, and she received preemptive rituximab (375 mg/m2) for six months. At eight months, the EBV load decreased to 375,412 copies/mL, but abdominopelvic CT showed new multifocal wedge-shaped low-enhancement lesions in the spleen, suggestive of infarction, with evaluation for thromboembolic causes (peripheral smear, echocardiography, coagulation studies) unrevealing. Nine months after transplantation, she was admitted with fever (40.0 °C), flank pain, abnormal liver function (ALT 161 IU/L), and an EBV load of 1,921,952 copies/mL. Abdominopelvic CT revealed para-aortic lymphadenopathy and progression of splenic lesion margins. PET/CT demonstrated increased metabolic activity in the spleen and iliac-chain lymph nodes.
title: T cell posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder after kidney transplantation progressing to acute liver failure: a case report

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of headache accompanied by incoherent speech, aggressive behavior, disinhibited conduct, and visual and auditory hallucinations. On the day before admission, she developed a progressive decrease in awareness. She had no significant past medical history, denied drug use, toxin exposure, or recent travel, and reported minimal oral intake of food and water over the preceding days.

On examination, she was tachycardic with a weak pulse, normal blood pressure, dry mucous membranes, and prolonged capillary refill. Neurologic examination revealed disorientation, retrograde amnesia, impaired judgment, and loss of abstract thinking. A chest radiograph and noncontrast head CT scan were unremarkable.

Laboratory evaluation showed severe hypernatremia (serum sodium 180 mEq/L) and acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.0 mg/dL; baseline 0.6 mg/dL). Serum electrolytes, liver function tests, complete blood count, urinalysis, and toxicology screen were otherwise normal. Spot urinary studies demonstrated a urinary sodium of 20 mEq/L with a fractional excretion of sodium of 0.5%, and the calculated electrolyte-free water excretion was inappropriately elevated at 805 mL in 24 hours on a total urine volume of 1 L. She was treated with enteral free water and hypotonic intravenous fluids. Although her intravascular volume and kidney function improved, she continued to exhibit hypernatremia (sodium 157 mEq/L), mild hypokalemia (potassium 3.2 mEq/L), a low urinary sodium (8 mEq/L), an inappropriately low urine osmolality (85 mOsm/kg), an electrolyte-free water excretion of 3.3 L, and a 24-hour urine volume of 4 L, consistent with polyuria and hypernatremia suggestive of diabetes insipidus.

Because water deprivation testing was contraindicated, MRI of the brain was performed and revealed a pituitary stalk lesion with extension into the optic chiasm and hypothalamus. Treatment with desmopressin achieved progressive normalization of serum sodium, urine volume, and volume status. Evaluation of pituitary function disclosed panhypopituitarism, prompting thyroid and glucocorticoid hormone replacement.
title: Neurosarcoidosis Presentation as Adipsic Diabetes Insipidus Secondary to a Pituitary Stalk Lesion and Association with Anti-NMDA Receptor Antibodies

case_prompt:
An 11-year-old Saudi boy with no prior medical history presented with a 5-year history of a right-sided, non-painful facial mass that had progressively enlarged and recurred after multiple interventions. He had undergone prior surgical excision with recurrence, a temporary reduction after intravenous steroids followed by regrowth one year later, and embolization of the right internal maxillary artery without resolution. There were no orbital or oral symptoms, no history of facial trauma or tattooing, and no family history of tumors or hematologic disease.

On examination, a 2 × 3 cm soft, mobile, non-tender mass was noted over the right zygomatic prominence; the overlying skin was hyperpigmented. There was no cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Ophthalmologic and dental evaluations were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal urea and electrolytes, and normal coagulation profile; serum IgE was elevated at 8977 IU/mL (normal < 200). 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the facial bones demonstrated a 2.6 × 7 × 8 cm hypo- to iso-dense soft-tissue mass in the right buccal region without bone or skin involvement. MRI of the face revealed a heterogeneously hyperintense mass on T2-weighted images and heterogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images, with no intraorbital extension. 

Given the non-specific imaging and persistent nature of the lesion, a transoral biopsy via a sublabial approach was performed.
title: Kimura disease

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of bilateral limb weakness that began in her legs and gradually involved all extremities. The weakness was constant, did not fluctuate with activity or rest, and progressed to difficulty walking two days before admission. She denied sensory changes, speech difficulties, palpitations, sweating, polyuria, edema, or bulbar symptoms. She had a history of hypertension diagnosed previously but had not taken any antihypertensive medications. Her mother died of hypertension-related complications. She was a nonsmoker, did not drink alcohol, and consumed a high-salt, high-fat diet.

On examination, blood pressure was 190/100 mmHg, heart rate 79/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 36.4°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. There was no conjunctival pallor. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. Mild right upper quadrant tenderness was noted without guarding or rebound. Extremities were warm, with normal capillary refill and no edema. Neurologic examination showed symmetric motor strength of 2/5 in all four limbs, normal sensation, physiologic reflexes, and intact cranial nerves without fasciculations or atrophy.

Laboratory studies showed AST 81 U/L (0–34), ALT 192 U/L (0–34), LDL cholesterol 247 mg/dL (57–130), serum sodium 143 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 1.00 mmol/L (3.5–5.5), and aldosterone 18 pg/mL (20–230). Arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.48, pCO2 38 mmHg, and HCO3– 28 mmol/L, consistent with metabolic alkalosis. An electrocardiogram demonstrated bigeminy premature ventricular contractions with multifocal couplets. Echocardiography showed mild left ventricular dilatation with an ejection fraction of 58.7%, normal right ventricular systolic function, and mild mitral regurgitation. Abdominal ultrasound revealed grade 1 fatty liver.
title: Challenges in diagnosing and treating Liddle syndrome in resource-limited settings: A case report from Indonesia

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old woman with no prior medical history experienced emotional stress at a family funeral. Four days later, she developed sudden-onset chest pain and shortness of breath. In the local health centre, her blood pressure fell to 60/30 mmHg, and troponin-T was elevated. The ECG demonstrated widespread ST-elevations in the anterior and inferior leads consistent with Grade 3 ischaemia. Lung auscultation revealed fine crepitant rales; cardiac examination was otherwise unremarkable. She received ticagrelor, enoxaparin, and aspirin and was transferred for primary percutaneous coronary intervention.  

On arrival at the hospital, she remained hypotensive (60/30 mmHg) with an oxygen saturation of 75% and continued to report intense chest pain. The ECG showed extensive ST-elevations in all precordial leads and the inferior leads, with a triangular (lambda-shaped) appearance of the QRS-ST-T waveform in leads II, III, aVF, and V3–V6. Telemetry revealed repeated episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia at 165 b.p.m., during which she transiently lost consciousness. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%.
title: The electrocardiographic ‘triangular QRS-ST-T waveform’ pattern: a marker of severe haemodynamic compromise in Takotsubo syndrome—a case report

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department after a syncopal episode at work. She reported a 2-week history of fever and cough and a 2-month history of anorexia and weight loss. On arrival, she was tachypneic and dyspneic. Examination revealed palpable cervical lymph nodes, generalized coarse crackles, and bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs. Vital signs were: blood pressure 100/40 mm Hg, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air.

An electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia with nonspecific T-wave inversion in the precordial leads and intermittent complete right bundle branch block. Chest radiography revealed diffuse bilateral miliary changes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severely reduced global left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction, 15%), an apical mural thrombus, and a small pericardial effusion. High-sensitivity troponin I was elevated at 85 pg/mL, and C-reactive protein was 9.85 mg/dL. Tests for COVID-19 and HIV were negative.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed disseminated disease involving the lungs, intestines, and bones, with possible tuberculomas in the liver and spleen. The scan also confirmed the presence of a left ventricular apical thrombus.
title: Disseminated Tuberculosis With Myocarditis and Intracardiac Thrombus in a Previously Young Healthy Woman

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old male presented with a 1-week history of acute onset abdominal pain. He had undergone a previous laparotomy for acute abdomen, though no records were available. Family history was notable for his mother and sister having pigmented macules on the lips, but no abdominal complaints. On examination, multiple hyperpigmented macules were present on the lips, palms, and soles. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse tenderness without palpable masses or organomegaly. An emergency ultrasound demonstrated a large mass in the periumbilical region. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a heterogeneous, peripherally enhancing mass in the mesentery just above the renal hilum that was inseparable from jejunal loops and abutting the superior mesenteric artery with preserved fat plane; the lesion was presumed malignant based on heterogeneous enhancement and infiltration of adjacent jejunum and mesentery. The study also revealed two sites of colonic telescoping: the descending colon into the sigmoid colon and the cecum into the ascending colon, each with a large enhancing polypoid mass at its lead point. Additional intraluminal enhancing polyps were seen in the stomach, jejunum, and colon. 

Subsequent upper endoscopy confirmed multiple polyps in the stomach and duodenum.
title: A rare case of synchronous colocolic intussusception in association with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old woman presented after a routine examination revealed a hepatic lesion. She had a >20-year history of hepatitis B but no symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed: AFP 1.22 ng/mL (normal <7), positive HBsAg, HBeAb, and HBcAb; negative HBeAg; HBV DNA 5.29×10^4 IU/mL; normal liver-function tests.  
Abdominal ultrasound showed a 19.9×14.2 mm heterogeneous hypoechoic nodule with clear margins in the right hepatic lobe.  
Contrast-enhanced ultrasound demonstrated slight hyperenhancement of the lesion at 11 seconds, peak at 14 seconds with a wedge-shaped hyperenhanced rim, followed by rapid central washout at 22 seconds; the portal and delayed phases showed low enhancement.  
MRI revealed an 18×14 mm mass in segment 6 that was T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense, and diffusion-weighted hyperintense. On Gd-BOPTA–enhanced sequences, there was heterogeneous arterial-phase enhancement with vague margins, rapid washout in portal and delayed phases, low signal in the hepatobiliary phase, and pseudocapsule enhancement.  
After multidisciplinary discussion, malignancy could not be excluded and surgical resection was planned.
title: Lymphoepithelioma-Like Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma Associated with Epstein–Barr Virus and Hepatitis Virus: Case Report and a Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old woman (gravida 3, para 1) was referred after an ultrasound performed during follow-up for a missed abortion revealed an intrauterine cystic lesion. She had no menorrhagia, chronic pelvic pain, or dysmenorrhea. Initial hematologic testing showed a CA125 level of 175 U/ml and a CA19-9 level > 1000 U/ml. Abdominal CT scanning and gastroscopy showed no evidence of gastrointestinal malignancy. She then developed sudden pelvic pain. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Menarche occurred at age 14 with 28-day regular cycles. Pelvic exam revealed an enlarged, retroflexed uterus displaced to the right, with a normal vagina, vulva, and adnexa, and no tenderness or nodules. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin of 102 g/l, CA125 of 642 U/ml, and CA19-9 > 1000 U/ml. 

Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a multilocular cystic mass in the posterior uterine wall; color Doppler imaging was not consistent with a leiomyoma. Ultrasound of the liver, bile ducts, pancreas, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract was unremarkable. Abdominal CT confirmed no abnormal density lesions in the liver, bile duct, pancreas, spleen, or gastrointestinal tract.

Pelvic MRI revealed a 53 × 48 × 41 mm lesion in the posterior uterine wall with high intensity on T2-weighted images and internal fluid levels on T1- and T2-weighted images, consistent with hemorrhagic and simple fluid layering. Hysteroscopy showed a normal uterine cavity and bilaterally patent tubal ostia.
title: Uterine adenomyotic cyst with markedly elevated serum CA19‑9 and CA125 levels: A case report

case_prompt: A 67-year-old man was evaluated for progressive dysphagia and a painless skin nodule on his left shoulder, first noted one month earlier. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperuricemia, and a remote myocardial infarction. He had a 50-pack-year smoking history. On examination, there was a 30 × 25 mm hard, stone-like, red mass on the left shoulder without other skin lesions or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for a mildly elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level of 5.4 ng/mL (normal <5.0 ng/mL). Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT demonstrated hypermetabolic foci in the middle thoracic esophagus (SUVmax 11.0), the right recurrent laryngeal nerve lymph node (SUVmax 4.4), and the left shoulder skin lesion (SUVmax 5.0). Esophagogastroscopy revealed an ulcerative, infiltrative lesion in the middle thoracic esophagus. Endoscopic biopsy of the esophageal lesion showed nests of atypical cells with round to oval or short spindle-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei and scant keratinization. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for cytokeratin 19 and Bcl-2, supporting a diagnosis of basaloid rather than conventional squamous cell carcinoma.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Cutaneous metastasis from esophageal basaloid squamous cell carcinoma: A case report

case_prompt: A 90-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain and coffee-ground emesis. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a tortuous, dilated esophagus with large amounts of retained undigested food. A barium swallow demonstrated markedly decreased lower-esophageal peristalsis with a characteristic bird’s-beak appearance, consistent with achalasia. Manometry was not performed. She underwent endoscopic injection of 80 units of botulinum toxin around the lower esophageal sphincter without intraprocedural complications. The patient initially noted symptomatic improvement and tolerated a diet. Within hours, however, she developed profound neuromuscular weakness of her upper extremities. Neurologic examination revealed 0/5 deltoid strength, 3/5 biceps, 2/5 triceps, 4/5 wrist extension, and 4/5 intrinsic hand muscle strength bilaterally, with decreased tone and absent reflexes in the upper extremities. Sensation was intact. Lower extremity and cranial nerve examinations were unremarkable, and the patient remained alert and conversant.
title: Rapidly Progressive Muscle Paralysis and Acute Respiratory Failure Following Endoscopic Botulinum Toxin Injection

case_prompt:
A male newborn, the third child of healthy nonconsanguineous parents and a twin pregnancy, was referred at 5 days of life for persistent axial hypotonia and poor feeding. He was born at 38+1 weeks by vaginal delivery; birth weight was 2560 g (10th percentile), length 49 cm (25–50th percentile), and head circumference 35 cm (50–75th percentile). Apgar scores were 9 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes due to hypotonia. 

On examination, the infant was alert but hypotonic with poor head control and weak sucking. Notable findings included joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, finger joint contractures, and transient right genu recurvatum. He had a “senile” facial appearance with hypertelorism, down-slanting palpebral fissures, ocular exotropia, arched nose with bulbous tip, high-arched palate, short philtrum, down-turned mouth, thin upper lip, micrognathia, low-set ears, and translucent, lax skin. Cardiac auscultation was normal; peripheral pulses were symmetric.

Ophthalmologic and abdominal ultrasound examinations were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed dilation of the aortic root at the sinuses of Valsalva (13 mm; Z score +3) without insufficiency; the remainder of the aorta was within normal limits. A small patent foramen ovale and patent ductus arteriosus with a hemodynamically insignificant left-to-right shunt were noted.
title: Neonatal presentation of Loeys-Dietz syndrome: two case reports and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 16-month-old pair of twin boys was admitted for persistent skin lesions that began at 12 months of age. They are the product of a non-consanguineous, full-term pregnancy and were breastfed for 7 months before weaning. The parents noted sequential onset of erythema around the mouth in each twin, followed by large areas of sharply demarcated erythema with peeling in the perianal region. Prior topical treatments had been ineffective.

On examination, both boys had normal growth parameters (9–10 kg, 78–79 cm) and no developmental delay. The skin was dry and hyperpigmented, and both appeared lethargic with weak crying; alopecia was absent. They exhibited intermittent episodes of increased irritability. Symmetrical erythematous lesions were present in the perioral region, hands, wrists, knees, feet, genital, and perianal areas.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests. Serum zinc was 4.2 mg/L (reference range 3.7–7.3 mg/L), and alkaline phosphatase was 45 U/L (reference range 37–147 U/L), both within normal limits.
title: Analysis of the relationship between the mutation site of the SLC39A4 gene and acrodermatitis enteropathica by reporting a rare Chinese twin: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 62-year-old man presented with sudden right upper limb weakness and loss of consciousness. Brain MRI revealed a well-defined lesion in the left parietal lobe, which was excised. Histopathology of the brain lesion showed glandular and papillary architecture with high-grade nuclei and frequent mitoses, and the tumor was diffusely positive for CK7 and thyroid transcription factor 1, consistent with metastatic adenocarcinoma. He underwent whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT for staging. PET/CT demonstrated focal FDG uptake in a prevascular mediastinal node and low-grade uptake in a left lung consolidation. Additionally, there was a large, well-defined enhancing soft-tissue mass arising from the prostate and seminal vesicle that showed no FDG uptake. Serum prostate-specific antigen level was 0.3 ng/mL.
journal: Indian Journal of Nuclear Medicine : IJNM : The Official Journal of the Society of Nuclear Medicine, India
title: Primary Neuroendocrine Tumor of Prostate in a Case of Metastatic Adenocarcinoma of Lung: Rare Entity with Histopathological and Gallium 68 DOTANOC Positron Emission Tomography Correlation

case_prompt: A 45-year-old Chinese woman presented with anterior chest pain of 10 days’ duration. Review of systems was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, vital signs, physical findings, and routine laboratory tests were normal. Enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a 2.4×1.4×2.8 cm nodule beneath the left thyroid lobe, mild bilateral pulmonary inflammation, and a 4.0×2.5 cm mass in the anterior mediastinum; both lesions demonstrated increased density on enhanced images similar to thyroid tissue. Serum thyrotropin and free thyroid hormone levels were within normal limits, and antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies were negative. Neck ultrasonography showed multiple hypoechoic nodules in the left upper lobe (largest, 0.6×0.4 cm) and right lower lobe (largest, 1.2×1.0 cm) with normal color Doppler flow; a separate 2.4×1.4×2.8 cm nodule under the left lobe had low-level Doppler flow and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy demonstrated no increased uptake in either the left-lobe nodule or the anterior mediastinal mass.
title: Ectopic thyroid mass in the left lateral neck and anterior mediastinum: a case report

case_prompt: A 26-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman was referred at 24 weeks’ gestation for routine fetal ultrasonography. The fetal presentation was breech. The maximum amniotic fluid pocket measured 34 mm. On cardiac imaging, a bidirectional flow with an interval of about 1.2 mm was seen at the muscular ventricular septum. In the abdominal view, the fetal bladder was not visualized, the external genitalia appeared ambiguous, and the “target loop” sign of the anus was obscured. Through a defect in the right anterior abdominal wall adjacent to the umbilical cord insertion, a 35 × 23 mm herniation of intestine and part of the liver was observed, partially encapsulated. No right kidney was detected in the renal fossa or elsewhere. The conus medullaris was low-lying, with a 9.3 × 5.0 mm anechoic cyst connecting to the spinal canal at the lumbosacral level. The left thigh ended blindly without a lower leg; a long bone arose from the thigh root into the pelvis and connected distally to a foot with a fixed posture and only two toes. The right foot also demonstrated fixed posture and clubbing. A single umbilical artery was present. Fetal cordocentesis revealed a normal female karyotype, 46,XX.
title: Prenatal ultrasound‐based diagnosis of fetal OEIS complex associated with lower limb polymelia and cardiac, hepatic dysplasia: A case report

case_prompt: A 65-year-old woman presented with a self-palpated small lump in the left breast. Her history included three prior lumpectomies for benign lesions; she took no medications and had no family history of breast cancer. On examination, a 19 × 14 × 19 mm nodule was palpable medially at 9 o’clock in the left breast. Mammography and ultrasound showed a spherical, homogeneous, non-cystic, well-defined mass situated close to the pectoralis major muscle, with imaging features suspicious for muscle invasion. Doppler ultrasonography revealed prominent perilesional and peripheral vascularization. Several enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes were noted. Core needle biopsies (CNBs) were obtained from the breast lesion and one enlarged axillary lymph node. The breast CNB showed a sharply defined spindle cell lesion separated from surrounding fat: variable cellularity with bland spindle cells in dense collagenous stroma or loose myxoid areas, no infiltrative permeation, and absent mitotic figures. The axillary lymph node biopsy showed no malignancy. Due to discordance between the radiological suspicion of malignancy and the bland CNB findings, a complete local excision was performed. Grossly, the 19 mm nodule was sharply delineated, white, and firm, with regular borders and an 8 mm surgical margin. Histologically, the resection specimen showed small clusters of epithelioid cells with vesicular nuclei and occasional mitoses, focal invasion into adipose tissue with entrapped ducts and lymphocytes, and a central scar-like sclerotic zone. Immunohistochemical studies of the spindle cells revealed diffuse positivity for α-SMA, p63, and cytokeratin AE1/AE3; focal positivity for S100, desmin, and caldesmon; negativity for ER, PR, HER2, CD34, Bcl-2, CD10, and ALK; β-catenin showed cytoplasmic but no nuclear staining; and the Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 2%.
title: Fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 54‐year‐old Caucasian woman presented with a 10‐year history of mild postprandial abdominal pain and a sensation of fullness. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hypercholesterolemia. She was obese (body‐mass index, 31 kg/m2). On examination, abdominal inspection and palpation were unremarkable; there was mildly increased tympany on periumbilical percussion, and bowel sounds were normal. The remainder of the physical examination and routine laboratory tests were normal.

An abdominal CT scan with oral contrast revealed a well‐circumscribed, retroperitoneal mass measuring 16 × 14 × 7 cm arising from the left adrenal gland and surrounded by a thin capsule. The lesion exhibited both adipose‐tissue density and soft‐tissue elements, with Hounsfield units consistent with fat. It abutted but did not invade adjacent structures, including small intestine, pancreas, spleen, and left kidney. No lymphadenopathy or vascular invasion was noted.
title: A giant adrenal lipoma presenting in a woman with chronic mild postprandial abdominal pain: a case report

case_prompt: A previously healthy 2-year-old girl from rural Telangana presented with a 5-day history of fever, 1 day of altered sensorium, and a single 10-minute generalized tonic–clonic seizure. There was no rash, recent vaccination, or toxin exposure. On arrival she was stuporous but hemodynamically stable, with no respiratory compromise. Funduscopic examination was normal, and there were no signs of meningeal irritation. Initial laboratory studies showed normal liver and renal function, electrolytes, blood glucose, serum albumin, and ammonia. A complete blood count revealed 7170 leukocytes/mm3 and 210 000 platelets/mm3. Dengue NS1 antigen and serum IgM were positive. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated 90 cells/mm3 (80% lymphocytes), protein 90.45 mg/dL, and glucose 62 mg/dL (67% of blood glucose), consistent with viral encephalitis. Electroencephalography showed generalized slowing. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast was normal.
title: Dengue Encephalitis in Children “Not an Uncommon Entity but Is Rarely Thought of”: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old Indian woman presented with a 2-year history of a swelling on the right side of her neck. Two years earlier, she underwent a wide local excision of a similar lesion, with histopathology revealing a granular cell tumor that extended to the excision margin. She was lost to follow-up. Her medical history is notable for moderately controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and glimepiride and a remote thyroidectomy for colloid goiter. She is normotensive, does not smoke or drink, and has no family history of cancer.

On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm nodular, mobile, firm swelling on the right side of the neck. It did not move with tongue protrusion or swallowing. No other swellings were found, and systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, WBC 8000/mm³ (70% neutrophils), fasting blood sugar 166 mg/dL, and post-prandial blood sugar 179 mg/dL. Given her history and clinical findings, there was a high suspicion for recurrence of a granular cell tumor.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Recurrent primary cutaneous granular cell tumor of the neck in an Asian women: A case report

case_prompt: A 63-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a waxing and waning, tender rash in the intergluteal cleft. He had applied topical terbinafine 1%, tolnaftate 1%, clotrimazole 1%, triple antibiotic cream, and hydrocortisone 1% without improvement. His medical history was notable for primary sclerosing cholangitis status post liver transplantation 5 years earlier (on mycophenolate mofetil and tacrolimus) and melanoma in situ on the left heel 3 years earlier. On examination, there were pink plaques with numerous coalescing “punched out” erosions symmetrically affecting the superior intergluteal cleft and bilateral buttocks in a “kissing” distribution; no satellite lesions were seen. The differential diagnosis included herpetic infection, extramammary Paget disease, intertrigo, and allergic or irritant contact dermatitis. Initial work-up included a viral swab, which was negative for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus.
title: Skin-limited Langerhans cell histiocytosis in an adult presenting as isolated, eroded, “kissing” intergluteal plaques

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and disseminated tuberculosis, including tuberculous meningoencephalitis, was readmitted 80 days after initiation of anti-TB therapy and 4 weeks after her last intravenous cyclophosphamide infusion for lupus nephritis. She had a 2-week history of progressive postural instability, diplopia, inattention, vertical gaze palsy, and myoclonic jerks. Vital signs were stable. Neurologic examination confirmed vertical gaze palsy, dysmetria, and profound inattention but no focal motor weakness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mild hyperproteinorrachia (68 mg/dL) without pleocytosis. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed:
• A T1-hyperintense, T2/FLAIR-hypointense lesion in the left lateral sulcus at the frontotemporal junction, with perilesional vasogenic edema and ring contrast enhancement abutting the middle cerebral artery at the M1–M2 transition  
• Smaller contrast-enhancing lesions adjacent to the left cavernous sinus and in the right lateral sulcus  
• Contrast enhancement of the left oculomotor nerve in its cisternal segment  
• Bilateral thalamic ischemic lesions
title: Paradoxical Reaction during Treatment of Tuberculous Meningoencephalitis in a Patient with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman with spina bifida and congenital proximal femoral focal deficiency has been wheelchair-bound for 40 years. She had a chronic right buttock pressure ulcer, previously treated surgically with initial healing followed by recurrence. She self-managed the wound for the past 29 years without specialist care. Several months before presentation, she noted severe pain and progressive enlargement of the ulcer and sought help from community nurses.

On examination, the buttock and sacral wound measured 17 cm × 8 cm × 9 cm. The ulcer bed was 100% granulation tissue with rolled edges and surrounding chronic blanching purple skin changes. The wound edges showed excessive granulation, were nodular, fragile, and easily bled. There was no foul odor, sinus drainage, or other clinical signs of infection.

Magnetic resonance imaging was attempted but not tolerated, so computed tomography was performed. CT showed a large circumferential pressure ulcer on the right buttock with markedly hypertrophied, lobulated margins and extension to the posterior cortex of the proximal femur. Chronic periosteitis and cortical sclerosis were present, with new cortical erosions compared to prior imaging. A few enlarged regional lymph nodes were noted.

MRI findings of the ulcer margins demonstrated a 4-cm-thick mass-like appearance with low signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on T2-weighted and STIR images. The posterior femoral cortex showed mild subcortical edema at STIR but no marrow replacement on T1WI.

The imaging findings were not conclusive for osteomyelitis, but the unusual ulcer margins prompted referral for specialist opinion and incisional biopsy of the ulcer edge.
title: Radiological appearances of metastatic Marjolin ulcer in a chronic pressure sore: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 49-year-old woman presented with painless swelling in her right inguinal region. She had a history of a cesarean section and no history of infantile inguinal hernia. On physical examination, there was a soft, egg-shaped mass extending from the right inguinal region to the labia majora; the mass was visible when she stood and disappeared when she lay down. Ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, hypo-echoic, elongated mass that extended from the superficial inguinal canal, with no solid component. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 55 × 34 × 95 mm oval fluid collection in the right inguinal region adjacent to the cecum and retroperitoneum. Total colonoscopy demonstrated no mucosal abnormalities but revealed an extrinsic mass pushing against the cecal wall.
final_diagnosis_raw: Hydrocele of the canal of Nuck
title: Large hydrocele of the canal of Nuck diagnosed and treated using conventional and laparoscopic methods

case_prompt: A 41-year-old African-American woman presented with an enlarging, painful mass in the right knee area. Four years earlier, she had been treated for osteosarcoma of the same leg with neoadjuvant docetaxel and gemcitabine, radical resection, and hinge-knee replacement. Six months after an initial biopsy of the new mass (reported elsewhere as a high-grade soft-tissue sarcoma), she returned with marked growth of the right-knee mass and increased pain, with decreased range of motion. On examination, there was a 150×200 mm hard, fixed, tender mass around the right knee and a 15×20 mm hard, mildly tender right inguinal lymph node. No rash, edema, or sensory deficits were present; distal pulses were intact. Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 126.7×10^9/L with neutrophils 57.02×10^9/L and eosinophils 60.82×10^9/L, peaking on hospital day 5 with eosinophils 77.79×10^9/L. A bone-marrow biopsy revealed marked eosinophilia and neutrophilia without increased blast cells. Testing for JAK2 mutation was negative as was flow cytometry. Additional investigations included IgE 3 IU/mL, C3 174 mg/dL, C4 35 mg/dL, haemolytic complement 276 units, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody negative.
title: Eosinophilic and neutrophilic leukemoid reaction in a woman with spindle cell sarcoma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive difficulty swallowing. She had no other neurological complaints. On examination, she was found to have right hypoglossal nerve palsy; no other deficits were noted. Her medical history was notable for breast cancer, treated successfully several years earlier.

A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed bone erosion extending from the right hypoglossal canal to the anterior aspect of the foramen magnum. MRI of the brain demonstrated a lesion within the right hypoglossal canal that was hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images and iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted images. After administration of gadolinium, the lesion exhibited irregular peripheral enhancement. A cerebral angiogram showed no tumor stain. PET-CT revealed no abnormal uptake in the lesion or elsewhere.

Based on these findings, the preoperative differential diagnosis included schwannoma of the hypoglossal nerve, chordoma, breast cancer metastasis, and chondroma.
title: Chondroma in the hypoglossal canal: A case report

journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A case report on POEMS syndrome with high parathyroid hormone and repeated surgery, a rare presentation of a rare disease

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a cyclically painful suprapubic lump beneath the scar of a prior laparoscopic port. Her medical history was notable for a laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy for leiomyomas performed 1 year earlier; no endometriosis was noted at the time, and the morcellated uterine corpus was removed in a sealed bag through the right iliac port. On examination, there was a hard, fixed mass adherent to the underlying layers of the abdominal wall under the suprapubic trocar scar.

An ultrasound scan revealed a 4-cm inhomogeneous mass with mild vascularization, extending from the rectus muscle to the subcutaneous fat. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a 36×32×26 mm solid, irregularly shaped mass with heterogeneous high contrast enhancement, infiltrating from the subcutaneous tissue to the transversalis fascia.

To rule out malignancy, a through-cut needle biopsy was performed, yielding a diagnosis of endometriosis. The patient was started on dienogest (2 mg daily). Over the next two months, her pain resolved, but the mass remained stable in size.
title: Trocar scar abdominal wall adenomyoma following laparoscopic hysterectomy: case report

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old Bangladeshi man with no prior medical history was referred with a 4-day history of fever and a 1-month history of progressive fatigue and a 6-kg weight loss. He denied night sweats, respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms, viral prodrome, sick contacts, and recent travel. On examination, he had painless bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, jaundice, and pallor. 

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 5.9 g/dL, reticulocyte count 5.4%, total bilirubin 57.1 µmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 546 U/L, haptoglobin <10 mg/dL, and a positive direct antiglobulin test. Platelet count was 108 × 10^3/µL, ferritin 1222 µg/L, with low serum iron, transferrin, and total iron-binding capacity, and low vitamin B12. Peripheral smear revealed anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, target cells, spherocytes, red-cell fragments, and nucleated red cells. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated centrilobular lung nodular opacities, bilateral hilar, mediastinal, and abdominal lymphadenopathy, and marked osteopenia. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia secondary to lymphoma was suspected, and the patient underwent an excisional biopsy of a left cervical lymph node.
title: An atypical presentation of Kikuchi‐Fujimoto disease: A case report & literature review

case_prompt: A 42-year-old Chinese woman with no prior medical history presented with 8 days of bilateral progressive blurring of vision without pain, photophobia, headache, or systemic symptoms. Examination revealed visual acuity of hand motion in the right eye and finger counting in the left, bilateral red desaturation, sluggish pupillary light reflexes with a right relative afferent pupillary defect, normal intraocular pressures, and normal anterior segments. Fundoscopic exam showed pink discs with sharp margins and 0.3 cup-to-disc ratios bilaterally. Neurologic examination was unremarkable, with intact cranial nerves, full limb strength, brisk symmetric reflexes, downgoing plantar responses, and no cerebellar signs. MRI of the brain with contrast demonstrated bilateral optic nerve enlargement with T2-weighted hyperintensity and enhancement, radiologic evidence of limbic and cortical encephalitis, subcortical and pontine myelitis, and leptomeningitis. Blood tests revealed normal blood counts, liver and renal function, and inflammatory markers; nonreactive VDRL; negative Lyme serology; and negative antinuclear, anti–double-stranded DNA, anti-extractable nuclear antigen, rheumatoid factor, anti–aquaporin 4, anti–myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, anti–voltage-gated potassium channel, and anti–N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antibodies. Paraneoplastic antibody screen, including anti–neuronal nuclear antibodies types I and II, anti-CRMP5, anti-Yo, anti-Ri, and anti-Hu, was negative. Tumor markers were within normal limits. CSF analysis showed normal opening pressure, cell count, and biochemistry, absence of oligoclonal bands, and negative microbiological studies including bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, cryptococcal antigen, HSV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, and VDRL. Whole-body PET-CT demonstrated no hypermetabolic lesions or tumor foci.
title: Optic neuritis as the initial clinical presentation of limbic encephalitis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of nausea, vomiting, and epigastric discomfort. She denied weight loss, additional gastrointestinal symptoms, fevers, or night sweats. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Physical examination was normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a normal-sized spleen with heterogeneous parenchyma and multiple hypoechoic nodules up to 1.0 cm in diameter. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI confirmed multiple splenic nodules with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and homogeneous enhancement; the largest lesion measured 1.0 cm.  
PET-CT demonstrated no fluorodeoxyglucose uptake. An extensive work-up for occult malignancy and infectious disease was negative.
journal: JSLS : Journal of the Society of Laparoendoscopic Surgeons
title: Laparoscopic Splenectomy for Isolated Splenic Sarcoidosis

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old man initially presented with daily vertigo triggered by head movements, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and difficulty maintaining balance in confined spaces. His examination was notable only for right-sided high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss; half a year later, an MRI of the cerebellum and cerebellopontine angle was normal. He was diagnosed with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo and given home exercises.  

Three years later, he re-presented with a persistent, non-positional balance disturbance and reported difficulty detecting fast-moving objects in his lateral visual fields. Neurologic evaluation showed bilateral horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, a tandem gait below age expectation, unsteadiness with eyes closed, and a right-predominant positive Dix–Hallpike test. Audiometry again confirmed right high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and repeat contrast-enhanced MRI with thin slices remained unremarkable.  

Six months after that, he developed progressive balance difficulty, slowed information processing with typing errors, dysarthria, decreased vision with diplopia, and photophobia. Neurologic examination revealed a broad-based ataxic gait; right-eye hypometria; spontaneous torsional nystagmus with left-eye extorsion that increased on downward right gaze; horizontal saccades; and dysdiadochokinesis on the right. There was no hypotonia, dysmetria, headache, or vomiting. Caloric testing showed bilateral hyperreactivity. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and serum studies, including Borrelia testing, were normal.  

Repeat MRI demonstrated a diffuse T2-hyperintense signal on the dorsolateral aspect of the fourth ventricle extending into the cerebellar vermis bilaterally, subtle diffusion restriction, and nodular contrast enhancement. Compared with earlier scans, the lesion had progressed but exerted no clear mass effect.
title: Adult-onset medulloblastoma presenting as slow-growing, atypical mass: a case report

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old man with refractory mixed‐cellularity classical Hodgkin lymphoma began nivolumab at 3 mg/m2 every two weeks after progression on multiple lines of therapy. The medication was well tolerated until after the sixth infusion, when he noted new skin lesions.

On examination, there were raised, non‐itchy, erythematous, scaly papules with a silver-white coating and some annular plaques with collarettes of scale of varying sizes on the anterolateral shins, dorsae of the hands, distal forearms, and both tibias. The Köbner phenomenon was not observed.

The clinical differential diagnosis included psoriasis vulgaris, erythema annulare, and tinea circinata. To confirm the diagnosis, a 5 mm punch skin biopsy was obtained from the right tibia.
title: De Novo Psoriasis Vulgaris Diagnosed after Nivolumab Treatment for Refractory Hodgkin's Lymphoma, Completely Resolved after Autologous Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation

case_prompt: A 55-year-old postmenopausal, nulligravida woman presented with a 2-month history of a protruding umbilical mass. She had no personal or family history of gynecologic or breast cancer. On examination, she was afebrile, pale, and asthenic. The umbilical lesion measured 5 × 4 cm, appeared necrotic, and bled on contact. Laboratory studies revealed severe hypochromic microcytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 5 g/dL. Pelvic ultrasonography showed an enlarged uterus (12 × 7 cm) with an indistinct endometrial outline and nonvisualized adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a pelvic soft-tissue mass measuring 93 × 80 × 90 mm, peritoneal carcinomatosis nodules, secondary involvement of the cutaneous umbilical region, and a large umbilical hernia. MRI depicted a large pedunculated mass on the anterior cervical wall (95 × 80 mm). A skin-punch biopsy of the umbilical lesion revealed a proliferation of atypical tumor cells exhibiting both epithelial and mesenchymal characteristics, suggesting a biphasic neoplasm.
title: The discovery of uterine carcinosarcoma through a sister mary joseph's nodule: A case report
