case_prompt: A 4-year-old child presented with a 1-week history of oliguria, weakness, anorexia, vomiting, and abdominal pain. There was no significant past medical history. On examination, the child had mild edema and hypertension (blood pressure 125/80 mm Hg). Laboratory studies showed: normal complete blood count; serum creatinine 130 µmol/L (normal 27–60); blood urea nitrogen 11 mmol/L (normal 2.5–6.4); uric acid 6.5 mg/dL (normal 1.7–5.9); sodium 140 mmol/L; potassium 4.5 mmol/L; lactate dehydrogenase 540 IU/L (normal 150–500); and normal liver enzymes. Urinalysis revealed no leukocytes, blood cells, or proteins. Renal ultrasound demonstrated diffuse enlargement of both kidneys, hypoechoic with loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed bilateral nephromegaly with multiple hypoenhancing areas of poorly defined margins relative to normal parenchyma and no hydronephrosis. No lesions were seen in other organs, and there were no enlarged abdominal lymph nodes. Differential diagnoses included acute tubular necrosis, pyelonephritis, acute papillary necrosis, and renal lymphoma.
title: A rare case of bilateral primary renal Burkitt lymphoma presenting with acute renal failure

case_prompt: A 71-year-old man was referred after a routine chest radiograph showed abnormal shadows. He was asymptomatic and had no significant medical history. Vital signs were within normal limits, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed slight elevations in angiotensin-converting enzyme (21.7 U/L), KL-6 (778 U/mL), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (743 U/mL); lysozyme was normal. Urinalysis showed mildly increased N-acetyl-β-glucosaminidase and β2-microglobulin without hypercalcemia or pyuria. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated multiple low-density lesions of variable sizes in the spleen. Chest CT revealed patchy consolidations in the right upper lobe and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial lung biopsy yielded no specific diagnostic findings.
title: Sarcoidosis with Splenic Involvement Diagnosed with Endoscopic Ultrasound-guided Fine-needle Aspiration

case_prompt: A 32‐year‐old man presented with a 1‐year history of slow‐growing, painless swelling around his right eye. The patient had sustained facial injuries in a motor‐vehicle accident 1 year earlier but did not seek treatment. He reported no visual disturbance or breathing difficulty. On examination, there were two swellings—one measuring 3×2 cm at the lower lateral aspect of the right eye and another 4×3 cm lateral to the right nasolabial groove. Both were fluctuant, mobile, non‐tender, with normal overlying skin. Visual acuity was intact, extraocular movements were full, and there was no diplopia. Fine‐needle aspiration via an intraoral route yielded a cheesy‐white granular aspirate, which was sent for cytological analysis. Non‐contrast CT of the face showed a cystic lesion extending from the lateral globe through a fracture line at the lateral orbital wall into the temporal fossa, and a second 4×3 cm cystic lesion below the inferior orbital rim. A 1‐cm bone discontinuity at the lateral orbital wall indicated a non‐union of an inferiorly displaced zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture, with increased right orbital volume but no prior visual symptoms.
title: Posttraumatic Epidermoid Inclusion Cyst Following Untreated Orbital‐Zygomaticomaxillary Fracture: Case Report

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old woman presented with 3 weeks of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by shortness of breath, cough, fatigue, and loss of appetite. She denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Three days before symptom onset, she had undergone a medical termination of pregnancy. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable.

On examination, blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, pulse 72/min, respiratory rate 28/min, temperature 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation 85% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed dullness and decreased air entry over the lower thirds of both posterior lung fields. Abdominal examination showed marked distension with positive shifting dullness and a fluid thrill. The skin was coarse and dry on trunk and extremities; there was no palpable thyroid enlargement.

Laboratory studies showed moderate anemia, normal liver enzymes and creatinine, a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 49 μIU/mL, free T3 of 1.1 pg/mL, and free T4 of 0.3 ng/mL. Tests for antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and HIV were negative. Analysis of pleural fluid revealed 1 200 cells/μL (93.3% lymphocytes), protein 5.6 g/dL, LDH 704 U/L, and glucose 47 mg/dL, consistent with an exudative effusion. Echocardiography showed mild pericardial effusion, and abdominal ultrasound confirmed ascites. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions. Thyroid ultrasound revealed heterogeneous echogenicity of both lobes measuring 0.4 mL, suggesting atrophy.
title: Polyserositis caused by tuberculosis in a young female patient with hypothyroidism: A diagnostic challenge

case_prompt: A 58-year-old African-American woman presented with several months of left lower quadrant abdominal pain. She had no jaundice or weight loss. Vital signs were stable. Physical examination was unremarkable except for mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed carcinoembryonic antigen 6.5 ng/mL (normal 0–5.0) and CA 19-9 of 39 U/mL (normal 0–37). Functional endocrine hormone studies revealed a gastrin level of 214 pg/mL (mildly elevated) with normal insulin, glucagon, and vasoactive intestinal peptide levels. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 3.8 cm hypervascular, well-circumscribed mass in the head of the pancreas without evidence of vascular invasion or distant metastasis. Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration was nondiagnostic.
title: Solitary fibrous tumor of the pancreas

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old woman was referred in February 2021 for evaluation of an adnexal mass. Her history was notable for HCV-related hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosed in 2009 (Edmonson and Steiner grade 2, pT2 N0 M0, G2, V1), treated with left hepatectomy and cholecystectomy. Preoperative AFP had been 8600 ng/mL and fell to 2.7 ng/mL postoperatively; there was no cirrhosis and no other disease localization at that time.

At routine follow-up in October 2020, serum AFP had risen to 467 ng/mL and CA-125 was borderline at 37.4 U/mL. Liver function tests were normal and imaging of the residual liver showed no lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed bilateral ovarian enlargement, more pronounced on the left (55 × 33 × 58 mm) with solid-cystic features and calcifications; there was a small pelvic fluid collection but no lymphadenopathy or peritoneal disease. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed a left multilocular-solid ovarian cyst measuring 62 × 23 × 34 mm with a color score of 2 (IOTA risk of malignancy 59.6%) and mild pelvic effusion.

After multidisciplinary review, the patient underwent laparoscopic left ovariectomy and peritoneal biopsies. Intraoperative frozen section demonstrated a tumor with solid trabecular architecture and atypical cells with a high mitotic index, requiring further characterization. A laparotomic hysterectomy, right oophorectomy, pelvic peritonectomy, and omentectomy were then performed, with no residual macroscopic disease.
title: A Rare Case of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Recurrence in Ovarian Site after 12 Years Mimicking a Hepatoid Adenocarcinoma: Case Report

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old previously healthy man was referred for evaluation of a suspected inguinal hernia after noticing a right lower quadrant abdominal mass 5 days earlier. He reported no abdominal pain, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal palpation revealed a non-tender mass in the right lower quadrant that did not enlarge with Valsalva maneuver.  
Ultrasonography demonstrated a 10.4 × 6.6 cm mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 9.5 × 7.1 × 9.1 cm pear-shaped intra-abdominal mass lying along the right ureter and surrounded by loops of small bowel, without apparent invasion of adjacent structures. A congenital malrotation of the small intestine was noted incidentally.  
Before tissue diagnosis, the differential diagnosis included sarcoma, lymphoma, and desmoid-type fibromatosis.
title: Spontaneous regression of a sporadic intra-abdominal located desmoid-type fibromatosis

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old boy presented with unsteady standing since age 1. Over three years, he developed gradually worsening restriction of movement in the right knee and a slowly enlarging mass on the inner aspect of the right distal femur and adjacent soft tissues. On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm firm, tender mass at the medial right knee.  
Plain radiographs of the right femur showed irregularly reduced medullary density in the metaphysis. CT imaging confirmed asymmetrical medullary hypodensity with multiple small cystic areas, irregular cortical thickening, and proximal soft-tissue swelling, without an obvious periosteal reaction.  
The lesion was curetted. Seventeen months later, MRI revealed a local recurrence at the operative site.
title: Clinical and pathological characteristics of giant cell angioblastoma: a case report

case_prompt: A 29-year-old man with ulcerative colitis presented two months after re-induction with vedolizumab for a disease flare. Laboratory tests showed alanine aminotransferase 348 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 238 U/L, gamma glutamyl transferase 308 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 89 U/L, and total bilirubin 15 μmol/L. His complete blood count was notable for an absolute eosinophil count of 3.22 × 10^9/L. A workup revealed positive hepatitis A total antibody (IgM-negative) and negative hepatitis B and C serologies; normal ceruloplasmin, alpha-1 antitrypsin, immunoglobulins, and ferritin; and negative anti-mitochondrial and anti–smooth muscle antibodies, with antinuclear antibodies positive at a titer of 1:160. An infectious screen—including human immunodeficiency virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Toxoplasma, Fasciola, Toxocara, and Trichinella—was negative, and although previous exposure to schistosomiasis was identified, it was not believed to be causing this presentation. Parasitic infections and myeloproliferative neoplasia were excluded. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver and biliary system. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided liver biopsy demonstrated multifocal, predominantly portal chronic inflammation consistent with early primary sclerosing cholangitis and foci of inflammation containing small-to-moderate numbers of eosinophils.
title: Vedolizumab-Associated Hypereosinophilia and Hepatoxicity

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 20-month-old boy was evaluated for progressive generalized swelling. Two weeks before presentation, his parents noted mild periorbital edema that steadily progressed to abdominal distension and bilateral lower-extremity edema. Around the time the edema began, he developed up to 5 to 6 loose, nonbloody stools per day. His diet routinely included more than 28 ounces of cow’s milk per day. 

At a pediatrician’s office, laboratory studies showed an albumin level of 1.8 g/dL and a urinalysis negative for protein. On transfer to the emergency department, results were notable for hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 69 fL, ferritin 4.9 ng/mL, albumin 1.6 g/dL, total protein 3.0 g/dL, and fecal α-1-antitrypsin beyond the upper limit of quantification (>1.13 mg/g). Stool tested positive for occult blood. 

Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy were performed. The mucosa lining the upper and lower gastrointestinal tract appeared grossly normal. Histologic examination revealed only a mild increase in eosinophils in the gastric antrum and otherwise normal-appearing mucosa without acute or chronic inflammation in the esophagus, duodenum, colon, or rectum.
final_diagnosis_raw: Protein-losing enteropathy secondary to iron deficiency anemia
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Protein-Losing Enteropathy in the Setting of Severe Iron Deficiency Anemia

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of anemia. Over the prior month, she had experienced progressive fatigue and malaise but denied fever or weight loss. Her medical history included mild mitral and aortic valve insufficiency and atrial fibrillation, managed with digitalis, an ACE inhibitor, and acenocoumarol (target INR, 2.5). 

On examination, she was pale and afebrile, with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. 

Laboratory studies revealed:  
– Hemoglobin, 7.2 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 94.8 fL  
– White blood cell count, 3,400/µL (56% neutrophils, 38% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, 1% eosinophils)  
– Platelet count, 756,000/µL; peripheral smear showed giant platelets without dysplastic features or leukoerythroblastic changes  
– Serum ferritin, 12× upper limit of normal; lactate dehydrogenase, 1.8× upper limit of normal; other chemistries within normal limits  

Bone marrow aspiration yielded a “dry tap.” Core biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow with marked reticulin fibrosis; prominent megakaryocytic hyperplasia with clustering and dysplastic under- or non-lobulated nuclei; few (<5%) small CD61-positive cells with prominent nucleoli lacking CD34 expression; myeloid hyperplasia with left shift and normal blast count; and diminished erythroid precursors.  

Molecular testing for BCR-ABL and JAK2 V617F mutations was negative.
title: Successful Control of Acute Myelofibrosis with Lenalidomide

case_prompt: A 29-year-old woman at 28 weeks’ gestation, with an unremarkable medical history and well-documented prenatal care, presented with a 2-day history of right iliac fossa pain and nausea. She denied fever, gastrointestinal disturbances, or urinary symptoms. On examination, she appeared distressed but was afebrile; blood pressure was 120/70 mm Hg and heart rate 80 bpm. Abdominal palpation elicited tenderness in the right iliac fossa; the gravid uterus extended to the supraumbilical region, and no mass was palpable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 11,900/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 23 mg/L; renal function and electrolytes were normal. An emergency abdominal ultrasound revealed aerocolia, failure to visualize the appendix, no free fluid, and poorly visualized adnexa. A gynecological consultation including pelvic examination and transvaginal ultrasound showed no adnexal masses, no ovarian tenderness, a closed cervix with no discharge or bleeding, and a uterus consistent with gestational age; fetal heart tones were present and regular. There was no evidence of pelvic inflammatory disease or ectopic pregnancy. Gynecological emergencies were thus ruled out, and a presumptive diagnosis of appendicitis was made, prompting a laparotomy via a McBurney incision.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare case report: Management of paratubal cyst torsion in the second trimester and literature review

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old previously healthy man presented with 1 day of worsening tachypnea and dyspnea. He reported intermittent fevers, myalgia, and headache for 1 week after returning from a 2-week trip to Costa Rica, with initial symptoms beginning 1 day before his return flight. On examination in the emergency department, his temperature was 38.6 °C, blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 35 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 82% on room air. He was alert (GCS 15) but in respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest radiograph showed bilateral pulmonary opacities. He was intubated after failing to improve on 100% nonrebreather. Arterial blood gas on 100% FiO₂ showed PaO₂ 65 mmHg. Basic blood tests, including electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, and coagulation studies, were normal.

In the ICU, he met Berlin criteria for ARDS with a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 110, bilateral infiltrates, and no evidence of cardiac dysfunction. Ventilation followed a low–tidal volume strategy (5 mL/kg ideal body weight, target pH >7.25) with PEEP up to 10 cm H₂O. Blood, urine, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cultures were sent. Bronchoscopy revealed no pulmonary hemorrhage or purulent secretions. Chest CT confirmed bilateral edema without focal consolidation. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated normal biventricular function and no valvular abnormalities. Empiric piperacillin–tazobactam, azithromycin, and vancomycin were started. Initial blood, urine, and BAL cultures were negative. Malaria thick and thin smears were repeatedly negative. Dengue serology, HIV, and hepatitis A, B, and C tests were all negative. Despite broad-spectrum antimicrobials, his respiratory status worsened, necessitating prone ventilation.
title: Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure from Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Secondary to Leptospirosis

case_prompt: A previously healthy 1-year-old boy was referred with a 15-day history of 6–7 mucoid, nonbloody diarrheal stools per day, abdominal distension, irritability, and fever spikes up to 39.8 °C. On examination, he appeared ill, with marked abdominal distension, a palpable abdominal mass, decreased bowel sounds, and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Initial laboratory tests showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, a C-reactive protein level of 97.1 mg/dL, and mild hyponatremia; liver and renal function, electrolytes (apart from sodium), and blood glucose were within normal limits, and stool examination revealed no parasites. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a multiseptate fluid collection occupying the right abdomen and displacing bowel loops; plain abdominal radiography showed opacification of the right hemiabdomen with displacement of bowel loops to the left without air-fluid levels or calcifications.
title: Male infant patient with a mesenteric cyst in the greater and lesser omenta: a case report

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old premenopausal woman presented with a 3-month history of distal hypesthesia and pricking paresthesia in the upper extremities that progressed to severe distal-accentuated weakness (Medical Research Council grade 3/5 in upper and 2/5 in lower extremities). All extremities were affected by severe hypesthesia; vibration sense was preserved. She became wheelchair bound and required assistance for activities of daily living (modified Rankin score 4).  

Her medical history was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal electrolytes, coagulation profile, renal and liver function, thyroid‐stimulating hormone, C‐reactive protein, and homocysteine, with elevated lipase (68 U/L) and leukocytosis (20.6 G/L). Extended immunologic tests were negative for antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, ANCA, AMA/LKM-1, cryoglobulins, cold agglutinins, and antineuronal antibodies (anti-Yo, ‑Hu, ‑Ri). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild protein elevation (0.59 g/L; normal 0.21–0.42 g/L) without evidence of active infection.  

Nerve conduction studies demonstrated absent sensory potentials in the radial and sural nerves and reduced conduction velocities with decreased compound muscle action–potential amplitudes in the tibial and median nerves. Electromyography of the anterior tibial muscle showed no spontaneous activity. Cranial and spinal MRI and CT of the chest and abdomen were unremarkable.  

To further evaluate, a sural nerve biopsy was performed, revealing advanced axonal neuropathy with moderate microangiopathy. High-dose corticosteroid therapy (75 mg daily) and pregabalin were initiated.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Endometrial Carcinoma Presenting as Vasculitic Sensorimotor Polyneuropathy

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old female with obesity, prediabetes, and marijuana use presented with a 1-month history of left frontotemporal and retro-orbital headaches accompanied by photophobia, nausea, vomiting, and localized numbness over the left temple. The headaches, which often awakened her from sleep, became constant over the 3 weeks before presentation. Over the preceding 2 weeks she developed persistent binocular diplopia progressing to complete ophthalmoplegia. She also reported 1 week of intermittent left mandibular pain and new sensory changes over the maxillary (V2) division of the left trigeminal nerve.

On examination, she was afebrile with a blood pressure of 156/83 mmHg and otherwise normal vital signs. She appeared mildly ill. Pupils were 5 mm and briskly reactive to direct light, with sluggish left‐eye consensual response. Funduscopic examination was normal. Extraocular movements of the left eye revealed near‐complete ophthalmoplegia with minimal upward and downward gaze, and marked ptosis consistent with severe oculomotor and abducens nerve palsies. Visual fields were full bilaterally, and there was no facial asymmetry. Trigeminal sensory testing showed left‐sided hyperesthesia in the V1 and V2 distributions.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel (glucose 170 mg/dL), hemoglobin A1c 6.1%, angiotensin‐converting enzyme 14 U/L (reference, 16–85), and negative autoimmune serologies (ANA, CCP, anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, Sm, RNP, Scl-70, Jo-1, RF, MPO, PR3). Lactate dehydrogenase and uric acid were normal; serum electrophoresis showed no monoclonal proteins. Infectious workup was negative for Borrelia burgdorferi, syphilis IgG, CSF VDRL, and QuantiFERON-TB Gold; bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures and acid-fast smear were negative. Lumbar puncture revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid except for lymphocytosis (92%); CSF ACE, IgG index, albumin, and flow cytometry were unremarkable.

MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated an extra-axial enhancing, ill-defined lesion centered in the left cavernous sinus, with extension into Meckel’s cave, superior orbital fissure, orbital apex, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, and the middle cranial fossa, and mild narrowing of the patent right cavernous internal carotid artery.
title: Ophthalmoplegia and cranial nerve deficits in an adolescent with headache

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old girl presented with a one-year history of gradually increasing abdominal swelling. Over the past few months she had experienced urinary urgency and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. She reported intermittent cyclic lower abdominal cramps and denied any episodes of menses. She had no fever, diarrhea, constipation, vomiting, or weight loss. Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, there was a large, non-tender, non-pulsatile abdominal mass extending from the pelvis to the xiphisternum, predominantly on the right side but crossing the midline. Secondary sexual characteristics were appropriate for her age (Tanner stage IV). Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, urinalysis, and pregnancy test, were all within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a large cystic lesion with a thick echoic collection extending from the epigastric region to the pelvis, posterior to the urinary bladder, filling nearly the entire abdominal cavity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a hypodense, non-enhancing, fluid-filled mass within the vaginal canal measuring 28.5 × 11.3 × 12.0 cm, with a small fluid collection in the uterine cavity, and compression of the urinary bladder and distal ureters resulting in moderate bilateral hydroureteronephrosis.
title: Abdominal swelling and obstructive uropathy due to hematometrocolpos secondary to imperforate hymen: a case report

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman with hypertension presented during the COVID-19 pandemic with three weeks of progressive shortness of breath on minimal exertion and fatigue. On arrival she was hypoxic (SpO2 74%) and tachypneic (30 breaths/min), prompting endotracheal intubation. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Soon afterward she developed persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support.

Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm at 70 bpm, a tall R wave in V2, and symmetric T-wave inversions in the precordial leads. A chest radiograph after intubation demonstrated bilateral patchy infiltrates. The initial SARS-CoV-2 PCR test was negative; a repeat test 24 hours later was positive. Laboratory studies revealed a troponin T of 0.07 ng/ml (peak 0.22 ng/ml; reference < 0.01 ng/ml), an NT-proBNP of 12 945 pg/ml, a white-cell count of 21.1 × 10^3/µl, creatinine 1.45 mg/dl, C-reactive protein 25.9 mg/dl, ferritin 546 ng/ml, and D-dimer 4.34 mg/l (reference ≤ 0.63 mg/l). Serial ECGs remained stable. The PaO2/FiO2 ratio was 85, consistent with severe ARDS, and the central venous oxygen saturation was 62%, suggesting mixed shock. A computed tomographic pulmonary angiogram was deferred due to hemodynamic instability and refractory hypoxemia. Broad-spectrum antibiotics and systemic anticoagulation with heparin were initiated.

A focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS) showed mildly increased right ventricular size with septal flattening in both systole and diastole, and bowing of the interatrial septum toward the left, indicating right ventricular strain. Given clinical suspicion for massive pulmonary embolism, alteplase (50 mg IV over 120 minutes) was administered, resulting in marked improvement in hemodynamics, perfusion, and oxygenation within 12 hours; vasopressor support resolved despite ongoing high-PEEP ventilation.

Twenty-four hours later, while off sedation, the patient was noted to be unresponsive. Urgent noncontrast head CT revealed multifocal infarcts in both cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres with mass effect. A follow-up CT 12 hours later showed hemorrhagic transformation, and anticoagulation with heparin was held.
title: One clot after another in COVID-19 patient: diagnostic utility of handheld echocardiogram

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman from northern India presented with an 8-month history of swelling at the right ankle. One year earlier, she had sustained trauma to the ankle; two months after that, a gradually enlarging, mildly painful swelling appeared. Three months before evaluation, a second swelling developed over the dorsolateral aspect of the right foot. In recent weeks, she noted tingling over the dorsal right foot on prolonged standing and walking. 

On examination, there were two smooth, soft, mildly tender swellings measuring 8×6 cm at the anterolateral right ankle and 5×4 cm at the proximal right foot. The overlying skin was normal, and neither lesion was adherent to skin or underlying bone. 

Vital signs were within normal limits. Routine blood tests were unremarkable except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/hr. Chest radiograph showed no signs of pulmonary tuberculosis. 

MRI of the right ankle demonstrated a lesion with altered signal intensity along the extensor tendons, with multiple small “rice bodies” and surrounding inflammatory changes, but no involvement of adjacent bones or joints.
title: Tubercular Tenosynovitis of Extensor Tendons of Ankle : A Case Report

case_prompt: A 64-year-old Japanese man with no stigmata of tuberous sclerosis underwent routine follow-up after ileocecal cancer resection, with no evidence of metastasis and normal tumor markers (α-fetoprotein, PIVKA-II, CEA, CA 19-9). He reported no symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C virus antibodies were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 25-mm low-density tumor with a high-density area in segment 2 of the liver. Gadolinium ethoxybenzyl diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid–enhanced MRI showed a 22×12-mm lesion in segment 2 that was slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1-weighted images. On dynamic imaging, the lesion demonstrated marked heterogeneous high signal intensity in the arterial phase with visible central filiform vessels and capsular enhancement, relative reduction of signal in the portal venous phase (still slightly higher than surrounding liver), and lower signal than liver parenchyma in the equilibrium phase. There was no uptake in the hepatobiliary phase at 20 minutes.
title: Primary hepatic angiomyolipoma: immunohistochemistry and electron microscopic observations: a case report

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old African-American man with a 4-year history of metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma presented with a 1-week history of bilateral lower extremity weakness, lethargy, several falls, hyperthermia, confusion, and gait abnormalities. His cancer history included a partial nephrectomy for papillary RCC with clear cell component, excisional biopsy confirming metastatic CCRCC, treatment with pazopanib and sunitinib, and ultimately a left radical nephrectomy. A positive QuantiFERON TB Gold test had excluded him from earlier immunotherapy trials. He then received seven cycles of nivolumab (240 mg) without prior complications.

On this admission, he became hypothermic, was transferred to the ICU, and required endotracheal intubation. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a lymphocytic pleocytosis (white blood cell count 27/mm3, 78% lymphocytes; protein 70 mg/dL). CSF virus culture and Gram stain showed no growth; a CSF pathogen panel and cryptococcal antigen were negative. Blood cultures and AFB smear were negative. Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and a 1.7 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm focus of T1-hypointensity at the midbrain–pons junction that had been stable for four years. A CSF MTB PCR test was negative.
title: Immune-Related Meningoencephalitis following Nivolumab in Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma

case_prompt: A 38‐year‐old woman presented with a painless right‐sided neck mass. She had no significant past medical history. On examination there was a palpable, firm, semi‐mobile, pulsatile 1 cm mass at level II/III on the right. Neck ultrasound showed a 2 × 1.3 × 2 cm hypoechoic, vascular solid nodule just anterior to the carotid bifurcation. MRI of the neck demonstrated a well‐circumscribed, homogeneous, T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, gadolinium‐enhancing mass anterior to the right carotid bifurcation, appearing to contact and possibly encase the external carotid artery without significant luminal narrowing. A preliminary diagnosis of paraganglioma was made, and the patient underwent digital subtraction angiography. Angiography revealed a moderately vascular, rounded mass anterior‐medial to the right common carotid bifurcation supplied by multiple branches of the superior thyroid artery, mildly displacing the external carotid artery. The carotid bifurcation was not splayed.
final_diagnosis_raw: Giant cell tumor of soft tissue
title: Case report of a giant cell tumor of the carotid sheath

case_prompt:
A 2-year-6-month-old girl presented with a 10-day history of fever, cough, and tachypnea. On admission, her temperature was 38.5 °C and SpO2 was 67% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed fine crackles in the posterior lung fields. Examination showed clubbing of the fingers, pigeon-breast deformity, and a chilblain-like rash on the face; her anterior fontanelle measured 0.3×0.3 cm. Growth parameters were below average (height 87 cm [–1.08 SD], weight 11.5 kg [–0.82 SD]). She had monthly respiratory infections since age 6 months and activity-related fatigue since age 2. Her 27-year-old father developed exertional dyspnea at age 22, has finger clubbing, facial tissue loss, and was diagnosed with CTD-associated ILD based on positive ANA and SRP autoantibody; his HRCT showed interstitial pneumonia with pulmonary cysts.  
Laboratory studies in the child showed CRP 54.2 mg/L, ESR 89 mm/H, WBC 16.3×10^3/mm^3; normal liver, renal, and thyroid function; IgG 25.3 g/L, IgA 3.26 g/L, IgM 1.69 g/L; normal complement levels; decreased CD4+ T lymphocytes; positive ANA (1:1000), ANCA, RF, and anti-CCP antibodies; IL-6 62.4 pg/mL; and negative pathology for malignancy. Chest HRCT showed diffuse ground-glass opacities; brain MRI revealed widened sulci and enlarged extra-axial spaces; echocardiogram and abdominal/vascular ultrasounds were normal.  
She was diagnosed with ILD and severe pneumonia and received IVIG, antibiotics, mechanical ventilation, and methylprednisolone pulse therapy; her respiratory symptoms improved and the ventilator was withdrawn on day 22.
title: Case report: JAK1/2 inhibition with baricitinib in the treatment of STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old Ethiopian woman presented with a 3-year history of a left axillary swelling that was initially small but had progressively increased in size. She reported mild local discomfort but denied cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats, or other constitutional symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable; she had no surgeries, no use of hormonal contraception, and no family history of cancer or chronic disease. She had regular menstrual cycles and no pregnancies.

On examination, vital signs were normal. In the left axilla there was a solitary 5 × 4 cm firm, nontender, well-defined, mobile mass completely separate from the breast; overlying skin was normal with no nipple, areola, or ulceration. Examination of the breasts, right axilla, other lymph node regions, chest, cardiovascular system, abdomen, genitourinary system, musculoskeletal system, and neurologic system was unremarkable.

A provisional clinical impression of axillary lymphadenopathy due to either lymphoma or tuberculosis was considered. Laboratory studies including complete blood count (WBC 5900/mL with normal differential, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, platelets 247 000/mL), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (13 mm/h), renal and liver function tests, urinalysis, and chest radiograph were within normal limits.
title: Fibroadenoma in axillary accessory breast tissue: a case report

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old white female healthcare worker with a history of diverticulosis presented with acute abdominal pain and a 10-week history of severe night sweats, progressive weight loss, and fever. On examination, she was febrile and cachectic, with no palpable lymphadenopathy. A chest radiograph was normal. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed dilated small-bowel loops with gas–fluid levels, distal small-bowel circumferential wall thickening, extensive mesenteric fat edema, a large volume of pelvic free fluid, and a 5.0×3.6 cm low-density right adnexal lesion with a thick enhancing rim. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 16,500 cells/mm3 with 58% bands, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, CA-125 39 U/mL, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, chloride 93 mmol/L, CO2 26 mmol/L, and creatinine 0.93 mg/dL. Pelvic inflammatory disease leading to a tubo-ovarian abscess was suspected, and gynecology performed a diagnostic laparoscopy followed by laparotomy. Findings included an enlarged right ovary with multiple small mucinous-appearing cysts, approximately 50 mL of pus drained from a right pyosalpinx, a normal left ovary, and extensive peritonitis with granulomas on the left upper abdominal wall. Biopsy showed chronic inflammation without malignancy. Cultures of the pyosalpinx fluid were negative for aerobes and anaerobes; acid-fast staining and cytology were not performed. The patient was discharged with postoperative diagnoses of right pyosalpinx and clinical tuberculous peritonitis.  

Ten days later, she returned with pleuritic chest pain. CT of the chest revealed a calcified granuloma in the right lower lobe and nonspecific pleural thickening. Electrocardiogram and cardiac enzymes were normal. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay was equivocal. Disseminated tuberculosis was suspected, and a second diagnostic laparoscopy revealed extensive granulomatous lesions throughout the peritoneum. Biopsies were obtained, and cultures for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Actinomyces, and fungi were sent and returned negative.
title: Disseminated histoplasmosis presenting as pelvic inflammatory disease

case_prompt:
An 86-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of diarrhea and bloody stool that began two weeks after his third dose of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA-1273 vaccine. His medical history was notable only for mild hypertension and hyperuricemia treated with febuxostat; there had been no changes in medications for years and no use of as-needed drugs. Nine years earlier, colonoscopy had been normal.

At the first evaluation, colonoscopy showed continuous coarse, erythematous mucosa with loss of vascular markings extending from the ascending colon to the rectum. Given the recent onset, he was managed with probiotics. Ten days later, he was admitted because of worsening symptoms.

On admission, laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 23 390/µL, hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, total protein 8.2 g/dL, albumin 3.1 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen 40.7 mg/dL, creatinine 1.24 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 25.1 mg/dL. Stool cultures were negative for pathogens. Sigmoidoscopy demonstrated marked erythema and loss of vascular translucency from the rectum to the sigmoid colon. Biopsy specimens showed dense inflammatory cell infiltration, crypt distortion, cryptitis, and goblet cell depletion.
title: An Elderly Patient Developed Ulcerative Colitis after SARS-CoV-2 mRNA Vaccination: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 0, with two prior embryonic arrests and known low-level 45,X/46,XX mosaicism, conceived spontaneously. First- and second-trimester screening, including nuchal translucency measurement and noninvasive prenatal testing, were normal. Fetal growth and amniotic fluid were normal at 22 and 26 weeks. At 29 weeks 6 days’ gestation, she was referred for suspected fetal anomaly. Ultrasonography showed:

• Oligohydramnios (AFD 1.2 cm; AFI 3.0 cm)  
• Bilateral hydronephrosis and right hydroureter  
• A 4.1 × 2.1 × 3.3 cm retrovesical pelvic cyst  
• A potential fistulous connection between the bladder and the cyst

Fetal MRI confirmed persistent oligohydramnios and demonstrated a gourd-shaped cyst arising from the pelvic floor, extending toward the umbilicus, compressing the rectum, with normal meconium signal in the intestines. These findings were felt to represent hydrometrocolpos, hypothesized to be secondary to a cloacal malformation.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?
title: Isolated hydrometrocolpos and cloacal malformation: can we prenatally distinguish them?—A case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 46-year-old man with hypertension and obesity was referred for excision and curettage of a lesion in the right proximal tibia, presumed to be chronic osteomyelitis. Two and a half years earlier, he noted acute localized pain, warmth, and swelling in his right knee after moving furniture. He received an intra-articular corticosteroid injection with transient relief, but no synovial fluid analysis was performed. One year later, symptoms recurred; radiographs showed a lytic lesion of the right proximal tibia, and a bone biopsy demonstrated necrosis with acute inflammation. The patient was afebrile. Laboratory studies revealed a CRP of 13.9 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L), an ESR of 30 mm/h (normal 0–22 mm/h), and a WBC count of 7.2 × 10^9/L. He underwent excision and curettage with placement of vancomycin- and tobramycin-impregnated beads. Intraoperatively, the bone appeared grossly abnormal and malodorous, but cultures were negative. He completed an 8-week course of empirical vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole, with normalization of inflammatory markers. One month later, radiographs showed only postsurgical sclerosis without lesion progression. Four months after surgery, he again developed right knee pain, swelling, and impaired ambulation. He denied trauma, unusual exposures, or IV drug use. MRI revealed a rim-enhancing fluid collection in the proximal tibia with cortical breakthrough and adjacent soft-tissue extension. His CRP was 24.6 mg/L, ESR 31 mm/h, and WBC count 4.0 × 10^9/L. A second excision and curettage was performed; operative findings again included friable, abnormal tissue. Empirical intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam were started postoperatively, but intraoperative bone and blood cultures remained negative. The patient faced the prospect of another prolonged course of antibiotics and possible above-the-knee amputation if symptoms recurred.
title: Going Bone Deep: Osseous Rosai–Dorfman Disease in an Adult with Recurrent, Culture-Negative Osteomyelitis

case_prompt:
A 12-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder was brought by his parents for evaluation of a 2-month history of intermittent nosebleeds, reduced oral intake, dysphagia, and decreased speech. He has no prior medical or surgical history. Because of his autism, history was obtained entirely from his parents.

On examination, there was a nontender, midline sublingual mass protruding into the oral cavity, displacing the tongue superiorly. No mucosal abnormalities, bluish discoloration, bleeding, or oozing were noted. The patient had no dyspnea or dysarthria. There were no palpable neck masses or lymphadenopathy. He was afebrile and had no weight loss.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a homogeneous, well-circumscribed, capsulated cystic lesion measuring 6.5 × 5.4 × 4.6 cm, located centrally in the sublingual space anterior to the hyoid bone. MRI demonstrated a thin-walled unilocular cyst with uniformly high protein content and peripheral enhancement after gadolinium administration in the sublingual space. Fine-needle aspiration yielded only squamous cells and was otherwise nondiagnostic.
title: Challenges in Diagnosing Dermoid Cyst in a Neurocognitive Patient

case_prompt: A 57-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of coughing without hemoptysis, dyspnea, or chest pain. He was a former smoker (quit 14 years earlier) and had no history of weight loss, fever, or tuberculosis exposure. Physical examination and vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, metabolic panel, and coagulation profile, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed an opacity in the right middle lobe. After a 10-day course of antibiotics with only partial symptom relief, a follow-up chest radiograph demonstrated persistent middle-lobe opacity. A CT scan revealed right middle-lobe consolidation and a small, round lesion in the right intermediate bronchus that contained calcification and fat and exhibited low enhancement. The next day, bronchoscopy demonstrated a smooth, round, yellowish mass subtotally occluding the intermediate bronchus without hypervascularization. Multiple endobronchial biopsies were obtained, and the histopathological examination showed chronic inflammation without evidence of malignancy.
title: A rare cause of bronchial obstruction: Endobronchial hamartoma case report

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman presented with a 10-year history of dull, aching pain, progressive swelling, and limited movement in her left knee. The pain arose insidiously and worsened over time without any history of trauma. Two years after symptom onset, she noted a gradually enlarging swelling over the lateral aspect of her left knee accompanied by a reduction in knee flexion. Activities involving knee flexion elicited pain. She had no significant medical or family history.

On examination, the lateral aspect of the left knee was swollen without erythema or warmth. A 15 × 5 cm hard, bony-feeling, non-tender mass extended from the lateral distal femur to the fibular head; it was not attached to underlying bone. The left knee’s range of motion was restricted to 0–40°, with no distal neurovascular deficits. No similar lesions were found elsewhere.

Plain radiographs of the left knee showed an irregular extraosseous radiolucent mass extending across the lateral aspect of the knee to the fibular head, with no bony contact. In addition, dense cortical hyperostosis resembling dripping candle wax covered the full length of the fibula, featuring large, thick, undulating, and irregular hyperostotic areas. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, alpha-fetoprotein, and carcinoembryonic antigen, were all within normal limits.
title: A Rare Case of Melorheostosis Presenting with Extra-osseous Lesions Around the Knee: Case Report

case_prompt: A 17-year-old man was referred after an orthodontic evaluation revealed an incidental mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion in the right anterior maxilla. He was asymptomatic, with no history of trauma, pain, paresthesia, or lymphadenopathy. Extraoral examination was normal. Intraorally, there was slight hard swelling from the right maxillary central incisor to the first molar; the anterior portion was slightly tender and fluctuant. All teeth in the area responded normally to cold testing. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion extending from tooth 11 to tooth 16 with root resorption of teeth 11, 12, 14, and 15. CT scan demonstrated a 2.7 × 2.1 cm hypodense lesion displacing the floor of the right maxillary sinus, containing internal hyperdense foci and confirmed the root resorption. Under local anesthesia, cyst decompression was performed. Fine-needle aspiration yielded lemon-yellow fluid. An incisional biopsy was obtained and a decompression tube placed. Based on the history, clinical and radiographic findings, and aspiration results, provisional diagnoses included adenomatoid odontogenic tumor; calcifying odontogenic cyst; calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor (Pindborg tumor); and juvenile cemento-ossifying fibroma in the intermediate stage.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Calcifying odontogenic cyst of anterior maxillary: Case report and review

case_prompt:
A 7-month-old female spayed Siberian cat was evaluated for a 4-day history of progressive dullness, left-sided hemiparesis, and ataxia. There was no history of trauma. Vaccinations were up to date; the cat lived exclusively in the UK and was fed a grain-free chicken-based kitten diet. The owner reported intermittent mixed-pattern diarrhea since adoption; prior fecal PCR had detected Giardia species and feline coronavirus. Giardia was treated first with fenbendazole and subsequently metronidazole, with improvement in fecal consistency. No medications had been given in the 3 weeks before presentation.

On examination, the cat was lean (body condition score 4/9), weighing 2.3 kg. Ophthalmic examination showed bilateral iris pigment changes suggestive of uveitis. Neurologic assessment revealed depressed mentation, ataxia, and absent proprioception in the left forelimb and hindlimb, resulting in left-sided hemiparesis; other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed a moderate, microcytic, non-regenerative anemia; lymphopenia; neutrophil toxicity; marked hyperproteinemia (total protein 121 g/L) due to extreme hyperglobulinemia (100.6 g/L; albumin:globulin ratio 0.2); mild hypoalbuminemia; mildly elevated ALT, AST, and CK activities; low creatinine; and mild hyperglycemia. Serology was negative for Toxoplasma gondii, feline leukemia virus, and feline immunodeficiency virus; feline coronavirus antibody titer was high.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and cervical spine revealed dorsal and ventral dilation of the subarachnoid space from the obex to C1, with abrupt narrowing at C2–C3 causing dorsoventral flattening of the spinal cord (more marked on the right). Caudal to this lesion, the cord appeared swollen with T2-weighted hyperintensity in the left dorsal compartment at C1 and surrounding the central canal from C2 to C6. There was marked leptomeningeal contrast enhancement around the cranial cervical cord and along the brainstem, suggestive of an inflammatory process.
title: Subarachnoid diverticulum associated with feline infectious peritonitis in a Siberian cat

case_prompt: A 34-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of dyspnea on exertion (stage II) and intermittent chest pain without cough or hemoptysis. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, he was afebrile, conscious, with a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, heart rate 85 beats per minute, and blood pressure 135/80 mm Hg. Pulmonary examination revealed dullness to percussion over the left basal hemithorax. A chest radiograph showed an opacity occupying the lower half of the left hemithorax, silhouettes the left heart border and diaphragm, suggesting an anterior mediastinal mass without pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a large, well-defined heterogeneous mass with predominant fat attenuation mingled with focal areas of soft-tissue density, extending from the anterior mediastinum to the left diaphragm and displacing the adjacent lung superiorly, with no signs of pulmonary or adjacent-tissue infiltration.
title: Rare mass of the anterior mediastinum: Thymolipomas

case_prompt: A 61-year-old man presented with a 4–5-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling on the left chin region without pain, paresthesia, or mastication difficulty. He reported no trauma or dental procedures in the area. He chewed tobacco 3–4 times daily for 10–15 years. Physical examination revealed a 5 cm × 3 cm smooth, soft, nonfluctuant, non-tender swelling near the left oral commissure without lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there was a 3 cm × 2 cm round, yellowish, sessile mass with smooth surface in the lower left labial vestibule, extending from the canine to the first molar. An incidental 1 cm × 0.5 cm sessile, erythematous, lobulated lesion with irregular borders was noted on the ventral tongue. Neither lesion blanched on pressure. Panoramic radiograph was unremarkable. Ultrasonography of the vestibular mass showed a well-defined echogenic intramuscular lesion measuring 2.2 × 0.8 cm, with no calcification or vascularity; surrounding bone and muscle appeared normal. Fine-needle aspiration twice yielded no material. A provisional diagnosis of lipoma was made, and the patient was referred for excisional biopsy under general anesthesia.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Co-existence of oral intra-muscular lipoma and lobular capillary hemangioma: A rare case report

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of continuous pain in the neck and bilateral shoulders. She had no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or appetite change. Her past medical history was notable only for a stable pulmonary nodule under observation. On examination, cervical range of motion was markedly reduced (forward flexion 20°, extension 20°, side bending 25°, rotation 30°) with paravertebral muscle spasm and tenderness; there were no neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, tumor markers, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the cervical spine showed collapse of the C6 vertebral body with mild malalignment, suggesting a pathologic fracture. Contrast-enhanced CT of the cervical spine demonstrated extensive bone erosion involving nearly the entire C6 body, destruction of the upper endplate and anterior and posterior walls, without adjacent disc involvement or significant intraosseous enhancement. MRI with contrast revealed diffuse T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, and contrast-enhanced infiltration of the C6 vertebral body; the C5–6 and C6–7 discs appeared normal. PET–CT showed focal hypermetabolism in C6 only (SUVmax 11.4).

Based on these findings, a neoplastic lesion with a pathologic fracture of C6 was suspected. Differential diagnoses included giant cell tumor, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, infection, and primary or metastatic bone tumor.
title: A solitary osteolytic lesion with pathological fracture in the cervical spine - a case report

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old South Asian woman presented with multiple generalized tonic–clonic seizures characterized by eye‐rolling, tongue biting, and frothing at the mouth. She had a history of bacterial meningitis at age 1, complicated by febrile seizures treated with carbamazepine for two years, after which she was seizure-free until five years ago when she had another brief course of carbamazepine. She remained well until the current episode. 

On examination, she was fully alert (GCS 15), with intact sensation. Motor strength was 4/5 in the right upper and lower limbs, which also showed mild atrophy and hyperreflexia. A right upper motor neuron facial palsy was present. Laboratory studies, including serum electrolytes, were within normal limits. Electroencephalography did not reveal any active seizure focus.

Brain MRI with 3D-TOF MRA demonstrated diffuse atrophy of the left cerebral hemisphere, including deep gray structures, with ex vacuo dilatation of the left lateral ventricle and widening of left sulci. There was unilateral calvarial thickening on the left, hypertrophy of the left frontal sinus and mastoid air cells, and elevation of the left petrous ridge. Atrophy of the left cerebral peduncle and pons was consistent with Wallerian degeneration; diffusion‐weighted and FLAIR sequences showed no abnormal signals. Crossed cerebellar diaschisis was noted in the right cerebellar hemisphere. Magnetic resonance angiography showed normal cerebral vessels.
title: Adult Presentation of Dyke–Davidoff–Masson Syndrome, a Radiological Enigma: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 47-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and fever of 24 hours’ duration. She had localized tenderness and rebound at McBurney’s point, along with a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa. Vital signs were notable for low-grade fever. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 14.0×10^9/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 90 mm in the first hour. She was managed conservatively for one day without improvement. Abdominal ultrasonography was inconclusive. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a large soft-tissue mass in the right lateral pelvis with adherent loops of bowel, thickened intestinal walls, and three enlarged regional lymph nodes. A radiological differential diagnosis of inflammatory versus neoplastic mass was made, and the patient was taken for exploratory laparotomy.
title: Cytological diagnosis of xanthogranulomatous appendicitis

case_prompt: A 64-year-old woman from central Nepal presented with a slowly growing, skin-covered, gray-brown mass in her right inguinal region of 1 year’s duration and bleeding from the mass for the past 4 days. She reported a dull, aching pain at the site but denied fever, weight loss, or other similar lumps. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she was not on any medications. On examination, there was a single, non-tender, globular, smooth, mobile mass measuring 7.5 cm by 6.0 cm in the right inguinal region, with bleeding from its tip. The mass was nonpulsatile, and there was no impulse on coughing. Ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous echogenicity mass with irregular margins and slightly increased vascularity.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Myopericytoma in right inguinal region: A rare case report from Nepal

case_prompt: A 76-year-old Syrian man presented with a 6-hour history of urinary frequency, dysuria, and gross hematuria. His medical history included hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On examination, vital signs were stable, and findings were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 20,000/μL, hemoglobin 11 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 82 fl, platelets 254,000/μL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, and urea 130 mg/dL. Renal ultrasonography demonstrated severe right-sided and mild left-sided hydronephrosis without stones, and a bladder-wall thickness of 1.5 cm. Cystoscopic biopsy of the bladder revealed denuded cystitis, low-grade dysplasia, and severe interstitial cystitis without invasive tumor. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed right hydronephrosis with a nonenhancing hypodense filling defect in the renal pelvis and inferior calyces. Chest CT revealed band-like opacities in the right upper lobe. On the basis of these findings, a primary diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma was made, and the patient underwent an open right radical nephrectomy and ureterectomy.
title: Urinary tract tuberculosis misdiagnosed and treated as renal carcinoma in the presence of diffuse interstitial nephritis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 3-year-old Hispanic girl with no prior systemic disease was referred for evaluation of bilateral granulomatous uveitis. She had a 3-month history of a nonpruritic skin eruption and left knee arthralgia. Her father and uncle both had psoriatic arthritis. 

On ophthalmologic examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/60 in both eyes; intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg OD and 14 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp examination revealed bilateral band keratopathy, large mutton-fat keratic precipitates, multiple posterior synechiae, and 4+ anterior chamber cells. Fundus views were poor due to band keratopathy and limited dilation; B-scan ultrasound showed no vitreous opacity.

Physical examination showed left knee edema and a right axillary eruption of irregular erythematous papules and plaques with thin scale. No dactylitis, enthesitis, or nail changes were noted.

Chest radiograph was normal. Laboratory tests revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm/h. Complete metabolic panel and urinalysis were unremarkable. Immunology studies showed a positive antinuclear antibody titer (1:1280, homogeneous) with negative anti–double-stranded DNA, anti-Smith, rheumatoid factor, and cyclic citrullinated peptide IgG. Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption, VDRL, and tuberculosis interferon-gamma release assay tests were negative. Tests for HLA-B27, HIV, hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B core IgG, and hepatitis C antibody were negative.

A punch biopsy of a skin lesion revealed psoriasiform acanthosis, thin suprapapillary plates, neutrophils in the stratum corneum, and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.
title: Bilateral Granulomatous Iridocyclitis Associated with Early-Onset Juvenile Psoriatic Arthritis

case_prompt: A 25-year-old man with no past medical history presented to the emergency department with chest pain, shortness of breath, and throat tightness. Six days earlier, he had had similar symptoms, a normal chest radiograph and laboratory tests, and was discharged with symptomatic treatment for a presumed viral syndrome. He returned with persistent chest pain and shortness of breath, now accompanied by acute visual loss in the right eye and weakness in the legs. On examination, his blood pressure was normal; auscultation revealed a loud, holosystolic murmur; and both radial and femoral pulses were diminished. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. A ventilation–perfusion scan demonstrated homogeneously decreased perfusion throughout the entire left lung, which was interpreted as high probability for pulmonary embolism.
title: Pulmonary artery dissection complicating aortic dissection in a patient with bicuspid aortic valve and aortic coarctation

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of intermittent acute epigastric pain radiating to the back and associated with abdominal fullness. She also reported fevers up to 101.2°F for 2 days. She had a history of cervical spine surgery 10 years earlier and a lower-segment cesarean section followed by copper-T insertion 2 years ago. She denied alcohol use, smoking, substance abuse, diabetes, viral infections, abdominal trauma, and use of steroids, estrogens, or other potential pancreatitis-inducing medications. Her family history was negative for pancreatitis, dyslipidemia, gallstones, or autoimmune disease.

On examination, she was tachycardic (116 bpm) with normal blood pressure; BMI was 32. Abdominal examination showed distention, epigastric tenderness, and sluggish bowel sounds. Laboratory tests revealed serum amylase 451 U/L, lipase 603 U/L, calcium 8.1 mg/dL, and triglycerides 579 mg/dL; liver enzymes, bilirubin, and renal function were unremarkable except for mildly elevated creatinine. ANA testing was negative. 

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated hepatomegaly with grade III fatty infiltration, significant free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, an enlarged pancreas with peripancreatic fluid, and no cholelithiasis. Non-contrast CT of the abdomen showed a diffusely enlarged pancreas with marked stranding and peripancreatic fluid, consistent with acute pancreatitis, and minimal bilateral pleural effusions.
title: Acute pancreatitis secondary to moderate hypertriglyceridemia: A case report

case_prompt: A 40-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with sudden onset of severe lower abdominal and pelvic pain. Ultrasonography revealed a right-sided 7 cm mass with both cystic and solid components. Diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal biopsies showed a spindle cell proliferation with a dense vascular network, scant nuclear atypia, and occasional mitotic figures. On immunohistochemical staining, tumor cells were focally positive for SMA, EMA, Cytokeratin AE1/AE3, and DOG1, and negative for C-KIT, CD34, S100, Melan A, PAX8, p53, WT1, calretinin, mesothelin, and D2-40. A presumptive diagnosis of gastrointestinal stromal tumor was made, and the patient underwent a contrast-enhanced CT scan, which demonstrated a large (20 × 15 × 10 cm), heterodense, multilobulated lesion occupying the pelvis and extending to the supra-umbilical region. There was no clear invasion of adjacent viscera or vascular structures, and the mass was deemed resectable.
title: A case of primary mesenteric synovial sarcoma: a challenging presentation

case_prompt: A 72-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of a lesion in the macula of his right eye. He was asymptomatic, and visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. The left eye examination was unremarkable. In the right eye, funduscopic examination revealed an orange-red, serpentine, track-like lesion inferior to the fovea extending temporally to the equator, with overlying retinal pigment epithelium changes. Near-infrared imaging showed alternating hyper- and hyporeflective spots along the lesion. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated early filling of the large branching lesion and no leakage in the late phase. Enhanced depth imaging optical coherence tomography through the lesion showed a hyporeflective structure originating at the choroid–scleral junction, elevating the overlying retina, with focal disruption of the Bruch’s–retinal pigment epithelium complex and a few hyperreflective foci in the outer retina. En face swept-source OCT angiography with a custom slab through the full choroidal thickness revealed a large, tortuous vessel-like lesion with a signal similar to that of adjacent physiological choroidal vessels.
title: Choroidal Macrovessel Diagnosed on Multimodal Imaging, including Swept-Source Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old Hispanic man with obesity and hypertension presented with a 3-month history of abrupt episodes of weakness and altered mental status. He described anxiety, aggressiveness, agitation, diaphoresis, visual blurring, and a burning sensation throughout his body, sometimes leading to loss of consciousness; symptoms occurred at any time of day and improved with eating. He reported worsening frequency and severity of attacks, which disrupted his work as a truck driver and led to suicidal thoughts. He had no tobacco or excessive alcohol use and took candesartan and hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension.

He was hospitalized briefly at a local hospital for recurrent irritability and aggression; psychiatric evaluation yielded no diagnosis. A subsequent 3-hour postprandial test revealed a blood glucose level of 58 mg/dL, prompting transfer. On admission, he was afebrile, heart rate 93 beats/min, blood pressure 161/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination was normal, including a neurologic evaluation.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 9.51 K/µL, and calcium 9.6 mg/dL. During a supervised 72-hour fast, he became symptomatic after 20 hours; laboratory testing revealed a blood glucose level of 29 mg/dL, insulin 426 mIU/L, and C-peptide 12.83 ng/mL. Sulfonylurea levels were undetectable. Abdominal ultrasound and contrast magnetic resonance imaging of the pancreas showed no abnormalities. Prolactin, parathyroid hormone, albumin, and calcium levels, as well as brain MRI, were normal, effectively ruling out multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.
title: Altered behavior with an organic cause: a case report

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old woman presented with recurrent, progressively enlarging, painless swellings of the left thigh. She first noted a mid-thigh swelling in 2001, which was excised in 2005; a new distal-thigh swelling was removed in 2009. Three years later, she again noted a slowly enlarging mass over the left distal medial thigh, now measuring approximately 8 cm × 4 cm. On examination, there was a healed scar over the medial thigh, quadriceps wasting, and a firm, intramuscular, non-tender mass in the left distal thigh. Systemic examination was unremarkable.  
Plain radiographs of the left femur and tibia revealed cortical thinning with radiolucent areas consistent with fibrous dysplasia. A full skeletal survey confirmed polyostotic involvement of the left femur and tibia. MRI of the entire left thigh showed three well-defined intramuscular lesions that were homogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted and STIR images, the largest in the distal thigh measuring 51 mm × 48 mm × 73 mm.  
What is your differential diagnosis?
title: Mazabraud’s Syndrome – A Diagnosis Commonly Missed

case_prompt: A 32-year-old man presented with acute onset of severe upper abdominal pain for 3 hours, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. He reported normal bowel movements earlier in the day and was still passing flatus. He had no history of abdominal surgery, took no regular medications, and smoked cannabis and cigarettes daily. On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits; he was afebrile. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the upper abdomen but a soft abdomen without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13.8×10^9/L and a lactate level of 2.5 mmol/L. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen suggested an internal hernia involving the small intestine. He was taken urgently for diagnostic laparoscopy. On entry, milky-white fluid was observed in the pelvis and between small-bowel loops, which was aspirated and sent for analysis. Inspection revealed a segment of ileum twisted as a volvulus, which was reduced with gentle traction; the bowel regained normal color and peristalsis. The mesenteric border of the small intestine appeared white, suggesting lymphatic congestion. Analysis of the peritoneal fluid showed a triglyceride concentration of 360 mg/dL.
journal: Middle East Journal of Digestive Diseases
title: Chylous Ascites Associated with Small Bowel Volvulus: Case Report on a Laparoscopic Diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of acute urinary retention and a 10-day history of bilateral lower-limb numbness and weakness. He also reported a 2-month history of productive cough, unintentional weight loss, and decreased appetite. Two years earlier, he had household exposure to a brother with tuberculosis. 

Laboratory evaluation showed a normal complete blood count and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Sputum testing for acid-fast bacilli was positive on two occasions. 

Multiplanar thoracolumbar MRI performed before and after gadolinium administration demonstrated a 12 × 16 mm intradural, extramedullary lesion at the L2 level. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, isointense to hypointense on T2-weighted and STIR images, and contained a small focus of central hyperintensity on long-TR sequences. Postcontrast images showed homogeneous enhancement with a small central nonenhancing focus.
title: Magnetic resonance imaging in diagnosing spinal cord tuberculoma: A case series and literature review

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of left flank pain. On initial evaluation in the emergency department, she was hemodynamically stable, and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits.  
Renal ultrasonography demonstrated a large cystic mass with multiple internal septations and lobulated margins in the lower pole of the left kidney, measuring approximately 12.3 × 8.6 cm.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a single, well-defined, thin-walled, parapelvic complex cystic lesion arising from the lower pole of the left kidney, measuring 11.9 × 9.3 × 8.8 cm (craniocaudal × transverse × anteroposterior). The lesion had thick internal septations, showed no significant post-contrast enhancement, and contained no solid nodules. There was no adjacent fat stranding, regional lymphadenopathy, or involvement of the renal veins, and the remainder of both kidneys and their vascular structures appeared normal.
title: Renal hydatid cyst: A case report

case_prompt: A 17-year-old Caucasian female presented with 5 days of right eye redness, pain, blurred vision, and intermittent photopsia. She reported vague systemic symptoms including nausea, headaches, left shoulder pain, and long-standing night sweats. Her ophthalmic history included recurrent right eye conjunctivitis and papillary edema since 2017, responsive to topical corticosteroids, with preserved visual acuity. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in both eyes. Slit lamp exam of the right eye showed non-necrotizing scleritis, endothelial haze, and 1+ anterior chamber cells. Fundus examination revealed vitreous turbidity, inferior condensations, vitreous snowballs, papillary edema, and peripheral white-yellow chorioretinal lesions. Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated peripheral vasculitis, hyperfluorescent chorioretinal lesions, a “hot disc,” and peripheral hypofluorescent spots. Spectral-domain OCT was normal. The left eye was unremarkable. Initial treatment included hourly topical prednisolone, twice-daily tropicamide, and oral ibuprofen. Over one week, right eye pain worsened, visual acuity dropped to 0.8, scleritis and vitreous condensations persisted, papillary edema progressed, and new peripheral lesions appeared. A multidisciplinary workup showed normal lymph nodes on exam and normal systemic imaging apart from ocular findings. A broad infectious and systemic inflammatory panel was negative for toxoplasmosis, Whipple’s disease, syphilis, Lyme disease, cat-scratch disease, HSV, VZV, CMV, sarcoidosis, Behçet’s disease, and SLE. Interferon-gamma release assay was positive, but Quantiferon testing was negative. Oral corticosteroids were started with gradual symptomatic and anatomic improvement. A whole-body PET-CT revealed hypermetabolic left supraclavicular and bilateral mediastinal lymph nodes, leading to a differential diagnosis of lymph node tuberculosis, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, IgG4–related disease, or Castleman’s disease.
title: Unmasking an unusual presentation of Hodgkin’s lymphoma masquerading as ocular inflammation: a case report

case_prompt: A 24-year-old man presented with gradually progressive, diffuse swelling of his right lower limb since childhood without paresthesia or motor impairment. He also had multiple, asymptomatic facial papules since early childhood; his sister had similar facial lesions and seizures. On examination, the right lower limb was diffusely swollen from the groin to mid–leg with multiple dilated, tortuous veins but no visible capillary or venous malformations. On the face, there were multiple firm, discrete reddish-brown telangiectatic papules over the nasolabial folds and cheeks. On the trunk, there were multiple ash leaf–shaped hypopigmented patches and soft, skin-colored papules coalescing into a plaque on the left lateral aspect. Oral examination revealed dental pits and gingival fibromas. Fine-needle aspiration from the thigh swelling showed lobules of mature adipose tissue. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right lower limb demonstrated T1- and T2-hyperintense signals throughout the musculature of all compartments, consistent with fatty infiltration, along with multiple prominent tortuous vessels and cortical thickening of the right femur and tibia with anterior bowing of the femur. Doppler ultrasonography revealed multiple incompetent perforators in the great saphenous vein territory.
title: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex and Diffuse Lipomatosis: Case Report of a Rare Association

case_prompt: A 66‐year‐old woman presented with 2 days of shortness of breath and chest pain. Her medical history included rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, for which she took prednisolone (6 mg/day) and hydroxychloroquine (200 mg/day). She frequently worked with potting soil in her garden and reported orange‐coloured sputum. On admission, temperature was 36.1 °C; blood pressure, 109/69 mmHg; pulse, 111/min; respiratory rate, 30/min; and oxygen saturation, 96% on 9 L/min via reservoir mask. She was alert and had coarse crackles bilaterally. Laboratory tests showed WBC 30,510/μL (99.5% neutrophils), hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, platelets 5.0 × 10^4/μL, LDH 341 U/L, BUN 30 mg/dL, creatinine 1.21 mg/dL, and CRP 41.06 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pH 7.397, pCO2 34.4 torr, pO2 46.5 torr, and HCO3– 21.8 mEq/L. Chest radiography showed bilateral consolidation in the upper and middle lung fields, and CT revealed consolidation of the right upper, middle, and lower lobes, left upper lobe, and atelectasis of the left lower lobe. Sputum Gram stain was not diagnostic. Both pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigen tests were negative. Empiric IV levofloxacin and meropenem were started. Given her immunosuppressed state, differential diagnoses included viral or fungal infection, alveolar hemorrhage, and interstitial pneumonia. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) performed under intubation yielded orange‐coloured fluid with a neutrophil predominance (90%), a negative Gram stain, and cytology showing numerous neutrophils and a few macrophages without hemosiderin.
title: Non‐pneumophila Legionella species pneumonia with orange‐coloured sputum

case_prompt:
An 86-year-old man with a history of stroke, hypertension, and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma presented with several months of fatigue, dizziness, generalized weakness, and weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

A chest radiograph showed multiple bilateral noncalcified lung nodules. Whole-body CT imaging revealed multiple hypervascular hepatic nodules and a 12.3 × 9 × 8 cm right renal mass that was well-encapsulated and partially necrotic, findings that were interpreted as suspicious for primary renal cell carcinoma with pulmonary and hepatic metastases. 

A CT-guided renal biopsy yielded only scant vascular fragments and was nondiagnostic. A repeat biopsy again showed extensive necrosis with few tissue fragments containing multiple vascular channels lined by pleomorphic endothelial cells with increased mitotic figures. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34 and CD31 and negativity for AE1/3, CK8/18, CD10, and RCC antigen.
title: Primary Renal Angiosarcoma with Extensive Necrosis: A Difficult Diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 3-month history of progressive dyspnea, hacking cough, and distended neck veins. Seven years earlier, he had been diagnosed with early polycythemia vera (JAK2 V617F–positive) and treated with hydroxyurea. He denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. 

On examination, he had a facial rash with periorbital and facial edema, bilateral obliteration of the supraclavicular fossae, prominent jugular venous distension, and mild right-sided ptosis. Neurologic examination was otherwise normal, and there were no signs of Horner syndrome or phrenic nerve involvement. A firm 3-cm mass was palpable over the right sixth rib.

Laboratory studies showed relative lymphocytosis (17.5%), absolute lymphocyte count 1.57×10^3/μL, lactate dehydrogenase 423 U/L, C-reactive protein 1.8 mg/dL, fibrinogen 414 mg/dL, immunoglobulin A 549 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 27 mm/h, and β2-microglobulin 2.6 mg/dL. Serologic tests were negative for hepatitis C virus, HHV8, and HIV, and positive for hepatitis B core IgG and for EBV.

Chest radiography revealed upper mediastinal widening with rightward tracheal deviation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 9.7×8.0×5.7 cm polylobulated anterior–middle mediastinal mass compressing the right internal jugular vein and superior vena cava, along with a chest wall lesion of similar appearance. One month later, the mediastinal mass had enlarged to 12×14×7.5 cm. Ultrasound of the neck showed nonocclusive thrombosis of the right internal jugular vein despite anticoagulation, with a patent left vein.

A percutaneous ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mediastinal mass and resection of the chest wall lesion were performed under local anesthesia, and samples were sent for histopathology and immunophenotyping.
title: Mediastinal syndrome from plasmablastic lymphoma in human immunodeficiency virus and human herpes virus 8 negative patient with polycythemia vera: a case report

case_prompt: A 44-year-old man with a 29-month history of moderately differentiated esophageal adenocarcinoma (treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and surgical resection, ypT3N0) presented with a 3-day history of floaters in the left eye. Visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes. The right eye was unremarkable. Examination of the left eye revealed a normal anterior segment, grade-1 vitritis, and a focal area of localized periphlebitis superonasally around the equator. Serologic testing for toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus was negative. Brain and orbital MRI scans were normal. Rheumatologic evaluation for systemic diseases, including sarcoidosis and Behçet disease, was unremarkable. Idiopathic inflammatory retinal vasculitis was suspected, and the patient was treated with oral steroids. On follow-up, the intraocular inflammation regressed and remained stable for 3 months while he received palliative chemotherapy for progressive lung metastases. The patient then discontinued chemotherapy. Three weeks later, he returned with a significant decrease in left-eye visual acuity to 6/60. Dilated fundus examination showed new severe vitritis with vitreous clouds, dense white-to-yellow vitreous clumps in the inferior retina, and increased perivascular infiltrates at the previous periphlebitis site.
title: Metastatic esophageal carcinoma to the eye masquerading as inflammatory vitreo-retinitis: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 1-month-old corrected-age male infant (birth weight 1,070 g at 32 + 1 weeks, small for gestational age) was transferred for respiratory insufficiency. He had a 50-day neonatal admission with pneumonia requiring O₂ for 4 days; chest imaging then excluded hyaline membrane disease or bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
