On examination, breath sounds were bronchial with rhonchi; cardiac examination revealed regular rate and rhythm with a grade 2 systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border.

Echocardiography showed a secundum atrial septal defect (7 × 12 mm), right-sided volume overload, tricuspid regurgitation with a peak gradient of 55–60 mmHg, a dilated main pulmonary artery (19 mm), branch pulmonary arteries (11–12 mm), and estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 58–65 mmHg. 

At first admission, he required intubation and mechanical ventilation for progressive respiratory distress. Chest radiographs demonstrated severe collapse of both lungs. CT at 1 month revealed collapse of the dependent right lung and total collapse of the left lower lobe, with narrowing of the main bronchus and right intermediate bronchus; “intrinsic cause like bronchomalasia was suspected.” Viral cultures (RSV, adenovirus, influenza A) were negative.

After two weeks of ventilator support, he was weaned and discharged on digoxin, furosemide, spironolactone, and lung physiotherapy. Up to 4 months corrected age, he had three additional admissions for recurrent respiratory infections; on the fourth admission, he required 40 days of mechanical ventilation. Follow-up echocardiography showed persistent pulmonary hypertension (tricuspid regurgitant gradient 60 mmHg). 

After extubation at 8 months corrected age, repeat CT demonstrated a dilated pulmonary artery compressing the left main bronchus and right intermediate bronchus, with improvement of lung consolidation and mild improvement of right bronchial stenosis.
title: Bronchial compression in an infant with isolated secundum atrial septal defect associated with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension

case_prompt: A 26-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of a left vulvar mass, irregular vaginal bleeding, and night sweats. She had no significant past medical or family history. On pelvic examination, the left vulva, vagina, and cervix were swollen, and bimanual examination revealed a mass fixed to the pelvic wall. Serum α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, CA-125, CA19-9, and β-hCG were within normal limits. Initial complete blood count showed a white-cell count of 3.7×10^9/L with blasts on peripheral smear; hemoglobin and platelet counts were normal. A biopsy of the vulvovaginal mass demonstrated a malignant small round cell tumour. Two weeks later, the white-cell count rose to 18.9×10^9/L, hemoglobin was 102 g/L, platelets were 24×10^9/L, and peripheral smear revealed 79% blasts. Contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI showed an ill-defined, irregular 10.5×9.0-cm diffuse mass involving the vagina, paravaginal tissue, urethra, posterior bladder wall, left ischiorectal fossa, pelvic diaphragm, and pelvic floor; the lesion was homogeneously isointense on T1-weighted images, slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images with restricted diffusion, and showed homogeneous enhancement greater than muscle. Bilateral obturator lymph nodes were enlarged. PET/CT demonstrated high FDG uptake in the pelvic mass and enlarged obturator nodes; thoracic CT was unremarkable.
title: Vulvovaginal myeloid sarcoma with massive pelvic floor infiltration: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 15.5-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat was evaluated for a 4-month history of progressive right pelvic limb lameness, with left pelvic limb involvement over the preceding 2 weeks. Treatment with meloxicam (0.05 mg/kg q24h) provided no appreciable improvement. On neurologic examination, the cat was ambulatory paraparesis with proprioceptive deficits in both pelvic limbs (right > left) and marked hyperesthesia on palpation over L6. Hematology and serum biochemistry results were within normal limits except for a hematocrit of 25.7% (reference range, 30.3–52.3%).

Orthogonal radiographs of the lumbar spine revealed a right-sided osteolytic lesion affecting the L6 vertebra. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the lumbosacral spine showed a 2.2 × 2.0 × 2.9 cm expansile mass in the dorsal lamina of L6, with bilateral (right > left) pedicle infiltration. The lesion exhibited central soft-tissue attenuation, a thin mineralized peripheral rim, mildly irregular but well-defined borders, and severe spinal canal stenosis. The soft tissue component demonstrated diffuse contrast enhancement. Differential diagnoses based on the CT findings included primary bone tumors such as fibrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, or chondrosarcoma. A fine-needle aspiration of the lesion was non-diagnostic. Surgical excision was planned.
journal: Animals : an Open Access Journal from MDPI
title: Vertebral Osteosarcoma in Two Cats—Diagnosis, Treatment, and Outcome

case_prompt: A 29-year-old Caucasian man presented with 3–4 months of right upper-quadrant and right flank discomfort. He denied gastrointestinal, urinary, or endocrine symptoms. His history was notable for latent tuberculosis diagnosed 3 months earlier, for which he was taking rifampicin and isoniazid. On examination, a palpable mass in the right hypochondrium displaced the liver anteriorly; blood pressure was normal. Laboratory evaluation showed normal results on a dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urine catecholamine and metanephrine assays, and plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Abdominal ultrasound and CT scans revealed a 15-cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass compressing the liver, findings that raised the possibility of a primary adrenal carcinoma. A metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan with SPECT showed no significant tracer uptake, making a pheochromocytoma less likely. A fluorodeoxyglucose–PET scan demonstrated an intensely metabolically active right adrenal mass measuring 14.5 × 9.5 × 17.2 cm, with dystrophic calcification and central necrosis, features consistent with either adrenal cortical carcinoma or tuberculosis. The left adrenal gland was normal, there were no features to suggest active tuberculosis elsewhere, and there was no evidence of metastatic disease. Because of the large size of the mass, he underwent an open right adrenalectomy; the postoperative course was uneventful.
title: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour arising in the adrenal gland: a case report

case_prompt: A 49-year-old woman presented in March 2024 with a 3-week history of a new, solitary, 2-cm erythematous, pruritic plaque in the right axilla that continued to enlarge despite twice-daily application of polymyxin B–gramicidin ointment. She had been treated for ipsilateral stage III breast cancer (T3N0) in June 2022 with neoadjuvant trastuzumab deruxtecan followed by paclitaxel/trastuzumab/pertuzumab, total mastectomy, adjuvant trastuzumab, and radiation confined to the breast. In September 2023 she underwent a deep inferior epigastric perforator flap reconstruction. She reported no history of other skin, nail, or hair disease, no family history of dermatologic conditions, and otherwise had a negative review of systems. On examination, the solitary axillary plaque was the only skin finding. After 2 weeks of progression, two punch biopsies were obtained to rule out local cancer recurrence. Initial histopathologic interpretation by a breast pathologist was benign epidermoid cyst, a diagnosis considered discordant with the clinical presentation, prompting referral to dermatology for further evaluation.
title: Transient and unique lesion of acantholytic dyskeratosis of the axilla

case_prompt: A 24-year-old woman with no significant medical or gynecological history presented with moderate, intermittent suprapubic cramp-like pelvic pain and dysuria. She denied abnormal uterine bleeding. Pelvic MRI revealed a well-demarcated vaginal mass measuring 10 × 8.3 × 5.6 cm, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on T1, with areas of high signal on fat-saturated sequences, compressing the bladder; no pelvic lymphadenopathy was seen. On physical examination, she was afebrile and in good condition; the abdomen was soft, with no palpable mass; vulvar and perineal inspection was normal, and there was no inguinal adenopathy. Diagnostic hysteroscopy revealed a large exophytic mass on the anterior cervical lip filling the vagina. Directed biopsy showed moderate cellularity with patches of round cells having irregular hyperchromatic nuclei and mitotic figures, occasional large cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm suggestive of rhabdomyoblastic differentiation, and a loose, edematous, highly vascular stroma.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A challenging diagnosis and treatment of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma in the cervix of an adult woman: A surgical case report

case_prompt: A 59-year-old Caucasian man was evaluated for generalized chorea of 1.5 years’ duration. He had no relevant family history. As a child, he was diagnosed with celiac disease, adhered to a gluten-free diet with resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms, but as an adult returned to a normal diet without issues until recent months, when he reported recurrence of abdominal pain and diarrhea. His psychiatric history included possible schizotypal personality disorder, depression, anxiety, and past alcohol dependence. His medications for the past three years were trazodone 100 mg/day, venlafaxine 375 mg/day, and mirtazapine 15 mg/day; quetiapine 100 mg/day had been added six months earlier for paranoid ideation without change in his movements. On examination, he had moderate generalized chorea with dystonic facial movements and right-hand posturing. His motor score on the United Huntington’s Disease Rating Scale was 9. Laboratory evaluations including blood chemistry, peripheral blood smear, creatine kinase, liver enzymes, thyroid function tests, ceruloplasmin, and Huntington’s disease gene were unremarkable. He had a mild microcytic anemia with low ferritin but no ferritin mutations. Anti-gliadin antibodies were markedly elevated (IgG 139 U [normal 0–20 U], IgA 72 U [normal 0–20 U]). Non-contrast brain MRI showed mild–moderate cerebral atrophy, periventricular and pontine microvascular changes, an old right subinsular hemorrhage, and a chronic left frontoparietal infarct.
title: Further Evidence for Celiac Disease-associated Chorea

case_prompt: A 43-year-old Hispanic man from Peru with remote travel in the Peruvian and Brazilian jungles two decades prior was diagnosed with Bell’s palsy three weeks earlier and started on prednisone 50 mg twice daily without follow-up. He presented with a three-week history of diarrhea, a 10-kg weight loss, intermittent fevers, and three days of hematochezia. On examination he was pale and tachycardic, had mild abdominal tenderness, and blood on rectal examination; the remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 16 000 cells/mm^3 (82% neutrophils, 2% eosinophils, 7% bands), hemoglobin 8 g/dL, and platelets 700 000/mm^3. He was presumed to have diverticulitis and was started on intravenous ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. One week after admission, he became drowsy with bradylalia and bradypsychia, developed nuchal rigidity with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, fever, right lower‐lobe crackles, abdominal distension, and constipation. A lumbar puncture yielded cloudy fluid with a protein of 179 mg/dL, glucose of 5 mg/dL, 2070 leukocytes/mm^3 (92% neutrophils), and Gram‐negative rods on Gram stain. Repeat blood count showed 25 000 leukocytes/mm^3 (84% neutrophils, 0% eosinophils, 7% bands). A CT scan of the abdomen revealed a dilated ascending colon.
title: E. coli Meningitis Presenting in a Patient with Disseminated Strongyloides stercoralis

case_prompt:
An 11-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and snoring. He also reported a 2-week history of progressive left visual field loss, initially as a small black dot that evolved to complete blackness. On examination, he had a high-arching, floppy posterior soft palate and inflamed nasal turbinates. Vital signs were within normal limits.

He was referred for an immediate dilated ophthalmologic examination and an MRI of the brain and orbits, and he was also referred to otolaryngology for evaluation of persistent allergic rhinitis versus bacterial sinusitis. He was discharged with cetirizine and oxymetazoline and instructed to return if symptoms worsened.

Four days later, an MRI of the orbits and sinuses showed a 7 × 7 × 7 cm, multi-spatial mass centered in the nasopharynx and nasal cavity. The mass involved the left sphenopalatine foramen, extended anteriorly along the turbinates into the nasal passage, invaded and replaced the bony sella posteriorly, tracked laterally through the pterygomaxillary fissure, and extended caudally anterior to the adenoids, causing complete nasopharyngeal airway obstruction. A CT scan of the facial bones confirmed the large, destructive, expansile bony changes associated with the mass.

He was admitted and underwent bilateral nasal endoscopy with biopsy of the left nasal mass, which revealed extensive involvement under the inferior turbinate. Histopathology showed a highly vascular, benign-appearing mesenchymal proliferation most suggestive of capillary hemangioma. The differential diagnosis included solitary fibrous tumor and juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.
title: Radiation Therapy Improves Local Control in Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma following Disease Progression after Embolization and Surgical Resection: A Case Report

case_prompt: A previously healthy 4-year-old boy presented with high-grade fever. On day 1 of illness, he was prescribed oral cefditoren-pivoxil for presumed group A streptococcal infection. On day 2, he developed left neck swelling, with a white blood cell count of 26.3 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein of 88.4 mg/L. He was hospitalized for acute purulent cervical lymphadenitis and treated with intravenous ampicillin–sulbactam, but fever and lymphadenopathy persisted, and torticollis appeared on day 4. Echocardiography showed tricuspid regurgitation without coronary artery abnormalities. On day 7, he met criteria for incomplete Kawasaki disease based on erythema and edema of the hands and feet, cervical lymphadenopathy, anemia for age, thrombocytosis after day 7, elevated ALT, and WBC ≥15 × 10^9/L. Intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) and high-dose aspirin were started, leading to resolution of fever and lymphadenopathy, but torticollis persisted. Plain cervical radiographs (anteroposterior and lateral views) showed head tilting with a normal atlanto-dental interval. An orthopaedic consultation noted marked restriction of cervical rotation and recommended additional imaging.
title: Torticollis in incomplete Kawasaki disease: a case of atlantoaxial rotatory fixation

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of low-grade fever, epigastric pain with episodic nausea and vomiting, anorexia, and unintentional weight loss. He had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis 30 years earlier, treated with a full course of antitubercular therapy. He denied tobacco, alcohol, or illicit-drug use and had no high-risk behaviors.

On examination, he was febrile; other vital signs were normal. He had non-tender hepatomegaly without splenomegaly, clubbing, edema, or lymphadenopathy. Cardiopulmonary examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 6500/mm3, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 70 mm/hr. Renal function was normal. Liver-function tests revealed total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 290 U/L, AST 132 U/L, and ALT 181 U/L.

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a large heterogeneously hypoechoic lesion with internal echoes in segment 6 of the liver, suggestive of an abscess. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a right-lobe liver abscess without lymphadenopathy, effusions, or other focal lesions; other abdominal viscera were normal.

He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole, but his condition did not improve after 1 week. Follow-up ultrasonography showed no reduction in abscess size. Under ultrasound guidance, a pigtail catheter was inserted and approximately 100 mL of thick, cream-colored fluid was aspirated. The fluid was negative for gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, and fungal stain was negative.
title: Unusual presentation of tuberculosis in an elderly male: a case report

case_prompt:
An 81-year-old woman was found on the floor of her home after being missing for two days. Firefighters measured 180 ppm CO in the atmosphere and 234 ppm in her exhaled air. On arrival at the emergency department, her blood pressure was 143/92 mmHg, pulse 97 beats/min, temperature 35.7 °C, and Glasgow Coma Scale score was 13 (eyes to voice, confused but able to answer questions). Her medical history included left breast carcinoma resected 30 years earlier and a known duplicate superior vena cava. She had no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

On examination, both temples were swollen and tender; palpation of the scalp over the left parietal bone worsened the pain. Temporal pulses were palpable, and sinus palpation was nonpainful. Cardiopulmonary and upper airway examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a carboxyhemoglobin level of 13% (normal 0.5–1.5%), arterial blood gas with PaO₂ 31.3 mmHg (35–40 mmHg), PaCO₂ 38.9 mmHg (36–44 mmHg), oxyhemoglobin 61% (68–73%), oxygen saturation 70.6% (68–73%), and lactate 2.1 mmol/L (0.6–1.4 mmol/L). White blood cell count was 14.34 ×10³/μL (3.8–9.1) with neutrophils 12.81 ×10³/μL (1.5–5.4), C-reactive protein 129 mg/L (< 5), creatine phosphokinase 968 IU/L (< 170), troponin 0.26 ng/L (< 0.10), creatinine 83 μmol/L (eGFR 57 mL/min), and NT-proBNP 13 294 ng/L (< 125). Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with a normal ST segment. Oxygen therapy and intravenous isotonic saline were initiated.
title: Bilateral superficial temporal vein thrombosis after acute carbon monoxide poisoning and prolonged immobilisation: a case report

case_prompt: A 35-year-old woman was evaluated for what was thought to be an intramural pregnancy. Her obstetric history included an elective cesarean delivery in 2016, an abortion for a blighted ovum (histology unremarkable) in October 2020, and a repeated evacuation 7 days later without histologic sampling. Two months after the abortion, a urine pregnancy test was positive. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a 30 mm hypoechoic lesion in the posterior uterine wall with a peripheral structure resembling a yolk sac. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated well-defined peripheral and central blood flow. Her serum β-hCG was 1092 mIU/ml, and an intramural pregnancy was diagnosed. She underwent open resection of the uterine lesion and excision of a right ovarian cyst, with an uneventful postoperative course. One week after surgery, her β-hCG had fallen to 245.7 mIU/ml and returned to normal by 2 months.
title: Placental site trophoblastic tumour mimicking an intramural pregnancy: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 3-year-old girl presented with a 1½-month history of a painful, ulcerated swelling in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. On examination, there was a soft-to-firm, ill-defined, ulcerated mass measuring 3.0 × 2.2 × 1.5 cm. Doppler ultrasonography showed a well-circumscribed, hypoechoic lesion with scant internal vascularity. Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed cellular clusters and single cells with round, centrally placed nuclei, bland chromatin, abundant granular cytoplasm, and indistinct cytoplasmic borders; the background contained occasional macrophages. The cytologic impression was a fibrocystic lesion of the breast with apocrine metaplasia. The skin nodule was excised. Grossly, the specimen measured 4.5 × 2.5 × 1.4 cm with a central 1 × 1 cm skin ulceration; on sectioning, there was a solid, light-gray, well-circumscribed subcutaneous nodule measuring 3.0 × 2.2 × 1.5 cm. Histologic examination showed sheets of polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei. Mitoses were sparse (<1 per 10 high-power fields), and there was no necrosis. The tumor cells were Periodic Acid–Schiff positive and diastase resistant.
title: Pediatric Granular Cell Tumor of the Breast: An uncommon neoplasm in an uncommon site and age group

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a several-month history of bilateral blurry vision, eye pain, redness, photophobia, and floaters, worse in the right eye. His ocular history was unremarkable. He had HIV infection and had been noncompliant with antiretroviral therapy for the past 4 months, and he was recently diagnosed with hepatitis C. He reported a history of unprotected sexual encounters with men; his last sexual partner was over a year ago. Two weeks before presentation, baseline laboratory tests revealed a serum VDRL titer of 1:256 (negative 5 years earlier), a CD4 count of 241 cells/mm3, and high HIV and hepatitis C viral loads. He denied neurologic symptoms, gummatous lesions, or cardiac signs. He received a single dose of intramuscular penicillin and was referred to ophthalmology. He had restarted antiretroviral therapy 1 week before his eye examination.

On ophthalmic examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Anterior segment assessment showed 1+ diffuse non-granulomatous keratic precipitates and 2+ flare with trace cells in both eyes. Dilated fundus examination demonstrated grade 2 optic disc edema in both eyes without evidence of infectious retinitis. Fluorescein angiography revealed early and late hyperfluorescence of both optic discs with low-grade periphlebitis, greater in the left eye than the right. These findings were interpreted as papillitis, possibly related to neurosyphilis. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. On neurologic examination, he had hyperreflexia of the upper and lower extremities and a positive right Babinski sign. A noncontrast CT scan of the head was unremarkable.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Bilateral papillitis as the initial presentation of neurosyphilis in a patient previously treated for primary and secondary syphilis

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman was referred for an enlarging neck mass and hoarseness of 5 days’ duration. She reported a very hard, fixed lump on the right side of her neck that had been present for months. She had intermittent treatment for hyperthyroidism over the past 30 years but no recent follow-up, and she denied symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.  
On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure 130/90 mm Hg, pulse 76 beats/min, and respirations 20 breaths/min. A firm, non-tender thyroid nodule approximately 5 × 4 cm was palpated on the right. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6460/mm^3, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, platelets 295 × 10^3/mm^3, ESR 19 mm/hr, CRP <0.2 mg/dL. Thyroid studies: TSH 0.07 µIU/mL (0.4–4.5), free T4 3.86 ng/dL (0.7–2), TBII 51% (0–15), thyroglobulin 493 ng/dL (2–60), antithyroid microsomal antibody 3.1 U/mL (0–8), thyroglobulin antibody 22 U/mL (negative).  
Chest radiograph showed a right-to-left tracheal shift. Thyroid ultrasound revealed a 4 cm irregular, hypoechoic nodule with scattered dense calcifications in the right lobe and no lymphadenopathy.  
Fine-needle aspiration with aspiration technique yielded scant cytologic material; no malignant cells were seen, and an adenomatous goiter was suspected.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a 4.3 × 4.0 cm nodular lesion occupying most of the right thyroid lobe with peripheral calcification and severely calcified margins. The right vocal cord was fixed in a paramedian position, consistent with paralysis.  
Given the large, solid lesion with evidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, a surgical approach was planned for diagnosis and treatment.
title: Riedel Thyroiditis in a Patient with Graves Disease

case_prompt:
A three-week-old African American female was referred for evaluation of “cysts in her gums.” She was born at term via vaginal delivery with an unremarkable prenatal history and had no other medical problems. Her mother noted the lesion in the mouth at birth and reported that it appeared to be decreasing in size over the past three weeks.  
On intra-oral examination, there was a bilobed, sessile nodular lesion approximately 1.5 cm in greatest dimension on the right maxillary alveolar ridge in the region of the unerupted canine. The surface was smooth, healthy pink, and non-hemorrhagic. There was no pain, discomfort, or cervical lymphadenopathy.  
A maxillary periapical radiograph showed no bony or dental abnormalities. Urine vanillylmandelic acid was measured to exclude a neuroectodermal tumor of infancy and was negative. A complete blood count with differential was within normal limits.  
The patient’s mother preferred non-surgical management, and in consultation with pathology, the decision was made to observe the lesion with weekly visits for one month followed by monthly follow-up.
title: Spontaneous regression of congenital epulis: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 1-year-9-month-old girl with no significant past medical or surgical history was referred for evaluation of an intra-abdominal mass versus abscess. She had a 10-day history of severe epigastric pain radiating to the left upper quadrant, fever up to 39 °C responsive to paracetamol, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. On examination, she had epigastric tenderness with left upper quadrant guarding; her abdomen was otherwise soft and lax, and no mass could be palpated.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 21.8×10^3/mm^3, hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, platelets 832×10^3/mm^3, C-reactive protein 203 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 83 mm/h, lipase 10 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 633 U/L, carcinoembryonic antigen 2.78 ng/mL, and a negative Quantiferon test. Blood cultures were negative.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined, multiloculated cystic lesion in the epigastrium extending to the left upper quadrant, the largest locule measuring 4.8×4.0×5.6 cm with swirling debris and foci of calcification, and no hyperemia. CT with contrast confirmed a multiloculated, thick, enhancing-walled fluid collection in the mesentery extending to the left flank, the largest locule measuring 6.7×6.2 cm with tiny calcifications displacing adjacent bowel loops. Mild pelvic fluid and subcentimetric enhancing mesenteric lymph nodes were noted.

Findings were interpreted as an organized abscess secondary to an infected mesenteric cyst or a lymphangioma. A true-cut biopsy yielded only fibrinoid material without viable cells, precluding a definitive diagnosis.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Mesenteric cystic lymphangioma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old woman presented after an accidental fall causing an occipital laceration. She reported months of fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, intermittent abdominal pain, and severe weight loss. On examination, blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and cardiac auscultation revealed no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Surface ECG showed sinus rhythm at 85 bpm with diffuse low QRS-wave amplitude and QT prolongation (600 ms by Bazett’s formula). Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 18,590/mm3 (70% neutrophils), C-reactive protein of 154 mg/L, procalcitonin of 2.64 ng/mL, and creatinine of 1.75 mg/dL. 

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large pericardial effusion without tamponade and marked thickening of the right atrial free wall (1.65 cm) and interatrial septum; left ventricular systolic function was preserved. Abdominal CT revealed bilateral hydronephrosis, thickening of the perirenal soft tissue, and adrenal gland enlargement.

During her first hospital night, she had a self-limited episode of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with Torsade-de-Pointes morphology. Continuous monitoring then showed junctional rhythm at 50 bpm. Over subsequent days she developed persistent QT prolongation, paroxysms of atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response, extreme sinus bradycardia, bouts of junctional rhythm, and recurrent Torsade-de-Pointes. A temporary pacemaker was placed, stabilizing the rhythm, but she later experienced ventricular fibrillation requiring external DC shock.

Brain MRI revealed T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity of the neurohypophysis, cerebellum, and brain stem. Her marked polyuria and polydipsia promptly responded to desmopressin, confirming central diabetes insipidus.
title: Cardiac electrical instability in Erdheim-Chester disease: a case report

case_prompt: A 55-year-old man presented with atony of both lower extremities and malaise for over 6 months. He reported progressive fatigue and thirst for 2 months, night sweats, a 5-kg weight loss, and intermittent fever. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed a white-cell count of 38.22×10^9/L, a platelet count of 390×10^9/L, and an LDH level of 1122 U/L. A bone marrow aspirate demonstrated hypercellularity with prominent dysgranulopoiesis: 0.5% myeloblasts, 3.5% promyelocytes, 9% myelocytes, 3% metamyelocytes, 10% eosinophils, 4.5% lymphocytes, 2% nucleated red cells, and 9.5% monocytes. A manual peripheral-blood differential confirmed granulocytosis with circulating myelocytes and metamyelocytes. Bone marrow biopsy showed marked neutrophilic leukocytosis (84%) with left shift, 6–8 megakaryocytes per high-power field without karyolobism, and grade 1 fibrosis. Immunohistochemistry was MPO+, CD71+, CD61+, CD117–, and CD34+/–. Testing for the BCR-ABL fusion gene was negative, and JAK2 V617F was detected. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a normal karyotype (46, XY). A preliminary diagnosis of prefibrotic primary myelofibrosis was considered, with other myeloid neoplasms to be excluded.
title:
A rare atypical chronic myeloid leukemia BCR-ABL1 negative with
concomitant JAK2 V617F and SETBP1 mutations: a
case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old white man with hypertension and no diabetes presented with a large, painful, malodorous mass on his left heel. He reported that the lesion began as a nonhealing wound after trauma in a motor‐vehicle accident 20 years ago; over the past 4 years it had progressively enlarged. He denied recent trauma, weight loss, night sweats, or systemic symptoms. 

On examination, temperature was 98.5 °F, heart rate 102 beats/min, blood pressure 131/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The left heel had a 15 × 20 cm hypergranular, fungating mass with areas of necrosis, mild erythematous margins, and serosanguinous drainage. The lesion extended proximally to the ankle, distally to the midtarsal region, and medially and laterally to the malleoli. There was severe pain on palpation; ankle motion was limited in a fixed equinus position. Peripheral pulses were palpable bilaterally. There was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Plain radiographs of the left foot showed a lytic lesion in the lateral posterior calcaneus without evidence of bone resorption. CT scans of the chest and abdomen showed no masses, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly.
title: A Rare Case of Invasive Keratinizing Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Foot

case_prompt: A 42-year-old Egyptian man with no comorbidities presented with moderate voiding and storage lower urinary tract symptoms without hematuria. Physical examination and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Flexible cystoscopy showed a clear urethra and prostate, but granulomatous reaction and bullous edema at the bladder neck and trigone obscured the ureteric orifices. Urine cytology was negative for high-grade malignancy. Transurethral resection of the bladder-neck and trigonal lesions revealed florid cystitis glandularis without malignancy. On follow-up, serum creatinine rose and ultrasound demonstrated worsening hydronephrosis; a renogram showed left renal function of 85% and right of 15%, indicating obstructive uropathy. A right percutaneous nephrostomy revealed severe hydroureteronephrosis with obstruction at the lower ureter. After failed antegrade stenting, the nephrostomy was maintained and further imaging was obtained. Abdominopelvic MRI T2-weighted imaging showed severe bilateral hydroureteronephrosis with thinning of the right renal cortex. A CT cystogram demonstrated urinary bladder wall thickening accompanied by extensive fat stranding.
title: Pelvic lipomatosis—a rare diagnosis and a challenging management: a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 39-year-old man with a two-year history of seronegative rheumatoid arthritis treated with azathioprine and etanercept (last dose three weeks earlier) presented with sudden-onset severe, progressive neck and left shoulder pain radiating down the left arm and a decreased range of shoulder movement. He denied trauma. On examination, he guarded the left neck and shoulder; he was febrile (38.3°C) but haemodynamically stable. The left shoulder was oedematous with an erythematous rash and diffuse tenderness both anteriorly and posteriorly. Passive range of motion was painful, active range of motion was very limited, and neurological and vascular examinations were normal. There was no clinical evidence of toxic shock. Laboratory studies showed neutrophilia and an elevated C-reactive protein; blood cultures were negative. A chest radiograph and plain films of the left shoulder and cervical spine were normal. The initial differential diagnosis included septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and localized skin abscess. Intravenous cefotaxime was started and immunosuppressive therapy was discontinued. Over the next 24 hours he remained febrile and developed a diffuse macular blanching rash over the left shoulder with a non-fluctuant boggy swelling in the left supraclavicular area. Antimicrobial therapy was broadened to include intravenous cefotaxime, metronidazole, vancomycin, and ciprofloxacin. Serial examinations showed persistent tenderness and progression of the erythematous rash without blistering, skin eruption, or discharge.
title: Necrotising fasciitis of the shoulder in association with rheumatoid arthritis treated with etanercept: a case report

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old boy presented with a left mandibular mass first noted 4 years earlier, slowly enlarging over time. He had no history of trauma or toothache. Over the past year, he experienced pain on mouth closure due to contact between his upper teeth and the lesion. Physical examination revealed a 16 × 12 cm hard, non‐tender mass involving the left mandible, extending from the zygomatic arch to 5 cm below the mandibular border. The overlying skin and oral mucosa were intact and of normal appearance. Intraorally, the lesion displaced adjacent teeth peripherally and pushed the tongue to the contralateral side, causing difficulty chewing and speaking. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Vital signs and routine laboratory studies were normal.

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a large, well‐defined expansile mass arising from the left mandible with cortical erosion, loosening of adjacent teeth, a unilocular radiolucent area, and multiple internal calcifications. The surrounding soft tissues, airway structures, and intracranial contents were unremarkable. CT scans of the chest and abdomen were normal.

Based on the clinical findings, history of presenting illness, and radiological features, differential diagnoses of ossifying fibroma, ameloblastoma, and fibrous dysplasia were entertained.
title: Massive ossifying fibroma of mandible: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 34-year-old man presented with a one-year history of progressive, painless proptosis of the left eye without preceding trauma or systemic illness. He also reported frontal headaches and occasional left eye pain over the same period. On examination, there was left eccentric proptosis with inferotemporal displacement of the globe, fullness in the superonasal orbit, and left-sided forehead prominence. Visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes, with a normal anterior segment and unremarkable fundus. Extraocular movements were full. Contrast-enhanced multidetector CT of the orbits showed a large multilobulated ossified mass (73 × 60 mm) centered in the frontal sinuses and extending into the ethmoid sinuses. The lesion involved the orbital roofs bilaterally with focal thinning and erosions. On the left, it extended superomedially into the extraconal space, compressing the globe and superior rectus muscle, correlating with the proptosis. Post-contrast images showed no enhancement of the mass lesion.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: An unusual encounter in ophthalmology: Fronto-Ethemoido-Orbital Osteoma with the art of precise referral and management of PEEK implant infection- A rare case report

case_prompt: A 67-year-old Iranian man presented with a 3-month history of weakness and epigastric pain. On examination, his blood pressure was 115/80 mm Hg and pulse rate was 88 beats per minute; no other abnormalities were noted. Laboratory studies revealed severe anemia (hemoglobin, 3 g/dL), a serum iron level of 65 μg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a suspicious collection at the lesser omentum. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an 81 × 73 mm polypoid mass involving the gastric antrum and duodenum, as well as a 54 × 45 mm enhancing lesion in the left posterior mediastinum suggestive of lymphadenopathy. Gastroendoscopy revealed a large, pedunculated duodenal mass. Endoscopic biopsy identified a poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm, suggestive of an epithelioid gastrointestinal stromal tumor, but was deemed inconclusive. The patient underwent total gastrectomy with gastrojejunostomy. Gross examination showed a brownish, polypoid tumor in the duodenum. On hematoxylin and eosin staining, the tumor was highly pleomorphic, composed of bizarre eosinophilic, round, and spindle cells with apparent skeletal muscle differentiation, extending into the submucosa without lymphovascular invasion. Based on morphology alone, the differential diagnoses included lymphoma, mucosal melanoma, undifferentiated carcinoma, epithelioid GIST, and sarcoma. Immunohistochemical stains and molecular studies are pending.
title: Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma in adults: a case report

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old Caucasian man with a family history of prostate and breast cancer presented with a 6-month history of a right upper medial thigh mass. There was no trauma history; the mass was nontender and had not changed in size. He denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, nausea, or malaise and had no history of immunocompromise.  
On examination, he had a firm, nonmobile, irregular 4 cm subcutaneous mass on the right upper outer thigh without inguinal lymphadenopathy. The abdomen was soft and nontender, with no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Strength and range of motion in the affected leg were normal.  
Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 7.9×10^3/μL (normal 4.8–10.8), an RBC count of 5.84 M/μL (4.70–6.10), a hematocrit of 50.7% (42.0–52.0), and a platelet count of 243×10^3/μL (164–446). Electrolytes and liver and renal function tests were normal.  
Ultrasound of the thigh revealed a vascularized heterogeneous subcutaneous mass measuring 5.9×3.8×1.3 cm, suggesting a primary soft-tissue or metastatic tumor. MRI of the right lower extremity showed a 5.4×3.4×1.5 cm T2-hyperintense, slightly T1-hyperintense lesion with uniform contrast enhancement, superficial to the rectus femoris without invasion; several small inguinal nodes were within normal limits. Findings raised concern for a soft-tissue sarcoma or metastasis.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy, multiple enlarged gastrohepatic lymph nodes (up to 5×3 cm), and mildly prominent retroperitoneal nodes (up to 10 mm), with otherwise unremarkable solid organs. Differential diagnosis included metastatic adenopathy and lymphoma.
title: Mantle Cell Lymphoma Presenting as a Subcutaneous Mass of the Right Leg

case_prompt: A 44-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of generalized weakness, fatigue, an urticarial rash without pruritus, fever up to 39°C, and bilateral leg and knee pain. Initial diagnoses of chronic allergic urticaria were treated unsuccessfully with antihistamines and then with prednisone, which led to temporary improvement; symptoms recurred upon tapering steroids. On admission, he had no focal neurologic deficits or signs of arthritis, and vital signs showed fever. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytes 23.2×10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 35 mm/h, C-reactive protein 107 mg/L, serum amyloid A 174 mg/L, ferritin 717 µg/L, and interleukin-6 37.8 pg/mL; rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies were negative. Serum lactate dehydrogenase, liver transaminases, interleukin-1β, and complement components C3 and C4 were within normal limits. Ultrasonography demonstrated minimal pericardial and left pleural fluid collections.
title: Increasing the Interval of Canakinumab Administration Effectively Supports the Remission of Schnitzler's Syndrome

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent, colicky central abdominal pain and altered bowel habits characterized by constipation, nausea, postprandial bloating, and easy fatigability. Over the past 2 days, her pain worsened and was accompanied by vomiting, progressive abdominal distension, and obstipation. She denied anorexia, weight loss, fever, or lower gastrointestinal bleeding. She reported that her father had been treated for abdominal tuberculosis 10 years earlier.

On examination, the abdomen was distended with palpable bowel loops and hyperactive bowel sounds; digital rectal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies were within normal limits; serum carcinoembryonic antigen was 0.65 ng/mL (reference range, 0–2.5 ng/mL). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen showed short-segment circumferential thickening and a stricture in the proximal descending colon with adjacent fat stranding and multiple enlarged mesocolic lymph nodes. The proximal large bowel was grossly dilated (approximately 6 cm) with fecal-loaded transverse colon, ascending colon, and cecum.
title: Left-Sided Colonic Tuberculosis Presenting as Colonic Stricture: A Rare Presentation of a Common Disease

case_prompt: A 3-year-old girl presented with progressive shortness of breath of several months’ duration. She had no fever, night sweats, weight loss, vomiting, flushing, hypertension, or abdominal pain. Physical examination was notable only for low oxygen saturation; routine laboratory tests were normal. A chest radiograph showed opacity of the entire right hemithorax and scoliosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a well-circumscribed solid mass measuring 10.2 × 9.2 × 11.8 cm in the right posterior mediastinum, extending from the first thoracic vertebra to the level of the heart. The mass was hypodense and mildly heterogeneous, contained punctate calcifications, caused contralateral displacement of mediastinal structures and trachea, demonstrated mild heterogeneous contrast enhancement, and showed no invasion of adjacent organs or the chest wall. There was no evidence of spinal destruction, and nerve involvement could not be assessed.
title: A Rare Case of Giant Mediastinal Ganglioneuroma in A 3-year-old

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man presented after tripping and falling onto his left side with persistent pain over the left clavicle. He had a 4-year history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension, treated with metformin, furosemide, and captopril. He had a 30-pack-year smoking history but had quit 5 years earlier. He denied any family history of cancer or exposure to environmental toxins. 

On examination, he was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 135/80 mmHg and a normal pulse rate. The only abnormal finding was tenderness over the left clavicle. 

Radiographs of the shoulder revealed a lytic lesion in the left clavicle and an asymptomatic lytic lesion in the left humeral head. CT imaging demonstrated multiple osteolytic lesions throughout the axial and appendicular skeleton. 

A whole-body bone scintigraphy with technetium-99m-MDP showed diffusely increased uptake in both axial and appendicular skeleton, absent urinary activity, prominent calvarial and periarticular uptake, and focal accumulation of tracer at the left clavicle.
title: Unusual pathological fracture of the clavicle revealing primary hyperparathyroidism: a case report

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 23 weeks of gestation was admitted emergently with acute abdominal pain and signs of hemodynamic shock. Her blood pressure was 80/05 mm Hg, pulse 115 bpm, and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute. She reported progressive abdominal distension over 10 days. Her obstetric history included one prior cesarean delivery for a placental anomaly; there was no other significant medical history. Fetal cardiac activity was present at 132 bpm. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness and a positive Flot’s sign indicating free fluid in the abdomen.  

One week earlier, a transabdominal ultrasound at a primary care facility confirmed a 23-week intrauterine mono-fetal pregnancy with normal fetal heart activity. The ovaries were not visualized, and no ascites or adnexal mass was reported.  

On admission, laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin level of 8.9 g/dL, urea 0.18 g/L, creatinine 8 mg/L, blood glucose 0.85 g/L, and prothrombin level 97%. Renal and coagulation studies were otherwise normal. The patient was resuscitated with two large-bore intravenous lines, macromolecule infusions, and supplemental oxygen.  

Given the patient’s hemodynamic instability and persistent abdominal fluid, an exploratory laparotomy was planned for definitive diagnosis and management.
title: Ovarian Dysgerminoma Associated With Pregnancy Presenting as Hemoperitoneum: An Obstetric Case Report

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old woman presented six weeks after a cesarean delivery with a sudden episode of heavy vaginal bleeding. Ten years earlier, she had undergone a lower transverse cesarean section. In the current pregnancy, she was diagnosed with marginal placenta previa and at 28 weeks of gestation developed significant vaginal bleeding, premature rupture of membranes, and chorioamnionitis (white cell count 19,980/mm3; C-reactive protein 50.2 mg/L). She underwent a repeat lower transverse cesarean section, during which small adherent placental fragments were manually removed. Histologic examination of the placenta had shown chorionic villi implanted directly on the myometrium without intervening decidua and extravillous trophoblasts between villi and myometrial fibers. Her immediate postoperative course was unremarkable, and she was discharged on day five.

Over the next six weeks, she noted intermittent light vaginal spotting until the recent heavy bleeding. On clinical examination, the uterus was enlarged to approximately 12–13 cm with a soft consistency. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a homogeneous uterine body measuring 67 × 52 × 61 mm, with a 72 × 30 × 75 mm nonhomogeneous hyperechoic mass in the lower uterine cavity and upper cervical canal. Color Doppler demonstrated numerous intralesional vessels. Serum β-hCG was 15.5 IU/L. Pelvic MRI confirmed that the uterine mass consisted solely of placental tissue without involvement of the myometrium or adjacent organs.
title: Unexpected Dramatic Evolution of Placenta Increta: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 52-year-old man with a 6-year history of sporadic abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss was treated intermittently with budesonide for presumed inflammatory bowel disease but had poor follow-up. He presented after several weeks of increasing diarrhea, abdominal pain, vomiting, and a 6.8-kg weight loss. On examination he was afebrile, hypotensive (systolic blood pressure 93 mmHg), and appeared chronically ill with somatic muscle wasting (BMI 21 kg/m2). The abdomen was modestly distended, diffusely tender without peritoneal signs, and bowel sounds were cavernous. Plain abdominal radiographs and CT of the abdomen demonstrated diffuse dilation of the small and large bowel with significant edema of a large segment of the distal ileum. Laboratory studies revealed iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, iron 38 µg/dL, ferritin 13 ng/mL) and hypoproteinemia (albumin 2.5 g/dL, total protein 5.1 g/dL). Serum immunoglobulin levels were normal. Neuromuscular markers for IPO—including anti-neuronal nuclear antibodies (ANNA-1), striational antibodies, N-type calcium channel antibodies, acetylcholine receptor antibodies, ganglionic neuronal AChR antibodies, and GAD65 antibodies—were negative.
title: Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction and Total Villous Atrophy of the Terminal Ileum: An Unusual Presentation of Untreated Celiac Disease

case_prompt: A 29‐year‐old man with HIV, end‐stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and hypertension presented with a 2‐day history of generalized, nonthrobbing headache and blurred vision. He reported compliance with antiretroviral and antihypertensive medications and denied tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. On examination, he was afebrile, alert, and oriented; blood pressure was 245/141 mm Hg; visual acuity was 20/80 in both eyes without scotomas or field deficits; cranial nerves II–XII were intact; muscle strength and sensation were normal; reflexes were 2+; and there were no cerebellar findings. CBC was within normal limits. His CD4 count was 325 cells/mm3 and HIV‐1 RNA was 5100 copies/mL. Noncontrast CT of the head was negative. Lumbar puncture showed normal opening pressure and clear cerebrospinal fluid with a white cell count of 2 cells/μL and protein of 39 mg/dL; CSF studies (Indian Ink, cocci, cryptococcus, HSV, VDRL) were all negative. Urine toxicology screening was negative.
title: Atypical presentation of cerebellar posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in a patient with HIV

case_prompt: A 57-year-old Japanese man with stage IVB ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma had initially received cisplatin plus pemetrexed followed by pemetrexed maintenance. Upon progression after nine months, he was started on alectinib (300 mg daily) as second-line therapy. Three months into alectinib treatment, he developed dyspnea on exertion. On room air, his oxygen saturation was 82%; arterial blood gas measurement showed a PaO2 of 58.2 torr. Pulmonary function testing revealed a restrictive ventilatory defect (vital capacity 2.11 L, 57.1% predicted) and a diffusion impairment (DLCO 4.84 mL/min/mmHg, 22.8% predicted). Chest CT demonstrated shrinkage of the left upper lobe primary lesion but new bilateral ground-glass opacities and areas of consolidation. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis showed a lymphocyte proportion of 34.4%, and cultures were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy revealed an organizing pneumonia/nonspecific interstitial pneumonia overlapping pattern without evidence of malignant infiltration. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 9300/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 1.41 mg/dL.
title: Efficacy of lorlatinib after alectinib-induced interstitial lung disease in a patient with anaplastic lymphoma kinase-positive non-small cell lung cancer: a case report

case_prompt:
A 6-year-6-month–old girl was referred for a routine dental examination. Her height and weight were below the fifth percentile, with a notably short neck and mild scaphocephaly. She walked with an abnormal gait but had normal speech and no neurologic deficits. Four years earlier, laboratory evaluation had shown elevated urinary keratan sulfate levels and markedly reduced N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfate sulfatase activity in leukocyte cultures; no genetic tests were performed, and she has not received enzyme therapy. Family history was unremarkable. Dietary history revealed low daily carbohydrate intake.

On examination, she had pectus carinatum, stubby hands, kyphosis, and mild rotation of the lower extremities. Craniofacially, she had brachycephaly, a convex and biprotusive facial profile, a flat nasal bridge, a closed nasolabial angle, an apparently large mouth, and broad lips.

Intraoral findings included mixed dentition with deep caries in all primary molars, ovoid dental arches, an anterior crossbite, a mild anterior open bite, macroglossia with tongue thrusting, generalized moderate gingivitis, and a high labial frenum. Oral hygiene was poor. She exhibited thumb-sucking and mouth-breathing habits. Both temporomandibular joints were normal on clinical examination. She was anxious and had difficulty maintaining a supine position.
title: Pediatric Dental Management of an Uncommon Case of Mucopolysaccharidosis Type IV A (Morquio A Syndrome): A Case Report of a Three-Year Follow-Up

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of migratory arthralgia (knees, ankles, small joints of toes) with rest pain and morning stiffness, accompanied by intermittent low-grade fever, dysphagia, and dyspnea for 4 days. She had a history of iron-deficiency anemia treated with oral iron and a 1-month course of prednisolone, which she stopped several days before presentation.  
On examination, vital signs were normal. She appeared pale and had pharyngitis. Fine crackles were heard at the right lung base. Joints showed synovial thickening of both knees, ankles, and select interphalangeal joints, with pain on movement of wrists, knees, and ankles.  
Laboratory studies revealed WBC 15,200/mm3 (64% neutrophils, 22% lymphocytes, 22% eosinophils), RBC 2.6×106/mm3, Hb 6.6 g/dL, Ht 20.3%, MCV 77.5 fL, MCH 25.5 pg. Serum creatinine was 1.8 mg/dL, CRP 8.3 mg/L, ESR 75 mm/h, serum iron 12 µg/dL. Urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria (800 RBCs), proteinuria, 70 WBCs, and positive bacteria.  
Chest CT demonstrated multifocal patchy centrilobular consolidative opacities in bilateral middle and lower lobes, consistent with acute hemorrhage or infection. Sputum culture grew Staphylococcus aureus; blood cultures were negative. Urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to amikacin, imipenem, and meropenem.  
Despite antibiotic therapy, purpura developed on the lower extremities and pulmonary infiltrates persisted on chest radiograph. Serologic testing revealed ANA 1:40, negative anti–double-stranded DNA, normal C3 and C4, negative rheumatoid factor, negative anti–citrullinated protein antibodies, and negative p-ANCA and c-ANCA on repeat testing.
title: Pauci‐immune necrotizing glomerulonephritis in a 24‐year‐old female with negative ANCA antibodies: A rare case report

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of chest tightness and dyspnea at rest. He had no history of pulmonary infection or asthma in childhood or adulthood and a 5-pack-year smoking history. On examination, his respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Pulmonary auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds over the left lung. Complete blood count, urinalysis, D-dimer, and blood chemistry results were within normal limits. Pulmonary function tests showed an obstructive pattern with a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 2.76 L (64% predicted) and a forced vital capacity of 4.93 L (110.8% predicted). 

Chest radiography demonstrated unilateral hyperlucency of the left lower lung with a small hilar shadow and reduced bronchovascular markings. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a hyperlucent left lung without anteroposterior gradient attenuation, hypoplasia or absence of the left pulmonary artery and peripheral vascular bed, and overall reduction in the left inspiratory lung volume; there was no mass or evidence of pulmonary embolism, and no abnormalities in the right lung. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction showed reduced airway branching and cylindrical and cystic bronchiectasis scattered throughout the left lung, most prominently in the left lower lobe. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed no bronchial stenosis.
title: Multimodal imaging findings in an adult case of Swyer‐James‐MacLeod syndrome

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old woman with a history of morbid obesity underwent multiple bariatric procedures over a 3-year period: initial endoscopic gastric bypass, subsequent banded gastric bypass for inadequate weight loss, and finally conversion to a distal gastric bypass. Her body-mass index decreased from 59 to 32 kg/m2, with a total weight loss of 46%. Over the year after her last surgery, she was hospitalized four times for malnutrition (serum albumin 12 g/L), generalized edema, and depression, during which she refused psychiatric evaluation.  

At the most recent admission, she had abstained from food for over one week, was markedly somnolent, and exhibited signs of hypoalbuminemia and anasarca. Initial laboratory studies included:  
– Serum albumin 12 g/L (normal >35)  
– Total bilirubin 53 μmol/L (normal <17)  
– Alkaline phosphatase 103 U/L (normal <120)  
– AST 25 U/L (normal <31)  
– ALT 21 U/L (normal <31)  
– γ-GT 76 U/L (normal <35)  
– Antithrombin III 10% (normal >80%)  
– Platelets 105×10^9/L (normal 150–400×10^9/L)  
– PT-INR >7  
– Blood glucose low  
– Serum ammonia 224 μmol/L (normal 10–45)  

No urea cycle disorders were identified. Abdominal imaging showed normal hepatic parenchyma and patent portal flow. Common causes of liver disease were excluded.
title: Liver failure caused by prolonged state of malnutrition following bariatric surgery

case_prompt: A 29‐year‐old woman with treated hypothyroidism presented with a five‐year history of a right nasal mass that had gradually increased in size. The mass was painless, nonpulsatile, and primarily caused cosmetic concern. She denied nasal obstruction, bleeding, rhinorrhea, or changes in skin pigmentation. There was no family history of similar lesions. General and neurologic examinations were normal. On nasal inspection, there was a spherical, cystic, movable, nontender enlargement of the right nasal ala extending from the lower to upper lateral cartilage, without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the nose showed an isolated, poorly defined soft‐tissue swelling in the right anterior lateral nasal wall with mild heterogeneous enhancement and no expansion into adjacent structures. MRI demonstrated an oval, 0.5 × 0.7 cm lesion that was isointense on all sequences, with homogeneous postcontrast enhancement, distinct surrounding fat planes, and no invasion of the septum or nearby tissues; comparison with an MRI from 2018 showed only modest growth. The patient opted for surgical excision after discussion of risks and benefits.
title: Schwannoma at an Unusual Site: Case Report and Surgical Technique Discussion for Nasal Dorsum

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old Han Chinese boy presented with a 2-week history of fever, weakness, pallor, edema, dyspnea, and progressively increasing abdominal girth. He was the product of a full-term, non-consanguineous pregnancy with markedly slow growth and development, but good school performance. At age 9, he underwent splenectomy for an unexplained splenomegaly. Since then he had multiple hospital admissions for fever of unknown origin without a clear diagnosis.

On examination, his height was 135 cm and weight 30 kg, with no secondary sexual characteristics. His temperature fluctuated between 37.2 °C and 39.7 °C. He appeared pale and distressed. There was no jaundice or rash. Superficial inguinal lymph nodes were palpable. He had periorbital edema, large bilateral tonsils without pharyngeal congestion, harsh breath sounds with bilateral crackles, and a heart rate of 114 beats/min without murmur. His abdomen was distended; the liver was firm, nontender, and palpable 10 cm below the costal margin. He had shifting dullness and marked pitting edema of the lower limbs. Neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory testing over several days showed a white blood cell count > 20 × 10^9/L, progressive anemia and thrombocytopenia, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (301 U/L), AST 45 U/L, ALP 218 U/L, total bilirubin 72.9 μmol/L, hypoalbuminemia (29 g/L), and slight prolongation of PT and APTT with an elevated D-dimer. Renal function and urinalysis were unremarkable. Other positive findings included procalcitonin ~ 0.2 ng/mL, ASO 259 IU/mL, Widal’s TH 1:160 and TO 1:320, CA-125 384 U/mL, CA724 38.8 U/mL, ferritin 550 ng/mL, hepatitis E virus IgG(+), and Legionella pneumophila IgM(±). Tests for thyroid function, ESR, CRP, CD64 index, T-lymphocyte subsets, and G6PD were normal. Coombs test; interferon-γ release assay; ANA; HAV, HBV, HCV, HIV antibodies; and HSV, CMV, and EBV DNA were negative. Blood and fungal cultures were negative. Bone marrow smear showed an infectious pattern with occasional atypical lymphocytes.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a grossly enlarged liver (164 mm), gallbladder wall swelling, left renal calculi, and massive ascites; the portal vein and common bile duct were normal. There was slight pericardial effusion. Enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated severe pulmonary interstitial fibrosis with infection, multiple lymph node enlargement, and an irregularly shaped enlarged liver without vascular abnormalities.

He received empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, antiviral therapy, diuresis, liver-protective measures, human serum albumin, intravenous immunoglobulin, and blood transfusions, with gradual improvement of fever. Given the multisystem presentation and difficulty attributing all findings to a single etiology, a rare genetic metabolic disorder was suspected. To pursue a definitive diagnosis, archived splenic tissue was retrieved for pathological examination.
title: Fever, pulmonary interstitial fibrosis, and hepatomegaly in a 15-year-old boy with Gaucher disease: a case report

case_prompt: A 25-year-old Caucasian man presented with a skull defect over the left frontotemporal region that had progressively enlarged over a 3-year period. He reported mild dull local aching headaches, short-term memory impairment for one year, occasional visual symptoms, and subjective hearing decrease. His past medical history was significant for depression and polysubstance abuse. On examination, general physical findings were unremarkable except for a clearly visible osseous depression of the left frontoparietotemporal region with mild tenderness, interspersed softness, and thinning yet firm skull. He was neurologically intact. Plain skull radiographs showed widespread loss of calvarial structure consistent with an osteolytic process. Head CT revealed patchy erosive osteolysis of the left frontoparietotemporal skull region, with patent coronal, sagittal, and lambdoid sutures. Postcontrast MRI demonstrated marginal enhancement of the calvarial defect without brain invasion or soft tissue component. A bone survey and chest radiograph showed no additional skeletal or pulmonary lesions. Metabolic and endocrine laboratory studies were within normal limits.
title: Complex single step skull reconstruction in Gorham’s disease - a technical report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 10-month history of right upper quadrant pain. The pain was sharp, intermittent, radiated to the back, and was associated with nausea and vomiting. She noted that the pain was exacerbated by fatty meals; there was no change in bowel habits or urinary symptoms. She denied other medical conditions or a family history of gastrointestinal problems. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the upper abdomen without guarding or rebound. Routine laboratory studies, including a metabolic profile and liver function tests, were within normal limits.

An abdominal ultrasound of the right upper quadrant was performed. It demonstrated a contracted, shrunken gallbladder that was not visualized on imaging; the biliary tree appeared normal. There was no sonographic Murphy’s sign, gallbladder wall thickening was 2 mm, no pericholecystic fluid was present, and there was no intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile duct dilatation.

Based on the clinical presentation and ultrasound findings, a laparoscopic cholecystectomy was planned.
title: Gallbladder Agenesis without Additional Biliary Tracts Abnormality

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old woman was under routine surveillance ten months after total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, appendectomy, para-aortic lymph node dissection, and adjuvant chemotherapy for papillary serous ovarian adenocarcinoma. Surveillance abdominal CT demonstrated a cystic lesion in the midportion of the pancreas, which was confirmed on follow-up MRI. To assess for malignancy, endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the cyst yielded fluid containing malignant cells but did not identify the tumor’s origin. 

On referral, she reported vague abdominal discomfort but had an otherwise normal physical examination and unremarkable laboratory studies. At laparotomy, a 4×2-cm cystic mass was found confined to the midpancreas without local invasion or distant spread. Intraoperative fluid cytology again showed malignant epithelial cells without a definable primary source. Operative findings led to a spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy.
title: Pancreatic Metastasis of High-Grade Papillary Serous Ovarian Carcinoma Mimicking Primary Pancreas Cancer: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 57-year-old man presented with binocular horizontal diplopia for 2 weeks, noted only when gazing to the left, and progressively worsening. He denied pain, redness, discharge, trauma, or prior infection. Corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. External examination showed no inflammation, mass, proptosis, or asymmetry on exophthalmometry. Extraocular movements were full bilaterally. On eversion of the upper eyelid, a small, smooth, translucent cystic mass was seen on the anterior aspect of the palpebral lobe of the lacrimal gland. Orbital magnetic resonance imaging revealed an 11 × 6.5 mm, well-circumscribed, cystic lesion adjacent to the lateral rectus muscle and contiguous with the inferior palpebral lobe of the lacrimal gland; the globe and remaining lacrimal tissue appeared normal, with no surrounding inflammation.
title: Diplopia due to Dacryops

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old woman was referred for an electrophysiological study because of recurrent palpitations refractory to beta-blockers. She reported palpitations since adolescence, frequently terminated by a 6 mg adenosine bolus. She had no other comorbidities. A 12-lead ECG during symptoms showed a narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia. Resting ECG in sinus rhythm, transthoracic echocardiography (normal left ventricular function), and 24-hour Holter monitoring (no sustained arrhythmias) were unremarkable.

Under conscious sedation, catheters were placed in the right atrium/right ventricle, at the His bundle, and in the coronary sinus. Incremental ventricular pacing revealed 1:1 ventriculoatrial conduction (earliest activation in proximal coronary sinus) down to a cycle length of 600 ms. Incremental atrial pacing showed an atrioventricular Wenckebach point at a cycle length of 380 ms. There was no pre-excitation on the surface ECG, and the HV interval was normal.

Programmed atrial stimulation from the high right atrium induced a supraventricular tachycardia associated with a critical jump in the AH interval. During tachycardia, there was a progressive prolongation of the RP interval culminating in a blocked P wave, resembling a Wenckebach cycle in the upper common pathway. A spontaneous atrial contraction then reset the tachycardia circuit. As the tachycardia cycle length increased, atrial activation occurred every other cycle (2:1 VA block) with upper-axis P waves on the frontal ECG leads. A few seconds later, the 2:1 VA block alternated with a 2:1 AV infra-Hisian block. Subsequently, 1:1 AV conduction resumed with a left bundle branch–type QRS morphology alongside continued 2:1 VA conduction. During tachycardia, isolated His-bundle depolarizations were also recorded.
title: Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia and the dilemma of reentry circuit components: A proof of concept

case_prompt:
An 11.5-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of facial and dental abnormalities. She was born at term (3500 g) to a first pregnancy with an unremarkable perinatal course. In the neonatal period, she was noted to have an extra digit on the left hand, torticollis, flexion contractures of digits in the right hand, and a malformed right thumb. Psychomotor development was mildly delayed in infancy. 

Her history included multiple osteoarticular abnormalities, structural inner ear anomalies, facial dysmorphism, frontal bone thinning, lumbar vertebral deformities, and underweight status. She required ongoing care by pediatricians, audiologists, pulmonologists, and rehabilitation specialists.

On orthodontic examination, she had bilateral Angle class II malocclusion, an overjet of 7.7 mm, and an overbite of 12.7 mm. Facial features included exophthalmos, hypertelorism, full cheeks, and prominent superciliary ridges. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated absence of the right second molar tooth germs (upper and lower), the right second lower premolar, and all third molars, with a retained deciduous tooth in the position of the right lower second premolar. 

Cephalometric analysis revealed a reduced mentolabialis sulcus angle, skeletal class II with upper incisor proclination (WITS index 8.6 mm), a retrognathic facial type, and mandibular hypoplasia resulting in an oblique retrognathic profile.
title: Craniofacial and Dental Manifestations of Melnick–Needles Syndrome: Literature Review and Orthodontic Management

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman presented with a painless swelling on the anterior aspect of her left leg. She reported that a small oval bulge had been present since birth and had gradually enlarged to approximately 10×6 cm. There were no associated symptoms such as fever, warmth, or overlying skin changes. Her medical, family, drug, and allergy histories were unremarkable.

On examination, the mass was smooth, soft, and mobile in all directions. There was no fluctuation, translucency, reducibility, compressibility, or pulsatility. A lateral radiograph of the left leg below the knee showed a localized soft-tissue swelling. MRI of the same region demonstrated a large, solitary, well-defined, heterogeneously isointense lesion measuring 13×9×6 cm in the subcutaneous plane over the diaphysis of the tibia, with an identifiable feeding vessel.

Based on the imaging findings, a subcutaneous hemangioma was diagnosed. The patient was treated with propranolol, but no improvement was observed. Surgical excision and biopsy were then planned.
title: Lower li1mb mesenchymal hamartoma masquerading as hemangioma: a case report of AA2 atypical presentation and diagnostic challenges

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with 7 days of fever, malaise, and arthralgia. He was febrile (39°C) on arrival; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. He reported drinking unpasteurized camel’s milk, and a serological test for brucellosis was positive. Initial laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 145 g/L, white cells 7.6 × 10^9/L (45.6% lymphocytes, 49.2% neutrophils), and platelets 4 × 10^9/L. Other tests, including renal and liver function, were within normal limits. He denied any medication use and left against medical advice on doxycycline and rifampicin.

Two days later, he returned with epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and hematuria. He was febrile (38.7°C), with blood pressure 110/75 mmHg and heart rate 72 beats/min. A nonpruritic, flat purpuric rash was noted on the lower extremities; other examinations were normal. Repeat CBC showed hemoglobin 128 g/L, white cells 4.9 × 10^9/L (51.8% lymphocytes, 41.1% neutrophils), and platelets 2 × 10^9/L. Peripheral smear revealed normal red and white cell morphology, marked thrombocytopenia with occasional giant platelets, and no platelet clumps. To evaluate thrombocytopenia, malaria blood film, coagulation profile, fibrinogen, antinuclear antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA antibody, and serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein–Barr virus were all unremarkable. The Brucella agglutination titer was 1 : 1280.
title: Acute Brucellosis Presenting with Bleeding Tendency due to Isolated Severe Thrombocytopenia

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old woman presented with an 8-day history of binocular vertical diplopia and a subjective restriction in elevation. Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism and polycystic ovarian syndrome; she had no prior ocular surgery or trauma. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 6/4.5 bilaterally, intraocular pressures were normal, and pupils were equal and reactive. Extraocular motility testing showed mild (–1) limitation of elevation in adduction of the left eye with pain on right gaze, and cover testing revealed a left hypotropia of 4 prism diopters. Anterior and posterior segment exams were unremarkable.

A contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated normal superior oblique muscles and trochlear tendon complexes. Given suspicion for acquired Brown syndrome of inflammatory origin, she was started on ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily. Five days later, she returned with increased trochlear-region pain and worsening diplopia. Examination revealed moderate (–2) limitation of elevation in adduction of the left eye; other findings were stable. Oral prednisolone 25 mg daily was initiated, with subjective pain relief but persistent motility deficit.

One month after presentation, her motility deficit progressed to bilateral moderate (–2) elevation limitation in adduction. A repeat orbit MRI again showed no superior oblique hypertrophy, tendon inflammation, or trochlear attachment abnormalities. Rheumatology evaluation and serologic testing for mixed connective tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis were negative. She remained symptomatic over the next 11 months while receiving up to 50 mg daily of oral prednisolone, which was tapered and replaced with methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine.
title: Novel association of ocular myasthenia gravis with Brown syndrome in an adult

case_prompt: A 21-year-old phenotypic female presented with primary amenorrhea and a desire for fertility. She was 146 cm tall, weighed 67 kg (BMI 31.3 kg/m2), and had cubitus valgus and a webbed neck; external genitalia were unambiguously female. Her medical history was notable only for multiple childhood tympanoplasties. There was no family history of gynecologic disease or short stature. Transabdominal ultrasound showed uterine hypoplasia. Contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI demonstrated a 30 mm-long uterus with vaginal thinning and no identifiable gonads. CT of the chest and abdomen was normal. Serum studies revealed estradiol ≤ 5.0 pg/ml, luteinizing hormone 25.5 mIU/ml, and follicle-stimulating hormone 98.4 mIU/ml. Peripheral-blood karyotyping showed 45,X/46,XY mosaicism (8 of 30 cells 45,X; 22 of 30 cells 46,XY).
title: Mixed gonadal dysgenesis with gonadoblastoma diagnosed by prophylactic laparoscopic gonadectomy: A case report

case_prompt: A 14-year-old boy presented with a 3-day history of severe right lower–quadrant abdominal pain, anorexia, and fever. His only past medical history was spontaneously descended undescended testes at age 4. On examination, his temperature was 37.4 °C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Abdominal examination revealed guarding and tenderness in the right iliac fossa; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal blood count and metabolic profile, with a C-reactive protein level of 41 mg/L; urinalysis was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated fat stranding in the right iliac fossa, and the appendix was not visualized. He was observed with analgesia, but after 6 hours his pain persisted and increased in intensity. A decision was made to proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy.
title: Torsion of the Omentum: A Rare Cause of Acute Abdomen in a 14-Year-Old Boy

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old man was evaluated for a 1-year history of recurrent palpitations consisting of sudden-onset, regular tachycardia episodes lasting approximately 5 minutes, which had increased in frequency over the past few weeks. He had no prior cardiac disease, took no medications, and had no exercise limitation or cardiovascular risk factors. Vital signs and a general physical examination were unremarkable.  
Baseline ECG showed sinus rhythm at 75 bpm, a PQ interval of 160 ms, QRS duration 107 ms with an incomplete right bundle branch block, no signs of ventricular pre-excitation, and a QTc of 441 ms. Transthoracic echocardiography and stress echocardiography were normal. A 48-hour Holter recording captured one non-sustained atrial tachycardia at 147 bpm without symptoms; clinical tachycardia remained undocumented. In the absence of malignant arrhythmia, supraventricular re-entrant tachycardia was suspected, and the patient was taught vagal maneuvers and instructed on using a wearable smart device to record single-lead ECG tracings during palpitations.  
Subsequently, the patient recorded episodes of regular wide QRS complex tachycardia at 145–160 bpm with a left bundle branch block morphology. On one occasion, he traced a wide LBBB tachycardia at 160 bpm (CL 375 ms) and, during the same symptomatic period, a narrow-complex tachycardia at 200 bpm (CL 300 ms).
title: Case report: orthodromic atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia with left lateral accessory pathway—smart diagnosis with a smart device

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old man was referred to the ENT outpatient clinic on an urgent two-week-wait pathway with a history of intermittent exertional stridor, dysphonia, and dysphagia. His symptoms had recurred over multiple emergency department visits, and an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal. He had undergone a partial thyroidectomy for multinodular goitre in 2006 and a revision right hemithyroidectomy in 2017 for compressive symptoms. He was prescribed thyroxine and calcium supplements but admitted to poor adherence with calcium.

On examination, there were well-healed thyroidectomy scars. Flexible nasendoscopy revealed tongue-base fullness with symmetrical vocal-cord mobility and no mucosal lesions. A CT scan of the neck and thorax showed a small mucous-retention cyst at the tongue base and residual thyroid tissue bilaterally but no evidence of malignancy.

He was scheduled for panendoscopy under general anaesthesia, and routine pre-operative blood tests were obtained.
title: Simultaneous dysphagia and stridor: an unreported presentation of hypocalcaemia

case_prompt:
