A 53‐year‐old woman presented with a two‐year history of a gradually enlarging mass in her right breast. She had no comorbidities or family history of cancer but had undergone right hemimandibulectomy with bone grafting for ameloblastoma 15 years earlier. 

On examination, the lesion measured 16 × 13 cm, involved the upper chest wall and the right side of the neck, and there was no palpable lymphadenopathy. 

Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography of the chest demonstrated a heterogeneous solid and cystic mass in the superior region of the right breast measuring 15 × 15 × 10 cm, with extension into the pectoralis major muscle but no other masses or lymphadenopathy. 

A punch biopsy of the breast lesion was performed, yielding a spindle‐cell neoplasm.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Metastasizing ameloblastoma of the breast: A case report

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old man with diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension (managed with metoprolol) presented with a 4-month history of a generalized, intensely pruritic, erythematous rash involving the bilateral upper and lower extremities, lower back, and trunk. He denied fever, chills, joint pain, bullae, mucosal lesions, new medications, or changes in personal care products.

Two separate skin biopsies (left distal posterior upper arm and right superior lateral lower back) showed confluent parakeratosis, epidermal acanthosis with eosinophilic spongiosis, and no microscopic subepidermal splitting. A perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes and numerous eosinophils was noted. The initial differential diagnosis included contact dermatitis, eczematous drug eruption, Ofuji disease, T cell lymphoma, and nonbullous pemphigoid.

Patch testing revealed a positive fragrance mix, but exposure was deemed unlikely and clinically irrelevant. The patient was treated with topical triamcinolone and 60 mg of oral prednisone daily for 2 weeks, with minimal improvement. A second 3-week course of prednisone (60 mg daily) also failed to provide relief, and over the next 3 months the rash progressed to erythroderma.

Given the absence of vesicles or mucosal involvement and persistent severe pruritus despite high-dose systemic steroids, a paraneoplastic process was considered. A computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed florid lymphadenopathy concerning for systemic lymphoma.
title: Nonbullous erythrodermic pemphigoid with florid lymphadenopathy, response to dupilumab

case_prompt: A 24-year-old pregnant woman (G2P1) was referred at 8 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of bilateral pelvic cysts. Her history was notable for two prior open ovarian cystectomies, one for a mature cystic teratoma and one for a mucinous cystadenoma. Transvaginal ultrasound and pelvic MRI showed a unilocular left cyst measuring 9 cm and a multilocular right cyst measuring 5 cm. Serum tumor markers (CA-125, CA19-9, and CEA) were within normal limits for pregnancy. At 14 weeks, an attempt at cyst resection was converted to laparotomy because of dense adhesions around the cysts and posterior uterus; no metastatic lesions or lymphadenopathy were found, and peritoneal fluid cytology was negative for malignancy. At 32 weeks, repeat MRI demonstrated that the left cyst had enlarged to 27 cm and appeared to merge with the right cyst, forming a single large pelvic cyst without any solid components or papillary projections. Tumor markers remained normal. Given the remaining uncertainty about malignancy and the risks of preterm delivery with relaparotomy, the team elected to defer surgical intervention until term.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Rapid Growth of Pelvic Cyst during Pregnancy: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 23-year-old woman with no significant medical or psychiatric history presented with convulsions, agitation, and rapidly progressive disorientation. Three weeks earlier she had a mild viral prodrome with dry cough and rhinitis. On examination her vital signs were normal; Glasgow Coma Scale was 12/15. She had fluctuating cognition, confusion, disorientation, and involuntary facial and limb movements. Initial blood tests—including a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid function tests, and viral serologies—were unremarkable. Despite treatment with risperidone, her agitation and psychosis persisted. A lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic pleocytosis with a predominance of CD4+ T cells, elevated protein, and normal glucose. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral multifocal high T2 signal changes surrounding the ventricles and in the basal nuclei with vasogenic edema.
title: A case report of anti‐NMDA receptor encephalitis in a 23‐year‐old female with acute psychiatric symptoms

case_prompt: A patient was referred to the hospital in March 2022 with a leukocyte count of 105×10^9/L. Initial laboratory assessment showed normal to slightly increased levels of C-reactive protein and procalcitonin and markedly increased lactate dehydrogenase. Tests for autoimmune disease were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography and computed tomography revealed a spleen measuring 14 cm, normal liver size, and no lymphadenopathy. A peripheral blood smear showed proliferative myelopoiesis with a pathologic left shift and a myelocyte peak; basophilic and eosinophilic granulocytes were underrepresented. Bone marrow puncture revealed hypercellularity, dominating granulopoiesis left shifted with myelocyte predominance, a blast count of 15%, underrepresentation of basophilic and eosinophilic granulocytes (<2%), erythroid precursors comprising 27–31% of hematopoiesis, and trilinear dysplasia. Conventional cytogenetic analysis demonstrated a normal male karyotype (46,XY). PCR analysis of BCR::ABL1 major and minor breakpoints and fluorescence in situ hybridization were negative.
title: Differential diagnoses and the mutational landscape of myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm with neutrophilia: A case report

case_prompt: A 43-year-old woman presented with progressively worsening right-sided neck pain for 3 days that did not respond to paracetamol. She had no recent upper respiratory infection or trauma. On examination, there was focal tenderness over the right side of the neck and mild right cervical lymphadenopathy without masses or bruits. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 6.35×10^9/L (neutrophils 57.1%, lymphocytes 29.6%, eosinophils 4.4%), platelet count of 134×10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 3.6 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/hr. Initial ultrasound of the neck demonstrated a few prominent reactive lymph nodes at Level II but otherwise normal neck anatomy. She was treated empirically with oral co-amoxiclav and metronidazole for a presumed dental infection and given celecoxib for pain. After 4 days, the pain persisted, and on reassessment a focal tender point was noted over the right carotid pulse at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. A focused second-look ultrasound with a 7.5-MHz transducer showed increased echogenicity of the anterior and lateral perivascular tissues surrounding the distal right common carotid artery, carotid bulb, and proximal external carotid artery with obliteration of normal fat planes; no carotid wall thickening, plaques, luminal stenosis, or abnormal Doppler flow was seen. The left carotid region was normal.
title: Transient perivascular inflammation of the carotid artery; a rare cause of intense neck pain

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old previously healthy Middle Eastern man presented with a 4-year history of a painless bulge in the left iliac fossa that arose 6 months after repair of a left inguinal hernia. The mass was initially small but grew gradually, becoming more uncomfortable when he walked over the past 5 months. He denied pain, skin ulceration, pigment changes, systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), trauma, or infections. He had no other medical or surgical history, did not smoke or drink alcohol, and had a BMI of 28 kg/m2.

On examination, he was mildly tachypneic with borderline tachycardia; other vital signs were normal. The abdomen moved normally with respiration; there was a fixed, hard, well-demarcated bulge in the left inguinal region that was irreducible, had no cough impulse, and did not change with position. The overlying skin was adherent and mildly erythematous but showed no induration, telangiectasia, ulceration, or pigmentation. There was no tenderness, guarding, or regional lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Ultrasound of the left iliac fossa demonstrated a 7.0 × 2.7 cm hypoechoic lesion. The radiological interpretation favored a lipoma, although malignant etiologies could not be excluded.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A unique case of Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans arising from an inguinal hernial repair scar in a Middle Eastern male - A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old woman presented with mild blurring of vision in the right eye and interest in refractive surgery. She denied any history of ocular inflammation, trauma, surgery, or use of topical or systemic medications. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.05 in the right eye (improving to 0.5 with −3.00 to +2.00 × 15) and 0.5 in the left eye (improving to 0.8 with plano −0.75 × 170). Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg bilaterally. 

Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a clear cornea, a deep and quiet anterior chamber without iris transillumination defects, and confluent stellate pigment deposits on the anterior lens capsule over the pupillary axis. After pupillary dilation, there were no pigment deposits on the peripheral capsule, zonules, posterior lens capsule, or anterior hyaloid face. The left eye anterior segment was normal before and after dilation. Gonioscopy showed an open angle in the right eye with mild pigmentation and prominent iris processes; the left eye angle was open and unremarkable. Ophthalmic examination of the posterior segment was normal in both eyes.
title: Unilateral Congenital Lenticular Pigmentation

case_prompt: A 36-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of severe, retrosternal chest pain that worsened when lying flat, associated with progressive dyspnea, high-grade fevers, and episodes of delirium. His medical and family histories were unremarkable; he had a 40–pack-year smoking history. On examination, he was febrile to 39.2 °C, tachypneic, and had facial and upper-limb edema. Laboratory testing revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL), a slightly elevated monocyte percentage (13.7%), and a normocytic red‐cell distribution width of 18.4%. Chest radiography showed widening of the mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest demonstrated a 12-cm anterior mediastinal mass compressing and infiltrating both right and left brachiocephalic veins and the superior vena cava, with an intraluminal filling defect consistent with thrombus, and a separate nodule on the right diaphragm suggestive of metastasis.
title: Wide en-bloc thymectomy and venous axis reconstruction in Masaoka stage IIIB thymoma: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old man presented with a recent decrease in vision in his left eye. He had undergone cataract extraction with intraocular-lens implantation in the right eye at age 10 after trauma; vision in that eye remained light perception before and after surgery. He also reported prior laser treatment to the left eye. He was born full term, with no parental consanguinity and no family history of ocular disease.

On examination, the right eye had light-perception vision; the left eye’s visual acuity was 20/60. The right anterior segment showed pseudophakia with pupillary occlusion; the left anterior segment was normal. The left eye was exotropic. Fundus examination of the left eye revealed disc dragging with a thick vitreoretinal traction band extending from the disc to the inferotemporal periphery; there were old laser marks in an area of peripheral avascular retina, minimal vitreous hemorrhage, and condensed vitreous.
title: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy complicated with macular hole retinal detachment

case_prompt: A 70-year-old Asian man presented with a 2-year history of intermittent dysuria characterized by a thin urine stream, decreased urinary volume, prolonged urination, and a sense of incomplete emptying, accompanied by urinary urgency and frequency. His symptoms had gradually worsened over the past few months. He had no significant past medical or family history. On physical examination, vital signs were stable, and the only abnormal finding was a diffusely enlarged prostate on digital rectal examination. Laboratory tests revealed a serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level of 0.404 ng/mL (reference range 0–4 ng/mL). Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging showed a mass occupying the peripheral zone of the prostate, with apparent invasion of both seminal vesicles, the posterior bladder wall, and the anterior rectal wall, as well as enlarged pelvic lymph nodes.
title: Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the prostate: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 25-year-old Japanese woman was referred for evaluation of a 4-week history of a painless nodule in her lower lip thought to be malignant. She was in good health until she noted the lesion and had no history of tobacco or alcohol use. Three weeks before the lesion appeared, she had unprotected orogenital contact with her steady partner. Physical examination revealed a 2.0-cm nodule of the lower lip with a central ulcer and a slightly elevated, indurated, erythematous margin. There was no fever or cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel except for a C-reactive protein level of 6.48 mg/dL (reference < 0.30 mg/dL). Serum squamous cell carcinoma antigen and carcinoembryonic antigen were within normal limits. Tests for HIV I/II, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody were negative. Ultrasonography of the lesion demonstrated an oval 17 × 11 × 12 mm mass in the left lower lip with heterogeneous internal echoes, an indistinct border, and very abundant blood flow on color Doppler except at the center. Probe‐pressure testing revealed that the tumor was soft. Magnetic resonance imaging could not be performed because of a metal crown on a front tooth.
title: Sonographic appearance of syphilitic induration mimicking squamous cell carcinoma in the lower lip: a case report

case_prompt:
An 18-year-old right-handed man presented with asymptomatic, gradually increasing fusiform swelling of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the left middle finger over the past 5 years. He reported no pain, no functional limitation, and denied any repetitive movements or compulsive habits. His family history was noncontributory, and psychiatric evaluation excluded emotional distress. 

On examination, there was diffuse thickening of the soft tissues over the radial and ulnar aspects of the left middle-finger PIP joint, with intact overlying skin, no pigmentation, and no neurologic deficits. The range of motion was full, and there were no signs of inflammation. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and rheumatoid factor, were within normal limits or negative. 

Plain radiographs of the hand showed fusiform soft-tissue swelling around the PIP joint without joint-space narrowing, bony erosions, or other structural abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated circumferential and longitudinal soft-tissue thickening that was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on postcontrast fat-suppressed T1-weighted images, with no joint effusion, tenosynovial fluid, or hemorrhagic changes.
title: Surgical Management of Unilateral Soft Tissue Swelling around the Proximal Interphalangeal Joint in an Adolescent: A Case Report of Pachydermodactyly

case_prompt: A 41-year-old woman presented with acute abdominal and back pain. Two days earlier, she had been treated at an outside hospital for a presumed urinary tract infection with systemic antibiotics, but her abdominal pain worsened and she developed high fever. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, her temperature was 40.0 °C; she had mild abdominal tenderness with rebound and marked pallor of the conjunctiva. Laboratory studies showed: Hb 7.3 g/dL, WBC 16,500/μL, platelets 18,000/μL, CRP 18.0 mg/dL, AST 146 IU/L, ALT 79 IU/L, LDH 899 IU/L, total protein 4.6 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, prothrombin time 44.1 %, fibrin/fibrinogen degradation products 239.4 μg/mL, D-dimer 75.1 μg/mL, antithrombin III activity 53 %, base excess −13.0 mmol/L, and lactate 12.9 mmol/L. Tumor markers and viral hepatitis serologies were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed thick-walled multilocular cystic lesions of both ovaries without pelvic ascites. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated an 11.1 × 7.9-cm left ovarian cystic mass and a 6.3 × 4.4-cm right ovarian cystic mass, both with low echogenicity and septations. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of one of the cystic masses yielded purulent fluid.
title: Emergency surgery for tubo-ovarian abscess identified extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli: the first case presentation revealing causative bacteria

case_prompt: A 19-year-old woman was admitted with acute, severe left upper-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and nonbloody vomiting unresponsive to oral medications. Three months earlier, she had experienced milder abdominal pain radiating to the right shoulder and scapula, relieved by nonopioid analgesics. She reported a 5 kg weight loss over eight weeks. Her only medication was an oral contraceptive; she denied fever, substance use, prior surgery, and relevant travel. Examination revealed a tender, palpable mass from the epigastrium to the left hypochondrium. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, mild elevations in AST (50 U/L), ALT (40 U/L), GGT (321 U/L), ALP (390 U/L), INR 1.5, and albumin 2.9 g/dL. AFP was 1.3 ng/mL, CA19-9 11 U/mL, and CEA 0.5 ng/mL. Contrast CT and MRI demonstrated an 18 × 12.1 × 12.5 cm lobulated, multilocular, cystic-solid, heterogeneous liver mass with a fibrous pseudocapsule, sparing only segment 6. There was no portal or arterial thrombosis. The three major hepatic veins were not visualized, but an inferior right hepatic vein (9.3 mm in diameter) drained segment 6. After multidisciplinary discussion, early resection was planned, with consideration of ruptured hepatocellular adenoma, atypical hemangioma, and mucinous cystadenocarcinoma.
final_diagnosis_raw: undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver
title: Undifferentiated Embryonal Sarcoma of the Liver Involving All Major Hepatic Veins Treated by Left Extended Trisectionectomy

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old woman presented with a 10-year history of primary amenorrhea. At age 15, pelvic ultrasonography showed absence of the uterus and part of the vagina, as well as a missing left kidney. She reports normal breast development and pubic hair (Tanner stage 5), and denies cyclic abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, headaches, visual changes, galactorrhea, or weight fluctuations. Her mother and sister have normal menstrual histories; there was no maternal exposure to substances or radiation during pregnancy.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. She was 155 cm tall and weighed 56 kg. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Genital examination revealed normal external genitalia and pubic hair distribution, with a blind vaginal dimple on perineal inspection. Perirectal examination confirmed the absence of a palpable uterus.

Laboratory studies showed a 46XX peripheral blood karyotype. Serum levels of luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, prolactin, progesterone, and testosterone were all within normal ranges. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed absence of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina, with a blind-ending distal one-third; both ovaries were visualized high in the pelvis anterior to the iliopsoas muscles. MRI of the abdomen confirmed absence of the left kidney with a normal right kidney. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no cardiac abnormalities.
title: McIndoe Vaginoplasty in MRKHS: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a four-week history of progressive unsteadiness and ataxia, initially diagnosed as labyrinthitis. Her only past medical history was a total thyroidectomy in 1993 for papillary carcinoma, with subsequent levothyroxine replacement and no residual disease. She had no allergies, occupational exposures, or relevant family history, and she neither smoked nor drank alcohol.

On examination, she was afebrile and disoriented, with marked gait ataxia and horizontal nystagmus; muscle strength, tone, and deep tendon reflexes were normal. Chest, abdominal, and other physical examinations were unremarkable.

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral parenchymal edema and leptomeningeal and cortical enhancement involving the cingulate gyri and the region of the superior sagittal sinus. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure greater than 34 cm H₂O, reactive cytology (lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, and occasional eosinophils) with no cells detected on automated count, and an elevated protein concentration of 742 mg/L. A staging CT of the chest identified a right upper lobe mass with a satellite nodule. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was within the normal range, and EEG showed no epileptiform activity.

Further history obtained from the patient revealed a two-year history of intermittent joint pains responsive to NSAIDs, two episodes of inflammatory eye disease treated with topical steroids, and occasional nosebleeds.
title: A Presentation of Cerebritis Secondary to Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Wegener)

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent headaches and episodes of blurred vision. Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, osteoarthritis, and Raynaud syndrome. Medications included aspirin, diltiazem, losartan, gabapentin, baclofen, tramadol-acetaminophen, calcium, fish oil, and others. She had no focal neurologic deficits on examination, with pupils equal and reactive, intact extraocular movements, and no lymphadenopathy. 

Visual evaluation by a retinal specialist showed visual acuity of 20/80 bilaterally, intraocular pressures of 17 mmHg (right) and 14 mmHg (left), thinning of the macula on fundus exam, and bitemporal visual field loss. 

An MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed an inhomogeneously enhancing mass in the pituitary fossa measuring approximately 1.8 × 1.8 × 1.5 cm, extending into the suprasellar region with cavernous sinus involvement, partially displacing the optic chiasm and hypothalamus superiorly. No acute infarct or hemorrhage was seen. A separate focus of gadolinium enhancement (<6 mm) was noted in the left caudate head adjacent to the internal capsule. 

A comprehensive pituitary hormone panel—including ACTH, cortisol, FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH, free T4, and IGF-1—was within normal limits.
title: Unusual Presentation of Craniopharyngioma Pituitary Mass in a 71-Year-Old Female: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 36-year-old nulliparous woman presented with 11 years of primary infertility, progressive hirsutism since age 25, recent secondary amenorrhea, deepening voice, clitoral enlargement, and male-pattern baldness. She had no medication use or relevant family history. On exam, BMI was 21 kg/m2, blood pressure normal, Ferriman-Gallwey score was 22, and clitoromegaly was noted. Laboratory studies showed total testosterone 1.71 ng/mL (normal 0.3–0.75), androstenedione 4.1 ng/mL (normal 0.4–3.5), normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, prolactin, cortisol, TSH, and hCG. A 17-hydroxyprogesterone level was normal after ACTH stimulation. Serum CA 125, CEA, CA 19-9, CA 15-3, and AFP were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound showed no adnexal masses. Laparoscopic ovarian biopsy and drilling were nondiagnostic, and postoperative testosterone rose to 10 ng/mL. A follow-up pelvic ultrasound showed a right ovarian cyst measuring 42 × 34 mm. MRI demonstrated multiple ovarian cystic formations and no adrenal mass.
final_diagnosis_raw: Steroid cell tumor not otherwise specified
title: Ovarian Steroid Cell Tumor (Not Otherwise Specified): A Case Report of Ovarian Hyperandrogenism

case_prompt: A 71-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of slowly enlarging swelling and diffuse pain in the left posterior mandibular region. She had undergone mastectomy for breast cancer 15 years earlier and had insulin-dependent diabetes. On examination, there was a smooth-surfaced, soft, well-defined mass in the left mandibular region that was tender but not fixed to the overlying skin or underlying bone. Panoramic radiography showed a retained root fragment in the left maxillary molar area. For further evaluation of possible metastasis, inflammatory swelling, or benign salivary-gland tumor, ultrasonography of the neck was obtained. Ultrasonography revealed normal thyroid and submandibular glands but showed a 40 × 18 mm, well-defined, hypoechoic solid lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland with echogenic septa and posterior acoustic enhancement. Hence, a pleomorphic adenoma was suspected, and contrast-enhanced CT was requested.
title: Differential Diagnosis of Parotid Lipoma in a Breast Ca Patient

case_prompt:
A woman in her mid-70s with a history of left-sided diverticulosis presented with 2 months of worsening nonbloody diarrhea, left lower-quadrant abdominal pain, decreased appetite, and fever. She had been treated empirically for diverticulitis without improvement. She denied recent travel, infectious contacts, or medication changes. Outpatient blood tests showed leukocytosis (WBC 23.63 × 10^9/L) and anemia (hemoglobin 81 g/L). The automated differential flagged immature granulocytes; a manual smear revealed a left shift to the blast stage with approximately 6% circulating blasts. She was referred to the emergency department. 

Abdominal computed tomography demonstrated extensive sigmoid diverticulosis but no bowel wall thickening or mass. Blood and urine cultures showed no microbial growth. Stool culture and parasite enzyme immunoassay were negative. Clostridioides difficile serology was negative. Repeat blood counts showed persistent blasts. Bone marrow biopsy revealed 65%–80% myeloblasts, consistent with acute myeloid leukemia; flow cytometry confirmed 47% myeloid blasts.

Because of her persistent severe diarrhea, she underwent flexible sigmoidoscopy without full bowel prep. Endoscopy showed grossly normal mucosa with scattered petechiae and surface friability, but no discrete lesions or masses. Random biopsies were obtained from the rectosigmoid colon.
title: Non-Mass-Forming Myeloid Sarcoma of the Colon Presenting With Diarrhea

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old man was referred for a 3-day history of painless visual loss in the right eye. He also reported 3 months of asthenia and occasional vomiting. He had a 45 pack-year smoking history and otherwise no relevant medical history.  
On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/63 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. A subtle right relative afferent pupillary defect was present. Visual field testing showed a severe diffuse defect in the right eye; the left visual field was normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed only an edematous right optic disc. Neurologic examination demonstrated diminished reflexes and mild gait instability, prompting hospital admission.

Laboratory studies showed normal C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Serologic tests for Treponema pallidum, HIV, hepatitis B and C viruses, Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella henselae, Coxiella burnetti, and Toxoplasma gondii were negative. CMV, EBV, and VZV serologies were IgG-positive but IgM-negative. QuantiFERON-TB Gold and blood cultures were negative. Visual evoked potentials revealed increased latency in the right eye. MRI of the brain and orbits was unremarkable. The patient was discharged without a definitive diagnosis.

On follow-up, visual acuity worsened to hand motion in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. A right afferent pupillary defect persisted, and bilateral optic disc edema was noted. Neurologic signs progressed to instability and dysmetria of all limbs, confirmed by sensory evoked potentials and electromyography. He was readmitted. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 170 mm H₂O, protein 137.5 mg/dL, 94% lymphocytes, and negative cytology and cultures. A chest radiograph was abnormal, and thoracic CT revealed mixed emphysema with a right hilar adenopathy of malignant appearance.

While awaiting PET-CT, visual acuity declined to 20/40 in the left eye. Slit-lamp exam showed no anterior chamber cells or flare. Fundoscopy revealed vitreous haze (RE +3, LE +2) and creamy-yellow deep retinal lesions: a perifoveal circular pattern in the right eye and a placoid parafoveal lesion in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated papillitis and peripapillary phlebitis. SD-OCT of the right eye showed severe disorganization of outer retinal layers with focal granular hyperreflectivity in Henle’s fiber layer and outer nuclear layer coalescing into wedge-shaped and band-like lesions at the fovea; the RPE and ellipsoid segment layers were granular, with atrophy and a hyperreflective deposit at the fovea. Vitreous hyperreflective dots were present. SD-OCT of the left eye showed vitreous hyperreflective dots and a single hyperreflective tangential band at the fovea with granular disorganization of outer retinal layers.
title: Paraneoplastic Focal Outer Retinitis and Optic Neuropathy in a Patient with Small Cell Lung Carcinoma and Anti-CRMP5, Anti-HU and Anti-Amphiphysin Antibodies

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman (BMI 29.1) underwent two separate surgeries, each followed by inspiratory stridor and respiratory distress shortly after extubation. 

First surgery (cervical laminectomy for C2–C3 extradural tumor): 
– Induction with propofol and rocuronium; easy intubation with a 7.5 mm armored tube (Cormack–Lehane grade 1).  
– Maintenance: desflurane/50% O₂ for 3 h 30 min; no intraoperative events.  
– Reversal with pyridostigmine/glycopyrrolate; extubation was uneventful, with SpO₂ 99%.  
– Five minutes later in the PACU, she developed tachypnea, respiratory difficulty, and inspiratory stridor despite accessory-free lungs; SpO₂ remained 99% on 2 L/min nasal O₂.  

Second surgery (laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ten months later):  
– Preoperative ENT evaluation showed normal vocal cord structure and movement.  
– Induction with propofol/rocuronium; lidocaine given before intubation; intubated with 6.5 mm cuffed tube; dexamethasone given before extubation.  
– Maintenance: desflurane/50% O₂ plus remifentanil infusion for 50 min; uneventful.  
– Adequate neuromuscular recovery confirmed by TOF; extubation performed; shortly thereafter she developed respiratory difficulty with inspiratory stridor and maintained SpO₂ ≥ 98% with 100% O₂.  

Laboratory studies during the second event showed mild respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.48, PaCO₂ 31.6 mmHg, PaO₂ 106 mmHg).
title: Paradoxical vocal fold motion masquerading as post-anesthetic respiratory distress: A case report

case_prompt:
A term male infant (birth weight 4.17 kg) was delivered by cesarean for antenatally detected fetal ascites and abdominal distension. At 20 weeks’ gestation, ultrasound showed fetal ascites with normal morphology; amniocentesis and karyotype were normal, and viral studies (cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis) were negative. At 23 weeks, ultrasound demonstrated increased ascites, peritoneal thickening, and an irregular solid mass arising from the left posterolateral peritoneal surface. Fetal MRI showed a T1- and T2-isointense soft‐tissue mass in the left lower quadrant, without cystic or fatty components, separate from visceral organs but inseparable from the left peritoneal lining, along with a large amount of ascites. At 35 weeks, ultrasound showed enlargement of the mass and multiple subdiaphragmatic peritoneal deposits. These findings raised suspicion for a malignant soft‐tissue tumor of peritoneal origin, with differential diagnoses of fibrosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and peritoneal neuroblastoma.

The infant was born at term with marked abdominal distension and respiratory distress requiring mechanical ventilation; he was extubated on day 2. A postnatal CT scan revealed a large multilobulated enhancing mass (5.8×4.3×8.6 cm) along the left paracolic gutter extending to the left iliac fossa, a tortuous draining vein into the inferior vena cava, and multiple small (up to 1.6 cm) avidly enhancing subphrenic and perihepatic lesions. The bowels were displaced, and no lymphadenopathy was seen. These features were described as suggestive of a malignant soft‐tissue tumor with peritoneal deposits. Tumor markers, including alpha-fetoprotein, HCG, and urine catecholamines, were unremarkable. Ultrasound‐guided paracentesis yielded chylous exudate without malignant cells. The infant was fed a medium-chain triglyceride–based formula. On day 13 of life, a laparoscopic biopsy was performed to obtain tissue for histologic diagnosis.
title: Neonatal Abdominal Hemangiomatosis: Propranolol beyond Infantile Hemangioma

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old man presented with two days of sudden bilateral chest pain, sharp and pleuritic in nature, associated with shortness of breath and a mild cough. He reported progressive dyspnea over the past month. He also noted a lesion on his scalp that had enlarged over 6 weeks; a dermatologist had performed a biopsy one week earlier, and the histopathology was pending. He had no hemoptysis, no history of cancer, diabetes, or tuberculosis, and no known family history of these conditions.

On examination, he appeared acutely ill. Blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, pulse 130 beats per minute, temperature 37.6 °C, respiratory rate 35 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80% on room air. A nonpainful, violet-colored lesion measuring 8 × 10 cm with dome-shaped elevation and irregular borders was present in the right occipito-parietal scalp region. Breath sounds were diminished bilaterally with scattered crackles at the lung bases. Other findings were unremarkable.

Initial laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 14,500/mm³ (80% neutrophils, 25% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, and platelet count 278,000/mm³; serum biochemistry was within normal limits. Differential diagnoses included tuberculosis, Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, Nocardia, fungal infection, malignancy, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pneumothorax. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed multiple cystic lesions in both lungs, patchy ground-glass opacities, and nodules, in the setting of bilateral pneumothorax. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for infectious pathogens.
title: Bilateral pneumothorax in a patient with angiosarcoma of the scalp: a case report

case_prompt: A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of generalised abdominal pain that had localised to the right iliac fossa. She reported nausea and constipation, but her bowels had opened on the day of presentation. She had no urinary symptoms, significant medical history, or regular medications. On examination, she was haemodynamically stable and apyrexial. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa but no signs of peritonitis. Laboratory studies showed a mild leukocytosis (11.2 × 10^9/L); the remainder of the complete blood count and serum biochemistry were within normal limits. She was discharged home but returned the following day with persistent symptoms and was referred to the surgical team. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal, with no appendix mass identified. After two more days of observation with non-resolving pain, the decision was made to perform a diagnostic laparoscopy for suspected appendicitis.
journal: World Journal of Emergency Surgery : WJES
title: A diagnostic challenge: primary omental torsion and literature review - a case report

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old Hispanic woman with Down syndrome, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and obesity (body mass index, 32 kg/m2) presented with epigastric abdominal pain and nausea of one month’s duration. She denied vomiting, changes in bowel habits, dysphagia, odynophagia, gastrointestinal bleeding, or weight loss. She had no history of pancreatitis, pancreatic surgery, or endoscopic procedures. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, she had tenderness to palpation in the epigastric region without peritoneal signs. A complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel were normal. Empiric therapy with famotidine provided no relief.  
One month later, she returned with persistent pain. Abdominal ultrasound showed a dilated pancreatic duct. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 12 mm hypoenhancing mass in the inferior pancreatic head, with upstream ductal dilation (5 mm) and mild hepatic steatosis. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a 15 mm mass in the pancreatic head, and four ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsies were obtained. Histopathology demonstrated marked acute inflammation with areas of necrosis and no dysplasia or malignancy.
title: A Rare Case of Pancreatic Actinomyces

case_prompt: A 67-year-old German woman with no prior illnesses presented to ENT colleagues with an intraoral laceration in the upper left wisdom-tooth region. She felt faint and had a high fever. Laboratory testing showed a normal leukocyte count (5.88 × 10^3/μl) and an elevated C-reactive protein level (224 mg/l). She was treated with intravenous penicillin V (10 mega units once daily) and underwent extraction of the impacted upper left wisdom tooth on the same day. Despite this regimen, her condition did not improve; she developed higher fevers and progressive swelling of cervical lymph nodes. Twenty-five days after tooth extraction, her cervical lymph nodes had enlarged to approximately 30 mm in diameter, and she was hospitalized for repeat intravenous antibiotics (penicillin V 10 mega units once daily plus metronidazole 0.5 g twice daily). Sonography at that time demonstrated markedly enlarged cervical lymph nodes without clear fluid collections.
title: Lymph node abscess caused by Francisella tularensis – a rare differential diagnosis for cervical lymph node swelling: a case report

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man was referred after routine health screening revealed a right retroperitoneal mass. He had a 5-year history of hypertension (up to 180/100 mmHg), managed with telmisartan; he was asymptomatic. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including CA 72-4, α-fetoprotein, CEA, CA 19-9, CA 12-5, and NSE, were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed an 8.0 × 7.0 × 5.0 cm oval mass in the right perinephric space with homogeneous isodensity and a clear margin. In the arterial phase, the lesion demonstrated intense heterogeneous enhancement, followed by rapid homogeneous washout in the portal-venous and delayed phases. There was no evidence of renal invasion, and the tumor compressed the adjacent duodenum. Multiplanar reconstruction revealed that the blood supply arose from the right testicular artery.

MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a perinephric mass with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, slightly high signal on T2-weighted images, and restricted diffusion on DWI. On dynamic gadolinium-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted sequences, the enhancement pattern mirrored CT, with a conspicuous enhancing capsule. A hyperintense central stellate area on T2-weighted images showed delayed enhancement in the portal-venous and delayed phases.
title: Primary extra-pancreatic pancreatic-type acinar cell carcinoma in the right perinephric space: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 66-year-old woman, a life-long non-smoker, presented with hemoptysis. Seven years earlier, chest CT had shown a pyramid-shaped pulmonary hemorrhage in the right upper lobe (segment 1). She was well until a second episode of hemoptysis, when chest CT revealed a 9-mm, well-demarcated, round nodule in segment 4 of the right middle lobe against a background of interstitial pneumonia. She underwent further evaluation. Sputum cultures showed no bacterial pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen and cytokeratin 19 fragments, were within normal limits. A complete blood count did not reveal eosinophilia. During 3 months of observation, the nodule increased in size to 11 × 10 × 8 mm. An ^18F-FDG PET/CT scan showed low uptake in the nodule, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 0.94.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare case of human pulmonary dirofilariasis with a growing pulmonary nodule after migrating infiltration shadows, mimicking primary lung carcinoma

case_prompt: A 72-year-old man was referred for evaluation of xerostomia and bilateral upper eyelid and salivary gland swelling that had persisted for eight months. He had no significant past medical history or medication use. On examination, both the lacrimal and salivary glands were swollen. Laboratory tests revealed: white blood cell count 7.8×10^3/μL, hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 139 U/mL, total protein 8.8 g/dL, soluble interleukin-2 receptor 5295 U/mL, C-reactive protein 1.30 mg/dL, total IgG 3880 mg/dL, and IgG4 3580 mg/mL, with the IgG4 subclass accounting for 92% of total IgG. Labial salivary gland biopsy showed lymphocytic infiltration, but anti–SS-A and anti–SS-B antibodies were negative, and a definitive diagnosis of Sjögren’s syndrome could not be made. Lip biopsy and excisional biopsy of the left submandibular gland confirmed MALT lymphoma. To assess disease extent, ^18F-FDG PET/CT was performed, showing abnormal uptake in the bilateral lacrimal and salivary glands, duodenum, pancreas, retroperitoneum, and multiple lymph nodes (mediastinal, bilateral bronchopulmonary, abdominal para-aortic, and mesenteric), with SUVmax values ranging from 2.5 to 6.8. Elevated serum IgG4 raised the possibility that these lesions could represent either MALT lymphoma or IgG4-related disease.
journal: Asia Oceania Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Biology
title: 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging of IgG4-producing MALT lymphoma with multiple site involvement

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old postmenopausal woman was referred to gynecologic oncology after a right salpingo-oophorectomy performed by her general gynecologist for an incidentally discovered complex ovarian mass. She had presented complaining of pelvic “heaviness” and increased urinary frequency. Her obstetric history included three vaginal deliveries and two spontaneous abortions; she underwent menopause at age 54. She had a remote history of left salpingo-oophorectomy at age 29 for ovarian torsion, with a benign pathology.

Laboratory evaluation showed a CA-125 level of 31 U/mL. A preoperative colonoscopy was normal. Pelvic ultrasound and subsequent MRI demonstrated an 11-cm complex right adnexal mass; there was no ascites, lymphadenopathy, or carcinomatosis, and the endometrial thickness was 3.9 mm.

Histologic examination of the ovarian specimen revealed an infiltrative neoplasm with a mixture of tubular, glandular, papillary, corded, and solid growth patterns. The tumor cells had scant cytoplasm, moderately atypical vesicular nuclei with overlap, variably prominent nucleoli, increased mitotic activity, and focal intraluminal eosinophilic secretions.

Immunohistochemical stains showed that the tumor cells were strongly positive for CK7 and PAX8, and focally positive for HNF1B, GATA3, TTF1, CD10, and p16. They were negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, WT1, and calretinin. Staining for p53 was wild-type, and DNA mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, PMS2, MSH6, MSH2), PTEN, and ARID1A were retained.
title: Mesonephric-like adenocarcinoma of the ovary with co-existent endometriosis: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 54-year-old farmer presented with a 2-year history of a left parotid swelling. On examination, there was a firm, mobile, painless, well-circumscribed mass measuring 3 cm in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland; the overlying skin was normal, and there was no cervical adenopathy or facial nerve palsy. Cervical ultrasonography revealed a 3 cm cystic lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 33 mm cystic mass with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, no diffusion restriction, and no enhancement of the cyst wall after gadolinium administration. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion yielded clear fluid containing occasional epithelial cells.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Hydatid cyst in the parotid gland, a rare localization of the disease: A case report

case_prompt: A 45-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with acute-onset swelling and mild pain of her right upper extremity during a high-intensity exercise routine. After initial resolution over 48 hours with rest and ice, she returned to exercise but 15 days later developed a second episode, this time with severe pain. On examination in the emergency department, her right arm was cyanotic and swollen with paresthesia and muscle weakness (4/5) of all muscle groups; the left arm was normal. After 48 hours, the swelling improved but the weakness persisted. Wright’s hyperabduction test reproduced cyanosis and abolished the right radial pulse. Sensation and deep tendon reflexes were otherwise normal. A color Doppler sonogram failed to visualize the entire subclavian vein. Contrast venography of the right upper limb showed near-complete obstruction of the subclavian vein, venous stenosis, and thrombosis from the axillary to the subclavian vein. A computed tomography scan, electromyogram, and nerve conduction study were performed to evaluate for neurogenic involvement but showed no abnormalities.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Paget-Schroetter syndrome in an active young female after unsupervised exercise

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old man was admitted with a 2-day history of diffuse abdominal pain and hematochezia and a 4-day history of palpable purpura that began on the lower legs and spread to involve his torso. Nine days earlier he had completed mediastinal radiation after partial response of limited-stage small cell lung cancer to four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin. On admission he appeared ill, complained of vague abdominal pain, and was afebrile with stable vital signs.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 8,520/mm³ (72.7% neutrophils, 18.0% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 15 g/dL, and platelets 179,000/mm³. Total protein was 6.9 g/dL and albumin 3.2 g/dL; renal and liver function tests, lipid profile, and coagulation studies were normal. Direct and indirect Coombs’ tests were negative. Urinalysis showed 3+ hematuria and 2+ proteinuria; a 24-hour collection revealed protein excretion of 3.005 g/day. Complement levels were C3 68 mg/dL and C4 10.6 mg/dL (both low). Rheumatoid factor was 105.5 IU/mL. Tests for ANCA, anti-MPO, cryoglobulin, and ANA were negative; immunoglobulin levels and serologic tests for hepatitis B antigen, parvovirus, and HIV were normal or negative. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Abdominal CT showed diffuse edematous thickening of the duodenum to proximal jejunum with prominent mucosal enhancement.
title: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura with Concurrent Cytomegalovirus Duodenitis

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man was referred for prosthetic rehabilitation of his complete dentures. His medical history included uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension treated with beta blockers. He denied smoking and reported nocturnal denture wearing, instability of his dentures during mastication and speech, and no routine oral or prosthetic hygiene.

Extraoral examination revealed a reduced vertical dimension of occlusion and mandibular laterodeviation. Intraorally, he was completely edentulous in both arches, wearing complete dentures with poor hygiene. The maxillary denture-bearing area showed generalized palatal erythema. In the mandibular vestibular sulcus, there was a three-month history of an inflammatory lesion described as raised, sessile tissue; it was movable, non-hemorrhagic on palpation, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Prosthetic assessment found ill-fitting dentures with overextended, sharp borders contacting the mandibular lesion, an inverted articulation, and poorly distributed occlusal contacts. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated moderate resorption of both edentulous ridges.

One week after referral to his physician confirmed stable blood pressure and initiation of diabetic control, he was advised to discontinue his old dentures until new provisional prostheses were fabricated.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Prosthetic management of an epulis fissuratum with simple conditioning tissue: A case report

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old Filipino nurse presented with a one-year history of right-sided neck pain, right otalgia, and odynophagia. Initial examination revealed a right tonsillar cyst but no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Neck ultrasonography showed enlarged right cervical lymph nodes. Tonsillar cyst biopsy demonstrated chronic tonsillitis with dilated crypts. 

Two weeks later, she returned with uncontrolled right facial pain. A repeat ultrasound noted a mildly enlarged right parotid gland and larger right-sided reactive cervical lymph nodes. MRI of the head and neck showed a 3.8 cm × 2.5 cm × 1.2 cm mass encasing the right internal carotid artery just below the skull base, along with smaller lymph nodes at level V. 

Fine-needle aspiration of the level V nodes revealed atypical cells, and low-grade lymphoma could not be excluded. An excisional biopsy of these nodes was planned for definitive diagnosis.
title: Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 77-year-old woman presented with one month of abdominal pain and anorexia. On examination, she had right upper-quadrant tenderness and rebound tenderness in the lower abdomen. Laboratory tests showed an aspartate aminotransferase level of 75 IU/L (normal 7–38 IU/L), a lipase level of 63 U/L (normal 7–60 U/L), and an elevated carbohydrate antigen 125 level of 279.5 U/mL; carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and alpha-fetoprotein levels were normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT and MRI revealed a 10 × 5 cm mass arising from the tail of the pancreas, invading the spleen and adjacent bowel loop; the tumor wall showed slight enhancement, and no regional lymphadenopathy, ascites, or distant metastases were seen. The patient underwent a distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy, along with left hemicolectomy and partial gastrectomy for direct invasion.
final_diagnosis_raw: Undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclast-like giant cells of the pancreas
journal: Journal of the Korean Surgical Society
title: Undifferentiated carcinoma of the pancreas with osteoclast-like giant cells

case_prompt: A 52-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 2-week history of progressively worsening abnormal behavior and gait disturbance. On admission, nonenhanced brain MRI showed an oval lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum that was hyperintense on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images with decreased apparent diffusion coefficient. A small hyperintense lesion was also noted in the left frontal subcortical region on diffusion-weighted imaging. Laboratory testing revealed a lactate dehydrogenase level of 650 U/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/h. Cerebrospinal fluid examination showed 9 cells/µL and a protein level of 125 mg/dL; encephalitis was suspected, and antiviral, antibacterial, and antiepileptic therapy was initiated. The patient’s symptoms initially improved, but he subsequently developed fever, impaired consciousness, hypercalcemia, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. No tumor was identified on imaging studies or endoscopy. Follow-up MRIs at 2 weeks and 1 month showed reduction in size and signal of the splenial lesion. Two months after onset, MRI revealed mottled multiple hyperintense areas in the bilateral cerebral white matter on T2-weighted, FLAIR, and diffusion-weighted images—predominantly in watershed areas—while the splenial lesion continued to regress. T1-weighted images demonstrated diffuse low signal in the bone marrow, and gadolinium-enhanced images showed dural thickening and enhancement. Laboratory studies now showed hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, platelet count 192 × 10^3/µL, white-cell count 16.3 × 10^3/µL, lactate dehydrogenase 506 U/L, albumin 2.2 g/dL, C-reactive protein 10.05 mg/dL, and serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2956 U/mL.
title: A case of intravascular lymphoma presenting with a lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of progressive slurring of speech. Four weeks earlier, he had been hospitalized for a 15-day history of low-grade intermittent fever and mild to moderate right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. He denied diarrhea, vomiting, urinary symptoms, chest pain, cough, or dyspnea. He had no known comorbidities but reported consuming 70–80 g of alcohol daily for 10 years. 

On initial evaluation, abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple pyogenic liver abscesses, and he was treated with metronidazole (2.4 g/day in divided doses), meropenem, and supportive care. His symptoms improved, and serial ultrasounds showed reduced abscess size.

On neurologic presentation, he denied gait disturbance, tremor, sensory symptoms, confusion, or weakness. Vital signs were temperature 100.5 °F, pulse 102/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 112/68 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Abdominal examination showed tenderness in the right hypochondrium and hepatomegaly. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and mental-status examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed a scanning, explosive dysarthria, subtle dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, and impaired tandem walking; strength, sensation, and deep-tendon reflexes were normal.

Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed multiple liver abscesses. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed bilateral T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in the dentate nuclei with corresponding T1 hypointensities, without diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement.
title: A rare clinical presentation of metronidazole-induced dysarthria: A Case report with literature review

case_prompt: A 23-year-old woman fell from a height of 5 m and presented with severe low back and right foot pain. She had no head trauma and a Glasgow Coma Score of 15. On examination, she had left L5 root paresis (1/5 long toe extension) with diminished light touch and pinprick sensation, perianal hypoesthesia, and urinary retention; anal sphincter function was impaired. Radiographs and CT showed A3/AO fractures of L2, B1/AO fractures of L5, and a comminuted Sanders type 4 right calcaneal fracture. Thirty hours after admission, she underwent posterior minimally invasive stabilization from L1 to S2 with L5 decompression and Ilizarov fixation of the calcaneus; both procedures were done prone under one anesthetic, lasting 4.5 hours. Immediately postoperatively, the anesthesiologist noted that the left pupil was larger than the right with a slower, incomplete reaction to light, while visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally and the right pupil reacted normally.
title: Anisocoria after Posterior Spine Surgery: A Rare but Disastrous Complication – A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation refractory to medications underwent catheter-guided radiofrequency ablation with isolation of all four pulmonary veins. He was asymptomatic post-procedure and an ambulatory cardiac CT angiogram 3 months later showed approximately 60% stenosis of the left superior pulmonary vein. He remained on oral anticoagulation without intervention.

Two months after that follow-up CT (5 months post-ablation), he developed cough with hemoptysis, mild intermittent fever, mild left-sided pleuritic chest pain, and exertional dyspnea. A chest radiograph showed poorly marginated opacities in the left upper lobe and minimal left pleural effusion. Laboratory studies to rule out pulmonary tuberculosis were within normal limits, and he received broad-spectrum antibiotics without improvement.

He presented to our hospital 6 months after ablation. A non-enhanced chest CT scan revealed minimal left pleural effusion and multiple peripheral patchy consolidations in the apico-posterior and anterior segments of the left upper lobe.
title: Pulmonary vein occlusion and lung infarction complicating non-treated moderate single pulmonary vein stenosis after radiofrequency ablation of atrial fibrillation

case_prompt: A 32-year-old Bangladeshi man initially presented after left knee trauma. Radiographs showed no fracture but revealed a well-defined oval lucency in the medulla of the proximal tibial metaphysis with surrounding sclerosis. Further examinations were suggested, but the patient declined. Six months later, he returned complaining of intense low back pain, a 20-day history of weight loss, and intermittent fever up to 37.5 °C. On examination he had a large right paravertebral mass at the lumbosacral level, hepatomegaly, and enlarged cervical and axillary lymph nodes. No neurological deficits were noted. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13,200 mmc⁻¹ and a negative HIV test. A CT scan of the lumbosacral spine demonstrated a large abscess in the superficial soft tissues of the posterolateral abdominal wall at the L4–S2 level contiguous with a lytic lesion of the right iliac bone with cortical destruction and scattered calcifications. A second multiloculated abscess extended from the pre-sacral space into the left gluteal muscles, associated with bone destruction of S5. Additionally, there was a lytic lesion with cortical destruction in the left L1 pedicle. A chest radiograph was unremarkable.
title: Delayed diagnosis of extrapulmonary tuberculosis in a 32-year-old man with knee pain

case_prompt: A 55-year-old man with hypertension had an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest while at rest watching television. He had no preceding symptoms or family history of sudden cardiac death. His wife began CPR immediately. Emergency responders found ventricular fibrillation, delivered two shocks, and achieved return of circulation; he was intubated and transferred to our centre. On arrival his physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.3), which was corrected, and troponin I levels of 573 and 303 ng/L (<21). Noncontrast head CT was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild left ventricular hypertrophy with normal systolic function, no regional wall motion abnormalities, and no pericardial or valvular pathology. His initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia, a QTc of 490 ms, 1 mm ST depression in leads II, III, aVF, and V6, and subtle, variable <0.5 mm ST‐elevation in lead aVR. One hour later, inferolateral ST changes and QTc prolongation had resolved, and new subtle down‐sloping 1 mm ST‐elevation appeared in lead V1. Coronary angiography demonstrated unobstructed coronary arteries but revealed an anomalous right coronary artery originating from the left coronary sinus. Cardiac MRI showed borderline left ventricular hypertrophy, normal systolic function, and no late gadolinium enhancement. CT coronary angiography confirmed the anomalous artery had an acute takeoff, an intramural segment, and an interarterial course. Exercise stress echocardiography produced no symptoms, ECG changes, arrhythmias, or regional wall motion abnormalities, and QT analysis was also normal.
title: Two zebras and a cardiac arrest: a case report of concomitant Brugada syndrome and an anomalous coronary artery

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a small swelling on the anterior dorsal surface of her tongue, just left of the midline. She first noticed the lesion more than 2 years earlier; it remained unchanged and asymptomatic unless inadvertently bitten. Her medical history was notable only for depression treated with desvenlafaxine. She did not smoke and drank little alcohol.

On examination, there were no extraoral abnormalities or cervical lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there was a small, nonulcerated, sessile mass on the anterior dorsal tongue, not tender to palpation, with otherwise normal mucosa. A provisional diagnosis of fibroepithelial polyp was made, and the lesion was excised.

An elliptical specimen of oral mucosa measuring 10 × 8 × 8 mm was submitted for histopathology. Microscopic examination showed a semipedunculated, nonencapsulated but well-circumscribed submucosal mass covered by stratified squamous epithelium. Centrally, there were lobules of fibromyxoid stroma separated by fibrous septa. Within these lobules, numerous randomly distributed stellate and spindle-shaped cells were seen. Nuclear pleomorphism was minimal, and mitotic figures were inconspicuous.
title: Oral nerve sheath myxoma: a rare and unusual intraoral neoplasm

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old unmarried man presented with a soft, painless swelling at the tip of his penis that had been noted by his mother at age 3. The lesion increased in size over the first few years of life but had remained stable for the past 15 years. He denied pain, itching, burning, tenderness, discharge, trauma, or interference with urination or erection. He had no significant medical history or family history of similar lesions. His only concern was cosmetic and potential impact on future sexual activity.

On examination, there was a solitary, soft, translucent cystic lesion approximately 2 cm in diameter on the ventral aspect of the glans penis, close to but not involving the urethral meatus. The overlying mucosa was shiny with no central umbilication; the surrounding mucosa was normal. The cyst was nontender, and the urethral opening was patent. Examination of the penile shaft, scrotum, and perineum was unremarkable, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory tests, including a hemogram and urinalysis, were normal. Ultrasonography of the lesion demonstrated a well-circumscribed, isoechoic cystic structure without solid components, septations, or internal vascularity. The cyst lay entirely within the mucosa and was clearly separated from the underlying urethra.
title: Median raphe cyst of the penis: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt: A 34-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of acute, painless vision loss in the left eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 10/10 in the right eye and 3/10 in the left. Ocular motility and anterior segments were normal bilaterally without inflammation. Dilated fundus examination of the left eye revealed a geographic, pale lesion measuring approximately one disc area at the papillomacular bundle, including the nasal foveal region; the right fundus was unremarkable. Near-infrared reflectance imaging showed a geographic hyperreflective lesion at the left macula. Optical coherence tomography angiography demonstrated ellipsoid-zone discontinuity and a wedge-shaped choriocapillaris flow void in the affected area. Systemic evaluation, including purified protein derivative skin testing and infectious disease consultation, was unremarkable.
title: Atypical Acute Ischemic Choriocapillaritis: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman was referred for characterization of an incidentally discovered left adrenal mass. She was asymptomatic, and physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including serum catecholamines, were within normal limits. 

MRI with and without gadobenate dimeglumine showed a 9 × 6 × 7 cm, well-circumscribed solid heterogeneous mass in the left adrenal gland. The mass had low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously high signal intensity on T2-weighted images with cystic components, and progressive contrast enhancement of the periphery and septa. There was no signal drop on T1 opposed-phase imaging. The lesion abutted adjacent structures (kidney, bowel, pancreas, renal vein, aorta, diaphragm) without signs of invasion.

Unenhanced CT performed during FDG PET/CT revealed a heterogeneous adrenal mass with hypodense foci (<20 HU) and no calcifications. PET demonstrated increased FDG uptake in the mass.
title: Adrenal schwannoma: a case report

case_prompt: A 6-year-old boy with no personal or family history of tuberculosis presented with a 3-month history of intermittent left upper-quadrant pain, intermittent vomiting, and persistent low-grade fever without chills or night sweats. He was vaccinated with BCG. On examination, his temperature was 38.6 °C, and the spleen was palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin; there was no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory evaluation showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL; white blood cells 3 700/mm³; platelets 119 000/mm³). A bone marrow aspirate demonstrated hypersplenism with erythroid hyperplasia. The ESR was 54 mm/h, HIV serology was negative, and sputum smear and culture for acid-fast bacilli were negative. The Mantoux test produced a 6 mm induration. Chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed splenomegaly with multiple hypoechoic cystic areas and splenic-hilum lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed heterogeneous splenomegaly with multiple hypodense lesions and a 13 mm peri-hilar lymph node, findings primarily suggestive of lymphoma. The patient was scheduled for laparoscopic splenectomy for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Isolated splenic tuberculosis in an immunocompetent child: A case report

case_prompt: A 33-year-old woman presented with 1 month of asthenia, nonproductive cough, and chest pain and was initially treated as acute bronchitis. Three days later, she returned with worsening stabbing chest pain, pleuritic but exertion-related and improving at rest, associated with exertional and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Vital signs were: blood pressure 112/64 mmHg, heart rate 116 bpm, respiratory rate 19/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination showed no murmurs, fine bilateral crackles at the lung bases, no abdominal abnormalities, and no lower extremity edema. A D-dimer and chest X-ray were normal. ECG showed 2-mm ST depression in precordial leads. High-sensitivity troponin I rose from 0.06 to 2.25 ng/mL (normal 0–0.026). C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a severely dilated left ventricle with mid-ventricular and apical dyskinesia, an ejection fraction of 20%, diastolic dysfunction, severe functional mitral regurgitation, moderate functional tricuspid regurgitation, and an estimated pulmonary systolic pressure ≥80 mmHg. On transfer to the coronary care unit she was hypotensive (86/54 mmHg) and tachycardic (124 bpm), consistent with cardiogenic shock; she received intravenous norepinephrine. The working diagnoses were takotsubo cardiomyopathy or acute myocarditis, and she was started on enalapril, spironolactone, carvedilol, intravenous furosemide, and low-molecular-weight heparin; antiplatelet therapy was withheld due to the noncoronary distribution of wall motion abnormalities. The next day, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed mild left ventricular dilatation, ejection fraction 45%, and severe apical and mid-ventricular contractility abnormalities with normal basal function, resembling takotsubo cardiomyopathy; however, there was no myocardial edema, fibrosis, or scarring.
title: Cardiogenic shock as the first manifestation of large vessel vasculitis in a young patient: case report

case_prompt: A 67-year-old woman presented with a 7-month history of a left-sided neck “lump” and mild discomfort on palpation. She denied odynophagia, dysphagia, or hoarseness. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and age-related cataracts; she was a non-smoker with a BMI of 34 kg/m2 and no family history of malignancy. Physical examination revealed an elastic, tender, mobile mass in the left lateral cervical region; the remainder of the head and neck examination was unremarkable. Prior fiberoptic laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, and esophagoscopy were normal. Neck ultrasonography showed a 3.0 cm × 2.06 cm well-defined, hypoechoic mass with no intratumoral vascularity on Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a well-circumscribed 4.5 cm × 3.2 cm × 2.7 cm mass located deep to the internal jugular vein, carotid artery, and vagus nerve. An ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration was performed, but the result was non-diagnostic.
title: A Predictable Approach of a Rare and Frequently Misdiagnosed Entity: Laryngeal Nerve Schwannoma

case_prompt: A 42-year-old woman presented with a 30-minute episode of visual loss in her left eye one day earlier. On examination in our ophthalmology clinic, visual acuity was full in both eyes, and microscopic fundus examination was normal bilaterally. She reported that at another center the same presentation had prompted a diagnosis of left internal carotid artery occlusion on the basis of Doppler ultrasonography and angiography, and she requested a repeat extracranial carotid Doppler study. On Doppler ultrasonography, the right common carotid artery (CCA) measured 8 mm in diameter; the left CCA measured 4 mm. The right CCA, internal carotid artery (ICA), and external carotid artery (ECA) were normal. On the left side, spectral Doppler waveforms and branching patterns were consistent with the ECA, whereas no Doppler signal or gray-scale evidence of an ICA was seen.
title:
An Important Clue in the Sonographic Diagnosis of Internal Carotid
Artery Agenesis: Ipsilateral Common Carotid Artery Hypoplasia

case_prompt: A 51-year-old man from East Asia with hypertension was referred for evaluation of recurrent nephrolithiasis and elevated serum creatinine. He had kidney stones in 1989 and 2006 (spontaneously passed) and bilateral calcium stones requiring lithotripsy in 2017. Over the preceding two years, his creatinine fluctuated between 0.9 and 3.1 mg/dL; 24-hour urine calcium was 637 mg. In July 2019, laboratory studies showed serum calcium 11.9 mg/dL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, intact PTH 5 pg/mL (suppressed), calcitriol 80.4 pg/mL (elevated), calcidiol 15.1 ng/mL (low), PTHrP <2.0 pmol/L, ACE 2 U/L, normal SPEP, normal CBC, and normal urinalysis. A whole-body bone scan was normal. Neck ultrasound showed no parathyroid abnormality. Chest radiograph revealed a calcified granuloma. CT of the chest demonstrated an upper-lobe solid nodule concerning for malignancy; pulmonology evaluation including tests for tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and lung cancer was negative. On follow-up, serum calcium remained elevated at 11.3 mg/dL with an ionized calcium of 6.0 mg/dL.
title: Steroid responsive idiopathic calcitriol induced hypercalcemia: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old woman with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia receiving the CALGB-10403 chemotherapy protocol and ponatinib was admitted for evaluation of new skin findings, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Her course had been complicated by chronic thrombocytopenia requiring monthly platelet transfusions and acute renal failure treated with hemodialysis; after renal recovery she remained on a self-restricted low-protein diet for 8 months without fruits, vegetables, or supplementation. 

She reported 10 of 10 constant abdominal pain and 10–12 watery bowel movements per day. Concurrently, she noted progressive, asymptomatic peeling of large sheets of skin on the extremities and trunk. On examination she was afebrile with stable vital signs. Dermatologic exam revealed ichthyosiform, plate-like scale with minimal erythema over the trunk and large adherent sheets of desquamation over the limbs. 

Laboratory studies showed albumin 2.3 g/dL (3.7–5.3), copper 65 μg/dL (85–155), vitamin A 0.07 mg/L (0.30–1.20), vitamin B1 4 nmol/L (8–30), vitamin B6 8.6 nmol/L (20–125), vitamin D 7.5 ng/mL (>40), vitamin E 5.1 mg/L (5.5–18.0), and zinc 44 μg/dL (55–150). Folate, vitamins B2, B12, and C were normal.

Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed findings consistent with neutropenic enterocolitis and typhlitis. She was also treated for a Klebsiella urinary tract infection with intravenous meropenem. The initial differential diagnosis of her dermatosis included a paraneoplastic process, drug reaction, transfusion reaction, or nutritional deficiency.
title: “Peeling paint” dermatosis in a leukemia patient

case_prompt: A 50-year-old woman presented with vague right upper abdominal pain of several weeks’ duration. On examination, she had a firm, palpable mass in the right hypochondrium. Laboratory studies showed a normal haemogram and normal liver-function tests. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 9 × 8 cm mass in the gallbladder fossa with loss of a clear interface with the liver and evidence of gallstones. Biphasic computed tomography of the abdomen showed a grossly distended gallbladder containing a soft-tissue mass with multiple large intraluminal projections, findings suggestive of a polypoidal gallbladder malignancy in the setting of cholelithiasis. A provisional diagnosis of carcinoma of the gallbladder was made.
title: Primary Leiomyosarcoma of Gallbladder: A Rare Diagnosis

case_prompt: A 75-year-old Japanese woman presented with progressive dyspnea and back pain after eating for 2 months. Her past surgical history included an open appendectomy at age 17 and a laparotomy for adhesive small-bowel obstruction at age 69; there was no history of upper abdominal surgery or trauma. On examination, she was 155.2 cm tall, weighed 53.0 kg (BMI 22.0), and had lower abdominal surgical scars. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. A chest radiograph revealed gas-filled loops of bowel in the left hemithorax. Computed tomography showed prolapse of the stomach, small intestine, colon, pancreas, and spleen into the left thoracic cavity above the diaphragm, with marked compression of the left lung, leading to the diagnosis of a diaphragmatic hernia such as a para-esophageal hiatal hernia or Bochdalek hernia.
title: Laparoscopic repair of a Bochdalek hernia in an elderly patient: a case report with a review from 1999 to 2019 in Japan

case_prompt:
A 66-year-old woman presented with acute-onset dyspnea. She was diagnosed at an outside hospital with a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction complicated by congestive heart failure and was stabilized with parenteral nitroglycerin and noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation. She was referred for coronary angiography.

Her history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, smoking, and peripheral vascular disease. Coronary angiography revealed extensive disease, including a 95% lesion of the left main coronary artery; there were no procedural complications, and left ventricular pressure was 90/45 mm Hg.

While recovering, she developed acute dyspnea and tachycardia. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia without low-voltage complexes or recurrent ischemia. Chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary edema, and she received intravenous furosemide and nitroglycerin.

An urgent transthoracic echocardiogram showed a mildly dilated left ventricle, severe global systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction, 20–25%), mild mitral regurgitation, and a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 30 mm Hg. No mechanical complications of myocardial ischemia were evident. A moderate pericardial effusion (25 mm) was noted along the right ventricular free wall, with echodense material adherent to the right ventricle (presumed thrombus). The inferior vena cava was dilated without inspiratory collapse. Right atrial systolic collapse and mild right ventricular inversion suggested tamponade physiology.
title: Pseudo cardiac tamponade in the setting of excess pericardial fat

case_prompt: A 51-year-old woman with a history of recurrent abdominal pain presented with upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. She had no history of alcohol use, smoking, autoimmune disease, medications, surgeries, or ERCP. On examination, the abdomen was mildly tender in the epigastrium with rebound and decreased bowel sounds; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 13,500/mm3, amylase 228 U/L (normal 30–151), lipase 3150 U/L (normal 11–82), and C-reactive protein 62 mg/L (normal <5). Liver enzymes and bilirubin were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound showed no evidence of cholelithiasis, choledocholithiasis, biliary sludge, or ductal dilation. Because of a contrast allergy, MR imaging with MR cholangiopancreatography was performed. MRCP demonstrated duplication of the main pancreatic duct with two separate ducts that joined at the pancreatic head and drained via the minor papilla. Pancreatic parenchyma was bifurcated at the neck with a common head. On axial T2-weighted images, the body and tail segment of one ductal limb was enlarged and hyperintense without peripancreatic fluid collections. These findings were interpreted as acute pancreatitis confined to one limb of an anomalous ductal system.
title: Pancreas bifidum: an extremely rare cause of acute pancreatitis☆

case_prompt: A 38-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of dizziness, palpitations, and fatigue accompanied by inappetence, black stools, and tenesmus. She denied recent weight loss or abdominal pain. Three days earlier, gastroduodenoscopy at an outside hospital revealed gastric mucosal ischemia and spherical lesions in the duodenum. She had no prior surgeries. On arrival, her temperature was 36.8°C, pulse 88/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiration 18/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Physical examination was notable only for pallor; the abdomen was soft and nontender, and digital rectal examination confirmed black stool but no masses. Laboratory studies demonstrated hypoalbuminemia, hypocalcemia, a positive fecal occult blood test, and microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 58 g/L). Abdominal CT showed a heterogeneous, nonobstructing mass in the stomach extending into the second and third parts of the duodenum. Repeat gastroscopy revealed a large polypoid mass originating from the anterior wall of the gastric antrum and protruding through the pylorus into the second part of the duodenum; the surface was red but lacked mucosal ulcerations or stigmata of recent bleeding. Random biopsies showed mild acute and chronic inflammation with significant proliferation of blood vessels and fibroblasts.
journal: The Journal of International Medical Research
