title: Nonobstructive gastroduodenal intussusception characterized by severe anemia: a case report

case_prompt: A 25-year-old woman, G4P4, had an uncomplicated home vaginal delivery 5 days earlier without antenatal ultrasounds. She presents with severe right lower-quadrant abdominal pain and vomiting. Her temperature is 37.8°C, blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg, heart rate 110 beats/min, and respiratory rate 22 breaths/min. On examination, she is in severe distress; the abdomen is moderately distended with rebound tenderness and guarding, and bowel sounds are hypoactive. Laboratory tests show a white-cell count of 9.6×10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 34 g/dL. Transabdominal ultrasound reveals a well-defined hypoechoic lesion with internal echoes and posterior acoustic shadowing in the right adnexa, an echogenic mural nodule (Rokitansky protuberance), and absent vascularity on color Doppler. Contrast-enhanced CT shows a normal appendix, an enlarged postpartum uterus, and a heterogeneous lesion in the right adnexa containing fat, fluid-density areas, and peripheral calcifications.
title: Ovarian Torsion Due to Mature Cystic Teratoma During the Early Postpartum Period: A Rare Case Report

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old right-handed woman presented with unprovoked numbness and worsening sensation in the volar surface of her right thumb, index, middle finger, and radial half of her ring finger, along with progressive weakness of her opponens pollicis muscle. Over the past 12 months, she had only slight improvement with wrist splinting, physiotherapy, high-dose NSAIDs, and gabapentin. She reported a history of repetitive finger and wrist movements with chronic pressure on the right wrist. 

On examination, there was no swelling or erythema, but thenar muscle atrophy and hypoesthesia in the median nerve distribution were present. Phalen’s test and Tinel’s sign were positive on the right. Wrist and finger range of motion were normal. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated right median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel.

A plain radiograph of the right wrist revealed an oval radio-opacity on the volar side facing the carpal bones. MRI of the right wrist showed a 2.0 × 0.8 × 0.6 cm low-intensity oval lesion centrally within the carpal tunnel, between the flexor tendons at the lunatum-capitatum junction, with a clear boundary from surrounding tissues, a surrounding reactive fluid collection, subtle flexor tenosynovitis, and mild compression of the median nerve. 

Laboratory studies, including full blood count, vitamin D, calcium, phosphate, electrolytes, uric acid, urea, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, and a comprehensive endocrine and rheumatology panel, were all within normal limits.
title: Carpal tunnel syndrome secondary to tumoral calcinosis: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A woman in her early thirties with a history of ankylosing spondylitis, obstructive sleep apnea, and recently diagnosed hypertension (2‐month history) presented after an optometry appointment at which her blood pressure was 230/155 mmHg. She denied fever, headache, dizziness, chest pain, visual changes, or shortness of breath. Home medications included hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, sulfasalazine 1000 mg twice daily, and adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 14 days.

On admission, her blood pressure was 201/133 mmHg, heart rate was 107 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. Physical examination revealed 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities; cardiopulmonary and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Chest radiography and electrocardiography showed no acute pathology beyond sinus tachycardia, and head CT was negative.

Laboratory studies revealed a serum creatinine of 1.47 mg/dL (baseline, 0.7 mg/dL) and serum albumin of 1.8 g/dL. Urinalysis demonstrated a specific gravity of 1.028, heavy proteinuria (>500 mg/dL), glucosuria, and 5 red blood cells per high‐power field. A urine protein:creatinine ratio exceeded 6 g/g. A 24‐hour urine collection confirmed protein excretion of 11.3 g. Renal ultrasound showed symmetric kidneys of normal size with preserved cortical thickness and no hydronephrosis. An extensive workup including ANA, anti‐scleroderma antibody, paraproteinemia studies, C3, and C4 was non‐revealing. Her blood pressure was controlled with intravenous antihypertensives and transitioned to oral labetalol, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide, but serum creatinine did not return to baseline.

Due to lack of improvement in serum creatinine levels, she underwent a kidney biopsy.
title: Primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in a patient with ankylosing spondylitis: A rare presentation requiring a broad differential in nephrotic syndrome

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman underwent elective outpatient surveillance colonoscopy because her sister had colon cancer at age 36. Her history was notable for menorrhagia, hypertension, depression, and two cesarean deliveries. Her medications included nebivolol, venlafaxine, and amlodipine–valsartan. 

On colonoscopy, the appendiceal orifice appeared prominent with edematous changes, and multiple biopsies were obtained. Histologic examination of the biopsies showed mild neutrophilic inflammation and a dense lymphocytic infiltrate of the lamina propria. 

Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 2.4 × 2.6 cm mass in the cecal tip involving the proximal appendix. Magnetic resonance imaging failed to further characterize the lesion.
title: Schwannoma of the Appendix Orifice

case_prompt: A 4-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a swelling of the left anterior maxillary gingiva. The parents first noticed bilateral small gingival enlargements 5 months earlier; the right lesion resolved spontaneously, but the left continued to enlarge despite manipulation. Three months before presentation, the primary central and lateral incisors had been extracted by a general dentist for a presumed periapical abscess, but the gingival mass persisted and grew. The patient denied pain and spontaneous bleeding, reporting only occasional interference with mastication. His medical history was unremarkable. Examination revealed slight facial swelling over the left anterior maxilla without lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there was a 20 × 15 × 12 mm pedunculated, lobular soft‐tissue mass on the left maxillary gingiva at the incisor region. The lesion was firm, with tan, red, and bluish mucosal areas and a focal ulceration. A periapical radiograph showed superficial erosion of the underlying alveolar bone without deeper bony involvement. Based on these findings, a benign gingival lesion was suspected, and the differential diagnosis included parulis, pyogenic granuloma, peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and peripheral odontogenic fibroma. Malignancy was considered unlikely. The lesion was scheduled for excisional biopsy under local anesthesia.
title: A Review and Report of Peripheral Giant Cell Granuloma in a 4-Year-Old Child

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of a pruritic truncal rash. Her medical history included asthma, seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with hydroxychloroquine, and documented hypereosinophilia (3400/µL) two years earlier. The rash began as a scablike lesion on her upper back and evolved into large, red, annular and polycyclic plaques covering much of her trunk. She denied medication changes, insect bites, systemic symptoms (fever, chills, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, chest pain), oral or palmoplantar lesions, recent travel, or sick contacts.  
On examination, there were well-demarcated, nonscaly, erythematous annular and polycyclic plaques with indurated, raised borders on the trunk.  
A 4-mm punch biopsy from an advancing border showed a dense dermal infiltrate with numerous eosinophils and no flame figures.  
Laboratory studies revealed a peripheral eosinophil count of 8670/µL. Two stool examinations for ova and parasites were negative. The patient was negative for hepatitis B and hepatitis C.
title: Eosinophilic annular erythema: A striking clinical presentation with potential systemic implications

case_prompt: A 12‐year‐old girl presented with a 10‐day history of intermittent, crampy abdominal pain that intensified over the preceding week and was accompanied by non‐bilious vomiting the night before presentation. She denied urinary symptoms, constipation, diarrhea, fever, weight loss, or recent travel. She had previously undergone ultrasonography, CT scans, and routine blood tests at three other hospitals, all of which were reported as negative, and appendicitis was ruled out. On examination, she had a stooped posture and difficulty walking due to pain. She was afebrile with normal heart rate and blood pressure. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right iliac fossa with a positive McBurney’s sign but no rebound tenderness or guarding; Rovsing’s, psoas, and obturator signs were negative. The rest of the examination, including genitourinary and gynecological assessments, was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 6.9 × 10^9/L and a CRP level of less than 4 mg/L; liver and kidney function tests were normal. Urinalysis was within normal limits, and pregnancy test was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography did not visualize the appendix and revealed no abnormalities. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated minimal endometrial fluid, an appendix of average caliber measuring 5.2 mm in diameter, and mild hepatomegaly, without any appendiceal wall thickening, periappendiceal fat stranding, or appendicolith.
title: Noninflammatory obstructive appendicopathy: A rare presentation of abdominal pain

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man presented with a right scrotal and inguinal mass that had gradually enlarged over 2 years. He had no other medical conditions and was not immunosuppressed (HIV negative). On examination, there was a 10 cm × 15 cm warty, friable mass involving the scrotum, and bilaterally fixed, voluminous inguinal lymph nodes.  
 
An abdominal and pelvic CT scan, pelvic MRI, and PET scan showed marked uptake in the inguino-scrotal mass and metastatic inguinal and pelvic lymph nodes (largest measuring 7 cm on the left). No other primary lesions or distant metastases were identified.  

Multiple skin biopsies of the inguinal mass demonstrated a dense proliferation of atypical epithelial cells in the dermis with ulceration of the overlying epidermis. Numerous mitotic figures and apoptotic cells were noted, along with focal squamous and glandular differentiation. Immunohistochemical studies showed diffuse positivity for CK5/6 and CK AE1/AE3, p63 positivity except in cells bordering glandular lumina, and GATA3 positivity in a subset of tumor cells.  

Based on the histologic and immunophenotypic findings, the initial differential diagnosis included malignant adnexal carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and a urothelial carcinoma metastasis.
title: Atypical presentation of adenosquamous carcinoma: A case report

case_prompt: A 47-year-old man presented with an eight-year history of intermittent pain and a “slipping” sensation in his right lower ribs after a cycling trauma. The pain was aggravated by deep inspiration, bending, and further cycling. Initial evaluation at another institution, including chest and abdominal X-rays and a bone scan, revealed no abnormalities. Analgesics (paracetamol and NSAIDs) provided no relief, and a single intercostal nerve block offered only temporary improvement. On physical examination, the patient had reproducible pain and a palpable subluxation of the right tenth rib with the hooking maneuver: placing the hands under the right costal margin and drawing them anteriorly produced a slipping or clicking feeling associated with his typical pain.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: The slipping rib syndrome: A case report

case_prompt: A 45-year-old man with a history of confluent erythematous and violaceous patches and plaques on the scalp—initially diagnosed as photodermatitis—presented with a new skin lesion on the left upper chest. The chest lesion was a sharply demarcated plaque with raised dusky, violaceous, and erythematous borders, central clearing, and an overlying scaly crust. Similar erythematous plaques were noted behind both ears. The lesions were nonpainful, nonpruritic, and there was no sensory loss. He denied systemic symptoms and reported prior improvement with oral steroids. There was no family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, there was no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy, and hair and nail examinations were unremarkable.
title: Unusual case of adult-onset cutaneous lupus erythematosus mimicking early mycosis fungoides

case_prompt: A 34-year-old nulliparous woman at 37 weeks’ gestation, with a history of uterine fibroids treated by two previous myomectomies, presented for routine fetal assessment. Pregnancy had been uneventful until cardiotocography revealed a sinusoidal tracing. She was admitted and underwent cesarean delivery. Intraoperative findings included an irregular uterine contour with two bulky fibroids. A live male infant was delivered breech into meconium-stained amniotic fluid; Apgar scores were 6 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes, and neonatal resuscitation was required. Cord blood gas analysis showed a hemoglobin concentration of 4.3 g/dL, pH 7.32, and base excess −2.9 mmol/L. A neonatal blood sample confirmed severe anemia (RBC count 1.06 × 10^6/μL, hemoglobin 4.0 g/dL, hematocrit 12.7%), and the infant developed hypovolemic shock and pulmonary hypertension requiring transfusion and intubation. The placenta weighed 600 g, measured 16 cm in diameter, and had marginal umbilical cord insertion.
title: Massive Fetomaternal Hemorrhage Caused by an Intraplacental Choriocarcinoma: Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 16-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of esotropia and a white pupil in the right eye first noticed at 12 months of age. On examination, he was esotropic in the right eye. Slit-lamp evaluation of the anterior segment was normal in both eyes, but ophthalmoscopy revealed a total retinal detachment in the right eye, with the detachment close to the lens preventing visualization of the peripheral retina. B-mode ultrasonography showed a diffuse, high-echo area in the right vitreous cavity with no apparent sign of calcification. A computed tomography scan performed one month earlier also showed no evidence of calcification in the right eye. Magnetic resonance imaging at one hospital demonstrated high-intensity signals in T1-weighted images and low-intensity signals in T2-weighted images in the vitreous body of the right eye, and a repeat MRI three months later showed high-intensity signals in T2-weighted images in the same region. No evidence of a mass lesion was seen in either eye on the MRI studies.
title: Subretinal Fluid Drainage and Vitrectomy Are Helpful in Diagnosing and Treating Eyes with Advanced Coats' Disease

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old healthy woman (BMI 19.0) presented with a 5-month history of progressive left infraumbilical abdominal pain that worsened with exercise or physical strain. One month before presentation, she noted a painful, hard mass in that region. Her gynecologic history was notable for three cesarean sections (10, 7, and 6 years earlier); she had no known endometriosis or other comorbidities.  
On examination, there was a 3-cm, painful, firm, fixed mass in the left infraumbilical region, 10 cm above the cesarean scar, without overlying skin changes. Routine blood tests, including inflammatory markers, were normal.  
She was referred to general surgery with a suspicion of muscle injury. Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous, predominantly hypoechoic 2.0 × 1.5 cm lesion within the left rectus abdominis muscle; Doppler showed internal vessels without high flow. US-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded scant atypical cells but was inconclusive for a definitive diagnosis, prompting recommendation for biopsy.  
Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a 2.1 × 0.9 cm focal lesion within the left rectus abdominis muscle of unknown etiology; there were no other intra-abdominal lesions or connections to the cesarean scar.
title: Rectus Abdominis Muscle Endometriosis: A Unique Case Report with a Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 3, presented with intermittent postmenopausal spotting for 6 months, cough with expectoration, and significant weight loss over 2 months. She received 2 months of empirical antitubercular therapy elsewhere without improvement; instead, her vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain increased. She had no history of diabetes, hypertension, or estrogen exposure and had been postmenopausal for 3 years.

On examination, she appeared cachectic (weight 27 kg, BMI 15 kg/m2). Chest auscultation revealed decreased bilateral air entry with rhonchi. Abdominal examination showed a scaphoid abdomen and a hard, nonmobile, nontender mass corresponding to a 14-week gravid uterus in the suprapubic region. On speculum exam, the cervix could not be visualized. Bimanual exam confirmed the hard uterine mass. Hemoglobin was 7.1 g/dL; other blood tests were within normal limits.

Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined heterogeneous hypoechoic 20 mm × 17 mm intramural lesion in the fundal myometrium, suggestive of a fibroid, with a bulky uterus. Pelvic MRI was interpreted as endometrial carcinoma with more than 50% myometrial invasion. A CT scan of the chest showed traction bronchiectasis and discrete random nodules with feeding vessel signs in the right lower lobe, likely metastases.

Two weeks later, the uterine mass had grown to a 20-week size, her abdominal pain had worsened, and hemoglobin had fallen to 5.2 g/dL. Repeat ultrasonography revealed a large lobulated heterogeneous mass measuring 13.7 cm × 7.3 cm with increased Doppler vascularity, obscuring the uterus and adnexa. She also developed severe left leg pain with unilateral edema; Doppler ultrasonography was normal, excluding deep vein thrombosis. Given the rapid tumor growth and progressive anemia, a presumptive diagnosis of leiomyosarcoma was made, and she was scheduled for exploratory laparotomy.
title: A Case of High-grade Endometrial Stromal Sarcoma: A Poignant Allegory

case_prompt: A 10-year-old girl was referred for fever and painful genital ulcers. Three days before admission, she had fever, sore throat, and mild dry cough; a rapid group A streptococcal antigen test was negative. On day 3 of fever, she developed intense pain and burning in the genital area. At admission, she remained febrile with cough but had no abdominal pain or diarrhea. Examination showed painful ulcers of variable depth and diameter with elevated violaceous borders inside the labia majora; there were no oral ulcers or lymphadenopathy. She was not sexually active and had no prior history of similar lesions. She was treated with intravenous antibiotics and local antiseptic care. Cultures from the lesions were negative for bacteria, and PCR of tissue for herpes simplex virus was negative. Serologic tests for HSV-1 and HSV-2 antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase) were all negative. Four days later, the genital lesions had significantly improved, but fever and cough persisted. Chest radiography revealed a right-sided pneumonia, and oral azithromycin was added.
title: Mycoplasma pneumoniae as a cause of vulvar ulcers in a non-sexually active girl: a case report

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman was referred from a dental clinic for excessive gingival enlargement that had appeared abruptly 20 days earlier. She had a history of hypertension but was not taking any medications associated with gingival overgrowth. She also reported a severe upper respiratory infection 30 days ago. 

On examination, there was generalized gingival enlargement, most pronounced in the maxillary anterior region. In the anterior maxilla, discrete bulbous enlargements were noted in the interproximal areas; posteriorly, the enlargement was diffuse and extended onto the alveolar mucosa, especially on the palate where it extended beyond the cingula of the anterior teeth. The gingiva was pale blue with a glazed texture, loss of stippling, and was generally friable. Spontaneous bleeding was observed on the palatal surfaces of the canine and premolar regions.

A panoramic radiograph showed generalized horizontal bone loss, most marked in the anterior maxilla, although the clinical enlargement was notably more pronounced than the radiographic bone loss. Extraoral examination revealed a bruise adjacent to the right lower lip without any recalled trauma and mild tenderness and enlargement of the right cervical lymph nodes. The patient also reported ongoing general weakness and headache.

Given the disproportionate gingival findings and systemic symptoms, a complete blood count with differential was obtained.
title: Oral signs of acute leukemia for early detection

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old man with coronary artery disease (status post bypass), mitral regurgitation, left ventricular hypertrophy, and atrial fibrillation presented with insidious atraumatic right shoulder pain beginning at 0300 on the day of presentation. He reported body aches and chills but remained afebrile. The pain initially resolved then returned, prompting an ED visit. He had played 18 holes of golf the previous day, with no other precipitant. 

Medications included aspirin, Norvasc, Flomax, topical diclofenac, and Norco as needed. He had allergies to cephalexin and latex (rash). He was a former half-pack-per-day smoker; denied alcohol or drug use. 

On examination, he was afebrile; vital signs were normal. Inspection of the right shoulder showed no erythema, swelling, fluctuance, or lesions. There was minimal tenderness to palpation over the glenohumeral joint. Active range of motion was limited by pain. Passive flexion and abduction reached 100°, internal and external rotation 45°, with pain at extremes. Axial loading of the shoulder elicited pain.

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 33,100 c/µL (normal 4,800–10,800) and C-reactive protein of 11 mg/dL (normal 0–0.8). Plain radiographs of the right shoulder were unremarkable aside from acromioclavicular joint degenerative changes. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a supraspinatus tear, a moderate glenohumeral effusion, and a thickened capsule.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Bilateral shoulder septic arthritis due to suspected bacterial endocarditis: A case report

case_prompt:
A 90-year-old man was evaluated for a one-month history of progressive fatigue and abdominal and lower extremity edema. His medical history was notable for ischemic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction, 15%) with a dual-chamber pacemaker for resynchronization, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and frequent ventricular ectopy treated with amiodarone (200 mcg/day) initiated six months earlier, and stage IV chronic kidney disease (not on dialysis). He reported full compliance with his heart failure medications and denied dietary indiscretion, alcohol use, or anginal symptoms.

On examination, his weight had increased by 4.6 kg; the heart rate was 60 beats/minute, with jugular venous distension and a positive hepatojugular reflex. Inspiratory crackles were heard at the lung bases, and there was pitting edema to the mid-thigh level. The skin appeared dry, and the thyroid examination was unremarkable.

A chest radiograph showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly. Electrocardiography revealed a paced rhythm at 62 beats/minute, and cardiac biomarkers showed no evidence of myocardial infarction. Laboratory studies revealed an N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide level of 10,644 pg/mL and a serum creatinine level of 3.7 mg/dL (baseline, 2.3 mg/dL). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 12% with global hypokinesis, a right ventricular systolic pressure of 44 mmHg, and a moderate-sized concentric pericardial effusion.

He was treated with cautious intravenous furosemide, resulting in improved pulmonary, abdominal, and peripheral edema and a decrease in serum creatinine to 3.2 mg/dL; however, he remained severely fatigued.
title: Amiodarone-Induced Hypothyroidism Presenting as Cardiorenal Syndrome

case_prompt: A 29-year-old man with a history of asthma, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and stage IIIa chronic kidney disease was found unresponsive at home. He received intranasal naloxone, after which he had witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity. On arrival to the emergency department, his pupils were pinpoint. Laboratory studies revealed a troponin level of 837 ng/L (reference 0–22 ng/L), arterial blood gas with pH 7.15 (7.32–7.43) and pCO2 85 mmHg (41–54 mmHg), lactate 5.3 mmol/L (0.6–1.4 mmol/L), and a urine toxicology screen positive for opiates. Initial noncontrast head CT demonstrated ill-defined hypodensities in the subcortical white matter, bilateral basal ganglia, and cerebellar hemispheres. A repeat CT 12 hours later showed diffuse cerebral edema with partial effacement of the fourth ventricle and basilar cisterns, as well as mild tonsillar and uncal herniation. Brain MRI revealed restricted diffusion involving the cerebral white matter, caudate nuclei, internal capsules, lentiform nuclei, hippocampi, vermis, and cerebellar hemispheres, with relative sparing of the subcortical U-fibers. Gradient-echo sequences showed petechial hemorrhages within the basal ganglia and cerebellum. MR angiography was normal. The patient was admitted to the ICU for supportive care.
title: Heroin-induced leukoencephalopathy: Chasing the imaging findings

case_prompt:
A 15.8-year-old boy was referred for severe back pain and evaluation of low bone mass. Five days after starting deflazacort for autoimmune hepatitis in November 2020, he developed lumbar spine pain that became constant. On May 7, 2021, DXA revealed low bone mass (Z-score spine −4.2, Z-score total body less head −1.9). In June 2021, while still on steroids, he was admitted for further evaluation. 

He was the second child of nonconsanguineous parents, born at term with normal anthropometrics. He had intermittent vitamin D supplementation in infancy. There was no family history of bone disease. Physical examination showed short stature without dysmorphic features. His weight was 47.4 kg (3rd–10th percentile), height 162 cm (<3rd percentile), BMI 18.1 kg/m2 (10th–25th percentile), Tanner pubarche stage 4, and testicular volume 10–12 mL bilaterally. Growth charts showed deceleration from age 11.

Laboratory studies showed normal serum calcium, phosphorus, PTH, and 25(OH)D. Twenty-four–hour urine calcium was mildly increased. Bone age was 15 years. Peak spontaneous nocturnal GH, thyroid function tests, gonadotropins, and androgens were appropriate for puberty.

Spine radiographs revealed compression fractures of T5–T9 and upper endplate depression of L4–L5; MRI of the spine confirmed multilevel vertebral fractures. Osteoporosis was diagnosed. The parents declined bisphosphonate therapy, and he received calcium and cholecalciferol.

Given his growth retardation, endocrine testing of the cortisol axis was performed. Late-night serum cortisol at 24:00 was elevated (10.7 µg/dL). An overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test showed a morning cortisol of 3.4 µg/dL (unsuppressed), whereas a low-dose dexamethasone regimen (0.5 mg every 6 h for 48 h) normalized the 8:00 cortisol to 1.0 µg/dL. Pituitary MRI demonstrated a poorly demarcated 2.0×3.5×5.0 mm area in the anterior lobe.

Deflazacort was discontinued on October 1, 2021. In January 2022, repeat diurnal ACTH and cortisol measurements showed persistent nocturnal elevation without a normal rhythm. A repeat overnight dexamethasone suppression test and low-dose dexamethasone test again failed to suppress cortisol, whereas a high-dose dexamethasone test (1.5 mg every 6 h) achieved suppression.
title: Osteoporosis as the First Sign of Cushing’s Disease in a Thin 16-Year-Old Boy—A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old girl from Maranhão, Brazil, presented with a 3-year history of recurrent irritation, bleeding, and watering of her left eye. For the past 2 years she noted pain and a progressively enlarging mass in the upper nasal quadrant above the left cornea. She reported frequent swimming in ponds and rivers but denied any ocular trauma, epistaxis, animal contact, or similar lesions elsewhere. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable.

On examination, uncorrected Snellen visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye; best-corrected acuity in the left eye was 20/20 with a –4.75-diopter cylinder at 120°. In the left eye, slit-lamp biomicroscopy revealed an oval bluish scleral swelling measuring 10 × 10 × 5 mm in the upper nasal quadrant with congestion of overlying conjunctival and episcleral vessels. Scattered white corpuscular bodies (<1 mm) were visible at the posterior margin of the hyperemic conjunctiva. An anterior chamber reaction was +/4+ and intraocular pressure was normal. Fundus examination showed upper nasal subretinal hypopigmentation. An ENT evaluation revealed no lesions. A complete rheumatologic workup was negative for systemic disease. An incisional biopsy of the hyperemic conjunctiva was then performed.
title: Partial regression of large anterior scleral staphyloma secondary to rhinosporidiosis after corneoscleral graft - a case report

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old woman (gravida 0, para 0) presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging pelvic mass and heavy menstrual bleeding. On pelvic examination, the uterus was enlarged to approximately the size of a 5-month pregnancy, with an uneven surface and limited mobility. Hysteroscopic evaluation showed a bulging anterior uterine wall but no distinct fibroid nodules. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed multiple heterogeneous intrauterine masses measuring up to 10.0 × 8.8 × 7.4 cm. Hemoglobin was 80 g/L.

She underwent uterine myomectomy. Intraoperatively, the masses were soft, round, finger-like, and cord-like, with no clear boundary between the lesions and adjacent pseudo-envelope. Frozen-section pathology indicated degenerated leiomyoma; permanent pathology confirmed uterine leiomyoma. Postoperatively, she received 3 months of GnRH-agonist therapy. One month after therapy, her menstruation resumed with heavy bleeding similar to baseline, and ultrasound again demonstrated uterine fibroids. Over the next 3 years, fibroids gradually enlarged, and she developed severe anemia requiring intermittent transfusions.

In July 2020, she was readmitted for severe anemia. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated the uterine mass extending into the left iliac vein, the common iliac vein, and the inferior vena cava, with evidence of intraluminal tumor.
title: Intravenous leiomyomatosis: A case study and literature review☆

case_prompt: A 15-year-old girl with a 6-month history of recurrent acute and chronic pancreatitis, most recently complicated by infected walled-off pancreatic necrosis, was treated with 14 days of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics after admission for high-spiking fever and a C-reactive protein level of 600 mg/L. Three days after her fever resolved, she noted sudden, painless loss of vision in her left eye. She denied eye pain, floaters, or flashes and had no prior visual pathology. Visual acuity was 1/60 in the left eye and 6/6 in the right eye. An urgent ophthalmology evaluation included fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography (OCT). Findings in the left eye included blurred disc margins, macular edema with exudates, multiple retinal nerve fiber layer hemorrhages with interspersed cotton wool spots predominantly in the peripapillary and macular regions, and well-demarcated areas of retinal whitening between vessels (Purtscher flecken). OCT showed central macular thickness >700 µm with multiple exudates.
title: Purtscher-like retinopathy: Case report of a rare complication of acute on chronic pancreatitis

case_prompt: A 25-year-old Caucasian woman with type 1 neurofibromatosis underwent cesarean section for fetal distress. Within 18 hours postoperatively, she developed diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. She had not passed flatus or stool and denied hematemesis or melena. On transfer, she appeared acutely ill. Temperature was 38.8°C, pulse 120/min, blood pressure 154/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on 2 L/min nasal oxygen. The abdomen was markedly distended, diffusely tender without peritoneal signs, and bowel sounds were absent. Her white blood cell count was 25,000/mm3 with 91% neutrophils; electrolytes, amylase, lipase, and liver‐function tests were normal. CT of the abdomen showed marked gastric dilation, air in the wall of the stomach along the greater curvature, air in the portal venous system, and dilatation of both small and large bowel. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed diffuse mucosal congestion, extreme pallor, and ulceration on the posterior wall and greater curvature of the stomach.
title: Successful medical management of emphysematous gastritis with concomitant portal venous air: a case report

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of ocular melanoma was found incidentally on surveillance CT to have a 1.6 × 1.6 × 0.7 cm hypodense lesion in the head of the pancreas and a 2.8 × 1 cm porta hepatis lymph node. She was asymptomatic with no history of pancreatitis.  
On MRI, a 1.7 × 1.3 cm lobulated lesion in the pancreatic head effaced the distal common bile duct.  
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) revealed a 1.5 × 1.4 cm hypoechoic cyst not communicating with the pancreatic duct, with a thickened wall, luminal debris, and an 0.8 × 0.7 cm mural nodule.  
Fine‐needle aspiration (FNA) of the cyst yielded turbid, viscous fluid with inconclusive cytology.  
After developing right upper quadrant pain, dark urine, and acholic stools post‐EUS, ERCP showed a 7 mm biliary stricture relieved by stent placement, with resolution of symptoms.  
Repeat EUS‐guided FNA of the mural nodule demonstrated atypical cells.  
Clinically, the lesion was considered an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm or mucinous cystic neoplasm with worrisome features (lymphadenopathy and atypical cells), and resection was planned.
title: Lactoferrin amyloid presenting as a mural nodule in a pancreatic cystic lesion prompting pancreatoduodenectomy: a case report

case_prompt: A 61-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation refractory to antiarrhythmic therapy underwent pulmonary vein isolation with roofline and cavotricuspid isthmus ablation. He had an uncomplicated immediate postprocedural course and was discharged on dabigatran. Approximately 3 months later, he presented with progressive dyspnea. His electrocardiogram showed low QRS voltage in the limb leads. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved biventricular function and a mild circumferential pericardial effusion measuring 8 mm, without signs of hemodynamic compromise. Several examinations were performed for exclusion of phrenic nerve palsy, pulmonary vein stenosis, and anemia. Because of the possibility of effusive pericarditis, the patient was treated with colchicine and ibuprofen, and anticoagulation was continued. Over the next several months, his symptoms progressed, with clinical features of right-sided heart failure. A repeat transthoracic echocardiogram performed 9 months after the ablation revealed paradoxical interventricular septal motion and a restrictive transmitral filling pattern with an E/A ratio of 2.84, a septal e′ velocity of 0.16 m/s, and a lateral e′ velocity of 0.10 m/s.
title: Constrictive pericarditis following atrial fibrillation ablation – A rare complication

case_prompt: A 43-year-old woman presented with a 3–4-month history of a left adnexal cyst and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She had hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. Vital signs were normal, and the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Pelvic ultrasonography performed for the adnexal cyst incidentally revealed a well-defined, approximately 9 cm hypoechoic lesion in the right hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 9 × 8.7 × 8.4 cm well-circumscribed hypodense mass in segments VI and VIII of the liver, with arterial-phase enhancement and a central nonenhancing component, followed by progressive enhancement in the portal venous phase. On imaging, focal nodular hyperplasia was initially favored. The patient was admitted and underwent right hemihepatectomy.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Myopericytoma of the liver: A rare tumor - A case report

case_prompt: An 80-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidemia, and poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presented with a 1-hour history of right-sided, nonradiating, 10/10 chest pain accompanied by nausea and two episodes of maroon-colored emesis. He denied toxic ingestions or prior similar episodes. On arrival, he was afebrile; blood pressure 109/45 mm Hg; heart rate 75 beats/min; respiratory rate 18 breaths/min; SpO₂ 98% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed sodium 125 mEq/L, potassium 5.1 mEq/L, chloride 91 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 145.7 mg/dL, creatinine 2.95 mg/dL, blood glucose 492 mg/dL, WBC 13.5 × 10³/mm³, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, platelets 242 000/mm³, BNP 154 pg/mL, and troponin 0.062 ng/mL. ECG revealed normal sinus rhythm at 94 beats/min without ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. The patient received morphine and nitroglycerin without relief. Given persistent chest pain and risk factors for ischemic heart disease, he was started on heparin and antiplatelet therapy. Cardiac catheterization showed no critical stenosis and an ejection fraction of 55%. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast was unremarkable, and gastroenterology was consulted for ongoing nausea, vomiting, and hematemesis.
title: Acute esophageal necrosis masquerading acute coronary syndrome

case_prompt:
A 3-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of painful gingival growths in the upper and lower jaws, present for 1 month. The pain was sudden in onset, intermittent, nonradiating, worsened with chewing, and self-resolving. He had been treated with analgesics and antibiotics at a local clinic without improvement. His medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, he was healthy in general appearance. Extraorally, there was a firm, tender, diffuse 4×2 cm swelling over the left mandible from the inferior border of the body to the superior ramus, with palpable, firm, nontender left submandibular lymph nodes (~0.5×2 cm). Intraorally, there were diffuse, erythematous, ulcerated gingival swellings covered with necrotic slough and bleeding spots adjacent to teeth 55, 65, 75, and 85, with Grade II mobility of those teeth.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic anemia on peripheral smear; normal liver and urine tests; creatinine 0.3 mg/dL; C-reactive protein 2.5 mg/dL; negative HIV and hepatitis B surface antigen.

An orthopantomogram revealed multiple areas of bone loss in the left mandible. Axial and coronal CT showed multiple soft-tissue density lesions with irregular, punched-out bony destruction of the left mandible, left occiput, right maxilla, and right temporal bone. Three-dimensional CT confirmed multiple osteolytic lesions in the maxillary alveolar process and the body and ramus of the left mandible.
journal: Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology : JOMFP
title: A rare and unusual case report of Langerhans cell histiocytosis

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 22-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of worsening left lower abdominal pain. She had eaten raw chicken 7 days earlier and had no significant past medical history. On examination, she was alert, febrile (39.6 °C), tachycardic (125 beats/min), blood pressure was 108/63 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. She had lower abdominal and rebound tenderness without pharyngitis, skin lesions, or rash. Initial laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 12 × 10^3/mm^3 and a C-reactive protein level of 18 mg/dL; blood cultures were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed localized thickening of the peritoneum in the left lower quadrant. She was observed without antimicrobial therapy. 

On hospital day 5, she developed chest pain and persistent fever. Repeat CT demonstrated generalized peritoneal thickening, increased ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions. Overnight, she developed respiratory and circulatory failure. On hospital day 6, she was intubated for hypoxemia and started on epinephrine, norepinephrine, and vasopressin for shock. Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 12 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.3 × 10^3/mm^3, platelet count 6.8 × 10^4/mm^3, CRP 43 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 40 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, interleukin-6 4.0 × 10^4 pg/mL, and VEGF 1.4 × 10^3 pg/mL, indicating systemic inflammation, thrombocytopenia, and renal dysfunction. Because of septic shock of unclear source versus TAFRO syndrome, intravenous meropenem and methylprednisolone were initiated.
title: Successful treatment of streptococcal toxic shock syndrome complicated by primary peritonitis and bilateral empyema in a healthy young woman: Identification of uncommon clone emm103 and novel sequence type 1363

case_prompt: A 48-year-old woman presented with progressive swelling of the left cheek. Three years prior, she noted a painless palpable mass on the left cheek, initially the size of her fifth finger tip. Over the next three years, the mass enlarged to roughly an adult fist and became painful. She also developed left epiphora, exophthalmos, blurry vision, rhinitis, and lost 23 kg in six months. She denied headaches, seizures, prior malignancy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or surgery. On examination, there was a single 6 × 5 × 10 cm fixed, hard, irregular mass in the left maxillary-nasal-infraorbital region with intraoral ulceration of the left maxillary gingiva. Visual acuity was 5/5 in the right eye and 5/6 in the left, with normal intraocular pressures. Panoramic radiographs showed permeative maxillary sinus destruction with a sunburst periosteal reaction, a broad transitional zone, and a chondroid-type matrix. A CT scan suggested an aggressive primary malignant bone tumor, most likely chondrogenic osteosarcoma, with bilateral maxillary sinusitis and submandibular and posterior trigonum lymphadenopathy. Thoracic radiography showed no pulmonary metastases. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded hypercellular specimens with anaplastic oval-round pleomorphic nuclei, binucleation, hyperchromasia, and an eosinophilic matrix.
title: Case report of a very rare primary malignant bone tumor: Mixed type maxillary osteosarcoma

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of painless swelling over her left temporal region. Her past medical history was notable only for hypothyroidism treated for 10 years. She denied head trauma, dietary changes, bruxism, headaches, or recent surgery. She had received botulinum toxin A injections into both masseter muscles for cosmetic reasons one year earlier and reported severe personal stress over the preceding 3 to 4 months.

On examination, there was a soft, diffuse swelling of the left temporal area without tenderness. The prominence increased and became firm when she clenched her teeth. According to the patient, the swelling was larger in the morning and decreased in size as the day progressed. There were no signs of pain, fever, warmth, tenderness, or erythema. Oral, dental, and temporomandibular joint examinations were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed asymmetric, homogeneous enlargement of the left temporalis muscle, with normal appearance of the masseter muscles. No lymphadenopathy or intra- or extra-cranial abnormalities were identified.
title: Isolated unilateral temporalis muscle hypertrophy of unknown etiology: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 78-year-old woman presented with subacute, intractable left lower extremity neuropathic pain, back pain, and a two-week history of left foot drop. She had sustained a left acetabular fracture in a fall 20 years earlier, treated nonoperatively, and had intermittent left hip pain since. Over the past six months, she experienced increasing back pain, left-sided radicular discomfort, and excruciating pain over the left foot.

On examination, strength in the left lower extremity was 4/5 for hip flexion, 5/5 for knee extension, 0/5 for ankle dorsiflexion, 1/5 for great toe extension, and 4/5 for ankle plantarflexion. Hypersensitivity was present in the superficial peroneal, deep peroneal, sural, saphenous, and tibial nerve distributions. Distal perfusion was intact with brisk capillary refill and a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse.

A pelvic radiograph showed no acute fracture but significant hip arthrosis and sclerotic changes around the greater sciatic notch of the left innominate bone. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed post-traumatic changes in the left iliac bone with a 5.8 × 3.6 × 7 cm lytic lesion containing cystic or soft-tissue components, extending from the supra-acetabular region under the psoas, findings initially favored to represent tumor or infection. MRI with contrast demonstrated that the lesion had a nonaggressive appearance and was partially visualized on an examination performed in 2014.
title: Delayed Presentation of Sciatic Nerve Palsy Due to Post-traumatic Pseudoaneurysm Following Pelvis Fracture: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old Hispanic boy with no significant past medical history was found to have a scrotal nodule during a routine physical examination. He recalled the lesion had been present for 3–4 years, was nonpainful, and had shown no significant change in size. On examination, there was a firm, nodular lesion immediately beneath a yellowish, discolored area of scrotal skin; no other mucosal or cutaneous lesions were noted.

He underwent complete surgical enucleation of the lesion without complications. Grossly, the specimen was a 1.0 × 0.8 × 0.6 cm firm, nonencapsulated mass covered by loose fibrous tissue; on sectioning, it showed a whitish, homogeneous cut surface without hemorrhage or necrosis. Low-power histology demonstrated a poorly circumscribed nodular lesion that appeared completely excised. On higher-power hematoxylin and eosin staining, the lesion comprised polyhedral cells with abundant granular cytoplasm and small, uniform, dark nuclei arranged in nests and as single cells within fibrous connective tissue.
title: Granular cell tumor presenting in the scrotum of a pediatric patient: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old Asian man presented with 10 days of gradual-onset right hypochondrial and epigastric pain, vomiting, intermittent fever with chills, and progressive weakness. He had been treated 3 months earlier for a right-lobe liver abscess diagnosed as amoebic on the basis of positive serology. He had no history of tuberculosis or known TB contacts. 

On examination, he appeared ill, dehydrated, and anemic. Vital signs were: temperature 38.5 °C, pulse 92/min, blood pressure 106/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min. There was no jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination showed tenderness and guarding in the right upper quadrant and hepatomegaly (liver span 16 cm); there was no splenomegaly, ascites, or other masses. The cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable.

A chest radiograph showed elevation of the right hemidiaphragm and blunting of the right costophrenic angle, without focal pulmonary lesions. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 5.6×6.8×8.8 cm ill-defined, heterogeneous hypo-echoic lesion with cystic areas in the right lobe of the liver, consistent with an abscess; the liver was enlarged (span 16.6 cm), with no perihepatic fluid or other focal lesions.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL; white-cell count 22 600/mm³ (76% neutrophils); platelets 376 000/mm³; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 52 mm/h; blood urea 28 mg/dL; total bilirubin 1 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase 7 IU/L; AST 29 IU/L; ALT 39 IU/L; serum protein 6.6 g/dL; albumin 4.0 g/dL; and prothrombin time 15 s (control 10.1 s).

Under local anesthesia, pigtail catheter drainage yielded 150 mL of cream-colored pus, which was sent for Ziehl–Neelsen staining, mycobacterial culture, PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and routine bacterial, fungal, and parasitic studies.
title: Primary tubercular liver abscess in an immunocompetent adult: a case report

case_prompt: A 53-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of chronic productive cough with greenish sputum and intermittent fever. He denied dyspnea or hemoptysis. He worked in construction for 20 years, had no significant medical history, no tobacco use, and no family history of lung disease or malignancy. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics without improvement. Examination was unremarkable, with normal systemic and chest findings and no lymphadenopathy. A chest radiograph showed right middle zone consolidation. CT of the thorax revealed right middle lobe subsegmental collapse with bronchiectasis and nodular calcified excrescences protruding into the lumen of the trachea and main bronchi; there was no contrast-enhancing lung mass or pleural effusion. Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a patent but narrowed airway with numerous whitish granular nodules along the anterolateral walls of the trachea and main bronchi, sparing the posterior wall.
title: Tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica—stalactite of airways

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of intermittent swelling of her left deltoid, with four episodes each lasting about 2 months. Each episode was associated with pain and tenderness. She denied any trauma to the region and had no systemic illnesses, significant family history, or medications. On examination, she had full range of motion of the shoulder and neck, and her neurological and vascular findings were normal. Plain radiographs of the shoulder were unremarkable. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left shoulder showed diffuse oedematous signal changes within the deltoid muscle on proton density–weighted sequences; there was no evidence of plexiform neurofibroma. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography revealed an axillary nerve M-wave amplitude of 14.1 mV and normal motor action potentials in the deltoid, confirming the absence of an axillary nerve lesion. 

During symptomatic periods, her erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 26–73 mm/h and C-reactive protein was 12 mg/L; both returned to normal when symptoms subsided. She was screened for connective tissue disorders with antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, and extractable nuclear antigen antibodies, and for diabetes; all tests were negative. Creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase levels during the acute phase were within normal limits. 

A sequential MRI performed after symptom resolution showed a reduction in the oedematous signal within the deltoid muscle.
title: Focal Myositis of the Deltoid Muscle: The Role of Magnetic Resonance Imaging for Diagnosis

case_prompt: A 4-year-old boy was admitted for evaluation of acute exacerbation of presumed severe asthma. He had a history of four episodes of recurrent respiratory symptoms (one at 10 months, three after age 3) characterized by cough, fever, and wheeze. On admission he reported intermittent cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, orthopnea, fatigue, pallor, and sweating, all worse at night. The parents denied any foreign-body aspiration, weight loss, or trauma. Physical examination showed tachypnea, cyanosis, suprasternal retraction, and prolonged expiratory crackles. Oxygen saturation was 91% on supplemental oxygen. Skin-prick testing was negative, and serum IgE was not elevated. Pulmonary-function testing revealed airway hyperresponsiveness: V75 and V50 were mildly reduced, peak flow was moderately reduced, and there was no reversibility with bronchodilator. Bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids produced only partial improvement, and each outpatient episode lasted more than 20 days. After admission, flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated tracheal narrowing at the lower trachea without any internal airway lesion. A noncontrast chest CT scan showed no parenchymal lung disease.
title: Recurrent Wheezing and Cough Caused by Double Aortic Arch, Not Asthma

case_prompt: A 6-year-old castrated male Golden Retriever was evaluated for decreased activity and loss of appetite. Two years earlier, the dog had undergone jejunojejunostomy for foreign body ingestion. The dog spent time both indoors and outdoors and had a habit of eating soil and grass. On presentation, temperature was 39.4 °C, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 42 breaths/min. Complete blood count showed mild leukocytosis (21 120/μL). Serum biochemistry revealed elevated total protein (8.5 g/dL; reference 5.0–7.2) and C-reactive protein (>17 mg/dL; reference <1.0). Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple well-circumscribed spherical masses (30–65 mm) with heterogeneously mixed echogenicity throughout the peritoneal cavity. Fine-needle aspiration of the masses yielded numerous neutrophils, macrophages, and septate hyphae; no bacteria were detected. Samples were submitted for fungal culture and susceptibility testing.
title: Multiple intra-abdominal fungal granulomas caused by Scedosporium apiospermum effectively treated with voriconazole in a Golden Retriever

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old man with a history of unprovoked deep vein thrombosis on rivaroxaban, alcohol use, and 22 pack-year tobacco use presented with right lower-extremity swelling and right groin pain radiating to the right testicle. He was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Physical examination showed right lower-extremity edema and slight tenderness of the right testicle. 

Given concern for occult malignancy in the setting of recurrent unprovoked DVTs, a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained, which showed diffuse gastric wall thickening, extensive retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and nodularity with stranding along the peritoneal surfaces. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a 0.9 × 0.7 × 0.8-cm, well-marginated hypoechoic lesion in the upper pole of the right testicle. 

The patient underwent a right orchiectomy. Histopathological examination revealed infiltrating signet ring cell adenocarcinoma involving both the testicular parenchyma and spermatic cord with angiolymphatic invasion. Immunohistochemical studies were positive for cytokeratin (CK)-7, CK-20, CK AE1/AE3, and CDX2, and negative for Helicobacter pylori.
title: Gastric Signet Ring Cell Adenocarcinoma With Metastasis to the Testicles and Leptomeninges

case_prompt: An 82-year-old woman with coronary artery disease (status post stenting) and known gallstones presented with two weeks of postprandial abdominal pain, persistent nausea, and vomiting. On examination she was tachycardic (pulse 102 beats/min), hypotensive (blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg), and showed signs of extracellular dehydration (clammy skin, decreased skin turgor, sunken eyes). Laboratory evaluation revealed hypokalemia and hypochloremia. A urinary catheter showed reduced urine output. Following fluid resuscitation and placement of a nasogastric tube, 400 cc of gastric fluid was drained. After hemodynamic stabilization, esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated normal mucosa up to the second part of the duodenum, no dilatation, and retained bile. To investigate the cause of gastric outlet obstruction, an abdominal CT scan was performed, which revealed a cholecystoduodenal fistula, marked gastric distention with pneumobilia, and a 4 cm calcified stone impacted at the duodenojejunal junction.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Bouveret Syndrome: A rare form of gallstone ileus a case report☆

case_prompt: A 4-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of a swelling over the left angle of the mandible that had been present for several weeks. The lesion was noted to be painless, soft, and nontender, with normal overlying skin and no regional lymphadenopathy. An ultrasound examination of the left parotid region using a 4–7-MHz linear transducer demonstrated a largely homogeneous, isoechoic mass replacing the parotid gland, with lobulated margins and internal echogenic septae. Color Doppler imaging revealed multiple dilated vascular channels within the lesion. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the neck showed a lesion in the left parotid gland that was hyperintense on fat-suppressed T2-weighted and STIR sequences, contained thin internal septae, and demonstrated prominent flow voids. On post-contrast T1-weighted images, the mass enhanced homogeneously, with thin nonenhancing septae. The right parotid gland and overlying skin appeared normal.
title: Infantile Hemangioendothelioma of the Parotid Gland

case_prompt: A 55-year-old woman with a 4-year history of hypertension (on atenolol 50 mg daily) presented with 3 days of headache, 1 day of altered sensorium, and 4 hours of loss of consciousness. CT scan demonstrated a right sylvian fissure subarachnoid hemorrhage (Fisher grade 3). Angiography revealed an anterior communicating artery aneurysm without vasospasm. She underwent uneventful craniotomy and aneurysm clipping under general anaesthesia and was extubated in the operating room. Initially she remained alert and neurologically intact with mean arterial pressure 90–100 mmHg and CVP 10–12 mmHg. On postoperative day 2 she became drowsy and developed progressive dyspnoea with wheezing and crepitations; oxygen saturation was 85%. On 6 L/min O₂ by face mask, arterial blood gas revealed PaO₂ of 50 mmHg. She was intubated and mechanically ventilated. She was afebrile, with a normal blood count. Chest radiograph showed diffuse alveolar opacities in the right lung. CVP was 12 mmHg. Tracheal aspirate and blood cultures were sterile. Brain CT showed no new infarct. Echocardiogram revealed diastolic dysfunction but preserved systolic function. Pulmonary artery catheterization showed a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 28 cm H₂O. Repeat chest radiograph 6 hours later showed persistent right-sided haziness. There was no evidence of infection, major cardiac dysfunction, fluid overload, or other systemic cause for the pulmonary oedema.
title: Unilateral neurogenic pulmonary oedema: An unusual cause for post-operative respiratory dysfunction following clipping of ruptured intracranial aneurysm

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old girl was referred for asymmetry of the maxillary arch. She was in good health, with normal stature and no history of systemic disease, trauma, or surgery. Her mother had past orthodontic treatment, and both parents had full dental arches; there was no other family history of dental anomalies.

On examination, no teeth had erupted distal to the left maxillary canine. There was a left lateral open bite and a slight shift of the maxillary midline to the left. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated delayed intraosseous development of the left upper lateral teeth compared with the right and no sign of mechanical obstruction; agenesis of the left upper premolars was suspected but uncertain.

At 5 years and 3 months, a molar erupted in the left maxillary arch, presumed to be the primary second molar (tooth 65), but its crown shape and size differed markedly from that of tooth 55 on the right. A repeat panoramic radiograph suggested that tooth 64 could be mechanically impacted by the primary canine (tooth 63).

At 7 years and 10 months, tooth 65 had fully erupted with an atypically large crown. No premolar tooth buds were visible in the upper left quadrant. The unerupted permanent first molar (26) had reached the coronal stage, while the second molar (27) lagged behind its right counterpart. Tooth 64 appeared more intruded and again seemed to be impacted by tooth 63. Primary failure of eruption of the upper left permanent molars was suspected.
title: Rare Case of First Permanent Molar Primary Failure of Eruption with Agenesis of Premolars

case_prompt: A 27-year-old man presented with progressive abdominal swelling for two years, accompanied by loss of appetite, significant weight loss, and constipation. Over the past month, he noted worsening abdominal distension, new scrotal swelling, and dyspnea. He had no prior surgery, comorbidities, tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. On examination, he was emaciated and tachypneic (24–26 breaths/min); other vital signs were normal. The abdomen was hugely distended, tense, and shiny with visible veins; the umbilicus was everted, percussion was dull throughout, and no discrete mass could be palpated. There was bilateral pedal and scrotal edema. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL and albumin 2.5 g/dL; other values were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large, multiseptated cystic mass filling the abdominal and pelvic cavities; its origin could not be determined. Differential diagnosis on imaging was a mesenteric cyst.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare case of huge intra-abdominal cystic lymphangioma arising from rectovesical pouch; a case report

case_prompt: A 36-year-old woman with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma presented on day 17 of her sixth cycle of CHOP chemotherapy with a 2-day history of fever (maximum 38.1°C) and nonproductive cough. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed an absolute neutrophil count of 0.6×10^9/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein level of 12.3 mg/L. A chest radiograph was normal. Initial septic workup was negative, including sputum bacterial culture, sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and culture, bacterial and fungal blood cultures, and urine acid-fast bacilli studies. Because fever persisted, a noncontrast thoracic CT was performed, which showed bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities without zonal predominance.
title: Computed tomography features of Stenotrophomonas maltophilia pneumonia in patients with neutropenic fever: report of two cases

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old woman presented with worsening dyspnea on exertion. Her medical history included hypertension since age 4, hyperlipidemia, bicuspid aortic valve with severe aortic insufficiency, aortic root dilation, and left ventricular dilation with preserved ejection fraction. She was born at 37 weeks in a pregnancy complicated by gestational hypertension and diagnosed with bicuspid aortic valve and aortic insufficiency at 3 months. At age 6, evaluation of her short stature and hypertension included karyotyping (46,XX), array CGH (negative), and skeletal survey revealing diffuse brachydactyly.

On examination, she was 58 inches tall, weighed 87 pounds (BMI 18.2), and had a blood pressure of 137/83 mm Hg. She had bilateral brachydactyly of the hands and feet without facial dysmorphism. Transesophageal echocardiography showed a bicuspid aortic valve, left ventricular ejection fraction 60%, severe aortic insufficiency with eccentric left ventricular dilation, mild aortic stenosis, and moderate mitral regurgitation. Cardiac MRI demonstrated an enlarged ascending aorta relative to body size. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy. A 29-gene aortopathy panel and an 82-gene cardiomyopathy panel were both negative.
title: Hypertension and Brachydactyly Syndrome

case_prompt: A 55-year-old woman presented with a painless, gradually enlarging mass in the right superior orbit over 4 years. She denied vision loss or field defects but reported occasional diplopia on up gaze for 6 months. Visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. Examination of the right eye revealed a solid, non-tender, freely mobile 20 × 15 mm mass in the superior orbit causing proptosis; pupillary reactions, color vision, and visual fields were normal. Supraorbital, infraorbital, and corneal sensation were intact, and cranial-nerve and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Slit-lamp and fundus examinations showed no optic-nerve involvement. Subjective diplopia in up gaze correlated with inferior globe dystopia, but ocular motility was full, and no compensatory head posture was noted. The left eye and general physical examination were normal. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the orbits showed a well-defined, homogenous, nonenhancing mass measuring 20 × 12 mm in the right superior orbit displacing the globe. Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of an orbital dermoid or cyst was made, and the patient was scheduled for excisional biopsy.
title: Unilateral orbital schwannoma arising from the supraorbital nerve: Report of a rare case

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old G2P2 woman presented with a 5-month history of umbilical swelling, cyclic umbilical pain, and bleeding. Her menstrual cycles occur every 29 days, lasting 5 days with moderate flow. She denied lower abdominal pain, trauma to the abdomen or umbilicus, bleeding from other sites, and urinary or bowel symptoms. She had two prior spontaneous vaginal deliveries without complications and had stopped using levonorgestrel implants two years earlier. She had no other relevant medical, surgical, or gynecologic history.

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed a 2.0 × 1.5 cm brownish umbilical nodule that was non-tender. Speculum and bimanual examinations were unremarkable. The remainder of her physical examination, including cardiovascular, respiratory, lymphatic, and neurologic assessments, was normal.

An abdominopelvic ultrasound showed a 10.3 mm endometrial thickness. Chest radiography, complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and urinalysis were all within normal limits.
title: Coexistence of Primary Umbilical Endometriosis and Endometrial Hyperplasia: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 2-year-old boy was evaluated for a gradually enlarging, circumscribed swelling over the left body of the mandible, first noted approximately 1 year earlier. The lesion was painless, although the child cried when it was palpated, and there were no other associated symptoms. On examination, there was a firm-to-hard, mildly tender, 4.0 by 2.5 cm mass over the left mandibular body. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a soft-tissue mass eroding the underlying mandibular bone, suggestive of a neoplastic lesion. The complete blood count and routine biochemical tests were within normal limits. A tru-cut biopsy of the lesion revealed sheets of intermediate-sized mononuclear blast-like cells with round to oval nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, prominent nucleoli, and scant basophilic cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the blast cells were positive for CD45, CD68, and lysozyme and negative for CD3, CD20, CD99, TdT, MPO, and CD138.
journal: Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology : JOMFP
title: De novo myeloid sarcoma involving mandible in a child: Report of a rare occurrence

case_prompt:
A 74-year-old man with a history of metastatic superficial spreading melanoma (NRAS-mutant, BRAF wild-type) had received 27 cycles of pembrolizumab, with initial regression of lymph node and lung metastases. Pembrolizumab was discontinued, and shortly thereafter he developed progressive dyspnea and cough.  
   
Workup revealed bilateral pleural effusions (exudative fluid without malignant cells) and mesenteric panniculitis on CT; he was treated with high-dose prednisolone and pleural drainage. Two weeks later he presented with dyspnea, fever (38.5°C), and red, tearing eyes. He was hypoxic; CT of the thorax showed right-sided pulmonary emboli and recurrent pleural fluid, which was drained. He was started on low-molecular-weight heparin. On the ward, fever persisted and CRP rose to 102 mg/L; broad-spectrum piperacillin/tazobactam was begun and steroids were halved.  

On hospital day 4, he developed vomiting, severe diarrhea, oliguria, and blue discoloration of the fingers. CT of the abdomen demonstrated free intra-abdominal fluid, a distended transverse colon, and no occluded mesenteric arteries.  

On day 5, he was transferred to the ICU with acute respiratory distress requiring nasal positive airway pressure. Examination revealed a tense, silent abdomen with diarrhea, profound mottling of the legs extending to the abdomen, capillary refill >4 seconds, and blue-purple discoloration of all fingers. Laboratory studies demonstrated rising lactate, worsening renal function, and elevated transaminases. A multi-disciplinary team was convened to evaluate for an immune-related adverse event.
title: Severe mesenteric ischemia with multiple organ failure in a patient previously treated with a humanized monoclonal antibody against programmed death receptor-1 (pembrolizumab), a case of pembrolizumab associated catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome?

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old man with hypertension and non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus underwent elective tonsillectomy for suspected oropharyngeal malignancy. His medications included valsartan, amlodipine/atorvastatin, sulodexide, fenofibrate, aspirin, pregabalin, and glibenclamide/metformin. Preoperative evaluation showed normal laboratory tests, nonspecific ST changes on electrocardiogram, a normal transthoracic echocardiogram (LV ejection fraction 58%), and an equivocal stage-4 treadmill stress test. He denied chest pain or dyspnea. 

Preinduction blood pressure was 165/97 mmHg, heart rate 76 beats/min, and SpO₂ 97%. Anesthesia was induced with propofol, remifentanil, and rocuronium, and maintained with sevoflurane in 60% oxygen. The 25-minute surgery was uneventful. At emergence, after reversal of neuromuscular blockade and extubation, he developed inspiratory stridor and hypoxemia (SpO₂ 77%), with blood pressure 164/101 mmHg and heart rate 125 beats/min. He was reintubated 5 minutes later, and large volumes of pink, frothy secretions were suctioned. 

Arterial blood gas analysis on FiO₂ 1.0 showed pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 55.6 mmHg, PaO₂ 47.9 mmHg, and SaO₂ 74.1%. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral perihilar opacities. After suctioning and furosemide, his PaO₂ improved to 75.7 mmHg with FiO₂ 0.8 and PEEP 10 cm H₂O. He was transferred to the ICU on mechanical ventilation (FiO₂ 0.8, PEEP 12 cm H₂O) with SpO₂ 96%. Hypotension (77/51 mmHg) and tachycardia (106 beats/min) prompted dopamine and then norepinephrine infusions.
title: Stress-induced cardiomyopathy after negative pressure pulmonary edema during emergence from anesthesia -A case report-

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old Taiwanese woman presented with a painless mass of the right upper eyelid that had been present for 5 years. In her early 20s, she had undergone blepharoplasty for trichiasis. Two years earlier, at a local clinic, an incision and curettage was performed for a presumed chalazion, but the lesion did not subside after the procedure. 

On examination, there was a firm nodule with a crusted wound at the margin of the right upper eyelid. The fornix, anterior chamber, and fundus were normal. There was no palpable orbital mass and extraocular movements were full. 

Under local anesthesia, the eyelid skin was incised at the wound site, and necrotic tissue along with soft tissue above the tarsus was excised and sent for clinical pathology. The wound healed without complications.
title: Solitary neurofibroma of eyelid masquerading as chalazion

case_prompt: A 69-year-old man presented with a right infra-auricular neck mass that he first noticed more than 10 years ago, which had grown more rapidly over the past 4 months. He denied pain, facial asymmetry, trismus, or overlying skin changes. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was a well-defined, mobile, multilobulated, non-tender mass measuring approximately 10 × 10 cm, extending from the tail of the parotid gland superiorly to the level of the cricoid inferiorly. A T2-weighted fast spin-echo MRI of the neck (noncontrast) showed a large, discrete, rounded heterogeneous lesion with soft-tissue signal in the right parotid region, measuring 11.5 × 10.5 × 11.5 cm, causing mass effect on adjacent structures; the mandible appeared preserved and no lymphadenopathy was noted.
title: Oncocytic lipoadenoma of the parotid gland: a case report and a review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old Japanese woman with no smoking history and a 15-year history of presumed interstitial pneumonia was referred in January 2018 for progressive dyspnea. She had undergone uncomplicated coronary artery bypass grafting in her 50s. On presentation, her respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min, pulse 86 beats/min, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg, temperature 36.3 °C; SpO2 was 93% on room air at rest and 88% during ambulation. Chest auscultation revealed inspiratory fine crackles bilaterally, most prominent in the lower lung fields. There was no Raynaud phenomenon, skin rash, joint swelling, dry eyes or mouth, or digital clubbing.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 5400/μL without abnormal cells, LDH 306 IU/L, C-reactive protein 1.17 mg/dL (normal ≤0.14), soluble IL-2 receptor 1077 U/mL (normal 157–474), KL-6 1297 U/mL (normal <500), surfactant protein D 215 ng/mL (normal <110), and surfactant protein A 74.7 ng/mL (normal <43.8). 

Chest radiography demonstrated diffuse micronodules and ground-glass opacities in both lungs. Thin-section CT revealed numerous well-defined, uniform 1–3 mm micronodules distributed diversely (centrilobular, peribronchovascular, and perilobular), with interlobular septal thickening, ground-glass attenuation, and traction bronchiectasis/bronchiolectasis predominantly in the lower lobes. Air trapping in the lower lobes created a mosaic attenuation pattern. 

At this point, the team considered diseases causing lymphatic tract abnormalities—lymphoproliferative disorders, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, HTLV-1–associated bronchioloalveolar disorder, collagen vascular disease, and drug-induced lung injury—as well as fibrotic chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis. A surgical lung biopsy was planned for definitive diagnosis.
title: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1)-associated bronchioloalveolar disorder required differentiation from fibrotic chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old woman sought care in March 2020 with sore throat, a continuous dry cough, fever of 38–39 °C, chills, sweats, and myalgias. Two weeks later, she developed sinus congestion, enlarged tonsils, breathing difficulties, fevers up to 40–41 °C, chest pain with a burning sensation in her lungs, anosmia, and diarrhea. Her medical history was notable only for insulin resistance and mildly elevated cholesterol; she had no immunocompromise.

In April 2020, home visits led to a clinical diagnosis of COVID-19 with possible pneumonia; she received a course of amoxicillin and over-the-counter remedies. In May and September 2020, persistent symptoms prompted courses of doxycycline and metronidazole (the latter empirically for Blastocystis hominis given her husband’s diagnosis), but she experienced no improvement. A stool test in February 2020 had shown no parasites.

Between May 2020 and March 2021, she continued to have recurrent cough, right-sided nasal blockage, right tonsillar swelling, upper-right quadrant chest pain, and episodic fevers and chills. Diarrhea and abdominal cramps persisted. She saw ENT in February 2021 and pulmonology in March 2021, and she tried various medications—including naproxen and N-acetylcysteine—without benefit.

Relevant investigations:
• Chest radiographs remained clear.  
• Sputum cultures (Sept 2020) were negative for bacteria.  
• Echocardiogram showed a minor pericardial effusion.  
• ECG transiently showed P-wave and subtle ST-segment changes that later normalized.  
• Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, ferritin) remained within normal limits.  
• Comprehensive panels for autoimmunity, paraneoplastic antibodies, allergies, HIV, toxoplasma, and toxocara were negative.  
• HbA1c, electrolytes, liver and renal function tests were unremarkable.
title: Can Nitazoxanide and/or other anti‐viral medications be a solution to long COVID? Case report with a brief literature review

case_prompt:
A 62‐year‐old man presented with persistent epigastric pain of 4–5 weeks’ duration. The pain began after he noticed a rash in the right hypochondriac area and was described as constant with episodic worsening; it neither improved with defecation nor was exacerbated by food intake.  
Initially, the symptoms were managed as herpes zoster with aciclovir and pregabalin, but the pain continued to intensify. Over the following weeks, he developed nausea, lethargy, decreased appetite, constipation, reduced urinary‐stream force and caliber, and a 5–7 kg weight loss.  
A contrast CT scan of the abdomen revealed small gallbladder stones; biliary colic was considered, but surgery was deferred. His medical history included migraines, health‐anxiety–related cognitive therapy, and daily esomeprazole for reflux esophagitis. Family history was noncontributory.  
On examination, he was hemodynamically stable (BP 132/89 mmHg; HR 89/min; T 36.9°C; RR 10/min; O2 saturation 98%), but appeared unwell. Abdominal palpation elicited epigastric tenderness; no neurological deficits were noted.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, CRP, liver enzymes, amylase, bilirubin, and PSA, were all within normal limits. Gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and a repeat CT abdomen were unremarkable. No critical somatic disease was identified, and the patient suggested a functional etiology for his symptoms. He was discharged.  
One week later, he was readmitted with unchanged symptoms after his general practitioner doubted a purely anxiety‐driven cause. He reported living in a tick‐endemic area and recalled several tick bites in the past, though none recently.
title: Autonomous dysfunction in Lyme neuroborreliosis. A case report

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old man of low socioeconomic status was referred from the ENT department for evaluation of a recurring pustule at the base of his right nostril that healed spontaneously over approximately 15 days only to recur. He had been treated for the past 6 months by a private practitioner with systemic antibiotics and intralesional steroids without improvement. He is a chronic heavy smoker (≥20 cigarettes per day for 15 years). He recalled trauma to his upper front teeth in his late 20s but denied any dental pain or swelling.

On extraoral examination, there was a pustular opening inferior to the right nostril. Intraoral examination revealed a discolored, attrited, noncarious right maxillary central incisor with prominent enamel cracks and generalized attrition; oral hygiene was poor. Pulp-vitality testing of the right maxillary central incisor with heated gutta-percha was negative. An intraoral periapical radiograph demonstrated a distinct periapical radiolucency and compromised periodontal status associated with the same tooth.
