title: Nasal Sinus Tract of Odontogenic Origin: Report of a Case

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old woman presented with diffuse bone pain involving both shoulders and multiple ribs. She had a history of bilateral lung transplantation for emphysema six years earlier; her post-transplant course was complicated by severe Scedosporium apiospermum sepsis, and she has since been on chronic oral voriconazole prophylaxis. On examination, strength was slightly reduced in both upper extremities, range of motion in both shoulders was full but painful, and there was diffuse tenderness over both shoulders and several left-sided ribs. 

Laboratory evaluation revealed an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase level of 220 U/L (reference range, 30–130 U/L). 

Radiographs of the chest and shoulders showed new areas of sclerosis and juxtacortical mineralization at the left proximal humerus and clavicle compared with prior post-transplant imaging. A subsequent whole-body radionuclide bone scan demonstrated multifocal radiotracer uptake confined to the periosteum of both clavicles, both humeral heads (more pronounced on the left), the left scapula, and the left third through fifth ribs. SPECT CT confirmed periosteal new bone formation at these sites.
title: Voriconazole-induced periostitis post lung transplantation

case_prompt:
A woman in her mid-30s presented with a 2-year history of recurrent pain and swelling in the left proximal leg. She had undergone resection of a biopsy-proven chondromyxoid fibroma of the left proximal tibia 4 years earlier and was asymptomatic for 2 years postoperatively. The current swelling had a rapid onset and was accompanied by pain.

On examination, there was a 20 × 15 cm globular, hard, tender mass over the proximal tibia, adherent to bone. The previous surgical scar was healthy, and distal neurovascular examination was intact.

Plain radiographs of the left tibia showed a lytic, eccentric, expansile meta-diaphyseal lesion with cortical breach and a sunburst periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a T2 hyperintense, lytic, expansile lesion with chondroid matrix and periosteal elevation, with focal invasion of the tibialis anterior and posterior muscles and the medial gastrocnemius head. PET-CT demonstrated a metabolically active lesion in the proximal tibial shaft and subcentimetric left popliteal lymph nodes.

Core-needle biopsy of the lesion showed abundant cartilaginous matrix with chondrocytes in lacunae, moderate nuclear atypia, coarse hyperchromatic nuclei, mitoses, myxoid change, and areas of necrosis.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Chondrosarcoma proximal tibia secondary to chondromyxoid fibroma: A rare case report

case_prompt: A 72-year-old obese woman with hypertension and a history of ischemic stroke presented with progressive dyspnea over 2 years. Her heart rate was 55 beats/min and blood pressure was controlled. There was no jugular venous distention or parasternal lift. Auscultation revealed a 2+/6 midsystolic murmur at the mitral area. Pulmonary and abdominal examinations were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed right-chamber enlargement, a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 58 mm Hg, and an interatrial septal aneurysm with a patent foramen ovale; the estimated pulmonary/systemic flow ratio (Qp/Qs) was 2.2. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography demonstrated a dilated main pulmonary artery trunk (43 mm) and excluded thromboembolic events as well as intrinsic lung disease. Other causes of pulmonary hypertension were excluded by specialist evaluation.
title: Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection in a 72-year-old woman: A case report

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old Caucasian woman was referred to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon for evaluation of a firm, painless lump in her left cheek that had progressively enlarged over 12 months. She reported no constitutional symptoms, had no significant past medical history, and was a non-smoker who drank alcohol only rarely.

On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm firm, well-circumscribed mass adjacent to the left mandibular body, anterior to the parotid gland and masseter, with no overlying cutaneous or mucosal changes and no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination was unremarkable. A dental examination and an orthopantomogram excluded an odontogenic origin.

The lesion was excised intraorally under general anesthesia. The gross specimen measured 30 × 23 × 20 mm and appeared as a tan, fibrofatty mass. Microscopically, skeletal muscle fibers were infiltrated by epithelioid tumor cells with abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and mildly pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei with inconspicuous nucleoli. Patchy pseudoacini and rosette formation were present, along with increased apoptosis and geographic necrosis. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion was identified.
title: Ewing sarcoma of the facial soft tissues—a case report

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman with severe, steroid-refractory asthma began monthly omalizumab injections after tapering chronic oral corticosteroids (>9 courses per year over 3 years). Six months after starting omalizumab, she developed an erythematous, intensely pruritic cutaneous eruption that worsened with each dose, prompting discontinuation of the drug.

Initial dermatology evaluation revealed violaceous erythema in a photo-exposed distribution. A skin biopsy showed only non-specific features of dermatitis. Topical corticosteroids, gabapentin, and maximal‐dose antihistamines (diphenhydramine, cetirizine, hydroxyzine) failed to relieve the rash or pruritus.

At an 8-month follow-up, examination demonstrated erythematous papules over the dorsal metacarpophalangeal joints, violaceous erythema of the face and upper eyelids, photo-distributed poikiloderma on the neck and shoulders, scattered telangiectasias, cuticular hypertrophy with peri-ungual erythema, and symmetrical proximal muscle weakness (Medical Research Council grade 4+/5 at deltoids and hips).

Repeat skin biopsy revealed interface dermatitis with focal thickening of the basement membrane, dermal lymphocytic infiltration, and increased dermal mucin. Laboratory studies showed an antinuclear antibody titer >1:640 (speckled pattern); negative extractable nuclear antigen panel (including anti–Ro/SSA, anti–Jo-1, anti–Scl-70); undetectable anti-histone antibodies; no eosinophilia; and normal levels of creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and C-reactive protein.
journal: Allergy, Asthma, and Clinical Immunology : Official Journal of the Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
title: Dermatomyositis associated with omalizumab therapy for severe asthma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old woman with an uneventful pregnancy was referred after failure to progress in the second stage of labor for 4 hours. Her medical and family history were unremarkable, with no known genetic disorders. Vital signs were within normal limits. Obstetric examination revealed a full-term uterus, longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation in occipitoposterior position, head fully engaged, fetal distress, and complete cervical dilation. An emergency cesarean section was performed, and a healthy 3.0-kg infant was delivered with Apgar scores of 8 and 9.

During the operation, a right ovarian mass was found incidentally. A right oophorectomy was performed. On gross examination, the mass was encapsulated, ovoid, gray-brown, and firm, measuring 11.9 × 7.0 × 3.8 cm. The cut surface was heterogeneous, fibrous, and yellow-tan in appearance, without cystic changes.
title: Incidental Primary Angiomyolipoma of Ovary: A Rare Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 64‐year‐old male cattle farmer presented with an asymptomatic left‐sided neck swelling of 2 years’ duration, static over the past year. He denied voice changes, dysphagia, dyspnea, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Examination revealed a well‐defined, non‐tender nodular mass measuring 7 cm × 4 cm on the anterior left neck; it moved with swallowing but not with tongue protrusion, and the overlying skin was intact.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal thyroid function tests, normal renal function, an ESR of 11 mm/h, and a CRP of 0.25 mg/dL. Serologic testing by ELISA was positive for Echinococcus granulosus. Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated a large multiloculated heterogeneous anechoic lesion measuring 8.1 cm × 4 cm × 5 cm in the left thyroid lobe (TI-RADS 3); the right lobe and cervical lymph nodes appeared normal. CT scan confirmed that the lesion was confined to the thyroid gland. Ultrasound‐guided fine‐needle aspiration yielded 18 mL of clear, watery fluid, which was sent for cytologic evaluation.
title: Hydatid Cyst of Thyroid Gland: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old woman with hypertension presented with 30 minutes of severe, pressure-like substernal chest pain radiating to her left arm and jaw at rest, accompanied by nausea and acute dyspnea. She denied prior episodes, exertional dyspnea, trauma, new medications, sick contacts, or recent travel. Medical history included hypertension, generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, severe osteoarthritis, and an atypical polymyalgia rheumatica treated with a 6-month steroid taper. Family history was notable for a father who died suddenly from dilated cardiomyopathy. Home medications were buspirone, duloxetine, hydrochlorothiazide, valsartan, and meloxicam as needed.

On examination, she was normothermic, tachycardic (112 bpm), hypotensive (88/55 mmHg), and hypoxemic (SpO2 88% on 5 L nasal cannula). She was diaphoretic, in acute distress, with jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, a normal S1, diminished S2, and a holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Extremities were well perfused, with 1+ lower-extremity edema.

Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with diffuse ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6, and ST elevation in aVR. Initial labs revealed a lactate of 1.7 mg/dL and a troponin of 1.33 ng/dL. She received aspirin, ticagrelor, and a heparin infusion and was taken emergently for cardiac catheterization.

Coronary angiography demonstrated less than 30% obstruction in all vessels. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure was elevated at 31 mmHg, and ventriculography showed severe (4+) mitral regurgitation with a dilated left atrium. In the cath lab, transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65%, severe mitral regurgitation, a flail posterior mitral valve leaflet, and a flail head of the posterior papillary muscle. An intra-aortic balloon pump was placed, and she was intubated for severe hypoxemic respiratory failure. She was admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit, diuresed, and hemodynamically supported, with plans for surgical intervention on hospital day 3.
title: Idiopathic posterior papillary muscle rupture; a case report

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man with a 30–pack-year smoking history was admitted for refractory hypoglycemia attributed to a suspected insulinoma. His complete blood count showed a white blood cell count of 9.9 × 10^3/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 0.1 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, and platelets 442 × 10^3/µL. A metabolic panel revealed mild hyponatremia and a glucose level of 34 mg/dL; liver function tests were normal. Hormonal studies demonstrated an insulin level of 133 mIU/mL, proinsulin 46.5 pmol/L, C-peptide 9.3 ng/mL, and a random cortisol of 129.1 µg/dL. Vital signs were normal, and he was afebrile.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple pulmonary nodules, the largest measuring 1.4 × 1.2 cm in the left lung. Serologic testing for histoplasma, aspergillus, coccidioides, and blastomyces by immunodiffusion and complement fixation was negative. An interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was also negative. CT-guided core needle biopsy of the largest nodule revealed a necrotic granuloma on microscopy. Fungal and mycobacterial cultures of the biopsy specimen remained negative at 4 and 6 weeks, respectively. No sputum cultures were obtained. The patient had no fevers during hospitalization.

Further social history revealed ownership of three dogs, one of which had fatigue, weight loss, and hair loss; the patient was uncertain whether his dogs had received heartworm preventative treatment. He denied any travel history.
title: Man's best friend: How humans can develop Dirofilaria immitis infections

case_prompt: A 46-year-old woman presented with 1–2 months of persistent lower abdominal pain. On examination, a right lower abdominal mass approximating a 16-week gestation size was palpated. Serum levels of β-hCG, LDH, α-fetoprotein, CA-125, and CEA were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined, multilobulated 5.8×6.3×5.7 cm lesion in the pelvic cavity, separate from the uterus and ovaries. The mass was heterogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2/STIR sequences, with multiple T2-hypointense septae and cystic spaces. Mild diffusion restriction was noted in the solid component (ADC, 1.3×10⁻³ mm²/s). On dynamic contrast-enhanced study, the lesion demonstrated avid progressive enhancement with delayed washout. There was no abnormal enhancement or thickening of the adjacent peritoneum.
title: Solitary fibrous tumor of the Pelvic cavity: A rare entity with review of literature

case_prompt: A 71-year-old man was referred for evaluation of painless jaundice and pruritus without weight loss. Two months earlier his liver tests were normal. On presentation he was alert, without encephalopathy, and had normal coagulation studies. Laboratory results showed a total bilirubin of 5.8 mg/dL (direct 4.3 mg/dL), alanine aminotransferase 51 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 47 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 264 U/L. Abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated an 11-mm low-density lesion in the pancreatic body and no dilation of the biliary or pancreatic ducts. On further questioning, he reported a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate for a sinus infection about 3 weeks before the onset of jaundice. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed normal-caliber common bile and pancreatic ducts without stones or sludge, and the pancreatic lesion corresponded to a side-branch intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm not causing obstruction.
title: Cystic Mass on Computed Tomography With Acute Onset Painless Jaundice

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of intermittent tingling on the right side of her face without pain. There was no history of trauma, headache, fever, or other neurologic symptoms. Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were normal, and there were no motor deficits, cranial-nerve abnormalities, or signs of increased intracranial pressure. Given the focal sensory complaint and lack of systemic findings, intracranial pathology was suspected.  
Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined extra-axial cystic lesion in the right cerebellopontine angle extending into the ambient cistern. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was hypointense; on T2-weighted images, it was hyperintense. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences showed a “dirty” hyperintense signal within the lesion. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated marked diffusion restriction, and susceptibility-weighted imaging showed no evidence of blooming. The lesion caused mass effect on the right side of the pons and displaced the right trigeminal nerve.
title: Cerebellopontine angle epidermoid cyst masquerading as trigeminal neuralgia: A rare presentation and surgical outcome

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old homosexual man was referred to the colorectal clinic with a 2-week history of perianal pain, peri-anal skin changes, altered bowel habit with diarrhea and fecal incontinence, and occasional fresh blood on toilet paper. He also reported loss of appetite but no weight loss. His past medical history was unremarkable, and he took no medications.

On examination, there was a 3 × 1 cm ulcerated lesion at the 12 o’clock position in the perianal region and a firm nodule at the 9 o’clock position. A colonoscopy to the terminal ileum was normal. Abdominal CT scan revealed only a simple liver cyst; pelvic MRI confirmed an anal nodule without clear distal extent.

An initial biopsy under local anesthesia showed ulcerated, plasma cell–rich inflammation without a definitive mass effect, raising suspicion for a syphilitic lesion. After multidisciplinary discussion, a repeat biopsy demonstrated reactive epithelial changes with ulceration, fibrin deposition, acanthosis, prominent intraepithelial neutrophils, and a dense dermal plasmacytic infiltrate. There was no evidence of granulomas, fungal hyphae, herpetic viral inclusions, or definitive obliterative endarteritis, but the marked plasma cell infiltrate suggested syphilis as a likely possibility.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A case of syphilitic anal condylomata lata mimicking malignancy

case_prompt: A 23-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of left great-toe pain that prevented him from wearing shoes. Two years earlier, he had undergone nail‐bed excision for an ingrown toenail by a general surgeon; since then he had nightly throbbing pain relieved by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. He had also taken an unidentified antibiotic and etodolac 500 mg twice daily. On examination, the left great toe was noticeably enlarged compared with the right, and was warm and tender to palpation. His medical and family history were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and leukocyte count. Plain radiographs demonstrated a lytic bone lesion with a sclerotic rim in the medial part of the distal phalanx. Magnetic resonance imaging showed bone marrow and soft tissue edema in the distal phalanx, compatible with osteomyelitis. A 99mTc bone scan revealed increased uptake in the left great toe.
title: Osteoid Osteoma of the Great Toe Mimicking Osteomyelitis: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 14-month-old spayed female Ragdoll cat, kept strictly indoors and adopted online a year earlier, was evaluated for a 12-month history of pruritus. Within days of acquisition, the owner noted generalized scratching, alopecia of the tail and face, and dark cerumen in both ears. A primary veterinarian diagnosed otodectic mange and administered a single 45 mg spot-on selamectin treatment, leading to resolution of ear mites and skin lesions and marked but incomplete relief of pruritus. Over the following months, the cat continued to scratch at a low intensity and had intermittent vomiting and diarrhea. At 13 months of age, the owner observed a flare of pruritus shortly after rabies vaccination. The veterinarian prescribed an exclusion diet with hypoallergenic food and two doses of dexamethasone given 3 days apart. After 1 month, only slight improvement was noted, and the cat was referred for further evaluation. On examination, there was self-induced alopecia and papulosquamous lesions on the abdomen, as well as gingivitis. Skin scrapings and Scotch-tape tests were negative. However, stereomicroscopic examination of a coat brushing sample revealed several mites.
title: First case report of dermatitis associated with Leporacarus gibbus in cat

case_prompt: A 2.5-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department with a one-day history of high fever and frequent vomiting followed by decreased level of consciousness. He had two similar episodes at ages 10 and 21 months, previously treated as febrile seizure and meningitis. Born to consanguineous parents, he had normal growth and development and no family history of liver disease. On examination, his temperature was 38.8°C, pulse 125 bpm, and he was drowsy (modified Glasgow Coma Scale score 6) with flexor posturing to pain; there was mild hepatomegaly without splenomegaly. Initial laboratory tests showed hypoglycemia (16 mg/dL), which corrected with glucose; a serum ammonia level of 650 µg/dL; elevated transaminases (ALT 429 U/L, AST 65 U/L); hypoalbuminemia (2.8 g/dL); and coagulopathy (PT 20.7 s, INR 1.65). Metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap resolved with hydration. CSF analysis and cultures of blood, CSF, and urine were normal. Brain CT demonstrated bilateral symmetric low focal attenuation in the thalami and focal lesions in posterior parietal and occipital white matter. EEG showed no seizure activity. Initial differential diagnoses included genetic metabolic disorders, acute necrotizing encephalopathy of childhood, and Reye’s syndrome.
title: Acute infantile liver failure syndrome type 2 in a 2.5‐year‐old boy: A case report

case_prompt: A 59-year-old man with end-stage renal disease due to nephrosclerosis and a prior kidney transplant that failed after 10 years (chronic vascular rejection) was evaluated for a second living unrelated kidney transplant. His medical history included hypertension, coronary artery disease, deep venous thrombosis, a reversible ischemic neurologic deficit, and a central venous thrombosis of the right eye; he was maintained on phenprocoumon. Pretransplant testing revealed a panel-reactive antibody level of 34%, a negative T-cell crossmatch, and a positive B-cell crossmatch. He underwent induction with basiliximab and maintenance immunosuppression with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. The donor was a 53-year-old woman with normal renal anatomy and a calculated creatinine clearance of 80 mL/min. The left kidney (47% function) was procured uneventfully. After 143 minutes of cold ischemia, the graft was anastomosed to the left iliac vessels and urinary tract reconstruction was performed. Immediately after reperfusion, the kidney had normal turgor and produced urine at 150 mL/hour for the first three hours. Thereafter, urine output abruptly declined without hemodynamic instability. Duplex ultrasonography showed normal arterial and venous flow but signs of acute renal failure. Differential diagnosis included acute humoral rejection, acute tubular necrosis, and a thromboembolic event. During relaparotomy the graft appeared edematous, flaccid, and cyanotic, and it was removed.
title: Hyperacute Rejection of a Living Unrelated Kidney Graft

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a painless, slowly enlarging swelling in the anterior maxillary region. He denied trauma or pain, and his medical history was unremarkable.  
Extraoral examination showed diffuse swelling over the anterior maxilla, extending from the tip of the nose laterally toward the left ala and from just below the left inner canthus to the superior border of the upper lip. There was mild deviation of the nasal tip to the right and effacement of the left nasolabial fold. The swelling was firm and nontender.  
Intraorally, there was a well-circumscribed vestibular swelling measuring approximately 3.5 cm × 3 cm, extending from the right central incisor region to the distal line angle of the left canine, obliterating the labial mucobuccal fold. The overlying mucosa was intact, and the swelling was firm at its periphery but yielded centrally to pressure.  
All maxillary anterior teeth were vital on testing. A provisional diagnosis of nasolabial cyst was made.  
A maxillary occlusal radiograph revealed a well-defined, corticated, unilocular radiolucency extending mediolaterally from the right to the left central incisor region and anteroposteriorly from the apices of the incisors into the palate. An inverted impacted supernumerary tooth (mesiodens) was seen, with the radiolucency circumscribing its cemento-enamel junction. There was slight root resorption of the central incisors.  
Fine-needle aspiration yielded blood-tinged cystic fluid, and microscopy demonstrated cholesterol crystals.
journal: International Journal of Applied and Basic Medical Research
title: Dentigerous cyst in association with impacted inverted mesiodens: Report of a rare case with a brief review of literature

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman with a history of asthma since childhood and recurrent fever, arthralgia, and fatigue over the past two years presented with worsening chest pain of several weeks’ duration. Twelve months earlier, she had been diagnosed with idiopathic pericarditis associated with eosinophilia and treated with NSAIDs, with rapid symptom remission. Two weeks before admission she experienced angioedema, painful subcutaneous nodules of the arms and legs, and numbness and paresthesia of her toes and hands. 

On presentation, the chest pain was pleuritic and improved by sitting up and leaning forward. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac examination revealed a holosystolic regurgitant murmur at the apex; there were no skin rashes or focal neurologic deficits. ECG showed diffuse T-wave flattening in the inferior, lateral, and precordial leads. Laboratory studies demonstrated C-reactive protein 101 mg/L (normal <16 mg/L), eosinophils 2.14 × 10^9/L (normal <0.5 × 10^9/L), high-sensitivity troponin T 193 ng/L (normal <52 ng/L), and NT-proBNP 1153 ng/L (normal <300 ng/L). 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF 47%), severe mitral regurgitation due to posterior leaflet prolapse, and a small pericardial effusion without tamponade. Coronary angiography showed no obstructive lesions. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an LVEF of 47% with left ventricular dilatation, absence of late gadolinium enhancement, and normal T1 and T2 mapping values.
title: Eosinophilic perimyocarditis associated with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old man presented with metamorphopsia and decreased vision in his right eye. Four years earlier, he had noted these symptoms and, at that time, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20. Fundus examination showed a whitish lesion in the macula, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed serous retinal detachment (SRD) accompanied by a fibrin-like deposit. He was diagnosed with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC). Five months later, BCVA declined to 16/20, and OCT demonstrated recurrent SRD and macular edema. Laboratory studies did not suggest infectious or noninfectious inflammation. Solitary idiopathic choroiditis (SIC) was suspected, and oral prednisolone was given for over 2 months without change. 

On referral, slit-lamp examination and intraocular pressure were normal. Funduscopy showed a subretinal yellowish-white lesion, approximately 1.0-mm disc diameter, located between the fovea and optic disc. OCT disclosed SRD and intraretinal fluid extending to the foveal center, a dome-like elevation of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) corresponding to the lesion, and shallow RPE detachment. Beneath the RPE, a horizontal lamellar-like structure was seen within the choroid. Bruch’s membrane and the sclera–choroidal junction were intact around the lesion, and the choriocapillaris and part of the choroidal vessels were not visible within it. 

Fluorescein angiography showed late-phase staining of the plaque, and indocyanine green angiography revealed early hypofluorescence and late hyperfluorescence. B-scan ultrasonography through the eyelid suggested a thin hypoechoic shadow but was not diagnostic.
title: Small Symptomatic Unilateral Choroidal Osteoma Diagnosed with Enhanced-Depth Imaging Optical Coherence Tomography and Thin-Slice Computed Tomography: 2 Clinical Cases

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 7-month history of a gradually enlarging, non-tender, firm, mobile mass in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. There were no skin changes or palpable ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes. Routine laboratory tests were normal.

Mammography (craniocaudal, mediolateral oblique, and spot compression views) revealed an oval, circumscribed, isodense mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, measuring 3.5 × 2.5 × 3 cm (BI-RADS 4a), without suspicious calcifications.

Breast ultrasound showed an oval, circumscribed, complex solid-and-cystic heterogeneous mass at 2 o’clock in the left breast with posterior acoustic enhancement. The lesion contained floating curvilinear structures (“serpent sign”).

A complementary liver ultrasound demonstrated multiple, variably sized, anechoic lesions throughout the liver, suggestive of cysts. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen confirmed multiple nonenhancing, fluid-density liver cysts; the lungs were clear.
title: The “serpent sign”—A classical sign in a nonclassical location: A case report of breast hydatid cyst

case_prompt: A 5-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of high-grade fever, lethargy, headache, and vomiting. One month earlier, she had been treated elsewhere for presumed bacterial meningitis with vancomycin and ceftriaxone for 14 days. She had no history of head trauma. On admission, temperature was 38.6 °C, heart rate 144 beats/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 110/69 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Physical examination revealed severe neck stiffness and a patchy red discoloration with a small skin dimple at the midline of the occiput. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein of 140 mg/L (normal <5), leukocytosis (21 × 10^3 cells/mm^3) with 90% neutrophils. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 1920 white blood cells/mm^3 (88% neutrophils), 60 red blood cells/mm^3, glucose 11 mg/dL (normal 40–80), and protein 9.9 mg/dL (normal 10–60); CSF cultures and PCR assays for common bacteria and viruses were negative. Empirical therapy with cefepime and vancomycin was started. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a 21 × 13 mm oval hypodense collection with peripheral rim enhancement between the cerebellar hemispheres. Three-dimensional volume rendering demonstrated smooth, well-corticated funneling of the inner table of the occipital bone and a 1 mm midline defect in the outer table. Brain MRI with contrast revealed that the inter-cerebellar collection had restricted diffusion, heterogeneous T2 signal, and peripheral enhancement, and it communicated through the bone defect with a subcutaneous nodular lesion of low T2 signal intensity and homogeneous enhancement. There were additional signs of ventriculitis and early cerebellitis. Based on MR images, the differential diagnosis included an epidural abscess or an infected dermoid cyst.
title: Intradural dermoid cyst with complete dermal sinus of the posterior fossa: Contribution of 3D imaging with histopathological correlation☆

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a motor-vehicle accident. He sustained midshaft fractures of the right radius and ulna with a puncture wound over the proximal dorsal forearm. On initial examination, he had limited active flexion and extension of all four fingers, but finger abduction was intact. Thumb motion and sensation in the median and ulnar nerve distributions were normal. The forearm compartments were soft.

On day 1 after injury, he underwent open reduction and internal fixation of the radius via a volar (Henry) approach and of the ulna via a direct ulnar approach. Intraoperatively, the flexor digitorum superficialis muscle belly was noted to be impaled by a proximal radial fragment.

On postoperative day 3, he was noted to have a drop of the medial three fingers and radial deviation of the wrist. The tests for median and ulnar nerve function remained normal. Passive tenodesis testing was unreliable, and a partial PIN neuropraxia was diagnosed. He was managed with a splint and mobilization exercises; nerve conduction studies, electromyography, and ultrasound were planned.
final_diagnosis_raw: Recurrent branch posterior interosseous nerve palsy
title: Medial three-finger drop in high-energy forearm trauma: An unrecognized peripheral nerve injury. A report of two cases

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman was admitted for a 1-month history of daily episodes of dizziness, fatigue, cold sweats, tremors, changes in behavior, anxiety, and occasional seizures or altered consciousness. During a recent psychiatric hospitalization, a random capillary glucose measurement was 19 mg/dL. She denied alcohol use and any use of insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no diabetes, endocrine syndromes, or significant illnesses. Her body-mass index was 25.6 kg/m2, with abdominal obesity; the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.

On admission, she had repeated hypoglycemic episodes (plasma glucose < 55 mg/dL) not related to food intake, accompanied by confusion, dizziness, cold sweats, and tremor. Episodes were refractory to oral carbohydrates and required intravenous boluses of 33% glucose and continuous infusion of 10% glucose. Two incidental plasma glucose readings off infusion were ≥ 200 mg/dL (fasting 209 mg/dL, postprandial 227 mg/dL). During a hypoglycemic episode, laboratory values were: plasma glucose 44 mg/dL, serum insulin 16.3 µU/mL (2.2–24.9), C-peptide 3.72 ng/mL (1.1–4.4), HbA1c 4.99%, negative urinary ketones, and anti-insulin antibodies < 0.03 U/mL (< 0.4). Seven-month prior HbA1c was 5.1%. 

Further evaluation excluded adrenal insufficiency (normal 8 a.m. ACTH and cortisol), thyroid dysfunction (normal TSH, FT4, FT3), organ failure (normal renal and hepatic function), and sepsis (normal blood counts and inflammatory markers). Ophthalmoscopy, abdominal ultrasound, cranial CT, and chest CT were normal. Given the biochemical evidence of endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, cross-sectional abdominal imaging was performed.

Abdominal CT showed in the anterior part of the pancreatic body–tail a 15.3 × 15 mm isodense rounded lesion with intense enhancement in the arterial phase that persisted in the venous phase. Complementary MRI demonstrated a hypervascular pancreatic lesion, hypointense to isointense on T1, slightly hyperintense on T2, homogeneous post-contrast enhancement, and diffusion restriction.
title: Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors—Diagnostic Pitfalls of Non-Diabetic Severe Hypoglycemia: Literature Review and Case Report

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of progressive lethargy, easy bruising, and slow-healing lower limb lesions. Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia and coagulopathy. Peripheral blood film revealed numerous blasts with reniform nuclei and Auer rods. Interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization detected a PML/RARα fusion consistent with t(15;17). She was started on the APML4 induction protocol with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA; 45 mg/m²), idarubicin (12 mg/m² on days 2, 4, 6, and 8), and arsenic trioxide (0.15 mg/kg from day 9), along with prophylactic prednisolone (1 mg/kg on days 1–10).

On day 11 she became febrile, hypotensive, and reported a mild headache; she was treated empirically with piperacillin–tazobactam and vancomycin for febrile neutropenia. By day 14 she remained hypotensive and tachycardic, developed acute renal impairment, peripheral edema, and weight gain, and complained of decreased vision—worse in the right eye.

Ophthalmic examination showed visual acuities of 6/36 in the right eye and 6/18 in the left, with intraocular pressures of 36 mmHg and 27 mmHg, respectively. Gonioscopy revealed bilaterally shallow anterior chambers with closed angles, for which she underwent bilateral peripheral iridotomies and was started on topical pilocarpine and intraocular-pressure-lowering agents. Funduscopic examination demonstrated bilateral, multifocal pale yellow chorioretinal lesions at the posterior poles with superficial retinal hemorrhages. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed multifocal sub–retinal fluid with focal retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) elevations adherent to the overlying thickened neurosensory retina. Enhanced-depth OCT showed marked choroidal thickening with multiple small nodular RPE elevations. Fluorescein angiography disclosed multiple areas of early hyperfluorescence corresponding to the yellow lesions, with late leakage of fluid into the sub–retinal space.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Two cases of differentiation syndrome with ocular manifestations in patients with acute promyelocytic leukaemia treated with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old Middle-Eastern male adolescent was brought to the child and adolescent psychiatric emergency department by his mother and stepfather because of mutism, bizarre postures, salivary drooling, urine and fecal incontinence, and asymmetric convulsions of his arms and legs. He had been living in Sweden with his mother, stepfather, and younger brother since age 12, following his parents’ divorce. He had no family history of psychiatric disease and normal psychomotor development. 

He began using illicit drugs before age 13; over the past 4 years he had smoked cannabis daily (up to 3 g per day) and over the past 2 years had used tramadol (200–1000 mg daily). He had also tried LSD, cocaine, hallucinogenic mushrooms, ecstasy, inhalants, and various analgesics. Three weeks before presentation, he entered a youth programme for a conviction and abstained from cannabis and tramadol, but still tested positive for THC five days before admission.

On examination he was mute, unresponsive to questions, and displayed a depressed mood. A urine toxicology screen on admission was negative for THC and other illicit substances. Physical examination showed motor immobility with bizarre postures, asymmetric convulsions, and incontinence. Vital signs were within normal limits (blood pressure 130/60 mmHg; heart rate 80 bpm). Results of blood tests, a brain MRI, and an EEG were all normal. A pediatric neurological consultation found no signs of a primary neurological disorder.

Possible differential diagnoses included substance‐induced psychosis, depressive stupor, catatonic schizophrenia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS).
title: Atypical course in severe catatonic schizophrenia in a cannabis-dependent male adolescent: a case report

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of left knee pain that worsened after a Judo competition. He had no prior trauma, no relevant family or medical history. On examination, there was slight atrophy of the left thigh (42 cm versus 45 cm on the right) but no tenderness, swelling, warmth, redness, or limitation of motion.  
Plain radiographs of the knee showed a 1.7 × 2.4 cm soap bubble–like radiolucent area in the medial patella without periosteal reaction.  
MRI revealed a lesion in the patella that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed diffuse enhancement after gadolinium; the lesion was multicystic with fluid–fluid levels and no obvious invasion into adjacent muscle or joint.
title: Secondary Aneurysmal Bone Cyst Following Chondroblastoma of the Patella

case_prompt:
A 1½-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of progressive swelling over the right wrist and three discharging sinuses on the dorsal, volar, and ulnar aspects. Initial swelling developed after removal of a sacred thread from the wrist; one month later, purulent volar discharge prompted local debridement and a 1-month course of IV cefpodoxime, followed by IV linezolid for inadequate response. Two additional sinuses then appeared, and he was referred for persistent discharge.

On examination, he appeared well. There was a partially healed, indurated circumferential scar at the wrist with three subcentimetric sinuses exuding minimal seropurulent fluid and exuberant granulation tissue. The hand was swollen and erythematous. He demonstrated active finger movements but had a pointing index, suggesting median nerve palsy. Capillary refill was brisk.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 9500/mm3, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 32 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein level of 5.2 mg/L. Plain radiographs of the wrist were unremarkable. MRI of the wrist revealed diffuse synovial thickening and effusion in the intercarpal and wrist joints, bony erosions in these areas, and a circular, thin foreign body in the proximal wrist joint with three fistulous tracts extending to the skin.
title: Forgotten Foreign Bodies Mimicking Osteomyelitis, a Diagnostic Dilemma – A Report of Two Cases

case_prompt:
A 4-day-old female infant, born at 39 weeks’ gestation via uncomplicated vaginal delivery to a healthy 25-year-old mother, presented to the emergency department with a painful skin lesion on her back. Pregnancy and delivery had been uneventful; the infant’s birth weight was 3150 g, APGAR scores 9 and 10, and she was discharged on day 2 of life. On day 4, parents noted an extensive flat, firm, erythematous area with heat and edema on the back and left shoulder. There was no fever, feeding difficulties, irritability, or history of trauma. The infant was clinically well otherwise.

Laboratory studies on day 4 showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, leukocytes 6.8 × 10^3/uL (67% neutrophils), platelets 316 × 10^3/uL, C-reactive protein 5.58 mg/dL, and procalcitonin 1.41 ng/mL. She was admitted with a presumptive diagnosis of cellulitis and started on intravenous flucloxacillin and gentamicin.

Between days 5 and 6, the skin lesions progressed to the upper limbs, thighs, and abdomen and changed in color from erythematous to purplish plaques; irritability increased, and antibiotics were escalated to gentamicin, ampicillin, and cefotaxime. On day 7, multiple erythematous subcutaneous nodules appeared on the back, upper limbs, and thighs, and a serum calcium level of 14.7 mg/dL was detected. The infant was transferred to the neonatal ICU and started on intravenous fluids, oral furosemide, and prednisolone.
final_diagnosis_raw: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn
title: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn – An atypical case with typical complications

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old man presented with persistent chest pain during exercise and at rest, along with worsening dyspnea. He had a 12–pack-year smoking history but no other cardiovascular risk factors. One month earlier, he had been evaluated for weakness and dry cough and diagnosed with a viral respiratory infection.  
On admission, blood pressure was 150/103 mm Hg, heart rate 60 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The baseline ECG showed up to 1 mm of J-point elevation in leads V3 to V5 with peaked T waves, findings that were unchanged from ECGs obtained during his earlier viral illness. Repeat ECGs remained unchanged, and blood pressure normalized.  
Laboratory tests revealed a negative D-dimer result, normal inflammatory markers, and a negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR. Cardiac biomarkers were elevated: creatine kinase 219 U/L, high-sensitivity troponin T 101 ng/L rising to 350 ng/L over 24 hours, and N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide 182 ng/L.  
Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular function, no wall motion abnormalities (including the septum), and no relevant pericardial effusion.  
Coronary computed tomography angiography demonstrated no significant coronary artery disease of the main coronary arteries.
title: Spontaneous Dissection of a Septal Coronary Artery Mimicking Myocarditis

case_prompt: A 46-year-old Caucasian man presented with a several-month history of right proximal thigh pain. He had no significant past medical or family history. Physical examination revealed no neurological deficits. Radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging of the right femur showed a 10 cm permeative, lytic lesion in the proximal femur with cortical destruction and an adjacent soft-tissue mass. Whole-body staging with chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT scans showed no evidence of metastatic disease or a second primary tumor. Core-needle biopsy revealed a malignant fascicular spindle-cell proliferation. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated tumor cells positive for α-smooth-muscle actin, desmin, and caldesmon, and negative for cytokeratin and S-100.
title: Leiomyosarcoma of Bone: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old man with no significant medical or surgical history and a BMI of 29 presented with a first episode of sudden-onset, severe, noncolicky abdominal pain localized to the right iliac fossa and extending into the right upper quadrant. He remained hungry and denied any nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or other gastrointestinal symptoms. His temperature was 37.0 °C and other vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, he was tender over the right side of the abdomen without signs of generalized peritonism; Murphy’s sign was positive. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Urinalysis was normal. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 10.9 × 10^9/L and a C-reactive protein concentration of 98 mg/L; all other blood tests were normal.  
An abdominal ultrasound revealed a thin-walled gallbladder without gallstones, a normal common bile duct caliber, and a trace of free fluid in the right iliac fossa; the appendix could not be visualized. The following day, a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated fluid in the right iliac fossa and the rectovesical pouch; the appendix appeared normal, but there was soft-tissue stranding adjacent to the cecum and ascending colon extending to the tip of the liver.
title: Idiopathic omental infarction: One for conservative or surgical management?

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man with obesity presented to the emergency department with severe central abdominal pain radiating mildly to his back, accompanied by nausea and one episode of non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting. He denied fever, changes in bowel habits, or infectious symptoms. His past medical history was notable for hypertension, gout, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia, all managed with diet and lifestyle modifications; he took no medications. He drank minimally (three drinks in the past month) and had quit heavy alcohol use years earlier. He smoked for 15 pack-years but had switched to smokeless tobacco; he used marijuana only occasionally and denied other substances or supplements.

He reported following a 2000-calorie-a-day ketogenic diet for 3 weeks with “cheat days” on weekends during which he consumed a high-carbohydrate, unrestricted diet; after each cheat day, his abdominal symptoms recurred on the following Monday, with increasing severity. He had similar but milder episodes earlier in the diet; the current episode was the most severe and prompted his ED visit.

On examination, his blood pressure was 155/101 mmHg, heart rate 77 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and he was afebrile. He appeared in severe pain (10/10), was not jaundiced, and had moist mucous membranes. Cardiorespiratory examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed a non-tympanic abdomen with normal bowel sounds and no skin discoloration; he was exquisitely tender in the epigastrium without peritoneal signs, and had no right upper quadrant tenderness or Murphy’s sign.

Point-of-care ultrasound showed no abdominal free fluid, no gallstones, and no sonographic signs of cholecystitis. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 15.4 × 10^9/L, blood glucose 9.3 mmol/L, and lipase 2283 U/L; other values were within reference ranges. A comprehensive abdominal ultrasound demonstrated severe fatty infiltration of the liver, a normal gallbladder without gallstones, non-dilated bile ducts, patent portal and hepatic veins, and an ill-defined, heterogeneous pancreas without peripancreatic fluid or ductal abnormality.
title: Recurrent acute pancreatitis during a ketogenic diet—a case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 64-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of a scar-like lesion on the volar pulp of the left fifth digit. Over the past three months, the lesion enlarged rapidly, became occasionally painful, and darkened in color. He denied weight loss, anorexia, or fatigue. Physical examination revealed a healthy-appearing man with a 1 cm, mobile, nontender, darkish, round, firm mass on the distal volar surface of the left fifth digit. Vital signs were: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 162/98 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min. Laboratory studies showed a random blood sugar of 9 g/dL, hemoglobin 10 g/dL, a normal white-cell count with differential, body-mass index 28.6 kg/m2, and creatinine 24.1 mmol/L. An incisional biopsy of the lesion revealed infiltrating, hyperchromatic glandular structures with micropapillary formations within the dermis; the overlying skin was intact. These histomorphological features were highly suggestive of metastatic papillary adenocarcinoma, possibly originating from the breast, colon, or thyroid. A search for a primary tumor included thyroid-function tests and serum markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125), all within normal limits; esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound of the neck were unremarkable; and thoracoabdominal CT scan did not reveal a primary lesion.
title: Digital papillary adenocarcinoma: A case report

case_prompt: A 40-year-old woman presented with one month of progressive weakness in both lower limbs and two days of bladder and anal sphincter dysfunction. On examination, she had spastic paraparesis with motor strength 3/5 in both lower limbs, impaired sensation below the T4 dermatome, brisk tendon reflexes, and bilateral Babinski signs. MRI of the thoracic spine showed two well-defined round intramedullary cystic lesions at the T4 and T5 levels, which were homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with slight peripheral edema causing narrowing of the subarachnoid space at those levels. There were no other spinal or brain abnormalities. A diagnosis of intramedullary mass lesion was made.
title: Spinal Intramedullary Cysticercosis: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 3-month-old Chinese girl was referred for evaluation of a one-week history of diarrhoea followed by a single afebrile seizure. She had been previously healthy, born at term with unremarkable perinatal history, and had transitioned from exclusive breastfeeding to various cow’s-milk formulas because of recurrent loose stools and excessive flatulence. On examination, she was moderately dehydrated and tachycardic; her weight was 6.2 kg and length 61 cm. Abdominal exam revealed a ballotable right kidney. Initial laboratory studies showed sodium 117 mmol/L, chloride 90 mmol/L, potassium 9 mmol/L, and metabolic acidosis. She received IV normal saline bolus and controlled fluid correction, plus calcium resonium to lower the potassium; her electrolytes normalized over four days. Stool studies for rotavirus and reducing substances were negative. Cow’s-milk protein allergy was suspected; she was switched to extensively hydrolysed formula with resolution of diarrhoea. Neurologic exam and brain ultrasound were normal. Urine culture grew Enterobacter, and she completed a 7-day course of cefuroxime. Renal ultrasound showed a right duplex kidney with gross hydronephrosis and hydroureter, and a voiding cystourethrogram demonstrated grade 5 vesicoureteric reflux on the right side.
journal: Journal of the ASEAN Federation of Endocrine Societies
title: Transient Pseudohypoaldosteronism in an Infant: A Case Report*

case_prompt:
An 80-year-old man with terminal, poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the base of the tongue (cT2N2b), status post tracheostomy, gastrostomy, and arterial embolization of multiple branches of the bilateral external carotid arteries 2 weeks earlier for hemoptysis, presented with 3 days of left upper- and lower-extremity weakness. He denied sensory changes, headache, fever, or other neurologic symptoms. He took only acetaminophen. Vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in the left upper and lower extremities; NIH Stroke Scale score was 2. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. No blood cultures were obtained.

Noncontrast CT of the brain revealed a hypodense region at the right parietal vertex with a 15 mm focal circular lesion surrounded by edema, plus a smaller adjacent focus; there was no hemorrhage or acute infarct. CT angiography of the head and neck showed a newly developed large, eccentric, saccular aneurysm of the distal right common carotid artery with surrounding soft tissue asymmetry, gas, and bony displacement; these findings had enlarged since the embolization procedure two weeks prior. MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium demonstrated a 2 cm right parietal lesion with peripheral ring enhancement and avid central restricted diffusion, a medially adjacent 1 cm lesion, and an anterior subcentimeter lesion, all with extensive vasogenic edema. MRI of the neck confirmed an irregular aneurysm at the right carotid bulb with diffuse soft tissue enhancement.
title: Differential diagnosis of a ring-enhancing brain lesion in the setting of metastatic cancer and a mycotic aneurysm

case_prompt: A 70-year-old man with a long-standing history of complicated Crohn’s disease presented with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and constipation—symptoms similar to prior obstructions that had resolved with conservative management. His surgical history included bilateral iliac artery angioplasty with stent placement. Medications were loperamide, simethicone, and aspirin. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia and slight hypokalemia. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated focal mucosal thickening in the mid-descending colon and upstream colonic dilation with mild mucosal thickening. A colonic stricture and bowel obstruction were suspected, and he underwent exploratory laparotomy with lysis of adhesions, partial colectomy, and diverting loop ileostomy. At surgery, a stricture at the mid-descending colon was excised. Gross examination revealed an unusual mass-like lesion. Histologic examination of the specimen showed a fissuring ulcer typical for Crohn’s disease and a proliferation of spindle-to-stellate cells intermixed with mast cells, without appreciable mitotic figures. The cell proliferation extended from the subserosa into the muscularis propria and focally into the submucosa, protruding into the bowel lumen.
title: A Novel Cause of Bowel Obstruction in a Patient with Long-Standing Crohn's Disease

case_prompt:
A 33-year-old African American woman presented with sudden sharp, nonradiating peristernal chest pain of the morning onset, worsened by deep breathing and movement and partially relieved by sublingual nitroglycerin. She also reported progressive right foot pain for five days and bilateral hand pain for three days despite naproxen and propoxyphene. Her medical history was unremarkable; she drank two beers daily but denied tobacco or drug use. 

On examination, she had violaceous purpuric macules and patches, nonpalpable and nonblanchable, distributed bilaterally over her hands and right foot in a stocking‐like pattern, with coalescent ecchymoses on her lower leg and scattered petechiae. Pulses were palpable in the lower extremities. All involved areas were extremely painful with moderate nonpitting edema.

She was started on a heparin infusion and intravenous methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg/day). Her ESR decreased from >140 mm/h to 47 mm/h by hospital day 3. Laboratory tests including ANA, ANCA, cryoglobulins, hepatitis panel, RF, anti-CCP, dsDNA, HIV, C3, C4, uric acid, and TSH were within normal limits; SPEP showed a monoclonal gammopathy with elevated IgE. Platelet counts remained stable (200–380 ×10^3/µL). 

Arterial Doppler ultrasonography of the right leg showed biphasic waveforms with normal systolic flow. Radiographs of the hands and right ankle showed only soft tissue swelling. CT angiography of the aorta and lower extremities revealed abrupt occlusion of the right anterior tibial, posterior tibial, and peroneal arteries approximately 5 cm from origin, without proximal filling defects. 

Differential diagnoses included neutrophilic dermatosis, purpura fulminans with DIC, antiphospholipid syndrome or other coagulopathies. Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S levels were all normal. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed no cardiac vegetations or thromboembolic source.
title: Severe leukocytoclastic vasculitis secondary to the use of a naproxen and requiring amputation: a case report

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old Asian boy (70 kg) with no past medical history was admitted for exploratory vitreoretinal surgery under general anesthesia. He was ASA grade I; preoperative labs and chest radiograph were normal. Premedication included ondansetron, glycopyrrolate, midazolam, and fentanyl. Intraoperative monitoring comprised ECG, blood pressure, SpO₂, and end-tidal CO₂. He was preoxygenated for 3 minutes, induced with propofol, intubated easily after vecuronium, and maintained on oxygen, nitrous oxide, and isoflurane. The procedure was uneventful. At the end, neuromuscular blockade was reversed with neostigmine and glycopyrrolate, and extubation was uneventful with full recovery of consciousness.

While being transferred to the postoperative ward, he suddenly developed laryngospasm with paradoxical chest movements, his SpO₂ fell to 40%, and he became dusky. Mask ventilation with 100% oxygen was initially unsuccessful. He received 50 mg of intravenous suxamethonium, followed by bag-mask ventilation, after which SpO₂ improved. At that point, he was fully conscious and responsive, and pink, frothy sputum was noted along with bilateral crackles on lung auscultation.
title: Negative pressure pulmonary edema - a life-threatening condition in an eye care setting: a case report

case_prompt: A 62-year-old Kurdish man presented with a swelling on his left forearm of 10 years’ duration, which had increased in size over the past 2 months. He had hypertension and a remote inguinal hernia repair. On examination, there was a hard, non-tender 3 × 2 cm mass fixed to the skin on the posteromedial aspect of the mid-forearm. Routine hematologic tests, including an erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were normal. Doppler ultrasound of the left elbow showed an ill-defined intramuscular hypoechoic lesion measuring approximately 32 × 21 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined oval mass within the subcutaneous fat with mild post-contrast enhancement and no evidence of surrounding invasion. The working diagnosis was a benign cystic lesion, particularly a dermoid cyst or lipoma.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Porocarcinoma: A systematic review of literature with a single case report

case_prompt:
A 62-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of a slowly enlarging mass in the anterior aspect of his left lower leg. Forty-three years earlier, he had sustained a crush injury that injured his popliteal vessels; there was no documented compartment syndrome. Since that accident, he had noticed weakness of foot dorsiflexion. On examination, there was a 13×9×5 cm bulging, non-tender, elastic hard mass covered by thin, atrophic skin in the mid-portion of the anterior calf. The circumference of the affected calf was 45 cm versus 43 cm on the opposite side. He had hypesthesia on the lateral calf and could not actively dorsiflex the ankle or big toe. 

Plain radiographs of the left leg showed an anterolateral soft-tissue mass with extensive amorphous calcifications and erosion of the middle third of the tibia and fibula. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 4×6 cm mass with a central low-density area and peripheral high density, suggestive of fluid centrally with calcified margin, and enhancement of the space between the tibia and fibula. MRI revealed that the mass was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with peripheral low-signal foci corresponding to calcification, and postcontrast fat-suppressed T1-weighted images showed peripheral ring enhancement. Volume-rendered CT angiography of bone and vessels demonstrated numerous branches from the tibialis posterior and peroneal arteries surrounding a bone defect in the middle tibia.
title: Calcific myonecrosis and the role of imaging in the diagnosis: A case report

case_prompt: A 14-year-old boy with osteosarcoma of the right tibia (no known metastasis) presented to the emergency department with status epilepticus and altered mental status. Five days earlier, he had received a second course of intravenous high‐dose methotrexate (12 000 mg/m2). Twenty-four hours after that infusion, he had a 5-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure treated with midazolam; electroencephalography then was normal, and methotrexate levels at 24, 48, and 72 hours were 1.7, 0.13, and 0.06 µmol/L, respectively. He was discharged on levetiracetam, but one day later had another generalized tonic-clonic seizure en route to the hospital. In the ED, midazolam, diazepam, and levetiracetam stopped the seizure. On examination he was obtunded, responding only to pain. Initial glucose, electrolytes, kidney and liver function tests were all normal. Arterial blood gas showed respiratory acidosis that resolved postictally. White blood count was 21 600/µL (90% neutrophils) and C-reactive protein was 12 mg/L. Head CT was normal. Brain MRI showed subtle diffusion restriction in the posterior subcortical white matter, more prominent on the left, without evidence of territorial infarct or metastases. During his ED stay he spiked fevers to 39.5 °C. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 10 white cells/µL (75% neutrophils), normal glucose, and protein. He was started on broad‐spectrum antibiotics and acyclovir, and blood and CSF were sent for cultures and viral PCR. All cultures and PCR results were negative.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title:
A Case of Methotrexate Neurotoxicity Presented as Status Epilepticus,
Encephalopathy, and High Fever

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of central abdominal pain associated with loose stools, lethargy, and marked weight loss. He denied fever, night sweats, or respiratory symptoms. He had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis 10 years earlier, treated for 6 months, and known bilateral renal calculi with moderate renal impairment. He had no prior abdominal surgery. On examination, he appeared cachectic; the abdomen was soft with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies demonstrated macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.6 g/dl, MCV 102.6 fl), a low–normal folate level (2.7 ng/ml), and normal vitamin B12. Thyroid function tests and stool studies were normal. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a fistulous opening in the third part of the duodenum, and colonoscopy showed a fistulous opening in the proximal transverse colon; there was no evidence of malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed irregular thickening of the transverse and descending colon extending to the hepatic flexure, with contrast opacification of adjacent small bowel loops but no clear communication. Multiple subcentimeter hypodense lesions with focal calcification were present in both liver lobes, and a pulmonary granuloma was seen at the left lung base. These findings were interpreted as suggestive of disseminated tuberculosis. A subsequent barium enema could not delineate the fistula. 

Given the radiologic impression in an endemic region, empiric anti-tuberculosis therapy was initiated prior to surgical intervention.
title: Colo‐appendico‐duodenal fistula: Rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old woman presented in January 2024 with primary amenorrhea. Her developmental milestones were normal, and she had been developing phenotypically. She had not commenced sexual activity. There was no family history of genital ambiguity.

On examination, height was 177 cm, weight 53 kg, and the upper-to-lower segment ratio was 1 to 1. Waist circumference was 88 cm and hip circumference was 103 cm. She had a feminine voice with sparse axillary hair. Breast development was Tanner stage 3 and pubic hair Tanner stage 4. The external genitalia appeared normal; vaginal examination was not performed.

Laboratory studies revealed hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with an elevated FSH of 274 mIU/mL and LH of 35 mIU/mL, normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone (0.57 ng/mL), and normal testosterone (0.14 ng/mL). Pelvic ultrasound showed an anteflexed uterus with a normal endometrial stripe and no evidence of ovarian pathology, findings incongruent with the hormonal profile. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a hypoplastic uterus with absent ovaries.
title: 46, XY Complete Gonadal Dysgenesis (Swyer Syndrome) Presenting as Primary Amenorrhea in a Normomorphic Adult Female From Kakamega, Kenya

case_prompt: A 54-year-old woman presented with a 15-month history of progressively worsening dyspnea, wheezing, and occasional cough. Initially, her symptoms occurred only with strenuous exertion. She had a normal chest radiograph and a spirometry ratio (FEV1/FVC) of 0.76; she was diagnosed with asthma and treated for one year without improvement. Current spirometry showed FEV1 1.61 L, FVC 2.11 L, and negative bronchodilator reversibility. Over the past months, her dyspnea—predominantly inspiratory—worsened even with mild activities. On examination, there was a wheeze audible over both lung fields, loudest at the upper third of the trachea. Repeat spirometry demonstrated blunting of both the inspiratory and expiratory limbs of the flow–volume loop.
title: Challenges in diagnosis and management of central airway obstruction: Case series

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old man was admitted on December 20, 2020, after left pleural effusion was detected on examination two weeks earlier. He had no facial edema or muscle pain and a history of hypertension. Vital signs were normal. On exam, breath sounds were diminished at the left lung base. CT of the chest showed moderate left pleural effusion with partial collapse of the left lung and scattered solid nodules in the right lung. Laboratory studies revealed an absolute eosinophil count of 0.30×10^9/L, creatine kinase 48 U/L, serum protein 55.1 g/L, and LDH 141 U/L. Other serum tests were normal. Thoracentesis yielded red, turbid fluid with clots. Pleural fluid analysis: specific gravity 1.022, Rivalta test positive; nucleated cells 3180/µL (98.9% mononuclear, 1.1% multinuclear); glucose 5.52 mmol/L, protein 36.5 g/L, albumin 22.2 g/L, chloride 111.3 mmol/L, LDH 220 U/L, ADA 9 U/L. Cardiac and abdominal ultrasounds were unremarkable. Chest ultrasound confirmed a large left pleural effusion (maximum depth 7.6 cm). PET/CT showed no muscle involvement or malignant lesions.  
He received cefotaxime–sulbactam for 1 week with no decrease in effusion. Pleural fluid cytology showed a few lymphocytes and mesothelial cells and no atypical epithelial cells. On hospital day 11, he was treated empirically for tuberculosis (rifampicin, isoniazid, moxifloxacin) for 25 days; repeat imaging showed no fluid reduction, and anti-tuberculosis therapy was discontinued.
title: Pleural effusion caused by Trichinella spiralis infection: two case reports

case_prompt: A 59-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute right upper quadrant pain and a low-grade fever (maximum temperature, 37.8°C). On examination, she had localized signs of peritoneal irritation in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a normal liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts; the appendix was not visualized. In the subhepatic region, there was a 4-cm, noncompressible, heterogeneous, hyperechoic mass with a thin hypoechoic rim and absent internal blood flow on color Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a 43×33×56-mm ovoid lesion between the right colic flexure and the inferior margin of hepatic segment IVb, characterized by a heterogeneous adipose matrix with dense internal branching and a surrounding hyperdense enhancing rim. No other significant abdominal abnormalities were identified.
title: A rare cause of right-upper quadrant abdominal pain: Epiploic appendagitis of the hepatic flexure

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old Indian American man presented with five days of constant blurry vision, primarily in the lower visual field, of the right eye. His ocular history included bilateral LASIK and moderate myopia (−5.0 diopters). Medical history was significant for idiopathic cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis diagnosed five years earlier by skin biopsy, with direct immunofluorescence showing IgM, IgG, and C3 deposition in dermal vessels; the disease had flared twice, with purpuric rash and abdominal pain, and responded to colchicine, antibiotics for Helicobacter pylori, and systemic prednisone.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes; intraocular pressures were 13 mm Hg OD and 14 mm Hg OS. Slit-lamp examination showed no anterior chamber cells or flare. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye demonstrated mildly enlarged, tortuous veins, optic nerve hemorrhage, and intraretinal hemorrhages temporal to the macula. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography revealed hyperreflective, plaque-like lesions in the inner nuclear layer consistent with paracentral acute middle maculopathy. Wide-angle fluorescein angiography showed patchy hypofluorescence within the macula without significant perivascular leakage or ischemia and no delay in arteriovenous transit time.

Laboratory evaluation for bleeding diatheses, blood dyscrasias, and hyperviscosity syndromes—including antithrombin III, protein C, protein S, factor V Leiden, proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase antibodies, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, C1q binding, Raji cell assay, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, beta-2 glycoprotein, phosphatidylserine/prothrombin antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, and serum protein electrophoresis—was unremarkable. Testing for infectious causes (Treponema pallidum ELISA, QuantiFERON-TB Gold) was negative. Complete blood count, metabolic panel, lipid panel, ESR, CRP, urinalysis, and HbA1c were all within normal limits.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Impending central retinal vein occlusion in patient with idiopathic cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old man presented with chest tightness and exertional shortness of breath for two weeks. His surgical history was notable for correction of a double-chambered right ventricle and tricuspid valvuloplasty 10 years earlier, but he had not followed up regularly. On examination, blood pressure was 170/110 mm Hg, heart rate 90 beats/min irregular, with a variable first heart sound and a short pulse.  
Electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation, ectopic atrial rhythm, and complete right bundle branch block. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a markedly enlarged right atrium and a 40 × 48 mm strongly echogenic mass along the right atrial wall, a mildly regurgitant aortic valve, a dilated aortic root, and an ejection fraction of 59%. Chest CT revealed a hypointense shadow in the enlarged right atrium, interpreted as a possible mucinous tumor.  
Laboratory studies showed an international normalized ratio of 0.88 (below postoperative target) and markedly elevated blood glucose with an oral glucose tolerance test indicating type 2 diabetes. Following glucose control, surgical resection of the right atrial lesion was planned.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: The Patient With Right Atrial Thrombus With a Previous History of Double-Chambered Right Ventricular Surgery and Atrial Fibrillation: A Rare Association

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of fever, anorexia, and abdominal pain, followed by 1 week of progressive abdominal distension. Ultrasonography at an outside center revealed ascites, omental thickening, and bilateral pleural effusions. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded purulent fluid; a percutaneous catheter was placed. Ascitic fluid analysis showed 17,000 cells/mm3 with lymphocyte predominance, degenerated cells, and a normal adenosine deaminase level. Acid-fast bacilli staining and nucleic acid amplification testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative, and the Mantoux test was nonreactive. He was started on antitubercular therapy and antibiotics without improvement and was referred to our hospital.

On transfer, he had tachycardia and tachypnea without pallor or peripheral lymphadenopathy. The abdomen was distended and firm, with shifting dullness; no organomegaly or discrete mass was palpable. Initial laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 14.9 × 10^9/L, normal hemoglobin and platelet counts, and normal liver-function tests. Repeat ultrasonography showed a large peritoneal collection, omental thickening, and multiple hypoechoic lesions in the liver. Chest radiography showed bilateral pleural effusions; echocardiography revealed a small pericardial effusion. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated ascites, thickened and nodular omentum, enhancing soft-tissue thickening in the retroperitoneum extending into the mesentery and encasing the superior and inferior mesenteric vessels, and 2–3 hypodense bilateral renal nodules (largest, 2 cm) and hypodense hepatic lesions encasing portal-vein branches; no lymphadenopathy was noted.

A new peritoneal catheter drained white-colored fluid. The fluid had a total cell count of 2.56 × 10^12 cells/L with 90% atypical lymphocytes, a lactate dehydrogenase level of 2864 U/L, a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 0.9, total protein 3.7 g/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL, and glucose 24 mg/dL. Pleural fluid cytology similarly showed atypical lymphocytes.
title: Peritoneal Lymphomatosis Masquerading as Pyoperitoneum in a Teenage Boy

case_prompt:
A 28-day-old girl, born at term after an uneventful pregnancy, was noted at birth to have bluish, palpable nodular lesions (0.5–1 cm) on her face. At 21 days of age, she presented with irritability and progressive abdominal distention. On examination, she was pale and had 13 visible and 6 palpable skin nodules on her face, thorax, and extremities, along with massive hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Initial blood tests showed mild anemia and thrombocytopenia. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple nodular lesions throughout the enlarged liver. 

After transfer to a tertiary care center, her anemia and thrombocytopenia worsened (platelet count, 4,000–18,000/mm3; hemoglobin, 7.5–11.3 g/dL), but her leukocyte count remained normal. Serologic studies for HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and Toxoplasma were negative, and serum tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and carcinoembryonic antigen) were negative. Electrolytes showed persistent hyponatremia (124–133 mEq/L); renal function and potassium were within normal limits. 

Three days after admission, she developed anasarca. Liver function tests showed hypoalbuminemia (1.4 g/dL), coagulopathy (INR, 2.52), elevated aminotransferases (AST, 11–325 U/L; ALT, 1.1–55 U/L), hyperbilirubinemia (2.59–8.75 mg/dL), low alkaline phosphatase (38.5 U/L), and elevated C-reactive protein (47.7 mg/L). Serum immunoglobulins were IgG 169 mg/dL, IgM 14 mg/dL, IgA 3 mg/dL, and IgE 0.71 U/mL. Serologic testing for syphilis was negative. A repeat abdominal ultrasound showed retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and ascites; the kidneys appeared normal. Radiographs demonstrated elevated diaphragms and intestinal distention. 

On hospital day 4, a limited bone marrow aspirate showed no abnormal infiltrate or hemophagocytosis, and an excisional skin biopsy was performed. The patient died on day 5 from respiratory distress syndrome.
title: Infantile systemic juvenile xanthogranuloma case with massive liver infiltration

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old Mongolian man from rural Nepal presented with a six-year history of insidious, throbbing pain and swelling of both hands and feet unrelieved by over-the-counter medications. He also reported profuse sweating, progressive enlargement of his hands and feet, and gradual coarsening of facial features. His grandparents were consanguineous, but there was no similar illness in other family members. He denied fatigue, eye redness or dryness, chest pain, dyspnea, fever, palpitations, heat intolerance, tremors, scalp dandruff, or rashes.

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable. There were marked skin folds on the forehead, face, and eyelids. Clubbing of the fingers was noted, along with swelling of the bilateral knees and ankles. Cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological, and thyroid examinations were unremarkable. There were no psoriatic nail changes, subcutaneous nodules, or ocular findings.

Laboratory studies showed a normal full blood count (TLC 9.5 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 410 × 10^9/L), normal liver and renal function tests, and normal thyroid function tests. Rheumatoid factor and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies were negative. Insulin-like growth factor–1 levels were within the normal range, and an oral glucose tolerance test excluded acromegaly.

Radiographs demonstrated mild cortical and subperiosteal thickening of the skull; symmetrical, irregular periosteal hypertrophy with subperiosteal new bone formation in the proximal tibia, fibula, and distal femur; irregular subperiosteal new bone formation and cortical thickening of the distal tibia, fibula, calcaneum, and talus; and soft tissue tumefaction of the distal phalanges with periostitis and hyperostosis of the metacarpals and proximal phalanges.

Synovial fluid analysis of a knee effusion was non-inflammatory, non-hemorrhagic, and non-septic.
title: Pachydermoperiostosis (Touraine–Solente–Gole syndrome): a case report

case_prompt:
A 3-year-old Saudi girl was admitted with a 2-day history of fever, cough, and intermittent tonic-clonic seizures associated with up-rolling of the eyes. She had two prior admissions for febrile convulsions and had been treated for asthma and bronchopneumonia. Her parents noted generalized darkening of the skin beginning at 18 months of age. There was parental consanguinity and a brother with early-onset adrenal insufficiency treated with hydrocortisone, but no genetic testing.

On examination: temperature 38.3 °C, heart rate 130 bpm, respiratory rate 40 per min, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg. There was diffuse hyperpigmentation, most pronounced on the elbows, hands, knees, and buccal mucosa; hypotonia and hyporeflexia were noted. Lacrimation was normal and there were no signs of achalasia.

Laboratory studies showed a random blood glucose of 30 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.24, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, PaCO₂ 45 mmHg; serum sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium were normal. Liver and renal function tests, HbA₁c, free T₃, free T₄, TSH, insulin, and C-peptide were within normal limits. The 17-hydroxyprogesterone level was normal. A critical sample during hypoglycemia revealed plasma ACTH >2000 pg/mL and serum cortisol 53 nmol/L (reference 140–690 nmol/L).
