Serum androgens were 0.65 nmol/L (reference 0.5–2.4 nmol/L) and aldosterone was 50 pg/mL (reference 2–200 pg/mL). 

Ultrasound showed bilaterally small adrenal glands (right 5 × 6 mm, left 5 × 7.5 mm). A noncontrast CT scan of the brain was normal.
title: Familial Glucocorticoid Deficiency Presenting with Tonic-Clonic Seizure: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 9-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat was referred for acute hemodynamic collapse. The caretaker had noted weakness and possible signs of lower urinary tract disease over the previous days; there was no known trauma, and the cat was strictly indoors. On presentation, the cat was obtunded, bradycardic (70 beats/min), hypothermic (35 °C), with weak femoral pulses, prolonged capillary refill time, and non-detectable Doppler blood pressure. Point-of-care ultrasound revealed a moderate volume of free abdominal fluid in all four quadrants and no pleural or pericardial effusion. ECG showed atrial standstill with idioventricular escape rhythms. A jugular venous sample demonstrated severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.10), hyperkalemia (K⁺ 8.78 mmol/L), and azotemia (creatinine 510 μmol/L). Abdominocentesis yielded serosanguineous fluid with a fluid-to-serum creatinine ratio of 6.09 and a potassium ratio of 2.28, consistent with uroabdomen. The cat was managed with IV fluids, calcium gluconate, sodium bicarbonate, antibiotics, placement of a peritoneal dialysis catheter via a central venous line, and peritoneal dialysis, which improved electrolytes and pH. Eighteen hours after admission, diagnostic ultrasound and retrograde contrast cystography confirmed a dorsal urinary bladder rupture, which was surgically repaired. During routine postoperative focused ultrasound, a mild-to-moderate bilateral pleural effusion was unexpectedly noted. A complete echocardiogram showed no evidence of cardiac disease or fluid overload. The total fluid balance from admission to surgery was a negative 240 mL.
title: Successful resolution of urothorax secondary to non-traumatic uroabdomen in a cat managed with peritoneal dialysis as a bridge to surgery

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of left palatal swelling. She had self-extracted her upper left second molar 3 years earlier and underwent extraction of the first molar 5 months before presentation; the latter was reportedly traumatic, with possible involvement of the maxillary sinus floor. Her medical history included uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and anticoagulant therapy; she denied prior facial trauma, sinusitis, or maxillary surgery.

On examination, there was mild swelling of the left cheek, paresthesia of the left infraorbital region, and left nasal obstruction for 1 month. Intraorally, a 2.5×3.0-cm palatal swelling was present in the left premolar–molar area, with obliteration of the buccal vestibule and expansion of the alveolar segment; the overlying mucosa was normal and all teeth were vital.

Computed tomography revealed a unilocular, radiolucent, expansile lesion measuring 35×31×34 mm in the left maxillary sinus, with resorption of the anterior and posterior sinus walls, obliteration of the osteomeatal complex, and cortical expansion of the palatal and buccal walls. Aspiration yielded straw-colored fluid and temporarily reduced the lesion’s size. An incisional biopsy via the buccal vestibule disclosed an unspecified odontogenic cyst, and a provisional diagnosis of odontogenic keratocyst was rendered.
title: Surgical Ciliated Cyst of the Left Maxilla - A Case Report of Unusual Pathogenesis

case_prompt: A 42-year-old man presented with 4 days of progressive musculoskeletal weakness, bladder and bowel retention, blurred vision, and ascending hypoesthesia to the T8 level. He was anicteric and cardiopulmonary–stable. Neurologic examination showed spasticity in the lower limbs, nonexhaustive Achilles tendon clonus, and muscle strength graded 3/5 on the right and 4/5 on the left (BMRC scale); the upper limbs were normal. Admission blood tests showed elevated alanine transaminase (40.16 μmol/(s·l)), aspartate transaminase (16.45 μmol/(s·l)), γ-glutamyltransferase (9.71 μmol/(s·l)), and bilirubin (31.9 μmol/l). Serologic testing for hepatitides A, B, C, D, and E revealed acute HEV infection (positive IgM; HEV-RNA 4.09×10^2 IU/ml). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed pleocytosis (15 cells/mm^3, including 43% atypical lymphocytes), normal glucose, lactate, and protein, and HEV-RNA (333 IU/ml), with negative tests for CMV, VZV, HSV, and other hepatic pathogens. Serologic and CSF studies were negative for antinuclear, extractable nuclear, anti-ganglioside, anti-aquaporin-4, anti-VGCC, and anti-VGKC antibodies; HIV antibodies were negative. Blood cultures for Streptococcus pneumoniae, Legionella, and Treponema pallidum were negative. Cranial MRI showed T2/FLAIR white-matter lesions adjacent to the lateral ventricle and rostral corpus callosum, subcortical hyperintensities in the right superior frontal gyrus and right precentral lobe, and bilateral contrast enhancement of the optic nerve sheaths consistent with retrobulbar neuritis. Spinal MRI revealed small T2 hyperintensities at C7, T2, T5, T8/9, and T12 extending to the conus medullaris without contrast enhancement. Electrophysiologic studies demonstrated bilateral peroneal nerve axonal damage with absent F-waves.
title: Disseminated inflammation of the central nervous system associated with acute hepatitis E: a case report

case_prompt: A 5-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of torticollis and pain radiating to his left upper limb. He had no previous medical history. On examination, he had decreased sensation in both upper limbs, bilateral lower-extremity weakness (motor strength 4/5 in distal muscle groups), and hypoactive reflexes in all four extremities. There was no bowel or bladder dysfunction. Cervical CT and MRI revealed a 75 × 36 × 24 mm extradural, dumbbell-shaped mass with extra-spinal extension at the left C1–C6 level, containing calcifications and showing heterogeneous signal intensity with homogeneous intermediate enhancement after gadolinium administration. No other spinal cord lesions or osseous abnormalities were identified.
title: Peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumors of the spine: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old man with a 10-year history of hypertension and recent urinary difficulty underwent a TURP two months ago, which showed adenocarcinoma on prostate biopsy. Two weeks post-procedure, he developed right flank pain and gross hematuria without other symptoms. He has no family history of tumors and takes only antihypertensive medication.  
On presentation, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal and flank examinations were unremarkable, and he voided without difficulty.  
Laboratory studies were within normal limits.  
Renal ultrasound revealed a 6×6 cm mass in the right kidney; the left kidney was normal.  
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a heterogeneous 6×6×5 cm mass in the upper pole of the right kidney without vascular invasion or lesions elsewhere.
final_diagnosis_raw: Thyroid-like follicular carcinoma of the kidney
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare case of thyroid-like follicular carcinoma of the kidney in a 75-year-old male: Case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 4-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of diffuse left-sided cervical swelling. Multiple eczematous lesions were noted over the swelling. On examination, there were firm, tender, slightly mobile cervical lymph nodes measuring 0.8 × 0.8 to 1.2 × 1.5 cm in the anterior neck on both sides. He also had left ear discharge for 2 weeks but denied fever or weight loss. There was no hepatosplenomegaly and no known tuberculosis exposure.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 12 080/µL (45% neutrophils, 37% lymphocytes, 15% monocytes, 3% eosinophils), and a normal platelet count. The Mantoux test was negative. Bone marrow biopsy was unremarkable. A skeletal X-ray survey revealed no abnormalities.

PET scan demonstrated a conglomerate nodal mass in left cervical levels II, III, IV/V, and a supraclavicular mass extending to the superior mediastinum and left chest wall; no skeletal lytic lesions were identified. The thyroid gland appeared normal.

Fine-needle aspiration of the left supraclavicular swelling yielded a hemorrhagic whitish aspirate. Smears stained with Papanicolaou and Giemsa stains were highly cellular. They showed numerous atypical histiocytes, both singly and in loose clusters, that were binucleate or multinucleate with abundant dense cytoplasm and eccentric vesicular nuclei. The nuclei exhibited intranuclear pseudoinclusions and prominent indentations or grooves with a kidney- or coffee-bean appearance. The background contained lymphocytes, neutrophils, and a few eosinophils.
journal: Journal of Cytology / Indian Academy of Cytologists
title: Cytological diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis with cutaneous involvement

case_prompt: A 53-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of an asymptomatic, slow-growing, soft mass in her right breast. On examination, there was a palpable, non-tender, solitary, soft mass measuring approximately 10 cm × 10 cm × 8 cm in the upper-outer quadrant of the right breast; the contralateral breast and both axillae were unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests—including blood counts, electrolytes, coagulation parameters, and liver, renal, and cardiopulmonary function tests—were all within normal limits. There was no family history of breast cancer. Breast ultrasonography showed a well-circumscribed, hyperechoic nodule of dense fat in the upper-outer quadrant of the right breast. Mammography demonstrated a round, sharply demarcated, non-calcified mass occupying most of the upper outer and inner quadrants of the right breast. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a heterogeneous low-density lesion with a maximum cross-sectional diameter of approximately 70 mm by 40 mm and attenuation values ranging from –38 to 12 Hounsfield units.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Mammary hibernoma: A rare case report of a benign tumor

case_prompt: A 38-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of pain localized to the tailbone. She had no significant medical history. On neurologic examination, motor strength was 5/5 in both lower extremities; sensation and deep tendon reflexes were symmetrical and intact. She denied urinary or fecal incontinence. An MRI of the lumbar spine revealed a 17 × 12 × 15 mm intradural lesion posterior to the L3–4 disc and the upper part of the L4 vertebral body. On midsagittal T2-weighted images, the lesion had indistinct hypointense margins; on axial T2-weighted images it was hyperintense and compressed nerve roots against the dura, obliterating CSF signal. The lesion was isointense to vertebral body on T1-weighted images and showed homogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images.
title: A case of rare lumbar intradural tumor: paraganglioma

case_prompt: A 59-year-old woman presented with a small, slowly enlarging, painless tumor on the tip of her nose. She reported no other symptoms. On examination, there was an 8 mm hemispherical, immobile, sharply demarcated nodule at the upper border of the right nostril, with slight subcutaneous extension toward the tip and columella. The lesion had a smooth surface without ulceration or signs of irritation. Further head and neck evaluation, including laryngopharyngoscopy and cervical sonography, was unremarkable. Because the lack of irritation was inconsistent with acute infection, and the sharp demarcation, smooth surface, and absence of ulceration made a primary malignancy unlikely, an excision biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. The lesion and surrounding capsule were completely resected without macroscopic infiltration of adjacent structures, and postoperative healing was uncomplicated. Histopathologic examination revealed fibrous connective tissue partly covered by intact, nondysplastic squamous epithelium. The corial connective tissue was infiltrated by nonkeratinizing squamous cells with pleomorphism of size and nuclei. These findings corresponded to a moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.
title: Isolated Nasal Tip Metastasis from Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old man presented with a 12-year history of hoarseness. He denied dyspnea or dysphagia but reported symptoms of gastric acid reflux. He was a former smoker (quit 6 months earlier) and a politician with chronic voice overuse. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated a 0.5 cm pedunculated, cystic-appearing mass on the medial free edge of the middle third of the right true vocal fold; vocal-fold mobility was normal. The rest of the ENT examination was unremarkable. Given the long-standing hoarseness, history of voice abuse, and appearance of a solitary polypoidal lesion, a preoperative diagnosis of a laryngeal polyp was made. No imaging was performed. The patient underwent microlaryngeal surgery with lesion excision using cold instruments. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient reported near-normal voice at the one-week follow-up.  
On histologic examination, the lesion was a polypoidal tumor lined by hyperplastic stratified squamous epithelium. Beneath the epithelium was an unencapsulated, paucicellular lesion composed of small, bland spindle to stellate cells with indistinct cytoplasmic margins and hyperchromatic nuclei, set in an abundant myxoid matrix. There was no significant atypia, mitotic activity, or necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains were negative for CD34, smooth muscle actin, and S100.
title: Head and Neck Myxoma Presenting as Isolated Laryngeal Polyp

case_prompt:
A 41-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with intermittent right upper–quadrant pain for 20 days, associated with decreased appetite and lassitude. She denied fever, cough, weight loss, night sweats, or known tuberculosis exposure. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL), a slightly distended abdomen, and a palpable lump in the right upper quadrant; there was no lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 23,000 cells/mm3; liver and renal function tests were normal. Tumor markers were elevated: CEA 7.3 ng/mL (normal 0–2.9) and CA19-9 41 IU/mL (normal <37). 

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a distended, moderately thickened gallbladder containing a 37 mm calculus and two smaller stones; adjacent to the fundus was a 3.0×4.2×3.8 cm heterogeneous collection extending into the abdominal wall. The common bile duct was dilated to 14 mm proximally. 

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a distended gallbladder with a 5.1 mm thickened wall and multiple stones (largest 14 mm), a focal breach in the fundus, and an adjacent 3.5×5.7×4.3 cm peripherally enhancing collection reaching the subcutaneous plane. A large, irregular peripancreatic lymph node (8×1.1 cm) and hepatosplenomegaly were also noted. 

Given concern for neoplastic versus inflammatory etiologies, a laparoscopic cholecystectomy was planned.
title: Isolated tubercular cholecystitis: A rare diagnostic challenge

case_prompt: A 31-year-old woman presented with dissatisfaction regarding her facial and dental appearance and reported a year-long odyssey through multiple dental and orthodontic practices without resolution. Her medical history was notable for multiple vertebral compression fractures. On examination, she was 1.6 m tall and had lax, wrinkly skin most prominent on her hands, feet, and abdomen, with drooping cheeks giving an aged appearance disproportionate to her chronological age. Prior dentists had extracted several maxillary teeth to address crowding attributed to a hypoplastic maxilla, but occlusal normality was not achieved. Orthodontic evaluation showed a dental Class III occlusion with bilateral lateral open bite, a marked curve of Spee, and anterior head‐to‐head bite. Panoramic and cephalometric imaging revealed maxillary retrognathia, mandibular prognathism, a skeletal Class III relationship (ANB −2.2°, WITS −6.6 mm), a horizontal mandibular plane (ML-NL 11.9°), apical radiopaque halos from hypercementosis, and superimposition of dental roots on the mandibular canal.
title: Orthognathic Surgery with Interdisciplinary Digital Planning in Patients with Geroderma Osteodysplasticum: A Case Report

case_prompt: An elderly woman with a history of asthma and hypertension, well controlled on medication, presented with a 4-week history of intermittent left-sided lumbar pain radiating to her back. She also experienced three to four episodes of nonprojectile, non–blood-stained vomiting but denied urinary symptoms or weight loss. She had no relevant drug, family, or genetic history. On examination, she appeared mildly dehydrated. Abdominal palpation revealed mild tenderness in the left hypochondrial and left lumbar regions; pulmonary and spinal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hyponatremia (Na+ 128 mEq/L), hypokalemia (K+ 2.8 mEq/L), elevated blood urea nitrogen (50 mmol/L), and creatinine (2.80 mg/dL); urinalysis was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined, 4.5 × 3.0 × 3.5 cm hyperechoic lesion arising from the left suprarenal gland. Serum cortisol (17.60 μg/dL), urinary vanillylmandelic acid (11.4 mg/24 h), and serum metanephrines (243.26 μg/dL) were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a left suprarenal mass abutting the upper pole of the left kidney, spleen, and psoas muscle; there was no focal enhancement, and the mean attenuation was −28 to +10 HU in arterial, venous, and delayed phases, without calcification, hemorrhage, necrosis, or surrounding fat stranding.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: An unusual presentation of an adrenal tumour–a case report

case_prompt: A 47‐year‐old Caucasian Greek woman and her 48‐year‐old male relative, both residents of rural Crete, presented to the emergency department with nausea, dizziness, blurred vision, dry mouth, headache, gait instability, and vomiting that began several hours after consuming a home‐gathered leafy plant as a vegetable. Both patients were normotensive with normal temperature and oxygen saturation; the man’s pulse was 190 beats per minute with 25 breaths per minute, and the woman’s pulse was 170 beats per minute with 20 breaths per minute. On examination, both had flushed skin and reactive mydriasis. Electrocardiography in each patient showed supraventricular tachycardia (heart rate 180 beats per minute in the man and 173 beats per minute in the woman). Initial laboratory studies revealed normal white-cell counts and normal blood and urine screening; liver transaminases were mildly elevated (man: AST 75 U/L, ALT 65 U/L; woman: AST 63 U/L, ALT 55 U/L).
title: A two cases clinical report of mandragora poisoning in primary care in Crete, Greece: two case report

case_prompt: A previously healthy 19-year-old Chinese man presented with progressive weakness of his right limbs over six months. Initially, he had right lower limb weakness with a normal ankle radiograph and no treatment. Two months before presentation, he developed right upper limb weakness and worsening right lower limb strength, accompanied by fever up to 39.5°C, blurred vision in his left eye, and mild episodic headaches lasting several minutes; there was no nausea or vomiting. Computed tomography at an outside hospital revealed numerous well-circumscribed low-density cysts rimmed by high-density calcifications scattered throughout both cerebral hemispheres. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated extensive white matter hyperintensity consistent with leukoencephalopathy and multiple cysts of varying sizes in the hemispheres, thalamus, basal ganglia, and left ventricle; the cyst walls enhanced with gadolinium, and the contents were heterogeneously hyperintense on T1-weighted and FLAIR images. On examination, visual acuity was 0.15 in the left eye and 0.5 in the right; motor strength was grade 4/5 in the right limbs with a positive Babinski sign on the right. Initial differential diagnoses included parasitic infection, glioma, and leukoencephalopathy.
title: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy, brain calcifications and cysts: a case report

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old woman (BMI 29.6, weight 173 lb) with hyperlipidemia, anxiety, and depression presented for ultrasound-guided trigger point injections of the left trapezius, levator scapulae, and rhomboids using preservative-free 1% lidocaine without epinephrine. She reported anxiety about the injection but agreed to proceed. She denied allergies or prior injection reactions. Preprocedure vital signs were stable, and she was alert and oriented.

Under sterile conditions and ultrasound guidance, a 27-gauge, 1.5-inch needle was advanced into the first trigger point; aspiration was negative, and 1 mL of lidocaine was injected intramuscularly. The needle was then repositioned into an adjacent point. Shortly thereafter, she felt dizzy and moved from sitting to lying on her right side. She became unresponsive and pale, with no palpable pulse. A jaw thrust was performed while staff retrieved an AED, which reported an unshockable rhythm. CPR was initiated, and after approximately 1 minute of chest compressions, she regained consciousness and a pulse. She was diaphoretic and had urinary incontinence.

Postresuscitation vital signs were blood pressure 100/84 mm Hg, pulse 62 beats/min, respiratory rate 11 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. Emergency medical services arrived, and she was transported to the emergency department. In the ED, repeat ECG and cardiac biomarkers were normal.
title: Cardiac arrest in a 36 year-old after trigger point injection with lidocaine: Case report

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old Caucasian man with a history of a precancerous supraglottic mass treated with resection and radiation, compensated alcoholic cirrhosis, and a right hemicolectomy presented with a 4-month history of daily melena. He denied nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hematemesis, hematochezia, reflux symptoms, changes in bowel habits, weight loss, and the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Over the preceding 3 years he had intermittent melena requiring blood transfusions; it progressed to daily melena in the past 4 months despite two prior EGDs, two colonoscopies, and one video capsule endoscopy that identified no bleeding source. In the last 2 months his hemoglobin ranged from 6.2 to 7.4 g/dL, necessitating 2 units of packed red blood cells weekly and biweekly intravenous iron infusions; he had not received oral iron in the 6 months before admission. 

On presentation he was asymptomatic and hemodynamically stable. Rectal examination revealed black, tarry stool. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 4.4 g/dL and an acute kidney injury; he received two units of packed red blood cells. Iron studies were consistent with iron deficiency (ferritin 109 ng/mL; transferrin 194 mg/dL; TIBC 225 µg/dL; serum iron 38 µg/dL; iron saturation 16.9%). CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated cirrhosis. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a nonbleeding, clean-based ulcer in the gastric body and nonbleeding gastric varices.
title: Gastric Siderosis and Ulceration from Intravenous Iron Supplementation Manifesting as Chronic Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 28-year-old nonsmoking male prisoner presented with several weeks of fresh hemoptysis, fever, anorexia, and weight loss. He had known exposure to pulmonary tuberculosis but no risk factors for pulmonary embolism or bronchiectasis. On examination, he was tachycardic, ill-appearing, and underweight. Chest auscultation revealed bronchial breathing in both upper lobes and diffuse inspiratory and expiratory crackles. Chest radiography showed bilateral diffuse reticulonodular opacities with fibrotic changes in the apices. Sputum AFB and nucleic acid amplification confirmed pan-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and standard first-line therapy was started. Despite treatment, he continued to have significant hemoptysis and required three units of packed red blood cells to maintain a hemoglobin around 9 g/dL. Fibreoptic bronchoscopy showed normal airways without an endobronchial mass or obvious bleeding source; bronchoalveolar lavage and biopsies revealed acute inflammation and AFB. A CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated a thick-walled cavitary lesion filled with blood, surrounded by fibrotic and bronchiectatic changes.
title: Rasmussen's pseudoaneurysm- case report

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 3-year-old girl was brought in with a 5-day history of fever (up to 40.5 °C), anorexia, and weakness. She had no cough, vomiting, diarrhea, myalgias, or altered consciousness. She had played in grass near her grandmother’s house during a festival in Lu’an City, Anhui Province—an area known for tick-borne illness—and her grandfather had died of a tick-borne hemorrhagic fever in 2017. Initial treatment with acetaminophen and oseltamivir at a community hospital failed to resolve her fever.

On admission (July 5), temperature was 39.4 °C, pulse 100 bpm, respiratory rate 14/min, and blood pressure 110/90 mmHg. Examination revealed petechiae and ecchymoses on the trunk; neurologic exam was normal.

Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (1.91 × 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (78 × 10^9/L), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (1620 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (81 U/L), and alkaline phosphatase (160 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Chest CT demonstrated increased lung markings. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia. Empiric cefoperazone–sulbactam and ganciclovir were initiated.
title: Infection of Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome Virus as a Cause of a Child’s Fever of Unknown Origin: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 64-year-old man presented with six months of progressive dyspnea. He had a history of asthma but no smoking history. Cardiac evaluation, including echocardiogram and stress testing, was normal. Noncontrast CT of the chest showed bilateral mild ground-glass opacities, slightly more pronounced in the right middle and lower lobes. Laboratory studies revealed a p-ANCA titer of 1:640, a negative anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody, a myeloperoxidase level >8 units (normal <0.4), and a negative proteinase-3 level. Wedge biopsies of the right upper, middle, and lower lobes appeared red to purple grossly. Microscopic examination showed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage with numerous hemosiderin-laden macrophages but no definite vasculitis. An external expert review rendered a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis and commented that (1) the findings were consistent with a diffuse alveolar hemorrhage syndrome; (2) the absence of vasculitis and capillaritis argued against granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and microscopic polyangiitis; and (3) Goodpasture’s syndrome remained possible but required identification of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies.
title: Top Differential Diagnosis Should Be Microscopic Polyangiitis in ANCA-Positive Patient with Diffuse Pulmonary Hemorrhage and Hemosiderosis

case_prompt: A 63-year-old Korean woman with no significant medical history presented with a 1-year history of swelling in her right parotid region. Physical examination revealed a fixed, non-tender, round mass in the right parotid area. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Neck CT showed a 3.2-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass lateral to the mandibular ramus adjacent to the right masseter muscle. Neck MRI demonstrated a well-demarcated, 2.5×3.0-cm gadolinium-enhanced fungating lesion with internal hemorrhage and increased vascularity. Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass in the right parotid gland suspicious for a parotid gland tumor. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded fragments of relatively short spindle cells in a myxoid and bloody background; cytologists suggested that pleomorphic adenoma could not be excluded.
title: A low grade fibromyxoid sarcoma originating from the masseter muscle: a case report

case_prompt:
An 88-year-old Asian woman noted a mass in her right breast 1 month earlier. She had no history of trauma to the breasts. Her past medical history was notable for a left breast cancer treated surgically 12 years ago (T1N0M0, hormone-receptor–negative, no adjuvant therapy). 

On examination, there was a 20 mm, elastic-hard, less mobile mass in the lower outer quadrant of the right breast, 25 mm from the nipple; no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was palpable. 

Mammography showed a dense, round, microlobulated mass. Ultrasonography revealed an 18.1 × 16.2 × 14.4 mm, round, hypoechoic solid lesion with heterogeneous internal echoes, lateral shadowing, a partially broken anterior margin, and an intact posterior margin. 

A core needle biopsy demonstrated proliferating spindle cells but did not yield a definitive diagnosis of malignancy. Because imaging and needle-biopsy results could not exclude a malignant tumor, an excisional biopsy was planned.
title: Nodular fasciitis of the breast clinically resembling breast cancer in an elderly woman: a case report

case_prompt: A 33-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks’ gestation presented after spontaneous rupture of membranes. Labor was augmented, and 2 hours later fetal bradycardia prompted emergency cesarean delivery; intraoperatively, 50% placental abruption was noted without significant hemorrhage. A healthy female infant was delivered, weighing 3.3 kg (Apgar scores 8 and 9). Fourteen hours postoperatively, the patient became jaundiced, oliguric, and hypoglycemic (glucose 40 mg/dL). She was alert and hemodynamically unstable without evidence of obstetric bleeding. Vital signs were: heart rate 120 bpm, blood pressure 74/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.3 °C. Laboratory evaluation showed: total bilirubin 7.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.149 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, AST 170 U/L, ALT 149 U/L, prothrombin time 27 s, INR 2.56, fibrinogen 71 mg/dL, creatinine 2.7 mg/dL, ammonia 126 μmol/L, platelets 95 000/μL, white-cell count 33 030/μL, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, hematocrit 27.8%, and LDH 432 IU/L. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an echogenic liver with fatty infiltrates consistent with mild hepatic steatosis. The patient had no prior symptoms of liver disease and no history of viral exposures or hepatotoxic medication use.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: A Rare Disease Presenting Postpartum: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman with a history of severe obesity, myocardial infarction, hypertension, and prior uterine fibroid resection presented with progressive epigastric and right subcostal pain for 1 year. She denied tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, vital signs were normal; there was localized tenderness on peri-umbilical palpation without other abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed no infectious syndrome; the electrocardiogram was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed gallstones. A routine chest radiograph demonstrated an opacity in the right costophrenic angle. 

A subsequent thoraco-abdominopelvic CT scan showed a heterogeneous right pleural-based mass containing both fatty and soft-tissue components, without calcification and without apparent invasion of adjacent structures or the chest wall. Chest MRI confirmed an antero-inferior right subpleural heterogeneous mass with fat and tissue elements, with no signs of adjacent-organ or chest-wall invasion, and was reported as suggestive of liposarcoma. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan showed low metabolic activity in the lesion (SUV 1.8) and no other sites of abnormal uptake.
title: Hamartochondroma Pleural Lesion Mimicking Liposarcoma: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old woman presented with progressive right‐sided hemiparesis. Her first acute attack occurred in 2007, and she had similar relapses in 2012 and 2015, each treated with methylprednisolone pulses with partial recovery and mild residual weakness. Over the past 2 years, her right hemiparesis continued to worsen without further remissions or new relapses. She has no personal or family history of neurologic disorders and no toxic exposures.

On examination, cranial nerves were intact except for a right Babinski sign. Motor strength was 4/5 in the right upper and lower limbs, with a limping gait; the left side was normal.

Brain MRI (3D T2 FLAIR) showed no signal abnormalities. Cervical-spine MRI revealed a focal, anterocentral hyperintense lesion at C1–C2 without contrast enhancement; this lesion was unchanged in size, location, and signal intensity compared with the original studies from 2007.

CSF analysis: cell count <5 cells/μL; protein 45 mg/dL; oligoclonal bands absent; IgG index normal. Aquaporin-4 antibody and MOG antibody tests were negative. Blood tests, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver and kidney function, thyroid function, vitamin and mineral levels (including B12), and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), as well as ANA, lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, SSA, SSB, and ANCA, were all within normal limits. CT and FDG-PET imaging excluded neoplasm. Thoracic MRI and digital subtraction angiography of the brain and spinal cord showed no abnormalities.
final_diagnosis_raw: Progressive solitary sclerosis with relapsing attacks
title: First case of progressive solitary sclerosis with relapsing attacks: A 49‐year‐old woman

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat was referred for acute-onset paraplegia of less than 12 hours’ duration. History included hyperthyroidism diagnosed 20 months earlier (elevated total T4), chronic systemic hypertension, and ataxia; management comprised carbimazole, unilateral thyroidectomy, atenolol, and later amlodipine with recurrent elevated urea, phosphorus, and total T4.

Fourteen months after thyroidectomy, the cat had an ataxic gait, gallop rhythm, weight loss, and blood pressure of 208/140 mmHg. Ophthalmic examination then revealed bilateral mydriasis, pupillary reflexes present, bilateral retinal hemorrhage, and left retinal detachment.

At presentation for paraplegia: mental status was depressed; cranial nerves were intact except for absent bilateral menace responses with partially preserved vision; flaccid paraplegia with absent pelvic limb nociception and reflexes; absent cutaneous trunci reflex caudal to the thoracolumbar junction; normal thoracic limb reflexes; absent anal tone and perineal reflexes; overflow urinary incontinence; no tail movement or nociception. Neurolocalisation was multifocal (forebrain, thoracolumbar, lumbosacral). Differentials included vascular, infectious, inflammatory, and metabolic causes.

Heart rate exceeded 200 bpm; systolic blood pressure was 220 mmHg (mean of five readings). Biochemistry showed ALP 31 U/l, hematocrit 24.8%, potassium 2.6 mmol/l, chloride 130 mmol/l. Cardiac ultrasound revealed unclassified cardiomyopathy with biventricular dilation, mild left ventricular hypertrophy, moderate left atrial dilation, and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, which resolved when systolic blood pressure was reduced to 170 mmHg via up-titration of amlodipine.

MRI of the thoracolumbar spine (0.3 T) before and after gadolinium depicted a heterogeneous, ill-defined intramedullary area extending from T12 to L5, isointense on T1-weighted and hyperintense on T2-weighted and STIR images, with no contrast enhancement.
title: Ascending haemorrhagic myelomalacia associated with systemic hypertension in a hyperthyroid cat

case_prompt:
A 9-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of nontraumatic leg pain, worse on the left, and progressive difficulty ambulating. Initial radiographs of the left knee showed a benign nonossifying fibroma in the proximal tibial metadiaphysis without fracture or effusion; he was advised rest and acetaminophen. Three days later, he returned unable to walk, with posterior left knee pain; ultrasound of the left popliteal fossa demonstrated an ill-defined fluid collection with overlying soft-tissue swelling but no joint effusion. He also reported vague right leg and chest-wall pain and was transferred for further evaluation.

On arrival, he was afebrile, in no acute distress, but refused to ambulate due to pain posterior to the left knee. Height was 140 cm (84th percentile) and weight 40.6 kg (95th). Laboratory studies revealed microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 72.5 fL), mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.0 × 10^9/L with left shift), and elevated C-reactive protein (16.8 mg/L); the WBC count normalized on repeat. The clinical differential diagnosis included septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, ruptured Baker’s cyst, osteoid osteoma, and malignancy. An MRI of the knees was performed using T1 and T2 fat-saturated sequences.

MRI demonstrated confluent T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense signal in the metaphyses of the left distal femur and proximal tibia; extensive T2 hyperintense signal infiltrated the popliteal fossa, calf muscles (especially at myotendinous junctions), and subcutaneous tissues. An extended field-of-view study including the contralateral leg and proximal hips revealed symmetric metaphyseal marrow abnormalities in both distal femora and proximal tibiae, with milder changes in proximal femora. Gadolinium was not administered due to the symmetry of the marrow abnormalities indicating a systemic process rather than a focal lesion.
title: Pediatric scurvy MRI appearance

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old Caucasian woman with refractory hypertension underwent abdominal ultrasonography to exclude renal artery stenosis. She was asymptomatic with no abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, or other complaints. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including liver enzymes and blood counts, were within normal limits.

Gray-scale sonography demonstrated a 2 cm well-defined, solid, hypoechoic lesion in segment V of an otherwise homogeneous liver. Color Doppler ultrasound showed peripheral flow signals in the lesion. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound with SonoVue revealed marked homogeneous hyperenhancement in the arterial phase (28 seconds after injection), persistent isoenhancement during the portal venous phase, and mild central washout with a rim of enhancement in the late parenchymal phase.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a 2 cm lesion with a strongly accentuated rim in the early arterial phase and isoenhancement in the portal venous phase; no other liver lesions were seen. Chest CT revealed a 6 mm right lung nodule, reported as most consistent with a small granuloma. Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopies were normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
title: Hepatic perivascular epithelioid cell tumor (PEComa): contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) characteristics—a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old unmarried man with a known history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency since childhood presented with a 13-year history of insidious onset psychiatric illness characterized by a continuous course with multiple exacerbations. The most recent exacerbation lasted six weeks prior to admission. His symptoms included:  
• Muttering to himself and unprovoked aggression toward family members.  
• Irritability and over-talkativeness with pressured speech.  
• Delusional beliefs that rays from the sun and moon were entering his brain, causing him to become violent.  
• Beliefs that planets Mars and Saturn were inserting and removing thoughts against his will, causing transient blanking of his mind.  
• Auditory hallucinations: hearing voices of Pakistani troops threatening to kill him and destroy his nation.  
• Grandiose delusions of possessing special healing powers.  
• Behavior changes during exacerbations: unplanned charitable donations of shop inventory and income, excessive smoking, decreased sleep (by ~3 hours), and increased appetite.  

He had never been asymptomatic, though symptom severity fluctuated with treatment trials. He had three prior psychiatric admissions and trials of three classes of antipsychotics and mood stabilizers with only partial improvement. There was a family history of psychotic illness in his mother and two elder sisters. Developmental history and premorbid temperament were unremarkable.  

On examination, there was black discoloration of the upper and lower gingiva; all other physical findings were normal. Mental status examination revealed increased psychomotor activity, decreased reaction time, pressured speech, euphoric affect, delusions of persecution, control, grandiosity, thought insertion and withdrawal, second- and third-person auditory hallucinations, impaired judgment, and poor insight.  

Laboratory studies were within normal limits: hemoglobin 14 g/dL, hematocrit 40.6%, MCV 98.6 fl, MCH 32.4 pg, MCHC 32.9 g/dL, serum bilirubin 0.88 mg/dL, and no red blood cells detected on urinalysis.
title: Glucose-6 Phosphate Dehydrogenase Deficiency and Psychotic Illness

case_prompt:
A 51-year-old woman presented with recurrent episodes of nonmassive hemoptysis (20–30 mL of fresh blood per event) since 2020. She denied fever, weight loss, history of tuberculosis exposure, and smoking. Two years earlier, she was treated for bacterial pneumonia; bronchoalveolar lavage at that time showed no evidence of infection. After being lost to follow-up, she returned with recurrent hemoptysis. 

Physical examination was unremarkable. Chest radiographs showed irregular ground-glass opacities in the anterior aspect of the left lower lung zone, with a silhouette sign along the left heart border. Contrast-enhanced chest CT angiography demonstrated a uniform consolidation in the inferior lingular segment of the left upper lobe. Maximal intensity projection and three-dimensional volume-rendered images revealed arterial branches arising from the left gastric artery supplying the lesion and venous drainage into the left superior pulmonary vein.
title: Lingular intralobar pulmonary sequestration supplied by the left inferior phrenic artery arising from the left gastric artery – A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old Asian American woman presented with right-sided flank pain of recent onset. She had no other complaints and a normal physical examination. Laboratory studies revealed elevated liver enzymes, including alkaline phosphatase and aspartate aminotransferase. 

An abdominal ultrasound showed a 1.5-cm hypodense lesion in the left lobe of the liver with associated porta hepatis lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 1.8 × 1.4-cm hypodense mass in the left lateral section of the liver with minimal peripheral enhancement. MRI of the liver revealed a lesion that was T1 hypointense and T2 mildly hyperintense with indeterminate enhancement. No other abdominal abnormalities were identified.

A CT-guided biopsy of the lesion showed nodular collections of polyclonal T and B lymphocytes and plasma cells. Serum tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA 19-9) were within normal limits, and viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Serum antimitochondrial antibody levels were normal. Upper and lower endoscopies were unremarkable. 

Given the imaging findings and an indeterminate percutaneous biopsy, she was referred for evaluation in a hepatobiliary high-risk clinic, where a laparoscopic left lateral sectionectomy was recommended.
title: Intrahepatic Reactive Lymphoid Hyperplasia: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 60-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes presented with acute low back pain radiating bilaterally to the legs, progressing over several days to difficulty ambulating. He was initially treated for a presumed urinary tract infection without relief and later received a spinal steroid injection. Two weeks after onset, he developed urinary incontinence and bilateral leg paralysis. During a 2-week hospitalization, CT pulmonary angiography diagnosed a pulmonary embolism. MRI of the brain and spine revealed abnormal foci of enhancement in the lumbar spine and at T12. A skeletal survey was negative, and a CT-guided bone marrow biopsy showed no malignancy. Lumbar puncture demonstrated 13 white blood cells/mm3 (82% lymphocytes), protein 132 mg/dL, and negative PCR testing for herpes simplex virus and West Nile virus. One day of intravenous steroids improved pain but not weakness; steroids were stopped. He then developed bowel incontinence and was treated with IV immunoglobulin and transferred for further evaluation. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and scrotal ultrasound showed no solid tumor. Repeat spinal MRI showed cauda equina nerve root enhancement. Electromyography revealed an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Laboratory studies were notable for an ACE level of 83 U/L, ANA 1:160 speckled, and LDH 2722 IU/L. A second lumbar puncture showed normalized cell counts; CSF cytology and flow cytometry were negative for malignancy. He underwent plasma exchange for presumed acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy without improvement, and a repeat MRI showed a new 3-cm T2 hyperintense focus in the lower lumbar cord with worsening cauda equina enhancement, raising concern for neurosarcoidosis. He received high-dose methylprednisolone and plasmapheresis, with temporary improvement, then was discharged on prednisone. Outpatient PET revealed patchy thoracolumbar marrow uptake with focal increased uptake at the left lateral aspect of L2. Despite increased prednisone and gabapentin, his lower extremity strength declined, requiring a wheelchair, and bowel and bladder dysfunction persisted. A third spinal MRI showed new hyperintense lesions in the thoracic cord, diffuse paraspinal myositis, and leptomeningeal enhancement. After another course of methylprednisolone with mild relief, a muscle biopsy of the left vastus lateralis showed type 2 myofiber atrophy without overt myopathic features or granulomatous inflammation.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title:
Intravascular Large B-Cell Lymphoma Presenting as Acute Axonal
Polyneuropathy: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old Moroccan woman presented with an 8-week history of symmetric polyarthralgia and swelling involving the proximal interphalangeal joints, metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, knees, and ankles. She denied respiratory symptoms, gastrointestinal complaints, fever, or other constitutional signs. Past medical and family histories were unremarkable, and prior treatment with corticosteroids and NSAIDs for 1 month produced no relief.

On examination, temperature was 37°C, heart rate 70/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and blood pressure 120/10 mmHg. Joints were warm, swollen, and tender with restricted movement. No axial arthritis, enthesopathy, or other systemic findings were noted.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 7.6 g/dl, MCV 68 fl, normal leukocyte and platelet counts, C-reactive protein 126 mg/l, ESR 100 mm/h, polyclonal increase in beta and gamma globulins, elevated IgA, IgG, and IgM, ferritin 7 ng/ml, and vitamin D 10 ng/ml. Liver, renal, electrolyte, albumin, total protein, LDH, glucose, and thyroid function tests were normal.

Arthrocentesis of the left knee yielded an inflammatory, sterile fluid rich in white blood cells without microcrystals. Streptolysin O antibody titers and procalcitonin levels were normal. Cultures of blood, urine, and stool and serologic tests for hepatitis B and C, syphilis, HIV, and CMV were all negative. Antinuclear antibodies, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were all negative. HLA-B27 testing was negative.

Ultrasound of the hands showed synovitis without erosions. Radiographs of the hands, knees, ankles, spine, and sacroiliac joints were normal, and MRI of the sacroiliac joints was unremarkable. Echocardiography, electrocardiogram, and abdominal–pelvic ultrasound were normal.
title: Isolated polyarthritis revealing celiac disease: A case report

case_prompt: A 45-year-old farmer presented with a 1-week history of progressive tingling and weakness in both lower limbs and several days of difficulty with urination. He denied trauma, back pain, recent infections, vaccinations, or foreign travel. On examination, there was symmetric lower-limb paresis (MRC grade 4/5, more pronounced proximally), sensory loss to all modalities below the T10 dermatome, brisk deep-tendon reflexes in the legs, and bilateral Babinski signs. Over the next 2 days, he progressed to complete paraplegia, anesthesia of the lower limbs, and loss of bladder and bowel control. Spinal MRI showed an intramedullary T2-weighted hyperintensity from T4 to T10 without contrast enhancement. Brain MRI revealed multiple T2-weighted hyperintense lesions, the largest posterior to the left lateral ventricle; the supratentorial lesions enhanced with contrast, whereas the pontine lesion did not. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 25 leukocytes/μL (87% lymphocytes, 9% eosinophils), protein 33 mg/dL, glucose 62 mg/dL, a normal IgG index (0.62), and no oligoclonal bands. Peripheral blood eosinophils were elevated at 21% (total WBC count 8,300/mm3). C-reactive protein and routine biochemistry were normal. Ophthalmologic examination and thoracic and abdominal CT scans were also normal.
title: Toxocariasis Presenting as Encephalomyelitis

case_prompt:
A 4.7-year-old boy was evaluated for persistent elevations of liver enzymes and an episode of macrohematuria. At age 2, he had undergone CT and brain MRI for a scalp swelling; imaging showed craniolacunia and enlarged subarachnoid spaces. Routine blood tests then revealed AST 104 U/L and ALT 203 U/L. Autoimmune hepatitis was excluded since autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA, AMA-M2, M2-3E, Sp100, PML, gp210, LKM-1, LC-1, ALS/LP, Ro-52) were negative.

At age 4.6, he presented with gross hematuria. Laboratory tests showed AST 116 U/L, ALT 207 U/L, GGT 112 U/L, total bilirubin 0.52 mg/dL, ceruloplasmin 21.9 mg/dL (normal 20–60), and total serum copper 71 µg/dL (normal 80–155). Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatomegaly with hyperechoic parenchyma, no focal lesions or biliary tract abnormalities, and a 4 mm calculus in a left renal calyx.

When seen at our center at age 4.7, blood tests confirmed elevated transaminases; ceruloplasmin was 19 mg/dL. Hemoglobin, ferritin, serum iron, transferrin, and transferrin saturation were within or slightly above normal age ranges. Celiac antibodies and fecal calprotectin were negative, and lysosomal acid lipase activity was normal. An echo-guided liver biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with portal, interface, and lobular inflammation, portal-periportal fibrosis (Ishak 3, METAVIR F2), and severe panlobular micro- and macrovesicular steatosis, with no iron deposition. Intrahepatic copper was 637 µg/g (normal 0–200). A 24-hour urinary collection demonstrated copper excretion of 206 µg/24 h (normal < 40 µg/24 h).
title: Early Onset of Wilson's Disease and Possible Role of Disease-Modifying Genes: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
• A 62-year-old housewife presented with a four-month history of breathlessness on exertion. She denied drug or environmental inhalational exposures, chest pain, palpitations, ankle swelling, syncope, gastrointestinal symptoms, smoking, or alcohol use.  
• Past medical records revealed no previous clubbing or major illness. Menopause at age 45; two full-term vaginal deliveries; no family history of clubbing.  
• On examination: pulse 80/min, regular; respiratory rate 15/min; blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg; afebrile; SpO₂ 98–100% on room air. Bulbous enlargement of all toes bilaterally; fingernails unaffected. No swelling or skin changes at wrists or ankles. Chest auscultation disclosed bilateral fine end-inspiratory crepitations at the lung bases.  
• Laboratory tests: hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL; WBC 9400/mm³ (61% neutrophils); ESR 12 mm/h; normal serum chemistries; thyroid and liver function normal; ANA and rheumatoid factor negative; HIV negative.  
• Microbiology: sputum AFB smear negative; blood and sputum cultures sterile.  
• Pulmonary function testing: restrictive pattern.  
• Chest radiograph showed basal haziness. HRCT demonstrated basal interstitial thickening and honeycombing. Contrast CT of chest and abdomen showed no thoracic or abdominal aortic aneurysm.  
• Additional studies: abdominal ultrasound, fiberoptic bronchoscopy, and ECG were unremarkable; transthoracic and contrast echocardiography revealed no intracardiac shunt or pulmonary arteriovenous fistula.  
• Examination of her children and siblings revealed no clubbing.
title: Idiopathic Clubbing Confined to Lower Limb Digits and Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis: An Unusual Association

case_prompt: A 37-year-old woman with clinical stage 3A, grade 3, triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast received neoadjuvant carboplatin, paclitaxel, and pembrolizumab, with excellent clinical and radiologic response. She underwent bilateral skin-sparing mastectomies and axillary nodal staging with delayed reconstruction. Her immediate postoperative course was unremarkable until postoperative day 6 (POD 6), when she developed fever and cloudy drain output. Empiric trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole was started; cultures of the drain fluid grew pan-sensitive Staphylococcus lugdunensis. On POD 9, she was admitted with a large bulla, erythema at the right breast incision site, and ongoing drainage. Intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin–tazobactam were begun. Concern for an undrained infectious collection prompted surgical debridement and washout on POD 10, which revealed full-thickness skin necrosis beneath the bulla but no purulent or retained fluid. The wound was debrided to healthy tissue and closed primarily. Over the next 48 hours, she remained febrile with rising leukocytosis despite switching antibiotics to piperacillin–tazobactam and linezolid; repeat blood and wound cultures were negative. By POD 12, she developed progressive induration, wound breakdown, and skin necrosis, leading to a punch biopsy.
title: Postsurgical pyoderma gangrenosum after mastectomy with a familial component

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old woman presented with right upper quadrant discomfort and epigastric pain. She was a smoker with treated type 2 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, she had pallor, right upper quadrant tenderness, and palpable hepatomegaly.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed two hypoechoic liver masses (60×75 mm in segment VII and 60×55 mm in the hilum). CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed:  
• Hepatomegaly (24 cm)  
• A 53×77 mm mass infiltrating the head of the pancreas and duodenum, extending to the liver hilum  
• A 75×70 mm hypodense lesion in segment VII with contrast enhancement  
• Significant gallbladder dilatation without wall thickening  
• A 28×44 mm asymmetrical hyperperfused nodule adherent to the anterior bladder wall  
Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy demonstrated poorly differentiated carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CK20, focally positive for CK7, and negative for GATA3, TTF-1, Pax-8, and Hep-Par 1. Serum CA-125, CEA, AFP, and CA19-9 were within normal limits. Cystoscopy with curettage of the bladder dome nodule was performed to obtain tissue for diagnosis.
title: Urachal carcinoma initially presenting only as a liver metastasis, a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge: first case in literature

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man was admitted for management of an oropharyngeal mass, with a 2-month history of progressive dysphagia. He had a history of total laryngectomy and tracheostomy with chemoradiation 15 years earlier for laryngeal carcinoma, which was considered cured. He was breathing via tracheostomy and otherwise independent. He had quit smoking 15 years prior and took no medications. On admission, he was hemodynamically stable, with difficulty swallowing due to the mass. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia and serum sodium 128 mEq/L. ECG revealed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 70 bpm. An open gastrostomy was performed on hospital day 3 without immediate complications. Enteral feeding began postoperatively.

On day 8, he became intermittently confused and less responsive, though vital signs remained within normal limits. Examination showed facial puffiness and dry skin. Labs revealed TSH 15.056 mIU/L, free T4 0.04 ng/dL, undetectable free T3, and morning cortisol 19 µg/dL. Primary hypothyroidism was diagnosed, and oral levothyroxine 25 µg/day was started via gastrostomy.

Chemoradiation began on day 14. By day 19, free T4 remained 0.04 ng/dL, and confusion persisted. Sodium fell further to 125 mEq/L, and he developed hypoglycemia requiring dextrose. LT4 was given on an empty stomach with enhanced nutritional support, but his mental status did not improve.

On day 28, he was unarousable to voice. Temperature was 33.4°C, heart rate 40 bpm and irregular, blood pressure 80/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 12 bpm. Plasma glucose was 56 mg/dL, CK-MB 182 U/L, troponin T 102 ng/L. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 40 bpm without ischemic changes. Echocardiography demonstrated global hypokinesia without regional wall-motion abnormalities and a small pericardial effusion. Chest radiograph revealed right upper lung haziness.
title: Split high‐dose oral levothyroxine treatment as a successful therapy option in myxedema coma

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old African American woman with a more than 10-year history of Sjögren’s syndrome treated with corticosteroids was admitted with sudden onset chest pain. Computed tomography of the chest revealed a large anterior mediastinal mass and several enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes; the liver and spleen were unremarkable. HIV serology was negative. At surgery, the mass was found to extend from the right side of midline into the left chest, adhering to the pericardium and left pleura and involving the phrenic nerve; the mass and adjacent lymph nodes were excised. Permanent histologic sections were reported as lymphocyte-predominant thymoma and benign reactive lymph nodes. The postoperative course was uneventful.

Twelve months later, she reported night sweats, low-grade fever, flu-like symptoms, green sputum production, a 14-lb weight loss, and exertional dyspnea. Follow‐up CT showed multiple enlarged lymph nodes throughout the chest and upper abdomen, new noncalcified pulmonary nodules, and bilateral pulmonary consolidation.
final_diagnosis_raw: T cell/histiocyte-rich large B cell lymphoma
title: T Cell/Histiocyte-Rich Large B Cell Lymphoma of the Thymus: A Diagnostic Pitfall

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man presented with progressive left-sided flank pain of several years’ duration. The pain was mild, lasted only a few minutes per episode, did not radiate, and was not associated with voiding or gastrointestinal symptoms. He also reported intermittent hematuria without pain. He had undergone left varicocele embolization 11 years earlier with an uneventful recovery.

He had no significant medical history, and his family history was unremarkable. He denied tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. On examination, there was no flank tenderness or abdominal distention. Laboratory investigations, including renal function tests and urinalysis, were within normal limits.

A plain abdominal radiograph (KUB) showed bilateral coils consistent with his prior varicocele embolization. Renal ultrasonography demonstrated moderate left hydronephrosis and hydroureter, with a dilated pelvicalyceal system on the left.
title: Migration of varicocele coil leading to ureteral obstruction and hydronephrosis: A case report

case_prompt: A 50-year-old man presented with 2 months of mild periumbilical pain. His medical history was notable for poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and pulmonary tuberculosis treated 10 years earlier. On examination, vital signs were stable and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, leukocyte count 10.5 × 10^3/mm^3 with an absolute eosinophil count of 1,780/mm^3; renal and liver function tests were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a space-occupying lesion in the right iliac fossa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed diffuse symmetric wall thickening of the cecum, proximal ascending colon, appendiceal base, and terminal ileum with significant enhancement and focal nonenhancing areas, along with several mesenteric lymph nodes up to 11 mm in diameter. Colonoscopy revealed circumferential ulcers with thickened, edematous folds in the cecum and ascending colon, raising suspicion for malignancy. Given his tuberculosis history, colonic TB was considered, but colonoscopic biopsy did not reveal malignant cells or tubercular granulomas. Special staining of the biopsy demonstrated fungal hyphae with tissue reaction, primarily suggestive of mucormycosis.
title: Basidiobolomycosis of Right Colon Mimicking as Carcinoma of Colon

case_prompt:
A 48-year-old woman was brought to the hospital after an episode of loss of consciousness. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, vital signs were stable, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 35 mm mass in the right posterior mediastinum at the level of T7–T8. The mass showed heterogeneous enhancement, with no apparent extension into surrounding structures or into the spinal canal. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction identified a feeding vessel arising from the right eighth intercostal artery supplying the mass. 

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Within the mass, there was a localized area of high signal on T1-weighted images, suggesting a fatty component. 

Preoperatively, the differential diagnosis included schwannoma, hemangioma, or lipoma. Given the evidence of hypervascularity, preoperative embolization of the feeding intercostal artery was planned to reduce intraoperative bleeding risk, followed by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical resection.
title: Primary posterior mediastinal angiolipoma: a case report

case_prompt: A 26-year-old white woman presented with a 2-week history of fever, fatigue, migratory arthralgias, and four enlarging left posterior cervical lymph nodes. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 2.0×10^3/mm^3 (lymphocytes 900/μL, granulocytes 1000/μL), hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, mean cell volume 91.5 fL, and platelet count 100,000/μL. HIV-1 and ‑2 screening tests were non-reactive; anti–double-stranded DNA and anti-nuclear antibodies were negative. Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus serologies were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed normal cytogenetics (46,XX) without evidence of malignancy. Chest imaging demonstrated bibasilar infiltrates that resolved with antibiotics. Abdominal CT without contrast revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly and portal venous dilation. PET/CT showed hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy in bilateral cervical and left supraclavicular regions (SUV max 3.7–9.8) with no other sites of uptake.
journal: Mediterranean Journal of Hematology and Infectious Diseases
title: Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease in the Unites States: Three Case Reports and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man with end-stage renal disease of unknown etiology underwent deceased-donor kidney transplantation. Induction immunosuppression consisted of rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin and methylprednisolone; maintenance therapy included mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and prednisolone. The surgery was prolonged with significant hemorrhage and required blood transfusions and inotropic support. The patient remained anuric postoperatively; renal Doppler ultrasound showed patent arterial flow without obstruction. Tacrolimus trough levels were within target range.

On day 6, a biopsy showed acute tubular injury; diuresis began by day 10. On day 16, a urinary leak led to re-exploration; the accessory renal artery was thrombosed and the distal ureter necrotic. The necrotic tissue demonstrated only ischemic necrosis without rejection. Urine output recovered.

By day 28, the patient developed fever spikes and rising creatinine. Tacrolimus levels, blood counts, peripheral smear, and LDH were unremarkable. He received broad-spectrum antibiotics. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria; graft ultrasound was unremarkable. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. With concerns for graft pyelonephritis or antibody-mediated rejection, a second allograft biopsy was performed on day 34. Histologic examination revealed:
  • Fibrin thrombi within glomerular capillaries  
  • Dense sheets of neutrophils, macrophages, and lymphocytes with microabscess formation and tubular destruction  
  • Occasional tubular epithelial cells with hyperchromatic, smudged nuclei  
  • Focal cortical necrosis and extensive interstitial hemorrhage  
  • No evidence of vascular inflammation  
  • C4d staining negative  
These features raised suspicion for a viral etiology.
title: Adenovirus-Associated Thrombotic Microangiopathy and Necrotizing Interstitial Nephritis in a Renal Transplant Recipient: A Case Report and Review

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old Hispanic woman was admitted with a 3-day history of bluish-black discoloration and pain of the left second toe. She reported 2 months of intermittent claudication in the same limb, arthralgias involving proximal interphalangeal joints, shoulders, elbows, and knees with morning stiffness, and foamy urine. She denied trauma.  
Her medical history included hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, and aortoiliac atherosclerosis; she took amlodipine, captopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and gemfibrozil.  
On examination, the left second toe was necrotic, tender, and had delayed capillary refill, but pedal pulses were palpable bilaterally. Skin examination revealed livedo reticularis and scattered brown macules on the thighs; no ulcers were seen.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12 g/dL, hematocrit 37%, leukocytes 10 200/mm³ (76% neutrophils), platelets 564 000/mm³, creatinine 1.64 mg/dL, BUN 25 mg/dL, glucose 121 mg/dL, PT 14.7 s (INR 1.03), PTT 29/28.5 s, ESR 2 mm/h, and CRP 1.2 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed 300 mg/dL proteinuria, 6 RBCs/hpf, 4 WBCs/hpf, and RBC casts.  
Arterial and venous Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated patent vessels. Given the digital ischemia with renal findings, small-vessel vasculitis was suspected, and methylprednisolone pulses were initiated. Renal and skin biopsies were ordered, and serum protein electrophoresis was obtained.  
Serum protein electrophoresis did not show monoclonal spikes or any other abnormality, and despite immunosuppressive therapy, her condition worsened with progressive kidney injury requiring hemodialysis.
title: Multiple Myeloma Mimicking a Small Vessel Vasculitis Presentation

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old Caucasian man with a history of mantle cell lymphoma in remission after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant 5 years earlier presented with progressive renal failure. His post-transplant course was complicated by hypogammaglobulinemia managed with IVIG, chronic cutaneous graft-versus-host disease manifesting as diffuse scleroderma (now limited to the lower extremities on ibrutinib), and recurrent respiratory infections. His current medications included mycophenolate mofetil, sirolimus, acyclovir, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and prednisone.

Over the past year, his creatinine rose from a baseline of 1.0 mg/dL to 4.84 mg/dL, accompanied by fatigue and worsening dyspnea. On admission, he appeared chronically ill; examination was notable only for skin thickening and mottling of the lower extremities. Laboratory studies revealed hyperkalemia (5.7 mmol/L), metabolic acidosis, moderate to large hemoglobin on urine dipstick with >50 RBCs per high-power field, and only trace proteinuria. Medications potentially nephrotoxic were held. Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative; ANA <1:80; C3 and C4 were normal; ANCA was undetectable.

Quantitative viral studies showed BK virus in blood (>1,000,000 copies/mL) and in urine (>390,000,000 copies/mL).
title: Native kidney BK nephropathy: A case report

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman presented with insidious onset of right leg radicular pain without numbness, tingling, weakness, or bladder/bowel symptoms. Physical examination showed a positive right straight-leg–raise test at 45° (left at 70°). Lumbosacral MRI demonstrated a right L4–L5 lateral disc herniation with extrusion. After partial relief with conservative management, she underwent right L4–L5 hemilaminotomy and removal of extruded disc material, with immediate postoperative pain relief.

Two weeks after discharge, she experienced new, constant burning pain in the left pelvic region, with sharp, shooting pain in the left leg radiating in multiple trajectories without a specific dermatomal distribution. The pain worsened while sitting and was not aggravated by coughing or sneezing. On examination, there was no infection or dehiscence of the lumbar surgical scar. She had an antalgic, waddling gait and a significant Tinel sign over the left gluteal region at the sciatic nerve. The straight-leg–raise test was negative in supine, sitting, and prone positions. Spinal range of motion was full without pain; muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes were normal. The piriformis stretch test was significantly positive and reproduced her pain. Repeat lumbosacral MRI showed only postoperative changes without disc herniation.

Over the next weeks, she underwent a multimodality pain regimen (antiepileptic and antidepressant medications, muscle relaxant, short-acting narcotics, and physical therapy) without significant relief. A diagnostic ultrasound-guided injection of 5 cc 1% lidocaine into the left piriformis muscle produced immediate pain relief, and a second injection provided again only a short course of relief.
title: Acute Sciatic Neuritis following Lumbar Laminectomy

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 7.2%) presented with a one-month history of sudden, painless decreased vision, metamorphopsia, and color vision deficits in the left eye. Visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg OU. Examination of the left eye revealed a relative afferent pupillary defect, blurred optic nerve margin, creamy chorioretinal infiltration around the optic disc, and mild macular edema; the right eye examination was unremarkable. The patient denied drug use, smoking, or recent travel. 

Laboratory testing showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 28 mm/hr; results were normal for CBC, CRP, ANA, RF, ACE, viral hepatitis serologies, lysozyme, Histoplasma antibody, syphilis serology, HLA-B27, HIV, Bartonella serology, ANCA, QuantiFERON, and TSH. Chest radiograph was normal; chest CT with contrast demonstrated calcified mediastinal lymph nodes, but endobronchial ultrasound biopsy was nondiagnostic. MRI of the brain and orbits with gadolinium enhancement showed soft-tissue abnormality with enhancement in the left orbital apex involving extraocular muscles, anterior Meckel’s cave, and lateral cavernous sinus; dural-based lesions along the right sphenoid wing and inferior frontal convexity with cortical erosion; enhancement of the calvarium; and subtle leptomeningeal enhancement along the ventral pons.

Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 11 cm H2O; CSF analysis showed 45 WBC/µL (88% lymphocytes), protein 174 mg/dL, and glucose 59 mg/dL. CSF complement fixation (CF) for Coccidioides immitis was positive at a titer of 1:2; culture was negative. Flow cytometry of CSF excluded lymphoma. 

On this basis, a tentative diagnosis of coccidioidal meningitis was made, and fluconazole 800 mg daily was initiated; it was later changed to posaconazole 100 mg three times daily due to intolerance. Three months later, the patient had mild improvement in vision (20/25 OS), negative Coccidioides antibodies in CSF and blood, and stable MRI findings. He was maintained on posaconazole 100 mg twice daily.
title: Neurosarcoidosis, Coccidioidomycosis, or Both!

case_prompt:
A 73-year-old man, a retired farmer, was referred for evaluation of a 6-month history of progressive chest tightness, exertional shortness of breath and intermittent low-grade fevers (maximum 37.5 °C) without a clear pattern. He denied cough, hemoptysis or weight loss. He had smoked 20 cigarettes per day for 60 years but stopped 6 months ago. He had no known family history of hereditary disease. 

On admission, his respiratory rate was slightly elevated; other vital signs were within normal limits. Blood gas analysis showed PaO₂ 81 mmHg, PaCO₂ 34 mmHg, pH 7.44. Laboratory results revealed a leukocyte count of 9.82×10⁹/L, lymphocytes 2.62×10⁹/L, neutrophils 65.6%, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 60 mm/h and C-reactive protein 36.2 mg/L. Blood glucose and procalcitonin were 6.91 mmol/L and 0.1 ng/mL, respectively. Sputum smear demonstrated a few gram-positive cocci; throat swabs were negative for influenza A/B and cytomegalovirus.

Pulmonary function testing revealed FEV₁/FVC 73.6% and DLCO 68.2% of predicted, indicating small-airway dysfunction and impaired diffusion. Chest CT showed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities with well-defined subpleural margins, scattered cystic cavities, and a solitary solid nodule in the left lower lobe.

Given the imaging and clinical presentation, noninfectious diffuse cystic lung diseases—including PLCH, LIP, BHD syndrome and DIP—were considered. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) analysis and transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) were performed. BALF cultures were negative for pathogens. Histopathology of the biopsy revealed mildly thickened alveolar septa with sparse lymphocytes and neutrophils in the interstitium and aggregates of macrophages filling the alveolar spaces.
title: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia: A case report

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of paroxysmal periumbilical abdominal pain that was worse at night. He had no nausea, vomiting or other gastrointestinal symptoms and no significant past medical history. On examination, vital signs were normal and there were no abdominal masses or organomegaly.  
Complete blood count, lipase, amylase, liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Plasma and urine catecholamine and metanephrine levels, aldosterone–renin ratio, carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 concentrations were all normal.  
Multidetector computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a single, well-defined, heterogeneous, hypodense ovoid mass measuring 45 × 28 × 80 mm in the left suprarenal region, with no septations, calcification at the margin, and no enhancement after contrast administration.
journal: The Journal of International Medical Research
title: A retroperitoneal bronchogenic cyst clinically mimicking an adrenal mass: three case reports and a literature review

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old man was referred for evaluation of recurrent bacterial meningitis. He first presented at age 7 with culture-proven meningitis and was found to have otitis media with effusion in the left ear. Persistent otorrhea after myringotomy prompted CT, which showed a left-sided type I incomplete partition deformity and a congenital oval window defect. He underwent canal-wall-down mastoidectomy and repair of the oval window defect, with two additional repairs after meningitis recurrences at ages 10 and 11. Each surgery localized CSF leaks, once at the oval window and once at the tegmen tympani, with subsequent pneumococcal vaccination.

On the current admission, he had fever, headache, and neck stiffness but no focal neurologic deficits; Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs were negative. Otoscopic examination of the left ear revealed an intact tympanic membrane and a large collection of fluid pulsating in the mastoid cavity and middle ear. There was no vestibular deficit, and nasoendoscopy showed no frank fluid draining from the left Eustachian tube. Audiometry revealed profound left hearing loss with normal right-sided hearing.

He was started empirically on ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir. A lumbar puncture on hospital day 3 showed low glucose and high opening pressure consistent with bacterial meningitis, although cultures were negative. High-resolution CT of the temporal bones showed a widened left oval window and an absent stapes footplate with complete opacification of the middle ear and mastoid; the tegmen tympani appeared intact. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated fluid signals in the middle ear and mastoid that matched signals in the internal acoustic meatus and vestibule, along with an expanded internal acoustic meatus and distended Eustachian tube filled with similar fluid signal.
title: Recurrent Meningitis Following Previous Repair of Congenital Oval Window Defect

case_prompt: A 39-year-old gravida 1, para 1 woman presented with a positive home pregnancy test. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed no intrauterine gestational sac and a cystic mass in the extrauterine space. Initial serum β-HCG was 142.4 mIU/mL. MRI demonstrated a 7 cm cystic mass extending from the anterior wall of the lower uterine segment into the pelvic cavity, with high signal intensity on both T2- and T1-weighted images, suggestive of subacute hemorrhage. Hysteroscopy and laparoscopy revealed a cystic mass containing old hemorrhagic material in the left paracervical retroperitoneal space, with a fistulous tract from the lower uterine cavity into the mass and otherwise normal adnexa. Pathologic examination of the resected tissue showed necrotic tissue, hemorrhagic material, and decidua without definitive diagnosis. On postoperative day 21, serum β-HCG was 304.6 mIU/mL, and persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia was diagnosed; weekly methotrexate was administered for 8 weeks. By postoperative day 88, β-HCG remained elevated at 119.8 mIU/mL. On referral, β-HCG was 132.9 mIU/mL, MRI showed a 21 × 12 × 10 mm mass in the left myometrial portion of the lower uterus, slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging, and CT revealed no metastatic disease.
title: Characteristics of Epithelioid Trophoblastic Tumor: Endoscopic and Magnetic Resonance Imaging Findings

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of right flank pain, dysuria, urinary urgency and frequency, and occasional hematuria, associated with fever, chills, and rigors. Over the preceding 3 months, he had a 40-pound weight loss, drenching night sweats, and intermittent low-grade fevers. His history was notable for nephrolithiasis treated conservatively 3 weeks earlier and multiple past episodes of renal colic treated with lithotripsy. He was a 30 pack-year smoker and drank alcohol occasionally.
