On arrival, his blood pressure was 78/49 mmHg (MAP 59 mmHg), temperature 97.3°F, heart rate 80 beats/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98–99% on room air. Hypotension did not improve after 3 L of normal saline. He was diagnosed with urosepsis and admitted to the ICU, where he received norepinephrine and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Examination showed mild pallor, no icterus or edema, and right costovertebral angle tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (MCV 77.6 fL), WBC 5.1 k/µL (77% neutrophils), alkaline phosphatase 212 U/L, ALT 80 U/L, AST 96 U/L, total protein 3.6 g/dL, albumin 1.5 g/dL. Urinalysis showed 1+ blood, protein 30, glucose 50; microscopy revealed 109 RBC and 12 WBC. A random cortisol level was 182.6 mg/dL. Two sets of blood and urine cultures remained negative after 5 days.

CT of the abdomen demonstrated numerous ill-defined hepatic lesions not present on a CT performed 3 weeks earlier, along with a staghorn calculus without obstruction or abscess. After two days of pressor support, his MAP rose above 70 mmHg, but he had recurrent hypotensive episodes requiring fluid boluses. On hospital day 5 he developed fluid overload treated with intravenous furosemide.

He declined liver biopsy and was discharged with oral levofloxacin. Three days later he returned with acute weakness, fatigue, and a single fever. His temperature was 94.1°F, blood pressure 84/49 mmHg (MAP 60 mmHg), heart rate 59/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and SpO2 97% on room air. Examination was unremarkable. Repeat blood and urine cultures again showed no growth, and he was restarted on vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam.
title: Hypotension Associated with Advanced Hodgkin Lymphoma

case_prompt: A 30-year-old African-American woman, 28 weeks pregnant, with multidrug-resistant HIV infection presented with a 10-year history of asymptomatic hyperpigmentation of the gingiva and vermillion lip. Over the past 3 months—during her current pregnancy—she noticed the areas had darkened and coalesced. She denied pain, bleeding, or ulceration. Her medications included antiretroviral therapy. On examination, there was an asymmetric, ill-defined, 3-cm dark brown to black plaque involving the vermillion and mucosal lip, maxillary gingiva, and adjacent hard palate. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Laboratory evaluation showed a CD4 count of 177 cells per cubic millimeter and an HIV viral load of 624 copies per milliliter.
title: Oral melanoma in a gravid, HIV-positive woman

case_prompt: A 60-year-old man from rural southwestern Tunisia, with a history of an atrioventricular block treated with a pacemaker and type II diabetes for 10 years, presented with epigastric pain and recurrent vomiting over the past 2 years, worsening in the last 3 months. He had no fever or jaundice. Physical examination showed mild upper abdominal tenderness without palpable mass. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis (12 000/dL) and a lipase level five times the upper limit of normal; liver‐function tests were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged pancreas with a 40 mm cystic lesion in the tail and an 8 mm dilated pancreatic duct (Wirsung). A contrast‐enhanced CT scan performed 72 h later confirmed a globally enlarged pancreas with homogeneous enhancement, peripancreatic fat infiltration, three necrotic collections in the lesser sac and splenopancreatic region, an 8 mm dilated Wirsung duct communicating with a 3.7 × 2.5 cm peripherally enhancing cystic lesion in the tail, and moderate intraperitoneal fluid. MRI was not performed due to the pacemaker.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Hydatid cyst of the pancreas revealed by acute pancreatitis: A case report

case_prompt: A 32-year-old woman presented 4 months postpartum with intermittent fevers up to 38.5 °C, malaise, unclear blood loss, and right upper-quadrant flank pain. She had no significant past medical or family history. On exam, her temperature was 38.5 °C; she had right upper-quadrant tenderness without jaundice or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed a normal white blood cell count, C-reactive protein 181 mg/L, AST 31 U/L, ALT 49 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 466 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 424 U/L, and normal bilirubin (6 μmol/L). Serum CA 19-9, α-fetoprotein, hepatitis serologies, and echinococcosis markers were all negative. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a round, encapsulated 8 cm lesion in liver segment IVa/b. A noncontrast CT confirmed the 8 cm liver mass and excluded urolithiasis. Contrast CT and MRI of the upper abdomen demonstrated an 8 cm × 8 cm lesion in segment IVa/b “suspected to be a liver adenoma.” The case was discussed at a multidisciplinary tumor board, and a PET-CT was performed, which “showed the known lesion as a metabolically active tumor resembling an inflammatory pseudotumor of the liver or a malignant tumor of unclear origin.” No other lesions were identified.
title: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor of the liver: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 36-year-old woman with a 10-year history of ileocecal Crohn’s disease in clinical remission on azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) and infliximab (5 mg/kg every eight weeks) presented with a three-month history of painful skin eruptions. She described erythematous, erosive, crusted plaques on the perioral, perinasal, postauricular, and occipital regions that improved within days of each infliximab infusion but flared in the interval between doses. She also noted ill-defined, scaly, erythematous plaques on the trunk, axillae, buttocks, and inguinal regions that paradoxically worsened after each infliximab infusion. Examination revealed marked edema of the vulva and mons pubis with overlying erythema and scaling. Given the concern for metastatic cutaneous Crohn’s disease versus a paradoxical psoriasiform reaction to infliximab, biopsies were obtained from an erosive postauricular plaque and a scaly lumbar lesion.
title: Metastatic Crohn’s disease despite infliximab therapy*

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old nondiabetic white woman presented with intermittent numbness and tingling in all extremities. Four months earlier in Puerto Rico, she had confirmed Zika virus infection (IgM ELISA and plaque-reduction neutralization test positive; RT-PCR negative) with a generalized maculopapular rash, fever, headache, conjunctivitis, arthralgia, and myalgia. Tests for Dengue and Chikungunya viruses were negative, and she had evidence of prior West Nile virus exposure (IgG elevated, IgM negative). Her history included a remote episode of painful genital and oral ulceration of unknown etiology; tests for herpes, syphilis, HIV, tuberculosis, and toxoplasmosis were negative.

She denied visual symptoms. Uncorrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left. Confrontation visual fields, pupillary responses, anterior segment examination, and intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. Slit-lamp ophthalmoscopy of the right eye revealed microaneurysms in the macula. Infrared reflectance imaging demonstrated a hyporeflective lesion in the macula. Fundus fluorescein angiography showed perifoveal microaneurysms in the inner retinal circulation. Optical coherence tomography revealed a focal detachment of the retinal pigment epithelium adjacent to outer retinal and RPE irregularity underlying the region of inner retinal change, without macular edema. Fundus-controlled microperimetry showed preserved retinal sensitivity. These imaging findings remained stable over six weeks of follow-up.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Inner retinal vasculopathy in Zika virus disease

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman with a 10-year history of poorly controlled hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia presented with several hours of paroxysmal dizziness and right upper-extremity weakness. She sometimes discontinued her medications, and her diabetes control had been poor (hemoglobin A1c, 15.5%). On examination, she had mild dysarthria and right hemiparesis, more pronounced in the upper limb. Vital signs were: temperature 36.8 °C, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, SpO₂ 98%, and blood pressure 164/81 mmHg. Laboratory tests showed blood glucose 155 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 206 mg/dL, without inflammatory markers or coagulation abnormalities. Head CT was normal. MRI showed the following in the right lateral ventricle:
• Diffusion-weighted image: very high signal intensity in the choroid plexus  
• Apparent diffusion coefficient map: corresponding low signal  
• T1- and T2-weighted images: signal intensity equal to CSF  
• FLAIR sequence: slightly higher signal than CSF
title: Isolated choroid plexus infarction caused by multiple occlusive cerebrovascular lesions

case_prompt: A 37-year-old woman with two prior lower-segment cesarean deliveries presented with an absence of menstrual periods for 3 years. She reported cyclical episodes of gross hematuria coinciding with her expected menses and associated breast tenderness, but she had no vaginal bleeding or watery vaginal discharge at any time. Three years earlier, during her second cesarean section, she sustained a bladder injury that was repaired at that time. Her medical and family histories were otherwise unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were normal, and the physical and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a normal-sized retroflexed uterus with homogeneous myometrium, an endometrial thickness of 11 mm without intrauterine fluid, and normal bilateral ovaries. A tubular hyperechoic tract, measuring 8 mm in diameter, was seen between the posterior bladder wall and the lower uterine segment. A hysterosalpingogram demonstrated uniform filling of contrast material in the bladder and no opacification of the uterine cavity or fallopian tubes.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Vesicouterine fistula presenting with cyclical haematuria mimicking bladder endometriosis: A case report

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of a progressive, painful skin eruption that began on her torso and spread to her extremities. She reported anorexia, fatigue, and one episode of fever the day before presentation, but denied night sweats, chills, weight loss, recent infections, Raynaud’s phenomenon, oral ulcers, photosensitivity, or serositis. Her medications included amiloride for hypertension, used for 10 years, with no recent new drugs.

On examination, she was afebrile, non-toxic-appearing, and hemodynamically stable. Skin examination showed widespread erythematous papules coalescing into dusky, annular plaques with central erosions, distributed over the trunk and extremities; the face, palms, and soles were spared. There was no mucosal involvement, joint findings, or lymphadenopathy.

On hospital day 2, despite remaining afebrile and stable, she developed peripheral sheet-like detachment and desquamation over 30% of her body surface area, with a positive Nikolsky sign.

A punch biopsy of affected skin showed prominent epidermal necrosis with minimal superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates and no eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence studies were unremarkable.
title: A case of toxic epidermal necrosis–like cutaneous eruption as the first manifestation and clue to the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus: A case report

case_prompt:
A 23-year-old white man was admitted with a 2-week history of suddenly enlarged left cervical lymph nodes unresponsive to multiple antibiotics. One week before admission, he developed fever up to 39 °C, fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats. His medical history was notable for over 20 episodes of bacterial tonsillitis in the past 2 years; his brother died young of a nasopharyngeal malignancy. He denied travel to endemic regions. Physical examination revealed a few separate, slightly tender left cervical lymph nodes with normal overlying skin and asymmetric left palatine tonsillar enlargement without exudate. His temperature reached 39.5 °C, responsive only to intramuscular metamizole; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (2.2–3.3 × 10^3/μL), anemia (hemoglobin 12 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (127 × 10^3/μL), granulocytopenia, monocytosis, and 1% lymphoid cells on smear. Coagulation studies revealed aPTT 39.8 s and D-dimer 1.9 μg/mL. Inflammatory markers were elevated (CRP 17.6 mg/L, ESR 40 mm/h; procalcitonin negative), and LDH was 463 U/L, with both CRP and LDH rising further during hospitalization.

Serologic tests for toxoplasmosis (IgG, IgM), syphilis (VDRL), hepatitis B and C, EBV (VCA IgG, IgM), HIV, anti-streptolysin O, and ANA were negative; anti-HBs was positive from prior vaccination; CMV IgG positive, IgM negative. Blood and urine cultures and a tuberculin skin test were negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed multiple left cervical lymph nodes up to 2 cm, mostly supraclavicular, without other masses; chest CT revealed small axillary nodes but no mediastinal or pulmonary lesions. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of a lymph node was non-diagnostic.
title: A white man with Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease mimicking lymphoma, preceded by frequent episodes of tonsillitis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old man with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented with symptomatic bradycardia. A dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted in the left prepectoral region without intraoperative complications. He was discharged the next day on doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for prophylaxis. 

Four days later, he returned with severe pain at the pacemaker incision site, associated erythema, and purulent drainage. He was afebrile, and vital signs were stable. The device pocket appeared tender with surrounding erythema and a small amount of purulence. The patient was admitted, started on intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam, and scheduled for device removal.

Laboratory evaluation showed a white blood cell count of 10.9×10^3/µL with a normal neutrophil percentage. During explantation, swabs of the purulent material in the device pocket were sent for aerobic and anaerobic cultures, and three sets of blood cultures were obtained.
All culture results returned negative for bacterial growth.
title: Pyoderma Gangrenosum following Pacemaker Implantation: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 6-month-old female infant was brought by her family after her grandmother noted a palpable, left-sided solid abdominal wall mass. There was no history of trauma, fever, or family history of similar conditions. The patient was born at 39 weeks’ gestation with a birth weight of 3.2 kg after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery; prenatal ultrasounds were normal and she was otherwise healthy.

An outpatient ultrasound showed a well-defined, heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass measuring approximately 3.7 × 3.5 cm; it was unclear whether the lesion arose from the abdominal wall or intra-abdominally, but it was separate from the left kidney and spleen. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated detectable peripheral arterial vascularity; venous flow within the mass was not well assessed. The patient was referred for further evaluation.

On presentation, vital signs were normal, and physical examination was notable only for the firm mass in the left lateral abdominal wall. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated activated partial thromboplastin time of 58.5 s (normal, 30–40 s), a low mean corpuscular volume of 72.2 fL (normal, 80–95 fL), and a reversed neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (neutrophils 23.4% [normal, 55–70%]; lymphocytes 63.6% [normal, 20–40%]); all other values were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 4.3 × 4 × 4 cm round, heterogeneous mass in the left lateral abdominal wall with internal calcifications; there was significant peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase with centripetal filling in the delayed phase. Multiple feeding vessels arose from the left inferior epigastric artery, internal and external iliac arteries, and a descending vessel from the left lateral chest wall. The differential diagnosis at this stage included rhabdomyosarcoma, fibromatosis, hemangioma, and lymphatic malformation.

Subsequent coronal T2-weighted MRI confirmed a heterointense mass in the left lateral abdominal wall with peripheral enhancement consistent with a vascular malformation. The liver, spleen, and both kidneys appeared normal on imaging.
title: Hemangioma of the abdominal wall in infancy

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hypothyroidism and fatty liver was diagnosed in 2018 with myelodysplastic syndrome with multilineage dysplasia and very low risk. Initial blood counts showed leukocytes 3.9×10^9/L (neutrophils 1.5, monocytes 1.49), platelets 113×10^9/L, hemoglobin 115 g/L. Bone marrow blasts were 1.4%, normal cytogenetics, and NGS detected SETBP1 mutation (VAF 21%). He was observed without specific therapy.

In December 2019 he developed a 13 kg weight loss, night sweats, fatigue, and anorexia. Vitals: T 36.7 °C, HR 95 bpm, BP 103/64 mmHg, SpO2 100% RA. Exam was unremarkable. Labs: leukocytes 29.7×10^9/L (neutrophils 23.46, monocytes 1.78), platelets 83×10^9/L, hemoglobin 78 g/L. Bone marrow aspiration showed major dysplasia without excess blasts, consistent with CMML-0, and hydroxyurea was started.

In January 2020 he was admitted for psychomotor slowing. He then acutely worsened with decreased consciousness (Glasgow 11), bilateral nonreactive myosis, and right central facial paralysis; no definite limb deficits could be assessed. Labs: hemoglobin 77 g/L, platelets 36×10^9/L, leukocytes 37×10^9/L (neutrophils 31, monocytes 3). Infectious studies, including cultures and serologies (Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, HIV, HBV, HCV, CMV, EBV, syphilis) and β-D-glucan, were negative. Autoimmune markers including ANA were negative.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed multiple hyperdense nodular hemorrhagic lesions. MRI demonstrated multiple supra- and infratentorial heterogeneous hemorrhagic lesions of varying ages without gadolinium enhancement, with surrounding edema and early left temporal herniation.
title: Cerebral localization of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia: a case report

case_prompt:
A 10-year-6-month-old boy was referred from the rheumatology clinic for evaluation of generalized myalgia and arthralgia involving the back, hips, knees, and ankles for the past 3 to 4 months. The pain occurred daily, was worse in the morning, and interfered with activities of daily living, causing an antalgic gait. He reported a poorer appetite but denied prolonged fever or weight loss. He had a recent intercurrent illness with cough and diarrhoea. 

On examination, he was short for age and pale, with hepatomegaly. Cardiopulmonary and neurologic examinations were normal. Musculoskeletal examination was notable only for a left antalgic gait. There was no rash and no goitre. 

Growth-chart plotting showed height 119.5 cm (SDS −3.29), weight 26.2 kg (SDS −1.61), and BMI 18.3 kg/m2 (SDS 0.58). Laboratory studies revealed normochromic normocytic anaemia (hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (56 mm/hr), alanine aminotransferase 226 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 270 U/L, creatine kinase 479 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 965 U/L. A hand-wrist radiograph showed a bone age delayed by 4 years 1 month.
title: Atypical presentations of primary acquired hypothyroidism – a case series

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman with hypertension and obesity presented with 1 day of dyspnea and adynamia. Two days earlier she had experienced intense emotional stress. She denied syncope, chest pain, or palpitations. Her medications included spironolactone, losartan, and amlodipine. On examination, heart rate was 50 beats per minute, blood pressure 140/90 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 97 %, and there were no signs of heart failure.  
Electrocardiography showed second-degree (2:1) atrioventricular block, right bundle-branch block, left anterior fascicular block, biphasic and inverted T waves in multiple leads, QRS duration of 142 ms, and a corrected QT interval of 689 ms. Troponin I was 396 ng/L (normal < 40), and B-type natriuretic peptide was 307 pg/mL (normal < 100). Renal function, electrolytes, and thyroid function tests were normal.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40 %, with basal hypercontractility and midventricular and apical ballooning. Coronary CT angiography showed no coronary lesions and a calcium score of zero. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the echocardiographic findings and did not show late gadolinium enhancement.
title: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy Associated with High-Grade Atrioventricular Block and Ventricular Fibrillation: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 56-year-old man with an 18-month history of chronic sinusitis and otitis media was referred for right otomastoiditis complicated by facial nerve palsy. He underwent cortical mastoidectomy, facial nerve decompression, and ossicular chain reconstruction; mastoid histology revealed inflamed granulation tissue but was non-diagnostic. Postoperatively, his C-reactive protein remained elevated at 55 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate at 49 mm/h, and c-ANCA/proteinase 3 testing was strongly positive. He reported nocturia 6–7 times per night and polydipsia of 3–4 L/day. Renal ultrasound and urine studies were unremarkable. Chest CT showed nonspecific bilateral apical lung nodules. He was treated with prednisolone, methotrexate, and folic acid, but the polyuria and polydipsia persisted. An HbA1c was 6%, and serum and urine osmolalities with a water deprivation test were consistent with central diabetes insipidus in the setting of normal pituitary hormone tests. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the pituitary gland showed an enlarged, heterogeneously enhancing gland. After six months of monthly IV cyclophosphamide, his polydipsia increased to 8 L/day, and repeat MRI demonstrated interval enlargement of the pituitary with mild superior displacement of the optic chiasm. Visual fields remained normal.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Rare presentation of Wegener’s granulomatosis in the pituitary gland: Case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old man was referred 4 weeks after transurethral resection of a 2 cm × 2 cm bladder tumor, histologically confirmed as nested-variant transitional cell carcinoma. He reported 2 months of painless hematuria and, more recently, lower-limb weakness and progressive dyspnea with a nonproductive cough. 

On examination, he appeared pale, was febrile to 99.5°F, tachycardic, and tachypneic, and had motor weakness of both lower limbs. Oxygen saturation was 82% on room air, improving to 95% with 6 L/min of supplemental oxygen. Digital rectal examination revealed a normal prostate and decreased rectal tone. Despite a 22-Fr three-way Foley catheter, suprapubic fullness persisted; bladder washout yielded 200 mL of old clots.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 14 500/mm3 (neutrophilia), creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 300 IU/L, and PSA 4.2 ng/mL. Urinalysis revealed numerous pus cells, red blood cells, and leukocyte esterase positivity; culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated diffuse bladder-wall thickening with a right-sided diverticulum, intraluminal air, bilateral external iliac and para-aortic lymphadenopathy, and osteolytic lesions in the sacrum, right acetabulum, bilateral iliac bones, L5 vertebra, T4 and T9 vertebrae, and the right eighth costovertebral angle.

CT of the chest revealed thickened, nodular interlobular septa and polygonal arcades in both upper lobes and the right middle lobe.
journal: Indian Journal of Urology : IJU : Journal of the Urological Society of India
title: Pulmonary lymphangitis carcinomatosa in a patient with carcinoma of urinary bladder

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old man presented with a two-year history of painless, nonprogressive blurring of vision in his right eye. He had no systemic illnesses, medications, or relevant family history. Best corrected visual acuity was 6/18 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left. Intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg in the right eye; there was a right relative afferent pupillary defect. The anterior segment was unremarkable. Dilated funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed a dark brownish pigmented mass covering the entire optic disk and extending into the vitreous, with pigmentation into the surrounding retina including the papillomacular bundle and superotemporal area. The lesion measured 4.8 mm vertically and 4.6 mm horizontally. Neovascularization was noted on the superior aspect of the lesion. The superotemporal retinal vessels appeared white, and dot hemorrhages were present in the temporal macula.  
B-scan ultrasonography of the right eye showed an elevated echogenic mass projecting into the vitreous from the optic disk. Fundus fluorescein angiography revealed extensive nonperfusion in the superotemporal retina with absence of dye transit in the corresponding artery and vein; there was late leakage from neovascularization on the optic disk. Fundus autofluorescence demonstrated hypoautofluorescence of the disk and a peripapillary ring of hypoautofluorescence sparing the fovea. Optical coherence tomography through the lesion showed thinning and stretching of the adjacent retina at the base of the mass and a flattened top.
title: Intravitreal bevacizumab causes rapid regression of disc neovascularization associated with large optic disk melanocytoma: a case report

case_prompt: A 44-year-old Japanese woman underwent a routine ultrasound that identified a 5.9-cm uterine myoma–like lesion. Twelve months later, the lesion had nearly doubled in size, and she was referred for further evaluation. On internal examination, the uterus was enlarged to approximately the size of a newborn head; cervical and vaginal examinations were unremarkable, and no adnexal masses were palpable. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an isoechoic solid mass with an ill-defined boundary between the lesion and the uterus. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 110 × 90 × 80 mm lesion in the right pelvis with smooth margins, mild lobulation, T1 signal intensity similar to myometrium, low T2 signal intensity, and flow-void areas forming a bridging vascular sign. These findings suggested a subserous uterine myoma, but the continuity with the uterus was unclear and the right ovary was not visualized, prompting consideration of an ovarian fibroma or thecoma. The left ovary appeared normal. A preliminary diagnosis of subserous myoma was made, and laparoscopic myomectomy was planned. Intraoperatively, a 10-cm right ovarian mass was identified without adhesion or rupture; the uterus and left adnexa were normal. A right adnexectomy was performed, and serous ascitic fluid was collected—cytology was negative.
title: Rapid growth of mitotically active cellular fibroma of the ovary: a case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 46‐year‐old man with no significant past medical history underwent an elective day-case repair of a rectal prolapse and total hemorrhoidectomy. He was discharged the same evening with paracetamol, ibuprofen, and lactulose. The following morning, he returned with severe spasmodic lower abdominal pain and urinary retention for a few hours; he reported opening his bowels twice since discharge. 

On examination, he was afebrile but had sinus tachycardia; blood pressure and respiratory rate were normal. His lower abdomen was extremely tender on palpation, and bladder scanning showed 225 mL of residual urine, prompting catheterization. After initial analgesia and antispasmodics, he continued to have severe abdominal pain. On reassessment, a tender, palpable mass was noted in the right iliac fossa. 

Routine blood tests revealed only a borderline elevated white-cell count; other values were within normal limits. An urgent erect abdominal radiograph demonstrated massive dilation of the large intestine with a few air-fluid levels and no evidence of perforation. A provisional diagnosis of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction was made.
title: Ogilvie's syndrome after rectal prolapse repair and total hemorrhoidectomy: Case report and Discussion

case_prompt:
A 75-year-old woman was referred to the oral surgery clinic for a suspected dental infection. Her history included tuberculosis, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and neurogenic bladder. Four weeks earlier, she had otorrhea of the right ear diagnosed as otitis media and treated with antibiotics; on the same day, her right mandibular canine and lateral incisor were extracted by her family dentist. Two weeks before referral, she sought routine follow-up for fatigue, fever, dysgeusia, neck swelling with numbness, and backache, which persisted after the extraction. Initial laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 11.46 mg/dL and a white blood cell count of 11,000/μL; chest radiography and CT were unremarkable, and influenza testing was negative. She subsequently developed trismus and tongue-apex pain, prompting referral to oral surgery. On examination, her temperature was 38.5 °C and blood pressure 125/75 mmHg. She reported fever, tongue discomfort with dysgeusia, redness and numbness at the tongue apex, but no trismus. The tooth-extraction sites had healed well, salivary function was intact, and there were no other orofacial abnormalities. Orthopantomography was normal. Repeat labs showed a CRP of 19.4 mg/dL and WBC count of 14,700/μL. Given the history of extraction and ongoing fever, she was referred to cardiology for suspected infective endocarditis.  
Blood cultures were negative for bacteria, and transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed neither vegetations nor valvular regurgitation.
title: Microscopic Polyangiitis Initially Presumed to Be Endocarditis

case_prompt: A 68-year-old man was found on a routine health check to have an asymptomatic mass in the uncus of the pancreas. He had no history of chronic pancreatitis or other relevant medical conditions, and tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9) were within normal limits. Enhanced abdominal CT showed a well-demarcated 4.2 × 3.9 cm lesion comprising cystic areas of iso- to low-density surrounded by an area of extremely low density resembling adipose tissue. MRI and MRCP demonstrated multilocular cysts 1–several millimeters in diameter within the uncus; the main pancreatic duct was not dilated, and there was no communication between the lesion and the duct. On this basis, a benign tumor such as lipoma, dermoid cyst, or another rare benign cystic lesion was initially suspected. The patient developed a contrast allergy, so surveillance with plain CT and MRI was undertaken. Twenty-one months later, CT showed a slight decrease in overall size (3.9 × 3.6 cm) with smaller cysts and a larger solid component, and endoscopic ultrasound revealed a honeycomb-like appearance. At 28 months, plain CT showed an increase in size to 4.2 × 3.3 cm and MRCP revealed more and larger cysts without ductal invasion. On MRI at that time, the cystic component was low intensity on T1-weighted imaging, iso-intense on T2, and high on T2 fat-saturation, whereas the surrounding solid tissue was iso-intense on T1, iso- to high on T2, and suppressed on fat-saturated sequences—suggesting fluid-filled cysts enveloped by fat. Coronal T2 imaging showed ringed multilocular cysts with a smooth outer margin and a small internal nodule, findings that raised concern for malignant transformation of an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm.
title: Pancreatic hamartoma: a case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man, former smoker (20 cigarettes/day from ages 20 to 25), with a history of asthma treated with inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting β₂-agonists and an ECOG performance status of 0, was referred after an abnormal chest X-ray on routine screening. He was asymptomatic, and routine laboratory tests were normal.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a 6-cm mass abutting the anterior mediastinum and the right upper lobe, multiple nodular shadows along the right pleura, and a moderate right pleural effusion. The origin of the mass (mediastinal vs. pulmonary) was unclear. Bronchoscopic sampling with endobronchial ultrasound guidance of a right upper lobe lesion was non-diagnostic. CT-guided needle biopsy of the mass revealed a solid tumor composed of malignant, non-keratinized squamous cells with surrounding fibrosis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for p40 and CK5/6.

18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated intense uptake in the primary mass (SUVmax 10.95) and multiple pleural nodules (SUVmax 7.08), consistent with pleural dissemination. Molecular testing showed no EGFR mutations, ALK fusions, or ROS1 rearrangements. PD-L1 expression (22C3) was low at 5–10%. The lesion was deemed unresectable. A multidisciplinary team convened to determine whether this represented primary lung cancer or a thymic carcinoma.
title: Good Response of Advanced Thymic Carcinoma with Low PD-L1 Expression to Chemotherapy plus Pembrolizumab as First-Line Therapy and to Pembrolizumab as Maintenance Therapy: A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man with hypertension, arthritis, seizure disorder, Parkinson’s disease, hiatal hernia, and chronic anemia presented with three months of non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting, decreased oral intake, one month of progressive weakness, and new dyspnea that left him bed-bound by the day before presentation. He took excess NSAIDs for joint pain and had no history of alcohol, smoking, or illicit drugs. 

In the ED, he was hypotensive (65/30 mmHg), heart rate 84 bpm, respirations 20–22 /min, O₂ saturation 96% on 4 L, and afebrile. He appeared ill, with labored breathing and decreased right-sided breath sounds. Labs showed WBC 25.5 k/µL, hemoglobin 2.3 g/dL, mild ALT/AST elevations, and metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (venous pH 7.23, HCO₃ 13 mmol/L, albumin-corrected anion gap 21.3 mEq/L). 

Chest X-ray revealed a right-sided pneumothorax with >1 cm air gap and a moderate right-sided pleural effusion. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed diverticulosis without retroperitoneal hematoma or occult gastrointestinal bleeding. CT of the chest demonstrated air and fluid in the right pleural cavity. 

He received IV fluids and packed red cells, was transferred to the ICU, and started on cefepime. A right chest tube drained approximately 1 L of air and purulent fluid. Pleural fluid analysis showed: straw color; cloudy; pH 5.6; nucleated cells 11 133/mm³ (91% neutrophils); LDH 14 898 U/L; protein 3.1 g/dL; glucose <2 mg/dL; and amylase >10 000 U/L. Fluid cultures grew Candida tropicalis, Candida glabrata, and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; blood and urine cultures were negative. Antibiotics were broadened to meropenem and caspofungin.
title: Catastrophic right-sided Candida empyema from spontaneous esophageal perforation

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old man with hypertension and a history of heavy alcohol use (abstinent for 1 year) presented 7 days after a sudden holocranial “thunderclap” headache. He had 3–4 episodes of projectile vomiting over 2–3 days without improvement. On examination, he was alert, normotensive, and had no focal neurologic deficits.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed subarachnoid hemorrhage in the interhemispheric fissure and bilateral Sylvian fissures (modified Fisher grade 2) with dilated temporal horns consistent with hydrocephalus. CT angiography revealed a 3×4 mm saccular aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery. 

He underwent a left pterional craniotomy, aneurysm clipping, and lamina terminalis fenestration. Intraoperative indocyanine green angiography confirmed complete aneurysm occlusion and good distal flow. Postoperative CT angiography corroborated these findings.

He remained asymptomatic until postoperative day 5, when he developed sudden inability to see from the left eye, aphasia, and right-sided hemiplegia. On examination, his left pupil was dilated with an ipsilateral afferent pupillary defect. MRI of the brain showed infarcts in bilateral internal carotid artery and left middle cerebral artery territories. Fundus examination on postoperative day 3 was normal, but by day 15 the left optic disc appeared pallid with attenuated vessels.
title: Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy with acute monocular vision loss following clipping of anterior communicating artery aneurysm. A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent dull aching right flank pain and associated vomiting. She denied hematuria, dysuria, fever, weight loss, or appetite change. On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal palpation revealed a firm, ballotable mass measuring approximately 10 × 8 cm in the right hypochondrium extending into the right lumbar and umbilical regions; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Renal ultrasonography showed a 17 × 9 cm heterogeneous mass lesion with internal vascularity involving the lower half of the right kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a 12.6 × 13.2 × 15.4 cm heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue density mass arising from the right kidney, compressing the renal cortex, extending into the right retroperitoneal space, and displacing bowel loops. There were also suspicious soft-tissue deposits along the left thoracic paravertebral space and in the pericardium adjacent to the right atrium.

An FDG PET scan corroborated these findings, with a maximum SUV of 2.0 in the primary renal lesion and 1.9 in the suspected metastatic sites. An additional 5 × 5 mm heterogeneously FDG-avid subcutaneous soft-tissue thickening was noted on the medial aspect of the right thigh.
journal: Indian Journal of Urology : IJU : Journal of the Urological Society of India
title: Extranodal Rosai–Dorfman disease: A rare mimicker of metastatic renal cell carcinoma

case_prompt: A 53-year-old woman was admitted with a 4-day history of worsening lower-limb pain, fever, lower-limb weakness, and a rash. She had tested positive for COVID-19 by PCR 4 days before admission; her last vaccination (Pfizer booster) was 6 months earlier. Her past medical history was unremarkable; she took no regular medications and had a 10 pack-year smoking history. On examination, there was livedo reticularis of both lower limbs, non-palpable peripheral pulses, and profound, proximal, symmetric weakness of the lower limbs. Initial laboratory tests showed: D-dimer 444 mg/l (80–500), CRP 8.9 mg/l (<5), ESR 24 mm/hr (0–20), CK 524 U/L (25–200), WCC 14.9 ×10^9/l (4–10), neutrophils 10.6 ×10^9/l (2–7.5), creatinine 56 μmol/l (45–84), urea 5.7 mmol/l (2.5–7.8), eGFR >90 ml/min. A CT angiogram of the legs excluded acute arterial occlusion. Three days later, the CK had risen to 24 250 U/L. MRI of the lower legs showed diffuse, symmetrical muscle edema in all compartments with perifascial fluid and subcutaneous edema.
title: Diagnosis and imaging in COVID-19 induced myositis

case_prompt: A 71-year-old man presented with dyspnea and fatigue that had worsened over 3 weeks. Laboratory tests showed severe pancytopenia with a leukocyte count of 2.4 G/L (neutrophils 0.3 G/L), hemoglobin 75 g/L, platelet count 7 G/L, and reticulocyte count 13 G/L. He had no history of novel drug intake or overt infections. An iliac crest bone marrow biopsy revealed a cellularity of 5% without clonal blasts. He was started on G-CSF (filgrastim 4 µg/kg/day) and received erythrocyte and platelet transfusions. Further work-up by histology, next-generation sequencing, and flow cytometry was inconspicuous for myelodysplastic syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, or myeloproliferative disorders, supporting a diagnosis of very severe aplastic anemia. Computed tomography revealed an anterior mediastinal mass. For further evaluation, an [18F]FDG-PET/CT scan was performed, showing a moderately hypermetabolic mediastinal lesion (SUVmax 5.1) and multiple intensely FDG-avid focal skeletal lesions, predominantly affecting the ribs, with SUVmax values up to 14.7, which was interpreted as highly suspicious for skeletal metastases. At the time of the PET/CT scan, the patient had received G-CSF for 5 days, which was then discontinued.
title:
Disseminated focal 18F-fluoro-deoxyglucose uptake upon granulocyte
colony-stimulating factor therapy mimicking malignant bone infiltration: case report of a
patient with very severe aplastic anemia

case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man presented with a two-week history of progressively worsening fatigue, anorexia, vomiting, diarrhoea, exertional dyspnoea, and increasing oedema. His history was notable for a living-donor kidney transplant 15 years earlier complicated by recurrent IgA nephropathy and nephrotic syndrome. On examination, his blood pressure was 144/94 mmHg, and he had gross peripheral oedema of the upper and lower limbs and sacrum; pulmonary auscultation was unremarkable.

Two months before admission, laboratory studies showed a serum creatinine of 572 µmol/L, urea of 30 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, corrected calcium 1.96 mmol/L, and phosphate 2.82 mmol/L. On admission, he had acute-on-chronic kidney injury with a serum creatinine of 1439 µmol/L, urea 53.2 mmol/L, potassium 6.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L (pH 7.06), corrected calcium 1.67 mmol/L, phosphate 5.97 mmol/L, normal sodium and glucose, serum osmolality 337 mOsm/kg, and haemoglobin 98 g/L.

Over the first 36 hours, he received parenteral loop diuretics, oral bicarbonate, insulin–dextrose and potassium-exchange resins, oral calcitriol, and calcium carbonate. Despite this, bicarbonate remained 6 mmol/L (pH 7.13), phosphate increased to 6.03 mmol/L, serum potassium and calcium improved to 5.1 mmol/L and 1.72 mmol/L, and osmolality rose to 341 mOsm/kg. He then developed uremic encephalopathy with delirium, fluctuating consciousness, dysarthria, asterixis, and a widespread tremor.

He was initiated on haemodialysis. The first session (3 hours; ultrafiltration 3000 mL; Polyflux 140H dialyser; Baxter CX265G dialysate; dialysate flow 500 mL/min; blood flow 200 mL/min) led to resolution of cognitive and speech deficits within 24 hours, with a remaining tremor. A second session 24 hours later (4 hours; ultrafiltration 4000 mL; Polyflux 140H; Baxter CX275G; dialysate flow 500 mL/min; blood flow 250 mL/min) resulted in complete symptom resolution, and discharge was planned.

Six hours after the second session, he became stuporous with blood pressure 187/102 mmHg (143/92 mmHg post-dialysis), hyperreflexia, sustained clonus, and bilaterally absent response to visual threat despite following commands. He was intubated and transferred to the ICU. Noncontrast CT of the brain was normal. MRI showed bilateral symmetric diffusion restriction in the supratentorial white matter without overt cerebral oedema or features of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. Lumbar puncture demonstrated no evidence of meningoencephalitis or autoimmune encephalitis, and an EEG showed no features of seizure activity. Serum ammonia was normal, and cryptococcal testing was negative.
title: Dialysis Disequilibrium: Is Acidosis More Important than Urea?

case_prompt: A female infant was born at 35 weeks’ gestation by uncomplicated caesarian section to a G2P2 mother, weight 2460 g. Prenatal ultrasound had repeatedly shown a markedly distended bladder, which was drained in utero on three occasions. After birth, the patient exhibited abdominal distension, a palpable enlarged bladder, massive hematuria, failure to pass meconium, and feeding intolerance. On day 2 of life, she was referred for surgical evaluation for presumed Prune Belly Syndrome. Abdominal ultrasound showed a distended urinary bladder with bilateral uretero-hydronephrosis. Voiding cystography demonstrated a markedly enlarged bladder without vesicoureteral reflux. Initial labs were notable for hemoglobin 12 g/dL and white blood cell count 9800/mm3. A rectal tube was placed and bladder instillations with saline, antibiotics, and hemostatic agents were recommended twice daily. On day 4, the neonate developed bilious vomiting and marked abdominal distension. A thoraco-abdominal radiograph revealed pneumoperitoneum, and contrast studies confirmed perforations of the stomach and distal colon. Repeat labs showed a white blood cell count of 23 000/mm3 and C-reactive protein of 12.6 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 49 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.10 mg/dL.
title: Megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome associated with cystic fibrosis and meconium peritonitis in a female neonate 4 days of age – case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old man with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department with left-sided constricting chest pain and diaphoresis of 1 hour’s duration. He was anxious; pulse, 108 beats per minute; blood pressure, 120/80 mmHg; and respiratory rate, 16 breaths per minute. The systemic examination was unremarkable. An electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V4 and ST-segment depression in leads I and aVL. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a regional wall-motion abnormality of the anterior wall. He received loading doses of aspirin and clopidogrel and was thrombolysed with 1.5 million units of streptokinase. Chest pain resolved, and follow-up electrocardiography 90 minutes later showed substantial ST-segment resolution.

Six hours after thrombolysis, he developed massive hemoptysis and acute-onset dyspnea. His oxygen saturation fell from 99% to 86% on room air. Auscultation revealed bilateral fine end-inspiratory crackles in all lung fields; jugular venous pressure was normal, and there were no signs of heart failure. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral alveolar infiltrates, and high-resolution computed tomography of the thorax confirmed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. The hemoglobin concentration fell from 14.0 g/dL to 10.0 g/dL, with no other bleeding manifestations.
title: Pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage following thrombolytic therapy

case_prompt:
An 86-year-old male farmer with transfusion-dependent myelodysplastic syndrome, coronary artery disease with coronary stents, atrial fibrillation, and presumed amiodarone-induced interstitial lung disease on 2 L/min oxygen presented with several months of intermittent nonmassive hemoptysis and one week of progressive dyspnea and fatigue. His hemoptysis persisted despite discontinuation of dual antiplatelet therapy, and his anemia required transfusions beyond expectations for his myelodysplastic syndrome.

On examination, he was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had an oxygen saturation of 94% on 2 L/min oxygen. Breath sounds revealed fine bibasilar crackles; he had bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 21.1 × 10^3/µL with a left shift, hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL with microcytosis, creatinine 1.31 mg/dL, NT-proBNP 5,375 pg/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate >100 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 23.2 mg/dL. CT of the chest demonstrated bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities with central predominance and a small right pleural effusion.

He was treated with diuresis for presumed volume overload and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics but continued to deteriorate, requiring 6 L/min oxygen; arterial blood gas revealed a PaO₂ of 38 mm Hg. Further history elicited late-onset Raynaud’s phenomena, occasional arthralgias without swelling, and oral sicca symptoms; he denied photosensitivity, rashes, ulcers, or skin thickening. His sister has a history of SLE. Serologic testing showed an ANA titer 1:160 homogeneous, low C4, normal C3, anti–double-stranded DNA 194 IU/mL, anti-Ro (SSA) 6.0, anti-La (SSB) >8.0, and negative anti-Smith, anti-RNP, antichromatin, proteinase 3, myeloperoxidase, and anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies.
title: An Elderly Gentleman with Acute Lupus Pneumonitis as the Initial Manifestation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

case_prompt: An 81-year-old man was admitted with acute onset of abdominal pain. He reported loss of appetite and general weakness for several weeks without fever. His medical history was notable for stage IIIC ascending colon cancer treated by right hemicolectomy, partial duodenopancreatectomy, splenectomy, and adjuvant chemotherapy in 2006; he remained disease-free until March 2010. On examination, he had multiple purpura on the trunk and lower extremities and gum bleeding; there was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 15 × 10^9/L (70% neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 4% eosinophils), and platelet count 11 × 10^9/L. Serum biochemical tests were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated massive ascites, diffuse peritoneal and omental thickening, and bowel wall thickening. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded turbid fluid with a white blood cell count of 52,210/mm^3, protein 2.6 g/dL, ascitic albumin 2.5 g/dL (serum albumin 3.5 g/dL), and a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.0 g/dL.
title: Peritoneal lymphomatosis confounded by prior history of colon cancer: a case report

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old woman with a 3-year history of Crohn’s disease, previously treated with azathioprine and intermittent prednisolone after ileocolic resection, presented with a 2-week history of abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Physical examination was unremarkable aside from mild abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed no leukocytosis and normal renal function. 

MRI of the abdomen performed to assess enterocolitis demonstrated active inflammation of the small and large bowel and revealed an incidental mass in the inferior pole of the left kidney measuring 2.5×2.9×2.3 cm. On MRI, the lesion was slightly hypointense to renal cortex on T2-weighted images, isointense on pre-contrast T1, and exhibited a honeycomb appearance after contrast with irregular enhancing septa around small (1–5 mm) non-enhancing foci; diffusion weighted imaging showed restricted diffusion. A dedicated contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed a well-defined, isodense mass pre-contrast that was homogeneously hypoenhancing in the arterial phase with cystic non-enhancing foci in the portal venous and delayed phases; there was no calcification, adenopathy, perinephric stranding, or vascular invasion. On renal ultrasound, the lesion was slightly hypoechoic with no demonstrable internal vascularity.
title: Mass-forming renal Crohn’s disease: a case report with multimodality imaging

case_prompt: A 63-year-old white man presented with a 3-month history of headaches, vomiting, and episodes of blurred vision, consistent with intracranial hypertension. On admission, he had papilledema, nystagmus, and lethargy. A T1-weighted MRI of the brain showed a hypointense lesion in the anterosuperior posterior fossa at the falcotentorial junction, displacing the cerebellar vermis inferiorly and compressing the aqueduct of Sylvius, resulting in obstructive hydrocephalus. The mass enhanced homogeneously with gadolinium, and flow voids compatible with vessels were observed around it. MR angiography demonstrated intense tumoral vascularization. MRI of the neuroaxis showed no additional lesions. Whole-body contrast-enhanced CT scans were unremarkable. Serum levels of alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and carcinoembryonic antigen were within normal limits.
title: Hemangioblastoma located in the posterior incisural space mimicking a tentorial meningioma: a case report

case_prompt:
A 40‐year‐old man was evaluated for several episodes of brief unresponsiveness lasting approximately 30 seconds. He reported four seizure‐like events triggered by minor stimuli (blood draw, hot tub, minor trauma). He had no family history of neurologic disease. On examination, he was alert and oriented with normal cranial nerve and motor findings; gait was slightly antalgic from a recent ankle sprain. 

An unenhanced head CT showed a 1.7‐cm hyperdense nodule extending from the left tentorium. MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed a 2.2‐cm lobulated mass along the left tentorium that was T1 isointense, mildly T2/FLAIR hyperintense, and demonstrated homogeneous enhancement. Susceptibility‐weighted imaging showed small punctate areas of hypointensity within the lesion. No surrounding edema or significant mass effect was noted. 

Based on imaging characteristics, the differential diagnosis included meningioma and hemangiopericytoma. The patient was taken for surgical resection of the mass.
title: Extra-Axial Cavernous Angioma: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt:
A 43‐year‐old woman presented to the bariatric surgery clinic for evaluation of intermittent umbilical bleeding. She reported that the bleeding occurred in direct correspondence with her menstrual cycles. She had no prior diagnosis of endometriosis but recalled heavy menses in her youth. Her surgical history was notable for a laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in 2018 and two cesarean sections in 2003 and 2005. She initially lost weight after her bypass but later regained weight and was lost to follow-up.

On examination, there was a small, non‐tender mass deep to the umbilicus without overlying skin changes. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 2.5 × 1.4 × 1.4 cm complex solid and cystic mass located beneath the umbilicus, without internal vascular flow.
title: Cyclically bleeding trocar-site endometrioma without known history of endometriosis: case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 4-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of left upper eyelid ptosis and a superonasal orbital mass present since birth. He was otherwise healthy, and the parents denied any pain or change in the size of the lesion. On examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left eye. Mechanical left upper eyelid ptosis was noted secondary to a soft, non-tender, freely mobile superonasal swelling without overlying skin changes, pulsation, discharge, or tear reflux on palpation. Pupillary reactions were normal, with no afferent defect, and extraocular movements were full. Slit-lamp and funduscopic examinations were unremarkable. Autorefraction revealed +0.75–1.00 × 173 in the right eye and −8.75–8.75 × 31 in the left eye. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated an anechoic, fluid-filled cavity with no internal echoes. Computed tomography of the orbits revealed a well-defined, hypodense cystic lesion in the medial extraconal compartment of the left orbit, with mild orbital compression and minimal adjacent bony remodeling.
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
title: Congenital giant orbital eccrine hidrocystoma

case_prompt: A 70-year-old woman presents with several weeks of general fatigue and is noted to have intrahepatic bile-duct dilatation on ultrasound. Her serum tumour markers are: AFP 5 ng/mL (normal), PIVKA-II 25 mAU/mL (normal), CEA 3 ng/mL (normal), and CA19-9 843.6 U/mL (elevated). Liver biochemistry shows alkaline phosphatase 601 IU/L, γ-GT 318 IU/L, albumin 3.3 g/dL, and normal bilirubin. The indocyanine green retention rate at 15 minutes is 4.6%, and the Child-Pugh score is 6 (Grade A). Cross-sectional imaging with CT and MRCP reveals a right umbilical portion anomaly and a 25-mm mass adjacent to the RUP, with nearly complete occlusion of the RUP and dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts. The tumour appears to involve the confluence of the left lateral, left medial, and right anterior hepatic ducts, while the right posterior duct remains intact.
title: Major hepatectomy using the glissonean approach in cases of right umbilical portion

case_prompt: A 33-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent mid-epigastric pain and a 4-kg weight loss. She denied fever, cough, or jaundice and had no history of tuberculosis, BCG vaccination, or TB exposure. On examination, she had moderate splenomegaly, no hepatomegaly, and no ascites. Laboratory tests showed normal hemoglobin, leukocyte, and platelet counts; elevated serum amylase and lipase; an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and lactate dehydrogenase; normal bilirubin and carcinoembryonic antigen levels; and negative tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV. A chest radiograph was normal. Noncontrast abdominal CT revealed multiple solid-cystic masses in the pancreas and spleen with peripancreatic lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an inhomogeneous cystic mass with peripheral rim enhancement in the body and tail of the pancreas, periportal lymphadenopathy with central low attenuation, and an enlarged spleen containing multiple 1–3 cm hypodense lesions showing mild enhancement after contrast.
title: Isolated pancreatic tuberculosis with splenic tuberculosis mimicking lymphoma malignum: A case report

case_prompt: A 43-year-old woman presented to the oral and maxillofacial clinic in January 2023 with a 3-year history of a painless, slow-growing mass on her chin. It began as a small nodule that gradually enlarged and then ulcerated; she reported mild discomfort when eating but no history of trauma. She consumes alcohol but does not smoke and is otherwise healthy. On examination, there was no facial asymmetry or lymphadenopathy, and speech and swallowing were normal. Extraoral inspection revealed a fungating, whitish-pink, cauliflower-shaped lesion with an uneven surface, measuring 8 × 6 cm over the submandibular region and lower border of the mandible. Intraoral examination showed an ulcer on the lower border of the mandible in the chin area. An orthopantomogram and chest radiograph were normal.
title: Surgical management of a huge oral verrucous carcinoma: A case report and review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 25-year-old Laotian woman, resident in Thailand for 10 years, presented with a 5-day history of low-grade fever, sudden onset of headache, and rapidly progressive visual loss in both eyes. She denied prior headache, chronic cough, weight loss, prolonged fever, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Two years earlier, she had an uncomplicated second pregnancy and breast-fed for 9 months.

On examination, she was alert but appeared acutely ill. Temperature was 37.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse 60 beats/min, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Best corrected visual acuity was hand movements in the left eye and 20/40 in the right eye, with a right temporal hemianopia by Goldmann perimetry. Other cranial nerves and neurologic findings were normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a 1.4 × 2.5 × 2.2 cm rim-enhancing lesion in the sellar region with suprasellar extension; it was hypointense on T1, mixed hypo- and hyperintense on T2, with meningeal enhancement, thickened enhancing pituitary stalk, absence of the posterior bright spot, and compression of the optic chiasm. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. HIV and VDRL tests were negative.

Anterior pituitary evaluation showed panhypopituitarism: TSH 0.081 µIU/mL (0.35–4.94), free T4 0.71 ng/dL (0.70–1.48), morning cortisol <1 µg/dL, prolactin <0.6 ng/mL (5.18–26.53), IGF-1 81 ng/mL (117–329). Serum sodium was 124 mmol/L. After initiation of IV hydrocortisone for adrenal insufficiency, polyuria developed, consistent with central diabetes insipidus.

Because of the acute visual loss and mass effect on the optic apparatus, she underwent urgent endoscopic transsphenoidal pituitary surgery.
title: Pituitary tuberculoma: A consideration in the differential diagnosis in a patient manifesting with pituitary apoplexy-like syndrome

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old Albanian man presented with fatigue, cough, shortness of breath, progressive dyspnea, liver distention, and lower-extremity edema. He was initially treated for tracheobronchitis without improvement.  
His vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination showed jugular venous distention, hepatomegaly, and bilateral pitting edema.  
Laboratory testing revealed mild hyperbilirubinemia attributed to biliary stasis; parathyroid hormone, phosphate, and calcium levels were normal. Antithrombin III activity was mildly reduced at 60 U/ml (normal, 80 U/ml). There was no evidence of deep-vein thrombosis in the legs.  
Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 4 × 10 cm calcified mass in the right ventricle attached to the pulmonary valve, a dilated pulmonary trunk (4 cm diameter), and thrombosis at the origin of the right pulmonary artery; the pulmonary trunk and left pulmonary branch enhanced uniformly.  
Transthoracic echocardiography showed a 4 × 7 cm hyperechogenic, calcified right ventricular mass broad based on the papillary muscles and trabeculae, extending into the infundibulum and pulmonary valve, with slight tricuspid annular calcification. The mass moved with ventricular contraction and did not prolapse into the right atrium. The right atrium and ventricle were dilated with volume and pressure overload; estimated pulmonary arterial pressure was 70 mmHg. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed these findings.
title: Surgical treatment of a calcified, amorphous tumor of the right ventricle complicated with thrombosis of the right pulmonary artery in an adult male: a case report

case_prompt: A 70-year-old woman with a history of asbestos exposure and prior epithelioid mesothelioma presented with progressive exertional dyspnoea. Initial CT had shown a right hydropneumothorax requiring chest-tube drainage, and thoracoscopic biopsy confirmed epithelioid mesothelioma. Six weeks later, surveillance CT revealed mild enlargement of pleural nodules and new ground-glass opacities in the right middle and lower lobes. She reported a cough but had no fever, other infective symptoms, or peripheral leukocytosis. A course of antibiotics yielded no improvement. Four months after biopsy, repeat CT demonstrated significant progression of the right-sided pulmonary infiltrates and pleural disease, as well as intrathoracic lymphadenopathy. PET scan showed these infiltrates were FDG-avid. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 6.4 × 10^9/L and a CRP of 11 IU/L. Atypical infection, lymphangitis carcinomatosis, and tumour infiltration were considered.
title: Widespread pulmonary invasion by malignant pleural mesothelioma: an important diagnostic consideration

case_prompt: A 78-year-old woman with reported seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, maintained on prednisone (10 mg daily) and methotrexate, presented with acute onset of shortness of breath. She was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and hypoxic to 87% on room air. Admission laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9770 cells/mcL, procalcitonin 0.23 ng/mL (low likelihood for bacterial etiology), normal cardiac biomarkers, lymphocyte count 480 cells/mcL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 98 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 24.6 mg/dL. On examination, there were bilateral rhonchi and fine basilar crackles; an erythematous rash was noted on her chest, with oral and nasal mucositis and epistaxis. She had no history of lung disease and no smoking or occupational exposures. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest showed diffuse bilateral consolidations and ground-glass opacities with subpleural sparing. Echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 75% with no other abnormalities. Blood and sputum cultures, including Legionella, were negative, and the serum methotrexate level was normal at 0.13 mcmol/L. Methotrexate was discontinued, and she was started on empiric antibiotics, diuretics, and leucovorin; subsequently, she became neutropenic and encephalopathic.
title: Leflunomide-induced interstitial pneumonitis: A rare occurrence in a case without underlying lung disease

case_prompt: A man in his early 50s with a BMI of 29.9 kg/m2 and no history of dyslipidaemia, diabetes, or other comorbidities was treated for stage IIIC mucinous adenocarcinoma of the left colon (pT4a pN2a [5/22] cM0, MSS/pMMR). Preoperative blood tests, including a fasting triglyceride level, were within reference ranges. He underwent left hemicolectomy with R0 margins and began adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy (5-FU 400 mg/m2 bolus on day 1, 5-FU 2400 mg/m2 continuous infusion over 48 hours on days 1–2, leucovorin 200 mg/m2 on day 1, and oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2 on day 1) every 2 weeks. After five cycles he developed grade 1 peripheral neuropathy. On day 2 of the ninth cycle, a deep vein thrombosis of the right axillary vein was diagnosed, and low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) was started daily. Three weeks later, immediately before the tenth cycle, blood samples appeared markedly lipaemic despite fasting. Repeat sampling confirmed a milky plasma supernatant. A lipid panel revealed triglycerides of 37.1 mmol/L (3286 mg/dL), total cholesterol of 13.3 mmol/L (514 mg/dL), LDL cholesterol of 1.90 mmol/L (73 mg/dL), and HDL cholesterol of 0.50 mmol/L (19 mg/dL). There was no evidence of diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, renal impairment, pancreatitis, or cutaneous xanthomas on examination.
title: 5-Fluorouracil-associated severe hypertriglyceridaemia with positive rechallenge

case_prompt: A 4-year-old girl was brought for evaluation of a swelling in the maxillary anterior region present since 6 months of age and gradually enlarging. The swelling has been asymptomatic, with no pain or discharge. Her parents also noted delayed eruption of her primary teeth; there was no history of trauma. Medical and family histories were noncontributory. On extraoral examination, findings were unremarkable. Intraorally, a diffuse swelling measuring approximately 1 × 2 cm was observed above the gingival margin in the region of the right maxillary primary central incisor, lateral incisor, and canine. The swelling was nontender and bony hard on palpation. A periapical radiograph of the area showed multiple radiopacities of densities equal to or greater than tooth structure, arranged irregularly and each separated and surrounded by a thin radiolucent capsule; above these calcifications lay a developing permanent tooth bud.
journal: Annals of Medical and Health Sciences Research
title: Compound Odontoma in Deciduous Dentition

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman with recently diagnosed ulcerative colitis presented with 3 days of bloody diarrhea, diffuse abdominal pain, anorexia, and weight loss. She was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and on examination was cachectic with diffuse abdominal tenderness but no peritoneal signs. Initial laboratories showed: WBC 15.9 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, platelets 128 × 10^3/µL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, INR 1.3, PT 16.6 s, PTT 42.8 s, lactate 2.11 mmol/L, ESR 20 mm/h, CRP 6.37 mg/dL, ferritin 93 ng/mL. She was treated for an ulcerative colitis flare with IV methylprednisolone and oral mesalamine.  
Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed a new occlusive main portal vein thrombosis extending into right and left branches with hepatic hypoperfusion and moderate-to-severe pancolitis. Unfractionated heparin was initiated. Shortly thereafter, she developed large-volume hematochezia, hypotension, and was transferred to the ICU. Repeat labs showed WBC 51 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, PTT >150 s, lactate 7.4 mmol/L. CT imaging demonstrated ischemic enterocolitis. Heparin was held, she received red blood cells, and underwent successful TIPS placement. Her pain, leukocytosis, and lactic acidosis improved; hemoglobin and vital signs stabilized.  
Heparin was restarted days later. A hypercoagulable panel showed a positive lupus anticoagulant; anti-beta2-glycoprotein, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, FLAER for PNH, and JAK2 mutation were negative. She had a history of miscarriage. Hematochezia abated on corticosteroids, mesalamine, and heparin, and she was transitioned from IV methylprednisolone to oral prednisone.  
Shortly afterward she developed worsening abdominal pain and hematochezia, prompting a return to IV methylprednisolone and increased mesalamine. Over 24 h she became lethargic and platelet count fell from 152 × 10^3/µL to 50 × 10^3/µL; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia was confirmed and anticoagulation was switched to argatroban. While on argatroban she had another large-volume bleed and became obtunded; head CT was negative for hemorrhage. Blood cultures grew Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus species, and Candida tropicalis, and she was started on broad antimicrobials while steroids were tapered.  
Serial CT venography then showed an expanding superior sagittal sinus thrombus and new cerebral venous thromboses despite therapeutic anticoagulation. She was transitioned to bivalirudin but progressed to disseminated intravascular coagulation and septic shock, and ultimately died under comfort measures.
title:
A probable case of catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome: Should
high-dose steroids be given in the setting of polymicrobial
sepsis?

case_prompt: A 79-year-old Caucasian male field worker from São Paulo, Brazil, presented with a six-month history of irritative lower urinary tract symptoms—urgency, frequency, nocturia—and difficulty initiating urination that progressed to urinary retention requiring a catheter. His medical history included Chagas disease with cardiac impairment, coronary disease treated with a stent in the anterior interventricular artery, and dyslipidemia. Digital rectal examination revealed a 40-cm3 prostate, slightly hardened at the apex with no nodules. Prostate-specific antigen was 1.2 ng/mL. Examination of the penis, testicles, and epididymides was unremarkable. Initial treatment with an α-blocker failed to allow catheter removal, and transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) was performed. During hospitalization, laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, hematocrit 36%, leukocytes 9300/µL, urinalysis with leukocytes 33 000 cells/mL and erythrocytes >500 000 cells/mL, and a negative urine culture. Serum sodium was 133 mEq/L, potassium 4.3 mEq/L, glucose 128 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. Postoperatively, he was discharged with normal urinary function. Anatomopathological analysis of the TURP specimen revealed chronic granulomatous prostatitis of fungal etiology with extensive necrosis.
title: Prostatic paracoccidioidomycosis with a fatal outcome: a case report

case_prompt: A 37-year-old previously healthy man presented with a two-week history of severe lower back pain, accompanied by mild lower abdominal pain, dysuria, and perineal discomfort. Two weeks earlier, he had been diagnosed at another facility with a urinary tract infection and treated with antibiotics without improvement. He denied vomiting, flank pain, hematuria, testicular pain, or penile discharge. On admission, his temperature was 39 °C, blood pressure 126/80 mmHg, heart rate 95 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Abdominal examination showed mild lower abdominal discomfort without tenderness. Digital rectal examination revealed severe prostate tenderness without fluctuance or nodules. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 22 × 10^3/μL, C-reactive protein of 238 mg/L, and a prostate-specific antigen of 9 ng/mL; urinalysis, renal function tests, serum glucose, and HIV test results were all within normal limits. Abdominal and renal ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged, heterogeneous prostate measuring 90 cc. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the pelvis revealed a 6 × 7 cm fluid collection with wall enhancement, necrosis, and septations extending beyond the prostatic capsule, consistent with an abscess.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare case of prostatic abscess caused by MRSA in a healthy young male: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old woman presented as a new outpatient with a history of symptomatic thrombocytopenia causing mucosal bleeding and easy bruising. She had a prior diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) based on isolated low platelet counts. She reported heavy menstrual bleeding requiring 9–11 pads per day, bleeding gums with tooth brushing, and occasional painless bruises; she denied hematuria, hematemesis, hematochezia, and had no family history of blood disorders or cancer.

Laboratory studies showed:
• Platelet count 9 × 10^3/µL  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, hematocrit 31%, mean corpuscular volume 76 fL, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 33.9 g/dL, ferritin 101 mg/L  
• Negative platelet-bound and free anti-GP IIb/IIIa and anti-GPIb/IX autoantibodies  
• Negative hepatitis and HIV panels  
• Peripheral smear with hypochromic microcytosis but normal platelet and leukocyte morphology; no abnormal cells  

She was started on oral iron for iron-deficiency anemia. A review of her prior medical records revealed fluctuations in platelet counts, with nadirs around 10 × 10^3/µL and peaks around 400 × 10^3/µL.  

Treatment and response:
• Pulse oral dexamethasone 40 mg for 4 days: platelet count remained at 8–9 × 10^3/µL over three cycles  
• Rituximab 375 mg/m^2 weekly for 4 weeks: platelets 11, 230, 130, then 15 × 10^3/µL  
• Eltrombopag 50 mg orally for 2 weeks: platelet count 17 × 10^3/µL  
• Splenectomy: platelet counts continued to fall to 10–50 × 10^3/µL  
• Bone marrow biopsy: normal, without evidence of myelodysplasia  
• Two additional doses of rituximab were given before transfer of care
title: Cyclical Thrombocytopenia Synchronized With the Patient’s Menstrual Cycle Treated With Danazol

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old woman, G3P2 at 12 weeks’ gestation, presented with a 2-day history of gradual-onset vaginal spotting and crampy lower abdominal pain radiating to her back. She reported one episode of clot passage but did not observe any products of conception and denied fever, nausea, vomiting, or presyncope.  

Her medical and surgical histories were unremarkable. On examination she was alert with a blood pressure of 110/72 mmHg, heart rate of 84 bpm, and normal other vital signs. Abdominal examination revealed mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding or rebound. Speculum examination showed a slightly open cervical os with oozing blood; no products were visible.  

Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 4.6×10^9/L, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, and platelets 255×10^9/L. Transvaginal ultrasound confirmed retained products of conception within the uterine cavity.  

She was administered 600 μg sublingual misoprostol. Four hours later, her blood pressure was 78/52 mmHg and heart rate was 56 bpm, and she reported passage of additional clots. Resuscitation with 1 L normal saline via two large-bore IV lines was initiated, and a urinary catheter drained 900 mL of clear urine. Crossmatching for two units of blood was underway. Fifteen minutes later, her blood pressure fell to 62/40 mmHg with a heart rate of 51 bpm and cold extremities.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Cervical vasovagal shock: A rare complication of incomplete abortion case report

case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman without previous psychiatric or neurological disease presented to the emergency department with pervasive existential anxieties and delusional beliefs of thought insertion and external control, accompanied by audible thoughts. Examination required lorazepam for severe anxiety.  
Laboratory studies revealed mild hypothyroidism (status post–hemithyroidectomy) treated with levothyroxine and hyponatremia from excessive water intake treated with sodium supplementation. Complete blood count, folic acid, vitamin B12, ceruloplasmin, and serologies for HIV, Borrelia burgdorferi, and Treponema pallidum were unremarkable.  
Antipsychotic treatment with risperidone, later switched to chlorprothixene, failed to relieve her delusional ideas.  
Neurological examination showed dysdiadochokinesis (left hand), mild hyperkinetic movements, bradykinesia on finger tapping, and a broad-based gait without rigidity, tremor, or postural instability. She became disoriented to time and place and exhibited long-term memory deficits with episodes of fear, agitation, and perseveration.  
Neuropsychological testing (CERAD+ battery) demonstrated impaired verbal recognition, severe visuospatial dysfunction, reduced semantic and phonemic fluency, and decreased cognitive flexibility; the MMSE score was 22/30 and the FAB score was 10/18. SCID-II showed no personality disorder.  
EEG demonstrated a normal alpha rhythm without epileptiform potentials. Brain MRI revealed generalized cerebral atrophy with putaminal rim sign, a hyperintensity at the lateral margin of the putamen, and ventriculomegaly.  
CSF analysis showed normal tau and beta-amyloid levels, no intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, negative autoimmune encephalitis antibodies, and absence of protein 14-3-3.  
These findings raised suspicion for an underlying neurodegenerative process.
title: An unusual presentation of Huntington’s disease

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old Caucasian man presented to the emergency department with acute urinary retention and lower abdominal pain. He reported consuming approximately 1 L of wine and several beers in the hours before presentation. He had no prior urinary symptoms, no significant medical history, and no family history of genitourinary disease. He was a regular smoker and alcohol consumer, with no medication use. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. The lower abdomen was distended; digital rectal and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.  
   
Point‐of‐care ultrasound showed normal kidneys and a distended bladder without wall irregularities; the prostate appeared unremarkable (size not documented). A Foley catheter drained 1 L of clear urine. Urinalysis was normal. He was given diclofenac and, two days later, passed a trial without catheter.  
   
One month later, he returned with acute urinary retention without recent alcohol intake. Examination and ultrasound revealed an enlarged prostate (approx. 50 mL). Laboratory tests, including prostate-specific antigen and lactate dehydrogenase, were within normal limits. He was started on tamsulosin, but trial without catheter failed, requiring re-catheterization. He developed intermittent tenesmus treated with trospium chloride. Cystoscopy showed diffusely erythematous and villous prostatic urethral mucosa extending to the bladder neck, with large obstructive lobes. A transurethral resection was scheduled in one month.  
   
Before surgery, he developed persistent right-sided flank pain. Urinalysis showed leukocyturia, and right pyelonephritis was treated with ciprofloxacin. Two days later, he presented with hematuria and right-sided hydronephrosis; renal colic and hemorrhagic cystitis were suspected, and analgesics and antibiotics were continued. A low-dose CT scan showed no stones but identified a mass in the prostate. Repeat cystoscopy again revealed obstructive prostatic lobes and erythematous mucosa. The working diagnosis was passing ureteral calculus with cystitis superimposed on benign prostatic hyperplasia. A trial without catheter relieved symptoms temporarily.  
   
Over the next days, he developed left-sided flank pain and bilateral second-degree hydronephrosis with a slight rise in creatinine; lactate dehydrogenase remained normal.
