Cystoscopy now showed a partly villous and solid tumor in the prostatic urethra infiltrating the bladder trigone and ureteric orifices. Biopsies were taken endoscopically, and bilateral ureteral stents were placed.
title: Burkitt’s lymphoma of the prostate presenting as acute urinary retention: a case report

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man presented with 5 days of severe hematemesis and melena. He reported bright-red emesis, dizziness, and cold, clammy skin. A similar episode occurred one month earlier without further evaluation. He denied alcohol use, smoking, antiplatelet or NSAID use, and had no family history of GI disease.

On examination, blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 120 beats/min and weak, respiratory rate 22/min, and temperature 37 °C. There were no stigmata of chronic liver disease or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies were within normal limits, including hemoglobin 11 mg/dl, leukocyte count 10 000/mm³, platelets 400 000/mm³, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dl, ALT 40 U/l, AST 38 U/l, albumin 4.0 g/dl, and prothrombin time 12 s.

Despite fluid resuscitation, tranexamic acid, and pantoprazole, hematemesis persisted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed multiple dilated vascular channels in the fundic part of the stomach with normal liver parenchyma and portal vasculature. Upper GI endoscopy revealed an angiomatous nodular lesion in the fundus without ulceration, which was inadvertently disrupted during the procedure, leading to further bleeding.
title: Angiodysplasia simulating variceal bleeding: a challenging case report of diagnosis and intervention

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old female with no significant medical history presented with four months of dizziness, frequent vomiting, and weight loss. Four months after symptom onset, she developed right hearing loss and blurred vision, prompting referral. Neurological examination revealed right-dominant resting horizontal nystagmus, right facial nerve palsy, right hearing loss, and headaches triggered by head motion; there was no neck stiffness.

Noncontrast brain CT showed a 7×5 mm iso- to slightly hypodense nodule in the right frontal cortex containing a focal hyperattenuated region. Brain MRI demonstrated diffusely thickened, strongly enhancing leptomeninges over the bilateral cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres, with multiple contrast-enhanced nodules along the meningeal surfaces, including one in the right frontal lobe protruding into the parenchyma. That frontal lesion was heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging, hypointense on T1-weighted imaging, and markedly hypointense on T2*-weighted imaging; diffusion-weighted imaging revealed heterogeneously restricted diffusion with an ADC of 0.9×10⁻³ mm²/s. Spinal MRI showed similarly thickened leptomeninges without intraparenchymal abnormalities. FDG-PET revealed a mean SUV of 3.51 for the frontal nodule—lower than that of normal cortex—and no other sites of abnormal uptake. Detailed blood tests showed no evidence of infectious or autoimmune disease.
title: Primary diffuse leptomeningeal atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor (AT/RT) demonstrating atypical imaging findings in an adolescent patient

case_prompt:
An 89-year-old man with second-degree Mobitz II and intermittent third-degree AV block had a left-sided dual-chamber pacemaker implanted for syncope. He developed an abrupt rise in right ventricular lead impedance and high capture thresholds, consistent with impending lead fracture. Left innominate vein occlusion precluded lead extraction, so the left device was abandoned and a new right-sided dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted and programmed to DDD 60–130 ppm, with paced and sensed AV delays of 220 msec and 165 msec, respectively. Because he was pacemaker-dependent, the abandoned left device was programmed to VVI 40 ppm as a backup.  
One month later, interrogation revealed that the abandoned left device was pacing approximately 75% of the time. An intracardiac electrogram from the new right-sided pacemaker showed that every fourth ventricular complex was a paced beat by the new device, while the intervening beats formed a regular nontracking rhythm at approximately 75 ppm.  
Why might this be? Possibilities include rate response phenomenon, pacing behavior resulting from End of Life mode, interference or cross-talk from the other device, and a manufacturer-specific pacing algorithm, such as rate smoothing.
title: Duelling pacemakers: Unexpected pacemaker interaction resulting from a proprietary rate smoothing algorithm

case_prompt: A 45-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of painless swelling of both sides of his neck, followed by swellings in both axillae. He reported intermittent fevers and night sweats. Multiple courses of antibiotics produced no improvement. On examination, vital signs were stable (temperature 37°C, blood pressure 150/70 mmHg). He had generalized, non-tender lymphadenopathy involving preauricular, occipital, axillary, and inguinal regions, with nodes up to 8 × 5 × 4 cm in size, and mild splenomegaly. Initial laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 3.3 × 10^9/L with 1.5% monocytes, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, platelets 158 × 10^9/L, lactate dehydrogenase 684 U/L, and C-reactive protein 186 mg/L; liver and renal function tests were normal. Viral studies for EBV, HIV, HBV, and HCV were negative. Contrast CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed bilaterally enlarged cervical, axillary, mediastinal, hilar, intraparotid, para-aortic, retrocaval, portahepatis, mesenteric, iliac, and inguinal lymph nodes, the largest measuring 8 × 5 cm in the right axilla; the spleen was mildly enlarged (14 cm) without focal lesions. During admission his temperature peaked at 38°C, and he was started empirically on Augmentin and Tazocin.
title: Generalized Lymphadenopathy as the First Presentation of Granulocytic Sarcoma: A Diagnostic Challenge

case_prompt: A 53-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of vague, generalized abdominal pain, bloating, and several episodes of bloody-mucous rectal discharge accompanied by changes in bowel habits. Her medical history was unremarkable; she had never used an intrauterine device and was postmenopausal for 5 years. She was afebrile, and vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed mild generalized abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, MCV 82 fL), a normal C-reactive protein level, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 13 mm/hr. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable. Colonoscopy demonstrated a polypoid, mass-like lesion with surrounding necrotic material in the distal sigmoid colon, located 20 cm from the anal verge. Multiple biopsies were obtained for histopathological examination.
journal: Middle East Journal of Digestive Diseases
title: Clinical, Endoscopic, and Histopathological Aspects of Sigmoid Actinomycosis; A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of chronic back pain that began after epidural anesthesia for a cesarean delivery. The pain was constant, progressive, worse with sitting and walking, and temporarily relieved by analgesics. She denied fever or weight loss. Because of severe pain and progression, she became unable to walk or bear weight. Initial treatment with antibiotics and muscle relaxants provided no improvement. She also developed a perianal abscess related to constipation due to limited mobility.

On examination, there was tenderness over the thoracolumbar spine, most pronounced at T12–L2, and paraspinal muscle spasm. Neurologic examination was normal, with intact motor and sensory function of the lower extremities and preserved sphincter control.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed multiple endplate changes in the thoracic (especially T11–T12) and lumbar regions. Laboratory studies, including CBC, C-reactive protein, and ESR, were obtained to evaluate for septic or infective spondylodiscitis. Cultures, sensitivity testing, and gene Xpert of the lesion were negative for tuberculosis or any other infection. Serum vitamin D level was normal. A bone biopsy demonstrated inflammatory infiltrates without granuloma or malignancy.
title: A rare adult presentation of chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) in 38-year female with exclusive spinal involvement

case_prompt: A 64-year-old man presented with a 2.5-month history of fatigue, fever, chills, night sweats, and a 65-lb weight loss. CT imaging demonstrated hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. An outside hospital evaluation included lymph node and skin biopsies and cytologic examination of a pleural effusion; all sites showed a polymorphic population of T and B lymphocytes with occasional rare atypical CD20-positive B cells, but clonality studies were negative and no definitive diagnosis was made. On transfer, a second excisional lymph node biopsy showed a polymorphous infiltrate of medium-to-large lymphocytes with clumped chromatin, multiple nucleoli, scant to moderate cytoplasm, frequent mitoses, and intermixed T lymphocytes, immunoblasts, histiocytes, eosinophils, and plasma cells, extending into surrounding fibroadipose tissue. Immunohistochemical stains revealed that the atypical large cells were strongly CD20 positive, Bcl-2 negative, CD10 negative, and Bcl-6 negative, with a high Ki-67 proliferation index.
final_diagnosis_raw: EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the elderly
title: Pleural Fluid Cytology of the Polymorphous Variant of EBV-Positive Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma: First Report and Distinction from a Reactive Process

case_prompt:
A 46-year-old African-American man presented with progressive, bilateral blurring of vision—worse in the right eye—over 5 days. He denied eye pain, trauma, redness, headache, neurologic symptoms, fever, or recent travel. His history was notable for hepatitis B virus infection diagnosed 5 years earlier; family history was noncontributory.

Vital signs were blood pressure 132/59 mmHg, heart rate 72/min, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 98.6°F, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination revealed icterus and nontender hepatomegaly; cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic examination demonstrated significantly reduced visual fields in both eyes, with normal pupillary size and reaction and a normal funduscopic examination. Extraocular movements were intact without ptosis; motor, sensory, and other cranial-nerve examinations were normal.

Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated aminotransferases (AST 500–1600 IU/L; ALT 400–1500 IU/L), stable platelets (127–210 ×10^3/μL), positive hepatitis B e antigen, and a hepatitis B virus DNA load of approximately 1.5×10^8 IU/mL. Serologic tests for hepatitis A and C viruses, HIV, syphilis, Babesia, and Lyme disease were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, orbits, neck, and spine with and without gadolinium was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed no malignant cells or organisms, few lymphocytes and monocytes, an albumin index of 6.3, a CSF IgG/albumin ratio of 0.26, and identical oligoclonal bands in serum and CSF.
title: Recurrent optic neuritis as the only manifestation of chronic hepatitis B virus flare: a case report

case_prompt: A 60‐year‐old man with metastasized ascending colon cancer diagnosed 18 months earlier (initial hemicolectomy followed by XELOX; later FOLFOX/bevacizumab and FOLFIRI/aflibercept) and comorbid hypertension, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea, primary hypothyroidism, and asthma was hospitalized for febrile neutropenia. During his stay, he reported progressive thirst and polyuria. Initial capillary glucose reached 11.2 mmol/l with a hemoglobin A1c of 6.9%, leading to a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and initiation of insulin therapy. Despite euglycemia, he continued to have fluid intake up to 6.3 L/day and urine output up to 8.4 L/day, especially at night. Endocrine evaluation revealed complete panhypopituitarism: TSH 0.1 mU/l (0.4–4.0), free T4 8.0 pmol/l (10.0–22.7), baseline cortisol <35 nmol/l (>500), testosterone <0.15 nmol/l (5–32), LH <0.2 U/l (1.0–8.6), FSH 2.6 U/l (0.7–11), prolactin 34.5 μg/l (2.7–17), IGF‐1 11.4 nmol/l (7.7–25.5), and copeptin 3.6 pmol/l (1.2–16.4) at a sodium level of 143 mmol/l. After hydrocortisone, desmopressin, and increased levothyroxine, his thirst and urine output decreased to 2–3 L/day. MRI of the brain with contrast showed a round enhancing lesion in the pituitary stalk and another in the pineal gland, with no other intracranial abnormalities. Ophthalmological examination was normal.
title: Synchronous pituitary and pineal gland lesions presenting with panhypopituitarism in a patient with widespread colorectal cancer: a case report

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old woman (162 cm, 52 kg) underwent elective total elbow arthroplasty under general anesthesia. Her history included well-controlled diabetes, Parkinson’s disease, depression, anxiety, and dementia. Home medications were valproate, olanzapine, quetiapine, donepezil, diazepam, levodopa, pregabalin, and rasagiline (discontinued two weeks preoperatively). She had experienced delusions and intermittent drowsiness two years earlier but had five prior uneventful general anesthetics.

Preinduction, she was alert and oriented without parkinsonian tremor. Vital signs: BP 145/86 mmHg, HR 78 beats/min. Anesthesia was induced with propofol, remifentanil, and rocuronium and maintained with desflurane, remifentanil, and intermittent rocuronium targeting MAP > 70 mmHg, BIS 40–60, and TOF < 30%. Total anesthesia time was 510 minutes; 3100 ml crystalloid given; urine output 540 ml. Hemodynamics were supported with ephedrine and phenylephrine as needed. 

At the end, anesthetics were discontinued and neuromuscular block was reversed with sugammadex. Although TOF returned to ≥ 90% and spontaneous breathing resumed, her BIS repeatedly fell to 50–60. On examination, her eyelids were tightly closed with left- or downward-deviated eyes; she was semi-comatose with neck and right arm stiffness and no response to painful stimuli. Temperature was 37.1 °C and arterial blood gas results were normal. One hour postoperatively there was no change in mental status. A neurologic consultation was obtained, and computed tomographic angiography of the head showed no evidence of acute stroke.
title: Catatonia associated with prolonged stupor after general anesthesia in a patient with multiple neuropsychiatric disorders -a case report-

case_prompt: A 59-year-old postmenopausal woman (gravida 2, para 2) presented with vaginal bleeding. Initial cytological tests of the cervix and endometrium were negative. On referral, vaginal examination revealed an enlarged uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a large heterogeneous mass occupying the entire endometrial cavity. Repeat endometrial cytology remained negative, and fractional curettage yielded only fibrous tissue with epithelial-like cells. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 77 × 76 mm heterogeneous solid tumor filling the uterine cavity, and degenerated myoma, leiomyosarcoma, or endometrial stromal sarcoma was suspected. Serum CA125 was mildly elevated at 41.4 U/mL, whereas CA19-9 and CEA were within normal limits. The patient underwent total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy. At laparotomy, the uterus was fist-sized without serosal invasion, both ovaries appeared normal, and a tumor arising from the uterine body occupied the entire cavity.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: A Case of Adenosarcoma of the Uterus

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man from East Timor, residing in the UK for 6 years, presented with 4 weeks of progressive left testicular pain and swelling, preceded by lower abdominal pain and dysuria that was initially treated as a urinary tract infection. He re-presented with 3 days of left iliac fossa pain and dysuria. Urinalysis showed leukocytes and nitrites. Tumor markers (AFP, hCG) and testosterone levels were normal. C-reactive protein was mildly elevated (21.6 mg/L) and full blood count was normal except for mild eosinophilia (1.02 × 10^9/L).

Initial scrotal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous, hypervascular lesion centered on the left epididymis extending into the left testis. Three weeks later, ultrasound demonstrated progression of the left lesion, new hypoechoic lesions in the right testis, scrotal thickening, and a discharging sinus.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed: right apical pleuroparenchymal distortion with bronchiectasis; a solitary peripherally calcified retroperitoneal lymph node; ill-defined hypoenhancement of the left renal upper pole without hydronephrosis; a peripherally enhancing collection in the right seminal vesicle; and multiple small foci of gas within the prostate gland.
title: A rare case of disseminated genitourinary tract tuberculosis complicated by emphysematous prostatitis and seminal vesicle abscess

case_prompt: A 43-year-old man presented with a 12-hour history of high-grade fever, cough, and left-sided chest pain. He had no history of trauma. On examination, his temperature was elevated; auscultation revealed reduced air entry over the left upper and mid lung zones. A chest radiograph showed a triangular opacity in the left upper and mid zones laterally. The finding was interpreted as possible lung consolidation, and the patient was treated medically. Two follow-up chest radiographs, each obtained at two-week intervals, showed no change in the left-mid-zone opacity, although he was asymptomatic. Review of the radiographs also noted depression of the left third rib. To further evaluate the persistent opacity and rib abnormality, a helical CT scan of the chest with multiplanar and 3D reconstructions was obtained.
title: A Unique Case of Left Second Supernumerary and Left Third Bifid Intrathoracic Ribs with Block Vertebrae and Hypoplastic Left Lung

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old man who works as a rice-field farmer presented with a 1-year history of right-eye proptosis and a 2-month history of foul-smelling nasal discharge accompanied by episodes of nasal itching. He denied constitutional symptoms, and there was no relevant family history. 

On examination, there was proptosis of the lower right eyelid and a firm, round swelling near the medial canthus of the right eye. Nasal endoscopy revealed a friable, polypoidal reddish mass on the inferior turbinate extending into the opening of the nasolacrimal duct, and multiple friable, polypoidal reddish masses in the nasopharynx that bled on contact. Routine biochemical and hematological tests were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses and orbits showed an intensely enhancing extraconal mass lesion in the inferior right orbit, with rarefaction of the inferior orbital wall and bony nasolacrimal duct. The nasolacrimal duct was enlarged, and similar enhancing masses were seen in the inferior turbinate and nasopharynx, containing small areas of air and calcification. A leash of blood vessels originating from the nasopharyngeal wall was seen supplying the lesion.

MRI demonstrated on T2-weighted imaging a heterogeneously hyperintense, multilobulated mass originating in the nasal cavity and nasopharynx, extending into the oropharynx, with a few flow voids. On postcontrast T1-weighted images, there was an intensely enhancing multilobulated mass in the inferior right orbit and nasal cavity, with nonenhancing foci and a cerebriform appearance as well as extension via the nasolacrimal duct causing proptosis.
title: Rhinosporidiosis: A Rare Cause of Proptosis and an Imaging Dilemma for Sinonasal Masses

case_prompt: A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of morning stiffness in his lower back, bilateral wrist, shoulder, and knee pain, and new skin lesions on his fingers and knees. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs provided only temporary relief. On examination, he had pain and tenderness in both knees, the third proximal interphalangeal joint of the left hand, and bilateral wrist joints. Cutaneous examination revealed symmetric multiple small umbilicated or crusted erythematous papules and ulcerated erythematous papules on the knees, knuckles of the fingers, elbows, and left auricle, with some pustule-like yellow vesicles on the metacarpophalangeal joints. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 mm/h and a C-reactive protein level of 62.7 mg/L, with negative rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, anti-nuclear antibody, and HLA-B27. A pelvic radiograph demonstrated bilateral grade 2 sacroiliitis. Ultrasound revealed bilateral knee effusions, synovitis, and Achilles tendon enthesitis, and sacroiliac-joint MRI showed focal bone marrow edema in the left sacroiliac joint.
title: A Case of Palisaded Neutrophilic and Granulomatous Dermatitis Associated with an Initial Presentation in Ankylosing Spondylitis

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of nausea, vomiting, upper abdominal pain localized to the left hypochondrium and lumbar region, and unintentional weight loss. She has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus on insulin, hypertension, and thoracolumbar discopathy. She does not smoke, drinks alcohol occasionally, and has no family history of malignancy. On examination, she had epigastric tenderness without palpable masses. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed two sessile, crater-like ulcerated lesions in the gastric fundus measuring 2.5–3.0 cm in diameter; biopsies were obtained. 

Abdominal and pelvic MRI showed two irregular, enhancing masses in the gastric fundus measuring 1.45×1.9 cm and 2.8×2.4 cm, both with restricted diffusion. Additional findings included pelvic girdle bone lesions suggestive of metastases, bilateral adrenal adenomas, and uterine fibromatous nodules. 

Subsequent thoracoabdominal CT confirmed the gastric masses and demonstrated multiple bone and pulmonary metastatic lesions.
title: Primary Gastric Malignant Melanoma in a 68-Year-Old Woman: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: An 81-year-old man presented with 4 months of progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion. His medical history included chronic kidney disease and coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting. On examination, his blood pressure was 138/82 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats per minute, and respiratory rate was normal. An electrocardiogram was unremarkable. Chest radiography revealed a rounded mass measuring approximately 8 cm in the left lower lung zone. A noncontrast CT scan of the chest showed an enhancing soft-tissue mass along the left aspect of the pericardium, measuring 6.2 × 5.3 cm. At that time, the differential diagnosis included pericardial cyst, teratoma, lymphangioma, and branchial cyst. A dedicated CT heart angiogram demonstrated a 6.9 × 5.4 cm mass in the left inferior mediastinum with a stalk-like connection to the pericardium. A biopsy of the mass was performed.
title: An unusual location of solitary fibrous tumor in heart—A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 12-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of insidious onset of pain and swelling over both clavicles, which began bilaterally on the same day. The discomfort temporarily subsided with analgesics but recurred days after stopping medication. She had no fever, no history of trauma, no other swellings, no polyarthralgias or morning stiffness, and no weight loss, throat infections, or skin lesions. Her activities of daily living were unaffected, and there was no relevant family history.

On examination, both medial halves of the clavicles were enlarged. The swellings were hard, smooth, and ill-defined, without tenderness or warmth. The sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints were non-tender, shoulder range of motion was normal, and there were no distal neurovascular deficits. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

Plain radiographs of the clavicles showed expansile, sclerotic lesions involving the medial halves bilaterally. Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 90 mm/hr, C-reactive protein of 0.6 mg/dL, and a white-cell count of 8000 cells/mm³. An antistreptolysin O titer was negative, and peripheral blood smear was normal. Hemoglobin electrophoresis and sickling test were negative. Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies were negative. A Mantoux test and sputum acid-fast bacilli smear were negative. Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. A chest radiograph was normal, and abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the clavicles demonstrated bilateral expansile lesions of the medial thirds measuring approximately 5.7 × 1.8 cm on the right and 6 × 2 cm on the left, with signal alteration, trabecular coarsening, obliteration of the marrow cavity and fat, continuous periosteal reaction, and heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast sequences; there was no significant adjacent soft-tissue mass.
title: Chronic Recurrent Multifocal Osteomyelitis - A Rare Clinical Presentation and Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia diagnosed 7 years earlier and treated with fludarabine, idarubicin, and cytarabine, in clinical remission for the past year but lost to follow-up, presented with 2 months of rapidly progressive bilateral vision loss and diplopia. He also reported headaches, nausea, vomiting, and a 26-lb weight loss over 2 months. He had been evaluated by an optometrist who prescribed new glasses without improvement.

On examination, the right eye had restricted extraocular movements in all directions, ptosis, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and minimal light perception. The left eye had normal extraocular movements and pupillary responses but severely restricted visual fields and decreased foveal acuity. Visual findings fluctuated rapidly. Dilated fundoscopic examination revealed bilateral Grade IV papilledema.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a lobulated extra-axial mass centered in the sella turcica, extending anteriorly along the floor of the anterior cranial fossa, crossing both cavernous sinuses into the middle cranial fossae, and posteriorly into the suprasellar and prepontine cisterns. The mass also extended into bilateral orbital apices and the sphenoid and ethmoid sinuses, encasing both internal carotid arteries, cavernous sinus contents, and optic nerves. It was hypointense on T1, isointense on T2, with homogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1.

Computed tomography of the head demonstrated a hyperdense sellar mass with erosion of the ethmoidal portion of the anterior skull base. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation revealed decreased ACTH, FSH, and LH. The patient was started on dexamethasone for optic nerve compression and adrenal insufficiency.
title: Myeloid sarcoma of the skull base: A case report and systematic literature review

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old man with type II diabetes mellitus presented with a 2-week history of left-sided neck pain, especially on swallowing, and persistent low-grade fever. He had no response to nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs. Examination by otolaryngology revealed marked soft-tissue destruction of the left peritonsillar region and tonsillar fossa without active bleeding. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck demonstrated an extensive lesion in the left peritonsillar and pharyngeal region with a liquefied central component. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a mass in the left submandibular region, lateral to the major neck vessels, compressing the internal jugular vein. The lesion lay posterior to the submandibular gland, displacing it anteriorly, and there was a defect in the lateral oropharyngeal wall, heterogeneous thickening of the palatine tonsil, and a necrotic lymph node adjacent to the internal jugular vein. 

Differential diagnoses included abscess versus tumor. Biopsy specimens were obtained twice to exclude malignancy.
title: Microvascular flap reconstruction of pharynx in patient with actinomycosis

case_prompt: A 63-year-old man presented with an acute episode of blurry vision, along with a two-month history of headache and intermittent nausea. He denied pain or infectious symptoms. Examination revealed bilateral proptosis with lid retraction, ophthalmoplegia in all directions, and reduced visual acuity without visual field defects; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. A nonenhanced CT of the head showed symmetric enlargement of all extraocular muscles with sparing of the musculotendinous junctions. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits, and anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies were negative. On further history, he reported 22 kg of unintentional weight loss over 3 months and a 40 pack-year smoking history. A screening chest radiograph revealed a large right middle lobe mass. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head and orbits demonstrated symmetric extraocular muscle enlargement with intra- and extraconal edema, sparing of the musculotendinous junctions, and no evidence of an infiltrative process. Serum vasculitic studies, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, parathyroid hormone studies, and urinary paraprotein studies were unremarkable. Serum potassium and corrected calcium were borderline elevated at 5.5 mmol/L and 2.63 mmol/L, respectively; all other electrolytes, including ionized calcium, were normal. Paraneoplastic autoantibodies, including anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-Yo, anti-PCA-2, anti-VGCC, and anti-VGKC, were negative.
title: Bilateral extraocular muscle enlargement and proptosis associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

case_prompt: A 44-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a hepatic mass that had been discovered incidentally five years earlier. Initial ultrasound had shown a 4.24 × 2.63 cm hypoechoic nodule in the right liver lobe. Non-contrast CT revealed a well-circumscribed, low–density oval mass in segment 6; contrast-enhanced CT at that time suggested peripheral enhancement and a hemangioma. During four years of surveillance, the mass grew slowly. In January 2020, contrast-enhanced CT showed a 7.8 cm mass located between segment 6 of the liver and the right adrenal gland, with marked peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase and hypointensity in the portal and delayed phases compared with adjacent liver. The patient remained asymptomatic. Laboratory studies were notable for negative hepatitis B surface antigen, negative anti–hepatitis C virus, positive hepatitis B surface antibody, and normal levels of α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, liver disease, or relevant family history. Physical examination was unremarkable.
title: An ectopic adrenocortical oncocytic adenoma in the liver highly mimicking hepatocellular carcinoma: case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 5-year-old child with known bicuspid aortic valve (mild stenosis) and mild enlargement of the aortic root and ascending aorta presented for routine follow-up. The patient was asymptomatic, with no chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, fatigue, or syncope. Vital signs were stable. An ECG showed sinus arrhythmia and was otherwise unchanged from prior tracings. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed the bicuspid valve, an enlarged aortic root, and ascending aorta. In the suprasternal notch view, an apparent intimal flap was noted in the ascending aorta just proximal to the head and neck vessels, raising concern for a possible aortic dissection or aneurysm. 
A chest CT scan was obtained; it was interpreted as showing a dissection flap extending 2.7 cm from the level of the anterior aortic cusp distally. The patient was referred for further management. On arrival, the child remained asymptomatic. Repeat ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with left axis deviation. A repeat echocardiogram again showed what was interpreted as an intimal flap in the ascending aorta. A second CT scan was interpreted as an anterior ascending aortic aneurysm extending from above the sinotubular junction obliquely along the left side of the ascending aorta to the transverse arch. The images were suboptimal, with contrast opacification of both right and left heart chambers and motion artifact.
final_diagnosis_raw: left juxtaposition of the right atrial appendage
title: Left Juxtaposition of the Right Atrial Appendage: Pitfalls in Diagnosis

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old girl was admitted with a 5-day history of left-sided neck swelling, fever, and mild dysphagia. One day before admission she developed bilateral conjunctival injection despite 5 days of cefoperazone–sulbactam and metronidazole. Her medical, family, and social histories were unremarkable. 

On examination, she had low-grade fever, mild posterior pharyngeal wall congestion, grade II tonsillar enlargement, and a tender, erythematous swelling below the left earlobe extending anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Multiple thumb-sized lymph nodes were palpable in the left supraclavicular fossa. Conjunctival injection with scleral edema and scattered dry rales were also noted.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 35.3×10^9/L (83.4% neutrophils), HGB 124 g/L, PLT 441×10^9/L, CRP 30.2 mg/L, PCT 0.14 ng/mL, and urinalysis WBC 85.6/µL. Liver and kidney function and cardiac enzymes were normal.

Neck CT revealed an irregular soft-tissue density with partial cystic components deep to the left parotid gland and sternocleidomastoid muscle (13×25 mm), with mild rim enhancement but no enhancement of cystic areas. Chest CT was normal.

She was diagnosed with acute cervical lymphadenitis, left parapharyngeal abscess, and acute conjunctivitis. She received intravenous cefoperazone–sulbactam and underwent surgical resection of the left parapharyngeal mass with lymph node excision. 

Histopathology of the tissue showed proliferative lymphoid changes with abundant nuclear fragments in necrotic foci, suggestive of acute necrotizing lymphadenitis. Pathogen gene sequencing of the tissue did not identify any specific pathogens. 

On postoperative day 2, WBC was 22.5×10^9/L, neutrophils 67.8%, PLT 651×10^9/L, and CRP 28.3 mg/L. Despite surgery, her temperature continued to fluctuate and conjunctival injection persisted. MRI on day 3 demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral carotid sheaths, submandibular, and submental regions (largest 10 mm) and an oval T2-hyperintense lesion (31×19×23 mm) adjacent to the left carotid sheath, with poorly defined borders and increased signal in the left anterior cervical fascia.
title: A KD with multiple pseudocystic lesions in oropharynx and literature review

case_prompt: A 20-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a three-week history of nausea, multiple episodes of vomiting, and moderate headache partially relieved by analgesics. There were no focal neurologic deficits. On noncontrast computed tomography of the brain, there was a partially calcified, soft-tissue density mass in the left lateral ventricle, broad-based on the septum pellucidum and occupying the foramen of Monro, with marked ventricular dilatation, effacement of sulci, and transependymal edema. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a voluminous intraventricular lesion that was isointense to gray matter on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with subtle peripheral cystic components and septations bridging to the ventricular wall, giving a scalloped contour. Susceptibility-weighted images revealed signal voids within the lesion corresponding to vascular structures and calcifications. Diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient mapping demonstrated restricted diffusion. After intravenous contrast, the lesion enhanced heterogeneously, with prominent intralesional vessels. Digital subtraction angiography indicated multiple small arterial feeders from anterior and middle cerebral branches and venous drainage to the left internal cerebral vein. A dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion study showed a relative cerebral blood volume of 3.4 compared with contralateral white matter.
title: Intraventricular neurocytoma: A diagnostic challenge with prognostic value

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old woman with a 2-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus and a 1-week history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presented with 3 days of progressive bilateral weakness in her arms and legs. She denied prior thromboses. Her medications were mycophenolate 250 mg twice daily, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, and apixaban 5 mg twice daily. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Muscle strength by Medical Research Council grading was 1/5 in the right upper and lower extremities and 2/5 in the left upper and lower extremities; cranial nerves II through XII were intact, light touch sensation was preserved, and she was alert and oriented with normal speech. High-sensitivity troponin I was 2781 ng/mL, and the ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with nonspecific ST-segment abnormalities unchanged from prior tracings. She was started on clopidogrel and atorvastatin while continuing apixaban and metoprolol.

A CT angiogram of the head demonstrated subtle hypoattenuation in the left frontal convexity, and MRI of the brain with contrast showed acute ischemic changes in watershed regions among the anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries. MRI of the cervical spine with and without contrast was unremarkable. A transthoracic echocardiogram with bubble study revealed no intracardiac thrombus; a cardiac PET–CT showed no perfusion defect. On hospital day 2, the troponin level rose to 5472 ng/mL. Neurology recommended holding apixaban, starting intravenous heparin, and obtaining a lumbar puncture. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed protein 30.6 mg/dL, glucose 51 mg/dL, 82 red cells/mm3, 1 lymphocyte/mm3, 10 monocytes/mm3, and a clear appearance; there were no abnormal serological, cytological, or biochemical findings. Creatine kinase ranged from 29 to 46 U/L. Rheumatology was consulted and considered an SLE flare. They administered methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days followed by prednisone 60 mg daily, and they ordered serological studies. Results showed a positive ANA; anti–double-stranded DNA antibody >1000 IU/mL; elevated anti–Sjogren’s‐syndrome–related antigen A; atypical p-ANCA; complement C3 of 110.3 mg/dL (previously 82.7 mg/dL) and C4 of 26.8 mg/dL (previously 19.9 mg/dL); and unremarkable lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies.
title: The Diagnostic Dilemma of “The Great Imitator”: Heart and Cerebral Involvement of Lupus Manifesting as Bilateral Upper and Lower Extremity Weakness

case_prompt: A 61-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with acute, constant epigastric pain of 1-day duration, associated with a sense of abdominal distension, several episodes of diarrhea, and a low-grade fever. On examination, her temperature was 38.1 °C; cardiovascular and pulmonary exams were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness localized to the epigastrium without guarding; the remainder of the abdomen was soft and non-tender. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 15.4 × 10^3/µL (reference 4.8–10.8) and a C-reactive protein concentration of 80 mg/L. A frontal chest radiograph demonstrated crescentic radiolucency beneath the right hemidiaphragm, suggestive of free air. To further evaluate, a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan was obtained; it revealed interposition of the right colon between the liver and diaphragm with circumferential thickening of the sigmoid colon, suggestive of an inflammatory or infectious process, and no evidence of free intraperitoneal air.
title: Pneumoperitoneum and Chilaiditi syndrome: navigating a diagnostic conundrum

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension was brought to the emergency department with a decreased level of consciousness of unknown duration. He was last seen awake at 6 p.m. the previous evening after dinner and his usual medications, and was found unconscious at home at 2 a.m. Two recent falls were reported, one two days earlier and another the same morning. There was no history of fever, convulsions, chest pain, cough, rash, decreased urine output, or substance use.

On arrival, he was unresponsive with a snoring airway. Vital signs were: temperature 97 °F, blood pressure 140/70 mmHg, pulse rate 68 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Neurologic examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7 (E1V2M4); pupils were 2 mm bilaterally with sluggish reaction to light; deep tendon reflexes were hypoactive, and plantar responses were extensor bilaterally.

A point-of-care glucose measurement was 19 mg/dL. After administration of 50 mL of 50% dextrose, his blood glucose normalized to 110 mg/dL, but his Glasgow Coma Scale remained at E1V1M4. Arterial blood gas analysis showed compensated metabolic acidosis. A noncontrast CT scan of the head revealed no evidence of ischemic changes, intracranial hemorrhage, or space-occupying lesions. 

Subsequent brain MRI demonstrated signal changes with restricted diffusion in the bilateral cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and caudate nuclei, findings suggestive of ischemia with cortical necrosis likely due to hypoxic–ischemic injury.
title: Prolonged Hypoglycemic Encephalopathy: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 52-year-old African American man with a known diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis complex presented for evaluation of longstanding facial lesions. His extracutaneous manifestations included bilateral subependymal nodules, cortical tubers, a renal angiomyolipoma, and multiple renal cysts. On examination, there were multiple firm brown dome-shaped papules on the cheeks, nose, and chin; several skin-colored papules and plaques on the forehead and right cheek; and numerous hypopigmented macules on the thighs. The largest skin-colored nodule on the right cheek was removed by shave biopsy. Histopathologic examination of this nodule revealed multiple foci of thin epithelial strands radiating from the upper part of the isthmus, surrounded by compact thin collagen fibers containing fibroblasts that stained for CD34, consistent with multiple fibrofolliculomas. An elastic stain revealed an absence of elastic fibers in the stroma surrounding the epithelial strands within the fibrofolliculomas; between the fibrofolliculomas, elastic fibers were irregularly distributed with decreased amounts in some areas.
title: Multiple fibrofolliculomas within a fibrous cephalic plaque in a patient with tuberous sclerosis

case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman with no past medical or surgical history presented with a painless mass in the left parotid region of 2 years’ duration. She reported that the size fluctuated with head position.  
On examination, the swelling was not visible in the sitting position but became more pronounced when the head was tilted downward. The mass was soft, compressible, non-tender, and non-pulsatile. There was no facial palsy, and the remainder of the head and neck examination was unremarkable.  
Color Doppler ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic compressible lesion within the left parotid at the junction of the deep and superficial lobes, with a venous flux within; it filled in the proclive position and drained into the retromandibular vein.  
Cervical MRI demonstrated a varicose formation in the deep and superficial left parotid lobes (18 × 14 × 13 mm), hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images with gadolinium enhancement; the lesion showed high diffusion signal (ADC 2.6). Anteriorly it abutted the mandibular ramus without signal anomaly; medially it was separated from the lateropharyngeal fat; posteriorly it was clear of the jugulocarotid vessels with preservation of the fat plane.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Retromandibular venous ectasia presenting as a parotid mass: An interesting case report

case_prompt: A 42-year-old Japanese woman with iron deficiency anemia was brought to the emergency department 36 minutes after a high-energy head-on motor-vehicle collision while wearing a seatbelt and airbag. On arrival, she was alert; respiratory rate 30/min, heart rate 74/min, blood pressure 148/64 mmHg, temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on 10 L/min via reservoir mask. She complained of anterior chest pain and had a laceration on the left lower thigh and a contusion on the right groin. On abdominal examination she had mild to moderate tenderness in the right lower quadrant without guarding or rebound. Focused ultrasonography showed fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 14,030/mm3, hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, normal lactate (1.8 mmol/L), and normal coagulation parameters. Noncontrast CT of the torso identified fractures of the right clavicle, sternum, and left 6th–8th ribs, and complex fluid (mean attenuation 28 HU) around the Douglas fossa extending to the ileocecal area. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a slightly dilated appendiceal tip containing a coprolith and an unclear appendiceal wall at the tip, without pneumoperitoneum, solid-organ injury, or contrast extravasation. Her vital signs remained stable and hemoglobin did not decrease over one hour; however, serial CT scans showed an increase in peritoneal fluid extending from the appendix through the pelvis. Emergency laparotomy was then considered because of localized peritonitis and possible intraperitoneal hemorrhage.
title: Undetermined Ruptured Low‐Grade Appendiceal Mucinous Neoplasm Following High‐Energy Blunt Abdominal Trauma Requiring Emergency Laparotomy

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old girl in 10th grade presented to the emergency department with her father. She had no prior medical history but had great difficulty coping with her mother’s death from breast cancer three years earlier. On examination, she exhibited a depressed mood, high levels of vegetative anxiety, egosyntonic visual hallucinations, and a bizarre gait abnormality. There was perfectionistic and obsessive behavior, and she reported intrusive images of her mother’s funeral. Her father noted stress related to upcoming school evaluations. 

Neurologic and pediatric evaluations, including laboratory studies, electroencephalogram, and brain computed tomography, were all normal. In the child and adolescent psychiatry assessment, she was found to be depressed with pronounced anxiety and visual hallucinations. A diagnosis of affective psychosis was made under ICD-10 criteria, and a low dose of antipsychotic medication was initiated.

After approximately 15 days of apparent symptom resolution, she returned with acute allopsychic disorientation, psychomotor agitation, disorganized speech punctuated by irrational laughter, thought-control abnormalities, and recurrent bizarre visual hallucinations. A urine toxicology screen was negative. After emergency antipsychotic treatment and a brief hospitalization, she was alert, cooperative, and focused but reserved, with hypomimia and mild depressive affect. She had no current thought disorder or hallucinations but no recollection of the acute episode.

At this stage, a diagnosis of psychotic disorder with schizophrenic symptoms was made according to ICD-10, and her antipsychotic regimen was adjusted for long-term monitoring.
title: A psychotic experience during adolescence: reasoning about differential diagnosis. Case report

case_prompt: A 54-year-old man presented in April 2018 with a 2-month history of fever and persistent cough. He had a 17-year history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a 360-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination was unremarkable, and vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests showed a fasting blood glucose of 15.5 mmol/L with normal liver and renal function, normal C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and serum tumor markers. Sputum culture, sputum smear for acid-fast bacillus, and T-SPOT® TB were negative. Immunoglobulin levels, T cell subsets, and autoantibody screens were within normal limits; HIV serology was negative. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography revealed enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes and a mass-like lesion in the left hilum causing stenosis of the proximal left upper bronchus. Bronchoscopy showed reddening and thickening of the bronchial mucosa with stenosis of the left main bronchus. Bronchial membrane biopsy specimens were obtained, and endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration of stations 7 and 11L lymph nodes was performed.
title: Invasive aspergillosis presenting as hilar masses with stenosis of bronchus: A case report

case_prompt: A 46-year-old morbidly obese woman presented with 2–3 months of painful redness and swelling of her right medial thigh. She had no known medical history but was found to be hypertensive. An ultrasound of the right lower extremity to exclude deep vein thrombosis was negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the right thigh demonstrated skin thickening and reticular soft-tissue attenuation compatible with edema throughout the subcutaneous fat at the area of redness. The patient was treated for presumptive cellulitis with diuretics and intravenous antibiotics, then discharged on a 7-day course of oral antibiotics; a compressive stocking was recommended but not obtained. Over the next 2 years, she was admitted four times for recurrent right thigh pain, redness, and swelling; she remained afebrile with normal white-cell counts on all admissions. An ultrasound during this period showed a lobular contour of subcutaneous fat with edema but no organized abscess. Fifteen months later, she returned with 3 weeks of right thigh swelling, intermittent fevers, and a larger, more well-defined medial thigh mass. MRI showed a large exophytic mass arising from the subcutaneous fat of the medial thigh, isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on fat-suppressed fluid-sensitive sequences, minimal peripheral and dermal enhancement, and regions of interposed fat. An ultrasound-guided biopsy was nondiagnostic.
title: Massive localized lymphedema of the thigh mimicking liposarcoma

case_prompt: A 28-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of edema, gross painless hematuria, and uremic symptoms. He had no history of diabetes or hypertension and smoked 2–3 cigarettes per day for 2 years. On examination, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg; there was pallor and bilateral pitting edema. Urinalysis showed 3+ protein, numerous red blood cells, and red-cell casts. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, white-cell count 14 830/mm3, platelets 230 000/mm3, and serum creatinine 16.5 mg/dL. Serum electrolytes and complement levels were normal; total calcium was 7.1 mg/dL. Tests for hepatitis B and C, HIV, antinuclear antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Renal ultrasonography showed bilaterally enlarged echogenic kidneys (12.9 cm). A renal biopsy was performed. Light microscopy showed four glomeruli, each with circumferential cellular crescents, fibrinoid necrosis, and disruption of the glomerular basement membranes and Bowman’s capsules; there was severe acute tubular injury. Immunofluorescence in seven glomeruli demonstrated strong linear staining (4+) of glomerular capillary walls for IgG and kappa light chain, with negative staining for IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and lambda. Subclass staining showed linear IgG1 (3+) along capillary walls and negative IgG2, IgG3, and IgG4. Electron microscopy revealed no electron-dense or powdery deposits.
title: Circulating Monoclonal IgG1-kappa Antibodies Causing Anti-glomerular Basement Membrane Nephritis

case_prompt: A 65-year-old Chinese man with chronic hepatitis B (on entecavir) and longstanding hypertension (on metoprolol) was admitted for elective hemorrhoidectomy. Preoperative CT of the abdomen revealed multiple abnormal signals in the liver. Liver MRI showed numerous low-density circular lesions of varying sizes, the largest measuring 2.1 × 2.0 cm in the right posterior lobe. A PET/CT scan demonstrated intensely increased metabolic activity in regions of the intestinal wall, mesentery, omentum, and peritoneum (SUVmax 16.3), raising concern for a malignant process. Exploratory laparoscopy revealed a 5 × 4 cm polypoid mass in the omentum, which invaded through the muscularis propria into the subserosal soft tissue and exhibited lymphovascular invasion. A biopsy specimen was obtained for further analysis.
title: Jejunal sarcomatoid carcinoma: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old postmenopausal Middle Eastern woman with diabetes, hypertension, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with a 10-month history of painless enlargement of her right breast. She denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. She had no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer, and her gynecologic history included three cesarean deliveries and 1 year of oral contraceptive use. 

On examination, the right breast was diffusely enlarged and non-tender. Multiple firm, non-fixed, non-tender lymph nodes were palpable in the right axilla. There was no skin redness, discoloration, or palpable breast mass. 

Laboratory studies showed peripheral eosinophilia (14%; normal, 1–3%) and an elevated serum IgE level (2153 UI/mL; normal, 80–120 UI/mL). 

Initial differential diagnoses included primary breast carcinoma or sarcoma, breast metastasis, primary or secondary breast lymphoma, inflammatory disorders (including non-puerperal mastitis), and superior vena cava obstruction due to thrombosis or mediastinal mass. 

Mammography of the right breast demonstrated diffuse enlargement with increased density, trabecular and dermal thickening, and right axillary lymphadenopathy but no suspicious mass lesion or microcalcifications. Ultrasound showed skin thickening, multiple hypoechoic areas consistent with fat edema, and no focal mass; ipsilateral axillary nodes had thickened cortices and preserved fatty hila with mildly increased vascularity. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed diffuse right breast enlargement with fat stranding and dermal thickening, multiple right axillary lymphadenopathies, and no pulmonary or mediastinal mass, nodule, or lymphadenopathy. The patient declined breast MRI due to claustrophobia and concerns about gadolinium.
title: A rarely described Kimura’s disease of the breast

case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of gradually progressive blurred vision in his left eye and a 10-day history of blurred vision in his right eye. He denied headache, pulsatile tinnitus, or other symptoms suggestive of raised intracranial pressure. His medical history was notable for ischemic cardiomyopathy treated with a cardiac transplant 6 months earlier and chronic kidney disease. His medications included tacrolimus 3 mg twice daily, prednisone 7.5 mg daily, mycophenolate sodium 360 mg twice daily, voriconazole 200 mg twice daily, pantoprazole, pravastatin, and bisoprolol.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye, with a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Humphrey visual fields showed constriction in the right eye and an enlarged blind spot with a nasal step in the left eye. Dilated fundus examination revealed significant bilateral optic disc edema, more pallid in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fiber layer demonstrated average thicknesses of 442 μm in the right eye and 330 μm in the left eye.

Brain MRI and MR venography were normal, with no evidence of raised intracranial pressure or distal transverse sinus stenosis. Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position revealed an opening pressure of 12 cm H₂O, 3 nonerythroid cells, and normal glucose and protein. Cerebrospinal fluid studies were negative for cryptococcal antigen, varicella zoster virus, VDRL, and fungal culture. A repeat lumbar puncture two weeks later showed an opening pressure of 14 cm H₂O with otherwise normal contents. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 114 g/L, creatinine 181 μmol/L, and a tacrolimus level of 13.4 μg/L.
title: Tacrolimus Optic Neuropathy Mimicking Papilledema

case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man with a history of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (35%), pulmonary sarcoid, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, prior cerebrovascular accident, and active crack-cocaine use presented with 3 days of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea and vomiting. He denied chest pain, cough, dyspnea, fever, or chills. He was a former 8-pack-year smoker with remote alcohol use. He reported regular intranasal crack-cocaine use, most recently 3 days before presentation. His medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, and metoprolol tartrate; he denied any new medications or recent steroid use.

Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, he had tenderness to palpation in the epigastrium, normal breath sounds, and no peripheral edema. Laboratory testing revealed lipase 2300 IU/dL (reference 11–82), total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, AST 30 IU/L, ALT 16 IU/L, white blood cell count 5700 cells/mL, triglycerides 90 mg/dL, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, and IgG4 18 mg/dL (reference 1–123). A urine toxicology screen was positive for cocaine only. Electrocardiography showed more pronounced T-wave inversions in the inferolateral leads compared with a prior study. Chest radiography demonstrated lung base scarring and mild central pulmonary vascular congestion.

Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneously hypoechoic pancreas consistent with pancreatitis, a normal-sized common bile duct, and a distended gallbladder without gallstones. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed edematous enlargement of the pancreas, peripancreatic fat stranding and free fluid, and subcentimeter peripancreatic lymphadenopathy, consistent with acute pancreatitis.
title: Cocaine-Induced Acute Pancreatitis

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman presented with a 20-day history of throat foreign-body sensation and dysphagia. One month earlier she had developed an intermittent cough, and her oropharyngeal symptoms gradually worsened until she also noted sleep apnea. She had a 2-year history of hypertension managed with oral lisinopril–hydrochlorothiazide. 

On examination, there was a tender, smooth-mucosal mass palpable at the right base of the tongue. There were no palpable cervical lymph nodes and no thyroid tissue was palpable in the normal anterior neck region. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and thyroid function tests, were all within normal limits. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the oral and maxillofacial region showed a 2.3 cm × 2.0 cm right-sided nodule at the base of the tongue with homogeneous enhancement. Laryngoscopic examination revealed a 4 cm × 3 cm submucosal bulge at the tongue base. Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated absence of thyroid tissue in the normal anatomical location. Tc-99 thyroid scanning showed radiotracer uptake at the base of the tongue and none in the normal thyroid bed.
title: Transposition of the lingual thyroid gland to the submandibular region through a submandibular approach: A case report

case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman was referred to the hematology clinic with anemia, fatigue, malaise, weight loss, night sweating, and abdominal fullness. She had no family history of cancer or known carcinogen exposure. Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count above 90,000/μL, a platelet count above 550,000/μL, absolute neutrophilia, and normocytic anemia. Peripheral-blood flow cytometry demonstrated left-shifted neutrophils without blasts. Bone marrow biopsy was hypercellular for age with myeloid hyperplasia, rare erythroid dyspoiesis, and small hyperlobulated megakaryocytes; no increase in blasts was seen. Cytogenetic testing revealed der(22)t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) in all 20 metaphases, and FISH showed BCR::ABL1 fusion in 99.5% of interphase nuclei, establishing a diagnosis of chronic myelogenous leukemia.

Review of the record revealed that eight years earlier she had presented with anemia and mild cytopenia. Non-neoplastic causes of anemia and cytopenia were excluded. Bone marrow examination at that time was normocellular with no evidence of myeloid neoplasm or infiltration; differential counts showed no granulocytic increase and blasts and basophils were each <1%. Karyotype analysis and FISH then identified only an isolated del(20q) in all 20 metaphases. No treatment was given.
title: Archived Cytogenetic Cell Pellets Used to Detect a BCR::ABL1 Driver Mutation Eight Years before Disease Presentation

case_prompt: A 16‐year‐old Caucasian male with no significant medical history presented with a 1‐month history of left thigh muscle atrophy, decreased strength in the left lower limb, and progressive inability to bear weight. He denied any history of trauma. On examination, he had hypoesthesia in the femoral nerve distribution of the left thigh and 2/5 strength in the left quadriceps muscle. Radiographs of the lower limbs showed diffuse osteopenia of the femur and tibia. Electromyography demonstrated severe reduction in conduction of the left femoral nerve. Pelvic MRI revealed a fusiform mass deep within the left iliacus muscle, measuring 48 × 14 × 52 mm, with no contrast enhancement, accompanied by atrophy of the left psoas, iliacus, and thigh muscles.
title: Femoral Neuropathy Secondary to Compression by Spontaneous Iliac Hematoma

case_prompt: A 3-month-old full-term female infant was evaluated for a 3-month history of curvilinear and linear palpable hyperpigmented papules and plaques. The lesions developed shortly after birth and were asymptomatic. Her parents denied any skin trauma prior to the appearance of the lesions. On skin examination, there were hyperpigmented papules on the scalp, chest, and legs and a sharply demarcated curvilinear plaque on the left distal forearm. A 4-mm punch biopsy of a curvilinear lesion on the left arm was performed. Histologic evaluation showed epidermal melanosis and intraepidermal histiocytes with few eosinophils. Immunohistochemical staining revealed S100 positivity in the epidermis and focally in the dermis. The papillary dermis stained positively for CD68 and was negative for CD34.
title: Unusual presentation of maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis in an infant with skin of color

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old girl presented with 5 days of bilateral blurred vision, neck pain, and headache. She had no prior medical history or systemic infectious symptoms. Vital signs were normal. On examination, she had optic disc pallor consistent with optic neuritis and a 2×2-cm right cervical lymph node; the remainder of the neurologic and systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9,700/mm3, hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, platelet count 242,000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 50 mm/h, C-reactive protein 12 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 43 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.54 mg/dL. Brain MRI and vertebral imaging were normal. Spine MRI demonstrated an intramedullary lesion, isointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2, extending from the brainstem through the lumbar spine. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 160 mmH2O, 11 lymphocytes/mm3, protein 148 mg/dL, and glucose 59 mg/dL. CSF PCR assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, herpes simplex virus, and common bacterial pathogens, as well as CSF AFB stain and Brucella agglutination, were negative. CSF NMO-IgG antibodies and oligoclonal bands were negative. Serum serologies, including HIV, Lyme, and Brucella, were unremarkable.  
On follow-up, she developed persistent hypertension (220/110 mmHg) and progressive renal impairment (blood urea nitrogen 132 mg/dL, creatinine 3.0 mg/dL). Autoimmune and connective‐tissue serologic markers, echocardiography, urine calcium, and sarcoidosis testing were negative. Tuberculin skin testing was positive at 23 mm induration, but chest radiography was normal and three sputum specimens were AFB-negative by smear and PCR. Computed tomography of the chest revealed a calcified right paratracheal lymph node, and abdominal MRI showed several nodular lesions in the left hepatic lobe.
title: Occult Disseminated Tuberculosis with Holocord Longitudinally Extensive Transverse Myelitis: A Rare Phenomenon in a Child

case_prompt:
A 77-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-month history of right inguinal swelling. She had no personal or family history of malignancy. Physical examination revealed a hard, movable 12-cm right inguinal subcutaneous mass. Plain MRI of the mass showed a multilocular cystic structure with internal septa and a solid component; the solid areas had high signal on diffusion-weighted images and low signal on the apparent diffusion coefficient map. Serum tumor markers showed CA125 36 U/mL (reference ≤ 35 U/mL), with squamous cell carcinoma antigen and CA19-9 within normal limits. 

The mass was surgically excised. Histopathological analysis demonstrated a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with papillary architecture, hemorrhage, and necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for PAX-8, focally positive for WT-1, showed p53 overexpression, and was positive for cytokeratin 7, but negative for cytokeratin 20, CDX-2, and GATA3. Based on these findings, a gynecologic origin was suspected.

Transvaginal ultrasonography, contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI, and thoracoabdominal-pelvic CT revealed only hydrometra with no abnormal findings in the uterus or ovaries. Uterine cervical cytology was negative for intraepithelial lesions.
title: Primary Fallopian Tube Carcinoma Presenting with a Massive Inguinal Tumor: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 9-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of nonbilious vomiting and features of gastric outlet obstruction. He had undergone excision of a type I choledochal cyst with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy at 4 months of age. Preoperative MRCP at that time showed pancreaticobiliary malunion, a type I choledochal cyst, and a dilated pancreatic duct suggestive of chronic pancreatitis; no annular pancreas or pancreatic rests were noted. On examination, the abdomen was soft, with epigastric fullness and visible reverse gastric peristalsis. An upper gastrointestinal contrast study demonstrated near-total obstruction of the first part of the duodenum. Upper endoscopy revealed a large polypoidal mass completely obliterating the lumen of the first duodenal segment, and the endoscope could not be passed beyond this point.
journal: Journal of Indian Association of Pediatric Surgeons
title: Heterotopic pancreas causing duodenal obstruction in a patient previously treated for choledochal cyst

case_prompt: A 43-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-year history of persistent right lower rib pain. She described a popping, grinding, and clicking sensation in the right upper quadrant, worsened by activities such as heavy lifting. Prior evaluation at an outside facility included CT of the abdomen, a HIDA scan, and transvaginal ultrasound, all reported as negative. She underwent diagnostic laparoscopy to rule out endometriosis or other intra-abdominal pathology, which was unremarkable. Conservative measures—including over-the-counter analgesics, muscle relaxants, medical marijuana, and intercostal nerve blocks—failed to relieve her symptoms. On examination, there was focal tenderness to palpation over the right lower ribs. A chest ultrasound with Valsalva maneuver was ordered for further assessment.
title: Slipping rib syndrome presentation in a young woman

case_prompt: A 35-year-old woman with a history of recurrent oral ulcers and panuveitis presented with acute loss of consciousness. Five years earlier she had been treated with azathioprine and cyclosporine for Behçet’s disease but had been lost to follow-up for one year. Two weeks before admission she developed a sore throat and low-grade fever (38 °C) treated with antibiotics; the fever then rose to 39 °C, and over the ensuing three days she developed photophobia, right-sided weakness, and gait difficulty. On arrival she was unconscious (Glasgow Coma Scale 8/15: E2 V3 M3), with bilateral vertical nystagmus, right-foot myoclonus, brisk deep-tendon reflexes, and bilateral Babinski signs. Examination of other systems was unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, vitamin B12 and B9 levels, thyroid function tests, serum electrolytes, and renal and hepatic panels—were normal. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a hypodense lesion centered in the left thalamus, with no pathologic enhancement on contrast. MRI revealed bilateral asymmetric T2 and FLAIR hyperintense, T1 hypointense lesions in the corpus callosum (more pronounced on the left), internal capsules, left thalamus, meso-diencephalic junction, midbrain, and hippocampi, with heterogeneous contrast enhancement and surrounding vasogenic edema causing a 5 mm rightward midline shift; leptomeningeal enhancement was noted in the right internal temporal region. MR angiography of the head and neck showed no arterial occlusion or stenosis, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm. Lumbar puncture revealed elevated protein with otherwise normal cytochemistry. Fungal (cryptococcus), parasitic (toxoplasmosis), bacterial (syphilis and tuberculosis), and viral (HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C) studies were negative. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of malignancy.
title: Neuro-Behçet leading to coma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old Caucasian man was referred to the eye clinic for evaluation of multiple raised yellowish lesions in both fundi. He had noted occasional flashes and floaters. His medical history included diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily, and a history of heavy alcohol use complicated by chronic liver disease with ascites. His medications were paracetamol, dihydrocodeine, and omeprazole. 

On abdominal examination, he had hepatomegaly with the liver edge palpated three fingerbreadths below the right costal margin; there was no splenomegaly. Hepatic ultrasound showed increased echogenicity consistent with cirrhosis. CT of the abdomen confirmed cirrhosis and esophageal varices without focal hepatic lesions. Liver function tests (ALP, ALT, GGT) had been elevated for several years, and plasma viscosity was marginally raised at 1.81 mPa/s (normal 1.5–1.72 mPa/s) with no paraprotein detected.

Ocular examination revealed normal anterior segments and visual acuity of 6/6 in both eyes. Fundoscopy demonstrated dozens of variably sized, slightly yellowish, translucent raised lesions throughout both fundi. Optical coherence tomography showed serous neurosensory retinal detachments without retinal pigment epithelial detachment or retinal thinning. Fundus autofluorescence revealed corresponding areas of autofluorescence in both eyes. Given the preserved visual acuity and absence of choroidal neovascularization, conservative management was recommended.
title: Alcoholic liver disease and bilateral multifocal central serous retinopathy: a case report

case_prompt: A 38-year-old G2P4 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries presented after 37 days of amenorrhea with vaginal spotting and lower abdominal discomfort. Her serum β-hCG level was 22 200 mIU/ml. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a gestational sac at the anterior uterine isthmus within the prior hysterotomy site, consistent with a cesarean scar pregnancy. She underwent hysteroscopic resection without complications; her β-hCG level fell to 17 965 mIU/ml on postoperative day 2. At 24 days postoperatively, she was asymptomatic but had a β-hCG level of 76 196 mIU/ml; transvaginal ultrasound showed widening of the lower uterine segment by 6 mm but no discrete mass. She was observed closely. Twenty-seven days later (51 days postoperatively), she experienced three days of vaginal bleeding. Her β-hCG level was 2799 mIU/ml. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 5.8×2.7 cm hypoechoic, poorly marginated lesion in the myometrium of the lower uterine segment at the prior scar, with abundant Doppler flow. MRI revealed a 4.0×4.4×4.0 cm heterogeneous mass at the cesarean scar surrounded by prominent vascularity. Based on these findings, a gestational trophoblastic tumor was suspected, and the patient was diagnosed with low-risk stage I gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
title: Exaggerated placental site in a cesarean scar: Misdiagnosed as gestational trophoblastic neoplasia: A case report

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man reported one year of gradually worsening numbness and weakness in both lower extremities, with marked decline over the past four months leading to dependence on a walker. He also had intermittent urinary incontinence and chronic constipation.  

On examination, sensation to light touch, pinprick, and proprioception was diminished from the T2 level downward, more on the right than the left. Motor testing revealed 0/5 strength in the right leg and 4/5 in the left leg. Bilateral clonus and muscle spasms were noted in the lower extremities.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed an intramedullary lesion in the upper thoracic cord with diffuse contrast enhancement and cord expansion. Imaging of the remainder of the neuraxis was unremarkable. Testicular ultrasound and CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were normal. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid levels of α-fetoprotein and β-HCG were within normal limits.  

Differential diagnoses included primary spinal cord neoplasms (astrocytoma, ependymoma), hemangioblastoma, intradural metastasis, lymphoma, ischemia, and lupus myelitis. The patient was scheduled for an open spinal cord biopsy.
title: Primary Spinal Germ Cell Tumors: A Case Analysis and Review of Treatment Paradigms

case_prompt:
A 20-month-old Kuwaiti girl was evaluated for a 6-month history of an enlarging mass in the left supraclavicular area. There was no preceding trauma or illness. She was born at term after an uncomplicated delivery; vaccinations were up to date, and there was no family history of malignancy. She appeared well systemically. Physical examination revealed a 5-cm, firm, non-tender mass in the left supraclavicular fossa, fixed to underlying tissue but not to overlying skin; there was no erythema. Laboratory tests showed a serum calcium concentration of 2.52 mmol/L (reference range 2.17–2.44 mmol/L), an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 34 mm/h (1–10 mm/h), a normal serum phosphate level, and normal results on full blood count and renal-function testing.  
  
Neck ultrasonography demonstrated a large, complex, densely calcified mass. A plain radiograph of the chest showed a 4-cm lobulated mass with heterogeneous calcification in the left supraclavicular region. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 4.6 × 4 cm mass in the left retroclavicular area that was low in signal on T1, T2, and short tau inversion-recovery sequences; diffusion‐weighted imaging showed minimal restriction, suggesting a benign process. Metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) I-123 SPECT–CT imaging demonstrated no uptake in the lesion. Although the mass abutted the brachial plexus, there was no evidence of bony destruction or invasion. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy showed avid tracer uptake in the mass with normal uptake elsewhere in the skeleton.
title: Increased uptake on 99mTc bone scintigraphy in a case of tumoral calcinosis in a child

case_prompt: A 63-year-old black woman presented with intense vulvar pruritus of long duration and, three months earlier, noted a purplish lesion with white striae. Her medical history included controlled hypertension; she denied hormone therapy use, smoking, or family history of gynecological cancer. On examination she was afebrile and well appearing. Vulvar inspection revealed a hypertrophic right labium majus with a 4-cm ulcerated purple lesion with hyper- and hypochromic spots near the vaginal fourchette. Inguinal lymph nodes were not palpable. Colposcopic examination and cytologic smear of the vulva showed intense inflammation without neoplastic cells. Bilateral mammography and transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. An incisional biopsy of the lesion demonstrated malignant intraepidermal neoplasia composed of large cells with karyomegaly, visible nucleoli, and clear cytoplasm; focal periodic acid–Schiff positivity was present, and black pigment was noted in some basal-layer cells.
title: Paget Disease of the Vulva: Diagnosis by Immunohistochemistry

case_prompt: A 20-year-old primigravida, amenorrheic for approximately 6 months, presented with a 1-week history of lower abdominal pain accompanied by fatigue, dizziness, blurred vision, and vertigo. On examination, she was hypotensive (blood pressure 85/50 mmHg) and tachycardic (126 bpm), with pale conjunctiva and abdominal tenderness. Laboratory evaluation revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 4.3 g/dL. Obstetric ultrasonography demonstrated a 22-week gestation consistency, negative fetal heartbeat, an empty uterus, and free fluid in the pelvic and right upper quadrant peritoneal spaces. Given her unstable vital signs and imaging findings, she received three units of cross-matched whole blood and was taken to the operating room with a preoperative diagnosis of uterine rupture.
title: Second Trimester Spontaneous Fundal Rupture of Unscarred Bicornuate Uterus in Primipara: A Case Report and Literature Review; Jigjiga University Sheik Hassen Yabare Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, Jigjiga, Ethiopia

case_prompt: A 57-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, major depression, and trichotillomania presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of progressive dyspnea on exertion, shortness of breath, and generalized weakness. She also noted 2 months of dysphagia to solids, habitual snoring at night, and daytime drowsiness. On examination, she was obese and had a harsh voice. Vital signs were heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, blood pressure 135/87 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 75% on room air (89% on 50% FiO2). Initial differential diagnoses included obesity hypoventilation syndrome, obstructive airway disease, and pulmonary thromboembolism. A spiral chest CT scan revealed no parenchymal lesions. Venous blood gas analysis showed pH 7.30, PCO2 78.3 mm Hg, and HCO3– 37.8 mmol/L; the D-dimer level was >500 ng/mL. Pulmonary CT angiography was performed. During contrast injection, extravasation caused swelling of the hand, and the patient underwent an urgent fasciotomy. Ventilation remained inadequate with a laryngeal mask airway, prompting endotracheal intubation. During laryngoscopy, a foreign body was seen in the subglottic area.
title: Uncommon cause of respiratory failure due to a bezoar in the hypopharynx: a case report

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman presented with a painful mass in the left hypogastric area at the site of a Pfannenstiel incision from a cesarean section performed 3 years earlier.
