She reported that the intensity of pain and the size of the mass increased during menstruation. She had no other significant medical history. On examination, a firm, pseudotumorous mass approximately 2 cm in diameter was palpated at the left side of the postoperative scar. Serum CA 125 measured on the first day of her menstrual cycle was 25 U/mL (reference range, 0–35 U/mL).  
Ultrasound with Doppler imaging revealed a hypoechoic, heterogeneous, roundish nodule at the lateral end of the postoperative scar, with a single vascular pedicle entering at the periphery of the mass. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 21×23×28 mm heterogeneous mass within the lower left rectus abdominis muscle containing focal areas of high and low signal intensity, suggestive of old hemorrhage or fibrosis, with no involvement of the abdominal or pelvic cavities.
title: Rectus Abdominis Endometrioma after Caesarean Section

case_prompt:
An 84-year-old woman, previously healthy and functionally independent, noted abrupt onset of hand and foot stiffness 10 days earlier, quickly followed by painful swelling and functional impairment of both hands and feet. Over the prior 2 months she had developed progressive fatigue, generalized muscle weakness, and pain in her shoulder girdles, hip girdles, and neck. She had no family history of rheumatologic disease.

On examination, she appeared moderately ill. There was symmetrical swelling, erythema, and warmth of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, with pitting edema over the dorsal hands and wrists. Neurologic and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a CRP of 28 mg/L and an ESR of 42 mm/h without leukocytosis. Mild microcytic anemia was present (Hb 103 g/L, Hct 34%, MCV 79 fL, MCH 24.1 pg). Rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, MPO, and PR3 antibodies were negative.

A hand radiograph demonstrated moderate degenerative changes at MCP, PIP, and DIP joints without erosions or cartilage calcifications. A chest radiograph was normal.
final_diagnosis_raw: Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema syndrome
title: Idiopathic remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema syndrome mimicking symptoms of polymyalgia rheumatica: a case report

case_prompt: A 21-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with chest pain, shortness of breath, and an episode of near syncope. Three months previously she had developed a diffuse erythematous rash after a course of minocycline for acne; the antibiotic was discontinued and she was treated with oral prednisone, with improvement of the rash. On arrival, her blood pressure was 81/68 mmHg, heart rate 121 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7ºC, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. The physical examination was unremarkable. While in the ED, she had syncope during IV-line placement, then became unresponsive with pulseless electrical activity arrest. She received CPR with two doses of IV epinephrine and achieved return of spontaneous circulation but remained hypotensive, requiring norepinephrine and intubation for airway protection. A computed tomography pulmonary angiogram was unremarkable. A point-of-care echocardiogram demonstrated grossly reduced biventricular function. She experienced a second PEA arrest with return of spontaneous circulation after CPR and epinephrine but remained hypotensive despite multiple vasopressors. Initial laboratory tests revealed a troponin-T concentration of 8.56 ng/mL, a leukocyte count of 17.5 × 10^3 cells/mL, and an eosinophil count of 1.6 × 10^3 cells/mL. Formal transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 15%.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Use of Emergency Department Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Treatment of Acute Necrotizing Myocarditis

case_prompt: A 69-year-old man with a history of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma diagnosed in January 2021, treated with docetaxel, vincristine, Adriamycin, dexamethasone, and both intravenous and intrathecal methotrexate, presented in October 2021 with swelling in the left popliteal fossa, neuropathic pain, and weakness. On examination, there was a palpable mass in the left popliteal fossa. Ultrasonography demonstrated a heterogeneous echogenic mass with internal vascularity in the popliteal fossa, with the sciatic and tibial nerves appearing as a cable-like edematous structure within the mass. MRI of the left knee revealed a fusiform, infiltrating mass lesion measuring 83×44×35 mm with intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted and STIR images, and heterogeneous predominantly peripheral enhancement; perilesional edema and partial encasement of the popliteal artery were noted. The distal sciatic and proximal tibial nerves were enlarged, infiltrated, and coursed through the mass.
title: Recurrence of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in sciatic and tibial nerves: A case report

case_prompt:
A 67-year-old man was admitted with a 1-month history of recurrent gross hematuria, dysuria, left testicular pain and enlargement, lumbar and sacral back pain, night sweats, and a 3 kg unintentional weight loss. He had occupational asbestos exposure and a body mass index of 37.8 kg/m2.  

On examination, he had bilateral lower‐extremity edema and a uniformly enlarged, tender left testis without discrete nodules. Scrotal ultrasonography showed diffuse enlargement of the left testis without focal lesions.  

Laboratory studies revealed a serum β-subunit human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) concentration of 644.4 mIU/mL; lactate dehydrogenase, α-fetoprotein, and prostate-specific antigen were within normal limits.  

Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 62 mm mass in the posterior prostate gland infiltrating the seminal vesicles and anterior rectal wall, with bilateral iliac lymph node enlargement. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed pelvic lymph node metastases.
title: Urothelial carcinoma of the prostate with raised β-hCG levels: a case report

case_prompt: A 3-year-old Hispanic boy in Arizona with a baseline right facial palsy presented with 5 days of fatigue, abdominal pain, and right cheek pain. Outpatient treatment for presumed otitis and sinusitis with ear drops and penicillin yielded no improvement. He then developed intermittent fevers, speech changes, gait instability, and difficulty sitting up. A rapid Group A Streptococcus test was positive, and penicillin was changed to cephalexin. The next day, he had seizure-like activity unresponsive to voice and received midazolam en route to the Emergency Department. On arrival he was febrile, had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8, and altered mental status. He experienced a generalized tonic–clonic seizure treated with lorazepam and levetiracetam. Noncontrast head CT showed hypoattenuation consistent with edema in the right frontal and left frontoparietal lobes. He was started on ceftriaxone and vancomycin. Admission laboratory studies showed a normal metabolic panel, WBC 10.1 K/μL, hemoglobin 14.4 g/dL, and platelets 321 K/μL. CSF obtained by lumbar puncture demonstrated 75 WBC/μL, 5 RBC/μL, glucose 53 mg/dL, and protein 85 mg/dL. A multiplex CSF PCR panel was negative for bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens. Pending studies included CSF oligoclonal bands, serum aquaporin-4 receptor antibody, and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody. Empirical dexamethasone and IV immunoglobulin were begun. After transfer to the PICU, he was intubated without sedation and lacked brainstem reflexes. EEG showed diffuse slowing consistent with moderate encephalopathy. MRI four days after admission revealed extensive bilateral supratentorial and infratentorial diffusion restriction, T2 hyperintensity, necrosis, subarachnoid and parenchymal enhancement, and patchy frontal-lobe involvement. A follow-up MRI three days later showed marked progression of diffusion restriction and T2 FLAIR hyperintensity with increased involvement of the periventricular regions, cerebellum, basal nuclei, thalami, brainstem, leptomeninges, and petechial hemorrhages.
title: A devastating case of a Balamuthia mandrillaris pediatric brain infection

case_prompt: A 24-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of progressive headaches, episodes of syncope, and blurred vision. Her medical history was notable only for an uncomplicated appendectomy and a head injury in a traffic accident at age 6, which had not been investigated or treated. On examination, she was alert and oriented; all neurologic findings were normal except for a firm, non-tender, 5 cm × 5 cm bony mass in the left frontoparietal region. Routine laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated focal thickening of the diploic space in the left frontoparietal bone, extending to the orbital roof, without evidence of cortical destruction or periosteal reaction. MRI of the brain and skull showed a heterogeneous bony mass in the same region with no intracranial or dural invasion.
title: Huge osteoma in the frontoparietal bone caused by trauma from 18 years ago: a case report

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old, 48-kg woman with a 6-month history of temporomandibular joint pain was scheduled for bilateral temporomandibular meniscopexy. Her previous anesthesia included an uneventful appendectomy at age 10. On arrival, HR was 92 bpm, RR 16/min, BP 128/78 mmHg, and SpO₂ 91% on room air. Anesthesia was induced with midazolam 2 mg IV, remifentanil infusion, propofol 140 mg IV, and rocuronium 35 mg IV. Following topical vasoconstrictor and local anesthetic, nasotracheal intubation was confirmed uneventfully.

Shortly after securing the airway, the patient developed sinus bradycardia with ST changes that rapidly progressed to supraventricular tachycardia (HR 168 bpm), hypotension, desaturation, piloerection, and persistent ST changes. Airway pressures rose with rhonchi, and bronchospasm was suspected; she received four puffs of salbutamol and 100 mg IV hydrocortisone. Bloody fluid then appeared in the endotracheal tube, and chest radiography showed severe bilateral pulmonary edema.

An intraoperative transesophageal echocardiogram demonstrated severe left ventricular dysfunction with akinesia of the apical and mid anterolateral and septal segments, hypokinesia of the anterior and anteroseptal walls, and preserved basal segments; the right ventricle was moderately dilated with mild dysfunction and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Cardiac output was 1.8 L/min. Norepinephrine infusion was started, with gradual hemodynamic improvement, and the surgery was canceled. 

In the ICU, a pulmonary artery catheter revealed a cardiac index of 1.63 L/min/m², a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 20 mmHg, and normal resistances. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed severe biventricular dysfunction with hypokinesia of the distal third of the anterior and inferior septum, and milrinone 0.5 µg/kg/min IV was initiated. Troponin I was 3.7 ng/mL on day 1 and 0.7 ng/mL on day 2.
title: Transesophageal echo diagnosis of perioperative unusual transient left ventricular apical ballooning syndrome

case_prompt: A 47-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a non-painful swelling of the left cheek/preauricular region that developed over several weeks. She denied trauma, discharge, redness, or warmth. Her medical and family history were unremarkable. On examination, there was a firm mass causing facial asymmetry; intraoral inspection showed no dental pathology and salivary flow was normal. Because the site and origin of the lesion were uncertain, a CT scan was obtained. Imaging revealed a well-circumscribed lesion confined to the left mandibular condyle, measuring 32 × 23 × 29 mm, with partial lytic changes but no evidence of cortical breach or destructive effects on adjacent structures. The lesion had a benign appearance, but the diagnosis remained unclear. An incisional biopsy was then performed.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare case of a intraosseous arteriovenous malformation of the temporomandibular joint and mandible – Case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 72-year-old Caucasian man presented with a one-year history of worsening dyspnea on exertion and bilateral leg edema. He reported paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and orthopnea requiring him to sleep in a reclining chair and was limited to walking only a few steps before severe shortness of breath developed. He denied chest pain, and repeated measurements of cardiac enzymes were negative. An echocardiogram performed eight months earlier showed mild dilation and hypokinesis of the right ventricle. Trials of therapy for presumed obstructive lung disease and courses of antibiotics for erythema and leg edema had been ineffective, and evaluations excluded deep venous thrombosis and obstructive disease of the lungs, abdomen, or pelvis.
On examination, temperature was 37°C, blood pressure 126/75 mm Hg, heart rate 95 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91% on room air; ambulation reduced saturation to 87%, and he appeared cyanotic. Electrocardiography showed left atrial enlargement and nonspecific T-wave abnormalities. A chest CT scan revealed nodular thickening of the pericardium and bilateral pleura. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe dilation of the inferior vena cava with a central venous pressure of 30 mm Hg and intrahepatic venous dilation, marked interventricular septal shift with respiration and right ventricular compression, restrictive movement of the lateral ventricular walls with a septal bounce, and decreased mitral inflow during inspiration.
title: Blunt trauma as a suspected cause of delayed constrictive pericarditis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman with no prior medical history was admitted after a motor-vehicle collision. She was hemodynamically stable and all laboratory studies were within normal limits. Her only complaint was tenderness over the thoracic vertebrae. 

Because of persistent back pain, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest was obtained, which revealed an incidentally noted mass in the left anterior superior mediastinum. The mass was oval, vertically oriented, well defined, and homogeneous, measuring 78 × 64 × 103 mm in the prevascular space and extending anterior to the pericardium. There were no calcifications and no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. The patient denied any respiratory or systemic symptoms, and there were no other remarkable comorbidities.
title: Thymic lipofibroadenoma: A case report

case_prompt: A 35-year-old woman presented with two months of diarrhea, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, and cramps. She had studied in Nepal for one year; her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 105 g/L, hematocrit 0.34 L/L, erythrocytes 3.70×10^12/L), vitamin B12 deficiency (130 ng/L), elevated serum iron (35.3 μmol/L), increased ferritin (1042 μg/L), normal transferrin, and neutrophilic leukocytosis (leukocytes 11.52×10^9/L, neutrophils 9.30×10^9/L). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed mural thickening of the ileocecum and appendix, interpreted as inflammatory, and a 7.9-cm nonhomogeneous cystic mass of the left ovary. Gastroscopy and proctoscopy were unremarkable. Colonoscopy showed multiple well-circumscribed, ulcerated, tumor-like masses in the ascending colon, measuring 8–33 mm, with livid-colored peripheries and necrotic centers. A larger, more solid lesion (4.5 cm) was present at the ileocecal valve extending into the adjacent cecum and appendix. These endoscopic findings were inconclusive; while atypical for Crohn’s disease, the differential diagnoses included tuberculosis, lymphoma, and carcinoma.
title: Diagnosis of colonic amebiasis and coexisting signet-ring cell carcinoma in intestinal biopsy

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old Thai man presented with a 2-month history of sensitivity over the left ala of his nose. Two months earlier, he had undergone extraction of an upper left deciduous canine; one month after the extraction, he noted persistent swelling of the left cheek. Periapical radiography at a private clinic showed an impacted upper left permanent canine and small radiopaque foci inferior to it.

On examination, there was mild extraoral swelling of the left cheek with effacement of the nasolabial fold. Intraorally, there was mild buccal vestibular swelling from the left maxillary central incisor to the first premolar; the left maxillary canine was clinically absent, and palpation revealed a soft tissue mass on its palatal aspect. Electric pulp testing indicated non-vital teeth at the left maxillary central and lateral incisors.

Panoramic radiography demonstrated a unilocular radiolucent lesion surrounding the embedded canine, containing a few non-homogeneous radiopaque components, with indistinct margins and involvement of the roots of the left lateral incisor and first premolar. Periapical radiographs showed irregular widening of the periodontal ligament space around the lateral incisor root without root resorption, diffuse radiolucent trabeculations near the central and lateral incisor apices, and small radiopaque structures surrounded by thin radiolucent rims, resembling tooth-like fragments.

Axial cone-beam computed tomographic images revealed extension of the lesion into the incisive foramen and bilateral anterior nasal cavities, involvement of the nasal septum and left lateral nasal wall (medial wall of the left maxillary sinus), perforation of the labial cortical plate across the midline, and perforation of the palatal cortex from the left lateral incisor to the first molar region. Coronal views showed obliteration of the left ostiomeatal complex and presence of tooth-like structures between the roots of the lateral incisor and second premolar, with the impacted canine located superior-posteriorly. Sagittal sections demonstrated extension into the anterior half of the left maxillary sinus with mucosal thickening.
title: Ghost cell odontogenic carcinoma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old woman with hypertension, dyslipidemia, multinodular goitre, cholecystectomy, and long-standing, poorly controlled type II diabetes with retinopathy, neuropathy, and peripheral angiopathy presented in July 2021 with hematuria with clots and lower abdominal pain of two weeks’ duration. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including electrolytes, creatinine, hemoglobin, and white-blood-cell count, were within normal limits. Urinary sediment showed leukocytes and erythrocytes. On examination, she appeared well but had suprapubic and lower abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. 

In early August, bladder ultrasonography revealed an echogenic, target-shaped lesion approximately 8 cm in diameter, apparently adhered to the superior bladder wall. Review of a March 2021 CT (performed prior to her hemicolectomy) showed no bladder abnormalities. Four days after the ultrasound, cystoscopy demonstrated an oval, endoluminal mass occupying most of the bladder, which appeared lithiasis-like but was soft and disintegrated on contact with the cystoscope. 

One week later, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 9-cm bladder-occupying lesion with a liquid-density core, a thin homogeneous nonenhancing wall, and a second cystic lesion within, containing a hydroaerial level. Excretory-phase images confirmed a filling defect in the bladder at that location. MRI revealed thickened bladder walls hypointense on T2-weighted sequences; the lesion contained multiple concentric layers and no areas of hemorrhage or diffusion restriction on T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted sequences.
title: Layer upon layer: Imaging techniques of bladder matrix stone: A case report

case_prompt:
A 13-year-old girl, three days after an appendectomy, presented with fever and loss of appetite. On examination she was dehydrated, tachycardic, tachypneic, and febrile (38.8 °C); blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were normal. The abdomen was diffusely tender with rebound pain, normal bowel sounds, and a hyperemic surgical scar.  
An abdominal ultrasound showed a pericolic abscess that was surgically drained. Cultures grew multisensitive Escherichia coli and group G β-hemolytic Streptococcus; she was treated with ceftriaxone and metronidazole. On postoperative day 3 she continued to have abdominal pain and fever; antibiotics were changed to vancomycin, ceftazidime, and amikacin, but fever persisted. An abdominal CT scan showed no surgical complication; fluconazole was added.  
On postoperative day 12 (from the second surgery) she became hypotensive, tachycardic, and febrile to 39.4 °C and was transferred to the ICU for vasoactive support. Laboratory tests on ICU admission showed:  
• Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL; hematocrit 24.6%  
• Leukocytes 7.2 × 10^3/mm^3 (bands 14%, neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 8%)  
• Platelets 26.9 × 10^3/mm^3  
• INR 4.66; fibrinogen 98 mg/dL  
• Total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL  
• ALT 16 556 IU/L; AST 6126 IU/L; AP 926 IU/L; γGT 202 IU/L  
• Triglycerides 105 mg/dL; ferritin 1287 ng/mL  
Repeat abdominal CT ruled out abscess. Serologic studies revealed HIV negative; hepatitis B surface antibody positive, antigen negative; hepatitis C negative; anti-CMV IgG positive/IgM negative; anti-EBV IgG positive/IgM negative; other viral IgM studies negative. Blood, urine, catheter, and abdominal fluid cultures remained negative.  
On postoperative day 20 laboratory evaluation confirmed worsening thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged prothrombin time, and marked transaminase elevations.
title: Hemophagocytic syndrome: a dilemma chasing the intensivists

case_prompt: A 48-year-old Syrian woman, G0P0, presented with one week of diffuse abdominal pain varying from mild to severe, fatigue, debility, high fever, vomiting, and urinary retention. She had been treated empirically for cystitis without improvement. Her last menstrual period was 5 years ago. There were no night sweats or weight loss. On examination, her abdomen was distended with periodic tenderness; other systems were normal. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11 mg/dL (normal 12–14) and CA-125 333.75 U/mL (normal 1.7–32). Pelvic ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous lobulated mass on the anterior and superior uterine walls extending to both ovaries with mixed echogenicity and high perfusion on Doppler, and moderate free fluid in the abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a 112 × 191 × 160 mm irregular, heterogeneous, lobulated uterine mass extending to both ovaries, enlarged lymph nodes along the abdominal aorta and right iliac vessels with mesenteric involvement, moderate ascites, and a large right pleural effusion with right lower lobe atelectasis.
title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in the uterus with unexpected manifestations: a case report

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old man of Indian origin presented with a 3-month history of pain, limited mobility, and swelling over the anterior aspect of the right leg above the ankle. He reported a history of a recurrent ulcer at the same site. He denied any trauma, fever, sensory loss, comorbid illness, or gastrointestinal or respiratory symptoms. 

On examination, there was a well-demarcated erythematous firm lesion over the anterior lower leg with peripheral nodular areas and accompanying lymphedema of the distal foot. No other cutaneous or oral lesions were found on full‐body examination. He had no history of similar lesions, and tests confirmed he was not immunocompromised and had no sexually transmitted infections.

Plain radiographs of the right leg showed a lobulated soft-tissue swelling in the anterior lower one-third of the leg with a few calcific areas and periosteal reaction of adjacent bone. CT imaging demonstrated soft-tissue edema, heterogeneous linear densities, faint calcifications within the lesion, and a short segment of thick unicortical periosteal reaction of the tibia. MRI confirmed these findings and revealed an intramuscular lesion that was iso- to hypo-intense on T1‐weighted images, hyperintense on T2‐weighted images, with surrounding perilesional edema and no bone marrow involvement.
title: Unanticipated diagnosis of skeletal muscle Kaposi sarcoma: a case report

case_prompt: A 44-year-old woman (weight 103 kg; BMI 41.8) with hypothyroidism, borderline type II diabetes mellitus, gastroesophageal reflux disease, hypertriglyceridemia, and prior vertical banded gastroplasty 10 years earlier (initial weight 140 kg, nadir 80 kg) underwent laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. She was discharged uneventfully. On postoperative day 5, she reported epigastric discomfort and underwent an abdominal CT scan, which was reported as normal by the radiologist. On day 10, she presented with sudden massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding. In the emergency department she was hemodynamically stable (hemoglobin, 12 g/dL) and was intubated for endoscopy to prevent aspiration. A review of the CT images noted that the remnant stomach was fluid-filled. During endoscopy, a large clot was seen in the gastric pouch, but no bleeding source was identified; two clips were placed on a suspicious area, and hemostasis was managed endoscopically. She received 2 L of normal saline and was admitted to the ICU. Four hours later, she had recurrent oral bleeding, hypotension (blood pressure 80 mm Hg systolic, pulse 125 beats/min), abdominal distention with dull percussion, and a nasogastric tube returned 500 mL of bright blood. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, white blood cells 1.5 × 10^9/L, platelets 180 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 46 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 20 mm/h, and normal PT, PTT, and INR. Given ongoing hemorrhagic shock, surgical exploration was undertaken.
title: Multiple Complex Complications After Redo Bariatric Surgery (Infrequent Complication: Fistula Between the Splenic Artery and the Remnant of the Stomach): A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 47-year-old man presented with a 10-month history of pain and swelling over the posterior aspect of his left shoulder. The pain worsened with arm movement, particularly on raising the arm overhead, and he noted mild weakness of the left shoulder. He was otherwise healthy and had no respiratory symptoms.

On examination, there was a hard, tender swelling over the posterior left scapula measuring 11×15×8 cm, with a rough texture and diminished sensation in the left suprascapular nerve distribution. Active flexion and abduction at the left glenohumeral joint were painful. Distal neurovascular examination of the left upper limb was normal. Pain was rated 8/10 on a visual analog scale, and his Revised Musculoskeletal Tumor Society Score was 13/30.

Serum investigations were normal except for an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 178 IU/L.

Conventional radiographs of the left shoulder showed a large, homogeneous, expansile lesion of the scapula with irregular but well-defined margins and a ground-glass matrix; internal septations compartmentalized the lesion. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined expansile scapular mass with intact overlying cortices, endosteal scalloping, high central signal intensity, and scalloped low-signal rims.
title: Advanced Unilateral Fibrous Dysplasia of the Scapula: A Rare Clinical Entity and Surgical Challenge

case_prompt: A 25-year-old primigravida at 28 weeks of gestation presented with new‐onset facial acne and abdominal and facial hirsutism that began at 23 weeks. On examination, her Ferriman–Gallwey score was 18, and she had early clitoromegaly and a deepening of her voice. Ultrasound imaging showed a single viable fetus appropriate for gestational age and a 12 × 9 cm right adnexal mass with areas of necrosis and low color Doppler flow; the left adnexa appeared normal. Laboratory studies revealed mildly elevated transaminases, negative serum tumor markers, and markedly elevated androgen levels: total testosterone 6270 ng/dL (normal 0.4–4.1), SHBG 689.6 nmol/L (normal 18–114), androstenedione ≤200 ng/dL (normal 0.4–4.1), and DHEAS 645.9 μg/dL (normal 98.8–340). Magnetic resonance imaging was recommended but declined by the patient. Over the following weeks, her hirsutism and virilization progressed despite conservative management, and severe right hydronephrosis developed. At 34 weeks, because of worsening laboratory findings, symptom progression, suspected ovarian malignancy, and incomplete antenatal evaluation, a cesarean delivery with unilateral oophorectomy was performed.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Luteoma of Pregnancy Presenting with Severe Maternal Virilisation: A Case Report

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old boy was brought by his parents with concern about an unusually large and unattractive upper lip that had become progressively more prominent over the preceding 3 to 4 years. The patient had no difficulty with speech or eating but was self-conscious about the appearance. There was no history of trauma, oral habits, infection, or prior surgery involving the lip, and no family history of similar lip abnormalities. His medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, at rest the upper lip appeared normal, but when the patient smiled or spoke, there was a bilateral fold of excess mucosal tissue with a central constriction, giving a cupid’s bow appearance. The mucosal surface was intact without ulceration or induration. There were no other oral or facial anomalies, and eyelid appearance was normal. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were normal. Ultrasonography of the neck showed no thyroid enlargement.

A provisional diagnosis was made.
journal: International Journal of Clinical Pediatric Dentistry
title: Double Lip-An Atypical Facial Anomaly: Two Case Reports

case_prompt:
A 15-year-old boy had a one-month history of intermittent fever (37.4–38.0 °C), sore throat, and fatigue unresponsive to antipyretics and cefuroxime. Two weeks before admission, he developed nausea, vomiting, anorexia, jaundice, and dark urine. He met the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus and received intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg twice daily, which improved his fever and fatigue but only partially corrected leukopenia, anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and hyperbilirubinemia. He then had a six-minute generalized seizure with postictal unresponsiveness; EEG was normal, and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily was started.

On admission, he had nocturnal episodes of disordered speech, disorientation, inattention, auditory and visual hallucinations, and persecutory delusions, with daytime lethargy. Olanzapine 5 mg daily was initiated. Two days later, his hallucinations and delusions abated, but he began displaying intermittent abnormal movements: repetitive buttock elevation with sustained posturing, maintenance of passive limb positions, echolalia, mutism, fixed staring, resistance to passive movement, and minimal responses to pain or verbal stimuli.

Initial labs showed leukopenia, anemia, elevated transaminases, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated C-reactive protein, hypocomplementemia (C3 and C4), ANA 1:1280, and anti-dsDNA antibodies 311 IU/mL; abdominal ultrasound revealed mild splenomegaly. During hospitalization, anti-dsDNA titers fell to 105 IU/mL, ANA to 1:160, and complement levels normalized. Tests for antiphospholipid, anti-NMDA receptor, anti-GABA, and anti-VGKC antibodies were negative. CSF examination was normal. Brain MRI showed slight widening of the sulci and fissures.
title: Catatonia induced by antipsychotics in an adolescent male patient with systemic lupus erythematosus: A case report

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of abdominal discomfort and blood-tinged urine. Vital signs were normal, and laboratory testing confirmed hematuria. CT intravenous urography showed:
• A 13.4 × 11.7 × 7.3 mm well-defined hypodense lesion in the body of the right adrenal gland with homogeneous avid postcontrast enhancement.  
• An irregular heterogeneous exophytic lesion measuring 4.2 × 3.3 × 3.6 cm in the upper pole of the right kidney, with enhancing septations.  
• A 2.4 × 1.4 × 1.4 cm well-defined hypodense lesion (< 50% exophytic) in the upper pole of the left kidney, with enhancing septations.  
• Multiple simple cortical cysts in both kidneys.  
• A 10.5 × 8.4 mm well-defined hypodense lesion in the body of the pancreas without postcontrast enhancement.  

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain revealed a 3.3 × 3.3 cm cystic lesion with an avidly enhancing eccentric mural nodule in the right brachium pontis, consistent with a hemangioblastoma; no spinal lesions were seen. Twenty-four-hour urinary metanephrine, normetanephrine, and vanillylmandelic acid levels were all within normal limits.
title: Von Hippel Lindau Disease with central nervous system and multiple visceral manifestations: A case report

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive, sustained pain in her left forearm, radiating to the fourth and fifth fingers, and a slowly enlarging bulge on the dorsal aspect of the lower forearm. Physical examination revealed a 1.5 × 1.5 cm firm, tender mass on the lower dorsal surface of the left forearm; the overlying skin was normal. The elbow had a full range of motion, wrist and forearm strength were 5/5 bilaterally, and sensory testing (light touch, temperature, crude touch, two-point discrimination) was normal in all digits. There were no signs of paresthesia or neurologic deficit. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the left forearm (anteroposterior and lateral views) showed a well-defined, eccentric osteolytic lesion in the distal diaphysis of the ulna with cortical thinning and expansion but no cortical destruction, calcification, or marginal sclerosis. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed, ovoid intramedullary lesion measuring approximately 2 × 1 cm in the distal ulnar diaphysis, exophytically protruding from the medial cortex. The lesion was low signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on T2-weighted and fat-saturated fast spin-echo T2-weighted sequences.
title: Enchondroma Protuberans of Ulnar Bone: A Case Report and Review of Literature

case_prompt: A 54-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of progressively worsening neck pain and numbness of the left upper extremity and left face, without trauma. His symptoms fluctuated initially but gradually worsened over 2 months, prompting evaluation. Neurologic examination showed a mildly spastic gait and exaggerated deep tendon reflexes in all extremities; muscle strength and vibration sense were normal, and there was no Babinski sign. He reported mild dysuria and constipation. Laboratory tests, including peripheral blood studies, were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was within normal limits except for a slightly elevated protein concentration (65 mg/dl; normal, 10–40 mg/dl). Unenhanced computed tomography of the cervicothoracic spine revealed diffuse dorsal epidural calcification extending from C3 to T6, appearing as a crescent-shaped mass along the dura mater with a well-defined border at the vertebral arch. Magnetic resonance imaging showed the lesion to be hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted sequences, causing cervical spinal canal stenosis. Head imaging was normal. Based on these findings, CPPD crystal deposition of the ligamentum flavum was suspected, and a C5–6 laminectomy was planned for biopsy confirmation.
final_diagnosis_raw: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease
title: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease of the spinal dura mater: a case report

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old male postman from southwestern China presented with a 3-year history of brownish-black plaques symmetrically involving the dorsum of his hands, wrists, elbows, ankles, and dorsal feet. The lesions first appeared 3 years ago, worsened during warm, humid summers, and improved in winter. He noted that the plaques became white and macerated after approximately 5 minutes of water immersion or sweating, with gradual restoration of the original appearance after drying. He denied itching, pain, or other symptoms. He had no history of systemic disease, medication use, palmoplantar hyperhidrosis, or family history of similar conditions.

On examination, sharply demarcated, rough-surfaced, brownish-black keratotic plaques were present symmetrically on the specified acral sites; the palms and soles were completely spared. After a 5-minute water immersion challenge, the lesions exhibited transient whitish maceration. No other skin or mucous membrane abnormalities were noted.

Histopathological examination of a lesional skin biopsy showed hyperkeratosis, thickening of the stratum spinosum, and mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltration in the papillary dermis; sweat glands appeared normal.
title: Symmetrical Acrokeratoderma: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 30-year-old woman presented with 5 years of recurrent umbilical pain, most recently lasting 2 weeks before presentation. Pain was cyclical, occurring monthly, sharp, intermittent, and worsened during menstruation. It was associated with bloody discharge from the umbilicus and a palpable swelling. She denied abdominal distension, gastrointestinal symptoms, or any prior surgery. Menarche was at 15 years; she had 4–5-day menstrual flow every 28–30 days, was nulliparous, and used no contraceptives. On examination, she was in satisfactory condition. The abdomen was full and symmetrical. The umbilicus was everted (4 cm × 3 cm) with a hyperpigmented, tender, firm dome-shaped nodule (~1.5 cm) at its left margin. Full blood count and urinalysis were unremarkable. Abdominopelvic ultrasound showed a normal-sized uterus with preserved endometrial echo and an oval hypoechoic solid mass (6.82 × 5.04 cm) in the left adnexa, suggestive of a pedunculated subserosal myoma.
title: Umbilical nodule, a rare presentation of primary cutaneous endometriosis: Case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute onset of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain and associated vomiting that began while lifting weights. His medical history was notable for 6–7 years of anabolic steroids, human growth hormone, and testosterone use to gain muscle mass. He had no prior surgical history. On abdominal examination, the abdomen was nondistended with focal tenderness and guarding in the right upper quadrant. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 190/85 mm Hg, heart rate of 83 beats/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Laboratory investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 17.1 g/dL, neutrophilia, and a normal C-reactive protein level. Liver function tests revealed a mixed hepatitic and obstructive pattern: total bilirubin 35 µmol/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 443 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 848 U/L; the international normalized ratio was normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography demonstrated a 9.6-cm well-circumscribed abnormality in segment 5 of the liver and a smaller focal lesion in segment 6, findings interpreted as acute hemorrhage into two focal liver lesions, likely hepatic adenomas. Subsequent liver magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple hepatic adenomas and an increase in the size of the larger lesion to 12 cm.
title: Life-Threatening Intraparenchymal Hemorrhage of Steroid-Induced Hepatic Adenomas in a Healthy Man

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of high-grade fever, rigors, two episodes of vomiting, generalized headache, and brief altered sensorium a few hours before admission. On examination, temperature was 101°F, pulse 132/min, blood pressure 90/40 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg), and extremities were cold; oxygen saturation was 100% on room air. She appeared pale without rash, edema, icterus, or mucosal bleeding. Neurologic examination revealed no focal deficits or neck stiffness; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly.

She was resuscitated with crystalloids. Empirical intravenous third-generation cephalosporin and artesunate were administered. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.5 g/dl, packed cell volume 45%, white-cell count 7100/mm3 (64% neutrophils, 34% lymphocytes), platelet count 135,000/mm3, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/h. A malaria antigen rapid test was negative. Liver enzymes were elevated (AST 220 U/L, ALT 182 U/L), serum albumin was 3.65 g/dl, and INR was 2.0. Blood urea nitrogen was 39 mg/dl and creatinine 1.4 mg/dl. Electrolytes and ammonia (23 mg/dl) were normal. Arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis with lactate 2.0 mmol/L; chest radiograph and echocardiography were normal. Ultrasonography revealed minimal bilateral pleural effusions and mild ascites.

After initial stabilization, she had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure with prolonged unresponsiveness. She received lorazepam and fosphenytoin, and was intubated and mechanically ventilated. Emergency MRI of the brain demonstrated extensive parenchymal hyperintense lesions on T2 and FLAIR sequences in the bilateral cerebellar cortex, vermis, pons, midbrain, medial temporal lobes, and thalami; these areas were hypointense on T1, dark on ADC maps, with small hemorrhagic foci on T2* GRE images. These features were suggestive of Japanese encephalitis. She was started on acyclovir for possible herpes simplex encephalitis.
journal: Indian Journal of Critical Care Medicine : Peer-reviewed, Official Publication of Indian Society of Critical Care Medicine
title: Dengue encephalitis

case_prompt: An 82-year-old woman presented with recently aggravated inflammation of her right great toe. Her medical history was notable for systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus nephritis managed with mizoribine and prednisolone for 20 years, diabetes mellitus, and a remote right hallux valgus surgery; she denied any overt trauma to the great toe. On examination, the right great toe was moderately enlarged, tender, and erythematous, with pustules over the dorsal interphalangeal joint. Initial treatment with cefcapene pivoxil was followed over 6 months by sequential courses of levofloxacin, faropenem, amoxicillin/clavulanate, minocycline, meropenem, and metronidazole; despite wound irrigation and drainage, symptoms recurred after temporary improvement. She remained afebrile, and her white blood cell count and C-reactive protein level were normal. Wound cultures from the skin lesion grew Corynebacterium striatum, Finegoldia magna, and an anaerobic gram-positive bacillus. Radiographs and CT of the right great toe demonstrated an osteolytic lesion with cortical erosion, bone destruction, and a pathological fracture of the distal phalanx, with soft-tissue swelling but no abscess. Based on these clinical findings and the course of treatment up to that point, it seemed most likely to be a case of diabetic foot infection with chronic osteomyelitis.
title: Intraosseous epidermal cyst of the great toe that was difficult to distinguish from chronic osteomyelitis: A case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 21-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of a reddish-bluish swelling on the left inner cheek that had appeared after an accidental bite. She reported occasional similar episodes of cheek biting and bleeding, but no marked change in the lesion’s size. Her mother recalled a mild left-cheek swelling at age 5, which was monitored without intervention. 

On extraoral examination, there was slight left facial asymmetry with asymmetric nasolabial folds on smiling; facial movements were normal. Intraorally, a solitary 2 cm × 1 cm reddish-bluish swelling with a translucent yellow surface was noted on the left buccal mucosa, extending from the occlusal plane to 1 cm above the retromolar trigone and 2 cm from the corner of the mouth. The surface was irregular, showed tooth-indentation marks, and multiple pinhead-sized clear vesicles were seen near its superior border. Palpation revealed a soft, slightly tender, nonindurated, nonpulsatile submucosal mass that was not adherent to the skin; the surrounding mucosa was normal. A 1 cm × 1 cm nontender, movable left submandibular lymph node was palpable.

A provisional diagnosis of traumatic hematoma was made, with lymphangioma and hemangioma considered in the differential. After informed consent, the lesion was excised under local anesthesia without identification of a feeder vessel, and the specimen was sent for histopathological examination.
journal: Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology : JOMFP
title: Hemangiolymphangioma of buccal mucosa: A rare case report

case_prompt:
A 32-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a persistent resting heart rate of up to 140 bpm. He reported intermittent bilateral knee pain and swelling but denied palpitations or syncope. Three months earlier he had found an engorged tick on his left knee; Lyme serology at that time was negative. One week after the tick bite he developed a bull’s-eye rash over the posterior left knee that resolved with ibuprofen.  

On presentation he was afebrile, heart rate 143 bpm, blood pressure 122/78 mm Hg. Examination revealed only a small area of hyperpigmentation at the left knee; no rash or tick was seen. Laboratory studies, including CBC, metabolic panel, toxicology screen, and thyroid function tests, were normal. Echocardiogram showed normal ventricular function and no structural disease. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.  

Telemetry and serial ECGs were obtained. Initial ECG showed a narrow-complex tachycardia with retrograde P waves and short RP intervals, consistent with AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT). Intravenous adenosine (2 doses), IV diltiazem, and IV metoprolol failed to terminate the tachycardia. A diltiazem infusion was also ineffective. The patient was transitioned to oral metoprolol and given one dose of flecainide, resulting in brief conversion to sinus rhythm with evidence of first- and second-degree AV block (PR intervals 240–320 ms). He was then started on propafenone and continued metoprolol, which achieved more sustained rate and rhythm control.
title: Lyme carditis presenting with an incessant atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia masking a variable atrioventricular block

case_prompt: A 19-year-old woman with no significant past medical or family history presents with two weeks of progressive abdominal pain and distention. On examination, there is a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa. Contrast CT and MRI reveal a 23×19×14 cm abdominopelvic mass in the mesogastrium and right iliac fossa compressing the iliac vessels and psoas, with moderate ascites and clustered retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Serum ionic calcium is normal. Ultrasound-guided biopsy shows a neoplasm with a biphasic pattern, partly spindle-shaped and partly epithelioid. Immunohistochemical staining is negative for PAX-8, p53, WT-1, inhibin, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor; positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3; and shows focal calretinin positivity.
final_diagnosis_raw: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary hypercalcemic type
title: Case Report of Small Cell Carcinoma of the Ovary, Hypercalcemic Type (Ovarian Rhabdoid Tumor) with SMARCB1 Mutation: A Literature Review of a Rare and Aggressive Condition

case_prompt:
A 19-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with bulging of the left eye and progressively blurred vision over the past few months. He had no fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms, and there was no family history of cancer or known exposure to chemicals or radiation. Six months earlier, an orbital lesion of approximately 3 cm in diameter had been noted but not further evaluated because of the COVID-19 pandemic. More recently, the lesion enlarged rapidly and began bleeding, prompting evaluation.

On MRI, there was a 60 × 44 × 50 mm mass in the extraconal space of the left orbit. The lesion was isointense to extraocular muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on STIR sequences, and showed heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. No internal cysts or calcifications were seen. The borders with the medial rectus muscle and the adjacent ethmoid sinus wall were ill-defined. The mass compressed and deformed the globe but did not invade the eyeball, the intraconal compartment, or extend intracranially. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated strong restricted diffusion with a minimum apparent diffusion coefficient of 0.7 × 10⁻³ mm²/s.

A systemic workup—including complete blood count, urinalysis, serum electrolytes, bone marrow aspiration, lumbar puncture, bone scintigraphy, cervical and abdominal ultrasonography, and CT scans of the abdomen and chest—was unremarkable.
title: Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma in a 19-year-old male patient: A case report and literature review

case_prompt: An 18-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of bilateral Achilles and posterior calf pain that was dull and aching, worsened by running, and did not occur at rest. She had undergone physical therapy, NSAIDs, and night splints with minimal benefit. On examination, she had bilateral tenderness over the superficial posterior compartment at the musculotendinous junction and muscle belly, mild swelling, and 4/5 strength on dorsiflexion; range of motion was normal. Ankle radiographs demonstrated a mild Haglund deformity bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging showed subtalar synovitis and an os trigonum, but these findings did not reproduce her primary posterior leg pain. She was offered pre- and postexertional compartment pressure measurement but declined further testing.
title: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome of the superficial posterior compartment: Soleus syndrome

case_prompt: A 76-year-old woman with a history of dementia presented with a 1-month history of pruritus localized to her right nipple. Topical corticosteroids produced minimal improvement. On examination, there was no palpable breast mass or axillary lymphadenopathy. The right nipple was swollen, erythematous, and bled occasionally; the areola appeared normal. Mammography showed no abnormalities. Ultrasonography demonstrated swelling of the right nipple, an internal punctiform hyperechoic area, and increased blood flow. Based on these clinical findings, inflammatory changes in the right nipple and Paget’s disease of the breast were considered as differential diagnoses, and a punch biopsy of the right nipple skin was performed. Histopathological examination revealed proliferating, highly atypical squamous cells accompanied by occasional mitotic figures, with no evidence of Paget cells or invasion of atypical cells beyond the basement membrane.
title: Bowen's Disease of the Nipple

case_prompt: A 48-year-old woman with a penicillin allergy presented with a progressively enlarging right cheek mass. Five years earlier, a similar soft-tissue lesion had been excised and diagnosed as a lipoma. Eight months after that excision, she noted recurrence of a firm, rounded, well-circumscribed, non-tender mass of about 4.5 cm in the right lower jugal region, causing facial asymmetry but with normal overlying skin and mucosa. No regional lymphadenopathy was present. Facial CT showed a well-defined, oval, fat-density lesion in the right jugal soft tissues, measuring 44 × 20 mm and extending 48 mm, crossed by linear septa, abutting the superficial cervical fascia and contacting the masseter without invasion.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Well-differentiated liposarcoma of the cheek misdiagnosed for lipoma: A case report

case_prompt: A 4-year-old boy presented with a diffuse swelling of the left cheek and left upper lip since birth, which had gradually enlarged with his growth. There was no pain or bleeding. On examination, the lesion was diffuse, ill-defined, soft, non-compressible, and involved the left cheek and upper lip; overlying skin showed hyperpigmented spots, and no bruit was heard. Doppler ultrasonography revealed a vascular lesion with questionable communication to the left facial vein. Clinically, hemangioma and arteriovenous malformation were considered. Propranolol was initiated (up to 2 mg/kg), and three cycles of intralesional bleomycin were administered over 8 months, but the swelling persisted. Surgical exploration and debulking were then planned.
journal: Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery
title: Angiomatosis: A Rare Vascular Proliferation of Head and Neck Region

case_prompt:
An 11-month-old intact male Labrador retriever was evaluated for a four-week history of chronic perianal dermatitis. The dog lived in the southeastern United States with exposure to fields, ponds, and woods. On examination, the perianal region from 12 to 7 o’clock around the anus showed a well-demarcated, asymmetrical erythematous area of lichenification with papules, crusts, punctate ulcerations, and fistulae; the lesions measured up to 5.5 cm × 5 cm × 1 cm. Superficial and deep skin scrapings revealed no ectoparasites. Cytology of the lesion showed neutrophils and macrophages with intra- and extracellular cocci, consistent with pyogranulomatous inflammation and secondary bacterial dermatitis. During routine castration, four 6 mm full-thickness punch biopsies of the lesion were obtained. 

Histopathology revealed chronic, severe pyogranulomatous and necrotizing nodular dermatitis and panniculitis with intralesional hyphae 6–14 μm wide, with non-parallel walls, irregular non-dichotomous branching, frequent septation, and occasional bulbous terminal dilatations. Hyphae stained positively with Periodic acid–Schiff and Grocott-Gomori’s methenamine silver stains and had no immunoreactivity for Pythium sp. antigen on immunohistochemistry. Potassium hydroxide tissue digests demonstrated tissue invasion by irregular hyphae producing little to no branching. 

Aerobic culture grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus pseudintermedius; anaerobic culture was negative. Serum Pythium ELISA results were 7% positivity at 1:1000 dilution, 6% at 1:2000, and 1% at 1:4000, consistent with a negative result. On Day +42, thoracic and abdominal radiographs, abdominal ultrasonography, CBC, biochemistry profile, and urinalysis showed no evidence of systemic dissemination.
title: Successful management of cutaneous paralagenidiosis in a dog treated with mefenoxam, minocycline, prednisone, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman presented with 7 months of mild, nonprogressive fullness over her right cheek. She had no pain or other symptoms. General examination was unremarkable. Extraoral inspection showed an ill-defined 1×1-inch fullness over the right lower two-thirds of the face, with normal overlying skin. Intraorally, there was diffuse expansion of the right posterior maxillary region, from the distal of the upper right second premolar to the tuberosity (about 2.5 cm), causing partial obliteration of the buccal vestibule. The overlying mucosa appeared normal. Palatal expansion was minimal with slight blanching. The swelling was hard and nontender, except adjacent to the buccal aspect of the upper right second molar, where the bone felt “windowed.” The upper right second molar showed grade II mobility; all right upper molars were nonresponsive to pulp testing. Oral hygiene was good, and aspiration was negative. A benign neoplasm of the basal maxillary bone was suspected, with initial differential diagnoses of benign odontogenic, nonodontogenic, and maxillary antral tumors.  
Laboratory studies, including hematologic values, were normal. Rhinoscopy revealed a mass in the middle meatus nearly occluding the right nasal cavity. Intraoral periapical radiography showed a diffuse, hazy radiolucency from the right upper second premolar to the third molar with root resorption and multiple fine calcifications. Panoramic imaging confirmed haziness of the right maxillary sinus. A paranasal sinus view demonstrated nonuniform opacification of the right maxillary sinus with an intact orbital margin.  
CT imaging was then performed. The CT scan revealed an ill-defined expansile mass completely occluding the right maxillary sinus and extending inferiorly to the alveolus, measuring approximately 5.6×3.3×4.2 cm. There was destruction of the medial, anterior, and lateral walls of the sinus, as well as of the maxillary alveolus and turbinates. The middle and posterior ethmoidal air cells were occluded. The lesion contained cystic spaces, calcific specks, and areas of ground-glass appearance.
title: Asymptomatic Presentation of Aggressive Ossifying Fibroma:A Case Report

case_prompt:
A 40-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a retroperitoneal mass discovered incidentally during preoperative CT for umbilical hernia repair. She had a 3-year history of hypertension on antihypertensive therapy and complained of a mild headache. Vital signs were unremarkable except for elevated blood pressure.  

Abdominal CT showed a 4×3×3 cm homogenous round mass located just below the left renal vein, with gradual, weak enhancement beginning in its peripheral area. MRI demonstrated low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and very high signal intensity on T2-weighted images.  

Laboratory studies revealed a plasma norepinephrine level of 702 pg/mL (normal, 100–450), with normal plasma epinephrine and dopamine levels. A 24-hour urine collection showed a slight increase in normetanephrine. However, ^123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy did not show uptake in the tumor.
title: Successful treatment for retroperitoneal cavernous hemangioma adjacent to the renal hilum via the laparoscopic approach: a case report

case_prompt:
A male neonate was born at 30 weeks’ gestation by urgent cesarean delivery because of an abnormal nonstress test, oligohydramnios, and cerebral blood flow redistribution. The 25-year-old mother had developed severe anemia (hemoglobin 5.0 g/dL) from multiple episodes of vaginal bleeding beginning at 24 weeks’ gestation; she received eight red‐cell transfusions in total. Maternal screening for TORCH infections, parvovirus B19, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis was negative, and the indirect Coombs test was negative. Placental histology showed terminal villous hypotrophy, infarction, and intervillous fibrinoid deposition, consistent with chronic hypoxia.

At birth (weight 1530 g; Apgar scores 1 at 1 minute, improving to 8 by 20 minutes), the neonate required full ventilatory support (FiO₂ 100%). Umbilical pH was 6.97 with a base excess of –12.2 mmol/L. Physical examination revealed a red-violaceous, nonblanching macular rash on the head, neck, and trunk. During the first 24 hours, he developed multiorgan dysfunction (brain, heart, liver, kidneys, lungs) with disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Laboratory tests on day 1 showed platelet count 38×10⁹/L, markedly elevated leukocyte count with 270 nucleated red blood cells (NRBC) per 100 WBC, absolute NRBC 63 558/mm³, reticulocyte count 519×10⁹/L, prolonged prothrombin time (>2 minutes), and elevated D-dimer 9419 ng/mL. C-reactive protein, TORCH and viral serologies, and thrombophilia screening were all negative. Echocardiography demonstrated right ventricular distension, hypokinesis, tricuspid insufficiency, and a bidirectional patent ductus arteriosus. Brain ultrasound revealed edema, periventricular hyperechogenicities, and bilateral porencephalic lesions in the posterior temporal regions.

By day 4, respiratory support was weaned from mechanical ventilation to CPAP, with improving organ function and normalized platelets and coagulation parameters. The cutaneous rash began to fade and had completely resolved by day 7. Serial brain ultrasounds showed persistent porencephalic areas; MRI on day 10 confirmed bilateral parietal, temporal, and occipital porencephalic cysts. The infant was discharged on day 41 in good condition, with mild transient hypotonia and normal growth.
title: Fetal hypoxia secondary to severe maternal anemia as a causative link between blueberry muffin baby and erythroblastosis: a case report

case_prompt:
A 64-year-old man was brought to the emergency department with anorexia, diarrhea, and an episode of altered consciousness. Earlier that day, a computed tomography scan had revealed a large mass in the right upper lobe of his lung, and he was admitted for evaluation of the pulmonary lesion. Shortly after admission, he developed bloody diarrhea, lower abdominal pain, and hypotension. 

His medical history included hypertension and depression; he was a heavy smoker (44-year pack history) but denied alcohol use. On examination, he was severely emaciated, normothermic, and hypotensive; his abdomen was soft with mild tenderness in the lower quadrants. Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 15.4 × 10^3/μL (86.5% neutrophils), hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen 69.4 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, prothrombin time 27.4%, and activated partial thromboplastin time 46.1 s. HIV testing was negative.

An urgent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan demonstrated extensive intestinal ischemia, intestinal pneumatosis, free intra-abdominal gas, intussusception of a small-intestinal mass, and a small amount of ascites. Chest CT again showed a large right upper-lobe mass. 

The preoperative diagnosis was bowel necrosis and perforation with intussusception of a small intestinal tumor. Accordingly, emergency subtotal colectomy and enterectomy were undertaken.
title: Lethal multiple colon necrosis and perforation due to fulminant amoebic colitis: a surgical case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman with no significant medical history and a remote nine-year smoking history (quit 30 years ago) was transferred for evaluation of sudden discoloration and numbness of her left fourth finger. The evening before presentation, she felt a sharp pinch in the middle phalanx and noted a blue circular spot. On awakening, the entire middle phalanx appeared bruised, was tender to palpation, and she experienced numbness. She denied trauma, coagulopathy, drug use, or similar prior episodes. 

On examination, the volar aspect of the middle phalanx of the left fourth digit was bluish, warm, slightly tender, and had decreased sensation. The distal phalanx had normal color with brisk capillary refill. All fingers had full range of motion. Radial pulses were equal and strong bilaterally, and the remainder of the hand was normal.

An ultrasound arterial duplex of the left upper extremity was performed and was normal.
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
title: Achenbach Syndrome: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 30-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-month history of left-sided nasal obstruction, recurrent left epistaxis, and left-sided headache. She denied nasal trauma, nasal picking, or pregnancy. On anterior rhinoscopy, a smooth, reddish-bluish soft-tissue mass filled the left nasal cavity, was attached to the nasal septum, and bled on palpation. Findings on ear, throat, neck examination and fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy were unremarkable. Routine blood tests were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses revealed a 3.5 × 1.2 cm soft-tissue lesion with heterogeneous patchy enhancement, attached to both the lateral and medial nasal walls, causing mild septal deviation but no bone erosions. MRI showed the lesion to be hypointense on non-contrast T1, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2 with multiple flow voids, and to have peripheral inhomogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. Digital subtraction angiography demonstrated a hypervascular left nasal mass receiving 70–80% of its blood supply from bilateral anterior ethmoidal branches and the remainder from the internal maxillary artery.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Nasal lobular capillary hezmangioma: Report of a case managed by endoscopic excision and pre-operative angio-embolization

case_prompt: A 19-year-old primigravid woman at 38 weeks’ gestation presented with an 8-hour history of intermittent semi-rhythmic, repetitive waving movements of the abdominal wall. The movements were rapid, with brief interruptions, confined to the abdominal musculature, predominantly the upper abdomen, without spreading to other body regions. They were not associated with pain, dyspnea, fatigue, or sensory symptoms, although she described discomfort below the right subcostal margin after prolonged episodes. The contractions were not voluntarily suppressible, did not vary with position or respiration, and persisted during sleep, causing sleep disturbance. She had no history of trauma, spinal or abdominal surgery, medication exposure, personal or family neurologic disorders, or psychosocial stressors. On examination, vital signs were normal, general and obstetric examinations showed no fetal distress, and neurologic assessment revealed normal mental status, cranial nerves, motor and sensory functions, except for the observed involuntary undulating abdominal wall movements. Basic laboratory studies, including complete blood count; serum electrolytes (sodium, calcium, potassium, magnesium); liver enzymes; bilirubin; renal function tests; and thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, and free triiodothyronine levels, were all within normal limits.
title: A case report and a brief literature review of belly dancer’s dyskinesia in a pregnant patient

case_prompt: A 36-year-old gravida 4, para 2-0-1-2 Asian woman of Bengali descent presented for antepartum care. Her history included hypothyroidism on levothyroxine, gestational diabetes on metformin, one prior miscarriage, and two prior cesarean deliveries. Noninvasive prenatal testing was negative and indicated a female fetus. At 27 weeks 5 days, an anatomy ultrasound showed fetal weight at the 25th percentile, an enlarged heart, mild ascites, and a bladder with posterior diverticulosis; kidneys appeared normal. Fetal echocardiography confirmed hydrops with 2 mm pericardial effusion, ascites, and mild cardiomegaly. Serologic testing for parvovirus and CMV IgM was negative. At 27 weeks 6 days, fetal MRI demonstrated a midline pelvic cystic structure posterior to the bladder and anterior to the rectum, left urinary tract dilatation with a 7 mm anterior–posterior pelvic diameter, central calyceal dilatation, proximal ureteral dilatation, mild–moderate ascites, a normal-appearing rectum, and possible ambiguous genitalia. Subsequent ultrasound at 28 weeks showed persistent ascites, a 10 mm left renal pelvic diameter, mild ureteral dilation, polyhydramnios (AFI 27), and normal female external genitalia. Amniocentesis was declined, but expanded carrier genetic testing revealed that the mother was a carrier of BBS12 and the father had a variant of uncertain significance in BBS12. The patient underwent cesarean delivery at 37 weeks; the female newborn (2720 g) had abdominal ultrasound on day 1 showing an 11 cm cystic pelvic structure, poor bladder visualization, and bilateral moderate hydronephrosis with caliectasis.
title: Prenatal diagnosis of Bardet Biedl Syndrome: A case report

case_prompt:
A 22-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a painless, enlarging vulvar mass for two months. Examination showed a well-defined, firm, crusted 3-cm cyst on the right labia majora; there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy and a pelvic examination was otherwise normal. Laboratory evaluation, including a complete blood count, was unremarkable. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia.  

Histopathology demonstrated a dermal spindle-cell proliferation with lobulated cellular myxoid nodules and collagenous hypocellular areas exhibiting abrupt transitions. Tumor cells were arranged in short fascicles with plump spindled to ovoid nuclei, mild hyperchromasia, and rare atypical mitoses (<2 per 10 high-power fields). Foci of small, curved vascular arcades with perivascular sclerosis were noted. There was no tumor necrosis or lymphovascular invasion. Immunohistochemical studies showed no staining for AE1/AE3, EMA, hormone receptors, SMA, h-Caldesmone, Desmin, CD34, S-100 protein, or CD10. The Ki-67 index was approximately 10%. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of metastatic disease.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma of the vulva presenting as a cystic mass: A case report and review of literature

case_prompt: A 62-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B and treated hepatocellular carcinoma (segment VIII) underwent microwave ablation. Six months later, he presented with a 2-week history of shortness of breath, productive cough, and right-sided chest pain. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 37 mm/h (reference 0–10 mm/h), AST 30 U/L, ALT 33 U/L, and negative tuberculosis, fungal, and sputum cultures. Bronchoscopy was performed and was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated a fluid attenuation biloma at the prior ablation site with a tract extending cranially through the diaphragm into the right lower pleural space, accompanied by a right anterior basal mass-like consolidation. This imaging raised concern for a thoracobiliary fistula.
title: Use heat with caution! Pleurobiliary fistula after hepatocellular carcinoma microwave ablation in lymphoma patient: A case study

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man with a history of primary antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) presented for evaluation of sudden neurologic deficits. Eighteen months earlier, he had developed right-sided neck swelling, resting dyspnea, and small-volume hemoptysis. CT pulmonary angiography revealed pulmonary emboli in bilateral lower-lobe branches, and ultrasound showed right internal jugular vein thrombosis. Laboratory testing at that time showed antiphospholipid IgG 237 GPL (normal <10 GPL), lupus anticoagulant 164 s (normal 24–36 s), and factor V Leiden 49% (normal 78–152%). Secondary causes of APS were excluded, and he was treated with apixaban.

Over the following year, he remained on follow-up with occasional dyspnea until he developed dull, moderate left upper quadrant pain for three weeks. Abdominal CT showed splenomegaly with two hypodense lesions consistent with splenic infarctions. He was admitted and started on IV heparin, warfarin, and prednisolone 40 mg daily. Rheumatologic testing revealed positive extractable nuclear antigen, antiphospholipid antibodies, perinuclear ANCA, and anti-dsDNA >200 IU/mL; ANA and c-ANCA were negative. INR was 2.2, and PTT was 70 s (normal 25–35 s).

A few days later, he acutely developed right-sided weakness, dysarthria, vomiting, and diaphoresis. On examination, he was alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15; cranial nerves and sensation were intact. He had right upper and lower extremity weakness with an upgoing right Babinski sign. Brain CT was unremarkable. MRI of the brain showed acute ischemic infarction in the right brainstem, a lacunar infarct in the left occipital lobe, subacute cortical infarction with laminar necrosis, and an old superior sagittal sinus thrombus. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular thrombus with an ejection fraction of 55%.

To evaluate for other thrombotic microangiopathies, a peripheral blood smear was obtained and showed slightly reduced red cells with no nucleated or helmet cells and neutrophilia.
title: Dramatic devastative complications in a patient with catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome: A Case report and literature review

case_prompt:
A 28-year-old man presented with visual disturbance in both eyes. His right eye symptoms began 2 months earlier and his left eye symptoms 2 weeks earlier. He had a history of stage IV lupus nephritis diagnosed at age 14, complicated by renal failure requiring hemodialysis since age 23, and hypertension; systemic steroids had not been used since dialysis onset. 

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures and anterior-segment examinations were normal in both eyes. Posterior-segment examination revealed shallow subretinal fluid and serous retinal detachment in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography showed shallow subretinal fluid, serous retinal detachment, and RPE–choroidal undulation at the foveae without pigment epithelial detachment, double-layer sign, or diffuse atrophic RPE changes.

Before angiography, the presumed diagnosis was central serous chorioretinopathy. Fluorescein angiography in the late phase demonstrated multiple subretinal leakage points in both eyes. Late-phase indocyanine green angiography showed choroidal vascular engorgement and multiple hyperfluorescent plaques in both eyes. 

Laboratory evaluation revealed decreased C3 levels, hematuria, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, consistent with moderate systemic lupus erythematosus activity. Although typically seen in severely active SLE, lupus choroidopathy was considered in both eyes.
title: Subretinal fluid in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus

case_prompt:
A 43-year-old Filipino man first noted an indurated mass on the right breast 12 years before presentation. Over the next 2 years the lesion enlarged, followed by erythema and the development of slowly enlarging pendulous indurated masses on the left breast and in the lower abdominal fold. A biopsy at that time showed granulomatous dermatitis, and he was treated with three full courses of antituberculosis therapy without improvement. In the ensuing years he developed diffuse erythema and areas of induration on the neck, with reticulated violaceous and hypopigmented patches, atrophy, and telangiectasia. Prominent engorged veins with punched-out necrotic ulcers were noted, accompanied by severe skin pain. At presentation, he had bulky, indurated, sagging skin folds on the inframammary areas and lower abdominal fold.  

Multiple skin biopsies showed:
- A nodular-to-diffuse infiltrate of lymphocytes and histiocytes around dilated telangiectatic blood vessels, with granulomas composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, Touton, Langhans, and foreign-body giant cells throughout the dermis.  
- Granulomatous vasculitis of small- to medium-sized vessels, with fibrin deposition and swollen endothelial cells infiltrated by lymphocytes, histiocytes, and giant cells.  
- Broad areas of sclerotic collagen within the reticular dermis.  

Verhoeff Van Gieson elastic tissue staining demonstrated absence of elastic fibers in the infiltrative areas, scattered fibers at the periphery, and fragmented elastic fibers within giant cells, consistent with elastophagocytosis.
title: Granulomatous slack skin presenting as diffuse poikiloderma and necrotic ulcers, with features of granulomatous vasculitis and response to oral prednisone, acitretin, and oral psoralen plus ultraviolet light therapy—A case report

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old Hispanic G2P1001 woman at 38 1/7 weeks’ gestation with obesity (BMI 41) and gestational diabetes presented with 8 hours of progressive shortness of breath. On arrival, temperature was 102.2 °F, blood pressure 119/73 mm Hg, heart rate 144 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air; fetal heart rate was 211 bpm. Cervical examination showed 1 cm dilatation, 0% effacement, intact membranes, and a posterior, long, vertex fetus. A urine toxicology screen was negative. Intravenous hydration and broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam and vancomycin) were initiated for presumed sepsis.  

Because of a nonreactive fetal tracing with tachycardia and minimal variability (category 2), a stat primary low transverse cesarean delivery was performed under general anesthesia with rapid-sequence intubation. Induction agents included propofol 200 mg and succinylcholine 100 mg; the endotracheal tube was placed atraumatically, and bilateral breath sounds and end-tidal CO₂ confirmed placement. A healthy infant was delivered (Apgars 9 and 9) with meconium-stained fluid.  

Immediately after delivery, before placental extraction, the patient’s heart rate remained 140 bpm, but oxygen saturation dropped to 72%, blood pressure fell to 72/48 mm Hg, and end-tidal CO₂ fell from 32 to 0 mm Hg. Anesthesia equipment was checked, and phenylephrine boluses (total 1800 µg) were administered without sustained effect. The obstetrics team found no hysterotomy extensions, lacerations, or uncontrolled bleeding. Within one minute of symptom onset, the anesthesia team administered atropine 0.2 mg, ondansetron 8 mg, and ketorolac 15 mg intravenously. Over the next 2–3 minutes, the patient’s oxygen saturation rose to 97%, blood pressure to 138/68 mm Hg, and end-tidal CO₂ to 32 mm Hg, although tachycardia persisted at 140 bpm. She received additional intravenous fluids, uterotonics, and blood products, had an estimated blood loss of 2000 ml, and was transported intubated to the ICU for further monitoring.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Atypical Amniotic Fluid Embolism Managed with a Novel Therapeutic Regimen

case_prompt: A 39-year-old African American woman with a 20-year history of HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy (bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide) and hypertension presented with 2 weeks of abdominal pain and decreased urinary output. Two weeks earlier she suffered a mechanical fall and had taken ibuprofen for pain. On presentation, her serum creatinine was 5.5 mg/dL (baseline 0.91 mg/dL 3 months earlier). Urinalysis showed 3+ proteinuria and microscopic hematuria without casts; the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was >10 g/g. CD4 count was 267/µL and HIV viral load 1,220 copies/mL. Tenofovir was discontinued, and ART was adjusted. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed mild bilateral hydronephrosis, marked diffuse irregular bladder wall thickening, and ascites. Cystoscopy revealed diffuse nodules throughout the bladder wall without ureteral obstruction. Serologic workup—including complements, ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM antibody, and hepatitis B and C serologies—was negative. Serum protein electrophoresis showed no monoclonal protein, but serum free κ light chains were 1,988 mg/L with a κ/λ ratio of 36.4; urine immunofixation revealed monoclonal free κ light chains. A bone marrow biopsy was unsuccessful, and diagnostic paracentesis was negative for malignancy. Hemodialysis was initiated on hospital day 6 for progressive renal failure.
title: Light chain cast nephropathy caused by plasmablastic lymphoma of the bladder

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman with a 5-year history of infertility presented with progressively worsening lower abdominal pain and distension over 3 months. Initially intermittent, the pain became constant and severe, accompanied by bloating and mild nausea. Eight months earlier, she had undergone a laparotomy for a myometrial mass diagnosed as a smooth muscle tumor of uncertain malignant potential. The prior surgery was uncomplicated.
