She had no family history of malignancy or gynecological disorders and no known hereditary conditions.

On examination, she appeared uncomfortable because of abdominal distension but was hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation revealed diffuse tenderness without rebound or guarding. There was no palpable mass or signs of peritonitis, and bowel sounds were normal. Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count (8.5 × 10^3/µL), normal inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 5 mg/L; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 15 mm/hr), normal liver and renal function, and normal tumor markers (CA-125, 18 U/mL; CEA, 2.5 ng/mL). A pregnancy test was negative.

Abdominopelvic ultrasound demonstrated a complex intraperitoneal fluid collection with multiple septations and internal debris. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed a large, well-defined cystic lesion in the inter-uterorectal space measuring 14 × 8 cm, exhibiting T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, thin septa, and no solid components.
title: Uncovering a peritoneal inclusion cyst after surgery: A case report

case_prompt: A 10-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever and left hip pain. He had no chronic illnesses or predisposing factors. On examination, he held the left hip in about 20° of flexion and had a limited range of motion in internal and external rotation. His temperature was 38.5 °C. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14,100/mm^3 with 85% neutrophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 18 mm/hr, and a normal C-reactive protein concentration. Pharyngeal, urine, and blood cultures, as well as a chest radiograph, were obtained, but no other source of infection was identified. Because septic arthritis was suspected, a fluoroscopy-guided needle aspiration of the hip yielded no synovial fluid. A pelvis radiograph was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated a fluid collection within the tensor fascia lata muscle.
title: Pyomyositis of tensor fascia lata: a case report

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old male presented with a 4-year history of multiple asymptomatic skin lesions. He reported that the lesions began on his lower limbs and gradually spread to involve his face, trunk, and both upper and lower extremities. He had no relevant personal or family medical history.

On examination, there were numerous well-defined, soft to firm, pedunculated papulonodular lesions ranging up to 15 mm in diameter. The lesions were yellow-brown in color and nearly symmetrically distributed over the entire body, particularly the extensor surfaces of the joints. Examination of the mucous membranes, palms, and soles was unremarkable. A pigmented patch with increased hair growth was noted on his back. He also had a marked kyphosis.

Ophthalmologic assessment, abdominal ultrasonography, and chest radiography revealed no evidence of extracutaneous involvement.

The initial differential diagnoses included histiocytosis, neurofibromatosis, sarcoidosis, and xanthoma.
title: Juvenile Xanthogranuloma: Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 36-year-old Caucasian Greek man presented with a two-month history of gradually progressive right shoulder weakness and limited active abduction and elevation, notably while carrying heavy objects on his shoulder. He denied any neck or shoulder pain, specific trauma, or recent infection. He had no significant medical or surgical history.

On examination, his right shoulder was depressed with noticeable asymmetry and winging of the scapula, becoming most evident during abduction and disappearing in forward elevation. He was unable to abduct the right arm above 80° in either the frontal or scapular plane, though passive range of motion was full and comparable to the left side. There was marked wasting of the right trapezius muscle with decreased shrugging. The ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle appeared normal, and there were no other cranial nerve deficits or signs of brachial plexus involvement. His rotator cuff was judged to be intact.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and serum biochemistry, were all within normal limits. Initial shoulder radiographs were unremarkable. Computed tomography of the shoulder girdle demonstrated diffuse atrophy of the right trapezius muscle. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine, right shoulder joint, and skull base showed mild atrophy of the right sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles without other pathology.

Electrophysiological testing of the right spinal accessory nerve with surface stimulation and recording from the trapezius yielded no compound muscle action potential. Needle electromyography of the right trapezius revealed active denervation (fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves), marked reduction of insertional activity, and absence of motor unit recruitment, indicating severe axonal loss. Electromyography of the right sternocleidomastoid showed mild axonal injury, while the levator scapulae, serratus anterior, and rhomboid muscles were normal.
title: Unusual insidious spinal accessory nerve palsy: a case report

case_prompt: A previously healthy 6-year-old boy presented with a 2-day history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and persistent vomiting following an elective upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsies. The procedure was performed under analgosedation to evaluate for celiac disease—given intermittent dizziness, nausea, abdominal pain, elevated deamidated gliadin peptides, and HLA-DQ2 and ‑DQ8 positivity—by a senior pediatric gastroenterologist without periprocedural complications. Three duodenal biopsies were obtained; histology showed normal mucosa. His history was negative for bleeding disorders, anticoagulant use, trauma, or abuse. On examination, he appeared fatigued, diaphoretic, and pale, with tachycardia, high-pitched bowel sounds, abdominal distension, and marked upper-abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.2 mmol/L (nv 7.4–9.1), platelets 441 Gpt/L (nv 150–530), prothrombin time 94% (nv 70–130%), aPTT 24.1 s (nv 27–40 s), and INR 1.03 (nv 0.8–1.25). An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large intramural mass within the duodenal wall causing proximal small-bowel obstruction.
title: Large Duodenal Hematoma Causing an Ileus after an Endoscopic Duodenal Biopsy in a 6-Year-Old Child: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 36-year-old Caucasian woman at 21 weeks’ gestation (normal fetal ultrasound; no comorbidities or medications) presented with a 6-month history of left nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea, which worsened during the first trimester. She also reported episodes of sleep apnea and hyposmia. Nasal endoscopy revealed a grayish polypoid mass with a multinodular surface occupying the entire left nasal fossa. CT and MRI of the paranasal sinuses showed a 24×28×26 mm lesion that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images, displaying a convoluted cerebriform pattern. The mass completely obliterated the left maxillary sinus, obstructed the anterior osteomeatal unit, and was associated with ethmoidal sinusitis. Vital signs were within normal limits.
title: Safety and efficacy of remifentanil target-controlled infusion for conscious sedation in a pregnant woman: a case report

case_prompt:
A 2.5-year-old neutered male Boxer (36.3 kg) was evaluated for a 2-day history of coughing, lethargy, and decreased appetite. Physical examination revealed increased bronchovesicular sounds; other findings were normal. CBC showed leukocytosis (26,100 cells/µl; ref 6000–17 000) with marked eosinophilia (14,090 cells/µl; ref 100–1000). Venous blood gas and remaining CBC values were unremarkable.

Thoracic radiographs showed a mixed pulmonary pattern: a consolidated alveolar pattern in the right caudal lung lobe with two soft tissue–opaque masses, and a multifocal unstructured interstitial pattern coalescing to patchy alveolar opacity in the left cranial and caudal lobes. Differentials included eosinophilic granuloma, parasitic or fungal pneumonia, or neoplasia. Bronchoalveolar lavage from three lobes was consistent with marked eosinophilic inflammation. Mycoplasma PCR and aerobic culture of lavage fluid were negative. A percutaneous transthoracic fine‐needle aspirate of the right caudal masses was inconclusive.

The dog was treated for presumptive eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy with fenbendazole, prednisone, and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. One month later, minimal radiographic improvement prompted addition of cetirizine. Two months after presentation, repeat radiographs showed resolution of the right caudal masses but a new, well‐defined 4.3 cm diameter mass in the left caudal lung lobe. Thoracic CT confirmed a 6 × 6.5 × 6 cm contrast‐enhancing mass in the left caudal lobe, a 1.6 mm nodule in the same lobe, and tracheobronchial and cranial mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Lobectomy was recommended.
title: Autologous blood pleurodesis for surgical pneumothorax and outcome with multimodal cancer treatment in a dog with primary pulmonary mast cell tumor

case_prompt:
A 39-year-old man presented with acute abdominal pain, fever, and chills. Ten years earlier, he underwent a renal transplant for end-stage renal failure secondary to amyloidosis and had been maintained on prednisolone, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate sodium. Ten months ago, he was treated for presumed pneumonia after pleuritic chest pain, fever, and weight loss; TB workup (chest radiograph, chest CT, blood cultures, urinary antigen, tuberculin skin test) was inconclusive. He continued to experience night sweats and weight loss. His father had pulmonary tuberculosis treated with rifampicin seven years earlier.

On examination, he appeared septic with a temperature of 38.3°C, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. The abdomen was diffusely rigid with rebound tenderness. Digital rectal examination revealed painful rectal ulcers. Laboratory tests showed WBC 14,900 cells/mm3, hematocrit 28.7%, BUN 78 mg/dL, creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 168 U/dL; other results were normal. A chest X-ray demonstrated subdiaphragmatic free air. Abdominal CT revealed pericecal inflammation and bowel perforation without distal obstruction.
title: Cecum perforation due to tuberculosis in a renal transplant recipient: a case report

case_prompt: A 15-year-old girl presented with a tender, palpable right breast lump that she first noticed 4 months earlier. She denied fevers, night sweats, cough, recent vaccinations, animal bites, or trauma. On breast examination, there was a firm, tender, mobile 3-cm mass at the 9:00 position, 8 cm from the nipple, without overlying skin changes. Exam of both axillae revealed a single tender node in the right axillary tail; other nodes in both axillae were not enlarged. A diagnostic ultrasound of the breast mass demonstrated an enlarged intramammary lymph node measuring 2.9 cm with cortical thickening up to 7.5 mm, preserved fatty hilum, and maintained oval shape. A second enlarged lymph node with cortical thickening was identified in the right axillary tail. Other imaging of the contralateral axilla was unremarkable. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the intramammary node was performed.
title: Kikuchi Disease with enlargement of intramammary lymph node

case_prompt: A 58-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of gradually worsening right lower quadrant abdominal pain associated with profuse watery diarrhea, fever, nausea, and dysuria. Two weeks earlier, she had returned from a trip to Hawaii. Her medical history was notable for Addison’s disease, Sjögren’s syndrome, and rheumatoid arthritis treated with chronic corticosteroids. On admission, vital signs showed a temperature of 38.2 °C, heart rate 102 bpm, blood pressure 110/68 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. Physical examination revealed tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant without rebound or guarding; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed metabolic alkalosis with serum bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, potassium 2.8 mmol/L, and calcium 7.1 mg/dL. She was admitted and treated empirically with metronidazole, piperacillin–tazobactam, and ciprofloxacin while undergoing evaluation for pyelonephritis, appendicitis, and adrenal crisis. After several days, all routine imaging and laboratory evaluations for these conditions were unremarkable.
journal: Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports
title: Acquisition of Cholera Within the United States

case_prompt:
A 27-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of headache, vomiting, and blurring of vision, and a 1-month history of imbalance and swaying to the right. On examination, he had a dilated pupil and ptosis on the right side, a visual acuity of 6/24 in that eye, and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed a well-defined suprasellar mass measuring approximately 3.0×2.5×3.5 cm that was T1 isointense, T2 heterointense, and homogeneously contrast-enhancing with a lobulated appearance. The lesion compressed the midbrain, displaced the third ventricle upward with proximal ventriculomegaly and periventricular lucencies, was predominantly in the interpeduncular cistern extending across the midline, effacing the aqueduct and compressing the cerebral peduncle, and extended anteriorly along the cavernous sinus toward the superior orbital fissure with compression of the adjacent optic nerve.  
Differential diagnosis at that time included meningioma, schwannoma of cranial nerve, vascular pathology (thrombosed giant aneurysm), and lymphoma.
title: Sporadic Cisternal Oculomotor Nerve Schwannoma: A Rare Case with Review of Literature

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman presented with a lesion on her chin that began as pinkish plaques 7 years earlier. Over time, the lesion slowly enlarged, became tender to touch, and changed from pink to purple with overlying telangiectasia and increased perspiration. The patient noted that the enlarging lesion began to interfere with her speech. 

On examination, there was a poorly circumscribed, pinkish, infiltrated plaque measuring approximately 4 × 4 cm on the chin, with overlying telangiectasia and extension into the intraoral gingival mucosa. The remainder of the general and systemic examination was unremarkable. An iodine–starch test over the lesion demonstrated profuse hyperhidrosis.

A 5-mm punch biopsy was obtained. Histopathologic examination revealed nodular clusters of dilated vessels intimately associated with an increased number of mature eccrine glands, with an unremarkable epidermis. A closer view showed ectatic blood vessels admixed with dilated sweat glands and mature fat cells.
title:
Facial eccrine angiomatous hamartoma in a 52-year-old woman: A case
report

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a two-year history of vague, paroxysmal abdominal pain localized to the right hypochondrium, occurring throughout the day. She denied fever, vomiting, or jaundice but reported a 10-kg weight loss over this period. Her general condition was well preserved; vital signs were stable. On abdominal examination, a fixed, well-limited 4-cm mass was palpable in the right hypochondrium; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including liver and renal function, were within normal limits. Six months earlier, an abdominal ultrasound had shown no abnormalities. A contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a heterogeneous, lobulated soft-tissue mass arising from the anterior wall of the inferior vena cava, measuring 50 × 37 × 46 mm, with invasion of the right renal vein. On MRI, the lesion was of low signal on T1, T2, and diffusion sequences, demonstrated intraluminal extension, and showed enhancement after gadolinium injection. The mass abutted the duodenum, pancreatic head, and hepatic pedicle without definite invasion. No lymphadenopathy or metastatic lesions were identified.  
Differential diagnoses of a retroperitoneal mass affecting the inferior vena cava included cruoric thrombus, leiomyosarcoma, intimal sarcoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, adrenal tumors (such as pheochromocytoma) extending into the IVC, and paraganglioma. However, all the radiological findings were highly suggestive of a leiomyosarcoma of the inferior vena cava according to the opinion of the vascular and digestive surgery teams and radiologists.
final_diagnosis_raw: Leiomyosarcoma of the inferior vena cava
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Inferior vena cava resection for a leiomyosarcoma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 38-year-old white man with Crohn’s disease treated with adalimumab presented with a 1-month history of scalp irritation that was intermittently tender and pruritic. One year earlier, he had an erythema multiforme–like rash with hot and cold sweats; chest radiography at that time suggested right lower-lobe pneumonia, and he received a prednisone taper with rapid symptom resolution. 

On examination, there was a 1.5- to 2-cm adherent yellow-brown crust overlying an indurated, fluctuant plaque on the vertex of the scalp without alopecia; cervical lymphadenopathy was present. A swab for bacterial and fungal cultures grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, and he was treated for bacterial cellulitis with oral cefadroxil and 4% chlorhexidine gluconate shampoo. After 17 days of therapy, and despite the later addition of topical Liquor Carbonis Detergens 20%, the lesion persisted. 

At a 6-month follow-up, there was no improvement. Over the next 3 months, he received oral doxycycline, topical clindamycin lotion, intralesional triamcinolone, and clobetasol shampoo. The plaque continued to enlarge, areas of scarring alopecia developed, and tufts of hair were appreciated. A punch biopsy and tissue cultures for bacteria, atypical mycobacteria, and fungus were performed, and his immunosuppressive therapies were temporarily held.
title: Disseminated coccidioidomycosis mimicking cicatricial alopecia

case_prompt:
An 83-year-old Arabic man was brought to the emergency department after a transient episode of altered consciousness and urinary incontinence. Earlier that day he had symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection (runny nose and cough) and had taken one tablet of loratadine/pseudoephedrine 10 mg/240 mg and two tablets of paracetamol/caffeine 500 mg/65 mg. His family found him snoring loudly in bed with wet sheets; on arousal he was confused, dizzy, and fell from the bed without trauma. While awaiting evaluation, he had a witnessed tonic–clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes. He had no fever, recent travel, or sick contacts. His medical history was remarkable only for type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension for 20 years; his medications included linagliptin, metformin, rosuvastatin, and lisinopril. He did not smoke or drink alcohol. 

On examination, vital signs were normal; he was pale and disoriented to person, place, and time, with no focal neurologic deficits or meningeal signs. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, sodium 134 mEq/L, glucose 8.3 mmol/L, and a normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein. An electrocardiogram and noncontrast brain CT scan were normal. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral small white-matter hyperintensities on T2 consistent with chronic small-vessel ischemic changes. Electroencephalography did not reveal focal or generalized epileptiform discharges, even with hyperventilation or photic stimulation.
title: Seizures provoked by over-the-counter cough and cold medications in an elderly patient: a case report

case_prompt: A 37-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 20-minute episode of central chest tightness radiating to both arms, associated with diaphoresis that resolved spontaneously. He smoked 10–15 cigarettes per day, had a remote history of anabolic steroid use, and denied current drug use. His past medical history included asthma, pulmonary sarcoidosis, and an NSAID-induced anaphylaxis with respiratory arrest. On examination he was muscular, with no murmurs or signs of heart failure. Serial ECGs showed normal sinus rhythm without ischaemic changes. Full blood count and renal function were normal. High-sensitivity troponin-I was 63 ng/L (normal < 15) then 45 ng/L three and a half hours later. Lipids were elevated (total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.1 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.9 mmol/L). He was treated as an acute coronary syndrome. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal biventricular function without regional wall motion abnormalities. Twenty-four hours after admission, while pain free, invasive coronary angiography revealed severe stenoses in multiple vessels—including the ostium and proximal segment of a diagonal branch, the proximal intermediate artery, the non-dominant circumflex, distal right coronary artery, and posterior descending artery—and a moderate lesion in the mid-LAD at the diagonal bifurcation. The angiographic appearances were atypical for coronary plaque. Computed tomography coronary angiography demonstrated normal coronary arteries. A repeat invasive coronary angiogram confirmed resolution of the previously observed stenoses.
title: The role of computed tomography coronary angiography in multi-vessel coronary vasospasm: a case report

case_prompt: A 40-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of dull pain and purulent discharge in the left posterior maxillary region following extraction of teeth 24, 25, 26, 27, and 28. She also reported intermittent extraoral swelling over the left maxilla and numbness of the left upper lip. Six months earlier, she had been diagnosed with uncontrolled type II diabetes mellitus (fasting blood sugar, 300 mg/dL; postprandial, 402 mg/dL) during evaluation for facial cellulitis and began treatment. On examination, vital signs were normal. Extraoral inspection revealed mild swelling over the left middle face with obliteration of the nasolabial fold, skin discoloration, and left periorbital edema. Intraorally, there was necrotic alveolar bone with foul discharge and tenderness in the left maxillary edentulous region. Panoramic radiography showed opacification of the left maxillary sinus. CT scan demonstrated nonhomogeneous opacification of the left maxillary sinus, obstruction of the left osteomeatal unit, extension into the middle meatus, ethmoidal, and frontal sinuses, and bony destruction of the walls of the left maxillary and ethmoidal sinuses. Based on these findings, differential diagnoses included deep fungal infection and avascular necrosis of the maxillary bone.
title: Fulminant Mucormycosis Involving Paranasal Sinuses: A Rare Case Report

case_prompt: A 32-year-old man with no significant medical history presented for evaluation of chronic headaches. He was afebrile, with stable vital signs, and initial laboratory studies were unremarkable. Noncontrast CT of the head showed an indeterminate lytic defect in the bony clivus with a well-demarcated, smoothly corticated margin, raising concern for an underlying malignancy. Subsequent MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed a well-defined midline retroclival cystic lesion measuring 5 × 12 mm that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and followed cerebrospinal fluid signal on T2-FLAIR. The lesion did not restrict diffusion and did not demonstrate any abnormal contrast enhancement.
title: Ecchordosis physaliphora: Case report and brief review of the literature

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old Japanese man with hypertension and prior bilateral inguinal hernia repairs presented with 6 days of swelling and pain over his left inguinal incision. He was afebrile, and vital signs were normal. On examination, tender, elastic, hard masses were palpated in the left inguinal region without overlying skin or mucosal lesions; the genitalia and lower limbs were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 8350/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 10.19 mg/dL. Abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated a left inguinal hernia and five to six enlarged left inguinal lymph nodes (1–4 cm) with increased surrounding soft-tissue density; no other lymphadenopathy was seen. A clinical diagnosis of left inguinal infectious lymphadenitis was made, and an excisional biopsy was performed.  
Grossly, the lymph nodes were fragile and exuded pus. Histologically, there were multifocal abscesses with central suppuration and peripheral purulent exudate. Lymphoid follicles and the capsule were inconspicuous, and dense fibrosis was absent. Numerous histiocytes formed vague granulomas, and occasional multinucleated giant cells were seen. The cortex showed marked interfollicular hyperplasia with perivascular plasma cells. Neutrophils within vessel lumina suggested endarteritis and phlebitis. The findings were interpreted as suppurative granulomatous lymphadenitis.
title: Primary syphilis presenting as a painful unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, without cutaneous manifestations, in a 71-year-old Japanese man: A case report

case_prompt:
A 24-year-old woman was admitted with sudden headache and left-sided weakness 6 hours earlier. She had no history of hypertension. Initial head CT showed an irregular right frontal lobe hematoma. Laboratory studies revealed a serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) level of 2266 mIU/mL; CA 19-9 was 37.13 U/mL. She received mannitol and supportive care and was discharged.  

Two weeks later, she was transferred for a generalized seizure. On examination, she was alert; pupils were equal and reactive. She had limited leftward gaze bilaterally, symmetric forehead wrinkles, tongue deviation to the left, and left upper and lower limb strength of grade IV–; right limbs were grade V. Obstetric history included a normal delivery 2 years ago, an abortion 1 year ago, an intrauterine device placed 7 months ago, and regular menses for the last 2 months.  

During hospitalization, she had two more seizures and her serum β-HCG rose from 63 148 to 980 893 mIU/mL. Gynecologic ultrasonography showed a normal uterus and adnexa, with no evidence of intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy. Repeat head CT demonstrated a new hemorrhagic focus at the margin of the chronic hematoma, which had enlarged substantially 10 days later. Head MRA and digital subtraction angiography showed no aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. Chest radiograph revealed a 6-cm mass in the right lung; abdominal and pelvic CT scans were unremarkable.
title: Intracerebral hemorrhage as initial presentation of metastatic choriocarcinoma: A case report

case_prompt:
A 29-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizoaffective disorder was hospitalized after an intentional overdose of acetaminophen and lithium and began clozapine therapy. Eight days after starting clozapine, he developed substernal chest pain worse with deep inspiration that progressed over two days. He was transferred to cardiology when troponin and brain natriuretic peptide levels were found to be elevated.  
On examination, he was tachycardic but had no murmurs, rubs, or signs of heart failure; lungs were clear. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis, elevated troponin, elevated inflammatory markers, and elevated brain natriuretic peptide. Electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevations most prominent in leads V2–V3.  
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed global hypokinesis with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45% and subtle late gadolinium enhancement of the epicardial lateral wall and pericardium with abnormal parametric mapping, consistent with myopericarditis. A respiratory viral panel was negative.
title: Chest Pain in a Psychiatric Patient Due to Clozapine-Induced Myopericarditis

case_prompt: A 30-year-old man presented with several months of pain, tenderness, and swelling on the left side of his palate. On examination, the left palatine mucosa was diffusely swollen—most pronounced in the molar region—with poorly defined borders and increased pain on palpation. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated a high-signal-intensity lesion in that area. Panoramic radiography and CT scans of the maxilla and sinuses were unremarkable, and all left maxillary teeth appeared healthy. His medical and family histories were unremarkable, and he denied any history of trauma or inflammation in the head or neck. Empiric treatment with oral antibiotics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for 7 days produced no improvement. Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, a soft-tissue tumor was suspected, and an incisional biopsy was performed.
title: A diffuse traumatic neuroma in the palate: a case report

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old Chinese woman was referred for evaluation of a 2-month history of progressively enlarging right submandibular swelling. The mass was painless, persisted despite multiple courses of oral antibiotics and a recent dental extraction, and was not associated with fevers, respiratory symptoms, weight loss, or dysphagia. Her medical history was notable only for prior right submandibular sialadenitis excision; she took no regular medications.

On examination, there was a firm, non-tender swelling in the right submandibular region without overlying skin changes. There was no trismus or intraoral abnormality. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated eosinophil count of 1.8 × 10^9/L (normal 0.0–0.5 × 10^9/L) and a serum creatinine of 91 µmol/L (normal 49–90 µmol/L); other tests were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed multiple enlarged right submandibular lymph nodes. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion was non-diagnostic.
title: Kimura's disease: an uncommon cause of head and neck masses with potentially serious sequelae

case_prompt:
A 14-year-old boy was evaluated for a painless swelling of the tongue that he had first noticed three months earlier. He denied bleeding, pain, or trauma. His medical history was unremarkable, with no diabetes, hypertension, or allergies. He led a healthy lifestyle. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

On examination, there was a well-demarcated, firm mass measuring approximately 1.7 × 1.5 cm on the right side of the tongue involving the apex and body. The overlying mucosa was intact except for a small area of peripheral ulceration noted on gross inspection. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Given the size and location of the lesion, the patient underwent a wide surgical excision of the mass. The specimen measured 17 × 15 × 4 mm and on sectioning revealed a vaguely nodular, gray-to-red lesion with ill-defined borders and a 10-mm ulcerated area at the periphery.
title:
Granular cell tumour of the tongue in a 14-year-old
boy: case report

case_prompt: A 61-year-old non-smoking woman was admitted with a 2-week history of facial edema, dry cough, and dyspnea on exertion. She appeared tachypneic with moderate respiratory distress. Vital signs were: blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Examination revealed facial edema and distended non-pulsatile superficial veins over the neck and chest; no peripheral lymphadenopathy was noted and the remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory test results were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed marked widening of the mediastinum without lung parenchymal lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated enlargement of the right upper paratracheal lymph node (45 mm) and both lower paratracheal lymph nodes (20 mm on the right, 23 mm on the left), compressing the superior vena cava; each node had marginal contrast enhancement with low central attenuation. Positron emission tomography showed increased FDG uptake in the upper paratracheal (SUVmax 16.1), lower paratracheal (SUVmax 14.4), and hilar (SUVmax 11.0) lymph nodes. Because of the short history and SVC obstruction by mediastinal lymph nodes, the differential diagnosis included lymphoma, tuberculosis, and bacterial infection. Initial acid-fast bacillus staining of the sputum as well as blood cultures were all negative.
title: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome Due to Mediastinal Tuberculous Lymphadenitis

case_prompt: A 16-year-old unmarried Kashmiri schoolgirl was referred for a 5-month history of complete loss of personal memory. She did not recognize her name, parents, school friends, or basic academic knowledge expected of a 10th-grade student. She was unable to perform previously mastered skills such as playing computer videogames. Attendants noted regressive behaviors, including thumb sucking and childlike speech. She denied any history of trauma, sexual abuse, head injury, loss of consciousness, seizures, mania, psychosis, or substance use. Past medical, psychiatric, family, and social histories were unremarkable. On examination, she was cooperative, appropriately dressed, and described her mood as euthymic. Thinking was goal directed; she had no delusions, hallucinations, derealization, or thought disorder. She was oriented to time, place, and person, with intact attention, concentration, and memory on immediate testing, but she could not recall her name, home address, or life events preceding admission and confabulated when pressed. She lacked insight and appeared unconcerned. Physical and neurological examinations were normal. EEG, brain MRI, basic laboratory tests, and toxicology screen showed no abnormalities. The Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES) score was 50%. A DES score of ≥48% is indicative of dissociative identity disorder. Based on the history, mental-status examination, and high DES score, a diagnosis of dissociative identity disorder was made, and she was admitted for further management.
title: First Reported Case of Lorazepam-Assisted Interview in a Young Indian Female Presenting with Dissociative Identity Disorder and Improvement in Symptoms after the Interview

case_prompt: A 23-year-old man with no known medical history was found near the entrance of the emergency department, confused and sweating, with visible blood around him. On arrival, his vital signs were: heart rate 140 beats per minute, blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, respiratory rate 55 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and temperature 37.2 °C. A venous blood gas demonstrated severe lactic acidosis, which was confirmed on an arterial sample obtained five minutes later. He received 500 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride and was preoxygenated for intubation. A focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) showed no intrathoracic or intraabdominal fluid. His scalp laceration was closed with staples, and after sedation, a whole‐body CT scan revealed no acute injuries. One hour after admission, his respiratory rate began to improve. Repeat arterial blood gases at one and two hours showed a rapid decline in lactate levels, and by two hours he was asymptomatic.
title: Run or Die: A Didactique Case Report of a Rare Cause of Lactic Acidosis in Emergency Medicine

case_prompt:
A 26-year-old Asian American man with no significant medical or psychiatric history presented with three months of intermittent, sharp mid-back pain (5/10 intensity) radiating along the left T5 dermatome, partially relieved by NSAIDs. Examination, including a neurological evaluation, was normal; HIV, Lyme, and tuberculosis risk factors were absent. He was instructed to continue NSAIDs and undergo MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine without contrast.

During a 3T closed-scanner MRI at a tertiary center, he received ear plugs but, during the lumbar sequences, became acutely agitated. He reported feeling extremely hot, experienced tachypnea, tachycardia with palpitations, intense anxiety with a sense of impending doom, acute vertigo, and “areas of intense heat” over his body. He perceived the scanner as threatening serious injury, so the scan was aborted; he was unsteady and appeared frightened afterward. The cervical and thoracic images were normal; the lumbar study was incomplete and non-diagnostic.

Over the next two to four weeks, his back pain resolved. In the following three months, he developed difficulty sleeping, hypervigilance, recurrent “flashbacks” of the MRI experience with palpitations, tachypnea, dizziness, and anxiety, and he avoided further MRI scans, loud repetitive noises, and reminders of the scan. He also had trouble concentrating. He presented for evaluation three months after the MRI.
title: 3T MRI induced post-traumatic stress disorder: a case report

case_prompt:
A 6-year-old girl was evaluated for progressively worsening difficulty walking and left-sided foot drop of 1 month’s duration. She denied pain, paresthesia, sensory symptoms, headache, backache, or recent trauma. Her past history was significant for frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome treated with 5 mg of prednisolone and 60 mg of levamisole on alternate days; her last relapse was 6 months earlier.

On examination, she appeared of average build. Neurologic examination revealed:
• Wasting of the anterior compartment of the left leg.  
• Muscle strength (Medical Research Council scale): left ankle dorsiflexion 0/5, left ankle plantar flexion 3/5; proximal left lower-limb muscles 5/5; all right lower-limb and both upper-limb muscle groups 5/5.  
• Reflexes: left knee jerk diminished; left ankle jerk and left plantar response absent; all right-sided reflexes normal.  
• Sensation: loss in left L4 and L5 dermatomes.  
• Superficial abdominal reflexes: present on the right, absent on the left.  

Examination of other systems, including blood pressure, was normal.  

Basic laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level, were unremarkable; rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies were negative.  

Nerve conduction studies showed normal distal amplitude, latency, and conduction velocities in the common fibular nerve (left amplitude 3.3 mV; latency 2.8 ms; velocity 59 m/s; right amplitude 2.9 mV; latency 3.1 ms) and normal tibial nerve responses (left amplitude 20.8 mV; latency 4.2 ms); the sural nerve sensory response was normal.  

Electromyography of the left tibialis anterior revealed fibrillations and scanty motor unit potentials; electromyography of the left medial gastrocnemius and right tibialis anterior was normal.  

These findings prompted imaging of the spine.
title: Chiari malformation type 1 presenting as unilateral progressive foot drop: a case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old nulliparous woman presented to the emergency department with continuous dull lower abdominal pain. One week earlier she had a positive urine pregnancy test; her last menstrual period corresponded to 5 weeks 5 days of gestation. Her medical and surgical history were unremarkable, and she had not undergone any fertility treatments or had known risk factors for ectopic pregnancy.

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation revealed mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant without peritoneal signs. Pelvic examination elicited pain in the right adnexa; there was no vaginal bleeding.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits except for a serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin concentration of 5436 mIU/mL.

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple subserosal uterine fibroids (largest diameter 41 mm) and a single intrauterine gestational sac measuring 7.3 mm, with a fetal pole of 1.7 mm and visible cardiac activity. In the right fallopian tube, there was a 64 × 32 × 29 mm hypoechoic mass with minimal blood flow on Doppler. The pouch of Douglas was free of fluid, and both ovaries appeared normal.

Differential diagnosis included hydrosalpinx, hematosalpinx, ovarian torsion, and heterotopic pregnancy.
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
title: Vaginal Delivery at Term in a Woman with a Spontaneous Heterotopic Pregnancy Treated with Laparoscopic Salpingectomy

case_prompt:
A 76-year-old man presented with abdominal pain and constipation. His history included osteoporosis, Parkinsonism, prior L2–L3 arthrodesis for spondylodiscitis, chronic lumbar pain, and bent spine syndrome. Home medications were pantoprazole, aspirin (CardioASA), bromazepam, transdermal fentanyl, and bisoprolol.

On examination he was oriented, malnourished with muscle atrophy and hypotonia. Vital signs: HR 68 bpm, BP 120/70 mmHg, T 36°C. Abdominal exam showed diffuse tenderness without peritoneal signs.

Labs: Hb 11.2 g/dL; WBC 10.8×10^3/µL; total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL; AST 40 U/L; ALT 28 U/L; ALP 115 U/L; amylase 406 U/L; CRP 150 mg/L.

Abdominal ultrasound for suspected chronic pancreatitis showed multiple pancreatic calcifications and an irregular aortic caliber. CT angiography revealed dissection of the right common iliac artery with an ulcerated plaque, dilation of the gallbladder and extrahepatic biliary tract, and small (≤3 mm) hypodense lesions in the pancreatic head. Fondaparinux was started.

Ten days later he developed sudden anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and worsening cholestasis; the abdomen was now painless and there was no gastrointestinal bleeding. Bedside ultrasound showed a distended gallbladder with non-homogeneous hyperechoic material and mild intrahepatic biliary dilation; the common bile duct was obscured. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a markedly distended gallbladder filled with hyperdense, non-homogeneous content, regular wall thickness, and a focal area of suspected active bleeding along the anterior wall, with increased dilation of the intra- and extrahepatic ducts.
title: Gallbladder hemorrhage–An uncommon surgical emergency: A case report

case_prompt: A 44-year-old woman presented to the emergency department after multiple syncopal episodes, dyspnea, and progressive non-radiating right flank and epigastric pain. She reported a 3-week history of non-bloody emesis and chronic irregular menstrual bleeding. Her medical history was notable for obesity, hypothyroidism, and anemia treated with prior blood transfusions; she had undergone a cholecystectomy and one Caesarean section. On examination, she was hypotensive and dyspneic. The abdomen was soft, diffusely tender, and distended, with a large, ill-defined, firm, fixed mass palpable. Laboratory testing revealed a hemoglobin level of 4.9 g/dL, and she received three units of packed red blood cells. Due to ongoing hemodynamic instability and concern for intra-abdominal hemorrhage or gastrointestinal perforation, a non-contrast abdominal and pelvic CT scan was obtained, demonstrating a large hyperdense pelvic mass extending into the abdomen, diffuse hemoperitoneum, and possible capsular splenic rupture.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Ruptured granulosa cell tumor of the ovary presenting with catastrophic intra-abdominal hemorrhage: A case report

case_prompt:
An 11‐year‐old Mexican girl presented with a six-month history of an asymptomatic, generalized skin eruption involving the face, trunk, and extremities. The lesions began as tense blisters on the face that resolved spontaneously, leaving erythema and scaling. Topical corticosteroids and systemic antibiotics produced no improvement. Over time, the eruption progressed to involve her entire skin surface and was associated with general malaise, chills, and edema of the lower extremities. 

On examination, she had scaling erythroderma with yellow-greenish crusts covering her entire body and a single tense blister on the dorsal aspect of her right foot. A skin biopsy specimen showed a subcorneal bulla with upper epidermal acantholysis. Direct immunofluorescence was positive for C3 and IgG deposits in the stratum spinosum with a beehive pattern. A skin culture grew Staphylococcus aureus.
title: Pemphigus Foliaceus in an 11-Year-Old Mexican Girl with Response to Oral Dapsone

case_prompt:
A 69‐year‐old obese woman with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented with midsternal chest pain radiating to her right arm and right jaw, accompanied by dyspnea. Physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, TSH, and coagulation studies, were within normal limits except for elevated cardiac enzymes: CK 248 IU/L, CK‐MB 32.6 ng/mL, and troponin I 1.18 ng/mL (normal <0.04). She was diagnosed with a non–ST‐segment elevation myocardial infarction and treated with dual antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, a beta blocker, an ACE inhibitor, and a statin. Overnight, her chest pain resolved and cardiac enzymes down‐trended.

The next morning, left heart catheterization demonstrated no angiographic evidence of disease in the epicardial coronary arteries, but revealed mid‐cavitary akinesis with apical and basal hyperkinesis and an ejection fraction of 37%, along with a mildly elevated left ventricular end‐diastolic pressure. The patient reported significant emotional stress that peaked 48 hours before presentation. Her antiplatelet agents, anticoagulation, and statin were discontinued, and she remained on the beta blocker and ACE inhibitor. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed later the same day showed severe mid‐cavitary hypokinesis, an ejection fraction of 35–40%, and mild mitral regurgitation. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging the following day confirmed mid‐ventricular hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 38% and demonstrated no delayed gadolinium enhancement in the epicardium, myocardium, or endocardium.
title: A Rare Case Report of Mid Cavitary Takotsubo: The Role of Magnetic Resonance Imaging

case_prompt: A 46-year-old dairy farm worker was referred for evaluation of multiple painless soft-tissue masses of the left wrist that had been present for 1 year. He had no past medical history, denied trauma, injury, or any prior infection or inflammatory episodes of the hand, and had no constitutional symptoms of fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Examination revealed large, mobile masses on the dorsal and volar aspects of the left wrist with minimal tenderness, no overlying warmth or erythema, and a normal range of motion of the wrist and fingers. Tinel’s sign was negative, and sensory and motor examination of the left upper extremity was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, a negative C-reactive protein level, a normal white blood cell count, and an unremarkable rheumatologic panel. Soft-tissue ultrasonography of the left axilla demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes measuring up to 27 × 14 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left wrist revealed multiple hyperintense masses within the flexor and extensor tendon sheaths, each containing innumerable small, round hypo-intense bodies on T2-weighted sequences.
title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis‐induced multiple tenosynovial masses with rice bodies: A case report

case_prompt:
A 20-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a progressively enlarging, painful swelling of her left shoulder over the past 2 years. On examination, there was an 8-cm mass on the anterior aspect of the left shoulder without overlying erythema or warmth; the mass was tender, adherent to deep tissues, and mobile relative to the skin. Active shoulder movement was impossible; passive extension of the arm was limited to 90°. There was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the left shoulder revealed marked deformity of the scapula by a mixed lytic and sclerotic process involving the entire bone, with preservation of the humeral head and clavicle. Contrast-enhanced CT of the scapula demonstrated an expansile osteolytic lesion with thin sclerotic margins and internal bony septa delineating multiple cavities, each containing fluid–fluid levels, and cortical breaches without soft-tissue extension; the lesion measured 116 × 56 mm. MRI confirmed a multiloculated mass involving the coracoid process, glenoid cavity, neck, body, and spine of the scapula, with a surrounding rim of low T1 and T2 signal, internal fluid–fluid levels, and septal and peripheral enhancement after gadolinium administration.
title: Giant aneurysmal bone cyst of the scapula: A case report

case_prompt:
A 78-year-old man from Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, with hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and benign prostatic enlargement was admitted on April 10, 2021, with a 3-day history of fever and productive cough. A nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2. Initial laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 13.6×10^9/L (90% neutrophils, 8% lymphocytes), C-reactive protein 39.0 mg/L, D-dimer 1.02 µg/mL, and ferritin 301.5 ng/mL. Chest CT revealed bilateral basal ground-glass opacities, and he required supplemental oxygen. He was treated with IV dexamethasone 6 mg/day, remdesivir for 5 days, and oral baricitinib for 10 days. His oxygen requirement decreased, and he was discharged after 16 days on a 10-day dexamethasone taper.

Fourteen days after discharge, on April 30, 2021, he returned with high-grade fever and anorexia beginning after completion of the dexamethasone taper. Laboratory results showed a white-blood-cell count of 11.2×10^9/L (70% neutrophils, 8% lymphocytes, 2% eosinophils), C-reactive protein 126 mg/L, ferritin 637.4 ng/mL, and D-dimer 1.22 µg/mL. His oxygen saturation fluctuated on room air, and a repeat SARS-CoV-2 swab was positive. He was treated for presumed COVID-19 reinfection with oral prednisolone for 2 weeks and was discharged after 7 days.

Twenty days later, on May 28, 2021, he developed loose stools, generalized itching, and low-grade fever for 3–4 days and was admitted to another hospital. He was then transferred on June 2, 2021, to the original hospital. This time he did not require oxygen. Laboratory tests on admission revealed a white-blood-cell count of 26.5×10^9/L with 49% eosinophils. Differential diagnoses included Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome and Ankylostomiasis. Stool routine microscopic examination was advised.
title: Strongyloides Hyperinfection Syndrome Following Immunosuppressant Therapy for COVID‐19: A Case Report With Literature Review

case_prompt: A 12-year-old boy with HIV infection presented with widespread papules and fungating, ulcerating nodules on the skin. HIV had been diagnosed 7 months earlier, at which time antiretroviral therapy (ART) was initiated; his baseline CD4 count was 76 cells/µL (5%). One month after starting ART, the patient noted a rash that progressively worsened over the ensuing 6 months. He was referred to the Baylor Tanzania Center of Excellence in Mbeya, Tanzania, because of concern for Kaposi sarcoma. On evaluation, chest radiography and abdominal ultrasonography were normal. Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. A complete blood count showed severe anemia, with a hemoglobin level of 4.0 g/dL, requiring blood transfusion. A skin biopsy was performed.
title: Successful treatment of bacillary angiomatosis with oral doxycycline in an HIV-infected child with skin lesions mimicking Kaposi sarcoma

case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman presented with a 5–6-month history of persistent headache and new-onset slight diplopia. The headache was initially NSAID-responsive but progressively worsened. On neurologic examination, she had peripheral right facial-nerve and right abducent-nerve palsies. Vital signs and routine blood tests were normal.

Noncontrast CT of the brain with 2D multiplanar reconstructions and 3D volume rendering revealed a large expansile lesion in the right posterior cranial fossa extending through the foramen magnum into the middle cranial fossa. The mass displaced the right temporal lobe upward and laterally and shifted the brainstem to the left; the cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle were compressed, resulting in hydrocephalus. Bone windows demonstrated erosion of the right petrous apex and greater wing of the sphenoid with widening of the right inferior orbital foramen. Attenuation measurements showed a cranial portion of the lesion at −5 to −10 HU and a caudal portion at −50 to −60 HU, suggestive of a fatty component. Numerous additional markedly hypodense foci (−150 to −180 HU) were scattered throughout the supratentorial cisternal and cortical spaces.

MRI, including T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, T1-fat-suppression, postcontrast T1, and 3D-TOF angiographic sequences, showed the caudal portion of the mass to be homogeneously hyperintense on T1 and T2. The cranial portion exhibited heterogeneous hyper- and hypointense signals with internal dark areas consistent with hemosiderin. There was no contrast enhancement of the mass or the extra-axial foci. 3D-TOF angiography revealed displacement and stretching of the basilar artery, the right posterior cerebral artery, and the right posterior communicating artery.
title: CT and MR Studies of Giant Dermoid Cyst Associated to Fat Dissemination at the Cortical and Cisternal Cerebral Spaces

case_prompt:
A 21-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 2-month history of recurrent, dull upper abdominal pain lasting 1–2 days approximately twice weekly, often accompanied by fever and, on a few occasions, nausea and vomiting. The symptoms began after a 1-week episode of gastroenteritis on return from a backpacking holiday in Southeast Asia; she had no further diarrhea and no weight loss. She denied urinary or bowel changes and had no known aggravating or relieving factors.

On examination, she had localized tenderness in the right lower quadrant without palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 7.9×10^9/L (normal 3.5–8.8×10^9/L), C-reactive protein 37 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L), normal hemoglobin and liver enzymes, negative urine pregnancy test, and fecal calprotectin <30×10^−6 (normal <50×10^−6). Extensive microbiological investigations—including malaria testing (×3), blood cultures, stool cultures and PCR for bacteria, viruses, and parasites, and serologies for HIV, hepatitis A–C, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein–Barr virus—were all negative.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 10 mm thickened, hypoechoic, hyperemic appendix with moderate periappendicular edema and no abscess or perforation.
title: Chronic appendicitis: two case reports

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-day history of acute onset, progressively worsening sharp epigastric and left-sided “gripping” chest pain of severe intensity. The pain was pleuritic in nature, worsened by deep breaths, had no radiation, and was not relieved by positioning. She denied trauma, recent travel, or similar symptoms in family members. Her medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism; medications were aspirin, amlodipine, lovastatin, and levothyroxine.

On examination, she appeared uncomfortable, clutching her left chest and epigastrium. Blood pressure was normal; heart rate was 105 beats per minute; temperature 99.9°F; and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. The pain was not reproducible with palpation, and there was no rash. Lung examination revealed a left-sided pleural rub; the right lung and the remainder of the examination were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 9.4 × 10^3/µL with 54% neutrophils, normal hemoglobin and hematocrit, creatinine 0.75 mg/dL, and normal liver-function tests. Cardiac biomarkers were unremarkable: troponin T was <0.030 ng/mL on three measurements 6 hours apart, creatine kinase 122 U/L, and CK-MB 3.7 ng/mL. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ST-T wave changes. Chest radiograph demonstrated small bilateral pleural effusions without airspace disease. 

Because of persistent pleuritic pain and sinus tachycardia, a CT scan of the chest was performed; it was negative for pulmonary embolism, pulmonary infarction, aortic abnormality, or gastroesophageal pathology, and revealed no muscular edema. Inflammatory markers were elevated: erythrocyte sedimentation rate 65 mm/hr and C-reactive protein 17.2 mg/L. Complement levels (C3 161 mg/dL, C4 16 mg/dL) were normal. Testing for vasculitis and connective-tissue disease showed negative C-ANCA, p-ANCA, and antinuclear antibodies.
title: Unusual cause of chest pain, Bornholm disease, a forgotten entity; case report and review of literature

case_prompt:
A 65-year-old overweight man with a 20–year history of heavy smoking and known right pulmonary tumor with adrenal metastases presented in December 2019 with dyspnea (SpO2 77%), fatigue, and productive cough. Chest CT showed minimal right pleural effusion, a right pulmonary mass, mediastinal and retrocrural lymphadenopathy, and bilateral adrenal masses. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis, an inflammatory syndrome, severe azotic retention, low creatinine clearance, and an eGFR consistent with chronic renal failure. He was treated with antibiotics, diuretics, systemic corticosteroids, and expectorants, with transient improvement, but then rapidly deteriorated and died. 

At autopsy, there was a 4 × 3 cm poorly defined lesion in the middle lobe of the right lung and multiple bilateral necrotic pulmonary nodules (0.5–1.5 cm). The stomach harbored a 1 cm ulcerative-infiltrative lesion. Both kidneys and adrenal glands had multiple poorly defined lesions. 

Histopathology (H&E) showed:
• Lung lesions: malignant polygonal epithelial proliferation with pleomorphic nuclei, frequent atypical mitoses, clear nucleoli, moderately eosinophilic cytoplasm, solid growth pattern with focal papillary features, lymphovascular invasion, and necrosis.
• Renal and adrenal lesions: malignant epithelial proliferation with cytological and architectural features identical to the lung (alveolar growth, necrosis, lymphovascular tumor emboli).
• Gastric lesion: malignant epithelial proliferation of the mucosa with glandular differentiation extending into the muscular layer, with lymphovascular invasion, consistent with moderately differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma.

What is the most likely explanation for the multiple tumors in this patient?
title: Concurrent Tumors Revealed by an Autopsy-A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt: A 53-year-old Tai Dam farmer from northern Laos presented in August with 2 days of fever, chills, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, and productive cough. On admission he was alert, oriented, febrile (39.7°C), normotensive, with crepitations at the left lung base, no rash, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly. He was started on oral amoxicillin and paracetamol; when fever rose to 40.2°C, IV metamizole was added. Day 2 labs showed normochromic anemia (Hct 18%, Hb 6 g/dL), leukocytes 7.5×10^9/L (70% neutrophils), negative malaria smear and HRP-2 rapid test. Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatomegaly without focal lesions and mild splenomegaly. Chest radiograph showed slight cardiomegaly without infiltrates. He developed abdominal and back pain, dyspnea, pallor, jaundice, hypotension (90/60 mmHg), irregular tachycardia (120/min), tachypnea (42/min), bibasal crepitations, tender hepatomegaly, and axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Therapy was changed to IV ceftriaxone and he received a blood transfusion. Despite this, he progressed to central cyanosis, cold extremities, coma (GCS 7), diffuse maculopapular rash with petechiae, prolonged bleeding at IV sites, and on day 3 became apneic and died.
journal: Annals of Clinical Microbiology and Antimicrobials
title: Fatal Chromobacterium violaceum septicaemia in northern Laos, a modified oxidase test and post-mortem forensic family G6PD analysis

case_prompt:
A 7-year-old girl presented with 8 months of mild, non–activity-related pain and progressive swelling in the left distal third of the forearm. There was no history of trauma, fever, or weight loss. On examination, a 5 × 2 cm fusiform swelling over the diaphysis of the radius was firm, tender, and continuous with the bone; the overlying skin was normal, and there was no neurovascular deficit. Pronation and supination of the forearm were painfully restricted; finger movements were intact.  
Preoperative radiographs showed a well-defined, lytic, expansile lesion measuring approximately 4 × 2 cm in the diaphyseal region of the radius, with cortical thinning but no breach. MRI confirmed a sharply marginated intramedullary lesion without soft-tissue extension.
title: Chondroblastoma of Diaphysis of Radius in a Seven Year Old Child

case_prompt: A 62-year-old Caucasian man presented with sudden onset of severe burning pain in the left hemithorax, accompanied by several weeks of night sweats and weakness. He feared a heart attack owing to his father’s history of coronary disease. One year earlier he had consulted for similar upper-abdominal pressure but underwent no further workup. His only medication was escitalopram; he had no known history of pancreatic disease or trauma. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs; breath sounds were decreased on the left side, and there was no tenderness on abdominal palpation. An electrocardiogram was normal, and cardiac enzymes were within reference limits. Intravenous analgesia provided significant relief. Laboratory testing showed leukocytes 13.9 G/L (4.4–11.3 G/L), C-reactive protein 2.9 mg/dL (< 0.5 mg/dL), amylase 157 U/L (13–53 U/L), and lipase 232 U/L (13–60 U/L); renal and liver tests were normal. A chest radiograph revealed extensive left-sided pulmonary infiltrates and pleural effusion. Bedside ultrasound confirmed a left pleural effusion of approximately 400 mL and no free abdominal fluid. The provisional diagnosis was left-sided pneumonia with effusion, and intravenous penicillin was started. Two days later, diagnostic thoracentesis yielded a hemorrhagic pleural effusion with lipase 3000 U/L and amylase 4800 U/L.
title: Minimally invasive treatment of an internal pancreaticopleural fistula with massive pleural effusion: a case report

case_prompt: A 66-year-old Japanese woman with a 2-year history of SAPHO syndrome (diagnosed on the basis of palmoplantar pustulosis and multiple spondylitis on spine MRI and bone scintigraphy) presented with a 4-month history of bilateral blurred vision. She had previously developed exudative pleural effusions of unknown origin; cytology and CT/MRI imaging had excluded malignancy. On ophthalmic examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 0.6 in both eyes, and intraocular pressures were normal. Slit-lamp examination showed shallow anterior chambers without keratic precipitates or cells. Fundus examination revealed bilateral annular choroidal detachment with exudative serous retinal detachment involving the macula. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated subretinal fluid with a wavy retinal pigment epithelium line and increased choroidal thickness in both eyes. Fluorescein angiography showed multiple areas of pinpoint dye leakage from the retinal pigment epithelium. Indocyanine green angiography revealed multiple areas of choroidal hypoperfusion bilaterally. B-scan ultrasonography confirmed choroidal detachment without scleral thickening or intraocular masses.
title: Unusual Case of Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Disease Associated with SAPHO Syndrome: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 61-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain. She had mild epigastric tenderness on examination and a 32–pack-year smoking history but no history of tuberous sclerosis, malignancy, alcohol use, or diabetes. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, hematocrit 23.2 %, white cells 4600/mm3, platelets 232 000/mm3; normal CEA, CA 19-9, AFP, elastase 1, SPAN-1, and DUPAN-2; gastrin 370 pg/mL (normal < 200), somatostatin 23 pg/mL (normal 1–12), and normal glucagon, VIP, serotonin, and insulin levels. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 56 mm hypo- to iso-echoic, gourd-shaped mass in the pancreatic head and body with slight upstream duct dilation. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-circumscribed, low-density 7 cm mass in the pancreatic body with mild upstream duct dilation but no invasion or lymphadenopathy. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing round mass on T1- and T2-weighted images. Endoscopic retrograde pancreatography showed downward deviation of the main pancreatic duct from extrinsic compression without evidence of invasion. Neuroendocrine neoplasm, acinar cell carcinoma, ductal adenocarcinoma variants such as clear cell carcinoma, and solid-pseudopapillary neoplasm were suggested before operation.
title: Perivascular epithelial cell tumor (PEComa) of the pancreas: a case report and review of previous literatures

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 2-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of cold, cough, and runny nose. One day before presentation he developed a fever of 39.5 °C responsive to antipyretics. On the day of arrival, he had four episodes of vomiting and two episodes of loose stools and was treated elsewhere for presumed viral gastroenteritis with antiemetics and IV fluids. He was discharged but vomited again and became very drowsy en route, prompting admission to our emergency department. 

His parents denied neck pain, stiffness, rash, or photophobia. He had fluctuating levels of consciousness and fever en route. Notably, he had received no immunizations after age 4 months. There was no travel or sick contacts. 

On examination his Glasgow Coma Scale fluctuated between 10 and 11. Temperature was 38 °C, pulse 137 beats/min, blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, and capillary refill time 4 seconds. Pupils were 3 mm with slow reaction to light and accommodation. There was no neck stiffness or meningeal signs. Tonsils were mildly enlarged and erythematous. 

Laboratory results on admission showed: WBC 2.73 ×10^9/L (low), neutrophils 80.2% (high), C-reactive protein 72.9 mg/L (high), procalcitonin 95.7 ng/mL (very high), prothrombin time 19.4 s (high), partial thromboplastin time 41.2 s (high), INR 1.65 (high), lactate 3.0 mmol/L (high). 

A noncontrast head CT performed after initial resuscitation showed mild diffuse cerebral edema without evidence of raised intracranial pressure.
title: Beta-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis in partially immunized immunocompetent child: a case report

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old boy presented with a 5-day history of abdominal pain and 2 days of progressive abdominal distention. He was hemodynamically stable, with a heart rate of 116 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, and no fever. He had scleral icterus, yellowish urine, and poor appetite. There was no history of diarrhea, constipation, cough, or significant past medical or surgical history.

On examination, chest percussion was dull with decreased breath sounds basally. The liver was soft and palpable 3 cm below the costal margin; the spleen was not palpable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, hematocrit 29.0%, white blood cell count 9.3×10^9 cells/L, platelet count 221×10^9 cells/L, total protein 6.6 g/dL, albumin 3.13 g/dL, prothrombin time 17.2 s, total bilirubin 6.54 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.35 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 741.5 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 805.7 U/L. Serologies for hepatitis B and C were negative.

Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions, larger on the left. Thoracic ultrasound confirmed mild bilateral pleural effusion. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatomegaly, gallbladder wall thickening of 7 mm without calculi, and moderate free fluid in the abdomen.
title: Hepatitis A virus infection associated with bilateral pleural effusion, ascites, and acalculous cholecystitis in childhood: a case report

case_prompt:
A 17-year-old male with a history of asthma presented with 24 hours of progressive shortness of breath and chest tightness at rest that did not respond to bronchodilators. He denied recent illness; he had a dental cleaning 3 days earlier and no family history of cardiac disease or coagulopathy. On presentation, he was well appearing. Vital signs were blood pressure 107/56 mm Hg, heart rate 97 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 99.4 °F, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. Lungs were clear without wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles. There was no jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, or edema. Extremities were well perfused with symmetric pulses.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete metabolic panel and blood count. A urine toxicology screen for nine substances, including cocaine and amphetamines, was negative. Electrocardiography revealed ST-segment elevations in leads I and aVL and T-wave inversions in the inferior and lateral leads. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated regional wall motion abnormalities of the inferior left ventricular segments with preserved global systolic function. Two hours after presentation, his oxygen saturation fell to 91% on room air; he was placed on 4 L nasal cannula with improvement to 96%. Chest radiography showed scattered bilateral hazy opacities. A computed tomographic angiogram of the chest excluded pulmonary embolism but demonstrated multifocal ground-glass opacities in both lungs. 

He was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit for further evaluation. The working differential diagnosis included COVID-19–related myocarditis, non–COVID-19 myocarditis, and multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children.
title: Challenges of Diagnosing Viral Myocarditis in Adolescents in the Era of COVID-19 and MIS-C

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old Han man presented with a several-month history of a gradually enlarging mass on the left side of his tracheal stoma and progressive dyspnea. His history was notable for squamous cell carcinoma of the glottis treated with partial laryngectomy in September 2011, followed by recurrence in 2016 managed with total laryngectomy, cervical lymph node dissection, and 60 Gy of radiotherapy over 1½ months. He had healed uneventfully until April 2018, when the parastomal mass was first noted.

On examination in October 2018, there was an immobile, well-defined, partially compressible, non-pulsatile 4 cm × 4 cm mass at the left lateral margin of the tracheal stoma, causing tracheostomal stenosis. No other cervical lymphadenopathy was present. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 5 cm × 4 cm, well-circumscribed, non-enhancing, cystic–solid mass adjacent to the left side of the stoma. Fine-needle aspiration yielded about 10 mL of yellowish-white fluid with a triglyceride level of 26.5 mmol/L, protein 58.0 g/L, glucose 8.5 mmol/L, and a white-cell count of 1.0 × 10^9/L (96% lymphocytes), consistent with chyle. The mass shrank after aspiration but refilled by the next day, and a second aspiration yielded similar fluid. Neck ultrasonography revealed a 43 mm × 36 mm mixed-echoic mass between the left thyroid lobe and the great vessels. Other preoperative studies were unremarkable.
title: Invasion of the thoracic duct by postlaryngectomy stomal recurrence: a case report

case_prompt:
An 8-year-old spayed female Labrador retriever weighing 32.3 kg was evaluated for a 3-month history of progressive snoring, wheezing, and nasal obstruction. The owner reported that the dog frequently pawed at her nose, rubbed it on the ground, and exhibited sleep apnea with gasping episodes. Appetite and activity were normal, but the dog appeared more comfortable panting and had difficulty eating due to inability to breathe through the nose.

On presentation, the dog was bright and alert. Airflow through both nares was absent, and there was mucopurulent discharge from the right naris. Facial symmetry was intact, with no pain on palpation. Ocular examination, thoracic auscultation, and the remainder of the physical examination were unremarkable except for pronounced inspiratory snoring. Complete blood count, chemistry, and coagulation panels were within reference limits aside from mild elevation of alkaline phosphatase (257 IU/L; reference range 20–150 IU/L). Thoracic and cervical radiographs were normal.

A sedated oral examination revealed a functionally normal larynx, ruling out laryngeal paralysis. Skull computed tomography showed a soft-tissue/fluid-attenuated structure in the nasopharynx at the junction of the soft and hard palate, occluding most of the nasopharyngeal lumen, more prominently on the right side, with no turbinate destruction or bony lysis. Retrograde rhinoscopy revealed a red-yellow, tubular mass arising from the caudal nasopharynx and extending rostrally, with adjacent mucosa and turbinates appearing healthy.

Biopsies of the mass demonstrated chronic, severe lymphoplasmacytic nasopharyngitis. Nasal mucosa biopsies showed subacute to chronic edematous and lymphoplasmacytic rhinitis with purulent ulcerative changes. Regional lymph node aspirates revealed moderate eosinophilic and mild neutrophilic inflammation. The lack of turbinate destruction and benign histopathologic features made a malignant neoplasm less likely.

A ventral rhinotomy was performed, and a 4 cm × 2 cm red-yellow mass attached by a stalk to the nasal mucosa was removed en bloc. Grossly, the polypoid mass had a fibrovascular core covered by stratified squamous epithelium, which was ulcerated in several areas. Histopathology showed that the core contained numerous blood-filled sinusoidal structures, some with thrombi, and a moderate infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and scattered neutrophils.
title: Nasopharyngeal Vascular Hamartoma in a Dog

case_prompt:
A 68-year-old, left-hand-dominant man presented with a 3-year history of tingling in his left thumb, mainly at night, and difficulty with daily activities due to numbness. He reported being an avid bowler in the past and noted a weakened bowling grip since symptom onset. Two months before presentation, he noticed a tender, palpable mass on the flexor surface of the left thumb. He denied any hand trauma or prior nerve‐compression diagnoses. His medical history included gastroesophageal reflux disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and mild arthritis; he denied diabetes or hypothyroidism.

On examination, there was a positive Tinel’s sign over the thumb mass and at both carpal tunnels, and a positive carpal compression test on the left. Cervical range of motion was decreased, but Spurling’s maneuver was negative. Static two-point discrimination was at least 5 mm at all digits except greater than 15 mm at the ulnar digital nerve of the left thumb. Motor and vascular examinations were normal.

Electrodiagnostic testing was performed and showed no evidence of compressive neuropathy or cervical radiculopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left hand demonstrated no definite abnormal signal or lesion corresponding to the palpable thumb mass.
title: Bowler's Thumb: Case Report and Review of the Literature

case_prompt: A 63-year-old Caucasian man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and hypertension was referred for evaluation of a recurrent mass in the left inguinal region. He had undergone two prior surgical resections of left groin masses with clear margins and no postoperative adjuvant therapy. On examination, there was an oval 9 × 11 cm lobulated, firm, fixed, and nontender mass in the left inguinal area without overlying skin changes. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, renal, bone, hepatic, and coagulation profiles, as well as tumor markers (CEA, AFP, and CA 12–5)—were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed a large multilobulated heterogeneous mass in the left groin compressing and inseparable from the left common femoral vein and ventral adductor muscles; associated findings included local lymphadenopathy, multiple small subcutaneous nodules, and an enlarged left external iliac lymph node measuring 1 × 1.5 cm. PET imaging demonstrated a hypermetabolic, heterogeneous, lobulated lesion in the left groin measuring approximately 9.6 × 9 cm, with a few adjacent FDG-avid nodal lesions suggestive of regional metastatic involvement.
title: Merkel Cell Carcinoma of Left Groin: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_prompt:
A 70-year-old woman with coronary artery disease and a remote history of morbid obesity (preoperative BMI 52 kg/m2) presented with one month of persistent postprandial nausea, regurgitation, and mild dysphagia to solids and liquids. She had undergone laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass two years earlier, complicated by a gastro-gastric fistula and gastro-jejunal ulcer that required revision two months before presentation. She denied weight change, abdominal pain, or altered bowel habits.

On examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds; her recent surgical wound was healing well. Laboratory tests, including liver enzymes and stool studies for Clostridium difficile toxin, ova, and parasites, were unremarkable. A contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed enteric contrast within a dilated distal esophagus and was “suspicious for a mild stricture at gastroesophageal sphincter (GES),” with no peri-gastric inflammation. She was admitted for further evaluation.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy the next day revealed large amounts of thick esophageal secretions. “The esophagus was tortuous, dilated and had a ‘sigmoid esophagus’ appearance, but no strictures, stenosis or evidence of malignancy were noted.” A barium swallow study demonstrated “persistent narrowing of the gastroesophageal junction with a moderately dilated, debris-filled esophagus proximally and some tertiary esophageal contractions. These findings were suggestive of achalasia.”
title: Achalasia after bariatric Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery reversal

case_prompt: A 34‐year‐old HIV‐positive Caucasian man presented with recurrent episodes of fever, myalgia, and macroscopic hematuria, each lasting 1–3 days and resolving spontaneously, with normal urinalysis and serum creatinine between episodes. HIV infection had been diagnosed 12 years earlier; combination antiretroviral therapy had been initiated 5 years prior, and the plasma viral load had remained undetectable since. Over the preceding year, febrile hematuric episodes increased to once every 1–2 months. On assessment, the serum creatinine was 160 μmol/L (eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m2), up from 94 μmol/L (eGFR 90 mL/min/1.73 m2) one year earlier. Urinalysis during an episode showed proteinuria (urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio, 80 mg/mmol) and glomerular hematuria (>1000 × 10^6/L erythrocytes). Testing for co-existent infections (hepatitis B and C, syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, Brucella, Rickettsia, Q fever, strongyloides, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, parvovirus, and malaria) was negative, and screening for familial Mediterranean fever and porphyria was negative. Serology indicated past exposure to EBV and CMV without active infection. A renal biopsy demonstrated 36 glomeruli without global sclerosis; 10 glomeruli had mild segmental mesangial hypercellularity, with no endocapillary proliferation, crescents, or necrosis. Immunoperoxidase staining showed granular capillary basement membrane positivity for IgA, IgG, IgM, C3, and C1q, with weak focal mesangial staining for IgA, IgG, and C1q. Concurrent serological testing was negative for antinuclear antibodies, anti-Smith, and anti–double-stranded DNA; C3 and C4 levels were normal, and rheumatoid factor was undetectable.
