title: Successful treatment of HIV‐associated lupus‐like glomerulonephritis with mycophenolic acid

case_prompt: A 34-year-old woman with no significant medical history reported 3 months of dull, postprandial epigastric pain without systemic symptoms. Examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests including complete blood count, biochemistry, CEA (0.9 ng/ml), and CA 19-9 (2 U/ml) were normal. Upper endoscopy showed extrinsic compression near the lesser curvature. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 5 × 5 × 3 cm retroperitoneal mass thought to arise from the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 48 × 50 mm solid, homogeneous, hypervascular, well-circumscribed mass posterior to the pancreatic body, abutting celiac branches without invasion or additional lymphadenopathy. MRI confirmed a 5 × 5 × 4 cm lesion in the lesser sac, hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, with heterogeneous enhancement. A provisional diagnosis of retroperitoneal gastrointestinal stromal tumor or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor was made.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Retroperitoneal unicentric Castleman’s disease: A case report

case_prompt: A 35-year-old woman with no systemic illness presented with pain in her left eye. Her ocular history included retinal surgery and secondary intraocular-lens implantation after blunt trauma at age 5, followed by trabeculectomy at age 20 for glaucoma. She was on brimonidine 0.15%, dorzolamide 2%, and timolol 0.5% twice daily. On presentation, visual acuity in the left eye was hand motion, and intraocular pressure was 38 mmHg, which fell to 10 mmHg after stat topical therapy. Slit-lamp examination showed a flat bleb, decompensated cornea with edema, a mid-dilated pupil, a mildly dislocated IOL, and advanced optic-nerve cupping. Two weeks later, with intraocular pressure of 40 mmHg despite maximal medical therapy, she underwent micro-pulse cyclophotocoagulation under local anesthesia. The postoperative course was unremarkable, and intraocular pressure remained controlled. One year after the procedure, she reported pain and could not fully close her left eyelids because of a protruding white mass on the cornea that had been enlarging. Visual acuity was light perception only; intraocular pressure was estimated at 30–40 mmHg. Examination revealed a large, pedunculated, whitish corneal mass. Ultrasound biomicroscopy showed a cystic mass overlying the cornea, localized to the anterior space without invasion. Anterior-segment OCT revealed a hyperreflective lesion within the subepithelial space with cystic components.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Corneal myxoma following micro-pulse cyclophotocoagulation in a young female: A case report

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old man from Dhaka presented with an 18-day history of high-grade fever (maximum 104 °F) accompanied by chills, generalized body aches, and a maculopapular rash predominantly on the trunk. From day 8, he experienced persistent vomiting and diarrhea. On day 10, he developed headache, and by day 14 his wife noted incoherent speech; on day 15 he reported blurring of vision. He had no clear history of prior antibiotic use.

On examination, he was disoriented (GCS 14/15), mildly icteric, mildly dehydrated, and tachycardic (pulse 110/min) with a temperature of 99.7 °F. He had bilateral conjunctival congestion, a coated tongue, and a non-tender but palpable spleen; neurological examination revealed bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsies without neck stiffness. A provisional diagnosis of enteric fever was made, with dengue, leptospirosis, and malaria as initial differentials.

A noncontrast CT of the brain was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed hepatosplenomegaly (liver 16.2 cm, spleen 15.9 cm). Laboratory studies revealed elevated transaminases and bilirubin, proteinuria, and mild hematuria. Blood cultures grew Salmonella Typhi, and a Widal test showed a Salmonella Typhi H titer of 1:640. Dengue and Leptospira serologies were negative.

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated clear fluid with glucose 37.8 mg/dL, protein 173 mg/dL, total WBC count 79 cells/µL (75% mononuclear), RBC 0–2 cells/µL, adenosine deaminase 4 U/L; CSF culture yielded no growth, MTB PCR was negative, and a multiplex meningitis panel detected no organisms. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI was unremarkable. An ophthalmologic examination revealed bilateral optic neuritis.
title: A case of typhoid fever with neurological presentation

case_prompt:
A 31-year-old woman was referred for persistent dyspnea on exertion (NYHA class II) and presumed chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Four years earlier, she had acute chest pain and dyspnea; a second similar episode occurred three months ago and was attributed to pulmonary embolism. She had a history of hookworm infection; she used oral contraceptives and smoked.

On examination, she had digital clubbing, a prominent pulmonary component of the second heart sound, and a left parasternal systolic ejection murmur; blood pressure was 99/60 mmHg bilaterally, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests showed no inflammation; ECG was normal.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a thickened mitral valve, moderate tricuspid regurgitation with an estimated systolic pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg, and a markedly dilated, mildly hypocontractile right ventricle. Right-heart catheterization showed a mean pulmonary arterial pressure of 28 mmHg, a cardiac index of 2.91 L/min/m2, and a pulmonary vascular resistance of 450 dyn·s·cm−5. Six-minute walk distance was 553 m (69% predicted) with oxygen saturation falling from 96% to 90%. Lung volumes were normal but diffusion capacity was reduced to 46% of predicted.

Chest radiograph revealed enlarged pulmonary arteries and a right parahilar nodule. A ventilation–perfusion scan showed multiple lobar and segmental perfusion defects. Pulmonary angiography demonstrated cutoffs of the right lower lobe and left upper lobe arteries and multiple aneurysmal dilatations of branches of the right upper lobe artery. Contrast-enhanced chest CT confirmed a right upper lobe nodule, and PET imaging showed that the nodule was metabolically active.
title: Intima Sarcoma of the Pulmonary Artery Mimicking Takayasu Disease

case_prompt: A 33-year-old woman with an otherwise unremarkable medical history except for a complicated twin pregnancy conceived by in vitro fertilization four years earlier presented with chest pain and dyspnea. A computed tomographic angiogram of the chest was negative for pulmonary embolism but showed incidental pulmonary nodules, sclerosis of the T7 vertebral body, and multiple enhancing lesions in the liver and spleen. Her respiratory symptoms resolved, and she underwent outpatient evaluation. A triphasic CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated scattered sclerotic foci throughout the spine, a 9 mm nodule in the left lower lobe of the lung, multiple hypodense hepatic lesions (largest, 5.5 × 3.3 cm), and an enlarged spleen containing hypodense lesions (11.4 × 6.4 cm). No lymphadenopathy was identified. MRI of the abdomen confirmed multiple large hepatic lesions (largest, 9 cm) and splenic lesions (largest, 13 cm) that did not exhibit the typical MR characteristics of hemangiomas. Hemogram and chemistry profiles were within normal limits, and levels of CEA, CA 125, CA 19-9, and α-fetoprotein were all normal. On re-evaluation, she denied constitutional symptoms, her dyspnea had resolved, and physical examination was notable only for a palpable spleen without hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or spinal tenderness.
title: When Benign Tumors Mimic Malignancies: A Case of Lymphangiomatosis Masquerading as Metastatic Disease

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old previously healthy Persian male presented with a 3-month history of right hip pain. The pain began during physical activity, became persistent, was moderate in intensity, and was associated with a limp and limited function.  
Plain radiographs of the right hip showed a proximal femoral lesion. MRI demonstrated signal changes in the same region.  
An initial percutaneous biopsy of the proximal femur revealed fibromuscular and bony tissue involved by a neoplasm composed of large cystically dilated vessels with thin walls, and was interpreted as a cavernous hemangioma of bone.  
Laboratory studies showed normal serum calcium, phosphate, albumin, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and alkaline phosphatase.  
Because of ongoing pain, absence of evidence for a primary bone sarcoma, and the extent of the lesion, prophylactic fixation with a cephalomedullary nail was performed.  
One month later, the patient returned with severe hip pain. Radiographs revealed a fracture and extensive bone destruction in the right trochanteric region and femoral neck. Curettage, structural fibula allograft, and repeat cephalomedullary nailing were performed. Cultures were negative for infection.  
At a follow-up 2½ months later, radiographs showed decreased bone density in the proximal femur and resorption of the allograft. A second incisional biopsy again demonstrated cavernous hemangioma and was negative for malignancy.  
Eighteen months after the initial biopsy, the patient was referred to our center. He remained wheelchair-bound with severe hip pain. Physical examination was notable only for painful limitation of hip motion. Repeat laboratory studies, including inflammatory and bone-metabolic markers, remained within normal limits.
title: Gorham–Stout syndrome, the challenge in diagnosis and unique in treatment: a case report

case_prompt:
A 12-year-old boy was evaluated for recurrent upper-eyelid swelling. Since age 7, he has had four to five sudden episodes annually, each lasting 4–7 days. Episodes feature eyelid erythema without pain, fever, or prodromal symptoms, and resolve spontaneously. There is no family history of similar symptoms or any history of trauma.

On examination, there is bilateral mild ptosis (~2 mm) with marked laxity and thinning of the eyelid skin. Extraocular movements are full, and the corneas are clear. There is no lacrimation, hyperemia, or conjunctival injection.

Laboratory studies, including serum protein and albumin, liver and thyroid function tests, renal function tests, and urinalysis, are all within normal limits. C1-esterase-inhibitor levels are normal, and there are no systemic signs of angioedema. Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder is unremarkable.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: A rare sight: Childhood blepharochalasis presenting as recurrent eyelid swelling: A case report

case_prompt: A 20-year-old Caucasian man with no prior medical history presented with five days of intractable vomiting. In the emergency department he had multiple seizures requiring intubation. On examination he was tachycardic with dry mucous membranes. Laboratory evaluation showed metabolic alkalosis, acute kidney injury, and a positive urine drug screen for cannabis; he was treated for presumed cannabis‐induced cyclic emesis. On hospital day five he developed high-grade fevers to 39.5 °C and new bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. He was started on vancomycin and piperacillin–tazobactam. Bronchial aspirate cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, both sensitive to the prescribed antibiotics. Despite ten days of antibiotic therapy—including escalation to meropenem and addition of micafungin—his fevers persisted. His respiratory status worsened to acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Review of imaging revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed hypertriglyceridemia (379 mg/dL), hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, platelets 88 × 10^3/mm^3, and ferritin 1188 ng/mL.
title: Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis Presenting With ARDS in a Young Adult: A Case Report

case_prompt: A 59-year-old man was referred for evaluation of right groin bulging. He had hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and chronic pruritus; his child had atopic dermatitis. One week earlier, after heavy drinking, he developed upper abdominal pain and nausea and was diagnosed with acute pancreatitis; he also noted a mildly painful right groin mass that did not change in size. On examination the patient was afebrile. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended. The right groin mass measured approximately 4 cm, was elastic-hard, mildly tender, nonwarm, and irreducible. Laboratory tests showed slight elevations of lactate dehydrogenase (317 IU/L), C-reactive protein (1.0 mg/dL), creatine kinase (372 IU/L), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (45 mm/h); white-cell, neutrophil, and eosinophil counts were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a right groin mass appearing to connect the peritoneal cavity to the scrotum, suggestive of an inguinal hernia; the presumed hernial contents were fatty tissue without signs of ischemia, but there was inflammatory change in the inguinal canal. Scrotal ultrasonography excluded testicular torsion. CT also showed lymphadenopathy around the stomach, para-aortic region, and mesentery; prior gastroscopy had shown no gastric malignancy. On the basis of these findings, the mass was diagnosed as an irreducible but nonincarcerated right inguinal hernia, and elective surgical repair was planned.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Eosinophilic funiculitis initially diagnosed as irreducible inguinal hernia: A case report

case_prompt: A 27-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of sharp, continuous pain in his left fourth toe that was refractory to conservative measures and prevented wearing closed shoes or playing indoor soccer. His medical history included well-controlled type I diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.5%) and depression; he took insulin via pump and sertraline. He had no allergies. Examination showed moderate edema of the entire left fourth toe with tenderness along its length and mild discomfort at the metatarsal head; alignment was normal. Diagnostic ultrasound demonstrated a small amount of soft-tissue edema but no ganglion cyst, tenosynovitis, or bursitis. Plain radiographs of the foot revealed a well-defined lucent lesion measuring 15 mm × 7 mm within the proximal phalanx of the fourth toe. MRI confirmed an expansile lesion breaching the inferior and lateral cortex without a soft-tissue mass or features suggestive of malignancy.
title: Surgical management of an enchondroma of the proximal phalanx of the foot: An illustrative case report

case_prompt:
A 71-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by family members because of chronic dyspnea at rest of 2 months’ duration, worsened by minimal exertion. She also reported long-standing generalized fatigue and left lower-limb swelling. She had no other respiratory or abdominal complaints. Her medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus, hypertension, iron-deficiency anemia, and chronic kidney disease requiring hemodialysis; she had been noncompliant with her medications. 

On examination, she appeared pale. Her temperature was 101.3 °F, pulse 110 beats/min, and blood pressure 113/73 mm Hg. Respiratory examination disclosed bilateral basal crackles; the abdomen was distended but non­tender, and there was bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs. A COVID-19 PCR test was negative. 

An echocardiogram was normal. A frontal chest radiograph showed a large, lobulated, heterogeneously opaque mass in the right posterior mediastinum with splaying of the carina and an unfolded aortic arch. A nonenhanced CT scan of the chest revealed an 8.2 × 7.6 × 12.7 cm mid-thoracic posterior mediastinal mass with mixed fat and soft-tissue attenuation (soft-tissue components mean 34 HU). After hemodialysis, an enhanced CT scan showed homogeneous enhancement of the soft-tissue component (mean 95 HU), with encasement and displacement of the lower azygos vein and right main pulmonary trunk. There was no bony erosion, neural-foraminal narrowing, pleural effusion, surrounding invasion, or calcification.
title: A case of bilateral posterior mediastinal myelolipoma

case_prompt: A 49-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with right upper‐quadrant abdominal pain. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal liver function tests. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, CA19-9, and alpha-fetoprotein, were within normal limits. Viral hepatitis markers were negative. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a nodular formation in the right hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an 18 × 12 × 20 cm lobulated cystic mass with thin enhancing septa occupying the right liver lobe. MRI confirmed a heterogeneous mass with fluid levels and thin septa, findings described as suggestive of an atypical hemangioma; the right hepatic vein was inseparable from the lesion. Given the size of the lesion and risk of complications, a right hepatectomy was performed without intraoperative rupture, and the resected tumor measured approximately 20 cm in greatest dimension.
final_diagnosis_raw: Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver
title: Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver: a case report of a rare case in an adult patient

case_prompt: A 59-year-old man with hereditary spherocytosis underwent a routine chest radiograph, which revealed an unexpected right paraspinal opacity. He denied respiratory or neurologic symptoms. Physical examination was notable only for jaundice. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 8.04 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelet count 990 × 10^3/µL, aspartate aminotransferase 122 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 127 U/L, and total bilirubin 6.83 mg/dL; other results were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 68 mm mass in the right posterior mediastinum. MRI revealed that the lesion had a predominantly fatty component but could not exclude a malignant tumor. Given its location, imaging characteristics, and the patient’s underlying hemolytic disorder, the differential diagnosis included neurogenic tumor, liposarcoma, and other posterior mediastinal lesions. To establish a diagnosis and mitigate risks of hemorrhage or spinal cord compression, video-assisted thoracoscopic resection was planned.
title: Surgical resection of extramedullary haematopoiesis in the posterior mediastinum

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old primigravid woman with a 12-year history of chronic pulmonary disease presented for routine antenatal care. At age 8, she had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis and had chest tube drainage for empyema. Since that time, she reported recurrent episodes of fever, cough, and dyspnea. 

On examination, the trachea was deviated to the right. Auscultation revealed diffuse crackles over the right lung field. Spirometry showed moderate obstructive impairment (FEV1/FVC, 69%). 

A chest radiograph demonstrated cicatricial collapse and hyperlucency of the right lung. Computed tomography of the thorax revealed markedly decreased attenuation of the right lung and of the basal segment of the left lung, diminished right hilar vessels, and bronchiectasis.
title: Successful pregnancy outcome in Swyer-James-Macleod syndrome

case_prompt: A 79-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and atrial fibrillation presented with a 2-month history of intermittent left nocturnal otalgia, dull in character, 5/10 in severity, without ear discharge, hearing loss, facial nerve dysfunction, or nasal symptoms. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Examination of the left ear revealed a patent but erythematous canal without granulation tissue and a bulging tympanic membrane; the right ear was normal. He was prescribed oral moxifloxacin and ciprofloxacin, but discontinued therapy after pain improved. Soon thereafter he noted sudden left-sided hearing loss. Otoscopic examination then showed a normal canal and a dull tympanic membrane on the left. Tympanometry revealed type B on the left and normal type A on the right. Pure-tone audiometry demonstrated conductive hearing loss on the left with a normal right ear. Laboratory evaluation revealed WBC 12.6×10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, hemoglobin below normal, C-reactive protein 38.2 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 120 mm/hr. A left myringotomy with grommet insertion was performed; one week later the grommet was in place and the patient was doing well. One month later he returned with two weeks of left ear pain and intermittent yellow discharge, without tinnitus, dizziness, or facial palsy. Examination showed an inflamed canal with yellowish discharge and a dull tympanic membrane. Ear-swab culture grew no organisms. A bone scan showed increased radionuclide uptake in the left middle-ear ossicles extending to the mastoid air cells and sphenoid bone, suggestive of active bone infection and a necrotizing process originating from the ear.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Uncommon disease with unusual presentation: A case report of acute necrotizing otitis media

case_prompt: A 32-year-old man awoke with acute right-sided hemiparesis that evolved over minutes. He had no prior medical history, no vascular risk factors, did not smoke, and took no medications or illicit drugs. The weakness resolved spontaneously over three hours; examination at presentation was normal. MRI and MRA of the brain and neck were unremarkable. Electrocardiogram, electrolytes, glucose, thyroid function tests, and complete blood count were within normal limits. Carotid intima–media thickness measurements and Doppler ultrasound of both carotid arteries showed no abnormalities. Continuous Holter monitoring revealed no arrhythmias. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a serpentine, filiform strand attached to the coapting edge of the mitral valve.
title: The serpentine mitral valve and cerebral embolism

case_prompt:
An 11-year-old prepubertal boy, an active football player, presented with a 1-year history of barely itching chronic blistering, erosions, and scarring localized to the knees and scrotum. Physical examination showed erythematous, exfoliative lesions on both knees and a solitary blister on the scrotum with evident scarring and crusting. The oral mucosa was normal, and there were no gastrointestinal symptoms.

Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional scrotal skin demonstrated linear C3 deposits (+++) at the dermal–epidermal junction; IgG, IgG1, IgG4, IgA, and IgM were not detected. Mosaic indirect immunofluorescence on salt-split primate skin revealed IgG antibodies localized to the dermal side of the split at a titer of 1:10. Multiplex ELISA showed an elevated level of IgG antibodies against type VII collagen (2.55; cut-off, 1.0). A serologic ELISA for IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase was negative (below 0.6 RU/mL; cut-off, 20.0 RU/mL).
title: An Exceedingly Rare Case of Mechanobullous Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita in a Prepubertal Child: A Review of the Clinical and Laboratory Considerations

case_prompt:
A 58-year-old Caucasian man with a history of rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed by his primary care physician—characterized by a positive homogeneous ANA, negative rheumatoid factor, and joint pain and stiffness—was transferred for evaluation of acute renal failure and hypoglycemia. He also had hypertension and type 2 diabetes treated with lisinopril, metformin, and glipizide, and he denied use of NSAIDs.

He reported one week of generalized malaise, subjective fevers, poor oral intake, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. On arrival, he was euvolemic and afebrile, blood pressure was 126/72 mmHg, and examination showed no synovitis, warmth, or rash. Initial labs revealed a blood glucose of 30 mg/dL and a serum creatinine of 6.6 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL). BUN was 67 mg/dL and creatinine trended at 6.1 mg/dL on admission. Fractional excretion of sodium was 4.5%. Urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria and nephritic-range proteinuria (protein : creatinine ratio, 1.4), with no urine eosinophils.

Complete blood count showed WBC 11,000/mm3, hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, and platelets 422,000/mm3. ESR obtained on hospital day 12 was 2 mm/hr. Complement levels were C3 72 mg/dL (low-normal) and C4 18 mg/dL. Serum protein electrophoresis was normal, and tests for anti-streptolysin O antibody and viral hepatitis were negative. A vasculitis panel revealed a p-ANCA titer of 1:640, myeloperoxidase-ANCA >8.8 antibody index, and ANA 1:80; anti–glomerular basement membrane and anti–proteinase-3 antibodies were negative.
title: A Case Report Describing a Rare Presentation of Simultaneous Occurrence of MPO-ANCA-Associated Vasculitis and Rheumatoid Arthritis

case_prompt: A 23-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 12, poorly controlled, was transferred for evaluation of 2 months of progressive generalized swelling. She had no arthritis, arthralgia, hair loss, or family history of edema. Her weight increased from 70 kg to 140 kg. Examination showed massive anasarca of all extremities, abdominal wall, and back. Chest imaging revealed bilateral pleural effusions; echocardiography demonstrated a large pericardial effusion with impending tamponade and a normal left ventricular ejection fraction (> 55%). Admission laboratory studies: hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL; normal white-cell and platelet counts; normal renal and liver function; serum albumin 3.1 g/dL; urinalysis with no proteinuria; random urine sodium 8 mmol/L; B-type natriuretic peptide 18 pg/mL. Thyroid function showed TSH 5.18 μIU/mL, free T4 0.93 ng/dL, free T3 1.62 pg/mL. Inflammatory markers were low (C-reactive protein 0.8 mg/dL, ESR 8 mm/hr). Autoimmune testing: ANA positive 1:80 speckled; anti-dsDNA and ENA negative; complements normal. Infectious serologies (HBV, HCV, HIV) were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed total protein 4.9 g/dL, albumin 2.2 g/dL, and a small monoclonal IgG κ on immunofixation; κ/λ light-chain ratio 3.08. IgG subclasses showed low IgG2 and undetectable IgG4. C1 esterase inhibitor level was 33 mg/dL. Total vitamin D was 5.0 ng/mL. Abdominal fat biopsy was negative for amyloid on Congo red stain.
journal: Allergy, Asthma, and Clinical Immunology : Official Journal of the Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
title: Chronic idiopathic systemic capillary leak syndrome: a case report

case_prompt:
A 16-year-old male presented with a 1-year history of left knee pain associated with stiffness that interfered with daily activities. He reported no fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. On examination, there was diffuse tenderness of the left knee and a moderate joint effusion; the remainder of the musculoskeletal and systemic examination was unremarkable.  
Plain radiographs of the knee showed a lucent, rounded lesion with a sharp sclerotic margin involving the distal anterior femoral epiphysis and metaphysis. MRI with intravenous contrast demonstrated a lesion centered in the distal femoral epiphysis extending through the physis into the metaphysis. The lesion was T2 hyperintense and T1 hypointense, with extensive surrounding bone marrow edema, slight adjacent periosteal reaction, and hyperintense signal on both pre- and postcontrast T1 fat-suppressed sequences.
title: Chondroblastoma of the knee in a teenager

case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man with diabetes was thrown from a quad bike and briefly lost consciousness. In the Emergency Department his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 14/15; blood pressure, 165/110 mmHg; and pulse, 110 beats per minute. He had bilateral “raccoon eyes,” multiple rib fractures, a small pneumothorax treated with chest tube drainage, and a grade III splenic injury managed conservatively. Head CT showed a thin left subdural hematoma with a left parenchymal hemorrhagic contusion. He was observed in the ICU and then transferred to the ward. 

Forty-eight hours after injury, he complained of loss of vision in his left eye. Examination revealed raccoon eye, eyelid edema, and severe conjunctival ecchymosis on the left. The left pupil was dilated and nonreactive to light; the right eye was 20/20. There was no light perception in the left eye, and extraocular movements were intact bilaterally. Ophthalmoscopy of both fundi was normal. 

A clinical diagnosis of left optic nerve injury was made. Optic nerve transection or retro-bulbar hematoma was suspected. The initial trauma CT cuts were too thick to evaluate the optic nerves. A bedside surgeon-performed point-of-care ultrasound of both eyes was normal: there was no intraocular bleeding, the optic nerve was intact, and there was no retro-bulbar hematoma.
title: Surgeon-performed point-of-care ultrasound in severe eye trauma: Report of two cases

case_prompt: A 66-year-old Japanese woman was admitted for evaluation of melena ongoing for 3 days. Her medical history included diabetes, hypertension, cerebral infarction, and angina. On admission, her temperature was 36.2 °C, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, pulse 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She was alert. Physical examination revealed pale conjunctiva; the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender, with no palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 4.3 g/dL and blood urea nitrogen 33.6 mg/dL. Emergent upper GI endoscopy revealed no vascular abnormalities, mass lesions, or ulcerations. Colonoscopy showed no lesions but altered blood throughout the colon and terminal ileum, suggesting a small-bowel source. She received transfusions with initial stabilization, but on hospital day 5 she developed hypotension (BP 68/40 mm Hg) with renewed melena. Abdominal CT showed an ill-defined mass lesion in the small bowel, but its precise location and nature were unclear. The differential diagnosis included small intestinal tumor (such as GIST), inflammatory disease, and vascular abnormalities. On hospital day 7, capsule endoscopy was performed; by day 9, active bleeding was visualized in the upper small bowel. An emergency SMA angiogram localized a vascular tumor in a jejunal arterial branch, and coil embolization achieved hemostasis.
title: Small bowel GIST with hemorrhagic shock diagnosed by capsule endoscopy and double‐balloon endoscopy, angiography‐guided hemostasis, and laparoscopic‐assisted resection

case_prompt: A 54-year-old gravida 4, para 4 woman presented with two months of persistent abnormal vaginal bleeding. Her last pregnancy was 12 years earlier, and she had no personal or family history of gestational trophoblastic disease. Vital signs were stable. Cardiac, pulmonary, and extremity examinations were normal. Gynecological examination showed minimal vaginal bleeding and an enlarged, soft uterus approximately the size of an 8-week pregnancy, with mild adnexal tenderness. Laboratory testing revealed a β-hCG level of 199,217 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated an intracavitary mass measuring 8 × 4 cm with chaotic vascularization on color Doppler. Pelvic MRI confirmed a poorly defined, heterogeneous intrauterine mass measuring 96 mm along its longest axis, with invasion of the cervical stroma and myometrium.
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
title: Trophoblastic tumor in perimenopausal women: A case report and literature review

case_prompt: A 64-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of urinary difficulty and tightness across the upper back. Two months after onset she developed progressive right lower-extremity weakness, culminating in inability to walk over 2 weeks. On examination, she had monoplegia of the right lower extremity and an asymmetric decrease in light-touch and pain sensation below the nipples, worse on the left, with hyperreflexia and bilateral Babinski signs. Routine blood tests were unremarkable, and there was no personal or family history of cancer. Given the clinical findings suggestive of a Brown-Séquard syndrome at the thoracic level, an MRI of the spine was obtained, showing a 1.5-cm intradural extramedullary mass at T3. The lesion demonstrated intermediate T1 signal, mildly increased T2 signal, and avid enhancement after gadolinium administration. There was no evidence of bony involvement or other lesions on radiologic evaluation.
title: Primary intradural extramedullary spinal mesenchymal chondrosarcoma: case report and literature review
